inlineHeadings.text: The theme: After the tenth trial, the Akeidah, it says “now I know that you fear God” — for Avraham was then included in the middah of Yitzchak. This is love’s completion: he added his own vigor and striving upon the arousal from Above that had preceded him, until he could be called its author. Hence they said of him, “they chose him but did not bring him near — rather he brought himself near.”

p: (ט), — וּמַדְרֵגָה זוֹ הוּא עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
And this spiritual rung is attained through repentance out of love,
כַּיָּדוּעַ דְּהָאַהֲבָה יוֹתֵר בְּקֵירוּב שֶׁאַחַר הָרִיחוּק
as is known that love is experienced with far greater intensity in the reconciliation following estrangement,
וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּנִדָּה (לא עַמּוּד ב)
and in the manner that our Sages of blessed memory stated in Niddah (31b)
בְּטַעַם טוּמְאַת נִדָּה: כְּדֵי שֶׁתְּהֵא חֲבִיבָה עָלָיו
concerning the reason for the impurity of menstruation: so that she become beloved to her husband as at her wedding.
וְנִמְצְאוּ הַזְּדוֹנוֹת גַּם כֵּן כִּזְכִיּוֹת
And consequently, willful transgressions likewise turn into actual merits,
שֶׁהֵם הַגּוֹרְמִים הַקֵּירוּב
inasmuch as they were the very catalysts inducing this supreme closeness,
וְיֵשׁ לוֹ זְכִיּוֹת הַרְבֵּה אֲלֻמּוֹת אֲלֻמּוֹת
and he amasses abundant merits in towering sheaves upon sheaves,
מַה שֶּׁאֵין לְצַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים כָּךְ.
which completely righteous individuals do not possess in such abundance.
וּלְעָתִיד עַל יְדֵי מָשִׁיחַ יְתוּקַּן כֵּן בִּכְלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל
And in the ultimate future through the Messiah this will be rectified across all Israel,
שֶׁעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר : "יְבֻקַּשׁ עֲוֺן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ",
concerning which it is said (Jeremiah 50:20): 'the iniquity of Israel shall be sought for, and there shall be none,'.
וְגַם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה נַעֲשָׂה מִקְצָתוֹ לַשָּׁבִים מֵאַהֲבָה
and even in this world a portion of this unfolds for those who repent out of love.
וְאַף דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וַדַּאי שָׁב מֵאַהֲבָה הַגְּמוּרָה
And even King David, peace be upon him, surely repented out of absolute love,
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם נֶאֱמַר לוֹ: בְּחַיֶּיךָ אֵינִי מוֹדִיעַ
yet nonetheless it was said to him: in your lifetime I do not make known
(שֶׁנִּמְחַל לְךָ אוֹתוֹ עָווֹן, שַׁבָּת ל עַמּוּד א),
(that that iniquity has been forgiven unto you, Shabbat 30a),
דְּעָלָיו נֶאֱמַר (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים ב, ז): "אִם תָּעִירוּ וְאִם תְּעוֹרְרוּ אֶת הָאַהֲבָה עַד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּץ",
for concerning this state it is said (Song of Songs 2:7): 'if you awaken or stir up love until it please,'
דַּעֲדַיִן לֹא הִגִּיעַ זְמַן "שֶׁתֶּחְפָּץ".
since the destined time 'until it please' had not yet arrived.
כִּי הָאַהֲבָה עִיקָּרָהּ מֵאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָּא
For love is rooted essentially in the supernal awakening from Above,
וְצָרִיךְ לָזֶה זְמַן שֶׁתֶּחְפָּץ לֵירֵד שֶׁפַע הָאַהֲבָה מֵאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָּא
and this requires the appointed hour when it pleases the Divine to descend with the influx of love from Above.
וְאֵינוֹ בְּיַד הָאָדָם לְעוֹרֵר אַהֲבָה בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת וְאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא
and it is not within mortal power to stir love through human exertion and the awakening from below alone.
וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן דְּלֹא קֵרְבוֹ,
And King David, peace be upon him, is likewise considered one whom Hashem did not unilaterally draw near unearned,
וְהוּא קֵירֵב אֶת עַצְמוֹ וְאָמַר (תְּהִלִּים כו, ב): "בְּחָנֵנִי ה' וְנַסֵּנִי",
and he drew himself near and pleaded (Psalms 26:2): 'Examine me, Hashem, and test me,'
אַף שֶׁלֹּא עָלְתָה בְּיָדוֹ לְמַרְאִית עַיִן
and even though it did not outwardly succeed to superficial sight,
עַל הָאֱמֶת עָלְתָה בְּיָדוֹ
in ultimate truth it indeed succeeded for him,
שֶׁהֲרֵי זֶהוּ שֶׁהֱבִיאוֹ לְהָקִים עוּלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה
for this failure is precisely what led him to establish the yoke of repentance,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִיקַּר הִתְעַלּוּת מַדְרֵגָתוֹ מֵהֵ"א תַּתָּאָה – מִדַּת מַלְכוּת
which is the primary elevation of his spiritual station from the lower Hei—the attribute of Malchut—,
לַעֲשׂוֹתָהּ הֵ"א עִילָּאָה הָרוֹמֶזֶת לִתְשׁוּבָה כַּנּוֹדָע
to elevate it into the upper Hei which alludes to Teshuva/Binah as is known,
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה קֵירֵב אֶת עַצְמוֹ.
and through this inward labor he drew himself near.

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §53): “for fear is from near — when one stands before the King he fears Him… and as it says,”with great awe" — this is the revelation of the Shechinah." Exactly the se’if: fear operates in nearness, and therefore love is what is disclosed across distance — which is why the love of the returner, after estrangement, is the greater.

paragraphs.text: Niddah 31b: “Why did the Torah say a niddah is impure seven days? Because a husband becomes habituated to his wife and repelled by her; therefore the Torah said she is impure seven days, so that she be beloved to him as on the day of her wedding.” R’ Tzadok: love renewed after distance is greater — so teshuvah from love makes the very sins (the “distance”) the cause of a greater nearness, i.e. “merits.” Maharal — distance itself can generate a stronger return. Maharal, Nesiv HaTeshuvah 2:17–19, gives a conceptual analogue to R’ Tzadok’s use of the niddah interval: the one who comes to God “from afar” can reveal a more forceful attachment than one who was never distant, just as fire far below moves upward toward its natural place with greater force. Maharal therefore says that the sin, which was itself the distance, becomes a merit when that very distance is what reveals the depth of the return. R’ Tzadok develops the same principle here in relational language: the separation makes the renewed nearness more beloved, and so the z’donos themselves become the causes of kiruv.

R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §40): “The essence of teshuvah is until Hashem enlightens his eyes, that the willful sins become as merits — that he recognize and grasp that all he sinned was also by the will of Hashem” (as in Berachos 32a, and the Arizal’s reconciling of foreknowledge and free choice, “both true, each in its own domain”); “and when he attains this immense light, then all his willful sins are turned to merits.” This is the crown of the rung §1-6 opens toward: not the Chesed that pardons yet leaves shame, but the Gevurah-born light in which the past itself is re-read as Divine guidance — the “as if he had never sinned,” and beyond. Izhbitz-Radzin on yedi'ah and bechirah — and the boundary that prevents this doctrine from becoming an excuse for sin. Mei HaShiloach, Vayeilech 3, says that even though bechirah is given into human hands, one who sees deeply recognizes that human action is "רק דבר מועט כקליפת השום" relative to the encompassing Divine conduct. In Tazria 2 he can say simultaneously that a person's eventual attainment was prepared from the beginning of creation and, nevertheless, "מצד האדם יש לו בחירה." The two statements are intentionally held together: from the creature's lived standpoint, command, responsibility, restraint, and teshuvah are real; from the later Divine illumination, the person may discover a providential depth that was never visible at the moment of choice.

This is the key to R' Tzadok's use of the Arizal's yedi'ah/bechirah resolution and his statement that, at the highest teshuvah, a person can recognize that "all he sinned was also by the will of Hashem." The recognition belongs to the afterward of teshuvah — "until Hashem enlightens his eyes" — not to the beforehand of temptation. Mei HaShiloach, Devarim 2, sometimes reads the Torah's naming of places of Israel's sins as teaching that circumstances and spiritual "place" can radically narrow a person's field of choice. But Beis Yaakov, Bereshis 69:1, supplies the essential guardrail through its reading of Cain. Cain's "השומר אחי אנכי" is understood as the claim that overwhelming anger had removed his bechirah and therefore he should not be liable. The Divine answer rejects the self-exculpation: "קול דמי אחיך צועקים" proves that the deficiency is attributed to Cain and that he had a point of responsibility by which he could have guarded himself.

The Ishbitz doctrine therefore works in two directions at once. Before and during action, a Jew must regard himself as a baal bechirah, obey Torah, resist the yetzer, and never invoke hidden providence to legitimate a prohibited act. After a genuine teshuvah that has uprooted identification with the sin, Hashem may reveal a deeper yedi'ah: the fall itself can be integrated into a providential road by which the person came to a higher recognition. That latter illumination is what R' Tzadok associates with zedonos becoming zechuyos. It does not say the aveirah was permitted; it says that Divine omnipotence can reclaim even the prohibited past and make the teshuvah born from it part of the final good. This is the precise Izhbitz-Radzin frame in which the radical sentence of Tzidkas HaTzadik §40 should be read.

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §70): “like Yaakov’s flight to Chutz la-Aretz — which is in distance from the face-to-face recognition of Yitzchak — and this is what clarifies his wholeness; for his wholeness (‘his bed was whole,’ his own cleaving to Hashem) is not shown complete except when, even in distance of place, he holds fast.” This is §5-9’s “the greater love, in the nearness that comes after distance”: the bond is not fully revealed in unbroken closeness — it is the cleaving that survives a gulf that discloses love in its full force, so that the willful sins themselves become merits.

paragraphs.text: Shir HaShirim 2:7: “הִשְׁבַּעְתִּי אֶתְכֶם בְּנוֹת יְרוּשָׁלַ͏ִם (…) אִם תָּעִירוּ וְאִם תְּעוֹרְרוּ אֶת הָאַהֲבָה עַד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּץ” — “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem… do not stir up or awaken the love until it desires” (repeated at 3:5 and 8:4). In its plain love-allegory sense it warns against forcing love before its time; the Sages also read the adjurations as the “three oaths” of exile (Kesuvos 111a). R’ Tzadok’s use: the influx of love descends only “when it desires” — a time set from Above — and it is not in a person’s power to awaken it by his striving; hence even David, who returned from complete love, was told “in your lifetime I will not make (it) known,” the time not yet having “desired.”

paragraphs.text: Tehillim 26:2: “בְּחָנֵנִי ה׳ וְנַסֵּנִי, צָרְפָה כִלְיוֹתַי וְלִבִּי” — “Examine me, Hashem, and test me; refine my kidneys and my heart” — David HaMelech’s request that God prove and refine him. The Sages (Sanhedrin 107a) relate that David asked to be tested: “why do we say ‘God of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov’ but not ‘God of David’? — because they were tested and you were not; if so, examine me and test me” — the trial in which he then stumbled. R’ Tzadok’s use: David “brought himself near” by requesting the nisayon; though “to the eye” it did not succeed (he fell), “in truth it did succeed,” for it is what brought him to raise the “yoke of teshuvah” — the ascent of malchus (the lower heh) into teshuvah (the upper heh).

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 30a: the Gemara recounts that David said before the Holy One, “mechol li al oso avon — pardon me for that sin,” and He answered, “machul lach — it is pardoned you.” David then asked, “asei imi os be-chayai — make a sign of the pardon in my lifetime,” and He replied, “be-chayecha eini modia — in your lifetime I will not make it known; be-chayei Shlomo bincha ani modia — in the lifetime of Shlomo your son I will make it known.” (This was borne out when the Temple gates clung shut until Shlomo invoked “zochrah le-chasdei David avdecha,” whereupon all knew the Holy One had pardoned him.) R’ Tzadok’s use: even David, who returned from complete love, was told “in your lifetime I will not make known” — for “do not awaken love until it desires”: the influx of love descends only when its time has “desired,” and it is not in a person’s power to compel it by striving; yet David, by his very request, “brought himself near.”

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: This rung comes through teshuvah from love, in which the nearness that follows distance is the greater — as the Sages explained the impurity of niddah, “so that she be beloved to him anew.” The willful sins themselves become merits, being the very cause of the drawing-near. Even David returned from complete love, yet was told “in your lifetime I will not make it known” — for love’s hour must come from Above.

p: (י), — וְאַשְׁרֵי אַהֲרֹן בְּכִפְלַיִם שֶׁנִּבְחַר וְנִקְרַב
And fortunate is Aaron doubly in that he was chosen and brought near,
שֶׁהוּא לֹא קֵירֵב אֶת עַצְמוֹ בַּעֲבוֹדָה וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת
for he did not draw himself near through active service and self-effort,
רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ קֵרְבוֹ לַעֲבוֹדָה זוֹ.
rather Hashem, blessed be He, brought him close to this sacred service.
וְדָבָר זֶה לֹא הָיָה עֲדַיִן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And such an unearned gift had not yet existed in this physical world,
שֶׁהוּא זְמַן הָעֲבוֹדָה וְהַהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת וְ"הַיּוֹם לַעֲשׂוֹתָם",
which is the realm of divine labor, striving, and 'today to perform them,'.
וּמִי שֶׁנִּתְקָרֵב הַיְינוּ שֶׁאֵין צָרִיךְ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת
and one who is thus brought near without effort implies having no need for further striving.
וְזֶה הָיָה רַק בְּיִתְרוֹ וְרָחָב שֶׁקֵּרְבָם אֲבָל לֹא בְּחָרָם (בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה ג, ב),
And this occurred only with Jethro and Rahab, whom Hashem brought near but did not choose (Bemidbar Rabbah 3:2),
וְהַקֵּירוּב שֶׁלָּהֶם הָיָה שֶׁיָּבוֹאוּ לְהִתְגַּיֵּיר וְלִיטָּפֵל לָאוּמָּה יִשְׂרְאֵלִית
and their drawing near was that they came to convert and attach themselves to the Jewish nation:
שֶׁזֶּה לֹא הָיָה בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם כְּלָל
which was not through their own spiritual initiative at all:
רַק יִתְרוֹ עַל פִּי סִבָּה שֶׁהָיָה חוֹתֵן מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
rather Jethro through the circumstance of being the father-in-law of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him,
וְרָחָב בְּסִבַּת הַמְּרַגְּלִים שֶׁהָיוּ בְּבֵיתָהּ.
and Rahab through the circumstance of the spies being in her lodging.
וְזֶה קֵירוּב מֵה' בְּלֹא הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם
And this represents drawing near from Hashem without prior exertion,
וְיֶשְׁנוֹ בְּגֵרִים דְּעַל תְּחִלַּת הַהִתְגַּיְּירוּת שַׁיָּיךְ קֵירוּב
and it applies to converts where at the initial conversion drawing near applies.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ צָרִיךְ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת לִהְיוֹת בְּשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל מִתְכַּנֶּה, כֵּיוָן דְּלֹא נִבְחַר כְּלָל
and afterward strenuous effort is required to be truly designated by the name of Israel, since he was not intrinsically chosen from the outset.
אֲבָל מִי שֶׁהוּא נִבְחַר וְנִתְקָרֵב – אִם כֵּן אֵין צָרִיךְ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת
However, one who is both chosen and brought near—who consequently requires no effort—,
זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
this is impossible in this physical world.
רַק גַּבֵּי אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֵן שֶׁנִּבְחַר לָעֲבוֹדָה
except with regard to Aaron the Priest who was chosen for the divine service.
וְזָכָה לוֹ עַל יְדֵי עֲשִׂיַּת הָעֵגֶל
And he merited this uniquely through the making of the Golden Calf,
שֶׁהוּא אַדְּרַבָּה עֲבֵירָה
which was, on the contrary, an egregious sin,
וְעַל כֵּן הָיָה בּוֹשׁ דְּיָדַע בְּעַצְמוֹ שֶׁאֵינוֹ כְּדַאי וְהָגוּן
and therefore he was deeply ashamed, knowing within himself that he was unworthy and unfitting,
עַד שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ (סִפְרָא שְׁמִינִי א): לָמָּה אַתָּה בּוֹשׁ? לְכָךְ נִבְחַרְתָּ!
until Moses told him (Sifra, Shemini 1): Why are you ashamed? For this very role were you chosen!
וְרָאִיתִי הַפֵּירוּשׁ: דִּבְשְׁבִיל זֶה עַצְמוֹ שֶׁאַתָּה בּוֹשׁ – בִּשְׁבִיל זֶה נִבְחַרְתָּ,
And I have seen the profound interpretation: on account of this very humility that you are ashamed—for this reason were you chosen;
הַיְינוּ דִּלַעֲבוֹדָתוֹ אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ אֶלָּא בְּכֵלִים שְׁבוּרִים
meaning that for His holy service the Holy One uses only broken vessels (Vayikra Rabbah 7:2)
וּמִי שֶׁלִּבּוֹ שָׁבוּר וְדוֹאֵג בְּקִרְבּוֹ.
and one whose heart is crushed and contrite within him.

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Yisrael Kedoshim §6): “ruach ha-kodesh of this kind comes through an arousal from Above without an arousal from below isarusa di-l’eila be-lo isarusa di-l’tata; and so the first of the rungs of R’ Pinchas ben Yair — he did not name ‘learning’ or ‘engaging in Torah’ or human effort, such as zehirus and zerizus.” This is §5-10’s Aharon exactly: he “did not bring himself near to the service by striving; rather God brought him near” — the rung that comes purely by arousal from Above, without the labor of arousal-from-below, which “did not yet exist in this world,” the time of striving.

paragraphs.text: Yisro, Rachav, and Aharon — background: the se’if turns on two Midrashic categories (from Bamidbar Rabbah 3:2, cited in §8): “kervu aval lo bacharu” (brought near but not chosen) and “bacharu ve-kervu” (chosen and brought near). Yisro (Shemos 18) was the Midyanite priest and Moshe’s father-in-law; hearing of the splitting of the sea and the war with Amalek, he came to the wilderness, converted, and gave the counsel for the system of judges — his “nearness” arising by circumstance (being Moshe’s father-in-law), not by his own striving. Rachav (Yehoshua 2) was the innkeeper of Yericho who sheltered the two spies, declared “Hashem your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below,” was spared at the city’s fall, and converted; the Sages (Megillah 14b) say she married Yehoshua and became ancestress of prophets and priests — her “nearness,” too, came by circumstance (the spies who lodged in her house). Both are “brought near but not chosen”: converts, whose initial drawing-near is God’s doing, though afterward striving is needed. Aharon alone, in this world, is “chosen and brought near” — chosen for the avodah without striving; and R’ Tzadok’s paradox is that he merited it through the shame of the Golden Calf, “for the Holy One uses only broken vessels”: as the Midrash (Toras Kohanim / Vayikra Rabbah, Shemini) records, Moshe said to the abashed Aharon, “lamah atah bosh? le-kach nivcharta — why are you ashamed? for this you were chosen.”

paragraphs.text: Bamidbar Rabbah 3:2 (on “happy is the one You choose and bring near,” Tehillim 65:5): “Happy is he whom the Holy One chose, even if He did not bring him near; and happy is he whom He brought near, even if He did not choose him. Whom did He choose but not bring near? Avraham, of whom it says ‘You are Hashem the God who chose Avram’ (Nechemyah 9:7) — but He did not bring him near; rather he brought himself near. So too Yaakov and Moshe. And whom did He bring near but not choose? Yisro and Rachav the harlot. And who is ‘happy’ doubly? — one whom He chose and brought near: Aharon and Levi.” R’ Tzadok makes this the frame of the whole se’if: the Avos “brought themselves near” by striving (the way of Torah/this world), while Aharon was “brought near” without striving.

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Tetzaveh §3: “ורק לאחר הקלקול נבחר אהרן מתוך בני ישראל” — “Only after the damage was Aharon chosen from among the children of Israel.” It explains: “וקדושת אהרן נצרך רק אחר הקלקול דאם לא היה הקלקול היו כל ישראל ראוים לכהונה כנ"ל.” — “Aharon’s sanctity was required only after the damage, for had there been no damage all Israel would have been fit for the priesthood, as above.” The passage relates the differentiated priesthood to the repair needed after the Calf, directly illuminating the paradox here. Sefas Emes on Aharon’s shame — “for this you were chosen.” Sefas Emes, Shemini 7:3, directly interprets Rashi’s “קרב אל המזבח — למה אתה בוש? לכך נבחרת” through the same axis as this se’if. He distinguishes בחירה, the standing of the complete tzaddik, from קריבה, the drawing-near of the baal teshuvah, and writes that Aharon certainly returned from love, so that even deliberate sins become merits — all the more an inadvertent participation in the Calf. He goes further: it is close to say that Aharon’s very connection to that sin was arranged so that he could elevate the teshuvah of Klal Yisrael into teshuvah from love; thus “לכך נבחרת” means that precisely through repairing the fall into zechus, his kiruv itself becomes a form of bechirah. This is almost a direct Chassidic commentary on R’ Tzadok’s paradox here: what appeared to disqualify Aharon from avodah became the very ground of his being chosen and brought near.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: “Happy is Aharon doubly — that he was chosen and brought near”: he did not bring himself near by striving. Such a thing does not otherwise exist in this world, which is the time of labor; Yisro and Rachav were brought near but not chosen. Aharon alone was both — and he merited it through the making of the Calf, which is why he stood ashamed, until he was told, “for this you were chosen.”

p: (יא), — וְזֶהוּ מַדְרֵגַת "זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת" שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And this is the nature of the rung of 'willful sins become merits' in this world,
לֹא כִּלְעָתִיד דְּ"יְבֻקַּשׁ הֶעָווֹן וְאֵינֶנּוּ",
unlike the ultimate future when 'the iniquity will be sought and there will be none,'.
כִּי יִהְיֶה גָּלוּי לַכֹּל אֵיךְ הוּא זְכוּת וְאֵינוֹ עָווֹן כְּלָל, וְאֵין בּוֹשׁ כְּלָל
for it will then be revealed to all how it was pure merit and not sin at all, and there will be no shame whatsoever.
אֲבָל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין זֶה גָּלוּי וּמְבוֹרָר לָעַיִן אֵיךְ הוּא כֵּן
However, in this world it is neither manifest nor visibly clear to the eye how this is so,
שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָשַׁב לְאִיסּוּר וְכַוָּונָתוֹ מִיהַת לְאִיסּוּרָא
since even though he thought it forbidden and his subjective intention was for transgression.
לֹא יָצָא מִכְּלַל שׁוֹגֵג כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל דְּנִקְרָא חֵטְא
he has not left the category of an inadvertent sinner, as mentioned above, which is still termed a sin.
וּמַה שֶּׁמֵּבִיא לִידֵי זְכִיּוֹת אַחַר כָּךְ הָוֵי כְּמוֹ "עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ",
And the fact that it subsequently leads to merits makes it comparable to 'a transgression for Heaven's sake',
דְּנַמֵּי צָרִיךְ סְלִיחָה וְכַפָּרָה עַל הָעֲבֵירָה
where one likewise still requires forgiveness and expiation for the external deed of transgression,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאֲפָרֵשׁ לְקַמָּן (סִימָן יד) מִדִּבְרֵי תּוֹסָפוֹת נָזִיר (ב עַמּוּד ב) וְתַעֲנִית (יא עַמּוּד א)
and as I shall explain further on (Siman 14) from the words of Tosafot in Nazir (2b) and Ta'anit (11a),
גַּבֵּי נָזִיר חוֹטֵא וְיוֹשֵׁב בְּתַעֲנִית חוֹטֵא
regarding a Nazirite being a sinner and one who fasts being a sinner,
אַף דְּמִצְוָה רַבָּה עַל הַחֵטְא וְנִקְרָא נָאֶה
where despite the fact that a great mitzvah accrues over the sin and he is praised as handsome.
מִכָּל מָקוֹם נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן חוֹטֵא, עַיֵּין שָׁם
he is nonetheless also termed a sinner, see there.
וּלְכָךְ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה יֵשׁ לוֹ בּוּשָׁה מִזֶּה עֲדַיִן
Therefore in this world he still feels profound shame over this,
וְאָסוּר לוֹמַר לְבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה "זְכוֹר מַעֲשֶׂיךָ הָרִאשׁוֹנִים" ;
and it is strictly forbidden to say to a penitent 'Remember your past deeds' (Bava Metzia 58b);
אֲפִילּוּ לְמִי שֶׁשָּׁב מֵאַהֲבָה מִכָּל מָקוֹם יֵשׁ לוֹ בּוּשָׁה מֵעֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁקָּדְמוּ,
and even for one who repented out of love, he nonetheless experiences shame over earlier sins,
דְּעַל כָּל פָּנִים בִּשְׁעַת הָעֲבֵירָה הָיָה מְרוּחָק
because at any rate during the commission of the sin he was in a state of alienation.
אַף דִּבְאֶמֶת רִיחוּק זֶה קֵירוּב הוּא
even though in absolute truth that distancing was itself the catalyst for closeness.
וּלְעָתִיד יִתְגַּלֶּה זֶה בְּבֵירוּר
And in the ultimate future this will be revealed with absolute clarity,
שֶׁגַּם בִּשְׁעַת הָרִיחוּק וְהָעֲבֵירָה הָיָה מְקוֹרָב
that even during the time of estrangement and sin he was essentially held close.
וְזֶהוּ כִּזְכִיּוֹת לְגַמְרֵי
and this is the state of becoming entirely merits.
בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין זֶה נִגְלֶה עֲדַיִן
In this world, this is not yet revealed,
רַק בִּשְׁעַת עֲבוֹדָה דְּקָרְבָּנוֹת אוֹ עֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב זוֹ תְּפִלָּה
except during the sacrificial service or during service of the heart, which is prayer,
דְּהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא קָרוֹב יוֹתֵר לְמִי שֶׁלִּבּוֹ דּוֹאֵג בְּקִרְבּוֹ.
for the Holy One, blessed be He, is closer to one whose heart worries within him.
וּ"תְפִלָּה לֶעָנִי" מְעַטְּפָא כָּל צְלוֹתִין (זוֹהַר חֵלֶק א, כג עַמּוּד ב),
And 'the prayer of the afflicted man' envelops all prayers (Zohar I, 23b),
וְכַאֲשֶׁר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ קָרוֹב אֵלָיו הֲרֵי הוּא מִתְקָרֵב לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ גַּם כֵּן
and when Hashem is close to him, he in turn draws close to Hashem as well;
כִּי זֶהוּ הָעֲבוֹדָה: שֶׁהוּא כְּעֶבֶד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ שֶׁהוּא בֶּן בַּיִת אֵצֶל הַמֶּלֶךְ.
for this is the divine service: that he stands like a servant before the King who is an intimate of the royal household:
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (לד עַמּוּד ב) בְּרַבָּן יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּאי שֶׁאָמַר עַל רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא
And as our Sages recounted in Berakhot (34b) concerning Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai who said of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa:
אֶלָּא שֶׁהוּא כְּעֶבֶד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ,
rather he is like a servant before the King,
וְעַל כֵּן יָכוֹל לִפְעוֹל בִּתְפִלָּה יוֹתֵר
and therefore he is able to accomplish more through prayer,
דִּתְפִלָּה הוּא כְּעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ,
since prayer is defined as standing directly before the King,
וְהוּא לְשׁוֹן דִּיבּוּק וְחִיבּוּר כַּיָּדוּעַ.
and tefillah denotes cleaving and union (tofel), as is known.
וְאָז בְּעֵת הָעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ וּמְקוֹרָב אֵלָיו
And then at the moment of divine service when he stands before the King and is drawn close to Him,
וּמֵאִיר לְעֵינָיו אוֹר פְּנֵי מֶלֶךְ חַיִּים הָאֲמִיתִּיִּים
and there shines before his eyes the light of the King's countenance of true life,
שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶם מָוֶת וְרַע כְּלָל
wherein no death or evil exists at all,
אָז מִתְגַּלֶּה נוֹכַח עֵינָיו דָּבָר זֶה
at that moment there is disclosed before his very eyes this mystery.
אֵיךְ הַכֹּל זְכִיּוֹת גְּמוּרוֹת
how everything was transformed into absolute merits.

paragraphs.text: Cf. the same distinction across Chassidus: Me’or Einayim (Ha’azinu) — teshuvah from fear renders willful sins “as inadvertent,” teshuvah from love renders them “as merits,” exactly R’ Tzadok’s yirah/ahavah frame; and Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 7: “a teshuvah from a great love, from the depths of the heart, until the willful sins become like actual merits.” Chassidic and Maharal parallels — the mechanism of “z’donos as merits.” Maharal, Netivos Olam, Nesiv HaTeshuvah 2:17–19, explains that the sinner’s very distance becomes the measure of his later attachment: one who returns “from afar” displays a stronger deveikus, and therefore the z’don itself — the distance that he traversed — can be reckoned as a zechus. This closely complements R’ Tzadok’s claim here that teshuvah me-ahavah does not merely lighten the old act but reaches back to the will that generated it. Sefas Emes, Shabbos Shuvah 9:4, makes the distinction still more explicit: teshuvah from fear is awakened by the damage of sin and therefore weakens the sin into shogeg; teshuvah from love is awakened by longing to cleave to Torah and mitzvos, so that the sin itself becomes the cause of intensified love and added merit — “נמצא ממש זדונות נעשין כמו זכיות.” Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 7, gives the same causal structure: because the soul had been “in a dry and shadowed land,” its later thirst for God is stronger, and “since through this he came to this great love,” the deliberate sins become actual merits. Shelah, Asarah Ma’amaros, Ma’amar Asiri §12, uses this distinction to reconcile the two statements about whether the baal teshuvah or the complete tzaddik is higher: ordinary teshuvah from fear does not surpass the tzaddik, whereas the rare teshuvah from love does. Chiddushei HaRim, Chayei Sarah §1, adds the temporal point that teshuvah can repair earlier days retroactively “as though he had performed mitzvos and good deeds” in them. These sources do not replace R’ Tzadok’s sharper metaphysical claim; they supply the devotional and conceptual mechanism by which the past itself becomes productive of present holiness.

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Chalomot §19): “‘though your sins be as scarlet, they shall become white as snow’ (Shabbos 89b) — and they are transformed into merits, since it was the will of Hashem, from the six days of creation, that it be so; and it emerges that the essence of the holiness in them is only that it was Hashem’s will.” This is §5-11’s “revealed to all how it is a merit and no sin at all”: at the end the willful sins turn white and are seen to have been, all along, His will — merits, with “no shame at all.”

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §34): “in truth it is hidden and concealed — ‘the sin of Israel shall be sought and be no more, for I shall forgive’ — this is so only in Israel, whose sins are ‘like the scarlet threads’ set in order from the six days of creation… and they have a good fragrance from afar.” This is §5-11 precisely: in this world the merit hidden within the sin is “not revealed and clear to the eye,” concealed like a fragrance sensed only “from afar” — but at the end “the sin shall be sought and be no more,” disclosed to all as no sin at all. Izhbitz-Radzin on what is visible only after complete teshuvah. Sod Yesharim, Parashas Parah 2:1–2, draws a precise distinction between the sinner’s responsibility before teshuvah and the Divine disclosure afterward. From the human side, repentance clarifies that at the hour of sin his דעת was absent — like a body severed from its head — and he must attribute the deficiency to himself. But after complete teshuvah, when z’donos become zechuyos, Hashem can illuminate that the very act which had appeared dark was never outside the supernal will: “אותו הפעולה בעצמה… היתה נמי גם אז מלא אור.” The work insists on the sequence: first the person owns the failure and returns; only afterward is the deeper Divine connection disclosed. This maps closely onto R’ Tzadok’s distinction here between this world, where the former act still carries shame and cannot yet be seen with complete clarity, and the future, when it will be revealed that the apparent distance itself was a form of nearness. Beis Yaakov, Vayigash 11:1–3, develops the same point through the image of Torah as “living words”: after a person returns with his whole heart, he can see retroactively that what he passed through was encompassed within divrei Elokim chayim, and the earlier meaning of his history is “healed.” Again, this is a retrospective illumination granted by teshuvah, not a heter to define a prohibited act in advance as God’s will.

paragraphs.text: Tosafos, Nazir 2b, s.v. Ve-amai naeh discusses the term “נאה” — “fitting” — in the nazirite formula of the Mishnah; this is not a biblical title. Although the nazirite is also called a sinner for afflicting himself, Tosafos explains: “ומכל מקום המצוה רבה על החטא ולכך קרי ליה נאה” — “Nevertheless, the mitzvah is greater than the sin, and therefore it calls him fitting.” Likewise, Tosafos, Taanis 11a, s.v. Amar Shmuel says of fasting: “אבל מכל מקום המצוה שהוא עושה התענית גדול יותר מן העבירה ממה שהוא מצער נפשו” — “Nevertheless, the mitzvah he performs through the fast is greater than the transgression involved in afflicting himself”; yet “ומכל מקום יש קצת חטא” — “nevertheless, there is some sin.” The comparison there is a dream-fast on Shabbos, whose benefit does not remove the need to atone for the fasting. This supplies Rav Tzadok’s precise distinction between a greater mitzvah and a remaining element requiring atonement.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 34b: When R’ Chanina ben Dosa prayed for R’ Yochanan ben Zakkai’s sick son and he recovered, R’ Yochanan said, “Had ben Zakkai stuck his head between his knees all day, they would not have heeded him.” His wife asked, “Is Chanina greater than you?” He answered, “No — but he is like a servant before the King who may enter at any time, while I am like a minister before the King who does not regularly come before him.” R’ Tzadok: the “service” (prayer, “standing before the King”) is itself the nearness in which one sees that all is merit — and God is nearest to the broken, anxious heart.

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §17): “After the teshuvah and rectification, that willful sins become merits — behold the people of Shushan, who ‘added’ in the sin of the second feast (which was in Shushan alone), and so there was added to them the merit of vengeance from their enemies one more day; and such is the measure: after they rectified their sin, judgment reached to slay those nations, where there had been a chillul Hashem.” The se’if’s “willful sins and merits” attained in this world — as with the people of Shushan. Mei HaShiloach — why the baal teshuvah can stand higher. Mei HaShiloach II, Berachos 34b, reconciles the opposing statements about tzaddikim and baalei teshuvah by separating body from soul: the complete tzaddik possesses the more purified body, but the baal teshuvah’s nefesh is hewn from a higher place. He explains that in the future, when deliberate sins become merits, Hashem will show the baal teshuvah that through his cry of teshuvah he touched an “עומק עמוק מכל דעת שהאדם יכול להשיג.” This is an especially close complement to R’ Tzadok’s language here: in this world the merit concealed in the old sin is not yet fully visible; the future disclosure is not that sin ceased to have been sin from the human standpoint, but that the baal teshuvah’s broken-hearted return reaches a depth that the earlier, unbroken state could not reveal.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: This is “willful sins as merits” as attained in this world, not as it will be revealed in the future. Here it is not yet clear to the eye: since he intended the forbidden he does not leave the category of “inadvertent,” much as an aveirah lishmah still requires atonement. Therefore shame remains, and one may not remind a baal teshuvah of his former deeds — even one who returned from love.

And this is the lofty degree of Aaron whom Hashem chose and brought near in the occupation of the sacred service,
דְּלֹא עָשָׂה שׁוּם הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת לְהַגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵגָה זוֹ,
in that he made no personal striving to attain this level,
רַק הַבּוּשָׁה שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ מִמַּעֲשֵׂה הָעֵגֶל
save the deep shame he harbored over the making of the Calf,
שֶׁהָיָה לְמַרְאִית עַיִן הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת לְהֵיפֶךְ.
which had been to outward appearances an effort in the absolute opposite direction.
שֶׁהָיָה רָאוּי לְהִתְרַחֵק מֵחֲמָתוֹ מֵעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
For on account of it he should logically have been disqualified and expelled from Hashem's service,
כַּכֹּהֲנִים שֶׁשִּׁימְּשׁוּ לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה דְּנִפְסְלוּ לַעֲבוֹדָה אַף שֶׁשָּׁבוּ בִּתְשׁוּבָה
like the priests who ministered to idolatry who were invalidated from the Temple service even after repenting (Menachot 109a),
וְהַיְינוּ בִּתְשׁוּבָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה דְּאֵין מוֹעִיל לִהְיוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת לְגַמְרֵי מַמָּשׁ.
which pertains to repentance in this world which does not avail to transform sins into merits in complete tangible reality.
וְאֵצֶל אַהֲרֹן הָיָה לְהֵיפֶךְ,
Yet with Aaron it was the exact reverse,
דִּבְאֶמֶת רִיחוּק זֶה קֵירוּב הוּא
for in truth this estrangement was itself the catalyst for closeness,
דְּעַל יָדוֹ נִתְקָרֵב
since by means of it he was brought near.
וְרַק לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן וּמִצַּד הָאָדָם אָז הָיָה רִיחוּק
and only to outward perception and from the human perspective at that moment was it alienation.
וְקֵירוּב זֶה הוּא לְעִנְיַן הָעֲבוֹדָה
And this closeness applies specifically to the realm of divine service.
דִּבְעֵת הָעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ שַׁפִּיר שַׁיָּיךְ הַקֵּירוּב הַגָּמוּר גַּם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
for at the time of divine service when standing before the King, absolute closeness rightfully applies even in this world.
וְזֶהוּ נֶגֶד מִדַּת הַהוֹד אֲשֶׁר הוּא הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת מִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה
And this corresponds to the attribute of Hod which is the extension of the attribute of Gevurah,
דִּבְמִדָּה זוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא יָרוּי וּמְאוּיָּם
for in this attribute the Holy One, blessed be He, is revered and awesome,
וְכֵן בְּמִדַּת הַהוֹד
and likewise in the attribute of Hod,
שֶׁהֲרֵי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁזָּכָה לְקַרְנֵי הוֹד "וַיִּירְאוּ מִגֶּשֶׁת אֵלָיו" (שְׁמוֹת לד, ל).
for Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, who merited radiant beams of Hod, 'they feared to draw near unto him' (Exodus 34:30).
רַק שֶׁהַגְּבוּרָה הוּא מִדָּה עַצְמִית
Except that Gevurah is an intrinsic sefirotic essence,
וְהַהוֹד עִנְיָנוֹ זִיו הַמִּתְפַּשֵּׁט מִן הָעַצְמִיּוּת
whereas Hod denotes the outer splendor radiating forth from the essence,
וְהוּא מִתְפַּשֵּׁט מִצַּד מִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה
and it expands through the power of Gevurah,
שֶׁהִיא הַמְצַמְצֶמֶת כְּבוֹד הַמֶּלֶךְ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת כְּמִדַּת הַחֶסֶד
which contracts the glory of the King so that it does not expand unrestrictedly like Chesed.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְגַּלֶּה הַהוֹד וְהַזִּיו לְבַד
and through this constriction alone the Hod and outward splendor are revealed.
וְעַל יְדֵי הִתְעוֹרְרוּת מִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה מִתְפַּשֵּׁט הַיִּרְאָה
And through the stirring of Gevurah awe and fear expand;
וּבְהִתְעוֹרְרוּת מִדַּת הַהוֹד וְזִיו הַמֶּלֶךְ מִתְפַּשֶּׁטֶת מִדַּת הַבּוּשָׁה
while through the awakening of Hod and the splendor of the King the attribute of shame expands,
שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן עֲנַף הַיִּרְאָה
which is likewise a branch of fear,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּנְדָרִים (כ עַמּוּד א):
as they expounded in Nedarim (20a): ",
בַּעֲבוּר תִּהְיֶה יִרְאָתוֹ עַל פְּנֵיכֶם" – זוֹ הַבּוּשָׁה
''that His fear may be before your faces'—this refers to shame,'.
שֶׁהִיא יִרְאָה שֶׁעַל הַפָּנִים הַמְכַסָּה אֶת הַפָּנִים
which is awe manifested upon the face that covers the face.
וְהוּא הַהֵיפֶךְ מֵהוֹד שֶׁהַזִּיו מְכַסֶּה הַפָּנִים
And this is the inverse of Hod where radiant splendor covers the countenance;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהַיִּרְאָה הֵיפֶךְ מִגְּבוּרָה
just as fear is the inverse of might,
שֶׁהַגִּבּוֹר אֵינוֹ מִתְיָירֵא רַק זֶה יָרֵא מִפְּנֵי הַגִּבּוֹר
for the warrior is not afraid, rather the other cowers before the warrior;
וְכֵן הַבּוּשָׁה הוּא מִפְּנֵי זִיו הַמֶּלֶךְ,
and so shame arises before the splendor of the King,
שֶׁמַּכִּיר שֶׁזֶּהוּ דַּרְגָּא דְּ"שִׁוִּיתִי ה' לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד" (תְּהִלִּים טז, ח)
in that he recognizes this as the rung of 'I have set Hashem before me always' (Psalms 16:8)
הַמּוּזְכָּר בְּהַגָּהַת הָרַמָ"א (בְּרֵישׁ שֻׁלְחָן עָרוּךְ אֹרַח חַיִּים סִימָן א)
mentioned in the gloss of Rema (at the beginning of Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayyim, sec. 1).
שֶׁמֵּבִיא בּוּשָׁתוֹ מִמֶּנּוּ תָּמִיד
which brings his continuous shame and humility before Him.

Therefore the service belongs to the priests.” This directly connects Aharon’s sanctity and drawing-near to the Temple service.

paragraphs.text: Divrei Soferim §30 gives a related pattern concerning Moshe: “וע"כ אמר השם יתברך למשה רד במעשה העגל דנתנדה ונתרחק כדי שיצטרך גם הוא לישועה זו דהתקרבות ועל ידי זה קירב גם כל ישראל עמו” — “Therefore God said to Moshe, ‘Go down,’ at the making of the Calf: he was placed under a ban and distanced, so that he too would require this salvation of drawing-near; through this he drew all Israel near with him.” The passage concerns Moshe’s own need enabling him to draw the people near. It illuminates how a leader’s experience of distance can become the channel of renewed nearness, while Rav Tzadok’s account here specifically concerns Aharon.

paragraphs.text: Resisei Layla §4 contrasts the crown of Torah, available to all, with Aharon’s crown of priesthood and the distinct quality of prayer. It expressly qualifies the latter: “כי השם יתברך שומע תפלת כל פה וקרוב לכל קוראיו רק אתפלה עצמה שאין דומה תפלת זה לשל זה” — “For God hears the prayer of every mouth and is near to all who call Him; rather, concerning the prayer itself, the prayer of this person is not like that of that person.” It adds: “והכל הוא לפי זוך הלב” — “Everything is according to the heart’s purity”; yet “כי באמת יש תפלה לעני דמעטפא כל צלותין” — “In truth there is the prayer of a poor person that encompasses all prayers.” This illuminates the special quality of priestly service without making lineage a condition for God to hear prayer.

paragraphs.text: The sefiros — background: Kabbalah counts ten sefiros (divine “attributes” or channels): Keser, Chochmah, Binah; then the seven “lower” sefiros — Chesed (loving-kindness / expansion), Gevurah (might / din / contraction), Tiferes (harmony); Netzach (eternity / victory), Hod (splendor / radiance), Yesod (foundation); and Malchus (kingship / the nukva, the receiving side). R’ Tzadok maps the rungs of teshuvah onto these middos, this fifth rung standing over-against Hod. He defines Hod as the ziv (radiance) that spreads from the essence of Gevurah: Gevurah “contracts” the King’s glory (so that it is not in free expansion like Chesed), and from that contraction only the radiance — Hod — is revealed. Thus as fear (yirah) spreads from Gevurah, so shame (bushah) — “a branch of fear” — spreads from Hod. (In the standard scheme Netzach and Hod are the “two thighs” from which the prophets are nourished — Moshe corresponding to Netzach and Aharon to Hod, as the next se’if develops.) A parallel development in R’ Tzadok’s own writings — on Hod, bushah, and the “whitening of the face” — is given in the corpus note on this se’if.

paragraphs.text: Nedarim 20a teaches in a baraita: “תַּנְיָא: ״בַּעֲבוּר תִּהְיֶה יִרְאָתוֹ עַל פְּנֵיכֶם״ — זוֹ בּוּשָׁה. ״לְבִלְתִּי תֶחֱטָאוּ״ — מְלַמֵּד שֶׁהַבּוּשָׁה מְבִיאָה לִידֵי יִרְאַת חֵטְא. מִיכָּן אָמְרוּ: סִימָן יָפֶה בְּאָדָם שֶׁהוּא בַּיְישָׁן.” — “It was taught: ‘So that His fear may be upon your faces’—this is shame. ‘So that you do not sin’—this teaches that shame leads to fear of sin. Hence they said: it is a favorable sign in a person that he is bashful.” Rav Tzadok uses the verse’s fear upon the face to explain shame as the human response to the King’s radiance.

paragraphs.text: Tehillim 16:8: “שִׁוִּיתִי ה׳ לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד, כִּי מִימִינִי בַּל אֶמּוֹט” — “I have set Hashem before me always; because He is at my right hand I shall not falter.” The Rema opens the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chaim 1:1) by citing this verse: “‘I have set Hashem before me always’ — this is a great principle in the Torah and among the virtues of the righteous who walk before God,” for one who is ever mindful of standing before the King is filled with humility and awe. R’ Tzadok’s use: this “before me always” is the constant “face-to-face” of the radiance (Hod) — the rung that induces bushah (shame) before the King’s presence at every moment, the branch of fear that spreads from Hod.

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §28): “‘whoever is ashamed does not quickly sin’ (Nedarim 20a)” — shame is the guard set over the heart. This lights up §5-12’s “he brings his shame before Him always”: Aharon, drawn near not by striving but through the shame of his fall, keeps that shame ever before him — so the very shame that might have distanced him becomes his abiding safeguard, the trembling nearness of one who never forgets from where he was raised.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: This is Aharon’s rung — chosen and brought near without striving, the shame of the Calf being, to the eye, a striving toward the very opposite. In truth that distancing was itself the nearness through which he was drawn close. It answers to the middah of Hod, the radiance that spreads from Gevurah — a contracted glory, which is why they feared to approach Moshe’s rays.

And this cannot endure uninterruptedly as is known,
דְּעַל כֵּן כָּל הַבְּרָכוֹת מַתְחִילִין בִּלְשׁוֹן נוֹכַח וּמְסַיְּימִין בִּלְשׁוֹן נִסְתָּר
which is why all blessings begin in direct second-person address ('Blessed are You') and conclude in the third-person ('Who has sanctified us'),
דְּמִיָּד נֶעְלָם הַנּוֹכַח דִּפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ.
for the immediate second-person awareness of the King's face promptly conceals itself.
אֲבָל הַנּוֹכַח דְּזִיו אֶפְשָׁר לְקַיֵּים בּוֹ "לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד",
However, the perception of His radiant splendor can be sustained 'before me always';
וְזֶהוּ דַּרְגָּא דַּעֲבוֹדָה דְּכֹהֲנִים בְּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ
and this is the spiritual stature of the priests' divine service in the Holy Temple.
שֶׁשָּׁם נִיכָּר זִיו שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ תָּמִיד
where the splendor of His Shechinah was constantly perceived.
וְהִתְקָרְבוּת זֶה דְּזִיו הוֹדוֹ זָכָה לוֹ אַהֲרֹן עַל יְדֵי הַבּוּשָׁה
And this drawing near to the splendor of His Hod was merited by Aaron through shame,
שֶׁהוּא הֶעְלֵם זִיו הַהוֹד שֶׁבַּפָּנִים
which represents the withdrawal of the radiant Hod of the countenance,
דְּפָנָיו מַלְבִּינוֹת, וְעַל כֵּן הוּא כִּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים ,
wherein his face blanches white, and therefore shaming is likened to bloodshed (Bava Metzia 58b),
כִּי פָּנָיו כִּפְנֵי הַמֵּת שֶׁמִּשְׁתַּנֶּה זִיו הַפָּנִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי (סוֹף יְבָמוֹת) וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ.
for his face turns like a corpse whose facial luster changes, as stated in the Yerushalmi (end of Yevamot) and Midrash.
(וּכְעִנְיָן שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּבֵלְשַׁאצַּר : "זִיווֹהִי שְׁנוֹהִי"
(And along the lines of what is said of Belshazzar (Daniel 5:6): 'his countenance changed within him'
עַל יְדֵי שֶׁלָּבַשׁ בִּגְדֵי כְּהֻנָּה וְנִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בִּכְלֵי הַקֹּדֶשׁ,
because he put on priestly vestments and profaned the holy vessels,
שֶׁהֵם זִיו וְהוֹד פְּנֵי מֶלֶךְ יִתְבָּרַךְ).
which embody the luster and Hod of the face of the King, blessed be He).
וְזֶהוּ מִדָּה טוֹבָה שֶׁבַּנָּשִׁים
And this is the commendable trait among women,
שֶׁכְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (תְּהִלִּים מה, יד): "כָּל כְּבוּדָּה בַת מֶלֶךְ פְּנִימָה",
for as it is written (Psalms 45:14): 'All glorious is the king's daughter within,'
וְאֵין מְגַלֵּית זִיו פָּנֶיהָ.
and she does not brazenly expose her facial luster.
וְזֶהוּ מִדַּת הַהוֹד מִסִּטְרָא דְּנוּקְבָא
And this is the attribute of Hod from the feminine side.
וּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהִיא "אֵשֶׁת חַיִל" לְהַעֲלִים זִיוָוהּ וּבוֹשָׁה לִתְבּוֹעַ בַּפֶּה
and the Congregation of Israel is 'a woman of valor' who conceals her radiance and is too bashful to demand with her mouth.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה (מִשְׁלֵי ז, יג): "הֵעֵזָה פָנֶיהָ וַתֹּאמַר וְגוֹמֵר",
In contrast to a wanton harlot (Proverbs 7:13): 'she impudently hardened her face and said, etc.'
וְנֶאֱמַר (יִרְמְיָה ג, ג): "מֵצַח אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה הָיָה לָךְ מֵאַנְתְּ הִכָּלֵם",
and it is said (Jeremiah 3:3): 'You had a harlot's forehead, you refused to be ashamed,'
וְנֶאֱמַר (מִשְׁלֵי ט, יג): "אֵשֶׁת כְּסִילוּת הֹמִיָּה וְגוֹמֵר".
and it is said (Proverbs 9:13): 'A foolish woman is clamorous, etc.',
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אֵשֶׁת חַיִל עִיקַּר מִדָּתָהּ הַצְּנִיעוּת
However, with a woman of valor her primary trait is modesty;
וְהוּא מִדַּת רָחֵל בִּשְׁתִיקָה
and this is the attribute of Rachel expressed in silence;
וּמִדַּת לֵאָה כְּנֶגְדָּהּ בְּהוֹדָאָה
and the attribute of Leah corresponding to it is in thanksgiving and acknowledgment (Hodayah),
כָּל הִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁלָּהּ הָיָה רַק לְהוֹדוֹת לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם יִתְבָּרַךְ וּלְהִדָּבֵק בְּמִדַּת הַהוֹד שֶׁלּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,
her entire self-expression being solely to offer praise before the Omnipresent and cleave unto His attribute of Hod,
וְתָבְעָה בַּפֶּה לְהַרְבּוֹת בָּנִים שִׁבְטֵי יָ"הּ וְהוּא מִלֵּידַת יְהוּדָה וְיִשָּׂשׂכָר
and she spoke forth to multiply sons for the tribes of God, which unfolded from the birth of Judah and Issachar;
וְזֶה אַחַר לֵידַת לֵוִי שֶׁאָמְרָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית כט, לד): "הַפַּעַם יִלָּוֶה אִישִׁי אֵלַי",
and this was after the birth of Levi when she proclaimed (Genesis 29:34): 'Now this time my husband will be joined unto me,'
דְּזָכְתָה לְמִדַּת הַדְּבֵקִים לְגַמְרֵי וְלִהְיוֹת מֶרְכָּבָה לְמִדַּת הַהוֹד שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה
for she merited the attribute of absolute cleaving and becoming a chariot for the supernal attribute of Hod,
שֶׁכֵּן יָצָא מִמֶּנָּה אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֵן שֶׁהוּא נִלְוֶוה אֵלָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּעֶבֶד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ.
since from her issued Aaron the Priest who was intimately joined unto Him, blessed be He, like a servant before the King.
וְזָכָה לְמִדַּת הַהוֹד עַל יְדֵי שְׁלֵימוּתוֹ בְּמִדָּה זוֹ מִצַּד מַה שֶּׁהוּא בִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל
And he merited the attribute of Hod through his perfection in this attribute as it exists within the Congregation of Israel,
דְּהַיְינוּ הַעֲלָמַת הַזִּיו שֶׁנִּרְאֶה כְּבוּשָׁה
namely the inward concealment of radiance that appears outwardly as shame,
וּבֶאֱמֶת זֶה עִיקַּר זִיוָון וְהוֹדָן שֶׁל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהֵן בַּיְישָׁנִים
and in truth this is the quintessential luster and glory of the children of Israel, that they are shamefaced,
שֶׁהוּא מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה סִימָנִים דִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל – אֵשֶׁת חַיִל (יְבָמוֹת עט עַמּוּד א).
which is one of the three hallmark signs of the Congregation of Israel, the woman of valor (Yevamot 79a).
וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (יב עַמּוּד ב):
And therefore our Sages said in Berakhot (12b):
הָעוֹבֵר עֲבֵירָה וּמִתְבַּיֵּישׁ – מוֹחֲלִין לוֹ עַל כָּל עֲוֺנוֹתָיו
He who commits a transgression and feels ashamed of it, is forgiven for all his iniquities,
וְלָמְדוּ מִשָּׁאוּל דְּאָמְרוּ לוֹ (שְׁמוּאֵל א כח, יט): "מָחָר אַתָּה וּבָנֶיךָ עִמִּי" – בִּמְחִיצָתִי (עֵרוּבִין נג עַמּוּד ב).
and they derived this from Saul to whom Samuel said (I Samuel 28:19): 'Tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me'—in my spiritual compartment (Eruvin 53b).
וְיָדוּעַ דַּרְגָּא דִּשְׁמוּאֵל הַשָּׁקוּל כְּמֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן (בְּרָכוֹת לא עַמּוּד ב)
And it is known that the rung of Samuel is equated to Moses and Aaron together (Berakhot 31b),
שֶׁהֵם מִדַּת נֶצַח וָהוֹד
who embody the twin attributes of Netzach and Hod,
דְּמִשָּׁם יְנִיקַת הַנְּבִיאִים
whence is the spiritual nurture of all prophets,
וּשְׁמוּאֵל רַבָּן שֶׁל כָּל הַנְּבִיאִים
and Samuel was the master of all prophets;
שֶׁהוּא בָּא וְהוֹרִיד הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַנְּבוּאָה בָּעוֹלָם
who came and drew down the broad expansion of prophecy into the world.
וְ"עִמּוֹ בִּמְחִיצָתוֹ" – הַיְינוּ בִּמְחִיצַת הַהוֹד שֶׁזָּכָה לָהּ עַל יְדֵי הַבּוּשָׁה
and 'with him in his compartment' means in the compartment of Hod which Saul merited through genuine shame.

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Likkutei Maamarim §6): “‘I who sanctify them and give holiness in you’ — and this is in the language of nochach present, ‘in you’; and afterward, when it says in the language of nistar hidden, ‘and they shall keep… between Me and Bnei Yisrael,’ it speaks of the Shabbos of the Holy One Himself.” This is §5-13’s law of the blessings exactly: the recognition opens face-to-face, in nochach (“in you,” the present), and because that clarity cannot stay fixed it closes in nistar (“between Me and Israel,” the hidden) — the very present-then-hidden turn R’ Tzadok hears in the covenant of Shabbos.

paragraphs.text: Kometz HaMinchah II §32: “כי תמידות עול האדנות א"א לצ"ג רק לבעל תשובה זהו מקומו מרוב מרירותו על מה שקדם וזהו מדרגת חסיד המתחסד עם קונו” — “For constancy in the yoke of lordship is impossible for a perfectly righteous person, but only for a penitent; this is his place, because of his great bitterness over what preceded. This is the rank of a chasid who acts lovingly with his Maker.” It connects this to David: “וזהו דוד המלך ע"ה שהוא הסוף מעשה ביחוד לכך שייך אצלו תפלה שמיוחדת לעני” — “This is King David, who particularly represents the final deed; therefore prayer, which belongs especially to the poor, pertains to him.” This illuminates the broken heart’s continuing submission and nearness in service; it is not a source for Hillel’s policy on safeguards.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash §17: “ויש מדרגה יותר כשיצייר ע"י אמונה שממ"ה הקב"ה עומד עליו ואז יגדל הבושה יותר ויותר. וכ"ז בבחי' אמונה” — “There is a higher rank: when through faith he pictures that the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed is He, stands over him, his shame then grows greater and greater. All this is within the aspect of faith.” It contrasts this with the future: “ולעתיד שהכל יראו עין בעין שהש"י רואה כל מעשי בנ"א אז יבוש האדם במעשיו” — “In the future, when all will see eye to eye that God sees all human deeds, a person will then be ashamed of his deeds.” The passage’s distinction between faith-shaped awareness now and unveiled vision later helps explain why Rav Tzadok distinguishes abiding awareness of the radiance from full direct perception.

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 58b: in the sugya of ona’as devarim (wronging with words), the Gemara teaches that “one who whitens the face of his fellow in public ha-malbin penei chaveiro ba-rabbim — it is as though he sheds blood shefichus damim,” for one observes that the shamed man’s redness drains away and his face whitens, like the pallor of the slain. R’ Tzadok draws on this: the whitening of the face in shame is the concealment of the inner Hod-radiance — “his face is like the face of the dead, whose facial radiance is altered” — and this is the very mark of bushah, the branch of Hod.

paragraphs.text: Daniel 5:6: “אֱדַיִן מַלְכָּא זִיוֺהִי שְׁנוֹהִי, וְרַעְיֹנֹהִי יְבַהֲלוּנֵּהּ, וְקִטְרֵי חַרְצֵהּ מִשְׁתָּרַיִן, וְאַרְכֻבָּתֵהּ דָּא לְדָא נָקְשָׁן” — “then the king’s radiance was changed, and his thoughts alarmed him; the joints of his loins were loosened, and his knees knocked one against the other.” The scene is Belshatzar’s feast (Daniel 5): the Babylonian king drank from the sacred vessels plundered from the Beis HaMikdash, whereupon a hand wrote upon the wall “mene mene tekel u-farsin,” and his face blanched in terror. R’ Tzadok draws on “ziv apohi ishtani” — the changing (blanching) of his face-radiance through his misusing the holy vessels, “which are the radiance and Hod of the King’s face” — as the image of the whitening of the face, the concealment of the inner Hod-radiance, which is the essence of bushah (shame): the kohen’s face, too, “whitens.”

paragraphs.text: Tehillim 45:14: “כָּל כְּבוּדָּה בַת מֶלֶךְ פְּנִימָה, מִמִּשְׁבְּצוֹת זָהָב לְבוּשָׁהּ” — “all the honor of the king’s daughter is within; her raiment is of golden settings.” Meforshim: a woman’s true honor and beauty are inward and concealed; the Sages derive from here the value of tzniyus (modesty) — that a woman’s dignity lies in her inwardness (cf. Shevuos 30a, Yevamos 77a). R’ Tzadok’s use: this “inwardness” is the middah of Hod from the side of the nukva — Knesses Yisrael, the eishes chayil, conceals the radiance of her face; and this very concealing of the radiance is her splendor, appearing outwardly as shame.

R’ Tzadok’s use: the harlot is az panim (brazen-faced), the very opposite of the eishes chayil, whose middah is modesty and bushah; Knesses Yisrael’s true splendor is her shame, the concealed Hod.

paragraphs.text: Mishlei 31:30: “שֶׁקֶר הַחֵן וְהֶבֶל הַיֹּפִי, אִשָּׁה יִרְאַת ה׳ הִיא תִתְהַלָּל” — “Grace is false and beauty is vain; a woman who fears Hashem — she shall be praised.” This is a verse near the close of “Eishes Chayil” (Mishlei 31:10–31), the alphabetical hymn to the woman of valor with which Shlomo HaMelech closes the book. Meforshim: in its plain sense, outward charm and beauty are fleeting, and only yiras Hashem is the abiding ground of praise; the Midrash and meforshim also read Eishes Chayil allegorically (of the Torah, the soul, and the Shechinah). R’ Tzadok fastens on “isha yiras Hashem”: fear is the “feminine” principle — the nukva, the receiving-and-submitting side, malchus — and this is precisely David’s rung, “a woman who fears Hashem,” the middah of Gevurah that subdues the yetzer; over against Avraham’s “masculine” love that transforms it.

Meforshim: homiyah (clamorous, noisy) marks folly’s brazen loudness. R’ Tzadok’s use: the “boisterous” woman of folly is the brazen harlot, the antithesis of the silent, modest eishes chayil (the middah of Rachel, “in silence”).

paragraphs.text: Bereishis 29:34: “וַתַּהַר עוֹד וַתֵּלֶד בֵּן, וַתֹּאמֶר עַתָּה הַפַּעַם יִלָּוֶה אִישִׁי אֵלַי כִּי יָלַדְתִּי לוֹ שְׁלֹשָׁה בָנִים, עַל כֵּן קָרָא שְׁמוֹ לֵוִי” — at the birth of her third son Leah says, “now this time my husband will accompany yilaveh me, for I have borne him three sons; therefore he called his name Levi.” Rashi explains that the matriarchs knew prophetically that twelve tribes would come from Yaakov and that he would marry four wives; Leah therefore said that, with three sons, she had borne her full allotted share; Leah’s word “yilaveh” (accompany / attach) gave Levi his name — the tribe of liwuy (attachment). Kabbalah (which R’ Tzadok develops here): Leah is the middah of hoda’ah (thanksgiving) and Hod — all her “revealing” and “demanding with the mouth” was to give thanks before God and to cleave to His middah of Hod; from her issued Levi and Aharon, who are “attached nilveh to Him like a servant before the King,” a Chariot for the supernal Hod — over-against Rachel, the middah of modesty and silence (the corpus note on this se’if brings R’ Tzadok’s parallel on Leah / Rachel and Hod).

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas Shabbos §7: “וזהו שלימות מדת ההוד שא' בהרואה זה בהמ"ק שהוא תלפיות תל שכל פיות פונין לו. דכל ההודיות והקילוסין אינם עולים אלא דרך המקדש. וזו מדת אהרן הכהן שהוא העומד שם בעבודת הקרבנות” — “This is the perfection of the attribute of Hod, which the Gemara in HaRo’eh says is the Temple: talpiyyos, the hill toward which all mouths turn. All thanksgivings and praises ascend only through the Temple. This is Aharon the priest’s attribute, for he stands there in the service of the offerings.” It adds: “וכן התפלה במקום הקרבנות ברכות והודאות לשמו.” — “Likewise, prayer in place of the offerings consists of blessings and thanksgivings to His name.” This directly connects Hod, Aharon, avodah, and hodaah, illuminating the author’s chain from Leah’s thanksgiving to Aharon’s service.

paragraphs.text: Berachos31b explains Channah’s request as “זֶרַע שֶׁשָּׁקוּל כִּשְׁנֵי אֲנָשִׁים, וּמַאן אִינּוּן — מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן. שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן בְּכֹהֲנָיו וּשְׁמוּאֵל בְּקוֹרְאֵי שְׁמוֹ״.” — “Offspring who is weighed against two people—and who are they? Moshe and Aharon, as it is stated: ‘Moshe and Aharon among His priests, and Shmuel among those who call His name.’” Taanis5b likewise has Shmuel say to God: “שְׁקַלְתַּנִי כְּמֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן” — “You have weighed me as Moshe and Aharon.” Rav Tzadok further characterizes Shmuel as the master of the prophets and reads his combined rank through Moshe/Netzach and Aharon/Hod; that is the framework for Shaul’s place in his precinct.

paragraphs.text: Shmuel I28:19 records Shmuel’s warning to Shaul: “וּמָחָר אַתָּה וּבָנֶיךָ עִמִּי” — “Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me.” Berachos12b derives Shaul’s shame from the preceding account of his unanswered inquiries: “וְאִילּוּ ״אוּרִים וְתוּמִּים״ לָא קָאָמַר.” — “But he did not mention the Urim and Tumim”; the reason is “מִשּׁוּם דְּקַטְלֵיהּ לְנוֹב עִיר הַכֹּהֲנִים.” — “because he had killed the priests of Nov, the priestly city.” He was ashamed to mention the means of inquiry associated with the priests he had killed. The Gemara then proves that Heaven forgave him from “עִמִּי — בִּמְחִיצָתִי” — “‘With me’—in my precinct.” Rav Tzadok develops this precinct as Shmuel’s prophetic Hod, reached through shame. Vayikra Rabbah26:7 supplies the separate acceptance-of-judgment tradition: “וְאִם אַתְּ מְקַבֵּל עָלֶיךָ מִדַּת הַדִּין מָחָר אַתָּה וּבָנֶיךָ עִמִּי” — “If you accept upon yourself the attribute of judgment, tomorrow you and your sons will be with me”; it explains “עִמִּי בִּמְחִצָּתִי” — “with me, in my precinct.” Thus the two cited traditions connect Shaul’s nearness respectively with shame over Nov and willing acceptance of judgment.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The clear “face-to-face” recognition is the rung of Yitzchak, and it cannot be sustained — which is why blessings open in the present and close in the hidden. The face-to-face of the radiance, however, can be held constantly, and this is the priests’ service in the Temple. Aharon merited it through shame, the concealment of the inner radiance of Hod — the same middah by which “all the honor of the king’s daughter is within.”

p: (יד), — וְזֶהוּ מִדַּת "זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת" שֶׁזּוֹכִין בַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And this attribute of 'willful sins become merits' which penitents out of love merit in this world,
הוּא מִצַּד מִדָּה זוֹ,
emanates directly from this sefirotic attribute of Hod,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ מִדַּת אַהֲרֹן: "אוֹהֵב אֶת הַבְּרִיּוֹת וּמְקָרְבָן לַתּוֹרָה" (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק א מִשְׁנָה יב).
which is the exact character of Aaron: 'loving created beings and drawing them near to the Torah' (Avot 1:12).
וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (אָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן פֶּרֶק יב, ג)
And our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Avot DeRabbi Natan 12:3):
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה הָיָה מְקָרְבָן
that through this method he would draw them close:
עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהָיָה מִתְחַבֵּר וּמַרְאֶה אַהֲבָתוֹ לוֹ,
by associating with the person and showing him personal warmth and love.
וְהָיָה הַלָּה בּוֹשׁ מֵעֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁבְּיָדוֹ עַל יְדֵי זֶה וְעוֹזְבָן
and the person would feel utterly ashamed of his transgressions on account of this and abandon them.
וְאִם זֶהוּ עַל יְדֵי אַהֲבַת אָדָם כְּאַהֲרֹן
And if such shame is evoked through the love of a mortal like Aaron,
כָּל שֶׁכֵּן עַל יְדֵי אַהֲבָה שֶׁמַּרְאֶה לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
how much more so through the infinite love demonstrated unto him by Hashem, blessed be He.
שֶׁהוּא מוֹלִיד בּוּשָׁה גְּדוֹלָה בְּקִרְבּוֹ עַל יְדֵי זֶה עַל עֲוֺנוֹתָיו
which engenders overwhelming shame within him over his past iniquities.
וְעַל כֵּן עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה הוּא תּוֹקֶף הַבּוּשָׁה
Therefore through repentance out of love there arises the utmost intensity of shame.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְקָרֵב לַעֲבוֹדָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ וּמִתְפַּלֵּל וְנַעֲנֶה
and through that contrite humility he draws near to His sacred service, prays, and is answered.
וְכֵיוָן שֶׁהִתְקָרְבוּת זֶה, שֶׁהוּא הַדְּבֵיקוּת בֵּאלֹהִים חַיִּים, הוּא עַל יְדֵי הָעֲוֺנוֹת
And since this drawing near—which is living cleaving unto the living God—was occasioned by the sins,
הֲרֵי "עֲלֵיהֶם" וְעַל יָדָם חָיֹה יִחְיֶה
behold 'by them' and through their catalyst he shall surely live (Ezekiel 33:19),
וְנַעֲשָׂה אוֹתוֹ רִיחוּק דַּעֲבֵירָה דּוּגְמַת נִדּוּת דְּאִשָּׁה הַנִּזְכָּר
and that very estrangement of sin becomes like the aforementioned separation of menstruation
שֶׁהוּא לְחַבְּבָהּ עַל בַּעֲלָהּ.
which serves ultimately to render her beloved to her husband.
וְעַל יְדֵי כֵּן (אֵיכָה א, יג): "כָּל הַיּוֹם דָּוָה",
And on account of this Scripture states (Lamentations 1:13): 'all the day faint (davah)',
וְנוֹדַע דְּרוֹמֵז לָאֶלֶף הַחֲמִישִׁי שֶׁאוֹתוֹ יוֹם כֻּלּוֹ בַּגָּלוּת
and it is known that this alludes to the fifth millennium which was an entire thousand-year 'day' in exile,
שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד הַהוֹד דִּבְהִפּוּךְ אַתְוָון "דָּוָה".
which corresponds to Hod whose letters invert to spell davah (,
דָּוָה). וְהַיְינוּ כְּאִשָּׁה דָּוָה שֶׁהָרִיחוּק הוּא לְקֵירוּב אַהֲבָה
Meaning that like an ailing woman during separation where the distancing is for the sake of renewed passionate closeness:
שֶׁזֶּהוּ מִדַּת הַקֵּירוּב שֶׁל מִדַּת הַהוֹד
such is the distinctive mode of reconciliation belonging to the attribute of Hod:
לֹא אַהֲבָה מְפוֹרֶשֶׁת הַבָּאָה עַל יְדֵי אַהֲבָה גְּלוּיָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לֶעָתִיד
not an overt, direct love arising from explicit revelation as will be in the World to Come.
רַק אַהֲבָה הַבָּאָה מִכֹּחַ רִיחוּק
rather a love that is forged out of the very power of estrangement.
כִּי הוּא מֵהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת מִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד הָאַהֲבָה
For Hod is the extension of Gevurah which stands opposite love,
רַק שֶׁהִיא הַמְּבִיאָה לְאַהֲבָה
except that it ultimately gives birth to love;
וּבִשְׁעַת הָרִיחוּק טֶרֶם נִתְגַּלָּה הָאַהֲבָה נִקְרָא "דָּוָה",
and during the season of estrangement before love is overtly manifest, it is termed davah.
שֶׁהוּא הַהֵיפֶךְ מֵהוֹד
which is the exact inversion of Hod.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: שֶׁהוּא לְחַבְּבָהּ עַל בַּעֲלָהּ.

paragraphs.text: Avos 1:12: “הִלֵּל אוֹמֵר: הֱוֵי מִתַּלְמִידָיו שֶׁל אַהֲרֹן — אוֹהֵב שָׁלוֹם וְרוֹדֵף שָׁלוֹם, אוֹהֵב אֶת הַבְּרִיּוֹת וּמְקָרְבָן לַתּוֹרָה” — “Hillel says: be of the disciples of Aharon — loving peace and pursuing peace, loving the creatures and drawing them near to Torah.” Avos de-Rabbi Nasan (ch. 12) explains how he drew them near: Aharon would befriend even a known sinner and show him love and friendship, so that the man became ashamed of the transgressions in his hand and forsook them. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the engine of teshuvah from love — the love shown to a person (all the more, the love God shows him) begets shame over his sins, and through that shame he draws near to the avodah; and since the drawing-near comes through the sins, “by them he shall live,” and willful sins become as merits. Aharon’s love as the engine of teshuvah. Sefas Emes, Shemini 7:3, connects Aharon’s own teshuvah from love with the elevation of the entire people’s return, invoking “על כל פשעים תכסה אהבה.” Read beside Avos’ “אוהב את הבריות ומקרבן לתורה,” the two teachings illuminate one another: Aharon’s mode of kiruv is itself the logic of teshuvah me-ahavah. Love precedes the sinner’s shame; the shame then makes him abandon the sin; and the very path by which he had been distant becomes the cause of a deeper return. This fits R’ Tzadok’s point that in Aharon’s middah the z’donos become zechuyos specifically because the Divine or human love shown to the sinner is what produces the new nearness. Rav Tzadok further connects this shame awakened by love with the middah of Hod/bushah; that observation absorbs the distinct point of the shorter companion note.

paragraphs.text: Eichah 1:13: “מִמָּרוֹם שָׁלַח אֵשׁ בְּעַצְמֹתַי וַיִּרְדֶּנָּה … נְתָנַנִי שֹׁמֵמָה, כָּל הַיּוֹם דָּוָה” — “from on high He sent fire into my bones and it prevailed; … He has made me desolate and faint daveh all the day.” From the first kinah of Eichah, Yirmeyahu’s lament over the Churban, in the voice of stricken Jerusalem. Meforshim: “daveh” is languishing, sick — the faintness likened to the davah of niddah. R’ Tzadok’s use: “kol ha-yom daveh” alludes to the fifth millennium, the “day” wholly given over to exile, which corresponds to Hod — for in reverse of letters “Hod” (ה־ו־ד) is “Daveh” (ד־ו־ה); the languishing distance of exile is, like the niddah of a wife, a distancing that is ultimately for a drawing-near of love.

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Ki Tavo §17): “the middah of Hod, that Aharon the Kohen is a merkavah chariot for it; and in the fifth millennium, which corresponds to the middah of Hod, was the essence of the servitude and the yoke of exiles… ‘all the day daveh faint’ — for Hod was overturned into daveh.” This is the very axis of §5-14: Aharon bears Hod, and when Hod is not revealed it is overturned, letter-for-letter, into daveh — precisely the se’if’s “when it is not revealed it is called daveh, the reverse of Hod.” Aharon’s whole avodah is to keep Hod turned right-side-up.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The “willful sins as merits” that baalei teshuvah from love attain belongs to this middah of Hod — Aharon’s, “who loves the creatures and draws them near to Torah.” He drew them near by showing love, until a man grew ashamed of what was in his hand and forsook it. All the more so the love God Himself shows a person; and since the drawing-near comes through the sins, the distance works like the niddah that endears.

p: (טו) — וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר בְּדָנִיֵּאל (י, ח): "וְהוֹדִי נֶהְפַּךְ עָלַי לְמַשְׁחִית"
And concerning this it is stated in Daniel (10:8): 'and my splendor (hodi) was turned in me into corruption'.
כְּשֶׁבָּא אֵלָיו הַמַּלְאָךְ לְהַגִּיד מִמַּלְכוּת יָוָן וְרוֹמִי
when the angel came to inform him concerning the empires of Greece and Rome.
וְהָרוֹמִיִּים הֵם שֶׁגָּרְמוּ הִפּוּךְ הַהוֹד לְדָוָה
And the Romans are the ones who caused the inversion of Hod into davah,
שֶׁהֵם זֶרַע עֵשָׂו שֶׁהָיָה פְּסֹלֶת הַגְּבוּרָה
for they are the seed of Esau who was the dross of Gevurah,
וְהֵם הַפְּסֹלֶת דְּהַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת
and they represent the dross of outward extension,
שֶׁהוּא פְּסֹלֶת הַהוֹד דְּאַהֲרֹן שֶׁהָיָה "אוֹהֵב שָׁלוֹם וְרוֹדֵף שָׁלוֹם",
which is the distorted counterfeit of the Hod of Aaron who 'loved peace and pursued peace';
וְהֵם בְּהֵיפֶךְ זַרְעָא דְּעֵשָׂו דִּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ (בְּרֵאשִׁית כז, מ): "עַל חַרְבְּךָ תִחְיֶה",
whereas they are the exact antithesis, the seed of Esau concerning whom it is written (Genesis 27:40): 'by your sword you shall live'.
רַק לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן הָיוּ מְדַמִּים עַצְמָם גַּם הֵם כֵּן
only that to outward appearance they falsely portrayed themselves as pursuers of peace as well.
וּכְנוֹדָע מִדִּבְרֵי אוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע טִיטוּס הַכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר יוֹסִיפוֹן
And as is known from the words of that wicked Titus recorded in Sefer Yosippon,
אֵיךְ בִּדְבָרָיו הָיָה מְבַקֵּשׁ רַק שָׁלוֹם
how in his deceptive speeches he claimed to seek only peace,
אַף שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת כַּוָּונָתוֹ הָיָה רַק לְהָרַע
even though his true intent was purely malicious,
כְּדֶרֶךְ אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים הַחֲפֵצָה לְהִתַּקֵּן בְּתִיקּוּנָהָא בְּרָזָא דְּ"אֵשֶׁת חַיִל".
in the manner of a seductive harlot who seeks to disguise herself in the holy ornaments of the 'woman of valor'.
וּלְעוֹלָם כָּל אוּמָּה בְּאוֹתוֹ רַע שֶׁהֵם שְׁקוּעִים, שֶׁבָּהֶם הֵם הַהֵיפֶךְ מִכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל
And invariably every pagan nation, in the very evil in which they are immersed and in which they oppose Israel,
הֵם חֲפֵצִים בּוֹ דַּוְוקָא לְהִתְדַּמּוֹת לִכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל
they intensely desire specifically to imitate and counterfeit the Congregation of Israel,
כַּנּוֹדָע בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, קמח עַמּוּד ב) שֶׁהוּא כְּגוֹוְנָא דְּקוֹפָא דְּאָזֵיל בָּתַר בַּר נָשׁ,
as is known in the Zohar (Part II, 148b) that evil mimics holiness like an ape mimicking a human being,
וְהוּא בְּזֶרַע דְּעֵשָׂו בְּיִחוּד שֶׁנִּמְשַׁל לַחֲזִיר שֶׁפּוֹשֵׁט טְלָפָיו
and this applies uniquely to the seed of Esau who is likened to a swine displaying its split hooves,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה סה, א) דִּמְצַעַת הַבִּימָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ.
and as our Sages recounted in the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 65:1) concerning the judge's podium, see there at length.
וּבֶאֱמֶת בָּזֶה עַצְמוֹ הוּא הַהֵיפֶךְ מֵרָזָא דְּאֵשֶׁת חַיִל
And in truth, in this hypocrisy itself lies the exact antithesis of the mystery of the woman of valor,
שֶׁכָּל הוֹדָהּ וְזִיוָוהּ וּכְבוֹדָהּ פְּנִימָה בְּהֶעְלֵם וּצְנִיעוּת
whose entire Hod, splendor, and glory are internal, in hiddenness and modest chastity,
וּבַגִּלּוּי הוּא אַדְּרַבָּה מִדַּת בּוּשָׁה שֶׁהוּא הֵיפֶךְ הַזִּיו
while on the outside there manifests on the contrary the attribute of shame which is the concealment of radiant pride.
וְהַיְינוּ הָרִיחוּק שֶׁסִּבַּת הַקֵּירוּב
which is the state of estrangement that serves as the cause of closeness.
כִּי הָרִיחוּק וְהָעֲבֵירוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הֵם רַק לְמַרְאִית עַיִן וּכְפִי הַנִּגְלֶה
For the apparent estrangement and sins of Israel are only skin-deep and outward appearances.
אֲבָל בִּפְנִימִיּוּת מַעֲמַקֵּי לְבָבָם וּרְצוֹנָם הוּא רַק לְטוֹב
whereas in the innermost depths of their heart and true will they yearn only for good.
וְהֵם בְּהֵיפֶךְ: כָּל הָרַע שֶׁלָּהֶם פְּנִימָה
While the nations are the exact reverse: all of their evil is concealed within,
וּבְהִתְגַּלּוּת חֶפְצָם לְהַרְאוֹת עַצְמָם טוֹבִים וְלִפְשׁוֹט טְלָפַיִם
while in outward display they strive to project themselves as righteous and display split hooves.
וְזֶהוּ מַמָּשׁ הַהֵיפֶךְ מִמִּדַּת הוֹד דִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל
and this is literally the polar opposite of the attribute of Hod belonging to the Congregation of Israel.
וְעַל כֵּן עַל יְדֵי נִצּוּחָם לִהְיוֹת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּגָּלוּת תַּחַת יָדָם
Therefore through their temporary political dominance, causing Israel to languish in exile under their subjugation.
וְלִהְיוֹת הֵם הַמּוֹשְׁלִים לְפִי שָׁעָה, הָפְכוּ הַהוֹד לְדָוָה
and making them the rulers for the hour, they inverted Hod into davah.
וְגַם מַלְכוּת יָוָן הוּא הַשְׁחָתַת הוֹד וְזִיו דִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהוּא מִדַּת הַבּוּשָׁה
And likewise the empire of Greece represented the corruption of the Hod and luster of Israel which is the trait of holy shame,
וְהֵם כָּל כֹּחָם בְּעַזּוּת פָּנִים
for their entire power was rooted in brazen impudence,
דְּעַל כֵּן נִמְשְׁלוּ בְּנָמֵר
which is why Greece was allegorized as a leopard,
וְשָׁנִינוּ בְּאָבוֹת (פֶּרֶק ה מִשְׁנָה כ): "הֱוֵי עַז כַּנָּמֵר",
and we learned in Avot (5:20): 'Be brazen as a leopard,'
וְעַיֵּין רַשְׁבַּ"ץ בְּסֵפֶר מָגֵן אָבוֹת כִּי הוּא מַמְזֵר, וּמַמְזֵרִים עַזֵּי פָנִים (כַּלָּה רַבָּתִי ב).
and see Rashbatz in Sefer Magen Avot that the leopard is a hybrid bastard animal, and bastards are brazen-faced (Kallah Rabbati 2).
וְכֵן אַלֶכְּסַנְדֶּר מוֹקְדוֹן, רֹאשׁ וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ מֶמְשֶׁלֶת יָוָן, הָיָה מַמְזֵר
And likewise Alexander of Macedon, the head and founder of the Greek empire, was a bastard,
וּמִדָּתוֹ הֵיפֶךְ הַבּוּשָׁה
and his character was the absolute antithesis of shame.
וְרָצוּ לְהַכְנִיס קְלִיפָּה זוֹ בִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
and they sought to inject this impurity of impudence into the children of Israel.

paragraphs.text: Daniel 10:8: “וַאֲנִי נִשְׁאַרְתִּי לְבַדִּי, וָאֶרְאֶה אֶת הַמַּרְאָה הַגְּדֹלָה הַזֹּאת, וְלֹא נִשְׁאַר בִּי כֹּחַ, וְהוֹדִי נֶהְפַּךְ עָלַי לְמַשְׁחִית, וְלֹא עָצַרְתִּי כֹּחַ” — “and I alone was left, and I saw this great vision, and no strength remained in me; my Hod was turned within me to ruin, and I retained no strength.” From Daniel’s final vision (ch. 10) by the river Chidekel, where an angel comes to reveal “what shall befall your people in the end of days” — the succession of kingdoms, Yavan (Greece) and Edom (Rome) among them. Daniel describes his bodily strength and hod as overcome by the vision. Rashi explains “לְמַשְׁחִית” as “לְהַשְׁחָתָה” — “to destruction”; the particular reading of Hod as the radiance of Knesses Yisrael is developed here by Rav Tzadok. R’ Tzadok reads “ve-hodi nehpach alai le-mashchis” of the middah of Hod: the very turning of Hod into daveh foretold by the vision — the ruin of the Hod and radiance of Knesses Yisrael through the exiles of Greece and Rome (“Hod” reversed being “Daveh”).

paragraphs.text: Bereishis 27:40: “וְעַל חַרְבְּךָ תִחְיֶה וְאֶת אָחִיךָ תַּעֲבֹד, וְהָיָה כַּאֲשֶׁר תָּרִיד וּפָרַקְתָּ עֻלּוֹ מֵעַל צַוָּארֶךָ” — “and by your sword you shall live, and you shall serve your brother; but it shall be, when you are aggrieved tarid, that you will break his yoke from off your neck.” This is the blessing Yitzchak gave Esav, after Yaakov had received the primary blessing (ch. 27). Rashi explains “עַל חַרְבְּךָ” as “כְּמוֹ בְּחַרְבְּךָ” — “like ‘by your sword’”; on “תָּרִיד” he gives the condition “כְּשֶׁיַּעַבְרוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל הַתּוֹרָה” — “when Israel transgresses the Torah,” allowing Esav to cast off the yoke. The association with plunder belongs to the broader Esav/Edom exposition, rather than to Rashi’s grammatical gloss on sword. R’ Tzadok’s use: “by your sword you shall live” brands Esav (and his seed, Rome) as the dross of Gevurah — the way of the sword — the very reverse of Aharon’s Hod, “who loved peace and pursued peace.”

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §24): “and so did Esav — he stretches out his hooves like the swine (which has one kosher sign in its hooves, of the two signs that hint to deed and thought — the hooves to the deed).” This lays bare §5-15’s image exactly: the swine shows only the outer sign, the deed, and lacks the inner — so the nations “desire to show themselves good in revelation and to stretch out the hooves,” all their evil hidden within, the precise reverse of the eishes chayil whose radiance is within and whose revelation is shame.
