inlineHeadings.text: The theme: This verse is the haftarah of Kedoshim, which speaks of the holiness of the bris — “wherever you find a fence against immorality, you find holiness.” All Israel are holy; only outwardly are they “like the children of Kushites,” washed clean with a little water. This whole exile serves to clarify the holiness of Israel’s bodies — “and not a pebble shall fall to the ground,” for no spark is lost.

p: (עח) וְזֶהוּ שְׁלֵימוּת הַתִּיקּוּן דְּ"בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא אָקִים אֶת סֻכַּת דָּוִיד הַנֹּפֶלֶת וְגוֹמֵר" ,
And this is the total perfection of: 'In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, etc.' (Amos 9:11),
"וְנִגַּשׁ חוֹרֵשׁ בַּקֹּצֵר וְדֹרֵךְ עֲנָבִים בְּמֹשֵׁךְ הַזָּרַע" (שָׁם יג),
'and the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes him that sows seed' (v. 13),
וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל יְהוּדָה וְיוֹסֵף
and our Sages expounded this concerning Judah and Joseph.
וּ"מוֹשֵׁךְ הַזֶּרַע" רוֹמֵז גַּם כֵּן עַל שׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית וּמַמְשִׁיךְ זַרְעוֹ וְאֵינוֹ שׁוֹפֵעַ לַחִיצוֹנִים
and 'he that sows/draws the seed' alludes to the guardian of the Covenant who channels his seed properly and does not discharge unto external forces.
וִיהוּדָה תְּחִלָּתוֹ,
And Judah at his beginning,
שֶׁהוּא עֵר בְּכוֹר יְהוּדָה רֵאשִׁית אוֹנוֹ שֶׁבּוֹ רֵאשִׁית הִתְגַּלּוּת הַמְשָׁכַת כֹּחוֹתָיו לַפּוֹעַל
which was Er the firstborn of Judah, the beginning of his vigor in whom his faculties first emerged into actuality,
הָיָה נִרְאֶה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הֵיפֶךְ זֶה
appeared in this world as the very reverse of this,
וְנִקְרָא "דּוֹרֵךְ עֲנָבִים" כְּטַעַם עֲנָבִים סְחָטָהּ לוֹ שֶׁהַרְבֵּה יַיִן עוֹשֶׂה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה יט, ה).
and was termed 'treader of grapes' after the manner of Eve squeezing grapes for Adam, for wine produces intoxication (Bereishit Rabbah 19:5).
וְזֶהוּ עִיקַּר גְּרָם דְּעֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע
And this was the primary consequence of the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil,
דְּאַחַר כָּךְ הוֹלִיד רוּחוֹת שֵׁדִין וְלִילִין
for Adam subsequently fathered spirits, demons, and night-specters,
מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה דַּחֲזָא לְאוֹנְסוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק ב דְּ
through nocturnal emissions that befell him involuntarily, as they taught in Eruvin (18b).
וְהוּא עִיקַּר עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ בַּתַּאֲווֹת
and this represents the core instigation of the Serpent in physical lust.
וְיִשַׁי שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ (שַׁבָּת נה)
And Jesse who died solely through the instigation of the Serpent (Shabbat 55b)
נִתְבָּרֵר בְּלֵידַת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם דְּקָרֵי אַנַּפְשֵׁיהּ: "הֵן בְּעָווֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי" (תְּהִלִּים נא, ז),
was vindicated at the birth of King David, peace be upon him, who proclaimed of himself: 'Behold, in iniquity was I brought forth' (Psalms 51:7),
וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה : "בְּעָווֹן מָלֵא – אֲפִילּוּ חֲסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים וְכוּלֵי".
and our Sages expounded (Vayikra Rabbah 14:5): “in iniquity,” with avon written plene with an additional vav—“even the most pious among the pious,” etc.
וְיָדוּעַ מִטַּעַם הָאֲרִ"י זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה
And it is known according to the holy Ari, of blessed memory.
דִּבְכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁנּוֹסְפוּ אוֹתִיּוֹת מִשֵּׁם הֲוָיָ"ה מוֹרִים תּוֹסֶפֶת קְדוּשָּׁה וּמַעֲלָה וְטוֹבָה
that wherever letters of the Name Havayah are added (such as the Vav in
בעוון),
they indicate added holiness, virtue, and blessing.
וְאוֹת וָא"ו הוּא אוֹת אֱמֶת כַּיָּדוּעַ בַּזֹּהַר רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת וַיִּקְרָא (חֵלֶק ג, ב סוֹף עַמּוּד ב),
And the letter Vav is the letter of truth, as known from the Zohar at the beginning of Vayikra (III, 2b),
וְהַתַּאֲוָה נִקְרָא שֶׁקֶר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל מִקְרָא דְּ"עָרֵב לָאִישׁ לֶחֶם שָׁקֶר" (מִשְׁלֵי כ, יז),
and lust is termed falsehood as I cited above from 'Bread of falsehood is sweet to a man' (Proverbs 20:17),
כִּי כָּל הֲנָאָה שֶׁל שָׁעָה "וְאַחַר יִמָּלֵא פִיהוּ חָצָץ" וְאֵין קַיֶּימֶת לָעַד רַק עַד אַרְגִּיעָה
for every momentary pleasure 'afterward fills his mouth with gravel' and does not endure forever, only for a fleeting instant.
הוּא דְּבַר שֶׁקֶר כְּכָל הֲנָאוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה עָלְמָא דְּשִׁקְרָא
being false like all pleasures of this physical world, the World of Falsehood.
דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא הַשֶּׁקֶר בִּלְשׁוֹן הַקֹּדֶשׁ "כְּזָב",
Therefore falsehood is termed in the Holy Tongue 'kezav' (deceit),
דְּרוֹצֶה לוֹמַר דָּבָר הַפּוֹסֵק כְּמוֹ "נְהָרוֹת הַמְכַזְּבִין" (יְשַׁעְיָה נח, יא).
which means something that dries up and ceases, like 'waters that fail (mekhazvim)' (Isaiah 58:11).
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן "שְׂפַת אֱמֶת תִּכּוֹן לָעַד" (מִשְׁלֵי יב, יט),
Not so 'the lip of truth which is established forever' (Proverbs 12:19),
וְתַאֲווֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הַדְּבוּקִים בֵּאלֹהִים חַיִּים כְּמוֹ שֶׁהֵם קַיָּימִים לְעוֹלָם כָּךְ כָּל כֹּחוֹתֵיהֶם
and the deep longings of the children of Israel cleaving to the living God, just as they endure forever, so do all their faculties.
כִּי הַכֹּל דְּבוּקִים בִּקְדוּשָּׁה
for all of them are rooted in holiness.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר: "וּמִסְפָּר אֶת רֹבַע יִשְׂרָאֵל" (בַּמִּדְבָּר כג, י),
Therefore Balaam uttered: 'or number the fourth part/seed of Israel' (Numbers 23:10),
דְּעַל דָּבָר זֶה נִסְתַּמֵּית עֵינוֹ וְכוּלֵי
over which his eye was blinded, etc.
דְּאוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע לֹא הֵבִין אֵיךְ יִהְיֶה בָּזֶה קְדוּשָּׁה וּמִי שֶׁהוּא קָדוֹשׁ וְכוּלֵי
for that wicked one could not fathom how holiness could reside in this marital union, asking: can one who is holy gaze upon this?!
וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (סה.) גַּבֵּי בַּר שֵׁשַׁךְ:
And this parallels what is related in Avodah Zarah (65a) regarding Bar Sheshakh:
"עֵינָא דְּבָעֵי לְמֶחֱזֵי לָנוּ בִּישׁוּתָא תִּפְקַע", וּפָקְעָה עֵינוֹ.
'May the eye that wishes to see evil befall us burst,' and his eye burst.
כִּי עִיקַּר הַחֶמְדָּה מֵהָעַיִן כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "לֹא תָתוּרוּ אַחֲרֵי לְבַבְכֶם וְאַחֲרֵי עֵינֵיכֶם" (בַּמִּדְבָּר טו, לט),
For the primary stirring of covetous desire stems from the eye, as stated: 'you shall not seek after your own heart and your own eyes' (Numbers 15:39),
דְּ"עַיִן רוֹאָה וְלֵב חוֹמֵד" (רַשִּׁ"י שָׁם).
for 'the eye sees and the heart covets' (Rashi there).
וְעִיקַּר הַנִּיאוּף בָּעַיִן כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְעֵין נֹאֵף (שָׁמְרָה נֶשֶׁף)" (אִיּוֹב כד, טו),
And the essential root of adulterous lust is in the eye, as stated: 'The eye of the adulterer waits for twilight' (Job 24:15),
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסוֹטָה (ט:): שִׁמְשׁוֹן הָלַךְ אַחַר עֵינָיו
and as they stated in Sotah (9b): Samson went after his eyes.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (עד:): טוֹב מַרְאֵה עֵינַיִם בְּאִשָּׁה וְכוּלֵי
and as they taught in Yoma (74b): better is the sight of the eyes in a woman, etc.
וּבִלְעָם הָיָה חוֹשֵׁב עַצְמוֹ טְהוֹר עֵינַיִם מֵרְאוֹת בְּרַע
And Balaam considered himself pure of eyes from gazing upon evil.
וְתָמַהּ מִי שֶׁהוּא קָדוֹשׁ וְכוּלֵי יִסְתַּכֵּל, נַעֲשָׂה שְׁתוּם הָעָיִן
wondering how the Holy One could gaze upon conjugal unions, and he was struck blind in one eye.
כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת הוּא עִיקַּר הָרַע עַיִן
For in truth he was the very archetype of the evil eye,
וּפָרַץ גֶּדֶר שֶׁל זְנוּת
and breached the boundary of morality,
כִּי כָּךְ הוּא בְּאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם: מִי שֶׁנִּרְאֶה בְּגַוֶּון טְהוֹר עֵינַיִם וְנָקִי מֵאֵיזֶה דָבָר הוּא בֶּאֱמֶת בְּשָׁרְשׁוֹ בְּהֵיפֶךְ.
for such is the way among the nations: whoever displays an outward guise of pure eyes in a matter is in his root the exact opposite.
כִּי כָּךְ דֶּרֶךְ פְּשִׁיטַת טְלָפַיִם שֶׁלָּהֶם לְהַרְאוֹת עַצְמוֹ נָקִי בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁהוּא עִיקַּר חֶסְרוֹנוֹ בְּשָׁרְשׁוֹ.
For such is their practice of hypocritically displaying split hooves—to portray oneself as clean in the very place where his essential root-deficiency lies.
וְאֵצֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא לְהֵיפֶךְ,
While with the children of Israel it is the reverse.
דִּבְמָקוֹם שֶׁנִּרְאֶה לְמַרְאִית עַיִן לֹא טוֹב הוּא בֶּאֱמֶת בְּשָׁרְשׁוֹ בְּתַכְלִית הַטּוֹב
for where it appears outwardly unfavorable, it is in its ultimate root the pinnacle of good.
כִּי בְּאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם הַטּוֹב הוּא רַק לְפָנִים
Because among the nations goodness is merely a superficial facade,
וְהוּא לְעֻמַּת הָרַע שֶׁבָּהֶם לְהַעֲלִימוֹ וּלְכַסּוֹתוֹ מֵעֵין הָרוֹאִים בְּעָלְמָא דְּשִׁקְרָא שֶׁהָאֱמֶת נֶעְלָם
serving to mask the corruption within them from the eyes of onlookers in the World of Falsehood where truth is obscured;
וּבְיִשְׂרָאֵל הָרַע הוּא רַק לְפָנִים מִצַּד יֵצֶר הָרָע הַמְסַבֵּב אֶת הַטּוֹב וּמִתְגַּבֵּר וְרוֹצֶה לְהַעֲלִימוֹ.
whereas in Israel evil is merely a superficial crust stemming from the evil inclination that surrounds the good, struggling to conceal it.

paragraphs.text: Amos 9:13: “וְנִגַּשׁ חוֹרֵשׁ בַּקֹּצֵר וְדֹרֵךְ עֲנָבִים בְּמֹשֵׁךְ הַזָּרַע.” Translation: “The plowman will meet the reaper, and the treader of grapes the one drawing seed.” The plain context promises overflowing harvests. Rav Tzadok reads the paired roles figuratively, linking Judah and Yosef and the safeguarding of generative power; this is a further homiletic reading rather than the verse’s literal agricultural sense.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Pinchas §3: Rav Tzadok reports that Zimri imagined there was a spiritual connection: “ובאמת היה לו הרגשה שיש לה איזה שייכות אליו ... וטעה וסבר שבזה יתקן עון משפחתו.” Translation: “He did sense that she had some connection to him ... but he erred in thinking this would correct his family’s sin.” Rav Tzadok expressly calls the act a mistake and discusses subsequent repentance. This is a cautionary comparison to judging holiness or affinity by one’s feeling, not a justification of prohibited conduct or a direct exposition of Amos 9:13.

Abbahu asks about Bamidbar 23:10 and explains “שהקדוש ברוך הוא יושב וסופר את רביעיותיהם של ישראל” — “the Holy One sits and counts Israel’s reproductive acts,” awaiting the conception of a righteous child. inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The perfection of the rectification: “I will raise the fallen sukkah of David — the treader of grapes overtaking the sower of seed,” expounded of Yehudah and Yosef. Yehudah’s beginning appeared the very opposite, and from the Tree of Knowledge came the serpent’s counsel in desire. Yishai “died only through the serpent’s counsel,” a matter clarified at David’s birth — “in iniquity I was fashioned,” from which even the most pious is not free.

p: (עט) וְיָדוּעַ דִּבְטֶבַע בַּעַל תַּאֲוָה הוּא טוֹב עַיִן וְאִישׁ טוֹב לַבְּרִיּוֹת
And it is known that naturally a passionate person is generous of eye and benevolent to fellow creatures.
וּמִי שֶׁהוּא רַע עַיִן וְרַע לַבְּרִיּוֹת אֵינוֹ כָּל כָּךְ שָׁטוּף בְּתַאֲווֹת
while one who has an evil eye and is harsh to others is not so intensely swept by appetites.
אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת כָּל הָרָעוֹת מְחוּבָּרוֹת זֶה לָזֶה
Yet in truth all evils are bound up with one another,
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן כָּל הַטּוֹבוֹת
and all the more so all virtues;
וּבְשׁוֹרֶשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא הַכֹּל טוֹב וּבְשׁוֹרֶשׁ אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם לְהֵיפֶךְ.
and at the root of Israel all is good, while at the root of the nations it is the reverse.
וּבִלְעָם הָיָה עַיִן רָעָה מִצַּד הַלְּבוּשׁ שֶׁלּוֹ, שֶׁהָיָה מַרְאֶה עַצְמוֹ נָקִי מִתַּאֲווֹת
And Balaam possessed an evil eye in his external demeanor, presenting himself as free of bodily appetites,
וְנֶפֶשׁ רְחָבָה מִצַּד פְּנִימִיּוּת שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַטְּמֵאָה שֶׁבְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁהָיָה מָלֵא תַּאֲווֹת כַּהֲמוֹת יַמִּים
and an insatiable soul from the internal impure root of his heart which seethed with lusts like the roaring sea,
וְרוּחַ גְּבוֹהָה מִצַּד הַמּוֹחַ וְהַשֵּׂכֶל הַטָּמֵא שֶׁלּוֹ.
and an arrogant spirit from his defiled mind and intellect (Avot 5:19).
וְגוּף וְנֶפֶשׁ וְרוּחַ יֵשׁ לְאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם גַּם כֵּן
– And body, soul, and spirit the nations of the world possess as well—,
רוּחַ הַבְּהֵמָה וְנֶפֶשׁ הַבַּהֲמִית
the animal spirit and the animal soul,
אֲבָל לֹא נְשָׁמָה
but not the divine neshamah,
דְּהוּא רַק נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים שֶׁמִּצַּד הַקְּדוּשָּׁה בְּמִי שֶׁנִּקְרָא אָדָם
for that is solely the breath of life emanating from holiness within one termed Adam,
דְּעַל כֵּן אוֹמְרִים "טְהוֹרָה הִיא וְגוֹמֵר".
wherefore we recite: 'it is pure, etc.',
וּבַר שֵׁשַׁךְ שֶׁהָיָה שָׁטוּף בְּזִימָּה בְּעִנְיַן דְּזוֹנוֹת עֲרוּמּוֹת
And Bar Sheshakh who was immersed in licentiousness with shameless women.
דִּמָּה דְּגַם בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כֵּן וּמִתְעַנְּגִים בָּזֶה
imagined that the children of Israel were likewise so, taking delight in this.
זֶהוּ הַבִּישׁוּת דְּבָעֵי לְמֶחֱזֵי בִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
This was the evil that he sought to project upon the children of Israel,
וְהוּא לֹא חָשַׁב לְקַלֵּל עַצְמוֹ,
and he did not intend to curse himself.
אַךְ שֶׁדִּמָּה שֶׁזֶּה בֶּאֱמֶת עוֹנֶג וְטוֹבָה וְלֹא חָפֵץ לִרְאוֹת רָעָתָם כְּלָל
supposing that this was genuine pleasure and not wishing to see their misfortune;
אֲבָל עַל הָאֱמֶת זֶה בִּישׁוּת לַחְשׁוֹב עֵינָם חַס וְשָׁלוֹם גַּם כֵּן מְשׁוֹקֶקֶת לַתַּאֲווֹת הַגַּשְׁמִיּוֹת כְּעֵינוֹ שֶׁל אוֹתוֹ נוֹאֵף
yet in truth it is the ultimate evil to imagine that Israel's eye is lustful for physical pleasures like the eye of that adulterer;
וְעַל כֵּן עָנָה רָבָא בַּתְרֵיהּ: "אָמֵן",
wherefore Rava responded after him: 'Amen',
שֶׁיִּתְקַיֵּים בְּמִי שֶׁהוּא עַל הָאֱמֶת בָּעֵי בִּישׁוּתֵיהּ,
that this curse be fulfilled upon the one who in truth sought evil.
וּפָקְעָה עֵינוֹ שֶׁלֹּא יָכוֹל עוֹד לְהִתְעַנֵּג מִתַּאֲווֹתָיו בְּעֵינָיו
and his eye burst so that he could no longer take pleasure in his lusts through his eyes.
כִּי עֵין אִישׁ הַיְּהוּדִי אֵין לוֹ תַּעֲנוּג בֶּאֱמֶת אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי "שְׂאוּ מָרוֹם עֵינֵיכֶם וּרְאוּ מִי בָרָא אֵלֶּה" (יְשַׁעְיָה מ, כו),
For the eye of a Jewish man experiences no authentic pleasure except through: 'Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these' (Isaiah 40:26).
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה זוֹכֶה לְיִרְאָה שֶׁהִיא אוֹתִיּוֹת רְאִיָּה
through which he merits awe (yir'ah) which shares the letters of vision (re'iyah).
וְכֵן רְאִיַּת תְּכֵלֶת דְּצִיצִית הַדּוֹמָה לָרָקִיעַ מֵבִיא הַיִּרְאָה (מְנָחוֹת מג),
And similarly gazing upon the blue thread of tzitzit which resembles the firmament brings awe (Menachot 43b),
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל דְּגַוֶּון תְּכֵלֶת מוֹרֶה עַל זֶה
and as I wrote above that the blue hue signifies this.
וּבָזֶה נִסְתַּלְּקוּ כָּל מִינֵי תַּאֲווֹת
and through this all manner of lusts are banished.
כִּי אֲפִילּוּ יִרְאָה רָעָה וְיִרְאַת הָעוֹנֶשׁ מְבַטֶּלֶת תַּאֲווֹת רָעוֹת
For even external fear and fear of punishment dissolves base desires,
כַּנּוֹדָע עַל פָּסוּק "רַק אֵין יִרְאַת אֱלֹהִים בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה (וַהֲרָגוּנִי עַל דְּבַר אִשְׁתִּי)" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כ, יא).
as is known regarding the verse: 'Surely the fear of God is not in this place; and they will slay me for my wife's sake' (Genesis 20:11).
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ רָבָא: "אַתּוּן אִית לְכוּ אֵימְתָא דְּמַלְכוּתָא"
And this is what Rava said to him: 'You have the fear of the earthly monarchy',
וּבָזֶה מִסְתַּלֶּקֶת הַתַּאֲוָה
and through that worldly fear lust is restrained,
"אֲבָל אֲנַן לֵית לַן וְכוּלֵי".
'whereas we do not have this worldly dread, etc.',
כִּי יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא בֶּאֱמֶת תַּכְלִית הַתַּעֲנוּג שֶׁלָּהֶם
For the fear of Heaven of Israel is in truth their supreme delight,
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה זוֹכִים לְאַהֲבָה
through which they merit love,
וְהוּא דַּרְגָּא דְּיִצְחָק דִּ"מְחַוֵּי לְהוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעֵינַיְיהוּ" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא (שַׁבָּת פט).
and this is the level of Isaac, who shows them the Holy One before their very eyes, as they taught in chapter Rabbi Akiva (Shabbat 89b).
וְזֶהוּ תַּכְלִית עֵינַיִם "הָעַיִן רוֹאָה וְלֵב חוֹמֵד" דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
And this is the true purpose of eyes in 'the eye sees and the heart covets' for the people of Israel.
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: מַהוּ תַּאֲוָתָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל? הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
as our Sages of blessed memory expounded: What is the yearning of Israel? The Holy One, blessed be He.
וְיִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם מְבַטֶּלֶת כָּל מִינֵי יְרָאוֹת דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And fear of Heaven nullifies all secular fears of this world.
וְהִיא מוֹשֶׁכֶת אַחֲרֶיהָ אַהֲבָה וָעוֹנֶג
and it draws after it love and sacred delight.

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §6): “From them flow the two inclinations of jealousy and desire, which are two opposites: for one who is a ‘man of desire’ baal taavah is by nature good to his fellow creatures. And among the nations this appears to the outward eye — one whose eye is good to others and who has love for them; and this is the matter of the mitzvah of ‘sending portions’ mishloach manos — to declare that this generosity too is in truth only in Israel alone. For the love and ‘good eye’ of the nations toward their fellows is, likewise, only for some ulterior motive, for their own benefit.” (Exactly the se’if’s principle: ‘a man of desire is good-eyed’ — but only in Israel’s root do the traits interconnect wholly for the good, whereas in the nations the very same ‘good eye’ is self-serving, the reverse.)

paragraphs.text: Chabad parallel - Tanya, Likkutei Amarim, ch. 1: Tanya offers a parallel - though not identical - map for the structure R' Tzadok describes here. The Alter Rebbe teaches that every Jew, tzaddik or rasha, possesses two souls. The animal soul of Israel comes from kelipas nogah, which contains an admixture of good; even natural traits such as rachmanus and gemilus chasadim can therefore arise from it. He also traces the negative middos to different elements within that animal vitality: anger and pride to fire, appetite to water, frivolity and self-display to air, and lethargy and sadness to earth. The significance for this se'if is twofold. First, middos that appear separate on the surface are branches of one underlying life, which helps explain R' Tzadok's insistence that 'all the evils are connected' and, more deeply, that the good traits of Israel are interconnected at their root. Second, Tanya distinguishes the Jewish animal soul, whose kelipas nogah itself contains good, from the spiritual source he assigns to the nations. R' Tzadok uses a different terminology - body, nefesh, ruach and the uniquely holy neshamah - so the systems should not be mechanically identified. But both refuse to judge the spiritual root from a single visible middah. Bilaam can display an outward restraint while carrying ayin ra'ah, nefesh rechavah and ruach gevohah together within; conversely, the mixed outer life of a Jew can contain a good root that the revealed appearance has not yet disclosed.

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Purim 3: “המן היה עינו רעה בזה ולא האמין שנמצא איזה קדושה בעניני הנאת הגוף כמו אכילה ושתיה” — “Haman begrudged this and did not believe holiness could exist in bodily enjoyment, such as eating and drinking”. R. Tzadok immediately connects this to the serpent’s corruption of desire and to Bilaam’s refusal to believe holiness could belong to the union from which righteous children are born. The parallel concerns the denial of holiness in Israel’s physical enjoyment; it does not separate the evil eye from desire altogether.

paragraphs.text: Yeshayah 40:26: “שְׂאוּ מָרוֹם עֵינֵיכֶם וּרְאוּ מִי בָרָא אֵלֶּה” — “Lift your eyes on high and behold Who created these.” Rashi identifies “these” as the heavenly host seen above: “כל הצבא אשר תראו במרום.” Rav Tzadok goes further: the act of looking upward becomes awareness of the Creator, turning re’iyah (seeing) into yir’ah (awe), and transforming the direction of desire. This homiletic extension is Rav Tzadok’s, not a direct statement of Rashi.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis 20:11: Avraham explains, “כִּי אָמַרְתִּי רַק אֵין יִרְאַת אֱלֹהִים בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה וַהֲרָגוּנִי עַל דְּבַר אִשְׁתִּי.” Translation: “For I said: Surely there is no fear of God in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife.” Rashi comments on the inappropriate questions asked of an arriving traveler: “אכסנאי שבא לעיר, על עסקי אכילה ושתיה שואלין אותו או על עסקי אשתו שואלין אותו?” — “When a traveler enters a city, do they ask about his food and drink or about his wife?” Rav Tzadok independently develops the ethical inference that fear can restrain wrongful desire; Rashi does not explicitly make the earlier note’s broad generalization about fear of punishment.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Purim §7: Rav Tzadok expounds “ליהודים היתה אורה ושמחה וששון ויקר” and the rabbinic saying “שמחה זה יום טוב.” He distinguishes the sanctity revealed through Israel’s own action, that inherited from the ancestors, and that bestowed from above. This provides a thematic parallel to inner holiness becoming visible in joy and delight, though the passage does not itself say that awe produces love, which is Rav Tzadok’s present argument.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: By nature a man of desire is “good-eyed” and generous, while the “evil-eyed” man is not so steeped in desire — yet in truth all evils interconnect, and so do all goods. In Israel’s root everything is good, and in the nations’ the reverse: Bilaam appeared pure of desire outwardly while inwardly “broad of soul” and haughty. The nations have body, nefesh and ruach, but no neshamah, which belongs to holiness alone.

p: (פ) וְדַרְגָּא דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הוּא דַּרְגָּא דְּ"אִשָּׁה יִרְאַת ה'" כַּנּוֹדָע
And the spiritual rung of King David, peace be upon him, is the rung of 'a woman that fears Hashem' as is known,
וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא "טוֹב רֹאִי" (שְׁמוּאֵל א טז, יב).
therefore he was called 'of beautiful appearance' (I Samuel 16:12).
וּשְׁפִירָא דְּעַיְינִין הַתַּאֲוָה שֶׁלּוֹ הָיָה לְמִי שֶׁרְאוּיָה לוֹ מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית
And with beauty of eyes his holy desire was directed toward her who was destined for him since the six days of Creation (Bathsheba),
שֶׁמִּמֶּנָּה בִּנְיַן מַלְכוּת בֵּית דָּוִד שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹ: "כִּסְאוֹ כַשֶּׁמֶשׁ נֶגְדִּי" (תְּהִלִּים פט, לז),
from whom arose the Davidic monarchy concerning which it is stated: 'his throne shall be as the sun before Me' (Psalms 89:37),
וּמָשִׁיחַ בֶּן דָּוִד הַגּוֹאֵל אֲמִיתִּי לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל גְּאוּלַּת עוֹלָמִים
and Mashiach ben David, the true redeemer of Israel in eternal redemption.
וְנִתְאַוָּה לְדָבָר הַקַּיָּים לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד, לֹא לַהֲנָאַת שָׁעָה הַפּוֹסֶקֶת
and he yearned for that which endures for all eternity, not for a fleeting gratification that ceases.
וְכָךְ: "הֵן בְּעָווֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי" (תְּהִלִּים נא, ז) בְּעָווֹן מָלֵא
And so: 'Behold, in iniquity was I brought forth'—with avon written plene, with an additional vav,
אַף שֶׁמִּצַּד הִתְגַּלּוּת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה נִרְאֶה כַּוָּונָה לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ וְנִקְרָא עָוֹן
even though from the perspective of this world's appearance it seemed an intent for self-gratification and is termed iniquity,
וְאַף שֶׁהָיָה בַּמּוּתָּר לוֹ,
and even though it occurred within what was permissible to him;
וַאֲפִילּוּ מִי שֶׁאֵין מְקַדֵּשׁ עַצְמוֹ בַּמּוּתָּר לוֹ,
and even one who does not sanctify himself in that which is permitted,
אַף לְפִי דִּבְרֵי הָרַמְבַּ"ן בְּרֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת קְדוֹשִׁים דְּעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה "קְדֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ",
even according to the Ramban at the start of Parashat Kedoshim that regarding this the positive command 'You shall be holy' was spoken.
מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין לִקְרוֹא זֶה עָוֹן
nonetheless this cannot properly be termed 'iniquity'.
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בָּזֶה שֶׁאָמַר "אֲפִילּוּ חֲסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים וְכוּלֵי",
All the more so here where the Midrash states 'even the most pious among the pious, etc.'
דְּמַשְׁמָע שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְסַלֵּק הַהֲנָאָה לְגַמְרֵי לָא שַׁיָּיךְ לִקְרוֹת עָוֹן
implying that it is impossible to eliminate physical pleasure entirely, in which case it is inapplicable to call it iniquity.
וְגַם מַה שֶּׁאָמַר עַל אִמּוֹ "בְּחֵטְא" שׁוֹגֵג, וְעַל אָבִיו "עָוֹן",
And also in that David spoke of his mother using the term 'chet' (inadvertent sin) and of his father using 'avon' (iniquity),
הַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק "עַבְדְּךָ בֶן אֲמָתֶךָ" (תְּהִלִּים פו, טז),
this aligns with what our Sages taught on the verse 'Your servant, the son of Your handmaid' (Psalms 86:16),
שֶׁבִּקֵּשׁ יִשַׁי לָבוֹא עַל שִׁפְחָתוֹ.
that Jesse had originally intended to cohabit with his handmaid.
וְנִרְאֶה וַדַּאי לֹא הָיְתָה שִׁפְחָה כְּנַעֲנִית
And it is clear that she certainly was not a Canaanite bondwoman,
דְּצַדִּיק כְּיִשַׁי שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְיַיחֵס לוֹ חֵטְא גָּמוּר
for unto a righteous man like Jesse who died solely by the instigation of the Serpent it is impossible to ascribe an outright sin;
וַאֲפִילּוּ שֶׁנִּזְדַּמֵּן אִשְׁתּוֹ,
and even though his lawful wife was substituted,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הֲרֵי בְּכֵהַאי גַּוְונָא כְּתִיב: "וְד׳ יִסְלַח —   " (בַּמִּדְבָּר ל, ו) וְנִקְרָא חֵטְא
nonetheless in such a circumstance Scripture writes 'and Hashem will forgive her' and it is termed a sin (Nazir 23a),
וְאֵיךְ אָמְרוּ עָלָיו דְּמֵת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ?!
so how could they declare that he died solely by the instigation of the Serpent?!
וְנִרְאֶה דְּהָיְתָה אָמָה הָעִבְרִיָּה
Rather it appears that she was a Hebrew maidservant,
וְעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר בִּלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב "אֲמָתֶךָ",
which is why the text specifies 'Your handmaid' (amatekha),
וְהָיָה יָכוֹל לְיַיעֲדָהּ וְתִהְיֶה אִשְׁתּוֹ,
and he had the legal option to designate her as his wife,
אֶלָּא שֶׁהִרְגִּישׁ שֶׁאֵינָהּ בַּת זוּגוֹ.
except that he sensed she was not his destined soulmate.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם קָרֵי לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ "בֶּן אֲמָתֶךָ",
And nonetheless King David, peace be upon him, called himself 'the son of your handmaid',
עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהִיא בְּצִדְקָתָהּ גָּרְמָה לֵידָתוֹ נֶחְשַׁב לִבְנָהּ,
because through her righteousness she brought about his birth and he was reckoned as her son,
כְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם לְבֶן בִּתְיָה עַל יְדֵי שֶׁגִּדַּלְתּוֹ .
just as Moses was called the son of Bithiah because she raised him (Megillah 13a).
וְהִרְגִּישׁ יִשַׁי שֶׁבְּנוֹ שֶׁיּוֹלִיד יִהְיֶה נֶחְשָׁב בְּנָהּ,
And Jesse sensed that the son he would father would be associated with her,
עַל כֵּן חָשַׁב שֶׁתֵּלֵד מִמֶּנּוּ שֶׁלֹּא דֶּרֶךְ נִשּׂוּאִין רַק בְּבִיאַת זְנוּת
therefore he thought she would bear from him outside of formal marriage through an uncanonical union,
שֶׁאֵינָהּ זִיוּוּגוֹ לְאִישׁוּת
not being his designated marital mate;
וְאַף שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא בִּיאַת זְנוּת
and even though this is termed an uncanonical union,
נִרְאֶה דְּהַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁאֵין רְאוּיָה לוֹ דְּהוּא זְנוּת בְּעָלְמָא
it appears that this is so only when she is not spiritually designated for him, which is wanton licentiousness;
אֲבָל אִם בֶּאֱמֶת רְאוּיָה וּמְזוּמֶּנֶת לוֹ מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם
but if she is truly designated and summoned for him from Heaven,
וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא בִּיהוּדָה וְתָמָר "מִמֶּנּוּ יָצְאוּ כְּבוּשִׁים"
along the lines of Judah and Tamar where 'from Him emerged hidden decrees' (Makkot 23b),
וְרָמַז לַמַּלְאָךְ הַמְמוּנֶּה עַל הַתַּאֲוָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פה, ח),
and He signaled to the angel appointed over desire (Bereishit Rabbah 85:8).
אֵינָהּ קְדֵישָׁה כְּלָל
she was not a harlot at all.
וְחָשַׁב גַּם הוּא דְּכָל בִּנְיַן הַמַּלְכוּת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת עַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה
And Jesse likewise reasoned that the entire establishment of monarchy in Israel had to unfold through this concealed path,
כִּי עִיקַּר עִנְיַן הַמַּלְכוּת נִקְרָא "כְּכָל הַגּוֹיִם אֲשֶׁר סְבִיבֹתָי" (דְּבָרִים יז, יד),
for the concept of kingship is phrased: 'like all the nations that are round about me' (Deuteronomy 17:14),
כִּי הוּא שַׁיָּיךְ רַק לַגּוֹיִם דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵין לָהֶם מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
belonging strictly to the nations, for Israel has no true King but the Holy One, blessed be He;
וְכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב (כא) בְּמָשִׁיחַ דְּיָבוֹא רַק לְלַמֵּד לְאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם וְנָהֲרוּ אֵלָיו עַמִּים רַבִּים
and so they taught in Shocher Tov (Psalm 21) regarding the Messiah that he will come only to teach the nations and many peoples shall stream to him,
אֲבָל יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יִצְטָרְכוּ לוֹ.
while Israel will not need him.
וְעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר: "שׂוֹם תָּשִׂים עָלֶיךָ מֶלֶךְ" (דְּבָרִים יז, טו),
Therefore it is stated: 'You shall surely set a king over you' (Deuteronomy 17:15),
דְּאֵצֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא רַק מַה שֶּׁהֵם מְשִׂימִים אוֹתוֹ וּמְקַבְּלִים מַלְכוּתוֹ עֲלֵיהֶם עַל דֶּרֶךְ "עֲשֵׂה לְךָ רַב" (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק א מִשְׁנָה ו),
for with Israel it is merely that they appoint him and accept his sovereignty upon themselves, in the manner of 'make for yourself a master' (Avot 1:6).
דְּפֵירֵשׁ הָרַב מִבַּרְטְנוּרָא אַף שֶׁאֵינוֹ רַבּוֹ בֶּאֱמֶת
which the Bartenura explains: even if he is not inherently his master.
וְאֵינוֹ מְלוּכָה בְּעֶצֶם וּמִצַּד עַצְמוֹ אֶלָּא עַל אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם
And it is not monarchy in its true essence except over the nations of the world.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: יָדֶיךָ חַדּוֹת וַחֲרוּצוֹת לִרְדּוֹת עוֹלָם
as our Sages of blessed memory noted concerning King David, peace be upon him: your hands are sharp and incisive to rule the nations.
וְכֵן שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מָלַךְ עַל כָּל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ ,
And similarly King Solomon reigned over the entire world (Megillah 11b),
וְזֶה מִצַּד הַגְּבוּרָה וְהַיִּרְאָה, וְזֶה מִצַּד הַחָכְמָה וְהָאַהֲבָה
the former (David) from Gevurah and Awe, and the latter (Solomon) from Chokhmah and Love,
וְרָצָה לְאַהְפָּכָא לֹא לְאַכְפַּיָּא
and Solomon sought to transform (le-ahpacha) rather than merely to suppress (le-akpaya),
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כֵּן לֶעָתִיד: "אָז אֶהְפֹּךְ אֶל עַמִּים וְגוֹמֵר" (צְפַנְיָה ג, ט).
as will be fulfilled in the future: 'For then will I turn to the peoples, etc.' (Zephaniah 3:9).
וְחָשַׁב הוּא שֶׁזֶּה בֶּאֱמֶת עִיקַּר הַמַּלְכוּת רַק עַל אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם
And Jesse reasoned that this is the primary essence of kingship: strictly over the nations of the world;
וּמֵאַחַר דְּהוּא נִמְשָׁךְ מִמַּלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם
and since earthly kingship is drawn from the Kingdom of Heaven.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ לְבָרֵךְ "שֶׁחָלַק מִכְּבוֹדוֹ" (בְּרָכוֹת נח),
as instituted in the blessing 'Who has imparted of His glory' (Berakhot 58a).
הוּא הַחֵלֶק מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מוֹשֵׁל בַּגּוֹיִם וּמְחַיֶּה אוֹתָם גַּם כֵּן
this represents that aspect through which Hashem rules over the gentiles and sustains them as well.

paragraphs.text: 1 Shmuel 16:12: “וַיִּשְׁלַח וַיְבִיאֵהוּ וְהוּא אַדְמוֹנִי עִם יְפֵה עֵינַיִם וְטוֹב רֹאִי.” Translation: “He sent and brought him; he was ruddy, with beautiful eyes and goodly appearance.” Rav Tzadok interprets David’s vision in light of his ultimately enduring dynastic destiny rather than transitory pleasure (cf. Mishlei 31:30). In Agra DeKala, Matos, the author relates David’s recognition of Bas Sheva as his destined match; Be’er Mayim Chaim, Tazria explicitly recalls the tradition that she was destined from Creation but insists the matter was premature and warns that “I will sin and repent” is forbidden. These comparisons are retrospective interpretations, not permission to disregard the revealed Torah.

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §17): “for the sun dries and desiccates all the moisture of the water, which is the desiring power — and this is the assurance to Noach and his sons, for the nations reckon by the sun, and immediately after the Flood the nations arose and fenced themselves from immorality.” R’ Tzadok then contrasts Israel, who count by the moon and the trait of David. The moon’s smallness and humility do not merely dry up desire through its opposite; the correction works within desire itself. In David, the source says, modesty and restraint are hidden, while what is visible can appear to be desire — unlike the openly visible restraint of Shaul and the line of Rachel. This is the illuminating parallel to §80’s completed description of David’s actual longing; the source does not identify the two edges of the turning sword. The source states: “מה שאין כן מדת דוד המלך ע״ה הסוד וההצנע שבו שהיא ההגדרה לתאוה הוא מכוסה ונעלם. שהרי הנגלה שבו הוא אדרבה בעל תאוה והוא היה היפך משאול” — “With the trait of David HaMelech, by contrast, his secret and modesty—which are restraint of desire—are covered and hidden. For what is visible in him is, on the contrary, an appearance of desire, and in this he was the opposite of Shaul.”

paragraphs.text: Yalkut HaMachiri, Tehillim 118 (on Tehillim 51:7): Yishai separated from his wife for three years. Then, desiring a fair maidservant, he told her, “prepare yourself tonight, that you may come to me with a bill of freedom.” The maid told her mistress Yishai’s wife, “save yourself, and me, and our master from Gehinnom,” and revealed it; the mistress said, “prepare yourself, and so will I.” That night the maid extinguished the lamp, and when Yishai’s wife came to the door, the mistress entered and the maid went out; she was with him all night and conceived David. Because of his love for that maidservant, David came out “ruddy,” and his brothers wished to kill him and his mother — until Yishai said, “leave him to be our servant and shepherd.” When Hashem sent Shmuel to “Yishai the Bethlehemite,” Yishai said, “there yet remains the youngest, tending the flock”; when Shmuel came, the oil bubbled up and Hashem said, “arise, anoint him, for this is he.” And David’s mother “rejoiced within and grieved without,” until, when “he took the cup of salvations,” all rejoiced. Editorial source qualification: This episode is cited as Yalkut HaMachiri, Tehillim 118 (often identified as §28), concerning David’s birth. The original Yalkut Hebrew has not been collated line-by-line; the narrative is retained as previously transmitted, not certified here as a verbatim quotation.

paragraphs.text: Bamidbar 30:6: When a father annuls his daughter’s vow, the verse says “וַה׳ יִסְלַח לָהּ כִּי הֵנִיא אָבִיהָ אֹתָהּ.” Translation: “Hashem will forgive her, because her father restrained her.” Rashi and the discussion in Kiddushin 81b explain the need for forgiveness where one intended a forbidden act without knowing the vow was already annulled. Rav Tzadok therefore argues that Yishai merely encountering his wife while intending the maidservant would still have raised an issue of mistaken intent; he develops his own alternative account involving an amah Ivriyah who could have been designated for marriage. His inference is not the plain interpretation of Bamidbar or a blanket dispensation for improper conduct.

paragraphs.text: Deuteronomy 17:14: “וְאָמַרְתָּ אָשִׂימָה עָלַי מֶלֶךְ כְּכָל הַגּוֹיִם אֲשֶׁר סְבִיבֹתָי” — “And you shall say: I will set a king over me, like all the nations around me”. The following verse commands setting a king over Israel. Rav Tzadok develops the phrase “like all the nations” to distinguish inherent sovereignty over nations from Israel’s voluntary acceptance of a human king, likened here to “make yourself a teacher.” This distinction is Rav Tzadok’s argument; it is not attributed here to the Sifrei or Ramban.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: David’s rung is “a woman who fears Hashem”: his desire was for the mate fitted to him since Creation, the source of the eternal house of David — he desired the enduring thing, not a passing pleasure. So “in iniquity I was fashioned” is not truly iniquity. “Your handmaid” alludes to Yishai’s episode — a Hebrew bondwoman he could have designated as a wife, sensing she was not his true mate.

p: (פא) וְיָדוּעַ מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה  — בִּנְבִיאֵי אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם מָשָׁל לְבָא עַל פִּילַגְשׁוֹ בְּמַטְמוֹנִיּוֹת
And known is what our Sages taught (Vayikra Rabbah 1:13) regarding the prophets of the nations, a parable of one who visits his concubine in secret.
וְכֵן כָּל יְרִידַת שֶׁפַע לְאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ בְּעִילַת זְנוּת בְּמִי שֶׁאֵינָהּ אִשְׁתּוֹ,
And likewise all descent of divine influx unto the nations occurs in the manner of an uncanonical union with one who is not his wedded wife.
וְזֶהוּ שׁוֹרֶשׁ בִּנְיַן הַמַּלְכוּת
and this is the root of the structure of earthly sovereignty.
אַךְ זֶהוּ בֶּאֱמֶת בְּמַלְכֵי אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם
Yet this applies strictly to the kings of the pagan nations,
דְּנִקְרָא "שֶׁחָלַק מִכְּבוֹדוֹ לְבָשָׂר וָדָם" ,
concerning whom we say 'Who has imparted of His glory to flesh and blood' (Berakhot 58a).
שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שַׁיָּיכוּת לוֹ כִּבְיָכוֹל
who hold no intrinsic holy connection unto Him, so to speak.
אֲבָל מַלְכֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל "שֶׁחָלַק מִכְּבוֹדוֹ לִירֵאָיו" ,
However, regarding the kings of Israel we recite: 'Who has imparted of His glory to those who fear Him' (Berakhot 58a),
דְּהֵם תֹּקֶף הַיִּרְאָה דְּלֵית לְהוּ מִגַּרְמַיְיהוּ כְּלוּם
for they embody the ultimate reverence, possessing nothing of their own,
הֵם עִיקַּר "אִשָּׁה יִרְאַת ה'"  רָזָא דְּ"אֵשֶׁת חַיִל עֲטֶרֶת בַּעְלָהּ" (מִשְׁלֵי יב, ד).
they being the essence of 'a woman that fears Hashem' (Proverbs 31:30), the secret of 'a woman of valor is a crown to her husband' (Proverbs 12:4).
וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל, לֹא מֶלֶךְ הַגּוֹיִם כְּלָל
Therefore he is termed the King of Israel, not the king of the nations at all,
כִּי כָּל הַשְׁפָּעָתוֹ הוּא עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלֹא לַגּוֹיִם
for his entire bestowal flows upon Israel and not unto the nations.
דְּקוֹלֵט הַשֶּׁפַע מֵהֶם וְלֹא מַשְׁפִּיעַ לָהֶם כְּלָל
reclaiming the holy influx from them without channeling anything back to them.
וְרַק בִּיהוּדָה וְתָמָר שֶׁהֻוצְרַךְ לְתַקֵּן נַפְשׁוֹת עֵר וְאוֹנָן
And only with Judah and Tamar where he needed to rectify the souls of Er and Onan,
וּקְלִיטַת אוֹתָן נִיצוֹצוֹת מִיָּד לְהַכְנִיסָן לִקְדוּשָּׁה גְּמוּרָה
and the reclamation of those sparks to bring them immediately into complete holiness,
לֹא הָיָה אֶפְשָׁר אֶלָּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כְּעֵין בְּעִילַת זְנוּת
was impossible except through this hidden path resembling an uncanonical union,
וְגַם זֶה קוֹדֶם מַתַּן תּוֹרָה דְּלֹא הָיָה עֲדַיִן אִיסּוּר בִּבְעִילַת זְנוּת (רַמְבַּ"ם הִלְכוֹת אִישׁוּת פֶּרֶק א הֲלָכָה ד).
and this was prior to the Giving of the Torah when uncanonical cohabitation without formal betrothal was not yet prohibited (Maimonides, Laws of Marriage 1:4).
וְנִמְצָא כְּפִי הָאֱמֶת הָיָה נֶחְשָׁב מַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ זוֹ לְעָוֹן
Thus according to the absolute truth, Jesse's reasoning was accounted as an iniquity,
אַךְ מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין כָּאן עָוֹן בַּפּוֹעַל כְּלָל
yet nonetheless there was no actual iniquity in deed whatsoever.
דְּהוּא לֹא אִיכַּוֵּין לְאִיסּוּרָא רַק לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וּלְהוֹלִיד מַלְכוּת בֵּית דָּוִד
for he never intended anything forbidden, but acted purely for Heaven to father the Davidic dynasty.
וְגַם לֹא עָלְתָה בְּיָדוֹ אִיסּוּרָא אֶלָּא פְּעֻלַּת הֶיתֵּר
Nor did anything forbidden transpire in his hand, but a completely permissible act with his lawful wife,
וְעַל כֵּן חָשְׁבוּ הֶעָוֹן רַק מַה שֶּׁכִּיוֵּון לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ.
and therefore Scripture accounted as the iniquity solely the minute element of personal pleasure.
הַיְינוּ דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הָיָה זֶה טָעוּת מַה שֶּׁחָשַׁב שֶׁמֵּהָאָמָה יֵצֵא מַלְכוּת בֵּית דָּוִד, לֹא מֵאִשְׁתּוֹ.
That is: it was nonetheless an error to assume that Davidic royalty would issue from the maidservant rather than from his lawful wife.
וְיָדוּעַ דְּכָל טָעוּת בָּא עַל יְדֵי אֵיזֶה נְגִיעָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּלִבּוֹ לְגַרְמֵיהּ,
And it is known that every cognitive error stems from some subconscious self-interest in the heart,
שֶׁהוּא כְּמוֹ שֹׁחַד הַמְעַוֵּור עֵינֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשִּׂיג הָאֱמֶת ,
which acts like a bribe blinding the eyes of the wise from discerning the truth (Deuteronomy 16:19);
דְּלוּלֵי כֵן וַדַּאי אָדָם גָּדוֹל הָיָה מַשִּׂיג הָאֱמֶת
for without that bias, surely so great a man would have perceived the truth.
רַק מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ נְגִיעָה דַּהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ בָּזֶה
his error arising solely because there was a trace of personal gratification in it.
וּכְבָר אָמְרוּ בְּסוֹטָה (י):
And our Sages already taught in Sotah (10a):
"אִיהוּ בְּבוּצִינָא וְאִיתְּתֵיהּ בְּקָרֵי",
'He in small gourds, and his wife in large pumpkins',
וְלָאו דַּוְוקָא בִּזְנוּת גָּמוּר
and this applies not only to outright licentiousness,
אֶלָּא הוּא הַדִּין בְּכָל אַבַּיְזְרַיְיהוּ דְּתַאֲוָה וְכַוָּנָה דַּהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ
rather the same principle governs all subtle offshoots of lust and self-gratification,
כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא בָּאִישׁ כֵּן הוּא בָּאִשָּׁה עוֹד יוֹתֵר
which within the woman are even more intensely felt than within the man.
דְּהֵם לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד מִצַּד הַגּוּף הַמִּתְאַוֶּוה, וְעִיקַּר הַתַּאֲוָה מִמֶּנָּה
since they are one flesh through the desiring body, and the core of physical desire originates from her.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמַר עַל אִמּוֹ רַק "בְּחֵטְא",
And nonetheless David spoke of his mother using merely 'chet' (inadvertent error).
דְּכֵיוָן שֶׁהָיָה בַּמּוּתָּר לָהּ אֵינוֹ בְּגֶדֶר עָוֹן רַק חֵטְא וְחִסָּרוֹן בְּעָלְמָא מִיהַת
for since it was fully permissible for her, it is not in the category of iniquity, but merely a subtle lack.
אַךְ גַּבֵּי דִּילֵיהּ שֶׁיָּצָא לַפּוֹעַל בְּמַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ דָּבָר הַנֶּחְשָׁב לְעָוֹן, נִקְרָא "עָוֹן".
Yet regarding Jesse, in whose thought there arose a design accounted as iniquity, it was called 'iniquity'.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵינוֹ עָוֹן גָּמוּר
And nonetheless it was not a genuine iniquity,
דְּבֶאֱמֶת אֵין כָּאן עָוֹן כְּלָל כַּנִּזְכָּר
for in truth there was no actual sin here as noted,
וְהַכַּוָּנָה לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ אֵינוֹ מִצַּד עַצְמוֹ בְּגֶדֶר עָוֹן
and the natural intent for personal pleasure is not intrinsically an iniquity.
רַק מַה שֶּׁכָּאן הָיָה נִרְאֶה כְּמוֹ עָוֹן
only that in this unique context it appeared like an iniquity.
אֲבָל זָכָה עַל יְדֵי כַּוָּונָתוֹ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם דְּנִרְמַז כָּאן בְּ"עָווֹן" מָלֵא
However, through his intention for Heaven he merited that it be hinted here in 'avon' spelled fully with a Vav,
שֶׁנִּתּוֹסַף בְּעָוֹן זֶה אוֹת הַוָּא"ו דְּשֵׁם הֲוָיָ"ה בָּרוּךְ הוּא הַמַּבְרִיחַ מִקָּצֶה אֶל הַקָּצֶה
the letter Vav of the Tetragrammaton being added to this word, which reaches from one end to the other.
וְרוֹמֶזֶת דְּלֵית מִגַּרְמֵיהּ כְּלוּם וְאֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ וּמִמֶּנִּי יָצְאוּ כְּבוּשִׁים
alluding that mortal man has nothing of his own, there is none besides Him, and 'from Me came forth these hidden designs.'
וְעַל כֵּן דָּרְשׁוּ מִזֶּה "",
Therefore they expounded from this: 'even the most pious among the pious, etc.' (Vayikra Rabbah 14:5),
וְכִפְשָׁטֵיהּ גַּם מֵעָוֹן סְתָם נִדְרַשׁ זֶה
and according to the plain sense this could be derived from 'iniquity' generally,
אַךְ מִי יֹאמַר דְּיִשַׁי הוּא חֲסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים
yet who would have dared declare that Jesse is the foremost pious of the pious;
אַךְ מִמַּה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בְּ"עָווֹן" מָלֵא לָמַדְנוּ
rather, from the fact that it is written 'avon' fully with a Vav we learn,
דְּעָוֹן זֶה דְּכַוָּנָה לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ הוּא מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁרָצָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כֵּן
that this subtle iniquity of personal pleasure was orchestrated by Hashem Who willed it to be so.
וְיֶשְׁנוֹ אֲפִילּוּ בַּחֲסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים
and it exists even within the most pious of the pious.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 1:13: Two teachings appear here and should not be blended. First, R. Chama bar Chanina says: “אין הקדוש ברוך הוא נגלה על אומות העולם אלא בחצי דיבור” — “The Holy One reveals Himself to the nations only in a partial utterance.” Separately, the Sages (Rabbanan) give a parable: “משל למלך שהיה לו אשה ופילגש, כשהוא הולך אצל אשתו הולך בפרהסיא, וכשהוא הולך אצל פילגשו הולך במטמונים.” Translation: “A king had a wife and a concubine: he visited his wife openly, but his concubine secretly.” Rav Tzadok applies this Midrashic distinction to his interpretation of sovereignty and spiritual influx; that extension is not the Midrash’s own wording.

paragraphs.text: Mishlei 12:4: “אֵשֶׁת חַיִל עֲטֶרֶת בַּעְלָהּ, וּכְרָקָב בְּעַצְמוֹתָיו מְבִישָׁה” — “a woman of valor is the crown of her husband, but one who shames is like rot in his bones.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Ralbag — a worthy wife is her husband’s crown and glory; the Sages read the verse also of the Torah and of the God-fearing soul. R’ Tzadok’s use: the kings of Israel — “to whom He apportioned of His honor to those who fear Him, who have nothing of their own” — are the very “woman who fears Hashem,” the Malchus that “crowns her husband,” receiving all from Above and keeping nothing for itself; hence David is “king of Israel,” who absorbs the flow from Israel and bestows nothing upon the nations. Izhbitz-Radzin context - Sod Yesharim, Eighth Day of Pesach 2:1: R. Gershon Henoch of Radzin develops precisely the paradox of Malchus on which R' Tzadok is building. Malchus, he writes, is the final middah and 'leis lah migarmah klum' - it has nothing from itself - yet the essential act of Jewish kingship is that Israel crown Hashem through their own bechirah while living inside the concealment of this world. The person experiences his good choice as his own acquired 'kav,' and only after it has truly entered his possession is he taught to return even that acquisition to Hashem, recognizing that the very capacity to recognize and choose was itself illuminated by Him. Thus bittul does not abolish bechirah; it is its culmination. The same passage applies this to worldly possession: one who recognizes that even after something reaches his hand it has not passed from the Reshus of Hashem becomes a trustworthy vessel for blessing. This is a particularly exact complement to the present description of malchei Yisrael. Their kingship is not an autonomous transfer of Divine kavod to 'flesh and blood,' as though a second center of power had been created. It is the middah that receives everything and returns everything to its Source, 'eishes chayil ateres ba'alah.' David's Malchus can therefore be supremely powerful while remaining 'leis lei migarmei klum': the more completely the king receives the life of Israel and owns none of it independently, the more fully the kingship itself becomes a revelation of Malchus Shamayim. Sod Yesharim thus supplies the Izhbitz grammar for R' Tzadok's contrast between gentile sovereignty, which appears as independent possession, and Jewish Malchus, whose deepest acquisition is the knowledge that even its acquired power never left Hashem's domain.

paragraphs.text: Devarim 16:19: in the charge to judges — “לֹא תִקַּח שֹׁחַד, כִּי הַשֹּׁחַד יְעַוֵּר עֵינֵי חֲכָמִים וִיסַלֵּף דִּבְרֵי צַדִּיקִם” — “you shall not take a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and perverts the words of the righteous.” Meforshim: Rashi — once a judge accepts a bribe he can no longer see the case straight, for his heart inclines toward the giver; the verse teaches that any self-interest blinds even the wisest. R’ Tzadok’s use: “every error comes about through some self-interest negi’ah in the heart,” which is “like the bribe that blinds the eyes of the wise” — so that even a great man like Yishai, but for the flicker of “intent for his own pleasure,” would have attained the truth; the faintest personal stake bends the mind’s sight.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: God’s revelation to the gentile prophets is “a concubine met secretly” — every flow to the nations is a union of harlotry and not the bond of a wife, and this is the root of merely worldly kingship. But Israel’s kings, to whom “He apportioned of His honor to those who fear Him,” have nothing of their own: they are “a woman who fears Hashem,” the crown of her husband. So David is king of Israel alone — he absorbs the flow and never bestows it upon them.

p: (פב) וְהַיְינוּ כַּיָּדוּעַ מֵהַטִּבְעִים דְּכָל הוֹלָדָה הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי תַּאֲוָה,
This follows from what is known among naturalists: all procreation occurs through desire.
וְכַאֲשֶׁר הוּא בְּתֹקֶף הַתַּאֲוָה, אָז יִהְיֶה הַנּוֹלָד זָרִיז וּמְמוּלָּא וְחָכָם,
When desire is especially strong, the child born will be vigorous, well developed, and intelligent.
דְּעַל כֵּן רוּבָּן שֶׁל מַמְזֵרִים פִּקְחִים (מַסֶּכֶת סוֹפְרִים ט״ו, י׳).
Thus the Sages say that most mamzerim are perceptive (Maseches Soferim 15:10).
וְאִם לֹא בְּתַאֲוָה כָּל כָּךְ, יִהְיֶה עָצֵל וְסָכָל,
If the desire is less intense, the offspring will be sluggish and dull;
וְשֶׁלֹּא בְּתַאֲוָה כְּלָל, לֹא יוֹלִיד כְּלָל.
and without desire at all, offspring cannot be produced.
וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּמַסֶּכֶת יוֹמָא (דַּף ס״ט, עַמּוּד ב׳),
Similarly, the Gemara states in Yoma (69b)
דִּכְשֶׁכָּבְשׁוּ יֵצֶר הָרָע לֹא אִשְׁתְּכַח בֵּיעֲתָא בַּת יוֹמָא,
that when the Sages restrained the sexual inclination, not even a freshly laid egg could be found.
וְלֹא אָמְרוּ דְּלֹא הָיָה זִיוּוּג,
It does not say that marital union had ceased;
רַק לֹא הָיָה הוֹלָדָה, שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּלֹא יֵצֶר וְתַאֲוָה.
rather, procreation had ceased, for birth cannot occur without inclination and desire.
וְכָךְ רָצָה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה יְצִירַת הָאָדָם עַל יְדֵי תַּאֲוָה
Thus Hashem, blessed be He, willed that human beings should be formed through desire
וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה בּוֹ יֵצֶר דְּתַאֲוָה בַּתּוֹלָדָה
and that an inclination toward desire should be innate in them.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יִהְיֶה מָקוֹם לִבְחִירָה וּלְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת
In this way there would be room for moral choice and for spiritual effort,
וּמָקוֹם לַתּוֹרָה שֶׁהוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי הַיֵּצֶר
and a place for Torah, which is needed precisely because the inclination exists.
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, בְּמַסֶּכֶת שַׁבָּת (דַּף פ״ט, עַמּוּד א׳):
As our Sages teach in the chapter Rabbi Akiva (Shabbos 89a):
"כְּלוּם יֵצֶר רַע יֵשׁ בֵּינֵיכֶם?"
“Is there an evil inclination among you?”
וְאֵינְכֶם צְרִיכִים לַתּוֹרָה, שֶׁהִיא נִתְּנָה רַק לִהְיוֹת תַּבְלִין לַיֵּצֶר, עַל יְדֵי שֵׁשׁ מֵאוֹת וּשְׁלוֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה עֵיטִין שֶׁבָּהּ.
And you do not need the Torah, which was given as a remedy for the inclination through its six hundred and thirteen counsels.
(זוֹהַר, חֵלֶק שֵׁנִי, דַּף פ״ב, סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳).
(Zohar, Part II, end of 82b.)
וְעִיקַּר נְטִיעַת הַיֵּצֶר בָּאָדָם הוּא עַל יְדֵי תַּאֲוַת הָאָבוֹת בִּשְׁעַת יְצִירָה
The principal planting of the inclination in a person comes through the parents’ desire at the moment of conception.
וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ הַיֵּצֶר אֵינוֹ לְרַע,
Yet the root of the inclination is not inherently evil,
דַּהֲרֵי יֵשׁ יֵצֶר טוֹב, גַּם כֵּן נִקְרָא יֵצֶר,
for there is also a good inclination, which is likewise called a yetzer.
דְּחַשְׁקוּת הַלֵּב הוּא הַנִּקְרָא יֵצֶר.
The heart’s longing itself is what is called yetzer.
כַּאֲשֶׁר יֵשׁ בּוֹ תֹּקֶף חֵשֶׁק וַהֲמוֹן חֶמְדָּה וּתְשׁוּקָה לְאֵיזֶה דָבָר, טוֹב אוֹ רַע — זֶהוּ תֹּקֶף הַיֵּצֶר.
When the heart has intense yearning and an abundance of desire and longing for something, whether good or evil, this is the power of the inclination.
וְיֵצֶר זֶה לֹא יִתְבַּטֵּל גַּם לֶעָתִיד
That capacity for desire will not be nullified even in the future,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם (זוֹהַר חָדָשׁ, דַּף כ״ד, עַמּוּד ג׳),
as stated in Midrash HaNe’elam (Zohar Chadash 24c):
דְּנִקְרָא לָבָן דְּאִתְלַבַּן,
it is called “white,” for it will have been purified.
וְלֹא יִהְיֶה בּוֹ זוּהֲמָא, רַק "לֵב לְהוֹצִיא בָּשָׂר",
It will no longer contain defilement, but only “a heart for bringing forth flesh,”
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק: "וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב בָּשָׂר" (יְחֶזְקֵאל ל״ו, כ״ו).
as our Sages explain the verse, “And I will give you a heart of flesh” (Yechezkel 36:26).
וְעַל כֵּן יֵשׁ בְּעָוֹן זֶה אוֹת אֱמֶת דְּתִכּוֹן לָעַד.
Therefore, even within this sin there is a mark of enduring truth.
וְאָז כְּשֶׁיִּתְלַבֵּן וְיִתְבָּרֵר דְּכָל תַּאֲוָה דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
And when it is purified and clarified that every desire of the children of Israel, at its root, comes from Hashem, blessed be He,
יִהְיֶה הֲקָמַת סֻכַּת דָּוִד הַנּוֹפֶלֶת (עָמוֹס ט׳, י״א),
the fallen sukkah of David will be raised up (Amos 9:11),
דְּכָל הַפָּלָתָהּ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְשָׁעָה הָיָה עַל יְדֵי חֲטָאֵי הַתַּאֲוָה
for its fall in this world was temporary and came through sins of desire.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁטָּעֲנוּ בָּזֶה שׂוֹנְאֵי דָּוִד עַל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם.
This was the accusation raised against King David, peace be upon him, by his enemies.
וְאַף דְּהוּא נִתְבָּרֵר בְּחַיֵּי שְׁלֹמֹה בְּנוֹ, דְּנִמְחַל אוֹתוֹ עָוֹן וְלֹא חָטָא (שַׁבָּת דַּף ל׳, עַמּוּד א׳),
Although in the lifetime of his son Shlomo it was clarified that this sin was forgiven and that David had not sinned as alleged (Shabbos 30a),
הֵחֵלּוּ אָז לִטְעוֹן בָּזֶה נֶגֶד שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
they then began directing a similar accusation against King Shlomo, peace be upon him,
שֶׁגַּם הַכָּתוּב אוֹמֵר עָלָיו בָּזֶה בְּעִנְיַן הַנָּשִׁים נָכְרִיּוֹת
for Scripture itself speaks critically of his foreign wives.
וְנִכְתַּב סִרְחָנוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּכְתַּב סִרְחָן דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, כְּדֵי לְהוֹרוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה לַדּוֹרוֹת,
His failing was recorded, as David’s was recorded, in order to teach repentance to future generations,
דַּהֲרֵי מִמֶּנּוּ עִיקַּר שַׁלְשֶׁלֶת מָשִׁיחַ הַמְתַקֵּן לְגַמְרֵי תַּאֲוָה זוֹ.
for from him comes the principal lineage of Mashiach, who will fully rectify this desire.
כִּי כָּךְ הַמִּדָּה, שֶׁבִּמְקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין אֵין צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים וְכוּלֵי (בְּרָכוֹת דַּף ל״ד, עַמּוּד ב׳),
For this is the principle: in the place where penitents stand, the completely righteous cannot stand, and so forth (Berachos 34b).
כִּי הֵם מַמְתִּיקִים הָרַע בִּמְקוֹרוֹ וּלְהָפְכוֹ לְטוֹב
They sweeten evil at its very source and transform it into good.
שֶׁדָּבָר זֶה הוּא תַּכְלִית הַמְּכֻוָּון בִּבְרִיאַת הָאָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
This is the ultimate purpose of the creation of humanity in this world,
מְקוֹם הִתְגַּלּוּת הַשֶּׁקֶר וְהָרַע, וְשֶׁהוּא יַהֲפֹךְ הַכֹּל לְטוֹב
a place where falsehood and evil become manifest, so that a person may transform everything into good.
וְאָז יִהְיוּ כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָאִים גַּם כֵּן עַל שֵׁם יוֹסֵף: "שְׁאֵרִית יוֹסֵף" (עָמוֹס ה׳, ט״ו),
Then all Israel will also be called by Yosef’s name: “the remnant of Yosef” (Amos 5:15),
דְּיִתְבָּרֵר דְּכוּלָּם צַדִּיקִים
for it will be clarified that all of them are righteous,
וְ"אֶפְרַיִם לֹא יְקַנֵּא אֶת יְהוּדָה, וִיהוּדָה לֹא יָצֹר אֶת אֶפְרָיִם" (יְשַׁעְיָה י״א, י״ג).
and “Ephraim shall not envy Yehudah, and Yehudah shall not harass Ephraim” (Yeshayah 11:13).
כִּי בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֶפְרַיִם מְקַנֵּא לִיהוּדָה
For in this world Ephraim envies Yehudah,
כִּי הוּא צַדִּיק גָּמוּר
because he regards himself as wholly righteous
וִיהוּדָה רוֹאֶה שֶׁאֵינוֹ כֵן
and sees that Yehudah does not appear to be so:
וּתְחִלָּתוֹ עֵר וְאוֹנָן, וְגַם עָלָיו הָיָה טַעֲנָה בְּמַעֲשֶׂה דְּתָמָר,
his early history includes Er and Onan, and even Yehudah himself was criticized in the episode of Tamar.
וְכֵן כָּל הַנִּבְחָרִים מִשֵּׁבֶט יְהוּדָה, כְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וּשְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
The same outward criticism was directed against the chosen figures of Yehudah’s tribe, including King David and King Shlomo, peace be upon them.
וּמַחְשִׁיב עַצְמוֹ לְצַדִּיק נֶגְדּוֹ וּמְעוּלֶּה מִמֶּנּוּ,
Thus Ephraim considers himself a tzaddik, superior to Yehudah,
וְאַף עַל פִּי כֵן רוֹאֶה שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בּוֹחֵר בְּזֶרַע יְהוּדָה לִמְלוּכָה
yet he sees that the Holy One, blessed be He, chooses Yehudah’s descendants for kingship.
וְזֶה קִנְאָה גְּדוֹלָה, וְהוּא קִנְאַת יָרָבְעָם בִּשְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם.
This gives rise to intense jealousy—the jealousy of Yarovam toward King Shlomo, peace be upon him.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי דְּהוּא הָיָה נָקִי מִתַּאֲווֹת וְלֹא רָאָה קֶרִי מִיָּמָיו,
As I heard, Yarovam was free of such desire and never experienced a seminal emission in his life.
דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא "אִישׁ אֶפְרָתִי" (מְלָכִים א׳ י״א, כ״ו),
For this reason he was called “an Ephraimite” (I Melachim 11:26),
וְעַל כֵּן מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי אֲחִיָּה הַשִּׁילוֹנִי
and he found favor in the eyes of Achiyah HaShiloni.
וְעַל יְדֵי קִנְאָה זוֹ מְעוֹרֵר קִטְרוּג לְמַעְלָה,
Through this jealousy he aroused an accusation Above,
עַד שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה נֶחְלַק מַלְכוּת בֵּית דָּוִד,
until, as a result, the kingship of the House of David was divided,
וְעַד שֶׁנִיטְּלָה מֵהֶם בְּחוּרְבַּן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ,
and ultimately taken from them with the destruction of the Beis HaMikdash.
וְעַל יְדֵי כֵן יְהוּדָה צוֹרֵר לְאֶפְרָיִם.
Thus Yehudah became hostile to Ephraim.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר דִּלְעָתִיד כְּשֶׁיְּבוֹרַר צִדְקַת כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יִהְיֶה — לֹא זֶה יְקַנֵּא וְלֹא זֶה יָצוֹר.
Therefore, in the future, when the righteousness of all Israel is clarified, neither one will envy nor will the other harass.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: דְּכָל הַפָּלָתָהּ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְשָׁעָה הָיָה עַל יְדֵי חֲטָאֵי הַתַּאֲוָה

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §35): “As they said in Yoma (69b), that when they captured the yetzer of forbidden relations, ‘no egg was found’ lo ishtakach beitza — all birth ceased. And the yetzer of forbidden relations is the sinking into idle imagination, like sleep; and this is what will not be entirely nullified even in the Future, as the Zohar writes — for were it not for some residue of desire, ‘the craving for Torah would not be found’ either.” (This is the se’if’s naturalist principle carried to its root: ‘without desire, there is no birth’ — so that even the Future retains a measure of desire, redirected as the ‘craving for Torah.’) Chassidic context - Be'er Mayim Chaim, Tazria 13:2:2: The Be'er Mayim Chaim gives a remarkably close account of why the force of a middah is not itself the enemy. Discussing the Rambam's therapeutic uprooting of anger and pride, he distinguishes what he calls a lower teshuvah from a higher teshuvah. For the higher return it is not sufficient merely to stop using a powerful desire in the old direction; the person must take the very middah and its heat and turn it into avodas Hashem. He explains David's 'vechatasi negdi tamid' in this sense: David remembers the intensity and burning with which the inclination once drew him, so that the same force can now become an intense longing for Torah, mitzvos and closeness to Hashem. The defect is not the existence of energy, yearning or fire, but its object and its corrupted form. This directly illuminates R' Tzadok's definition of yetzer as 'chashkus halev' - a strong movement of desire that can be good or evil - and his insistence that the root-power will not simply disappear in the Future. What must disappear is the zuhama; the power itself is whitened and redirected. The Be'er Mayim Chaim also supplies an essential boundary for reading the se'if: he immediately warns that no one may deliberately sin in order to attain the superior intensity of teshuvah, for 'echtah ve'ashuv' is itself a corruption of avodah. The transformation is retrospective and therapeutic. Prospectively, the task is to govern the desire according to Torah; after a fall, teshuvah can reveal that the same human force that gave energy to the sin can be reclaimed as the very energy of holiness.

paragraphs.text: From the Ishbitzer (Mei HaShiloach): the teaching R’ Tzadok “heard” — that Yerovam was “clean of desire and never came to any emission,” the paradigm of the guarded tzaddik — is his rebbe’s, R’ Mordechai Yosef of Izhbitz (see §8 above). Navi context - Be'er Moshe on I Melachim 11:26: On the very verse cited here concerning Yerovam ben Nevat, the Be'er Moshe (ad loc., p. 198 of the uploaded Melachim volume) brings Sanhedrin 101b: 'Why did Yerovam merit kingship? Because he rebuked Shlomo; and why was he punished? Because he rebuked him publicly.' He uses this as a paradigm of 'mishpetei Hashem emes tzadku yachdav': one and the same historical act can contain a point deserving reward and another point deserving punishment, because Divine judgment weighs intention, substance and mode with the precision of a hair's breadth. The rebuke of Shlomo was, in itself, a good act and earned Yerovam kingship; the public manner, which amounted to raising a hand against Malchus Beis David, carried its own punishment. This is especially helpful beside R' Tzadok's treatment of Yerovam. The se'if is not presenting him as a flat villain: he could be extraordinarily clean in one sphere, find favor with Achiyah HaShiloni, and still be undone by jealousy and the form in which his opposition to Yehudah emerged. Be'er Moshe's reading of the exact Navi passage gives the same non-binary structure in legal-moral terms: genuine virtue in an act does not cancel its defect, and a defect does not require denying the genuine virtue that was also present. That makes Yerovam an apt illustration of R' Tzadok's broader thesis that future birur does not rewrite responsibility; it separates intertwined strands until the true good can be acknowledged without disguising the point that required judgment.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Every birth comes about through desire, and the stronger the desire the sharper the child; where the yetzer was captured, not even a day-old egg was found. So Hashem willed that man be formed through desire, with an inborn yetzer — making room for choice, for effort, and for Torah, which is only “seasoning for the yetzer.” Its root is therefore not evil, and it will not be nullified even in the Future.

p: (פג) וּבֵירוּר זֶה, הַיְינוּ לֹא בַּעֲרָיוֹת וְאִיסּוּרִין גְּמוּרִים חַס וְשָׁלוֹם
And this clarification concerns neither forbidden sexual relations nor outright prohibitions, Heaven forbid,
רַק בְּתַאֲווֹת דְּהֶיתֵּר וּבַעֲוֹן דְּהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה
rather to permissible desires and the sin of wasting seed,
דְּעַל כֵּן לֹא נִכְתַּב אִיסּוּרוֹ בְּפֵירוּשׁ בַּתּוֹרָה
which is why its prohibition was not explicitly formulated in the Torah,
דְּאִם כֵּן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁלֹּא נִתְבָּרֵר עֲדַיִן חֲזָרַת כָּל הַנִּיצוֹצוֹת לִקְדוּשָּׁה
for had it been so written, in this world where the restoration of all sparks unto holiness has not yet been clarified,
כָּל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא נִתְקַבְּצוּ נִדְחֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הָיָה נִרְאֶה כְּנִדָּח חַס וְשָׁלוֹם
as long as the dispersed of Israel have not been gathered, such a soul would appear utterly banished, Heaven forbid,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, ריט סוֹף עַמּוּד ב) דְּעַל עָוֹן זֶה אֵין מוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה
and as they stated in the Zohar (Part I, 219b) that for this sin repentance is ineffective,
דְּאֵין עָוֹן שֶׁמּוֹסִיף כֹּחַ וְשֶׁפַע לַחִיצוֹנִים רַחֲמָנָא לִצְלַן כָּמוֹהוּ.
for no sin like it adds strength and vitality to the external forces, may the Merciful One spare us.
אֶלָּא שֶׁכָּל זֶה לְמַרְאִית עַיִן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
Except that all this is merely to outward appearance in this world,
וְעַל כֵּן לֹא כָּתַב אַזְהָרָה עַל זֶה בַּתּוֹרָה דְּנִקְרֵאת תּוֹרַת אֱמֶת שֶׁהִיא קַיֶּימֶת לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד
and therefore Hashem did not inscribe an explicit negative prohibition regarding this in the Torah which is titled the Torah of Truth that endures for all eternity,
וְעָוֹן זֶה אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא מִצַּד הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁיֵּשׁ מָקוֹם לַחִיצוֹנִים
since this iniquity exists solely from the vantage point of this world where a temporary domain is afforded to external forces.
וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה זֶרַע קֹדֶשׁ נִשְׁפָּע לַחִיצוֹנִים, וְאֵין זֶה בֶּאֱמֶת כְּלָל
and where holy seed appears to discharge unto extraneous shells, whereas in ultimate truth this is not so at all.
וְעַל כֵּן אַף הָעוֹנֶשׁ עַל עָוֹן זֶה בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל וְעֵר וְאוֹנָן הוּא מִקּוֹדֶם מַתַּן תּוֹרָה
Therefore, even the retribution for this sin in the Generation of the Flood and with Er and Onan occurred prior to the Giving of the Torah,
שֶׁזֶּה מִצַּד מִדַּת דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ שֶׁקָּדְמָה לַתּוֹרָה
which belongs to the sphere of natural morality (derekh eretz) that preceded the Torah,
דְּהַזִּיוּוּג נִקְרָא בַּתַּלְמוּד (בְּסוֹף נְדָרִים צא: וּפֶרֶק מִי שֶׁאָחֲזוּ – גִּיטִּין ע. וְעוֹד טוּבָא) בִּלְשׁוֹן "דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ"
for marital union is termed “derekh eretz” in the Talmud (Nedarim 91b, Gittin 70a, and many other places).
וְהַמּוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה נִקְרָא שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ
and one who emits seed in vain is termed one who acts contrary to derekh eretz.
וְזֶהוּ דֶּרֶךְ עֵץ הַחַיִּים
And this is 'the way of the Tree of Life' (Genesis 3:24),
שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה (פֶּרֶק א): "דֶּרֶךְ" – זוֹ דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ
of which they expounded in Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah (chapter 1): 'way'—this is derekh eretz.
דְּמִי שֶׁהוּא בְּדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ בִּשְׁמִירַת הַבְּרִית כָּרָאוּי יוּכַל לְהַגִּיעַ לְעֵץ הַחַיִּים שֶׁיִּחְיֶה לְעוֹלָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לֶעָתִיד
that one who aligns with derekh eretz in properly guarding the Covenant could attain the Tree of Life to live forever as in the World to Come.
אֲבָל לֹא זָכָה לָזֶה עֲדַיִן אָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה זוּלַת אֵלִיָּהוּ דְּנִקְרָא מַלְאַךְ הַבְּרִית
Yet no mortal in this world has attained this pristine state save for Elijah who is titled the Angel of the Covenant,
וְאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, צג.) דְּהָיָה בֶּאֱמֶת מַלְאָךְ מִתְּחִלָּתוֹ וְנִשְׁלַח לָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
and they stated in the Zohar (Part I, 93a) that he was truly an angel from his inception sent down into this world.
וְזָכָה שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בוֹ יִצְרָא דְּתַאֲוָה כְּלָל
and merited to have no inclination for carnal desire whatsoever.
אֲבָל שְׁאָר כָּל אָדָם אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַגִּיעַ לָזֶה וַאֲפִילּוּ חֲסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים וְכוּלֵי
However, for all other human beings it is impossible to attain this, even the most pious among the pious, etc.
כִּי יֵשׁ כְּרוּבִים וְלַהַט הַחֶרֶב "לִשְׁמֹר אֶת דֶּרֶךְ (עֵץ הַחַיִּים) וְגוֹמֵר" (בְּרֵאשִׁית ג, כד)
for the cherubim and the flaming sword stand “to guard the way to the Tree of Life” (Genesis 3:24).
וְיָדוּעַ פֵּירוּשׁ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה
And the explanation given by our Sages is known:
עַל כְּרוּב – כְּרַבְיָא
“Keruv” is explained as “ke-ravya,” like a child (Sukkah 5b).
וְכָאן רַחֲמָנָא לִצְלַן חַטֹּאת נְעוּרִים
and here, may the Merciful One spare us, it points to the youthful transgressions,
כִּי "יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם רַע מִנְּעֻרָיו" (בְּרֵאשִׁית ח, כא)
for “the inclination of a person’s heart is evil from his youth” (Genesis 8:21).
וּבְיַלְדוּתוֹ אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִהְיוֹת נָקִי לְגַמְרֵי מִתַּאֲווֹת
and in his childhood and youth it is impossible to be completely clean from lusts.

paragraphs.text: Rav Tzadok parallel, qualified — Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Chiddushim al HaRambam, Hilchos Melachim, chapter 10 (in the October 8 Chassidus ZIP: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Novellae, Rambam, Melachim 10): "מנא לן דפטור דילמא באמת חייב" — ‘How do we know he is exempt; perhaps he is actually liable?’ Rav Tzadok reports Tosafos’ challenge and adds: "דכל מי שחייב בפריה ורביה חייב גם כן בלאו דהשחתת זרע" — ‘whoever is obligated in procreation is also subject to the prohibition of destroying seed.’ The immediate discussion there concerns enumerating the seven Noahide commandments and whether absence from a list settles a liability question. It is a comparison about inference from an enumeration, not direct proof about the biblical warning or the precise law discussed in this se’if. Rav Tzadok’s argument here must be understood from its own context, and the omission must not be taken to imply permission.

paragraphs.text: Zohar primary sources — Zohar I 219b, Vayechi (archived Zohar, Vayechi 25, final paragraph): "לית לך חובא בעלמא דלא אית ליה תשובה, בר מהאי" — “There is no transgression in the world without the possibility of repentance except this one.” Thus Rav Tzadok’s "אין מועיל תשובה" accurately paraphrases a severe, explicit statement of the Zohar, although it is not the identical Aramaic wording. Compare Zohar II 214b, Vayakhel (archived Zohar, Vayakhel 27, paragraph 5): "והני מלי כד לא עבד תיובתא שלימתא. תיובתא דאיהי אתחזייא לחפייא על כל עובדוי" — “These words apply where he has not undertaken complete repentance—repentance sufficient to cover all his deeds.” Rav Tzadok quotes both passages together in Pri Tzaddik, Noach, Ois 6, explaining the particularly demanding, root-level rectification of the primordial blemish. He clarifies in Takanas HaShavin, Siman 6, se’if 85: "אבל מכל מקום אין לך דבר שעומד בפני התשובה" — “Nevertheless, nothing stands in the way of repentance.” The impossibility he discusses is the complete rectification that would remove the guarding of the Tree of Life and mortality within this world, not the possibility of sincere teshuvah. Cf. Tanya, Likkutei Amarim, chapter 7, which also distinguishes the severity of the transgression from the possibility of raising fallen vitality through proper repentance. These citations must not be construed as denying the value or availability of teshuvah.

paragraphs.text: Sukkah 5b: discussing the faces of the Keruvim, the Gemara asks — “what is the face of a cherub keruv? R’ Abahu said: like that of a child ke-ravya, for in Babylonia they call a child ‘ravya’.” Meforshim: Rashi — the cherubs bore the faces of children; and the Gemara resolves the verse “the face of the keruv… the face of a man” (Yechezkel 10:14) as the small face of a child versus the large face of an adult. R’ Tzadok’s use: since “keruv” denotes a child, the “Keruvim and the ever-turning flaming sword to guard the way to the Tree of Life” (Bereishis 3:24) allude to the “sin of youth chatas ne’urim” — for “the inclination of man’s heart is evil from his youth” (Bereishis 8:21), and in childhood no one, save Eliyahu (an angel from his very origin), is wholly clean of desire.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: This clarification concerns not forbidden unions but the permitted desires of a permitted union, and the iniquity of wasting seed — whose prohibition the Torah did not write explicitly. In this world, before the sparks are gathered, such a spark appears an outcast lost forever. But that is only the outward view: the Torah of truth does not write it as a prohibition, for it is not truly so — which is why its punishment predates Sinai.

p: (פד) וְגַם אִם יִמָּצֵא הַנָּקִי לְגַמְרֵי גַּם מִיַּלְדוּתוֹ
And even should there be found one completely free of that flaw from childhood,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ עַל כָּרְחֲךָ מִי שֶׁבְּטֶבַע תּוֹלַדְתּוֹ אֵין בּוֹ חִסָּרוֹן זֶה דְּתַאֲוָה
which perforce applies solely to one in whose innate constitution this flaw of lust does not exist,
יֵשׁ לְעֻמָּתוֹ בּוֹ הַחִסָּרוֹן בְּכַעַס
there exists facing it within him the counter-deficiency in anger.
דְּהֵם תְּרֵין יִצְרִין הַהֲפָכִים שֶׁבָּאָדָם
these being the two polar inclinations in man.
וְזֶהוּ "לַהַט הַחֶרֶב הַמִּתְהַפֶּכֶת"
And this is “the flame of the turning sword.”
וְאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר וְתִיקּוּנִים (זוֹהַר חֵלֶק א, נג סוֹף עַמּוּד ב; תִּיקּוּן כב) דְּמִתְהַפֶּכֶת לְזִמְנִין חַיֵּי לְזִמְנִין מוֹתָא
and they taught in the Zohar and Tikkunim (Zohar I, 53b; Tikkun 22) that it turns at times unto life and at times unto death.
הַיְינוּ דְּמִי שֶׁנָּקִי לְגַמְרֵי מִתַּאֲוָה אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה בּוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ כַּעַס
Meaning: one who is completely clear of lust cannot avoid having within him a root of anger,
אֶלָּא דְּיֵשׁ רוּגְזָא דְּרַבָּנָן דְּאִיהוּ טָב בְּכָל סִטְרִין כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, קכח עַמּוּד א)
There is, however, the indignation of Torah scholars, which is good on every side, as stated in the Zohar (III, 128a),
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (תַּעֲנִית ד.) דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא מְרַתְּחָא לֵיהּ
and as our Sages taught (Ta’anis 4a), the Torah within him makes him seethe,
דְּ"הֲלוֹא כֹה דְבָרִי כָּאֵשׁ" (יִרְמְיָה כג, כט)
for “Is not My word like fire?” (Jeremiah 23:29).
וְהֵם דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים וְיֵשׁ בָּזֶה חַיִּים וְתוֹסֶפֶת חַיּוּת
and these are the words of the living God containing eternal life and enhanced vitality.
אַךְ מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַנָּקִי מִתַּאֲוָה לֹא יִמָּלֵט שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ חִסָּרוֹן בְּכַעַס
Yet nonetheless, one clear of lust cannot escape having an imperfection in anger,
דְּלוּלֵי כֵן הָיָה חַי לְעוֹלָם
for were it not so, he would live forever,
וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לֹא רָצָה בָּזֶה עַד עֵת קֵץ שֶׁיְּבוּלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח
and Hashem, blessed be He, did not will this before the End of Time, when death will be swallowed up forever (Isaiah 25:8).
וּבָרָא יֵצֶר הָרָע לִשְׁמוֹר דֶּרֶךְ חַיֵּי עוֹלָם
having created the evil inclination to guard the threshold of eternal life.
וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם רַבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל יוֹכִיחַ
And Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, the teacher of Israel, demonstrates this,
דְּנִקְבַּר מוּל בֵּית פְּעוֹר הָרוֹמֵז לְתַאֲווֹת שֶׁהָיָה נֶגֶד זֶה לְגַמְרֵי
being buried opposite Beit Peor which alludes to base lusts, he having transcended this entirely,
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת נה:) אַף הוּא בְּחֶטְאוֹ מֵת
and nonetheless our Sages stated (Shabbat 55b) that he too died on account of his sin,
מַה שֶּׁאָמַר: "שִׁמְעוּ נָא הַמֹּרִים" (בַּמִּדְבָּר כ, י)
in his saying, “Hear now, you rebels” (Numbers 20:10).
וְהַכָּאַת הַסֶּלַע שֶׁהָיָה מִכְּלַל כַּעַס וְרוּגְזָא שֶׁלֹּא בִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַנִּגְלֶה
and striking the rock, which partook of anger and wrath outside the revealed will of Hashem, blessed be He.

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §5): “the keruvim are love, and "the flame of the ever-turning sword" is fear — and therefore they said to recite Kerias Shema upon one’s bed (the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven, and fear)… holding a two-edged sword.” Exactly the se’if: the “ever-turning sword” is not simply a menace but the second of the two opposite inclinations — the fear set over against love, turning between them.

paragraphs.text: Kometz HaMinchah 2:63: “המיתה והתחיה שניהם מצד יצחק” — “Death and resurrection both proceed from Isaac’s side”. The passage explains that resurrection is purification of desire, whereas death in this world is the moment of that desire; fear and complete distancing from it here also belong to Isaac’s side. It further discusses the future inclination needed for procreation that will no longer be repulsive. This is the relevant parallel to the two outcomes of the turning sword, rather than an argument derived solely from the double meaning of gur.

paragraphs.text: Taanis 4a: “Rava said: If a young Torah scholar tzurva mei-rabbanan grows hot-tempered, it is the Torah within him that makes him seethe Oraisa hi de-ka marsecha lei, as it says (Yirmeyah 23:29), ‘is not My word like fire?’” Chabad clarification - Tanya, Iggeret HaKodesh 25:30: The Alter Rebbe draws almost the exact distinction needed for R' Tzadok's discussion of anger. He returns to Chazal's statement that anger is 'like serving avodah zarah' and explains that this applies to ordinary worldly matters: 'hakol bidei Shamayim chutz miyiras Shamayim,' so rage at the human agent treats that agent as though he possessed autonomous power outside Divine providence. But he then explicitly limits the rule: in 'mili diShmaya,' where one must separate another from prohibition, this reasoning does not apply, and he cites the very Torah expression 'vayiktzof Moshe.' Thus the Tanya does not flatten every manifestation of anger into one category. There is an anger born of wounded selfhood and denial of hashgachah, and there can be a forceful response whose entire content is responsibility to the revealed will of Hashem. This sharpens the present se'if's use of 'Oraisa ka-martecha lei.' The fire of Torah can make the scholar seethe, but that does not sanctify personal irritability; it means that the same faculty of gevurah can be requisitioned by Torah when the situation truly calls for it. R' Tzadok's reading of Moshe then becomes even more precise: Moshe's anger was not wrong merely because anger is always evil. Its defect lay in the fact that at Mei Merivah the force did not match the particular Divine revelation of that moment. The prospective test is therefore exacting: holy anger is not whatever the righteous person feels intensely, but anger subordinated to the command and measure of Heaven.

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 55b: “רבי שמעון בן אלעזר אומר אף משה ואהרן בחטאם מתו שנאמר יען לא האמנתם בי” — “R. Shimon ben Elazar says: Even Moshe and Aharon died through their sin, as it is stated: “Because you did not believe in Me””. The Gemara adds: had they believed, their time to depart would not yet have arrived. It then challenges the general claim that every death requires personal sin from the four who died through the serpent’s counsel. Rav Tzadok adopts the Moshe statement here while addressing the other position in the following paragraph.

paragraphs.text: Bamidbar 20:10: at the waters of Merivah — “וַיֹּאמֶר לָהֶם שִׁמְעוּ נָא הַמֹּרִים, הֲמִן הַסֶּלַע הַזֶּה נוֹצִיא לָכֶם מָיִם” — “and he said to them, ‘listen now, O rebels; shall we bring forth water for you from this rock?’” Meforshim: Rashi — “ha-morim” means fools / rebels (some render it “those who would instruct their teachers”); the commentators dispute what precisely Moshe’s sin was — Rashi holds it was striking the rock instead of speaking to it, while the Rambam (Shemonah Perakim, ch. 4) holds it was the anger betrayed in “shimu na ha-morim.” R’ Tzadok’s use: he follows the anger-reading — “shimu na ha-morim” and the striking of the rock “were part of anger and wrath, not according to Hashem’s revealed will”; and so even Moshe, buried opposite Pe’or as the utter opposite of desire, “died through his own sin” (Shabbos 55b) — the flash of that anger — proof that no one born clean of desire escapes some deficiency of anger.

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §92): “"as you rebelled" — as in the matter of the quarrel, where He said to the two of them, "and you shall speak to the rock"; and Aharon did not speak… but Moshe struck.” R’ Tzadok compares Aharon’s failure to speak with Moshe’s striking: Aharon also did not act against the command by striking, whereas Moshe did. He then considers two readings of Moshe’s being allowed to see the land when Aharon did not: either the sight intensified the pain of exclusion, or it was a partial reward for Moshe’s partial action. This is a direct parallel to §84’s completed discussion of the striking at Merivah and its consequence. The source states: “אבל משה רבינו ע״ה הכה. ולכך אהרן גם לא ראה. אבל משה ראה. עונש יותר בעיניו יראה ושם לא יבוא. או להיפך הראיתא שכר קצת” — “But Moshe Rabbeinu struck. Therefore Aharon also did not see, whereas Moshe did see: a greater punishment, that he should see it with his eyes but not enter there. Or, on the contrary, the sight was a partial reward.”
