inlineHeadings.text: The theme: For a community, however, the verdict is torn — for then it is an “hour of favor,” and favor is the opposite of wrath and judgment. When the community rouses such an hour, of itself there is no room for judgment. And this is no change in God at all: it is the revelation of the middah of His favor and goodness, which is always to do good.

p: (ד) וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה (י״ח עַמּוּד א
And examine there in Rosh Hashanah (18a),
פְּלִיגֵי תַּנָּאֵי גַּם בִּגְזַר דִּין דְּיָחִיד
where Tannaitic authorities dispute even regarding the decreed verdict of an individual;
וּלְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא שָׁם (ט״ז עַמּוּד א
and according to the alternative explanation there (16a),
הָא דִּמְצַלֵּינַן אַקְצִירֵי וּמְרִיעֵי
regarding our praying for the critically sick and ailing,
דְּקַיְימָא לָן כְּרַבִּי יִצְחָק
it is because we hold according to Rabbi Yitzchak.
דְּגַם לְאַחַר גְּזַר דִּין יָפָה צְעָקָה וְיִקָּרַע
that even after the decreed verdict, outcry is beneficial and it is torn up.
אַךְ מִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ דְּמוֹעִיל תְּפִלָּה וּצְעָקָה
Nevertheless, they stated that prayer and outcry are effective,
אֲבָל הַתְּשׁוּבָה לְבַדָּהּ לְדִבְרֵי הַכֹּל אֵין מוֹעִילָה
whereas repentance alone, according to all opinions, does not avail;
וְעַל כֵּן לֹא מוֹקֵי הָא דְּרַבִּי יִצְחָק גַּם בִּגְזַר דִּין דְּיָחִיד
and therefore the Gemara does not establish the statement of Rabbi Yitzchak regarding the verdict of an individual
כִּסְתִימוּת הַלָּשׁוֹן וּכְמַאן דְּאָמַר הָכִי כֵּיוָן דְּקַיְימָא לָן כְּוָותֵיהּ,
matching the plain formulation of the text and according to the authority who holds so, since we rule like him,
וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ מִשּׁוּם דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בִּתְשׁוּבָה לְבַד דִּבֵּר
and perforce you must say that this is because Rabbi Yochanan spoke strictly of repentance alone.
וּבָזֶה לֵיכָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר
and regarding this there is no dissenting authority.
וְהוּא מוּכְרָח גַּם כֵּן מִמַּה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי
And this is proven likewise from what I wrote.
דְּלָא מַהֲנֵי תְּשׁוּבָה לְמִיתַת בֵּית דִּין
that repentance does not remove liability for execution by a court.
וּבְנוֹדָע בִּיהוּדָה מַהֲדוּרָא קַמָּא (חֵלֶק אֹרַח חַיִּים) סִימָן ל״ה
And in Noda BiYehudah, first edition, Orach Chaim §35,
כָּתַב דְּאִם כֵּן בִּטַּלְתָּ כָּל עָנְשֵׁי תוֹרָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם
he wrote that if so, one would nullify all the penalties of the Torah; see there.
וְאֵין זֶה מַסְפִּיק לַעֲשׂוֹת דִּינָא בְּלֹא דִּינָא
Yet this argument is insufficient to establish a legal sentence without its proper legal basis,
וְאֵין אַחֲרָיוּת עֳנָשִׁין עָלֵינו
and the administration of punishments does not rest on our own discretion.
וּמַה שֶּׁחָשַׁב שֶׁהָעֳנָשִׁין כְּדֵי לִמְנוֹעַ הָעוֹבְרִין – אֵינוֹ כֵן
His claim that the penalties exist to deter transgressors is not sufficient,
דְּאֵין עֹנֶשׁ בֵּית דִּין אֶלָּא בְּעֵדִים וְהַתְרָאָה
for court penalties require witnesses and a formal warning,
וְאֵין זֶה מָצוּי כָּל כָּך
and such circumstances are not common.
וְסַנְהֶדְרִין הַהוֹרֶגֶת אַחַת לְשֶׁבַע שָׁנִים נִקְרֵאת חָבְלָנִית
A Sanhedrin that executes once in seven years is called destructive.
וְאִם יִהְיֶה הַדּוֹר פָּרוּץ וְהוּא צוֹרֶךְ שָׁעָה
(and if the generation is licentious and there is an emergency need of the hour,)
דָּבָר זֶה נִמְסַר לְבֵית דִּין לַעֲנוֹשׁ גַּם שֶׁלֹּא מִן הַתּוֹרָה
(this authority was handed over to the court to penalize even beyond biblical law,)
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּיבָמוֹת (צ׳ עַמּוּד ב
as they said in Yevamos (90b).
וְאֵין עָנְשֵׁי הַתּוֹרָה מִשְּׁלֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה מִדּוֹת וְצוֹרֶךְ שָׁעָה
(and the statutory penalties of the Torah do not derive from the thirteen hermeneutical principles or temporary exigency,),
אֶלָּא שֶׁכָּךְ קָצַב הָעֹנֶשׁ הַמַּגִּיעַ לְאוֹתוֹ עָוֺן
(rather such was the exact measure of retribution apportioned to that sin,),
וּכְשֶׁקִּבֵּל עָנְשׁוֹ נִתְכַּפֵּר
(and once he receives his punishment he is atoned for,)
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: כֵּיוָן שֶׁלָּקָה הֲרֵי הוּא כְּאָחִיך
as they said: once he has been flogged, he is again regarded as your brother.
וּנְהִירְנָא דְּרָאִיתִי בְּאֵיזֶה סֵפֶר
(And I recall seeing in a certain work,),
וּבְסֵפֶר הָרַב חִידָ״א בְּשֵׁם אַחֲרוֹנִים
(and in the book of the Chida in the name of later authorities,)
כָּתְבוּ הַטַּעַם
who wrote that the reason a penitent may still be executed
דְּשֶׁמָּא לֹא שָׁב בְּכָל לֵב
(is lest he did not repent with all his heart,)
רַק אִיעֲרוֹמֵי מַעֲרִים מִפְּנֵי פַּחַד הָעֹנֶשׁ.
(but was merely practicing deception out of dread of the penalty.),
וְגַם זֶה אֵין מַסְפִּיק לַהֲמִיתוֹ מִפְּנֵי הַסָּפֵק
(Yet even this reason is insufficient to put him to death on account of doubt,),
כֵּיוָן דְּאִם שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת פָּטוּר
(since if he truly repented he should be exempt,)
סְפֵק נְפָשׁוֹת לְהָקֵל
and a doubt in a capital case is resolved leniently,
וְאֵין לַהֲמִיתוֹ מִסָּפֵק שֶׁמָּא מַעֲרִים
(and he may not be put to death out of a doubt lest he is deceiving.):
וְלֹא שַׁיָּיךְ גַּם כֵּן לוֹמַר בָּזֶה
(Nor is it applicable to argue in this matter:)
אֵין סָפֵק תְּשׁוּבָה מוֹצִיא מִידֵי וַדַּאי חֵטְא
(“a doubtful repentance does not displace an established certainty of sin”);
לְהוֹצִיא הַלָּה לְמִיתָה עַל יְדֵי זֶה
(so as to execute this person on that account;)
דַּהֲרֵי לְקוּלָּא יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּלָא אָמְרִינַן כֵּן
(for when leading to stringency in taking life we do not apply this logic,)
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת פְּסָחִים (ט׳ עַמּוּד א׳ דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל: "כְּדֵי
as Tosafos wrote in Pesachim (9a, beginning “Kedei”),
וּבְחֻלִּין וּבְנִדָּה, יְעֻיַּין שָׁם
(and in Chullin and in Niddah, examine there;),
הֲרֵי דְּלָאו מִילְּתָא פְּסִיקָא הוּא גַּם בְּאִיסּוּרִין
(behold it is not a finalized principle even in ritual prohibitions,),
כָּל שֶׁכֵּן בְּדִינֵי נְפָשׁוֹת
how much more so in capital cases,
וְהַלָּה צוֹוֵחַ: "אֲנִי שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת
when the accused cries, “I have truly repented!”
וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּהַתְּשׁוּבָה
(And perforce you must conclude that repentance,),
אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמּוֹעֶלֶת
(even though it avails,)
הַיְינוּ רַק מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
(is effective strictly from the side of Hashem, blessed be He,);
שֶׁיָּדוֹ פְּתוּחָה לְקַבֵּל שָׁבִים
Whose hand remains open to receive penitents;
אֲבָל מִצַּד הַחָכְמָה
(however, from the perspective of Wisdom)
"הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַחֹטֵאת הִיא תָמוּת" (יְחֶזְקֵאל י״ח, ד׳),
(“the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4))

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Vayeishev §3: “בזעקך יצילוך קבוציך”—“When you cry out, let your gatherings save you.” He contrasts the gathered prayer of Yaakov and his children, with prayer arising from a person who has nothing of his own. A more direct explanation of the inward power of crying is in Pri Tzaddik, Shemos §8: “צעקה גדולה מכולן שצעקה היא בלב”—“Outcry is greatest of all, because outcry is in the heart.” The parallel illuminates the distinct operation of prayer and outcry here; it does not establish a separate legal rule that every judgment is cancelled.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The Tannaim differ over an individual’s verdict too. R’ Yitzchak holds that “a cry avails a person both before and after the verdict,” and we rule like him — which is why we pray even for the gravely ill after a verdict has been sealed. But that operates by prayer and mercy, not by the tearing that teshuvah itself accomplishes.

p: (ה) וְהַיְינוּ דְּוַדַּאי אִלּוּ הָיוּ מִצְוֹת הַתּוֹרָה
And this means: certainly, were the commandments of the Torah
רַק גְּזֵירַת מֶלֶךְ לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹנוֹ,
merely an arbitrary royal decree to carry out His will,
וְכָל חֲטָאֵי הָעוֹבֵר וְהָעֳנָשִׁין הַבָּאִין עָלָיו
and all sins of the transgressor and the penalties befalling him
רַק מִפְּנֵי שֶׁעָבַר מִצְוַת הַמֶּלֶךְ,
existed solely because he violated the sovereign's command,
אִם כֵּן הָיָה בַּדִּין
then it would be right to expect
לִכְשֶׁיָּשׁוּב וִיבַקֵּשׁ מְחִילָה וְכַפָּרָה שֶׁיּוֹעִיל
that when he repents and petitions for pardon and atonement, it should avail.
שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ בָּשָׂר וָדָם צָרִיךְ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה אַכְזָרִי מִלִּמְחוֹל כְּשֶׁמְּבַקֵּשׁ מְחִילָה
for even a mortal king should not be so cruel as to refuse forgiveness when it is requested;
כָּל שֶׁכֵּן מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
all the more so the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He;
שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכְּפִי גְּדוּלָּתוֹ
for although commensurate with His infinite greatness,
הַמְרָאַת רְצוֹנוֹ חֵטְא גָּדוֹל וְעָצוּם מְאֹד
defying His will is an immense and colossal sin,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא מֶלֶךְ מָלֵא רַחֲמִים
nonetheless He is a King brimming with compassion.
וּכְבוֹדוֹ לִמְחוֹל לַחוֹטְאִים הַמְבַקְּשִׁים מְחִילָה
and His very glory is to pardon sinners who plead for forgiveness.
וּבַדִּין הוּא כָּךְ לְמֶלֶךְ רַחֲמָן כְּמוֹתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ
And this is fully warranted for a compassionate King such as He, blessed be He,
שֶׁהוּא מְקוֹר הָרַחֲמִים שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּעוֹלָם
Who is the wellspring of all mercy in existence,
שֶׁגַּם הַיּוֹתֵר רַחֲמָנִי שֶׁבִּבְנֵי אָדָם
for even the most compassionate of human beings,
אֵין לוֹ שׁוּם שַׁיָּיכוּת וְעֵרֶךְ לְרַחֲמָנוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל הַנִּבְרָאִים
bears no comparison or proportion to His mercy toward creatures,
וְלֹא יַעֲלֶה עַל הַדַּעַת שֶׁיִּתְאַכְזֵר
and it is unthinkable that He would act cruelly;
וְלֹא יִמְחַל לַמִּתְחָרֵט וּמְבַקֵּשׁ מְחִילָה
and refuse to forgive one who is remorseful and asks for pardon;
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן שֶׁכְּבָר הִבְטִיחַ עַל הַתְּשׁוּבָה
all the more so since He already pledged the efficacy of repentance,
וְשֶׁהוּא חָפֵץ בִּתְשׁוּבַת רְשָׁעִים וּמַרְבֶּה לִסְלוֹחַ.
and that He desires the repentance of the wicked and is abundant in forgiveness.
אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בָּא בִּטְרוּנְיָא עִם בְּרִיּוֹתָיו
However in truth, the Holy One does not deal tyrannically with His creatures
לְהַטִּיל עֲלֵיהֶם גְּזֵירוֹת כְּדֵי לְהַעֲנִישָׁם אִם יַעַבְרוּ;
imposing decrees upon them merely to punish them if they transgress;
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ:
and concerning this they taught in the Midrash:
"שֶׁאַל תֹּאמַר לְרָעַתְכֶם נָתַתִּי הַתּוֹרָה, לֹא נִיתְּנָה אֶלָּא לְטוֹבַתְכֶם
“Do not say that I gave the Torah for your harm; it was given only for your good.”
וְאֵין רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר לְרָעַתְכֶם מַמָּשׁ
and this does not mean literal, deliberate harm,
דְּזֶה לֹא יַעֲלֶה עַל הַדַּעַת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם
for that is utterly inconceivable, Heaven forbid,
רַק רָצָה לוֹמַר שֶׁאֵינוֹ גְּזֵירָה בְּעָלְמָא
rather it means that it is not merely an external, arbitrary fiat,
דְּאִם כֵּן רָעָה הוּא לְגַבֵּי הָעוֹבְרִים שֶׁהֵם הָרוֹב
for if so, it would be detrimental for the transgressors who form the majority,
וְ"אֵין אָדָם צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ וְכוּלֵי" (קֹהֶלֶת ז׳, כ׳),
as “there is no righteous man on earth, etc.” (Ecclesiastes 7:20),
וּבְבָבָא בַּתְרָא (קס״ה עַמּוּד א
and in Bava Basra (165a):
רוּבָּן בְּגָזֵל, וּמִעוּטָן בַּעֲרָיוֹת, וְהַכֹּל בַּאֲבַק לָשׁוֹן הָרָע",
“the majority stumble in theft, a minority in illicit relations, and all in the dust of slander,”
וּמוּטָב הָיָה שֶׁלֹּא יִגְזוֹר וְלֹא יֵעָנְשׁוּ.
and it would have been better had He not decreed and they not been punished.
אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת הַתּוֹרָה הוּא דְּפוּס מַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית
Rather, the Torah is the very blueprint of Creation,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה א׳, א׳),
as they stated in Bereishit Rabbah (1:1),
וּכְפִי חוּקֵי הַבְּרִיאָה
and according to the organic laws of Creation;
הַהֶכְרֵחַ הוּא לִשְׁמוֹר חוּקֵי הַתּוֹרָה כְּדֵי לְקַיֵּים הָעוֹלָם
it is necessary to keep the Torah’s laws to sustain the world;
וְ"חַטָּאִים תְּרַדֵּף רָעָה" – הִיא הָעֲבֵירָה עַצְמָהּ רוֹדַפְתָּם
and “evil pursues sinners”—it is the sinful act itself that pursues and damages them,
וְאֵין לוֹ לְהִתְאוֹנֵן עַל חֵי עוֹלָמִים רַק עַל עַצְמוֹ.
and a person has no complaint against the Life of the Worlds, but only against himself.
וְטוֹבָה גְּדוֹלָה עָשָׂה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה
And Hashem, blessed be He, performed a tremendous kindness in the Giving of the Torah
שֶׁהוֹדִיעָנוּ הַדְּבָרִים "אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה אֹתָם הָאָדָם וָחָי בָּהֶם" (וַיִּקְרָא י״ח, ה׳),
by informing us of the actions “which a man shall do and live by them” (Leviticus 18:5),
וְהִזְהִיר כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים עַל הַבְּחִירָה בַּחַיִּים
and admonished us repeatedly concerning choosing life.
כִּי הֵם חַיֵּינוּ מִצַּד עַצְמָם
for they are our vitality by their very nature.
וְאִם כֵּן מַה מָּקוֹם לִתְשׁוּבָה וּבַקָּשַׁת מְחִילָה
If so, what functional room is there for repentance and requests for pardon
אִם גּוּף הַדָּבָר מִצַּד עַצְמוֹ רַע וָמָר וּמֵבִיא הָעֹנֶש
if the act itself is inherently harmful and brings about its punishment?
הָא לְמָה הַדָּבָר דּוֹמֶה
To what is this matter comparable?
לְאָדָם שֶׁפָּצַע בְּעַצְמוֹ,
To a person who has wounded himself:
הֲיוֹעִיל מַה שֶּׁיִּתְחָרֵט אַחַר כָּך
does his subsequent regret heal his wound?
וְעַל כָּרְחוֹ לָשׂוּם רְטִיּוֹת וְסַמְמָנִים מְרַפְּאִים
He must instead apply poultices and healing medicines.
וְאִם קָטַע יָדוֹ אֵין לוֹ תַּקָּנָה עוֹד
and if he has severed his limb, he has no remedy anymore.
וּמִצְוֹת הַתּוֹרָה הֵם חַיּוּת אֶבְרֵי הַנֶּפֶש
And the Torah’s commandments give life to the organs of the soul,
וְהַחוֹטֵא הוּא כְּפוֹצֵעַ אוֹ קוֹטֵעַ אֵבֶר כְּפִי גּוֹדֶל הַחֵטְא
and the sinner is like one who wounds or amputates an organ commensurate with the gravity of the sin;
וּלְפִיכָךְ מִצַּד הַחָכְמָה אֵין מָקוֹם לְתוֹעֶלֶת הַתְּשׁוּבָה
therefore from the perspective of Wisdom, there is no logical room for the efficacy of repentance.
לְהַצָּלַת הַמִּיתָה הָרְאוּיָה לַנֶּפֶשׁ הַחוֹטֵאת
to rescue from the organic death naturally due to the sinning soul.

The especially close Izhbitz–Radzin parallel is Tiferes Yosef, Chagigah §2: “כי נגד כל אבר שבאדם יש דברי תורה, נגד רמ״ח אברי אדם יש רמ״ח מצות עשה, ונגד שס״ה גידין יש שס״ה לא תעשה”—“Each human organ corresponds to Torah: 248 positive commandments to 248 limbs, 365 prohibitions to 365 sinews.” It relates the Torah to the very anatomy of life, directly illuminating Rav Tzadok’s subsequent wounded-limb analogy without attributing the Chassidic expansion to the Midrash.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Were the Torah’s mitzvos merely a king’s decree, and its penalties merely for transgressing the royal will, reason would demand that repentance and a plea for pardon should help — for even a flesh-and-blood king ought not be cruel. It is his honor to pardon sinners who ask. That the matter is not so simple shows that the mitzvos are of another order entirely.

p: (ו) אֶלָּא שֶׁכָּל זֶה מִצַּד חוּקִים שֶׁחָקַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּעוֹלָמוֹ,
Rather, all this applies strictly from the vantage point of the laws Hashem established in His universe,
וְהַמִּדּוֹת וּמַאֲמָרוֹת שֶׁבָּהֶם נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם בְּשִׁבְעַת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית
and the divine attributes and utterances through which the cosmos was created in the seven days of Creation,
הַנּוֹתְנִים גְּבוּל וְקִצְבָּה לְכָל דָּבָר
which assign boundaries and precise measures to everything,
וּכְפִיהֶם הֵם חוּקֵי הַתּוֹרָה הַמְגַדֶּרֶת הָאָדָם
and corresponding to them are the laws of the Torah which demarcate man.
שֶׁהוּא דּוּגְמַת הָעוֹלָם
who is a microcosm of the world.
אֲבָל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּרָא הַתְּשׁוּבָה קוֹדֶם לָעוֹלָם
However, Hashem, blessed be He, created teshuvah before the world,
וְקָדְמָה לַתּוֹרָה גַּם כֵּן
and it preceded the Torah as well;
כִּי יֵשׁ מַדְרֵגָה גְּבוֹהָה יוֹתֵר
for there exists a transcendent spiritual level,
שֶׁכְּשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לְשָׁם כְּבָר עָבַר לְמַעְלָה מִגְּבוּל הָעוֹלָם וְחוּקָיו
whereby when one reaches there, he has ascended far beyond the boundary of the world and its natural laws.
וְאֵין חֲטָאֵי יְצִיאַת הַחוּקִים מַגִּיעִים לְשָׁם
and the sins incurred by deviating from those lower laws cannot reach that altitude.
וְזֶהוּ פְּתִיחַת הַשַּׁעַר לַדּוֹפְקֵי בִּתְשׁוּבָה
And this is the opening of the gate for those knocking in repentance.
הֵם שַׁעֲרֵי תְּשׁוּבָה דִּלְמַעְלָה מִכָּל הַשְּׁעָרִים שֶׁל הַנְהָגוֹת הָעוֹלָם
which are the supernal gates of repentance towering above all the gates governing the conduct of the universe.
וְהֵם גַּם כֵּן הַשְּׁעָרִים הַנִּפְתָּחִים בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים
And these are likewise the gates that are unlocked on Yom Kippur,
דְּעַל יְדֵי כֵן יוּכַל הַכֹּהֵן הַגָּדוֹל לִכָּנֵס אָז לְבֵית קָדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים
whereby the High Priest is empowered to enter then into the Holy of Holies.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין יָכוֹל לִכָּנֵס כָּל הַשָּׁנָה
which he is not permitted to enter throughout the rest of the year.
וְיָדוּעַ בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (פָּרָשַׁת שְׁלַח קס״א עַמּוּד ב
as it is known from the holy Zohar (Shelach 161b):
דְּבֵית קָדְשֵׁי הַקֳּדָשִׁים הוּא לִבָּא דְּכָל אַרְעָא וְעָלְמָא, עַיֵּין שָׁם
that the Holy of Holies is the heart of all the earth and the universe, see there;
וְתַמָּן הַלֵּב מֵבִין, רָזָא דְּבִינָה עִילָּאָה
and there resides the understanding heart, the mystery of supernal Binah.
שֶׁהוּא עָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מֵהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת שֵׁשׁ קְצָווֹת דְּעָלְמָא דֵּין
which is the World to Come, above the six directions of this lower world.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Avos 5:1: “בעשרה מאמרות נברא העולם”—“The world was created through ten utterances.” The Mishnah says that the wicked undermine, and the righteous sustain, the world so created. Rav Tzadok relates those utterances and the seven days of Creation to the bounded framework of mitzvos; his next claim that teshuvah reaches a prior root is a further development, not a quotation from the Mishnah.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Vaeschanan §3: “שערי תפלה פעמים פתוחין פעמים נעולים אבל שערי תשובה לעולם פתוחים”—“The gates of prayer are sometimes open and sometimes shut, but the gates of teshuvah are always open.” He compares prayer to a seasonal mikveh and teshuvah to the sea which is always open, and links the fiftieth gate to Yom Kippur. This directly clarifies the “higher gates” in Rav Tzadok’s present paragraph.

paragraphs.text: Zohar, Shelach 161b: “והיכל לבית קדש הקדשים דתמן שכינה שריא וכפרת וכרובים וארון והכא הוא לבא דכל ארעא ועלמא ומהכא אתזנו כל אינון אתרי דישובא דאינון שייפי דגופא ולבא דא אתזן ממוחא דרישא ואתאחיד דא בדא.” — “And the Sanctuary surrounds the Holy of Holies, where the Shechinah dwells, together with the Ark-cover, the cherubim, and the Ark. This is the heart of all the earth and the world. From here all inhabited places, like the limbs of a body, draw sustenance; this heart in turn draws sustenance from the brain, and the two are joined.” Rav Tzadok gives an illuminating parallel in his Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvot §29 (Har Bracha, printed p. 65): “כמו שאמרו בזוהר ... דהלב מכוון כנגד בית קדשי הקדשים ששם השראת השכינה” — “As the Zohar teaches ... the heart corresponds to the Holy of Holies, where the Shechinah dwells.” In this Har Bracha edition the inserted parenthetical citation identifies the Zohar as Shelach 161b; the earlier archival Dover Tzedek text refers simply to the Zohar without naming the folio. The Zohar itself presents the Holy of Holies as the heart nourished by the brain, while Rav Tzadok develops its relation to the understanding heart and supernal Binah in his next line.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: “Days were fashioned, and one among them is His” — this is Yom Kippur, a day of a higher rung than the seven “building” days, as Shabbos too is “a taste of Olam Haba.” It is called “Shabbos Shabbason,” and it completes the count of ten, which is a complete stature. Hence it is then a time of teshuvah for all — “his heart understands and repents.”

The theme: All of that holds only from the side of the “laws” Hashem inscribed in His world — the middos and utterances by which it was made in the seven days, which give bound and measure to everything, and by which the Torah fences in man, who mirrors the world. There are gates above all the gates of the world’s governance, and the sins of “exiting the laws” do not reach there.

p: יָמִים יֻצָּרוּ וְלוֹ אֶחָד בָּהֶם" (תְּהִלִּים קל״ט, ט״ז) – זֶה יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים
“Days were fashioned, and one of them belongs to Him” (Psalms 139:16)—this refers to Yom Kippur,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְּבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה (פֶּרֶק א
as they said in Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah, chapter 1.
שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ קָבַע בַּשָּׁנָה שֶׁהוּא דּוּגְמַת הָעוֹלָם
which Hashem established in the yearly cycle, a counterpart to the world,
כִּי הוּא הַמְשַׁמֵּשׁ בָּעוֹלָם שֶׁתַּחַת הַזְּמָן
which functions within time,
יוֹם אֶחָד שֶׁהוּא מִמַּדְרֵגָה עֶלְיוֹנָה מִשְּׁאָר יָמִים
one single day that derives from a rung superior to all other days.
שֶׁהֵם שִׁבְעַת יְמֵי הַבִּנְיָן
which correspond to the seven days of worldly structure.
וְגַם עַל שַׁבָּת נִדְרַשׁ שָׁם
And this verse was also expounded there regarding Shabbat.
שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא
which is likewise a foretaste of the World to Come.
וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים נִקְרָא "שַׁבַּת שַׁבָּתוֹן
and Yom Kippur is called “Shabbos Shabbason,”
כִּי שַׁבָּת הוּא סוֹד הֵ״א תַּחְתּוֹנָה הַיּוֹנֶקֶת מֵהֵ״א עֶלְיוֹנָה
for Shabbat is the mystery of the lower Hei (Malchut) drawing nurture from the supernal Hei (Binah),
וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים סוֹד הֵ״א עֶלְיוֹנָה עַצְמָה
whereas Yom Kippur is associated with the supernal Hei itself;
וְעַל כֵּן אָז זְמַן תְּשׁוּבָה לַכֹּל
and therefore that is the universal season of repentance for all.
וּמוֹשֶׁכֶת עִמָּהּ כָּל עֲשֶׂרֶת יְמֵי תְּשׁוּבָה
And it draws along with it all the Ten Days of Repentance.
כִּי כָּל הַדְּבָרִים כְּלוּלִים בְּעֶשֶׂר שֶׁהֵם קוֹמָה שְׁלֵימָה כַּנּוֹדָע
for all entities are structured within ten sefirot which form a complete stature, as is known.
וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים בַּשָּׁנָה הוּא דּוּגְמַת קָדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים בָּעוֹלָם
And Yom Kippur in the dimension of time is the counterpart to the Holy of Holies in space,
וְלֵב בַּנֶּפֶשׁ,
and the heart in the dimension of the human soul;
וְשָׁם עִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה דְּ"לְבָבוֹ יָבִין וָשָׁב
and there lies the essence of teshuvah: “His heart understands and he returns.”
וְהוּא אַחַת מִמִּצְוֹת הַתּוֹרָה
And it is one of the commandments of the Torah,
שֶׁגַּם זֶה אַחַת מֵחוּקֵי הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁיּוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה
for it is also one of the statutory laws of the Torah that repentance should avail,
שֶׁגַּם זֶה מֵחוּקֵי הַבְּרִיאָה שֶׁחָקַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּעוֹלָמוֹ.
since this too is embedded in the laws of Creation which Hashem decreed in His universe.
אֶלָּא שֶׁהוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם בְּהַאי עָלְמָא כְּמוֹ קָדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים בָּעוֹלָם
Except that it is shrouded in concealment in this world like the Holy of Holies in space,
דִּבִזְמַן קְדוּשָּׁתוֹ שֶׁהָיָה שָׁם לֵב הָעוֹלָם הָיָה בְּתַכְלִית הַהֶעְלֵם
for during the era of its sanctity, when it stood as the heart of the world, it was in utter concealment,
דְּ"כָל אָדָם לֹא יִהְיֶה בְּאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד" (וַיִּקְרָא ט״ז, י״ז),
as “no man shall be in the Tent of Meeting” (Leviticus 16:17),
וַאֲפִילּוּ אוֹתָם מַלְאָכִים שֶׁדְּמוּת פְּנֵיהֶם פְּנֵי אָדָם
and even those angels whose faces bear the likeness of human faces,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דְּיוֹמָא (פֶּרֶק ה׳ הֲלָכָה ב׳).
as they stated in the Yerushalmi on Yoma (5:2).
וְכֵן הַלֵּב בָּאָדָם: "עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא מִי יֵדָעֶנּוּ" (יִרְמְיָה י״ז, ט
and so too the human heart: “The heart is deceitful above all, and desperately frail—who can know it?” (Jeremiah 17:9).
רַק "אֲנִי ה' חֹקֵר לֵב וְגוֹמֵר",
only “I, Hashem, search the heart, etc.”
וְנֶאֱמַר: "ה' יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב" (
and it is said: “Hashem looks to the heart” (I Samuel 16:7).
וְכֵן בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים יִשְׂרָאֵל מִתְדַּמִּים בּוֹ לְמַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת
And likewise on Yom Kippur Israel resemble ministering angels,
שֶׁמִּתְרַחֲקִים מִכָּל תַּאֲוַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַגּוּפָנִי
for they withdraw from the bodily desires of this world,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ הֶעְלֵם הַגּוּפָנִיּוּת
which is the transcendence of physical corporeality;
כִּי מִצַּד הַגּוּפָנִיּוּת אֵין שַׁיָּיכוּת לִקְדוּשַׁת יוֹם הַזֶּה
for from the perspective of bodily materiality there is no connection to the sanctity of this day.
כִּי הוּא נֶעְלָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
because it remains concealed within this physical world.

paragraphs.text: Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah 1:2: “ימים יוצרו ולא אחד בהם ... זה יום השבת לישראל”—“Days were fashioned, and one among them ... this is Shabbos for Israel.” The next unit, 1:3, explicitly says: “זה יום הכפורים לישראל”—“this is Yom Kippur for Israel.” Both interpretations occur in the chapter: neither should be represented as excluding the other. The higher-day application and relation of Shabbos to Yom Kippur are developed by Rav Tzadok.

paragraphs.text: Yerushalmi Yoma 5:2 (27a), and the parallel Yoma 1:5 (7b): “וכל אדם לא יהיה באהל מועד ... אפי׳ אותן שכתוב בהן ודמות פניהם פני אדם לא יהיו באהל מועד”—“No person may be present in the Tent of Meeting; even those beings described as having faces in the likeness of a human face may not be present.” Both Yerushalmi passages explicitly apply the prohibition to angelic beings, citing Vayikra 16:17; Ramban on Exodus 28:35, explicitly quotes Yoma 1:5. Thus the manuscript’s Yoma 5:2 citation is indeed correct, and the parallel Yoma 1:5 is now independently confirmed; the metaphysical application to the Kohen Gadol is Rav Tzadok’s development of the rabbinic exposition.

paragraphs.text: Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer §46: The Midrash compares Israel on Yom Kippur to ministering angels: “מה מלאכי השרת אין להם אכילה ושתיה כך ישראל אין להם אכילה ושתיה ביום הכיפורים”—“Just as ministering angels neither eat nor drink, so Israel do not eat or drink on Yom Kippur.” It also describes purity from sin and peace among them. The source text consulted says “אין להם קפיצין” regarding the angels’ feet, rather than the generalized claim “barefoot”; that particular gloss has therefore been omitted. Rav Tzadok applies the analogy to withdrawal from material bodily desires.

p: (ז) וְכָךְ בְּמִצְוֹת הַתּוֹרָה
And thus regarding the commandments of the Torah,
מִצְוַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם מִצַּד הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
the commandment of repentance is concealed from the perspective of this earthly world,
וּלְפִיכָךְ מִשְׁפְּטֵי הַסַּנְהֶדְרִין שֶׁהֵם מִשְׁפָּטִים שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
and therefore the judicial verdicts of the Sanhedrin, which govern this physical world,
אֵין הַתְּשׁוּבָה מוֹעֶלֶת לָהֶם
are not affected by repentance.
כִּי אֵין כֹּחַ לַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁיּוֹעִיל לְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם
For repentance lacks the overt authority to rectify the past
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כְּאִלּוּ לֹא חָטָא
so that it becomes as though he never sinned
אוֹ עוֹד כִּזְכִיּוֹת מְבוֹרָר בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
or even into merits in a manner manifest in this world,
שֶׁהוּא עָלְמָא דְּאִתְגַּלְיָא
which is the realm of manifest outward reality.
וַהֲרֵי כְּפִי הַהִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁל "אָדָם אֲשֶׁר יִרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם" הָיָה מַעֲשֵׂה הַחֵטְא
and according to the outward perception of “man who looks at appearances,” the sinful act was indeed committed.
וְאַף בְּדִינֵי שָׁמַיִם לְאַחַר גְּזַר דִּין שֶׁנִּמְסַר לַמַּלְאָכִים
And even in heavenly judgments, after a decreed verdict has been handed over to the angels,
וְהֵם אֵין יוֹדְעִין מַחֲשָׁבוֹת שֶׁבַּלֵּב
and they do not know the hidden thoughts of the heart,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "אֲנִי ה' חֹקֵר לֵב"
as it is stated: “I, Hashem, search the heart” (Jeremiah 17:10).
וּלְאַפּוֹקֵי מֵהַתּוֹסָפוֹת פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּשַׁבָּת י״ב עַמּוּד ב׳
in contrast to the view of Tosafos in the first chapter of Shabbos, 12b,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר
as I have written elsewhere.
לָא מַהֲנֵי אֶלָּא בַּעֲשֶׂרֶת יְמֵי תְּשׁוּבָה דְּהוּא "בְּהִמָּצְאוֹ"
repentance by itself does not annul the decree except during the Ten Days of Repentance, the time when He “may be found.”
שֶׁאָז מִתְגַּלֶּה מַלְכוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ
For then His sovereignty, blessed be He, is openly revealed,
דְּעַל כֵּן אוֹמְרִים "הַמֶּלֶךְ הַקָּדוֹשׁ" וְ"הַמֶּלֶךְ הַמִּשְׁפָּט"
which is why we say “the Holy King” and “the King of Judgment”;
וְהוּא יוֹשֵׁב עַל הַמִּשְׁפָּט
and He sits in judgment Himself,
וְהוּא יוֹדֵעַ מַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב
and He knows the innermost recesses of the heart;
וְסַגִּי בִּתְשׁוּבָה לְבַדָּהּ
and repentance alone is sufficient
לִהְיוֹת נִקְרָע מִמֵּילָא הַגְּזַר דִּין עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה
for the decreed verdict to be torn up automatically through repentance.
כֵּיוָן דְּשָׁב לַה' בְּכָל לִבּוֹ
Since he has returned to Hashem with all his heart,
אֵין מָקוֹם עוֹד לָעֹנֶשׁ שֶׁהוּא מֵהָעֲבֵירָה עַצְמָהּ דְּתִרְדְּפוֹ רָעָתוֹ
there is no longer a basis for punishment arising from the transgression itself, as the evil consequences pursue the offender;
וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הָרוֹאֶה לַלֵּבָב
and Hashem, blessed be He, Who sees into the heart,
רוֹאֶה דְּאֵין כָּאן עוֹד עֲבֵירָה
sees that the sin is no longer present in the penitent’s heart.
וְכֵן לְצִבּוּר בִּשְׁאָר יְמוֹת הַשָּׁנָה
And likewise for a community throughout the rest of the year,
כְּשֶׁשָּׁבִים לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
when they return to Hashem, blessed be He,
וּמַמְלִיכִים אוֹתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ עֲלֵיהֶם
and crown Him sovereign over themselves,
לִהְיוֹת "ה' שֹׁפְטֵנוּ וְכוּלֵי וְהוּא יוֹשִׁיעֵנוּ" (יְשַׁעְיָה ל״ג, כ״ב)
so that “Hashem is our Judge,” and “He will save us” (Isaiah 33:22).
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן יָחִיד
In contrast to an individual,
דְּ"אֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּלֹא עָם"
for “there is no king without a people,”
אֵין יָכוֹל לְהַמְשִׁיךְ הִתְגַּלּוּת מִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת
he cannot draw down the overt revelation of the attribute of Malchut,
אֶלָּא בַּעֲשֶׂרֶת יְמֵי תְּשׁוּבָה הַנִּמְשָׁכִים מֵרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה
except during the Ten Days of Repentance that extend from Rosh Hashanah;
שֶׁאָז הוּא הִתְגַּלּוּת מַלְכוּתוֹ שֶׁהָיָה בִּבְרִיאַת עוֹלָם מִצַּד עַצְמוֹ
for then His kingship is revealed as it was at creation, through His own initiative,
שֶׁהוּא בָּרָא לוֹ עָם כְּדֵי לְגַלּוֹת מִדַּת מַלְכוּתוֹ
when He created a people through whom to reveal the attribute of His kingship.
וְכֵן מִתְגַּלֶּה בְּכָל רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה מִדַּת מַלְכוּתוֹ עַל הַנִּבְרָאִים
And likewise on every Rosh Hashanah His Kingship is revealed over creatures,
מִצַּד עַצְמוֹ בְּלֹא אִתְעָרוּתָא שֶׁלָּהֶם
from His own sovereign initiative without their prior awakening.
וְיִשְׂרָאֵל מַמְלִיכִין אוֹתוֹ עַל עַצְמָם מֵרְצוֹנָם
and Israel crowns Him over themselves by their own willing devotion.
וְעַל יְדֵי הַתְּפִלָּה לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
And through prayer to Hashem, blessed be He,
דְּהוּא "קָרוֹב לְכָל קֹרְאָיו" (תְּהִלִּים קמ״ה, י״ח)
Who is “near to all who call upon Him” (Psalms 145:18),
יָכוֹל לִקְרוֹעַ הַגְּזַר דִּין שֶׁנִּמְסַר לַמַּלְאָכִים
one has the power to tear up the decreed verdict handed over to the angels.
גַּם בִּשְׁאָר יְמוֹת הַשָּׁנָה
even during the rest of the year.
כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יָכוֹל לְשַׁנּוֹת
For Hashem, blessed be He, can alter it;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן לִהְיוֹת נִקְרָע מֵעַצְמוֹ
unlike a decree being annulled of itself
עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה לְבַד
through the power of repentance alone,
כִּי זוֹ הַמַּדְרֵגָה הַגְּדוֹלָה שֶׁבַּתְּשׁוּבָה
for this great level of repentance
שֶׁאֵינָהּ מוּרְגֶּשֶׁת אֶלָּא בַּבִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב
which is perceptible nowhere except in the understanding (Binah) in the heart,
וְלִפְנֵי בּוֹחֵן לְבָבוֹת יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ לְבַד
and before the Searcher of hearts, blessed be His Name, alone.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי
as I have written.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 43b (Mishnah): “כל המומתין מתודין, שכל המתודה יש לו חלק לעולם הבא” — “All who are executed confess, for whoever confesses has a share in the World to Come.” A court-imposed sentence still goes forward even while confession benefits the offender in the World to Come. This is the distinction Rav Tzadok develops: the concealed spiritual change effected by sincere repentance does not erase an already established earthly judicial act. The Mishnah is an analogy for the distinction, not a statement that repentance has no spiritual efficacy.

She-ein malakhei ha-shares: “ותימה דאפי׳ מחשבה שבלב כל אדם יודעים ולשון ארמי אין יודעים” — “It is surprising: they know even a person’s inner thoughts, yet do not know Aramaic?” Tosafos assumes angelic knowledge of thoughts; Rav Tzadok expressly takes the contrary view when explaining a decree entrusted to angels. Shabbos 12b itself says that angels do not attend to a request in Aramaic; the assertion that they know concealed thoughts is Tosafos’s interpretation, not an explicit statement of the Gemara. paragraphs.text: Rosh Hashanah 18a: “התם ביחיד, הכא בצבור ... אלו עשרה ימים שבין ראש השנה ליום הכפורים” — “There the case is an individual, here a community ... these are the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.” Berachos 12b specifies “המלך הקדוש” and “המלך המשפט” during these days. Rav Tzadok explains the liturgical change in Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas Shabbos §7: “וכן המלך הקדוש והמלך המשפט לפי שאז מראה מלכותו” — “Likewise, ‘the Holy King’ and ‘the King of Judgment,’ because then He makes His kingship manifest.” The Gemara provides the stated temporal and liturgical bases; Rav Tzadok extends them into a teaching about disclosure of Divine kingship and the hidden heart.

paragraphs.text: Rosh Hashanah 18a:10–12: “אף על גב שנחתם נקרע ... התם ביחיד הכא בצבור” — “Even though it has been sealed, it is torn up ... there concerning an individual, here concerning a community.” This qualifies the difference Rav Tzadok is drawing between a community’s returning to Hashem all year and the individual’s special opportunity during the Ten Days. The Gemara also discusses a special exception for a decree accompanied by an oath (18a:6–8); therefore the communal teaching should not be overstated as a universal cancellation of every decree.

paragraphs.text: Rav Tzadok, Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berachos §1 (Har Bracha 5768, printed p. 21, PDF p. 25): “לפי שאין מלך בלא עם ועל ידי זה יהיה לו עם” — “For there is no king without a people, and through this He has a people.” In context Rav Tzadok explains the manifestation of the attribute of Malchus among created beings and the possibility of choice. The same idea appears in Har Bracha Kometz HaMinchah, printed p. 392, as “ואין מלך בלי עם.” Here the expression illuminates the collective acceptance of sovereignty; it does not mean that Hashem’s existence depends on created beings.

paragraphs.text: Rosh Hashanah 18a:3–4 distinguishes effective prayer and the cry that can help even after judgment: “יפה צעקה לאדם בין קודם גזר דין בין לאחר גזר דין” — “A cry is beneficial both before and after a decree.” Rav Tzadok’s own Pri Tzaddik, Vaeschanan §3 also states: “שערי תפלה פעמים פתוחין פעמים נעולים אבל שערי תשובה לעולם פתוחים” — “The gates of prayer are sometimes open and sometimes closed, but the gates of repentance are always open.” There is no contradiction: repentance is always available as return to Hashem; the issue here is the special power of repentance alone to annul a previously transmitted decree, whereas prayer invokes Hashem to change it even at other times. Neither source guarantees that every individual petition will be granted.

sections.en: The essence of teshuvah is in the heart's contemplation

items.h: The essence of teshuvah is in the heart's contemplation
עיקר התשובה בהרהור הלב.

p: (א), —   וְעִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא בְּהִרְהוּר בַּלֵּב בִּלְבַד
And the primary essence of repentance lies in contemplation in the heart alone,
שֶׁהֲרֵי נִקְרָא בְּכָךְ "צַדִּיק גָּמוּר"
for behold, by this inward return he is described as “completely righteous,”
אֲפִילּוּ הָיָה מִקּוֹדֶם רָשָׁע גָּמוּר
even if he was previously completely wicked,
כִּמְבוֹאָר בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (מ״ט עַמּוּד ב׳).
as explained in Kiddushin (49b).
וַאֲפִילּוּ הַוִּידּוּי דְּבָרִים
And even the verbal confession of words,
אַף עַל גַּב דְּהוּא מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה מִן הַתּוֹרָה: "וְהִתְוַדּוּ וְגוֹמֵר" (בַּמִּדְבָּר ה׳, ז׳),
even though it is a positive Torah commandment, as it says, “They shall confess,” etc. (Numbers 5:7),
זֶהוּ מִצְוָה בִּפְנֵי עַצְמָהּ,
this is a distinct mitzvah in its own right,
וְאֵינוֹ מְעַכֵּב הַתְּשׁוּבָה
and it does not prevent the essential act of repentance,
שֶׁעִיקָּרָהּ בַּלֵּב לְבַד
whose essence is in the heart alone,
שֶׁמִּתְחָרֵט עַל הֶעָבָר
wherein one feels remorse over the past.
וּמַסְכִּים בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁלֹּא לָשׁוּב עוֹד לְכִסְלָה וְשֶׁלֹּא יֶחֱטָא עוֹד
and firmly resolves in his heart never to return to folly and never to sin again.
וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּלֹא נִגְלָה לְשׁוּם אָדָם
And even though this is not revealed to any mortal person,
וַאֲפִילּוּ לְמַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת שֶׁאֵין יוֹדְעִים מַה שֶּׁבַּלֵּב
nor even to the ministering angels who do not know what is in the heart,
קַמֵּי שְׁמַיָּא גַּלְיָא
before Heaven it is openly manifest,
וְהוּא נִקְרָא צַדִּיק גָּמוּר בֶּאֱמֶת
and he is truly designated completely righteous at that moment,
אֲפִילּוּ הִגְדִּיל עֲבֵירוֹת עַד לְמַעְלָה
even if he multiplied severe sins towering upward;
דִּבְכָל רָשָׁע גָּמוּר אֲמָרוּהוּ שָׁם
for concerning any completely wicked person did they teach this there,
וַאֲפִילּוּ עָבַר עַל כָּל הַתּוֹרָה כֻּלָּהּ.
even if he has transgressed the entire Torah.
וּבְבֵית שְׁמוּאֵל וְחֶלְקַת מְחוֹקֵק (בְּאֶבֶן הָעֵזֶר סִימָן ל״ח) כָּתְבוּ
And Beit Shmuel and Chelkat Mechokek (Even HaEzer, section 38) write
דַּאֲפִילּוּ גָּזַל וְלֹא הֶחֱזִיר הַגְּזֵילָה
that even if one stole and has not yet returned the stolen property,
רַק שֶׁקִּבֵּל בְּלִבּוֹ לְהַחֲזִיר – מַהֲנֵי
merely that he resolved in his heart to restore it—it avails;
וְכֵן מַשְׁמַע בִּבְרָכוֹת (ה׳ עַמּוּד ב׳)
and so it is implied in Berakhot (5b).
בְּעוֹבָדָא דְּאַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת דַּנֵּי דְּחַמְרָא דְּסַגִּי בְּהָכִי
in the episode of Rav Huna’s four hundred barrels of wine, where accepting the obligation sufficed at that moment.
וּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (כ״ה עַמּוּד ב׳) בַּחֲזָרָתָן שֶׁל בַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה
And that which they taught in Sanhedrin (25b) regarding the formal restitution procedures of penitents,
הַיְינוּ לְעִנְיַן נֶאֱמָנוּתוֹ לְעָלְמָא
this applies strictly to his legal credibility before the public,
דְּחוֹשְׁשִׁין שֶׁמָּא לֹא שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת וּמְרַמֶּה הַבְּרִיּוֹת
for we suspect lest he did not repent in truth and is deceiving people.
וְצָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּרְאוּ בְּנֵי אָדָם מִמֶּנּוּ מַעֲשֵׂה תְּשׁוּבָה בַּפּוֹעַל
and human beings must witness concrete, actualized deeds of repentance from him.
וְהַהַגְדָּרוֹת בַּמּוּתָּר שֶׁהִזְכִּירוּ שָׁם
And the self-restraints in permissible matters mentioned there
הֵם עֵצוֹת טוֹבוֹת לַשָּׁב
are sound practical counsels for the penitent;
שֶׁלֹּא יִתְקְפֶנּוּ יִצְרוֹ לְהַבָּא עוֹד
so that his base inclination does not overpower him in the future;
וְעַל כֵּן צָרִיךְ לִגְדּוֹר עַצְמוֹ גַּם בַּמּוּתָּר
and therefore he must fence himself around even in permissible matters
כְּדֵי לְהַרְחִיקוֹ מֵהָאִיסּוּר שֶׁכְּבָר נִכְשַׁל בּוֹ,
in order to distance him from the prohibition in which he had already stumbled,
וּבְנָקֵל יוּכַל הַיֵּצֶר
for easily could the evil inclination,
אֲשֶׁר כְּבָר קָנָה לוֹ קֵן בְּלִבּוֹ
which has already established itself within his heart,
וְנַעֲשָׂה בַּעַל הַבַּיִת
and become the master of the house,
לְהַכְשִׁילוֹ,
cause him to stumble again.
וְלָכֵן צָרִיךְ לְהַגְדָּרוֹת יְתֵירוֹת
and for this reason he requires extra safeguards.
אֲבָל אֵין זֶה עִכּוּב לַהַתְּשׁוּבָה בִּשְׁעָתָהּ,
However, this does not invalidate the repentance that occurred at that moment,
שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ יַחֲזוֹר וְיַרְשִׁיעַ,
even if he subsequently returns to wicked conduct,
מַשְׁמַע מֵהַהִיא דְּקִדּוּשִׁין דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הָוֵי קִדּוּשִׁין
the passage in Kiddushin implies that the betrothal remains a matter of legal doubt,
וְאָמְרִינַן דְּנִקְרָא צַדִּיק גָּמוּר
and we maintain that he is termed completely righteous,
עַל יְדֵי הִרְהוּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁבְּלִבּוֹ בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה בֶּאֱמֶת
through the contemplation of repentance in his heart at that exact moment in truth,
וְאַחַר כָּךְ הוּא שֶׁתְּקָפוֹ יִצְרוֹ.
and only afterward was he overcome by his yetzer.
וְכֵן בְּדִבְרֵי בֵּית שְׁמוּאֵל וְחֶלְקַת מְחוֹקֵק הַנִּזְכָּר בְּגָזֵל
And likewise in the words of the aforementioned Beit Shmuel and Chelkat Mechokek regarding robbery,
אֲפִילּוּ אַחַר כָּךְ לֹא הֶחֱזִיר הַגְּזֵילָה
even if he afterward failed to return the stolen property,
וְלֹא הוֹעִיל לְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם
and it did not avail to rectify the past,
הַיְינוּ לִהְיוֹת נִמְחָל לְגַמְרֵי
meaning to be completely and permanently forgiven,
אֲבָל בִּשְׁעַת הַהִרְהוּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה
nevertheless at the instant of the contemplation of repentance,
שֶׁהָיָה בְּדַעְתּוֹ בֶּאֱמֶת לְהַחֲזִיר
when it was his sincere intention to restore it,
הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה
behold he is completely righteous at that hour,
וְאַחַר כָּךְ הוּא דְּאִתְרַע
and it is only afterward that a relapse occurred,
וּכְצַדִּיק גָּמוּר שֶׁהִרְשִׁיעַ.
like a person who was genuinely righteous at one moment but subsequently acted wickedly.
וְעַיֵּין בִּתְרוּמַת הַדֶּשֶׁן (סִימָן שמ״ט)
see Terumat HaDeshen (Part I, responsum 349),
דְּרַק כְּשֶׁלֹּא הָיָה הוֹכָחָה בִּשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁשָּׁב
that only when there was no corroborating proof at the time of the deed that he repented
אָמְרִינַן: הוֹכִיחַ סוֹפוֹ עַל תְּחִלָּתוֹ
we may infer from the person’s later behavior something about his former condition,
דְּלֹא שָׁב כְּלָל בֵּינְתַיִם
and that he did not genuinely repent in the interim,
כֵּיוָן דִּתְחִלָּתוֹ וְסוֹפוֹ בְּרִשְׁעוּת
since both his beginning and his end were in wickedness;
אֲבָל אִם הָיָה הוֹכָחָה מוֹעִיל
however, if there existed corroborating proof it avails,
וְהַיְינוּ לְהַאֲמִינוֹ עַל יְדֵי הַהוֹכָחָה
which means to believe him by virtue of the evidence.
דְּנִרְאֶה שֶׁהָאֱמֶת שֶׁשָּׁב – מַהֲנֵי
where there is evidence of genuine repentance, that repentance is effective.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Toldos §1.  “ואם עושה תשובה אחר כך נקרא בעל תשובה ולא צדיק” — “If he subsequently repents he is called a baal teshuvah, not [simply] a tzaddik.”  This is a deliberate distinction in Rav Tzadok’s own vocabulary: a lifelong untouched tzaddik is not identical to a penitent. The parallel qualifies rather than mechanically proves that terminology. (Sefaria)

paragraphs.text: Terumat HaDeshen, Part I 349, responsum (response §349:2).  “דְּתוֹכִיחַ סוֹפוֹ עַל תְּחִלָּתוֹ ... שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בּוֹ צַד הִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה” — “His end may show what he had been at the beginning ... that there had been no indication of contemplative repentance.”  The original responsum concerns disputed inheritance rights of children who abandoned Judaism and whether sustained visible apostasy allows retrospective evidentiary inference. It also explicitly discusses cases where the principle cannot be applied without proof. Rav Tzadok uses that evidentiary distinction: proven genuine intermediate repentance cannot simply be invalidated by later relapse. It is not a general rule that subsequent sin cancels the spiritual truth of earlier teshuvah. (Sefaria)

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The essence of teshuvah lies in the heart’s contemplation alone: a person is called a “complete tzaddik” even if a moment before he was wholly wicked. Even verbal viduy, though a Torah mitzvah, is a separate mitzvah and does not hold the teshuvah back. What is required is the resolve not to return to his folly — not that others see an act of teshuvah from him.

p: (ב) וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב רַמְבַּ״ם (פֶּרֶק ב׳ מֵהִלְכוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה הֲלָכָה ב׳):
And what Maimonides wrote (Laws of Repentance 2:2):
וְיָעִיד עָלָיו יוֹדֵעַ תַּעֲלוּמוֹת שֶׁלֹּא יָשׁוּב לָזֶה הַחֵטְא לְעוֹלָם
“And the Knower of hidden secrets shall testify concerning him that he will never return to this sin,”
עַל כָּרְחֲךָ כַּוָּונָתוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ בְּכֶסֶף מִשְׁנֶה וְלֶחֶם מִשְׁנֶה שָׁם
must mean, as Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh explain there,
דְּיִקַּח לוֹ אֶת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְעֵדוּת
that he takes Hashem, blessed be He, as his witness,
וְהַיְינוּ לְבָרֵר אֲמִיתַּת רְצוֹנוֹ אָז בְּרֶגַע הַתְּשׁוּבָה
namely, to establish the sincerity of his will at the moment of repentance,
דְּדַעְתּוֹ בֶּאֱמֶת שֶׁלֹּא יָשׁוּב וְכוּלֵי
that he genuinely resolves then never to return to the sin.
וְהֲגַם דְּקוּשְׁיַת לֶחֶם מִשְׁנֶה שָׁם לֹא קָשֶׁה מִידֵּי
Although the question raised by Lechem Mishneh there does not in itself present a difficulty,
דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הַיְדִיעָה וּבְחִירָה שְׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת
because Divine foreknowledge and human free choice are both true,
וּכְשֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת לֹא יֶחֱטָא הֲרֵי יָעִיד עָלָיו הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אָז
when he truly does not sin afterward, Hashem can testify concerning him even then.
וְגַם קוּשְׁיַת כֶּסֶף מִשְׁנֶה שָׁם לֹא קָשֶׁה
Nor does the question raised by Kesef Mishneh there present a difficulty.
דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר פֵּירוּשׁ: "וְלֹא נֹאמַר עוֹד (אֱלֹהֵינוּ לְמַעֲשֵׂה יָדֵינוּ)" (הוֹשֵׁעַ י״ד, ד׳),
For “we will no longer call the work of our hands our god” (Hoshea 14:4) can mean
הַיְינוּ דָּבָר בָּרוּר שֶׁלֹּא נֹאמַר עוֹד וְלֹא נַעֲשֶׂה זֶה
a firm, unreserved resolve not to say or do such a thing again.
וְזֶהוּ כַּוָּונַת לְשׁוֹן "וְיָעִיד וְכוּלֵי
This is the meaning of “and He shall testify,”
הַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּבֵירוּר שֶׁלֹּא יָשׁוּב וְכוּלֵי
namely that the decision not to return to the sin be unmistakably sincere.
מִכָּל מָקוֹם אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה זֶה מִתְּנָאֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה
Nevertheless, certain knowledge of all future conduct cannot be a condition of repentance.
וְרַק כְּשֶׁבְּדַעְתּוֹ גַּם בִּשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה לַחֲזוֹר וְלַחֲטוֹא
Only if, even while repenting, he already intends to return to the sin
הֲרֵי לֹא שָׁב בְּכָל לִבּוֹ כְּלָל
has he not repented wholeheartedly.
וְזֶהוּ מִדָּתָן שֶׁל פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הַמְּלֵאִים חֲרָטָה
Such is the condition of Jewish transgressors who are filled with remorse:
הַיְינוּ חֲרָטָה לְבַד בְּלֹא עֲזִיבַת הַחֵטְא
remorse alone, without abandoning the sin.
כִּי רַק עַל הֶעָבָר שֶׁכְּבָר חָלְפָה הֲנָאָתוֹ וְאֵינָהּ עוֹד מִתְחָרֵט
He regrets a past sin only once its pleasure has already passed,
אֲבָל אֵין דַּעְתּוֹ לַעֲזוֹב לְהַבָּא הֲנָאָה זוֹ
but does not intend to forgo that pleasure in the future
אִם יִזְדַּמֵּן לְפָנָיו אֲפִילּוּ בְּאוֹתָהּ רֶגַע
should the opportunity arise again, even at that very moment.
וְזֶה אֵין עָלֶיהָ שֵׁם תְּשׁוּבָה כְּלָל, רַק חֲרָטָה לְבַד
This is not yet called repentance, but only remorse,
שֶׁאַחַר הַחֵטְא שֶׁעָבְרָה הֲנָאָתוֹ מִתְחָרֵט חֲרָטָה בְּעָלְמָא
a passing regret after the pleasure of sin is over,
בְּלֹא מַחֲשֶׁבֶת עֲזִיבַת הַחֵטְא
without forming the decision to abandon it.
וְהִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב הַמּוֹעִיל
The inward contemplation of repentance that is effective
הַיְינוּ בַּעֲזִיבַת הַחֵטְא
consists in genuinely abandoning the sin;
שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא שֶׁשָּׁב לַה׳
this is what is called returning to Hashem.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash §2 — Yehudah’s sincere confidence. “וכיון שהתפלל יהודה תפלה זו ונתחרט בלב נשבר ... והוא בטוח שיהיה עבד ה׳ וזה עיקר התשובה שיעיד עליו יודע תעלומות שלא ישוב לזה החטא לעולם” — “After Yehudah offered that prayer and regretted with a broken heart ... he was confident he would be a servant of Hashem; this is the essence of repentance, that the Knower of secrets testify he will never return to this sin.” Rav Tzadok applies Rambam’s expression to Yehudah’s true resolve as manifested in his prayer and intended conduct. This is a more direct and precise parallel than treating a general statement about later repentance as a proof of guaranteed future behavior.  [Primary Rav Tzadok]

rich.text: Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash §2 — Yehudah’s sincere confidence.

“וכיון שהתפלל יהודה תפלה זו ונתחרט בלב נשבר ... והוא בטוח שיהיה עבד ה׳ וזה עיקר התשובה שיעיד עליו יודע תעלומות שלא ישוב לזה החטא לעולם” — “After Yehudah offered that prayer and regretted with a broken heart ... he was confident he would be a servant of Hashem; this is the essence of repentance, that the Knower of secrets testify he will never return to this sin.” Rav Tzadok applies Rambam’s expression to Yehudah’s true resolve as manifested in his prayer and intended conduct. This is a more direct and precise parallel than treating a general statement about later repentance as a proof of guaranteed future behavior.

paragraphs.text: Be’er Mayim Chaim, Bereishis on Genesis 3 — knowledge and choice. “אשר ודאי שניהם אמת ... ואף על פי כן אין הידיעה זו מכרחת האדם לאשר יבחר” — “Both are certainly true ... and yet Divine knowledge does not compel the choice a person will make.” This is a directly sourced parallel to the phrase הידיעה ובחירה שניהם אמת. The author rejects using that truth as a pretext to enter a forbidden trial. It supports Rav Tzadok’s distinction, without claiming to resolve the metaphysical problem by denying bechirah. paragraphs.text: Mei HaShiloach, Vayeilech §3 — human agency within Providence. “כל מעשי בני אדם, אף שניתן הבחירה ביד אדם, הוא רק דבר מועט כקליפת השום” — “In human action, although choice was entrusted to people, its independent portion is but a small thing, like the peel of garlic.” This is a philosophical parallel rather than a direct law of teshuvah: the Izhbitzer considers Divine action and human agency together. Rav Tzadok likewise keeps meaningful responsibility at the moment of choosing while refusing to treat God’s knowledge as coercion.

Rav Tzadok reads it as proof of the necessary clarity of commitment, not a claim that a finite person can guarantee every future choice.  [Hoshea]

paragraphs.text: Dover Tzedek, Kometz HaMinchah II §18, Tanya §11 — remorse is not yet departure. “דבלאו הכי גם פושעי ישראל מליאים חרטות ... וזהו פושעי ישראל מלאים חרטה אחר החטא” — “Even without that, the transgressors of Israel are filled with regrets ... the transgressors of Israel are filled with remorse after sin.” Rav Tzadok’s original parallel appears in Dover Tzedek, Likkutim, Har Bracha printed p. 137, and in Kometz HaMinchah II §18, Har Bracha printed p. 314. Tanya, Likkutei Amarim 11, distinguishes the inward good manifested by regret from the strength needed to abandon sin. paragraphs.text: Tzidkat HaTzadik §152 — a genuine resolve even for one moment. “שיהי ממעמקי לבו התעוררות גמור דעזיבת החטא ולעזוב כל עניני עוה״ז אפי׳ רגע א׳ די” — “There must be an arousal from the depths of his heart to abandon the sin completely and to leave worldly concerns behind—even for a single moment; that suffices.” This is Rav Tzadok’s own parallel to the key distinction: remorse at pleasure now past is not enough; teshuvah is a true present turning away from the sin. It does not exempt the penitent from future obligations, restitution or confession.  [Original Rav Tzadok]

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The Rambam’s phrase — “the Knower of secrets will testify about him that he will never return to this sin” — cannot be a condition of teshuvah. As Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh explain, he takes Hashem as witness to the truth of his present resolve: that his mind is genuinely not to return. Regret without any thought of abandoning the sin is not teshuvah at all.

p: (ג), — וּמִדָּתָן שֶׁל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים
And the trait of Torah scholars,
דְּעוֹבֵר עֲבֵירָה בַּלַּיְלָה
that if one commits a transgression by night (,
שֶׁאָז הוּא זְמַן עֲבֵירוֹת דְּתַאֲווֹת בִּזְנוּת
(for then is the time of sins of lust in immorality;
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "בְּנֶשֶׁף בְּעֶרֶב יוֹם וְגוֹמֵר" (מִשְׁלֵי ז׳, ט׳) דְּאֵין רוֹאֶה
as it is stated: “In the twilight, in the evening of the day, etc.” (Proverbs 7:9), where none sees;
וּבְשַׁבָּת פ״ט עַמּוּד ב׳ אִיתָא: "דַּל פַּלְגָא דְּלֵילְיָא"
and in Shabbat 89b it is taught: “Deduct half the night,”;
דְּאָז אֵין חוֹטְאִין
for during normal sleep hours people do not sin;
וּבַזֹּהַר הַגִּרְסָא אִיפְּכָא: "תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁעָבַר עֲבֵירָה בַּיּוֹם – אַל תְּהַרְהֵר בַּלַּיְלָה",
and in the Zohar the textual reading is the reverse: “a scholar who committed a sin by day—do not harbor suspicion by night,”
וְנִרְאֶה דְּדֶרֶךְ לָשׁוּב בַּלַּיְלָה לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁינָה
and it appears that it is customary to repent at night prior to sleep,
כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא בִּמְגִלָּה (כ״ח עַמּוּד א׳):
in the manner stated in Megillah (28a):
כִּי סָלֵיק לְפוּרְיֵיהּ אָמַר
when Mar Zutra went up to his bed he would say:
"שָׁרֵי לֵיהּ מָרֵיהּ לְכָל מַאן דְּצַעֲרַן";
“May the Master forgive anyone who caused me distress”;
כִּי אָז טָעֵים טַעֲמָא דְּמוֹתָא
for then one tastes a foretaste of death,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר וּבְהָרוֹאֶה (בְּרָכוֹת נ״ז עַמּוּד ב׳)
as they stated in the Zohar and in HaRoeh (Berakhot 57b),
דְּהוּא אַחַת מִשִּׁשִּׁים בְּמִיתָה
that sleep is one-sixtieth of death,
וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא בְּשַׁבָּת (קנ״ג עַמּוּד א׳):
and this is in line with what is taught in Shabbat (153a):
"שׁוּב יוֹם אֶחָד לִפְנֵי מִיתָתְךָ",
“Repent one day before your death,”
וְאָז שְׁעַת הַחֶשְׁבּוֹן לְמָארֵי דְּחוּשְׁבָּנָא
and then is the moment of reckoning before the Master of accounting
עַל כָּל מַה שֶּׁעָשָׂה בְּאוֹתוֹ יוֹם),
over all that he performed during that day),
"אַל תְּהַרְהֵר אַחֲרָיו בַּיּוֹם דְּוַדַּאי עָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה",
“do not harbor suspicion after him by day, for he certainly performed repentance,”
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (י״ט עַמּוּד א׳),
as they stated in Berakhot (19a).
לֹא בַּחֲרָטָה לְבַד, רַק בִּתְשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה
not with mere remorse alone, but with complete repentance.
וַאֲפִילּוּ רוֹאֵהוּ חוֹזֵר וְשׁוֹנֶה אַחַר כָּךְ בְּחֶטְאוֹ
And even if one sees him repeat his sin again afterward
(וּמִיהוּ אֶפְשָׁר דְּהַךְ "אַל תְּהַרְהֵר"
(however, it is possible that this rule “do not harbor suspicion”
הַיְינוּ קוֹדֶם שֶׁרוֹאֵהוּ שׁוֹנֶה בַּחֵטְא
applies only prior to seeing him repeat the sin;
דְּמַחֲזִיקִין שֶׁשָּׁב וְלֹא יֶחֱטָא עוֹד
where we presume he repented and will not sin again;
אֲבָל כְּשֶׁרָאוּהוּ שׁוֹנֶה וּתְחִלָּתוֹ וְסוֹפוֹ בְּחֵטְא
but when they saw him repeat it, so that his beginning and end are in sin,
אֶפְשָׁר גַּם בְּתַלְמִיד חָכָם לֹא מַחְזְקִינַן שֶׁשָּׁב
it is possible that even regarding a Torah scholar we do not presume he repented;
בִּדְלֵיכָּא הוֹכָחָה
in the absence of corroborating evidence;
אוֹ עַל כָּל פָּנִים אַחַר פַּעַם שְׁנִיָּה שֶׁשָּׁנָה בַּחֵטְא
or at least after the second time that he repeated the sin,
רַשַּׁאי לְהַרְהֵר אַחֲרָיו
one is permitted to harbor suspicion after him,
דַּהֲרֵי "עָבַר וְשָׁנָה – נַעֲשָׂה לוֹ כְּהֶתֵּר",
for “once he transgressed and repeated it, it becomes permitted to him,”
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (פ״ו עַמּוּד ב׳).
as they stated in Yoma (86b).
אֶלָּא דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר: אִם שָׁב בֵּינְתַיִם בִּתְשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה
However, one may argue: if he repented in the interim with complete repentance,
דַּהֲוֵי לֵיהּ בְּאוֹתוֹ שָׁעָה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר
so that he was at that moment completely righteous,
כְּשֶׁחוֹזֵר וְחוֹטֵא אֵין עָלָיו דִּין "עָבַר וְשָׁנָה",
when he sins again the status of “transgressed and repeated” does not apply to him,
רַק כִּתְחִלַּת חֵטְא
rather it is viewed as an initial sin,
דְּהָרִאשׁוֹנָה כְּבָר נִמְחֲקָה בַּתְּשׁוּבָה הַקּוֹדֶמֶת שֶׁבֵּינְתַיִם
for the first transgression was already erased by the earlier intervening repentance,
וַהֲרֵי זֶה כְּצַדִּיק גָּמוּר הַמַּתְחִיל בְּחֵטְא
and behold he is like a completely righteous person who begins a sin,
וְגַם כֵּן אַל תְּהַרְהֵר
and likewise do not harbor suspicion,
דְּגַם אַחַר כָּךְ יָשׁוּב, וְצָרִיךְ עִיּוּן),
for he will surely repent afterward as well; and this requires further analysis).
מִכָּל מָקוֹם בִּשְׁעָתוֹ שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת
nonetheless, at his initial hour he repented in truth.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ"הַבָּא לִטָּהֵר מְסַיְּיעִין אוֹתוֹ",
And even though “one who comes to purify himself is assisted,”
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (ל״ח סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳),
as they stated in Yoma (38b),
אֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר: מִדְּלֹא סִיְּיעוּהוּ, עַל כָּרְחֲךָ לֹא שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת
is it possible to argue: since they did not assist him to prevent future sin, perforce he did not truly repent?
וְהַךְ "מְסַיְּיעִין" הַיְינוּ בְּאוֹתָהּ רֶגַע שֶׁבָּא לִטָּהֵר
Rather, that divine assistance applies specifically at that very instant when he comes to purify himself,
וְאִלְמָלֵא בָּא לְיָדוֹ אָז בְּאוֹתָהּ רֶגַע דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה
and had a matter of transgression presented itself to his hand at that moment,
אִין הָכִי נַמֵּי שֶׁהָיָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ וְיָכוֹל לוֹ.
indeed yes, the Holy One, blessed be He, would have helped him and he would have prevailed.
וַאֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא דְּגַם בְּאוֹתָהּ רֶגַע לֹא יָכוֹל
And even if you say that at that very moment he could not have prevailed,
אִם הוּא גָּמַר בְּלִבּוֹ לְהִתְקוֹמֵם נֶגֶד יִצְרוֹ בְּכָל כֹּחוֹ
if he decisively resolved in his heart to rise against his inclination with all his strength,
(אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁוַּדַּאי אִלּוּ הָיָה בֶּאֱמֶת בְּכָל כֹּחוֹ הָיָה יָכוֹל לוֹ),
(even though certainly, had it been in truth with all his strength, he would have overcome it),
מִכָּל מָקוֹם אִם אַחַר כָּךְ יִצְרוֹ אַלְבְּשֵׁיהּ
nonetheless if afterward his base urge clothed him,
וְהִסִּיתוֹ לִדְבַר עֲבֵירָה
and incited him to a matter of transgression;
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּלֹא נִדְחָה עַל יְדֵי זֶה תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ הַקּוֹדֶמֶת שֶׁהָיְתָה בֶּאֱמֶת
it can be said that his earlier sincere repentance is not nullified on account of this;
דְּגַם בַּהַהוּא דְּקִדּוּשִׁין לֹא חִלְּקוּ
for in that case of Kiddushin they did not make a distinction
אֲפִילּוּ רָאוּהוּ תֵּיכֶף בְּרֶגַע אַחַר הַקִּדּוּשִׁין חוֹטֵא וּמַרְשִׁיעַ כְּדַרְכּוֹ.
even had they seen him immediately the moment after the betrothal sinning and acting wickedly as was his custom.
וּמַה דְּמִן הַשָּׁמַיִם לֹא סִיְּיעוּהוּ
And as for why from Heaven they did not actively shield him
אַחַר שֶׁהֵחֵל לִטָּהֵר בְּהִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב
after he began to purify himself through contemplation of repentance in the heart,
עַד שֶׁיֵּשׁ עָלָיו שֵׁם צַדִּיק גָּמוּר
to the point that the title of completely righteous rests upon him—,
הַרְבֵּה תְּשׁוּבוֹת לַמָּקוֹם
many reasons exist before the Omnipresent,
שֶׁהָיָה הַמִּשְׁפָּט לְנַסּוֹתוֹ וְשֶׁלֹּא לְסַיְּיעוֹ;
in that divine judgment deemed it fitting to test him and withhold overt assistance;
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא נִדְחָה מִשֵּׁם צַדִּיק גָּמוּר
and nonetheless he was not displaced from the title of completely righteous.
בְּאוֹתָהּ רֶגַע דְּהִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה
at that precise instant of the contemplation of repentance.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 89b (“subtract half the night”) and Mishlei 7:9 (“in the twilight, in the evening of day”) mark night as the time of concealed sins of desire. Megillah 28a: before sleep Mar Zutra would say, “may his Master forgive everyone who has troubled me.” Shabbos 153a: “Repent one day before your death” — i.e., every day, since one never knows. Sleep being “one-sixtieth of death,” nightfall is the fitting hour of nightly reckoning and return.

paragraphs.text: Me'or Einayim — 'one who comes to purify is helped' means added daas is drawn after the initial arousal (Toldos §32): The Me'or Einayim explains 'ha-ba le-taher mesay'in lo' through the structure of daas. A person first makes an awakening from below; then, precisely because he has come to purify himself, Heaven draws to him an added daas 'me-olam ha-ta'anug' so that he will be strengthened in his avodah. The help is therefore not a substitute for the first movement of the person but a response to it. This matches R' Tzadok's answer to the apparent difficulty in this se'if. If a talmid chacham later falls again, one cannot reason backward that no help was given and therefore the prior teshuvah must have been false. The maxim describes a living sequence: first a real human turn, then assistance that expands the person's capacity; later, new concealment or a new trial can still occur and require a renewed awakening. The Me'or Einayim even describes daas as sometimes being withdrawn so that it can later return in greater measure. That Chassidic pattern gives conceptual room for what R' Tzadok is defending halachically — a genuine spiritual state at one time need not be invalidated by a different state at another time. The truth of the earlier return is judged at the moment in which the heart actually turned.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 38b: “One who comes to purify himself is helped from Heaven.” R’ Tzadok resolves the apparent objection: the “help” is granted at the very instant of coming to purify; a later relapse (permitted by Heaven as a test) does not retroactively cancel the genuine teshuvah of that instant. Izhbitz — human effort in the revealed area, Divine help in the hidden area (Mei HaShiloach II, Nitzavim §3): On 'ha-nistaros la-Hashem Elokeinu ve-ha-niglos lanu u-levaneinu,' the Mei HaShiloach warns a person not to declare himself already clarified merely because he can blame the atmosphere around him for what he feels. Instead, 'yishtadel ha-adam leva'er ha-ra mi-kirbo ve-livdok ad makom she-yado maga'as ba-niglos' — a person must strive to remove the evil from within himself and examine as far as his hand reaches in the revealed matters — 've-Hashem yitbarach ya'azor lo ba-nistaros' — and Hashem will help him in the hidden matters. This is perhaps the cleanest Izhbitz formulation of 'ha-ba le-taher mesay'in oso' for the present discussion. The person is not asked to control every hidden layer of psyche and circumstance before his teshuvah can count. He is asked to do honestly what lies within the reach of his revealed choice. Once he turns there, the hidden work is not abandoned; it becomes the arena of Divine assistance. That makes R' Tzadok's position both demanding and merciful. The thought of teshuvah is sufficient when it is true because the human being is judged on the point genuinely in his hand; but sincerity requires that he actually use that point rather than invoke hidden causes as an excuse. The later assistance belongs to Hashem, and a later test does not retroactively erase the earlier human act of turning.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: This concerns the talmid chacham “who commits a sin at night” — night being the time of desire’s sins, and the hour before sleep being fitting for teshuvah, when one tastes a sixtieth of death. What is asked is not regret alone but complete teshuvah. And at its own moment his teshuvah was genuine, even if he afterward returned to his wont.

p: (ד) — וּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ: "הֵיכִי דָּמֵי בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה? וְכוּלֵי",
And that which they asked: “What is the definition of a penitent? etc.”
עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּיוֹמָא (פ״ו עַמּוּד ב׳),
examine there in Yoma (86b),
כְּפִי גִּרְסָא שֶׁלָּנוּ צָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּזְדַּמֵּן שְׁנֵי פְּעָמִים וְנִיצּוֹל
according to our textual version it requires that the opportunity present itself twice and he be delivered.
דִּבִתְרֵי הָוֵי חֲזָקָה שֶׁלֹּא יִכָּשֵׁל עוֹד
for twice establishes a legal presumption that he will stumble no more.
וְרִי״ף וְרֹא״שׁ וְרַמְבַּ״ם לֹא גָּרְסִי "פַּעַם רִאשׁוֹנָה וּשְׁנִיָּה"
And the Rif, Rosh, and Rambam do not read “a first and second time,”;
וּבְפַעַם אַחַת סַגִּי
holding that a single occasion suffices.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּזְדַּמֵּן לְיָדוֹ וְנִיצּוֹל
yet nonetheless it requires that the temptation present itself to his hand and he be spared.
כְּבָר יִשְּׁבָהּ רַמְבַּ״ם (בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ב׳ מֵהִלְכוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה הֲלָכָה א׳)
Maimonides already resolved this (Laws of Repentance 2:1),
דְּזֶהוּ לְעִנְיַן תְּשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה וּמִן הַמּוּבְחָר
in that this standard applies to complete, superlative repentance.
וְכָתַב: וְאִם וְכוּלֵי אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ תְּשׁוּבָה מְעֻלָּה מוֹעֶלֶת הִיא
and wrote: and if, etc. even though it is not superior repentance, it is effective.
וְאֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר גַּם כֵּן
And it is possible to suggest likewise
מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ "הֵיכִי דָּמֵי בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה",
that what they asked: “What is the definition of a ba’al teshuva?”
הַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נִקְרָא בְּשֵׁם זֶה דְּ"בַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה",
means: what qualifies him to be permanently titled by this designation of “master of repentance,”
וּקְרִיאַת הַשֵּׁם הַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה עַצְמוּתוֹ כָּךְ,
and bearing this permanent name signifies that his very essential being has become such.
דְּאָז נַעֲשָׂה לוֹ שֵׁם הָעֶצֶם קָבוּעַ וְקַיָּים
for then it becomes an enduring, permanent proper noun for him.
וְכָל בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה
And every penitent,
אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלִּשְׁעָתוֹ הוּא שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת
even though at his specific moment he repented in truth,
וְהוּא בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה לְשָׁעָה
and is indeed a penitent for that hour,
כֵּיוָן דְּאֵינוֹ בָּטוּחַ שֶׁלֹּא יִתְקַלְקֵל וְיַחֲזוֹר לְסוּרוֹ,
inasmuch as it is not guaranteed that he will not relapse and return to his former waywardness,
אֵינוֹ נִקְבָּע לוֹ לְשֵׁם עַצְמוֹ
it is not permanently fixed as his essential name,
עַד שֶׁיָּבוֹא לְיָדוֹ דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה פַּעַם אַחַת וּשְׁנִיָּה כְּגִרְסָא דִּילַן
until an opportunity for the sin presents itself to his hand once and twice according to our version.
דְּבָזֶה בָּטוּחַ דְּלָא יֶחֱטָא עוֹד
wherein it is certain that he will not sin again.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (ל״ח עַמּוּד ב׳)
And as they stated in Yoma (38b)
מִקְּרָא דְּ"רַגְלֵי חֲסִידָו יִשְׁמֹר" (שְׁמוּאֵל א ב׳, ט׳),
from the verse: “He will guard the feet of His pious ones” (I Samuel 2:9).
דְּ"חָסִיד" נִקְרָא כְּשֶׁמִּתְגַּבֵּר יוֹתֵר מִצַּדִּיק
for one is titled “chasid” when he overcomes evil to a greater degree than a standard tzaddik.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ בְּאוֹתִיּוֹת דְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
Therefore they expounded in Otiyot DeRabbi Akiva
עַל פָּסוּק "וַחֲסִידֶיךָ יְרַנֵּנוּ" (תְּהִלִּים קל״ב, ט׳)
– on the verse: “and Your pious ones shall sing for joy” (Psalms 132:9) –;
אֵלּוּ רִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁעֲתִידִים וְכוּלֵי
these are the wicked of Israel who are destined to repent, etc.;
כִּי יוֹתֵר תּוֹקֶף גְּבוּרָה בְּנִיצּוּחַ הַיֵּצֶר
for a greater intensity of might in defeating the inclination,
צָרִיךְ הָרָשָׁע כְּשֶׁשָּׁב
is required by the wicked person when he repents,
וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא "חֲסִידֶיךָ",
and therefore they are termed “Your chasidim,”
פֵּירוּשׁ חֲסִידֵי ה' הַיְינוּ מוּפְלָגֵי הַחֲסִידוּת
meaning the chasidim of Hashem—those who are extraordinary in piety,
כְּמוֹ "עֲצֵי ה'", "אַרְזֵי ה
'", like “the trees of Hashem,” “the cedars of Hashem,”.
וּבְכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁמַּסְמִיךְ אֶל ה' לְהַפְלָגַת הַדָּבָר בְּיוֹתֵר
and in every instance where Scripture appends an entity to the divine Name, it signifies the absolute superlative of the matter.
וּמִי שֶׁבָּא דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה לְיָדוֹ וְנִיצּוֹל
And one to whose hand an opportunity for sin comes and he is delivered
נִקְרָא בְּ "גִּבּוֹרֵי כֹחַ",
is designated in Kiddushin (40a) as “mighty in strength,”
וּבָזֶה מוּבְטָח לְהִשָּׁמֵר מֵעַתָּה
and through this he is guaranteed to be guarded from now on.
עַד שֶׁקָּנָה לוֹ שֵׁם עַצְמוֹ שֶׁל "בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה" עַל יְדֵי זֶה
so that he acquires the permanent proper title of “ba’al teshuva” through this accomplishment.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: דִּבִתְרֵי הָוֵי חֲזָקָה שֶׁלֹּא יִכָּשֵׁל עוֹד

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §114): “‘and behold, three flocks of sheep’ — he thought perhaps it is chance that this one wishes to sell his flock and gathered them; but in three times it is a chazakah — that is, that in three times it is impossible that it be chance.” This gives his explanation of the evidentiary force of recurrence: a pattern can establish what a single event leaves accidental. The numerical rules differ: Kometz discusses three, whereas the present passage discusses two according to our text and records the Rif, Rosh, and Rambam’s reading requiring one. The parallel concerns what a presumption establishes, rather than an identical required count.

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:1: “What is complete teshuvah? One who has the opportunity to repeat a sin he committed, and it is within his power to do it, yet he refrains and does not — out of teshuvah, not fear or incapacity. And even if he repented only in his old age, when he can no longer do what he once did — though it is not the choicest teshuvah, it avails, and he is a baal teshuvah.”

paragraphs.text: I Shmuel 2:9: “רַגְלֵי חֲסִידָיו יִשְׁמֹר, וּרְשָׁעִים בַּחֹשֶׁךְ יִדָּמּוּ, כִּי לֹא בְכֹחַ יִגְבַּר אִישׁ” — “He guards the feet of His pious ones, and the wicked are silenced in darkness; for not by his own strength does a man prevail” (from Chana’s prayer). Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — God protects the steps of the devout, while the wicked perish; a man triumphs not by his own power but by Hashem’s help. R’ Tzadok’s use: from “the feet of His pious ones chasidav He guards” the Sages derive that one is called a “chassid” when he strengthens himself beyond a mere tzaddik; and the verse’s close, “not by strength does a man prevail,” is why the one saved from sin is called “mighty of strength” (Kiddushin 40a) — his victory is by God’s help.

paragraphs.text: Tehillim 132:9 (and 132:16): “כֹּהֲנֶיךָ יִלְבְּשׁוּ צֶדֶק, וַחֲסִידֶיךָ יְרַנֵּנוּ” — “Your priests shall clothe themselves in righteousness, and Your pious ones shall sing.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak read it of the Temple — its priests and its devout rejoicing before Hashem. R’ Tzadok’s use: he cites the derashah Osios d’Rabbi Akiva that “and Your pious ones shall sing” refers to “the wicked of Israel who are destined to be counted among the pious” — for the returning wicked, needing greater might to subdue the yetzer, becomes God’s “chasid,” His exceedingly pious one, “the pious of Hashem” like “the cedars of Hashem.”

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 40a: “Anyone to whom a matter of forbidden intercourse presented itself and who was saved from it — a miracle is performed for him, as it says, ‘mighty of strength, who do His word’ (Tehillim 103:20) — such as Rabbi Tzadok and his colleagues” (whose accounts of withstanding temptation follow there). Hence one who faces the trial and is saved is a “mighty one of strength,” secured against relapse. Kedushas Levi — why the baal teshuvah can stand higher without manufacturing a new test (Kedushat Levi, Bereshit §24): R. Levi Yitzchak explains the superiority of the baal teshuvah through the work of transforming darkness itself: the fallen sparks are raised through Torah and mitzvos, and when they return to their root their light is intensified, 'ke-yisron ha-or min ha-choshech.' He therefore invokes Chazal's teaching that 'in the place where baalei teshuvah stand' the completely righteous cannot stand, comparing it to a son who wandered far from his father and whose return produces an added delight. This sharpens R. Tzadok's use here of the person who actually withstood the recurring temptation. The advantage is not that sin or exposure to sin is intrinsically valuable; the advantage lies in the transformation of a darkness that already existed. A baal teshuvah has confronted an energy that once carried him away and has now redirected that same life toward Hashem. The 'gevurah' praised in Kiddushin is therefore the strength of conversion and return, not the pursuit of danger. In the language of this se'if, repeated resistance can establish the enduring name 'baal teshuvah' because it shows that the earlier force no longer governs him; Kedushas Levi supplies the inner mechanism — the very distance becomes material for a stronger attachment once it has genuinely been brought back to its source.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: “Who is the true baal teshuvah?” By our text, the same sin must present itself twice and he refrain — for two times establish a chazakah that he will not stumble again. The Rif, Rosh and Rambam lack “a first and a second time.” Once the trial has been withstood, the name of the thing becomes fixed and enduring in him.

p: (ה): — וְהָעִיקָּר נִרְאֶה
And the essential truth appears to be:
מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ "כְּגוֹן וְכוּלֵי",
what they taught: “for example, etc.”:
פֵּירוּשׁ כַּגָּוֶון הַזֶּה
means: in this specific manner—
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ בַּלֵּב כַּגָּוֶון וְאֹפֶן הַזֶּה
that his repentance in the heart be of the identical quality and intensity,
שֶׁל מִי שֶׁבָּא וְכוּלֵי
as one who encountered the identical sin, etc.
שֶׁכָּל כָּךְ מִתְחָרֵט וְשָׁב מִן הַדָּבָר
in that he is so profoundly remorseful and detached from the act;
עַד שֶׁאִם הָיָה מִזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ אוֹתָהּ אִשָּׁה, בְּאוֹתוֹ פֶּרֶק, בְּאוֹתוֹ מָקוֹם – הָיָה נִמְנָע
that had the identical woman, at the identical time, in the identical place presented herself, he would refrain.
אֲבָל אֵין צָרִיךְ שֶׁיֶּאֱרַע לוֹ כֵּן בַּפּוֹעַל דַּוְוקָא
yet it is not strictly required that this occur to him in concrete practice.
וְעַל כֵּן אֲפִילּוּ עָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה בָּאַחֲרוֹנָה וּבְיוֹם מוֹתוֹ,
Therefore, even if one repented at the very end and on the day of his death,
וְלֹא נִזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ כְּלָל דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה
and a temptation to sin never presented itself to him at all,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם אִם הָיְתָה בְּכָל לִבּוֹ
nonetheless, if it was with all his heart, (,
וַאֲפִילּוּ נִזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ וְלֹא עָמַד בַּנִּסָּיוֹן
(and even if it presented itself afterward and he failed the test,
אִם בִּשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה הָיְתָה בְּכָל לִבּוֹ
if at the moment of his repentance it was with all his heart
וְאִלּוּ נִזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ בְּאוֹתָהּ רֶגַע לֹא הָיָה חוֹטֵא),
and had it presented itself at that exact second he would not have sinned),
הֲרֵי זֶה בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה גָּמוּר בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה
behold he is a complete penitent at that hour,
וְאֵין צֹרֶךְ לְדִבְרֵי רַמְבַּ״ם בָּזֶה
and there is no need to relegate him according to Maimonides' distinction here.
וְהַכֹּל תְּשׁוּבָה מְעֻלָּה
and all of it constitutes superlative repentance.
וּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (י״ט עַמּוּד א׳):
And that which they taught in Avodah Zarah (19a):
"אַשְׁרֵי שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה תְּשׁוּבָה כְּשֶׁהוּא אִישׁ",
“Happy is he who performs repentance while he is still a vigorous man,”
הַיְינוּ דִּבְזִקְנוּתוֹ אֵין לוֹ כֹּחַ בִּמְזִמּוֹת לְבָבוֹ
means that in his old age he lacks the psychological vigor in the designs of his heart,
לְהִתְגַּבֵּר עַל יִצְרוֹ לָשׁוּב בְּכָל לִבּוֹ בֶּאֱמֶת
to conquer his urge so as to repent with all his heart in absolute truth;
וּבִפְרָט שֶׁנִּשְׁתָּרֵשׁ בַּחֵטְא
especially after having become entrenched in sin;
וְכָתַב בְּלִקּוּטֵי מַהֲרִי״ל
and it is written in Likkutei Maharil,
דַּעֲבֵירָה שֶׁעָבְרוּ עָלָיו רוֹב שְׁנוֹתָיו מְלַפַּפְתּוֹ וְהוֹלֶכֶת
that a sin over which the majority of one's years have passed wraps around him continuously.
וְעַיֵּין בְּשַׁעֲרֵי תְּשׁוּבָה (סוֹף שַׁעַר ב׳) ט׳ טְעָמִים בָּזֶה
and see in Sha'arei Teshuvah (end of Gate 2) nine reasons for this.
אֲבָל כְּשֶׁשָּׁב – תְּשׁוּבָה מְעֻלָּה הוּא
However, when he does repent, it is superlative repentance.
וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לֵיהּ גַּבֵּיהּ בְּאוֹתוֹ פֶּרֶק
even though you cannot find the identical physical youthfulness in his case.
וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דְּאֵינוֹ רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר בַּפּוֹעַל מַמָּשׁ,
And perforce you must say that the Gemara does not mean literally in concrete reality;
דְּהֵיכִי מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לָהּ?
for how could you ever configure such a scenario permitted by halakhah?
וּבִשְׁעַת עֲבֵירָה בַּתְּחִלָּה נִתְיַיחֵד עִמָּהּ
For during the commission of sin, he initially secluded himself with her,
וְאַחַר כָּךְ שְׁאָר הִתְקָרְבוּת
and afterward engaged in further intimacy,
וַהֲרֵי אָסוּר לְהִתְיַיחֵד
and behold it is strictly forbidden to seclude oneself;
וְכִי סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ דְּהוּתַּר אִיסּוּר יִחוּד לְבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה
could it enter your mind that the biblical prohibition of yichud was permitted to a penitent?!
וְלָא מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לָהּ בְּאוֹתוֹ מָקוֹם
And thus you cannot find the identical scenario in that location!
וַאֲפִילּוּ אִם אֵירַע שֶׁהָיְתָה עִמּוֹ בְּיִחוּד, צָרִיךְ לִבְרוֹחַ מִיָּד
And even if it happened that she was in seclusion with him, he must flee immediately;
וְדָבָר זֶה חוֹבָה עַל כָּל אָדָם
and this obligation rests upon every single human being.
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן עַל בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לִגְדּוֹר עַצְמוֹ בְּיוֹתֵר
and all the more so upon a penitent who must fence himself in with extraordinary care.
וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין (ק״ז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳) דִּלְעוֹלָם לֹא יָבִיא עַצְמוֹ לְנִסָּיוֹן שֶׁלֹּא יִכָּשֵׁל
And in Sanhedrin (107a) it is taught that a person should never bring himself into a test lest he stumble;
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בְּבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה
and how much more so regarding a penitent;
וְכֵן הוּא בְּסֵפֶר חֲסִידִים (סִימָן קס״ז)
and so it is stated in Sefer Chassidim (sec. 167),
דְּלֹא יֹאמַר אָדָם: הֲרֵי אֲנִי בְּאוֹתָהּ וְכוּלֵי
that a person should never say: behold I am with the same woman, etc.
אֲקַיֵּים זֶה דְּשֶׁמָּא תִּתְרַצֶּה
“I will fulfill this [criterion]”—for she might consent [and he would sin].
וְלֹא אָמְרוּ שֶׁיָּבִיא עַצְמוֹ לֶעָוֺן, עַיֵּין שָׁם
for the Sages never told a person to bring himself near to sin, see there:
וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּהַכַּוָּונָה רַק שֶׁהַתְּשׁוּבָה יִהְיֶה עַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה
And perforce the intent is solely that the inward repentance be of such caliber:
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לִבּוֹ בָּטוּחַ שֶׁיִּצְרוֹ בְּיָדוֹ לִכְפּוֹתוֹ,
that his heart is confident that his inclination is within his grasp to subdue it.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא יִבְטַח עַל עַצְמוֹ בַּפּוֹעַל
and nonetheless he must not trust in himself in concrete practice.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהַהַרְחָקוֹת לְכָל אֶחָד כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא מַכִּיר בְּיִצְרוֹ,
And even though the distance required for each person corresponds to how well he knows his urge,
וּמִי שֶׁבּוֹטֵחַ בְּנַפְשׁוֹ אֵין צָרִיךְ כָּל כָּךְ הַרְחָקָה
and one who is truly secure in his soul does not require as broad a distance,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרִיטְבָ״א (בְּסוֹף קִדּוּשִׁין)
as the Ritva wrote (at the end of Kiddushin)
מֵהָא דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן יָתֵיב אַשַּׁעֲרֵי טְבִילָה וְעוֹד טוּבָא, יְעֻיַּין שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ,
from the fact that Rabbi Yochanan sat at the gates of the immersion mikveh and many other instances, examine there at length,
וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ בְּתוֹסָפוֹת שַׁבָּת (י״ג סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳ דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל: "וּפְלִיגָא"),
and similarly in Tosafot on Shabbat (13a, heading: “Ufeliga”);
וְכֵן בְּנִדָּה (י״ג סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳), עַיֵּין שָׁם
and likewise in Niddah (13a), see there;
זֶהוּ בְּהַרְחָקָה בְּעָלְמָא מִשּׁוּם גֶּדֶר וּסְיָיג
this applies only to standard distancing as a fence and safeguard,
וְלֹא לְהָבִיא עַצְמוֹ לִידֵי נִסָּיוֹן דְּזֶה אָסוּר
and never to intentionally bringing oneself into a trial, which is strictly forbidden,
דְּאָז הַיֵּצֶר גּוֹבֵר
for then the urge overpowers,
וְאָנוּ מְבַקְּשִׁין בְּכָל יוֹם: "אַל תְּבִיאֵנוּ לִידֵי נִסָּיוֹן וְכוּלֵי".
and we plead daily: “Do not bring us into temptation, etc.”,
וְגַם זֶה בְּצַדִּיק גָּמוּר שֶׁלֹּא חָטָא מֵעוֹלָם
Moreover, even that leniency applied only to a completely righteous person who never sinned;
וְלֹא בְּבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁכְּבָר טָעַם טַעַם חֵטְא
and never to a penitent who has already tasted the taste of sin;
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּדְמֶה לוֹ שֶׁכְּבָר שָׁב בְּכָל לִבּוֹ,
and even though it appears to him that he has already repented with all his heart.
וַדַּאי אֵין לוֹ לִבְטוֹחַ בְּעַצְמוֹ כְּלָל
he certainly must not trust in himself at all.

paragraphs.text: The prohibition of yichud seclusion (Kiddushin 80b): the Mishnah and Gemara forbid a man to be secluded with a woman forbidden to him — and with men “steeped in immorality” a woman may “not be secluded even with ten.” Meforshim: yichud with the arayos is a Torah prohibition, derived (Avodah Zarah 36b) from “your brother, the son of your mother may entice you” (Devarim 13:7) — implying a son may be secluded with his mother, but no other man with any of the forbidden relations; and yichud with an unmarried woman was decreed by David’s court after the affair of Amnon and Tamar (Sanhedrin 21a). R’ Tzadok’s use: this is his proof that Yoma 86b’s “k’gon” — “one who came to the same woman, place, and circumstance and refrained” — cannot describe a literal recurrence, “for would it enter your mind that the prohibition of seclusion was permitted for a baal teshuvah?!” Hence it means a teshuvah of that quality, not an actual repeated trial.
