paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 107a: “Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav: a person should never bring himself to a test nisayon, for David king of Israel brought himself to a test and stumbled.” David had asked why we say “God of Abraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov” but not “God of David,” and was told, “they were tested by Me, and you have not been”; he asked to be tested — and fell in the matter of Bathsheba. This is the proof-text against a penitent’s courting temptation. Izhbitz-Radzin safeguard against courting a test — Sod Yesharim, Shabbos HaGadol 3:1: Sod Yesharim gives a remarkably explicit formulation of the distinction R' Tzadok is laboring to preserve here. A nisayon can indeed raise a person: 'mi-sibas nisayon nis'aleh madreigas ha-adam,' because through the concealment of the test one who stands in it can discover that Hashem was present even within the hester. Yet the sefer immediately insists that this truth is only retrospective. 'Ha-adam mi-tzido eino rashai le-hachnis atzmo be-nisayon' — from his own side a person is not permitted to place himself into a test — and this remains so 'even in a case where he would stand in the test.' That is why we pray 'al tevi'einu lo lidei nisayon': a person is not authorized to desire a spiritual ascent purchased by deliberately entering danger. Only 'after Hashem has brought a person into some test without his knowledge' should he understand that the trial can be for his elevation and refuse to rebel against it. This is an exceptionally exact Radzin complement to R' Tzadok's rejection of a literal requirement that the baal teshuvah recreate the scene of his sin. The same hidden-Providence doctrine that can reveal holiness within a test also forbids turning that doctrine into a prospective heter. The trial may be read as Divine after it has arrived from Above; it may not be manufactured below in order to prove one's righteousness. Thus the deepest Izhbitz language of hashgachah itself becomes the strongest protection of ordinary halachic responsibility.

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh §2): He describes the primordial serpent’s deceptive advice: “‘lest they become sunk in evil’ — but in truth you shall have greater elevation when you know of good and evil, and afterward return to the good — and you shall have added praise; and this is what is said, ‘for on the day you eat… and you shall be as God, knowing good and evil.’” He immediately answers: “in truth Hashem warned them not to bring themselves to a test,” for that tree would not be fully clarified until the end. The promise of elevation through return therefore gives no permission to enter the sin deliberately. This closely parallels the author’s insistence here that confidence in one’s teshuvah never licenses self-testing.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The essential reading: when they said “such as” — the same woman, the same place, the same circumstance — they meant that his teshuvah should be of that quality, such that were the trial to present itself he would refrain. It need not actually befall him in fact. On this reading the Rambam’s words stand, and all of it is “the choicest teshuvah.”

paragraphs.text: Baal Shem Tov — a safer explanation of 'where baalei teshuvah stand' (Baal Shem Tov, Nitzavim §6:1): A teaching recorded in the name of the Baal Shem Tov explains the higher standing of the baal teshuvah without requiring him to recreate the scene of sin. The baal teshuvah, it says, has already known the 'heat and enthusiasm' of transgression; when he returns and turns to Torah and mitzvos, he can perform them with an unusually intense warmth and desire because he already knows what powerful yearning feels like. The tzaddik who never entered that terrain does not possess that same experiential transformation. This provides an important contextual counterweight to the striking report R. Tzadok records here from Rav Yeiva and the Kli Yakar. The special power of the baal teshuvah can be understood as the redirection of an already-experienced force, not as permission to create a forbidden encounter in order to prove himself. That reading also fits R. Tzadok's own hesitation — 'tzarich iyun me'od ve-lo nitan le-iamer klal' as a practical rule — and his later move to David's use of permitted desire to break the yetzer. The Chassidic advantage of teshuvah is thus preserved in its strongest form while ordinary halachic responsibility remains intact: one transforms the fire one has already known; one does not light a new forbidden fire for the sake of extinguishing it.

That reading also fits R. Tzadok's own hesitation — 'tzarich iyun me'od ve-lo nitan le-iamer klal' as a practical rule — and his later move to David's use of permitted desire to break the yetzer. The Chassidic advantage of teshuvah is thus preserved in its strongest form while ordinary halachic responsibility remains intact: one transforms the fire one has already known; one does not light a new forbidden fire for the sake of extinguishing it.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: R’ Tzadok recalls reported permissions to test a penitent, but subjects them to strong scrutiny and rejects applying them as stated. If any such permission is intended, he limits it to permissible matters, as in David’s struggle with his inclination. Even that is not a proof of repentance; David sought to break desire through the good inclination.

items.h: סִימָן י
Teshuvah from love transforms sins into merits
תשובה מאהבה מתקנת את החטא והופכתו לזכויות

p: הָרִאשׁוֹן: תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה, וּבָזֶה מְתַקֵּן אֶת הַקּוֹדֵם, וְעַיֵּין (שָׁם:) דִּתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה זְדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוּ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת
The first: teshuvah from love — and by it he rectifies the past; and see there, Yoma 86b that with teshuvah from love, “willful sins become like merits.”
וְאִם כֵּן פֵּירַשׁ״י שֶׁכָּתַב בְּד״ה ״דְּמֵעִיקָּרָא״ דְּ״שׁוֹבָבִים״ — כְּאִלּוּ תְּחִלַּת חֵטְא עַל יְדֵי נַעֲרוּת כו׳, צָרִיךְ עִיּוּן לִכְאוֹרָה
If so, Rashi’s comment (s.v. “d’me’ikara”) — that “shovavim” means it is reckoned “as if the beginning of the sin was through youthfulness,” etc. — requires study, at first glance.
(וִיעוּיַּן מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְקַמָּן רֵישׁ סִימָן י״א לְפָרֵשׁ בְּעִנְיָן אַחֵר, וְדִבְרֵי רַשִׁ״י צָרִיךְ יִישּׁוּב)
And see what I wrote below, start of Siman 11, to explain it in another way; and Rashi’s words require settling.

וְנִרְאֶה דְּ״מֵעִיקָּרָא שׁוֹבָבִים״ הַכַּוָּנָה קוֹדֶם הַתְּשׁוּבָה, דְּעַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה נִתְבָּרֵר דְּגַם שְׁעַת הַחֵטְא שֶׁקּוֹדֶם הַתְּשׁוּבָה לֹא עֲשָׂאוֹ מִלִּבּוֹ כְּלָל, רַק מַעֲשֵׂה נַעֲרוּת וּשְׁטוּת בְּעָלְמָא

And it appears that “me’ikara shovavim” means before the teshuvah: that through teshuvah from love it is clarified that even the moment of the sin, before the teshuvah, he did not do “from his heart” at all — only an act of “youthfulness and mere folly” —
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסוֹטָה ג.) דְּאֵין אָדָם עוֹבֵר עֲבֵירָה אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְנָס (בּוֹ) רוּחַ שְׁטוּת
as they said in Sotah 3a, “a person does not commit a transgression unless a spirit of folly ruach shtus has entered him.”

וְשָׁם אֲמָרוּהוּ דֶּרֶךְ כְּלָל עַל כָּל אֶחָד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל, לְפִי שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל לִבָּן לַשָּׁמַיִם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּשהש״ר) עַל פָּסוּק ״וְלִבִּי עֵר״ שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל

And there they said it as a general rule of every Jew — for in truth “the heart of all Israel is to Heaven,” as they said in Shir HaShirim Rabbah on the verse “and my heart is awake” (Shir HaShirim 5:2), that “the Holy One is the heart of Israel.”
וּבִבְרָכוֹת (יז.) ״גָּלוּי וְיָדוּעַ שֶׁרְצוֹנֵנוּ (לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹנְךָ), וּמִי מְעַכֵּב — שְׂאוֹר (שֶׁבָּעִיסָה וְשִׁעְבּוּד מַלְכֻיּוֹת)״, וְהוּא הָרוּחַ שְׁטוּת

And in Berachos 17a, “it is revealed and known before You that our will is to do Your will — and what prevents it? — the ‘leaven in the dough’ and the subjugation to the kingdoms” — and that leaven is the “spirit of folly.”

וְעַל כָּךְ אָמַר (סַנְהֶדְרִין מד.) דְּאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָטָא — יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא, מָשָׁל לַאֲסָא דְּקָאֵי בֵּינֵי חִילְפֵי, שֶׁמֵּעַצְמוּת לֵב אִישׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי לְעוֹלָם מֵרִיחַ רֵיחַ טוֹב כַּאֲסָא

And concerning this they said Sanhedrin 44a, “even though he has sinned, he is still a Jew” — a parable to “a myrtle standing among thorns chilfei” — for from the very essence of the heart of a Jewish man there always wafts a good fragrance, like a myrtle.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בב״ר וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין לז.) עַל פָּסוּק ״וַיָּרַח אֶת רֵיחַ בְּגָדָיו״ — ״רֵיחַ בּוֹגְדָיו״, וְהַחֲטָאִים הֵם רַק דֻּגְמַת חוֹחִים הַסּוֹבְבִים אֶת הַשּׁוֹשַׁנָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״כְּשׁוֹשַׁנָּה (בֵּין הַחוֹחִים)״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְהַחוֹחַ עוֹקְצָהּ לְפִי שָׁעָה

and as they said in Bereishis Rabbah and Sanhedrin 37a on the verse “and he smelled the fragrance of his garments begadav” — read “the fragrance of his traitors bogdav” — and the sins are only like the thorns that surround the rose, as it says, “like a rose among the thorns” (Shir HaShirim 2:2), the thorn pricking it only for a moment.
וְלֶעָתִיד יְבוֹרַר זֶה בְּכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁ״יְּבוּקַּשׁ עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ״, כִּי ״כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ״ שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הַלֹּבֶן וְהַבְּהִירוּת

And in the Future this will be clarified in all Israel — that “the iniquity of Israel shall be sought and there shall be none” (Yirmeyah 50:20) — for “though your sins be as scarlet they shall become white as snow” (Yeshayah 1:18), which is the ultimate of whiteness and radiance, —
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "בַּהֶרֶת עַזָּה כַּשֶּׁלֶג",
as it is stated: “a bright spot as white as snow,”
הַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת
meaning, that they become like merits.

וּבָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה מִי שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לָשׁוּב מֵאַהֲבָה זוֹכֶה לָזֶה, דְּנִתְבָּרֵר דְּגַם מִקּוֹדֶם בִּשְׁעַת הַחֵטְא הָיָה רַק שׁוֹבָבוּת וּמַעֲשֵׂה נַעֲרוּת, וְלֹא זָדוֹן גָּמוּר, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה נַעֲשָׂה עוֹד כִּזְכֻיּוֹת

And in this world, one who merits to repent from love merits this — for it is clarified that even beforehand, at the moment of the sin, it was only “waywardness and an act of youth,” and not full willful sin; and through this, after the teshuvah, it becomes further “like merits.”
וּמַהֲרְשָׁ״א בְּחִדּוּשֵׁי אַגָּדוֹת (שָׁם:) תָּמַהּ עַל זֶה אֵיךְ חוֹטֵא נִשְׂכָּר, וְנִדְחַק דְּרוֹצֶה לוֹמַר שֶׁמּוֹסִיף זְכֻיּוֹת
And the Maharsha, in Chiddushei Aggados there, Yoma 86b, wondered at this — “how is a sinner rewarded?” — and forced an answer, that it means only “that he adds merits.”

וְהָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר גַּם כֵּן מִפְּנֵי שֶׁכֹּחַ הַבַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה, שֶׁכְּבָר טָעַם טַעַם חֵטְא וְשָׁב לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר (שֶׁצָּרִיךְ הִתְגַּבְּרוּת נֶגֶד הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע בְּיוֹתֵר), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב רַמְבַּ״ם (פ״ז מֵהִלְכוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה ה״ד)

But he could also have said it is because the power of the baal teshuvah — who has already tasted the taste of sin and returned to Hashem — is greater for he needs a greater overcoming against the evil inclination, as the Rambam wrote Hilchos Teshuvah 7:4.
וְזֶה טַעַם מַאן דְּאָמַר (בִּבְרָכוֹת לד:) דְּבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה גָּדוֹל מִצַּדִּיק גָּמוּר, וְעַיֵּין בְּסֵפֶר הַיָּשָׁר הַמְיוּחָס לְרַבֵּינוּ תָּם (שַׁעַר י׳) עַיֵּין שָׁם
And this is the reasoning of the one who says Berachos 34b that “a baal teshuvah is greater than a complete tzaddik”; and see the Sefer HaYashar attributed to Rabbeinu Tam Shaar 10 — see there.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 17a; Rambam, Hilchos Gerushin 2:20; Resisei Layla §44. The prayer says “Our desire is to do Your will”; the leaven in the dough and subjection to foreign kingdoms hinder that desire. In his specific legal case of a divorce that the law requires, Rambam explains that lawful compulsion may expose the underlying will to observe the Torah, although the inclination obstructs it. Resisei Layla §44 explicitly places those texts together. Rav Tzadok reads these sources as evidence of the inward attachment that makes authentic repentance possible; the rule about a lawfully compelled divorce is not a general permission to coerce actions or excuse wrongdoing.

paragraphs.text: Maharsha, Chiddushei Aggados, Yoma 86b, on ‘נעשו לו כשגגות’. On the Gemara’s assertion that deliberate sins become merits through teshuvah from love, he asks ‘דנמצא חוטא נשכר’—how could the sinner profit? His first explanation is that the penitent ‘מוסיף במעשיו הטובים יתר מכדי הצורך לגבי אותו עון’—adds good deeds beyond those required to redress the sin. Yet his discussion continues: expounding Yeshayahu 40:2 (‘כי נרצה עונה’), he explicitly writes ‘כי החטא גופיה נעשה זכות’—the sin itself becomes a merit. Thus the first explanation is not Maharsha’s entire discussion. Rav Tzadok cites and challenges the ‘additional merits’ reading, then develops his own account of retrospective transformation through teshuvah from love. This note is placed only after Rav Tzadok has quoted Maharsha’s explanation.

paragraphs.text: Sefer HaYashar (musar), Shaar 10; Berachos 34b. The ethical work traditionally attributed to Rabbeinu Tam first describes teshuvah as cleansing sin, rendering the penitent like a newborn child. It offers several interpretations of the Sages’ ranking of penitents and the fully righteous. In one preferred explanation, an exceptionally wholehearted penitent whose righteousness has become firmly established has, in this sense, “doubled” his righteousness by returning after straying. The argument is not an unconditional ranking of every penitent over every tzaddik. The attribution of this ethical Sefer HaYashar to Rabbeinu Tam is traditional and disputed; it must not be confused with other books bearing that title.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The first — teshuvah from love — rectifies the past, for through it “willful sins become like merits.” R’ Tzadok’s key move: teshuvah from love reveals retroactively that even at the moment of the sin the person did not act “from his heart” but through a mere “spirit of folly” (Sotah 3a). For every Jew’s heart is truly “to Heaven” (the Holy One is “the heart of Israel”), and his sins are only the thorns encircling the rose, never touching its fragrant core.

p: (ב) אֲבָל לְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא מְבוֹאָר דְּהַזְּדוֹנוֹת עַצְמָן נַעֲשִׂין כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, וּכְפֵירַשׁ״י דַּ״עֲלֵיהֶם״ מַשְׁמַע עַל כָּל מַה שֶּׁעָשָׂה אַף עַל הָעֲבֵירוֹת
But the language of the Gemara is explicit that the willful sins themselves become “like merits.” As Rashi explains, “upon them” implies all that he did—even the transgressions.

כִּי נֶחְשָׁב עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ דַּחֲשִׁיבָא מִצְוָה (בְּנָזִיר כג:), וּכְמִצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ דְּמִתּוֹךְ שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ בָּא לִשְׁמָהּ, הָכִי נָמֵי מִתּוֹךְ עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ בָּא לְמִצְוָה לִשְׁמָהּ

For it is reckoned “a transgression for Heaven’s sake (aveirah lishmah),” which is considered a mitzvah Nazir 23b: and just as “a mitzvah not for its own sake — for out of doing it not for its own sake one comes to its own sake,” so too “out of a transgression for Heaven’s sake one comes to a mitzvah for its own sake.”

וְעַל כֵּן הָעֲבֵירָה עַצְמָהּ חֲשׁוּבָה מִצְוָה וּזְכוּת, דְּאִלּוּ כִּוֵּן תְּחִלָּה לְכָךְ הֲרֵי הָיָה מִצְוָה לְכַתְּחִלָּה גַּם כֵּן, בְּכָל עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ, ״עֵת לַעֲשׂוֹת לַה׳ הֵפֵרוּ תּוֹרָתֶךָ״, וְאֵלִיָּהוּ בְּהַר הַכַּרְמֶל

And therefore the transgression itself is considered a mitzvah and a merit — for had he intended it so from the outset, it would have been a mitzvah even initially, as in every “transgression for Heaven’s sake”: “it is a time to act for Hashem — they have voided Your Torah” (Tehillim 119:126), and as with Eliyahu on Mount Carmel who offered on a private altar.
וְאַף דִּבְנָבִיא יֵשׁ גְּבוּל, דְּבַכֹּל אִם יֹאמַר לַעֲבֹר עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שְׁמַע לוֹ חוּץ מֵעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה — זֶהוּ רַק עַל פִּי נָבִיא
And though for a prophet there is a limit — that “in everything, if he says to transgress the words of Torah, listen to him, except for idolatry” — that license is only “by the word of a prophet”;

אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם לְחֵטְא עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ תִּקּוּן לִהְיוֹת נֶחְשָׁב אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה כַּעֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ, דְּמָצִינוּ דֻּגְמָא גַּם בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין קז.) עַל פָּסוּק ״עַד הָרֹאשׁ״, שֶׁבִּיקֵּשׁ דָּוִד כו׳ עַיֵּין שָׁם

but nonetheless, even for a Jew’s sin of idolatry there is a rectification, to be reckoned after teshuvah as “a transgression for its own sake” — for we find an example even in idolatry of “a transgression for its own sake” Sanhedrin 107a on the verse “unto the top rosh” (II Shmuel 15:32), that “David sought to serve idolatry” — see there.

וּמֵאַחַר דְּאַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה זוֹכֶה עַל יְדֵי הַחֵטְא לְמַדְרֵגָה גְּדוֹלָה יוֹתֵר, מָקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין, וְהֶעֱבִירָהּ הוּא שֶׁהֱבִיאַתּוּ לָזֶה, אִם כֵּן אִגַּלַּאי מִילְּתָא לְמַפְרֵעַ דַּהֲפָרַת הַתּוֹרָה בַּעֲבֵירָה הָיָה לְטוֹב וְלַעֲשׂוֹת לַה׳

And since after the teshuvah he merits, through the sin, a greater rung — “the place where masters of teshuvah stand” — and the transgression is what brought him to it, then the matter is “revealed retroactively” that the “voiding of the Torah” through the transgression was “for good, and to act for Hashem.”

וְאַף דְּהוּא לֹא כִּוֵּן לְכָךְ בִּשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה, הַכֹּל הָיָה מְסֻדָּר וּבָא מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית מֵרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּבְּרִיאָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת פט:) עַל פָּסוּק ״חֲטָאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים״

And though he did not intend so at the time of the act, all was “arranged and came from the six days of Creation, from Hashem’s will in creation,” as they said Shabbos 89b on the verse “though your sins be like scarlet ka-shanim” (Yeshayah 1:18).
וְכֵן (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין שָׁם) ״רְאוּיָה הָיְתָה בַּת שֶׁבַע לְדָוִד מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית, אֶלָּא שֶׁבָּאת לוֹ בְּמַכְאוֹב״, שֶׁהֻצְרַךְ לִסְבּוֹל אַחַר זֶה יִסּוּרִין בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And so in Sanhedrin 107a, “Bas Sheva was fit for David from the six days of Creation — only that she came to him through pain” — for he had to bear, after this, sufferings in this world.
וְזֶהוּ הַאֲכִילַת פַּגָּה, שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ טַעַם כָּל כָּךְ לִפְנֵי זְמַנּוֹ, דְּלֹא הָיָה הַקְּדֻשָּׁה מֻרְגֶּשֶׁת עֲדַיִן בְּפֹעַל בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה לְעֵין כֹּל
And this is “the eating of unripe fruit pagah,” which has “not much taste before its time” — for the holiness was “not yet felt in actuality at that time, to every eye”;

אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם בְּלֵב דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה הָיָה מָלֵא קְדֻשָּׁה גַּם בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה, וְלֹא כִּוֵּן לְחֵטְא כְּלָל, דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא ״פַּגָּה״, שֶׁהוּא הַפְּרִי הַחֲשׁוּבָה עַצְמָהּ, רַק שֶׁלֹּא נִגְמְרָה עֲדַיִן לִהְיוֹת חֲשִׁיבוּתָהּ בְּפֹעַל

but nonetheless, in the heart of David HaMelech it was “full of holiness even at that time,” and he “did not intend to sin at all” — therefore it is called “pagah,” which is “the important fruit itself,” only that it “was not yet completed to have its importance in actuality.”

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין שָׁם) דְּאָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ דְּהָיָה יָכוֹל לִכְפּוֹת לְיִצְרוֹ אִם רָצָה, וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ד:) דְּלִבּוֹ הָיָה חָלָל בְּקִרְבּוֹ, וְלֹא הָיָה רָאוּי לְאוֹתָהּ מַעֲשֶׂה, רַק לְהוֹרוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה

And as they said in Sanhedrin 107a that he said of himself “he could have subdued his inclination had he wished,” and as they said in Avodah Zarah 4b that “his heart was hollow within him,” and “he was not fit for that deed — only to teach teshuvah.”
וְהוּא יָדַע זֶה דְּיֵשׁ בַּדָּבָר הֲסָתַת הַיֵּצֶר,
And he knew that there was an incitement of the base inclination in the matter,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַנָּבִיא אַחַר כָּךְ מִמְּשַׁל דְּהֵלֶךְ,
as the prophet Nathan subsequently told him through the parable of the traveler,
שֶׁדְּרָשׁוּהוּ בְּפֶרֶק הֶחָלִיל (סֻכָּה נ״ב עַמּוּד ב׳) אַיֵּצֶר הָרָע.
which they expounded in the chapter HeChalil (Sukkah 52b) as referring to the evil inclination.
אֲבָל יָדַע בְּרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ דִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה זֶה,
Yet he perceived through Ruach HaKodesh that the will of Hashem, blessed be He, was that he do this,
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא עֲבֵירָה וְשֶׁיֵּעָנֵשׁ עָלֶיהָ,
even though it was a transgression and he would be punished for it,
וְלֹא רָצָה לְמִזְכֵּי לְמָארֵיהּ;
and he did not wish to prevail against his Master;
וְכֵיוָן דִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה
and since it was the will of Hashem that he do it,
הֲרֵי זֶה עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ,
behold this constitutes a transgression for Heaven's sake,
דְּלֹא רָצָה לְמִזְכֵּי וְלִכְבוֹד שָׁמַיִם;
for he did not wish to prevail, and acted for the honor of Heaven;
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הָיָה צָרִיךְ לְיִסּוּרִין וְכַפָּרַת עָוֺן,
and nonetheless he still required suffering and the atonement of sin,
דְּגַם בְּכָל עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ כֵּן,
for so it is in every transgression for Heaven's sake,
שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ כַּפָּרָה עַל הָעֲבֵירָה.
that one nonetheless requires atonement for the transgression.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת בָּבָא קַמָּא (צ״א עַמּוּד ב׳ דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל: "אֶלָּא"),
And as Tosafot stated in Bava Kamma (91b, heading: “Ela”),
גַּבֵּי נָזִיר דְּנִקְרָא חוֹטֵא,
regarding a Nazirite who is termed a sinner,
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם יֵשׁ מִצְוָה הַגְּדוֹלָה מֵעֲבֵירָה,
and nonetheless there is an immense mitzvah greater than the transgression,
וְאַף עַל פִּי כֵן צָרִיךְ כַּפָּרָה עַל שֶׁחָטָא עַל הַנֶּפֶשׁ.
and despite this, he requires atonement for having sinned against the soul by abstaining from wine.
וְהֵבִיאוּ רְאָיָה מִתַּעֲנִית חֲלוֹם בְּשַׁבָּת,
And they brought proof from fasting over a bad dream on Shabbat,
דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּאֵין חוֹטֵא שֶׁיִּתְעַנֶּה,
where even though he is not a sinner for fasting,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם נִפְרָעִין מִמֶּנּוּ עֹנֶג שַׁבָּת,
nonetheless he is penalized for depriving himself of Shabbat delight,
וְצָרִיךְ כַּפָּרָה בְּתַעֲנִית לְתַעֲנִיתוֹ.
and he requires atonement through a subsequent fast to atone for his fast.
וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (כ״ו סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳)
And similarly in Sanhedrin (26b)
דְּסָבְרִי מִצְוָה עָבְדִי,
concerning those who thought they were performing a mitzvah,
וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכִי מְשַׁמְּתֵי,
and even so the Sages placed them under a ban,
דְּסָבְרִי כַּפָּרָה עָבְדוּ לְהוּ רַבָּנָן;
reasoning that the Rabbis administered an expiation on their behalf;
וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ יָדְעוּ כָּךְ הַדִּין:
and perforce they knew such to be the halakhic principle:
דְּמִצְוָה הַבָּאָה בַּעֲבֵירָה, אַף שֶׁמִּצְוָה לַעֲשׂוֹתָהּ,
that a mitzvah that comes through a transgression, even when it is a mitzvah to perform it,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם צְרִיכִין כַּפָּרָה עַל הָעֲבֵירָה שֶׁבָּהּ.
nonetheless requires expiation for the transgression within it.
וְגַם אֵלִיָּהוּ בְּהַר הַכַּרְמֶל,
And also Elijah at Mount Carmel,
מַה שֶּׁהֻוצְרַךְ לִבְרוֹחַ אַחַר כָּךְ מִפַּחַד אִיזֶבֶל
the fact that he had to flee afterward out of dread of Jezebel
הָיָה לְכַפָּרָה לְהַקְרָבָתוֹ בַּבָּמָה,
served as an expiation for his having sacrificed upon an outdoor altar (bamah),
אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה בִּדְבַר ה',
even though it was entirely by the word of Hashem,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק (מְלָכִים א י״ח, ל״ו): "וּבִדְבָרְךָ עָשִׂיתִי" –
as our Sages of blessed memory expounded on the verse (I Kings 18:36): “and that I have done all these things at Your word” –
דְּבַר ה' הָיָה שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה הַדָּבָר בַּעֲבֵירָה;
the word of Hashem was that he perform the act through a transgression;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק (בְּרֵאשִׁית ל״ה, י״א): "וּקְהַל גּוֹיִם" –
and as our Sages expounded on the verse (Genesis 35:11): “and a company of nations” –
עֲתִידִין לְהַקְרִיב בְּאִיסּוּר בָּמוֹת כַּגּוֹיִים.
they are destined to sacrifice under the prohibition of altars like the nations.
וְלֹא דָּמֵי לְכִלְאַיִם בְּצִיצִית וּמִילָה בְּשַׁבָּת
And this is not comparable to the juxtaposition of wool and linen in tzitzit or circumcision on Shabbat
וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ כָּל "עֲשֵׂה דּוֹחֶה לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה",
and similar cases where a positive commandment overrides a negative one,
דְּמִצְוָתוֹ בְּכָךְ לְעוֹלָם עַל פִּי חוּקֵי הַתּוֹרָה,
for its mandated performance is permanently ordained thus according to the laws of the Torah,
שֶׁבְּעִנְיָן זֶה יַעֲשֶׂה כָּךְ וְאֵין כָּאן עֲבֵירָה כְּלָל.
wherein in this configuration one acts thus and no sin exists whatsoever.
וְדַוְוקָא בְּדָבָר שֶׁאֵין מִצְוָתוֹ כָּךְ,
Rather it applies specifically to an act whose standard mitzvah is not structured thus,
רַק הוּתַּר וְנַעֲשָׂה מִצְוָה לְצוֹרֶךְ שָׁעָה זוֹ לְבַד;
having been permitted and made a mitzvah strictly for the urgent need of that hour alone;
וְעַל כֵּן קְרוּיָה "כַּגּוֹיִם",
and therefore it is termed “like the nations,”
וְדָיֵיק "כַּגּוֹיִם",
and the Midrash specifically emphasizes “like the nations,”
כִּי אוֹתוֹ דּוֹר חָטְאוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
because that generation had sinned in idolatry
וְלִהְיוֹת כְּכָל הַגּוֹיִם מַמָּשׁ.
and in seeking to become literally like all the nations.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: (ב) אֲבָל לְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא מְבוֹאָר דְּהַזְּדוֹנוֹת עַצְמָן נַעֲשִׂין כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, וּכְפֵירַשׁ״י דַּ״עֲלֵיהֶם״ מַשְׁמַע עַל כָּל מַה שֶּׁעָשָׂה אַף עַל הָעֲבֵירוֹת

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86b; Yechezkel 33:19; Rashi on Yoma 86b. The Gemara derives the transformation of deliberate sins into merits from “and he does justice and righteousness—upon them he shall live.” Rashi understands “upon them” to include the person’s former acts, even transgressions. Rav Tzadok therefore insists that the wording concerns the former sins themselves, not simply new good deeds added afterward. The further metaphysical account of their retroactive role is Rav Tzadok’s subsequent argument, not Rashi’s statement or a license to sin.

paragraphs.text: Nazir 23b; Shoftim 5:24. The Gemara initially says that an aveirah lishmah—a transgression for Heaven’s sake—is greater than a mitzvah performed with improper motive, but immediately corrects the comparison to equal to such a mitzvah. Yael is the example. Rav Tzadok draws a further analogy: just as mitzvah shelo lishmah can lead to mitzvah lishmah, he discusses how a transgression, assessed only after a genuine return, can become part of the account of ascent. The Gemara itself does not issue a general authorization to commit a prohibited act.

paragraphs.text: Yevamos 90b: ‘אליו תשמעון ... אפילו אומר לך עבור על אחת מכל מצות שבתורה, כגון אליהו בהר הכרמל, הכל לפי שעה שמע לו’—listen to an established prophet’s exceptional instruction to transgress a commandment, as with Eliyahu at Har HaCarmel, only for that occasion. Devarim 18:15 supplies ‘אליו תשמעון’. Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 9:3, expressly requires ‘נביא שנודע לנו שהוא נביא’, limits the departure to ‘לפי שעה’, and explains that Eliyahu sacrificed outside ‘בדבר ה׳ כדי להכחיש נביאי הבעל’. Rambam 9:5 separately states ‘אבל בעבודת כוכבים אין שומעין לו ואפילו לפי שעה’—idolatry is excluded even temporarily. See Kometz HaMinchah II §34 (Har Bracha printed p. 330) and Dover Tzedek, Acharei Mos (printed p. 139), both explicitly discussing the Carmel exception. This is a legal hora’as sha’ah, not a personal license for aveirah lishmah. Rav Tzadok’s subsequent claim about a sin’s possible retrospective rectification after teshuvah is his own interpretive development and must not be attributed to Rambam or presented as prospective authorization.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 107a; II Shmuel 15:32. The Gemara relates that David considered an appearance of idolatry while fleeing Avshalom so that observers would not suppose a righteous king had suffered an unjust fate; Chushai challenged and dissuaded him. It does not say that David actually worshiped idols or that such an act would have been halachically permitted. Rav Tzadok cites the contemplated episode as an example of ostensibly grave wrongdoing being conceived under an appeal to Heaven’s honor; that is his interpretive comparison, not a standing permission to transgress.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 34b; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:4; Peri Tzadik, Pesach Sheni 3:2 — the fall as the route to a higher return: The higher standing of the baal teshuvah is explained by the Rambam as the reward of one who tasted sin, separated from it, and conquered the inclination more forcefully. Peri Tzadik describes Pesach Sheni as a root-level rectification in which distance itself, when it awakens brokenhearted return, is transformed until willful sins become merits. These sources illuminate Rav Tzadok’s “revealed retroactively”: the transgression becomes the occasion and material of ascent only through the later teshuvah. The doctrine cannot be invoked prospectively to choose sin in order to attain a higher level.

paragraphs.text: Machshavos Charutz §4 (Rav Tzadok’s own parallel). Rav Tzadok connects Nazir 23b, the exceptional concept of aveirah lishmah, with Shabbos 89b, “sins like the years ordered since the six days of Creation”; he adds that in the future Israel’s history will be clarified in this way. In the present siman this retrospective understanding is connected to teshuvah; it is neither the literal language of the Gemara nor permission to transgress prospectively. The text of Machshavos Charutz compares the eventual disclosure to aveirah lishmah; it does not erase the legal distinction between forbidden conduct and an authorized exceptional act.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 89b. ״כַּשָּׁנִים״? ״כַּשָּׁנִי״ מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ! אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק, אָמַר לָהֶם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל: אִם יִהְיוּ חֲטָאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים הַלָּלוּ שֶׁסְּדוּרוֹת וּבָאוֹת מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְּרֵאשִׁית וְעַד עַכְשָׁיו — כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ. “‘Like scarlet’—it should have said ‘like a scarlet thread’! Rabbi Yitzchak said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: If your sins are like these years, which have been ordered and come from the six days of Creation until now, they will become white as snow.” The Gemara compares sins to the years since Creation; Rav Tzadok reads its language of ordering as disclosing, after teshuvah, the Divine ordering of the whole course.

Pri Tzaddik develops a related warning through the Avigail episode. The Har Bracha editorial notes point to the Sanhedrin passage and cross-reference Takanas HaShavin §10; these are useful editorial parallels, not additions to Rav Tzadok’s original words. Rav Tzadok’s teaching about holiness concealed at the time of the act extends the Gemara; it does not render premature conduct permissible.

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 5:1–5; Tzidkas HaTzadik §40 — divine ordering and human responsibility: The Rambam establishes free choice as a foundation of Torah, reward, punishment, and teshuvah, while acknowledging that divine knowledge is beyond ordinary human comprehension. Tzidkas HaTzadik §40 explicitly holds both perspectives together: in the realm of choice, the act is fully the person’s responsibility; in the higher realm of divine knowledge, nothing lies outside Hashem’s knowledge and will. Rav Tzadok’s language that the course was arranged from Creation belongs to that second perspective and becomes spiritually accessible through complete teshuvah; it does not erase culpability at the moment of choice.

paragraphs.text: Tosafos on Bava Kamma 91b, s.v. אלא שציער עצמו מן היין. Rabbeinu Tam explains that a Nazirite may fulfill a greater mitzvah even though the abstention involves a measure of sin: “דמצוה גדולה מן העבירה ... ומכל מקום קצת יש חטא.” Tosafos compares a fast undertaken for a troubling dream on Shabbos: despite its benefit, one must account for the loss of Shabbos delight. This is the precise parallel to Rav Tzadok’s assertion that a spiritually beneficial deed does not automatically eliminate the need for atonement. Sanhedrin 107a and Avodah Zarah 4b–5a separately treat David and the nation as examples through which the path of teshuvah is taught; they do not declare their actions halachically permitted. Rav Tzadok’s generalization about aveirah lishmah is his theological development, not the wording of Tosafos.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The Gemara’s wording is precise: the willful sins themselves become merits. For a sin done “for its own sake” (aveirah lishmah) is reckoned a mitzvah, on the model of “a mitzvah not for its own sake, from which one comes to its own sake.” Had the person intended it so, it would have been a mitzvah from the outset (“a time to act for Hashem”).

p: (ג) וְכָל חֵטְא הַדּוֹר צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת גַּם בְּרֹאשׁ הַדּוֹר שֶׁמֶץ מִמֶּנּוּ, כִּי כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל קוֹמָה שְׁלֵמָה, וְרֹאשׁ הַדּוֹר כּוֹלֵל כָּל הַדּוֹר, ״פַּרְנָס לְפִי הַדּוֹר״ כַּיָּדוּעַ

And every sin of the generation must have, even in the head of the generation, a “trace” of it — for all Israel are one “complete stature,” and the head of the generation includes the whole generation, “a leader according to the generation,” as is known.

וּכְשֶׁשִּׁיבֵּר מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה הַלּוּחוֹת בְּחֵטְא יִשְׂרָאֵל בָּעֵגֶל — שֶׁזֶּה גַּם כֵּן חֵטְא מֵעֵין דֻּגְמָא, אֲבָל הוּא כִּוֵּן לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם — וּכְשֶׁאָמַר לוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ ״יִישַׁר כֹּחֲךָ שֶׁשִּׁבַּרְתָּ״, אָז פָּעַל סְלִיחָה וְכַפָּרָה גַּם לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, כִּי נִתְבָּרֵר דְּגַם חֶטְאָם הָיָה כְּעֵין עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ

And when Moshe Rabbeinu broke the tablets at Israel’s sin of the calf — which is also a “sin of that kind,” but he intended it “for the sake of Heaven” — and when Hashem said to him afterward, “yishar kochacha that you broke them” (Shabbos 87a), then he effected “forgiveness and atonement for Israel too,” for it was clarified that “their sin too was like a transgression for Heaven’s sake.”

וְכֵן בְּדוֹר אֵלִיָּהוּ הֻצְרַךְ הוּא לְהַקְרִיב בַּחוּץ, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא ״כַּגּוֹיִם״ וּכְדֶרֶךְ עוֹבְדֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, אֲבָל הוּא עָשָׂה מְפוֹרָשׁ בִּדְבַר ה׳ וּלְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מָצָא מָקוֹם לִטְעוֹן גַּם בְּעַד יִשְׂרָאֵל ״וְאַתָּה הֲסִבּוֹתָ אֶת לִבָּם אֲחֹרַנִּית״

And so in Eliyahu’s generation he had to offer “outside” on a private altar — which is called “like the nations” and the way of idolaters — but he did it “explicitly by the word of Hashem and for the sake of Heaven”; and through this he “found room to plead for Israel too”: “and You turned their heart backward” (I Melachim 18:37) —

שֶׁגַּם חֶטְאָם הוּא עַל יָדְךָ וְאַתָּה רָצִיתָ שֶׁיַּעֲשׂוּ כֵּן, וְעַל כָּרְחָם הָיָה שֶׁיַּעֲשׂוּ כִּרְצוֹנְךָ, דְּלָא יֹאמְרוּ ״עַבְדָּא דְּזָכֵי לְמָרֵיהּ״, וּפָעַל לְעוֹרֵר תְּשׁוּבָה בְּקֶרֶב כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל

that “their sin too is by Your hand, and You willed that they do so,” and “against their will it was that they did Your will,” lest they say “a servant who prevailed over his Master” — and he effected the “arousal of teshuvah among all Israel.”

וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא נִפְטְרוּ מִן הָעֹנֶשׁ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה עַל חֲטָאִים הַגְּדוֹלִים הָהֵם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וְהָיָה הַנִּמְלָט מֵחֶרֶב חֲזָאֵל (יָמִית יֵהוּא)״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וְהִשְׁאַרְתִּי (בְיִשְׂרָאֵל שִׁבְעַת אֲלָפִים כָּל) הַבִּרְכַּיִם אֲשֶׁר לֹא (כָרְעוּ לַבַּעַל)״

And nonetheless they were not exempted from punishment in this world for those great sins, as it says, “and it shall be, whoever escapes the sword of Chazael, Yehu shall slay” and “I will leave in Israel seven thousand, all the knees that have not bowed to the Baal” (I Melachim 19:17–18).

וְכָל הַחוֹטְאִים נֶעֶנְשׁוּ, וּכְמוֹ בָּעֵגֶל ״וּבְיוֹם פָּקְדִי וּפָקַדְתִּי״, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁשָּׁבוּ בִּתְשׁוּבָה שְׁלֵמָה מֵאַהֲבָה דְּנַעֲשָׂה כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, מִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ כַּפָּרָה כְּכָל עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ

And all the sinners were punished — as with the calf, “and on the day of My reckoning I will reckon their sin upon them” (Shemos 32:34) — and even though they repented with complete teshuvah from love, which “becomes like merits,” nonetheless it requires atonement, like every “transgression for Heaven’s sake.”
וְעַל כֵּן הֻצְרְכָה יָעֵל לִבְרָכָה, דְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר ״תְּבֹרַךְ מִנָּשִׁים״ וְגוֹמֵר הוּא לְהָגֵן עָלֶיהָ מִיִּסּוּרִים
And therefore Yael needed a “blessing” — for what is said, “blessed above women shall Yael be” (Shoftim 5:24) is “to shield her from sufferings.”

וְאֵין לְךָ עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ גְּדוֹלָה מֵאֶסְתֵּר, וְנִכְתַּב בְּרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ מַה שֶּׁאָמְרָה עַל עַצְמָהּ ״כַּאֲשֶׁר אָבַדְתִּי אָבָדְתִּי״, דְּמִסְּתָמָא יֵשׁ בָּזֶה שֵׁם ״אֲבֵדָה״ בֶּאֱמֶת, מִצַּד עֲבֵירָה כָּזוֹ דְּנִבְעֶלֶת לַגּוֹי

And you have no “transgression for Heaven’s sake” greater than Esther’s; and it was written by ruach hakodesh what she said of herself, “and as I am lost, I am lost” (Esther 4:16) — for presumably there is in this a name of “loss” in truth, from such a transgression as “being bedded by a gentile,”
שֶׁזֶּהוּ תַּכְלִית הַטִּמּוּעַ בֵּין הָעַמִּים שֶׁנִּקְרָאִים ״אוֹבְדִים״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וּבָאוּ הָאֹבְדִים בְּאֶרֶץ אַשּׁוּר״ עַל אוֹתָם שֶׁנִּטְמְעוּ בֵּין הָעַמִּים

which is the ultimate of “assimilation among the peoples,” who are called “the lost ones,” as it says, “and the lost ones shall come from the land of Ashur” (Yeshayah 27:13) — said of those who were “assimilated among the peoples.”
וְדִינָה שֶׁנִּבְעֲלָה לְגוֹי, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁתְּחִלָּתָהּ בְּאֹנֶס,
And Dinah, who was taken by a gentile, even though it began with force,
מִפְּנֵי סוֹפָהּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עָלֶיהָ "הַנִּבְעֶלֶת לְגוֹי קָשָׁה לִפָּרֵשׁ",
because of its outcome, about which our Sages of blessed memory said, “One taken by a gentile finds it hard to separate,”
הוּצְרְכָה לְהִתְגַּלְגֵּל בְּגוֹיָה,
had to be reincarnated in a gentile woman,
כְּכָזְבִּי בַּת צוּר כַּיָּדוּעַ.
as Cozbi daughter of Tzur, as is known.
וְאֶסְתֵּר שֶׁכָּל כַּוָּנָתָהּ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם
But Esther, whose entire intention was for the sake of Heaven
וּלְהַצָּלַת כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל מִגְּזֵרַת "לְהַשְׁמִיד וְלַאֲבֹד",
and to save all Israel from the decree “to destroy and to obliterate,”
אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁהִיא תֹּאבַד חַס וְשָׁלוֹם.
it is impossible that she should perish, Heaven forbid.
אֲבָל הִיא תִּקְּנָה בָּזֶה כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל,
Rather, through this she rectified all Israel,
שֶׁחָטְאוּ אָז בְּהִשְׁתַּחֲוָיָה לַצֶּלֶם וַהֲנָאַת סְעוּדַת אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ,
who had sinned then by bowing to the idol and enjoying the feast of Achashverosh,
שֶׁהוּא הָעֵרוּב בַּגּוֹיִם וְטִמּוּעַ בֵּין הָאֻמּוֹת לִהְיוֹת כְּמוֹתָם חַס וְשָׁלוֹם,
which is mingling with the gentiles and assimilation among the nations, to become like them, Heaven forbid,
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה עוֹרְרוּ גְּזֵרַת אוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע לִכְתֹּב עַל הַיְּהוּדִים לְאַבְּדָם.
and through this they aroused the decree of that wicked one to write against the Jews to destroy them.
אֲבָל הֵם לֹא עָשׂוּ רַק לִפְנִים וּבְעַל כָּרְחָם,
But they acted only outwardly and under compulsion;
רַק חֶטְאָם שֶׁלֹּא מָסְרוּ נַפְשָׁם עַל קִדּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם כַּחֲנַנְיָה מִישָׁאֵל וַעֲזַרְיָה.
their sin was only that they did not give up their lives for the sanctification of the Name, like Chananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.
וְגַם הִיא חָטְאָה בָּזֶה שֶׁהֵשִׁיבָה תְּחִלָּה לְמָרְדֳּכַי
And she, too, sinned in this, that she at first replied to Mordechai
שֶׁאֵינָהּ רְאוּיָה לְהַכְנִיס עַצְמָהּ לְסַכָּנָה בִּשְׁבִיל הַצָּלַת כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל,
that she ought not to endanger herself for the sake of saving all Israel,
וְלֹא רָצְתָה לִמְסֹר נַפְשָׁהּ מַה שֶּׁהָיְתָה מְחֻיֶּבֶת עַל זֶה.
and she did not want to give up her life, which she was obligated to do for this.
וְעַל זֶה הֵשִׁיב: "וְאַתְּ (וּבֵית אָבִיךְ) תֹּאבֵדוּ",
And to this he replied (4:14): “And you (and your father’s house) will perish,”
שֶׁיִּתְקַיֵּם הַגְּזֵרָה בָּהּ,
meaning that the decree would be fulfilled in her,
כִּי חֶטְאָהּ גָּדוֹל מִשֶּׁלָּהֶם,
for her sin is greater than theirs,
דִּבְעַל כָּרְחָם וְלִפְנִים לֹא נִקְרָא עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כְּלָל בֶּאֱמֶת וְלֹא טִמּוּעַ בֵּין הָאֻמּוֹת,
since what is under compulsion and merely outward is not truly called idolatry at all, nor assimilation among the nations,
אֲבָל הִיא לֹא חָשָׁה לְהַצָּלַת אִבְּדוֹן כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּגְזֵרָה וַדַּאִית לְפָנֶיהָ.
but she gave no heed to saving all Israel from destruction in a decree that was certain before her.
וְהִיא שָׁבָה תֵּיכֶף וּמָסְרָה נַפְשָׁהּ,
But she immediately repented and gave over her life,
וְלֹא בְּסַכָּנַת הַגּוּף לְבַד
and not only into danger to the body,
רַק גַּם סַכָּנַת אִבְּדוֹן נֶפֶשׁ דְּהַטָּלַת זֻהֲמָא וְתַכְלִית הַטִּמּוּעַ בֵּין הָאֻמּוֹת,
but also the danger of the loss of the soul, of being cast into contamination and the ultimate assimilation among the nations,
רַק שֶׁהָיָה בְּעַל כָּרְחָהּ.
except that it was against her will.
וּבָזֶה תִּקְּנָה עַצְמָהּ וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל,
And through this she rectified herself and all Israel,
בְּמַה שֶּׁעָשְׂתָה עוֹד עֲבֵרָה חֲמוּרָה כָּזוֹ דְּלִכָּנֵס בִּרְצוֹנָהּ,
in that she committed yet another grave transgression, to enter of her own accord,
רַק שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם אֵינָהּ בִּרְצוֹנָהּ הָאֲמִתִּי כְּלָל,
though nonetheless it is not at all her true will,
וְהוּא עֲבֵרָה לִשְׁמָהּ שֶׁנֶּחְשָׁב אַדְּרַבָּא לְמִצְוָה גְּדוֹלָה כַּאֲשֶׁר קִבַּלְתִּי,
and it is a transgression for the sake of Heaven, which is considered, on the contrary, a great mitzvah, as I have received,
כִּי עַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה הוּא תַּכְלִית הַתִּקּוּן לְכָל חֵטְא
for in this manner is the ultimate rectification of every sin,
וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ.
and this is not the place for it.

paragraphs.text: Arakhin 17a; Machshavos Charutz §17:5 — the leader and generation as one organic stature: Arakhin states that “the generation follows the leader” or “the leader follows his generation,” but the Gemara limits that dispute to harshness and gentleness, explicitly noting that a righteous leader may stand over an unworthy generation and conversely. Machshavos Charutz describes Israel as one complete stature whose spiritual “head,” “eyes,” and “heart” transmit life to the whole body. Rav Tzadok’s claim that a trace of the generation’s sin appears in its head is therefore his organic-mystical synthesis of collective soulhood; it is broader than the literal scope of the Arakhin passage and does not erase each person’s individual responsibility.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 87a records that Moshe broke the Luchos on a kal vachomer after the calf and that the Holy One approved the decision—“יישר כחך ששיברת.” Menachos 99b calls this a case in which apparent suspension of Torah became its foundation. Rav Tzadok, in Pri Tzaddik, Sefer Kedushas Shabbos §7:7, links the broken and second Tablets with renewed Torah effort. In the present paragraph he goes beyond those sources, proposing that Moshe’s act served as a figure through which the nation’s fault could be reconsidered; the Gemara does not itself identify the sin of the calf as an aveirah lishmah.

paragraphs.text: I Melachim 18:37; Berachos 31b; Rashi on I Melachim 18:37; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 6:3; Tzidkas HaTzadik §40. Eliyahu pleads, “You turned their hearts backward,” an assertion Chazal interpret as a bold appeal to Heaven concerning Israel’s failure. Rashi says Heaven permitted room for their turning and could have prepared their hearts to return; he also records an alternative aggadic interpretation. Rambam treats the related language about a hardened heart as punitive concealment of the path of repentance after earlier sins committed freely—not the assertion that the initial sins were forced or guiltless. Rav Tzadok, by contrast, reads the Divine-knowledge dimension through the later spiritual revelation disclosed in repentance. His concluding insistence that earthly punishment remained necessary prevents this comparison from erasing culpability.

paragraphs.text: Shemos 32:34; Yoma 86a. “On the day of My reckoning, I shall reckon their sin” preserves an accounting for the calf even after Israel’s return. The Gemara on Yoma 86a distinguishes the act of repentance from completion of kapparah: for especially grave offenses, repentance and Yom Kippur can suspend punishment while suffering completes expiation. Rav Tzadok’s phrase “nevertheless atonement is required” concerns this continuing consequence even where repentance from love transforms the spiritual accounting. That does not imply that the original act was permissible.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Every sin of a generation must leave a trace even in the head of the generation — for all Israel are one “stature,” and the leader includes them all. So Moshe broke the tablets at the sin of the calf (himself performing a “sin of that kind,” yet for Heaven’s sake). And when God said “yishar kochacha that you broke them,” he thereby won atonement for Israel too, its sin being revealed as an aveirah lishmah.

p: (ד) וְכָךְ מִדָּתוֹ שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַמְתִּיק הַמַּר בְּמַר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל עַל פָּסוּק ״וַיַּשְׁלֵךְ (עֵץ)״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וַיִּמְתְּקוּ הַמַּיִם״, שֶׁהָיָה עֵץ הַרְדּוּפְנִי מַר, רַק שֶׁהָיָה בְּצִוּוּי וּבִרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּבָזֶה נִמְתַּק הַמְּרִירוּת הַזֶּה וְהַקּוֹדֵם

And so is the way of Hashem — to “sweeten the bitter with the bitter”: as the Sages said on the verse “and he cast a tree and the waters were sweetened” (Shemos 15:25), that it was a bitter oleander branch — only that it was “by Divine command and by the will of Hashem” — and by this the present bitterness and the earlier bitterness were sweetened.
וְהִיא הוֹסִיפָה עוֹד בַּאֲמִירַת ״כַּאֲשֶׁר אָבַדְתִּי״, לְקַבֵּל עָלֶיהָ עֹנֶשׁ הָאֲבַדּוֹן הַנִּגְזָר עַל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל
And she Esther added further, in saying “as I am lost,” to take upon herself the punishment of “loss” that was decreed upon all Israel.
וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל (בְּרֵישׁ פ״ב דִּנְגָעִים) ״כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲנִי כַּפָּרָתָן״, שֶׁרָצָה לְקַבֵּל עַל עַצְמוֹ הָעֹנֶשׁ דִּנְגָעִים בַּעֲבוּרָן, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּהָרַע״ב וְתוֹי״ט

in the way that R’ Yishmael said Negaim 2:1, “all Israel — I am their atonement,” wishing to take upon himself the punishment of nega’im on their behalf — see there in the Bartenura and Tosafos Yom Tov.

וּכְמוֹ מָשִׁיחַ שֶׁסּוֹבֵל עֲנִיּוּת יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְכֵן בִּיחֶזְקֵאל בִּשְׁעַת הַחֻרְבָּן, וְכֵן מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ ״לֵךְ רֵד״, דְּאָמְרוּ ז״ל שֶׁנִּתְנַזֵּף בְּבֵית דִּין שֶׁל מַעְלָה, הוּא לְכַפָּרַת יִשְׂרָאֵל וּלְקַבֵּל הָעֹנֶשׁ שֶׁעֲלֵיהֶם, כִּי רֹאשׁ הַדּוֹר הוּא הַדּוֹר

And like Mashiach, who “bears the poverty of Israel,” and likewise Yechezkel at the time of the Destruction, and likewise Moshe Rabbeinu, to whom God said “go down” (Shemos 32:7) — of which the Sages said that his being rebuked in the Heavenly court was “for the atonement of Israel and to receive the punishment that was upon them” — for “the head of the generation is the generation.”

וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרָה (אֶסְתֵּר) לְהַצִּיל בָּזֶה כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵעֹנֶשׁ הַגְּזֵרָה דִּלְאַבֵּד, כִּי כְּבָר נִתְקַיֵּים בָּהּ, דַּאֲבַדּוֹנָהּ מִגּוּף קָדוֹשׁ דְּמָרְדְּכַי — אַחַר שֶׁכְּבָר נֶאֶבְדָה מֵעַמָּהּ וּמוֹלַדְתָּהּ — נֶחְשָׁב אֲבַדּוֹן גָּמוּר לָהּ

And therefore (Esther) intended thereby to save all Israel from the punishment of the decree of “loss” — for it was already fulfilled in her: her “loss” from the holy body of Mordechai — after she had already been “lost” from her people and her birthplace — is reckoned a “complete loss” for her.

וְגַם דְּאִלּוּ לֹא נֶאֶסְרָה לְמָרְדְּכַי, אֶפְשָׁר הָיְתָה מוֹלִידָה מִמֶּנּוּ וְהָיָה הַוָּלָד טָהוֹר מֵאִמּוֹ וּמֵאָבִיו, וְאָז וַדַּאי ״זְרוֹק חוּטְרָא אַעִקָּרֵיהּ קָאֵי״, וְהָיָה נִשְׁאַר מִמֶּנָּה זֶרַע בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל

And moreover, had she not become forbidden to Mordechai, she might have borne from him, and the child would have been “pure from its mother and its father,” and then certainly “throw a stick and it lands on its root” i.e., it reverts to its origin, and seed of hers would have remained in Israel.

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אַחַר כָּךְ שֶׁהוֹלִידָה דָּרְיָוֶשׁ מֵאֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ, אַף שֶׁהָיָה טָהוֹר מֵאִמּוֹ וְהָיָה מֶלֶךְ כָּשֵׁר וּבָנָה בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הָיָה מִכְּלַל הַגּוֹיִם וְנִטְמַע בֵּינֵיהֶם, וְנִתְקַיֵּים הָאֲבַדּוֹן בְּזַרְעָהּ

Not so afterward, when she bore Daryavesh to Achashverosh — for although he was “pure from his mother,” and was a “fit king” who built the Beis HaMikdash, nonetheless he was of the category of the nations and was assimilated among them, and the “loss” was fulfilled in her offspring.
וְזֶהוּ אִבּוּדָהּ מֵעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״בְּכוּ לַהֹלֵךְ כִּי לֹא יָשׁוּב וְרָאָה״ וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁדְּרָשׁוּהוּ (בב״ב קטו.) עַל מִי שֶׁלֹּא הִנִּיחַ בֵּן

And this is her “loss” from this world, as it says, “weep for the one who goes, for he shall not return and see his birthplace” (Yirmeyah 22:10), which they expounded Bava Basra 116a of one who “left no son.”

וְעַל בִּיאַת גּוֹי מַגִּיעַ עֹנֶשׁ זֶה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין פב.) בְּבִיאַת אֲרַמִּית — אִם לֹא פָּגְעוּ קַנָּאִין — ״לֹא יִהְיֶה לוֹ עֵר וְעוֹנֶה״ וְכֵן ״מַגִּישׁ״ וְגוֹמֵר, כִּי זֶהוּ עִיקַּר חִלּוּל הַבְּרִית

And for the union with a gentile this punishment comes, as they said Sanhedrin 82a regarding one who “beds an Aramean woman” — if the zealous do not strike him — “may he have no ‘awakener er and answerer oneh’” and “‘one who brings near an offering’” (Malachi 2:12) — for this is the essence of the “profaning of the bris.”
וְנֶאֱמַר (תְּהִלִּים נה) ״אֲשֶׁר אֵין חֲלִיפוֹת לָמוֹ וְלֹא יָרְאוּ אֱלֹקִים״, וְדָרְשׁוּ (בב״ב שָׁם) ״אֵין חֲלִיפוֹת״ עַל בָּנִים הַמְמַלְּאִים מְקוֹמוֹ
And it says (Tehillim 55:20), “who have no ‘changes chalifos,’ and fear not God,” which they expounded Bava Basra 116a — “no changes” refers to sons who fill his place.

וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר ״וְלֹא יָרְאוּ אֱלֹקִים״, כִּי ״אִישׁ יָרֵא אֶת ה׳״ — ״גִּבּוֹר בָּאָרֶץ יִהְיֶה זַרְעוֹ״, וְנֶאֱמַר ״כָּל יְרֵא ה׳״ — ״אֶשְׁתְּךָ כְּגֶפֶן פֹּרִיָּה״ וְגוֹמֵר, ״כִּי כֵן יְבֹרַךְ גָּבֶר יְרֵא ה׳״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וּרְאֵה בָנִים לְבָנֶיךָ״

And this is why it says “and fear not God” — for of “a man who fears Hashem,” it is said, “his seed shall be mighty in the land” (Tehillim 112:2); and it says, “everyone who fears Hashem — your wife shall be as a fruitful vine in the recesses of your house, your children like olive shoots around your table; behold, for so shall the man who fears Hashem be blessed. May Hashem bless you from Zion, and may you see the good of Jerusalem; and see children to your children” (Tehillim 128).
כִּי הַיִּרְאָה הִיא הַגְּבוּרָה כַּיָּדוּעַ, וְכֵן הֵם בְּגִימַטְרִיָּא שָׁוֶה, כִּי הַיָּרֵא הוּא הַמִּתְגַּבֵּר עַל יִצְרוֹ, וְהַגִּבּוֹר מִתְיָרְאִין מִמֶּנּוּ
For “fear yirah is gevurah,” as is known, and they are equal in gematria — for the God-fearing one is “the one who overpowers his inclination,” and the mighty one is feared.

וְכֵן כָּל מִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם שֵׁם ה׳ נִקְרָא עָלָיו, וּמִתְקַיֵּים בּוֹ ״וְיִרְאוּ מִמְּךָ״ כַּיָּדוּעַ. וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יֵשׁ בּוֹ כֹּחַ גַּבְרָא לְהַזְרִיעַ זֶרַע לְמִינֵהוּ, דְּתָלוּי בִּגְבוּרָה

And likewise, whoever has fear of Heaven, “the Name of Hashem is called upon him,” and there is fulfilled in him “and they shall fear you” (Devarim 28:10). And through this he has the “power of a man” to sow “seed after its kind,” which depends on gevurah,
וְכמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "כְּחִצִּים בְּיַד גִּבּוֹר כֵּן בְּנֵי הַנְּעוּרִים" וְגוֹמֵר,
as it is stated, “Like arrows in the hand of a warrior, so are the sons of one’s youth,” and so on,
וְכמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּנִדָּה) "כָּל שֶׁאֵינוֹ יוֹרֶה כַּחֵץ" וְכוּלֵי,
and as they said (Niddah), “whoever does not shoot like an arrow,” etc.,
וּבְדִבְרֵי הַיָּמִים (א׳, ח׳, מ׳)
and in Chronicles (I, 8:40)
"וַיִּהְיוּ" וְגוֹמֵר "גִּבּוֹרֵי חַיִל דֹּרְכֵי קֶשֶׁת וּמַרְבִּים בָּנִים וּבְנֵי בָנִים",
“And they were mighty warriors, archers, with many sons and grandsons,”
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מִי שֶׁלֹּא יָרֵא אֱלֹקִים — ״אֵין חֲלִיפוֹת לָמוֹ״
Not so one who fears not God — “they have no ‘changes.’”
וּבַעֲמָלֵק דִּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ ״וְלֹא יָרֵא אֱלֹקִים״, וְנִצְטַוּוּ בִּמְחִיַּת כָּל זֵכֶר לוֹ, כִּי הוּא נִקְרָא ״רֵאשִׁית גּוֹיִם״, שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ (דְּ)גוֹיִם שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶם יִרְאַת אֱלֹקִים

And of Amalek it is written, “and he feared not God” (Devarim 25:18), and they were commanded to blot out every remembrance of him — for he is called “the first of the nations” (Bamidbar 24:20), the root of the nations who have no fear of God.

וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא הָעָרְלָה עַל שֵׁם אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּנְדָרִים לא:) מִקְּרָא דְּ״כָל הַגּוֹיִם עֲרֵלִים״, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּימּוֹל, וְהוּא חִלּוּל הַבְּרִית שֶׁהוּא לָהֶם מִצַּד שֶׁרָשַׁם, עַל יְדֵי הֶעְדֵּר יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם הַגּוֹרֵם שִׁיקּוּעַ בְּתַאֲוָה

And therefore the “orlah” is named for the nations, as they said Nedarim 31b from the verse “for all the nations are uncircumcised arelim” (Yirmeyah 9:25) — even one who is circumcised — and this is the “profaning of the bris” that is theirs by their root: through the absence of fear of Heaven, which causes immersion in desire.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ״רַק אֵין יִרְאַת אֱלֹקִים״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וַהֲרָגוּנִי עַל דְּבַר אִשְׁתִּי״
as Avraham said, “only there is no fear of God in this place, and they will slay me over my wife” (Bereishis 20:11).
דְּעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ (בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יז.) דְּפוֹשְׁעֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם בְּגוּפָן הוּא בַּעֲרָיוֹת, שֶׁהֵם מְשׁוּקָּעִים בָּזֶה
Therefore they said Rosh Hashanah 17a that “the sinners of the nations, in their body,” is in the domain of immorality, for they are “sunk” in it.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, דַּאֲפִילּוּ הָעֲרֵלִים נִקְרָאִים ״מוּלִים״, שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ הַחוֹטֵא אֵינוֹ מְשׁוּקָּע, כִּי שָׁרְשׁוֹ מֵרָזָא דְּ״אֵשֶׁת חַיִל״ — ״אִשָּׁה יִרְאַת ה׳״

Not so in Israel — for even the “arelim” among them are called “mulim circumcised,” for even the sinner is “not sunk,” since his root is from the secret of “a woman of valor” — “a woman who fears Hashem.”
לֹא נִקְרְאוּ פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן אֶלָּא ״קַרְקַפְתָּא דְּלָא מַנַּח תְּפִלִּין״, שֶׁהוּא הֶעְדֵּר שֹׁרֶשׁ הַיִּרְאַת שָׁמַיִם בִּקְרִיאַת שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם עָלָיו

“The sinners of Israel in their body” are called only “the skull that never donned tefillin” — which is merely the absence of the root of fear of Heaven in the “calling of the Name of Heaven upon him,”

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּמְגִלָּה) עַל פָּסוּק ״וְרָאוּ (כָּל עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ) כִּי שֵׁם ה׳ נִקְרָא עָלֶיךָ״ — ״אֵלּוּ תְּפִלִּין שֶׁבָּרֹאשׁ״, שֶׁזֶּהוּ הָאוֹת שֶׁמְּיוּחָד לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, לְקַבֵּל עֹל מַלְכוּתוֹ כְּעֶבֶד הַנּוֹשֵׂא עָלָיו חוֹתַם רַבּוֹ וְסִימָנוֹ

as they said Megillah 16b on the verse “and all the peoples of the earth shall see that the Name of Hashem is called upon you” (Devarim 28:10) — “these are the tefillin of the head” — which is “the sign dedicated to Hashem,” to accept the yoke of His kingship like a servant who bears upon himself his master’s seal and mark.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: (ד) וְכָךְ מִדָּתוֹ שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַמְתִּיק הַמַּר בְּמַר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל עַל פָּסוּק ״וַיַּשְׁלֵךְ (עֵץ)״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וַיִּמְתְּקוּ הַמַּיִם״, שֶׁהָיָה עֵץ הַרְדּוּפְנִי מַר, רַק שֶׁהָיָה בְּצִוּוּי וּבִרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּבָזֶה נִמְתַּק הַמְּרִירוּת הַזֶּה וְהַקּוֹדֵם

paragraphs.text: Shemos 15:25; Mekhilta deRabbi Yishmael, Vayassa 1:16–17; Shemos Rabbah 50:3. For the tree shown to Moshe at Marah, the Mekhilta records: Rabbi Yehoshua—willow; Rabbi Elazar HaModa’i—olive; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha—hardufani (oleander); others give different interpretations. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel contrasts healing bitter with sweet in human practice with Hashem’s healing bitter with bitter, giving the fig poultice of Yeshayahu and Elisha’s salt as analogies. Shemos Rabbah 50:3 independently preserves the varied tree identifications. The miracle did not demonstrate a general medicinal rule; it displayed the reversal effected by Divine instruction. Rav Tzadok applies the principle to the sweetening of Israel’s decree through Esther’s willingness to bear loss.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Negaim 2:1 records Rabbi Yishmael's phrase “בני ישראל אני כפרתן” within a dispute about judging tzaraas appearances against varying skin colors, where he calls Israel intermediate in complexion. Bartenura explains this loving expression as an offer to bear the punishment that might come upon Israel and atone for them; this is the interpretation Rav Tzadok invokes. Tosafos Yom Tov also cites the Maharam's alternative contextual explanation: Rabbi Yishmael used the affectionate protective phrase when he had to mention tzaraas concerning Jews, wishing no such harm upon them. The Mishnah itself does not explicitly describe transferring all the nation's guilt; that is the later interpretive application, and the Maharam's qualification should not be suppressed.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 32a; Arachin 17a; Yechezkel 4:4–6; Sanhedrin 98b; Rav Tzadok, Machshavos Charutz 17:5. In Berachos, Moshe's “go, descend” reflects his standing as Israel's leader and prompts his plea for them. Arachin records the two directions of the leader/generation comparison but does not equate a righteous leader's personal misdeeds with the generation's sins. Yechezkel is commanded symbolically to bear the house of Israel's iniquity, while the messianic suffering passage in Sanhedrin invokes Yeshayahu 53. Machshavos Charutz 17:5 describes Israel as one shared spiritual body, with leaders and other figures as its organs. Rav Tzadok's synthesis here is that the head may suffer on behalf of the whole; this does not mechanically assign another person's legal guilt to the leader.

paragraphs.text: Esther Rabbah 8:3; Rashi on Chaggai 1:1; Ezra 6:14–15; Pri Tzaddik, Purim §8. Esther Rabbah transmits Rabbi Yudan in the name of Rabbi Simon’s account that the later Daryavesh was Esther’s son, pure through his mother but belonging to the nations through his father. This is a Midrashic tradition, not a parentage claim explicit in Tanach. Rashi on Chaggai 1:1 invokes a Midrash that he was Esther’s son, and describes the rebuilding after Cyrus and Achashverosh; Ezra 6:14–15 explicitly describes completion of the Second Temple in Daryavesh’s reign. Pri Tzaddik, Purim §8 independently develops the hidden preparation for this rebuilding. Rav Tzadok’s conclusion concerning Esther’s lineage is his own spiritual reading.

paragraphs.text: Bava Basra 116a—not 115a—interprets Yirmeyahu 22:10 (“weep bitterly for him who goes”) as one who dies without leaving a son: Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav explicitly says “להולך בלא בן זכר”. Rav Tzadok applies this to Esther's “loss,” in the particular sense that her son Daryavesh did not continue a Jewish line through Mordechai. The Hebrew parenthetical of the manuscript reads “בב״ב קטו.”, but the quoted teaching appears at 116a; the English translation and this note identify the corrected location without altering the main Hebrew text. This is a bibliographic correction, not a change to Rav Tzadok's Hebrew.

This is a bibliographic correction, not a change to Rav Tzadok's Hebrew.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 82a interprets Malachi 2:11–12 in connection with “one who cohabits with a foreign woman”: the verse threatens removal of “ער ועונה ... ומגיש מנחה.” The Gemara parses the exclusions: for a Torah scholar, none awake among the Sages or answering among the students; for a priest, no son serving to bring an offering. The explicit denial of a son is in the priestly clause, not an unqualified Gemara statement that every offender is childless. Rav Tzadok connects this corruption of covenantal continuity with the subsequent “אין חליפות” verse about those lacking successors; these lines interpret and extend the cited punishment rather than silently equating the two texts.

paragraphs.text: Avos 4:1 defines a gibbor as one who conquers his inclination: “איזהו גבור הכובש את יצרו.” Rav Tzadok's own Pri Tzaddik, Masei §9, connects yiras shamayim, inner gevurah and aid in overcoming the inclination; Pri Tzaddik, Metzora §6, explains that “gevurah” lies in the heart and that yirah supports self-mastery. Mishlei 31:30 praises the “woman who fears Hashem”. The equality of the Hebrew gematrias yirah and gevurah and their extension to procreative strength are Rav Tzadok's present synthesis, not explicit statements in Avos. The note is located only after he connects the inward might of yirah with the capacity to transmit seed, rather than being held back until the later Israel-versus-nations contrast.

paragraphs.text: Nedarim 31b — The Mishnah states: “שאני נהנה למולים אסור בערלי ישראל ומותר במולי אומות העולם,” meaning that one who vows not to benefit from those designated “circumcised” is prohibited from benefiting even from physically uncircumcised Jews, but may benefit from circumcised gentiles. The distinction concerns the covenantal designation used in vows, not a change in anyone’s physical condition. Rav Tzadok cites it precisely at “הערלים נקראים מולים” and only then extends its significance to Israel’s enduring capacity for yiras shamayim.

paragraphs.text: Rav Tzadok’s parallel in Yisrael Kedoshim §10 states “הרי גם הערלים נקראים מולים” and distinguishes the visible condition from the inner covenantal root. Here he develops that teaching through “אשת חיל” and “אשה יראת ה׳” (Mishlei 31:30): the spiritual interpretation is his, not the literal legal rule of Nedarim. His Resisei Layla §44 and Pri Tzaddik, Shemos §1 offer related discussions of spiritual identity and moral correction; these are parallels, not excuses for transgression. The Har Bracha Dover Tzedek edition, printed pp. 103–105, similarly distinguishes inherited bris from tefillin acquired through one’s conscious conduct.

paragraphs.text: Rosh Hashanah 17a reads: “פושעי ישראל בגופן מאי ניהו אמר רב קרקפתא דלא מנח תפילין; פושעי אומות העולם בגופן אמר רב בעבירה.” Thus the Gemara explicitly identifies the Israelite example with failure to don tefillin and uses the more general term “בעבירה” for the other case. Rav Tzadok interprets that distinction through the brit and the religious meaning of head-tefillin. His explanation should not be presented as the Gemara’s verbatim characterization of the sexual behavior of whole populations. See his parallel in Dover Tzedek, Har Bracha, printed pp. 103–105.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: God’s way is to “sweeten the bitter with the bitter” — as at Marah, where a bitter branch was cast in to sweeten the bitter water. So Esther added “as I am lost,” taking the decree of “loss” hanging over all Israel upon herself. This is illustrated by R’ Yishmael (“I am Israel’s atonement”), Mashiach bearing Israel’s poverty, and Moshe rebuked “for Israel’s sake,” since the head of the generation is the generation.

p: (ה) וְזֶהוּ הַ״יְּקָר״ שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ שָׁם ״זֶה תְּפִלִּין״, שֶׁזָּכוּ עַל יְדֵי הַנֵּס דְּאֶסְתֵּר
And this is the “yekar precious honor” (Esther 8:16) that they expounded there means “this is tefillin” — which Israel merited through the miracle of Esther.
שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהִיא נִטְמְאָה עַל יְדֵי אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ, שֶׁזֶּה נִרְאֶה כְּ״אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים״ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם — וְהִיא הָיְתָה אָז בִּשְׁעַת נֵס זֶה כּוֹלֵל (כְּנֶסֶת) יִשְׂרָאֵל
For although she was defiled by Achashverosh — which appears, God forbid, like “an adulterous wife” — she was then, at the time of this miracle, the “inclusive gathering of Israel”;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (בִּמְגִלָּה) עַל פָּסוּק ״וַתִּלְבַּשׁ אֶסְתֵּר מַלְכוּת״ שֶׁלָּבְשָׁתָּהּ רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, הַיְינוּ מִדַּת מַלְכוּת הַיָּדוּעַ, שֶׁהִיא רָזָא דְּ״אֵשֶׁת חַיִל״

and as they said Megillah 15a on the verse “and Esther donned royalty malchus” (Esther 5:1), that “she donned ruach hakodesh” — namely, the known middah of Malchus, which is the secret of “a woman of valor.”

כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת גְּדוֹלָה עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ, וְאֵין זֶה מוֹרֶה חִילּוּל הַבְּרִית חַס וְשָׁלוֹם בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, אֶלָּא אַדְּרַבָּא עַל יְדֵי זֶה נִתְבָּרֵר דַּאֲפִילּוּ הַנִּרְאִים מְחַלְּלֵי הַבְּרִית בֶּאֱמֶת אֵינוֹ כֵּן

For in truth “great is a transgression for Heaven’s sake,” and this indicates no “profaning of the bris” in Israel, God forbid — rather, on the contrary, through it it is clarified that even those who appear to profane the bris are, in truth, not so.
וַאֲפִילּוּ בּוֹעֵל אֲרַמִּית, שֶׁזֶּהוּ תַּכְלִית הַחִילּוּל, שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּעֵירוּבִין יט.) דְּמִמַּשְׁכָא עׇרְלָתוֹ — הַיְינוּ רַק לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן, שֶׁאֵין נִיכָּר

And even one who “beds an Aramean woman,” which is the ultimate profanation, of whom they said Eruvin 19a that “his foreskin is drawn mimashcha” — that is only “to the outward eye,” that it is not discernible;

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּיבָמוֹת) שֶׁמָּשׁוּךְ צָרִיךְ לַחֲזוֹר וּלְמוּלוֹ רַק מִדְּרַבָּנָן מִטַּעַם מַרְאִית הָעַיִן, אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת גַּם זֶה מָהוּל, כִּי שֹׁרֶשׁ הַיִּרְאַת שָׁמַיִם קָבוּעַ בְּלִבָּם מִצַּד הִתְקַשְּׁרוּת שָׁרְשָׁם בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ

and as they said in Yevamos that one whose foreskin is drawn must be re-circumcised — but only rabbinically, for the sake of appearance — yet in truth he too is “circumcised,” for the root of the fear of Heaven is fixed in their heart by the binding of their root to Hashem.
וְזֶהוּ הַתְּפִלִּין שֶׁבָּרֹאשׁ,
And this is the tefillin of the head,
שֶׁהַתְחָלָתוֹ קָשׁוּר בַּשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
whose beginning is bound to the Blessed Name,
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה "וְיָרְאוּ מִמֶּךָ",
and through this “and they will fear you,”
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלְמַרְאִיּת הָעַיִן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין כֵּן, הוּא רַק לְמַרְאִיּת הָעַיִן.
and although in appearance in this world it is not so, that is only in appearance.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם מִצַּד הַמַּרְאִית הָעַיִן דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁצָּרִיךְ תִּיקּוּן לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן, הוּא צָרִיךְ עֹנֶשׁ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְכַפָּרָה
And nonetheless, from the side of “the outward appearance” of this world, which requires rectification “to the eye,” he requires punishment in this world for atonement.
וְהָאוּמּוֹת שֶׁהֵם בְּשָׁרְשָׁן כֵּן, לָכֵן יִהְיֶה הָעֹנֶשׁ כֵּן בְּשָׁרְשָׁן לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וְלִהֵט אוֹתָם״ וְגוֹמֵר ״אֲשֶׁר לֹא יַעֲזֹב לָהֶם שֹׁרֶשׁ וְעָנָף״

And the nations, whose root is evil so, therefore their punishment will be so, in their root, forever — as it says, “and it shall consume them, the coming day, that shall leave them neither root nor branch” (Malachi 3:19).

וּפְשָׁטֵיהּ בְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם קָאֵי; וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין (קי סע״ב) דְּדָרֵישׁ לֵיהּ אַרִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל — הַיְינוּ מִכָּל עוֹשֵׂי רִשְׁעָה, וְעַל זֶה פְּלִיג רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, אֲבָל בְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם מוֹדִים

And its plain sense refers to the nations; and in Sanhedrin 110b, where it is expounded of the wicked of Israel re their young children, that is of “any evildoer,” and on this R’ Akiva disputes — but regarding the nations, all agree,
כִּדְאִיתָא הָתָם מִ״וַתְּאַבֵּד כָּל זֵכֶר לָמוֹ״
as it is there, from “and You destroyed their every remembrance” (Yeshayah 26:14).

אֲבָל בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל בְּהֵפֶךְ: כָּל עֹנֶשׁ הוּא רַק לְמַרְאִית עַיִן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וַאֲפִילּוּ מִי שֶׁנִּגְזַר עָלָיו חַס וְשָׁלוֹם כִּילּוּי בָּנִים — הַיְינוּ רַק בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, אֲבָל נַפְשָׁם צְרוּרוֹת בַּה׳ וְקָמִים לִתְחִיַּית הַמֵּתִים וּלְעוֹלָם הַבָּא

But in Israel it is the reverse: every punishment is only “to the outward eye,” in this world; and even one upon whom, God forbid, “cutting off of children” was decreed — that is only in this world, but their souls are “bound in the bond of life” and rise for the resurrection of the dead and for Olam Haba.

וַאֲפִילּוּ מִי שֶׁלֹּא הוֹלִיד כְּלָל — הַיְינוּ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה; אֲבָל אָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר כְּתָב יָד (הֱבִיאוֹ הָרַב חִידָ״א בְּחַסְדֵּי אָבוֹת פ״ו מ״א) עַל פָּסוּק ״מִי יָלַד לִי אֶת אֵלֶּה״, שֶׁאֵין שׁוּם טִיפָּה שֶׁאֵינָהּ בְּאִיסּוּר הוֹלֵךְ לְאִיבּוּד, וּגְנוּזוֹת בְּהֵיכְלָא חַד, וְלֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא יִהְיֶה לוֹ בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת רַבִּים, וְיַכִּיר כָּל אֶחָד אָבִיו — עַיֵּין שָׁם

And even one who did not beget at all — that is only in this world; but they said in the Zohar (in manuscript, cited by the Rav Chida in Chasdei Avos 6:1) on the verse “who bore me these?” (Yeshayah 49:21), that “no drop of seed that is not emitted in prohibition goes to loss,” and they are “stored in one chamber,” and in the Future he will have “many sons and daughters, and each will recognize his father” — see there.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 15a says of “ותלבש אסתר מלכות” (Esther 5:1): “מלמד שלבשתה רוח הקודש” — Esther was clothed in Divine inspiration. Separately, Nazir 23b initially states “גדולה עבירה לשמה ממצוה שלא לשמה,” but the sugya challenges that ranking and concludes “אלא אימא כמצוה שלא לשמה,” comparing it to a mitzvah not performed for its own sake, and adduces Yael. Rav Tzadok’s identification of Esther with Malchus and his application of aveirah lishmah to her ordeal are his theological development, not a new blanket halachic permission in either Gemara. The context involves coercion, extraordinary circumstances, and the grave limits discussed earlier in this siman.

His separate teaching about the hidden root of Israel is also developed in Yisrael Kedoshim §10.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86a describes graded paths to full atonement: even after genuine repentance, some acts require Yom Kippur and suffering for the completion of kapparah. Rav Tzadok in Tzidkas HaTzadik §40 describes a higher illumination in which deliberately committed sins may be reconsidered as merits through repentance and Divine knowledge. In this siman he nonetheless maintains that the visible deed and its consequences in this world can demand purification and punishment. The distinction between an inner transformed spiritual root and the outer correction required in worldly life is Rav Tzadok's synthesis, not a conclusion stated by Yoma itself. Nothing here licenses wrongdoing or makes every painful event evidence of a particular sin.

Rabban Gamliel interprets “לא יעזב להם שרש וענף” as denial of a future share, whereas Rabbi Akiva disagrees and argues that they have a share. The sugya subsequently states a harsher view about young children of wicked non-Israelites, invoking “ותאבד כל זכר למו” (Yeshayahu 26:14). Rav Tzadok uses this contested aggadic discussion at the point where he has finished presenting its terms; his further theology of the continued inward root of Israel is developed in the following paragraph. Neither the individual disputants’ statements nor Rav Tzadok’s extension should be erased by a universalized paraphrase.

paragraphs.text: I Shmuel 25:29 speaks of David's soul being “bound in the bond of life with Hashem.” Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1 begins with the principle “all Israel have a share in the World to Come,” but immediately names defined exceptions; it is not a denial of judgment. Sanhedrin 44a says “Israel, though he has sinned, remains Israel,” establishing persistent covenantal identity despite an act. Rav Tzadok's parallel discussions in Machshavos Charutz §14 and Resisei Layla §52 use these foundations to distinguish the outward manifestation of loss and punishment from the enduring inner Israelite root. Here his conclusion extends that interpretation to the lost manifestation of offspring or life in this world. The original verses and sugyos do not themselves say that worldly penalties are illusory or unnecessary.

paragraphs.text: Rav Tzadok here cites a Zohar manuscript reported by the Chida in Chasdei Avos, sixth chapter, first mishnah, interpreting “מי ילד לי את אלה” (Yeshayahu 49:21). In his account, no seed from a non-prohibited union is truly lost: it is kept in a heavenly chamber, and will have its future offspring, each able to recognize its father. This is explicitly qualified by Rav Tzadok's Hebrew wording “שאינה באיסור”: it concerns seed not produced in a forbidden act, and cannot be used to excuse or spiritualize a prohibition. A direct corroborating witness to Rav Tzadok's citation appears in Resisei Layla §58:5, where he says that a manuscript Zohar quoted in Chasdei Avos teaches that no Israelite seed is ultimately wasted and all such seed will become holy souls in the future. The original Chida printing and manuscript-Zohar passage have not been separately collated in this audit; the detailed wording is quoted by Rav Tzadok here and remains an inherited source claim pending printed-witness verification.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: This is the “precious honor yekar” (expounded as tefillin) that Israel merited through Esther’s miracle. Though “defiled” by Achashverosh — seemingly an “adulterous wife,” God forbid — she was then the inclusive gathering of Israel, who “donned ruach hakodesh,” the middah of Malchus, the secret of “a woman of valor.” For “great is an aveirah lishmah,” and it signals no true profaning of the bris — on the contrary, it clarifies that even those who appear to profane it are, in root, “circumcised.”

p: (ו) וּבְוַדַּאי גַּם בְּאִשָּׁה בַּעֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ כְּיָעֵל וְאֶסְתֵּר כֵּן, וְכַיָּדוּעַ מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בְּיָעֵל דְּאָז קָלְטָה נֶפֶשׁ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא מִמֶּנּוּ, וְהָיְתָה אָז תְּחִלַּת יְצִיאָתוֹ מֵהַקְּלִיפָּה, וּמִסְּתָמָא גַּם בְּאֶסְתֵּר כֵּן

And certainly in a woman too, with a “transgression for Heaven’s sake” like Yael and Esther, it is so; and it is known what they said of Yael, that she then received from him, Sisera, the soul of R’ Akiva, and it was then the beginning of its emergence from the kelipah — and presumably so with Esther too.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהֵם לֹא עָשׂוּ אֶלָּא לִפְנִים, כָּךְ הָיָה הָעֹנֶשׁ רַק לְפָנִים וּלְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְבַד
And just as they acted only “outwardly,” so the punishment was only outward and “to the eye,” in this world alone.

וְגַם בְּפֹעַל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, הֲרֵי אָמְרוּ עַל פָּסוּק ״וְאֵלֶּה בְּנֵי בִּתְיָה״ דְּכָל הַמְגַדֵּל בֶּן חֲבֵירוֹ (מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב כְּאִלּוּ יְלָדוֹ, סַנְהֶדְרִין יט:), וְכֵן מִקְּרָא דְּ״אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדוֹת מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן״ עַל הַמְלַמֵּד בֶּן חֲבֵירוֹ תּוֹרָה

And even in actuality in this world: they said on the verse “and these are the sons of Bisya” (I Divrei HaYamim 4:18) that “whoever raises the child of his fellow, Scripture reckons it as if he bore him” (Sanhedrin 19b), and likewise from the verse “these are the offspring of Moshe and Aharon” (Bamidbar 3:1) — said of one who teaches his fellow’s son Torah.
וְאָמְרוּ גַּם בְּנֶפֶשׁ יְחִידָה, דְּכָל הַמְקַיֵּים נֶפֶשׁ אַחַת כִּמְקַיֵּים עוֹלָם מָלֵא, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן הַמְקַיֵּים עוֹלָם מָלֵא וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל
And they said even of a single soul, that “whoever sustains one soul is as one who sustains a whole world” (Sanhedrin 37a) — all the more one who sustained a “whole world” and all Israel;
וְ״לַיְּהוּדִים הָיְתָה אוֹרָה״ — זוֹ תּוֹרָה, דַּהֲדַר קִבְּלוּהָ אָז מֵאַהֲבָה, וְהַכֹּל הָיָה עַל יָדָהּ, דַּהֲרֵי הוּא כְּהוֹלִידָהּ עוֹלָם מָלֵא וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל
and “the Jews had light orah” — “this is Torah” (Megillah 16b), which they then “re-accepted from love,” and all was through her — for it is as if she “bore” a whole world and all Israel,
דְּאַחַר שֶׁנִּגְזַר עֲלֵיהֶם לְהַשְׁמִיד וְנִיצּוֹלוּ, הֲרֵי הֵם כִּבְרִיָּה חֲדָשָׁה, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל (ויק״ר ל, ג) עַל פָּסוּק ״וְעַם נִבְרָא״ וְגוֹמֵר

for after it was decreed upon them to be destroyed and they were saved, they are “like a new creation,” in the manner the Sages said (Vayikra Rabbah 30:3) on the verse “and a people yet to be created shall praise God” (Tehillim 102:19).

וְגַם זָכְתָה לְ״יָד וְשֵׁם טוֹב מִבָּנִים וּבָנוֹת״, שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין צג:) ״זֶה סֵפֶר דָּנִיֵּאל שֶׁנִּקְרָא עַל שְׁמוֹ״, וְכֵן הוּא מְגִילַּת אֶסְתֵּר נִקְרֵאת עַל שְׁמָהּ, וְזֶה נִקְרָא ״טוֹב מִבָּנִים וּבָנוֹת״

And she also merited “a memorial yad va-shem better than sons and daughters” (Yeshayah 56:5) — for they said Sanhedrin 93b “this is the book of Daniel, called by his name” — and likewise Megillas Esther is called by her name, and this is “better than sons and daughters.”

וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁקִּיבְּלָה עֹנֶשׁ עַל עַצְמָהּ בְּעַד הָעֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ, וְכֵן עַל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל — אַחַר שֶׁשָּׁבוּ דְּנַעֲשָׂה כִּזְכוּיוֹת מֵעֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ — זָכְתָה עַל יְדֵי זֶה לְשָׂכָר הַטּוֹב מֵהָעֹנֶשׁ, וְכָל הָעֹנֶשׁ הוּא רַק בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְהַשָּׂכָר לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד

And even though she received punishment upon herself for the “transgression for its own sake,” and likewise for all Israel — after they repented, so that it became “like merits” from a “transgression for Heaven’s sake” — she merited through this the good reward that emerged out of the punishment; and all the punishment is only in this world, while the reward is forever.

paragraphs.text: Gittin 57b says only that descendants of Sisera taught children in Jerusalem: “מִבְּנֵי בָנָיו שֶׁל סִיסְרָא לָמְדוּ תִּינוֹקוֹת בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם”; it does not name Rabbi Akiva. The identification of Rabbi Akiva's soul-spark entering the holy side through Yael and Sisera belongs to a separate kabbalistic tradition. It is explicitly described by Rema MiPano in Asarah Maamarot, Maamar Chikur Din, part V, chapter 11 (directly checked against the supplied printed scan, pp. 382–383), and in Megalleh Amukkot, Va'etchanan §88. The Chida, Petach Einayim on Gittin 57b, records Maharam Schiff's objection to identifying the unnamed descendants with Rabbi Akiva and defends the received tradition, citing Sha'ar HaGilgulim literature. These works do not turn the identification into an explicit statement of the Gemara, nor do the witnesses need to have identical accounts of the soul's transmission. Rav Tzadok invokes the kabbalistic parallel to illustrate his opening statement concerning Yael; his tentative extension to Esther is his own inference.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 19b. לְלַמֶּדְךָ שֶׁכׇּל הַמְגַדֵּל יָתוֹם בְּתוֹךְ בֵּיתוֹ מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב כְּאִילּוּ יְלָדוֹ. … וְכִי בִּתְיָה יָלְדָה? וַהֲלֹא יוֹכֶבֶד יָלְדָה! אֶלָּא יוֹכֶבֶד יָלְדָה וּבִתְיָה גִּידְּלָה, לְפִיכָךְ נִקְרָא עַל שְׁמָהּ. … אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן: כׇּל הַמְלַמֵּד בֶּן חֲבֵירוֹ תּוֹרָה, מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב כְּאִילּוּ יְלָדוֹ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וְאֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת אַהֲרֹן וּמֹשֶׁה״, וּכְתִיב: ״וְאֵלֶּה שְׁמוֹת בְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן״. לוֹמַר לָךְ: אַהֲרֹן יָלַד וּמֹשֶׁה לִימֵּד, לְפִיכָךְ נִקְרְאוּ עַל שְׁמוֹ. “This teaches that whoever raises an orphan within his home, Scripture credits him as though he gave birth to him.” Rabbi Yochanan brings Bityah as another proof: “Did Bityah give birth? Surely Yocheved gave birth! Rather, Yocheved gave birth and Bityah raised him; therefore he was called by her name.” Separately, “Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in Rabbi Yonatan’s name: Whoever teaches his fellow’s son Torah, Scripture credits him as though he gave birth to him, as it is said, ‘These are the offspring of Aharon and Moshe,’ and ‘These are the names of Aharon’s sons.’ That is: Aharon gave birth and Moshe taught; therefore they were called by his name.” The Bityah verse is I Divrei HaYamim 4:18; the teaching verse is Bamidbar 3:1.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 37a (Mishnah): “Whoever destroys a single soul of Israel, Scripture reckons it as though he destroyed a whole world; and whoever sustains a single soul of Israel, Scripture reckons it as though he sustained a whole world.” R’ Tzadok applies the latter to Esther — who “sustained” all Israel, and so is as one who “bore a whole world.”

paragraphs.text: Megillah 16b on Esther 8:16: Rav Yehudah explains “לַיְּהוּדִים הָיְתָה אוֹרָה” — “אוֹרָה זוֹ תּוֹרָה”: “light” means Torah, based on Mishlei 6:23, “for the mitzvah is a lamp and Torah is light.” This source explains Rav Tzadok's phrase “אורה—זו תורה.” The later statement here about reacceptance from love has its own source, Shabbos 88a, and the “new creation” comes from Vayikra Rabbah 30:3; those are not asserted by this particular Megillah line.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 88a records Rava's teaching that Israel “again accepted” the Torah in the days of Achashverosh (הֲדוּר קַבְּלוּהָ), “they fulfilled what they had already accepted.” Rashi explains: “מֵאַהֲבַת הַנֵּס שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה לָהֶם” — from love of the miracle performed for them. Rav Tzadok here applies this renewed acceptance to Esther's salvation of Israel. In Resisei Layla §43:2 and Pri Tzaddik, Purim §2, he develops a related but further teaching about the emergence of Torah Shebe'al Peh; that is a cross-reference, not something explicitly stated in this Gemara or yet developed in this passage.
