paragraphs.text: Machshavos Charutz §20 develops a close Rav Tzadok parallel in which Esther’s work within the palace of Achashverosh participates in the rectification of earlier spiritual entanglements, alongside the national renewal of Torah at Purim. Here its correct anchor is after Rav Tzadok has concluded “דהרי הוא כהולידה עולם מלא וכל ישראל,” not prematurely beside the subsequent Midrashic quotation about “ועם נברא.” This is a parallel to Rav Tzadok’s theological interpretation of Esther’s service, not an independent halachic authorization for forbidden conduct.

paragraphs.text: Tehillim 102:19; Vayikra Rabbah 30:3 — Mordechai’s generation as a “new creation”: The Midrash first derives from “a people yet to be created shall praise Hashem” that penitents are created anew, and then applies the same verse specifically to the generation of Mordechai, who had stood on the verge of death and were recreated after their deliverance. Rav Tzadok’s language here is therefore nearly literal Midrash: the rescued nation was not merely spared but received the standing of a newly created people. His further conclusion—that Esther is consequently as one who bore all Israel—joins this Midrash to the preceding rabbinic principles concerning raising, teaching, and sustaining another.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 93b. בִּשְׁלָמָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר סָרִיסִים מַמָּשׁ, הַיְינוּ דִּכְתִיב ״בְּבֵיתִי וּבְחוֹמֹתַי יָד וָשֵׁם טוֹב מִבָּנִים וּמִבָּנוֹת״. אֶלָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר שֶׁנִּסְתָּרְסָה עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה בִּימֵיהֶם, מַאי ״טוֹב מִבָּנִים וּמִבָּנוֹת״? אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: מִבָּנִים שֶׁהָיוּ לָהֶם כְּבָר וּמֵתוּ. מַאי ״שֵׁם עוֹלָם אֶתֶּן לוֹ אֲשֶׁר לֹא יִכָּרֵת״? אָמַר רַבִּי תַּנְחוּם: דָּרַשׁ בַּר קַפָּרָא בְּצִפּוֹרִי, זֶה סֵפֶר דָּנִיֵּאל שֶׁנִּקְרָא עַל שְׁמוֹ. “According to the one who says they were actual eunuchs, this explains ‘in My house and within My walls a memorial and a name, better than sons and daughters.’ But according to the one who says that idolatry was made barren in their days, what does ‘better than sons and daughters’ mean? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: Better than the sons they already had, who died. What does ‘an everlasting name I will give him, which will not be cut off’ mean? Rabbi Tanchum said: Bar Kappara expounded in Tzippori: This is the book of Daniel, which is called by his name.” Rav Tzadok applies the named-scriptural-memorial principle to Esther’s Megillah.

paragraphs.text: Yeshayah 56:5; Megillah 7a; Resisei Layla §52 — Esther’s memorial “better than sons and daughters”: Yeshayah promises the faithful “a hand and a name better than sons and daughters.” Sanhedrin applies the phrase to Daniel’s book, as noted in the preceding footnote. Megillah records Esther’s requests, “Establish me for generations” and “Write me for generations,” and the Sages’ eventual inclusion of the Megillah within the scriptural memorial of Amalek. Resisei Layla reads this enduring institution as Esther’s service to the Shechinah and as an “eternal sign” of Israel’s hidden bond with Hashem. Rav Tzadok accordingly treats the Megillah bearing her name as a lasting spiritual progeny that exceeds ordinary biological continuity.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 12a; Eichah 3:33; Resisei Layla §52 — “outwardly” answered “outwardly”: When asked why Israel was saved after bowing to Nevuchadnetzar’s image, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai answers: “They acted only outwardly; likewise the Holy One acted with them only outwardly,” citing “He does not afflict from His heart.” The Gemara refers to the threatened annihilation in the Purim story. Rav Tzadok extends the same pattern to the temporal punishment associated with Yael and Esther: an act whose deepest intent was not separation from Hashem produces a punishment that remains on the plane of this-worldly appearance. That extension is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis; the Bavli itself does not formulate a general rule that every such punishment is confined to this world.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Certainly the principle of aveirah lishmah applies to women as well, as shown by Yael and Esther. The Sages say that R’ Akiva’s soul was drawn out from the kelipah through Yael, and R’ Tzadok suggests a similar process in Esther’s case. Because these women acted improperly only on the outward level, their punishment in this world was likewise only outward.

p: (ז) וְגַם מִצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ הוּא כֵּן, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב קַדְמוֹן אֶחָד בִּתְשׁוּבוֹת מהר״ח אוֹר זָרוּעַ הַנִּדְפָּס מֵחָדָשׁ (סוֹף סִימָן קס״ג), דְּכָל שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ חַד הוּא וְכוּלָּם ״עֲבֵירָה״, אַךְ אוֹתָהּ עֲבֵירָה הוּתְּרָה שֶׁסּוֹפָהּ לָבוֹא לִידֵי מִצְוָה כו׳

And a mitzvah not for its own sake is also so; as one early authority wrote in the Responsa of Maharach Or Zarua (newly printed, end of §163), that “everything ‘not for its own sake’ is one category, and they are all in a sense ‘a transgression’ — but that transgression was permitted whose end is to come to a mitzvah,” etc.
וְכֵן מַשְׁמַע (בְּנָזִיר) שֶׁמְּדַמֶּה אוֹתָהּ לְמַעֲשֵׂה דְּיָעֵל כו׳ עַיֵּין שָׁם
And so it is implied in Nazir 23b that the Gemara compares a mitzvah not performed for its own sake with the deed of Yael, etc. — see there.
וּדְבַר ה׳ בְּפִיו אֱמֶת,
And the word of Hashem in his mouth is truth,
כִּי וַדַּאי אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָמְרוּ (פְּסָחִים נ׃) "לְעוֹלָם יַעֲסֹק שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ",
for certainly, although they said (Pesachim 50b), “One should always engage in Torah even not for its own sake,”
לָאו הֶתֵּר גָּמוּר הוּא,
it is not a complete permission,
וְעוֹבֵר עַל לָאו מִדִּבְרֵי סוֹפְרִים "אַל תַּעֲשֵׂם עֲטָרָה לְהִתְגַּדֵּל" אוֹ "אַל תִּהְיוּ כַּעֲבָדִים הַמְשַׁמְּשִׁים עַל מְנָת לְקַבֵּל פְּרָס".
and one transgresses a rabbinic prohibition: “Do not make them a crown with which to aggrandize yourself,” or “Do not be like servants who serve in order to receive a reward” (Avot).
וּבַזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ צָוַח הַרְבֵּה עַל אוֹתָם דְּעָבְדִין לְגַרְמַיְיהוּ,
And the holy Zohar cries out much against those who act for themselves,
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין עוֹנְשִׁין עַל זֶה בְּפֹעַל,
and although one is not punished for this in actuality,
דְּהֲרֵי אֲפִילוּ מַחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה דַּעֲבֵרָה אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְצָרְפָהּ לְמַעֲשֶׂה (בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל),
for even an evil thought of transgression the Holy One, blessed be He, does not join to a deed (among Israel),
מִכָּל מָקוֹם נֶחְשָׁב לְחֵטְא לְגַבֵּי מַעֲלַת קְדֻשַּׁת הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל עַם קָדוֹשׁ לַה׳,
it is nevertheless considered a sin relative to the elevated holiness of the souls of Israel, a people holy to Hashem,
אֶלָּא שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי כֵן "לְעוֹלָם יַעֲסֹק (אָדָם בַּתּוֹרָה וּבְמִצְוֹת אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ) שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ (שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ בָּא לִשְׁמָהּ)".
except that nevertheless “one should always engage (in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake), for from (not for its own sake one comes to its own sake).”
וּמִמַּה שֶּׁאָמַר הַטַּעַם רַק "שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ" וְכוּלֵי,
And from the fact that they stated the reason only as “for from…,” etc.,
מְבוֹאָר גַּם כֵּן דִּבְעַצְמוּתוֹ, לוּלֵי הָא דְּ״מִתּוֹךְ״ וְכוּלֵי,
it is also clear that in itself, were it not for this principle of “from…,” etc.,
לֹא הָיָה רָאוּי לַעֲסֹק שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ.
it would not be proper to engage not for its own sake.
אֶלָּא שֶׁכְּבָר הֵעִידוּ לָנוּ חֲכָמִים שֶׁ"מִתּוֹךְ" וְכוּלֵי,
But the Sages have already testified for us that “from…,” etc.,
כִּי מַעֲשֵׂה הַמִּצְוָה בְּעַצְמָהּ בְּלֹא כַוָּנָה לִשְׁמָהּ גַּם הִיא נוֹתֶנֶת קְדֻשָּׁה בְּלֵב הָאָדָם,
for the act of the mitzvah itself, without intention for its own sake, also imparts holiness into a person’s heart,
עַד שֶׁעָתִיד לִפָּתֵחַ עַל יְדֵי זֶה שַׁעֲרֵי קְדֻשָּׁה בִּלְבָבוֹ כְּפִתְחוֹ שֶׁל אוּלָם
until through this the gates of holiness are destined to open in his heart as wide as the entrance of the Temple Hall,
וְלִכָּנֵס לְלִשְׁמָהּ הַגָּמוּר,
and he enters into complete “for its own sake,”
וְדִבְרֵי חֲכָמִים נֶאֱמָנִים וְקַיָּמִים לָעַד.
and the words of the Sages are faithful and enduring forever.
וַאֲפִילוּ אִם אֵין רוֹאִים בְּפֹעַל כֵּן,
And even if one does not see this in actuality,
אִם לֹא זָכָה לָזֶה בַּגִּלְגּוּל הַזֶּה מִפְּנֵי אֵיזֶה חֵטְא הַגּוֹרֵם,
if he did not merit this in this incarnation because of some causative sin,
יִזְכֶּה בְּגִלְגּוּל אַחֵר.
he will merit it in another incarnation.
אוֹ גַּם בְּגִלְגּוּל זֶה אִם לֹא זָכָה בִּקְבִיעוּת,
Or even in this incarnation, if he did not merit it permanently,
זוֹכֶה לָזֶה בְּאַקְרַאי וּבְשָׁעָה וְרֶגַע אַחַת
he merits it incidentally, in a single hour and moment
שֶׁיִּמָּצֵא יַחַל לִבָּבוֹ מוּכָן לְאַהֲבָה וּלְיִרְאָה אֶת שְׁמוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ וּלְעָבְדוֹ בֶּאֱמֶת.
when his heart happens to be ready to love and revere His blessed Name and to serve Him in truth.
וּמִמֵּילָא גַּם כָּל הָעֵסֶק שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ,
And automatically, all the engagement not for its own sake,
כֵּיוָן שֶׁהוּא גָּרַם לְהָבִיאוֹ לִידֵי הָרֶגַע דְּלִשְׁמָהּ,
since it caused him to arrive at the moment of “for its own sake,”
הֲוֵי כֻּלּוֹ נַעֲשָׂה כְּהַכָּנָה לְכָךְ וּמַכְשִׁירֵי מִצְוָה שֶׁנֶּחְשָׁב כְּגוּף הַמִּצְוָה,
is entirely made into a preparation for that, like preparatory acts of a mitzvah, which are considered part of the mitzvah itself,
וְלֹא גָּרַע מֵעֲבֵרָה לִשְׁמָהּ
and it is no lesser than a transgression for Heaven’s sake,
וְכְדִקְדּוּק דִּמְיוֹן רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה לְהַדְדֵי.
in accord with the precise comparison of our Sages of blessed memory of the two to each other.
וּלְמַאן דְּאָמַר שָׁם "עֲדִיפָא" מִמִּצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ,
And according to the one who says there that it is “greater” than a mitzvah not for its own sake,
לְמַאי דְּלֹא יָדַע הָא דְּ"מִתּוֹךְ" וְכוּלֵי,
that is, according to the one who is not aware of the principle of “from…,” etc.,
דְּמִתּוֹךְ עֲבֵרָה לִשְׁמָהּ בָּא דָּבָר גָּדוֹל כְּהַצָּלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּימֵי יָעֵל וְאֶסְתֵּר וְכַדּוֹמֶה,
it is because from a transgression for Heaven’s sake comes something great, like the rescue of Israel in the days of Yael and Esther and the like,
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה הֻתְּרָה הָעֲבֵרָה וְנִקְרָא לִשְׁמָהּ.
whereby, in that exceptional case, the act was deemed permitted and was called “for Heaven’s sake.”
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר דְּגַם בְּמִצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ כֵּן, דְּמִתּוֹךְ וְכוּלֵי,
And therefore he said that with a mitzvah not for its own sake it is also so, since “from…,” etc.,
וְלָכֵן הֵם שָׁוִים.
and therefore they are equal.
וְגַם כָּל עֲבֵרָה כְּשֶׁשָּׁב כֵּן,
And every transgression, when one repents, is likewise so,
כֵּיוָן דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּא לְמַדְרֵגָה הַגְּדוֹלָה דִּתְשׁוּבָה,
since through this he came to the great level of repentance,
וְהַחֵטְא הוּא שֶׁגָּרַם לְהָבִיאוֹ לְכָךְ וְהוּא הַכָּנָה לוֹ,
and the sin is what caused him to arrive at it and is a preparation for it,
שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ זֶה בָּא לְמָקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין,
for through this he came to the place where penitents stand,
הֲרֵי אוֹתוֹ הַחֵטְא כִּזְכֻיּוֹת וּמִצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ.
that sin is thus like merits, and like a mitzvah not for its own sake.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Yitzchak ben Rabbi Eliyahu, reply preserved in Maharach Or Zarua Responsa §163:4 (Leipzig 1860 edition). The reply opens: 'ושלא לשמה הואיל ואתא לידן נימא ביה מילתא כי ר״ת אומר שני עניני שלא לשמה יש, חד אסיר וחד שרי, ואני הדיוט ופעוט אומר דכל שלא לשמה חד הוא וכולם עבירה אז אותה עבירה הותרה שסופה לבא לידי מצוה'. Translation: 'Now that service not for its own sake has arisen, let us discuss it. Rabbeinu Tam distinguishes a forbidden kind and a permitted kind; in my humble opinion, all such service is one category, all involving a transgression, and that transgression is tolerated because it ultimately leads to a mitzvah.' The responsum explicitly identifies its speaker as Rabbi Yitzchak son of Rabbi Eliyahu; it is preserved in Maharach Or Zarua's collection, not stated in the compiler's own name. Rav Tzadok uses this striking opinion to distinguish an existing deficient motive that can lead to proper service from choosing a Torah prohibition. Compare Nazir 23b, which concludes that aveirah lishmah is like mitzvah shelo lishmah, not categorically superior.

Berachos 17a warns that one acting שלא לשמה would have been better off not created. Tosafos explains that learning to provoke others differs from imperfect pursuit of honor. paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 10:5 — a beginning that must lead beyond itself: “כָּל הָעוֹסֵק בַּתּוֹרָה כְּדֵי לְקַבֵּל שָׂכָר ... הֲרֵי זֶה עוֹסֵק שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ” — one who studies for reward serves with an imperfect motive. Yet the Rambam directs teachers to introduce beginners to service through fear or reward, and gradually lead them to service from love. Rav Tzadok develops the distinct point that the mitzvah-act can itself impart sanctity and ultimately bring the heart to true lishmah. The Rambam's pedagogic allowance is not a declaration that the ulterior motive is ideal.

paragraphs.text: In Pri Tzaddik, Shoftim §1, Rav Tzadok cites Rabbeinu Chaim Or Zarua as distinguishing the fault in a שלא לשמה motive, for which there may be punishment, from the mitzvah-content of Torah study, which earns reward because it leads toward lishmah. His analogy is fasting a dream-fast on Shabbos: its good aspect can still be efficacious while the improper aspect needs atonement. That parallel illuminates Rav Tzadok's completed explanation here: prior imperfect study can subsequently be counted as preparation for the sincere mitzvah, yet the original defective intention was not itself the ideal.

paragraphs.text: Nazir 23b — Yael and the Gemara’s final formulation: The Gemara first states that an aveirah lishmah is greater than a mitzvah shelo lishmah, but challenges this from the rule that shelo lishmah leads to lishmah and revises the conclusion: an aveirah lishmah is “like” a mitzvah shelo lishmah. Yael is then compared to Sarah, Rivkah, Rachel, and Leah, the “women in the tent.” The comparison explains the spiritual valuation of Yael’s exceptional act after the fact; it is not a general authorization to choose a prohibition in the hope of producing a mitzvah.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: A mitzvah not for its own sake works the same way: an early authority (Responsa of Maharach Or Zarua) holds that all “not for its own sake” is one category and is, in a sense, “a transgression.” But that transgression was permitted whose end is to come to a mitzvah. And Nazir likens it to the deed of Yael.

p: (ח) וְהַחִילּוּק בֵּינֵיהֶם רַק לְעִנְיַן לְכַתְּחִלָּה, דְּבָזֶה אָמְרוּ ״לְעוֹלָם יַעֲסֹק (אָדָם בַּתּוֹרָה וּמִצְוֹת אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ)״ כו׳, שֶׁהַמִּצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ יֵשׁ בָּהּ מַעֲשֵׂה מִצְוָה גְּלוּיָה הַמַּכְנֶסֶת קְדֻשָּׁה בַּלֵּב, שֶׁבְּהֶכְרֵחַ וּבְבֵירוּר בָּא מִכֹּחָהּ וְעַל יָדָהּ לִשְׁמָהּ

And the distinction between them is only regarding l’chatchilah — for concerning a mitzvah not-lishmah they said, “let a person always occupy himself with Torah and mitzvos, even not for their own sake,” for a mitzvah not-lishmah has in it a revealed act of mitzvah that “brings holiness into the heart,” so that necessarily and certainly, by its power and through it, one comes to lishmah.

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הָעֲבֵירָה, אַדְּרַבָּא גּוֹרֶרֶת עֲבֵירָה הַמַּכְנֶסֶת טוּמְאָה בַּלֵּב וְהֵיפֶךְ הַקְּדֻשָּׁה, וְהָאוֹמֵר ״אֶחֱטָא וְאָשׁוּב״ אֵין מַסְפִּיקִין (בְּיָדוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה, יוֹמָא פה:)

Not so a transgression — on the contrary, it “drags along another transgression,” bringing impurity into the heart, the opposite of holiness; and “one who says ‘I will sin and repent’ is not given the opportunity (to do teshuvah)” (Yoma 85b).
וְלֹא דִּיבְּרוּ חֲכָמִים בְּשׁוֹפְטָנֵי — שׁוֹטִים וּרְשָׁעִים הַחוֹטְאִים לְמַלֹּאות תַּאֲוַת יִצְרָם וִידַמּוּ שֶׁיָּשׁוּבוּ אַחַר שֶׁיִּמְלְאוּ תַּאֲוָתָם — דְּזֶה שְׁטוּת גָּדוֹל

And the Sages did not speak of “fools” — the foolish and wicked who sin to fill the desire of their inclination and imagine that they will repent after they sate their desire — for that is great folly:
כִּי אִם בִּתְחִלַּת כְּנִיסַת הַיֵּצֶר לְלִבּוֹ לֹא יָכוֹל לְנַצְּחוֹ, עַד שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה אִישׁ וּבַעַל הַבַּיִת וְחֵטְא בְּפֹעַל — אֵיךְ יְחַכֶּה אַחַר כָּךְ לְנַצְּחוֹ

for if at the very entry of the inclination into his heart he could not overcome it, then once it has become a “man” and a “master of the house” and a sin in actuality — how will he then hope to overcome it?
אֲבָל הַכַּוָּונָה עַל הַטּוֹעִים הַחוֹשְׁבִים לַחֲטוֹא כְּדֵי לָשׁוּב אַחַר כָּךְ לְהַגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵיגַת בַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה
Rather, the intent is regarding the erring ones who think to sin in order to repent afterward and reach the rung of baalei teshuvah —
וְגַם זֶה בְּהַסָּתַת הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע לְמִי שֶׁלֹּא יָכוֹל לְהַסִּיתוֹ לַחֵטְא גָּמוּר,
and this too is through the instigation of the evil inclination, toward one whom it cannot incite to a complete sin,
לַעֲבֹר עַל רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
to transgress the will of Hashem, blessed be He;
מַסִּיתוֹ שֶׁזֶּהוּ כְּמוֹ עֲבֵרָה לִשְׁמָהּ.
it incites him, saying that this is like a transgression for Heaven’s sake.
וְהַגַּם דְּלִשְׁעָה זֶה חֵטְא וּמֶרִי גָּדוֹל,
And although for the moment this is a sin and great rebellion,
הַטּוֹעִים הַלָּלוּ הַבּוֹטְחִים בְּנַפְשָׁם לָשׁוּב אַחַר כָּךְ יַחְשְׁבוּ בְּטָעוּתָם שֶׁזֶּה כְּעֵין עֲבֵרָה לִשְׁמָהּ.
these mistaken ones, who trust themselves to repent afterward, will think in their error that this is a kind of transgression for Heaven’s sake.

וְעַל זֶה הֵעִידוּ חֲכָמִים דְּאֵין מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ, כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת זֶה הַחוֹטֵא לְכַתְּחִלָּה עַל מְנָת לָשׁוּב אֵין הַחֵטְא נֶחְשָׁב בְּעֵינָיו לִכְלוּם, וְאֵיךְ יִזְכֶּה לִתְשׁוּבָה הַגְּמוּרָה שֶׁהִיא הַהִתְמַרְמְרוּת וְהַחֲרָטָה הַגְּמוּרָה בַּלֵּב עַל מַה שֶּׁעָשָׂה

And of this the Sages testified that “he is not given the chance” — for in truth, this one who sins l’chatchilah “on condition to repent,” the sin is reckoned as nothing in his eyes; and how will he merit the complete teshuvah, which is the bitter embittering and complete regret of the heart over what he did?

וּלְעִנְיַן לְכַתְּחִלָּה בְּוַדַּאי אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְדַמּוֹתָם כְּלָל, שֶׁזֶּה מִצְוָה גְּמוּרָה וְזוֹ עֲבֵירָה גְּמוּרָה. אֲבָל אַחַר שֶׁחָטָא, וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עֲזָרוֹ שֶׁשָּׁב לַה׳ בְּכָל לְבָבוֹ וּבְכָל נַפְשׁוֹ בֶּאֱמֶת, שַׁפִּיר עַל הָעֲבֵירוֹת עַצְמָן ״חָיֹה יִחְיֶה״, דְּיַעֲשׂוּ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת

And regarding l’chatchilah, certainly they cannot be likened at all — this being a complete mitzvah and that a complete transgression. But after he has sinned, and Hashem helped him so that he returned to Hashem with all his heart and all his soul in truth — well then, upon the transgressions themselves “he shall surely live,” that they become like merits,

וְכַמִּצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ דַּחֲשִׁיבִי כְּמוֹ לִשְׁמָהּ גָּמוּר, וְכַמְבוֹאָר (בַּעֲרָכִין טז:) גַּבֵּי עֲנָוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ ״מִי לָא מוֹדֵית דְּלִשְׁמָהּ עֲדִיפָא״, הָכִי נָמֵי שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם

like a mitzvah not-for-its-own-sake which is reckoned like complete lishmah; and as is explained Arachin 16b regarding “humility not-for-its-own-sake” — “do you not concede that for-its-own-sake is preferable?” — so too “not-for-its-own-sake” is good — see there.
וְהַהוּא דְנָזִיר דְּאָמַר כְּמִצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ,
And that passage in Nazir which says “like a mitzvah not for its own sake,”
דְּמַשְׁמַע הָא לִשְׁמָהּ עֲדִיפָא,
implies that for its own sake is preferable,
וְלֹא אָמְרִינַן כֵּיוָן דְּלִשְׁמָהּ עֲדִיפָא הָכִי נָמֵי שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ,
and we do not say that since for its own sake is preferable, so too not for its own sake,
וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר דַּעֲבֵרָה נָמֵי מְבִיאָה לִידֵי מִצְוָה לִשְׁמָהּ בְּאוֹתוֹ הָעִנְיָן דַּעֲבֵרָה.
but one can say that a transgression too brings to a mitzvah for its own sake, in that same matter of the transgression.
וְזֶהוּ דְּיָעֵל דִּתְבֹרַךְ מִנָּשִׁים בָּאֹהֶל,
And this is that Yael is “blessed above women in the tent,”
כִּי הֵיכִי דִּבְהוּ סוֹף בָּא לְמִצְוָה לִשְׁמָהּ, הָכִי נָמֵי בִּדִידֵיהּ,
just as in those cases the end comes to a mitzvah for its own sake, so too in hers,
וְשַׁפִּיר הֲוֵי כְּמִצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ.
and it is properly like a mitzvah not for its own sake.
וּמַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הָתָם תּוֹכָחָה לִשְׁמָהּ אֵין מֵבִיא לַעֲנָוָה לִשְׁמָהּ,
Not so there: reproof for its own sake does not bring to humility for its own sake,
וְעַל כֵּן עֲנָוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ עֲדִיפָא, דִּמְבִיאָה לַעֲנָוָה לִשְׁמָהּ,
and therefore humility not for its own sake is preferable, because it brings to humility for its own sake,
וְשַׁפִּיר הַשֶּׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ הוּא כְּמוֹ לִשְׁמָהּ.
and properly the not-for-its-own-sake is like for its own sake.

וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה ד.) דִּבְיִשְׂרָאֵל ״הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״ (דְּהָא דְּ״מִתּוֹךְ״ כו׳ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, דְּאָנוּ מְבָרְכִין ״אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ״, שֶׁמַּעֲשֵׂה הַמִּצְוָה גַּם שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ מַמְשֶׁכֶת קְדֻשָּׁה לַלֵּב לְהָבִיא לִשְׁמָהּ, ״וְלֹא עָשָׂה כֵן לְכָל גּוֹי״)

And so they said Rosh Hashanah 4a that in Israel one who gives charity so that his sons live or that he merit the World to Come “is a complete tzaddik” for “from not-lishmah one comes to lishmah” applies only in Israel — for we bless “who sanctified us with His mitzvos and commanded us,” so that the mitzvah-act, even not-lishmah, draws holiness to the heart to bring him to lishmah — “and He did not do so for any other nation”.
וְאֵין צֹרֶךְ לְמַה שֶּׁדָּחֲקוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם מֵהָא דְּאַל תִּהְיוּ כַּעֲבָדִים וְכוּלֵּי, עַיֵּן שָׁם.
and there is no need for what the Tosafot strained there on account of “Do not be like servants,” etc.; see there.
דְּזֶה הוּא בִּשְׁבִיל דְּמֵאַחַר דְּזוּלַת זֶה לְעוֹלָם יַעֲסֹק וְכוּלֵּי,
for this is because, since otherwise “one should always engage,” etc.,
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעוֹבֵר בְּאַל תִּהְיוּ וְכוּלֵּי,
and although he transgresses “Do not be…,” etc.,
וּמִשּׁוּם שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ וְכוּלֵּי שַׁפִּיר הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר כְּמוֹ בְּלִשְׁמָהּ,
because of “from…,” etc., he is properly a completely righteous person, as with “for its own sake,”
וְהָכִי נָמֵי בַּעֲבֵרָה לִשְׁמָהּ נָמֵי דְּכוּתֵּיהּ,
so too with a transgression for Heaven’s sake, likewise,
הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר בַּעֲבֵרָה זוֹ שֶׁהִיא לִשְׁמָהּ,
he is a completely righteous person in this transgression, which is undertaken for Heaven’s sake,
וְשַׁפִּיר אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הֵן עַצְמָן כִּזְכֻיּוֹת.
and properly, after repentance, they themselves are like merits.
וְזֶהוּ בַּקָּשַׁת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה ״(הֶרֶב) כַּבְּסֵנִי מֵעֲוֹנִי וּמֵחַטָּאתִי טַהֲרֵנִי״, שֶׁמֵּהַחֵטְא וְהֶעָוֹן עַצְמוֹ יִהְיֶה הַכִּיבּוּס וְהַטָּהֳרָה

And this is the request of David HaMelech, “wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” (Tehillim 51:4) — that from the sin and the iniquity itself will come the washing and the purification;

שֶׁכָּךְ מִדָּתוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, בַּמֶּה שֶׁהוּא מַכֶּה בּוֹ מְרַפֵּא, וּבְדָבָר שֶׁקִּלְקְלוּ בּוֹ נִתַּקְּנוּ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין ע ע״ב) וּמַמְתִּיק הַמַּר בְּמַר; וְאֵין הַכִּיבּוּס וְהַטָּהֳרָה לְחֵטְא בְּדָבָר אַחֵר, רַק בְּהַחֵטְא עַצְמוֹ, דְּאַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא עַצְמוֹ הַגּוֹרֵם הַטָּהֳרָה

For this is the way of the Holy One, blessed be He: He heals with the very thing through which He strikes, and the very thing through which they were damaged becomes the means of rectification, as in the teaching about the fig leaves (Sanhedrin 70b). He sweetens the bitter with the bitter. The washing and cleansing of the sin are not brought about by an unrelated element: after teshuvah, the history of the sin itself becomes a means of purification.

paragraphs.text: Pirkei Avos 4:2: “מִצְוָה גּוֹרֶרֶת מִצְוָה, וַעֲבֵרָה גּוֹרֶרֶת עֲבֵרָה” — a mitzvah draws another mitzvah, while a transgression draws another transgression. Rav Tzadok distinguishes their direction at the outset: even Torah study שלא לשמה contains the actual commanded act and can lead toward its sincere fulfillment, whereas a freely chosen sin implants the contrary tendency. In Tzidkas HaTzadik §59 he says Torah not yet learned lishmah does not yield its full inner light, though speaking words of Torah remains a mitzvah; Resisei Layla §38 explicitly describes the initial enticement growing into habitual sin. Neither parallel grants permission to sin now in expectation of later repentance.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Yoma 8:9, printed at Yoma 85b, says: “הָאוֹמֵר אֶחֱטָא וְאָשׁוּב ... אֵין מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה” — one who says “I shall sin and repent” is not afforded the opportunity for repentance. It separately says that one who plans to sin relying on Yom Kippur’s atonement is not atoned for by that day. This is the prohibition against planning a transgression on the strength of future teshuvah. Rav Tzadok’s deeper explanation of why such a person cannot readily attain true remorse follows in this paragraph; it is not being anticipated in this note.

paragraphs.text: Sukkah 52b; Resisei Layla §38 — the evil inclination gains a dwelling: The Gemara says, “בַּתְּחִלָּה קְרָאוֹ הֵלֶךְ, וּלְבַסּוֹף קְרָאוֹ אוֹרֵחַ, וּלְבַסּוֹף קְרָאוֹ אִישׁ” — at first a passerby, then a guest, and ultimately a man established in the house. The Gemara does not itself use the expression 'master of the house' here. In Resisei Layla §38 Rav Tzadok expands the image to “אִישׁ וּבַעַל הַבַּיִת עַצְמוֹ” — a man and the householder himself. His point is that repeated sin hardens the habit, so one cannot confidently plan to overcome the inclination later.

paragraphs.text: Mishneh Torah, Hilchos Teshuvah 4:1 lists “הָאוֹמֵר אֶחֱטָא וְאָשׁוּב” among serious impediments to repentance. Chapter 2:2 requires abandonment of sin, regret, and sincere resolution for the future. Crucially 4:6 adds: “אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמְעַכְּבִין אֶת הַתְּשׁוּבָה אֵין מוֹנְעִין אוֹתָהּ” — although these matters obstruct teshuvah, they do not absolutely prevent it if the person truly repents. Rav Tzadok here explains the inner difficulty: one who deliberately treats a sin as a device for spiritual gain undermines the honest grief that full teshuvah requires. This is a diagnosis of the temptation to plan sin, not denial of Heaven’s acceptance of a person who truly turns back.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86b — Reish Lakish teaches that willful sins can become like merits through teshuvah, and the Gemara distinguishes teshuvah from love, which transforms them into merits, from teshuvah from fear, which renders them like unwitting sins. The prooftext is Yechezkel 33:19: “וּבְשׁוּב רָשָׁע מֵרִשְׁעָתוֹ וְעָשָׂה מִשְׁפָּט וּצְדָקָה עֲלֵיהֶם חָיֹה יִחְיֶה.” Rav Tzadok introduces the transformation only after the sinner has actually returned “with all his heart and all his soul”; its retrospective result can never furnish prospective permission to commit the sin.

paragraphs.text: Arachin 16b asks which is better: “תּוֹכָחָה לִשְׁמָהּ” (sincere rebuke) or “עֲנָוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ” (humility with an imperfect motive). The answer prefers imperfectly motivated humility, since “מִתּוֹךְ שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ בָּא לִשְׁמָהּ.” Nazir 23b independently concludes that an “עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ” is like a mitzvah שלא לשמה, after first suggesting “greater than.” Rav Tzadok’s distinctive resolution here is that an imperfect act of humility can grow into sincere humility in precisely the same area, whereas rebuke for Heaven’s sake is not itself the natural precursor of genuine humility. The Gemara does not itself spell out that further psychological comparison.

paragraphs.text: Rosh Hashanah 4a and Tosafos there — reward-motivated tzedakah: The Gemara says, “הָאוֹמֵר סֶלַע זוֹ לִצְדָקָה בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁיִּחְיוּ בָנַי ... הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר” — a giver who hopes that his children will live may be termed fully righteous in this act. Tosafos asks about Avos 1:3, which warns not to serve for reward, and answers “הַיְינוּ בְּאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם שֶׁתּוֹהִין עַל הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת” — the latter warning concerns those who regret their earlier good deeds when reward is withheld. Rav Tzadok expressly develops an alternative account: imperfect motivation is tolerated because it can lead onward to lishmah. He is not simply repeating Tosafos's answer.

paragraphs.text: Tzidkas HaTzadik §174 says: “הגם דחלילה לומר אחטא ואשוב ולעשות כן בבחירתו ... מ״מ מעצמו נעשה כן” — Heaven forbid that one elect to sin on the plan of later repentance, yet a fall may occur without such a plan and be followed by genuine return. Rav Tzadok contrasts darkness that is later transformed by teshuvah with choosing darkness as a spiritual method. Here the original sins are counted as merits after the wholehearted turning, not during the forbidden act or merely because the sinner intended eventual benefit.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 70b; Shemos Rabbah 50:3 — repairing through the source of the damage: Rabbi Nechemiah says, “תְּאֵנָה הָיָה, שֶׁבַּדָּבָר שֶׁקִּלְקְלוּ בּוֹ נִתַּקְּנוּ” — the Tree of Knowledge was a fig, for with the very thing through which Adam and Chavah were harmed they found a remedy, as the fig leaves covered them (Bereishis 3:7). Shemos Rabbah 50:3 similarly says, “בְּמַה שֶׁהוּא מַכֶּה הוּא מְרַפֵּא” — Hashem heals through that with which He strikes. Rav Tzadok applies these teachings specifically after teshuvah: the remembered sin becomes material for purification, not permission to sin. The Sanhedrin passage is on 70b; its appearance as 71b in the Hebrew working witness is a folio discrepancy, not an alternate teaching.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The distinction between a mitzvah shelo lishmah and an aveirah lishmah applies only as an ideal at the outset. A revealed act of holiness, even when done with an imperfect motive, can draw a person toward serving God for its own sake. A transgression normally pulls toward further sin, which is why one who plans to sin and then repent is not granted the opportunity.

p: (ט) וּבְבָבָא מְצִיעָא (פד.) בְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ ״מַאי אַהֲנֵית לִי, הָתָם רַבִּי קָרוּ לִי (וְהָכָא רַבִּי קָרוּ לִי)״ כו׳, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י
And in Bava Metzia 84a, concerning Reish Lakish, who said to Rabbi Yochanan, “What benefit did you do me? there they called me ‘Rebbi,’ and here they call me ‘Rebbi’!” — see there in Rashi.
וְלִכְאוֹרָה תָּמוּהַּ מְאֹד,
And at first glance it is very puzzling,
דְּאַחַר שֶׁשָּׁב רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אֵיךְ יֹאמַר מַאי אַהֲנֵיתָ לִי בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁהָיָה רַבִּי בֵּין הַלִּסְטִים.
for after Reish Lakish repented, how could he say “What benefit did you do me?” on account of having been a “rabbi” among the bandits?
וְגַם לְפִי דִּבְרֵי הַתּוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם,
And even according to the words of the Tosafot there,
דְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ מֵעִקָּרָא כְּשֶׁהָיָה תַּלְמִיד חָכָם,
that Reish Lakish, originally, when he was a Torah scholar,
מַאי אַהֲנֵיתָ לִי דְּקָאָמַר כֵּיוָן דְּסוֹף סוֹף אַחַר כָּךְ נַעֲשָׂה עַם הָאָרֶץ וְלִסְטִים עַד שֶׁהֶחֱזִירוֹ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן,
“What benefit did you do me?” that he said, since in the end he afterward became an ignoramus and a bandit until Rabbi Yochanan brought him back,
וְעַל דָּבָר זֶה שֶׁהֶחֱזִירוֹ וְאַקְרְיֵיהּ וְאַתְנְיֵיהּ וְשַׁוְּיֵיהּ גַּבְרָא רַבָּה הוּא שֶׁאָמַר זֶה דְּמַה אַהֲנֵיתָ,
and it is about this matter, that he brought him back, taught him Scripture and Mishnah, and made him a great man, that he said this, “What benefit?”
וְאֵיךְ הַלָּשׁוֹן אוֹמֶרֶת כֵּן עַד שֶׁהוּצְרַךְ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן לְהָשִׁיבוֹ אַהֲנֵאי וְכוּלֵּי,
and how can the wording say so, so that Rabbi Yochanan needed to answer him, “I did benefit you,” etc.,
כְּאִלּוּ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ לֹא יָדַע אוֹ לֹא הֶחְשִׁיב זֶה.
as if Reish Lakish did not know, or did not value, this.
וְיוֹתֵר קָשֶׁה מַה שֶּׁאָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ חַלְשָׁא דַעְתֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן,
And still more difficult is what it says afterward, “Rabbi Yochanan’s mind was weakened (he was offended),”
וּבְכָל מָקוֹם חֲלִישׁוּת דַּעַת הוּא כְּשֶׁהַלָּה מֵשִׁיב לוֹ דָּבָר שֶׁל מַמָּשׁ לְהַגְדִּיל מַעֲלָתוֹ נֶגְדּוֹ,
for everywhere offense occurs when the other replies to him with something substantive, to magnify his own stature against him,
שֶׁמִּפְּנֵי זֶה נֶחֱלַשׁ דַּעְתּוֹ כְּשֶׁרוֹאֶה הַקָּטָן מִמֶּנּוּ מִתְרַבְרֵב וְגָדוֹל נֶגְדּוֹ,
for because of this his mind is weakened when he sees one lesser than himself puffing up and acting great against him,
אֲבָל כָּאן דְּהַדְּבָרִים כִּפְשָׁטָן נִרְאִין לִכְאוֹרָה דִּבְרֵי הֶבֶל מַמָּשׁ,
but here, where the words as they stand appear at first glance to be sheer nonsense,
לוֹמַר דְּמַאי דְּהֶחֱזִירוֹ מִלִּסְטִיּוּת לִהְיוֹת גַּבְרָא רַבָּה לָא אַהֲנִי לֵיהּ כְּלוּם,
saying that his having brought him back from banditry to be a great man did not benefit him at all,
וְהֵם דְּבָרִים שֶׁלֹּא נִתְּנוּ לֵאָמֵר כְּלָל,
and these are things that should not have been said at all,
מַה חֲלִישׁוּת דַּעַת גָּרַם בָּזֶה לְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בִּדְבָרִים שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם שַׁחַר כָּאֵלּוּ לִכְאוֹרָה.
what offense did this cause Rabbi Yochanan, with seemingly baseless words such as these?

וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּדָבָר גָּדוֹל דִּיבֵּר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ בָּזֶה: כִּי בְּוַדַּאי אָדָם גָּדוֹל כְּמוֹתוֹ זָכָה לִתְשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה מֵאַהֲבָה, שֶׁכָּל זְדוֹנוֹתָיו נַעֲשׂוּ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת לִהְיוֹת מְאִירִים וּמַזְהִירִים מַמָּשׁ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת

And perforce Reish Lakish spoke a great matter here: for certainly a great man like him merited complete teshuvah from love, such that all his willful sins became like merits — literally shining and radiant like merits —
וּמַה שֶּׁהָיָה קוֹדֶם ״רַבִּי בֵּין הַלִּיסְטִים״ נֶחְשָׁב לוֹ לִגְדֻלָּה וּמַעֲלָה מַמָּשׁ כְּמוֹ עַכְשָׁיו שֶׁהוּא רַב בֵּין הַחֲכָמִים
and what he was before — “Rebbi among the bandits” — was reckoned to him as greatness and elevation, literally like now, when he is a master among the Sages.
כִּי כָּךְ הוּא יְשׁוּעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְמִי שֶׁזּוֹכֶה, שֶׁמֵּאִיר אֶת עֵינָיו לְהַשִּׂיג זֶה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵיךְ הָעֲוֹנוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת מַמָּשׁ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהֶם קְדֻשָּׁה
For such is Hashem’s salvation to one who merits: that He illumines his eyes to attain, in this world, how the iniquities are literally like merits that have holiness in them.

דְּעַל כֵּן נִכְתְּבוּ כָּל חֲטָאֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּתּוֹרָה הַקְּדוֹשָׁה הַקַּיֶּימֶת לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד; וַהֲרֵי לֶעָתִיד נֶאֱמַר דִּיבוּקַּשׁ עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ וְחַטַּאת יְהוּדָה וְלֹא תִמָּצֶאנָה — וְאֵיךְ נִכְתְּבוּ בַּתּוֹרָה לִהְיוֹת לְמַזְכֶּרֶת עָוֹן לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד

Therefore all the sins of Israel were written in the holy Torah, which endures forever — yet of the Future it is said, “the iniquity of Israel shall be sought and be no more, and the sins of Yehudah, and they shall not be found”; so how were they written in the Torah to be “a remembrancer of iniquity” forever?

וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּאַחַר הַתִּיקּוּן הַגָּמוּר שֶׁהַכֹּל נַעֲשֶׂה כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, וְיָאִיר זֶה לְעֵינֵי הַכֹּל אֵיךְ הֵם זְכֻיּוֹת, אֵין כָּאן גְּנוּת וּמַזְכֶּרֶת עָוֹן, אֶלָּא שֶׁבַח וּמַזְכֶּרֶת זְכוּת

And perforce, after the complete rectification, when everything becomes like merits, and this shines to all eyes how they are merits — there is here no disgrace or “remembrancer of iniquity,” but praise and a “remembrancer of merit.”

וְלֹא לְחִנָּם לָמְדוּ (בע״ז נב.) עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל טְעוּנָה גְּנִיזָה מִמִּזְבֵּחַ, ״מָה מִזְבֵּחַ טָעוּן (גְּנִיזָה אַף אֲשֵׁרָה טְעוּנָה גְּנִיזָה)״, כִּי כְּבָר הִבְטִיחָנוּ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ דְּ״לֹא יִדַּח מִמֶּנּוּ נִדָּח״, וְהַכֹּל יְתוּקַּן לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא בְּתַכְלִית הַתִּיקּוּן, וַאֲפִילּוּ חָטָא עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה

And not for nothing did they learn Avodah Zarah 52a that Israel’s idolatry “requires genizah burial” from the law of the altar — “just as the altar requires burial, so the asheirah requires burial” — for Hashem already assured us “that no outcast shall be cast away from Him” (II Shmuel 14:14), and all will be rectified in the Future in the ultimate rectification, even the sin of idolatry.

דְּיִהְיוּ ״כַּשָּׁנִים״ הַלָּלוּ שֶׁסְּדוּרוֹת וּבָאוֹת מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית, דְּהַכֹּל מְסֻדָּר מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְּחִלַּת הַבְּרִיאָה, וּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הָיָה לְכָךְ, דְּ״גַם כָּל מַעֲשֵׂינוּ פָּעַלְתָּ לָּנוּ״, ״וְאַתָּה הֲסִבּוֹתָ אֶת לִבָּם אֲחֹרַנִּית״, וְהוּכְרְחוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת כִּרְצוֹנְךָ ״לְמַעַן תִּצְדַּק בְּדָבְרֶךָ תִּזְכֶּה בְשָׁפְטֶךָ״

for they will be like these “shanim scarlet/years,” arranged and coming from the six days of Creation — for all is arranged by Hashem from the beginning of Creation, and Hashem’s will was so: “also all our deeds You have wrought for us” (Yeshayah 26:12), “and You turned their heart backward,” and they were compelled to do Your will, “so that You be justified when You speak, and be right when You judge” (Tehillim 51:6).

וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עַל פָּסוּק זֶה בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קז.) דְּ״לָא לֵימְרוּ עַבְדָּא דְּזָכֵי לְמָרֵיהּ״, שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ יָכוֹל לָנֶצַח יִצְרוֹ לֹא הָיָה רַשַּׁאי, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יַחֲשִׁיבוּ לְחֵטְא וְיֵעָנְשׁוּ עַל זֶה, כֵּיוָן דִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כָּךְ

in the manner they said on this verse regarding David Sanhedrin 107a — “lest they say, a servant who prevailed over his Master” — that even though he could have conquered his inclination, he was not permitted to, and even though he knew Hashem would reckon it a sin and they would be punished for it, since Hashem’s will was so.

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 84a, Rashi and Tosafos — Reish Lakish's earlier standing: Reish Lakish says, “הָתָם רַבִּי קָרוּ לִי, הָכָא רַבִּי קָרוּ לִי” — there they called me 'Rabbi,' and here they call me 'Rabbi.' Rashi explains his earlier title as the leader of bandits; Tosafos, citing Rabbeinu Tam, maintains that he had studied Torah earlier and later cast off its yoke. Rav Tzadok does not merely quote either explanation: after developing the topic of teshuvah from love, he reads Reish Lakish's former eminence as retrospectively transformed into merit. This last claim belongs to Rav Tzadok's interpretation rather than to the Gemara's explicit statement.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86b distinguishes teshuvah from fear, which reduces willful sins to inadvertent acts, from teshuvah from love, in which they become “כִּזְכֻיּוֹת.” In Tzidkas HaTzadik §40 Rav Tzadok adds a higher description: “עִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא עַד שֶׁיָּאִיר ה׳ עֵינָיו שֶׁיִּהְיוּ זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת”; enlightenment reveals how the past comes to be understood within Divine knowledge. This is his further interpretation of the Gemara, not a claim that sin was licit or meritorious at the moment of deliberate choice. The insight becomes intelligible here only once Rav Tzadok has said that the penitent’s eyes are illuminated.

Yirmeyahu promises, 'יְבֻקַּשׁ אֶת עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ' — Israel's wrongdoing will be sought and not found — although the historical episodes remain recorded in Scripture. Rav Tzadok joins these teachings: the written record endures, but after complete rectification it can illuminate the Divine service that eventually emerged from the episode rather than stand forever as disgrace. This is his explanation of a future completed process, not a claim that sin was already meritorious when committed.

Rav Chisda in Rav’s name learns from “לֹא תִטַּע לְךָ אֲשֵׁרָה כָּל עֵץ אֵצֶל מִזְבֵּחַ”: just as the altar requires genizah, so the asheirah requires genizah. Rashi explains that the forbidden altar cannot be used for benefit, and that an idol remains concealed in the ground. The Gemara states a law of forbidden property; the further idea that genizah hints to eventual spiritual rectification belongs to Rav Tzadok, not to the Gemara’s plain meaning.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 89b reads Yeshayah 1:18, “אִם יִהְיוּ חֲטָאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים,” as “like these years ordered and coming from the six days of Creation”: even sins spanning that long may be whitened like snow. The Gemara itself promises forgiveness; it does not explicitly state that deliberate sin was commanded, excused or made a mitzvah at the time.

Sanhedrin 107a records David's extraordinary remark on 'לְמַעַן תִּצְדַּק בְּדָבְרֶךָ': he could have restrained his inclination, 'דְּלָא לֵימְרוּ עַבְדָּא זַכְיָה לְמָרֵיהּ'. The same sugya begins by forbidding a person to invite a test. Avodah Zarah 4b–5a discusses David's lapse as a precedent opening the path of teshuvah for individuals. Rav Tzadok reads these aggadic passages together retrospectively, to investigate Divine foreknowledge and human responsibility. His severe description of David's experience is not a rule allowing someone to commit a known prohibition.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: In the story of Reish Lakish (Bava Metzia 84a), his cry to R’ Yochanan — “what benefit did you do me? there they called me ‘Rebbi,’ and here they call me ‘Rebbi’!” — is astonishing after his teshuvah. R’ Tzadok’s reading: Reish Lakish spoke something great. A man of his stature merited teshuvah from love, whereby his willful sins literally shine as merits. So that his former “chief of the bandits” was reckoned an elevation, truly like his present eminence among the Sages.

p: (י) וְזֶהוּ עֲבוֹדַת ״בְּכָל נַפְשְׁךָ״ שֶׁזָּכָה לָזֶה דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה (לְתַקֵּן דַּרְגָּא דִּידֵיהּ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (לֵךְ פד.) ״מַאן נַפְשִׁי — דָּא דָוִד״, וּבְפָרָשַׁת וַיִּגַּשׁ ״נֶפֶשׁ — דָּא נֶפֶשׁ דָּוִד״ עַיֵּין שָׁם ר״ו א) — לִמְסוֹר גַּם הַנֶּפֶשׁ לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ

And this is the service of “with all your soul,” which David HaMelech merited to rectify his own rung — as they said in the holy Zohar (Lech Lecha 84a), “who is ‘my soul’? — this is David,” and in Parashas Vayigash, “‘nefesh’ — this is the nefesh of David,” see there 206a — to surrender even the soul to Hashem:
שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ שֶׁחוֹטֵא עַל הַנֶּפֶשׁ בָּזֶה, אִם רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְאַבֵּד אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם נִתְרַצָּה גַּם לָזֶה, שֶׁלֹּא לִנְטוֹת מֵרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
that even though he knows he “sins against the soul” in this, if Hashem’s will were to destroy his soul, God forbid, he consents even to this — not to deviate from Hashem’s will.

וְהוּא הַגֶּבֶר שֶׁהֵקִים עוּלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה לְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל, דְּ״יָחִיד שֶׁשָּׁב מוֹחֲלִין לוֹ וּלְכָל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ״, שֶׁמְּעוֹרֵר הִרְהוּרֵי תְּשׁוּבָה בְּכָל קוֹמַת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל וּבְכָל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל

And he is “the man who raised the yoke of teshuvah” for all Israel — “an individual who repents, they forgive him and the whole world with him” — who arouses stirrings of teshuvah in the whole stature of Knesses Yisrael and in all the souls of Israel.

וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא נִגְלֶה אֶצְלָם בְּפֹעַל, הֲרֵי גַּם מִשֶּׁהִרְהֵר תְּשׁוּבָה בְּלִבּוֹ הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר, וּמִמֵּילָא יִהְיֶה הַתִּיקּוּן לְכָל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ, דִּיבוּקַּשׁ עֲוֹן (יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ) כו׳, דְּלֵיכָּא עָוֹן עוֹד, כִּי הַכֹּל זְכוּת מֵאַחַר שֶׁהָיָה רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כָּךְ

And even though it is not revealed among them in actuality, behold, even from when he contemplated teshuvah in his heart, he is a complete tzaddik, and of itself the rectification will be for the whole world — “the iniquity of Israel shall be sought and be no more” — for there is no iniquity anymore, since all is merit, once Hashem’s will was so.

וַהֲרֵי הָיָה בָּזֶה עוֹבֵד לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ; וַאֲפִילּוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה הַחֲמוּרָה, הֲרֵי זֶה כְּעֵין הַשָּׂעִיר לַעֲזָאזֵל, שֶׁאִלּוּ עָשִׂינוּ מֵעַצְמֵנוּ כְּמוֹ זֶה הָיָה נֶחְשָׁב הַקְרָבָה לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם
And indeed he was, in this, “serving Hashem”; and even in grave idolatry, it is like the sa’ir la-Azazel: had we done such of our own accord, it would be reckoned an offering to idolatry, God forbid,
אֲבָל מֵאַחַר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ צִיוָּה כָּךְ, הֲרֵי אָנוּ עוֹבְדִין בָּזֶה גַּם כֵּן לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁאָמַר וְנַעֲשָׂה רְצוֹנוֹ, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה אוֹתוֹ הַשָּׂעִיר נוֹשֵׂא כָּל עֲוֹנֹתָם
but since Hashem commanded so, we are thereby also “serving Hashem,” who spoke and His will is done — and through this that goat “bears all their iniquities.”

כִּי כֵן הֵם כָּל עֲוֹנֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל — אֵין יוֹצְאִים מֵאֲמִיתּוּת רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ; וְכָל חֲטָאֵי הַצִּבּוּר וְהַיְּחִידִים מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁנִּכְתְּבוּ בַּתַּנַ״ךְ וּבְתַלְמוּד הַמְקוּדָּשׁ הַקַּיָּם לָעַד, וַדַּאי לֹא לְשֵׁם גְּנוּת נִכְתַּב, דַּאֲפִילּוּ בִּגְנוּת בְּהֵמָה טְמֵאָה לֹא דִּיבֵּר הַכָּתוּב

For so are all the iniquities of the Children of Israel — they do not depart from the truth of Hashem’s will; and all the sins of the community and the individuals of Israel written in Tanach and in the sanctified, eternal Talmud were certainly not written for disgrace, for “Scripture did not speak even in the disgrace of an impure animal” (Pesachim 3a).

וַאֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא שֶׁהָיָה זֶה מִכְּלַל עוֹנְשֵׁי הַחֵטְא, שֶׁיִּתְפַּרְסֵם הַגְּנוּת לְכָל הַדּוֹרוֹת — מִכָּל מָקוֹם אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּשָּׁאֵר גְּנוּת קַיָּם לָעַד, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּלָא נִכְתַּב אֶלָּא לְשִׁבְחָן

And even if you say it was part of the punishment of the sin, that the disgrace be publicized to all generations — nonetheless, it is impossible that a disgrace remain forever, as I wrote; and perforce it was written only for their praise.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהַחֲטָאִים הָהֵם הָיוּ גְּדוֹלִים בִּשְׁעַת הַחֵטְא בְּעִנְיַן חֶטְאָם, כָּךְ הֵם גְּדוֹלִים אַחַר הַתִּיקּוּן בְּעִנְיַן הַזְּכוּת הַנַּעֲשֶׂה מֵהֶם, כִּי ״שְׁלִיטַת הָאָדָם בְּאָדָם לְרַע לוֹ״: כְּפִי תֹּקֶף הַשְּׁלִיטָה בְּרֶגַע הַשְּׁלִיטָה, כָּךְ הוּא תֹּקֶף הָרַע הַנִּמְשָׁךְ לוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ מִזֶּה, כְּשֶׁמּוֹצִיאִין ״בָּלְעוֹ מִפִּיו״

And just as those sins were great at the time of the sin in the matter of their sin, so they are great after the rectification in the matter of the merit made from them — for “man ruled over man to his own harm” (Koheles 8:9): as the intensity of the evil rule at the moment of ruling, so is the intensity of the harm that afterward befalls the dominator, when what he swallowed is extracted from his mouth (Iyov 20:15).

paragraphs.text: Zohar, Lech Lecha 84a and Vayigash 206a; Tehillim 25:1. The Zohar identifies 'נַפְשִׁי' with David and the first spiritual rung, nefesh: 'נַפְשִׁי, מַאן נַפְשִׁי? דָּא דָוִד' (Lech Lecha 84a); Vayigash 206a similarly says 'נֶפֶשׁ, דָּא נֶפֶשׁ דָוִד'. These are direct sources for Rav Tzadok's description of David's task of rectifying the level of nefesh. His subsequent claim about surrendering even one's spiritual standing is a further theological development, rather than language directly stated in these Zohar passages.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 61b records Rabbi Akiva’s explanation of “בְּכָל נַפְשְׁךָ” (Devarim 6:5): “אֲפִלּוּ נוֹטֵל אֶת נַפְשְׁךָ” — even if Hashem takes your life. Rabbi Akiva embodied that reading while accepting the yoke of Heaven as he was executed for Torah study. Rav Tzadok extends the motif to David’s exceptional willingness to surrender even his own spiritual condition to the Divine will, a much more radical statement that is not itself present in the Gemara. It cannot be read as permission for anyone to choose a Torah prohibition and declare it the will of Hashem; an actual command must not be confused with a human assumption about hidden providence.

paragraphs.text: Avodah Zarah 4b–5a teaches that David’s fall, though not expected for a person of his standing, opened a “door to repentance” for individuals. On 5a, Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in Rabbi Yonasan’s name interprets “נְאֻם הַגֶּבֶר הֻקַם עָל” as “שֶׁהֵקִים עוּלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה.” Yoma 86b adds Rabbi Meir’s teaching that through one person’s teshuvah forgiveness reaches the whole world. Rav Tzadok joins these sources with his view that the head of Israel includes the whole people, so David’s return awakens an inner potential for teshuvah throughout Knesses Yisrael. The final collective process is Rav Tzadok’s interpretation, not a guarantee that every individual has already completed personal repentance.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 49b; Rambam, Hilchos Ishus 8:5. The Gemara states: 'עַל מְנָת שֶׁאֲנִי צַדִּיק — אֲפִלּוּ רָשָׁע גָּמוּר מְקֻדֶּשֶׁת, שֶׁמָּא הִרְהֵר תְּשׁוּבָה בְּדַעְתּוֹ.' Rambam rules that the kiddushin remain in doubt because sincere repentance might have occurred in the heart. This gives legal weight to the possibility, not certainty, of an unseen inner turn. Rav Tzadok develops it into the potential for hidden teshuvah throughout Israel, while the practical requirements of repentance and restitution remain binding.

paragraphs.text: Ramban on Vayikra 16:8; Pirkei deRabbi Eliezer 46; Tzidkas HaTzadik §40. Ramban insists that the Yom Kippur goat sent to Azazel is not an independent offering to another power: both goats are presented before Hashem, and the extraordinary dispatch is performed solely by His explicit command. Pirkei deRabbi Eliezer connects the ritual with the accuser's testimony concerning Israel. Rav Tzadok draws an analogy in Tzidkas HaTzadik §40. The decisive distinction is an actual revealed command; a person cannot transform an independently chosen forbidden act into permitted worship by assuming a hidden Divine purpose.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 3a — a comparison in language, not a direct proof. Pesachim 3a teaches, 'לְעוֹלָם אַל יוֹצִיא אָדָם דָּבָר מְגוּנֶּה מִפִּיו', citing Scripture's preference for refined expression where possible (Bereishis 7:8). This illuminates Rav Tzadok's question: why should sacred Scripture continue to narrate earlier wrongdoing if its final purpose is permanent disgrace? His answer is that complete future rectification allows the account to become praise. The Gemara itself concerns refined speech, not the retroactive conversion of every recorded sin into merit; that is Rav Tzadok's argument.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהַחֲטָאִים הָהֵם הָיוּ גְּדוֹלִים בִּשְׁעַת הַחֵטְא בְּעִנְיַן חֶטְאָם, כָּךְ הֵם גְּדוֹלִים אַחַר הַתִּיקּוּן בְּעִנְיַן הַזְּכוּת הַנַּעֲשֶׂה מֵהֶם, כִּי ״שְׁלִיטַת הָאָדָם בְּאָדָם לְרַע לוֹ״: כְּפִי תֹּקֶף הַשְּׁלִיטָה בְּרֶגַע הַשְּׁלִיטָה, כָּךְ הוּא תֹּקֶף הָרַע הַנִּמְשָׁךְ לוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ מִזֶּה, כְּשֶׁמּוֹצִיאִין ״בָּלְעוֹ מִפִּיו״

paragraphs.text: Koheles 8:9; Zohar, Mishpatim 3; Iyov 20:15; Divrei Chalomot §22. Koheles says 'עֵת אֲשֶׁר שָׁלַט הָאָדָם בְּאָדָם לְרַע לוֹ'. The Zohar, Mishpatim 3, describes oppressed souls and states 'לְרַע לוֹ וַדַּאי'. Rav Tzadok provides an especially close parallel in Divrei Chalomot §22: an 'אָדָם בְּלִיַּעַל' temporarily rules a holy person 'לְרַע לוֹ כִּי סוֹף לְהוֹצִיא בִּלְעוֹ מִפִּיו'. Iyov 20:15 supplies the imagery of swallowed wealth drawn back out. This describes a later overturning of evil's apparent triumph, never a recommendation to perform the initial wrongdoing.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: This is the service of “with all your soul,” which David merited (the Zohar: “‘my soul’ — this is David”). The aim is to surrender even the soul to God: knowing he thereby “sins against the soul,” yet if God’s will were to destroy his soul he would consent, never to deviate from God’s will. He is “the man who raised the yoke of teshuvah” for all Israel — the individual whose repentance is forgiven “him and the whole world” — arousing teshuvah in the whole stature of Knesses Yisrael.

p: (יא) וּבְיוֹמָא (פו סע״ב) דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה בִּיקֵּשׁ שֶׁיִּכְתּוֹב סוּרְחָנוֹ, וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה אָמַר ״אַל יִכְתּוֹב״ — הַיְינוּ כָּל אֶחָד כְּפִי מַדְרֵגָתוֹ
And in Yoma 86b, the account that Moshe Rabbeinu asked for his misdeed (surchan) to be recorded, whereas David HaMelech said, “Let it not be written,” reflects the different spiritual rung of each.

כִּי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה הוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב דִּכְתִיבָא וּמַנְּחָא גָּלוּי לְכָל אֶחָד, וְהוּא מִדַּת ״יוֹם״ וְנֶגֶד הַחַמָּה בָּעוֹלָם, וּ״מַאן דִּבְחַמָּה — רוּזִין גַּלְיִין״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קנו.)

For Moshe is the root of the Written Torah, “written and set, revealed to each one,” and he is the middah of “day” and corresponds to the sun in the world — and “one who is born under the sun — his secrets are revealed,” as they said Shabbos 156a.
וְלָכֵן אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחֶטְאוֹ סוֹד גָּדוֹל וְכָמוּס, כִּי אֵיךְ אֶפְשָׁר לְשֶׁכְּמוֹתוֹ שֶׁיֶּחֱטָא כְּלָל, וּכְבָר נִזְדַּכֵּךְ גּוּפוֹ כְּמַלְאֲכֵי מָרוֹם שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶם חֵטְא
And therefore, although his sin is a great and hidden secret — for how is it possible for one like him to sin at all, his body already refined like the angels on high, who have no sin?

וְגַם מִקְרָא מְפוֹרָשׁ ״לְמַעַן תִּהְיֶה יִרְאָתוֹ עַל פְּנֵיכֶם לְבִלְתִּי תֶחֱטָאוּ״, שֶׁמִּי שֶׁיִּרְאַת ה׳ עַל פָּנָיו אֵינוֹ חוֹטֵא כְּלָל, וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיֶּחֱטָא אָדָם אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁנִּסְתַּלֵּק יִרְאַת ה׳ מֵעַל פָּנָיו בְּאוֹתָהּ רֶגַע, וַהֲרֵי אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת לג סע״ב) דְּ״יִרְאָה — לְגַבֵּי מֹשֶׁה מִילְּתָא זוּטַרְתִּי״

And an explicit verse: “so that His fear be upon your faces, that you not sin” (Shemos 20:17) — for one upon whose face is the fear of Hashem does not sin at all, and it is impossible for a person to sin except when the fear of Hashem departs from his face at that moment; and they said Berachos 33b that “fear — regarding Moshe — is a small matter.”

וּבְוַדַּאי מְצִיאוּת עִנְיַן חֵטְא אֶצְלוֹ הוּא ״מִכְּבָשַׁי דְּרַחֲמָנָא״, שֶׁהוּא ״נוֹרָא עֲלִילָה עַל בְּנֵי אָדָם״, ״וּבְמַלְאָכָיו יָשִׂים תְּהִלָּה״, וְקָאֵי עַל מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״מַלְאָךְ״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וַיִּשְׁלַח מַלְאָךְ וַיּוֹצִיאֵנוּ מִמִּצְרָיִם״

The very existence of what is called a “sin” in his case belongs to the hidden counsels of the Merciful; God is “awesome in His dealings with mankind” (Tehillim 66:5), and “in His angels He places fault” (Iyov 4:18). Rav Tzadok applies this to Moshe, who is called an angel, as it says: “He sent an angel and brought us out of Egypt” (Bamidbar 20:16).

וּבְמִלַּת ״תְּהִלָּה״ שְׁתֵּי מַשְׁמָעוּת — לְשׁוֹן גְּנוּת וְחֶרְפָּה, וּלְשׁוֹן אוֹר וְנֹגַהּ — וּשְׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת, שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמִּצַּד מַרְאִית הָעַיִן לְשָׁעָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הָיָה בָּזֶה גְּנוּת וְנִגְזַר עָלָיו מִיתָה, בֶּאֱמֶת יֵשׁ בָּזֶה נַחַת רוּחַ גָּדוֹל

And in the word “tehillah” are two meanings — a term of disgrace and reproach, and a term of light and radiance — and both are true: for although, from the side of outward appearance, for a moment in this world, there was in it disgrace and a decree of death upon him, in truth there is in it great “contentment of spirit.”

וְזֶהוּ הָרָז הַגָּנוּז בְּאוֹתָהּ מַעֲשֶׂה, שֶׁעַל זֶה בִּיקֵּשׁ שֶׁיִּכָּתֵב סוּרְחָנוֹ, דְּ״רָזוֹהִי גַּלְיִין״, שֶׁמִּצַּד מִדָּתוֹ מִדַּת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב גַּם הָאוֹר וְהָרָז שֶׁבְּדָבָר זֶה נִתְגַּלָּה לְכָל הַלְּבָבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, לְהַמְשִׁיךְ אוֹר הַנֶּעְלָם לִלְבָבָם עַל יְדֵי זֶה

And this is the secret hidden in that deed, over which he asked that his “misdeed” be written — for “his secrets are revealed” — that from the side of his middah, the middah of the Written Torah, even the light and the secret in this matter was revealed to all the hearts of Israel, to draw the hidden light to their hearts thereby.

וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר ״הֵמָּה מֵי מְרִיבָה״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וַיִּקָּדֵשׁ בָּם״, שֶׁנִּמְשַׁךְ הִתְגַּלּוּת קְדֻשַּׁת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּעוֹלָם וּבִלְבָבוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל יְדֵי דָּבָר זֶה, כְּמוֹ עַל יְדֵי מַעֲשֵׂה מִצְוָה גְּדוֹלָה

And this is the meaning of “these are the waters of Merivah, where Israel quarreled with Hashem, and He was sanctified through them” (Bamidbar 20:13) — that the revelation of Hashem’s holiness was drawn into the world and into the hearts of Israel through this matter, as through the act of a great mitzvah.
וַהֲרֵי נִתְגַּלָּה גַּם הַסּוֹד בַּתּוֹרָה,
and thus the secret was also revealed in the Torah,
שֶׁהָיָה עַל יְדֵי מַעֲשֵׂה הִתְגַּלּוּת קְדֻשָּׁה עַל יְדָם,
that it came about through an act of revelation of holiness by them,
וְלֹא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם חֵטְא שֶׁהוּא הַגּוֹרֵם וּמַמְשִׁיךְ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם הֵיפֶךְ מִקְּדֻשָּׁה.
and not, God forbid, a sin, which causes and draws, God forbid, the opposite of holiness.

וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה — מִדַּת מַלְכוּת ״פֶּה״, תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״מִסְטוֹרִין שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא״, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּתַנְחוּמָא פָּרָשַׁת תִּשָּׂא) עַל פָּסוּק ״כְּתָב לְךָ״ — ״מִי שֶׁמִּסְטוֹרִין שֶׁלּוֹ בְּיָדוֹ — אֵלּוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל״

And David HaMelech — the middah of Malchus, “the mouth peh,” the Oral Torah, which is called “the mysteries of the Holy One,” as they said in Tanchuma, Parashas Tisa on “write for yourself these words” (Shemos 34:27) — “the one whose mysteries are in his hand — these are Israel.”

וְהוּא מִדַּת ״לַיְלָה״ שֶׁהִיא בְּהֶעְלֵם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּתַרְגּוּם שה״ש) דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב לְמֵדִין בַּיּוֹם וְתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה בַּלַּיְלָה, וְכֵן אִיתָא בַּמִּדְרָשׁ גַּבֵּי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה; וּ״מַאן דִּבִלְבָנָה — רוּזִין כַּסְיִין״

And it is the middah of “night,” which is in concealment, as they said in the Targum of Shir HaShirim that the Written Torah is learned by day and the Oral Torah by night — and so it is in the Midrash regarding Moshe; and “one who is born under the moon — his secrets are hidden.”
וְעַל כֵּן בִּיקֵּשׁ שֶׁלֹּא יִכְתּוֹב סוּרְחָנוֹ, וְאָמַר לוֹ דְּאִי אֶפְשָׁר, ״וּמַה יוֹ״ד שֶׁנָּטַלְתִּי מִשָּׂרַי״ כו׳, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין קז סע״א)
And therefore he asked that his “misdeed” not be written; and God told him that it is impossible: “and what of the yud that I took from Sarai,” as they said Sanhedrin 107a.

וּמִזֶּה גַּם כֵּן דְּנִכְתְּבָה הַפָּרָשָׁה לְשִׁבְחָן, דְּאִי לִגְנוּתוֹ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ, מָה רְאָיָה מִיּוֹ״ד דְּשָׁרֵי, דְּזָכָה שֶׁהָיָה בִּשְׁמָהּ שֶׁל אוֹתָהּ צַדֶּקֶת, וּבַדִּין הוּא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה עוֹמֵד וְצוֹוֵחַ עַל מַה שֶּׁהוֹרִידוּהוּ מִמַּעֲלָתוֹ לִינָּטֵל מִשָּׁם

And from this too we learn that the portion was written for their praise — for if it were for his disgrace, God forbid, in its plain sense, what proof is there from the yud that “cried out”? For the yud merited to be in the name of that righteous woman Sarah, and it is right that it stand and cry over being lowered from its elevation, taken from there;

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אוֹתָהּ פָּרָשָׁה דַּהֲרֵי הִיא מְדַבֶּרֶת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם בִּגְנוּת אוֹתוֹ הַצַּדִּיק — אַדְּרַבָּא שֶׁבַח וְנוֹחַ הָיָה לְאוֹתָן אוֹתִיּוֹת שֶׁלֹּא יִכְתְּבוּ; אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת רְאוּיָה הִיא לוֹ מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית, כִּדְאִיתָא הָתָם

By contrast, had the portion concerning Bathsheba merely been the public disgrace of this righteous man, those letters should have preferred not to be written. But in truth, Bathsheba was designated as fitting for him from the six days of Creation, as taught there.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86b — the different recorded misdeeds of Moshe and David. The Gemara says 'שני פרנסים טובים עמדו להם לישראל: משה ודוד': Moshe asks 'יכתב סורחני', but David asks 'אל יכתב סורחני'. Its parable explains the concern that one episode not be confused with another, graver disgrace. Rav Tzadok adds a distinct explanation, contrasting the revealed quality of Moshe's Written Torah with David's hidden mode of revelation. The day-and-night interpretation is Rav Tzadok's, not the Gemara's own conclusion.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 10a reports Chizkiyahu’s refusal to have children because he foresaw wicked descendants. Yeshayahu rebukes him: “בַּהֲדֵי כִּבְשֵׁי דְּרַחֲמָנָא לָמָּה לָךְ? מַאי דְּמִפַּקְּדַת אִיבְּעִי לָךְ לְמֶעְבַּד” — hidden Divine arrangements are not the measure of a person’s revealed obligations. Takanas HaShavin 3:9 uses the same expression regarding the ultimately unrevealed order of teshuvah. Rav Tzadok applies the distinction here retrospectively to the concealed reason that an event involving Moshe could occur. The sugya emphatically requires fidelity to the revealed command; it provides no permission to plan a forbidden act on the theory that a hidden Divine purpose requires it.

paragraphs.text: Tehillim 66:5; Midrash Tanchuma, Vayeshev §4; Tzidkas HaTzadik §100. 'לְכוּ חֲזוּ מִפְעֲלוֹת אֱלֹהִים נוֹרָא עֲלִילָה עַל בְּנֵי אָדָם' (Tehillim 66:5). Tanchuma, Vayeshev §4, explains that the Divine decree concerning Moshe's entry into the Land is intimated earlier and only afterward connected openly with his saying 'שְׁמְעוּ נָא הַמֹּרִים' at Mei Merivah: 'וְכֵיוָן שֶׁאָמַר לָהֶם שִׁמְעוּ נָא הַמֹּרִים ... לָכֵן לֹא תָבִיאוּ אֶת הַקָּהָל הַזֶּה'. Rav Tzadok uses the theme in Tzidkas HaTzadik §100. This is a teaching about hidden providence; the Midrash does not revoke the revealed command or its consequences.

paragraphs.text: Machshavos Charutz §2 — the revealed Written Torah and the day. Rav Tzadok writes: ״התורה שבכתב מדת יום שהוא מצד השם יתברך שרוצה להאיר לאדם שישיג האמת גלוי לעין בבירור גמור״ — the Written Torah belongs to day, for Hashem desires that a person recognize truth openly and unmistakably. He contrasts this clarity with the present world and particularly exile, which are likened to night and therefore demand emunah. This is a direct parallel to his interpretation of Moshe as a mode of open, sunlike revelation; it is not an assertion that a person may know in advance that an act of wrongdoing will later provide illumination.

Rashi explains the public sanctification when strict judgment was carried out even against Moshe and Aharon, recalling ״בִּקְרֹבַי אֶקָּדֵשׁ״ (Vayikra 10:3); Zevachim 115b discusses that phrase in the account of Nadav and Avihu. This further teaching belongs to Rav Tzadok and does not cancel either the historical decree or Rashi’s plain explanation.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Tisa §34, on Shemos 34:27, reports that Moshe wished the Mishnah to be put in writing. Because other nations might translate the Written Torah and claim to be Israel, the Midrash identifies the Oral Mishnah as the distinguishing hidden teaching: “מִי שֶׁמִּסְטוֹרִין שֶׁלִּי אֶצְלוֹ, הֵם בָּנַי” — “Those who possess My mysteries are My children.” Rav Tzadok applies this hidden dimension of Torah to David, Malchus, and the mouth; the Midrash itself does not address David’s personal conduct.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 156a speaks of one born under the sun, “רָזוֹהִי גַּלְיָין” — his secrets are revealed — and one born under the moon, “רָזוֹהִי כַּסְיָין” — his secrets are hidden. The Aramaic Targum to Shir HaShirim 5:10 depicts the Holy One occupied with the twenty-four books of Scripture by day and the six orders of Mishnah by night; it is an interpretive portrayal of Divine study, not a direct halachic instruction governing human study hours. Tanchuma, Ki Tisa §36, likewise describes Moshe recognizing day when he learned Written Torah and night when he learned Mishnah and Talmud. Rav Tzadok joins these separate images to contrast Moshe’s openly revealed mode with David’s concealed mode; Shabbos 156a does not itself expound their roles.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 107a: David asks “שֶׁלֹּא יִכָּתֵב סִרְחוֹנִי”; God answers that even the yud removed from Sarai’s name cried until it was restored in Yehoshua’s name, “כָּל הַפָּרָשָׁה כֻּלָּהּ — עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה.” Rav Tzadok draws a further argument: if the written section were only shame, its letters should not resist omission; the comparison implies a deeper worth in its inclusion. That inverse inference is his, not the Gemara’s explicit rationale. The very same Sanhedrin passage describes David’s acceptance of suffering and departure of the Shechinah; its record must not be characterized as a simple declaration that no wrong was committed in the ordinary public order.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Moshe asked that his “misdeed” be written; David asked that his not be — each according to his rung. Moshe is the root of the Written Torah, “revealed to all,” the middah of day/sun, “whose secrets are revealed”; how could such a one truly “sin”? His body was already refined like an angel’s, and “the fear of God upon his face” makes sin impossible — so the very existence of his “sin” is “from the hidden things of the Merciful,” “awesome in deed,” who “places tehillah in His angels.”

p: (יב) וְתֵדַע דַּהֲרֵי כָּל שַׁלְשֶׁלֶת מַלְכוּת בֵּית דָּוִד וְהַמָּשִׁיחַ הַמְקוּוֶה בִּמְהֵרָה בְּיָמֵינוּ הוּא מִמֶּנָּה, מִשְּׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה; וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה רָאָה זֶה בְּרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, וְהִבְטִיחָהּ דְּזַרְעָהּ יִמְלֹךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל

(12) Know that the whole royal line of the House of David and the Mashiach for whom we await redemption, speedily in our days, comes through her — Bathsheba — through Shlomo HaMelech. David HaMelech perceived this through ruach hakodesh and promised her that her son would reign, as the Sages taught.
וְעַל זֶה צָם וְהִרְבָּה בִּתְפִלָּה שֶׁיִּחְיֶה אוֹתוֹ יֶלֶד, וְאִלּוּ הָיָה שֶׁמֶץ חֵטְא אַדְּרַבָּא הָיָה לוֹ לִשְׂמוֹחַ כְּשֶׁמֵּת, שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ כְּמַזְכִּיר עָוֹן

And over this he fasted and prayed much that the child would live — and had there been even a trace of sin, on the contrary he should have rejoiced when it died, so that it not be for him “a reminder of iniquity.”

אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת, אִלּוּ הָיָה אוֹתוֹ יֶלֶד חַי וְהָיָה הוּא הַמֶּלֶךְ אַחֲרָיו וְהַבּוֹנֶה בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, נִמְצָא לֹא הָיָה אוֹתוֹ מַעֲשֵׂה אֲכִילַת פַּגָּה גַּם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, שֶׁהֲרֵי בְּהֶכְרֵחַ הָיָה אוֹתוֹ וָלָד לְהִיוָּלֵד אָז

But in truth, had that child lived and been king after him and the builder of the Beis HaMikdash, then that act of “eating unripe fruit” would not have been a lapse even in this world — for that child necessarily had to be born then;

וְהָיָה בָּזֶה תִּיקּוּן גָּמוּר לְחֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁהָיָה גַּם כֵּן בַּאֲכִילַת פַּגָּה כַּנּוֹדָע, וְהָיָה גְּמַר הַתִּיקּוּן וְעֵת קֵץ, וְאוֹתוֹ וָלָד הָיָה מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן דָּוִד, וְהַבַּיִת שֶׁהָיָה נִבְנֶה עַל יָדוֹ הָיָה קַיָּים לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד

and there would have been in it a complete rectification of the sin of Adam HaRishon — which too was an “eating of unripe fruit,” as is known — and it would have been the finish of the rectification and the End of Days; and that child would have been Mashiach ben David, and the House built by him would have stood forever.
וּבְוַדַּאי שֶׁהָיָה אוֹתוֹ וָלָד נִשְׁמַת מָשִׁיחַ וּמוּכָן לָזֶה, אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא הִגִּיעַ הַקֵּץ עֲדַיִן
And certainly that child bore the soul of Mashiach and was ready for it — only that the End had not yet arrived.

וְזֶהוּ הָאֲכִילָה פַּגָּה טֶרֶם הִגִּיעַ הַזְּמַן וְהַקֵּץ, שֶׁהוּא הָיָה עָסוּק בְּאוֹתָהּ מַעֲשֶׂה לִבְרוֹא אוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בברא״ר ר״פ פה) בְּעִנְיַן יְהוּדָה ״וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא הָיָה עוֹסֵק בּוֹרֵא אוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם; אֶלָּא שֶׁחָשַׁב לְמַהֲרוֹ לִפְנֵי זְמַנּוֹ

And this is “the eating of unripe fruit before the time and the End came” — for he was engaged in that act to “create the light of Mashiach,” as they said Bereishis Rabbah 85:1 regarding Yehudah, “and the Holy One was engaged in creating the light of Mashiach,” see there — only that he thought to hasten it before its time.

וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר (תְּהִלִּים נא) ״מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד בְּבוֹא (אֵלָיו נָתָן הַנָּבִיא) כַּאֲשֶׁר בָּא (אֶל בַּת שֶׁבַע)״, דִּכְמוֹ אָז הָיָה עָסוּק בְּבוֹרֵא אוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ, כֵּן ״בְּבוֹא״ כו׳ לֹא חָשׁ לְעַצְמוֹ וּלְאַבְּדָן נַפְשׁוֹ בַּחֲשַׁאי, רַק כָּל מְגַמָּתוֹ לְהַצָּלַת כְּלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״אֲלַמְּדָה פוֹשְׁעִים (דְּרָכֶיךָ)״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְסִיֵּים ״בִּישׁוּעַת צִיּוֹן, הֵיטִיבָה (בִרְצוֹנְךָ אֶת צִיּוֹן, תִּבְנֶה) חוֹמוֹת יְרוּשָׁלִָם״

And therefore he said Tehillim 51, “A psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, as he came to Bas Sheva” — for just as then he was engaged in “creating the light of Mashiach,” so too, “when Nathan came to him,” he did not care for himself and the loss of his own soul in secret, but his whole aim was the salvation of all Israel, as it says, “I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners shall return to You,” and he concluded, “in the salvation of Zion” — “do good in Your favor to Zion, build the walls of Jerusalem.”

וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר ״מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד״, שֶׁהוּצְרַךְ לְעוֹרֵר רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ עָלָיו עַל יְדֵי הַשִּׁירָה וְהַזֶּמֶר, וְכִדְאִיתָא (פְּסָחִים קיז.) — הַיְינוּ לְפִי שֶׁאָז נִסְתַּלְּקָה מִמֶּנּוּ רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, וְעַל זֶה אָמַר ״הָשִׁיבָה לִּי שְׂשׂוֹן יִשְׁעֶךָ״ וְכִדְאִיתָא (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין שָׁם)

And this is why it says “Mizmor l’David” rather than “l’David Mizmor” — that he had to rouse the ruach hakodesh upon himself through song and melody, as it is stated Pesachim 117a — because then the ruach hakodesh had departed from him, and of this he said, “restore to me the joy of Your salvation,” as it is stated in Sanhedrin 107a.

וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי הָעַצְבוּת מֵהַחֵטְא, כִּי עֶצֶם הַחֵטְא לֹא הָיָה חֵטְא כְּלָל, רַק אַדְּרַבָּא קְדֻשָּׁה גְּדוֹלָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה כּוּלּוֹ קֹדֶשׁ לַה׳, וְאֵין שׁוּם דָּבָר אֶצְלוֹ מִלְּבַד (ה׳) חַס וְשָׁלוֹם

The departure of the Divine Spirit came about through sorrow over the sin. For in Rav Tzadok’s inward interpretation, the essential act was not a sin at all but rather great holiness: David HaMelech was wholly consecrated to Hashem, with nothing in his heart apart from Him.

אֲבָל לְפִי שֶׁלְּמַרְאִית הָעַיִן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הָיָה חֵטְא, וְהָיָה חִילּוּל הַשֵּׁם בְּפִי הַבְּרִיּוֹת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַנָּבִיא (ש״ב יב) ״אֶפֶס כִּי נִאֵץ נִאַצְתָּ״ וְגוֹמֵר ״גַּם הַבֵּן הַיִּלּוֹד לְךָ מוֹת יָמוּת״

But because, to the outward eye in this world, it was a sin and a “profaning of the Name” in people’s mouths — as the prophet said to him II Shmuel 12, “However, because you have shown such great contempt, also gam the child born to you shall surely die” —

וּלְשׁוֹן ״גַּם״ מְבוֹאָר דְּבָא לְהוֹסִיף וְלוֹמַר שֶׁכְּמוֹ שֶׁעָשִׂיתָ כֵּן יִהְיֶה לְךָ גַּם כֵּן נֶגֶד זֶה דָּבָר זֶה; כִּי מֵאַחַר דְּרָזוֹהִי (כַּסְיָין), וְאֵין הִתְגַּלּוּת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה עֲדַיִן מֵאוֹר הַבָּהִיר שֶׁלְּךָ, בְּהֶכְרֵחַ אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּתְגַּלֶּה אוֹר הַוָּלָד הַזֶּה, דְּאִם כֵּן אֵינוֹ אֲכִילַת פַּגָּה וְלֹא הָיָה כָּאן חֵטְא בְּעֵינֵי הַבְּרִיּוֹת גַּם כֵּן

and the word “gam also” is precise — coming to add: that as you did, so shall correspondingly be done to you in this matter — for since “his secrets are hidden,” and there is not yet, in this world, a revelation of your “radiant light,” necessarily the light of this child cannot be revealed; for if it were revealed, it would not be “eating unripe fruit,” and there would have been no sin in people’s eyes either.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּא לוֹ הָעַצְבוּת אַחַר כָּךְ בְּבִיאַת הַנָּבִיא לוֹ לְהַגִּיד שֶׁלֹּא עָלָה בְיָדוֹ,
And through this the sadness came to him afterward, at the prophet’s coming to tell him that he had not succeeded,
כִּי נֶחְשָׁב חֵטְא וְצָרִיךְ לְעֹנֶשׁ.
because it was considered a sin and requires punishment.
וּבָזֶה נִסְתַּלֵּק מִמֶּנּוּ רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ עַד שֶׁהוּצְרַךְ לְעוֹרְרוֹ בְּשִׂמְחָה שֶׁל מִצְוָה,
And through this the Divine Spirit departed from him, until he needed to arouse it with the joy of a mitzvah,
הַיְנוּ מִצְוַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁזָּכָה לָהּ עַל יְדֵי חֵטְא זֶה,
that is, the mitzvah of repentance, which he merited through this sin,
לִהְיוֹת מֵקִים עֻלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה,
to be one who raises up the yoke of repentance,
וַאֲלַמְּדָה פֹשְׁעִים וְגוֹמֵר לְהוֹרוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה לָרַבִּים.
“and I will teach transgressors,” etc., to teach repentance to the many.
וְזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן כַּאֲשֶׁר בָּא וְגוֹמֵר,
And this is also “when he came,” etc.,
דְּגַם אָז הָיָה כֵּן תְּחִלַּת הַהֲסָתָה הָיְתָה עַל יְדֵי הַיֵּצֶר,
for then too the beginning of the incitement was through the inclination,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַמָּשָׁל מִבִּיאַת הַהֵלֶךְ לָאִישׁ הֶעָשִׁיר,
as the parable told him of the coming of the wayfarer to the rich man,
אַף שֶׁהוּא הָיָה כְּבָר לִבּוֹ חָלַל בְּקִרְבּוֹ,
although his heart was already “hollow within him,”
בִּשְׁבִיל הַנִּסָּיוֹן שָׁלַח לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵחָדָשׁ כֹּחַ הֲסָתַת הַיֵּצֶר.
for the sake of the test Hashem, blessed be He, sent him anew the power of the inclination’s incitement.
וְעַל זֶה אָמַר וַיָּבֹא הֵלֶךְ — שֶׁבָּא מֵחָדָשׁ וְלֹא הָיָה מָצוּי שָׁם מִקֹּדֶם כְּלָל,
And about this it says, “and a wayfarer came”—that he came anew and was not found there at all beforehand,
וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ דָּרְשׁוּ (בְּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה כ״ב וּבְשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה) עַל פָּסוּק וּבוֹאִי תֵימָן, דָּבָר שֶׁל חִדּוּשׁ.
and similarly they expounded (Bereishis Rabbah 22 and Shir HaShirim Rabbah) on the verse “and come, south wind,” as a matter of novelty.
וּבְוַדַּאי בְּהִתְעוֹרְרוּת יֵצֶר הָרָע וְהִתְגַּבְּרוּתוֹ מֵהֵלֶךְ לְאוֹרֵחַ וּלְאִישׁ גָּרַם הִסְתַּלְּקוּת שְׁכִינָה וְרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ,
And certainly the arousal of the evil inclination and its strengthening, from wayfarer to guest to man, caused the departure of the Shechinah and the Divine Spirit,
כִּי אֵין טוֹב וָרָע אוֹר וְחֹשֶׁךְ מִתְקַיְּמִים יַחַד וּמְצוּיִים בְּמָקוֹם אֶחָד.
for good and evil, light and darkness, do not coexist and are not found together in one place.
וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יְבָמוֹת קי״ב ע״ב) אֵין אָדָם דָּר עִם נָחָשׁ בִּכְפִיפָה אַחַת,
In the manner that they said (Yevamot 112b), “A person does not dwell with a snake in one basket,”
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּשַׁבָּת קמ״ט ע״ב) עַל פָּסוּק לֹא יְגֻרְךָ רָע, לֹא יָגוּר בִּמְגוּרְךָ רָע.
and as they said (Shabbat 149b) on the verse “Evil shall not sojourn with You”: no evil shall sojourn in Your dwelling.
וְיֵצֶר הָרָע הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא קְרָאוֹ רַע, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסֻכָּה נ״ב ע״א),
And the Holy One, blessed be He, called the evil inclination “evil,” as they said (Sukkah 52a),
וְהַיְנוּ הַיֵּצֶר שֶׁמִּצַּד הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא,
that is, the inclination from the side of the Holy One, blessed be He,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא ט״ז ע״א) בָּרָאתָ רְשָׁעִים וְכוּלֵּי, בָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא יֵצֶר הָרָע וְכוּלֵּי, עַיֵּן שָׁם,
as they said (Bava Batra 16a), “You created the wicked,” etc., “the Holy One, blessed be He, created the evil inclination,” etc.; see there,
וְהוּא הַיֵּצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם שֶׁמִּנְּעוּרָיו בְּתוֹלָדָה וּמִשֶּׁנִּתְנַעֵר מִמְּעֵי אִמּוֹ.
It is the inclination of a person’s heart from youth, implanted in his nature, present from the time he emerges from his mother’s womb.
זֶהוּ הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ הַנִּקְרָא רַע שֶׁהָיָה בְּעֵר בְּכוֹר יְהוּדָה, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹ וַיְהִי (עֵר בְּכוֹר יְהוּדָה) רַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳.
This is the root called “evil” that was in Er, Yehudah’s firstborn, of whom it is said, “And (Er, Yehudah’s firstborn) was evil in the eyes of Hashem.”
וְיָדוּעַ מֵהָאֲרִי זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה שֶׁבּוֹ הָיְתָה רִאשׁוֹנָה הִתְגַּלּוּת נֶפֶשׁ הַמָּשִׁיחַ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
And it is known from the Ari, of blessed memory, that in him was the first revelation of the soul of Mashiach in this world,
וְזֶהוּ בְּכוֹר יְהוּדָה וְרֵאשִׁית אוֹנוֹ.
and this is “Yehudah’s firstborn,” “the first of his strength.”
וְרָמוּז גַּם כֵּן בִּלְשׁוֹן הַבְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל עַל פָּסוּק וַיֵּרֶד יְהוּדָה, דְּעָסוּק בִּבְרִיאַת אוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ.
And it is also hinted in the language of Bereishis Rabbah mentioned above, on the verse “and Yehudah went down,” that the Holy One was engaged in the creation of the light of Mashiach.
וְאָז הָיָה נִשּׂוּאֵי בַּת שׁוּעַ, וְאֵין הַמָּשִׁיחַ מִזַּרְעָהּ, אֲבָל לֵדַת עֵר הוּא בְּרִיאָה הָרִאשׁוֹנָה דְּאוֹר שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
And then was the marriage to Bat-Shua; and Mashiach is not from her offspring, but the birth of Er is the first creation of the light of Mashiach in this world.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא נִתְקַיֵּם וּמֵת, מִכָּל מָקוֹם כְּבָר הִתְחִיל אָז בְּרִיאָתוֹ וְהִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹרוֹ,
And although he did not endure and died, nevertheless his creation and the revelation of his light had already begun then,
אֶלָּא דְּשָׁלַט בּוֹ כֹּחַ הָרַע שֶׁבַּבְּרִיאָה וּבַתּוֹלָדָה.
except that the power of evil that is in creation and in birth ruled over him.
וְהוּא חֵטְא דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל, דְּגַם אָז הָיוּ מוּכָנִים לְקַבָּלַת הַתּוֹרָה אִלְמָלֵא זָכוּ.
And that is the sin of the generation of the Flood, for then too they were prepared for the receiving of the Torah had they merited.
וְגַם מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הָיָה שָׁם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא פִּנְחָס רי״ו ע״ב) וְנִרְמַז גַּם כֵּן בַּתַּלְמוּד (חֻלִּין קל״ט ע״ב),
And Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, was also there, as they said (Ra’aya Mehemna, Pinchas 216b), and it is also hinted in the Talmud (Chullin 139b),
אֶלָּא שֶׁגָּרַם הַחֵטְא וְנִטְבַּע גַּם הוּא בְּמֵי הַמַּבּוּל,
except that the sin caused him too to be drowned in the waters of the Flood,
דְּעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר עָלָיו מִן הַמַּיִם מְשִׁיתִיהוּ,
for about this it is said of him, “From the water I drew him,”
דְּעַתָּה בְּגִלְגּוּל זֶה נִצַּל וְנִמְשַׁךְ מִשָּׁם.
for now, in this incarnation, he was saved and drawn from there.

paragraphs.text: I Melachim 1:13, 17, 30 recounts the oath concerning Bathsheba’s son Shlomo: “שְׁלֹמֹה בְנֵךְ יִמְלֹךְ אַחֲרַי” — “Shlomo your son shall reign after me.” Nasan asks Bathsheba to remind David of the promise; she repeats it, and David confirms it. This establishes succession through Bathsheba and Shlomo, the part of Rav Tzadok’s claim developed at this point. The verses do not state that the oath was disclosed through ruach hakodesh or identify the earlier child with Mashiach; those are Rav Tzadok’s subsequent interpretive conclusions.

paragraphs.text: II Shmuel 12:14–23 relates that David prayed and fasted for his first child while the child was still alive: “וַיְבַקֵּשׁ דָּוִד אֶת הָאֱלֹהִים בְּעַד הַנָּעַר וַיָּצָם דָּוִד צוֹם” (v. 16) — “David sought God for the child and fasted.” After the child died, David explained: “בְּעוֹד הַיֶּלֶד חַי צַמְתִּי וָאֶבְכֶּה” (v. 22) — “While the child was alive, I fasted and wept.” The narrative proves his hope for the child’s survival, not that his earlier conduct was without sin. Rav Tzadok’s additional connection between that hope, the End of Days, and the child’s possible messianic role is an interpretation beyond the verse.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 40a records Rabbi Nechemiah’s view: “תְּאֵנָה הָיְתָה, שֶׁבַּדָּבָר שֶׁנִּתְקַלְקְלוּ בּוֹ נִתְקְּנוּ” — the Tree of Knowledge was a fig, for what brought corruption was also used for repair. The sugya preserves other opinions about the tree. Akeidas Yitzchak, Shaar 60, reads “נֹצֵר תְּאֵנָה יֹאכַל פִּרְיָה” (Mishlei 27:18) as delaying present gratification for future spiritual fruit, contrasting patient self-restraint with Adam; the available Hebrew transcription reads “לא כמוהו שאכלת פגה” — unlike one who ate the unripe fruit. Rav Tzadok applies this moral image to obtaining a destined good before its appointed time. Neither source grants permission to take something forbidden in expectation of its later rectification.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 107a contains two distinct, consecutive teachings rather than a single combined quotation. Rava teaches: “רְאוּיָה הָיְתָה בַּת שֶׁבַע בַּת אֱלִיעָם לְדָוִד מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְּרֵאשִׁית, אֶלָּא שֶׁבָּאת עָלָיו בְּמַכְאוֹב” — Bathsheba was destined for David from Creation, but came to him through pain. The school of Rabbi Yishmael adds: “רְאוּיָה הָיְתָה לְדָוִד בַּת שֶׁבַע בַּת אֱלִיעָם, אֶלָּא שֶׁאֲכָלָהּ פַּגָּה” — she was fitting for David, but he partook of her prematurely. Rav Tzadok extends the figure of unripe fruit to an attempted hastening of redemption. The sugya does not license action before its permitted time.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 85:1, introducing Yehudah and Tamar’s ancestral story, contrasts the brothers’ concern over Yosef with Yehudah’s efforts to marry and says: “וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא הָיָה עוֹסֵק בּוֹרֵא אוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מֶלֶךְ הַמָּשִׁיחַ” — “The Holy One was occupied creating the light of the King Mashiach.” Rav Tzadok applies that model of hidden redemptive development to David and Bathsheba. The Midrash’s direct subject is Yehudah, not David, and it does not determine that David’s first child was Mashiach or authorize premature action.
