paragraphs.text: Divrei Soferim §28 is a direct parallel in Rav Tzadok’s own writing. After citing Sanhedrin 107a concerning Bathsheba’s destined union and “אֲכָלָהּ פַּגָּה,” he states: “אוֹתוֹ וָלָד הָיָה נִשְׁמַת מָשִׁיחַ ... לְפִי שֶׁהָיָה פַּגָּה דַּעֲדַיִן לֹא הִגִּיעַ הַקֵּץ עַל כֵּן לֹא נִתְקַיֵּם” — that child bore the soul of Mashiach, but, being premature before the End, could not endure. This confirms Rav Tzadok’s own linkage of the first child with a premature messianic possibility. It is not a quotation from Sanhedrin, and the parallel’s theology is not permission to undertake forbidden conduct for a concealed goal.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 117a distinguishes “לְדָוִד מִזְמוֹר,” when the Shechinah came first, from “מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד,” when song came first and the Shechinah followed. The passage insists that Shechinah rests through “דְּבַר שִׂמְחָה שֶׁל מִצְוָה,” not sadness. Sanhedrin 107a records that David endured six months of affliction and that “וְנִסְתַּלְּקָה הֵימֶנּוּ שְׁכִינָה,” reading “הָשִׁיבָה לִּי שְׂשׂוֹן יִשְׁעֶךָ” from Tehillim 51:14. Rav Tzadok supplies the further causal explanation: sadness upon the failure of the earlier messianic possibility, and the reawakening through the mitzvah of teshuvah, enabled David to teach repentance to the many. The Gemaras do not explicitly say the event was no sin at all; Rav Tzadok acknowledges here that it was judged a sin requiring punishment in the revealed order.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The royal line of David and the awaited Mashiach descends from Bas Sheva through Shlomo, a destiny David perceived through ruach hakodesh. This explains why David fasted and prayed that his first child with Bas Sheva should live. Had their union retained a true trace of sin, the child’s death would have relieved rather than distressed him.

p: (יג) וְכָךְ מִדָּתוֹ שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בִּבְרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם, דִּבְרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא וַהֲדַר נְהוֹרָא; וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (בברא״ר) דְּהָיָה בּוֹרֵא עוֹלָמוֹת וּמַחֲרִיבָן כו׳ — וְהֵן עוֹלָמוֹת הַתֹּהוּ עַד שֶׁיָּצָא עוֹלָם הַתִּיקּוּן כַּנּוֹדָע

And so is the way of Hashem in the creation of the world — “first darkness, and then light”; and so they said in Bereishis Rabbah that “He was creating worlds and destroying them,” these being the worlds of tohu, until the world of tikkun came forth, as is known.

וְכֵן הוּא בְּכָל דָּבָר; וְכָל גִּלְגּוּלֵי הַמָּשִׁיחַ שֶׁהָיוּ כְּבָר בָּעוֹלָם הֵם דֻּגְמַת ״בּוֹרֵא עוֹלָמוֹת וּמַחֲרִיבָן״, וְעַל יְדֵי אוֹתָן חוּרְבָּנוֹת דַּוְקָא הָיָה בִּנְיַן עוֹלָם הַתִּיקּוּן, בְּהַעֲלָאַת אוֹתָן אוֹרוֹת דְּשִׁבְרֵי כֵלִים כַּנּוֹדָע; וּמָשִׁיחַ הוּא הַבָּא לְתַקֵּן שֹׁרֶשׁ הָרַע שֶׁבִּבְרִיאָה

And so it is in everything; and all the “reincarnations of Mashiach” that were already in the world are a “likeness” of “creating worlds and destroying them” — and through those very destructions was the building of the world of tikkun, by the raising of those “lights of the broken vessels,” as is known; and Mashiach is the one who comes to rectify the root of the evil in Creation.
וְזֶהוּ חֵטְא דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל וְחֵטְא עֵר וְאוֹנָן, שֶׁבִּמְקוֹם הִתְעוֹרְרוּת אוֹר הַקְּדֻשָּׁה הוּא כְּנֶגְדּוֹ הִתְגַּבְּרוּת כֹּחַ הָרַע, דְּ״זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה״

And this is the sin of the generation of the Flood and the sin of Er and Onan: that in the place of the arousal of the light of holiness there is, opposite it, the intensification of the power of evil — “this-against-that.”

וְהוּא נִקְרָא ״רַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״, וְכֵן בְּאוֹנָן נֶאֱמַר ״וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״, וְכֵן אוֹמֵר עַל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה (ש״ב יא) ״וַיֵּרַע הַדָּבָר״ וְגוֹמֵר ״בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״, וְכֵן אָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ (תְּהִלִּים נא) ״וְהָרַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ עָשִׂיתִי״

And it is called “evil in the eyes of Hashem”; and so of Onan it says, “and it was evil in the eyes of Hashem” (Bereishis 38:10), and so it says of David II Shmuel 11, “and the thing was evil in the eyes of Hashem,” and so he said of himself Tehillim 51, “and I did the evil in Your eyes.”

וְהָעִנְיָן כְּמוֹ דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין נִקְרָאִים ״עֵינֵי הָעֵדָה״ בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁמְּדַבֵּר מֵהַשְׁגָּחָתָם עַל הָעֵדָה, כִּי הָעַיִן הוּא הַמַּשְׁגִּיחַ; וְכֵן אֵצֶל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״דֵּעוֹת ה׳״, ״עֵינֵי ה׳ הֵמָּה מְשׁוֹטְטוֹת״, וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר (תְּהִלִּים לג) ״עֵין ה׳ אֶל יְרֵאָיו״

And the matter is like the Sanhedrin being called “the eyes of the congregation” where it speaks of their oversight hashgachah over the congregation — for “the eye is the overseer”; and so with Hashem, as it says, “a God of knowledge,” “the eyes of Hashem range over the earth” (Zechariah 4:10), and it says Tehillim 33, “the eye of Hashem is to those who fear Him.”

וּבַזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית נז רע״א) ״רַע״ לֹא אָמְרוּ אֶלָּא ״מַאן דִּמְחַבֵּל אוֹרְחֵיהּ (זַרְעוֹ)״ כו׳ ״וְיָהֵיב חֵילָא״ כו׳, ״דִּבְהַאי אִסְתְּלִיק שְׁכִינְתָּא מֵעָלְמָא״ כו׳, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם

And in the holy Zohar (Bereishis 57a), the designation “evil” (ra) is applied specifically to “one who corrupts his way” — who gives strength to the spirit of impurity — “for through this the Shechinah departs from the world.” Rav Tzadok will now explain the meaning of that withdrawal.

הַיְינוּ סִילּוּק הַהַשְׁגָּחָה הַפְּרָטִית הַגְּלוּיָה עַל יְדֵי שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּתַּחְתּוֹנִים, שֶׁכָּל כֹּחַ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת דְּרַע בָּעוֹלָם הוּא מִצַּד הִתְעַלְּמוּת הַשְׁגָּחָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּמַרְאִים כְּאִלּוּ הַכֹּל בְּמִקְרֶה

that is, the removal of the revealed particular providence through His Shechinah among the lower ones — for all the power of the spread of evil in the world is from the concealment of His providence, which makes it appear as if all is “by chance mikreh.”

וְזֶהוּ שֹׁרֶשׁ הָרַע וְכָל כֹּחַ עֲמָלֵק שֶׁהוּא ״רֵאשִׁית גּוֹיִם״, דִּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ ״אֲשֶׁר קָרְךָ״, שֶׁרָצָה לְהַכְנִיס בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל דָּבָר זֶה; ורז״ל דְּרָשׁוּהוּ לְשׁוֹן ״קֶרִי״, כִּי גַּם זֶה נִקְרָא בִּלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב ״מִקְרֵה לַיְלָה״

This is the root of evil and of Amalek, the “first of the nations,” concerning whom it says “who happened upon you” (asher karcha; Devarim 25:18). Amalek sought to introduce this sense of chance into Israel. The Sages also expound karcha as connected to keri, and Scripture speaks of a nocturnal emission as a “happening of the night” (mikreh laylah).

שֶׁכַּאֲשֶׁר אֵינוֹ בִּקְדֻשָּׁה וּלְשֵׁם מִצְוָה, רַק עַל יְדֵי הַיֵּצֶר הַנִּקְרָא ״רַע״, נֶחְשָׁב לְ״מִקְרֶה״, שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה כִּבְיָכוֹל עַיִן שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה כְּאִלּוּ אֵינוֹ רוֹאֶה, שֶׁעַל דָּבָר זֶה נִסְמֵית עֵינוֹ שֶׁל אוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע, אָמַר ״מִי שֶׁהוּא קָדוֹשׁ וְטָהוֹר״ כו׳ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּנִדָּה לא סע״א)

for when it is not in holiness and for the sake of a mitzvah, but through the inclination called “evil,” it is reckoned a “chance-happening” — making, as it were, “the eye above” as if it does not see; over which matter the eye of that wicked one Bilaam was blinded, who said, “shall He who is holy and pure gaze at this?” — as they said Niddah 31a.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 77b: Asked why goats go first and sheep follow, the Gemara answers, “כברייתו של עולם, דברישא חשוכא והדר נהורא” — in the order of the world's creation, darkness first and light afterward. This supports only the opening sequence Rav Tzadok invokes here: an obscured beginning can precede illumination. His further application of that pattern to the broken vessels, the unfolding of Mashiach, and teshuvah is a later stage of his own explanation, not a statement made by this Gemara.

paragraphs.text: Tzidkas HaTzadik §206 is a precise parallel in Rav Tzadok's own writings. He writes that “שורש הרע הוא מעולם התוהו ושבירת הכלים”, and connects the shattering with “אנא אמלוך” — the assertion of self-rule — and with the beginning of the yetzer as a movement of thought in the heart. These are Rav Tzadok's kabbalistic formulations, not claims explicitly found in Bereishis Rabbah. The present passage goes on to explain Mashiach as rectifying the root of evil by raising what fell amid shattering; the parallel bears on this completed stage of the argument.

paragraphs.text: Koheles 7:14 reads “גם את זה לעומת זה עשה האלהים” — God made this corresponding to that. The verse juxtaposes a day of prosperity and a day of adversity. Rav Tzadok applies its “זה לעומת זה” wording to the opposed rise of holiness and evil, using the generation of the Flood and Er and Onan as examples. Those instances and the account of opposite spiritual forces are his explanation here; they should not be attributed as the direct content of Koheles.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I, Bereishis 57a distinguishes a person called “רשע” from one called “רע”. It reserves the latter term here for “מאן דמחבל ארחיה וסאיב גרמיה וסאיב ארעא” — someone who corrupts his conduct, himself, and the land — and says that such conduct strengthens “רוח מסאבא”, the unclean spirit, and causes the Shechinah's departure. This is the text Rav Tzadok cites. He next understands the Shechinah's departure as concealment of clearly manifested particular providence, making events seem chance occurrences. That second explanation is Rav Tzadok's; it is not to be inserted into the quoted Zohar itself.

paragraphs.text: Resisei Layla §18 explicitly links Amalek with apparently random events: “לכאורה הגורל נראה מקרה” but in truth “ומה׳ כל משפטו”; Amalek's own pattern is “אשר קרך”, for he “תולה הכל במקרה”. Pri Tzaddik, Emor §13 makes the next implication explicit: Amalek seeks withdrawal of revealed providence from Israel “ויניח אותם למקרה”. These are independently checked parallels in Rav Tzadok's writings. They illuminate the claim made up to this point — Amalek tries to introduce the worldview of chance — before Rav Tzadok develops the additional wordplay concerning keri in the next part of the sentence.

paragraphs.text: Rashi on Devarim 25:18 gives three readings of “אֲשֶׁר קָרְךָ”: “לשון מקרה” — a chance encounter; “לשון קרי וטמאה” — the language of sexual impurity; and “לשון קר וחם” — Amalek cooled the other nations' fear of Israel. Rav Tzadok draws together the first two readings with “מקרה לילה” (Devarim 23:11). The Torah and Rashi establish the wordplay, whereas the suggestion that concealment of Divine providence underlies the bodily phenomenon is Rav Tzadok's further interpretation, which continues into the following phrase.

paragraphs.text: Niddah 31a: R. Abbahu interprets “וּמִסְפַּר אֶת רֹבַע יִשְׂרָאֵל” to mean that the Holy One counts Israel's acts of conception, awaiting the drop from which a righteous child will be formed. When Bilaam objected, “מי שהוא טהור וקדוש ... יציץ בדבר זה”, the Gemara says his eye was blinded, drawing on “שתום העין” (Bamidbar 24:3). The passage thereby directly supports the issue Rav Tzadok raises: how the seemingly bodily can be under the Divine gaze and directed toward holiness. Rav Tzadok's broader contrast of concealment, chance, and holiness is his own development, not an additional ruling of Niddah.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: So is God’s way in creating the world — “first darkness, then light”; He “created worlds and destroyed them” (the worlds of tohu) until the world of tikkun emerged. And precisely through those “destructions” was the world of rectification built, by raising the lights of the “broken vessels.” Mashiach comes to rectify the root of evil in Creation. Hence the sin of the Flood-generation and of Er and Onan: opposite the arousal of holiness rises “this-against-that,” the intensified power of evil — “evil in the eyes of Hashem.”

p: (יד) וּבֶאֱמֶת הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא ״טְהוֹר עֵינַיִם מֵרְאוֹת בְּרָע״; אֲבָל דָּבָר זֶה שֶׁהוּא כְּלַל בְּרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם, דְּ״לֹא תֹהוּ בְרָאָהּ״ וְגוֹמֵר, וּמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה רִאשׁוֹנָה שֶׁצִּיוָּה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְמִין הָאָדָם — אֵיךְ אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בּוֹ רַע וְטוּמְאָה

And in truth the Holy One is “too pure of eyes to look upon evil” (Chavakuk 1:13). Yet this generative act is integral to Creation — “He did not create it for chaos, but formed it to be inhabited” (Yeshayah 45:18) — and to the first affirmative command given to humanity, to be fruitful and multiply. How, then, could it inherently be evil or impure?
אֲבָל כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁעָשָׂה הָאָדָם יָשָׁר נֶאֱמַר ״וְלֹא יִתְבּוֹשָׁשׁוּ״, כִּי לֹא הָיָה בּוֹ תַּאֲוָה גּוּפָנִית שֶׁמִּזֶּה הוּא הַטּוּמְאָה שֶׁבּוֹ, עַל כֵּן לֹא הִרְגִּישׁ בּוּשָׁה

Rather, according to how “God made man upright,” it says “and they were not ashamed” (Bereishis 2:25) — for there was in it no bodily desire, from which is the impurity in it; therefore he felt no shame,

רַק כְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה שֶׁלֹּא בּוֹשׁ לוֹמַר ״הָבָה (אֶת אִשְׁתִּי)״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וְאָבוֹאָה (אֵלֶיהָ)״, מַה שֶּׁקַּל שֶׁבַּקַּלִּים אֵין אוֹמֵר כֵּן, רַק שֶׁהוּא לֹא יָדַע מִכַּוָּנָה אַחֶרֶת אֶלָּא לְהַעֲמִיד תּוֹלָדוֹת, וְלֹא שַׁיָּיךְ בָּזֶה בּוּשָׁה

like Yaakov Avinu, who was not ashamed to say, “give me my wife, that I may come to her” (Bereishis 29:21) — which the lightest of the light would not say — only that he knew no other intent than to raise up offspring, and shame does not apply to that.

אֶלָּא אַחַר הַטָּלַת הַזּוּהֲמָא דְּנָחָשׁ, שֶׁהוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הָרַע שֶׁנִּבְרָא בָּעוֹלָם, וְזֶהוּ ״עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בשוח״ט (ויק״ר יד, ה)) עַל פָּסוּק ״בְּעָוֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי״ ״אֲפִילּוּ חָסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים (אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ צַד אֶחָד מֵעָוֹן)״, ״אִישִׁי אֲבִי דָוִד שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּשַׁבָּת נה:)

This shame arises only after the injection of the “filth zuhama of the serpent,” which is the root of the evil created in the world — and this is “the counsel of the serpent,” as they said in Shocher Tov / Vayikra Rabbah 14:5 on the verse “in iniquity I was fashioned” (Tehillim 51:7), “even the most pious of the pious cannot be entirely without some trace of iniquity”; “my father Yishai, who died only through the counsel of the serpent,” as they said in Shabbos 55b.

וְזֶהוּ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁעָמְדוּ עַל הַר סִינַי שֶׁפָּסְקָה זוּהֲמָתָן כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם קמו רע״א), וְלֵיכָּא רַק ״עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ״; אֲבָל בְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם הוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הַזּוּהֲמָא הַהִיא שֶׁלֹּא פָּסְקָה כְּלָל, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם דְּהֵם מְזוֹהָמִים

And this is the case with Israel who stood at Har Sinai, whose “filth ceased,” as they said Shabbos 146a — leaving only “the counsel of the serpent”; but in the nations it is the root of that filth, which never ceased at all, and as they said there that they are “filthy.”

וּבִלְעָם וַעֲמָלֵק מִשֹּׁרֶשׁ אֶחָד כַּנּוֹדָע וּמוּבָא (בְּלִיקּוּטִים שֶׁבְּסוֹף סֵפֶר דָּן יָדִין) וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ דִּבְאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם קָם (נָבִיא כְּמֹשֶׁה), וּמַנּוּ — בִּלְעָם, שֶׁהָיָה דֻּגְמַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה בִּקְדֻשָּׁה

Bilaam and Amalek are of one spiritual root, as discussed in the Likkutim at the end of Sefer Dan Yadin, and in the Sages’ statement that a prophet arose among the nations comparable to Moshe — Bilaam. Rav Tzadok presents this as a counterpart on the side of impurity, not an equivalence in holiness.

שֶׁהוּא (מֹשֶׁה) שֹׁרֶשׁ הֲסָרַת הַזּוּהֲמָא מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל בְּהוֹרָדַת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁהִיא הַתַּבְלִין לְיֵצֶר הָרָע שֶׁבִּבְרִיאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִידּוּשִׁין ל:) ״בָּרָאתִי יֵצֶר הָרָע בָּרָאתִי תּוֹרָה (תַּבְלִין)״; וְזֶהוּ כֹּחַ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה שֶׁהוֹרִיד לָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה דָּבָר זֶה שֶׁל נִיצּוּחַ הַיֵּצֶר שֶׁבַּתּוֹלָדָה וּבִבְרִיאָה

Moshe, by contrast, is the root of removing this impurity from Israel through bringing the Torah, the antidote to the evil inclination inherent in human existence. As they said (Kiddushin 30b), “I created the evil inclination, and I created the Torah as its remedy.” This is the power Moshe brought into the world: the means of overcoming the yetzer.

וְכֹחַ בִּלְעָם זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה מִצַּד הָרַע, לְהַמְשִׁיךְ וּלְפַשֵּׁט יוֹתֵר כֹּחַ הָרַע שֶׁבַּתּוֹלָדָה, כִּי בּוֹ הָיָה שֹׁרֶשׁ זוּהֲמָא זוֹ דְּנָחָשׁ, דְּעַל כֵּן פָּרַץ גָּדֵר שֶׁל עֲרָיוֹת שֶׁנִּגְדַּר מִימוֹת הַמַּבּוּל

And Bilaam’s power is “this-against-that,” from the side of evil — to draw out and spread further the power of evil in human birth, for in him was the root of that “filth of the serpent”; therefore he “breached the fence of immorality” that had been fenced off since the days of the Flood.
וּמִי שֶׁהוּא מָלֵא זוּהֲמָא אֵין יָכוֹל לְהַאֲמִין כְּלָל שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בָּזֶה קְדֻשָּׁה
And one who is full of filth cannot believe at all that there is holiness in this act.

(וְכֵן אִיתָא (בבר״ר) עַל פָּסוּק ״וַיִּשַּׁק יַעֲקֹב לְרָחֵל״, דְּהָרוֹעִים אָמְרוּ עָלָיו שֶׁבָּא לִפְרוֹץ גָּדֵר עֲרָיוֹת, וְלֹא הֶעֱלוּ עַל לִבָּם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נְשִׁיקָה שֶׁל קוּרְבָה בְּלִי שׁוּם מַחְשָׁבָה לְתַאֲוָה כְּלָל)

And so it is in Bereishis Rabbah on the verse “and Yaakov kissed Rachel” (Bereishis 29:11), that the shepherds said of him that he came “to breach the fence of immorality,” and it did not enter their hearts that it could be a kiss of kinship, with no thought of desire at all.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר עֲמָלֵק ״טוֹל מַה שֶּׁבָּחַרְתָּ״, כִּי אוֹת בְּרִית קֹדֶשׁ שֶׁבִּבְשָׂרָם הוּא הַמֵּעִיד שֶׁגַּם תַּשְׁמִישׁ אֵבֶר זֶה אֵצֶל זֶרַע יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא רַק לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וּבִקְדֻשָּׁה

And therefore Amalek said, “take what you chose” — for the sign of the holy bris in their flesh is what testifies that even the use of this organ, by the seed of Israel, is only for the sake of Heaven and in holiness.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis 1:28 gives the command “פרו ורבו”; Yeshayah 45:18 says of the world, “לא תהו בראה, לשבת יצרה” — God created it to be inhabited. Gittin 41b cites that very verse in the discussion of fulfilling procreation, saying “לא נברא העולם אלא לפריה ורביה”. These texts support Rav Tzadok's opening difficulty: how can a generative act that fulfills a Divine command and a purpose of Creation be intrinsically unclean? His answer, which follows, distinguishes the act from desire affected by the serpent; the cited texts themselves do not supply that later answer.

paragraphs.text: Rashi on Bereishis 2:25 explains “וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ”: although Adam had the intelligence to name animals, “לא נתן בו יצר הרע עד אכלו מן העץ” — the inclination to evil did not enter him until eating from the Tree. Rashi connects the new awareness of good and evil with modesty. Rav Tzadok specifies the theological application here: before the serpent's influence, the bodily faculty existed without a lustful intention that would produce shame. This is his explanation of Rashi, not a claim that the verse itself mentions the serpent's impurity in the sexual sphere.

paragraphs.text: Rashi on Bereishis 29:21 asks how Yaakov could say “וְאָבוֹאָה אֵלֶיהָ” when even a coarse person would not ordinarily speak that way. He explains: “אלא להוליד תולדות אמר כן” — Yaakov intended to establish offspring. Bereishis Rabbah 70:18 provides the fuller discussion of the twelve tribes and Yaakov's age. Rav Tzadok's point is not permissiveness or an ordinary coarse expression: the statement reflects Yaakov's intention of procreation rather than sensual gratification. The source and the explanatory conclusion have both appeared by the end of this phrase.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 14:5 says that even the most pious cannot be wholly independent of the circumstances of conception and explains David’s “בְּעָוֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי” by distinguishing a child’s origin from the parents’ own intention or pleasure. It does not assert that every pious person has personally committed a particular sin. Shabbos 55b, separately, names Yishai among the four who died “בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ” — by consequence of the primordial serpent rather than their own sin. Rav Tzadok combines these separate teachings into his account of a trace of the serpent affecting bodily life even in exceptionally righteous people; this combination is his explanation, not the Midrash’s wording.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 146a teaches: “בָּא נָחָשׁ עַל חַוָּה הֵטִיל בָּהּ זוּהֲמָא” — the serpent introduced spiritual defilement into Chavah — and states that Israel’s defilement ceased at Sinai. The Gemara then explicitly asks about converts and answers “אַף עַל גַּב דְּאִינְהוּ לָא הֲווֹ, מַזָּלַיְיהוּ הֲווֹ” — although they were not physically present, their spiritual destiny was. This mystical teaching is not a biological claim or an exclusion of converts. Rav Tzadok’s distinction between residual “עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ” and the root of this defilement is his own extension, read alongside Shabbos 55b.

paragraphs.text: Likkutei Shoshanim, supplemental gloss ג* (gimel-star) among the “additional selections of R. Shimshon” printed at the end of Sefer Karnayim with the Dan Yadin apparatus, quotes a passage attributed there to “Limmudei HaAri”: “בִּלְעָם וַעֲמָלֵק מִצַּד הַטֻּמְאָה, יִרְאָה אַהֲבָה בַּטֻּמְאָה נֶגֶד יִרְאָה אַהֲבָה בַּקְּדֻשָּׁה. וְהִנֵּה בְּקֶשֶׁר אֶחָד תִּמְצָאֶנּוּ.” Translation: “Bilaam and Amalek belong to the side of impurity; fear and love on the impure side oppose fear and love on the holy side. Behold, you will find them linked in a single configuration.” The supplemental gloss then sets the letters of Bilaam and Amalek in a diagram alongside yirah and ahavah. The editor R. Eizik explicitly presents these materials as additional texts, so this is not an independently verified quotation from the main body of Dan Yadin or from an extant Ari manuscript. The direct text has been verified in the digitized supplement; a facsimile collation of the original printed page remains a separate bibliographic check, not a reason to leave this passage uncited. paragraphs.text: Sifrei Devarim 357:40 explains “וְלֹא קָם נָבִיא עוֹד בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמֹשֶׁה” by saying that among the nations Bilaam arose, immediately contrasting their prophetic modes. It does not equate their moral or spiritual standing. Rav Tzadok's own Pri Tzaddik, Bo §12 calls Bilaam akin to Amalek's kelipah and explains his inability to perceive sanctity in human generation, with reference to Niddah 31a. The preceding Dan Yadin parallel is documented in its own footnote immediately after Rav Tzadok's explicit citation, rather than being repeated late here. The present marker follows the fully developed Bilaam-versus-Moshe argument. Sources: Sifrei Devarim 357:40; Pri Tzaddik, Bo 12; Niddah 31a.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Teitzei §9 reports that the Amalekites “הָיוּ מְחַתְּכִין מְלוֹתֵיהֶם שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל וְזוֹרְקִין כְּלַפֵּי מַעְלָה” — severed Israelites’ circumcisions and cast them upward — taunting: “בָּזֶה בָחַרְתָּ, טַל לְךָ מַה שֶׁבָּחַרְתָּ” — “Is this what You chose? Take what You chose!” The Midrash text reads “טל”; Rav Tzadok cites the expression as “טול”, the equivalent form. Rav Tzadok’s Machshavos Charutz §16 (Har Bracha printed pp. 134–135), together with Peri Tzadik, Bo §12, interprets this derision as an assault on Israel’s covenantal holiness in the physical realm. This theological reading is Rav Tzadok’s, not the Midrash’s literal claim. The note follows Rav Tzadok’s fully developed explanation of the sign of bris; it does not imply that every act is thereby permissible.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: In truth God is “pure of eyes, too pure to look on evil” — but this act is the very foundation of Creation (“He did not create it tohu”) and the first positive commandment. How could it hold evil or impurity? As Adam was made upright, “they were not ashamed,” for there was no bodily desire in it. This is illustrated by Yaakov, who felt no shame saying “give me my wife, that I may come to her,” knowing no intent but to raise offspring.

p: (טו) וְזֶהוּ הַמַּבְדִּיל בֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לָעַמִּים, דְּכָל הַגּוֹיִם עֲרֵלִים, שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לָהֶם לִהְיוֹת נִימּוֹלִים כְּלָל (אִם לֹא שֶׁיִּתְגַּיְּירוּ, דְּאָז הֵם כְּקָטָן שֶׁנּוֹלַד וּבְשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכַנֶּנּוּ)

And this is the distinction between Israel and the nations: even those of the nations who are physically circumcised are not thereby called “circumcised” in the covenantal sense. Upon a genuine conversion, however, a convert is regarded as a newborn and is included in the people called Israel (cf. Yeshayah 44:5).
וַעֲמָלֵק לֹא יָכוֹל לְהַאֲמִין שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אֵצֶל יִשְׂרָאֵל גַּם כֵּן קְדֻשָּׁה בְּדָבָר זֶה כְּלָל, כִּי הַגּוֹיִם לֹא יוּכְלוּ לְהָבִין שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מְצִיאוּת קְדֻשָּׁה כְּלָל בָּזֶה
And Amalek could not believe that there is, by Israel too, holiness in this matter at all — for the nations cannot grasp that there could be any existence of holiness in it.
וּמִזֶּה בְּהֶכְרֵחַ לָהֶם לְסַלֵּק הַשְׁגָּחָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְגַמְרִי,
And from this they are necessarily compelled to remove His blessed providence from this world entirely,

כֵּיוָן שֶׁכְּלַל מְצִיאוּת הַנִּבְרָאִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה דְּלָשֶׁבֶת יְצָרָהּ, לְפִי דַּעְתָּם הַמְזֻהָּם, אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בָּזֶה הַשְׁגָּחַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, דְּאֶפְשָׁר מִי שֶׁהוּא וְכוּלֵּי.

since the whole existence of creatures in this world—“He formed it to be inhabited”—according to their filthy opinion cannot have the providence of Hashem, blessed be He, in it; for, as Bilaam said, “Is it possible that One who is holy and pure would gaze upon this?”
וּמִמֵּילָא כֵּיוָן שֶׁעִקָּר הַהִתְהַוּוּת מִקְרֶה, הֲרֵי הַכֹּל מִקְרֶה,
And automatically, since the origin of coming into being is happenstance, everything is happenstance,
וְזֶהוּ הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ וְהָרֵאשִׁית גּוֹיִם בְּכֹּחַ עֲמָלֵק וּבִלְעָם.
and this is the root, “the first of the nations,” in the power of Amalek and Bilam.

וַעֲמָלֵק הָיָה מֶלֶךְ, כִּי הוּא הַכֶּתֶר דִּקְלִיפָּה, וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא ״רֵאשִׁית״, וְהוּא הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מִכָּל קוֹמַת הַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת דְּרַע, שֶׁבָּא מִזֶּרַע עֵשָׂו הַנִּקְרָא ״יִשְׂרָאֵל מוּמָר״ (בְּקִידּוּשִׁין יח.)

And Amalek was “a king,” for he is “the keser of the kelipah,” and therefore is called “first,” and he is the root above the whole stature of the spread of evil — coming from the seed of Esav, who is called “a Jewish apostate Yisrael mumar” Kiddushin 18a.

וּבִלְעָם שֶׁהִתְפָּאֵר דְּ״יוֹדֵעַ דַּעַת עֶלְיוֹן״ (שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה שֶׁהָיָה בְּסוֹד הַדַּעַת דִּקְדֻשָּׁה) הוּא כֹּחַ הַדַּעַת דִּקְלִיפָּה כַּנּוֹדָע, וְהוּא הַמְחַבֵּר חׇכְמָה וּבִינָה, שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ כֹּחַ הָעַיִן שֶׁמִּתְיַיחֵס לַלֵּב וְלַמּוֹחַ

And Bilaam, who boasted “he knows the knowledge of the Most High” (Bamidbar 24:16) which is over-against Moshe, who was in the secret of holy Da’as, is the power of the Da’as of the kelipah, as is known — the one “joining Chochmah and Binah,” whence comes the power of the eye, which relates to the heart and the brain,
כְּעִנְיַן וְלִבִּי רָאָה הַרְבֵּה חָכְמָה.
as in “and my heart has seen much wisdom.”
וּבַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (כ״ח ע״ב) דְּשׁוּרְיָינָא דְעֵינָא בְּאוּבְנְתָּא דְלִבָּא תָּלֵי,
And Avodah Zarah 28b says: “The vessels of the eye are connected with the membranes of the heart.”
הַיְנוּ בִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמְּקוֹמוֹ בָּרֹאשׁ נֶגֶד הַמֹּחַ.
that is, the Binah in the heart, although its place is in the head, opposite the brain.
כִּי הוּא מִחִיבּוּר שְׁנֵיהֶם, וְאֵל אַחֵר אִסְתָּרֵס, שֶׁאֵין שָׁם הַדַּעַת הַמְחַבֵּר חָכְמָה וּבִינָה כַּנּוֹדָע.
For it comes from the joining of the two, and “the other god is sterile,” for there is no Daas there joining Chochmah and Binah, as is known.

וּלְפִיכָךְ כָּל הַשָּׂגַת בִּלְעָם הָיָה מִצַּד הַקְּדֻשָּׁה, שֶׁהֲרֵי דְּבָרָיו נֶאֶמְרוּ בַּתּוֹרָה הַקְּדוֹשָׁה, וְהוּא נְבוּאַת אֱמֶת, וְכָל נְבוּאָתוֹ עַל מַעֲלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהִכִּיר הָאֱמֶת וּבִיקֵּשׁ עַל נַפְשׁוֹ ״תָּמֹת נַפְשִׁי מוֹת יְשָׁרִים וּתְהִי (אַחֲרִיתִי כָּמֹהוּ)״

And therefore all of Bilaam’s apprehension was from the side of holiness — for his words were said in the holy Torah, and it is “true prophecy,” and all his prophecy was about the greatness of Israel; for he recognized the truth and begged for his own soul, “let my soul die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his” (Bamidbar 23:10).
וּבָנָיו יַנֵּס וִימְבְּרוֹס יָצְאוּ עִם יִשְׂרָאֵל מִמִּצְרַיִם, דְּהֵם הָעֵרֶב רַב שֶׁעָשׂוּ הָעֵגֶל כַּיָּדוּעַ בַּזֹּהַר (וְהוּא כְּמַאן דְּאָמַר שֶׁהוּא הָיָה מִיוֹעֲצֵי פַּרְעֹה)

And his sons Yonos and Yombros joined Israel in leaving Egypt; according to the Zohar, they belonged to the Erev Rav and participated in making the Golden Calf. Rav Tzadok notes that this account follows the tradition that Bilaam was among Pharaoh’s advisers.
וְהִכִּירוּ מַעֲלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּצַּד שָׁרְשָׁם בְּרַע וְזוּהֲמָא לֹא יָכְלוּ לְהַפְרִיד עַצְמָם מִמֶּנָּה.
and they recognized Israel’s greatness, except that due to their root in evil and filth they could not separate themselves from it.

וְעַל כֵּן עַל דָּבָר זֶה נִסְמֵית עֵינוֹ, כִּי כָּל כֹּחַ עֵינוֹ וְהַשָּׂגָתוֹ הוּא מִצַּד שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ אֲחִיזָה מַה בִּקְדֻשָּׁה, עַל יְדֵי מַה שֶּׁיֵּשׁ מְצִיאוּת רַע בָּעוֹלָם, וְ״אַתָּה מְחַיֶּה אֶת כּוּלָּם״ כְּתִיב כַּנּוֹדָע

And therefore over this matter his eye was blinded — for all the power of his eye and apprehension was from the side that he had some grasp in holiness, through the fact that there is an existence of evil in the world, and “You give life to them all” (Nechemiah 9:6) is written, as is known.

וְהוּא הָיָה נֶגֶד הָעַיִן דִּקְדֻשָּׁה, כְּמוֹ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה שֶׁהָיָה רֹאשׁ לְכָל הַסַּנְהֶדְרָאוֹת שֶׁבְּכָל הַדּוֹרוֹת, דְּעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ ״לֹא כָהֲתָה עֵינוֹ״ — כָּךְ הוּא זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה, הִתְפָּאֵר ״אֲשֶׁר מַחֲזֵה (שַׁ-דַּי יֶחֱזֶה)״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וּגְלוּי עֵינָיִם״

And he Bilaam was over-against “the eye of holiness” — like Moshe, who was “head of all the Sanhedrins of all generations,” of whom it says “his eye did not dim” (Devarim 34:7); so is this one, “this-against-that,” who boasted, “who sees the vision of Sha-dai, falling, yet open of eyes” (Bamidbar 24:4).

paragraphs.text: Nedarim 31b; Yevamos 48b — “arelim” and “mulim” as covenantal identity, and conversion as a new birth: The Mishnah rules that one who vows not to benefit from “arelim” may nevertheless benefit from uncircumcised Jews, while he may not benefit from circumcised members of the nations; conversely, a vow concerning “mulim” includes even an uncircumcised Jew and excludes a circumcised non-Jew. It explains that the Torah’s language calls the nations “arelim.” Yevamos states the complementary rule that “a convert who converts is like a newborn child.” These sources supply the precise halachic language behind Rav Tzadok’s opening distinction: the terms here mark covenantal identity, not merely physical condition. This does not exempt an uncircumcised Jew from the mitzvah of milah; it explains why he nevertheless remains within the covenantal category called “mul.”

paragraphs.text: Devarim 25:18 describes Amalek as “אֲשֶׁר קָרְךָ בַדֶּרֶךְ.” Rashi reads “לְשׁוֹן מִקְרֶה” — an encounter by chance — alongside other readings concerning impurity and the cooling of Israel’s fearsome reputation. In Resisei Layla §18 (Har Bracha printed pp. 22–23), Rav Tzadok writes both “שֶׁנִּתְלִים בַּמִּקְרֶה” and, more explicitly, “הוּא תּוֹלֶה הַכֹּל בַּמִּקְרֶה,” contrasting Amalek’s ideology of chance with the Purim lot, whose judgment is from Hashem. Rav Tzadok applies these sources only after he has developed his argument that denying providence at creation makes all subsequent events seem random. Neither the verse nor Rashi alone asserts his full theological argument.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 18a. רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָבִין אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: נׇכְרִי יוֹרֵשׁ אֶת אָבִיו דְּבַר תּוֹרָה, דִּכְתִיב: ״כִּי יְרֻשָּׁה לְעֵשָׂו נָתַתִּי אֶת הַר שֵׂעִיר״. וְדִלְמָא יִשְׂרָאֵל מְשׁוּמָּד שָׁאנֵי? אֶלָּא מֵהָכָא: ״כִּי לִבְנֵי לוֹט נָתַתִּי אֶת עָר יְרֻשָּׁה״. Rav Chiya bar Avin said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name: “A gentile inherits his father by Torah law, as it is written, ‘For I gave Mount Seir to Esav as an inheritance.’ But perhaps a Jewish apostate is different? Rather, derive it from ‘For I gave Ar to the children of Lot as an inheritance.’” The Gemara itself treats Esav as a Jewish apostate and therefore distinguishes him from the ordinary gentile in that proof.

paragraphs.text: Avodah Zarah 28b: “עין שמרדה — מותר לכוחלה בשבת ... דשורייני דעינא באובנתא דליבא תלו.” In the medical discussion, a dangerous eye condition may justify treatment on Shabbos because the eye’s vessels are connected with the heart. Rashi explains this as “מאור העין מעורין ואחוזין בטרפשי הלב.” The Gemara does not itself identify the “heart” with the sefirah of Binah or the eye with the union of Chochmah and Binah. Those are the subsequent symbolic interpretations Rav Tzadok develops, and should not be placed in the source quotation.

paragraphs.text: Bamidbar 24:20 calls Amalek “רֵאשִׁית גּוֹיִם.” Rav Tzadok, Machshavos Charutz §16 (Har Bracha printed pp. 134–135), explicitly writes “כִּי עֲמָלֵק הוּא הָרֵאשִׁית וְהַכֶּתֶר דִּקְלִיפָּה” — Amalek is the beginning and crown of the kelipah — and associates Bilaam, who says “יֹדֵעַ דַּעַת עֶלְיוֹן,” with “הַדַּעַת דִּקְלִיפָּה.” Resisei Layla §52:7 likewise develops the cosmic opposition of Amalek and Bilaam to Moshe. These are Rav Tzadok’s own interpretive parallels, not the literal content of Bamidbar 24:20. The note follows his completed Daas/Chochmah/Binah argument so that it is neither too early nor too late.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II, Ki Tisa 191a, identifies the Egyptian sorcerers leading the Erev Rav as “יוֹנוֹס וְיִמְבְּרוּס.” Zohar III, Balak 194a, identifies them as “תְּרֵין בְּנוֹהִי” — two sons of Bilaam — and discusses their role in the Golden Calf episode. These are the precise conventional folio locations, verified against the Zohar text; alternate digital numbering reads Ki Tisa 11:61 and Balak 13:174. Rav Tzadok’s next conclusion, that their root in evil prevented their separation from it despite recognizing Israel’s greatness, is his theological interpretation, not a claim quoted verbatim from these Zohar lines.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:6; Devarim 34:7; Bamidbar 24:4 — Moshe over the seventy elders and the undimmed “eye of holiness”: The Mishnah derives the seventy-one-member Great Sanhedrin from “gather Me seventy men” together with “Moshe over them,” placing Moshe at the head of the foundational court. The Torah then closes his life with “his eye had not dimmed.” Bilaam, by contrast, boasts of himself as one who sees the vision of Sha-dai, “falling, yet open of eyes.” Rav Tzadok joins these verses typologically: Moshe’s undimmed eye represents the governing eye of holy da’as, while Bilaam is its opposing imitation. The phrase “head of all the Sanhedrins of all generations” is Rav Tzadok’s extension of the Mosaic model; the Mishnah itself speaks directly of Moshe standing over the original seventy elders.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: This is what divides Israel from the nations: “all the nations are arelim,” unable to be truly “circumcised” (save by conversion, when they are “as a newborn”). Amalek cannot believe holiness could inhere in this act, and so must strip all providence from the world, reducing everything to “chance mikreh.” Amalek is the “keser of the kelipah,” root of all evil’s spread, of Esav’s seed (“a Jewish apostate”).

p: (טז) אֲבָל כָּל מַה שֶּׁנִּתְגַּלָּה לוֹ הָיָה רַק לְצֹרֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְעַל כֵּן נִכְתַּב בַּתּוֹרָה עַל יְדֵי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה שֶׁהוֹצִיא ״בָּלְעוֹ מִפִּיו״, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה פָּעַל שֶׁלֹּא תִּשְׁרֶה עוֹד שְׁכִינָה עַל אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם

But all that was revealed to him was only for the sake of Israel; therefore it was written in the Torah through Moshe Rabbeinu, who “brought forth the swallowed prey from his mouth” (cf. Iyov 20:15) — and through this he effected that the Shechinah would no longer rest upon the nations.

וְאַף בִּלְעָם, אַחַר שֶׁנִּקְלַט מִמֶּנּוּ הַנִּיצוֹצוֹת קְדוֹשׁוֹת, חָזַר לִהְיוֹת קוֹסֵם (וְהוּא רַבָּן שֶׁל כָּל הַקּוֹסְמִים וְהַמְכַשְּׁפִים, שֶׁכּוּלָּם מְקַבְּלִים מִבִּלְעָם וּמִמְּקוֹם קִבְרוֹ וְעַצְמוֹתָיו כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ, וְדֻגְמַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה בִּקְדֻשָּׁה, רַבָּן שֶׁל כָּל הַנְּבִיאִים, וְכוּלָּן מְקַבְּלִין נְבוּאָתָן מִמֹּשֶׁה, וְנִרְמְזוּ בִּלְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא (נְדָרִים לח.) ״וְכוּלָּן מִמֹּשֶׁה״ וְכַנּוֹדָע)

Even Bilaam, after the holy elements had been drawn out of his prophecy, returned to being a diviner. Rav Tzadok describes him, on the side of impurity, as the counterpart to Moshe, the master of the prophets, and says that all diviners draw from Bilaam, even from his grave and bones, as he cites from the Zohar. He further finds an allusion to the prophets receiving through Moshe in the Gemara’s phrase “and all from Moshe” (Nedarim 38a). The Gemara itself uses that phrase for qualities learned from Moshe; the prophetic meaning is Rav Tzadok’s allusion.
וְעַצְמוּתוֹ הָיָה ״שְׁתוּם הָעַיִן״, כִּי אֵין לוֹ הַשָּׂגָה בְּעַיִן דִּקְדֻשָּׁה כְּלָל
And his essence was “blind of eye shesum ha’ayin,” for he has no apprehension in the “eye of holiness” at all.
וּבֶאֱמֶת לְגַבֵּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נֶאֱמַר ״כָּל חֹשֶׁךְ לֹא יַחְשִׁיךְ (מִמֶּךָּ)״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְנֶאֱמַר ״אֲנִי ה׳ הַשּׁוֹכֵן אִתָּם בְּתוֹךְ טוּמְאֹתָם״
Concerning Hashem, the verse says, “Even darkness is not dark to You” (Tehillim 139:12), and Scripture speaks of Him “dwelling with them amid their impurity” (Vayikra 16:16).

שֶׁאַף דְּהַטּוּמְאָה הוּא הֵפֶךְ דְּטָהֳרָה וְהַקְּדֻשָּׁה, וּמִצַּד הַהִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה נִרְאֶה שֶׁהַטּוּמְאָה מְסַלֶּקֶת קְדֻשָּׁה — זֶהוּ מִצַּד הַאי עָלְמָא דְּשִׁקְרָא; אֲבָל יִשְׂרָאֵל זֶרַע אֱמֶת מַכִּירִים הָאֱמֶת, דְּאִי אֶפְשָׁר מְצִיאוּת שׁוּם דָּבָר בְּלֹא כֹּחַ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַמְּחַיֵּיהוּ

For although impurity is the opposite of purity and holiness, and from the side of revelation in this world it appears that impurity “removes” holiness — that is only from the side of this “world of falsehood”; but Israel, “seed of truth,” recognize the truth: that it is impossible for anything to exist without the power of Hashem that enlivens it.

וַאֲפִילּוּ הוּא בְּתַכְלִית הַהֶעְלֵם וּמְשׁוּקָּע בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁנִּשְׁתַּקַּע, וְגַם ״כִּי אֵלֵךְ בְּגֵיא צַלְמָוֶת״, שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הַחוֹשֶׁךְ דְּ״אַחְשֵׁךְ אַנְפֵּי בִּרְיָיתָא״, ״לֹא אִירָא רָע״ — שֶׁהוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הָרַע הַנּוֹתֵן כֹּחַ לְטוּמְאָה וְצַלְמָוֶת וּמְסַלֵּק הַשְּׁכִינָה — לֹא אִירָא מִזֶּה, ״כִּי אַתָּה עִמָּדִי״ גַּם שָׁם

And even if it is in the ultimate concealment, sunk in the place where it sank, and even “though I walk in the valley of the shadow of death” — which is the ultimate darkness that “darkened the face of Creation” — “I will fear no evil”: no fear of the root of evil that gives power to impurity and death-shadow and removes the Shechinah — “I will fear” it not, “for You are with me” even there.
וּמִמֵּילָא כְּשֶׁמַּאֲמִין וּמַכִּיר זֶה נִסְתַּלֵּק הָרַע, דְּ״לֹא יְגוּרְךָ רָע״; וְעַל כֵּן אֲפִילּוּ עַרְלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָאִים ״מוּלִים״, דַּאֲפִילּוּ חָטָא, יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא

Consequently, when a person recognizes this Divine presence, the notion that evil constitutes a power independent of Hashem falls away, as in “evil shall not sojourn with You” (Tehillim 5:5). Therefore even uncircumcised Israelites are termed “circumcised” in covenantal language: although a Jew may sin, he remains a Jew. This does not nullify the prohibition or the need for teshuvah.

paragraphs.text: Bava Basra 14b: “משה כתב ספרו ופרשת בלעם ואיוב” — Moshe wrote his book, the portion concerning Bilaam, and Iyov. Sifrei Devarim 357 distinguishes Moshe’s prophecy from Bilaam’s, while acknowledging that a prophet arose among the nations. These sources establish that the truthful portion of Bilaam’s words is preserved in the Torah through Moshe; Rav Tzadok’s image of drawing the swallowed element from Bilaam is his interpretation. The baraisa does not itself teach the extraction of “sparks.”

paragraphs.text: Berachos 7a; Bava Basra 15b; Peri Tzadik, Kedushas Shabbos 7:32 — Moshe’s request that prophecy cease from the nations, and Bilaam’s revelation only for Israel: Berachos records that Moshe asked that the Shechinah not rest upon the nations, and that his request was granted from “and we shall be distinguished, I and Your people” (Shemos 33:16). Bava Basra therefore reasons that after Moshe’s death the Shechinah no longer rested upon a prophet of the nations. Rav Tzadok supplies the inner complement: in Peri Tzadik he writes that Bilaam, “head of the sages of the nations,” attained the truth of Israel’s greatness, but the nations apprehend only what Hashem reveals to them “for the sake of Israel.” This closely parallels the opening of the present se’if: Bilaam’s true prophetic content was extracted into Israel’s Torah, while the independent channel of gentile prophecy was closed.

paragraphs.text: Zohar, Balak III 194b, paragraphs 181–182, supplies the source behind Rav Tzadok's description of sorcery connected with Bilaam's remains. It says “וְגַרְמוֹי כֻּלְּהוּ אִתְרְקָבוּ” — all his bones decayed — and describes the resulting serpents. It then says “אִי יְדַע טִנָּרָא דְּנָפַל תַּמָּן בִּלְעָם, יִשְׁכַּח מֵאִינּוּן חִוְיָין דַּהֲווֹ מִגַּרְמוֹי” — one who knew the rock at which Bilaam fell could find serpents produced from his bones, associated there with sorcery. Critically, the immediately preceding Zohar states “וְלָא אִתְקְבִיר לְעָלְמִין” — Bilaam was never buried. Thus Rav Tzadok's “מִמְּקוֹם קִבְרוֹ וְעַצְמוֹתָיו” is an expansive description of the site and remains, not an exact Zohar quotation asserting a literal grave. Separately, Nedarim 38a's “וְכוּלָּן מִמֹּשֶׁה” refers in its straightforward setting to four qualities inferred from Moshe; the application to all prophets' reception through Moshe is Rav Tzadok's allusive contrast with Bilaam's followers. Sources: Zohar, Balak III 194b, §§181–182; Nedarim 38a.

paragraphs.text: Tehillim 139:12 says “גַּם חֹשֶׁךְ לֹא יַחְשִׁיךְ מִמֶּךָּ,” and Vayikra 16:16 describes the One “הַשֹּׁכֵן אִתָּם בְּתוֹךְ טֻמְאֹתָם.” Yoma 57a — not 56b — expressly teaches “אֲפִלּוּ בִּזְמַן שֶׁהֵן טְמֵאִין שְׁכִינָה שְׁרוּיָה בֵּינֵיהֶן.” Rav Tzadok, Sichat Malakhei HaSharet 4:29, gives a direct parallel: “שֶׁהַשְּׁכִינָה ... שׁוֹכֵן בְּתוֹךְ טֻמְאוֹתָם ... טָמוּן בְּלֵב כָּל אִישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל אַף בְּעֵת הֱיוֹתוֹ בְּתַכְלִית הַמֶּרְחָק” — the Divine presence remains concealed in a Jew’s heart even in profound distance. This is a description of Divine indwelling, not permission to transgress or a denial of the laws of impurity; the following paragraphs develop Rav Tzadok’s explanation.

paragraphs.text: Tehillim 23:4 declares: “גם כי אלך בגיא צלמות לא אירא רע כי אתה עמדי”; Tehillim 5:5 adds “לא יגורך רע.” Divrei Soferim §32 makes a careful distinction: one deliverance is removal from darkness, whereas another is the discovery “כי אתה עמדי” even while still in darkness; the latter is a genuine salvation without yet asserting that all external difficulty has vanished. Machshavos Charutz §9 says that recognizing Hashem’s presence in the valley makes return possible. This clarifies Rav Tzadok’s point that evil has no independent domain beside Hashem, without interpreting it as permission for wrongdoing.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: All that was revealed to Bilaam was only for Israel’s sake — hence written in the Torah by Moshe, who “drew the swallowed prey from his mouth,” ending the resting of prophecy on the nations. Once the holy sparks were absorbed from him, Bilaam reverted to mere sorcery (the kelipah-counterpart of Moshe, master of the prophets). His essence is “blind of eye” — no grasp of the “eye of holiness.”

p: (יז) אֲבָל דָּבָר זֶה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַדּוֹמֶה לְלַיְלָה הוּא בְּתַכְלִית הַהֶעְלֵם, דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא בְּסָבָא דְּמִשְׁפָּטִים (צה.) ״עוּלֶמְתָּא שַׁפִּירְתָּא דְּלֵית לָהּ עַיְינִין״ — אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעִיקַּר הַיֹּפִי בָּעֵינַיִם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ״כָּל כַּלָּה שֶׁעֵינֶיהָ יָפוֹת (אֵין כָּל גּוּפָהּ צָרִיךְ בְּדִיקָה)״ כו׳, אֲבָל הֵם בְּהֶעְלֵם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

But in this world, which “resembles night,” that reality is concealed to the utmost. Thus the Saba deMishpatim (Zohar II 95a) speaks of “a beautiful maiden who has no eyes.” Although the main beauty is in the eyes, as our Sages say, “When a bride’s eyes are beautiful, her entire body requires no examination,” those eyes are concealed in this world.

וְזֶה שֹׁרֶשׁ הֲסָתַת הַנָּחָשׁ ״וְנִפְקְחוּ עֵינֵיכֶם וִהְיִיתֶם (כֵּאלֹקִים יֹדְעֵי טוֹב וָרָע)״ — הַיְינוּ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא יוֹדֵעַ טוֹב וָרַע בְּשָׁוֶה, דְּיוּכַל לְהִסְתַּכֵּל עַל שְׁנֵיהֶם יַחַד, וְכוּלָּן בִּסְקִירָה אַחַת, כִּי הַשְׁגָּחָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל הַכֹּל, דְּהוּא מְחַיֶּה אֶת הַכֹּל וְאֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ, וַאֲפִילּוּ בִּמְקוֹם טוּמְאָה

And this is the root of the serpent’s enticement: “and your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be like God, knowing good and evil” (Bereishis 3:5) — that is, Hashem “knows good and evil equally,” able to gaze upon both together, all in a single glance, for His providence is over all, for He enlivens all and “there is none besides Him,” even in a place of impurity.

אֲבָל עַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר ״קְדוֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ, יָכוֹל כָּמוֹנִי? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר (כִּי קָדוֹשׁ אֲנִי — קְדֻשָּׁתִי לְמַעְלָה מִקְּדֻשַּׁתְכֶם)״ (ויק״ר כה, ט) — הַיְינוּ דְּלֹא יַעֲלֶה עַל דַּעַת אָדָם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה גַּם כֵּן קָדוֹשׁ כִּבְיָכוֹל כָּמוֹהוּ, שֶׁכָּל טוּמְאָה לֹא תְּטַמְּאֶנּוּ, דְּזֶהוּ רַק קְדֻשָּׁתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ

But regarding this it says, “you shall be holy” — could it mean “like Me”? — Scripture teaches otherwise: “for I am holy” — My holiness is above your holiness (Vayikra Rabbah 24:9) — meaning, let it not enter a person’s mind that he could be holy, as it were, like Him, whom no impurity defiles, for that is His holiness alone.

אֲבָל הָאָדָם הַמְשׁוּקָּע בְּרַע כְּאוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע אֵין יָכוֹל לִרְאוֹת וּלְהַשִּׂיג הַטּוֹב; וּמִי שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ דָּבוּק בַּטּוֹב כְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע״ה וְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא, אֵינוֹ רוֹאֶה וּמַשִּׂיג הָרַע, וּלְפִיכָךְ לֹא הָיָה לוֹ בּוּשָׁה, כִּי לֹא הִשִּׂיגוּ צַד רַע שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּזֶה כְּלָל

But the person “sunk in evil,” like that wicked one, cannot see and attain the good; and one wholly cleaving to the good, like Avraham Avinu and Adam before the sin, does not see or apprehend the evil — and therefore he had no shame, for they apprehended no “evil side” in this at all.

וְהַנָּחָשׁ הִסִּיתָם שֶׁיּוּכְלוּ לְהִתְדַּמּוֹת לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁהֵם בִּקְדֻשָּׁה כָּזוֹ שֶׁיּוּכְלוּ לִהְיוֹת פִּקּוּחֵי עֵינַיִם כֵּאלֹקִים, לָדַעַת וּלְהַשִּׂיג טוֹב וָרַע יַחַד, וְכָל טִינּוֹפֶת לֹא תְּטַנְּפֵם

And the serpent enticed them that they could liken themselves to Hashem — that they are in such holiness that they could be “open of eyes like God,” to know and apprehend good and evil together, and no filth would soil them.

אֲבָל תֵּיכֶף מִשֶּׁנִּפְקְחוּ עֵינֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם לְהִסְתַּכֵּל בְּרַע, דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּאוּ לִידֵי בּוּשָׁה, בִּיקְּשׁוּ לְסַמּוֹת רַחֲמָנָא לִיצְלַן ״עֵינוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם״, שֶׁחָשְׁבוּ כִּבְיָכוֹל עַיִן שֶׁל מַעְלָה כְּאִינוֹ רוֹאֶה, שֶׁיּוּכְלוּ לְהִתְחַבֵּא מִמֶּנּוּ — וְזֶהוּ שֹׁרֶשׁ הַזּוּהֲמָא וְהָרַע שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם

But immediately when the eyes of both were opened to gaze on evil — through which they came to shame — they sought to blind, God spare us, “the eye of the world,” for they thought, as it were, that “the eye above” does not see, that they could hide from it — and this is the root of the filth and the evil in the world.

וּבִירוּשַׁלְמִי (דִּבְרָכוֹת) ״עַיִן וָלֵב שְׁנֵי סַרְסוּרֵי (דַּעֲבֵירָה)״, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״לֹא תָתוּרוּ (אַחֲרֵי לְבַבְכֶם וְאַחֲרֵי עֵינֵיכֶם)״, וְהַהַתְחָלָה הוּא מֵהָעַיִן רוֹאָה, וְאַחַר כָּךְ לֵב חוֹמֵד, וּכְלִי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה גּוֹמְרִים

The Yerushalmi (Berachos 1:5) calls “the heart and the eye two intermediaries of sin,” based on “Do not go astray after your heart and after your eyes” (Bamidbar 15:39). Rav Tzadok then states the order: the eye sees, the heart desires, and the bodily organs complete the action.

וְכֵן הָיָה חֵטְא הָרִאשׁוֹן עַל יְדֵי הָעַיִן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וַתֵּרֶא הָאִשָּׁה״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וְכִי תַאֲוָה הוּא לָעֵינַיִם״; וְאַחַר כָּךְ בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל בָּאוּ לַלֵּב הַחוֹמֵד, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וְכָל יֵצֶר מַחְשְׁבֹת לִבּוֹ רַק (רַע)״ וְגוֹמֵר

And so the first sin was through the eye, as it says, “and the woman saw that the tree was good for food and that it was a delight to the eyes” (Bereishis 3:6); and afterward, in the generation of the Flood, they came to “the coveting heart,” as it says, “and every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil” (Bereishis 6:5).

paragraphs.text: Zohar, Saba deMishpatim (Zohar, Mishpatim 3:15; II 95a) asks: “מַהוּ עוּלֵימְתָּא שַׁפִּירְתָּא, וְלֵית לָהּ עֵיינִין” — “What is a beautiful maiden who has no eyes?” The riddle is genuinely present at this location. Rav Tzadok applies this Zoharic image to the hidden beauty of spiritual vision in the world that resembles night; the Zohar’s question alone does not assert all his later conclusions.

paragraphs.text: Ta’anis 24a:13 teaches: “כָּל זְמַן שֶׁעֵינֶיהָ יָפוֹת — אֵין כָּל גּוּפָהּ צְרִיכָה בְּדִיקָה,” in the parable of a bride whose sound eyes indicate that her entire body does not need examination. Shir HaShirim Rabbah 4:1:3 also gives this saying while discussing the Sanhedrin. The metaphor concerns perception and leadership, not a literal test of physical beauty. Rav Tzadok takes the image of beautiful eyes as a way of speaking about spiritual apprehension, which he has just contrasted with concealment.

paragraphs.text: Devarim 4:35 declares “אֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ.” In Sanhedrin 67b Rabbi Chanina applies the principle “אַפִּלּוּ לִדְבַר כְּשָׁפִים.” The Gemara then qualifies the incident by distinguishing Rabbi Chanina’s exceptional merits, “דְּנָפִישׁ זְכוּתֵיהּ”; it does not instruct others to seek danger or transgression. Rav Tzadok invokes Hashem’s unique all-encompassing providence, including over places described as impure. This is a theological account of Divine sovereignty, not a license for a person to expose himself to sin.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 24:9, commenting on Vayikra 19:2, asks “קְדֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ — יָכוֹל כָּמוֹנִי?” and answers “כִּי קָדוֹשׁ אֲנִי — קְדֻשָּׁתִי לְמַעְלָה מִקְּדֻשַּׁתְכֶם.” The inherited Hebrew manuscript currently labels this “ויק״ר כה, ט”, an inaccurate chapter number; the verified citation is 24:9. The Hebrew source wording is preserved pending comparison with a printed Takanas HaShavin witness; the revised scholarly note supplies the accurate locus. Rav Tzadok's prohibition against imagining oneself immune to spiritual impurity is his explanation of the Midrash and the immediately developed issue, not a quotation from it. paragraphs.text: Bereishis 2:25; Rashi — Adam’s lack of shame before the sin: On “they were both naked … and were not ashamed,” Rashi explains that Adam and Chavah did not yet know the mode of modesty that distinguishes good from evil. Adam certainly possessed intellect — he had already named the creatures — but the yetzer hara had not entered him until he ate from the tree; only then did experiential knowledge of good and evil enter. This closely matches Rav Tzadok’s formulation: before the sin Adam could not “see” the evil side in the bodily reality, and therefore nakedness did not yet produce shame.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis 3:7–10; Tehillim 139:7–12 — opened eyes, shame, and the attempt to hide: The Torah itself places the stages in immediate sequence: “the eyes of both were opened,” they knew they were naked and made coverings; they then heard Hashem in the garden and “the man and his wife hid,” with Adam explaining, “I was afraid because I was naked, so I hid.” Tehillim states the opposite theological truth: there is nowhere to flee from His presence, and even darkness is not dark before Him. Rav Tzadok reads the narrative sequence homiletically as the first attempt to behave as though the “eye above” could be screened from human conduct; that deeper characterization is his interpretation of the Torah’s juxtaposition.

paragraphs.text: Yerushalmi, Berachos 1:5:3: Rabbi Levi says, “לִיבָּא וְעֵינָא תְּרֵין סַרְסוּרֵי דְחַטְאָה” — the heart and eye are two intermediaries of sin. Rashi on Bamidbar 15:39 explains the causal sequence: “הָעַיִן רוֹאָה וְהַלֵּב חוֹמֵד וְהַגּוּף עוֹשֶׂה אֶת הָעֲבֵרָה” — the eye sees, the heart desires, and the body acts. The Yerushalmi names the two intermediaries; Rashi supplies the explicit ordered sequence cited by Rav Tzadok. The next paragraph will then apply that order to Adam and the Flood generation.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: This matter, in this world “resembling night,” is in ultimate concealment — hence in the Saba d’Mishpatim it is “a beautiful maiden who has no eyes,” for though beauty’s essence is in the eyes, here they are hidden. This was the serpent’s enticement: “your eyes will be opened, and you shall be like God, knowing good and evil.” For God “knows good and evil equally,” gazing on both in a single glance, His providence over all, “there is none besides Him” even amid impurity.

p: (יח) וּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל מִתְפָּאֶרֶת ״אֲנִי יְשֵׁנָה וְלִבִּי עֵר״, וְדָרְשׁוּ רז״ל (בשהש״ר) ״זֶה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא״, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״צוּר לְבָבִי״ וְגוֹמֵר

And Knesses Yisrael boasts, “I am asleep, but my heart is awake” (Shir HaShirim 5:2), which the Sages expounded in Shir HaShirim Rabbah, “‘my heart’ — this is the Holy One,” as it says, “the Rock of my heart and my portion is God forever” (Tehillim 73:26).

דְּאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיְּשֵׁנִים מִן הַמִּצְוֹת וְלֵית לְהוּ עַיְנִין, כִּבְעֵת הַשֵּׁינָה דְּהָעַיְנִין סְתוּמִים וְהַלֵּב מְשׁוּקָּע בְּדִמְיוֹנוֹת, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מֵאַחַר שֶׁשֹּׁרֶשׁ הַנֶּפֶשׁ ״חֵלֶק אֱלוֹקַּ״, וּמַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב דָּבוּק בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, הֲרֵי גַּם כָּל הַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת דָּבוּק בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ

For although they “sleep from the mitzvos” and “have no eyes” — as in the time of sleep, when the eyes are shut and the heart is sunk in imaginings — nonetheless, since the root of the soul is “a portion of God,” and the depths of the heart cleave to Hashem, then even all the imaginings cleave to Hashem.

וְאַף בְּעֵת תַּכְלִית הַהִשְׁתַּקְּעוּת בְּדִמְיוֹנוֹת הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַמַּעֲלִימִים הָאֱמֶת לַאֲמִיתּוֹ, יֵשׁ בּוֹ כֹּחַ הִתְעוֹרְרוּת לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִצַּד דְּבֵיקוּת הַלֵּב בֵּאלֹקִים חַיִּים

And even in the moment of the ultimate sinking in the imaginings of this world, which conceal the absolute truth, there is in him a power of “awakening” to Hashem, from the side of the cleaving of the heart to the living God.
וְזֶה טַעַם קְרִיאַת יְהוּדָה שֵׁם בְּנוֹ ״עֵר״ עַל שֵׁם ״וְלִבִּי עֵר״
This is why Yehudah called his son “Er” (עֵר), evoking the words “but my heart is awake” (וְלִבִּי עֵר).

דְּאַחַר מְכִירַת יוֹסֵף שֶׁהוֹרִידוּהוּ מִגְּדֻלָּתוֹ — דִּלְעוֹלָם אַחַר הַמַּעֲשֶׂה, וּבִפְרָט צַדִּיקִים כְּמוֹהֶם, הִרְגִּישׁוּ הָאֱמֶת — דְּיוֹסֵף הָיָה קְדֻשַּׁת הַיְסוֹד בְּרִית קֹדֶשׁ שֶׁבְּקוֹמַת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה וּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל

For after the sale of Yosef, when his brothers brought Yehudah down from his greatness — for always, after the deed, and especially tzaddikim like them, they felt the truth — that Yosef was the holiness of Yesod, the holy bris, in the stature of Yaakov Avinu and Knesses Yisrael.
דְּעַל כֵּן אָמַר "כִּי אֵרֵד (אֶל בְּנִי אָבֵל שְׁאֹלָה)",
Therefore he said, “for I will go down (to my son mourning, to the grave),”
שֶׁחָשַׁב שֶׁחָזַר הַקִּלְקוּל לִמְקוֹמוֹ,
for he thought that the damage had returned to its place,
וְשֶׁחַיָּה רָעָה אֲכָלָתְהוּ לְאֵבֶר הַבְּרִית קֹדֶשׁ הַמַּבְדִּיל בֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לָעַמִּים.
and that “a wild beast devoured him”—the organ of the holy covenant, which distinguishes between Israel and the nations.
כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם עַל יְדֵי הַמְּכִירָה, שֶׁהָיָה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם נִטְמָע בֵּין הָעַמִּים אִלְמָלֵא דְמוּת דְּיוֹקְנוֹ שֶׁל אָבִיו שֶׁהִצִּילַתּוּ.
As it would have been, Heaven forbid, through the sale—that he would, Heaven forbid, have been absorbed among the nations, had the image of his father not saved him.
הַיְנוּ הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ שֶׁהָיָה בּוֹ מֵאָבִיו יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם דְּמִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵמָה בֶּאֱמֶת, שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ פְּסֹלֶת כְּלָל.
That is, he was saved by the root inherited from his father, Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, whose “bed”—his offspring—was spiritually complete, without any defective branch.
וְלֹא כְּמוֹ עֵשָׂו שֶׁנִּמּוֹל גַּם כֵּן לִשְׁמוֹנָה וְהָיָה מִלֵּידָה יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲבָל נִקְרָא "יִשְׂרָאֵל מוּמָר",

Unlike Esav, who was circumcised on the eighth day and whom Rav Tzadok describes as an “Israelite from birth” at that earlier stage of the patriarchal lineage, yet whom Kiddushin 18a refers to hypothetically as “an apostate Israelite,”
שֶׁהָיָה בְּיָדוֹ עֲדַיִן לְהָמִיר וְלַעֲקֹר עַצְמוֹ מִשֹּׁרֶשׁ הַקְּדֻשָּׁה שֶׁהָיָה בּוֹ מֵאֲבוֹתָיו.
for it was still in his power to apostatize and uproot himself from the root of holiness inherited from his forefathers.
מָה שֶׁאֵין כֵּן זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב, אֲפִילוּ יַגְדִּיל עֲוֹנוֹת זוֹ לְמַעְלָה מִזּוֹ וְיִטְמַע בָּעַמִּים, אִי אֶפְשָׁר לַעֲקֹר מִמֶּנּוּ שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּלָל.
Not so the seed of Yaakov: even if he were to pile up sins one above the other and be absorbed among the nations, it is impossible to uproot the name Israel from him at all.

וְאָז בְּהַתְחָלַת בִּנְיַן הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל הָיָה עֲדַיִין דָּבָר זֶה צָרִיךְ לְבֵירוּרִים, וְעַד שֶׁלֹּא נִתְבָּרֵר בְּיוֹסֵף שֶׁעָמַד בַּנִּסָּיוֹן — שֶׁעַל שְׁמוֹ נִקְרָא כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל ״שְׁאֵרִית יוֹסֵף״ — לֹא יָדְעוּ זֶה עֲדַיִין

And then, at the beginning of the building of Knesses Yisrael, this matter still required clarifications; and until it was clarified through Yosef, who “withstood the test” — for whom all Israel is called “the remnant of Yosef” (Amos 5:15) — they did not yet know this.

וּלְפִיכָךְ חָשְׁבוּ הַשְּׁבָטִים שֶׁמִּמֵּילָא יֵשׁ הוֹרָדָה גַּם כֵּן לִגְדֻלַּת יְהוּדָה, שֶׁהוּא הַמֶּלֶךְ בָּעָם — שֶׁבִּמְקוֹם הַלֵּב בַּגּוּף כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֵפֶר יְצִירָה — וְאֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּלֹא עָם וְלֹא לֵב בְּלִי גּוּף

And therefore the tribes thought that, consequently, there is a “lowering” also to Yehudah’s greatness — he being “the king among the people,” who is “in the place of the heart in the body,” as they said in Sefer Yetzirah — and “there is no king without a people,” nor a heart without a body;
וְכֵיוָן שֶׁחָשְׁבוּ שֶׁנִּתְקַלְקֵל חַס וְשָׁלוֹם כָּל בִּנְיַן קוֹמַת הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְהָעָם אֶחָד, מִמֵּילָא אֵין מָקוֹם וּמְצִיאוּת לְמַלְכוּתוֹ גַּם כֵּן
and since they thought that the whole building of the stature of Knesses Yisrael and “the one people” was corrupted, God forbid, then of itself there is no place or existence for his kingship either.

וִיהוּדָה, דְּיָדַע בְּנַפְשֵׁיהּ דִּלְבָבוֹ דָּבוּק בֶּאֱמֶת בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ — דְּעַל כֵּן כּוּלּוֹ נִקְרָא עַל שֵׁם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְכֵן ״כָּל הַכּוֹפֵר בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה נִקְרָא יְהוּדִי״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל (מְגִילָּה יג.) — יָרַד מֵאֵת אֶחָיו לְתַקֵּן זֶה בְּעַצְמוֹ

And Yehudah, who knew in himself that his heart truly cleaves to Hashem — for which reason he is wholly “called by the Name of Hashem,” and likewise “whoever denies idolatry is called a Yehudi,” as the Sages said (Megillah 13a) — “went down from his brothers” to rectify this in himself.
דְּחָשַׁב שֶׁאֶחָיו וַדַּאי כַּדִּין הוֹרִידוּהוּ, דְּהֵם הִרְגִּישׁוּ קִלְקוּל בְּנַפְשָׁם מִזֶּה, אֲבָל הַקִּלְקוּל לֹא נָגַע עֲדַיִין עַד הַלֵּב וְלֹא הִגִּיעַ לוֹ
for he thought his brothers had certainly rightly brought him down, since they felt a corruption in their soul from this — but the corruption did not yet reach the heart and did not touch it;
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכָּל קוֹמַת הַגּוּף הוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם וְהַסְתֵּר פָּנִים מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, עֲדַיִין ״לִבִּי עֵר״ וְדָבוּק בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ; וְזֶה הָיָה הַמְשָׁכַת נֶפֶשׁ ״עֵר״ בָּעוֹלָם

and although the whole “stature of the body” is in concealment and “hiding of the face” from Hashem, still “my heart is awake” and cleaves to Hashem — and this was the drawing-down of the soul of “Er” into the world.

paragraphs.text: Iyov 31:2 says “וּמֶה חֵלֶק אֱלוֹהַּ מִמָּעַל” — “What portion from God above [would remain]?” The biblical verse is a rhetorical question in Iyov’s argument, not an explicit proposition that every soul is part of the Divine. Rav Tzadok uses the phrase in a theological sense and develops it in Resisei Layla §40, where he writes of an enduring point of the Jewish heart attached to Hashem, “נְקוּדָה ... בַּלֵּב שֶׁדָּבוּק ... בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,” linked to “אֲנִי יְשֵׁנָה וְלִבִּי עֵר.” The complete present sentence has already described both the soul’s source and the heart’s attachment.

paragraphs.text: Shir HaShirim 5:2 says “אֲנִי יְשֵׁנָה וְלִבִּי עֵר.” Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2 expounds Israel as asleep from commandments yet still awake in its capacity for goodness; in another reading “לִבּוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עֵר לְגָאֳלֵנִי,” and Rabbi Chiya bar Abba appeals to Tehillim 73:26, “צוּר לְבָבִי.” Rav Tzadok combines those readings to argue that the inner bond of the Jewish heart can remain awake even when the outer faculties are immersed in concealment. The Midrash supplies the words; the structure of enduring inner attachment is his extension.

paragraphs.text: Sotah 13b: Rabbi Elazar says one who begins a mitzvah but fails to finish it may be “מוֹרִידִין אוֹתוֹ מִגְּדֻלָּתוֹ,” citing “וַיֵּרֶד יְהוּדָה.” Rashi on Bereishis 38:1 explains that Yehudah’s brothers demoted him upon seeing Yaakov’s grief, arguing that they would have listened had he advised returning Yosef instead of selling him. Rav Tzadok accepts the tradition of Yehudah’s descent, then explains it through the brothers’ apprehension of the injury done to the covenantal stature of Israel; the Talmud does not itself present the Yesod symbolism.

paragraphs.text: Sotah 36b — Yosef’s test and the image of Yaakov: In the account of Yosef and Potiphar’s wife, one opinion says that Yosef entered the house intending to satisfy his desire. At that moment “the likeness of his father appeared to him in the window” and warned him that the names of his brothers were destined to be engraved on the stones of the Ephod: did he wish his own name erased from among them? The Gemara then reads “his bow remained firm” as Yosef recovering his restraint. This is the direct source for Rav Tzadok’s reference to the dmus dyokno that prevented Yosef from being swallowed into the nations and preserved the holiness of the bris.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 13a asks why Mordechai, of Binyamin, is called “יְהוּדִי”; Rabbi Yochanan answers: “עַל שׁוּם שֶׁכָּפַר בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה,” concluding “שֶׁכָּל הַכּוֹפֵר בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה נִקְרָא יְהוּדִי.” The Talmud’s immediate discussion concerns Mordechai’s title rather than Yehudah’s personal biography. Rav Tzadok applies this title’s meaning to Yehudah’s inward attachment to Hashem and only then explains Yehudah’s independent act of descending to effect a tikkun.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Knesses Yisrael boasts “I am asleep, but my heart is awake.” Expounded of the Holy One (“the Rock of my heart”): though Israel “sleep” from the mitzvos and have “no eyes,” the soul’s root is “a portion of God,” and the depths of the heart cleave to Him. So even the sleeper’s imaginings cleave to God, and in the deepest sinking there remains the power to awaken to Him.

p: (יט) וְלֹא לְחִנָּם בְּכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁנִּכְתַּב תּוֹלְדוֹתֵיהֶם הִזְכִּיר גַּם עֵר וְאוֹנָן (בְּפָרָשַׁת וַיִּגַּשׁ וּבְפָרָשַׁת פִּנְחָס וּבִדְהֵ״א ב), אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהֵם כְּבָר מֵתוּ וְלֹא הֶעֱמִידוּ תּוֹלָדוֹת, וּמַאי נָפְקָא מִינַהּ בְּזִכְרוֹנָם

And not for nothing does Scripture, wherever their genealogies are written, mention Er and Onan too in Vayigash, in Pinchas, and in I Divrei HaYamim 2 — even though they had already died and raised no offspring; and what difference does their remembrance make?

וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דִּשְׁמָם נִשְׁאַר קַיָּים לָעַד, דְּעִנְיַן הַתּוֹלָדָה שֶׁמּוֹלִיד וּמֵבִיא נֶפֶשׁ כָּזוֹ לָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְאוֹר שֶׁל כָּל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת שֶׁהָיוּ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, אַף שֶׁנִּסְתַּלְּקוּ, נִרְשַׁם הָאוֹר, וְכַיָּדוּעַ בְּהָנֵי דְּשָׁבַק חַיִּים

And perforce their name “remains forever” — for the matter of offspring, that one begets and brings such a soul into this world, and the light of all the souls that were in this world, even after they departed, “the light is inscribed,” as is known regarding “those who left life behind.”

וְכֵן אֵלּוּ שְׁתֵּי הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּעֵר וְאוֹנָן, שֶׁהָיָה יְהוּדָה עָסוּק בָּהֶם לְתַקֵּן קִלְקוּל הַקּוֹדֵם; אֶלָּא שֶׁהוּא חָשַׁב שֶׁהַבְּרִית קֹדֶשׁ כְּבָר נִתְקַלְקֵל וְנִטְמַע בֵּין הָעַמִּים לְגַמְרֵי, וּדְאֶפְשָׁר עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ תִּקְוָה מִצַּד דְּבֵיקוּת הַלֵּב בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ

And so these two souls of Er and Onan, with whom Yehudah was occupied, to rectify the earlier corruption — only that he thought the holy bris had already been corrupted and wholly assimilated among the nations, and that there might still be hope from the side of the heart’s cleaving to Hashem.

דְּעֵר וְאוֹנָן נֶגֶד שְׁנֵי מַפְתְּחוֹת הַלֵּב: ״עֵר״ הוּא נֶגֶד ״לֵב חָכָם לִימִינוֹ״, שֶׁבּוֹ עִיקַּר הַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ; וְהַשְּׂמֹאל הוּא מִסִּטְרָא דְּנוּקְבָּא, שֶׁשָּׁם הַתְחָלַת הָרַע

For Er and Onan correspond to the two “entrances of the heart”: “Er” corresponds to “the heart of the wise is to his right” (Koheles 10:2), where the essential awakening toward Hashem begins; while the left is from the aspect of the feminine side, from which evil begins.
וְעַל כֵּן הִיא קָרְאָה שְׁמוֹ מִסִּטְרָא דִּידָהּ אוֹנָן, לְשׁוֹן אֲנִינוּת,
and therefore she called him, from her own side, Onan, an expression of mourning,
כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קט סֵפֶא ב׳) עַל "אוֹן בֶּן פֶּלֶת" דְּנִקְרָא כֵּן שֶׁיָּשַׁב כָּל יוֹם בְּאֲנִינוּת, וְהוּא הַחֲרָטָה וְהַתְּשׁוּבָה לְתַקֵּן הָרַע הַקָּדֵם.
as our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 109b, end) about “On ben Pelet,” who was so called because he sat every day in mourning, which is regret and repentance to repair the earlier evil.
וּלְפִי שֶׁכָּל זֶה הָיָה כְּפִי הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה בַּאֲבֵידַת יוֹסֵף לְגַמְרֵי חַס וְשָׁלוֹם,
And since all this was according to the thought of Yosef’s complete loss, Heaven forbid,

וּבֶאֱמֶת אִלּוּ הָיָה כֵּן (שֶׁנֶּאֱבַד יוֹסֵף לְגַמְרֵי) לֹא הָיָה תִּיקּוּן בִּמְצִיאוּת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אָז כְּלָל, דְּ״עַמֵּךְ כּוּלָּם צַדִּיקִים״ דַּוְקָא — דַּרְגָּא דְּצַדִּיק הֵם דְּיָרְשׁוּ אֶרֶץ; וּלְפִיכָךְ גַּם הֵם (עֵר וְאוֹנָן) חָטְאוּ בַּבְּרִית

And in truth, had it been so that Yosef was wholly lost, there would have been no rectification in reality in this world then at all — for “your people are all tzaddikim” specifically: it is the rung of tzaddik Yesod that “inherited the land”; and therefore they too Er and Onan “sinned in the bris.”
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁתִּיקֵּן הַלֵּב, לֹא תִּיקֵּן עֲדַיִין הָעֵינַיִם שֶׁהוּא עִיקַּר הַהַתְחָלָה, וּלְפִיכָךְ הָיוּ ״רָעִים בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״
And even though he rectified the heart, he did not yet rectify the eyes, which are “the essential beginning”; and therefore they were “evil in the eyes of Hashem.”

וּבְעִנְיַן תָּמָר שֶׁהָיָה עַל יְדֵי הָרְאִיָּה — ״וַיִּרְאֶהָ יְהוּדָה״ וְגוֹמֵר — הִתְחִיל לְתַקֵּן הָעֵינַיִם, וְכַיָּדוּעַ דְּהֵם נִתְגַּלְגְּלוּ וְנִתַּקְּנוּ בְּפֶרֶץ וְזֶרַח, וְעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר בָּהּ ״וַתֵּשֶׁב בְּפֶתַח עֵינַיִם״ — הוּא הַכְּנִיסָה לְתִיקּוּן הָעֵינַיִם

And in the matter of Tamar, which came about through seeing — “Yehudah saw her,” etc. (Bereishis 38:15) — he began to rectify the eyes. As is known, the souls of Er and Onan were reincarnated and rectified in Peretz and Zerach. Accordingly, the verse says of Tamar, “she sat at pesach einayim” (Bereishis 38:14): for Rav Tzadok, the expression also alludes to the entrance to the rectification of the eyes.

Rav Tzadok explains that the light of a soul that once entered this world leaves a lasting impression even after departure. That inference is his theological interpretation of the repeated names.

paragraphs.text: Resisei Layla §53:4 explicitly teaches “כָּל אוֹרוֹת שֶׁנִּתְגַּלּוּ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, אַף דְּנִסְתַּלְּקוּ ... לֹא נִסְתַּלְּקוּ לְגַמְרֵי, רַק נִשְׁאֲרוּ בְּהֶעְלֵם” — spiritual lights that appeared in this world may cease to be revealed, yet are not completely extinguished, remaining concealed. The exact wording was checked against the Har Bracha Resisei Layla edition, printed p. 159 (PDF page 163). Later in the same discussion Rav Tzadok writes that this influence can be “נֶחְקַק ... בְּמַעֲמַקֵּי לִבְבוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל” and invokes “שְׁבִיק חַיִּין לְכָל חַי”. Machshavos Charutz §17:5 supplies a further Rav Tzadok parallel regarding the life-force left to Israel by the deceased. This note is appropriately anchored at “נִרְשַׁם הָאוֹר ... שְׁבַק חַיִּים”, separately from the earlier genealogy note. paragraphs.text: Berachos 61a states: “יֵצֶר הָרָע דּוֹמֶה לִזְבוּב וְיוֹשֵׁב בֵּין שְׁנֵי מַפְתְּחֵי הַלֵּב.” The same sugya distinguishes the right and left kidneys as inclining toward good and evil and adduces Koheles 10:2, “לֵב חָכָם לִימִינוֹ וְלֵב כְּסִיל לִשְׂמֹאלוֹ.” In Pri Tzaddik, Shavuos 6:1 and Rosh Chodesh Shevat 5:1, Rav Tzadok explicitly relates the right/left heart-symbolism to Torah entering the heart and the yetzer’s interference. Here he interprets the names Er and Onan through these two openings of the heart. The specific identification of the sons with the two aspects is Rav Tzadok’s present reading.

Rav Tzadok borrows the wordplay on aninus — mourning and regret — to interpret Onan’s name as the aspect through which the earlier wrong might be addressed by repentance.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Scripture records Er and Onan in the genealogies (Vayigash, Pinchas, I Divrei HaYamim) though they died childless. Teaching that their “name endures forever,” for the light of every soul that entered this world remains inscribed. Yehudah was occupied in rectifying these two souls, thinking the holy bris had been wholly lost among the nations, with hope only from the heart’s cleaving to God.

p: (כ) וּגְמַר הַתִּיקּוּן בְּדָוִד, דִּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ (ש״א טז) ״יְפֵה עֵינַיִם וְטוֹב רֹאִי״; וְאִלּוּ הָיָה הַדּוֹר רָאוּי הָיָה אָז גְּמַר הַתִּיקּוּן וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה הוּא מָשִׁיחַ, דִּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ ״יָרוּם וְנִשָּׂא וְגָבֹהַּ מְאֹד״, וְדָרְשׁוּ רז״ל מֵאָבוֹת וּמִמֹּשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה

And the completion of the rectification is in David, of whom it is written I Shmuel 16:12, “of beautiful eyes and goodly to look upon”; and had the generation been worthy, it would then have been the completion of the rectification, and that he be Mashiach, of whom it is written, “he shall be high and lifted up and very lofty” (Yeshayah 52:13), which the Sages expounded to be higher than the Avos and than Moshe Rabbeinu.

וּלְפִיכָךְ בִּיקֵּשׁ לְיַחֵד שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם עָלָיו כְּמוֹ עַל הָאָבוֹת, וְכִדְאִיתָא (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין שָׁם) דְּאָמַר ״מִפְּנֵי מָה אֵין אוֹמְרִים אֱלֹקֵי דָּוִד״, כִּי הִכִּיר שֶׁהוּא הַמְתַקֵּן הַכֹּל, וְיִיחוּד שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם עָלָיו הוּא יוֹתֵר מִכּוּלָּם

And therefore he sought to have the Name of Heaven unified upon him as upon the Avos, as it is stated Sanhedrin 107a, that he said, “why do they not say ‘God of David’?” — for he recognized that he is the rectifier of all, and the unification of the Name of Heaven upon him is greater than upon them all.

וְזֶהוּ ״וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ עַל גַּג בֵּית הַמֶּלֶךְ״: הַ״בַּיִת״ הוּא הַמָּקוֹם לְקוֹמַת הָאָדָם כְּפִי מַדְרֵגָתוֹ, וּ״בֵית הַמֶּלֶךְ״ מְתוּקָּן לְמִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת, וְהַ״גַּג״ הוּא הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מִמְּקוֹם מַדְרֵגָתוֹ

And this is “and he walked upon the roof of the king’s house” (II Shmuel 11:2): the “house” is the “place” for a person’s stature according to his rung; “the king’s house” is fitted to the middah of Malchus; and the “roof” is the place above the place of his rung.

כִּי כְּפִי מַדְרֵגָתוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה בַּמַּלְכוּת שֶׁבְּאוֹתוֹ דּוֹר, ״דְּפַרְנָס לְפִי הַדּוֹר״, הָיָה בַּקָּשַׁת דָּבָר זֶה דָּבָר שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מִמַּדְרֵגָתוֹ, כִּי עֲדַיִין לֹא הִגִּיעַ עֵת קֵץ שֶׁיּוּכַל לָבוֹא לִגְמַר הַתִּיקּוּן בְּפֹעַל גָּלוּי בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

For according to his rung in this world, in the kingship of that generation (“a leader according to the generation”), the request of this thing was something above his rung — for the End had not yet come, that he could reach the completion of the rectification in revealed actuality in this world.

וְזֶה גָּרַם קְצָת קִלְקוּל בִּרְאִיָּה, דְּ״וַיַּרְא אִשָּׁה״ וְגוֹמֵר, ״וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״ — חָזַר הַקִּלְקוּל בָּעֵינַיִן עַל יְדֵי הָרַע דִּפְגַם הַבְּרִית, שֶׁהָיָה לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן דְּאוֹיְבֵי ה׳ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

This caused some impairment in the realm of seeing — “he saw a woman,” and “the thing was evil in Hashem’s eyes.” The corruption of sight returned through the evil associated with the blemish of the bris, as it appeared to the eyes of “the enemies of Hashem” in this world.

וְהוּא (דָּוִד) שֶׁיָּדַע דִּרְאוּיָה לוֹ, וְרָאָה כָּל הַשַּׁלְשֶׁלֶת שֶׁיָּצָא מִמֶּנָּה, לֹא עָלָה בְּלִבּוֹ דָּבָר רַע כְּלָל; רַק כְּשֶׁהִרְגִּישׁ שֶׁהַדָּבָר בָּא מֵהֲסָתַת הַיֵּצֶר וְגָרַם סִילּוּק שְׁכִינָה, וְהוּא יָדַע דְּ״לִבּוֹ חָלָל בְּקִרְבּוֹ״ רַק שֶׁרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כָּךְ — עַל יְדֵי זֶה הִכְנִיס שִׂמְחָה שֶׁל מִצְוָה בְּלִבּוֹ, שֶׁהֲרֵי עוֹשֶׂה בָּזֶה רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ דִּ״לְמַעַן תִּצְדַּק״ וְגוֹמֵר, וַעֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ כְּמִצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ

And he (David), who knew that she was fit for him, and saw the whole chain that would issue from her, no evil thing arose in his heart at all; only when he sensed that the matter came from the yetzer’s enticement and caused the removal of the Shechinah — and he knew that “his heart was hollow within him,” only that Hashem’s will was so — through this he introduced “the joy of a mitzvah” into his heart, for he is thereby doing Hashem’s will, “so that You be justified when You speak,” and a “transgression for its own sake” is like a mitzvah not-for-its-own-sake.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה חָזַר לוֹ גַּם אָז רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ מַמָּשׁ, בִּנְבוּאַת נָתָן הַנָּבִיא לוֹ וּבִשְׁעַת תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ
And through this the ruach hakodesh literally returned to him even then, in the prophecy of Nathan the prophet to him, and at the time of his teshuvah.

כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת מִצִּידּוֹ הָיָה מָלֵא קְדֻשָּׁה גַּם בִּשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה וְלֹא הָיָה חֵטְא כְּלָל, וּלְפִיכָךְ הוּא לֹא הִתְעוֹרֵר לִתְשׁוּבָה כְּלָל עַל זֶה מֵעַצְמוֹ, כִּי לֹא עָלָה בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁיַּחְשׁוֹב לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עָוֹן בְּדָבָר זֶה, שֶׁהָיָה יוֹדֵעַ כָּל כַּוָּונָתוֹ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם

For in truth, from his side he was “full of holiness” even at the time of the act, and there was no sin at all; therefore he was not aroused to teshuvah at all of himself over this, for it did not enter his heart that Hashem would reckon it an iniquity, since he knew his whole intent was for the sake of Heaven —

עַד שֶׁהוּצְרַךְ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לִשְׁלֹחַ אֵלָיו נָתָן הַנָּבִיא לְהַגְדִּיל הֶעָוֹן וְשֶׁהוּא צָרִיךְ לִתְשׁוּבָה, שֶׁזֶּה הָיָה כָּל הַכַּוָּונָה: לִיתֵּן פִּתְחוֹן פֶּה לַשָּׁבִים וּלְהָקִים עוֹלָהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בע״ז ה רע״א) עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת ד״ה ״וּצְרִיכָא״, פֵּירוּשׁ לִכְתּוֹב חֶטְאָם וְקַבָּלַת תְּשׁוּבָתָם

until Hashem had to send him Nathan the prophet, to “magnify the iniquity” and teach that he needs teshuvah — for this was the whole intent: to give an “opening of the mouth” to penitents and to raise the yoke of teshuvah, as they said Avodah Zarah 5a — see there in Tosafos, s.v. “u-tzricha” — meaning, to write their sin and the acceptance of their teshuvah.

וּלְפִיכָךְ לֹא הוֹעִיל בְּבַקָּשָׁתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא יִכְתּוֹב סוּרְחָנוֹ, כִּי בַּכָּתוּב נֶאֱמַר שֶׁחָטָא, וְשֶׁהוּא הוֹדָה וְאָמַר ״חָטָאתִי לַה׳״, רַק שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הִזְכִּיר חַטָּאתוֹ עַל יְדֵי וִידּוּיוֹ וּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ

And therefore his request that his misdeed not be written did not avail — for in Scripture it says that he sinned, and that he confessed and said “I have sinned to Hashem” (II Shmuel 12:13) — only that Hashem “mentioned his sin” through his confession and his teshuvah.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 107a records David’s question “מִפְּנֵי מָה אוֹמְרִים אֱלֹהֵי אַבְרָהָם ... וְאֵין אוֹמְרִים אֱלֹהֵי דָּוִד?” Hashem explains that the Avos were tested, David asks for a test, and the sugya moves immediately to “וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ עַל גַּג בֵּית הַמֶּלֶךְ וַיַּרְא אִשָּׁה.” The Gemara explicitly warns against inviting a test; it does not assign the house and roof the spiritual levels that Rav Tzadok derives. The present explanation identifies David’s wish to complete the messianic tikkun with rising beyond the level of kingship available in his generation.

paragraphs.text: Arachin 17a states “דּוֹר לְפִי פַרְנָס” and “פַרְנָס לְפִי דּוֹרוֹ.” In Likkutei Maamarim, On the Book of Yehoshua §10, Rav Tzadok writes: “פַּרְנַס הַדּוֹר נַפְשׁוֹ כּוֹלֶלֶת כָּל נַפְשׁוֹת הַדּוֹר,” and immediately cites both orders of the saying in Arachin. This supplies the direct parallel: even David’s royal spiritual reach is read here in relation to what the generation could receive, so his wish to complete the final tikkun in revealed actuality was ahead of its appointed time.

paragraphs.text: II Shmuel 11:27 says explicitly, “וַיֵּרַע הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה דָוִד בְּעֵינֵי ה׳.” II Shmuel 12:14 refers to the “אֹיְבֵי ה׳.” Shabbos 56a offers the interpretive statement “כָּל הָאוֹמֵר דָּוִד חָטָא אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא טוֹעֶה,” while continuing to discuss David’s serious failings in the episode. Rav Tzadok distinguishes the outward appearance of the bris/eyes blemish from David’s inward intention, without deleting Scripture’s express judgment or Nathan’s later rebuke. These sources contain differing emphases, which should not be flattened into a claim that the narrative records no wrong.

paragraphs.text: Horayos 10b first says “גְּדוֹלָה עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָה מִמִּצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָה” but then qualifies the comparison: “אֵימָא: כְּמִצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָה,” taking Yael as the example; the sugya also contrasts Tamar and Zimri. Nazir 23b gives the same qualified teaching. In Tzidkas HaTzadik §100, Rav Tzadok explains that after complete teshuvah the penitent recognizes Hashem’s providence even in the earlier failing and cites David’s “לְמַעַן תִּצְדַּק בְּדָבְרֶךָ,” describing the temporary loss of heavenly assistance. Here his analysis is a retrospective interpretation of David’s unique test, completed by Nathan’s rebuke and David’s teshuvah; it is not a general license to commit transgression for an alleged higher purpose.

paragraphs.text: In Pri Tzaddik, Vaeschanan §2:2, Rav Tzadok says that Nathan confronted David with “אַתָּה הָאִישׁ.” David knew that through his struggle he had reached “לִבּוֹ חָלָל בְּקִרְבּוֹ,” yet the episode showed that even such efforts did not preserve him from a failing. The awareness of his distance drove an inward cry “לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא לִי אֱלֹהִים”: he asked for a newly created pure heart and depended on Divine mercy. This is a close original parallel to the present movement from David’s confidence in his intention to Nathan’s warning and the necessity of genuine teshuvah.

rich.text: 2, Rav Tzadok says that Nathan confronted David with “אַתָּה הָאִישׁ.” David knew that through his struggle he had reached “לִבּוֹ חָלָל בְּקִרְבּוֹ,” yet the episode showed that even such efforts did not preserve him from a failing. The awareness of his distance drove an inward cry “לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא לִי אֱלֹהִים”: he asked for a newly created pure heart and depended on Divine mercy. This is a close original parallel to the present movement from David’s confidence in his intention to Nathan’s warning and the necessity of genuine teshuvah.
