footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: עַד שֶׁהוּצְרַךְ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לִשְׁלֹחַ אֵלָיו נָתָן הַנָּבִיא לְהַגְדִּיל הֶעָוֹן וְשֶׁהוּא צָרִיךְ לִתְשׁוּבָה, שֶׁזֶּה הָיָה כָּל הַכַּוָּונָה: לִיתֵּן פִּתְחוֹן פֶּה לַשָּׁבִים וּלְהָקִים עוֹלָהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בע״ז ה רע״א) עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת ד״ה ״וּצְרִיכָא״, פֵּירוּשׁ לִכְתּוֹב חֶטְאָם וְקַבָּלַת תְּשׁוּבָתָם

paragraphs.text: Avodah Zarah 4b–5a says that the recorded failings of David and the wilderness generation were meant to “לִיתֵּן פִּתְחוֹן פֶּה לַשָּׁבִים”: if an individual has sinned, he is directed to David, while a community is directed to Israel after the Golden Calf. Tosafos, Avodah Zarah 5a, s.v. “וּצְרִיכָא,” explicitly comments: “פֵּירוּשׁ לִכְתּוֹב חֶטְאָם וְקַבָּלַת תְּשׁוּבָתָם.” The Tosafos quotation explains why both sin and accepted teshuvah were written down. Rav Tzadok connects this to why David’s plea that his wrongdoing not be recorded did not succeed: the confession and its acceptance had to remain accessible as a paradigm of teshuvah.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The completion of the rectification is in David — “of beautiful eyes and goodly to look upon.” Had the generation been worthy, this would have been the final tikkun and David would have been Mashiach (“high and lifted up and exalted, very lofty,” higher than the Avos and Moshe). Hence he sought to have God’s Name unified upon him as upon the Avos (“why do they not say ‘God of David’?”).

p: (כא) ורז״ל גִּילּוּ הַדָּבָר שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת נו.) דְּהָאוֹמֵר ״דָּוִד חָטָא״ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא טוֹעֶה; וְאָמְרוּ בְּלָשׁוֹן זֶה לוֹמַר שֶׁהוּא דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין לְהַעֲלוֹתוֹ עַל הַדַּעַת כְּלָל שֶׁאִישׁ כְּמוֹתוֹ יֶחֱטָא, וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיֹּאמַר כֵּן אֶלָּא מִי שֶׁהוּא טוֹעֶה וּמְשׁוּבָּשׁ בְּדַעְתּוֹ

And the Sages revealed the matter, saying Shabbos 56a that “whoever says David sinned is merely erring”; and they said it in this language to convey that it is a thing that cannot be entertained at all — that a man like him should sin — and it is impossible to say so except one who is “erring and confused in his mind.”
וְדָבָר זֶה פָּעַל בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ, ״דְּלָא לִשְׁתָּעֵי בֵּיהּ רַבָּנָן״ — שֶׁלֹּא יִרְצוּ אַדְּרַבָּא לְהַגְדִּיל הַחֵטְא כְּדֵי לְהוֹרוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה אֲפִילּוּ לְחֵטְא גָּדוֹל
And this thing he effected by his prayer, “that the Rabbis not speak of it” — that they not wish, on the contrary, to magnify the sin, in order to teach teshuvah even for a great sin.
וְזֶהוּ ״אַל יִמְשְׁלוּ בִי״, דְּפֵירַשׁ״י שָׁם לְשׁוֹן ״מָשָׁל״, אַל יִדְרְשׁוּ (בְּחַטָּאתִי חַכְמֵי הַדּוֹרוֹת); וְלֹא פֵּירֵשׁ לָמָּה קָרֵי לִדְרָשָׁתָם בִּלְשׁוֹן ״מָשָׁל״

And this is “let them not rule over me al yimshelu bi” (Tehillim 19:14), which Rashi there interprets as a term of “mashal parable”: “let them not expound my sin, the sages of the generations”; and he did not explain why he calls their expounding by a term of “mashal.”

אֲבָל לְפִי שֶׁעִיקַּר הַכַּוָּונָה בְּחֶטְאוֹ וּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מָשָׁל וְדֻגְמָא לַאֲחֵרִים שֶׁיִּלְמְדוּ מִמֶּנּוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה, עַל זֶה אָמַר שֶׁלֹּא יִמְשְׁלוּ בּוֹ בְּעִנְיַן הַחֵטְא, רַק בְּעִנְיַן הַתְּשׁוּבָה לְבַד, וּדְהַתְּשׁוּבָה מוֹעֶלֶת, שֶׁיְּבוֹרַר אַחַר כָּךְ דְּלָא חָטָא, וְהָאוֹמֵר כו׳ טוֹעֶה

But because the essential intent in his sin and teshuvah was that it be “a mashal and example” for others, that they learn from him to do teshuvah — on this he said, that they not “use him as a mashal” in the matter of the sin, only in the matter of the teshuvah alone; and that the teshuvah avails, so that it be clarified afterward that he did not sin, and “whoever says he sinned is erring.”

אֲבָל זֶהוּ בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, שֶׁהוּא גִּילּוּי הַמִּסְתּוֹרִין; אֲבָל בַּכָּתוּב בַּנְּבִיאִים נֶאֱמַר שֶׁחָטָא, דְּמַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב כְּאִלּוּ חָטָא. וְכֵיוָן שֶׁהוּא כְּאִלּוּ חָטָא, שֶׁהֲרֵי הַכָּתוּב קְרָאוֹ ״חוֹטֵא״, הוּא צָרִיךְ לִתְשׁוּבָה, וְיָלְפִינַן הוֹרָאַת תְּשׁוּבָה

But this pertains to the Oral Torah, which reveals what is concealed. In the written account of the Prophets, however, David is described as having sinned, for Scripture reckons it to him as though he sinned. And since Scripture calls him a sinner in this account, he requires repentance, and from it we learn the teaching of teshuvah.
וּלְפִי שֶׁהוּא פָּעַל שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה הַלִּמּוּד דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל וְדוּגְמָא מִמֶּנּוּ,
And because he brought about that the learning would not be by way of mashal and example from him,

וְהַכּוָּנָה דְּוַדְאַי אִם הָיָה בְּזֶה תּוֹעֶלֶת לְהָשִׁיב רַבִּים מֵעָוֹן עַל יְדֵי זֶה, וָדַאי גַּם הוּא עַצְמוֹ הָיָה מַסְכִּים לְזֶה, וְהָיָה מְוַתֵּר כְּבוֹדוֹ בִּשְׁבִיל כְּבוֹד שָׁמַיִם וְתִקּוּן הַרַּבִּים.

and the intent is that surely, had there been benefit in this to return the many from sin through it, surely he himself would also have agreed to this, and would have forgone his honor for the sake of the honor of Heaven and the rectification of the many.
אֲבָל תְּפִלָּתוֹ הָיָה שֶׁלְהִתְעוֹרֵרוּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה עַל יָדוֹ לֹא יִצְטָרְכוּ לִדְרוֹשׁ הַגְדָּלַת חֵטְאוֹ וְלַהַמְשִׁיל מִמֶּנּוּ,
But his prayer was that for the arousal of repentance through him they would not need to expound the magnification of his sin and to make a mashal of him,
רַק לִהְיוֹת הוּא "הַגֶּבֶר הֻקַם עָל מָשִׁיחַ" וְגוֹמֵר, הוּא הַיָּחִיד שֶׁשָׁב,
but rather that he alone be “the man raised on high, the anointed one,” etc., the singular one who repented,
שֶׁבְּהִתְעוֹרְרוּת תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ בְּלַבָּד מִתְעוֹרֵר מִמֵּילָא תְּשׁוּבָה בְּכָל הַלְּבָבוֹת דְּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל,
so that through the arousal of his repentance alone, repentance is automatically aroused in all the hearts of the Children of Israel,
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה פָּעַל דְּלָא לִשְׁתַּעִי כּוּלֵּי.
and through this he brought about “that they should not speak of him,” etc.
וּלְפִיכָךְ חָשַׁב גַּם כֵּן לִפְעוֹל דְּלֹא יִכְתֵּב גַּם כֵּן,
And therefore he also thought to bring about that it not be written either,
וְיִהְיֶה הַתִּעֹוֹרְרוּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה בְּלֹא הַכְּתִיבָה כָּלָל וּבְלִי זִכָּרוֹן הַמַּעֲשֶׂה גַּם כֵּן.
and the arousal of repentance would be without the writing at all and without the remembrance of the act as well.
וְעַל זֶה אָמַר לוֹ דְּאַי אֶפְשָׁר,
And about this He said to him that it is impossible,
כִּי כְּבָר הַדָּּבָר מְסֻדָּר כָּךְ, שֶׁמִּכֹּחַ קְדֻשַּׁת אוֹתָה פָּרָשָׁה וְאוֹתָן אוֹתיוֹת שֶׁל סִפּוּר חֵטְא דָּוִד וְתְשׁוּבָתוֹ לִגְרֹם הִתְעוֹרְרוּת תְּשׁוּבָה בָּעוֹלָם,
for the matter is already arranged thus: that through the holiness of that portion and those letters of the account of David’s sin and his repentance, to cause the arousal of repentance in the world,
אֶי אֶפְשָׁר עוֹד לְשַׁנּוֹת וּלְבַטֵּל שִּׁימּוּשָׁם וְשֶׁיִּעָקְרוּ מִן הַכְּתוּבִים,
it is no longer possible to change and nullify their use and to have them uprooted from the Scriptures,
שֶׁדִּבְרֵיהֶם תּוֹרָה שְׁלֵמָה, וְהֲרֵי זֶה כְּעֲקִירַת אוֹת מִן הַתּוֹרָה,
for their words are a complete Torah, and this is like uprooting a letter from the Torah,
שֶׁבְּקְדֻשַּׁת נְבִיאִים וּכְתוּבִים כְּקְדֻשַּׁת הַתּוֹרָה דְּקַיָּמִים גַּם כֵּן לָעַד.
since the holiness of the Prophets and Writings is like the holiness of the Torah, which also endure forever.
וְעִקַּר הוֹרָאַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה הַיִנוּ שֶׁיַּגִיעַ לִמְדַרְגָּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה כָּזוֹ, שֶׁיִּהְיוּ הַזֵּדוּנוֹת כְּזְכוּיוֹת,
And the essence of the teaching of repentance is that one reach such a level of repentance that the willful sins become like merits,
וְחֵטְא זֶה שֶׁנִּכְתַּב עָלָיו בָּכָּתוּב, עַל כָּרְחֲךָ שֶׁתִּקְנוּ כָּךְ שֶׁנִּעֱשָׂה כְּזְכוּיוֹת, דְּלוּלֵי כֵּן לֹא הָיָה נִכְתָּב וְכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְּתִּי.
and this sin that was written about him in the text, you must say that it was rectified so that it became like merits, for otherwise it would not have been written, and as I have written.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 107a understands David’s “אַל יִמְשְׁלוּ בִי” as “דְּלָא לִישְׁתַּעוּ בִּי רַבָּנָן” — that the Sages should not recount his disgrace. Rashi there adds: “אַל יִמְשְׁלוּ לְשׁוֹן מָשָׁל, שֶׁלֹּא יִדְרְשׁוּ בְּחַטָּאתִי חַכְמֵי הַדּוֹרוֹת” — the word is interpreted in the sense of making him an illustrative example. Rav Tzadok develops the distinction: David seeks to remain a model of the power of repentance, not to require an embellished depiction of his failing as the lesson’s center.

paragraphs.text: Resisei Layla 51:2 gives the close original parallel: “אֲבָל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הוּא מְסְטוֹרִין שֶׁלּוֹ, מַה שֶּׁבְּמַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, דְּזֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהִתְגַּלּוֹת בִּכְתָב כְּלָל, רַק עַל יְדֵי חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּדוֹר דּוֹר.” Translation: Oral Torah is His hidden counsel, what lies within the Blessed One’s thought; that cannot be disclosed in writing at all, but only through the sages of Israel in every generation. This illuminates Rav Tzadok’s “גִּילּוּי הַמִּסְתּוֹרִין”: the Sages unfold an inward meaning that is not transparent from the prophetic narrative’s outward wording; it does not deny the sanctity of the Prophets or their record.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 56a states: “כָּל הָאוֹמֵר דָּוִד חָטָא אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא טוֹעֶה” — whoever says that David sinned is mistaken. It asks: “אֶפְשָׁר חֵטְא בָּא לְיָדוֹ וּשְׁכִינָה עִמּוֹ?” — could sin come into his hand while the Shechinah was with him? The sugya construes the biblical reproach in David’s favor, while still discussing specific serious failings, including his treatment of Uriah. II Shmuel 11:27 nevertheless declares that the deed was evil in Hashem’s eyes. Rav Tzadok distinguishes the prophetic narrative, which teaches repentance, from the Sages’ disclosure of an inward level of David’s story; this is his reconciliation and should not be stated as though the Gemara erased the prophetic rebuke.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 107a presents two successive requests: “אַל יִמְשְׁלוּ בִי” — “דְּלָא לִישְׁתַּעוּ בִּי רַבָּנָן” (that the Rabbis not discuss him), followed by “וְנִקֵּיתִי מִפֶּשַׁע רָב” — “שֶׁלֹּא יִכָּתֵב סוּרְחָנִי” (that his disgrace not be written). Hashem replies: “אִי אֶפְשָׁר,” invoking the yud removed from Sarai and restored in Yehoshua’s name. Yad Ramah to Sanhedrin 107a instead reads “אַל יִמְשְׁלוּ” as the request not to write, explaining “שֶׁמִּשָּׁעָה שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה מַעֲשֶׂה עָלָה בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה לְהִכָּתֵב וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְעָקְרָהּ.” These are differing verse assignments, not a contradiction in the story. Rav Tzadok’s further claim that the established prophetic letters have enduring sanctity and a purpose in awakening teshuvah is his present explanation of why their writing could not be undone.

paragraphs.text: Earlier in this siman (Takanas HaShavin 10:11), Rav Tzadok distinguishes Moshe, the root of Written Torah, who asked that his failure be recorded, from David, whose level is “מַלְכוּת פֶּה, תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה,” who requested that the incident not be written. The present paragraph completes the argument: the written account of David’s failing remains holy because its very preservation can awaken complete teshuvah. Yoma 86b teaches: “גְּדוֹלָה תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁזְּדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוֹת לוֹ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת,” and expressly distinguishes repentance from love from repentance from fear. Rav Tzadok here understands the recorded episode as having been rectified so deeply that it can function in the Scriptural teaching of teshuvah.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The Sages revealed it: “whoever says David sinned is merely erring” (Shabbos 56a) — phrased so, to say it is unthinkable that such a man sinned; only one “confused in mind” could say it. David effected this by his prayer “that the Rabbis not speak of it” — that they not magnify the sin to teach teshuvah. “Let them not rule over me al yimshelu bi” — Rashi reads mashal: “let them not expound my sin.”

p: (כב) וְזֶהוּ שְׁלֵימוּת הִתְעוֹרְרוּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּמַדְרֵגָה זוֹ; וְזֶהוּ עִיקַּר שֹׁרֶשׁ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה, שֶׁהוּא עַצְמוֹ נִשְׁמַת מָשִׁיחַ — הוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הַתִּיקּוּן דְּרַע שֶׁבַּתּוֹלָדָה, וּבִיטּוּל הַיֵּצֶר וְעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ שֶׁבַּתַּאֲווֹת, וּשְׁמִירַת הַבְּרִית

And this is the perfection of the arousal of teshuvah, and that it be at this rung; and this is the essential root of David HaMelech, who is himself the soul of Mashiach — the root of rectifying the evil in human birth, and the nullification of the inclination and the serpent’s influence in the realm of desire, and the guarding of the bris.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּתִיקּוּנֵי זֹהַר תִּיקּוּן לז) ״לָא תְּצַפֵּי לְרַגְלָא דִּמְשִׁיחָא עַד דְּתֶחֱזֵי קֶשֶׁת בִּגְוָונִין נְהִירִין, אוֹ עַד דְּאִתְגַּלְיָא אוֹת בְּעָלְמָא — מַאי אוֹת? — אוֹת בְּרִית״

And as they said in Tikkunei Zohar, tikkun 37, “do not await the footstep of Mashiach until you see a rainbow in shining colors, or until the ‘sign’ is revealed in the world — what ‘sign’? — the sign of the bris.”
וְיָדוּעַ הַקֶּשֶׁת הוּא גַּם כֵּן סִימַן תִּיקּוּן הַבְּרִית, שֶׁבָּזֶה הוּא הַהֲגָנָה מֵעֹנֶשׁ חֵטְא דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל
And it is known that the rainbow keshes is also a sign of the rectification of the bris, whereby is the protection from the punishment of the sin of the generation of the Flood.
רַק הַחִילּוּק, דְּקֶשֶׁת הוּא סִימָן שֶׁצְּרִיכִין הֲגָנָה מִצַּד הַבְטָחַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְלוּלֵי רֹב רַחֲמָיו הָיוּ חַיָּיבִים
The difference is that the rainbow signifies the need for protection through Hashem’s promise; were it not for His abundant mercy, they would be liable.
וְזֶה עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא (סַנְהֶדְרִין צח.) ״אֵין בֶּן דָּוִד בָּא אֶלָּא בְּדוֹר שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ (זַכַּאי) כו׳ שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ חַיָּיב כו׳, לְמַעֲנִי אֶעֱשֶׂה״, עַיֵּין שָׁם
And this is in the manner it is stated Sanhedrin 98a, “the son of David comes only in a generation that is wholly worthy or wholly liable — ‘for My own sake I will do it’” — see there.

וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר וּמַרְאֶה לְעֵין כֹּל אֵיךְ הַכֹּל ״מִמֶּנּוּ יָצְאוּ כְּבוּשִׁים״, וְשֶׁאֵין חֵטְא בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּלָל; וְזֶהוּ הַקֶּשֶׁת בְּגַוְונֵי נְהִירִין, הַיְינוּ הַהֶאָרָה גְּמוּרָה בַּהֲגָנַת יִשְׂרָאֵל לְמַעֲנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ; אוֹ בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹת הַבְּרִית בָּעוֹלָם בְּפֹעַל, וְהַיְינוּ בְּדוֹר שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ זַכַּאי

And Hashem illuminates and reveals before all eyes how the concealed things “came forth from Him,” and that there is no sin in Israel at all; this is the rainbow in radiant colors — the full illumination of the protection of Israel for His own sake — or else the actual revelation in the world of the sign of the bris, namely in a generation wholly worthy.

וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה כּוֹלֵל שְׁנֵיהֶם: דְּמִצַּד עַצְמוּתוֹ כּוּלּוֹ זַכַּאי, וּמִצַּד מַרְאִית הָעַיִן אֵצֶל אוֹיְבָיו הוּא לְהֵפֶךְ, שֶׁאָמְרוּ ״רַע לוֹ״ (שֶׁהוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הָרַע חַס וְשָׁלוֹם), ״מָתַי יָמוּת וְאָבַד שְׁמוֹ״ וְגוֹמֵר

And David HaMelech includes both: from the side of his essence, “wholly worthy”; and from the side of the outward eye, by his enemies, the reverse — who said “evil to him” that he is the root of evil, God forbid, “when will he die and his name perish” (Tehillim 41:6).
וּבְבָבָא מְצִיעָא (נט רע״א) דְּאָמְרוּ לוֹ ״הַבָּא עַל אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ, מִיתָתוֹ בַּמֶּה״
And in Bava Metzia 59a, where they said to him, “A man who has relations with a married woman — by what manner of death is he punished?”

paragraphs.text: In Pri Tzaddik, Pinchas 8:1, Rav Tzadok writes: “דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הוּא מֶרְכָּבָה לְמִדַּת מַלְכוּת וְהוּא רֶגֶל רְבִיעִי שֶׁבַּמֶּרְכָּבָה”; and “אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁהָיָה נִשְׁמַת דָּוִד כַּיָּדוּעַ, אָדָ״ם רָאשֵׁי תֵּבוֹת אָדָם דָּוִד מָשִׁיחַ.” He presents Adam, David and Mashiach as one chain in the soul-root of Malchus. This is a close parallel to the opening of our paragraph: David bears the root of the final rectification, especially in regard to desire and guarding the covenant. The specific tikkun of congenital evil and the serpent’s influence is Rav Tzadok’s development here, not a direct quotation from Pri Tzaddik.

paragraphs.text: The full original, including BOTH alternatives, is Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 37, fol. 78a:7 (not merely the abbreviated rainbow statement at 36b:3): “לָא תִצְפֵּי לְרַגְלָא דִמְשִׁיחָא עַד דְּתֶחְזֵי קֶשֶׁת בְּגַוְּונוֹי נְהִירִין, אוֹ עַד דְּאִתְגַּלְיָיא אוֹת בְּעָלְמָא, מַאי אוֹת ... דָּא אָת י׳ אוֹת בְּרִית.” Translation: Do not expect Mashiach’s footsteps until the rainbow appears with radiant colors, or until a sign is revealed in the world; that sign is the yud, the sign of the covenant. The passage reads “אֶלָּא דָּרַךְ כּוֹכָב מִיַּעֲקֹב” between “מַאי אוֹת” and “אוֹת בְּרִית”; Rav Tzadok abridges it. Related, shorter presentations of the shining rainbow also occur in Tikkunei Zohar 36b:3 and Zohar, Noach 35:290. These witnesses are not identical word-for-word; the two-part teaching quoted here is verified in the 78a text. Sources: Tikkunei Zohar 78a:7 (Tikkun 37); cf. Tikkunei Zohar 36b:3; Zohar, Noach 35:290; Numbers 24:17.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: רַק הַחִילּוּק, דְּקֶשֶׁת הוּא סִימָן שֶׁצְּרִיכִין הֲגָנָה מִצַּד הַבְטָחַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְלוּלֵי רֹב רַחֲמָיו הָיוּ חַיָּיבִים

paragraphs.text:
Genesis 9:12–17 calls the rainbow the sign of a Divine covenant: “אֶת קַשְׁתִּי נָתַתִּי בֶּעָנָן וְהָיְתָה לְאוֹת בְּרִית בֵּינִי וּבֵין הָאָרֶץ” — “I have placed My bow in the cloud as a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth”; and “וְלֹא יִהְיֶה עוֹד הַמַּיִם לְמַבּוּל לְשַׁחֵת כָּל בָּשָׂר” — the waters shall no longer become a flood destroying all flesh. Zohar, Pinchas III 215a (section 9:35), explains “קֶשֶׁת אָתָא לְאַגָּנָא עַל עָלְמָא” — “the rainbow comes to protect the world.” It distinguishes protection manifest in the presence of a tzaddik, himself identified with the covenant, from protection signaled by the rainbow when no such protective tzaddik is present: “וּבְשַׁעֲתָא דְּאִית צַדִּיק בְּעָלְמָא, אִיהוּ בְרִית ... וְאָגִין עַל עָלְמָא; לָא הֲוִי צַדִּיק, הָא קֶשֶׁת.” Rav Tzadok applies this distinction to the difference between mercy granted through the promise and the fully revealed covenantal holiness. The verses do not, on their own, teach that every physical rainbow proves a generation’s culpability; the Zohar’s teaching is mystical interpretation, not an empirical weather criterion. Sources: Genesis 9:12–17; Zohar, Pinchas III 215a, §9:35; cf. Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 37 (folio 36b on the bright colors of the messianic rainbow).
Additional original Talmudic parallel: Ketubot 77b relates that R. Shimon bar Yochai asked R. Yehoshua ben Levi, “נִרְאֲתָה קֶשֶׁת בְּיָמֶיךָ?” — “Did a rainbow appear in your days?” Although he answered yes, the Gemara explains that no rainbow appeared and that he did not wish to attribute credit to himself: “לָא אֲחַזֵּיק טִיבוּתָא לְנַפְשַׁאי.” This illustrates the protective merit of a tzaddik without the visible covenantal sign and complements the Zohar, Pinchas III 215a explanation above. It is an aggadic distinction, not a modern meteorological test. Sources also: Ketubot 77b.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר וּמַרְאֶה לְעֵין כֹּל אֵיךְ הַכֹּל ״מִמֶּנּוּ יָצְאוּ כְּבוּשִׁים״, וְשֶׁאֵין חֵטְא בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּלָל; וְזֶהוּ הַקֶּשֶׁת בְּגַוְונֵי נְהִירִין, הַיְינוּ הַהֶאָרָה גְּמוּרָה בַּהֲגָנַת יִשְׂרָאֵל לְמַעֲנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ; אוֹ בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹת הַבְּרִית בָּעוֹלָם בְּפֹעַל, וְהַיְינוּ בְּדוֹר שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ זַכַּאי

paragraphs.text: At Yehudah’s acknowledgment of Tamar, “צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי” (Bereishis 38:26), Makkos 23b reports: “יָצְאָה בַּת קוֹל וְאָמְרָה: מִמֶּנִּי יָצְאוּ כְּבוּשִׁים” — a heavenly voice declared that the concealed matters came forth from Me. Sotah 10b records the same expression in its discussion of Yehudah and Tamar. The phrase is a statement of Divine direction behind a concealed process, not a general endorsement of transgression. Rav Tzadok draws upon Yehudah and Tamar — ancestors of the Davidic dynasty — when reading the revealed inner purpose of apparently discrediting events. The present phrase explains the hidden direction as part of the mode of luminous covenantal mercy.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה כּוֹלֵל שְׁנֵיהֶם:

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 98a teaches in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: “אֵין בֶּן דָּוִד בָּא אֶלָּא בְּדוֹר שֶׁכֻּלּוֹ זַכַּאי אוֹ כֻּלּוֹ חַיָּיב.” The wholly worthy generation is supported by Yeshayah 60:21, “וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים”; the wholly liable by Yeshayah 59:16, “וַיַּרְא כִּי אֵין אִישׁ,” together with 48:11, “לְמַעֲנִי לְמַעֲנִי אֶעֱשֶׂה.” Rav Tzadok reads the two possible generations as two modes of redemption: radiant rainbow/mercy for Hashem’s sake, and revealed bris for a wholly worthy generation. David “includes both” in the contrast between inward righteousness and the hostile view of his deeds; this two-symbol correspondence is Rav Tzadok’s interpretation, not Sanhedrin’s wording.

paragraphs.text: Resisei Layla 49 gives a related, but different, emphasis: “אֵין נוֹפֵל אֶלָּא בְּיַד זַרְעוֹ שֶׁל יוֹסֵף, שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד אוֹת בְּרִית הַקֹּדֶשׁ ... וְהוּא שׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית שֶׁגַּם לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן אֵין שׁוּם טַעֲנָה נֶגְדּוֹ.” Translation: Amalek falls to Yosef’s descendants, who correspond to the holy covenantal sign; Yosef guards the bris in a way that leaves no charge even to the outward eye. Rav Tzadok there contrasts inward covenantal identity with what is visibly contestable. In our paragraph, David’s inward spiritual standing is likewise distinguished from the accusations made by his enemies. This is a thematic parallel, not a statement that Yosef and David occupy the same role.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: וּבְבָבָא מְצִיעָא (נט רע״א) דְּאָמְרוּ לוֹ ״הַבָּא עַל אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ, מִיתָתוֹ בַּמֶּה״

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 59a describes David’s public humiliation: “אֲפִלּוּ בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁעוֹסְקִין בִּנְגָעִים וְאֹהָלוֹת, אוֹמְרִים לִי: דָּוִד, הַבָּא עַל אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ, מִיתָתוֹ בַּמֶּה?” — even while studying technical laws they taunt him by asking the penalty for relations with a married woman. David replies that such a person incurs strangulation but can still have a share in the World to Come, whereas one who humiliates another publicly forfeits that share. Rav Tzadok cites the taunt as evidence of David’s hostile public image; the Gemara also condemns the cruelty of those who wielded the accusation.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: This is the perfect arousal of teshuvah at its highest rung. And the essential root of David, who is himself the soul of Mashiach: the root of rectifying the evil of human birth, nullifying the yetzer and “the counsel of the serpent,” and guarding the bris. As the Tikkunei Zohar says: “do not await the footstep of Mashiach until you see a rainbow in shining colors, or until the ‘sign’ of the bris is revealed.”

p: (כג) וּמַה שֶּׁאָמַר בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁעוֹסְקִים בִּנְגָעִים וְאֹהָלוֹת, הַכַּוָּונָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּפְסָחִים נ רע״א) ״אוֹר יְקָרוֹת וְקִפָּאוֹן — אֵלּוּ נְגָעִים וְאֹהָלוֹת״, שֶׁ״יְּקָרִים״ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וּ״קְפוּאִים״ לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא

And what he said about “when they are engaged in nega’im and ohalos”: he means the statement in Pesachim 50a on “precious things and congealing” (Zechariah 14:6) — “these are nega’im and ohalos,” which are valued in this world but of comparatively diminished significance in the World to Come.
וְהַעִנְיָן דְּקָרִי לְהוּ "אוֹר יָקָר",
And the question is why they are called “precious light,”
וְגַם אִם רָצָה לוֹמַר מִשֶּׁוֹם דְּאָז יְבֻלַּע הַמָּוֶת וְגַם לֹא יִהְיוּ נְגָעִים,
and even if one wanted to say it is because then death will be swallowed up and there will also be no Negaim,
כְּמוֹ כֵן לֹא יִהְיוּ זָבִים וּשְׁאָר טֻמְאוֹת, וְהָיָה לוֹ לֹאמַר בְּכְלָל סֵדֶר טָהֲרוֹת,
likewise there will be no zavim and other impurities, and he should have said “the whole Seder Taharos”,
וְכֵן כָּל דִּינֵי נְפָשוֹת יִתְבַּטֵּל אָז, שֶׁלֹּא יִחֱטָאוּ שֶׁיִּצְטָרְכוּ לְדוּנָם,
and likewise all capital cases will be nullified then, since they will not sin so as to need to be judged,
וְהָיָה לוֹ לֹאמַר גַּם כֵּן סַנְהֶדְרִין וּמַכּוֹת וּכְדוֹמֶה.
and he should have said Sanhedrin and Makkos as well, and the like.
אֲבָל כְּבָר אָמְרוּ (בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה) עַל פָּסוּק "זֹאת קוֹמָתֵךְ" שְׁנֵי יְצָרִים בָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעוֹלָמוֹ, יֵצֶר עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְיֵצֶר זְנוּת,

But they already said (in Shir HaShirim Rabbah) on the verse “this is your stature”: two inclinations did the Holy One, blessed be He, create in His world — the inclination for idolatry and the inclination for immorality,
וְכֵן נִזְכָּר שְׁנֵי יְצָרִים אֵלּו (בְּיוֹמָא ס׳ט עַמּוּד ב).
and likewise these two inclinations are mentioned (in Yoma 69b).
וְנְגָעִים רוֹמֵז לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה,
And Negaim allude to idolatry,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה סוֹף פֶּרֶק י״ז) "כְּנֶגַע נִרְאָה לִי בַּבָּיִת — זֶה טִינּוּפֶת עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה",
as they said (in Vayikra Rabbah, end of chapter 17): “‘like a lesion has appeared to me in the house’ — this is the filth of idolatry,”
וּבְסֵפֶר יְצִירָה דְּאֵין בָּרָעָה לְמָטָּה בְּנֶגַע,
and in Sefer Yetzirah, that there is no evil lower than the lesion,

וְכֵן עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה הִיא תַּכְלִית הָרַע שֶׁבְּכֹחַ הַיֵּצֶר לְהָבִיא אֶת הָאָדָם "הַיּוֹם עֲשֵׂה כָּךְ וְלָמָחֳרָה" (אוֹמֵר לוֹ עֲשֵׂה כָּךְ) עַד שֶׁאוֹמֵר לוֹ "לֵךְ עֲבוֹד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה" כּוּלֵּי (שַׁבָּת ק׳ה עַמּוּד ב),

and likewise idolatry is the utmost of the evil that is in the power of the inclination to bring a person — “today do this and tomorrow” (he tells him “do this”) — until he says to him, “go and serve idols,” etc. (Shabbos 105b),
שֶׁזְּהוּ סוֹף הַכְּפִירָה בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לַגְמַרִי, שֶׁאֵין בָּרַע לְמָטָּה מִזֶּה.
which is the end of denial of Hashem, blessed be He, entirely, for there is no evil lower than this.
וְאֹהָלוֹת הוּא כְּטוּמְאַת מֵת שֶׁבָּא עַל יְדֵי יֵצֶר דְּתַאֲוָה, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִגְזַר הַמִּיתָה, וְעִיקַּר הַטּוּמְאָה שֶׁבְּגוּף הַמֵּת הוּא מִצַּד הַתַּאֲוָה שֶׁבַּגּוּף שֶׁבּוֹ הַטּוּמְאָה

And ohalos concerns corpse impurity, which comes about through the inclination toward desire: through this, death was decreed. In Rav Tzadok’s account, the principal impurity remaining in the dead body derives from bodily desire, where that impurity is found.
וְאֲפִילּוּ הַצַּדִּיקִים הַמֵּתִים בְּעִטּוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ, הֲרֵי יֵשׁ בָּהֶם אוֹתָה טֻמְאָה דְּעִטּוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ וְזוּהֲמָתוֹ שֶׁהִטִּיל בְּחַוָּה,
And even the righteous who die through the effect of the serpent — there is in them too that impurity of the effect of the serpent and his filth that he cast into Chavah,
דְּזֶהוּ שֹׁרֶשׁ הַטֻמְאָה שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם,
for that is the root of the impurity in the world,
וְכֶשֶּׁנִּפְרְדָה נָשָׁמָה הַקְּדוֹשָׁה דְּטָהוֹרָה הִיא מִהַגּוּף נִשְׁאַר הַטּוֹמְאָה בּוֹ.
and when the holy soul, which is pure, separates from the body, the impurity remains in it.
וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה ״אֹהָלִים״, וּמַעֲלִים אֶת הָאָדָם מִטּוּמְאָה לְטָהֳרָה וּמִכַּף חוֹבָה לְכַף זְכוּת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת טז רע״א)
And therefore words of Torah too are called “ohalim tents,” and they raise a person from impurity to purity and from the scale of guilt to the scale of merit, as they said Berachos 16a.
וְהַיְנוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִדּוּשִׁין ל׳) "אִם פָּגַע בְּךָ מְנוּוָל זֶה — מִשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ", וְמְנוּוָל הַיְנוּ יִצְרָא דְּעֲבֵירָה, שֶׁאֵין נִיוּוּל גָּדוֹל מִזֶּה,
And that is as they said (Kiddushin 30b): “If this vile one encounters you, drag him to the Beis HaMidrash,” and the “vile one” is the inclination to sin, for there is no greater vileness than this,
וְכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קְנִ״ב סוֹף עַמּוּד א) "אִשָּׁה חֵמָת מָלֵא צוֹאָה",
And as they said in Shabbos 152a, “A woman is a skin flask filled with excrement.”
וּבִמְשְׁנָה (רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ב׳ דְּסוֹטָה י״ד סוֹף עַמּוּד א) שֶׁמַּעֲשֶׂיהָ מַעֲשֵׂה בְּהֵמָה,
And in the Mishnah regarding the sotah (Sotah 14a), her conduct is described as “the act of an animal.”
וְכֵן מִדָּה כְּנֶגֶּד מִדָּה צִוָּה הַכָּתוּב לְנַוּלָה וְכִדְתְנַן (סוֹטָה ז׳: ח׳:).
and likewise, measure for measure, the verse commanded to disgrace her, as we learned (Sotah 7b, 8a).
וְעִקַּר הַתּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין הוּא לַיֵּצֶר הָרַע זֶה,
And the essence of the Torah is a spice for this evil inclination,
וְכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב רַבֵּנוּ מֹשֶׁה בֶּן מַיְמוֹן (סוֹף הִלְכוֹת אִסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה) דְּאֵין הַתַּאֲווֹת מְצוּיוֹת אֶלָּא בְּלֵב פָּנוּי מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, יָעוּיַּן שָׁם.
and as Rabbeinu Moshe ben Maimon wrote (end of Hilchos Issurei Bi’ah) that desires are found only in a heart free of words of Torah, see there.

וְעַל כֵּן דָּרְשׁוּ (בְּרָכוֹת סג:) מֵ״אָדָם כִּי יָמוּת בְּאֹהֶל״ — לְהָמִית עַצְמוֹ עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כִּי זֶהוּ זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה, נֶגֶד הַמִּיתָה בְּאֹהֶל שֶׁהוּא עַל יְדֵי הַתַּאֲווֹת, וּבִיטּוּלָן עַל יְדֵי הַ״מִּיתָה בְּאֹהֶל״ עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה

And therefore they expounded Berachos 63b from “a man, when he dies in a tent ohel” (Bamidbar 19:14) — that one should “put himself to death over words of Torah” — for this is “this-against-that,” over-against the “death in a tent” that is through the desires, and their nullification by the “death in a tent” of words of Torah.
וְזֶה אֵינוֹ מִיתָה גְּמוּרָה, רַק שֶׁהוּא נִקְרָא מֵמִית עַצְמָן, הַיְנוּ שֶׁמְקַבֵּּל עַל עַצְמוֹ לָמוּת גַּם כֵּן עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
And this is not a complete death, only that he is called one who “puts himself to death,” that is, who accepts upon himself to die as well over words of Torah.
אֲבָל בְּאֱמֶת אַדְרָבָה הִיא הַנּוֹתֶנֶת לוֹ חַיֵּי עוֹלָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּשַׁבָּת י׳.),
But in truth, on the contrary, it is what gives him eternal life, as they said (in Shabbos 10a),
וְגַם חַיֵּי שָׁעָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם ל׳ רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב) בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
and also temporal life, as they said (there, 30b) regarding David the King, peace be upon him,
וּבְבָבָא מְצִיעָא (פְּו.) בְּרַבָה בַּר נַחְמָנִי שֶׁכָּל כָּךְ הָיוּ דְּבוּקִים בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה (וְלָכֵן מַלְאָךְ הַמָּוֶת לֹא יָכֹל לְהֹרְגָם).
And in Bava Metzia 86a, regarding Rabbah bar Nachmani: both he and David were so profoundly attached to Torah study that the Angel of Death could not take them while their recitation continued.

וְיֵצֶר הָרָע הוּא מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בב״ב טז.), וּכְמוֹ שֶׁמַּצִּיל מִיֵּצֶר הָרָע כֵּן מַצִּיל מִמַּלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת, וְכִבְמַתַּן תּוֹרָה שֶׁהָיוּ ״חֵירוּת מִיֵּצֶר הָרָע״ וּמִמַּלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת

And the evil inclination is the Angel of Death, as they said Bava Basra 16a; and just as Torah saves from the evil inclination, so it saves from the Angel of Death — as at the Giving of the Torah, when they were “free of the evil inclination” and of the Angel of Death.
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר נַחְמָנִי (שָׁם בב״מ) ״אֲנִי יָחִיד בִּנְגָעִים, אֲנִי יָחִיד בְּאֹהָלוֹת״, שֶׁהוּא כֹּחַ הַתּוֹרָה הַמַּצֶּלֶת בִּשְׁנֵי יְצָרִים אֵלּוּ
And this is what Rabbah bar Nachmani said there in Bava Metzia, “I am unique in nega’im, I am unique in ohalos” — which is the power of the Torah that saves in the matter of these two inclinations.

(וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּבִיטְּלוּ אַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה יִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, יָדוּעַ דְּיִצְרָא דְּכַעַס עוֹמֵד בִּמְקוֹמוֹ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת קה: ״הַמְקָרֵעַ כְּסוּתוֹ בַּחֲמָתוֹ כו׳ כְּעוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה״, וְכֵן עִיקַּר הַמְּצֹרָע עַל כַּעַס וַעֲנָפָיו כַּיָּדוּעַ)

And although the Men of the Great Assembly abolished the inclination of idolatry, it is known that the inclination of anger stands in its place, as they said in Shabbos 105b, “one who tears his garment in his anger or scatters his money in his anger is like one who serves idols”; and so the essence of the metzora is over anger and its branches, as is known.

וּבַחֲגִיגָה (יד.) וְסַנְהֶדְרִין (סז סע״ב) דְּאָמַר לוֹ לְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא ״כְּלָךְ אֵצֶל נְגָעִים וְאֹהָלוֹת״ — גַּם כֵּן לְכַוָּונָה זוֹ; כְּמוֹ שֶׁקִּיבַּלְתִּי כִּי שֹׁרֶשׁ נִשְׁמַת רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא (שֶׁהָיָה יְסוֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה) הוּא מִדִּיבּוּר ״לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ״, שֶׁהוּא כּוֹלֵל כָּל מִינֵי בֵּירוּרִים וְהַפְרָדָה לְסִטְרָא דְּרַע

And in Chagigah 14a and Sanhedrin 67b, where they said to R’ Akiva, “turn to the study of nega’im and ohalos” — that too is for this intent; as I have received, that the root of R’ Akiva’s soul who was the foundation of the Oral Torah is from the utterance “you shall have no other gods” — which includes all kinds of “clarifications” and the separation of holiness from the side of evil.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 50a expounds Zechariah 14:6, “אוֹר יְקָרוֹת וְקִפָּאוֹן”; R. Yochanan says: “אֵלּוּ נְגָעִים וְאֹהָלוֹת, שֶׁיְּקָרִין הֵן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וּקְפוּיִין הֵן לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא” — these laws are esteemed in this world and relatively diminished in the World to Come. Rashi on Pesachim 50a explains the “frozen/floating” image as “קָפוּי וְקַל,” light or diminished, not as a concealed store of power awaiting future discovery. The Gemara does NOT itself equate nega’im and ohalos with the two primal inclinations; Rav Tzadok asks why these two subjects are named and develops that distinctive interpretation in the following paragraphs. Sources: Pesachim 50a and Rashi ad loc.; Zechariah 14:6.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 17:7 expounds “כְּנֶגַע נִרְאָה לִי בַּבָּיִת” as “זוֹ טִינֹפֶת עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה” — “the filth of idolatry.” Sefer Yetzirah 2:4 adds: “אֵין בָּרָעָה לְמַטָּה מִנֶּגַע” — “There is nothing lower in evil than nega.” These are the two textual hinges for Rav Tzadok’s link between nega’im and the drive toward idolatry; the full identification is his exegetical synthesis, rather than a simple equivalence stated in either text.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 105b states of the yetzer hara: “הַיּוֹם אוֹמֵר לוֹ עֲשֵׂה כָךְ, וּלְמָחָר אוֹמֵר לוֹ עֲשֵׂה כָךְ, עַד שֶׁאוֹמֵר לוֹ עֲבוֹד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְהוֹלֵךְ וְעוֹבֵד” — today it tells a person to act in one way, tomorrow another, until he is drawn to idol worship. Rav Tzadok cites this as an escalating sequence in which successive concessions to the yetzer culminate in the deepest denial of Hashem; the Gemara does not say that every lesser lapse invariably ends in idol worship.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 30b records: “בָּרָאתִי יֵצֶר הָרָע, וּבָרָאתִי לוֹ תּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין” — “I created the evil inclination and created Torah as its antidote”; and, “אִם פָּגַע בְּךָ מְנֻוָּל זֶה, מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ” — “if this vile one confronts you, draw him into the study house.” These are connected teachings in the same sugya. footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: וְכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב רַבֵּנוּ מֹשֶׁה בֶּן מַיְמוֹן (סוֹף הִלְכוֹת אִסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה) דְּאֵין הַתַּאֲווֹת מְצוּיוֹת אֶלָּא בְּלֵב פָּנוּי מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, יָעוּיַּן שָׁם.

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot Issurei Bi’ah 22:21, writes: “גְּדוֹלָה מִכָּל זֹאת ... יְפַנֶּה עַצְמוֹ וּמַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה ... שֶׁאֵין מַחֲשֶׁבֶת עֲרָיוֹת מִתְגַּבֶּרֶת אֶלָּא בְּלֵב פָּנוּי מִן הַחָכְמָה” — above all, direct one's thought to Torah, for thoughts of prohibited relations intensify only in a heart empty of wisdom. Rav Tzadok condenses the last phrase as “בְּלֵב פָּנוּי מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה”: this communicates the Rambam’s meaning but is not its verbatim final wording. Rav Tzadok further explains in Machshavos Charutz §3 (Har Bracha edition, printed p. 7; PDF p. 11): “כְּשֶׁהַלֵּב שָׁקוּעַ בְּמַחְשְׁבוֹת דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְמַחֲשָׁבָה אַחֶרֶת וְהִרְהוּר אַחֵר לִכָּנֵס בְּקִרְבָּהּ כְּלָל” — when the heart is absorbed in Torah thoughts, an opposing thought cannot enter. Both the exact Rambam quotation and Rav Tzadok’s own illuminating parallel thus belong together; the symbolic link to Ohalos is developed by Rav Tzadok here, not stated by Rambam. Sources: Mishneh Torah, Forbidden Intercourse 22:21; Machshavos Charutz §3, Har Bracha p. 7.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 30b recounts that David’s constant Torah study prevented the Angel of Death from approaching until the sound of the trees disrupted his recitation. Bava Metzia 86a similarly relates of Rabbah bar Nachmani: “לָא הֲוָה מָצֵי מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת לְמִקְרַב לֵיהּ, מִדְּלָא הֲוָה קָא פָסֵיק פּוּמֵיהּ מִגִּירְסֵיהּ” — the Angel of Death could not come near because he did not cease his learning. Both narratives concern a temporary protection that ended; they do not teach general bodily immortality through study. Rav Tzadok connects these stories to Torah’s spiritual power against the yetzer, which he identifies with the Angel of Death.

paragraphs.text: Shemos Rabbah 41:7 explains “חָרוּת עַל הַלֻּחֹת” (Exodus 32:16) as “חֵרוּת,” citing distinct teachings: R. Yehudah — freedom from exiles; R. Nechemiah — “חֵרוּת מִמַּלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת,” freedom from the Angel of Death; and the Sages — freedom from afflictions. Vayikra Rabbah 18:3 offers a related treatment, with its own attributions. Neither of these specific lists should be misquoted as a single source saying “freedom from both the yetzer hara and the Angel of Death.” Rather, Bava Basra 16a identifies the yetzer hara with the Angel of Death (“הוּא שָׂטָן, הוּא יֵצֶר הָרָע, הוּא מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת”), and Rav Tzadok applies that identification to the liberation of Sinai. Sources: Exodus 32:16; Shemos Rabbah 41:7; Vayikra Rabbah 18:3; Bava Basra 16a.

paragraphs.text: Shir HaShirim Rabbah 7:8:1, on “זֹאת קוֹמָתֵךְ,” states: “שְׁנֵי יְצָרִים בָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעוֹלָמוֹ, יֵצֶר עֲבוֹדַת כּוֹכָבִים וְיֵצֶר זְנוּת” — God created two inclinations, for idolatry and illicit sexual desire. It continues that the first was uprooted while the second endures. Yoma 69b narrates the Men of the Great Assembly’s suppression of idolatry and the failed attempt to eliminate sexual desire entirely, since reproduction ceased. Rav Tzadok additionally argues here that anger can occupy the idolatrous impulse’s place; Shabbos 105b compares a destructive act of anger to idol worship. That identification of anger as a remaining analogue is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive extension; it is not stated in Yoma 69b.

paragraphs.text: Chagigah 14a and Sanhedrin 67b each report Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah telling Rabbi Akiva: “עֲקִיבָא, מַה לְּךָ אֵצֶל הַגָּדָה? ... אֵצֶל נְגָעִים וְאֹהָלוֹת” — “Akiva, why occupy yourself with aggadah? Turn to nega’im and ohalos.” In Chagigah the dispute concerns the interpretation of divine thrones; in Sanhedrin it concerns the plague of frogs. The two rebukes do not themselves identify Rabbi Akiva’s soul with the second commandment. Rav Tzadok reads an additional allusion into the repeated instruction, supported by the original Mei HaShiloach teaching.

paragraphs.text: Mei HaShiloach I, Bo §5, gives an exceptionally close original parallel: “מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ ... הָיָה נֶגֶד אָנֹכִי, וְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא בֶּן יוֹסֵף ... נֶגֶד לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ” — Moshe’s soul corresponded to “I am Hashem,” while Rabbi Akiva’s corresponded to “You shall have no other gods.” The passage continues that Rabbi Akiva’s halachic boundaries in permitted/forbidden and pure/impure clarify and separate evil from good. The parallels are strikingly close to Rav Tzadok’s “כְּמוֹ שֶׁקִּבַּלְתִּי”; this note cites the original Izhbitz teaching, not a later commentary, but does not assert that the phrase is a verbatim personal transmission without textual evidence.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: David’s taunters raise “nega’im and ohalos” — which (Pesachim 50a) are “precious light or yekaros, congealed for the World to Come.” Why these two? Because the Sages taught that God created two root inclinations — idolatry and licentiousness. And nega’im alludes to idolatry (the “filth of idolatry,” the utter denial of God, than which nothing is lower), while ohalos (corpse-impurity) alludes to desire, through which death and the body’s impurity came.

p: (כד) וְזֶהוּ הַלִּימּוּד דִּנְגָעִים וְאֹהָלוֹת שֶׁהוּא ״אוֹר יְקָרוֹת״ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, דְּכָל הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא בְּנִיצּוּחַ הַיֵּצֶר, דְּ(לַ)צַּדִּיקִים דּוֹמֶה לְהַר, וּכְשֶׁזָּכוּ לְנַצְּחוֹ הוּא דָּבָר גָּדוֹל וְיָקָר, וּמַשִּׂיגִים מִזֶּה אוֹר גָּדוֹל

And this is the study of nega’im and ohalos, which is “precious light” in this world — for all a person’s labor in this world is in conquering the inclination, which “to the righteous appears like a mountain”; and when they merit to conquer it, it is a great and precious thing, and they attain from it a great light.
וּבָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, דְּלֹא יִהְיֶה יֵצֶר הָרָע, אֵינוֹ כְּלוּם, וְאֵין מוּשָּׂג שׁוּם אוֹר מִזֶּה, כְּמוֹ לַמַּלְאָכִים
And in Olam Haba, where there will be no evil inclination, it is nothing, and no light is attained from it — as is the case for the angels.

וְהַמָּשִׁיחַ הוּא תַּכְלִית הַשְׁלָמַת נִיצּוּחַ הַיֵּצֶר, עַד דְּ״חַיִּים שָׁאַל מִמְּךָ נָתַתָּ לּוֹ״, שֶׁיְּבוּלַּע גַּם כֵּן הַמָּוֶת, עַל יְדֵי דְּהָא בְּהָא תַּלְיָא, וְהוּא יֵצֶר הָרָע הוּא מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת

And Mashiach is the ultimate completion of the conquest of the inclination, until “he asked life of You, You gave it him” (Tehillim 21:5) — that death too be swallowed up, since “this depends on that,” and the evil inclination is itself the Angel of Death.
וְדָוִד מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּעָצְמוּתוֹ וְמִצַּד עָצְמוֹ זָכָה כְּבָר לָזֶה.
And David, king of Israel, in his essence and from his own side, had already merited this,
דְּנִקְרָא חַי וְקַיָּם.
for he is called “alive and enduring.”
רַק שֶׁאוֹיְבָיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה מִאוֹתָה מַעֲשֶׂה, כְּשֶׁעָסְקוּ בְּנְגָעִים וְאָהֳלוֹת שֶׁהוּא הָאוֹר יְקָרוֹת דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
Only that his enemies in this world, from that incident, when they were engaged in Negaim and Ohalos, which is the “precious light” of this world,
וְיָדְעוּ דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הִתְפָּאֵר דְּלִבּוֹ חָלָל בְּקִרְבּוֹ וְכָבָר הוּא קָפוּי אֶצְלוֹ,
and knew that David the King, peace be upon him, boasted that “my heart is slain within me” and that it was already congealed in him,
וְהָיָה חוֹשֵׁב לַשִּׂיג חַיֵּי עוֹלָם,
and he thought he would attain eternal life,
עַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ לוֹ לְהַקְנִיטוֹ דְּבָא עַל אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ,
therefore they said to him, to provoke him: “He committed adultery with a married woman,”
שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הָרַע דְּיֵצֶר הַתַּאֲוָת,
which is the utmost evil of the inclination of desire,
וְשֶׁהוּא מְחֻיָּב מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין מִיָּד,
and that he is liable to the death penalty of the court immediately,
וְגֶבֶרָא קְטִילָא הוּא שֶׁאֵין לוֹ חַיִּים כְּלָל.
and a “slain man” who has no life at all.
וְכָךְ הָיָה רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיֹּאמְרוּ כֵּן עַל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
And such was the will of Hashem, blessed be He, that they should say so about David the King, peace be upon him,
כֵּדֵי שֶׁיִהְיֶה הוּא הַמְזַכֶּה לְחַיָּיֲבַיָּא גַּם לְדוֹר שֶׁכֻּלּוֹ חַיָּב,
so that he would be the one who gives merit to the guilty, even to a generation that is entirely guilty,
שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם אֲהַבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִיִשְׂרָאֵל אֵין נִיתֶּקֶת,
for in any case the love of Hashem, blessed be He, for Israel is never severed,
שֶׁהֵם עָצְמוּתָם "עַמֵּךָ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים" וְגוֹמֵר,
for in their essence “Your people are all righteous,” etc.,
דְּכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא.
for all Israel have a share in the World to Come.
וְאֲפִילּוּ הַבָּא עַל אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ דְּמִיתָתוֹ בְּחֶנֶק יֵשׁ לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא,
And even one who commits adultery with a married woman, whose death is by strangulation, has a share in the World to Come,
וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּנִקְרָא צַדִּיק,
so you must say that he is called righteous,
דִּבְהָא תַּלְיָא עוֹלָם הַבָּא כְּפִי הַמִּשְׁנָה (דר״פ חֵלֶק), וּמִשּׁוּם דְּגַם עַרְלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָאִים מוּלִים
For upon this rests the share in the World to Come, according to the Mishnah at the beginning of Perek Chelek; and likewise even uncircumcised Israelites are designated “circumcised.”

וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה זָכָה לְהוֹלִיד תֵּיכֶף אַחַר כָּךְ מִמֶּנָּה שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה, שֶׁכָּתוּב מִיָּד בְּלֵידָתוֹ ״וַה׳ אֲהֵבוֹ״, וְשָׁלַח לִקְרוֹא שְׁמוֹ ״יְדִידְיָהּ בַּעֲבוּר ה׳״, שֶׁהוּא יְדִידוֹ וְאוֹהֲבוֹ מִלֵּידָה וּבֶטֶן, אֲפִילּוּ יִהְיֶה אַחַר כָּךְ מַה שֶּׁיִּהְיֶה

And through this he merited to beget, immediately afterward, Shlomo HaMelech from her, of whom it is written at once, at his birth, “and Hashem loved him,” and He sent to call his name “Yedidyah, for the sake of Hashem” (II Shmuel 12:24–25) — that he is His beloved and friend “from birth and womb,” whatever he might be afterward,
וְכַאֲשֶׁר הִבְטִיחוֹ גַּם כֵּן מִקּוֹדֶם עַל זַרְעוֹ (ש״ב ז) ״וְהוּא יִהְיֶה לִּי לְבֵן, אֲשֶׁר בְּהַעֲוֹתוֹ וְהוֹכַחְתִּיו״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וְחַסְדִּי לֹא יָסוּר מִמֶּנּוּ״

as He assured him beforehand too regarding his seed II Shmuel 7, “and he shall be to Me a son; when he sins, I will chastise him with the rod of men and the afflictions of the sons of men, but My kindness shall not depart from him.”

וְהוּא כּוֹלֵל כָּל הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְכֵן חֶטְאוֹ הָיָה תִּיקּוּן לְכָל חֲטָאֵי כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל בִּשְׁבִירַת הַלּוּחוֹת שֶׁהָיָה תִּיקּוּן לְחֵטְא הָעֵגֶל עַל יְדֵי שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא ״יִישַׁר כֹּחֲךָ״ עַל חֶטְאוֹ, וְזֶהוּ הַיִּצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה

And he—Shlomo—encompasses the entire Congregation of Israel; similarly, his sin served to rectify the sins of the Congregation of Israel. As I wrote above concerning Moshe’s breaking of the Tablets, this brought about a rectification of the sin of the Golden Calf when the Holy One said to him, “Well done that you broke them,” concerning that act. And this concerns the inclination toward idolatry.

paragraphs.text: Sukkah 52a teaches: “צַדִּיקִים נִדְמֶה לָהֶם כְּהַר גָּבוֹהַּ ... וְאוֹמְרִים הֵיאַךְ יָכֹלְנוּ לִכְבּוֹשׁ הַר גָּבוֹהַּ כָּזֶה” — to the righteous the evil inclination appears as a towering mountain, and they marvel that they overcame it. The passage also describes the yetzer’s future slaughter. Rav Tzadok draws the further conclusion: the very struggle makes its conquest a precious spiritual light in this world; after the yetzer ceases, that particular kind of achievement is no longer possible. This is his interpretation, not an assertion about the value of Torah in general in the World to Come.

paragraphs.text: Sukkah 52a relates that Mashiach ben David asks for “חַיִּים,” life, and is answered: “עַד שֶׁלֹּא אָמַרְתָּ כְּבָר הִתְנַבָּא עָלֶיךָ דָּוִד אָבִיךָ ... חַיִּים שָׁאַל מִמְּךָ נָתַתָּה לּוֹ” — before you asked, David your ancestor had already prophesied, “He asked life of You; You granted it.” Isaiah 25:8 promises “בִּלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח,” the swallowing of death forever. The connection of the Mashiach teaching to David’s inward attainment of enduring life is Rav Tzadok’s interpretation in this paragraph; the Gemara does not state that David escaped physical death.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 90a, the opening Mishnah of Perek Chelek, states: “כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא ... וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים” — “All Israel have a share in the World to Come ... Your people are all righteous” (Isaiah 60:21). The Mishnah immediately identifies exceptions (“וְאֵלּוּ שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם”), so this is not an unconditional ruling that no person can lose that share. Nedarim 31b says “מוּתָּר בְּעַרְלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל,” permitting those called “uncircumcised Israelites” under a vow against “uncircumcised,” since Israel retains its covenantal designation. Bava Metzia 59a reports David’s answer when mocked in the beis midrash: “מִיתָתוֹ בְּחֶנֶק, וְיֵשׁ לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, אֲבָל הַמַּלְבִּין אֶת פְּנֵי חֲבֵירוֹ בָּרַבִּים אֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא” — the guilty adulterer faces the prescribed penalty yet may retain a share, whereas public humiliation may forfeit it. Rav Tzadok draws from these sources his further point about an enduring Jewish covenantal root; this in no way excuses adultery, annuls punishment, or negates teshuvah. Sources: Sanhedrin 90a; Isaiah 60:21; Nedarim 31b; Bava Metzia 59a (the latter already discussed in the earlier David narrative).

paragraphs.text: II Samuel 12:24–25 says of the newborn Shlomo: “וַה׳ אֲהֵבוֹ ... וַיִּקְרָא אֶת שְׁמוֹ יְדִידְיָהּ בַּעֲבוּר ה׳” — Hashem loved him, and the name Yedidyah was sent through Nathan. II Samuel 7:14–15 promises concerning David’s heir: “אֲנִי אֶהְיֶה לוֹ לְאָב וְהוּא יִהְיֶה לִּי לְבֵן ... וְחַסְדִּי לֹא יָסוּר מִמֶּנּוּ” — I shall be to him a father and he a son; chastisement will occur when he acts wrongly, but My kindness will not depart. The verses explicitly preserve both love and discipline. Rav Tzadok interprets this as an enduring covenantal bond; it should not be described as Scripture’s approval of every subsequent act.

paragraphs.text: Rav Tzadok writes in Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua §10 that Shlomo, as king, belonged to “כָּל הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל” and that “פַּרְנַס הַדּוֹר נַפְשׁוֹ כוֹלֶלֶת כָּל נַפְשׁוֹת הַדּוֹר” — the leader’s soul embraces all the souls of the generation. This explains why the present sentence’s “וְהוּא כּוֹלֵל” refers to Shlomo and why Rav Tzadok understands his deeds through a collective lens. The immediate earlier parallel is Takanat HaShavin 10:3, where Moses’ breaking of the Tablets rectified the Golden Calf. Shabbos 87a records the Divine assent: “יִישַׁר כֹּחֲךָ שֶׁשִּׁבַּרְתָּ” — well done that you broke them. The description of this paradox as a rectification of an “aveirah” is Rav Tzadok’s theological analysis; the Gemara does not offer general license to transgress.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The study of nega’im and ohalos is “precious light” in this world, for a person’s whole labor here is conquering the yetzer (which “appears to the righteous like a mountain”) — a great and precious attainment. In Olam Haba, with no yetzer, it is “nothing,” yielding no such light (as for the angels). Mashiach is the ultimate completion of conquering the yetzer — “he asked life of You, You gave it him” — so that death too is swallowed, “for this depends on that,” the yetzer being the Angel of Death.

p: (כה) וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה לֹא פָּעַל לְעָקְרוֹ (לְיִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה) לְגַמְרֵי, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לוֹ זְכוּת דְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בַּעֲרָכִין לב:); וְנִגְמַר עַל יְדֵי אַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה, וְהָעִיקָּר עֶזְרָא כִּדְאִיתָא (שָׁם בַּעֲרָכִין), כִּי הוּא הָיָה כְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין כא:) דְּהָיָה רָאוּי שֶׁתִּינָּתֵן תּוֹרָה עַל יָדוֹ

And Moshe Rabbeinu did not effect to uproot it (the inclination of idolatry) completely, because he did not have “the merit of Eretz Yisrael,” as they said Arachin 32b; and it was completed by the Men of the Great Assembly, chiefly Ezra, as it is there in Arachin — for he was “like Moshe,” in the manner it is stated Sanhedrin 21b that “he was worthy that the Torah be given through him.”

וְזֶה הָיָה תֹּקֶף רִיבּוּי הַתְּפִלּוֹת דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה לִיכָּנֵס לָאָרֶץ, דְּאָז הָיָה עוֹקֵר יִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, וְלֹא עָבְדוּ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְלֹא כָּלוּ, וְהָיָה כִּיבּוּשׁ עוֹלָם, אֲבָל לֹא הִגִּיעַ הַזְּמַן עֲדַיִין, כִּי לַכֹּל זְמָן

And this was the intensity of Moshe Rabbeinu’s many prayers to enter the Land — for then he would have uprooted the inclination of idolatry, and they would not have served idolatry and would not have been destroyed, and it would have been an everlasting conquest; but the time had not yet come, “for everything has its time.”

וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה הַמְתַקֵּן לְיִצְרָא דִּזְנוּת — עַל יְדֵי שֶׁיְּבוֹרַר חֶטְאוֹ, מַה שֶּׁגַּם כֵּן מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב חֵטְא גָּמוּר וְשֶׁ״רַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״, וְהוּא מָלֵא קְדֻשָּׁה בֶּאֱמֶת, דַּהֲרֵי רְאוּיָה לוֹ מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית

And David HaMelech, peace be upon him, is the one who rectifies the inclination toward sexual immorality, through clarification of his sin — concerning which Scripture indeed attributes to him a complete sin and says that the matter was “evil in the eyes of Hashem”; yet he was truly full of holiness, for Bat Sheva was destined for him from the six days of Creation.

וְכָךְ כָּל חֲטָאֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל סְדוּרִים וּבָאִים מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית, וְאָז ״כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ״, וְהַגּוֹמֵר יִהְיֶה מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן דָּוִד שֶׁבְּיָמָיו יְבוּלַּע הַיֵּצֶר לְגַמְרֵי

and so all the sins of the Children of Israel are “arranged and come from the six days of Creation,” and then “they shall become white as snow”; and the one who completes it will be Mashiach ben David, in whose days the inclination will be wholly swallowed up.

וְנִרְאֶה לִי דִּכְמוֹ דִּלְמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה הָיָה הַחִסָּרוֹן מִפְּנֵי שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, לְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה הָיָה הַחִסָּרוֹן שֶׁלֹּא גָּמַר הוּא עֲקִירַת הַיֵּצֶר לְגַמְרֵי, מַה שֶּׁלֹּא נִבְנָה בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ עֲדַיִין

And it appears to me that, just as for Moshe the deficiency was because he was not in Eretz Yisrael, for David the deficiency was that he did not complete the uprooting of the inclination entirely — in that the Beis HaMikdash was not yet built.

שֶׁאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל מְיוּחֶדֶת לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״אֱלֹקֵי הָאָרֶץ״ וַ״אֲשֶׁר הוּא דּוֹרֵשׁ אֹתָהּ״, שֶׁהַשְׁרָאָתוֹ וֶאֱלֹקוּתוֹ נִיכָּר בָּהּ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּכְתוּבּוֹת קי סע״ב) שֶׁהַדָּר בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ אֱלוֹהַּ, וְהַדָּר בְּחוּץ לָאָרֶץ כְּעוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם

For Eretz Yisrael is dedicated to Hashem — called “the God of the land,” “which He seeks out” — where His indwelling and Godliness are recognized; and as they said Kesubos 110b, one who dwells in Eretz Yisrael is “like one who has a God,” and one who dwells outside the Land is “like one who serves idols” — see there.
וּלְכָךְ אִי אֶפְשָׁר עֲקִירַת יִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה אֶלָּא בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל; וּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ הוּא מְקוֹם מִשְׁכַּן הַקְּדֻשָּׁה שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם, דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא ״מִקְדָּשׁ״

And therefore the uprooting of the inclination of idolatry is impossible except in Eretz Yisrael; and the Beis HaMikdash is the “place of the dwelling of holiness in the world,” and therefore called “Mikdash Sanctuary.”
וְעִיקַּר הַקְּדֻשָּׁה הוּא בִּפְרִישׁוּת מִתַּאֲווֹת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ״כָּל מָקוֹם שֶׁאַתָּה מוֹצֵא גֶּדֶר עֶרְוָה שָׁם אַתָּה מוֹצֵא קְדֻשָּׁה״
And the essence of holiness is “abstinence from the desires,” as they said, “wherever you find a fence against immorality, there you find holiness.”
וּבִבְרָכוֹת (י׳:) “אִישׁ קָדוֹשׁ” שֶׁלֹּא רָאֲתָה שׁוּם קֶרִי אַסְדִּינוֹ, וּמְשָׁרְתוֹ אֵינוֹ קָדוֹשׁ שֶׁאֲחָזָהּ וְכוּלֵּי.
And in Berakhot (10b), a “holy man” was identified by the fact that she had never seen a seminal emission on his bed-linen, whereas his attendant was not holy, for he seized her, and so forth.
וּבִירוּשַׁלְמִי (פֶּרֶק ב׳ דִּיבָמוֹת הֲלָכָה ד׳) דְּהַפּוֹרֵשׁ מֵעֶרְיוֹת נִקְרָא קָדוֹשׁ.
And in the Yerushalmi (Yevamos, chapter 2, halachah 4): one who separates from forbidden relations is called holy.

וְעַד שֶׁלֹּא נִבְנָה בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, שֶׁלֹּא הָיְתָה הִתְגַּלּוּת הַקְּדֻשָּׁה דְּמָקוֹם בָּעוֹלָם, גַּם בַּנֶּפֶשׁ לֹא הָיְתָה הִתְגַּלּוּת הַקְּדֻשָּׁה בְּפֹעַל, וּלְפִיכָךְ לֹא יָכוֹל לְהָבִיא לְיָדוֹ גְּמַר דַּעֲקִירַת הַיֵּצֶר דַּעֲרָיוֹת

And before the Beis HaMikdash was built, when the holiness of a particular place had not yet been revealed in the world, holiness had likewise not become manifest in the soul in actual practice; therefore David could not himself bring about the final uprooting of the inclination toward forbidden relations.

וְזֶהוּ הִשְׁתּוֹקְקוּת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה לְבִנְיַן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, וְאִלְמָלֵא זָכוּ שֶׁהוּא יִבְנֶנּוּ הָיָה עֵת קֵץ בַּעֲקִירַת הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע וְלֹא הָיָה נֶחֱרָב עוֹד, אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא הִגִּיעַ הַקֵּץ

And this is David’s yearning for the building of the Beis HaMikdash; and had they merited that he build it, it would have been the End of Days in the uprooting of the evil inclination, and it would never have been destroyed again — only that the End had not yet come.

paragraphs.text: Arakhin 32b describes the returnees under Ezra: “דְּבָעוּ רַחֲמֵי עַל יֵצֶר דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וּבַטְּלֵיהּ” — they prayed for mercy concerning the urge toward idol-worship and abolished it. The same passage asks why Yehoshua had not sought its abolition and expressly distinguishes Moshe: “בִּשְׁלָמָא מֹשֶׁה לָא בָּעֵי רַחֲמֵי דְּלָא הֲוָה זְכוּתָא דְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל” — Moshe did not possess the merit of the Land. Separately, Sanhedrin 21b says: “רָאוּי הָיָה עֶזְרָא שֶׁתִּינָתֵן תּוֹרָה עַל יָדוֹ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, אִלְמָלֵא לֹא קְדָמוֹ מֹשֶׁה” — Ezra was worthy of giving Torah had Moshe not preceded him. Rav Tzadok connects these statements to explain why the correction was historically completed in Ezra’s era; the additional claim about what would have followed had Moshe entered the Land is developed in the next passage, not stated by either Gemara. Sources: Arakhin 32b; Sanhedrin 21b.

paragraphs.text: Sotah 14a asks, “מפני מה נתאוה משה רבינו ליכנס לארץ ישראל?” — why did Moshe long to enter the Land? The answer is that Israel was commanded many mitzvos performable only there and he sought to fulfill them himself: “אכנס אני לארץ כדי שיתקיימו כולן על ידי.” Rav Tzadok supplies a second, inner reading of the yearning: the Land could have become the setting for Moshe to remove the urge toward idolatry from Israel, as clarified by his interpretation of Arakhin 32b. This is a spiritual extension of the teaching about land-dependent commandments, not the explicit reason given in Sotah.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 107a records Rava’s teaching: “ראויה היתה בת שבע בת אליעם לדוד מששת ימי בראשית, אלא שבאת עליו במכאוב” — Bat Sheva had been destined for David from the six days of Creation, but came to him through suffering. The school of Rabbi Yishmael adds: “ראויה היתה לדוד בת שבע ... אלא שאכלה פגה” — she was destined for him, yet he took her before the proper time, like unripe fruit. II Samuel 11:27 nevertheless says of the episode, “וירע הדבר אשר עשה דוד בעיני ה׳” — the thing David did was evil in Hashem’s eyes. The destined zivug does not annul the historical wrongdoing. Rav Tzadok’s distinctive claim here is that its innermost holiness becomes comprehensible in the subsequent unfolding of teshuvah and the final rectification.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 89b reads Isaiah 1:18, “אִם יִהְיוּ חֲטָאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים ... כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ,” in R. Yitzchak's derashah “כַּשָּׁנִים הַלָּלוּ שֶׁסְּדוּרוֹת וּבָאוֹת מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית וְעַד עַכְשָׁיו” — like the years ordered and arriving since Creation. Rav Tzadok’s Tzidkas HaTzadik §228 quotes the same teaching and develops the goal “לְאִתְהַפְּכָא מִנֶּגַע לְעֹנֶג” — to transform affliction into delight. Sukkah 52a separately describes Hashem's future removal of the evil inclination. Rav Tzadok here joins these teachings in the final rectification through Mashiach ben David. This is an interpretation of teshuvah and ultimate transformation, not permission to sin or a claim that the Gemara exempts wrongdoing. Sources: Shabbos 89b; Isaiah 1:18; Tzidkas HaTzadik §228; Sukkah 52a.

paragraphs.text: Ketubot 110b teaches, “כל הדר בארץ ישראל דומה כמי שיש לו אלוה, וכל הדר בחוצה לארץ דומה כמי שאין לו אלוה” — one dwelling in Eretz Yisrael is like one who has a God, while one dwelling outside is likened to one who does not. The Gemara further qualifies the comparison: “כל הדר בחוצה לארץ כאילו עובד עבודה זרה” — it is as if he serves idols, and it cites David’s lament (I Samuel 26:19), “כי גרשוני היום מהסתפח בנחלת ה׳ ... לך עבד אלהים אחרים” — “they have driven me today from attachment to Hashem’s inheritance ... ‘Go, serve other gods.’” This is an aggadic comparison, not an assertion that residents outside the Land literally worship idols. Rav Tzadok infers that removing the idolatrous impulse requires the distinctive revelation of Divine sovereignty in Eretz Yisrael.

paragraphs.text: Rashi on Vayikra 19:2 writes on “קְדֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ”: “הֱווּ פְרוּשִׁים מִן הָעֲרָיוֹת וּמִן הָעֲבֵרָה, שֶׁכָּל מָקוֹם שֶׁאַתָּה מוֹצֵא גֶדֶר עֶרְוָה אַתָּה מוֹצֵא קְדֻשָּׁה” — separation from forbidden relations is itself an expression of holiness. Maharal's Gur Aryeh on Shemos 22:30 distinguishes this from refraining from forbidden food: “שֶׁפְּרִישַׁת הָעֶרְוָה בְּעַצְמָהּ הוּא הַקְּדֻשָּׁה,” since this restraint directly disciplines desire, whereas abstaining from nonkosher food primarily preserves an existing sanctity. Berakhot 10b gives the Shunammite woman's contrasting tests of Elisha's holiness and Gehazi's misconduct. These sources explain Rav Tzadok's connection of holiness with inward restraint; the historical claim that the Temple's later construction was needed to complete the rectification is his further interpretive conclusion. Sources: Rashi on Leviticus 19:2; Gur Aryeh on Shemot 22:30, first comment; Berakhot 10b. Gur Aryeh exact original text checked on Sefaria and Wikisource.

paragraphs.text: Psalms 132:1–5 describes David vowing to forego rest “עד אמצא מקום לה׳” — “until I find a place for Hashem.” In I Chronicles 22:7–10 David tells Shlomo “אני היה עם לבבי לבנות בית לשם ה׳ אלהי” — “It was in my heart to build a House for the Name of Hashem my God,” yet the task was given to his son, a man of rest. Chronicles also supplies its stated historical reason: David had shed much blood. Rav Tzadok adds a distinct theological interpretation: David could begin the rectification of desire, but the moment in history had not arrived for him to finish it by establishing a permanent Sanctuary. His counterfactual that a Temple built by David would not be destroyed is his interpretation, not a direct claim in these verses.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Moshe did not fully uproot the inclination of idolatry, lacking “the merit of Eretz Yisrael.” It was completed by the Men of the Great Assembly — chiefly Ezra, “like Moshe” (worthy that the Torah be given through him). This was the intensity of Moshe’s prayers to enter the Land: there he would have uprooted idolatry, and Israel would never have been destroyed.

וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סֻכָּה מה:) "שֶׁמָּא תֹאמַר אָבַד סִבְרָן וּבָטַל סִכּוּיָן, תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר עוֹמְדִין, שֶׁעוֹמְדִין לְעוֹלְמֵי עוֹלָמִים".
and our Sages, of blessed memory, expounded (Sukkah 45b): “Lest you say their hope is lost and their prospect nullified, the verse says ‘upright’ — they stand forever and ever.”
וּכְלָשׁוֹן הַזֶּה (בְּעֵרוּבִין כא רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב) עַל רְשָׁעִים גְּמוּרִים, "שֶׁמָּא תֹאמַר אָבַד סִבְרָן וּבָטַל סִכּוּיָן, תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר וְכוּלֵּי עֲתִידִין שֶׁיִּתְּנוּ רֵיחַ".

And in this language (in Eruvin 21b, beginning of the amud) regarding completely wicked people: “Lest you say their hope is lost and their prospect nullified, the verse says, etc. — they are destined to give forth fragrance.”
וְכַיּוֹצֵא בּוֹ (בְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא לג:) עַל עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ שׂוֹנְאֵי הַתַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים עַיֵּן שָׁם.
And similar to it (in Bava Metzia 33b) regarding ignoramuses who hate Torah scholars, see there.
וְהַיְנוּ דְּעִקַּר קְדֻשַּׁת הַמִּשְׁכָּן הוּא שֶׁשְּׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרֵךְ תּוֹךְ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל,
That is, the main holiness of the Mishkan is that His Presence, blessed be He, is among the Children of Israel,
דְּכָל הָעֵדָה כֻּלָּם קְדוֹשִׁים וּבְתוֹכָם ה'.
for “the whole congregation, all of them are holy, and Hashem is in their midst.”
הַיְנוּ מֻגְדָּרִים בַּעֲרָיוֹת וְתַאֲוַת יֵצֶר הָרָע הַמּוֹנֵעַ שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרֵךְ,
That is, fenced off from forbidden relations and from the desire of the evil inclination which prevents His Presence, blessed be He,
וְכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "פֶּן יִרְאֶה בְךָ עֶרְוַת דָּבָר וְשָׁב מֵאַחֲרֶיךָ",
as it is said, “lest He see in you an unseemly thing and turn away from you,”
וְכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סַנְהֶדְרִין קט סוֹף עַמּוּד ב) "יָדַעְנָא דְּכוּלָּה וְכוּלֵּי" עַיֵּן שָׁם.
and as they said (Sanhedrin 109b, end of the amud): “I know that all of it, etc.,” see there.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּתְבַּטֵּל לְשָׁעָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, דְּנִרְאֶה שֶׁלֹּא כֵן,
And even though it was nullified for a time in this world, in which it appears not to be so,
בֶּאֱמֶת קְדֻשָּׁה זוֹ קַיֶּמֶת לְעָלְמֵי עַד, וַעֲתִידִים לִתֵּן רֵיחַ,
in truth this holiness endures forever, and they are destined to give forth fragrance,
הַיְנוּ עַל יְדֵי טָהֳרָה מִטֻּמְאַת הַיֵּצֶר,
that is, through purity from the impurity of the inclination,
וְכִדְתַנְיָא (סוֹטָה מט.) דְּטָהֳרָה נָטְלָה הָרֵיחַ, וְשָׁם ״טָהֳרָה יֵשׁ בָּךְ״,
as they taught (Sotah 49a), that the loss of purity took away fragrance; and there, “you possess purity,”
וְהַיְנוּ הֶעְדֵּר הִרְהוּרֵי תַאֲוָה,
and that is the absence of thoughts of desire,
וְכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּיוֹמָא עב:) עַל פָּסוּק "יִרְאַת ה' טְהוֹרָה", זֶה (הַלּוֹמֵד תּוֹרָה בְּטָהֳרָה), מַאי הוּא (נוֹשֵׂא אִשָּׁה וְאַחַר כָּךְ לוֹמֵד תּוֹרָה) עַיֵּן שָׁם.
and as they said (in Yoma 72b) on the verse “the fear of Hashem is pure”: this is (one who learns Torah in purity); what is it? (one who marries a wife and afterward learns Torah), see there.
וְכֵן (בְּסוֹף מְנָחוֹת קי) עַל פָּסוּק "וּמִנְחָה טְהוֹרָה",
And likewise (at the end of Menachos 110) on the verse “and a pure meal-offering,”
וְכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּעֵרוּבִין שָׁם) "הַדּוּדָאִים נָתְנוּ רֵיחַ — אֵלּוּ בַּחוּרֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁלֹּא טָעֲמוּ טַעַם חֵטְא".
and as they said (in Eruvin there): “‘the mandrakes give forth fragrance’ — these are the young men of Israel who have not tasted the taste of sin.”
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעִקַּר תַּבְלִין הַיֵּצֶר הוּא הַתּוֹרָה,
And although the main spice for the inclination is the Torah,
גַּם עַמֵּי הָאָרֶצוֹת וְשׂוֹנְאֵי תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים לֹא יֵבוֹשׁוּ, כִּי יִהְיוּ לַאֲגֻדָּה אַחַת.
even the ignoramuses and the haters of Torah scholars will not be ashamed, for they will be one bond.
וְהָאָרוֹן שֶׁהוּא מִשְׁכַּן הַתּוֹרָה, רוֹמֵז לְתַלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים,
And the Ark, which is the dwelling of the Torah, alludes to Torah scholars,
גַּם הוּא מֵעֲצֵי שִׁטִּים אֶלָּא שֶׁמְּצֻפֶּה זָהָב מִבַּיִת וּמִבַּחוּץ,
it too is of acacia wood, but overlaid with gold inside and outside,
וְדָרְשׁוּ מִזֶּה (יוֹמָא עב:) לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה תּוֹכוֹ כְּבָרוֹ.
and from this they expounded (Yoma 72b) that a Torah scholar should have his inside like his outside.
הַיְנוּ יִרְאָתוֹ הַקּוֹדֶמֶת לְחָכְמָתוֹ,
That is, his fear of Heaven preceding his wisdom,
כַּיָּדוּעַ מִזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ דְּזָהָב דַּרְגָּא דְיִצְחָק רוֹמֵז לְיִרְאָה, וְהוּא מִבַּחוּץ,
as is known from the holy Zohar, that gold, the level of Yitzchak, alludes to fear, and it is on the outside,
וְכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק קִנְיַן תּוֹרָה) "וּמַלְבַּשְׁתּוֹ עֲנָוָה וְיִרְאָה",
and as they said (at the beginning of the chapter Kinyan Torah), “and it clothes him with humility and fear,”
וְזֶהוּ הַמָּשָׁל לַמַּפְתְּחוֹת הַחִיצוֹנוֹת (בְּשַׁבָּת לא רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב).
and this is the parable of the outer keys (Shabbos 31b).
וְגַם בִּפְנִימִיּוּתוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּיוֹמָא שָׁם) עַל פָּסוּק "וְלֵב אַיִן", דְּיִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם בְּמַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב.
And also in his inwardness, as they said (in Yoma there) on the verse “and a heart is lacking,” for fear of Heaven is in the depths of the heart.
וּבָזֶה נִתְקַן הָעֲצֵי שִׁטִּים שֶׁבֵּינְתַיִם, שֶׁאֵין נִרְאֶה כְּלָל וְכְאִלּוּ הַכֹּל זָהָב.
And through this the acacia wood in between is rectified, so that it is not seen at all, as if everything were gold.

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 30a relates that when Shlomo built the Temple and sought to bring the Ark into the Holy of Holies, “דבקו שערים זה בזה” — the gates clung together. They did not yield to his previous pleas. Only when he said “זכרה לחסדי דוד עבדך” — “remember the loving deeds of David Your servant” (II Chronicles 6:42) — was he answered. Then “וידעו כל העם וכל ישראל שמחל לו הקדוש ברוך הוא על אותו עון” — all Israel learned that God had forgiven David for that sin. The “sign for good” alludes to Psalms 86:17. Rav Tzadok’s point is about when forgiveness was publicly revealed, not a claim that David could not have received Divine forgiveness before the Temple’s construction.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 21b enumerates “חמשה דברים שהיו בין מקדש ראשון למקדש שני” — five differences between the First and Second Temples — including “ארון וכפורת וכרובים ... ושכינה” — the Ark, cover and cherubs, and the Shechinah. Rav Tzadok draws on this loss of the Ark and the absence of the First Temple’s manifest Shechinah to explain why the First Temple had special revelatory sanctity. The Gemara’s list should not be expanded into the unqualified theological claim that no Divine Presence existed anywhere in the Second Temple era.

paragraphs.text: Bava Batra 14a–14b describes the Luchos within the Ark and records a dispute about the place of Moshe’s Torah scroll: according to Rabbi Meir it was inside, and according to Rabbi Yehudah it lay at the Ark’s side. Thus the Ark is the place of the covenantal Tablets, and also closely associated with the Torah scroll. Rav Tzadok’s “ארון רומז לתורה” — the Ark alludes to Torah — is symbolic exposition built upon that concrete association, not a claim that the disputed placement of the scroll was unanimously accepted.

paragraphs.text: Bamidbar Rabbah 20:22 and Midrash Tanchuma, Balak 17 describe the old “מַעְיָן שִׁטִּים” as a spring that fostered licentiousness: “וּמַעְיַן שִׁטִּים שֶׁל זְנוּת הָיָה.” The Midrash says this polluted spring is destined to dry up, quoting Joel 4:18: “וּמַעְיָן מִבֵּית ה׳ יֵצֵא וְהִשְׁקָה אֶת נַחַל הַשִּׁטִּים” — a spring shall issue from the House of Hashem and water the brook of Shittim. Rav Tzadok resolves the distinction: the former destructive influence ends, while the same place becomes nourished by a holy stream. This is now a developed idea in the Hebrew text, which explicitly says the new spring will be holy and the acacia trees themselves allude to that transformation. Peri Tzaddik, Terumah §8 similarly teaches the future “חֲמִידוּ דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא,” desire redirected toward Torah. The biblical wording and the Midrashic explanation are cited separately; the synthesis is Rav Tzadok's. Sources: Bamidbar Rabbah 20:22; Midrash Tanchuma, Balak 17; Joel 4:18; Pri Tzaddik, Terumah §8.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 30b declares: “בָּרָאתִי יֵצֶר הָרָע וּבָרָאתִי לוֹ תּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין” — “I created the evil inclination and created Torah as its remedy”; it also advises, “אִם פָּגַע בְּךָ מְנֻוָּל זֶה מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ.” Rav Tzadok then goes beyond this individual remedy to the destiny of all Israel, including those alienated from learning. Eruvin 21b, using the good and bad figs, says even those considered utterly wicked are not without hope: “שֶׁמָּא תֹּאמַר אָבַד סִבְרָם וּבָטַל סִיכּוּיָם ... אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ עֲתִידִין שֶׁיִּתְּנוּ רֵיחַ” — both are destined to give fragrance. Bava Metzia 33b separately enumerates Torah scholars and different groups including the “עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ”; it does not itself promise the future rectification. Rav Tzadok joins the former hopeful derashah with the latter distinctions to explain the eventual “one bond” of Israel. Sources: Kiddushin 30b; Eruvin 21b; Bava Metzia 33b.

rich.text: Kiddushin 30b declares: “בָּרָאתִי יֵצֶר הָרָע וּבָרָאתִי לוֹ תּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין” — “I created the evil inclination and created Torah as its remedy”; it also advises, “אִם פָּגַע בְּךָ מְנֻוָּל זֶה מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ.” Rav Tzadok then goes beyond this individual remedy to the destiny of all Israel, including those alienated from learning. Eruvin 21b, using the good and bad figs, says even those considered utterly wicked are not without hope: “שֶׁמָּא תֹּאמַר אָבַד סִבְרָם וּבָטַל סִיכּוּיָם ... אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ עֲתִידִין שֶׁיִּתְּנוּ רֵיחַ” — both are destined to give fragrance. Bava Metzia 33b separately enumerates Torah scholars and different groups including the “עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ”; it does not itself promise the future rectification. Rav Tzadok joins the former hopeful derashah with the latter distinctions to explain the eventual “one bond” of Israel. Sources: Kiddushin 30b; Eruvin 21b; Bava Metzia 33b.

paragraphs.text: Sotah 3a derives from “כִּי תִשְׂטֶה” that “אֵין אָדָם עוֹבֵר עֲבֵירָה אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְנַס בּוֹ רוּחַ שְׁטוּת” — transgression follows a spirit of folly. Rav Tzadok's Machshavos Charutz §4 (Har Bracha printed p. 14; PDF p. 18) directly develops the Ark analogy: “וְהָאָרוֹן הָיָה מֵעֲצֵי שִׁטִּים, דְּזֶהוּ הָעֵצָה דְּמָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ, לְהַמְשִׁיךְ הַחֵשֶׁק וְהַתַּאֲוָה שֶׁלּוֹ לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה” — the Ark's acacia represents redirecting desire into Torah; he further says its inner and outer gold symbolize “תֹּקֶף הַיִּרְאָה הַקְּדוֹשָׁה הַמְבַטֶּלֶת תַּאֲווֹת רָעוֹת,” holy awe that overcomes destructive desire. Pri Tzaddik, Terumah §8 develops the same symbolism and speaks of “חֲמִידוּ דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא,” longing for Torah. The Talmudic words and Rav Tzadok's added metaphysical interpretation must be distinguished. This note is placed only after Rav Tzadok has explained the acacia core, gold covering, and yirah both externally and internally. Sources: Sotah 3a; Kiddushin 30b; Machshavos Charutz §4, Har Bracha p. 14; Pri Tzaddik, Terumah §8; Yoma 72b.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Therefore the pardon of David’s iniquity was likewise not revealed to all — “a sign for good, that his enemies see and be ashamed.” Until the Beis HaMikdash was completed, when “they could not bring the Ark into the Holy of Holies” until David’s merit was invoked. This is the essence of the First Temple’s holiness — for the Second, lacking the Ark, lacked the Shechinah; and the Ark alludes to the Torah.

p: (כז) וְזֶהוּ תַּכְלִית הַמְתָּקַת הַיֵּצֶר עַל יְדֵי תַּבְלִין דְּתוֹרָה. וּבְסוֹטָה (ט סע״א) דְּמֹשֶׁה וְדָוִד לֹא שָׁלְטוּ שׂוֹנְאִים בְּמַעֲשֵׂה יְדֵיהֶם, כִּי הֵם הַמַּתְחִילִים בַּעֲקִירַת הַיֵּצֶר לְגַמְרֵי מִלֵּב

This is the ultimate sweetening of the inclination through the seasoning of Torah. Sotah 9a teaches that the enemies of Moshe and David never gained mastery over the work of their hands; Rav Tzadok explains that these two began to uproot the inclination entirely from the heart.
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה הוּא הַחֵירוּת מִמַּלְכֻיּוֹת גַּם כֵּן, דִּ״שְׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָה״ וְשִׁעְבּוּד מַלְכֻיּוֹת הָא בְּהָא תַּלְיִין
for through this is also “the freedom from the kingdoms,” since “the leaven in the dough” and the subjugation to the kingdoms are interdependent.

וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא הִגִּיעַ הַזְּמַן שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּפֹעַל כֵּן בְּכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מַעֲשֵׂה יְדֵיהֶם וְהַהַתְחָלָה שֶׁלָּהֶם לֹא נִתְבַּטֵּל כְּלָל, רַק נִגְנַז, וּלְעָתִיד יִתְגַּלֶּה דְּ״לֹא אָבַד סִבְרָן וּבָטֵל סִיכּוּיָן״, רַק הֵם קַיָּימִין לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד

Although the time had not yet arrived for this to become actual throughout Israel, the works of their hands and the beginnings they established were not annulled at all, but were only concealed. In the future it will be revealed that their hope was not lost and their expectation had not come to an end; rather, those works endure forever.

וְהַמִּשְׁכָּן — קְדֻשַּׁת שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּאֹהֶל אֲרַעַי — הָיָה עַל יְדֵי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה שֶׁהָיָה בַּמִּדְבָּר, דַּעֲדַיִין לֹא הָיָה לוֹ קְבִיעוּת מָקוֹם; וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה הוּא שֶׁהִתְחִיל בְּבִנְיַן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ

And the Mishkan — the holiness of His Shechinah in a “temporary tent” — was through Moshe, who was in the wilderness, when there was not yet a fixed place; and David HaMelech is the one who began the building of the Beis HaMikdash.

וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא נִבְנָה עַל יָדוֹ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא הָיָה הַמַּתְחִיל עַל יְדֵי הִשְׁתּוֹקְקוּתוֹ וְחִשְׁקוֹ וַהֲכָנָתוֹ, וְהַכֹּל לוֹ; גַּם קָנָה הַמָּקוֹם, וּקְדֻשַּׁת הַמָּקוֹם קִידְּשָׁהּ לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא וְקַיָּים לָעַד, וְעַל פִּי צִיוּוּיוֹ לִשְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה נִבְנָה

And although it was not built by him, nonetheless he was the initiator, through his yearning and desire and preparation, and all is his; he also acquired the “place,” and the holiness of the place he sanctified for the Future — enduring forever — and by his command to Shlomo HaMelech it was built.

וּלְפִיכָךְ הַשְּׁעָרִים — הַיְינוּ פֶּתַח הַכְּנִיסָה לִקְדֻשַּׁת הַמִּקְדָּשׁ — הֵם מַעֲשֵׂה יָדָיו; וְזֶה ״טָבַע בָּאָרֶץ״ וְנִגְנַז לִהְיוֹת קַיָּים לָעַד, וְלֹא יוּכְלוּ אוֹיְבִים לִשְׁלוֹט בָּהֶם וּלְהוֹצִיאָם לְחוּלִּין כְּלָל

Accordingly, the gates — the entrance to the holiness of the Mikdash — are the work of his hands. These “sank into the earth” and were concealed so as to endure forever, beyond the power of enemies to control or profane them.
דְּמִשֶּׁבָּאוּ פָּרִיצִים חִלְּלוּהוּ, לְפִי שֶׁ״דָּוִד מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל חַי וְקַיָּים״ וּקְדֻשָּׁתוֹ קַיֶּימֶת, וְלֹא אָבַד סִבְרוֹ, רַק שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם וּבִגְנִיזָה

For once marauders entered, they profaned what they seized. Yet “David, king of Israel, lives and endures”; his holiness endures and his hope has not vanished, but remains hidden and stored away in this world.

וְעַל כֵּן כְּשֶׁבָּא לְהַכְנִיס הָאָרוֹן לְבֵית קָדְשֵׁי הַקֳּדָשִׁים — דְּהָאָרוֹן רוֹמֵז לִקְדֻשָּׁה זוֹ דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה, שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיֵּשׁ עֲצֵי שִׁטִּים בָּאֶמְצַע הֵם מְצוּפִּים זָהָב מִבַּיִת וּמִחוּץ — וְעַל כֵּן מְקוֹמוֹ בְּבֵית קָדְשֵׁי הַקֳּדָשִׁים, שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הַקְּדֻשָּׁה שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר לָאָדָם לְהַשִּׂיג, שֶׁהוּא לְמַעְלָה מֵהַשָּׂגַת הַמַּלְאָכִים, שֶׁהֲרֵי הַמַּלְאָכִים אֵין יְכוֹלִים לִיכָּנֵס שָׁם

And therefore, when Shlomo came to bring the Ark into the Holy of Holies — for the Ark alludes to this holiness of David, in that although there is acacia wood in the middle, it is “overlaid with gold within and without” (Shemos 25:11) — and therefore its place is in the Holy of Holies, which is the ultimate holiness a person can attain, above the attainment of the angels, for the angels cannot enter there,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּירוּשַׁלְמִי (פ״ה דְּיוֹמָא) עַל פָּסוּק ״וְכָל אָדָם לֹא יִהְיֶה בְּאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד״ אֲפִילּוּ אוֹתָם שֶׁדְּמוּת פְּנֵיהֶם פְּנֵי אָדָם, עַיֵּין שָׁם, וּכְמוֹ לֶעָתִיד דִּמְחִיצַּת הַצַּדִּיקִים יִהְיֶה לִפְנִים מִמְּחִיצַת מַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּירוּשַׁלְמִי (סוֹף פֶּרֶק ו׳ דְּשַׁבָּת)

As the Yerushalmi, Yoma chapter 5, teaches on “no person shall be in the Tent of Meeting” — even those “whose faces are the face of a man,” meaning the angelic beings. And in the future the enclosure of the righteous will be inward of that of the ministering angels, as the Yerushalmi says at the end of Shabbos chapter 6.
וְדָבְקוּ הַשְּׁעָרִים שֶׁהֵם מַעֲשֵׂה יְדֵי דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה, דְּהוּא שַׁעַר הַכְּנִיסָה לִקְדֻשָּׁה הַקַּיֶּימֶת לָעַד
And the “gates,” which are the work of David’s hands — the gate of entry to the holiness that endures forever — clung shut.

וְזֶה לֹא הָיָה מַדְרֵיגַת שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה, דִּבְמַעֲשֵׂי יָדָיו שָׁלְטוּ אוֹיְבִים, וּלְפִיכָךְ לֹא יָכוֹל לִפְתּוֹחַ עַד שֶׁאָמַר ״זָכְרָה לְחַסְדֵי דָּוִד״, שֶׁהֵם הַנֶּאֱמָנִים וְקַיָּימִים לָעַד; וְיָדוּעַ דְּ״תַאֲוַת אָדָם חַסְדּוֹ״, וְאֶצְלוֹ הָיָה הַכֹּל מִצַּד הַחֶסֶד דִּקְדֻשָּׁה

And this was not the rung of Shlomo, over whose handiwork enemies did rule; therefore he could not open them until he said, “remember the pious deeds chasdei of David,” which are “faithful and enduring forever”; and it is known that “the desire of a man is his kindness chesed” (Mishlei 19:22), and by him all was from the side of the chesed of holiness.

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 17a gives R. Alexandri’s petition: “רצוננו לעשות רצונך, ומי מעכב? שאור שבעיסה ושעבוד מלכיות” — “we desire to do Your will; what prevents us? The leaven in the dough and the subjugation of kingdoms.” This is a pair of impediments in the prayer, not a statement of their causal identity. Rav Tzadok makes the relationship explicit in Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:2 (“שאור שבעיסה ושעבוד מלכיות הכל אחד”) and 16:18 (“דהא בהא תליא”); the latter contrasts the absence of both forms of freedom under Ahasuerus with the freedom at Sinai. The present linkage of purification of the yetzer and release from foreign dominion belongs to Rav Tzadok’s developed reading.
