paragraphs.text: Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Beit HaBechirah 6:14 attributes the formal first consecration of the Temple precincts and Jerusalem to Shlomo: “בקדושה ראשונה שקדשה שלמה.” In 6:15–16 the Rambam rules that offerings may be brought even without a standing Temple, because that sanctity endured, “שכינה אינה בטלה” — the Divine Presence does not cease. The legal attribution to Shlomo must not be replaced by David. Rav Tzadok’s description of David as sanctifying the site for the future concerns his purchase and the enduring spiritual root disclosed by it, not a correction to the Rambam’s legal history.

paragraphs.text: I Chronicles 21:22–22:5 gives David’s acquisition and preparation of the site: “לא כי קנה אקנה בכסף מלא” — he insists on purchasing Ornan’s threshing floor for full payment; the heavenly fire answers his offerings, he declares “זה הוא בית ה׳ האלהים,” and prepares stone, iron, bronze, and cedar for the future building. David’s role is therefore not a claim that he physically completed the Temple. Rav Tzadok reads his yearning, purchase, preparations and guidance to Shlomo as its enduring spiritual beginning.

paragraphs.text: Sotah 9a expounds Psalms 33:1 by reading “נָוֶה תְהִלָּה” (“a dwelling of praise”) and says of Moshe and David: “שלא שלטו שונאיהם במעשיהם” — their enemies did not gain control over their works. For David it cites “טבעו בארץ שעריה” (Lamentations 2:9), the gates sunk into the earth; for Moshe it says that the Mishkan, including its boards, clasps, bars, pillars and bases, was hidden beneath the tunnels of the Sanctuary after the First Temple was built. The Gemara supplies two examples of works preserved from the conqueror. Rav Tzadok extends this to their enduring, initially concealed achievement in uprooting the yetzer and to David’s gates as entry into a holiness that cannot be profaned. The extension is his explanation, not an explicit statement of Sotah.

paragraphs.text: Avodah Zarah 52b applies Ezekiel 7:22, “ובאו בה פריצים וחללוה” (“marauders entered and profaned it”), to sacred Temple property seized by invaders; Nedarim 62a likewise uses the passage in its discussion of Belshazzar’s use of Temple vessels. Rav Tzadok draws a specific contrast: the gates associated with David were concealed rather than seized, and so he describes their holiness as guarded against the conqueror’s profanation. Neither Gemara makes a general statement that all works of David are physically indestructible.

paragraphs.text: Jerusalem Talmud Yoma 5:2 expounds Leviticus 16:17, “וכל אדם לא יהיה באהל מועד,” to include even those of whom Ezekiel 1:10 says “ודמות פניהם פני אדם” — a reference to angelic beings. In its story about Shimon HaTzaddik, the Yerushalmi concludes that the companion he saw was the Holy One, not an ordinary person. Jerusalem Talmud Shabbat 6:9 explicitly says, “עתיד הקדוש ברוך הוא לעשות מחיצתן שלצדיקים לפנים ממחיצתן שלמלאכי השרת” — in the future, the righteous will have an enclosure inward of that of the ministering angels. Rav Tzadok sets these two sources together to explain the exceptional holiness of the Holy of Holies in relation to the righteous. They establish the two premises; their use to explain the Ark and David is Rav Tzadok’s interpretation.

paragraphs.text: Isaiah 55:3 calls the enduring covenant “חַסְדֵי דָוִד הַנֶּאֱמָנִים” — “the steadfast mercies of David”; Proverbs 19:22 states “תַּאֲוַת אָדָם חַסְדּוֹ” — literally, “a person’s desire is his kindness.” Shabbos 30a and Sanhedrin 107b recount that the gates of the Holy of Holies did not open for Shlomo until he invoked “זָכְרָה לְחַסְדֵי דָוִיד עַבְדֶּךָ.” At that moment, “וְיָדְעוּ כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁמָּחַל לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עַל אוֹתוֹ עָוֹן” — all Israel knew Hashem had forgiven David that transgression. This later public vindication is not the same argument as Shabbos 56a’s interpretive teaching that whoever says “David sinned” errs; both teachings are kept distinct. Rav Tzadok identifies David’s longing for the enduring Mikdash with chesed rooted in holiness, whose spiritual effect survives Shlomo’s era. Sources: Isaiah 55:3; Proverbs 19:22; Shabbat 30a; Sanhedrin 107b; cf. Shabbat 56a.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: This is the ultimate “sweetening” of the yetzer through the Torah’s “seasoning.” Of Moshe and David it is said that “enemies did not rule over the work of their hands” (Sotah 9a). For they began the complete uprooting of the yetzer from the heart (which brings, too, “freedom from the kingdoms,” since the “leaven in the dough” and the subjugation to kingdoms are interdependent). Though the time had not come for this in actuality in all Israel, their beginning was not nullified, only “stored away,” to be revealed in the Future — enduring forever.

p: (כח) וְאָז נֶהְפְּכוּ פְּנֵי שׂוֹנְאֵי דָּוִד ״כְּשׁוּלֵי קְדֵרָה״, הַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (ר״ה יז.) עַל אוֹתָן שֶׁפָּשְׁטוּ יְדֵיהֶם בִּזְבוּל, דִּפְנֵיהֶם דּוֹמִין לְשׁוּלֵי קְדֵרָה, וְשׂוֹנְאֵי דָּוִד הֵן הֵן הֵם שֶׁפָּשְׁטוּ כו׳, כִּי כָּל חֵשֶׁק דָּוִד לִבְנוֹת בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ הַקָּבוּעַ וְקַיָּים לָעַד

Then the faces of David’s enemies turned “like the bottom of a pot,” as Rosh Hashanah 17a says of those who “stretched forth their hands against the zevul,” that their faces resemble the bottom of a pot. Rav Tzadok identifies David’s enemies with those who stretched forth their hands, because David’s entire longing was to build the fixed and enduring Mikdash.

וְזֶהוּ הַנִּקְרָא ״זְבוּל״, וּכְמוֹ ״הַפַּעַם יִזְבְּלֵנִי אִישִׁי״, שֶׁעִיקַּר קְבִיעוּת דִּירָתוֹ אֶצְלָהּ לָעַד — דְּגַם בִּקְבוּרָה נִקְבַּר עִמָּהּ בִּמְעָרַת הַמַּכְפֵּלָה — וְכֵן לְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב ״בֵּית זְבוּל לָךְ מָכוֹן לְשִׁבְתְּךָ עוֹלָמִים״

This is what is called “zevul,” as in “this time my husband will dwell with me,” meaning that his principal dwelling will be with her forever — since even in burial he lies beside her in the Cave of Machpelah. So too Scripture says, “I have surely built You a lofty dwelling, a place for You to abide forever.”

וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנֶּחֱרַב, מִכָּל מָקוֹם נִכְתַּב דִּבְרֵי שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה שֶׁאָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ ״בָּנִיתִי בַיִת״ וְגוֹמֵר, מִשּׁוּם דִּקְדֻשָּׁה רִאשׁוֹנָה קִידְּשָׁה לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא וְסוֹפוֹ לַחֲזוֹר וְלִבְנוֹת, וְהַבִּיטּוּל הָיָה רַק לְשָׁעָה

And even though it was destroyed, nonetheless Shlomo’s words were recorded, that he said of himself, “I have built a house of habitation for You,” because the first holiness “sanctified for the Future,” and it is destined to return and be rebuilt, and the nullification was only for a time.

וְאִלּוּ בְּנָאוֹ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה לֹא הָיָה נֶחֱרַב בֶּאֱמֶת, אֶלָּא שֶׁשּׂוֹנְאָיו שֶׁיֹּאמְרוּ ״רַע לוֹ״ גָּרְמוּ דְּלֹא נִתְגַּלֵּית קְדֻשָּׁתוֹ בְּפֹעַל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה בְּיָמָיו, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה לֹא זָכָה לִבְנוֹתוֹ

And had David built it, it truly would not have been destroyed; only that his enemies, who said “evil to him,” caused that his holiness was not revealed in actuality in this world in his days, and through this he did not merit to build it.

וּלְפִיכָךְ הֵם פָּשְׁטוּ יְדֵיהֶם בִּזְבוּל, וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא ״אוֹיְבֵי ה׳״, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״נִאֵץ נִאַצְתָּ (אֶת) אוֹיְבֵי ה׳״, וְהַכַּוָּונָה עַל אוֹיְבָיו, רַק דְּהֵם נֶחְשָׁבִים לְאוֹיְבֵי ה׳ עַל יְדֵי זֶה; וְכֵן אוֹמֵר ״מְשַׂנְאֶיךָ ה׳ אֶשְׂנָא״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְהוּא הָיָה שׂוֹנֵא מִסְּתָמָא לְשׂוֹנְאָיו, דִּ״כְמַיִם הַפָּנִים לְפָנִים״

Therefore they stretched forth their hands against the zevul, and are called “enemies of Hashem.” Thus the verse says, “you have greatly given the enemies of Hashem cause to blaspheme”; Rav Tzadok understands this here as referring to David’s enemies, who thereby count as enemies of Hashem. Likewise David says, “Do I not hate those who hate You, Hashem?” He would naturally hate those who hated him, as “water reflects face to face.”
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּיְבָמוֹת קיז סוֹף עַמּוּד א) דֶּרֶךְ כְּלָל בְּכָל אָדָם,
and as they said (Yevamos 117a, end of the amud) as a general rule regarding every person,
אֶלָּא שֶׁשּׂוֹנְאָיו הֵם שׂוֹנְאֵי ה׳.
except that his enemies were the enemies of Hashem.
וְעַל כֵּן פְּנֵיהֶם כְּשׁוּלֵי קְדֵרָה,
And therefore their faces are like the bottoms of a pot,
הַיְנוּ תַּכְלִית הַשְּׁחֹרוּת וְהַחֹשֶׁךְ,
that is, the ultimate blackness and darkness,
עַל יְדֵי תַּכְלִית רִחוּקָם מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ דִּנְהוֹרָא עִמֵּיהּ שָׁרֵי,
through their ultimate distance from Hashem, blessed be He, "for light dwells with Him,"
וּבְאוֹרוֹ נִרְאֶה אוֹר,
and "in Your light we see light,"
הוּא אוֹר תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה דַּרְגָּא דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
which is the light of the Oral Torah, the level of David the King, peace be upon him,
וְהוּא "חָכְמַת אָדָם"
and it is "the wisdom of man"
(דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הוּא מַה שֶּׁנּוֹבֵעַ מִלִּבּוֹת בְּנֵי אָדָם חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל)
for the Oral Torah is that which springs forth from the hearts of human beings, the sages of Israel
דְּ"תָּאִיר פָּנָיו" וּ"בְאוֹר פְּנֵי מֶלֶךְ חַיִּים".
that illuminates his face, and “in the light of the king’s countenance is life.”

paragraphs.text: On Genesis 30:20, Rashi explains “יזבלני” as an expression related to “בית זבול,” a dwelling house: “מעתה לא תהא עיקר דירתו אלא עמי” — henceforth Yaakov’s principal dwelling will be with Leah. In I Kings 8:13 Shlomo calls the Temple “בית זבל לך מכון לשבתך עולמים” — a dwelling prepared for an enduring Divine presence. The further association with Yaakov’s burial beside Leah is Rav Tzadok’s own extension of the idea of lasting habitation, not part of Rashi’s gloss.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Eduyot 8:6 teaches, “מקריבין אף על פי שאין בית” — offerings can be brought even when there is no standing Temple; it explains that “קדושה ראשונה קידשה לשעתה וקידשה לעתיד לבוא.” Rambam, Hilkhot Beit HaBechirah 6:14–16, likewise distinguishes the enduring sanctity of Jerusalem and the Mikdash from the physical existence of their buildings, and attributes the original formal consecration to Shlomo. Rav Tzadok therefore calls the physical destruction a temporary concealment or interruption, not a cancellation of the sacred place. The texts establish continuity of sanctity; Rav Tzadok’s assertion about the eternal significance of the Temple’s building goes beyond their literal halakhic statement.

paragraphs.text: Yalkut Shimoni, II Shmuel, remez 145 (קמה), states directly: “שאם אתה בונה אותו הוא קיים ואינו חרב” — “If you [David] build it, it will endure and not be destroyed.” The Yalkut continues that Hashem foresaw Israel’s future sins and allowed the Temple to be destroyed rather than the people; David’s desire to build it nevertheless earned him credit in the title of Psalm 30. Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:1:6 distinguishes David, who laid the foundations, from Shlomo, who raised the upper structure. Rav Tzadok’s own precise parallel, Dover Tzedek, Likkutim 4:134 (Har Bracha printed p. 249; PDF page 253), cites the Yalkut but adds “ומה שלא בנה על ידי שלא היה עדיין מבורר בחייו” — “The reason he did not build was that his level had not yet been clarified in his lifetime.” Machshavos Charutz 20:2 treats David’s acquisition and preparation of the site as the enduring root. Thus the Yalkut's explanation, and Rav Tzadok's additional explanation of delayed spiritual disclosure, must be distinguished rather than attributed interchangeably. Sources: Yalkut Shimoni on Nach 145 (II Samuel, remez קמה); Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:1:6; Dover Tzedek, Likkutim 4:134; Machshavos Charutz 20:2; cf. Sotah 9a.

paragraphs.text: II Samuel 12:14 uses the difficult expression “נִאֵץ נִאַצְתָּ אֶת אֹיְבֵי ה׳.” Rashi says it is a euphemism (“כינוי ... דרך כבוד למעלה”) and cites Targum Yonatan: “מיפתח פתחתא פומא דסנאי עמא דה׳” — you opened the mouths of the enemies of Hashem’s people. Thus the verse does NOT plainly mean “you scorned the enemies of Hashem,” as the older English suggested. Rav Tzadok then reads the hostile slanderers as adversaries of David and of Hashem’s cause. His further association with reciprocal hatred draws on Proverbs 27:19 and Yevamot 117a, where the verse is invoked in a discussion of mutual animosity. This is an interpretation, not an excuse for David’s earlier conduct.

paragraphs.text: Rosh Hashanah 17a speaks of grave offenders who are judged and specifically of those “שפשטו ידיהם בזבול” — “who stretched out their hands against the zevul,” which it identifies with the Temple through I Kings 8:13. R. Yitzchak bar Avin adds: “ופניהם דומין לשולי קדירה” — “their faces resemble the bottom of a pot.” The Gemara does NOT itself identify these people as David’s enemies. Rav Tzadok applies its image to those whose hostility blocked David’s aspiration for the enduring Mikdash; in the following phrases he develops the blackening as a metaphor for spiritual darkness and distance from the Divine light. This theological application should not be mistaken for the Gemara’s explicit identification.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: R’ Tzadok interprets the darkening of David’s enemies’ faces through the image of a pot’s blackened bottom. Rosh Hashanah applies that image to those who stretch out their hands against the zevul, the fixed and enduring Temple. David’s enemies opposed the sanctuary he longed to establish, while his own bond with enduring holiness continued even after death.

p: (כט) וְנִתְבָּרֵר אָז דְּהַחַיִּים שֶׁשָּׁאַל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה נִיתַּן, כִּי הוּא בֶּאֱמֶת חַי וְקַיָּים לָעַד, וְשֶׁנִּמְחַל אוֹתוֹ עָוֹן, דְּנִתְבָּרֵר דְּ״שִׁטִּים״ דִּידֵיהּ הוּא הַשּׁוֹתֶה מִמַּעְיָן הַיּוֹצֵא מִבֵּית ה׳ וּמְצוּפֶּה זָהָב מִבַּיִת וּמִבַּחוּץ

At that time it became clear that the life King David, peace be upon him, had asked for was granted to him: in truth he lives and endures forever. It was also made clear that his sin was forgiven, for his “shittim” proved to be nourished by the spring issuing from the House of Hashem and overlaid with gold on the inside and the outside.
וּלְפִיכָךְ נִכְתַּב חֶטְאוֹ לִהְיוֹת ״אוֹת וְסִימָן״ לְכָל חֲטָאֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וּמַעֲשֵׂה רוּחַ שְׁטוּת שֶׁלָּהֶם אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה וְהַתִּיקּוּן
Therefore his sin was written as “a sign and indication” for all the sins of Israel, and for the actions arising from their spirit of folly, after repentance and rectification.

בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב (מִזְמוֹר לד) דְּאָמַר דָּוִד ״הֲשָׁטוֹת שֶׁבָּרָאתָ מַה הֲנָאָה יֵשׁ״ כו׳, אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא ״חַיֶּיךָ שֶׁתִּצְטָרֵךְ לוֹ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם — הַכַּוָּונָה עַל הָרוּחַ שְׁטוּת שֶׁבִּבְרִיאַת הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע

In Shocher Tov on Psalm 34 it is said that David asked, “What benefit is there in the folly You created?” The Holy One answered him, “By your life, you will need it” — see there. Rav Tzadok understands the deeper meaning to concern the spirit of folly involved in the creation of the evil inclination.
וּבֶאֱמֶת יֵשׁ בָּזֶה צֹרֶךְ וְתוֹעֶלֶת, וְ״יִתְרוֹן אֶרֶץ בַּכֹּל הוּא״, שֶׁלִּפְעָמִים צָרִיךְ לְשַׁנּוֹת אֶת טַעְמוֹ, וְהוּא כְּמוֹ עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ

And indeed there is a need and a benefit in this, for “the profit of the earth is in all things” (Koheles 5:8): sometimes a person must alter his usual manner of conduct, just as in the concept of an act that appears a transgression but is undertaken for the sake of Heaven.

וְסִיּוּם אוֹתוֹ מִזְמוֹר ״פּוֹדֶה ה׳ נֶפֶשׁ עֲבָדָיו״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְקִיבַּלְתִּי דְּנֶאֱמַר (עַל) פְּגַם הַבְּרִית, דְּלִפְנֵי זֶה שֶׁאָמַר ״וְשֹׂנְאֵי צַדִּיק יֶאְשָׁמוּ״ (וְכֵן מַה שֶּׁאָמַר ״פְּנֵי ה׳ בְּעֹשֵׂי רָע״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְאָמַר ״צָעֲקוּ״ וְגוֹמֵר דְּהַתְּשׁוּבָה מוֹעֶלֶת, ״וְאֶת דַּכְּאֵי רוּחַ יוֹשִׁיעַ״, כִּי הַשָּׁב מִפְּגָם זֶה הוּא בִּשְׁבִירַת לֵב וְדִכְאוּת רוּחַ בְּיָדְעוֹ גּוֹדֶל הַפְּגָם הֵיכָן מַגִּיעַ)

The same psalm concludes, “Hashem redeems the soul of His servants,” and so forth. I have received a tradition that this concerns a blemish of the covenant. The preceding verse says, “Those who hate the righteous will be condemned”; the psalm also says, “The face of Hashem is against evildoers,” and relates that they cried out and were heard, showing that repentance is effective. It says that Hashem “saves the crushed in spirit,” for one who repents of this blemish experiences a broken heart and a crushed spirit, recognizing its gravity.
אֲבָל ״עֲבָדָיו הַחוֹסִים בּוֹ״ לֹא יֶאְשָׁמוּ אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁפְּגָמוֹ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, דְּיֵשׁ לָהֶם פִּדְיוֹן עַל זֶה
but “His servants who take refuge in Him” shall not be condemned, even though he blemished, God forbid — for they have a “redemption” for it.
וְקִיבַּלְתִּי דִּפְעָמִים ״מִקְרֶה״ שֶׁיֶּאֱרַע לָאָדָם הוּא הַצָּלָה מִמִּיתָה רַחֲמָנָא לִיצְלַן שֶׁנִּגְזַר עָלָיו, וְהוּא לְפִדְיוֹן נַפְשׁוֹ, וְזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן שְׁטוּת שֶׁנִּבְרָא לְצֹרֶךְ

And I have received that sometimes an involuntary nocturnal occurrence — a “mikreh” — that happens to a person can be a deliverance from a death, Heaven spare us, that had been decreed against him, acting as a redemption for his soul. This too is an instance of folly that was created for a purpose.

וְכָל עֲסָקָיו שֶׁל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה הָיָה בָּזֶה, לְבָרֵר וּלְתַקֵּן כָּל הַחֲטָאִים שֶׁל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל; וְכֵן כָּל רָאשֵׁי הַדּוֹרוֹת שֶׁלְּאַחֲרָיו, דּוֹר דּוֹר עַד בִּיאַת הַמָּשִׁיחַ, עִסְקָם בָּזֶה, לְתַקֵּן חֲטָאֵי הַדּוֹר שֶׁיִּהְיוּ זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, עַד עֵת קֵץ שֶׁיְּבוֹרַר זֶה לְגַמְרֵי

All the work of King David, peace be upon him, was directed toward this: to clarify and rectify the sins of all Israel. Likewise, the heads of the generations after him, generation by generation until Mashiach arrives, engage in rectifying the sins of their generations so that deliberate transgressions may become like merits, until the final End when this will be fully clarified.

paragraphs.text: Psalms 21:5 reads “חַיִּים שָׁאַל מִמְּךָ נָתַתָּה לּוֹ, אֹרֶךְ יָמִים עוֹלָם וָעֶד” — “He asked You for life; You granted it, length of days forever and ever.” Rosh Hashanah 25a records the lunar-sanctification signal “דוד מלך ישראל חי וקים,” “David, King of Israel, lives and endures”; Sukkah 52a applies the life requested in Psalms 21:5 to Mashiach ben David. Rav Tzadok explains specifically in Machshavos Charutz 7:14: “חיים שאל ממך נתתה לו — על ידי השאלה דוקא” — the life was granted through the very act of requesting. His further discussion of David's enduring kingship is in Machshavos Charutz 20:3. This is a spiritual and dynastic teaching, not an assertion that David was never physically deceased. The marker is placed immediately after Rav Tzadok completes the assertion that David's asked-for life endures, before he develops the separate Shittim/acacia image. Sources: Psalms 21:5; Rosh Hashanah 25a; Sukkah 52a; Machshavos Charutz 7:14; 20:3.

paragraphs.text: Exodus 25:10–11 commands an Ark of “עצי שטים” (acacia wood) and “מבית ומחוץ תצפנו” — “you shall overlay it within and without” with pure gold. Joel 4:18 speaks of a spring flowing from the House of Hashem to water “נחל השטים” — “the Valley of Shittim.” Yoma 72b derives from the Ark that a Torah scholar’s inward life must match the outward: “כל תלמיד חכם שאין תוכו כברו אינו תלמיד חכם.” In Pri Tzadik, Terumah 8, Rav Tzadok reads the Ark’s wood as an image of the inclination redirected: “למשוך החמדה להיות חמידו דאורייתא” — drawing desire into desire for Torah. Here “his shittim” is Rav Tzadok’s symbolic synthesis of these distinct verses: the seemingly disordered drive becomes an instrument of holiness after teshuvah. Neither Joel nor Yoma by itself comments on David’s sin.

paragraphs.text: Psalms 34:22–23 juxtaposes “ושנאי צדיק יאשמו” — “those who hate the righteous will be held guilty,” with “פודה ה׳ נפש עבדיו ולא יאשמו כל החסים בו” — “Hashem redeems the souls of His servants; none who take refuge in Him will be condemned.” Rav Tzadok labels the interpretation “וקיבלתי” — “I have received,” explicitly reporting a tradition rather than the plain meaning of the verse. His direct parallel Tzidkat HaTzadik 243 says of “מזמור לדוד בשנותו” that he heard it applied to “ענין ראיית קרי,” an involuntary nocturnal emission, and continues “שיש בזה פדיון והצלה ממיתה” — “that it can involve redemption and deliverance from death.” Berakhot 57b lists a nocturnal emission among six favorable signs for a sick person; that aggadah does not assert that every emission averts a literal death sentence. Rav Tzadok also says there that this comfort applies after the event and one should not seek such an event deliberately.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tehillim (Shocher Tov) 34:1 reports that David questioned why God had created “השטות” (madness/folly): “השטות שבראת מה הנאה יש לפניך?” — “What benefit is there before You in the folly You created?” God replies “חייך שתצטרך לו” — “By your life, you will need it.” The Midrash then tells how David feigned madness before Achish to escape danger (I Samuel 21:14–16); it is not describing a sinful act, let alone an involuntary nocturnal occurrence. Rav Tzadok separately reads this event as illustrating how an apparently disordered faculty, and ultimately the human inclination, can serve a hidden purpose. Only after Rav Tzadok discusses a “מקרה” and its possible redemption does the full analogy reach its conclusion. The comparison belongs to Rav Tzadok and his received teaching, not to a literal statement of the Midrash.

paragraphs.text: Earlier in this same siman, Takanat HaShavin 10:3 says “כל ישראל קומה שלימה וראש הדור כולל כל הדור” — “All Israel is a single complete spiritual form, and the head of the generation encompasses the generation.” Rav Tzadok states the underlying principle in Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua 10: “כי דבר ידוע שפרנס הדור נפשו כוללת כל נפשות הדור” — “It is known that the soul of the generation’s leader includes all the souls of that generation.” These are direct, demonstrably relevant Rav Tzadok parallels. The application here is his teaching that a leader’s teshuvah and clarifications can open the way for his generation; it does not mean that the leader’s deeds remove the responsibility of individuals to repent. The inherited general pointer to Yisrael Kedoshim 5 is replaced by precise verified internal parallels rather than treated as proof without a matching passage.

paragraphs.text: Sotah 3a says “אין אדם עובר עבירה אלא אם כן נכנס בו רוח שטות” — no person sins unless a spirit of folly has entered. Avodah Zarah 4b–5a says “לא דוד ראוי לאותו מעשה ... אלא למה עשו?” and answers that an individual who has sinned may be directed toward David’s precedent for teshuvah; David “הקים עולה של תשובה” — raised the yoke of repentance. These sources do not turn the original sin itself into a permissible act. Rav Tzadok’s further argument is that after genuine teshuvah and correction, David’s episode can be written as an “אות וסימן” for Israel, with the generation’s leaders working toward the eventual clarification of what is redeemable. The conversion of deliberate sins to merits is conditional upon repentance from love in Yoma 86b; it is not a license to sin.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: It was then clarified that the “life” David asked for was granted — he is “alive and enduring forever.” And that iniquity pardoned, his “Shittim” being the one that “drinks from the spring going forth from the House of Hashem,” gold-overlaid within and without. So their sin was written as a “sign and token” for all Israel’s sins and their “act of spirit-of-folly,” after teshuvah.

p: (ל) וְגַם רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ וַדַּאי מַה שֶּׁאָמַר שֶׁהָיָה לִיסְטִים — עַל יָדוֹ הָיָה תִּיקּוּן לְכָל הַלִּיסְטִים דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
Similarly, when Reish Lakish was said to have been a bandit, Rav Tzadok understands that through him there was a rectification for the bandits among Israel.

וּבְוַדַּאי אִם הוּא הָרַג אָדָם, לֹא הָרַג אֶלָּא מֵאוֹתָן הַ״מּוֹרִידִין וְלֹא מַעֲלִין״ שֶׁדָּמוֹ מוּתָּר (וּמָמוֹנוֹ מוּתָּר מִקַּל וָחֹמֶר, וְאַף לְמַאן דְּפָלֵיג בְּסוֹף בָּבָא קַמָּא וְאוֹסֵר, דְּהַיְינוּ לְאַבְּדוֹ, אֲבָל מוּתָּר לִיקַּח לְעַצְמוֹ)

And Rav Tzadok maintains that if Reish Lakish had killed anyone, he would only have killed someone in the exceptional category described by the old expression “those whom one lowers but does not raise,” whose blood the cited legal discussion treats as permitted; he extends this by a fortiori reasoning to that person’s property. Even the dissenting view at the end of Bava Kamma, which forbids this, he interprets as forbidding its destruction, not its taking for oneself.

וְקוֹצִים הָיָה מְכַלֶּה מִכֶּרֶם ה׳, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא (שָׁם בב״מ פג:) אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן, וְכֵן אַחַר כָּךְ אַרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי, וּבְוַדַּאי מִפְּנֵי זֶה סָמְכוּ עִנְיָן לוֹ (הַלִּיסְטִיּוּת דְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אֵצֶל מַעֲשֵׂה ר׳ אֶלְעָזָר)

In his reading, Reish Lakish was “clearing thorns from the vineyard of Hashem,” as R. Elazar son of R. Shimon says in Bava Metzia 83b; the following account likewise concerns R. Yishmael son of R. Yosei. Rav Tzadok proposes that the Talmud juxtaposes these narratives with the story of Reish Lakish’s earlier reputation for banditry.
וְלֹא הִזְכִּירוּ בְּהַדִּיא בַּגְמָרָא שֶׁהָיָה לִסְטָים כָּלָל,
And they did not mention explicitly in the Gemara that he was a bandit at all,
רַק בְּרֶמֶז וּמִכְּלָלָא אִתְמַר,
only by allusion and by implication was it stated,
מִמָּה שֶׁאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן לִיסְטָאה וְכוּלֵּי וּמַה שֶׁאָמַר אָז הַדַּרְתָּ,
from what Rabbi Yochanan said, “bandit,” etc., and the statement, “Then you returned,”
וְרַק רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן קְרָאוֹ לִיסְטָאה.
and only Rabbi Yochanan called him a bandit.
אֲבָל רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָמַר הַתָּם "רַבִּי קָרֵא לִי" וְכוּלֵּי,
But Reish Lakish said there, “They called me Rabbi,” etc.,
כְּבָר בִּירֵר עַצְמוֹ שֶׁגַּם אָז הָיָה רַבִּי וּמְלַמֵּד לְהוֹעִיל לַלִּיסְטִים שֶׁיֵּלְכוּ בְּדֶרֶךְ ה׳,
he had already clarified for himself that even then he was a Rabbi and a teacher, to benefit the bandits that they would go in the way of Hashem,
שֶׁלֹא לְבַעֵר אֶלָּא קוֹצִים,
he aimed to remove only the thorns, not to uproot the vineyard itself,
וְשֶׁדָּבָר גָּדוֹל עָשׂה גַּם אָז שֶׁהָיָה נֶחְשָׁב כְּמוֹ לִמּוּדוֹ תּוֹרָה שֶׁאַחַר כָּךְ, עַד דְּלֹא אַהֲנָא כּלוּם.

and in his account, Reish Lakish had already accomplished a great thing in that earlier period, which he regarded as comparable in its purpose to his later Torah learning; this, Rav Tzadok argues, is why he could say that R. Yochanan had added nothing for him in that respect.

paragraphs.text: Avodah Zarah 26b uses “מורידין ולא מעלין” for exceptional ancient categories such as “מינין” and “מסורות”; the sugya itself discusses category boundaries rather than indiscriminate violence. Rambam, Hilkhot Rotzeach uShemirat HaNefesh 4:10–11 likewise distinguishes sharply among classes; it cannot be generalized to ordinary wrongdoers. Bava Kamma 119a records a DISPUTE over “ממון מסור”: one sage permits “לאבדו ביד” — deliberately destroying the property, saying “לא יהא ממונו חמור מגופו”; another forbids its destruction for the sake of possible righteous heirs. That passage does NOT explicitly authorize taking property for private benefit. The assertion in Rav Tzadok’s parenthesis that one may “take it for oneself” is his own inference within a historical, hypothetical discussion of Reish Lakish; it must not be represented as a ruling of Bava Kamma or as contemporary guidance.

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 83b records that R. Elazar son of R. Shimon helped officials identify thieves. R. Yehoshua b. Korchah protested: “חומץ בן יין עד מתי אתה מוסר עמו של אלהינו להריגה?” — “Vinegar, son of wine, how long will you hand our God's people over for execution?” R. Elazar said “קוצים אני מכלה מן הכרם” — “I remove thorns from the vineyard”; the protest answered “יבא בעל הכרם ויכלה את קוציו” — “Let the vineyard's Owner remove His own thorns.” The Talmud does not endorse R. Elazar's justification unconditionally. Rav Tzadok's extension of this disputed image to Reish Lakish's earlier conduct is his interpretive reading of adjacent narratives, not a historical assertion made by Bava Metzia. Source: Bava Metzia 83b.

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 84a continues the related narrative about R. Yishmael b. R. Yosei. In response to Elijah's objection to handing people over for execution, he says “הרמנא דמלכא הוא” — “It is the king's directive”; Elijah replies “אבוך ערק לאסיא, את ערוק ללודקיא” — “Your father fled to Asya; flee to Ludkya.” This narrative, adjacent in the Gemara to that of Reish Lakish, likewise questions the practice, rather than legitimizing it. Rav Tzadok treats the literary adjacency as meaningful and rereads Reish Lakish's history through a spiritual-rectification framework; the proposed connection is Rav Tzadok's, not the Bavli narrator's assertion. The source is cited at the completion of Rav Tzadok's juxtaposition argument. Source: Bava Metzia 84a.

paragraphs.text: The narrative of Bava Metzia 84a does not itself announce, in its narrator’s voice, that Reish Lakish was a robber. R. Yochanan says “לסטאה בלסטיותיה ידע” — “A bandit knows his own trade”; Reish Lakish replies “התם רבי קרו לי, הכא רבי קרו לי” — “There they called me rabbi, and here they call me rabbi.” Rashi, however, explicitly glosses the earlier meeting “חזייה ריש לקיש” with “שהיה לסטים” — “for he had been a robber,” and interprets “רבי קרו לי” as “רבן של לסטים וראש להן הייתי” — “I was the leader and chief of the bandits.” Thus Rav Tzadok is making a narrow claim about the Bavli narrator, not denying that Rashi identifies him as a bandit. Rav Tzadok’s following reading of his earlier conduct as later redirected to good remains his interpretation.

paragraphs.text: Tosafos on Bava Metzia 84a, s.v. “אי הדרת בך”, quotes Rabbeinu Tam: “דר״ל מתחלה ידע הרבה אלא שפרק עול תורה ונעשה עם הארץ ועסק בלסטיות” — Reish Lakish had learned much Torah earlier, subsequently abandoned its yoke and entered banditry. Maharsha, Chidushei Aggados to Bava Metzia 84a, s.v. “מאי אהנית לי”, reads “התם רבי קרו לי” as referring to knowledge he had even before his bandit period, not as a claim that banditry was Torah teaching; Maharsha also distinguishes Reish Lakish's intention from Rabbi Yochanan's understanding. Rav Tzadok goes beyond both: after teshuvah, Reish Lakish could interpret his earlier actions as a misguided effort to draw those around him toward Hashem. This is Rav Tzadok's theological reading, not a statement in Tosafos or Maharsha validating violent wrongdoing. Sources: Tosafos, Bava Metzia 84a, s.v. “אי הדרת בך”; Maharsha, Chidushei Aggados, Bava Metzia 84a, s.v. “מאי אהנית לי”; Bava Metzia 84a.

paragraphs.text: Isaiah 5:7 calls Israel “כרם ה׳ צבאות” — “the vineyard of Hashem of Hosts.” In Isaiah 27:4–6, “שמיר שית” (briers and thorns) appears in the prophetic vineyard imagery. Bava Metzia 83b records R. Elazar b. R. Shimon’s claim “קוצים אני מכלה מן הכרם” — “I remove thorns from the vineyard,” followed immediately by the rebuke “יבא בעל הכרם ויכלה את קוציו” — “Let the owner of the vineyard remove His own thorns.” The Gemara thereby challenges rather than unconditionally approves the practice of handing people over for execution. Rav Tzadok extends the metaphor to Reish Lakish’s past, imagining a possible corrective intention; that theological reinterpretation is not stated in Isaiah or the Gemara.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Reish Lakish, too — his having been “a bandit” means that through him was a rectification for all the bandits of Israel. Certainly, if he killed, he killed only those “lowered and not raised” (whose blood is permitted). And he was “clearing thorns from the vineyard of Hashem,” in the very manner of R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon (and later R’ Yishmael b’Rabbi Yosei), who caught thieves — which is why the Gemara juxtaposes the Reish Lakish narrative to theirs.

p: (לא) וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הֱשִׁיבוֹ ״אַהֲנַאי (לָךְ)״ כו׳, וּלְגַנּוֹתוֹ אָמַר הַלָּשׁוֹן ״תַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַשְּׁכִינָה״ — וְיָדוּעַ מֵהָאֲרִיזָ״ל דְּשָׁם מִשְׁכַּן נַפְשׁוֹת הַגֵּרִים — וְשֶׁאָמַר לוֹ עַל נֶפֶשׁ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל כֵּן, דְּמוֹרִידוֹ לְמַטָּה, וְהוּא אָמַר עָלָיו כֵּן כְּאִלּוּ הָיָה כְּגֵר שֶׁנִּתְגַּיֵּיר, וּלְהַקְנִיטוֹ אָמַר זֶה

And although R’ Yochanan answered him, “I benefited you,” etc., and, to disparage him, used the expression “beneath the wings of the Shechinah” — and it is known from the Arizal that there is “the abode of the souls of converts” — and he said this of a soul of Israel, meaning that he lowers him in status, saying it of him as though he were “like a convert who converted,” and to needle him he said this —
וְעַל כֵּן לֹא הֱשִׁיבוֹ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָז כְּלוּם, וְלָכֵן חָלַשׁ דַּעְתֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, דְּהִרְגִּישׁ דִּתְשׁוּבָה נִיצַּחַת הֱשִׁיבוֹ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
Therefore Reish Lakish gave him no further answer, and Rabbi Yochanan became distressed because he sensed that Reish Lakish had already given him a conclusive reply.

וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהֶעֱנִישׁ לְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁהֶחְלִישׁ דַּעְתּוֹ וְהוּא הָיָה רַבּוֹ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם סוֹף נֶעֱנַשׁ הוּא עַל יָדוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ, כִּדְאִיתָא הָתָם סִיּוּם הַסִּיפּוּר; אֶלָּא שֶׁאֶצְלוֹ הָיָה זֶה מִתּוֹךְ צַעֲרוֹ בִּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ וַחֲרָטָתוֹ עַל מַה שֶּׁחֲבֵירוֹ נֶעֱנַשׁ עַל יָדוֹ

Although he brought punishment upon Reish Lakish for having caused his distress, and Rabbi Yochanan was his teacher, nevertheless in the end he himself suffered punishment on account of Reish Lakish, as told at the end of that narrative. In Rabbi Yochanan’s case it came through his anguish, repentance, and regret that his fellow had suffered through him.
וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא בְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַשִׁי (קִדּוּשִׁין פא עַמּוּד ב)
and it is along the lines of what is found regarding Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi (Kiddushin 81b),
דְּכָל יָמָיו הִתְעַנָּה עַד שֶׁמֵּת בְּאוֹתָהּ מִיתָה.
For the rest of his days he fasted, until he died “by that death.”
וּמִתְּחִלָּה רָצָה לְהָמִית אֶת עַצְמוֹ,
And at first he wanted to put himself to death,
וְאֶפְשָׁר דְּהָיְתָה אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ אוֹתָהּ זוֹנָה שֶׁחָשַׁב עָלֶיהָ
and it is possible that the harlot he thought of was a married woman
(אוֹ פְּנוּיָה נִדָּה דִּבְכָרֵת וּמִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם)
(or an unmarried menstruant woman, where the penalty is karet and death at the hands of Heaven)
אוֹ גּוֹיָה דִּבְמִיתָה לַקַּנָּאִים דְּפוֹגְעִין.
or a non-Jewish woman, which could have been a case described in the older halakhic terminology as “zealots may strike.”
וְאַחַר כָּךְ דְּהוּא צָרִיךְ סְלִיחָה רַק מִפְּנֵי הַכַּוָּנָה לְאִסּוּרָא,
And afterward, that he needed forgiveness only because of the intention toward the prohibition,
כֵּיוָן דְּהוּא אִסּוּר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ חִיּוּב מִיתָה הִתְעַנָּה כָּל כָּךְ עַד שֶׁמֵּחֲמָתָם נִגְרַר מִיתָה.
Since he had imagined a prohibition that he regarded as carrying a death penalty, he fasted so intensely that death followed as a consequence.
וְכֵן בְּהַהוּא דְּהֶעֱנִישׁוֹ זֶה מֵאַבִיזְרַיְיהוּ דִּרְצִיחָה,
Similarly, in Rav Tzadok’s analysis, the punishment Rabbi Yochanan brought upon Reish Lakish was related to the subsidiary aspects of bloodshed.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת קנו עַמּוּד א)
and as they said (Shabbos 156a),
"מָאן דִּבְמַאְדִּים אָשִׁיד דְּמָא" וְכוּלֵּי,
"One born under Mars will spill blood," etc.,
"מַר נָמֵי עָנִישׁ וְקָטִיל".
"The master too punishes and kills."
וּלְפִי שֶׁהוּא זִלְזֵל לְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ שֶׁהוּא רוֹצֵחַ,
And because he disparaged Resh Lakish as a murderer,
הֶרְאוּ לוֹ שֶׁהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ "כָּל הַפּוֹסֵל בְּמוּמוֹ פּוֹסֵל",
they showed him that the principle “whoever disqualifies another does so with his own blemish” could be applied to him,
מֵאַחַר שֶׁאֵין זֶה אֱמֶת בְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי.
since this is not true of Resh Lakish, as I have written.
וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הָיָה מִזַּרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף כְּדְאִיתָא הָתָם,
And Rabbi Yochanan was from the seed of Yosef, as is found there,
וּבְמַכּוֹת (ט סוֹף עַמּוּד ב) דִּבְגִלְעָד שְׁכִיחֵי רוֹצְחִים,
and in Makkos (9b, end of the amud), that in Gilad murderers are common,
וְשָׁם (י רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א) דְּכֵן בִּשְׁכֶם
and there (10a) that so too in Shechem,
וְהֵם מִנַּחֲלַת בְּנֵי יוֹסֵף,
and they are from the inheritance of the sons of Yosef,
וּבִשְׁכֶם הוּא קְבוּרָתוֹ,
and in Shechem is his burial place,
דְּעַצְמוֹתוֹ הוּא מִשָּׁם,
for his bones belong to that place,
וְעַל כֵּן מִשָּׁם נִמְכַּר, דְּשָׁם מָצְאוּ טַעֲנָה עָלָיו.
and therefore, in Rav Tzadok’s telling, it was from that region that Yosef was sold, for there his brothers found their pretext against him.
כַּיָּדוּעַ דְּתַאֲוָה וּרְצִיחָה הֵם שְׁנֵי הֲפָכִים,
As is known, desire and murder are two opposites,
שֶׁהֵם חֶסֶד וּגְבוּרָה דִּקְלִפָּה.
for they are the chesed and gevurah of the kelipah.
וְיוֹסֵף הַצַּדִּיק שׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית הַמֻּגְדָּר בְּתַאֲוֹת הָיָה צָרִיךְ בֵּרוּרִים בְּעִנְיַן הַכַּעַס וּרְצִיחָה,
And Yosef the Righteous, guardian of the covenant, who was fenced in against desires, needed clarifications in the matter of anger and murder,
שֶׁמִּזֶּה הוּא גַּם כֵּן חֶטְאוֹ בִּלְשׁוֹן הָרָע בְּדִבַּת אֶחָיו.
from which also came his sin of evil speech with the report about his brothers.
וְהֵם עַצְמוֹ יִצְרָא דַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל,
And they themselves are the inclination to idolatry, as I have written above,
שֶׁנִּמְשָׁךְ מִזַּרְעוֹ בְּיָרָבְעָם,
which was drawn from his seed in Yeravam,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה) עַל פָּסוּק "בַּעַל הַחֲלֹמוֹת",
and as the Sages said in Bereishis Rabbah, commenting on “the master of dreams,”
"זֶה עָתִיד לְהַשִּׁיאֵנוּ לַבְּעָלִים".
“This one is destined to lead us toward the Baalim.”

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 31a records the converts’ gratitude to Hillel: “קרבתני תחת כנפי השכינה” — “You brought me near beneath the wings of the Shechinah.” In Bava Metzia 84a, Rabbi Yochanan similarly tells Reish Lakish, “אהנאי לך דאקרבינך תחת כנפי השכינה” — “I benefited you by bringing you beneath the wings of the Shechinah.” The Bavli itself treats that idiom as spiritual closeness, not an insult. In the exact parallel Dover Tzedek, Likkutim 4:138, Rav Tzadok says, “ולשון זה בכמה מקומות בגמרא על הגרים” — “This expression occurs in several places in the Gemara concerning converts,” and cites an Arizal tradition connecting that realm with converts’ souls. It is Rav Tzadok, not the Bavli, who interprets the expression here as a pointed challenge to Reish Lakish’s already-Jewish spiritual root. Preserve the distinction between literal report, Rav Tzadok’s inference, and his attribution to the Arizal.

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 84a records the dispute in the beis midrash: “לסטאה בלסטיותיה ידע” — “A bandit knows the trade of bandits”; Reish Lakish answers “התם רבי קרו לי, הכא רבי קרו לי” — “There they called me rabbi and here they call me rabbi.” After Rabbi Yochanan responds that he brought Reish Lakish beneath the wings of the Shechinah, “חלש דעתיה דרבי יוחנן, חלש ריש לקיש” — “Rabbi Yochanan became distressed, and Reish Lakish became ill.” Following Reish Lakish’s death, Rabbi Yochanan mourned him until his own death. The Gemara reports the sequence, but does not label Rabbi Yochanan’s later suffering a Divine punishment or a formal act of repentance. Rav Tzadok provides that interpretation explicitly in Dover Tzedek, Likkutim 4:138 (Har Bracha printed page 253; PDF page 257): “בדבור זה עורר רבי יוחנן קטרוג על שורש הנעלם דריש לקיש” — “By this statement Rabbi Yochanan awakened an accusation concerning Reish Lakish's concealed root”; and “אך מכל מקום לרבי יוחנן הגיע גם כן ענש אחר כך” — “Nevertheless Rabbi Yochanan also experienced punishment afterward.” Rav Tzadok here links Rabbi Yochanan's later pain and remorse to teshuvah; that explanatory inference is his own, not a direct assertion of the Bavli. Sources: Bava Metzia 84a; Dover Tzedek, Likkutim 4:138.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 81b relates the case of Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi: his wife disguised herself as the woman called “Charuta,” he believed he had sought a forbidden partner, and he later attempted to cast himself into a heated oven. When she established that she herself was the woman, he continued to agonize over the event. The Gemara closes: “כל ימיו של אותו צדיק היה מתענה עד שמת באותה מיתה” — “Throughout the rest of that righteous man’s life he fasted, until he died by that death.” The source does not describe an actual forbidden encounter with the supposed stranger; this was his wife. The precise wording of “that death” is preserved rather than silently glossed into a medically certain cause of death. Rav Tzadok uses this episode as a comparison for contrition that profoundly affects the penitent.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi tells his wife, even after recognizing her, “אנא מיהא לאיסורא איכווני” — “Nevertheless, I intended a prohibited act” (Kiddushin 81b). The Gemara immediately illustrates how a person who intends to eat pork but actually eats permitted lamb still requires atonement; the law of intention is the direct point of the comparison. Rav Tzadok then conjectures several possible identities and prohibitions the man might have supposed (a married woman, a niddah or a non-Jewish woman), using them to explain why his inward repentance was so severe. The Gemara does not determine which of those conditions he imagined, or establish that an actual prohibited relationship occurred. These proposed cases and their penalties are Rav Tzadok’s speculation; none is a practical halakhic ruling here.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Though R’ Yochanan “prodded” Reish Lakish — “what benefit did I do you?” And, to disparage him, used the phrase “beneath the wings of the Shechinah” (which, per the Arizal, is the abode of converts’ souls — implying, needlingly, that Reish Lakish was a mere “returnee” lowered in status). Reish Lakish’s silence was itself a “winning answer,” which is why R’ Yochanan’s mind was pained.

p: (לב) וְשָׁם (בב״מ) הִתְחִילוּ בְּסִיפּוּר שֻׁפְרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן דְּאִשְׁתַּיֵּיר מִשַּׁפִּירֵי יְרוּשָׁלַיִם, וְהוּא הַיֹּפִי לַצַּדִּיקִים שׁוֹמְרֵי הַבְּרִית, כְּעִנְיַן ״יוֹסֵף יְפֵה תֹאַר וִיפֵה מַרְאֶה״

And there in Bava Metzia they began with the account of the “beauty shufreih” of R’ Yochanan, who “remained from the beautiful ones of Jerusalem” — and this is the beauty belonging to the tzaddikim who guard the bris, in the manner of “Yosef, of beautiful form and beautiful appearance” (Bereishis 39:6).

כִּי לֹא דִּיבְּרָה תוֹרָה בַּמֵּתִים מְיוּפֵּי הַדִּמְיוֹן שֶׁל עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וּמִי שֶׁעֵינַיִם לוֹ יִרְאֶה שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הַכִּיעוּר וְכִבְנֵי כּוּשִׁיִּים, וְאֵין יֹפִי בִּבְשַׂר הַגּוּף אֶלָּא בִּבְשַׂר קֹדֶשׁ זֶרַע יִשְׂרָאֵל

For Scripture is not speaking, in relation to the mortal body, of the imagined beauty prized in this world; whoever has eyes to see will recognize the repulsiveness of merely transient flesh, likened here to “the children of Kush,” whereas the body has true beauty only as the holy flesh of the seed of Israel.
וְהֵם ״תִּשְׁעָה קַבִּין יֹפִי שֶׁנָּטְלָה יְרוּשָׁלַיִם״ מֵעֲשָׂרָה קַבִּין שֶׁיָּרַד לָעוֹלָם, כִּדְאִיתָא (בְּקִידּוּשִׁין מט:), הַיְינוּ מַה שֶּׁנִּקְרָא יֹפִי עַל דֶּרֶךְ הָאֱמֶת
And they are the “nine kav of beauty that Jerusalem took” of the ten kav that descended to the world, as it is stated Kiddushin 49b — namely, that which is called “beauty” by way of truth.

וְזֶהוּ דְּיָתֵיב אַשַּׁעֲרֵי טְבִילָה, ״דְּלֶהֱווֹ בְּנֵי שַׁפִּירֵי כְּוָותִי, גְּמִירֵי אוֹרָיְיתָא כְּוָותִי״; וְאִם רָצָה לוֹמַר יֹפִי גּוּפָנִי לְבַד, לָא הֲוָה לֵיהּ לֵישֵׁב מִשּׁוּם זֶה בְּשַׁעֲרֵי טְבִילָה, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לֵיהּ לְהַקְדִּים זֶה לִגְמִירֵי אוֹרָיְיתָא

This is why Rabbi Yochanan sat at the gates of immersion, saying, “So that they might have children beautiful like me and learned in Torah like me.” If he had meant only physical attractiveness, he would not, for this reason alone, have sat at the immersion gateway—and certainly would not have placed beauty before Torah learning.

וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, דְּרוֹצֶה לוֹמַר מַה שֶּׁנִּקְרָא אֵצֶל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְהַתּוֹרָה וְיִשְׂרָאֵל הַהוֹלְכִים בְּעִקְבוֹתָיו ״יֹפִי בַּגּוּף״; וְזֶה הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַיִּרְאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״לְמַעַן תִּהְיֶה יִרְאָתוֹ״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְנֶאֱמַר ״כִּי אָמַרְתִּי רַק אֵין יִרְאַת אֱלֹקִים״ וְגוֹמֵר, כִּי יִרְאַת אֱלֹקִים מְבַטֶּלֶת תַּאֲווֹת רָעוֹת

Rather, as I have explained, he means what Hashem, the Torah, and the people of Israel following His ways call “beauty of the body.” It comes through fear of God, as it says, “so that His fear should be upon your faces” (Shemos 20:17), and, “Surely there is no fear of God in this place” (Bereishis 20:11); for fear of God restrains evil desires.
וְזֶהוּ יִרְאָתוֹ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת קוֹדֶמֶת לְחָכְמָתוֹ, וְעַל כֵּן הִקְדִּימוּ לִגְמִירֵי אוֹרָיְיתָא
And this is the “fear” that must precede his wisdom, and therefore they placed it before “learned in Torah.”

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 84a and Berachos 20a report Rabbi Yochanan's appearance and his stated hope that women who saw him at the immersion gateway would have children “שפירי כוותי, גמירי אורייתא כוותי” — “beautiful like me and learned in Torah like me.” The Talmud also describes his connection to Yosef and the protection against the evil eye (Bereishis 49:22). These reports alone do not explicitly identify bodily beauty with holiness of the covenant. Rav Tzadok supplies that interpretation in his exact parallel, Pri Tzaddik, Kedoshim §12: “שפורי מרמז על היופי, מצד שהיה בשלימות בקדושת הברית” — “Shufrei signifies beauty by virtue of his completeness in kedushas habris,” and connects it to Yosef's “יפה תואר גוף נקי ומהודר” — “handsome in form, with a purified and refined body.” Thus the first term of Rabbi Yochanan's wish, beauty, denotes a spiritual quality in Rav Tzadok's own reading, rather than simply physical appearance. Sources: Bava Metzia 84a; Berachos 20a; Bereishis 49:22; Pri Tzaddik, Kedoshim 12.

paragraphs.text: Rashi on Leviticus 19:2 interprets “קדשים תהיו” as “הוו פרושים מן העריות ומן העבירה” — “Be separate from forbidden sexual relations and from transgression”; and adds, “כל מקום שאתה מוצא גדר ערוה אתה מוצא קדושה” — “Wherever you find a fence around sexual immorality, you find holiness.” This is the classical textual basis for connecting the sanctification of the body with restraint, not merely with pleasant looks. It does not say that all outward beauty necessarily implies holiness: Rav Tzadok’s stronger statement here is his developed understanding of beauty measured by Torah, fear of Heaven and bris.

paragraphs.text: Shemos 20:17 teaches “וּבַעֲבוּר תִּהְיֶה יִרְאָתוֹ עַל פְּנֵיכֶם לְבִלְתִּי תֶחֱטָאוּ” — “so that fear of Him be upon your faces and you not sin.” Nedarim 20a expounds “זו בושה” — that this refers to modest shame; Yevamos 79a lists Israel's traits as “הרחמנים והביישנין וגומלי חסדים” — merciful, modest, and charitable. Bereishis 20:11 separately reports Avraham's warning in Gerar: “רַק אֵין יִרְאַת אֱלֹקִים בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה וַהֲרָגוּנִי עַל דְּבַר אִשְׁתִּי” — “There is no fear of God in this place; they will kill me because of my wife.” The verses and sugyos respectively associate yirah with restraint and its absence with threatened violence and desire. Rav Tzadok combines them to explain spiritual beauty as inward yiras Elokim checking destructive appetites; the full combined doctrine is his own application, not a verbatim statement in one source. Sources: Shemos 20:17; Nedarim 20a; Yevamos 79a; Bereishis 20:11.

paragraphs.text: Pirkei Avos 3:9 states, “כל שיראת חטאו קודמת לחכמתו חכמתו מתקיימת” — “Whose fear of sin comes before his wisdom, his wisdom endures.” Rabbeinu Yonah explains: “המשתדל לדעת חכמה כדי שידע לשמור את נפשו מן החטא ... חכמתו מתקיימת” — “One who strives to learn wisdom in order to know how to protect himself from sin ... his wisdom endures.” Rav Tzadok uses this to explain Rabbi Yochanan’s choice to say “beautiful like me” before “learned in Torah like me”: in Rav Tzadok’s reading the first virtue signifies the inward refinement and fear that give Torah knowledge its proper foundation. The Mishnah itself does not discuss Rabbi Yochanan’s beauty.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The Bava Metzia passage opens with R’ Yochanan’s “beauty shufreih” — “I remained from the beautiful ones of Jerusalem” — which is the beauty of the tzaddikim who guard the bris (like “Yosef, of beautiful form”). For the Torah does not mean the imagined bodily beauty of this world (which, truly seen, is “the ultimate ugliness, like the children of Kushites”). Real beauty is only in “the holy flesh of the seed of Israel” — the “nine kav of beauty that Jerusalem took” (Kiddushin 49b), beauty by way of truth.

p: (לג) וְשָׁם מִקּוֹדֶם, בַּר׳ אֶלְעָזָר בַּר׳ שִׁמְעוֹן וְר׳ יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּר׳ יוֹסֵי, סִיפְּרוּ מַה שֶּׁהָיוּ בַּעֲלֵי בָּשָׂר — נִרְאֶה לִי גַּם כֵּן הַכַּוָּונָה לְהוֹדִיעַ מִקְּדֻשַּׁת בְּשַׂר גּוּפָם, שֶׁגַּם כָּל גּוּפָנִיּוּתָם הָיָה כּוּלּוֹ קֹדֶשׁ לַה׳

Earlier there, regarding Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei, the Gemara recounts that they were men of abundant flesh. It seems to me that this, too, is intended to make known the holiness of the very flesh of their bodies: all their bodily nature was wholly holy to Hashem.
דְּזוּלַת זֶה מַה שַּׁיָּךְ לְהַזְכִּיר בָּהֶם דָּבָר זֶה דְּהָיוּ בַּעֲלֵי בָשָׂר כְּלָל,
For apart from this, what relevance is there to mention this thing about them, that they were possessors of flesh at all,
וְהָא וַדַּאי וּפָשׁוּט דְּרִבּוּי בָשָׂר הַנַּעֲשֶׂה רִמָּה וְתוֹלֵעָה אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא לִגְנַאי,
for it is certain and simple that an abundance of flesh that becomes worm and maggot is only a disgrace,
וְכִדְתְנַן בְּאָבוֹת "מַרְבֶּה בָשָׂר מַרְבֶּה רִמָּה".
As we learned in Avos: “One who increases flesh increases worms.”
אֲבָל רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן שֶׁהָיָה בָּטוּחַ דִּבְשָׂרוֹ יִשְׁכֹּן לָבֶטַח כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם פג סוֹף עַמּוּד ב).
But Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon was confident that “even his flesh would dwell securely,” as stated there at the end of Bava Metzia 83b.
וְכֵן רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי מִסְתַּמָּא הָיָה כְּיוֹצֵא בוֹ,
And so too Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yose presumably was like him,
דְּמַה שֶּׁאֵרַע לָזֶה אֵרַע לָזֶה
for what happened to this one happened to that one,
וְזִכְּכוּ גּוּפָם כָּל כָּךְ עַד שֶׁהָיָה בְּשַׂר גּוּפָם כֻּלּוֹ קָדוֹשׁ לַה',
and they refined their bodies so much that the flesh of their bodies was entirely holy to Hashem,
אֶצְלָם שַׁיָּךְ לְסַפֵּר שֶׁהָיוּ בַּעֲלֵי בָשָׂר,
with them it is relevant to relate that they were possessors of flesh,
שֶׁתּוֹסֶפֶת בְּשַׂר הַגּוּף הוּא אֶצְלָם תּוֹסֶפֶת קְדֻשָּׁה.
For in their case, an increase of bodily flesh was an increase of holiness.
וּמַה שֶּׁהוּא אֵצֶל כָּל אָדָם בְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לִגְנַאי,
And what is, for every person in this world, a disgrace,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סוֹטָה ה סוֹף עַמּוּד א) "בָּשָׂר — בּוּשָׁה סְרוּחָה (רִמָּה)",
As the Sages said (Sotah 5a, end of the page), “basar — shame, decay, and worms.”
דְּזֶה עִקַּר הַבּוּשָׁה שֶׁל הָאָדָם מַה שֶּׁהוּא בָּשָׂר,
for this is the main shame of man, that he is flesh,
וְאֶצְלָם הָיָה לְשֶׁבַח
and with them it was for praise,
וּכְמוֹ לֶעָתִיד שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לְשֶׁבַח "וַהֲסִרֹתִי" וְגוֹמֵר "וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב בָּשָׂר",
Similarly, of the future Scripture speaks of flesh in praise: “I will remove . and give you a heart of flesh.”
וְכֵן "יָבוֹא כָל בָּשָׂר לְהִשְׁתַּחֲוֹת" וְגוֹמֵר,
and likewise "all flesh shall come to bow down," etc.,
כֵּיוָן שֶׁכָּל גּוּפָנִיּוּתוֹ קֹדֶשׁ לַה'.
since all his physicality is holy to Hashem.
וְלְפִי שֶׁסִּפֵּר מֵהֶם שֶׁנִּתְפְּסוּ לְבַעֵר קוֹצִים,
And since he related about them that they were seized for clearing away thorns,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ מִצַּד הַגְּבוּרָה דִּקְדֻשָּׁה,
which is from the side of the gevurah of holiness,
"וְאֵיזֶהוּ גִּבּוֹר — הַכּוֹבֵשׁ יִצְרוֹ" בְּהַגְדָּרַת תַּאֲוַת הַגּוּפָנִית,
and "who is mighty? He who conquers his inclination," in the fencing-in of physical desire,
עַל כֵּן סִפֵּר גַּם מִזֶּה אַחַר כָּךְ וְדַאֲבָרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי וְכוּלֵּי.
Therefore the Gemara afterward also relates the description of Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei’s male organ, and so forth.
וּבְוַדַּאי סִפּוּר זֶה אֵינוֹ דָּבָר רֵיק,
And certainly this story is not an empty matter,
וּלְאֵיזֶה צֹרֶךְ יַזְכִּירוּ דְּבָרִים כָּאֵלּוּ בַּתַּלְמוּד הַמְקֻדָּשׁ,
and for what purpose would they mention such things in the sanctified Talmud,
וְגַם שֶׁזֶּה נִרְאֶה כְּעֵין מוּם דְּבַעַל גֶּבֶר
And this even seems to resemble the physical blemish termed ba’al gever, an unusually large male organ,
(בִּבְכוֹרוֹת מד עַמּוּד ב).
(Bechoros 44b).
וַאֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא דְּלֹא הָיָה כְּשִׁעוּר הַפּוֹסֵל גְּנַאי הוּא,
And even if you say that it was not of the measure that disqualifies, it is a disgrace,
וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין (צג סוֹף עַמּוּד ב) דְּלֹא מִשְׁתַּעֵי קְרָא בִּגְנוּתָא דְּצַדִּיקֵי בִּסְרִיסִים
And Sanhedrin 93b raises the objection that Scripture would not describe righteous men disparagingly as eunuchs,
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בָּזֶה,
and all the more so in this,
וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתְבוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם עַל זֶה דָּחוּק.
In Rav Tzadok’s judgment, the explanation Tosafos gives there is strained.

paragraphs.text: Avos 2:7: “מרבה בשר מרבה רמה” — “One who increases flesh increases worms.” Rabbeinu Yonah explains that indulgence does not preserve life and that flesh ultimately decays. Maharal, Derekh Chayim on Avos 2:7, clarifies: “אין הכונה פה על רבוי הבשר בלבד” — “The intent is not only an increase in flesh”; the broader target is preoccupation with materiality and its eventual loss. Thus Rav Tzadok is not stating a blanket medical rule about body size: he quotes the ethical warning to set up the contrast with the two Sages. The exception must be understood in that context.

paragraphs.text: Tehillim 16:8–9 joins “שויתי ה׳ לנגדי תמיד” — “I set Hashem before me constantly” with “אף בשרי ישכן לבטח” — “even my flesh shall dwell securely.” Bava Metzia 83b quotes the second phrase after reporting R. Elazar b’R. Shimon’s claim “מובטח אני בכם שאין רמה ותולעה שולטת בכם” — “I am confident that worms and maggots will not rule over you,” and the test in which his fat did not decay despite the heat. Rav Tzadok then extends this particular report to the pair of Sages and interprets their larger quantity of flesh as greater sanctity. The Gemara explicitly records the events concerning R. Elazar; it does not say the second Sage underwent the same test.

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 83b–84a reports R. Elazar b. R. Shimon's confidence that his flesh would not succumb to worms, an account of separated fat resisting decay, and the physical size of R. Yishmael b. R. Yosei and R. Elazar. In response to a challenge about parenthood, a reply is “אהבה דוחקת את הבשר” — “Love presses the flesh aside” (84a). The Bavli relates these events but does not itself conclude that all the Sages' bodily substance was holy; that is Rav Tzadok's interpretation after distinguishing them from the usual warning of Avos 2:7, “מרבה בשר מרבה רמה.” A directly illuminating parallel is his Pri Tzaddik, Vayeshev §7: “כשמתקן פגם זה שיהיה הגוף בקדושה ונקרא בשר קודש אז גם עינוגי הגוף בקדושה” — “When this defect is rectified so that the body becomes holy flesh, even its bodily pleasures are holy.” He extends the principle of sanctifying corporeality to the Sages here, without making ordinary body size a spiritual test. Sources: Bava Metzia 83b–84a; Avos 2:7; Pri Tzaddik, Vayeshev 7.

paragraphs.text: Two earlier commentators illuminate the unusual physical detail without explicitly teaching Rav Tzadok’s full thesis. Midrash Shmuel to Avos 2:7 distinguishes indulgence-driven enlargement from the case of R. Elazar b’R. Shimon: “זה לא היה מרבה בשר רק מטבעו היה שמן ולזה לא הבאיש ורמה לא היתה בו” — “He did not deliberately increase his flesh; he was naturally stout, and therefore it did not decay and was not subject to worms.” Maharal, Be’er HaGolah, Well 5, §4:3–4, explains that marital union is not intrinsically contemptible, because it participates in a God-given bond; “אהבה דוחקת הבשר” is understood as a higher union overcoming bodily hindrance. Tosafos on Bava Metzia 84a, s.v. “אמר רבי יוחנן איבריה,” explains the Talmudic descriptions as preventing slander: “אלו דברים נכתבו שלא להוציא לעז על בני אדם שהם כך.” Rav Tzadok, in the closing line here, expressly judges that narrower Tosafos explanation insufficient; the conclusion of bodily holiness is his own. Sanhedrin 93b raises an analogous challenge regarding apparently disparaging descriptions of the righteous but also entertains the literal reading; it is not a general rule that such descriptions can never be literal.

rich.text: Two earlier commentators illuminate the unusual physical detail without explicitly teaching Rav Tzadok’s full thesis. Midrash Shmuel to Avos 2:7 distinguishes indulgence-driven enlargement from the case of R. Elazar b’R. Shimon: “זה לא היה מרבה בשר רק מטבעו היה שמן ולזה לא הבאיש ורמה לא היתה בו” — “He did not deliberately increase his flesh; he was naturally stout, and therefore it did not decay and was not subject to worms.” Maharal, Be’er HaGolah, Well 5, §4:3–4, explains that marital union is not intrinsically contemptible, because it participates in a God-given bond; “אהבה דוחקת הבשר” is understood as a higher union overcoming bodily hindrance. Tosafos on Bava Metzia 84a, s.v. “אמר רבי יוחנן איבריה,” explains the Talmudic descriptions as preventing slander: “אלו דברים נכתבו שלא להוציא לעז על בני אדם שהם כך.” Rav Tzadok, in the closing line here, expressly judges that narrower Tosafos explanation insufficient; the conclusion of bodily holiness is his own. inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Earlier in that passage, the Sages recount that R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon and R’ Yishmael b’Rabbi Yosei were “corpulent ba’alei basar.” R’ Tzadok reads this too as making known the holiness of their bodily flesh — that even all their physicality was wholly “holy to Hashem.” For otherwise, why record of them that they were fleshy at all? — since an abundance of flesh, which becomes “worm and maggot,” is plainly only a disgrace (as the Mishnah in Avos teaches, “one who increases flesh increases worms”).

p: (לד) אֲבָל הַכַּוָּונָה לְסַפֵּר בִּקְדֻשַּׁת הַבְּרִית שֶׁלָּהֶם, וְ״כְּחֵמֶת בַּת תִּשְׁעָה קַבִּין״ הוּא קְדֻשַּׁת הַתִּשְׁעָה דַּרְגִּין שֶׁמֵּרֵישׁ כָּל דַּרְגִּין עַד הַיְסוֹד

But the purpose is to describe their holiness in guarding the covenant. The comparison “like a wineskin of nine kav” alludes, in Rav Tzadok’s reading, to the holiness of nine spiritual levels, from the head of all the levels down to Yesod.

וְדַרְכָּן לְכַנּוֹת הַמִּדּוֹת בְּקַבִּין, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּקִידּוּשִׁין מט:) ״עֲשָׂרָה קַבִּין״ עַל כַּמָּה דְּבָרִים, וְכַוָּונָתָם עַל עֶשֶׂר מִדּוֹת וּמַדְרֵיגוֹת שֶׁל כָּל קוֹמָה הַיְּדוּעִים

The Sages also describe various qualities in measures of kav, as in Kiddushin 49b, which speaks of “ten kav” in several connections; Rav Tzadok understands this as alluding to the ten attributes and levels within each spiritual configuration.

וּבַת חֲמִשָּׁה קַבִּין אוֹ שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּר׳ יוֹחָנָן, הַיְינוּ מֵהַגְּבוּרָה עַד הַיְסוֹד, אוֹ נֶגֶד נֶצַח הוֹד יְסוֹד; וְזֶהוּ פָּחוֹת מִדְּר׳ יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּר׳ יוֹסֵי שֶׁהִגִּיעַ בֵּירוּר קְדֻשָּׁתוֹ עַד הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ, וּדְרַב פַּפָּא בְּפָחוֹת עוֹד, כִּי הַדּוֹרוֹת הוֹלְכִין וּמִתְמַעֲטִין

The five-kav — or, alternatively, three-kav — measure attributed to Rabbi Yochanan represents levels from Gevurah through Yesod, or Netzach, Hod, and Yesod. In this reading, that reflects a lesser spiritual attainment than Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei, whose clarification of holiness reached the root; Rav Pappa was yet less, as later generations progressively diminished.
וְכָל אֶחָד שֶׁהָיָה גַּם הוּא בְּעִנְיָן זֶה הָיָה יָכוֹל לְהַבְחִין וּלְהַשִּׂיג מַדְרֵיגַת הַקּוֹדֵם לוֹ, שֶׁהָיָה גַּם כֵּן מֵעִנְיַן מַדְרֵגָתוֹ וְגָדוֹל מִמֶּנּוּ קְצָת

And each one who was himself engaged in this matter of guarding the bris could discern and apprehend the rung of the one before him — who was also of the character of his rung, and somewhat greater than him.

וְאָמְנָם כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁאִיתָא (בְּשַׁבָּת קכז עַמּוּד א) דְּדִיקוּלֵי דְּהַרְפְּנְיָא שְׁלוֹשָׁה מִקּוּפָּה, וּבְתוֹסָפוֹת (שָׁם קכו סוֹף עַמּוּד ב) דִּיבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "מְפַּנִּין" מִהַיְרוּשָׁלְמִי דְּקוּפָּה שְׁלוֹשָׁה סְאִין, אִם כֵּן דִּיקוּלָא סְאָה

Yet from Shabbos 127a Rav Tzadok infers that three small Harpanya receptacles can be reckoned to one kupah, while Tosafos to Shabbos 126b, s.v. “Mefanin,” cites the Yerushalmi that a kupah holds three se’ah; on that calculation each smaller vessel is one se’ah.

(וְכֵן מַשְׁמַע גַּם מִמַּה שֶּׁאִיתָא שָׁם דְּשִׁיעוּר תְּבוּאָה צְבוּרָה דְּלֹא יַתְחִיל לֶתֶךְ, וּמַשְׁמַע דְּהַיְנוּ שִׁיעוּר אוֹצָר דִּתְנַן דְּלֹא יַתְחִיל. וְשָׁם קכו סוֹף עַמּוּד ב ״אַרְבַּע מֵחֲמִשָּׁה, וַחֲמִשָּׁה מֵאוֹצָר גָּדוֹל״, מַשְׁמַע דַּחֲמִשָּׁה הוּא שִׁיעוּר אוֹצָר קָטָן, וְהַיְנוּ חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה סְאִין, וּמוּכָח דְּקוּפָּה שָׁלוֹשׁ סְאִין וַחֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה דְּקוֹרֵי דְּהַרְפַּנְיָא לֶתֶךְ.)

(This is also suggested by the measure stated there for heaped-up grain that may not initially be cleared: a letekh. Rav Tzadok identifies this as the size of a storehouse which the Mishnah says one must not initially clear. At the end of Shabbos 126b, “four from five, and five from a large storehouse” implies to him that five baskets represent a smaller storehouse, equivalent to fifteen se’ah. On his calculation, each kupah is three se’ah, and fifteen smaller Harpanya receptacles form a letekh.)
וְהוּא שִׁשָּׁה קַבִּין וְטָפֵי מִדְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן.
Each such small vessel would therefore hold six kav, numerically more than the five- or three-kav measure attributed to Rabbi Yochanan.
אֲבָל מִדְּלֹא אָמַר גַּם בְּזֶה "חֵמֶת בַּת שִׁשָּׁה קַבִּין" נִרְאֶה דַּהַכּוּנָה לְהַקְטִין אֶת הַשִּׁעוּר,
But since he did not say in this case also "a wineskin of six kavim," it appears that the intention is to diminish the measure,
דְּאַעַגָּב דְּשִׁשָּׁה קַבִּין הוּא מְרֻבָּה, וְהוּא רוֹמֵז עַל הַמְשָׁכַת קְדֻשַּׁת הַיְסוֹד מִן הַחֶסֶד,
for although six kavim is a larger amount, and it alludes to the drawing down of the holiness of Yesod from Chesed,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם מִצַּד הַחֶסֶד יֵשׁ הִתְפַּשְׁטוּת וְאֵין מְצוּמָצָּם כָּל כָּךְ.
in any case, from the side of Chesed there is expansion and it is not so constricted.
וְזֶהוּ "דְּהַרְפְּנְיָא" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּיבָמוֹת יז עַמּוּד א) דְּהוּא מָקוֹם פְּסוּלִים,
And the name “Harpanya” itself is relevant, for Yevamos 17a describes the town as associated with disputed genealogical standing.
וְכָל פְּסוּלִים נִמְשָׁכִים מִקִּלְקוּל הַבְּרִית,
And Rav Tzadok understands such genealogical disqualification as connected to blemishes of the covenant,
וְהוּא הִמְשִׁיךְ קְדֻשָּׁה גַּם לִמְקוֹמוֹת הַמְקוּלָקִּים מִצַּד הַהִתְפַּשְׁטוּת כְּמִדַּת הַחֶסֶד,
whereas in his symbolic reading Rav Pappa drew holiness even toward spiritually damaged settings, through the expansive aspect of Chesed,
וְאַעַל פִּי שֶׁזֶּה מוֹרֶה תּוֹסֶפֶת קְדֻשָּׁה מִצַּד הַהִתְגַּלּוּת בְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
and although this shows an addition of holiness from the side of revelation in this world,
כָּל הַמְצַמֵּצַּא בְּתַאֲוֹתָיו מוּרְגָשׁ קְדֻשָּׁתוֹ יוֹתֵר.
For a person who restrains his desires, the holiness is more distinctly perceptible.

paragraphs.text: Sefer Yetzirah 1:3–4 establishes the tenfold framework: “עשר ספירות בלימה ... עשר ולא תשע, עשר ולא אחת עשרה” — “Ten sefirot of belimah ... ten, not nine and not eleven.” Kiddushin 49b likewise measures particular qualities in “עשרה קבים” (“ten kav”): e.g., “עשרה קבים יופי ירדו לעולם, תשעה נטלה ירושלים” — “Ten measures of beauty descended to the world; Jerusalem received nine.” Bava Metzia 84a uses a nine-kav wineskin to describe R. Yishmael b. R. Yosei, but it does not identify any kav with a sefirah. Rav Tzadok explicitly supplies the interpretive bridge in Pri Tzaddik, Vayikra §5: “אדם רוצה בקב שלו מט׳ קבין של חבירו ... שמרמז על ט׳ מדות שהוא הקדושה מצד השי״ת. ומדת מלכות קב אחד שלו מצד האדם” — “A person prefers his own kav to nine belonging to another ... it alludes to nine attributes of holiness from Hashem and one kav of Malchus from human effort.” Rabbeinu Bahya on Bereishis 17:13:6 similarly connects the embodied bris with “ברית עולם” and Yesod. Here Rav Tzadok reads the specific figures nine, five, and three in Bava Metzia as graded spiritual attainments, finally explaining the ability of a Sage to discern a prior level. That final comparison and its numerical assignment are Rav Tzadok’s own reading, not the Bavli’s literal teaching. Sources: Sefer Yetzirah 1:3–4; Kiddushin 49b; Bava Metzia 84a; Pri Tzaddik, Vayikra 5:2; Rabbeinu Bahya on Bereishis 17:13:6.

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 53a: Rabbi Yochanan says, “לבן של ראשונים כפתחו של אולם ושל אחרונים כפתחו של היכל ואנו כמלא נקב מחט סידקית” — “The hearts of the earlier Sages were like the opening of the Ulam, those of the later ones like the opening of the Heikhal, and ours like the eye of a fine needle.” Shabbos 112b says: “אם ראשונים בני מלאכים אנו בני אנשים ואם ראשונים בני אנשים אנו כחמורים” — “If the earlier ones were like angels, we are like people; if they were like people, we are like donkeys.” These sayings concern spiritual and scholarly stature in general. Rav Tzadok applies that theme to differing degrees of kedushas habris and the progression across three Sages; this application is not a direct teaching of the two Talmudic statements.

paragraphs.text: The measurement chain is an inference assembled by Rav Tzadok, not a single explicit measurement in the Bavli. Yerushalmi Shabbos 18:1, citing the Shekalim collection rite, states “בשלש קופות של שלש שלש סאין” — three kupot, each holding three se’ah (also Mishnah Shekalim 3:2). Tosafos to Shabbos 126b, s.v. “מפנין”, cites this as the size of a kupah. Shabbos 127a separately refers to three-at-a-time loads “בדקורי דהרפניא” — Harpanya receptacles, while Bava Metzia 84a uses such a vessel for Rav Pappa’s comparison. Rav Tzadok reasons that if three smaller Harpanya receptacles fit into one three-se’ah kupah, each would hold one se’ah, equivalent to six kav (explicit conversion in Rashi to Shemos 16:36). He also infers this capacity via a letekh (fifteen se’ah; Rambam, Hilchos Arachin 4:4). The Yerushalmi does NOT say that three baskets total three se’ah: it says each of three larger baskets holds three se’ah. The combination of different vessels is Rav Tzadok’s argument and remains an interpretive inference. He then recognizes that six is numerically greater than the five or three attributed to Rabbi Yochanan and resolves that tension in the following sentences.

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 84a gives the physical comparison “כחמת בת תשע קבין” for R. Yishmael b’R. Yosei; R. Yochanan is compared to five kav, or alternatively three, and Rav Pappa to “דקורי דהרפניא” — Harpanya baskets. The text does not offer a sefirah-based interpretation, and it does not assert that a larger physical size always equals greater spiritual merit. Rav Tzadok first interprets the measures as differing degrees of kedushas habris, then explains why even an apparently larger size for Rav Pappa may signify a more diffuse and therefore less perceptible degree of holiness. The last line of this paragraph completes that qualification.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rather, the intent is to tell of the holiness of their bris: “wisdom of nine kav” is the holiness of the “nine rungs,” from the top of all the rungs down to the Yesod. The Sages denote the middos by “kav” (Kiddushin 49b, “ten kav”), meaning the ten middos of every “stature.” R’ Yochanan’s “five kav” (or “three”) is the span from Gevurah to Yesod (or Netzach-Hod-Yesod) — less than R’ Yishmael b’Rabbi Yosei, whose clarification of holiness reached the root; and Rav Pappa’s, less still, for “the generations go and diminish.”

p: (לה) וְזֶהוּ שֻׁפְרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, שֶׁקְּדֻשַּׁת הַיְסוֹד שֶׁלּוֹ נִמְשָׁךְ מֵהַגְּבוּרָה, דַּרְגָּא דְּיִצְחָק ״יוֹשֵׁב בְּאֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב״ מְנוּגָּב מִכָּל תַּאֲוָה, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא (בִּתְמוּרָה טז.) עַל פָּסוּק ״אֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב נְתַתָּנִי״

(35) This explains R. Yochanan’s beauty: the holiness of his Yesod drew from Gevurah, the quality of Yitzchak, who “dwelt in the land of the Negev” — spiritually parched of all desire, as the Gemara interprets the expression “You have given me the land of the Negev” (Temurah 16a).
וְזֶהוּ הַיֹּפִי דִּירוּשָׁלַיִם שֶׁהוּא מַדְרֵגַת שְׁלֵימוּת הַיִּרְאָה כַּנּוֹדָע
And this is the beauty of Jerusalem: the spiritual level of perfected awe of Heaven, as is known.
וּלְפִי שֶׁהָיָה מִתֹּקֶף הַגְּבוּרוֹת, עַל כֵּן אָמַר דְּ״הַדְרַת פָּנִים זָקָן״ לֹא הָיָה לוֹ, דְּהַדִּיקְנָא מוֹרֶה עַל מִדּוֹת הָרַחֲמִים כַּנּוֹדָע
Because his quality was rooted in intense Gevuros, he was said to lack “hadras panim” — the splendor of a beard — for, in this symbolism, the beard signifies the attributes of Rachamim, mercy.
וְאַף דְּהָיָה אֶצְלוֹ רוֹגְזָא דְּרַבָּנַן דְּטָב מִכָּל סִטְרֵין,
Even though he possessed the Sages’ holy ardor — rogza d’rabbanan — which is good in every respect,
לְפִי שֶׁזִּלְזֵל בְּרוֹגְזֵּיהּ דְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ שֶׁהָיָה גַּם כֵּן רוֹגְזָא דְּרַבָּנַן,
because he diminished the significance of Reish Lakish’s holy ardor, which likewise belonged to rogza d’rabbanan,
דְּעַל זֶה כִּוֶּן גַּם כֵּן בְּמַה שֶׁאָמַר הָתָם "רַבִּי קָרֵא לִי",
and this was also what Reish Lakish meant when he answered there, “They called me Rabbi even then”:
שֶׁהָיָה גַּם אָז רַב וְרַבִּי, וְשֶׁהָיָה רוֹגְזָא דְּרַבָּנַן, וּ"סְבִיבָיו נִשְׂעֲרָה מְאֹד",
he was a teacher and a rabbi even in his former life, and that earlier force was also a holy ardor — “around Him the storm rages exceedingly.”
נִמְצָא פַּגָם בְּרוֹגְזָא דִּילֵיהּ גַּם כֵּן.
Thus a blemish was found in R. Yochanan’s own holy anger as well.

וּמִפְּנֵי שֶׁבָּא לוֹ עַל יְדֵי הֶעְדֵּר יְדִיעָתוֹ בְּמַעֲלַת וּמַדְרֵגַת רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ, שֶׁלֹּא הֶחֱזִיקוֹ בְּמַדְרֵגָה כָּל כָּךְ שֶׁתִּיקֵּן כָּל כָּךְ הַקּוֹדֵם, עַד דְּגַם הָתָם ״רַבִּי קָרוּ לֵיהּ״ — עַל כֵּן שָׁף מִדַּעְתּוֹ

Because the defect arose from his failure to recognize Reish Lakish’s spiritual level — not realizing how completely his former conduct had been rectified, so that “they called him Rabbi” even then — R. Yochanan ultimately lost his reason.
וְזֶה הָיָה בִּירוּר דְּנָח רוֹגְזָא זֶה נֶגֶד רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ,
This was the process of clarification through which that anger directed against Reish Lakish was brought to rest:
שֶׁהָיָה לִטְעוֹן נֶגְדּוֹ לֹא עִינָה מִלִּבּוֹ רַק מִצַּד חִסְרוֹן יְדִיעָה,
R. Yochanan could argue that he had not caused hurt willingly, but only from a failure of knowledge;
אֶלָּא שֶׁהַשּׁוֹגֵג צָרִיךְ גַּם כֵּן סְלִיחָה וְכַפָּרָה.
nevertheless, even one who errs inadvertently requires forgiveness and atonement.
וְכֵן רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ גַּם כֵּן לְפִי שֶׁלֹא הָיָה מִן הַנִּעֱלָבִים וְאֵין עוֹלְבִים,
Likewise, Reish Lakish was not yet among those who hear an insult without returning it,
וְאַעַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה זֶה לְצֹרֶךְ לֹאמַר דְּלֹא עָבַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן חָס וְשָׁלוֹם מִאִיסּוּר אוֹנָאַת דְּבָרִים,
although his reply was necessary to establish that R. Yochanan had not, Heaven forbid, violated the prohibition against hurtful speech,
דְּלֹא יֹאמַר לְבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה "זְכוֹר מַעֲשֶׂיךָ הָרִאשׁוֹנִים".
for one must not tell someone who has repented, “Remember your former deeds.”

אֲבָל וַדַּאי גַּם רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הֶחֱזִיקוֹ תְּחִלָּה כָּךְ, דְּגַם מַעֲשָׂיו הַקּוֹדְמִין נֶחְשָׁבִין כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, וְאֵין כָּאן גְּנוּת כְּלָל (וְעַיֵּין לְעֵיל סִימָן א׳), וְלֹא נִתְכַּוֵּון לְגַנּוֹתוֹ מִתְּחִלָּה

Yet R. Yochanan had certainly regarded Reish Lakish’s former deeds as having become merits, so that no disgrace remained in referring to them (see above, Siman 1); he had not originally intended to shame him.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁקְּרָאוֹ ״לִיסְטָאָה״, לְפִי שֶׁהָיָה בֵּין הַלִּיסְטִים, וְגַם דְּהַמַּעֲשֶׂה הָיָה דּוֹמֶה לְלִיסְטִיּוּת
And even though he called him “bandit listaa,” it was because he had been among the bandits, and also because the deed resembled banditry.

וּבִלְעָם הָרָשָׁע קָרְיֵיהּ לְפִינְחָס ״לִיסְטָאָה״, ורז״ל הֶעְתִּיקוּ הַלָּשׁוֹן (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין קו רע״ב), וְהוּא עַל הֲרִיגָתוֹ לְזִמְרִי שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה חַיָּיב מִיתָה בְּבֵית דִּין וְלֹא נִצְטַוָּוה עַל זֶה, דְּ״אִם בָּא לִשְׁאוֹל אֵין מוֹרִין לוֹ״, רַק שֶׁקִּינֵּא קִנְאַת ה׳

Even the wicked Bilaam called Pinchas “a bandit,” as the Sages preserve the expression (Sanhedrin 106b), in connection with Pinchas’s killing of Zimri, who had not been condemned to death by a court. Pinchas had not been instructed beforehand to act, for “if one comes to consult, one is not instructed to do it”; he acted from zeal for Hashem.
וְהַהוֹרֵג לְמִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ חַיָּיב מִיתָה מִן הַדִּין אֶלָּא שֶׁכַּוָּונָתוֹ לַשָּׁמַיִם ״לְכַלּוֹת קוֹצִים״ וְכַיּוֹצֵא, זֶהוּ מַעֲשֵׂה לִסְטִיּוּת לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם
A killing not ordered as a judicial punishment, even when undertaken with an intention for Heaven, can outwardly resemble what Rav Tzadok calls “banditry for the sake of Heaven.”
אֶלָּא דְּבִמַעֲשֵׂה דְּפִנְחָס שָׁם הַהֲלָכָה כֵּן דְּקַנָּאִים פוּגְעִים, וְאִם כֵּן דִּין גָּמוּר הוּא לַקַּנָּאי לִפְגֹּע.

In Pinchas’s case, however, there is the specific halachic rule that zealots may intervene in the prescribed circumstances; it is an exceptional rule permitting the zealot’s intervention, not a court-imposed death sentence.
וְאוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע שֶׁלֹא יָדַע זֶה קָרְיֵה לִיסְטָאה אַף שֶׁיָדַע כַּוָּנָתוֹ שֶׁלְשָׁמַיִם הָיָה,
And that wicked one, who did not know this, called him a bandit, even though he knew his intention was for the sake of Heaven,
דְּהֲרֵי הוּא עַצְמוֹ הוּא שֶׁהָיָה בְּאוֹתָה עֵצָה לְהַכְשִׁילָם וְשֶׁיִּפְלוּ עֶשְׂרִים וְאַרְבָּעָה אֶלֶף,
for he himself was the one who was in that plan to cause them to stumble, so that twenty-four thousand would fall,
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם שַׁיָּךְ עַל זֶה שֵׁם לִסְטוּת כֵּיוָן שֶׁאֵינוֹ בָּדִּין.
Nevertheless, the term “banditry” can be applied to its extra-judicial appearance, since it does not proceed from a court’s imposed sentence.

paragraphs.text: Temurah 16a expounds Achsah's “כִּי אֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב נְתַתָּנִי” (Yehoshua 15:19) as “בַּיִת שֶׁמְּנוּגָב מִכָּל טוֹבָה” — “a household dried out of all good.” Bereishis 24:62 separately describes Yitzchak living in the Negev. The Gemara concerns material lack, not an explicit claim that Yitzchak was without desire. Rav Tzadok draws a deliberate spiritual analogy: Yitzchak's Gevurah, free of bodily craving, is the root of R. Yochanan's sanctified beauty. This note therefore belongs immediately after the developed Negev analogy, before Rav Tzadok turns to the next idea, Jerusalem's perfected yirah. Sources: Temurah 16a; Yehoshua 15:19; Bereishis 24:62.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 56:10 joins Avraham’s “ה׳ יראה” (“Hashem will see”) and Shem’s “שלם” (“Shalem”) into the name Yerushalayim: “יראה שלם, ירושלים.” Rav Tzadok’s Pri Tzaddik, Pesach §44, explicitly says, “ושם ירושלים נקרא ע״ש ירא שלם ... והיינו דשם יראה שלימה” — “Jerusalem is called after Yireh-Shalem ... meaning complete awe is found there.” He also connects it with maaser sheni’s “למען תלמד ליראה.” The Midrash supplies the name’s combination; the identification of Jerusalem’s beauty with perfected yirah is the interpretation being developed here.

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 84a says of R. Yochanan “דְּהַדְרַת פָּנִים לָא הֲוָה לֵיהּ” — “he lacked hadras panim”; Rashi explains “הדרת פנים — זקן” — “splendor of the face: a beard.” The Arizal's Shaar HaKavvanot, Derushei Vaya’avor, Derush 5, explicitly organizes the thirteen tikkunei dikna alongside the thirteen Divine attributes of mercy, with names such as “אל”, “רחום”, “וחנון”, and “ורב חסד.” This independently supports the link between the dikna and merciful attributes. Rav Tzadok then interprets R. Yochanan's lack of a beard as corresponding to his stronger Gevuros rather than the outward aspect of Rachamim. That individual application is Rav Tzadok’s interpretation, not a statement of the Gemara, Rashi, or Arizal. Sources: Bava Metzia 84a; Rashi ad loc.; Shaar HaKavvanot, Derushei Vaya’avor, Derush 5 (Hebrew textual witness: https://he.wikisource.org/wiki/שער_הכוונות/דרושי_ויעבר/דרוש_ה).

paragraphs.text: Zohar, Tetzaveh, II 182b (Sefaria, Zohar, Tetzaveh 6:57) explicitly distinguishes Torah-born righteous anger from ordinary anger: “רוגזא דרבנן טב איהו לכל סטרין” — “The anger of the Sages is good on all sides,” precisely because “אורייתא קא מרתחא ליה” — “the Torah makes him ardent”; the text specifies that such anger is over Torah and for Divine service. Taanis 4a supplies the Bavli formulation yet immediately adds that one must learn to act gently. Rav Tzadok’s Tzidkas HaTzadik §199 explains: “שגם בעת כעסו אינו אלא מצד התורה וזוכר ומשתדל ברחמים” — “Even at a moment of anger, it is for Torah alone, while he remembers and strives for mercy.” Thus the fault in R. Yochanan is not holy intensity itself but his failure to recognize holy intensity in Reish Lakish.

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 84a describes the illness and death of Reish Lakish, R. Yochanan's grief, and “וְהָוָה קָא צָוַח עַד דְּשָׁף דַּעְתֵּיהּ מִינֵּיהּ” — “he cried out until his mind became dislodged.” It does not identify this as a punishment for failing to discern Reish Lakish's earlier spiritual level. Rav Tzadok gives that interpretation in Dover Tzedek, Likkutim 4:138 (Har Bracha, printed p. 253), saying “בדבור זה עורר רבי יוחנן קטרוג על שורש הנעלם דריש לקיש” — “By this statement R. Yochanan awakened an accusation concerning the concealed root of Reish Lakish.” Here he adds that the hurt was not deliberate but arose from “חסרון ידיעה” (lack of knowledge), and that even such an unwitting mistake may require forgiveness and atonement. The Torah's “נֶפֶשׁ כִּי תֶחֱטָא בִשְׁגָגָה” (Vayikra 4:2) provides an analogy, not a ruling that every inadvertent remark requires a sacrificial chatas: Rambam, Hilchos Shegagos 1:1, limits the prescribed chatas to particular unwitting prohibitions involving an act and kareis. Sources: Bava Metzia 84a; Dover Tzedek, Likkutim 4:138; Vayikra 4:2; Mishneh Torah, Hilchos Shegagos 1:1.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 88b praises “עֲלוּבִין וְאֵינָן עוֹלְבִין, שׁוֹמְעִין חֶרְפָּתָן וְאֵינָן מְשִׁיבִין” — “those insulted who do not insult in return, who hear their disgrace without replying.” Yoma 23a cites the same teaching while weighing its relationship to righteous indignation, underscoring the difference between feeling pain and responding in kind. Rav Tzadok finds in Reish Lakish’s defensive reply evidence that the exceptional restraint of the silent, insulted righteous was not yet complete in him. The Gemara does not directly pronounce judgment on Reish Lakish; this is Rav Tzadok’s reading of the episode.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86b reports two teachings of Reish Lakish: repentance may turn deliberate sins into inadvertent ones, or into merits. The Gemara resolves the difference: “לָא קַשְׁיָא: כָּאן מֵאַהֲבָה, כָּאן מִיִּרְאָה” — “No difficulty: here from love, there from fear.” Rav Tzadok applies the repentance-from-love principle to Reish Lakish himself, arguing that R. Yochanan initially viewed his former deeds as reinterpreted into merits, making his reference to the past non-disparaging. The independent norm against invoking a penitent’s former sins is explicit in Bava Metzia 58b: “אם היה בעל תשובה לא יאמר לו זכור מעשיך הראשונים” — “If he has repented, do not say: Remember your former deeds.” Rav Tzadok explains how he thinks the two points coexist in this special instance; the Gemara does not itself grant a general exception.
