paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 106b does NOT record Bilaam himself speaking to Pinchas. A heretic says that he saw “פנקסיה דבלעם” — “Bilaam’s ledger” — recording “פנחס ליסטאה” — “Pinchas the bandit” — as the one who killed Bilaam. Rav Tzadok treats the insulting epithet as Bilaam’s outlook and extends it to Pinchas’s killing of Zimri, not a court-imposed punishment. The Gemara in Sanhedrin 82a limits this event to the special rule “הבועל ארמית קנאין פוגעין בו” and explicitly adds “הבא לימלך אין מורין לו” — “If someone comes to ask, we do not instruct him to do it.” It adds that if Zimri had stopped, Pinchas would have been liable for killing him. Thus the author’s paradox—an act resembling extra-judicial banditry while specifically permitted under a narrow, non-court-ordered rule—must not be flattened into a license for privately motivated violence. Bamidbar 31:16 attributes the Peor enticement to Bilaam’s counsel; Bamidbar 25:9 gives 24,000 deaths.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: R’ Yochanan’s beauty stems from the holiness of the yesod the guarded covenant drawn from Gevurah — the rung of Yitzchak, “dwelling in the parched Negev,” dried of all desire. This is the beauty of Jerusalem, the level of perfected yirah. Because he was of the intense Gevuros, “he had no hadras panim beard” — the beard signifies the middos of Rachamim.

p: (לו) וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִתְּחִלָּה לֹא כִּיוֵּון לִגְנוּת וְאוֹנָאַת דְּבָרִים חַס וְשָׁלוֹם בְּמַעֲשָׂיו רִאשׁוֹנִים, רַק חָשַׁב דְּאֵין לוֹ גְּנוּת מִזֶּה
(36) At first, R. Yochanan had not meant to disgrace Reish Lakish or cause him verbal hurt, Heaven forbid, by referring to his earlier deeds; he thought there was no disgrace attached to them.

אֲבָל רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ ״מַאי אַהֲנֵית״ כו׳ שֶׁהִרְגִּישׁ גְּנוּת, וְסָבוּר דְּכִיוֵּון לְגַנּוֹתוֹ — עַל כֵּן אַף עַל פִּי דְּיָדַע בְּנַפְשׁוֹ דְּבֶאֱמֶת הַכֹּל נֶחְשָׁב לוֹ לִזְכֻיּוֹת, מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא נִתְגַּלָּה וְנִתְבָּרֵר זֶה עֲדַיִין לְעֵין כֹּל וּלְעֵינֵי בְּנֵי אָדָם עֲדַיִין

But Reish Lakish, who replied, “What benefit did you bring me?”, felt dishonored and thought that R. Yochanan had intended to disgrace him. Although he knew within himself that his earlier deeds truly had become merits, this had not yet been revealed and clarified before everyone.
וּמִמֵּילָא דַּעֲדַיִין לֹא הִגִּיעַ לְתַכְלִית גְּמַר הַתִּיקּוּן הַגָּמוּר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מְבוֹרָר לַכֹּל
And consequently he had not yet reached the ultimate completion of the perfect rectification that would be clear to all.

דְּגַם מַה שֶּׁבְּנֵי אָדָם חוֹשְׁדִין בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, אִם אֵינוֹ מִצַּד אֵיבָה וְשִׂנְאָה, עַל כָּרְחֲךָ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ שֶׁמֶץ מַה מִזֶּה עֲדַיִין בַּלֵּב עַל כָּל פָּנִים, כָּל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא פָּסַק הַחֲשָׁד וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּמוֹעֵד קָטָן יח:)

For when people in this world suspect someone of a matter — unless the suspicion arises from enmity or hatred — Rav Tzadok reads the Sages as indicating that a subtle trace of it may remain in the heart as long as suspicion persists; compare Moed Katan 18b.
וּבִגְמַר הַתִּיקּוּן דְּ״יְבוּקַּשׁ עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ״, יִפָּסֵק גַּם הַחֲשָׁד מִפִּי הַבְּרִיּוֹת
When the rectification is complete, “the iniquity of Israel will be sought and it will not be found,” and even the suspicion voiced by others will cease.
וְכָל זְמַן שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּזֶה גְּנוּת לְעֵינֵי הַבְּרִיוֹת,
And as long as there is in this a disgrace in the eyes of people,
עַל כֵּן אַעַל פִּי שֶׁמִּצַּד עַצְמוֹ שֶׁהוּא מִצַּד הָאֱמֶת לְאֲמִיתוֹ הוּא נָקִי וָזַךְ לַגְמַרִי,
therefore, although from his own side, which is the side of truth in its truth, he is clean and pure entirely,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם עַדַיִן צָרִיךְ בִּירוּרִים לָבוֹא לִידֵי גִּילּוּי לַכֻּלָּם, דְּלֹא יִתְבֻּשׁוּ עוֹד.
in any case he still needs clarifications to come to revelation to all, that they will no longer be ashamed.

וּמִצַּד הַזֶּה בָּא לַחְשׁוֹד אֶת רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן שֶׁבָּא לְאוֹנָאוֹתוֹ בִּדְבָרִים, דְּמִי שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ שׁוּם שֶׁמֶץ חִסָּרוֹן לֹא יָכוֹל לַחְשׁוֹד אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ גַּם כֵּן בְּחִסָּרוֹן, דְּאֵין מַרְגִּישׁ בִּמְצִיאוּת חִסָּרוֹן וְדָן הַכֹּל לְכַף זְכוּת

For that reason Reish Lakish came to suspect that R. Yochanan intended to wound him with words. In Rav Tzadok’s account, someone entirely free of a particular inner defect would not attribute that defect to another, but would interpret others favorably.

וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ ז״ל ״כָּל הַפּוֹסֵל בְּמוּמוֹ פּוֹסֵל״, דְּאֵין אָדָם פּוֹסֵל לַחֲבֵירוֹ בְּמַה שֶּׁאֵין בּוֹ, אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן יֵשׁ בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁמֶץ מִזֶּה, וְאָז רוֹאֶה גַּם בַּחֲבֵירוֹ מֵאוֹתוֹ חִסָּרוֹן שֶׁבּוֹ, כִּי הַנְּפָשׁוֹת כְּמַרְאוֹת כַּנּוֹדָע

And therefore the Sages said, “whoever disqualifies, disqualifies with his own blemish” — a man does not disqualify his fellow with what is not in himself, unless there is in his own soul a trace of it, and then he sees in his fellow, too, that same defect that is in him; for souls are like mirrors, as is known.
וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ שְׁנֵיהֶם הָיוּ מִתֹּקֶף הַגְּבוּרוֹת הַקְּדוֹשׁוֹת, וְהָיוּ נְקִיִּים לְגַמְרֵי מִכָּל תַּאֲוָה וְחֶמְדָּה גּוּפָנִית דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And R’ Yochanan and Reish Lakish were both of the intensity of the holy Gevuros, and were completely clean of all desire and bodily craving of this world.
דְּעַל כֵּן נָסֵיב רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ לַאֲחָתֵיהּ, וְלֹא חָשׁ שֶׁיֹּאמְרוּ כו׳ כְּמוֹ שֶׁהִרְגִּישׁוּ הַתּוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם (ד״ה ״אִי״), וְלֹא פֵּירְשׁוּ הַטַּעַם

Thus Reish Lakish married R. Yochanan’s sister and was not concerned that people might say he had returned to the Torah merely in order to marry her, a question raised but not resolved by Tosafos there, s.v. “אי הדרת בך.”

אֲבָל הוּא מְבוֹאָר דְּשָׁם הָיָה חֵטְא בְּתַאֲוָה שַׁיָּיךְ ״שֶׁמָּא יֹאמְרוּ״ כו׳, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אֵצֶל רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא יָדְעֵי דְּהָיָה נָקִי מִזֶּה וְלֹא יַחְשְׁדוּהוּ בְּכָךְ, כִּי לֹא הָיָה בְּלִבּוֹ שׁוּם שֶׁמֶץ מִדָּבָר זֶה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מָקוֹם לְחָשְׁדוֹ

Rav Tzadok explains that such a concern would arise where repentance from an offense rooted in desire could appear motivated by a prospective marriage. But everyone knew Reish Lakish was completely free of that motive; nobody would suspect him of repenting merely to obtain the marriage, for not a trace of such desire remained in his heart.
וְאֵין חוֹשְׁדִין לְאָדָם אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן יֵשׁ בּוֹ שֶׁמֶץ מַה וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, וַהֲרֵי דְּהָיָה נָקִי לְגַמְרֵי בְּתַאֲוָה בְּלִי שׁוּם מַשֶּׁהוּ שֶׁמֶץ מַה בַּמַּעֲמַקִּים גַּם כֵּן

Thus, in Rav Tzadok’s analysis, suspicion does not arise without some subtle ground of which a person is conscious. Reish Lakish had, he says, been purified of bodily desire completely, without even the faintest trace hidden in his depths.

paragraphs.text: Moed Katan 18b says “אין אדם נחשד בדבר אלא אם כן עשאו” and develops possibilities involving action, thought or delight in another's conduct. The same passage immediately questions any unqualified inference by citing innocently suspected people and Moses himself, and limits the concern to a rumor that does not cease and is not propagated by enemies: “אִית לֵיהּ אוֹיְבִים — אוֹיְבִים הוּא דְּאַפְּקוּהּ לְקָלָא” — “If he has enemies, it is the enemies who spread the report.” Meiri to Moed Katan 18b likewise states “ומכל מקום יצא מכלל זה כל שחושדין אותו מחמת קנאה או שנאה” — “This excludes anyone suspected because of jealousy or hatred.” Rav Tzadok uses this explicitly qualified teaching to explain why public recognition of Reish Lakish's inward rectification was not yet complete; it must not be treated as a factual test establishing guilt from gossip. The subsequent prophecy of the end of suspicion is addressed separately at the next Hebrew citation (Yirmeyahu 50:20). Sources: Moed Katan 18b; Meiri, Beis HaBechirah ad loc.

paragraphs.text: Pirkei Avos 1:6 instructs “וֶהֱוֵי דָן אֶת כָּל הָאָדָם לְכַף זְכוּת” — “Judge every person favorably.” Rambam on Avos 1:6 explains that even when an apparently bad action of a known righteous person can only with difficulty be understood positively, one must accept a credible positive possibility; he also addresses the morally unknown and the known wicked differently. Shabbos 97a warns that one who suspects the righteous can be punished; Shabbos 127b says one who judges others favorably is judged favorably. Rav Tzadok’s psychological claim that one who is entirely free of a blemish cannot even perceive it in another is a further interpretive premise, not a direct statement of Avos, Rambam, or Shabbos.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 70a states “כָּל הַפּוֹסֵל — פָּסוּל ... בְּמוּמוֹ פּוֹסֵל” — “Whoever disqualifies others is disqualified ... he does so by his own blemish.” Its immediate context concerns impugning lineage; it is not a general proof that suspicions reveal actual wrongdoing. Rav Tzadok explicitly generalizes it in Dover Tzedek, Likkutim 4:149 (Har Bracha, printed p. 264): “וכנודע מאמר החכם הנפשות כמראות ... כי הכלל בכל אדם כפי מה שהוא כך היא תפיסתו בחבירו” — “As in the sages' saying, souls are like mirrors ... each perceives another according to what he himself is.” He continues by explaining “הוי ... שתהיה דן חבירך לכף זכות” — “Become such that you judge your fellow favorably” (cf. Avos 1:6). A related but distinct application appears in Pri Tzaddik, Vayeshev §7: Yosef's brothers, thinking themselves innocent, suspect him instead — “וע״כ במומו פוסל”. These are Rav Tzadok's moral and psychological readings, not literal pronouncements of Kiddushin or evidence that any particular allegation is true. Sources: Kiddushin 70a; Dover Tzedek, Likkutim 4:149 (printed p. 264); Avos 1:6; Pri Tzaddik, Vayeshev 7.

paragraphs.text: Tosafos on Bava Metzia 84a, s.v. “אי הדרת בך”, observes that Reish Lakish later married R. Yochanan’s sister and asks “וְלֹא חָשׁ לְשֶׁמָּא יֹאמְרוּ בִּשְׁבִיל זוֹ חָזַר זֶה” — “Was he not concerned that people would say he returned because of this woman?” Tosafos does not supply a resolution here. Rosh, quoted in Shitah Mekubetzes to Bava Metzia 84a, suggests that his earlier learning made the return intelligible. Rav Tzadok instead distinguishes a return from sins grounded in bodily desire: Reish Lakish was so clearly free of that motive that nobody would suppose his teshuvah was undertaken for the marriage. His answer is his own, not the wording of Tosafos or Rosh. This note belongs immediately after that explanation is completed in Se’if 36, not after the later restatement of his purified inner life. Sources: Tosafos, Bava Metzia 84a, s.v. “אי הדרת בך”; Shitah Mekubetzes ad loc.; Rav Tzadok, Takanas HaShavin, Siman 10, Se’if 36.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: R’ Yochanan at first did not intend disgrace or ona’as devarim — he thought there was no disgrace in it. But Reish Lakish, who felt the shame (“what benefit have I gained”), supposed he did intend to shame him. So although Reish Lakish knew within himself that in truth all was reckoned to him as merits, this had not yet been revealed and clarified to every eye — hence he had not yet reached the utter completion of the rectification, manifest to all.

p: (לז) וְכֵן שֻׁפְרֵיהּ דְּר׳ יוֹחָנָן שֶׁהָיָה רַבּוֹ דְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ, וְכֵן הָיָה רַבּוֹ דְּר׳ אַבָּהוּ, שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם דְּשֻׁפְרֵיהּ מֵעֵין דְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה, שֶׁהוּא צוּרַת אָדָם שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה

(37) So too the beauty of R. Yochanan, the teacher of Reish Lakish and also of R. Abbahu. The Sages said that R. Abbahu’s beauty resembled that of Yaakov our father, whose form corresponds to the supernal human image.

וּבְוַדַּאי הוּא תַּכְלִית הַיֹּפִי דְּצוּרַת אָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אַחַר חֵטְא דְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן; וּמַה שֶּׁאָמַר ״מֵעֵין שֻׁפְרֵיהּ דְּאָדָם״, הַיְינוּ קוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא, דְּאַחַר כָּךְ נִיטַּל מִמֶּנּוּ זִיו פָּנָיו, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בברא״ר פ׳ י״ב) מִקְּרָא דְּ״מְשַׁנֶּה פָנָיו וַתְּשַׁלְּחֵהוּ״

Certainly, that form represents the utmost beauty of the human appearance in this world after Adam’s sin. The statement that it resembled Adam’s beauty refers to Adam before the sin, for afterward the radiance of his face was removed, as Bereishis Rabbah chapter 12 teaches from “You change his face and send him away” (Iyov 14:20).

וְיַעֲקֹב תִּיקֵּן חֶטְאוֹ לְגַמְרֵי מִצַּד עַצְמוֹ, דְּעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ (תַּעֲנִית ה:) דְּלֹא מֵת; אֶלָּא שֶׁכְּפִי הַהִתְגַּלּוּת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הָיָה רַק ״מֵעֵין״, כְּמוֹ שַׁבָּת ״מֵעֵין הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא״

Yaakov himself completely rectified that original sin; therefore the Sages say in Taanis 5b that he did not die. Yet in what was revealed in this world, his perfection was only a semblance, just as Shabbos is a semblance of the World to Come.

כִּי כָּל הַשָּׂגָה דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, גַּם לְמִי שֶׁמַּשִּׂיג עוֹלָמוֹ בְּחַיָּיו כְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה, אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא ״מֵעֵין״ דְּעוֹלָם הַבָּא, הַיְינוּ בְּתַכְלִית קוֹטֶן הַהַרְגָּשָׁה הָאֶפְשָׁרִית

For every apprehension possible in this world—even one who attains his own World to Come during his lifetime, like Yaakov our father—is but a semblance of the World to Come, meaning the smallest degree of perception possible.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת נז:) ״שַׁבָּת אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא״, דְּיָדוּעַ הַפֵּירוּשׁ מִשּׁוּם דְּבִיטּוּל הַטַּעַם בְּשִׁשִּׁים וְאֶחָד, וְשִׁשִּׁים וְאֶחָד אֵין עוֹד הֶרְגֵּשׁ; אֲבָל אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים, שֶׁהוּא רַק חֲמִשִּׁים וָתֵשַׁע פַּעַם כְּמוֹתוֹ, יֵשׁ הֶרְגֵּשׁ, וְהוּא הַיּוֹתֵר מוּעָט וְקָטָן, עַד שֶׁבְּפָחוֹת מִמֶּנּוּ אֵין עוֹד הֶרְגֵּשׁ נִיכָּר — זֶה נִקְרָא ״מֵעֵין״ הַדָּבָר

As the Sages said (Berachos 57b), “Shabbos is one-sixtieth of the World to Come.” The familiar explanation is that taste is treated as nullified where a single part is mixed with sixty opposing parts, becoming one in sixty-one of the total. But when it is one in sixty of the whole, there are only fifty-nine other parts, and some taste is still perceptible. This is the faintest detectable trace; less than that is not discernible. Such a trace is called a “semblance” of the thing.
וְדְּרַבִּי אַבָּהוּ מֵעֵין דְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁגַּם הוּא בְּתַכְלִית הַיֹּפִי מֵעֵין דְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קֹדֶם הַחֵטְא, וְלֹא הָיָה רָאוּי לָמוּת.
R. Abbahu’s beauty likewise resembled that of Yaakov, whose own extraordinary beauty resembled that of Adam before the sin, when Adam had not yet incurred the decree of death.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ עָלָיו (בִּירוּשַׁלְמִי רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ג׳ דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה) דְּהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא הֶרְאָה לוֹ מַתַּן שְׁכָרוֹ וְנַפְשוֹ שָׂבְעָה לוֹ וְיָשֵׁן, עַיֵּן שָׁם.

For this reason, the Yerushalmi at the beginning of chapter 3 of Avodah Zarah relates of R. Abbahu that Hashem showed him his reward. It then teaches that the soul of the righteous is satisfied and they fall asleep; see the passage there.
וְשּׁוּפְרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הָיָה בְּיוֹתֵר, שֶׁהֲרֵי אָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ "אֲנָא אַשְׁתִּייָרֵי" (מִשְׁפִירֵי יְרוּשָׁלַיִם), מַשְׁמַע הוּא לְבַדוֹ,
But R. Yochanan possessed an even greater beauty, for he said of himself, “I remain from among the beautiful people of Jerusalem,” which Rav Tzadok understands as referring to himself alone.
וְרַבִּי אַבָּהוּ הָיָה תַּלְמִידוֹ וּבְדוֹרוֹ, אֲבָל שּׁוּפְרֵיהּ יוֹתֵר מִמֶּנּוּ, וְאִם כֵּן יוֹתֵר קִרּוּב לוֹ עִם שּׁוּפְרֵיהּ דְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
R. Abbahu was his disciple and lived in his generation, yet R. Yochanan’s beauty, Rav Tzadok argues, surpassed his. If so, R. Yochanan’s beauty was even closer to that of Yaakov our father.
וְלֹא חֲשָׁבֵיהּ מִשּׁוּם דְּ"הַדַּרְת" כּוּלֵּי? וְכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל.
Why, then, was R. Yochanan omitted from that comparison? Because he lacked “hadras panim,” as explained above.
כִּי הוּא הָיָה מִתּוֹקֶף הַגְּבוּרוֹת דִּקְדֻשָּׁה, וּבְזֶה הָיָה הַחֶסְרוֹן שֶׁלוֹ, שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּכָל אֶחָד מִעֲטִיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ "דְּאֵין אָדָם צַדִּיק" וְגוֹמֵר.

For his spiritual quality sprang from the intense Gevuros of holiness; there too lay his remaining deficiency, since everyone still bears some trace of the serpent’s counsel: “For there is no righteous person,” and so forth.

אֲבָל בְּתַאֲוֹת הָיָה נָקִי לְגַמְרֵי, וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר (בִּירוּשַׁלְמִי שָׁם) דְּ"כַּד דְּמַךְ אִתְכַּפִּין אוּקְנַיָּא" (כְּשֶׁמֵּת נִכְפְּפוּ הַצּוּרוֹת שֶׁעוֹשִׂים עַל הַכְּתָלִים), דְּלֹא הֲוַת אִיקוֹנִין דְּכוּתֵיהּ.

From physical desires, however, he was entirely pure. Accordingly, the Yerushalmi there says that when he died, the images bent over—the figures fashioned upon the walls bowed—because there was no image equal to his.
כִּי הָאָדָם הוּא אִיקוֹנִין שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה לד, ג) "מָה אִם אִיקוֹנִין שֶׁל מְלָכִים וְכוּלֵּי, אֲנִי שֶׁנִּבְרֵאתִי בְּצֶלֶם וּבִדְמוּת וְכוּלֵּי".
For a person is an image of the supernal form, as Vayikra Rabbah 34:3 relates: “If even the images of earthly kings [are honored] . how much more I, who was made in the Divine image and likeness!”
וְזֶהוּ זִיו אִיקוֹנִין דְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קֹדֶם הַחֵטְא שֶׁנִּקְרָא (בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא נח.) "דִּיוֹקְנִי עַצְמָהּ"
This is the radiance of Adam’s image before the sin, called in Bava Basra 58a “My image itself.”

(דְּאַחַר שֶׁקִיבֵּל עוֹנְשוֹ הַמִּיתָה שֶׁנִּגְזַר עָלָיו נִתְכַּפֵּר לוֹ, דְּמִשְׁלָקָה הֲרֵי הוּא כְּאָחִיךָ, וְאֵין לָךְ עָוֹן שֶׁלֹא נִתְכַּפֵּר אַחַר קִבּוּל עוֹנֶשׁ הַנִּגְזָר עָלָיו, דְּעַל זֶה הוּא גְּזֵירַת הָעוֹנֶשׁ, וְעַל כֵּן אַחַר מוֹתוֹ חָזַר לְזִיווֹ וְדִיוֹקְנִי עַצְמָהּ)

For after Adam underwent the decreed punishment of death, Rav Tzadok explains, the sin was atoned for: “Once he has received lashes, he is considered your brother.” On this reasoning, the prescribed punishment effects atonement, and after Adam’s death his radiance returned, so that he was again called “My image itself.”
וְדִיעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נִקְרָא "דְּמוּת דִּיוֹקְנִי",
Yaakov our father, peace be upon him, is called “the likeness of My image,”
וְכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ הֵם בְּחוֹתָמוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן כְּדַתְנַן (סַנְהֶדְרִין לז סוֹף עַמּוּד א) וְהֵם אִיקוֹנִין שֶׁלוֹ,
whereas all humanity bears the imprint of Adam’s seal, as taught at the end of Sanhedrin 37a, and all are images derived from him.
אֲבָל אֵין דּוֹמִין לוֹ בְּכָל הַדּוֹרוֹת כְּמוֹ יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם.
Yet among all generations, no one resembled Adam as fully as Yaakov our father did.

וּבְדוֹרוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן לֹא הָיָה אִיקוֹנִין כְּמוֹהוּ, שֶׁהוּא הַיוֹתֵר דוֹמֶה בְּאִיקוֹנִין שֶׁלוֹ לְמִי שֶׁהוּא אִיקוֹנִין מִמֶּנּוּ, כִּי כָּל שִׁינּוּי זִיו הַפָּנִים וְהָאִיקוֹנִין הוּא מִצַּד הַתַּאֲוָה שֶׁהוּא חֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן.

And in R. Yochanan’s generation there was no human likeness equal to his; his appearance most closely reflected the original image from which such likenesses derive. Rav Tzadok explains every diminution of facial radiance as arising from desire, the root of Adam’s sin.

paragraphs.text: Ta'anis 5b records R. Yochanan's “יעקב אבינו לא מת” (“Our father Yaakov did not die”). Challenged that Yaakov was eulogized, embalmed, and buried, he answers “מקרא אני דורש” (“I expound Scripture”), citing Yirmeyahu 30:10 and its continuation: “מקיש הוא לזרעו, מה זרעו בחיים אף הוא בחיים” (“He is compared with his descendants: as they live, so he lives”). The Gemara gives this scriptural derashah, but does not say that Yaakov's rectification of Adam's sin is the reason for his continuing life; that is Rav Tzadok's interpretation in this paragraph. Sources: Ta'anit 5b; Yirmeyahu 30:10–11.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 17a blesses “עולמך תראה בחייך” — “May you see your world in your lifetime.” Bava Basra 16b–17a says “שלשה הטעימן הקדוש ברוך הוא בעולם הזה” (at the end of 16b), continuing on 17a with “מעין העולם הבא, אלו הן אברהם יצחק ויעקב” — “The Holy One gave three a taste in this world of the World to Come: Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov.” Its prooftexts are “בכל”, “מכל”, and “כל”. This taste pertains to all three Avos, not Yaakov alone. Rav Tzadok associates the traditions with Yaakov's exceptional rectification but emphasizes that even earthly attainment of Olam HaBa remains only “me'ein,” not the fullness of the World to Come. Sources: Berakhot 17a; Bava Batra 16b–17a.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 57b records two distinct but closely adjacent descriptions: “שלשה מעין העולם הבא” (“Three things resemble the World to Come”), including Shabbos, and “חמשה אחד מששים ... שבת אחד מששים לעולם הבא” (“Five are one-sixtieth ... Shabbos is one-sixtieth of the World to Come”). The Gemara itself does not explain these aggadic descriptions through the halachos of food-mixture nullification. Rav Tzadok develops that additional explanatory analogy immediately afterward; see the following note on the completed numerical argument. Source: Berakhot 57b.

paragraphs.text: Chullin 98a–b and Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 98 discuss the halachic framework of taste and nullification in mixtures. In the usual sixty-to-one comparison, one prohibited unit with sixty permitted units is one part of sixty-one total; with only fifty-nine permitted parts it is one of sixty total. Rav Tzadok applies this arithmetical distinction homiletically to the faintest perceptible “me'ein”: the Torah’s account of taste/nullification is not an experimentally fixed perception threshold, nor does every mixture follow one unconditional rule. Compare the adjacent “one-sixtieth” teaching in Berachos 57b. Sources: Chullin 98a–b; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh Deah 98; Berakhot 57b.

paragraphs.text: Yerushalmi Avodah Zarah 3:1 first reports, on R. Abbahu’s passing, “רבי אבהו מי דמך עברון קומוי י״ג נהרין דאפרסמון” — “When R. Abbahu died, thirteen rivers of balsam passed before him.” Asked who they were for, he learned they were his reward and exclaimed, “ואני אמרתי לריק יגעתי” — “Yet I had said that I had labored in vain.” Immediately thereafter the Yerushalmi offers a general teaching: “הקדוש ברוך הוא מראה להן לצדיקים מתן שכרן בעולם הזה ונפשם שביעה והן ישינין להן” — “The Holy One shows the righteous their reward in this world; their souls are satisfied and they fall asleep.” The second sentence speaks of the righteous generally, NOT as a verbatim biographical sentence exclusively about R. Abbahu. Rav Tzadok connects the adjoining general teaching with R. Abbahu’s account and his own interpretation of radiant beauty.

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 84a gives the actual sequence: “שופריה דרב כהנא מעין שופריה דרבי אבהו; שופריה דרבי אבהו מעין שופריה דיעקב אבינו; שופריה דיעקב אבינו מעין שופריה דאדם הראשון” — Rav Kahana's beauty resembled R. Abbahu's, R. Abbahu's resembled Yaakov's, and Yaakov's resembled Adam's. The Gemara then asks why R. Yochanan is not counted and answers “שאני רבי יוחנן דהדרת פנים לא הויא ליה”; Rashi explains that hadras panim means a beard. Elsewhere on this daf R. Yochanan says “אנא אשתיירי משפירי ירושלים” — “I remain among the beautiful people of Jerusalem.” Tosafos there, s.v. “אנא אשתיירי,” understands this as descent from Jerusalem's beautiful families, not necessarily that he was the single surviving exemplar. Rav Tzadok reads R. Yochanan's remark as implying beauty exceeding his disciple R. Abbahu's, yet understands the absence of a beard in terms of his Gevurah. Neither ranking nor its spiritual explanation is asserted by the Bavli or Tosafos. Sources: Bava Metzia 84a; Rashi and Tosafot ad loc.

paragraphs.text: Bava Basra 17a enumerates four who died “בעטיו של נחש” (“through the serpent's counsel”)—Binyamin, Amram, Yishai, and Kilav—without an individual transgression. Shabbos 55b cites this against R. Ami's “אין מיתה בלא חטא” (“There is no death without sin”) and concludes “תיובתא דרב אמי, תיובתא” (the claim is refuted). Rav Tzadok's close parallel is Dover Tzedek, Likkutim 4:10, NOT the inherited Likkutim 4:77: “ובבבא בתרא (דף י״ז עמוד א׳) חשבינן ארבעה שמתו בעטיו של נחש, ואצלו גם עטיו של נחש נתקן מצדו” — “Bava Basra lists four who died through the serpent's counsel; in Eliyahu's case even that trace was rectified.” Rav Tzadok's application here to R. Yochanan's residual Gevurah is interpretive, not a Gemara ruling about all people. Sources: Bava Batra 17a; Shabbat 55b; Dover Tzedek, Likkutim 4:10 (direct original parallel).

paragraphs.text: Bereshis Rabbah 12:6 names six features lost by Adam after the sin, the first being “זיוו” (“his radiance”), and cites Iyov 14:20, “משנה פניו ותשלחהו” — “You alter his countenance and send him away.” The Midrash then speaks about their restoration in the future. Rav Tzadok goes further: he interprets Adam’s death as completion of a decreed punishment and the return of his luminosity after death, applying the legal formula “ונקלה אחיך לעיניך” as explained by R. Hananya ben Gamliel in Makkos 23a, “כשלקה הרי הוא כאחיך” (“Once he has been flogged, he is your brother”). Makkos concerns an appropriately administered court penalty and is not a universal rule that every spiritual blemish disappears merely because someone died. The after-death restoration is Rav Tzadok’s particular metaphysical reasoning.

paragraphs.text: Rav Tzadok expressly writes in Yisrael Kedoshim 10:11, “שצורתו חקוקה בכסא הכבוד ... שמשם מחצב כל הנפשות דישראל מצורת אדם שעל הכסא” — “Yaakov's form is engraved upon the Throne of Glory ... whence the souls of Israel are hewn from the human form upon the Throne” (compare Bereshis Rabbah 68:12 and Yechezkel 1:26). Bava Basra 58a distinguishes Yaakov's “דמות דיוקני” from Adam's “דיוקני עצמה”; Sanhedrin 37a teaches that humanity is stamped with Adam's image while each individual remains distinct. Rav Tzadok uses these ideas to explain the physical radiance of R. Yochanan as an expression of spiritual purity. The Bavli itself does not teach that outward beauty proves freedom from craving. Sources: Yisrael Kedoshim 10:11; Bava Batra 58a; Sanhedrin 37a.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: R’ Yochanan’s “beauty” — teacher of Reish Lakish and of R’ Abbahu (whose beauty was “a semblance of Yaakov Avinu’s,” which is the supernal “form of Adam”) — is the ultimate beauty of the human form after Adam’s sin. “A semblance of Adam’s beauty” means Adam before the sin, whose facial radiance was then taken. Yaakov rectified his portion fully (“he did not die”), yet in this world only a semblance remained — as Shabbos is “a semblance of Olam Haba” (one-sixtieth: the faintest still-perceptible trace).

p: (לח) וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר (שָׁם בב״מ) ״לְמִחְזֵי שֻׁפְרֵיהּ דְּר׳ יוֹחָנָן״ בְּ״כָסָא דְּכַסְפָּא״ — יָדוּעַ דְּ״כֶסֶף״ רוֹמֵז לְתַאֲוָה, לְשׁוֹן ״כִּיסּוּפִין״, וְהוּא נֶגֶד הַחֶסֶד לְאַבְרָהָם
(38) This explains the comparison in Bava Metzia: to glimpse R. Yochanan’s beauty, take a “silver goblet.” Silver, kesef, alludes to yearning, kisufin, and corresponds to Avraham’s quality of Chesed.
וּ"מִבֵּי סַלְקֵי" עַיֵּן שָׁם בְּרַשְׁי הַפֵּרוּשׁ,
“From the house of the silversmith”—see Rashi there for the expression “bei salkei.”
וּפָשׁוּט דְּמִבֵּית הָאוּמָּן שֶׁעַדַיִן לֹא נִשְׁתַּמַּשׁ בּוֹ, וּבִהְיוֹתוֹ חָדָשׁ הוּא בְּתַכְלִית זִיווֹ וְזָהֲרוּרִיתוֹ.
Plainly, it should be a vessel brought straight from its maker, not yet used; being new, its luster and brilliance are at their height.

אֲבָל אוֹתוֹ זַהֲרוּרִית לְבָנָה, וְעִיקַּר הַיֹּפִי בְּתָקְפּוֹ, הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַכָּאַת זִיו הָאֹדֶם בּוֹ — הַיְינוּ מִדָּתוֹ שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה שֶׁמְּמוּזָּג הַגְּבוּרוֹת בַּחֲסָדִים, וְאֵין מָקוֹם לִפְסֹלֶת דְּתַאֲווֹת רָעוֹת לְהִתְפַּשֵּׁט

But the silvery-white radiance reaches the height of its beauty when the red glow strikes it: this represents Yaakov’s quality, in which Gevuros are blended with Chasadim, so that the dross of wrongful cravings can no longer spread.

(כְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע״ה שֶׁיָּצָא מִמֶּנּוּ פְּסֹלֶת דְּיִשְׁמָעֵאל; וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאַחַר שֶׁיָּצָא נִתְבָּרֵר גַּם הוּא וְנִשְׁאַר נָקִי, דְּיִשְׁמָעֵאל אֵין נִקְרָא עוֹד זַרְעוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא בִּנְדָרִים לא)

By contrast, Yishmael emerged from Avraham as dross. Nevertheless, after that dross had separated, Avraham too was clarified and remained pure, since in the specific sense discussed in Nedarim 31a, Yishmael is no longer termed his “seed.”

וְזֶהוּ ״פַּרְצִידֵי דְּרוּמָּנָא סוּמָּקֵי״ — רִימּוֹן רוֹמֵז לְמִילֵּי דְּתוֹרָה וּמִצְוֹת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּבְרָכוֹת נז.); וְכֵן ״כְּלִילָא דְּוַרְדָּא סוּמָּקָא״ — הַ״כֶּתֶר״ הוּא הָרֹאשׁ וְהַשֹּׁרֶשׁ שֶׁבִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, הַנִּמְשָׁל בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים לְשׁוֹשַׁנָּה

Thus the “red pomegranate seeds” signify matters of Torah and mitzvos, as the Sages say in Berachos 57a. Likewise, the “wreath of red roses” points to the crown, the head and root of Knesses Yisrael, which is compared in Shir HaShirim to a rose.

וְכָל הַמִּילּוּי שֶׁבִּפְנִים, שֶׁזֶּהוּ אוֹר פְּנִימִי, וְכָל הַהַמְשָׁכָה עַד הַכֶּתֶר, הָיָה אֶצְלוֹ מִצַּד הַגְּבוּרוֹת וְהָאֹדֶם, רַק הָאוֹר מַקִּיף הוּא דְּכֶסֶף; וּמִצַּד זֶה הָיָה אֶצְלוֹ תֹּקֶף הַיֹּפִי בְּהַגְדָּרַת (הַ)תַּאֲווֹת

All the filling within—that is, the inner light—and all the emanation up to the crown were, in R. Yochanan, from the Gevuros and the red. Only the surrounding light was represented by silver. In this way his beauty manifested the strength with which he restrained physical desire.
וּלְפִי שֶׁרָצָה לְסַפֵּר אַחַר כָּךְ דָּבָר שֶׁגָּרַם מוֹתוֹ, מַזְכִּיר מִקּוֹדֶם שִׁבְחוֹ, ״דְּבַאֲשֶׁר מִשְׁפָּטוֹ שָׁם פָּעֳלוֹ״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּיבָמוֹת עח סע״ב)

Because the Gemara will next recount the event that brought about R. Yochanan’s death, it first speaks in his praise. As the Sages say in Yevamos 78b, “Where his judgment occurs, his meritorious deeds are mentioned.”

וּבְכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁנִּזְכַּר בַּכָּתוּב, וְכֵן בַּתַּלְמוּד, מִיתָה מִפְּנֵי אֵיזֶה דָּבָר — לֹא הָיָה בּוֹ שׁוּם דָּבָר וְחֵטְא אַחֵר זוּלַת זֶה, רַק זֶה לְבַדּוֹ נִשְׁאַר בּוֹ מֵ״עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ״ שֶׁבַּעֲבוּרוֹ הוּכְרַח לָמוּת, ״דְּאֵין מִיתָה בְּלֹא חֵטְא״

Whenever Scripture or the Talmud mentions that someone died on account of a particular event, Rav Tzadok understands this to mean that no other sin remained in that person: only this final trace of “the serpent’s counsel” made death necessary. He relates this to the saying “There is no death without sin.”

וְאָמְרוּ (בתנדב״א) ״אִם יֹאמַר לְךָ אָדָם אִלּוּ לֹא חָטָא (אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן)״ כו׳ — הֲרֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ שֶׁלֹּא חָטָא וְחַי לְעוֹלָם, וְהוּא ״מַלְאַךְ הַבְּרִית״; וּ״פִנְחָס זֶה אֵלִיָּהוּ״ שֶׁכָּל קִנְאָתוֹ הָיְתָה רַק ״קִנְאַת ה׳ צְבָאוֹת״ וְ״רוּגְזָא דְּרַבָּנָן״

The Sages taught: “If someone tells you that, had Adam not sinned, he would have lived forever,” point to Eliyahu, who did not sin and remains alive. He is the “messenger of the covenant,” and “Pinchas is Eliyahu”; all his zeal was for Hashem alone—the pure ardor of the Sages.
וְהֵם זָכוּ לִקְדֻשַּׁת הַבְּרִית דֻּגְמַת אֵלִיָּהוּ, וְהַחִסָּרוֹן מֵ״עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ״ שֶׁלָּהֶם הָיָה מִפְּסֹלֶת הַגְּבוּרוֹת
These Sages attained holiness of the covenant resembling that of Eliyahu. Their remaining trace of the serpent’s counsel, however, was associated with the dross of the Gevuros.
וְלִפְי שֶׁהוּא דָּבָר קָטָן מְאֹד נִכְתַּב סוֹרְחָנוֹ, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶּׁאִיתָא בְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם "מָשָׁל לְשְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים" וְכוּלֵּי.
Precisely because their failing was so slight, the text records it explicitly, as in the account of Moshe our teacher and the parable of two women.
וּבְחֵטְא שֶׁל תַאֲוָה יֵשׁ בּוּשָׁה, וְעַל כֵּן דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר "אַל יִכָּתֵּב" שֶׁהוּא חֵטְא שֶׁבָּבָשָׂר שֶׁבּוֹ הַבּוּשָׁה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסוֹטָה ה סוֹף עַמּוּד א).

A sin rooted in desire, on the other hand, entails shame. Thus King David said, “Let my fault not be written,” for such a sin concerns the flesh, which is associated with shame, as the Sages say at the end of Sotah 5a.
דְּעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר "וְאֶתְנָה בְּרִיתִי בְּבִשְׂרֲכֶם" לְקִדֻשַּׁת הַבָּשָׂר גַּם כֵּן כְּקוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן, דְּלֹא יִתְבֻּשׁוּ מִהַבָּשָׂר הָעָרוּם,

It is for this reason that the Torah says, “My covenant shall be in your flesh,” pointing toward the sanctity of the body itself as it was before Adam’s sin, when the naked human body did not evoke shame.
דְּהוּא נוֹלַד מָהוּל, רַק אַחַר הַחֵטְא מָשַׁךְ עָרְלָתוֹ וְעָבַר בְּרִית בָּשָׂר כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין לח עַמּוּד ב), וְאָז הוּצְרַךְ לִלְבּוֹשׁ הַמְכַסֶּה הַבּוּשָׁה שֶׁבָּבָשָׂר.

Adam, the Sages teach, was created circumcised; only after his sin did he draw forward his foreskin, thereby violating the covenant of the flesh (Sanhedrin 38b). Only then did he need garments to cover the shame of the body.
וּבְחֵטְא דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל בְּזְנוּת נֶאֱמַר "בְּשַּגָּם הוּא בָשָׂר", הַיְנוּ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ זֶה בְּתוֹלָדָה.

Concerning the generation of the Flood and its sexual wrongdoing, the verse says, “Inasmuch as he too is flesh” (Genesis 6:3), indicating in Rav Tzadok’s interpretation that such susceptibility can exist from birth.

וְאָמְרוּ (חוּלִין קלט עַמּוּד ב) דְּ"בְּשַּגָּם" זֶה מֹשֶׁה, הַיְנוּ דְּהוּא הַמְתַקֵּן זֶה דְּאַעַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא בָשָׂר הָיָה יָכוּל לַעֲלוֹת לָמָרוֹם מָקוֹם שֶׁאֵין שַׁיָּכוּת לַתַּאֲוֹת כְּלָל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת פט רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א) "יֵצֶר הָרָע יֵשׁ בֵּינֵיכֶם".

The Sages say in Chullin 139b that the word “beshaggam” alludes to Moshe: he is the one who rectified this condition, so that although made of flesh, he could ascend to the heavenly realm, where physical cravings have no place. As he asked the angels, “Is there an evil inclination among you?” (Shabbos 89a).
וְהֵם אָמְרוּ עַל מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם (שָׁם פח:) "מַה לִילוּד אִשָּׁה" וְלֹא אָמְרוּ "מַה לְבָשָׂר וָדָם",
The angels had initially asked about Moshe (Shabbos 88b), “What is one born of a woman doing among us?” They did not formulate that opening question as “What is flesh and blood doing here?”
אֲבָל הוּא כְּבָר נִזְדַּכְדֵּךְ בְּשָׂרוֹ וְדָמוֹ עַד שֶׁהָיָה כְּמַלְאֲכֵי מָרוֹם וְלֹא יָכְלוּ לְזַלְזְלוֹ בְּזֶה רַק בְּמַה שֶּׁמִתּוֹלָדְתוֹ הוּא יְלוּד אִשָּׁה.

For Moshe had already purified his flesh and blood until it resembled the angels above. In Rav Tzadok’s explanation, they could not disparage his present physical condition; their challenge instead concerned the fact that he was born of a woman.
וְהַשִּׁי״ת מָצָא עֲלִילָה בּוֹ רַק בְּעִנְיָן הַכַּעַס, וְאַעַל פִּי שֶׁוַדַּאי גַּם זֶה הָיָה רַק קִנְאַת ה׳ צְבָאוֹת וְרוֹגְזָא דְּרַבָּנַן, לֹא נִתְבָּרֵר עַדַיִן.

Hashem thus found grounds for judgment against him only in the matter of anger. Rav Tzadok maintains that even this anger arose solely from zeal for Hashem—the Sages’ holy ardor—but that it had not yet been fully clarified.
וּבְזֶה אֵין בּוּשָׁה, כִּי כְּאִישׁ גְּבוּרָתוֹ, וּבְרוֹב חָכְמָה רוֹב כַּעַס דְּאוֹרַיְתָא דְּמִרְתַּחָא לֵיהּ, דְּהִנֵּה "כֹּה דְּבָרִי כָּאֵשׁ" וְהוּא הַגְּבוּרוֹת דְּקְדֻשָּׁה.

In such anger there is no inherent shame, for “as a man is, so is his strength,” and “with much wisdom comes much anger.” Torah arouses such intensity, as in the verse “Is not My word like fire?”—the Gevuros of holiness.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 57a discusses dreaming of split pomegranates: “אם תלמיד חכם הוא — יצפה לתורה ... ואם עם הארץ הוא — יצפה למצות” — “If one is learned, anticipate Torah; if unlearned, anticipate mitzvos”; and “אפילו ריקנין שבך מלאים מצות כרמון” — “Even the emptiest among you are full of mitzvos like a pomegranate.” The dream interpretation and the image of seeds provide Rav Tzadok’s textual basis for reading the pomegranate as Torah and mitzvos. The Gemara does NOT discuss red pomegranate seeds in R. Yochanan’s goblet here; that visual image is in Bava Metzia 84a.

paragraphs.text: The opening of Zohar, Introduction 1:1, asks “מאן שושנה? דא כנסת ישראל” — “Who is the rose? It is Knesses Yisrael,” and compares the rose’s red and white with “דין ורחמי” — “judgment and mercy”; its thirteen petals are likened to thirteen attributes of mercy. Rav Tzadok’s Pri Tzaddik, Shushan Purim §1, repeats that the shoshana represents Knesses Yisrael and its thirteen mercies. These passages verify the symbolic rose; Rav Tzadok alone applies the wreath of red roses of Bava Metzia 84a to the Keser, head, and root of Knesses Yisrael here. paragraphs.text: In Bava Metzia 84a, R. Yochanan compares his beauty to an artisan's polished silver goblet containing red pomegranate seeds and ringed by red roses, set between sunlight and shade. Rav Tzadok reads the red interior and rose crown as Gevurah and inner light (or penimi), while silver represents enveloping light (or makif), from Chesed. His own Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh 12 says “כסף מרמז לאהבה מדת חסד לאברהם” — “Silver alludes to love, Avraham's attribute of Chesed.” Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash 7 says “דהשמלות הם בחי׳ אור מקיף בסוד עוטה אור כשלמה” — “Garments signify surrounding light, in the mystery of 'He clothes Himself in light as a garment'.” Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 5 independently distinguishes “והמזון היא בחינת אור פנימי, והלבושים בחינת מקיפים” — “Nourishment is inner light, garments are encompassing lights.” These sources illuminate Rav Tzadok's conceptual application; the Gemara itself describes the imagery but does not assign sefirot to its colors or vessels. Nedarim 31a separately derives the particular halachic use of Avraham's 'seed' from “כי ביצחק יקרא לך זרע.” Sources: Bava Metzia 84a; Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh 12; Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash 7; Tanya, Likkutei Amarim 5; Nedarim 31a.

paragraphs.text: Yevamos 78b, when describing Divine judgment concerning Shaul, cites “באשר משפטו — שם פעלו” — “Where a person's judgment is discussed, the person's merits are also mentioned”; Rashi explains “במקום שדנים האדם שם מזכירין פועל צדקותיו.” Rav Tzadok applies this to the placement of praise of R. Yochanan's beauty before the narrative of his final suffering, then goes further and proposes that whenever Scripture or the Gemara names a specific cause of death it represents a remaining defect. A qualification is indispensable: R. Ami says “אין מיתה בלא חטא” in Shabbos 55a, but Shabbos 55b cites the four who died “בעטיו של נחש” without personal transgression and concludes “תיובתא דרב אמי, תיובתא.” Therefore the blanket principle is NOT the Bavli's final rule. The account of merits at judgment, the aggadic refutation, and Rav Tzadok's metaphysical reading must remain distinct. Sources: Yevamot 78b; Rashi ad loc.; Shabbat 55a–b; Bava Batra 17a.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 27:4 asks whether Adam could have lived perpetually had he not sinned and answers by pointing to Eliyahu, “כבר היה אליהו שלא חטא, הוא חי וקים לעולם” — “Eliyahu, who did not sin, is already alive and enduring.” Pesikta de-Rav Kahana 9:4 also preserves the teaching, but in its Oxford-manuscript recension it is phrased as a rhetorical question: “אליהו זכור לטוב שלא חטא אינו חי וקיים עד עכשיו” — “Is not Eliyahu, of blessed memory, who did not sin, alive and enduring to this day?” These two witnesses must not be presented as identical verbal quotations. The Hebrew here cites Tanna d'Vei Eliyahu; an exact parallel at that location has not been independently established, so the verified early witnesses are cited instead without silently changing Rav Tzadok's Hebrew. Yalkut Shimoni on the Torah §771 connects “פינחס הוא אליהו”; Malachi 3:1 speaks of the “מלאך הברית” and 3:23–24 of Eliyahu's return. Rav Tzadok's own Tzidkas HaTzadik §218 interprets Eliyahu's freedom from sin specifically in terms of purifying bodily desire and applying holy Gevurah. That spiritual analysis is Rav Tzadok's, not an exact Midrash quote. Sources: Vayikra Rabbah 27:4; Pesikta de-Rav Kahana 9:4; Yalkut Shimoni on Torah 771; Malachi 3:1, 3:23–24; Tzidkat HaTzadik 218.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: “To see R’ Yochanan’s beauty in a silver goblet”: silver (kesef, “yearning”) alludes to desire, over against Avraham’s Chesed; “fresh from the smith” means new, at its full luster. But that white radiance reaches its peak of beauty only when the red glow of the pomegranate seeds strikes it. Yaakov’s middah, in which Gevuros are blended with Chasadim, leaving no room for the “dross” of evil desire to spread (unlike Avraham, from whom the dross of Yishmael issued and was then purged).

p: (לט) וְזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן בַּר׳ יוֹחָנָן וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ, שֶׁנִּכְתַּב בַּתַּלְמוּד סִיבַּת מִיתָתָם עַל יָדוֹ — אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁתְּחִלָּה לֹא נִתְכַּוֵּון לְבַזּוֹתוֹ וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא דִּיבֵּר בְּלָשׁוֹן נְקִיָּה כָּל כָּךְ

(39) The same applies to R. Yochanan and Reish Lakish: the Talmud records how their deaths came about through R. Yochanan. Although he did not initially intend to humiliate Reish Lakish, as I explained, he nevertheless did not speak with sufficient refinement.

וְזֶה דְּשָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ כְּשֶׁהֵשִׁיב רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ ״מַאי אַהֲנֵית״ כו׳ — דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ דְּלֹא עַל יְדֵי מַה שֶּׁהֶחֱזִירוֹ בִּתְשׁוּבָה הוּא שֶׁתִּיקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם (דְּבָזֶה עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ גְּנַאי, כֹּל שֶׁלֹּא נִתְקַן לְגַמְרֵי, כֵּיוָן דְּבִשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה הָיָה חֵטְא, וְשֶׁהוּא הֶהֱנָהוּ שֶׁהֱבִיאוֹ לְכָךְ)

That is why, when Reish Lakish later responded, “What did you benefit me?” and so forth, he meant that his earlier life was not rectified merely because R. Yochanan had brought him back through repentance. Were that the whole explanation, an element of disgrace would remain as long as the earlier acts were not fully rectified: they would have been sinful at the time, and R. Yochanan would then have benefited him by bringing about his repentance.

אֲבָל בַּתְּחִלָּה וּבִשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה גַּם כֵּן הָיְתָה כַּוָּונָתוֹ לַשָּׁמַיִם בֶּאֱמֶת, וְ״רַבִּי קָרוּ לֵיהּ״, וְאֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק בּוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁבְּכֹחוֹ וְעַל יָדוֹ הוּא שֶׁשָּׁב, כִּי הוּא לֹא הוֹסִיף לוֹ כְּלוּם

Rather, his intention had been genuinely for the sake of Heaven even at the outset and during those very actions; already then they called him “Rabbi.” R. Yochanan therefore could not claim that Reish Lakish returned solely through his own power, for he had added nothing to that original inward intention.
הוֹסִיף ר׳ יוֹחָנָן לְזַלְזְלוֹ בְּפֵירוּשׁ וְאָמַר ״אַהֲנֵית״ כו׳, הַיְינוּ דְּהַשְׁתָּא דְּרוֹאֶה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ בּוּשָׁה מִזֶּה, עַל כָּרְחֲךָ לֹא תִּיקֵּן לְגַמְרֵי

R. Yochanan then went further and provoked him openly, saying, “I benefited you,” and so forth: now that he saw that Reish Lakish felt shame about his past, he reasoned that the past could not yet have been fully rectified.

וְהוּא יָדַע עוֹצֶם הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ בַּתּוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה, דְּהָיָה רָאוּי שֶׁיְּתוּקַּן לְגַמְרֵי, דְּעַל כֵּן לֹא עָלָה בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אוֹנָאַת דְּבָרִים וּבוּשָׁה לוֹ בַּאֲמִירַת ״לִיסְטָאָה״; וּכְשֶׁרָאָה דְּאֵינוֹ כֵן, חָשַׁב דְּוַדַּאי יֵשׁ בּוֹ חִסָּרוֹן בָּזֶה מִתּוֹלָדָה שֶׁאֵין יָכוֹל לְתַקְּנוֹ

He knew how intensely Reish Lakish had subsequently labored in Torah and avodah, enough that complete rectification seemed fitting. Therefore it had never occurred to him that calling him “bandit” might constitute verbal wronging or cause shame. When he saw that it did, he supposed there must be some inborn deficiency that Reish Lakish could not correct.
וְחִסָּרוֹן זֶה אֵינוֹ רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת בְּשֹׁרֶשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל, כַּיָּדוּעַ דִּמְצוֹרָע מִשְׁתַּלֵּחַ חוּץ לְמַחֲנֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל, כִּי חִסָּרוֹן זֶה אֵין רָאוּי לְיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּלָל
Such a deficiency, he thought, could not be part of Israel’s essential root. The metzora is therefore sent outside the camp of Israel, for this quality has no proper place within its spiritual root.
וְהַצָּרַעַת אֵינָהּ אֶלָּא פְּרִיחָה בְּעוֹר בָּשָׂר, וְלֹא בַּעֲצָמוֹת שֶׁהֵם עַצְמוֹת גּוּף הָאָדָם, וּמֵהֶם הוּא הָעֶצֶם הַקָּטָן שֶׁבַּשִּׁדְרָה הַקַּיָּים לָעַד

Tzaraas is a manifestation in the skin of the flesh rather than the bones, which constitute the body’s enduring structure. Among them is the small bone of the spine, the luz, described as persisting for the resurrection.
וְ״רָקָב עֲצָמוֹת קִנְאָה״, שֶׁהוּא גּוֹרֵם כִּילָּיוֹן הָעֲצָמוֹת גַּם כֵּן; וּבְאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם, שֶׁהוּא בְּשָׁרְשָׁם כֵּן, נִגְלֶה הַכֹּל וְאֵין קָמִים בִּתְחִיַּית הַמֵּתִים

But “envy is the rot of the bones” (Mishlei 14:30), meaning that envy reaches even the bones and causes their decay. Among the nations, where Rav Tzadok understands this defect as touching the root, its full effect is manifest; he accordingly speaks here of their not rising at the resurrection.

אֲבָל אֵצֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כָּל עִנְיְנֵי קִנְאָה וְכַעַס אֵין לוֹ שַׁיָּיכוּת לְעַצְמִיּוּתוֹ, רַק מִצַּד הַמַּלְבּוּשׁ דְּ״כָתְנוֹת עוֹר״ בָּשָׂר שֶׁעַל גַּבָּיו, שֶׁבּוֹ זוּהֲמַת הַנָּחָשׁ הָאַרְסִי, הַנּוֹשֵׁךְ וּמֵמִית בְּלֹא שׁוּם הֲנָאָה לְגַרְמֵיהּ, דְּכָל כַּוָּונָתוֹ לְהָרַע לְבַד מִצַּד הַקִּנְאָה שֶׁבּוֹ

For the children of Israel, however, envy and anger have no essential connection to their inner nature. They arise from the outer garment of the “coats of skin” covering the person—the serpent’s poison, which bites and kills without deriving any benefit, desiring only to harm through envy.
שֶׁמִּזֶּה הָיָה הַתְחָלַת הֲסָתָתוֹ
This envy was the starting point of the serpent’s seduction,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ
as the Sages taught
(בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין נט:)
(Sanhedrin 59b):
דְּנִתְקַנֵּא בִּכְבוֹדוֹ דְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן.
the serpent envied the honor bestowed on Adam HaRishon.
וְזֶהוּ הַזֻּהֲמָא שֶׁהִכְנִיס בְּחַוָּה,
That is the contamination it introduced into Chavah,
וְשֶׁפָּסְקָה זֻהֲמָתָן דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל בְּהַר סִינַי,
which ceased for Israel at Mount Sinai,
דְּאֵין עוֹד בְּמַחֲנֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל
so that in the camp of Israel there is no longer
זֻהֲמָא כָּזוֹ בְּעֶצֶם.
such contamination in the very essence.
וּלְפִיכָךְ אָמַר לְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
For this reason, he said to Reish Lakish,
אַהֲנָאִי
“I did you a service,”
(לָךְ דְּאַקְרִבִּינָךְ)
“in that I brought you close,”
תַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַשְּׁכִינָה,
“beneath the wings of the Shechinah.”
דְּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל
for as I wrote above
דְּהוּא מְקוֹם הַגֵּרִים,
that this expression refers to the place of converts.
שֶׁהֶחְשִׁיבוֹ כְּגֵר
He was thus treating Reish Lakish as if he were a convert,
וְכְאִלּוּ אֵינוֹ מִשֹּׁרֶשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל
as though he did not originate in Israel’s spiritual root
שֶׁאֵין יָכוֹל לְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם.
and could not completely rectify what had preceded his repentance.
כִּי גֵּר אֵין יָכוֹל לְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם
A convert, in this comparison, does not retroactively transform his earlier life
וּמַה שֶּׁהָיָה בְּגִיּוּת
when he was not yet Jewish
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כְּמִי שֶׁנּוֹלַד בַּיַּהֲדוּת.
into a life as though he had already been born Jewish.
דְּזָכָה לָזֶה רַק אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
Only Avraham our father, peace be upon him, merited this,
דְּנִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֶזְרָחִי,
who is also called “Israel” and an ezrachi, a native-born member of the people,
כְּאִלּוּ הוּא אֶזְרָח בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל,
as if he were a native in Israel;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן גֵּר אֵינוֹ אֶזְרָח
unlike an ordinary convert, who is not called a native from birth
וְהוּא רַק כְּנוֹלָד מֵעֵת שֶׁנִּתְגַּיֵּר וְלֹא מִקֹּדֶם.
but is considered newly born from the moment of conversion, not from the time before it.
וְקִנְטֵר אֶת רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
He thus taunted Reish Lakish by implying
דְּגַם הוּא כֵּן
that the same was true of him:
שֶׁאֵין יָכוֹל לְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם
that he could not fully correct the past
שֶׁלֹּא יֵבוֹשׁ מִזֶּה,
so that its memory would no longer cause him shame,
וְהוּא אַהֲנִי לֵיהּ
and that he had benefited him
בְּמַה שֶּׁהֶחְזִירוֹ בִּתְשׁוּבָה,
in that he returned him to repentance,
רַק דְּמִקְרֵי גֵּרִים.
but only became comparable to a convert.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ חָלַשׁ דַּעְתֵּיהּ מִזֶּה,
Afterward R. Yochanan himself became distressed,
כִּי כְּפִי דְּבָרָיו
for according to his words
שֶׁהוּא הֶחְזִירוֹ וְאַהֲנִי לֵיהּ,
since according to his own claim that he had restored Reish Lakish and thereby benefited him,
אִם הוּא הָיָה נָקִי לְגַמְרֵי
if he himself had been entirely purified,
הָיָה מַחְזִיר אֶת רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
he would have restored Reish Lakish
גַּם כֵּן לִהְיוֹת נָקִי לְגַמְרֵי.
to complete spiritual purity as well.
וְהִרְגִּישׁ דְּעַל כֵּן
And he sensed that therefore
גַּם בּוֹ יֵשׁ חִסָּרוֹן בָּזֶה,
there was a deficiency in himself concerning this matter,
וְהַיְנוּ בְּדָבָר זֶה עַצְמוֹ
namely in this very matter,
מַה שֶּׁקִּנְטֵר לְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ בְּמַה שֶּׁאֵינוֹ.
that he had reproached Reish Lakish over something that was not true of him.
כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
For in truth Resh Lakish
מִזֶּרַע אַבְרָהָם יִצְחָק וְיַעֲקֹב,
is of the seed of Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov,
וְגַם אָמַר אֱמֶת וַדַּאי
and he also certainly spoke the truth
מַה שֶּׁאָמַר מַה אַהֲנִית וְכוּלֵּי.
when he said, “What benefit have you given me?” etc.
אַף דְּגַם רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וַדַּאי
Although Rabbi Yochanan too certainly
הֵשִׁיבוֹ בֶּאֱמֶת אַהֲנִית וְכוּלֵּי,
answered truthfully, “I benefited,” etc.,
דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם יֵשׁ יִתְרוֹן בָּזֶה לְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
nevertheless he really did benefit Reish Lakish in another respect:
בְּמַה שֶּׁחָזַר לַעֲסֹק בַּתּוֹרָה
in that he returned to engage in Torah
וְלִקָּרֵא רַבִּי מִצַּד לִמּוּד הַתּוֹרָה,
and to be called Rabbi on account of Torah study,
דְּנִשְׁאֲרוּ מִמֶּנּוּ כַּמָּה הֲלָכְתָא גְּבוּרְתָּא
for many powerful halachic teachings from Reish Lakish were preserved
בְּתַלְמוּד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה,
through his learning and transmission of the Oral Torah.
שֶׁגַּם זֶה נִקְרָא תַּחַת כַּנְפֵי שְׁכִינָה.
which is also called under the wings of the Shechinah.
מִכָּל מָקוֹם שְׁנֵיהֶם דִּבְּרוּ בָּזֶה
Nevertheless both of them spoke in this
דֶּרֶךְ קִנְטוּר,
by way of provocation,
וְנִתְבָּרֵר עַל עִסְקֵיהֶם בִּדְבָרִים אֵלּוּ
and what happened to them over this exchange demonstrated
דִּ"סְבִיבָיו נִשְׂעֲרָה מְאֹד".
the verse, “Around Him the storm rages mightily” (Tehillim 50:3).

paragraphs.text: Clean speech and the dignity of a baal teshuvah are separate, verified standards. Pesachim 3a teaches “לעולם אל יוציא אדם דבר מגונה מפיו” — “A person should never utter a degrading expression,” and adds “לעולם יספר אדם בלשון נקיה” — “One should always speak in refined language.” Bava Metzia 58b states “אם היה בעל תשובה, לא יאמר לו: זכור מעשיך הראשונים” — “If he is a penitent, do not tell him: Remember your former deeds.” R. Tzadok does not initially accuse R. Yochanan of intending humiliation: he argues that “ליסטאה,” even spoken without that intent, was insufficiently guarded language. Later (§39, phrase 4) he explains why R. Yochanan had thought Reish Lakish beyond such embarrassment. These texts supply the standards, not a formal finding by the Gemara that this particular exchange violated the prohibition.

paragraphs.text: Tosafos, Bava Metzia 84a, s.v. “אי הדרת בך” (Sefaria's Tosafos 84a:12), infers that Reish Lakish had been learned before his association with R. Yochanan: “דר״ל מתחלה ידע הרבה אלא שפרק עול תורה ונעשה עם הארץ ועסק בלסטיות”; it explains his “מאי אהנית לי ... התם קרו לי רבי” with “מעיקרא נמי הוו קרו לי רבי אלא ששכחתי” — “At first I was also called Rabbi, but I forgot [my studies].” Tosafos explicitly disputes Rashi's explanation that “Rabbi” meant leader of bandits. Rav Tzadok goes considerably beyond Tosafos, understanding Reish Lakish's inner orientation to Hashem as pure even during that earlier period and therefore taking “what did you benefit me?” as a challenge to R. Yochanan's presumption of creating his holiness. That is Rav Tzadok's theological interpretation, NOT a statement by Tosafos: Tosafos says he had cast off the yoke of Torah. Sources: Bava Metzia 84a; Tosafos on Bava Metzia 84a, s.v. “אי הדרת בך”; Rashi ad loc.; Dover Tzedek, Likkutim 4:138.

paragraphs.text: Rav Tzadok makes this precise symbolic correspondence in Peri Tzadik, Nasso 1:3: “שמצורע משתלח חוץ לג׳ מחנות שזה כנגד הקנאה והכעס שאין לו חלק כלל בישראל” — “The metzora is sent outside all three camps, corresponding to jealousy and anger, which have no essential share in Israel.” Compare Bamidbar 5:2 for the actual camp law. In Tzidkas HaTzadik §233, Rav Tzadok calls envy a root of the serpent and describes its concealment as an exterior garment, not the soul’s original identity. These are Rav Tzadok’s ethical/metaphysical interpretations of the Torah’s law, not the Torah’s own express proof that Jews cannot experience jealousy. They do not excuse real misconduct. Sources: Peri Tzadik, Nasso 1:3 (original Hebrew); Tzidkat HaTzadik 233; Numbers 5:2.

paragraphs.text: Bereshis Rabbah 28:3 describes “לוז של שדרה, שממנו הקדוש ברוך הוא מציץ את האדם לעתיד לבוא” — “the luz of the spine, from which the Holy One causes the person to sprout at the resurrection.” In its exchange with Hadrian, R. Yehoshua ben Chananyah describes the luz’s extraordinary endurance under grinding, fire, water, and striking. However, the SAME Midrash’s Flood exposition explicitly says “אפלו לוז של שדרה ... נמחה” — “even the luz of the spine was erased.” Zohar, Toldos 6:50 calls it “ההוא גרמא דשדרה ... דאשתאר בקברא” — “that bone of the spine ... which remains in the grave.” Thus the sources do NOT claim unconditional physical indestructibility. Rav Tzadok uses ordinary postmortem endurance symbolically to distinguish the enduring spiritual root from external skin affliction; the latter application is his interpretation. Sources: Bereshit Rabbah 28:3; Zohar, Toldot 6:50; Leviticus 13:2.

paragraphs.text: Mishlei 14:30 states “חיי בשרים לב מרפא ורקב עצמות קנאה” — “A tranquil/healing heart gives life to the flesh, but envy is rot in the bones.” Shabbos 152b makes it literal within an aggadic account: “כל מי שיש לו קנאה בלבו עצמותיו מרקיבים; כל שאין לו קנאה בלבו אין עצמותיו מרקיבים” — “One who harbors envy has bones that decay; one without it has bones that do not decay.” The passage concerns a righteous person whose body was found intact in the grave. Rav Tzadok reads the bones as the more enduring spiritual root and then contrasts Israel with the nations. That last categorical eschatological contrast is his theological construction, not a direct universal ruling of this Gemara or the Mishlei verse. Do not turn the text into a factual declaration about the fate of individual people.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis 3:21 calls Adam’s coverings “כתנות עור” — “garments of skin.” In Peri Tzadik, Nitzavim §14, Rav Tzadok expressly contrasts “כתנות אור בא׳ ... כתנות עור” — “garments of light, spelled with aleph ... [later] garments of skin,” treating the body as a garment of the soul. Shabbos 146a says “ישראל שעמדו על הר סיני פסקה זוהמתן” — “Israel’s contamination ceased when they stood at Sinai,” and specifically clarifies that although converts were not physically at Sinai, “מזלייהו הוו” — “their spiritual root was present.” Sanhedrin 59b reports that the serpent saw Adam’s honor and envied it; Zohar Toldos 19:142 says “נחש נושך וממית ולית ליה הנאה מניה” — “the serpent bites and kills yet derives no pleasure.” Together they supply the individual images. Rav Tzadok’s claim that envy is extrinsic to Israel’s inner root rather than an immutable trait is his synthesis; the sources must not be paraphrased as excluding converts.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: So too with R’ Yochanan and Reish Lakish, whose cause of death was recorded through R’ Yochanan’s not speaking “in fully clean language.” Reish Lakish’s “what benefit?” meant: it was not R’ Yochanan’s returning him in teshuvah that rectified the past (for that would leave disgrace, the act having been a sin). Rather, at the very time of the act his intent was for Heaven, and “Rebbi they called him,” so R’ Yochanan “added nothing.”

p: (מ) וְגוּף הַלִּסְטִיּוּת דְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ לֹא נִזְכַּר כְּלָל בַּתַּלְמוּד בְּסִיפּוּר בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ, שֶׁזֶּה כְּבָר נִמְחַק לְגַמְרֵי, כִּי לֹא הָיָה חֵטְא כְּלָל

(40) Reish Lakish’s alleged banditry is never recounted in the Talmud as an independent episode. In Rav Tzadok’s understanding, it had already been entirely erased as sin because its true inward purpose had not been sinful at all.

וְנִרְאֶה לִי דְּגַם הָעוּבְדָּא דִּ״זְבַן נַפְשֵׁיהּ לְלוּדָאֵי״ (בְּגִיטִּין מז.) אֵינוֹ מִכְּלַל הַדָּבָר שֶׁעָשָׂה שֶׁלֹּא כַּהוֹגֶן, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ הַתּוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם דְּהָיָה קוֹדֶם שֶׁחָזַר לְמוּטָב, דְּלֹא הָיָה מְזַלְזֵל בְּנַפְשֵׁיהּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם

It seems to me that even the story “he sold himself to the Ludaei” (Gittin 47a) should not be counted among deeds he performed improperly. Tosafos there places it before he had returned to the right path, reasoning that afterward he would not have so demeaned himself; see there.
וּבֶאֱמֶת לֹא זִלְזוּל לְבַד הוּא, אֶלָּא גַּם אִיסּוּר ״מְאַבֵּד עַצְמוֹ לְדַעַת״, כִּי לֹא יָדַע תְּחִלָּה שֶׁיִּתְרַצּוּ בְּהַהַכָּאוֹת וְשֶׁיִּנָּצֵל מִיָּדָם

In truth, the concern is far more than self-disparagement: it approaches the prohibition of deliberately destroying one’s own life, since he did not know in advance that his captors would agree to the proposed blows or that he would escape them.

וְאִם כְּפִי דִּבְרֵי תּוֹסָפוֹת שֶׁלֹּא חָזַר לְמוּטָב, דְּמַשְׁמַע דְּבֶאֱמֶת עָשָׂה שֶׁלֹּא כַּהוֹגֶן — לָמָּה לָהֶם לרז״ל לְהַזְכִּיר גְּנוּתוֹ, וּלְאֵיזֶה צֹרֶךְ הִזְכִּירוּ כְּלָל סִיפּוּר הַהוּא, שֶׁכְּפִי הַנִּרְאֶה פְּשָׁטֵיהּ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא סִיפּוּר דְּבָרִים בְּעָלְמָא, לְסַפֵּר (אַחַר) מִיטָּתָן שֶׁל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים וּלְדַבֵּר בִּגְנוּת דְּצַדִּיקִים

If, according to Tosafos, this happened before he had returned to the right path—apparently implying that he had truly acted improperly—why would our Sages record it to his discredit? What purpose could there be in repeating an otherwise incidental story that would speak ill of a Torah scholar after his death and disgrace a righteous man?

אֲבָל הַפָּשׁוּט בְּעֵינַי דְּהוּא עָשָׂה זֶה בְּכַוָּונָה גְּדוֹלָה לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, דְּאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁבְּכָל לִסְטִיּוּתוֹ הָיָה רַק מְכַלֶּה קוֹצִים וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הָיָה יָרֵא לְנַפְשׁוֹ

The straightforward explanation in my view is that he acted with a great intention for the sake of Heaven. Even if his earlier banditry had, as I argued, been only a removal of thorns, he nevertheless feared for his own spiritual standing.

שֶׁהֲרֵי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע״ה שֶׁהָרַג אוּכְלוּסֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם הָיָה מִתְפַּחֵד, עַד שֶׁהִבְטִיחוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ ״אַל תִּירָא״ דְּכוּלָּם ״קוֹצִים כְּסוּחִים״, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בברא״ר מד)

For even Avraham our father, peace be upon him, feared that among the great multitudes he had killed there might have been a worthy person, until Hashem reassured him, “Do not fear”: they were “thorns already cut down,” as Bereishis Rabbah 44 explains.
וְכֵן בַּר׳ אֶלְעָזָר בַּר׳ שִׁמְעוֹן (בב״מ שָׁם פג:) אַף אַחַר שֶׁאָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ ״וּמַה סְפֵקוֹת שֶׁלָּכֶם״ כו׳, אֲפִילּוּ הָכֵי לָא מְיַתְּבָא דַּעְתּוֹ וְחוֹזֵר לְנַסּוֹת וּלְבָרֵר

Likewise, R. Elazar bar R. Shimon (Bava Metzia 83b), even after saying, “If even your doubtful cases were like this, how much more your certain cases,” was still not at ease and continued to examine his actions.
וְגַם אַחַר כָּךְ
And also afterward,
אַחַר שֶׁקָּרָא עַל עַצְמוֹ
after he applied to himself
אַף בְּשָׂרִי יִשְׁכֹּן לָבֶטַח
“Even my flesh shall dwell securely,”
חָזַר לְהִסְתַּפֵּק בְּנַפְשֵׁיהּ
he again had doubts about himself,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ
as they said
(שָׁם פד רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב)
there, 84b
וַאֲפִילוּ הָכִי לֹא סָמַךְ אַדַּעְתֵּיהּ
“Even so, he did not rely upon his own judgment,”
וְקִבֵּל עָלָיו יִסּוּרִים.
“and he accepted sufferings upon himself.”
וְגַם רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ לֹא סָמַךְ אַדַּעְתֵּיהּ.
Reish Lakish, too, did not confidently rely upon his own judgment.

וּמָצִינוּ דְּמוּתָּר גַּם לְאַבֵּד נַפְשׁוֹ לִתְשׁוּבָה, וְלָא מִיבַּעְיָא לַעֲבֵירוֹת חֲמוּרוֹת בְּמֵזִיד שֶׁחַיָּיב עֲלֵיהֶם מִיתָה בְּבֵית דִּין, כְּיוֹיָקִים אִישׁ צְרוֹרוֹת (בברא״ר ס״פ סה, שֶׁחָזַר בִּתְשׁוּבָה וְקִיֵּים בְּעַצְמוֹ אַרְבַּע מִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין), אֶלָּא גַּם בַּעֲבֵירוֹת קַלּוֹת כְּהַהוּא כּוֹבֵס (בִּכְתוּבּוֹת קג:)

We also find exceptional accounts of deliberately surrendering one’s life in the course of repentance—not only over grave willful offenses punishable by a court, as with Yekum Ish Tzerorot (Bereishis Rabbah, end of chapter 65), who repented and subjected himself to the four forms of court death, but even for seemingly lesser offenses, as in the story of the laundryman (Kesubos 103b).
וְאַף לְפִי דִּבְרֵי מוֹרֵנוּ הָרַב יוֹסֵף מִטְרָאנִי בַּחִדּוּשָׁיו שָׁם
Even according to R. Yosef of Trani, the Maharit, in his commentary there,
דְּעָשָׂה מִשּׁוּם חִלּוּל שַׁבָּת דִּבְסְקִילָה,
who explained that the laundryman acted because of an inadvertent desecration of Shabbos, which ordinarily carries the court penalty of stoning,
הֲרֵי הָיָה שׁוֹגֵג בָּזֶה
his offense had been inadvertent,
כֵּיוָן דְּרָאָה חַמָּה זוֹרַחַת.
because he had seen the sun still shining.
וּבְסֵפֶר מִצְוֹת קָטָן (סִימָן ג׳)
And Sefer Mitzvot Katan, mitzvah 3,
מֵבִיא מֵרַבִּי יְהוּדָה חָסִיד
relates in the name of Rabbi Yehudah HeChasid
שֶׁצִּוָּה לְתַלְמִידָיו
that he instructed his disciples,
עַל שֶׁנִּשְׁתַּמְּשׁוּ בַּשֵּׁם
after they had invoked the Divine Name
לְהִנָּצֵל מִלִּסְטִים
to escape highway bandits,
לַחֲזוֹר לֵילֵךְ בְּלֹא שֵׁם
to travel that route again without invoking the Name,
וְלִמְסוֹר נַפְשָׁם, נֶהֶרְגוּ,
and to expose themselves to death; they were killed.
עַיֵּן שָׁם.
see there.
וְאִם כֵּן יֵשׁ לוֹמַר
And if so, it can be said
דְּגַם רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ עָשָׂה כֵּן,
that Reish Lakish likewise acted for this purpose,
וּבִפְרָט בַּעֲוֹן רְצִיחָה.
especially in relation to the possibility that his earlier acts amounted to murder.
דְּדִין בֵּית דִּין דְּדָמוֹ יִשָּׁפֵךְ,
The punishment imposed by a duly constituted court for deliberate murder is that the murderer’s blood be shed.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלְּדַעְתּוֹ עָשָׂה מִצְוָה
Although he himself thought he had performed a mitzvah,
לֹא בָּטַח בְּלִבּוֹ עַל זֶה.
he was unwilling to rely upon his own heart as proof.
וּבְלָאו הָכִי נַמִּי
And even without this,
מֵאַחַר דְּלֹא נִדּוֹנוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין
because those people had not been judged by the Sanhedrin
לְחַיְּבָם מִיתָה
and sentenced to death,
הֲרֵי הֲרָגָם שֶׁלֹּא כְדִין,
putting them to death would have been contrary to the ordinary judicial procedure;
דַּאֲפִילוּ דִּין,
for even a lawful judgment,
מִשֶּׁבָּטְלוּ סַנְהֶדְרִין
after the Sanhedrin ceased functioning in that capacity,
אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהָרְגָם.
those court executions could no longer be carried out.
וְאַף דְּכוּלָּם קוֹצִים
And even though they are all thorns,
הָוֵי כְּכָל עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ,
it would belong to the category of a transgression claimed to be for the sake of Heaven:
דְּאַף דְּמִצְוָה עָבֵיד
for even though he performs a mitzvah,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ כַּפָּרָה
according to this reasoning it would nevertheless require atonement,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל.
as I wrote above.
וְלֹא רָצָה לֵילֵךְ לִמְקוֹם גְּדוּדֵי חַיּוֹת וְלִסְטִים,
He did not choose to seek out bands of wild beasts or robbers,
דְּהוּא הָיָה גִּבּוֹר בְּיוֹתֵר
for he was exceedingly mighty,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר חֵילָךְ לְאוֹרַיְיתָא,
as it was said, “Your strength be for the Torah,”
וְיָדַע דְּיוּכַל לְהַצִּיל עַצְמוֹ מֵהֶם
and he knew that he could save himself from them
אִם יִרְצֶה,
if he wished,
וְשֶׁלֹּא יַעֲמֹד נֶגְדָּם
and that if he did not stand against them
הָוֵי כִּמְאַבֵּד עַצְמוֹ מִדַּעַת
to refrain from defending himself would have been tantamount, in his view, to deliberately bringing about his own death,
וְזֶה גַּם כֵּן לֹא רָצָה,
and this too he did not want,
כִּי הֲרֵי בֶּאֱמֶת מִצְוָה עָבֵיד
for truly he is performing a mitzvah
וְאֵין חַיָּב כְּלוּם עַל זֶה.
and is not liable for anything for it.
וְלָנִסָּיוֹן וּבֵרוּר בְּעָלְמָא
Instead, simply as a test and clarification,
וְגַם לְכַפָּרָה
and also for atonement
עַל יְדֵי הַמְּסִירַת נֶפֶשׁ בִּסְפֵק שֶׁלּוֹ,
through putting his life in danger while remaining uncertain of his earlier deeds,
עַל כֵּן זְבִין לְלוּדָאֵי
he sold himself to the Ludaei,
שֶׁהֵם יַאַסְרוּהוּ בְּיָדָם
that they would bind him with their hands
וְלֹא יוּכַל לְהִנָּצֵל
and he would not be able to be saved
אִם לֹא עַל יְדֵי תַּחְבּוּלָה שֶׁחָשַׁב,
except by a stratagem he devised,
וּמִי יוֹדֵעַ אִם יַעֲלֶה בְּיָדוֹ.
without knowing whether that plan would succeed.
וְזֶהוּ בֵּרוּר,
This, in his understanding, would serve as a test:
אִם עָשָׂה שֶׁלֹּא כַהֹגֶן
if his earlier actions had been wrongful
וְחַיָּב מִיתָה לֹא יִנָּצֵל,
and he truly deserved death, he would not be saved;
וְאִם לָאו
and if not,
מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם יַעַזְרוּהוּ וְיִנָּצֵל.
Heaven would aid him and he would escape.
וְעָלְתָה בְּיָדוֹ
The stratagem in fact succeeded,
דְּגַם בָּזֶה אַדְּרַבָּה
for in this too, on the contrary,
הוֹסִיף לְכַלּוֹת קוֹצִים כְּסוּחִים
and in the course of escaping he also eliminated those he regarded as destructive thorns,
כְּאֵלֶּה אוֹכְלֵי אָדָם,
such as these man-eaters,
וּבָזֶה נִתְבָּרְרוּ כָּל עִנְיָנָיו
Thus, in Rav Tzadok’s reading, what happened brought Reish Lakish’s earlier intentions into focus:
שֶׁהָיָה רַק לְכַלּוֹת הַקּוֹצִים
his actions had been directed at clearing away the thorns
הַסּוֹבְבִים הַשּׁוֹשַׁנָּה הָעֶלְיוֹנָה.
around the supernal rose.

paragraphs.text: Gittin 47a records “ריש לקיש זבין נפשיה ללודאי” — Reish Lakish sold himself to the Ludaei, used a stratagem against his captors, escaped, and subsequently ate and drank. Tosafos, s.v. “ר״ל זבין נפשיה,” expressly writes “קודם שחזר למוטב, דמסתמא לא היה מזלזל בעצמו כל כך” — “Before he returned to the good, for presumably he would not so demean himself afterward.” Rav Tzadok, by contrast, proposes that his inward intention was directed to Heaven, a reconstruction not stated by the Gemara. A printed parallel in Dover Tzedek (Har Bracha edition, Acharei Mos, printed p.248 / PDF p.252) explicitly mentions “ריש לקיש דזבין נפשיה ללודאי”; his later discussion, printed pp.252–254 (PDF pp.256–258), further develops the Ludaei and the root of eating. These printed passages are parallels to, not a replacement for, the Gittin/Tosafos sources. Sources: Gittin 47a; Tosafot on Gittin 47a; Dover Tzedek, Har Bracha, Acharei Mot pp.248, 252–254.

paragraphs.text: The Gittin 47a account does not say Reish Lakish knew in advance whether he would survive; Rav Tzadok therefore raises the severe concern of putting oneself deliberately in mortal danger. Bava Kamma 91b cites “ואך את דמכם לנפשתיכם אדרש” — “Your lifeblood I shall require” — in a discussion distinguishing loss of life from other forms of self-injury. Rambam, Hilchos Rotzeach uShmiras HaNefesh 11:5, directly states: “הרבה דברים אסרו חכמים מפני שיש בהם סכנת נפשות ... הריני מסכן בעצמי ומה לאחרים עלי בכך” — “The Sages prohibited many acts because they endanger life ... [one cannot simply say,] ‘I endanger myself; what concern is that of others?’” These sources establish the legal seriousness of danger but DO NOT adjudicate Reish Lakish’s particular aggadic case or permit self-endangerment for repentance. Rav Tzadok’s proposed exceptional interpretation must not be converted into practical guidance. Sources: Gittin 47a; Bava Kamma 91b; Mishneh Torah, Murderer and the Preservation of Life 11:5.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 19a has two distinct teachings: “כל המספר אחר מטתן של תלמידי חכמים נופל בגיהנם” — “Whoever disparages Torah scholars after their death falls into Gehinnom,” and “אם ראית תלמיד חכם שעבר עבירה בלילה אל תהרהר אחריו ביום ... ודאי עשה תשובה” — “If you see a scholar transgress at night, do not suspect him the next day ... he certainly repented.” The Gemara immediately restricts the latter presumption to bodily matters: for monetary offenses restitution remains necessary. Rav Tzadok invokes this ethic to ask why Chazal would include a seemingly purposeless story that could only shame Reish Lakish. It is a methodological and reverential question, not an absolute rule that Chazal never report true failures of great figures, nor proof of the specific motive he later proposes.

paragraphs.text: The exact “clearing thorns” metaphor occurs at Bava Metzia 83b when R. Elazar bar R. Shimon defended his role in apprehending thieves: “קוצים אני מכלה מן הכרם” — “I am clearing thorns from the vineyard.” R. Yehoshua ben Korcha rejected the presumption that this justified handing Jews over for execution: “יבא בעל הכרם ויכלה את קוציו” — “Let the Owner of the vineyard come and clear His own thorns.” Rav Tzadok uses the same motif to reconstruct what he believes Reish Lakish intended in the earlier episode. Precisely because the original sugya includes the rebuke, this allusion cannot be used as a blanket moral or legal endorsement of private violence. R. Tzadok’s point here is the risk of judging one’s own intentions, even when one thinks one has removed harmful people.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 44:4, not merely “chapter 44” generally, reports R. Levi’s explanation of Avraham’s fear after defeating the kings: “תאמר אותן אוכלוסין שהרגתי שהיה בהם צדיק אחד וירא שמים אחד” — “What if among the multitudes I killed there had been even one righteous or God-fearing man?” The Holy One reassures him that those combatants were “קוצים כסוחים” — “thorns already cut down,” echoing Yeshayahu 33:12. This is a close and exact primary-source parallel for a righteous person’s uncertainty about violent acts, not evidence that Reish Lakish himself received a divine verdict or that one may decide without lawful adjudication whom to harm.

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 83b records that R. Elazar bar R. Shimon, even after apparently reassuring evidence, still felt uneasy: “ואפילו הכי לא מייתבא דעתיה” — “Even so, his mind was not settled.” The continuing account opens on 84b, “ואפילו הכי לא סמך רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון אדעתיה, קביל עליה יסורי” — “Even so, he did not rely on his own assessment and accepted suffering.” These are statements about R. Elazar; extending them to Reish Lakish is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive parallel. Avos 2:4 advises “ואל תאמין בעצמך עד יום מותך”; Pri Tzaddik, Behar 2 says that even one who experiences an anticipatory taste of Olam HaBa may fear the yetzer while evil remains present in the world. Neither a narrator’s self-doubt nor Rav Tzadok’s comparison proves guilt. Sources: Bava Metzia 83b–84b; Pirkei Avot 2:4; Peri Tzadik, Behar 2.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 65:22 identifies “יקום איש צרורות” — Yekum Ish Tzeroros — as the nephew of R. Yosei ben Yoezer. It narrates that after being affected by his uncle’s rebuke, he “הלך וקים בעצמו ארבע מיתות בית דין” — “went and subjected himself to the four forms of judicial death”; R. Yosei subsequently perceived his bier ascending and declared “בשעה קלה קדמני זה לגן עדן” — “In one brief hour, he preceded me to Gan Eden.” This is the actual exceptional Midrashic narrative, not a normative statement authorizing self-destruction as a means of repentance. Rav Tzadok draws a theoretical comparison, which must not be taken as practical halachic advice. The separate account of the laundryman in Kesubos 103b and the other later sources is documented in the next note rather than folded into this Midrash. Source: Bereshit Rabbah 65:22.

paragraphs.text: Two narratives and a later interpretation must be distinguished. Kesubos 103b reports that a laundryman absent from Rebbi’s funeral went onto a roof, fell, died, and was proclaimed destined for Olam HaBa; the Bavli itself does not say he violated Shabbos. Yerushalmi Kilayim 9:3 and Yerushalmi Kesubos 12:3 independently recount Rebbi’s funeral on erev Shabbos, the miraculous prolongation of daylight, people’s fear “דילמא דחללינן שבתא” (“perhaps we desecrated Shabbos”), and the separate proclamation “בר מן קצרא” (“except the laundryman”). Later explanations, including the interpretation attributed by Rav Tzadok to Maharit, associate the laundryman with a Shabbos lapse. A secondary source transcribes the Maharit explanation, but the original Maharit printed page was not directly collated, so this is a marked print-witness qualification. Separately, Sefer Mitzvos Katan, mitzvah 3, paragraph 4, directly recounts R. Yehudah HeChasid’s disciples and the perilous journey after their initial recourse to the Divine Name; it is not the Yekum Midrash or the funeral narrative. These extraordinary medieval/aggadic accounts are presented as historical texts, not normative permission to put oneself in danger. Sources: Ketubot 103b; Jerusalem Talmud Kilayim 9:3; Jerusalem Talmud Ketubot 12:3; Sefer Mitzvot Katan 3:4; Maharit on Ketubot 103b (exact original printing not collated).

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Reish Lakish’s actual “banditry” is never told in the Talmud as a story in its own right — it was wholly erased, being no sin at all. Even his “selling himself to the Ludaei” (Gittin 47a) is, R’ Tzadok argues, no improper deed: not mere “self-disparagement” (Tosafos) but bordering on suicide (he could not know in advance he would be spared). Yet if he truly acted improperly, why would the Sages record his disgrace, “speaking ill of tzaddikim”?

p: (מא) וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ ״נְפַק וַאֲתָא יָתֵיב אָכֵיל וְשָׁתֵי״, ורש״י פֵּירֵשׁ ״כָּל יָמָיו״ כו׳, מַשְׁמַע דִּמְפָרֵשׁ דְּהוּא עִנְיָן בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ, וְלֹא מַשְׁמַע כֵּן רַק דְּהוּא נִמְשָׁךְ לְהַקּוֹדֵם

(41) This is why the Gemara then says, “He went out, returned, sat, ate and drank.” Rashi explains this as “throughout his days,” etc., indicating that he understands it as a separate matter. But that is not how it reads; rather, it continues what came before.
וְגַם אִי מִלְּתָא בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ הוּא
and even if it is a matter in its own right,
מַה שַׁיָּכוּתֵּיהּ הָכָא.
what is its relevance here?
וְאִם רָצָה לוֹמַר דְּגַם סִיפּוּר הַקּוֹדֵם מַה דְּזָבַן נַפְשֵׁיהּ הָיָה בִּשְׁבִיל אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה, אִם כֵּן הַכֹּל הוּא לְגַנּוֹתוֹ וְשֶׁהָיָה רַעַבְתָן חַס וְשָׁלוֹם

And if someone wanted to say that even the earlier account of his selling himself was for the sake of food and drink, the entire story would be to his discredit, suggesting he was ravenous, Heaven forbid.
וְאֵיךְ אָמַר ״כָּל יָמָיו״ כו׳, וַהֲרֵי אַחַר כָּךְ חָזַר וְהָיָה תַּלְמִיד חָכָם וּבְוַדַּאי כָּל אֲכִילָתוֹ בִּקְדֻשָּׁה
How, then, could Rashi say “all his days,” when later Reish Lakish returned to Torah and became a Torah scholar, so that surely all his eating was conducted in holiness?
וְאֵיךְ הִסְמִיךְ זֶה לְהַקּוֹדֵם שֶׁמָּכַר עַצְמוֹ לְמִיתָה בִּשְׁבִיל אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה, וְאֵין לְךָ ״זוֹלֵל וְסוֹבֵא״ גָּדוֹל מִזֶּה
How could the Gemara place such eating next to the account of his selling himself into mortal danger for food and drink? There would be no greater “glutton and drunkard” than that.
וְדֶרֶךְ רָשָׁע
That would be the conduct of a wicked person
אֲשֶׁר יֶעֱרַב לוֹ לֶחֶם שֶׁקֶר
to whom “false bread is sweet,”
וְאַחַר יִמָּלֵא פִיהוּ חָצָץ.
“but afterward his mouth is filled with gravel.”
וְגַם הַלָּשׁוֹן
Moreover, consider the wording
אָמְרָה לֵיהּ בְּרָתֵּיהּ וְכוּלֵּי,
“His daughter said to him,” and so forth:
אִם הַסִּפּוּר דַּאֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה הוּא
If the mention of eating and drinking describes
דֶּרֶךְ תְּמִידוּת
something that occurred continually,
כְּפֵירוּשׁ רַבִּי שְׁלֹמֹה יִצְחָקִי,
as Rashi interprets it,
וְכִי תָּמִיד אָמְרָה לֵיהּ כָּךְ.
did his daughter really speak to him in this way every time?
וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּהַכֹּל סִיפּוּר אֶחָד, דִּכְשֶׁיָּצָא מִמַּה שֶּׁהָיָה, יָתֵיב וְאָכַל וְשָׁתָה בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה לְשִׂמְחָתוֹ שֶׁנִּיצוֹל מֵהֶם
Rather, necessarily the entire passage describes one event: after he came out of that danger, he sat and ate and drank at that very moment, rejoicing that he had been saved from them.

וּכְפִי הַנִּרְאֶה דְּהוּקְשָׁה לְרַשִׁ״י לְאֵיזֶה צֹרֶךְ יַזְכִּיר זֶה דְּאָכַל וְשָׁתָה כֵּיוָן דְּלֹא נִזְכַּר שׁוּם סִיפּוּר וְהֶמְשֵׁךְ עִנְיָן עַל זֶה, וְעַל כֵּן מְפָרֵשׁ דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר כָּל יוֹם כָּל מַה שֶּׁמִּשְׁתַּכֵּר כו׳, וְנִמְשָׁךְ לְמַה שֶּׁאָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ ״כִּי נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ״ כו׳

Apparently Rashi found it difficult to understand why the Gemara would say that he ate and drank at all, since it provides no further event or narrative continuation about that meal. Therefore Rashi explains it to mean “every day, whatever he earned,” etc., linking the passage to what follows: “When he died,” etc.
אֲבָל לְפִי זֶה הָעִיקָּר דְּאָכַל וְשָׁתָה כָּל מַה שֶּׁמִּשְׁתַּכֵּר וְשֶׁלֹּא הִשְׁאִיר כְּלוּם חָסֵר מֵהַסֵּפֶר
But according to that explanation, the very substance of the point—that he ate and drank everything he earned and left nothing aside—is missing from the text itself.

paragraphs.text: Rashi on Gittin 47a explains the Bavli’s “יתיב קאכיל ושתי” with the exact gloss “כל ימיו כל מה שהיה משתכר לא היה מצמצם להצניע ליום מחר” — “Throughout his life, whatever he earned, he would not ration or put aside for the next day.” The Bavli itself says only “נפק ואתא, יתיב קאכיל ושתי” — “He went out, returned, sat, ate and drank”; it then reports the exchange with his daughter and his eventual bequest of a kav of saffron. Rav Tzadok objects to Rashi’s construal as a habitual pattern and instead argues that the plain sequence records a single meal immediately after Reish Lakish escaped mortal danger. That contextual interpretation is Rav Tzadok’s, not a competing explicit Gemara gloss. This note belongs at the first complete juxtaposition of the Gemara and Rashi; the later phrases develop Rav Tzadok’s arguments against the gloss.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Avos 2:12 instructs “וכל מעשיך יהיו לשם שמים” — “Let all your actions be for the sake of Heaven.” Rambam, Hilchos De’os 3:2–3, applies this to eating, drinking, sleep and caring for the body as means toward knowing and serving Hashem. Rav Tzadok, Pri Tzaddik, Tu BiShvat 2:2, gives the precise parallel of Hillel’s eating: “שלא עלה על דעתו שום הנאת הגוף רק כמו שמאכיל לאכסניא” — “He had no thought of bodily pleasure; it was like feeding a guest.” Thus ordinary permitted eating may itself be avodah through its intention. The claim that every meal Reish Lakish ate after teshuvah was holy is Rav Tzadok’s application, not a separate recorded historical fact. Sources: Pirkei Avot 2:12; Mishneh Torah, Human Dispositions 3:2–3; Peri Tzadik, Tu BiShvat 2:2.

paragraphs.text: The phrase “זולל וסובא” (“glutton and drunkard,” Devarim 21:20) has a precise, restricted legal meaning in the laws of a ben sorer u’moreh. Sanhedrin 70a–71a specifies a particular consumption of meat and wine, and Rambam, Hilchos Mamrim 7:1–3, requires numerous conditions (including theft of the father’s money, purchase of meat and wine, and eating outside his house in a specified company). Rashi’s lifetime eating explanation would not, by itself, prove these halachic conditions. Rav Tzadok invokes the expression here rhetorically, as a critique of an interpretation that would present self-endangerment and eating for appetite as a sage’s defining habit. His point is a literary and spiritual reductio, not an accusation of the biblical statutory offense.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 54b states “ארבעה צריכין להודות” — “Four categories must give thanks,” including “מי שהיה חבוש בבית האסורים ויצא” — “one who was imprisoned and was released,” citing Psalm 107 (especially verses 10–16). The verse says “יודו לה׳ חסדו ונפלאותיו לבני אדם” — “Let them thank Hashem for His kindness and His wonders for humanity.” The Bavli’s Gittin account does not call Reish Lakish’s meal a prescribed seudas hoda’ah or discuss his obligation to recite hagomel. Rav Tzadok interprets the immediate post-rescue eating and drinking as rejoicing on deliverance. The classical thanksgiving pattern makes that literary reading comprehensible but must not be misattributed to Gittin.

paragraphs.text: Beitzah 16a distinguishes Shammai’s continuous Sabbath preparations from Hillel: “אבל הלל הזקן מדה אחרת היתה לו, שכל מעשיו לשם שמים, שנאמר ברוך ה׳ יום יום” — “Hillel the Elder had another practice: all his deeds were for the sake of Heaven, as it says ‘Blessed is Hashem, day by day.’” Ramban on Shemos 20:8 discusses this same distinction, and Rav Tzadok interprets it in Pri Tzaddik, Tu BiShvat 2 as an expression of holy eating without bodily self-indulgence. Thus Rashi’s picture of not saving tomorrow’s food need not itself imply vice. Rav Tzadok’s criticism here is textual: if that habit was the intended main point of Gittin 47a, the Bavli would have had to say more about his earnings. The note therefore distinguishes the possibility of holy trust from Rav Tzadok’s objection to Rashi’s reading of this specific story.
