inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The Gemara continues, “he went out, came, sat, ate and drank.” Rashi glosses “all his days whatever he earned he did not save for tomorrow,” taking it as a matter in its own right. R’ Tzadok objects: read plainly, it is continuous with the rescue — Reish Lakish sat and ate in joy at having been saved from the Ludaei.

p: (מב) וּכְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי ״טוֹבִי״ קָא מַשְׁמַע לָן לְהֶמְשֵׁךְ הַסִּיפּוּר כַּמָּה לִיסְטִים רַעַבְתָנִים הֵם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּפְסָחִים יב:) ״שָׁעָה שְׁנִיָּה מַאֲכַל לִיסְטִים״, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י דְּהֵם רַעַבְתָנִים כְּלוּדִים לֶאֱכוֹל מִיָּד שֶׁנֵּיעוֹרִים

(42) As I have written, the expression “tovi” is brought to teach, in connection with the continuation of the account, how ravenous bandits can be. Thus Pesachim 12b says, “The second hour is the mealtime of bandits.” See Rashi there: they are ravenous, like the Ludim, eating as soon as they wake.

וְעִיקַּר הַלִּסְטִיּוּת בָּא מֵרַעַבְתָנוּת שֶׁאֵין מוֹצִיא כָּל צָרְכּוֹ מֵאֻמָּנוּת אוֹ לְהָטִיל עַצְמוֹ עַל הַצִּבּוּר, וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין עב רע״א) בְּבֶן סוֹרֵר וּמוֹרֶה ״סוֹפוֹ עוֹמֵד וּמְלַסְטֵם הַבְּרִיּוֹת״

The root of banditry also comes from ravenousness: one does not earn enough through one’s craft to meet one’s needs, or would cast oneself upon the community. Thus Sanhedrin 72a says concerning a rebellious son, “In the end he will stand and rob other people.”

וְהוּא שֶׁחָשַׁד עַצְמוֹ לְלִיסְטִים גַּם אֲכִילָתוֹ חָשַׁב שֶׁהוּא רַעַבְתָנוּת בְּעָלְמָא כְּמַאֲכַל כָּל לִיסְטִים; וּלִכְשֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵר דְּאֵינוֹ לִיסְטִים כִּי כָּל מַעֲשָׂיו לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם לְבַעֵר הָרַע, מִמֵּילָא גַּם אֲכִילָתוֹ וּשְׁתִיָּיתוֹ בִּקְדֻשָּׁה

Because Reish Lakish suspected himself of being a bandit, he likewise regarded his eating as mere ravenousness, as bandits eat. But when it became clear, in Rav Tzadok’s interpretation, that he was no bandit—that all his actions had been for Heaven’s sake to remove evil—his eating and drinking too could be seen as holy.
וְגַם עִיקַּר קְדֻשַּׁת הָאֲכִילָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה דּוֹמֶה לַמִּזְבֵּחַ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (חֲגִיגָה כז רע״א) ״פָּתַח בְּמִזְבֵּחַ וְסִיֵּים בְּשֻׁלְחָן״ כו׳
Moreover, the central sanctity of eating is that it should resemble the altar. Thus Chagigah 27a says, “It begins with an altar and ends with a table,” and so forth.

וּבִפְרָט בְּתַלְמִיד חָכָם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּיוֹמָא עא סע״א) ״לְנַסֵּךְ עַל גַּבֵּי הַמִּזְבֵּחַ — יְמַלֵּא גְּרוֹנָם שֶׁל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים״, וּבִכְתוּבּוֹת (קה סע״ב) ״הַמֵּבִיא דּוֹרוֹן לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם כְּמַקְרִיב בִּיכּוּרִים״, דְּכָל אֲכִילוֹתָיו וּשְׁתִיּוֹתָיו כְּקָרְבָּנוֹת

This applies particularly to a Torah scholar. Thus Yoma 71a teaches, “Whoever wishes to pour a libation upon the altar should fill the throats of Torah scholars,” and Kesubos 105b says, “One who brings a gift to a Torah scholar is as one who offers firstfruits,” since all his eating and drinking can be compared to offerings.
וּבִבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּא (פָּרָשָׁה ס״ה) ״אִם לְקָרְבָּנְךָ הִמְצִיא כו׳ לְמַאֲכָלְךָ עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה״, מַשְׁמַע דְּחָשׁוּב טְפֵי מִקָּרְבָּנוֹת
Bereishis Rabbah, chapter 65, states, “If He provided for your offering, how much more so for your food,” which implies to Rav Tzadok that holy eating is even more significant than offerings.
וְזֶהוּ כָּל עִנְיַן אֲכִילָה דִּקְדֻשָּׁה
This is the whole idea of eating in holiness:
שֶׁבָּרָא הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֶת הָאָדָם
that the Blessed One created the human being
שֶׁיִּצְטָרֵךְ לַאֲכִילָה לְקִיּוּם חַיָּיו,
to require food for the preservation of life,
כִּי יֵשׁ בָּזֶה עֲבוֹדָה כְּמוֹ בְּקָרְבָּנוֹת.
because eating involves divine service, as sacrifices do.
וּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר לְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן
And what was said to Adam HaRishon,
מִכֹּל עֵץ הַגָּן אָכֹל תֹּאכֵל,
“From every tree of the garden you shall surely eat,”
זוֹ מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה כְּמוֹ קָרְבָּנוֹת.
is, in this interpretation, a positive commandment, like the sacrificial commandments.

וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁהַלִּיסְטִים מָמוֹנָן גֶּזֶל וְכָל אֲכִילָתָן מִגְּזֵילוֹת וַחֲמָסִים, אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לְרָצוֹן וְהַקְּדֻשָּׁה, ״דַּאֲנִי ה׳ שׂוֹנֵא גָּזֵל בְּעוֹלָה״, וּבְוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּא (פָּרָשָׁה ג) ״הַזֶּפֶק שֶׁמָּלֵא גְּזֵילוֹת וַחֲמָסִין אַל יִקְרַב לְגַבֵּי הַמִּזְבֵּחַ״

Since bandits’ wealth derives from theft and their food from robbery and coercion, such eating cannot be acceptable before Heaven or sanctified: “For I, Hashem, hate robbery in a burnt offering.” Vayikra Rabbah, chapter 3, says that the crop filled with stolen and forcibly taken food must not approach the altar.
וְעוֹד דְּכֵיוָן שֶׁדּוֹמֶה לְקָרְבָּן וְהוּא לִיסְטִים וְשׁוֹפֵךְ דָּמִים, הֲרֵי קְרָא צָוַוח ״לָמָּה לִּי רוֹב זִבְחֵיכֶם וְגוֹ׳ יְדֵיכֶם דָּמִים מָלֵאוּ״

Moreover, if their eating is compared to an offering while their conduct involves banditry and bloodshed, Scripture cries out, “Why do I need your many sacrifices?” and “Your hands are full of blood” (Yeshayah 1).
וּבְאוֹר זָרוּעַ גָּדוֹל (חֵלֶק א׳ סוֹף סִימָן קי״ב)
And in the great Or Zarua, part I, at the end of section 112,
מַשְׁמַע דְּכֹהֵן רוֹצֵחַ
it appears that a kohen who committed murder
(בְּמֵזִיד וְלֹא שָׁב)
deliberately and without returning in repentance
פָּסוּל לַעֲבוֹדָה
is disqualified from the Temple service
כִּנְשִׂיאַת כַּפַּיִם.
as he is from raising his hands in the priestly blessing.
(וְכֵן לִהְיוֹת שְׁלִיחַ צִבּוּר
The same question is raised about his service as prayer leader;
עַיֵּן שָׁם
see there
דִּמְדַמֶּה לָעֲבוֹדָה
for he likens it to the service
מִשּׁוּם דְּכְנֶגֶד תְּמִידִין,
because it corresponds to the daily offerings,
וְהוּא מְבֹאָר מִפְּשַׁטּוּת לְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב
and this is clear from the plain wording of the verse
דִּישַׁעְיָה הַנִּזְכָּר
of Yeshayah mentioned:
גַּם כִּי תַרְבּוּ תְפִלָּה וְגוֹמֵר
“Even when you multiply prayer,” etc.,
יְדֵיכֶם וְגוֹמֵר.
“your hands,” etc.
וְצָרִיךְ עִיּוּן
This still requires further examination.
אַךְ רַבִּי מֹשֶׁה אִיסֶרְלֶס
but Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema)
בְּאוֹרַח חַיִּים סִימָן נ״ג סָעִיף ה׳
in Orach Chaim, sec. 53, par. 5,
בְּהַגָּהָה
in his gloss
הֶעְתִּיק דִּבְרֵי אוֹר זָרוּעַ
quoted the words of the Or Zarua
דִּבְשׁוֹגֵג כָּשֵׁר לִשְׁלִיחַ צִבּוּר,
that an inadvertent one is fit to be prayer leader,
וּבְסִימָן קכ״ח סָעִיף ל״ה
and in sec. 128, par. 35,
שָׁתַק לַשֻּׁלְחָן עָרוּךְ
the Rema, Rav Tzadok writes, did not add a comment to the Shulchan Arukh’s ruling
דְּסָתַם כָּרַמְבַּ״ם
which ruled without qualification according to the Rambam
דְּגַם בְּשׁוֹגֵג פָּסוּל לִנְשִׂיאַת כַּפַּיִם,
that even when the killing was inadvertent, the kohen is disqualified from the priestly blessing.
וַהֲרֵי אוֹר זָרוּעַ מְדַמֶּה
yet the Or Zarua likens
שְׁלִיחַ צִבּוּר וַעֲבוֹדָה לִנְשִׂיאַת כַּפַּיִם,
prayer leader and service to the priestly blessing,
וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ סְבִירָא לֵיהּ
so of necessity he holds
דְּגַם לִנְשִׂיאַת כַּפַּיִם כָּשֵׁר שׁוֹגֵג,
that even for the priestly blessing an inadvertent one is fit,
וּלְדִידַן דְּפָסְלִינַן לִנְשִׂיאַת כַּפַּיִם
and according to us, who disqualify for the priestly blessing,
הָוֵי לֵיהּ לִפְסֹל גַּם לִשְׁלִיחַ צִבּוּר,
he should disqualify also for prayer leader,
וְאֵין כָּאן מָקוֹם לְהַאֲרִיךְ בָּזֶה)
and this is not the place to elaborate on this)
וַאֲפִילוּ לְפִי דַּעַת הַתּוֹסָפוֹת (יְבָמוֹת ז.)
And even according to Tosafos on Yevamos 7a,
דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר
s.v. “shene'emar”
דְּלַעֲבוֹדָה כָּשֵׁר עַיֵּן שָׁם,
who maintain that such a kohen remains valid for the Temple service—see there—
וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין (לה:)
and in Sanhedrin (35b)
דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר,
s.v. “shene'emar,”
מִכָּל מָקוֹם וַדַּאי
nevertheless surely
פְּשָׁטֵיהּ דִּקְרָא
the plain sense of the verse
דִּ״יְדֵיכֶם וְגוֹמֵר״
“your hands,” etc.,
אַלְמָה לִי רֹב זִבְחֵיכֶם
“Why do I need your many sacrifices”
דְּרֵישָׁא קָאֵי,
refers to the beginning,
דְּאֵין מְרֻצֶּה כָּל כָּךְ מִיהַת.
the offerings are, at the least, not fully acceptable in this prophetic image.
וּבְשַׁבָּת (לג.) ״דְּבַעֲוֹן שְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ חָרֵב וּשְׁכִינָה מִסְתַּלֶּקֶת״, הֲרֵי דְּאֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא רוֹצֶה בַּעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁל שׁוֹפֵךְ דָּמִים
Shabbos 33a says that “because of bloodshed, the Temple is destroyed and the Shechinah departs.” Rav Tzadok therefore concludes that Hashem does not desire the service of someone guilty of bloodshed.
וְאַף דְּהָתָם בְּצִבּוּר כֻּלָּם כֵּן,
And although there it is a community, all of whom are so,
הַיְנוּ לְעִנְיַן חֻרְבַּן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ
that is regarding the destruction of the Beis HaMikdash
וּבִטּוּל עֲבוֹדָה לְגַמְרֵי מִכָּל הַצִּבּוּר,
and total cancellation of service for the entire community,
וְהוּא הַדִּין לְיָחִיד בְּחֵטְא דִּידֵיהּ.
the principle also bears upon an individual’s own transgression.
וּבְיוֹמָא (פה סע״א) אִיתָא גַּם אַשְּׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים דְּיָחִיד דְּגוֹרֵם לַשְּׁכִינָה שֶׁתִּסְתַּלֵּק מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל
Yoma 85a also says that bloodshed by an individual defiles the land and causes the Shechinah to withdraw from Israel.
וְגַם מַה שֶּׁאָמַר שָׁם
And also what it says there,
דְּמִטַּמֵּא הָאָרֶץ
that it defiles the land,
הוּא מִקְּרָא דְּלֹא תְטַמֵּא
is from the verse “do not defile,”
כְּדִפֵּרֵשׁ רַשִׁ״י שָׁם,
as Rashi explained there,
וְהַהוּא קְרָא מַיְיתֵי נַמֵּי בְּשַׁבָּת שָׁם,
and that verse is also brought in Shabbos there,
וְעִקַּר קְרָא נַמֵּי בְּרוֹצֵחַ יָחִיד כְּתִיב.
and the biblical warning itself speaks of the bloodshed of an individual murderer.

וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן לְעִנְיַן קְדֻשַּׁת הָאֲכִילָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נֶחְשָׁב כְּקָרְבָּנוֹת, דְּצָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה גּוּפוֹ מוּכָן לְהַשְׁרָאַת שְׁכִינָה, דְּאָז יוּכַל לְדַמּוֹת לְקָרְבָּנוֹת דְּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ

How much more must the sanctity of a person’s eating, when it is to be reckoned as like an offering, depend on a body prepared to receive the Shechinah. Only then can such eating be compared to the Temple offerings.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: (מב) וּכְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי ״טוֹבִי״ קָא מַשְׁמַע לָן לְהֶמְשֵׁךְ הַסִּיפּוּר כַּמָּה לִיסְטִים רַעַבְתָנִים הֵם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּפְסָחִים יב:) ״שָׁעָה שְׁנִיָּה מַאֲכַל לִיסְטִים״, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י דְּהֵם רַעַבְתָנִים כְּלוּדִים לֶאֱכוֹל מִיָּד שֶׁנֵּיעוֹרִים

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 12b explicitly distinguishes “שעה ראשונה — מאכל לודים; שניה — מאכל ליסטין” — “The first hour is the Ludim’s mealtime; the second, the bandits’.” Rashi explains “לודים ולסטים רעבתנים הן אלא שהליסטים נעורין כל הלילה וישנים שחרית שעה ראשונה ואוכלין בשניה” — both groups are ravenous, but bandits stay awake at night, sleep during the first morning hour, and eat in the second. Rav Tzadok discusses precisely this distinction in the Har Bracha printing of Dover Tzedek, Acharei Mot, p.253–254 (PDF pp.257–258): the Ludim belong to the first hour and bandits to the second, in his interpretive framework of the root of appetite. The spiritual explanation is Rav Tzadok’s, not a universal assertion by the Gemara about all persons with hunger. Sources: Pesachim 12b; Rashi ad loc.; Dover Tzedek, Har Bracha, Acharei Mot pp.253–254.

rich.text: Pesachim 12b explicitly distinguishes “שעה ראשונה — מאכל לודים; שניה — מאכל ליסטין” — “The first hour is the Ludim’s mealtime; the second, the bandits’.” Rashi explains “לודים ולסטים רעבתנים הן אלא שהליסטים נעורין כל הלילה וישנים שחרית שעה ראשונה ואוכלין בשניה” — both groups are ravenous, but bandits stay awake at night, sleep during the first morning hour, and eat in the second. paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 72a explains the feared future of the ben sorer u’moreh: “סוף מגמר נכסי אביו ומבקש למודו ואינו מוצא ויוצא לפרשת דרכים ומלסטם את הבריות” — he will exhaust his father’s property, seek the consumption to which he has become accustomed, fail to find it, and rob passersby. Avos 2:2 warns that Torah without a livelihood “סופה בטלה וגוררת עון” — “will ultimately cease and lead to sin”; Bartenura explains that lack of food may lead someone to rob, and Rambam, Hilchos Talmud Torah 3:10, ends “וסוף אדם זה שיהא מלסטם את הבריות” — “In the end this person will rob people.” The Rema to Yoreh De’ah 246:21 expressly mentions exceptions and support for scholars. paragraphs.text: Chagigah 27a quotes the juxtaposition “פתח במזבח וסיים בשלחן” — “It began with an altar and ended with a table.” Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish jointly teach: “בזמן שבית המקדש קיים מזבח מכפר על אדם עכשיו שלחנו של אדם מכפר עליו” — “When the Temple stood the altar atoned for a person; now a person’s table atones for him.” This is the Gemara’s actual altar/table comparison. Rav Tzadok applies it to the broader program of kedushas ha-achilah; it does not say that every individual meal automatically has the legal status of an offering or absolves bloodshed. The later sections distinguish holy food from robbery and violence.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 65:19 comments on “כי הקרה ה׳ אלהיך לפני” (Genesis 27:20). Of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, one says “אם לקרבנך המציא לך הקדוש ברוך הוא ... למאכלך על אחת כמה וכמה” — “If God provided for your offering ... how much more so for your food”; the other argues analogously from the providential arrival of Rivkah as a bride. The Midrash asserts divine providence in supplying food. Rav Tzadok infers a further comparison—food prepared in holiness may be considered more important than offerings—but the Midrash does not expressly rank the holiness of regular meals above sacrifices. This interpretation is grounded in, but conceptually develops, the cited passage.

paragraphs.text: In Pri Tzaddik, Tu BiShvat 1:2, Rav Tzadok states “והש״י ברא את האדם שיצטרך אכילה לקיום החיים שהוא חיות הקדושה והיה בהאכילה קדושה” — “The Blessed One created man to require food to sustain life, which is holy vitality, and there was holiness in eating.” He connects this with the primordial nourishment of Eden: “מכל עץ הגן אכל תאכל” (Bereishis 2:16). paragraphs.text: Yeshayah 61:8 has “שֹׂנֵא גָזֵל בְּעוֹלָה” — “I hate robbery in a burnt offering.” The precise midrashic locus is Vayikra Rabbah 3:4 (not merely an unspecified paragraph of chapter 3): because a bird takes food from many places, “הואיל והזפק הזה מלא גזלות וחמסין אל יקרב לגבי המזבח” — “Since this crop is full of things stolen or seized, it should not approach the altar”; hence the bird-offering’s crop is removed. These sources explain why offerings cannot be formed from stolen food. Yeshayah 1:11–15 separately denounces many sacrifices, prayers and bloodstained hands. Rav Tzadok joins these to argue that a bandit’s stolen food cannot serve the sanctity of the altar, but the texts must not be collapsed into a single direct quotation or used to assume every accused person is guilty.

paragraphs.text: Critical printed-source reconciliation. The complete original Hebrew of Ohr Zarua, vol. I §112 begins “אדם שהרג נפש בשוגג אם יכול ליעשות שליח צבור” (whether a person who caused a death inadvertently may serve as prayer leader). The responsum distinguishes deliberate killing from inadvertent killing and the effect of repentance. Regarding the proposed shaliach tzibbur, it explains: “ולענין ליעשות לו שליח צבור ... אם הי׳ כהאי גונא כהן פסול להקריב אז גם הוא לא הי׳ יכול ליעשות שליח צבור ... אבל השתא שכה״ג כהן כשר להקריב גם הוא ראוי להעשות שליח צבור” — because prayer corresponds to offerings, eligibility for avodah is used as the analogy. This is NOT a blanket explicit ruling in the Or Zarua that a killer may perform nesias kapayim. Compare Berachos 32b, Rambam Hilchos Tefillah 15:3, Mechaber and printed Rema on OC 128:35 (Rema explicitly permits leniency after repentance), and Tosafos Yevamos 7a / Sanhedrin 35b (s.v. שנאמר), which distinguish invalidity of birkas kohanim from Temple service. Rav Tzadok’s “שתק” cannot mean that the extant OC 128:35 prints no Rema gloss; it may address the specific inadvertent-homicide distinction, and his original Hebrew wording is retained pending any separate edition collation. Sources: Berakhot 32b; Ohr Zarua I §112; Tosafot Yevamot 7a; Tosafot Sanhedrin 35b; Rambam, Prayer 15:3; Shulchan Arukh and Rema OC 128:35.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 33a states “בעון שפיכות דמים בית המקדש חרב ושכינה מסתלקת מישראל” — “For bloodshed, the Temple is destroyed and the Shechinah departs from Israel,” quoting the Torah’s warning not to defile the land in which God dwells (Bamidbar 35:33–34). Yoma 85a says “ושפיכות דמים מטמא את הארץ וגורם לשכינה שתסתלק מישראל” — “Bloodshed defiles the land and causes the Shechinah to depart from Israel,” in Rabbi Yishmael’s argument concerning saving life on Shabbat. Those exact sources concern communal sanctity and the seriousness of bloodshed. Rav Tzadok extends their underlying principle to an individual’s bodily fitness for God’s indwelling and thence to a sacred meal resembling Temple offerings. Neither Gemara independently rules that a particular person’s meal is legally a sacrifice or that an accusation alone makes it invalid. This note accompanies the completed theological conclusion rather than anticipating it midway.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: On R’ Tzadok’s reading, the extra word “better” comes to teach, for the flow of the story, how ravenous bandits are. For example, in Pesachim 12b, “the second hour is the bandits’ mealtime,” ravenous like the Ludim who eat the instant they wake. The root of banditry is ravenousness — failing to draw one’s needs through faith, or casting oneself upon the community (so a ben sorer u’moreh “ends up robbing people,” Sanhedrin 72a).

p: (מג) וּבְתַעֲנִית (יא רע״ב) ״דְּיִרְאֶה כְּאִלּוּ קָדוֹשׁ שָׁרוּי בְּתוֹךְ מֵעָיו״, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה אָסוּר לְהִתְעַנּוֹת, וְהַיְינוּ דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה הוּא קְדֻשַּׁת הָאֲכִילָה כְּקָרְבָּנוֹת וְהוּא כְּמַקְרִיב קָרְבָּנוֹת עַל מִזְבַּח ה׳

In Taanis 11a–11b it is said that one should regard himself as though a Holy One dwells within his innards. On this basis, fasting is prohibited in the circumstances discussed there. This means that eating may itself possess a sanctity comparable to offerings, as though one were bringing offerings upon the altar of Hashem.
וְהָרוֹצֵחַ שֶׁגּוֹרֵם לְסִילּוּק שְׁכִינָה מִכָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל כָּל שֶׁכֵּן שֶׁאֵין קָדוֹשׁ שָׁרוּי תּוֹךְ מֵעָיו
And the murderer, who causes the departure of the Shechinah from all Israel, certainly has no “holy one dwelling within his innards.”

וְנִרְאֶה דְּזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בַּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן (בב״מ שָׁם פג:) ״שִׂישׂוּ בְּנֵי מֵעַי״ כו׳, כִּי כְּשֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵר שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ עֲוֹן דִּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים עַל יְדֵי זֶה יוּכַל לִהְיוֹת קָדוֹשׁ תּוֹךְ מֵעָיו וְכָל אֲכִילָתוֹ כְּקָרְבָּנוֹת, וּמִמֶּנּוּ הִתְהַוּוּ חֶלְבּוֹ וּבְשָׂרוֹ

This, it seems, is the meaning of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon’s statement (Bava Metzia 83b): “Rejoice, my innards!” Once it was clarified, in Rav Tzadok’s reading, that he bore no guilt for bloodshed, a holy presence could dwell within him, and all his eating could be like offerings; from that eating his fat and flesh were formed.
וַהֲרֵי תְנַן (בְּפֶרֶק ה׳ דְּאָבוֹת וְיוֹמָא כא.),
For we learned in the fifth chapter of Avos and in Yoma 21a
דְּלֹא הִסְרִיחַ בְּשַׂר הַקֹּדֶשׁ מֵעוֹלָם
that the flesh of sacred offerings never putrefied;
וְזֶהוּ אֲפִילוּ בְּחֶלְקָן שֶׁל כֹּהֲנִים,
and this included even the priests’ portions,
וְכָל שֶּׁכֵּן בְּקָרְבָּן עַצְמוֹ,
all the more so the offering itself,
וְכָל שֶּׁכֵּן בִּבְשַׂר הָאָדָם הַקָּדוֹשׁ,
and all the more so, Rav Tzadok reasons, the flesh of a holy person,
שֶׁמֵּעָיו בִּמְקוֹם הַמִּזְבֵּחַ
whose innards serve in place of an altar
וְגִדּוּל בְּשָׂרוֹ מֵאֲכִילָה קְדוֹשָׁה שֶׁכְּקָרְבָּן
and whose flesh grows from eating made holy like an offering.
דְּאֵין שַׁיָּכוּת לִסְרָחוֹן אֵלָיו כְּלָל.
Decay, accordingly, has no connection with such flesh at all.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר מֻבְטָח אֲנִי וְכוּלֵּי,
Therefore, he said, “I am confident,” and so forth:
דְּבְשָׂרוֹ יִשְׁכֹּן לָבֶטַח
his flesh would dwell securely,
שֶׁלֹּא יַסְרִיחַ,
without decaying,
וּמִמֵּילָא לֹא יִהְיֶה רִמָּה וְתוֹלֵעָה
and thus without the maggots and worms
הַבָּאִים אַחַר הַסִּרְחוֹן,
that follow putrefaction.
עַיֵּן שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל בְּשִׁמְשָׁא
See Rashi there, s.v. “בשמשא,”
וּבְרַשִׁ״י (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא יז.)
and in Rashi (Bava Basra 17a),
דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל כִּדְאָמְרַן.
s.v. “כדאמרן.”

וְעַל כֵּן רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ כִּדְנָפַק מִלּוּדָאֵי, דַּה׳ עֲזָרוֹ שֶׁנִּיצוֹל מִיָּדָם, נִתְבָּרֵר לוֹ דְּאֵין בְּיָדוֹ שֶׁמֶץ עֲוֹן דִּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים, דְּאָז לֹא הָיָה נִיצוֹל דְּלָא עָבֵיד קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא נִיסָּא לְשִׁקְרָא, וְגַבְרָא מִיבַּדְקֵי בְּכָל מְקוֹם סַכָּנָה כִּדְאִיתָא (בְּשַׁבָּת לב.)

Consequently, when Reish Lakish emerged from the Ludaei, having been saved from them with Hashem’s help, Rav Tzadok understood it as a clarification that no trace of the sin of bloodshed remained in his hands. Otherwise, he reasons, he would not have been saved: the Holy One does not perform a miracle to support falsehood, and a person is tested wherever danger is encountered, as stated in Shabbos 32a.
וּכְשֶׁנִּבְדַּק וְנִמְצָא נָקִי אָז הָלַךְ לֶאֱכוֹל בְּשִׂמְחָה לַחְמוֹ וְלִשְׁתּוֹת בְּלֵב טוֹב יֵינוֹ, כִּי כְּבָר רָצָה אֱלֹקִים אֶת מַעֲשָׂיו וְקָדוֹשׁ שָׁרוּי בְּמֵעָיו

And once he had been tested and found clear, he went to eat his bread joyfully and drink his wine with a glad heart, because God had already accepted his deeds and a Holy One dwelt within his innards.

וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ ״כְּרֵיסִי כָּרִי״, שֶׁחֶלְבּוֹ וּבְשָׂרוֹ נֶחְשָׁב לוֹ רַק כְּמוֹ כַּר וְכֶסֶת וְדָבָר שֶׁחוּץ מִמֶּנּוּ, כִּי עַצְמוּתוֹ עִנְיָן אַחֵר שֶׁהָיָה כּוּלּוֹ קָדוֹשׁ לַה׳ בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַגַּשְׁמִיּוּת, וְהַגּוּף אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בְּשַׂר אָדָם לְבוּשׁ לְעֶצֶם הָאָדָם שֶׁהוּא הַנַּעֲשֶׂה בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹקִים

This is also what he meant afterward by “my belly is my pillow”: he regarded his fat and flesh only as a cushion or pillow, something external to his true self. His essential being was something else—wholly dedicated to Hashem, divested of attachment to materiality—while the body was merely “human flesh,” the garment of the essential human being, fashioned in the Divine image.
וְנֶחְשָׁב אֶצְלוֹ רַק כְּמוֹ כַּר,
He considered it no more than a pillow,
וְלוֹמַר דְּאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה אוֹכֵל וְשׁוֹתֶה לֹא הָיָה מַרְגִּישׁ מִזֶּה הֲנָאָה, כִּי לֹא הָיָה לוֹ שַׁיָּיכוּת עִם הֲנָאָה הַגּוּפָנִית כְּלָל —
meaning that although he ate and drank, he did not feel self-directed pleasure in it, for he had no attachment to bodily enjoyment at all.

paragraphs.text: Taanis 11b records: “לעולם ימוד אדם עצמו כאילו קדוש שרוי בתוך מעיו” — one should regard oneself as though a Holy One dwells within the body. The surrounding discussion of voluntary fasting distinguishes one able to endure it from one unable (“הא דמצי לצעורי נפשיה הא דלא מצי לצעורי נפשיה”); it does not impose a blanket prohibition on every fast. Rav Tzadok develops the additional idea that eating undertaken in holiness can resemble altar service. Compare his own Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah, Ois 9, discussing “בקרבך קדוש” and the yetzer associated with eating: original-Hebrew paragraph 2 / interlinear Reader paragraph 4. The korban interpretation belongs to Rav Tzadok, not the explicit Talmudic wording. Sources: Taanit 11b; Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 9 (original Hebrew §9:2; Reader §9:4).

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 83b records Rabbi Elazar b. Rabbi Shimon regretting his part in the execution of the laundryman. After hearing of the man's grave offenses, he laid a hand on his belly and said: 'שישו בני מעי, שישו! ומה ספיקות שלכם כך, ודאות שלכם על אחת כמה וכמה'—rejoice, my innards; if this is the outcome of a doubtful case, all the more certain cases. Yet the Gemara adds 'ואפילו הכי לא מייתבא דעתיה': even so, he remained troubled. The report next describes his fat not decaying in summer heat. Rav Tzadok makes the interpretive step from his moral ordeal to the purity of his body and its eating; the Gemara does not expressly equate acquittal from every bloodshed offense with a guarantee of bodily incorruptibility.

paragraphs.text: Rav Tzadok gives a direct parallel in Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah, Ois 9: “וכשיש בו ברכת ה׳ מסיר המחלה שהוא היצר הרע ומביא קדושה ואור כי טוב” — when Hashem’s blessing is in one’s eating, it removes the illness of the yetzer hara and brings holiness and the “good” light. The corresponding passage is in PARAGRAPH 2 OF THE ORIGINAL HEBREW EDITION, but PARAGRAPH 4 OF THE LATER INTERLINEAR READER; these editorial divisions must not be confused. The passage invokes Taanis 11b, “כאילו קדוש שרוי בתוך מעיו,” and explains the sanctification of physical nourishment. It does NOT expressly assert that flesh grown through holy eating cannot decay: that additional connection is Rav Tzadok’s further explanation in the present Takanas HaShavin passage. Sources: Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah, Ois 9 (original-Hebrew §9:2; Akiva Publishing interlinear §9:4); Taanit 11b.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Avos 5:5 and Yoma 21a list 'לא הסריח בשר הקדש מעולם'—the flesh of the sacred offerings never putrefied—as one of the miracles at the Temple. Bava Basra 17a separately identifies seven exemplary figures over whom 'רמה ותולעה' had no power; Rashi s.v. כדאמרן relates their state to death without the angel of death's destructive drop. Rashi on Bava Metzia 83b, s.v. בשמשא, says Rabbi Elazar's exposed fat was tested 'לנסות אם יסריח וירום תולעים'—to see whether it would decay and raise worms. Neither Mishnah nor Gemara asserts Rav Tzadok's general inference that a holy person's flesh must behave like sacred meat; that is the theological analogy he develops here.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 32a asks 'וגברי היכא מיבדקי?'—where are men put to the test? Reish Lakish answers 'בשעה שעוברים על הגשר,' while the Gemara extends it to any situation analogous to crossing a dangerous bridge. Crucially, Rabbi Yannai cautions: 'לעולם אל יעמוד אדם במקום סכנה לומר שעושין לו נס'; one must not enter danger in reliance on a miracle. Rav Tzadok reads Reish Lakish's survival of the Ludaei as retroactive clarification of his spiritual state. This is not a literal Talmudic declaration that escaping danger proves innocence of a specific offense, nor permission to seek deadly tests.

paragraphs.text: Koheles 9:7 states: 'לך אכל בשמחה לחמך ושתה בלב טוב יינך כי כבר רצה האלהים את מעשיך'—Go, eat your bread with joy and drink your wine with a glad heart, for God has already accepted your deeds. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:7, likewise cites the verse when describing the renewed acceptance of a penitent's actions. Rav Tzadok applies the verse to the single meal described after Reish Lakish's escape: the joy signals, for Rav Tzadok, his recognition of Divine favor rather than greedy appetite. The Gemara in Gittin 47a reports the meal but does not expressly give it this meaning. A previously cited, unspecific Zohar Vaera '138–139' parallel was not verified at a precise location and is therefore not quoted as evidence here.

paragraphs.text: Gittin 47a records Reish Lakish’s words “כריסי כרי” — “My belly is my pillow,” after his escape; the Gemara does not supply Rav Tzadok’s mystical explanation. Dover Tzedek, Likkutim 4:138 (Reader: Miscellany 4:138), directly connects Reish Lakish’s clarification to his Ludaei ordeal: “ובירורו היה על ידי דזבין ללודאי” — “his clarification came through selling himself to the Ludaei.” That passage does NOT itself elaborate the later meal or body-as-pillow as a korban; those are developed in the present Takanas HaShavin paragraph. A precise parallel for BODY AS GARMENT is Rav Tzadok, Pri Tzaddik, Nitzavim 14: “בגדי מרמז על הגוף שהוא לבוש להנפש” — garments symbolize the body as a garment for the soul; “שעיקר אדם הוא הנפש והגוף נקרא רק בשר אדם” — the person’s essential self is the soul, while the body is called human flesh. This supports his interpretation that the physical belly sustains, yet is external to, spiritual identity. An inherited reference to Dover Tzedek Likkutim 4:104 as a near-identical body-and-meal parallel remains unsupported; use 4:138 only for the Ludaei episode. Sources: Gittin 47a; Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:138; Pri Tzaddik, Nitzavim 14; Takanat HaShavin 10:43.

paragraphs.text: Kesubos 104a reports that Rabbeinu HaKadosh said near death: 'יגעתי בעשר אצבעותי בתורה, ולא נהניתי אפילו באצבע קטנה'—I labored with ten fingers in Torah and did not enjoy this world even with my little finger. Avodah Zarah 11a nevertheless states that rich foods did not cease from his table; Tosafos there, s.v. צנון וחזרת, propose that many people ate at his table. Rav Tzadok, Yisrael Kedoshim 5, offers a different explicit explanation: the foods really were present, but 'לא הרגיש הנאת עצמו כלל'—he did not experience enjoyment as self-directed bodily appetite—and he compares Hillel's care for the body to caring for a guest (Vayikra Rabbah 34:3). This original Rav Tzadok parallel illuminates the ideal he attributes to Reish Lakish; neither Gemara literally certifies Reish Lakish's state of mind.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: In Taanis 11a, “one should ever regard himself as though a holy one dwells within his innards” — and therefore he may not fast. Through this his eating is holy like korbanos, as though offering them on God’s altar. By contrast, a murderer, who drives out the Shechinah, surely has no “holy one” within.

p: (מד) וְתוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם מַיְיתֵי מִזְּבָחִים (ה רע״א) ״רָמֵי אַמְּעוֹהִי״, וּמַקְשֶׁה דְּהָיָה דַּרְכּוֹ (וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתְבוּ שָׁם ״דַּרְכָּן״ כו׳, טָעוּת סוֹפֵר, וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דַּרְכּוֹ, דְּרַק רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ דַּרְכּוֹ כָּךְ וְלֹא מָצִינוּ כֵן בִּשְׁאָרֵי)

Tosafos there, on Gittin 47a, cite Zevachim 5a: “Reish Lakish lay upon his belly,” רמי אמעוהי, and explain that this was their custom. But, Rav Tzadok argues, the word “their” is a scribal error and should read “his,” since it is only Reish Lakish whom we find doing this, not the other Sages.
וּלְפֵרוּשׁ הָעָרוּךְ
And according to the explanation of the Arukh
הַמּוֹבָא בַּתּוֹסָפוֹת (נִדָּה יד.)
cited in Tosafos on Niddah 14a,
דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל אַפְרָקִיד
s.v. “אפרקיד,”
רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי לִיֵּיט עֲלַהּ,
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi condemned that posture;
וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר
one must say
דְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ פְּלִיג עֲלֵיהּ
that Reish Lakish disagreed with him,
אוֹ דְּהוּא בָּטַח בְּנַפְשֵׁיהּ
or that he was certain about his own condition
שֶׁלֹּא יִתְחַמֵּם עַל יְדֵי זֶה.)
and would not be aroused by it.)
כֵּן,
so,
וְגַם שָׁם אֵין מוּבָן כְּלָל
Even there, however, it is entirely unclear
לְאֵיזֶה צֹרֶךְ הִזְכִּירוּ זֶה,
why this detail needed to be mentioned,
דְּכְשֶׁהִקְשָׁה אוֹתָה קֻשְׁיָא דְּהָתָם
when he posed his question in that sugya:
אִם כְּשֵׁרִים וְכוּלֵּי
“If the offerings are valid,” and so on,
כִּדְרָמֵי אַמְעוֹהִי,
why add that he was “lying upon his belly”?
וּמַאי נָפְקָא מִינָּא בָּזֶה.
What bearing does the posture have on the question?
וַאֲפִילוּ בְּעִנְיַן הַמַּשָּׂא וּמַתָּן שֶׁל הֲלָכָה עַצְמָהּ
And even in the give-and-take of halachah itself
אָמְרוּ (פְּסָחִים ג:)
the Sages said in Pesachim 3b:
לְעוֹלָם יִשְׁנֶה אָדָם לְתַלְמִידוֹ דֶּרֶךְ קְצָרָה,
“A person should always teach his student in a concise manner,”
כָּל שֶּׁכֵּן בְּסִפּוּר שֶׁלֹּא לְצֹרֶךְ.
all the more so when narrating an otherwise unnecessary detail.
וְנִרְאֶה טַעַם דֶּרֶךְ שְׁכִיבָתוֹ עַל בִּטְנוֹ בַּפָּשׁוּט
The straightforward reason for his practice of lying on his belly appears
הָיָה לְפִי מַה שֶּׁרָאיִיתִי
to be what I have seen
בְּסֵפֶר אוֹצַר הַחַיִּים (שַׁעַר א׳ חֲקִירָה ו)
in Sefer Otzar HaChaim, Gate 1, Inquiry 6,
וּבְפֵרוּשׁ דִּבְרֵי הָרַמְבַּ״ם (הִלְכוֹת דֵּעוֹת)
and in an explanation of Rambam’s Hilchos Deos:
דְּהוּא עוֹזֵר וּמְסַיֵּעַ הָעִכּוּל,
that it assists digestion.
וּלְפִי שֶׁהָיָה אוֹכֵל הַרְבֵּה, כַּנִּרְאֶה מִדִּבְרֵי רַשִׁ״י ״כָּל מַה שֶּׁהִרְוִיחַ״, הוּצְרַךְ לָזֶה עַל דֶּרֶךְ הָרְפוּאָה
Since he ate a great deal, as Rav Tzadok infers from Rashi’s phrase “everything that he earned,” he needed this posture for digestive reasons.

וְזֶהוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי שֶׁכָּל אֲכִילָתוֹ כְּקָרְבָּנוֹת הַכֹּל בִּקְדֻשָּׁה וְלֹא לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ, וְאֵינוֹ מִדַּת רַעַבְתָנוּת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, רַק כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא בַּאֲכִילַת קָרְבָּנוֹת (בִּפְסָחִים נז סע״א) בְּיוֹחָנָן בֶּן נַרְבָּאי ״וְיֹאכַל בְּקָדְשֵׁי שָׁמַיִם״

This accords with what I have written: all his eating was like offerings, entirely holy and not for self-gratification—far removed, Heaven forbid, from mere gluttony. It resembled the sacred consumption mentioned in Pesachim 57a concerning Yochanan ben Narbai, who “filled his belly from the holy offerings of Heaven.”
וְכָל שֶּׁכֵּן מַה שֶׁהוּא כְּקָרְבָּן עַצְמוֹ עַל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ.
How much more so in the case of what Rav Tzadok compares to the offering placed upon the altar itself.

וְהִנֵּה כְּמוֹ כָּל הַזְּבָחִים שֶׁנִּזְבְּחוּ שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָן כְּשֵׁרִין כִּדְתְנַן (רֵישׁ זְבָחִים), דִּלְשֵׁם חוּלִּין אֲפִילּוּ בְּחַטָּאת כְּשֵׁרָה, דְּלָא מִינָּהּ לָא מַחְרִיב בָּהּ כִּדְאִיתָא (שָׁם ג.)

Now, just as offerings slaughtered with an intention other than their designated purpose generally remain valid, as taught at the beginning of Zevachim—and even a sin-offering slaughtered with an intention for unconsecrated meat remains valid, because what is outside its category does not undermine it (Zevachim 3a)—
הָכִי נַמֵּי מִי שֶׁזּוֹכֶה
so too one who attains the level
דְּכְאִלּוּ קָדוֹשׁ שָׁרוּי בְּמֵעָיו
at which a Holy One dwells within his innards,
דַּאֲכִילָתוֹ כְּקָרְבָּנוֹת,
and whose eating is comparable to offerings:
אֲפִילוּ יִהְיֶה לוֹ אֵיזֶה פַּעַם כַּוָּנַת הֲנָאָה,
even if on some occasion he eats with an intention of bodily pleasure,
דְּלֹא הַכֹּל זוֹכִין לִהְיוֹת כְּרַבִּי
for not everyone merits to reach the level of Rabbeinu HaKadosh,
שֶׁאָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ (כְּתֻבּוֹת קד.)
who testified about himself in Kesubos 104a,
וְלֹא נֶהֱנֵיתִי וְכוּלֵּי
“I did not derive enjoyment,” and so forth.
עַיֵּן שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת
see there in Tosafos
דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל לְשֵׁם
s.v. “lesheim”
(וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתְבוּ שֶׁלֹּא יִכָּנְסוּ,
As for Tosafos’ suggestion, “that they should not enter,”
הַיְנוּ לְשֵׁם הֲנָאַת גּוּפוֹ,
it concerns entry for the sake of one’s own physical gratification;
וְרַבִּי עַצְמוֹ הָיָה שֻׁלְחָנוֹ שֻׁלְחַן מְלָכִים
Rabbeinu HaKadosh himself maintained a table fit for kings,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה יא.)
as they said (Avodah Zarah 11a)
שֶׁלֹּא פָּסַק מֵעַל שֻׁלְחָנָם וְכוּלֵּי
that those foods never ceased from their tables.
עַיֵּן שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל שֶׁלֹּא,
see there in Tosafos, s.v. “shelo,”
וְאֵין צֹרֶךְ לְמַה שֶּׁדָּחֲקוּ שָׁם
There is no need for the strained explanation offered there
סוֹף דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל צְנוֹן,
at the conclusion of Tosafos, s.v. “צנון,”
דְּפָשׁוּט דְּהַכַּוָּנָה
because the meaning is straightforward:
דְּלֹא נֶהֱנֵיתִי
“I did not derive enjoyment”
שֶׁלֹּא הִרְגִּישׁ הֲנָאַת גּוּפוֹ
means that he did not experience the pleasure of his body as self-gratification,
רַק כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר הִלֵּל
just as Hillel explained
בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ל״ד
in Vayikra Rabbah, chapter 34,
לִגְמֹל חֶסֶד עִם הָדָא עֲלוּבְתָּא.)
that he was “showing kindness to this unfortunate guest.”

paragraphs.text: Niddah 14a says: 'רבי יהושע בן לוי לייט אמאן דגני אפרקיד'—Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi condemned sleeping aparkeid. Tosafos ad loc., s.v. אפרקיד, quote Rashi's reading 'פניו למעלה' (face-up) and contrast the Arukh, 'פניו מטה' (face-down); the distinction is central to Rav Tzadok's question about Reish Lakish lying on his belly. Berachos 13b discusses a slight side-tilt and distinguishes sleeping from reciting Shema. Rambam, Hilchos Deos 4:5, advises sleeping neither face-down nor face-up but on one's side. Rav Tzadok offers two possible explanations of Reish Lakish, not a blanket exception to the sleeping guidance: he either disagreed with that identification of posture or did not face the specific danger. The texts do not establish that he routinely slept face-down; Zevachim only depicts him lying in the beis midrash while discussing Torah.

paragraphs.text: Source-critical qualification to Rav Tzadok’s observation “אוצר החיים (שער א׳ חקירה ו)” regarding lying prone to aid digestion. Jacob Tsahalon (Zahalon), Otzar HaChaim (Venice 1683), in his discussion of Rambam, Hilchos Deos 4:4–5, first reproduces Rambam’s instruction NOT to sleep face-down or face-up, but on one’s side. Tsahalon then describes a separate exception in historical humoral medicine: “One who has a feeble belly should sleep on his belly, in order to heat it and thereby aid the digestion” (English translation by Avi Steinhart, Posen Library, vol. 5; credits identify the 1683 edition, ch. 4, p. 6 [vav]). Thus the purported prone digestion practice IS attested in the work Rav Tzadok names, but it is Tsahalon’s exception, NOT the Rambam’s recommendation. Rambam Deos 4:3 discusses posture while eating, and 4:5 addresses sleep; Zevachim 5a (“רמי ריש לקיש על מעוהי”) does not itself explain health. The 1683 Hebrew facsimile has not been collated word-for-word; this verification is via a credited scholarly translation, not a claim of inspection of the printed Hebrew folio. These are early modern historical beliefs, not modern medical advice. Sources: Otzar HaChaim, Gate 1, Investigation 6 (Venice 1683), translated in https://www.posenlibrary.com/entry/otsar-ha-hayim-treasury-life; Rambam Hilchos Deos 4:3–5; Zevachim 5a.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 57a says the courtyard of the Temple proclaimed: 'ויכנס יוחנן בן נרבאי ... וימלא כריסו מקדשי שמים'—Let Yochanan ben Narbai enter and fill his belly with the holy offerings of Heaven. The account goes on to ascribe to him extraordinary eating and concludes 'כל ימיו של יוחנן בן נרבאי לא נמצא נותר במקדש'—in his days no sacrificial leftover was found in the Temple. Rav Tzadok uses this specifically as a precedent for considerable consumption that serves sacred purposes. The numerical quantities in the story are aggadic, not a diet prescription; the Gemara does not directly compare Yochanan ben Narbai with Reish Lakish.

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Maaseh HaKorbanos 10:1, explicitly states 'אכילת החטאת והאשם מצות עשה'—eating the sin- and guilt-offerings is a positive commandment—and 'הכהנים אוכלים ובעלים מתכפרים': the priests eat and the offerers receive atonement. The eating of other priestly sacred portions is likewise a mitzvah. This provides a precise halachic analogue for Rav Tzadok's notion of holy eating. It does not itself classify ordinary food consumed by a righteous person as an actual consecrated offering; that further step is his spiritual analogy. The case of the Temple priest Yochanan ben Narbai is a more literal example of sacrificial eating.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Zevachim 1:1 distinguishes validity from discharge of obligation: 'כל הזבחים שנזבחו שלא לשמן, כשרים, אלא שלא עלו לבעלים לשם חובה'—offerings slaughtered not for their own sake generally remain valid but do not fulfill the owner's obligation. The Mishnah immediately excepts the chatas and the korban Pesach at its appointed time; it also records Rabbi Eliezer's additional view about the asham. These qualifications matter: the rule is not unconditional acceptance of any non-lishmah intent. Rav Tzadok applies the category only analogically to a person whose eating is fundamentally directed to holiness; the Mishnah itself addresses literal animal offerings.

paragraphs.text: Zevachim 3a reports Rav's distinction: 'חטאת ששחטה לשם עולה פסולה, שחטה לשם חולין כשירה'—a sin-offering slaughtered for the sake of an olah is invalid, whereas one designated for ordinary unconsecrated meat remains valid. The Gemara states 'דמינה מחריב בה, דלאו מינה לא מחריב בה'; Rashi explains that the alien non-sacred designation 'אין שמו נתפס על הזבח לעקור שמו ממנו'—does not take hold to uproot its sacrificial identity. Rav Tzadok applies that mechanism as a metaphor: when eating is essentially holy, a passing thought of bodily pleasure need not uproot that identity. This is his application, not a ruling made about human eating in Zevachim.

paragraphs.text: The passage draws together two separate rules, which must not be conflated. Mishnah Zevachim 1:1 says that most offerings slaughtered shelo lishmah remain valid without discharging the owner's obligation; chatas and the timely korban Pesach are exceptions. Zevachim 3a separately says that a chatas slaughtered for the sake of chullin is nevertheless valid because a designation outside the category of sacrifices does not displace its identity. Rav Tzadok's comparison is not a technical legal ruling for ordinary eating. He sees a holy person's bodily nutrition as analogous to sanctified service, so occasional self-directed pleasure does not automatically erase that central character; this is an interpretive analogy, not a universal assurance.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 50b quotes Rav Yehudah in Rav's name: 'לעולם יעסוק אדם בתורה ומצות אף על פי שלא לשמה, שמתוך שלא לשמה בא לשמה'—one should engage in Torah and mitzvos even with imperfect motives, for such involvement can lead to lishmah. Tosafos there, s.v. וכאן בעושים שלא לשמה, distinguishes such motives from studying 'כדי להתיהר ולקנטר ולקפח את חביריו בהלכה'—to boast, provoke, or humiliate others. Rav Tzadok's shelo-lishmah metaphor concerns a basically sanctified act into which personal pleasure occasionally intrudes; it is not a license for harmful intent or conduct. Zevachim 5a records Reish Lakish's distinct technical objection: 'אם כשרים הם ירצו ואם אין מרצין למה באין?'—If offerings are valid, why do they not effect acceptance; if not, why bring them? These are separate Talmudic questions that Rav Tzadok interprets together.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Tosafos there adduces from Zevachim 5a that Reish Lakish “would lie on his belly rami a’me’ohi” (and R’ Tzadok emends the printed “their way” to “his way” — this was Reish Lakish’s practice alone), asking why the Gemara mentions it. R’ Tzadok answers: he lay on his belly medicinally — it aids digestion (as in Sefer Otzar HaChaim and Rambam, Hilchos De’os). And since he ate a great deal (per Rashi, all that he earned), he required it as a remedy.

but as a formula for resolving a difficulty,
אֵין טַעַם בְּלָשׁוֹן זֶה)
this expression seems unwarranted.)

וּלְמַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי דְּעִיקַּר קֻשְׁיָא דְּ״רָמֵי אַמְּעוֹהִי״ הַיְינוּ ״לְצֹרֶךְ נַפְשֵׁיהּ״, דְּהוּא רָצָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לְרָצוֹן גַּם כֵּן, וְעַל זֶה אָמַר שַׁפִּיר לְשׁוֹן ״אֶפְתַּח״ כו׳ שֶׁזֶּה פֶּתַח לְנַפְשׁוֹ הַצְּמֵאָה וּתְאֵבָה לְדָבָר זֶה

According to what I explained, however, the core of the question asked while Reish Lakish was “lying upon his belly” was for the need of his own soul: he wanted the act to be acceptable as well. Thus he fittingly said “I shall open,” for this was an opening for his soul, thirsty and yearning for just this assurance.

וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא בִּמְגִילָּה (י: יא.) ״פָּתַח לָהּ פִּתְחָא לְהַאי פָּרָשְׁתָא״, דְּהַכַּוָּונָה שֶׁאוֹתוֹ מַאֲמָר הוּא פֶּתַח פָּתוּחַ לְשֹׁרֶשׁ כָּל עִנְיַן פָּרָשַׁת הַמְּגִילָּה — וְכָךְ בֵּירוּר דָּבָר זֶה הוּא פֶּתַח פָּתוּחַ לְשֹׁרֶשׁ קְדֻשַּׁת נַפְשׁוֹ, בִּהְיוֹת גַּם הַשֶּׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ קָדוֹשׁ לֵאלֹקָיו וּמְרוּצֶּה גַּם כֵּן

This resembles the formula in Megillah 10b–11a, “he opened an opening to this passage”: the saying provides an entrance to the root meaning of the entire Megillah narrative. In the same way, clarification of this issue opens the root of Reish Lakish’s soul’s holiness, so that even what was done not wholly for its own sake could be holy to his God and acceptable before Him.
וְהָא דְּלֹא עָלָה לְחוֹבָה הַיְינוּ רַק לָצֵאת יְדֵי נִדְרוֹ, אֲבָל נְדָבָה הָוֵי, וְהוּא כְּקָרְבַּן נְדָבָה שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן לְרָצוֹן לִפְנֵי ה׳
That the offering “did not discharge the obligation” means only that he did not fulfill his vow; it nevertheless counts as a voluntary offering, which is also acceptable before Hashem.

וְכֵן אֲכִילַת הַתַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁכְּקָרְבָּנוֹת, וְהַפֶּה הוּא פֶּתַח הַגּוּף, וְכֵן ״כָּל עֲמַל אָדָם לְפִיהוּ״, וְ״אָדָם לַעֲמַל פֶּה יוּלָּד״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין צט רע״ב), וְהָעִיקָּר לַעֲמַל תּוֹרָה כִּדְאִיתָא הָתָם

The same applies to a Torah scholar’s eating, which may be likened to offerings. The mouth is the body’s entrance; hence “all of man’s toil is for his mouth,” and “man is born for the toil of the mouth,” as explained in Sanhedrin 99b—above all, for the toil of Torah.

אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ הַמּוּבָא בַּתּוֹסָפוֹת (כְּתוּבּוֹת קד רע״א) דְּעַד שֶׁמִּתְפַּלֵּל שֶׁיִּכָּנְסוּ דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה יִתְפַּלֵּל שֶׁלֹּא יִכָּנְסוּ מַעֲדַנִּים, דְּאַף דְּעִיקַּר הַכֹּל הוּא כְּנִיסַת הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה בַּלֵּב, מִכָּל מָקוֹם צְרִיכָה לִהְיוֹת יִרְאָתוֹ קוֹדֶמֶת לְחָכְמָתוֹ הַמַּגְדִּירָתוֹ בְּסוּר מֵרָע

Nevertheless, the Midrash cited by Tosafos on Kesubos 104a says that before praying that words of Torah enter his body, a person should pray that delicacies do not enter it. Though the ultimate aim is for Torah to enter the heart, fear of sin must precede wisdom and restrain it through the discipline of turning away from evil.

דְּלוּלֵי זֶה ״לָמָּה זֶּה מְחִיר בְּיַד כְּסִיל״ כו׳; וְהָעִיקָּר בַּתַּאֲווֹת, וְהַהַתְחָלָה בַּאֲכִילָה שֶׁבָּזֶה הָיָה חֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן, וְכָל אֲכִילָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ עֲבוֹדָה בִּקְדֻשָּׁה הוּא פֶּתַח הַכְּנִיסָה לְכָל רַע, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת לב.) ״מְלֵי כְּרֵיסֵיהּ זָנֵי בִּישֵׁי״, וְהַהֵיפֶךְ בַּאֲכִילָה דִּקְדֻשָּׁה הוּא פֶּתַח הַכְּנִיסָה לְכָל טוֹב

Otherwise, “Why should there be a price in a fool’s hand?” The principal danger lies in desire, beginning with eating, through which Adam HaRishon sinned. Eating that is not an act of holy service opens the way to every evil, as the Sages say in Berachos 32a: “A full belly breeds evils.” Conversely, eating with holiness opens the way to every good.

paragraphs.text: Zevachim 5a: “אלא אמר ריש לקיש, אפתח אנא פתחא לנפשאי” — “Rather, Reish Lakish said: I shall open an opening for myself.” Nedarim 22b: “נפק רב סחורה ופתח פיתחא לנפשיה” — “Rav Sechora went out and found an opening for himself.” The second expression refers specifically to an opening for release of a vow, not a proof that every Talmudic question is an inward spiritual inquiry. Rav Tzadok reads the unusual wording of Zevachim in light of Reish Lakish’s own concern: can a valid but non-discharging sacrifice be acceptable before God? He applies this to the sanctification of his eating. The spiritual autobiographical reading is Rav Tzadok’s, not the Gemara’s explicit conclusion.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Zevachim 1:1: “כל הזבחים שנזבחו שלא לשמן, כשרים, אלא שלא עלו לבעלים לשם חובה” — “Offerings slaughtered with a different designated intent remain valid, but do not discharge the owner’s obligation.” Bartenura on Mishnah Zevachim 1:1: “יהא נדבה, כלומר כשר הוא כאלו הביאו לנדבה, אבל לא יצא ידי נדרו” — “It shall be as a voluntary offering—valid as though brought voluntarily—but he has not discharged his vow.” This is the precise halachic analogy: validity and nonfulfillment coexist. The rule has exceptions, notably Pesach and chatas when wrongly designated; it must not be generalized to every offering. Rav Tzadok further applies the accepted, non-discharging korban to eating without wholly perfect inner intent, as a homiletic analogy rather than a ruling about ordinary food.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 99b: “כשהוא אומר כי אכף עליו פיהו הוי אומר לעמל פה נברא. ועדיין איני יודע אם לעמל תורה אם לעמל שיחה” — “From the verse that his mouth drives him, man was created for toil of the mouth; the question remains whether speech or Torah.” Sanhedrin 99b: “כשהוא אומר לא ימוש ספר התורה הזה מפיך הוי אומר לעמל תורה נברא” — “From “the Torah shall not depart from your mouth,” he was created for toil in Torah.” The Gemara’s conclusion is Torah labor, not an endorsement of bodily indulgence. Rav Tzadok uses the mouth as the gateway of both Torah and food and insists that physical intake be sanctified as it becomes part of a person’s service.

paragraphs.text: Tosafot on Ketubot 104a: “עד שאדם מתפלל שיכנס תורה לתוך גופו יתפלל שלא יכנסו מעדנים לתוך גופו” — “Before one prays that Torah enter his body, let him pray that delicacies not enter his body.” Tanna Debei Eliyahu Rabbah 26: “אם לא זכה אדם לבקש רחמים על ד״ת שיכנסו לתוך מעיו מכל מקום יבקש רחמים על אכילה ושתיה יתירה שלא יכנסו לתוך מעיו” — “If one has not merited to pray that Torah enter his innards, he should at least pray that excessive eating and drinking not enter them.” Tosafot quotes a midrash; Tanna Devei Eliyahu records a close, more detailed formulation. They warn against excess and distraction, not all eating. Rav Tzadok sees restraint as the boundary that permits the greater purpose, Torah entering the heart; Rambam Hilchos Talmud Torah 3:12 likewise warns that Torah does not endure amid indulgence.

paragraphs.text: Pirkei Avot 3:9: “כל שיראת חטאו קודמת לחכמתו, חכמתו מתקימת” — “Whoever’s fear of sin precedes wisdom has wisdom that endures.” Yoma 72b: “אוי להם לשונאיהן של תלמידי חכמים, שעוסקין בתורה ואין בהן יראת שמים” — “Woe to scholars who engage in Torah yet lack fear of Heaven.” The Yoma passage expounds “למה זה מחיר ביד כסיל לקנות חכמה ולב אין,” Proverbs 17:16. Rav Tzadok gives the same point in Peri Tzadik Kedoshim §3: even learning Torah does not remove the label kesil if fear of Heaven is missing. Yirah and sur mera protect the Torah-learning from becoming an instrument of bodily desire.

Yirah and sur mera protect the Torah-learning from becoming an instrument of bodily desire.

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 32a: “היינו דאמרי אינשי: מלי כרסיה זני בישי” — “As people say: when he fills his belly, evil breeds.” Berakhot 32a: “כמרעיתם וישבעו שבעו וירם לבם על כן שכחוני” — “When they had pasture and became sated, their hearts became exalted, and therefore they forgot Me.” This is the precise proverb quoted in the Bavli: abundance and the fullness of the belly can open the way to moral failure. It is not a claim that normal sustenance is sinful; Rav Tzadok applies it specifically to eating outside the discipline of kedushah.

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Pesach 1: “וכן בא מצוה ראשונה בתורה באכילת פסח אכילת מצוה שבא לתקן הקלקול של אדם הראשון שהוא שורש הסתת הנחש להכניס תאוה באכילה” — “The first mitzvah of holy eating comes in eating the Pesach offering, which repairs Adam’s corruption rooted in the serpent introducing desire into eating.” Peri Tzadik, Tazria 3: “ושורש הסתת הנחש היה להכניס תאוה באכילה, ומי שהוא מוגדר באכילה שמאכלו בקדושה ממילא שומר כל המצות שבתורה” — “The serpent’s root seduction brought appetite into eating; one who disciplines eating in holiness consequently guards the Torah’s mitzvot.” These are direct passages of Rav Tzadok, not later editors’ glosses. They explain both sides of the closing contrast: consumption pursued for appetite may open wrongdoing, while eating ordered toward a mitzvah can repair that original breach. Do not flatten this into the claim that every desire or meal is evil.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: “Upon this Reish Lakish said, ‘I will open an opening for myself eftach ana pischa l’nafshai’” (Zevachim 5a) — a phrase both needlessly long and awkward. Per R’ Tzadok’s reading — that the whole “rami a’me’ohi” question is “for his own soul’s sake,” wishing his eating to be favorable. The phrase fits perfectly: “I will open” an opening for his soul, which thirsts and craves this.

p: (מו) וּמִצְוָה רִאשׁוֹנָה שֶׁנִּצְטַוּוּ בִּיצִיאַת מִצְרַיִם,
The first mitzvah that marked the Exodus from Egypt
שֶׁהוּא הַתְחָלַת כְּנִיסַת הַיַּהֲדוּת
—the beginning of entering Jewish life
וּבִנְיַן אֻמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית,
and establishing the nation of Israel—
הָיְתָה מִצְוַת אֲכִילָה דְּקָרְבַּן פֶּסַח
was the mitzvah of eating the korban Pesach,
דְּעִקַּר מִצְוָתוֹ הוּא אֲכִילָתוֹ,
because eating is its essential purpose.
וְכִדְתְנַן (פְּסָחִים עו סוֹף עַמּוּד ב)
Thus we learned in Pesachim 76b
שֶׁתְּחִלָּתוֹ לִבְנֵי אָדָם לַאֲכִילָה,
that from its very inception it was intended for human consumption.
וְכֵן אֲכִילַת מַצָּה.
The same is true of the mitzvah of eating matzah.

וְאַזְהָרַת אֲכִילַת חָמֵץ הוּא אַזְהָרַת אֲכִילָה שֶׁמִּצַּד הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע הַנִּקְרָא (בִּבְרָכוֹת יז רע״א) ״שְׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָּה״, שֶׁהוּא הַמְרוֹמֵם הָעִיסָּה יוֹתֵר מִמַּה שֶּׁהִיא, וְזֶהוּ בַּקָּשַׁת הַמּוֹתָרוֹת יוֹתֵר מֵהַשַּׁיָּיךְ לְחֶלְקוֹ

The prohibition against eating chametz guards against eating under the sway of the evil inclination, called “the leaven in the dough” in Berachos 17a. Just as leaven lifts the dough beyond its original measure, so the impulse seeks excess beyond one’s allotted portion.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מַצָּה
Matzah, by contrast,
הוּא הָאֲכִילָה בִּקְדֻשָּׁה
represents eating with holiness,
שֶׁהִיא לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם,
for the sake of Heaven,
וְאֵין לַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִסָּה חֵלֶק בָּהּ.
in which the “leaven in the dough” has no share.
וְזֶהוּ הַפִּתְחָא לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ
This is the “opening for himself”
דְּפָתַח רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ,
that Reish Lakish opened:
דְּגַם הַנֶּפֶשׁ לֹא תִמָּלֵא
the soul, too, is never filled
(שֶׁהוּא סִיּוּמָא דִּקְרָא
—as the verse concludes,
דַּעֲמַל אָדָם לְפִיהוּ
“All a man’s toil is for his mouth,”
קֹהֶלֶת ו, ז)
Koheles 6:7—
בְּתַאֲוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
by the desires of this world.

וְכֵן בִּקְדֻשָּׁה ״אוֹהֵב מִצְוָה לֹא יִשְׂבַּע מִצְוָה״, וְ״צַדִּיק אוֹכֵל לְשׂוֹבַע נַפְשׁוֹ״, דְּיֵשׁ לוֹ שְׂבִיעָה בְּמַה דְּשַׁיָּיךְ לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ; מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן ״בֶּטֶן רְשָׁעִים״ דְּ״קֶבֶר פָּתוּחַ גְּרוֹנָם״ הוּא לְעוֹלָם חָסֵר דְּאֵין לוֹ מִילּוּי, וְהַשְּׂבִיעָה שֶׁלּוֹ אֵינוֹ שְׂבִיעָה אֶלָּא מִילּוּי הַכֶּרֶס לְבַד

In the realm of holiness, too, “one who loves a mitzvah is not sated with mitzvot”; yet “a righteous person eats to the satisfaction of his soul,” because he finds satisfaction in what truly belongs to his soul. This is unlike the “belly of the wicked,” whose “throat is an open grave.”
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מִי שֶׁמְּמַלֵּא כְרֵיסוֹ
By contrast, one who fills his belly
מִקָּדְשֵׁי שָׁמַיִם,
from the sacred things of Heaven
הִיא אֲכִילָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ שְׂבִיעָה,
engages in eating that truly satisfies.
דְּמַה דְּלֹא יִשְׂבַּע מִצְוֹת
Being “never sated with mitzvot”
הַיְנוּ שֶׁהוֹמֶה וּמְהַמֶּה לְהַשִּׂיג יוֹתֵר
means that he longs and strives to accomplish more;
אֲבָל כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁאֶפְשָׁר,
yet insofar as he is able to act,
וּבָזֶה יֵשׁ לוֹ שְׂבִיעָה.
he experiences genuine satisfaction.

וְזֶהוּ אֲכִילַת אוֹתוֹ צַדִּיק — רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ, דִּכְפִי דִּבְרֵי רַשִׁ״י דְּאָכַל כָּל מַה שֶּׁמִּשְׁתַּכֵּר נִרְאֶה כְּמִלֵּי כְּרֵיסֵיהּ, אֲבָל הָיָה מִקָּדְשֵׁי שָׁמַיִם, וְזֶהוּ הַפֶּתַח לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ דְּהַכֹּל לְרָצוֹן לִפְנֵי ה׳

This was the eating of that righteous sage, Reish Lakish. Although Rashi’s explanation that he consumed what he earned could make it appear to be merely “filling his belly,” his eating was of the holy things of Heaven. This was the opening for his soul: all was pleasing before Hashem.

וְעַל כֵּן לֹא רָצָה לְהַנִּיחַ לַאֲחֵרִים יְגִיעוֹ, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר רַב לְרַב הוּנָא (עֵירוּבִין נד רע״א) ״אִם יֵשׁ לְךָ הֵיטֵב לְךָ״ וְגוֹ׳, ״וְאִם תֹּאמַר אַנִּיחַ לְבָנַי״ כו׳ — כִּי מֵאַחַר דְּבָטוּחַ בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁכָּל הֲנָאוֹתָיו בִּקְדֻשָּׁה, לָמָּה לֵיהּ לְהַנִּיחַ לַאֲחֵרִים שֶׁאֵין יוֹדֵעַ מַה יִּהְיוּ

Therefore he did not wish to leave his earnings to others, following Rav’s saying to Rav Huna in Eruvin 54a: “If you have means, do good for yourself,” and, “If you say, ‘I shall leave it to my children,’” and so on. For since he was confident that his pleasures were holy, why leave them to others whose conduct he could not know?

וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (קֹהֶלֶת ב, יח–יט) ״וְשָׂנֵאתִי אֶת כָּל עֲמָלִי שֶׁאַנִּיחֶנּוּ לְאָדָם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אַחֲרַי וּמִי יוֹדֵעַ הֶחָכָם יִהְיֶה אוֹ סָכָל״ וְגוֹ׳, וְאָמַר (שָׁם ג, כב) ״אֵין טוֹב מֵאֲשֶׁר יִשְׂמַח הָאָדָם בְּמַעֲשָׂיו כִּי הוּא חֶלְקוֹ״

Thus it says in Koheles 2:18–19: “I hated all my labor, which I must leave to the person who will come after me; and who knows whether he will be wise or foolish?” And in 3:22: “There is nothing better than that a person rejoice in his works, for that is his portion,”
כִּי מִי יְבִיאֶנּוּ לִרְאוֹת (בְּמָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אַחֲרָיו).
“for who will bring him to see what will be after him?”
וּמִדַּת רְשָׁעִים הוּא
The characteristic of the wicked, however, is
יָכִין וְצַדִּיק יִלְבָּשׁ,
that “he prepares, but the righteous will wear,”
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר גַּם כֵּן (קֹהֶלֶת ב, כו)
as it also says in Koheles 2:26,
וְלַחוֹטֶא נָתַן עִנְיָן לֶאֱסוֹף וְלִכְנוֹס
“To the sinner He assigns the task of gathering and amassing,”
לָתֵת לְטוֹב (לִפְנֵי הָאֱלֹקִים),
“to give to one who is good before God.”
שֶׁהֵם עִקָּרָם רַק לִכְנוֹס
Their purpose is merely to accumulate,
וְשֶׁלֹּא לֵהָנוֹת בְּעַצְמָם,
rather than to enjoy their possessions themselves,
וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בַּכְּנַעֲנִים
as the Sages said concerning the Canaanites
קֹדֶם שֶׁנִּכְנְסוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל לְאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל.
before Israel entered the Land.
דְּמִדַּת כָּל אָדָם גַּם כֵּן
An ordinary person, however, normally
אַף שֶׁהוּא נֶהֱנֶה גַּם כֵּן וְיָגַע לְעַצְמוֹ,
enjoys the fruit of his own labor
יָגַע גַּם לְבָנָיו
while also working for his children,
לְהַשְׁאִיר בְּרָכָה אַחֲרָיו
to leave a blessing behind
בְּקִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
through the possessions of this world.
דְּכָל פָּרָשַׁת נַחֲלוֹת נֶאֱמַר עַל זֶה,
The Torah’s laws of inheritance address this purpose.
וְאָמְרוּ (בְּאֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה פֶּרֶק כה)
Thus they said in Eliyahu Rabbah, chapter 25,
מֵאוֹתוֹ זָקֵן שֶׁאָמַר
of the elder who declared,
כְּשֵׁם שֶׁיָּגְעוּ לִי אֲבוֹתַי
“Just as my fathers labored for me,”
כָּךְ אֲנִי יָגֵעַ לְבָנַי.
“so I labor for my children.”

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 76b: “הפסח שבא בטומאה נאכל בטומאה, שלא בא מתחילתו אלא לאכילה” — “The Paschal offering brought in impurity may be eaten in impurity because it was brought from the outset for eating.” Peri Tzadik, Pesach 1: “וכן בא מצוה ראשונה בתורה באכילת פסח אכילת מצוה שבא לתקן הקלקול של אדם הראשון” — “The first mitzvah of holy eating is the Pesach consumption that repairs Adam’s corruption.” The Mishnah is specifically explaining why Pesach differs from other public offerings regarding eating in impurity; it is not a blanket ruling about all sacrifices. Rav Tzadok reads the inauguration of national holy eating as an answer to the primordial misuse of appetite. Exodus 12:2 already commands calendrical sanctification, so “first commandment” here expresses Rav Tzadok’s thematic focus, not a denial of that earlier command.

Rav Tzadok reads the inauguration of national holy eating as an answer to the primordial misuse of appetite. paragraphs.text: Yoma 39a: “ונשתלחה ברכה בעומר, ובשתי הלחם, ובלחם הפנים. וכל כהן שמגיעו כזית, יש אוכלו ושבע, ויש אוכלו ומותיר” — “Blessing rested on the Omer, Two Loaves and showbread; a priest receiving an olive’s bulk could eat and be satisfied, even leaving over.” This direct account is a parallel to the motif of actual satiation from sacred food, in the era of Shimon HaTzaddik. paragraphs.text: Midrash Mishlei and Maharal illuminate “צדיק אוכל לשובע נפשו” (Proverbs 13:25). Midrash Mishlei 13:5: “צדיק אוכל לשובע נפשו — זה הממלא נפשו מדברי תורה. ובטן רשעים תחסר — זה שאין בו דברי תורה” — the righteous person's satisfaction is nourishment of the soul through Torah, whereas the wicked person lacks it. Maharal, Ohr Chadash on Esther 5:13, unit 6: “כי הצדיק שיש לו השלמה, לכך אוכל לשובע נפשו” — the righteous is inwardly whole, and hence experiences satisfaction; the wicked, being inwardly deficient, is represented by an unsatisfied material belly. Together they illuminate Rav Tzadok’s distinction between the ever-increasing desire for additional mitzvot and actual spiritual satiety within one’s allotted portion, without reducing this passage to ordinary gluttony. The Maharal passage is directly in Ohr Chadash 5:13:6, not merely an unverified general cross-reference to Netiv HaOsher. Sources: Mishlei 13:25; Midrash Mishlei 13:5; Maharal, Ohr Chadash, Esther 5:13:6.

Eruvin 54a reads: “אמר ליה רב לרב המנונא: בני אם יש לך היטב לך, שאין בשאול תענוג ... ואם תאמר אניח לבני — חוק בשאול מי יגיד לך” — “Rav said to Rav Hamnuna: My son, if you have resources, make good use of them, for there is no enjoyment in the grave ... And if you say, I shall leave it to my children, who will tell you what will happen there?” Rav Tzadok's inherited Hebrew reads רב לרב הונא, whereas the consulted Bavli and its parallel textual witnesses read רב לרב המנונא. The manuscript Hebrew and newest English are preserved; this difference is recorded as a textual attribution question rather than silently repaired. Rav Tzadok applies the counsel to Reish Lakish only because he believes this particular sage's benefit was wholly sanctified. The Gemara does not instruct others to neglect their dependents. Compare Koheles 2:18–19 and 3:22, which Rav Tzadok cites in the next paragraph.
Sources: Eruvin 54a; Koheles 2:18–19; Koheles 3:22.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The very first mitzvah commanded at the Exodus — the beginning of entering Jewishness and building the Israelite nation. Was the mitzvah of eating the korban Pesach (whose essence is its eating, Pesachim 76b), and likewise the eating of matzah. The prohibition of eating chametz is the warning against eating from the side of the yetzer hara, called “the leaven in the dough” (Berachos 17a), which “raises the dough higher than it is” — the craving for excess beyond one’s portion.

p: (מז) אֲבָל זֶהוּ מִדַּת עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ הָעוֹסְקִים בְּיִשּׁוּבָהּ שֶׁל אֶרֶץ, אוֹ מִי שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁפִּיעַ לוֹ הַרְבֵּה וְהוּא אֵין רַשַּׁאי לְהוֹצִיא בְּמוֹתָרוֹת וְרַק הוּא צִינּוֹר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁפִּיעַ עַל יָדוֹ לַאֲחֵרִים — וְזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן חֶלְקוֹ מַה שֶּׁגְּנָזוֹ לוֹ לְמַעְלָה, וְכֵן לְהַנִּיחַ לְבָנָיו חוֹק

This is the way of ordinary people engaged in cultivating and settling the land, or of someone whom Hashem grants considerable abundance but who may not spend it on luxuries. He is instead a channel through whom Hashem bestows resources on others. This, too, is his allotted portion and what is stored for him above, as is leaving a rightful share for his children.
אֲבָל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁתּוֹרָתוֹ אוּמָּנוּתוֹ וְאֵין עוֹסֵק בִּמְלָאכָה אֶלָּא כְּדֵי פַּרְנָסָתוֹ וְכָל הֲנָאוֹתָיו בִּקְדֻשָּׁה, אֵין לוֹ לְצַמְצֵם עַצְמוֹ לְהַנִּיחַ לְבָנָיו

A Torah scholar, however, whose Torah is his occupation, who works only to provide his livelihood, and whose pleasures are all sanctified, need not deprive himself merely in order to leave more to his children.
וְקַבָּא דְּמוֹרִיקָא שֶׁהִנִּיחַ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ קָרֵי אַנַּפְשֵׁיהּ ״וְעָזְבוּ לַאֲחֵרִים חֵילָם״, שֶׁחָשַׁב זֶה לְעֹנֶשׁ לוֹ שֶׁעָזַב יְגִיעוֹ לַאֲחֵרִים אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא דָּבָר מוּעָט

Of the kav of saffron Reish Lakish left behind, he said of himself: “They leave their wealth to others” (Tehillim 49:11). He regarded even this small remainder, which he had to leave to others, as a punishment.

כִּי מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁפִּיעַ לְאָדָם הוּא כְּדֵי שֶׁיֵּהָנֶה הוּא בּוֹ, וּמַה שֶּׁלֹּא זָכָה לֵיהָנוֹת הוּא בִּשְׁבִיל אֵיזֶה חֵטְא; וְאוֹתוֹ חֵטְא קַל שֶׁבִּשְׁבִילוֹ מֵת, דְּאֵין מִיתָה בְּלֹא חֵטְא, אוֹתוֹ הַחֵטְא גָּרַם גַּם כֵּן לְאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר מוּעָט שֶׁלֹּא יָכוֹל לֵיהָנוֹת מִמֶּנּוּ בְּעַצְמוֹ

For the abundance Hashem gives a person is intended for that person’s benefit. In Rav Tzadok’s interpretation, what Reish Lakish did not merit to enjoy was withheld because of some slight fault; that same fault, he explains, caused his death—on the premise that “there is no death without sin”—and left that little portion for others.
וְנִמְצָא כָּל הַסִּיפּוּר דְּשָׁם בְּ״הַשּׁוֹלֵחַ״ כּוּלּוֹ לְשִׁבְחוֹ שֶׁל רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ, וְחָלִילָה לָהֶם לְהַזְכִּיר דָּבָר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ גְּנוּת לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם

Thus the entire account in the chapter HaSholeach is, in Rav Tzadok’s view, a tribute to Reish Lakish. Far be it from the Sages to record a disgraceful matter about a Torah scholar merely to diminish him.

וְגַם לְפִי דִּבְרֵי הַתּוֹסָפוֹת דְּהַמַּעֲשֶׂה הָיָה קוֹדֶם שֶׁחָזַר, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מַה שֶּׁסִּיפְּרוּ זֶה עַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּאַחַר שֶׁחָזַר תִּיקֵּן גַּם מַעֲשֶׂה זוֹ עַד שֶׁגַּם זֶה נַעֲשֶׂה זְכֻיּוֹת וְיֵשׁ בָּהּ שֶׁבַח

Even if, as Tosafos explain, the incident occurred before Reish Lakish returned to the good, the fact that it is recorded must, Rav Tzadok argues, mean that afterward he also repaired that event, until it too became counted among his merits and could be recounted to his praise.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי דְּמַה דְּנִיצוֹל מִיָּדָם מוֹכִיחַ כִּי אֵין בּוֹ חֵטְא דִּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּם, וְהַמְּכִירָה הוּצְרְכָה לְבָרֵר זֶה, כִּי כְּפִי דַּעַת בְּנֵי אָדָם הָיָה רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת מִשְׁפָּטוֹ כֵּן לְהִמָּסֵר לַלּוּדִים שֶׁהֵם רָאשֵׁי הַשּׁוֹפְכִים דָּמִים

As I explained, his escape from their hands demonstrates, in this interpretation, that no guilt for bloodshed remained with him. His sale into their power was necessary to clarify this: by ordinary human reckoning, he would have been considered liable to such a fate, delivered to the Ludaei, the foremost of blood-shedders.

וְעִיקַּר אַזְהָרַת שְׁפִיכוּת דָּם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לִבְנֵי נֹחַ נִסְמְכָה לְהֶתֵּר אֲכִילַת בְּשַׂר בַּעֲלֵי חַיִּים, עַל זֶה אָמַר ״וְאַךְ אֶת דִּמְכֶם וְגוֹ׳ שֹׁפֵךְ דָּם וְגוֹ׳״, לְפִי שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ שֶׁהוּתַּר אֲכִילַת בָּשָׂר הוּתַּר גַּם כֵּן לְהָרְגוֹ לִשְׁאָר צָרְכֵי בְּנֵי אָדָם

The fundamental prohibition against shedding blood given to the children of Noach immediately follows permission to consume animal flesh. Scripture therefore says: “But your own blood, for your lives, I will require” and “Whoever sheds human blood, by man shall his blood be shed” (Bereishis 9:5–6). Having permitted the consumption of animals, the Torah also permits killing them for certain other human purposes.
דְּמָה נָפְקָא מִינָּה אֲכִילָה אוֹ שְׁאָר הֲנָאָה.
For what essential difference would there be between eating and some other benefit?

וְאָמַר דְּאָדָם אֵין מָסוּר לְאָדָם אַחֵר לְהָרְגוֹ לְצָרְכּוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁהוּתַּר אֲכִילַת בַּעֲלֵי חַיִּים, וְזֶהוּ עִיקַּר הָרְצִיחָה לְצֹרֶךְ אֲכִילָה וּבִכְלָלוֹ לִשְׁאָר הֲנָאוֹת, וְיוֹתֵר אַכְזָרִיּוּת הוּא גַּם כֵּן לִרְצוֹחַ לְאָכְלוֹ; וּלְפִיכָךְ הֵם רָאשֵׁי הָרוֹצְחִים, וְהוּא נִמְכַּר לָהֶם, וְנִתְכַּפֵּר בְּמַה שֶּׁנִּיצוֹל מִיָּדָם כִּי אֵין לוֹ מִשְׁפַּט מָוֶת

But one human being is not placed at another’s disposal to be killed for personal needs, as animals were permitted for food. This is murder for the sake of eating or other benefit; to kill a human being in order to eat him is still more cruel. Rav Tzadok therefore identifies these Ludaei as leading blood-shedders, and interprets Reish Lakish’s delivery into, and rescue from, their hands as an ordeal that established he deserved no death sentence.

וְדָבָר זֶה כְּלָל גָּדוֹל בְּכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁנִּזְכַּר בַּתַּלְמוּד כַּיּוֹצֵא בּוֹ וּבִשְׁאָר מְקוֹמוֹת בְּדִבְרֵי רז״ל, וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר בַּמִּקְרָאוֹת: מֵחֵטְא אָדָם גָּדוֹל הוּא מַה שֶּׁכְּבָר נִתְקַן עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה שְׁלֵימָה מֵאַהֲבָה עַד שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, וְלֹא נִכְתַּב אֶלָּא לְשִׁבְחָן

This is a great principle, Rav Tzadok says, for comparable reports in the Talmud, in the other teachings of Chazal, and in Scripture: if a great person’s failure has been completely repaired through repentance from love until the transgressions are transformed into merits, its being recorded can itself serve as praise.
וְזֶהוּ תֹּקֶף הַתְּשׁוּבָה בַּמַּדְרֵגָה הַגְּדוֹלָה הָרִאשׁוֹנָה, וְהוּא מַה שֶּׁגְּדוֹלִים בּוֹ מִצַּדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים, כִּי הַזְּדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת
Such is the strength of repentance on this highest initial level, where penitents may attain a rank beyond those who were always wholly righteous—because intentional sins are transformed into merits.

The exact saying inherited under “באליהו רבה פרק כה” is attested in Vayikra Rabbah 25:5, in the account of the hundred-year-old planter questioned by Hadrian: “אם זכית אכלית, ואם לאו כשם שיגעו לי אבהתי, כך אני יגע לבני” — “If I merit, I shall eat; if not, just as my forefathers labored for me, so I labor for my children.” This exact planter story and formulation were not located in the consulted Tanna Devei Eliyahu Rabbah, chapter 25; the inherited attribution in Rav Tzadok's Hebrew remains untouched pending edition collation. Taanis 23a offers a distinct but close parallel: “כי היכי דשתלו לי אבהתי — שתלי נמי לבראי” — “As my fathers planted for me, so I plant for my children.” Bava Basra 133b adds that diverting an estate away from one's children is ordinarily disapproved. Together these illuminate Rav Tzadok's distinction between a person's appropriate responsibility to posterity and his exceptional portrayal of Reish Lakish, not a general license to abandon those responsibilities.

Gittin 47a reports of Reish Lakish: “כי נח נפשיה שבק קבא דמוריקא, קרא אנפשיה: ועזבו לאחרים חילם” — “When he died he left a kav of saffron, and said about himself, ‘They leave their wealth to others’” (Tehillim 49:11). Rav Tzadok takes this small unused remainder as evidence, in this exceptional case, of a subtle spiritual deficiency. Compare Koheles 5:18: “והשליטו לאכל ממנו ולשאת את חלקו ולשמח בעמלו” — being granted the ability to enjoy one's rightful portion; and Koheles 6:2: “ולא ישליטנו האלהים לאכל ממנו כי איש נכרי יאכלנו” — having wealth but not being enabled to enjoy it. A crucial source qualification is required: Rav Tzadok invokes the maxim “אין מיתה בלא חטא,” but the conclusion of Shabbos 55b explicitly states “יש מיתה בלא חטא ויש יסורין בלא עון” and refutes Rav Ami's unrestricted claim. Thus the specific moral reading of Reish Lakish's remainder belongs to Rav Tzadok; one cannot infer another person's guilt from death, deprivation, or inheritance.
Sources: Gittin 47a; Tehillim 49:11; Shabbos 55a–b; Koheles 5:18; Koheles 6:2.

paragraphs.text: Tosafot on Gittin 47a: “קודם שחזר למוטב דמסתמא לא היה מזלזל בעצמו כל כך” — “The episode occurred before he returned to the good, for presumably he would not have degraded himself so.” Gittin 47a: “ריש לקיש זבין נפשיה ללודאי” — “Reish Lakish sold himself to the Ludaei.” Tosafot establish their chronological judgment from the episode; the Gemara itself reports the encounter without assigning Rav Tzadok’s full inner motives. Rav Tzadok argues that a fully repaired past can be recounted to honor the sage. His claim that rescue from the Ludaei definitively establishes spiritual innocence is an individual homiletic conclusion, not ordinary evidence of legal innocence or authorization to risk life.

Shabbos 55b teaches “כל האומר ראובן חטא אינו אלא טועה,” explaining the particular act through a more exact reading; Shabbos 56a likewise says “כל האומר דוד חטא אינו אלא טועה,” while identifying narrower questions surrounding the narrative. These statements do not mean that every wrong act by a great person was blameless. Rav Tzadok develops a broader hermeneutic: after complete teshuvah from love has genuinely transformed the past, recording a former failure may itself reveal praise. His direct parallel is Resisei Layla §9, Har Bracha printed pp. 8–9: “וכל מעשי אדם הוא מעשי השם יתברך ... וזה ודאי מה גדלו, כטעם זדונות נעשו כזכיות” — a theological reflection on providence and the transformative power of repentance, not a claim that wrongdoing is desirable before repentance. Compare Yoma 86b, which attributes the conversion of intentional wrongdoing into merits to repentance from love. The Gemara's specific rereadings and Rav Tzadok's generalization must be kept distinct.
Sources: Shabbos 55b; Shabbos 56a; Resisei Layla §9, Har Bracha printed pp. 8–9; Yoma 86b; Yeshayahu 26:12.

Berachos 34b: “מקום שבעלי תשובה עומדין — צדיקים גמורים אינם עומדין” — “The place where penitents stand cannot be attained by those who were always wholly righteous.” The Gemara identifies this as the view of Rav Abbahu and explicitly places it in dispute with Rav Yochanan, who interprets the verse differently. Rav Tzadok himself draws a close parallel in Yisrael Kedoshim 7:9: concerning Eliyahu, “כִּי לֹא חָטָא מֵעוֹלָם וְעַל כֵּן לֹא זָכָה לְחֵילָא יַתִּיר דְּבַעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁמּוֹשְׁכִין בְּכֹחַ טְפֵי” — “Because he never sinned, he did not attain the added strength of penitents, who draw with greater force.” This supports Rav Tzadok's description of a spiritual rung accessible through true return, but is not an uncontested hierarchy asserted by all of Chazal. Place the note at the phrase concerning penitents' height above complete tzaddikim; the separate Yoma 86b note follows the subsequent clause about sins becoming merits.
Sources: Berachos 34b; Yisrael Kedoshim 7:9.

Yoma 86b places two teachings in the name of Reish Lakish side by side. First, “גדולה תשובה שזדונות נעשות לו כשגגות” — repentance can make deliberate sins count like inadvertent mistakes; then, “גדולה תשובה שזדונות נעשות לו כזכיות” — repentance can make deliberate sins count as merits. The Gemara resolves the contrast: “לא קשיא: כאן מאהבה, כאן מיראה” — the second transformation is through repentance from love, the lesser through repentance from fear. This is Rav Tzadok's specific closing principle about genuine retrospective transformation, not an exemption from accountability and not a recommendation to commit the original transgression. The note belongs immediately after the Hebrew phrase “כי הזדונות כזכויות,” following the separate note about the spiritual standing of penitents.
Sources: Yoma 86b.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: But leaving an estate for one’s children is the way of the amei ha’aretz who occupy themselves with settling the land, or of one to whom God grants abundance and who is but a “channel” through whom God provides to others. For such a person, that is his portion, what is stored up for him above, and so too leaving his children their statute. A talmid chacham whose Torah is his craft, however, who works only for his sustenance and whose every pleasure is holy, need not stint himself to leave for his children.

items.h: סִימָן יא
Teshuvah from fear and the path to love
תשובה מיראה והעלייה לאהבה

p: (א) הַשֵּׁנִי
The second:
תְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה
repentance out of fear,
מְרַפֵּא מִכָּאן וּלְהַבָּא
heals from now onward,
אֲבָל עַל הַקּוֹדֵם
but for what came before,
אֵין מְתֻקָּן לְגַמְרֵי
it is not fully repaired,
רַק כְּבַעַל מוּם
only like one with a blemish
שֶׁנִּתְרַפֵּא
who was healed,
שֶׁמִּקְצָת שְׁמוֹ עָלָיו
whose name partly remains on him;
כֵּן הוּא בְּרַשִׁ״י
so it is in Rashi,
דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל “וּכְתִיב”
in the entry beginning “and it is written”;
וּבַגְּמָרָא (רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב)
and in the Gemara (beginning of side b)
דְּמוֹעִיל עַל הַקּוֹדֵם גַּם כֵּן
that it also avails for what came before.
לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ כִּשְׁגָגוֹת
to make it like inadvertent sins.
וְלוּלֵי דִּבְרֵי רַשִׁ״י
And were it not for Rashi’s words,
הָיָה נִרְאֶה לְפָרֵשׁ אִיפְכָּא
it would seem to explain the reverse,
דְּשׁוֹבָבִים
that “wayward ones”
דְּמֵעִיקָּרָא שׁוֹבָבִים
at first, “wayward ones,”
זֶהוּ מִיִּרְאָה
this is out of fear,
שֶׁנַּעֲשֶׂה כִּשְׁגָגוֹת
which is made like inadvertent sins,
וְעַל יְדֵי שׁוֹבָבוּת
and through waywardness.
הַיְנוּ כְּשׁוֹגֵג
meaning as inadvertent.
וְאֶרְפָּא
And “I will heal,”
דְּסִיֵּם “אֹהֲבֵם נְדָבָה”
which ends “I will love them freely,”,
הַיְנוּ מֵאַהֲבָה
means out of love,
וּרְפוּאָה דִּמְשׁוּבָתָם
and the healing of “their backsliding”
הַיְנוּ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה
means that he will not be,
כְּמוֹ שׁוֹבָב גַּם כֵּן
like one wayward either,
רַק שֶׁמֵּאַהֲבָתָם
but that out of their love
יַחֲשִׁיב הָעָוֹן
He will count the sin.
לִנְדָבָה וּלְמִצְוָה וּזְכִיּוֹת
as a freewill offering, a mitzvah, and merits.
וְאַף עַל פִּי
And although
שֶׁאֵין הַסֵּדֶר כָּאן וְכוּלֵּי
the order here, etc.
מְכֻוָּן לְסֵדֶר הַכְּתוּבִים
is not aligned with the order of the verses,
שֶׁסִּדֵּר תְּחִלָּה בְּקֻשְׁיָא
which he first arranged in the question,
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר
one can say.
דְּבְמָה דְּסִיֵּם פָּתַח
that with what he ended, he began.
וְגַם יֵשׁ לוֹמַר
And one can also say
דְּהַכְּתוּבִים נָקַט
that he took the verses,
כְּסִדְרָן בִּנְבִיאִים וּכְתוּבִים
in their order in Prophets and Writings,
וּתְרֵי עָשָׂר מְאֻחָּר
and the Twelve (Minor Prophets) come later
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ
as they said
(בָּבָא בַּתְרָא יד עַמּוּד ב),
(Bava Batra 14b),
וּבְתֵרוּץ הִקְדִּים
and in the answer he put first
מֵאַהֲבָה
“out of love,”.
שֶׁהִיא הַמְּעֻלָּה
which is the superior one.
וְזֶהוּ כְּפִי הַגִּרְסָא
And this is according to the version
שֶׁבְּעֵין יַעֲקֹב
in Ein Yaakov
(שֶׁלִּפְנֵי דְפוּס פִירְדָא)
in the copy before me, the Fürth printing
שָׁם (סִימָן עַ״ג)
there (section 73)
“וּכְתִיב אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבָתָם”,
“and it is written, ‘I will heal their backsliding,’”
וְכֵן הוּא בְּרַשִׁ״י
and so it is in Rashi
שֶׁבְּעֵין יַעֲקֹב שָׁם
in Ein Yaakov there,
וְכֵן בְּיַלְקוּט
and so in Yalkut
(יִרְמְיָה סוֹף סִימָן רִס״ט)
(Jeremiah, end of section 269)
וְהַיְנוּ קְרָא דְהוֹשֵׁעַ.
and that is the verse in Hosea.
וּלְפִי גִּרְסָא זוֹ
And according to this version
נִרְאֶה וַדַּאי הַפֵּירוּשׁ
the explanation certainly appears
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי
as I wrote,
מִדִּכְתִיב “אֹהֲבֵם”,
since it is written “I will love them,”
וְגַם מִדְּלָא מַקְשֶׁה
and also since he does not ask
מִסִּיּוּם לְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב
from the end of the verse’s wording
דְּיִרְמְיָה עַצְמוֹ
of Jeremiah itself,
אֶלָּא דְּמַיְיתֵי הָאי
but rather brings this one
מִשּׁוּם הַתֵּרוּץ
because of the answer
דְּבֵיהּ מְפֹרָשׁ אַחַר כָּךְ “אֹהֲבֵם”.
in which “I will love them” is afterward stated explicitly.
וְגַם יֵשׁ לוֹמַר
And one can also say
דְּעִקַּר הַקֻּשְׁיָא מֵהָא
that the main question is from this,
מִדִּכְתִיב “אֹהֲבֵם נְדָבָה”
since it is written “I will love them freely,”
מַשְׁמָע
implying,
דְּאֵינָם כְּשׁוֹבָבִים גַּם כֵּן
that they are not like wayward ones either,
רַק נֶחְשָׁב עוֹד לִנְדָבָה
but are further counted as freewill,
וְעַל כֵּן “אֹהֲבֵם”
and therefore “I will love them”,
וְכמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי
as I wrote;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן
which is not so
קְרָא דְיִרְמְיָה
for the verse in Jeremiah,
דְּחַד קְרָא הוּא
which is a single verse
לֹא מַפְסִיקֵיהּ לֵיהּ.
that he does not split.
וְגַם סֵיפֵיהּ
And also the end of it,
דְּ“אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבוֹתֵיכֶם”
“I will heal your backslidings,”
קָאֵי אַמִּיִּרְאָה
refers to fear,
וְאֵין רְפוּאָה גְּמוּרָה
and there is no complete healing,
רַק מִקְצָת שְׁמוֹ עָלָיו
only his name partly remains on him,
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן
which is not so
רְפוּאַת הוֹשֵׁעַ
for the healing in Hosea.
הוּא לְגַמְרֵי
which is complete.
וְנִרְאֶה סִיּוּעַ
And support appears
לְמַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי
for what I wrote
מִמֵּימְרָא הַקּוֹדֶמֶת שָׁם
from the preceding statement there
דְּמֵבִיאָה רְפוּאָה
that brings healing
מִקְּרָא דְ“אֶרְפָּא” וְגוֹמֵר
from the verse “I will heal,” etc. “,
נְדָבָה”, עַיֵּין שָׁם
“freely,” see there,
וְאַמַּאי לֹא מַיְיתֵי
and why does it not bring
קְרָא דְ“אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבוֹתֵיכֶם”
the verse “I will heal your backslidings”?
דְּיִרְמְיָה דְּקָדִים
of Jeremiah, which comes first?
אֲבָל לְמַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי נִיחָא
But according to what I wrote it is fine,
דְּהָתָם שֶׁבָּא לְבָאֵר
for there, where he comes to explain
גְּדֻלַּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה
the greatness of repentance,
נָקַט הָאִי קְרָא
he took this verse
דִּתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה הַגְּדוֹלָה
of repentance out of love, the greater.
שֶׁמְּרַפֵּאת הַקּוֹדֵם לְגַמְרֵי
which heals the earlier completely.
וְעַיֵּין בַּחִדּוּשֵׁי הָרִי״ף
And see the novellae of the Rif
שֶׁבְּעֵין יַעֲקֹב שָׁם
in Ein Yaakov there,
דִּקְדֵּק בֶּאֱמֶת
who indeed scrutinized
לְפֵירוּשׁ רַשִׁ״י
according to Rashi’s explanation
לָמָּה נָקַט הָתָם
why there he took
מִמַּעֲלַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה
the merit of repentance out of fear,
דְּאֵינָהּ כָּל כָּךְ גְּדוֹלָה
which is not so great,
עַיֵּין שָׁם
see there.
וּלְמַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי נִיחָא
and according to what I wrote it is fine.
