Rashi on Yoma 86a, s.v. “וכתיב ארפא”, writes: “משמע מכאן ואילך כבעל מום שנתרפא שמקצת שמו עליו” — “This implies healing from now onward, like a person cured of a blemish who still bears something of its former designation.” In the following gloss, “כאן מאהבה”, Rashi explains that return from love uproots the sin from its beginning. Rav Tzadok first states Rashi’s distinction and then considers reversing the reading of the verses. This note distinguishes his proposed interpretation from Rashi’s actual words; Yoma 86b separately distinguishes deliberate sins becoming inadvertent through fear from their transformation into merits through love.

paragraphs.text: Bava Basra 14b — order of Nevi’im: the baraisa lists Yirmiyah, Yechezkel, Yeshayah and then Trei Asar. It asks why Hoshea, who prophesied earlier, was not placed first, and answers that his short book was joined to the single scroll of the Twelve; if written separately it might be lost. Rashi notes that Chaggai, Zecharyah and Malachi were the last prophets, so Hoshea is counted with their collected scroll. R’ Tzadok therefore distinguishes historical chronology from canonical book-order: the Gemara’s question can cite Yirmiyah before Hoshea because that is their order in the received sequence, while its answer gives priority to love because love is the higher spiritual rung.

paragraphs.text:
Rav Tzadok reports that the Fürth Ein Yaakov before him read 'וכתיב ארפא משובתם'—the phrasing of Hoshea 14:5—rather than the received Bavli wording 'ארפא משובותיכם' from Yirmeyahu 3:22. This is a reported printed-text variant, not something we may silently impose upon the Gemara. Crucial qualification: the currently accessible Yalkut Shimoni on Yirmeyahu, remez 269, actually introduces the teaching with 'שובו בנים שובבים' and quotes 'ארפא' under that Yirmeyahu passage; it does not independently establish the Hoshea reading. Rav Tzadok himself discovers and explains that very difficulty in Se'if 2. The Fürth Ein Yaakov typography and its Rif commentary still require direct facsimile collation. The conceptual distinction he develops is his proposed interpretation, not the unopposed received text.
Sources: Hoshea 14:5; Yirmeyahu 3:22; Yoma 86a; Yalkut Shimoni on Nach, remez 269; Takanas HaShavin 11, Seif 1–2; Ein Yaakov, Fürth imprint (original variant requires facsimile collation).

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 9: וההבדל בין שוגג למזיד שהמזיד הוא עם מחשבה ורצון וזה נתבטל ע״י הדיבור ונשאר רק המעשה לבד ולכן נעשית לו כשגגות. — “The difference between an inadvertent sinner and an intentional sinner is that the intentional act is accompanied by thought and desire; this is nullified through speech, and only the act remains, so it becomes like inadvertent sins.” This directly explains why fear leaves a residue requiring fuller healing. The parallel is an explanation of Rav Tzadok’s distinction, not a quotation from RoshHashanah8.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86a and Hoshea 14:2-5: “Great is teshuvah, for it brings healing to the world,” derived from “I will heal their backsliding; I will love them freely.” The prophetic context moves from Israel’s command, “Return, O Israel,” and its verbal confession (vv. 2-4), to Hashem’s answer of healing and renewed love (v. 5). Meforshei Tanakh: Radak explains that Hashem heals the rebellion committed until now and then loves Israel with a freely given love once His anger has turned away. Metzudas David sharpens the distinction: confession can remove enmity, but it cannot by itself produce love; the renewed love is a divine gift even when Israel is not yet worthy. Malbim likewise reads a sequence — first the wound of backsliding is healed, and afterward Hashem returns not merely to pardon but to love. R’ Tzadok’s distinctive move: he reads ohavem nedavah not only as undeserved divine love but as the sign that the past itself has been transvalued: the avon becomes a nedavah, mitzvah and merit. In Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah §§9 and 11, he repeats the same order — human return, divine assistance toward complete love, and finally the former bad deeds yielding a pleasing fragrance. That parallel shows why this verse, rather than Yirmiyah’s more limited “healing,” bears the se’if’s idea of total retroactive repair.

rich.text: -5: “Great is teshuvah, for it brings healing to the world,” derived from “I will heal their backsliding; I will love them freely.” The prophetic context moves from Israel’s command, “Return, O Israel,” and its verbal confession (vv. 2-4), to Hashem’s answer of healing and renewed love (v. 5). Meforshei Tanakh: Radak explains that Hashem heals the rebellion committed until now and then loves Israel with a freely given love once His anger has turned away. Metzudas David sharpens the distinction: confession can remove enmity, but it cannot by itself produce love; the renewed love is a divine gift even when Israel is not yet worthy. Malbim likewise reads a sequence — first the wound of backsliding is healed, and afterward Hashem returns not merely to pardon but to love. R’ Tzadok’s distinctive move: he reads
not only as undeserved divine love but as the sign that the past itself has been transvalued: the avon becomes a
Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah §§9 and 11

, he repeats the same order — human return, divine assistance toward complete love, and finally the former bad deeds yielding a pleasing fragrance. That parallel shows why this verse, rather than Yirmiyah’s more limited “healing,” bears the se’if’s idea of total retroactive repair.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Teshuvah from fear heals only “from here onward” and, reaching back, recasts willful sins (zedonos) as inadvertent ones (shegagos). Yet it leaves the penitent “like a healed baal mum, a trace of whose name remains” (Rashi). Complete healing — turning the sin itself into nedavah and merit — belongs to teshuvah from love, which the verse sets after the return from fear.

p: (ב) אַךְ רָאִיתִי בְּיַלְקוּט
But I saw in Yalkut
(יִרְמְיָה שָׁם)
(Jeremiah, there)
הַגִּרְסָא בֶּאֱמֶת
that the version, indeed,
בַּמֵּימְרָא הַקּוֹדֶמֶת
in the preceding statement
מִקְּרָא דְּ“שׁוּבוּ” וְגוֹמֵר
is from the verse “Return,” etc. “,
אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבוֹתֵיכֶם” דְּיִרְמְיָה
“I will heal your backslidings” of Jeremiah,
וְשָׁם אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַגִּיהַּ,
and there it is impossible to emend,
מִדְּמַיְיתֵי לֵיהּ
since he brings it
לְהָךְ מֵימְרָא שָׁם בְּיִרְמְיָה
for that statement there, in Jeremiah,
אַמִּקְרָא זֶה
on this verse
וְלֹא בְּהוֹשֵׁעַ,
and not in Hosea;
עַל כָּרְחָךְ
you must say
דְּכָךְ הָיְתָה הַנֻּסְחָא
that so was the text
לִפְנֵי הַמְחַבֵּר
before the author.
בַּגְּמָרָא שָׁם
in the Gemara there.
וְנוּסַח הַגְּמָרָא הוּא
And the Gemara’s text is
גַּם בְּהָךְ רוּמְיָא גַּם כֵּן
also in this contradiction as well:
“וּכְתִיב אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבוֹתֵיכֶם”
“and it is written, ‘I will heal your backslidings,’”
וְהַיְנוּ סֵיפָא
and that is the end.
דְּאוֹתוֹ מִקְרָא דְּיִרְמְיָה
of that verse of Jeremiah.
וְכֵן הוּא בְּהָרִי״ף
And so it is in the Rif,
בְּעֵין יַעֲקֹב
in Ein Yaakov,
וְהוּא הִקְשָׁה
and he asked
מִקְּרָא דְּ“אֹהֲבֵם נְדָבָה”
from the verse “I will love them freely,”
דִּמְשְׁמָע מֵאַהֲבָה
which implies out of love,
וּכְתִיב גַּם כֵּן “אֶרְפָּא”
and “I will heal” is also written,
וְהַיְנוּ לְפֵירוּשׁ רַשִׁ״י
that is, according to Rashi’s explanation.
וְנִדְחָק
and he is forced into a strained reading.
אֲבָל גַּם זֶה מוֹכִיחַ
But this too proves,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי
as I wrote,
דְּהַקֻּשְׁיָא דְּ“אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבוֹתֵיכֶם”
that the question from “I will heal your backslidings”,
מַשְׁמָע דִּמְרַפֵּא גַּם הַשּׁוֹבָבוּת
implies it heals waywardness too.
וְזֶהוּ מֵאַהֲבָה
and this is out of love.
וְסֵדֶר הַכְּתוּבִים
And the order of the verses
הוּא כְּפִי סֵדֶר הַמַּדְרֵגוֹת
is according to the order of the levels,
לְאָדָם הַשָּׁב
of a person who returns,
דְּתְחִלָּה הוּא מִיִּרְאָה
for first it is from fear.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ בָּא לְמֵאַהֲבָה
and afterward he comes to love.
וּמִיִּרְאָה אָמַר “שׁוּבוּ”,
And regarding fear He said “Return,”,
תָּלָה בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם
relying on human effort,
דְּהַכֹּל בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם
for everything is in Heaven’s hands
חוּץ מִיִּרְאַת שָׁמַיִם
except fear of Heaven,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּבְרָכוֹת ל״ג סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳)
as they said (Berachos 33b, end)
מִקְּרָא דְּ“כִּי אִם לְיִרְאָה”.
from the verse “but only to fear.”
וְאַחַר כָּךְ “אֶרְפָּא”
And afterward “I will heal”
תָּלָה בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
He attributed to the Blessed Name,
כִּי מַה שֶּׁזּוֹכֶה אַחַר כָּךְ
for what one afterward merits
לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
of repentance out of love
הוּא מַה שֶּׁמִּן הַשָּׁמַיִם מְסַיְּעִין אוֹתוֹ.
is what Heaven helps him with.
וְכַיָּדוּעַ הַטַּעַם
And as the reason is known,
דְּלְאַהֲבָה אֵין צָרִיךְ
that for love there is no need for
הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם כָּל כָּךְ,
so much human effort,
רַק בָּאָה מֵמֵּילָא
but it comes of itself
אַחַר הַיִּרְאָה
after fear,
שֶׁהִיא נוּקְבָּא
— which is feminine —
“אִשָּׁה יִרְאַת ה׳”,
“a woman who fears the Lord,”,
וְאַהֲבָה בְּרָזָא דִּדְכוּרָא
and love is in the secret of the masculine.
וְדֶרֶךְ אִישׁ לַחֲזֹר וְכוּלֵּי
and it is the way of a man to go seeking (a wife), etc.
וְכָךְ בְּהוֹשֵׁעַ
And so in Hosea
פָּתַח “שׁוּבָה יִשְׂרָאֵל” וְגוֹמֵר
He began “Return, Israel,” etc.
תָּלָה בְּדִידְהוּ,
placing it on them,
וְסִיֵּם עַל זֶה
and concluded on it
“כִּי כָשַׁלְתָּ בַּעֲוֺנֶךָ”
“for you have stumbled in your iniquity,”
דְּדָרְשִׁינַן מִזֶּה (שָׁם בְּיוֹמָא)
from which we derive (there in Yoma),
דְּנַעֲשִׂין כִּשְׁגָגוֹת
that they become like inadvertent sins.
וְהַיְנוּ מִיִּרְאָה
and that is from fear.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ אָמַר “אֶרְפָּא” וְגוֹמֵר
And afterward He said “I will heal,” etc.
שֶׁיִּזְכּוּ מֵמֵּילָא אַחַר כָּךְ
that they will merit of themselves afterward
עַל יְדֵי זֶה לְאַהֲבָה
through this, to love
וְלָשׁוּב מֵאַהֲבָה
and to return out of love
עַד דְּיֵרָפֵא
until it is healed.
גַּם הַשּׁוֹבָבוּת
even the waywardness.
וְעִקַּר לְשׁוֹן רְפוּאָה
And the essence of the term “healing”,
הַיְנוּ כְּשֶׁנִּתְרַפֵּא לְגַמְרֵי
is when one is healed completely,
דְּאִם הוּא כִּשְׁגָגוֹת
for if it is like inadvertent sins
הֲרֵי גַּם הַשּׁוֹגֵג צָרִיךְ
then even the inadvertent sinner needs
סְלִיחָה וְכַפָּרָה
forgiveness and atonement,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּנָזִיר כ״ג עַמּוּד ב׳)
as they said (in Nazir 23b),
וַעֲדַיִן הוּא צָרִיךְ
and he still needs.
רְפוּאָה דִּסְלִיחָה
the healing of forgiveness.
וְעַל כֵּן מִ“אֶרְפָּא” גּוּפֵיהּ
And therefore from “I will heal” itself,
נַמִּי מְדַיֵּק
he also infers,
דִּמְשְׁמָע דְּנִתְרַפֵּא לְגַמְרֵי
that it implies one is healed completely,
וְאֵין צָרִיךְ עוֹד סְלִיחָה
and needs no further forgiveness,
וְאִם הוּא מִשּׁוֹבָבוּת וְשִׁטּוּת
whereas if it is from waywardness and folly
עַל יְדֵי רוּחַ שְׁטוּת
through a spirit of folly
דְּיֵצֶר הָרָע
of the evil inclination
עֲדַיִן נֶחְשָׁב כְּשׁוֹגֵג
it is still considered as inadvertent,
וְצָרִיךְ עוֹד לִרְפוּאָה
and still needs healing,
וְ“אֶרְפָּא” מַשְׁמָע
while “I will heal” implies
רְפוּאָה שְׁלֵמָה
complete healing
שֶׁלֹּא צָרִיךְ עוֹד אַחַר כָּךְ
so that afterward one needs no further.
לִרְפוּאָה שְׁנִיָּה
second healing.

paragraphs.text: Yalkut Shimoni, the Rif on Ein Yaakov, and R’ Tzadok’s framework: Yalkut Shimoni is a medieval anthology arranged along the verses of Tanakh. In Yirmiyah, remez 269, it places the teaching upon “Return, wayward children; I will heal your backslidings” (Yirmiyah 3:22). Because the material is attached to that verse rather than to Hoshea, its location is textual evidence that the compiler’s Gemara read the Yirmiyah wording; R’ Tzadok therefore reopens and qualifies the variant discussed in the previous se’if. The “Rif” here is R’ Yoshiyahu Pinto’s aggadic commentary Me’or Einayim on Ein Yaakov, not R’ Yitzchak Alfasi. His difficulty is that Rashi associates “I will heal” with the lesser teshuvah from fear, while “I will love them freely” plainly denotes love. R’ Tzadok turns that strain into a sequence: the human call “Return” begins in fear, and the divine “I will heal” culminates in love. Compare Machshavos Charutz §7, where he describes lower and upper teshuvah as the two heh’s of the Divine Name. The lower return prepares the vessel; the upper return completes the healing. Se’if Beis thus joins textual criticism to R’ Tzadok’s recurring two-stage map of teshuvah.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 33b — free choice, fear, and divine assistance: R’ Chanina teaches, “Everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven,” deriving it from Devarim 10:12. Rashi explains that a person’s natural circumstances — long or short life, poverty or wealth, wisdom or foolishness — are decreed, but whether one becomes righteous or wicked is entrusted to the person, before whom two paths are placed. Rambam, Shemoneh Perakim ch. 8, similarly limits “everything” to natural conditions and insists that mitzvah and aveirah remain matters of choice. Rashi to Megillah 25a adds the important nuance: Hashem can transform the heart, yet the initial preparation of the heart toward fear was handed to man. R’ Tzadok develops exactly this progression in Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Galus Mitzrayim 4:4-6: yirah is the arena of human choice and effort; ahavah can then enter the heart “of itself.” Human awakening from below is the gate, and afterward “the Holy One helps him.” Accordingly, “Return” is phrased as an imperative to man, while “I will heal” is Hashem’s answering gift.

paragraphs.text: Zoharic background to fear as “female” and love as “male”: Mishlei 31:30 supplies the phrase “a woman who fears Hashem,” while Kiddushin 2b states that it is the way of the man to seek the woman. R’ Tzadok reads these as a spiritual metaphor. In the kabbalistic map, yirah aligns with restraint, gevurah and the receptive/feminine principle; ahavah aligns with chesed, the right side and the bestowing/masculine principle. Zohar II 216a gives the controlling order: after fear rests upon a person, love — identified there with the right side — is awakened, and through love the worshipper rises and cleaves above. The metaphor therefore describes movement from disciplined receptivity to an overflowing gift; it is not a claim about the relative spiritual worth of men and women. Compare Tzidkas HaTzadik §200: revealed yirah can be awakened through a person’s own self-rebuke, whereas revealed “great love” is a gift of Hashem and is not attained by effort in the same way. Together with Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Galus Mitzrayim 4:4, this is the closest parallel to the present se’if: fear is cultivated; love comes afterward from Heaven and completes the return.

paragraphs.text: Hoshea 14:2-5, Yoma 86b, and the meforshim: The prophecy begins with Israel’s own act — “Return, O Israel, to Hashem your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity” — and proceeds through confession to Hashem’s response, “I will heal their backsliding; I will love them freely.” Yoma 86b reads “you have stumbled” as a willful sin reduced to a mere stumbling: teshuvah from fear turns zedonos into shegagos, while teshuvah from love turns them into merits; Rashi states this distinction directly. Radak explains that Hashem first heals the earlier rebellion and then loves Israel after His anger has turned away. Metzudas David notes that removal of enmity does not itself create love, so the renewed love is a divine gift. Malbim likewise reads a progression from healing to positive love. Maharsha to Yoma 86b emphasizes the added good generated by the penitent’s return. R’ Tzadok’s sharper reading is that the verse’s order maps the penitent’s ascent: human yirah first strips the sin of deliberate rebellion, and the divinely granted ahavah then heals and transforms the remaining deed. Compare Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah §§9 and 11, where he repeats the sequence of human return, heavenly assistance, and the former bad deeds ultimately producing a pleasing fragrance.

Nazir 23a (the standard daf checked directly) teaches 'אישה הפרם וה׳ יסלח לה — באשה שהפר לה בעלה והיא לא ידעה ... שהיא צריכה כפרה וסליחה': a wife who knowingly acts against her vow after her husband already annulled it, without knowing of the annulment, still needs forgiveness for her wrongful intention. R. Akiva draws the parallel of someone intending forbidden food but receiving permissible food. Thus intention may require atonement even when the intended forbidden result does not occur; an actual inadvertent act likewise cannot simply be called complete healing. Rav Tzadok's printed citation here appears as Nazir 23b, but the passage is on 23a in the verified text. Preserve the inherited Hebrew citation while recording the corrected daf in the note.
Sources: Nazir 23a, Mishnah and following baraita; Bamidbar 30:13; Takanas HaShavin 11, Seif 2 (inherited reference: Nazir 23b).

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: In the Yalkut the proof-verse of the earlier statement really is the Yirmiyah verse, and there it cannot be emended. So the Rif’s difficulty (why “I will heal” — from fear — is paired with “loving them freely” — from love) actually confirms R’ Tzadok’s reading. The order of the verse mirrors the order of the penitent’s ascent: first “Return” — from fear, which depends on man’s own effort, “for all is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven”; then “I will heal” — from love, which Heaven grants him.

p: (ג) וְגַם לְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל
And also according to what I wrote above
(רֵישׁ סִימָן א)
(beginning of section 1),
דִּרְפוּאָה מַשְׁמָע לְהַבָּא
that “healing” implies going forward,
וְעַד הֵנָּה הָיָה
and until now it was as it was
וְלֹא שֶׁנֶּעֱקַר לְמַפְרֵעַ
and not uprooted retroactively,
עַיֵּין שָׁם
see there,
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר גַּם כֵּן
one can say as well
דְּהוּא מְכֻוָּן לְמַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי
that it aligns with what I wrote
דְּקָאֵי אִרְפוּאָה
that it refers to the healing
דִּתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
of repentance out of love.
הַבָּאָה אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה
which comes after the repentance out of fear.
דְּעַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה
For through repentance out of fear,
נֶעֱקַר מַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ הָרָעָה הַקּוֹדֶמֶת
his earlier evil thought is uprooted,
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה נַעֲשֶׂה
for through this are made
מִזְּדוֹנוֹת שְׁגָגוֹת
from willful sins, inadvertent ones,
שֶׁהוּא מַעֲשֶׂה
which is an act.
בְּלֹא כַּוָּנָה וְרָצוֹן לָרָע
without intent or desire for evil.
וְדָבָר זֶה הוּא עֲקִירָה לְגַמְרֵי
And this is a complete uprooting
לְמַפְרֵעַ,
retroactively,
דְּהַמַּחֲשָׁבָה שֶׁהָיָה לָרָע
for the thought that was for evil
הוּא כְּמִי שֶׁאֵינָהּ.
is as though it does not exist.
וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר
And about this it is said
“בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא יְבֻקַּשׁ עֲוֺן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ
“On that day the iniquity of Israel will be sought, and it will not be,
וְחַטֹּאת יְהוּדָה וְלֹא תִמָּצֶאנָה”,
and the sins of Judah, and they will not be found,”
דְּעָוֺן דְּהַיְנוּ בְּמֵזִיד
for “iniquity,” meaning willful,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא ל״ו עַמּוּד ב׳)
as they said (Yoma 36b),
אֵינֶנּוּ כְּלָל
is gone entirely,
כֵּיוָן דְּנֶעֱקַר הָרָצוֹן דְּרָע
since the desire for evil is uprooted
לְגַמְרֵי לְמַפְרֵעַ.
completely, retroactively.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן “חַטֹּאת”
Not so “sins,”
דְּהוּא שׁוֹגֵג
which is inadvertent
שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה מִקֹּדֶם מֵהַמֵּזִיד
made earlier from the willful,
עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה הַקּוֹדֶמֶת
through the earlier repentance out of fear,
שֶׁהוּא הַשְׁאָרַת הַמַּעֲשֶׂה הַגּוֹלְמִית
which is the leftover raw deed,
בְּלֹא כַּוָּנָה
without intent;
זֶה נִתְרַפֵּא אַחַר כָּךְ
this is healed afterward.
עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
through repentance out of love.
וְלֹא שֶׁנֶּעֱקַר לְמַפְרֵעַ
And not uprooted retroactively
כְּאִלּוּ לֹא הָיָה מֵעוֹלָם וְאֵינֶנּוּ,
as if it never was and is gone,
דְּאִם כָּךְ
for if so,
מָה נַעֲשֶׂה כִּזְכִיּוֹת
how is it made into merits,
וְעַל כָּרְחָךְ
and you must say
דְּהַמַּעֲשֶׂה אֵין נֶעֱקֶרֶת כְּלָל
that the deed is not uprooted at all.
רַק נִתְרַפֵּאת
but healed.
וְזֶהוּ “דְּלֹא תִמָּצֶאנָה”,
And this is “they will not be found,”
לֹא דְּאֵינָהּ
not that it does not exist
רַק דְּנִתְהַפְּכָה לִזְכוּת
but that it was turned into merit,
וְאֵין הַחַטָּאת נִמְצֵאת
and the sin is not found,
שֶׁאִם הַמְקַטְרֵג יְחַפֵּשׂ אַחֲרֶיהָ
for if the accuser searches for it
לֹא יִמְצָא
he will not find it.
כֵּיוָן שֶׁנִּשְׁתַּנֵּית לִזְכוּת
since it has changed into merit.
וְאָמַר תְּחִלָּה “יִשְׂרָאֵל”,
And He said first “Israel,”
כִּי תְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה
for repentance out of fear
נִתְעוֹרְרוּ כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל לָזֶה
all Israel were awakened to
בְּמַעֲשֵׂה דָעֵגֶל
in the incident of the calf,
שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ רְאוּיִים לְאוֹתָהּ מַעֲשֶׂה
who were not fit for that act
אֶלָּא לְהוֹרוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה
but to teach repentance,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ד׳ סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳)
as they said (Avodah Zarah 4b, end),
וּתְשׁוּבָתָם הָיְתָה מִיִּרְאָה
and their repentance was out of fear
כְּשֶׁהִגִּיד לָהֶם מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
when Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, told them.
חֶטְאָם הַגָּדוֹל וְעָנְשָׁם
their great sin and its punishment.
וְעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר (שָׁם בְּפָרָשַׁת תִּשָּׂא)
And therefore it is said (there, in Parashas Tisa)
“בְּיוֹם פָּקְדִי וּפָקַדְתִּי עֲלֵיהֶם חַטָּאתָם”.
“On the day of My reckoning, I will reckon upon them their sin.” “.
חַטָּאת” הַיְנוּ שׁוֹגֵג
“Chatas” means inadvertent.
לְפִי שֶׁלֹּא נִמְחַל לְגַמְרֵי
Since it was not forgiven fully
רַק נַעֲשָׂה כְּשׁוֹגֵג
but made like inadvertent
דְּצָרִיךְ עֲדַיִן סְלִיחָה
which still requires forgiveness.
וְעֹנֶשׁ לְכַפָּרָה
and punishment for atonement.
וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
And Moses, peace be upon him,
בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ פָּעַל סְלִיחָה
by his prayer effected forgiveness,
לְאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה לְגַמְרֵי
for that hour completely,
וְעַל זֶה הָיוּ כָּל תְּפִלּוֹתָיו
and for this were all his prayers
לִסְלֹחַ לְגַמְרֵי
to forgive completely.
שֶׁלֹּא יֵחָשֵׁב גַּם שׁוֹגֵג
so that even inadvertent not be counted.
דְּגוּף הַמְּחִילָה אַחַר שֶׁשָּׁבוּ
For the forgiveness itself, after they repented,
אֵין צָרִיךְ לְהַרְבּוֹת בִּתְפִלָּה
needs no abundant prayer,
דִּכְבָר יָדוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ פְּתוּחָה
for His blessed hand is already open
לְקַבֵּל שָׁבִים
to receive returnees,
וְהַשָּׁב וּמִתְוַדֶּה מוֹחֵל לוֹ.
and one who returns and confesses is forgiven.
רַק לִהְיוֹת דַּעֲדַיִן נִשְׁאַר שׁוֹגֵג
Only because inadvertent sin still remained,
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר
therefore he said “,
חֲטָאתֶם חֲטָאָה גְדֹלָה” וְגוֹמֵר
“you have sinned a great sin,” etc. “,
בְּעַד חַטַּאתְכֶם” וְגוֹמֵר
“on behalf of your sin,” etc. “,
חָטָא הָעָם הַזֶּה חֲטָאָה” וְגוֹמֵר
“this people has sinned a sin,” etc. “,
תִּשָּׂא חַטָּאתָם” וְגוֹמֵר
“bear their sin,” etc.
הַכֹּל לְשׁוֹן חֵטְא שׁוֹגֵג
all the language of inadvertent sin,
דִּכְבָר שָׁבוּ וְנִתְחָרְטוּ בָזֶה
for they had already repented and regretted,
מִיָּד בְּבִיאַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
immediately upon Moses’s arrival.
וְדָבָר זֶה בְּדִידְהוּ תָּלְיָא
and this depends on them.
וְהַתְּפִלָּה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
And the prayer to the Blessed Name
הוּא לְזַכּוֹתָם
is to merit them
לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
to repentance out of love,
שֶׁהוּא בְּסִיּוּעַ מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם
which is with Heaven’s help,
וְשֶׁיְּכֻפַּר לְגַמְרֵי
and that it be atoned completely,
שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה עוֹד חֵטְא וְשׁוֹגֵג גַּם כֵּן
so there be no further sin, nor inadvertent either,
וְעַל זֶה לֹא הֻבְטַח לְגַמְרֵי
and about this he was not fully promised,
רַק “בְּיוֹם פָּקְדִי” וְגוֹמֵר
only “on the day of My reckoning,” etc..
דְּעֲדַיִן נִשְׁאַר חֵטְא שׁוֹגֵג שָׁמוּר
for an inadvertent sin remains reserved.

paragraphs.text:
Yirmeyahu 50:20 distinguishes the fate of iniquity from the continued existence of the person: “יבקש את עון ישראל ואיננו ... ואת חטאת יהודה ולא תמצאינה, כי אסלח לאשר אשאיר” — Israel’s iniquity will be sought and will not be, and Yehudah’s sins will not be found, because Hashem pardons the remnant. Metzudas David says the remaining guilt is cleansed through the hardship of exile and forgiven. Malbim distinguishes “avon,” associated here with idolatry and distortion of understanding, from “chatas,” the sin of appetite: the former ceases when that inclination is removed, while the latter no longer incurs a charge because of forgiveness. Yoma 36b distinguishes inadvertent chata’os, deliberate avonos, and rebellious pesha’im in the order of vidui; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1, codifies the confession. Rav Tzadok develops a further distinction: “איננו” can express uprooting of sinful will, whereas “לא תמצאינה” can express a past act whose spiritual meaning has changed through teshuvah from love. These are Rav Tzadok’s inferences, not direct statements of the verse’s commentators. A separate, illuminating parallel is Berachos 10a: Beruriah corrects Rabbi Meir with “יתמו חטאים” — “Let sins cease,” not “Let sinners cease” — and asks him to pray for his tormentors’ repentance; they repent. Maharsha on Berachos 10a raises the question how prayer for another’s teshuvah relates to free choice. Zohar, Balak 15:193–194, explains that one who confesses turns away from the side of impurity and attaches to the outstretched right hand receiving penitents; confession does not fix the person permanently as wicked. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:6–7, describes the penitent as beloved and close instead of distant. Thus the person is not identical with the sin, and the historical event need not be denied in order for the accusation to disappear. Compare Tzidkas HaTzadik §100, the related interpretation in Takanas HaShavin 15:77, and the earlier footnote’s additional parallel in Peri Tzadik, Shemini §4 (last parallel retained for printed-edition collation).
Sources: Yirmeyahu 50:20; Metzudas David and Malbim ad loc.; Yoma 36b; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1, 7:6–7; Berachos 10a; Maharsha ad loc.; Tehillim 104:35; Zohar, Balak 15:193–194; Tzidkas HaTzadik 100; Takanas HaShavin 15:77; cf. Peri Tzadik, Shemini 4 (edition collation outstanding).

Yoma 86b records two teachings of Reish Lakish. Teshuvah from fear makes “זדונות נעשות לו כשגגות” — deliberate sins become like inadvertent sins; return from love can make “זדונות נעשות לו כזכיות” — deliberate sins become merits. The Gemara reconciles the teachings as “כאן מאהבה, כאן מיראה.” Rav Tzadok explains the difference between removing culpable intent and repairing the past at its spiritual root. In Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah §9, his wording is “וההבדל בין שוגג למזיד שהמזיד הוא עם מחשבה ורצון וזה נתבטל ע״י הדיבור ונשאר רק המעשה לבד ולכן נעשית לו כשגגות” — “The difference between inadvertent and deliberate sin is that the deliberate act has thought and will; these are nullified through words of return, leaving only the action, which is therefore like inadvertent sin.” The higher completion is stated in Tzidkas HaTzadik §100: “ועל ידי זה, אחר התשובה הגמורה, הוא זוכה שזדונות נעשין זכיות” — “Through this, after complete return, he merits that deliberate sins become merits.” This is retrospective rectification, not permission to choose sin. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2, still requires abandonment of the sin, remorse, firm resolve not to repeat it, and spoken confession. In Rav Tzadok’s application, the fall can become the occasion for deeper longing, humility, and closeness; the act is not retroactively declared permissible.
Sources: Yoma 86b; Hoshea 14:2; Yechezkel 33:19; Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 9; Tzidkas HaTzadik 100; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2.

rich.text: Yoma 86b records two teachings of Reish Lakish. Teshuvah from fear makes “זדונות נעשות לו כשגגות” — deliberate sins become like inadvertent sins; return from love can make “זדונות נעשות לו כזכיות” — deliberate sins become merits. The Gemara reconciles the teachings as “כאן מאהבה, כאן מיראה.” Rav Tzadok explains the difference between removing culpable intent and repairing the past at its spiritual root. In Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah §9, his wording is “וההבדל בין שוגג למזיד שהמזיד הוא עם מחשבה ורצון וזה נתבטל ע״י הדיבור ונשאר רק המעשה לבד ולכן נעשית לו כשגגות” — “The difference between inadvertent and deliberate sin is that the deliberate act has thought and will; these are nullified through words of return, leaving only the action, which is therefore like inadvertent sin.” The higher completion is stated in Tzidkas HaTzadik §100: “ועל ידי זה, אחר התשובה הגמורה, הוא זוכה שזדונות נעשין זכיות” — “Through this, after complete return, he merits that deliberate sins become merits.” This is retrospective rectification, not permission to choose sin. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2, still requires abandonment of the sin, remorse, firm resolve not to repeat it, and spoken confession. In Rav Tzadok’s application, the fall can become the occasion for deeper longing, humility, and closeness; the act is not retroactively declared permissible.
Yoma 86b; Hoshea 14:2; Yechezkel 33:19; Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 9; Tzidkas HaTzadik 100; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2.

Avodah Zarah 4b–5a says that the Golden Calf became a communal precedent through which later sinners learn that teshuvah remains open. In the paired teaching, David serves as the example for the individual. The Gemara emphasizes that the nation was not disposed to such a fall in its elevated state, and frames the story as opening the path of return; it does NOT declare idolatry permissible or eliminate human responsibility. Rav Tzadok applies this to the two stages of the Golden Calf's repair: repentance from fear first converts the intentional quality into an inadvertent sin, while the subsequent prayers of Moshe seek the further forgiveness still needed. Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah §18 states this distinction explicitly, including the remaining liability conveyed by 'וביום פקדי'.
Sources: Avodah Zarah 4b–5a; Shemos 32:30–34; Yoma 86a–b; Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 18; Takanas HaShavin 11, Seif 3.

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 18: וכאשר המזיד מתחרט במחשבתו אחר החטא אז נמחה החטא של המחשבה ונשאר רק המעשה בלבד כשוגג. ועל גוף מעשה העון נצרך לזה הד׳ חילוקי כפרה כמו שאז״ל. וכמו כן מצינו בתוה״ק במעשה העגל שמיד ביקש משה רחמים ויחל משה וגו׳ מפני שידע שמיד הרהרו ישראל בתשובה ולכן פעל וינחם ה׳ על הרעה שנעשה כשגגות. — “When the intentional sinner regrets the sin in his thought, the sin of thought is erased, and only the act remains, like an inadvertent sin. The act of the sin itself requires the four divisions of atonement, as our Sages said. Likewise, in the Torah’s account of the Golden Calf, Moses immediately sought mercy—“Moses pleaded”—because he knew that Israel immediately entertained repentance; he therefore achieved “the Lord relented of the evil,” since it had become like inadvertent sins.” This is the precise parallel for Rav Tzadok’s distinction between immediate acceptance and the still unrectified deed; the following sentence there expressly connects the latter with “on the day I visit.”

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Teshuvah from fear uproots the evil intention that accompanied the earlier act. The willful sin is therefore reclassified as inadvertent, leaving the deed without its former rebellious will. This is a genuine retroactive uprooting, as expressed in the promise that Israel’s iniquity will be sought and not found (Yirmiyah 50:20).

p: (ד) אֲבָל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
But King David, peace be upon him,
הֵקִים עֻלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה הַגְּמוּרָה
raised up the yoke of complete repentance,
לְתַקֵּן לְגַמְרֵי
to repair completely,
וְזֶהוּ מִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת
and this is the attribute of kingship
שֶׁזָּכָה יְהוּדָה
that Judah merited,
אֲשֶׁר גָּבַר בְּאֶחָיו
who prevailed over his brothers
בִּכְבִישַׁת הַיֵּצֶר
in conquering the inclination.
לְהוֹדוֹת אַחַר הַחֵטְא
to confess after the sin.
דְּזֶה נֶחְשָׁב יוֹתֵר
For this is considered greater,
מִכְּבִישַׁת הַיֵּצֶר דְּיוֹסֵף
than Joseph’s conquering of the inclination,
שֶׁכָּבַשׁ בְּלֹא חֵטְא כְּלָל
who conquered without any sin
וְנוֹסַף לוֹ רַק אוֹת אֶחָד
and only one letter was added to him,
מִשְּׁמוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
from the name of the Holy One, Blessed Be He,
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן יְהוּדָה
unlike Judah,
דְּנִקְרָא כֻּלּוֹ
who is called entirely
עַל שְׁמוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
by the name of the Holy One, Blessed Be He,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסוֹטָה י׳ עַמּוּד ב׳)).
as they said (Sotah 10b).
כִּי הוּא זָכָה
For he merited
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה
that
חֶטְאוֹ נֶחְשָׁב לִזְכוּת גָּדוֹל
— his sin would be counted as a great merit —
בְּרִיאַת אוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ
the creation of the Messiah’s light,
שֶׁיָּצָא מֵאוֹתָהּ מַעֲשֶׂה
which came out of that act,
דְּאֵין זְכוּת גָּדוֹל מִזֶּה
for there is no greater merit than this,
וְזֶהוּ גְּבוּרָה יוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלָה
and this is a greater strength,
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה גַּם הָרַע עַצְמוֹ
that even the evil itself.
נֶהְפָּךְ לְטוֹב מְאֹד
be turned into very good.
וְיוֹסֵף כְּשֶׁנִּקְרָא יְהוֹסֵף
And Joseph, when he was called Yehosef,
עֲדַיִן חָסֵר לוֹ הֵ״א אַחֲרוֹנָה
still lacked the final Hei,
שֶׁבּוֹ נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
with which this world was created,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּמְנָחוֹת ק״ט עַמּוּד ב׳),
as they said (Menachos 29b),
שֶׁשָּׁם הַפֶּתַח פָּתוּחַ לָצֵאת
for there the opening is open to exit,
לָבֹא לִטַמֵּא דְּפוֹתְחִין לוֹ,
for one who comes to defile himself, they open for him,
וְתָלְיָא כַּרְעֵיהּ
and its leg hangs.
לְבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה
for the penitent.
וּכְבִישַׁת הַיֵּצֶר לְגַמְרֵי
And conquering the inclination completely
וְלִהְיוֹת צַדִּיק גָּמוּר
and being a perfect tzaddik,
לֹא כָּל אָדָם זוֹכֶה
not every person merits,
וְ"אֵין אָדָם צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ",
“and there is no righteous man on earth,”,
וּמָה יַעֲשֶׂה מִי שֶׁעָבַר וְחָטָא
and what shall one do who has transgressed and sinned,
וַהֲרֵי הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כֻּלּוֹ
and this world, entirely,
לְפִי זֶה מְרֻחָק מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
by this account is distant from the Blessed Name
מִצַּד הַחֲטָאִים שֶׁבּוֹ.
because of the sins in it.
אֲבָל יְהוּדָה גָּבַר לְבָרֵר
But Judah prevailed to clarify
דְּאֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ
that there is nothing else besides Him
וְהַכֹּל מֵאֲמִתּוּת רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,
and everything stems from His blessed true will,
כְּשֶׁמִּתְבָּרֵר אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה
when it becomes clear after repentance
דְּהַחֲטָאִים הֵם זְכֻיּוֹת גְּדוֹלוֹת
that the sins are great merits
וַעֲשִׂיַּת רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ.
and the doing of His will, blessed be His name.
וּבָזֶה נִתְמַלֵּא הַשֵּׁם שָׁלֵם אֶצְלוֹ,
And by this the Name was filled whole with him,
שֶׁגַּם עִנְיְנֵי הָאַרְצִיִּים וְגַשְׁמִיִּים שֶׁלּוֹ
for even his earthly and bodily matters
בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
in this world
שֶׁנִּרְאִים כְּרִחוּק מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
that appear as distance from the Blessed Name.
אַדְּרַבָּא הֵן הֵם תַּכְלִית הַקֵּרוּב
on the contrary, they are the ultimate closeness.
וְהוּא הָיָה הַמַּתְחִיל
And he was the one who began,
בְּוִדּוּי וְהוֹדָאָה עַל חֵטְא
with confession and admission of sin,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסוֹטָה י׳ עַמּוּד ב׳)
as they said (Sotah 10),
"מִי גָּרַם לִרְאוּבֵן שֶׁיּוֹדֶה, יְהוּדָה".
“Who caused Reuben to confess? Judah.”
וְזֶהוּ עִקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה
And this is the essence of repentance:
הַוִּדּוּי דְּבָרִים
verbal confession,
לְהִתְחָרֵט וְלִכָּלֵם
to regret and be ashamed
עַל יְדֵי זֶה מֵעֲוֺנוֹ,
through this over one’s sin,
וְכמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
and as it is said of King David, peace be upon him,
כְּשֶׁאָמַר לְנָתָן "חָטָאתִי לַה׳",
when he said to Nathan, “I have sinned to the Lord,”
מִיָּד אָמַר לוֹ
immediately he told him ".
גַּם ה׳ הֶעֱבִיר חַטָּאתְךָ" וְגוֹמֵר
“The Lord has also removed your sin,” etc.
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁקָּפַץ שִׁבְטוֹ שֶׁל יְהוּדָה
And this is why the tribe of Judah
תְּחִלָּה לַיָּם
first leaped into the sea,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם לז עַמּוּד א).
as they said (there, 37a).
דְּהַיָּם
For the sea,
אֲרוֹנוֹ שֶׁל יוֹסֵף רָאָה וַיָּנֹס
saw Joseph’s coffin and fled,
כִּי עֹנֶשׁ הַטְּבִיעָה בַּמַּיִם
for the punishment of drowning in water
הוּא בִּשְׁבִיל קִלְקוּל הַבְּרִית
is for corruption of the covenant,
כְּדַאֲשְׁכַּחְנָן בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל
as we find in the generation of the Flood,
וְכֵן עֹנֶשׁ אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ בְּחֶנֶק
and so the punishment for adultery with a married woman is strangulation,
וְדִינוֹ לִטְבֹּעַ בַּנָּהָר
and its corresponding heavenly punishment is drowning in the river,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין ל״ז עַמּוּד ב׳)
as they said (Sanhedrin 37b),
וְיוֹסֵף דְּלֹא חָטָא כְּלָל
and Joseph, who did not sin at all,
בָּרַח מִמֶּנּוּ.
fled from it.
וִיהוּדָה שֶׁחָטָא וְשָׁב
And Judah, who sinned and repented,
קָפַץ לְתוֹכוֹ
leaped into it,
קֹדֶם שֶׁנִּקְרַע וְאַחַר כָּךְ נִקְרַע
before it split, and afterward it split,
וְהַקְּפִיצָה הָיָה
and the leap was
דִּמְקַבֵּל עַל עַצְמוֹ
that he accepted upon himself
עֹנֶשׁ שָׁמַיִם
Heavenly punishment
אִם הוּא מְחֻיָּב בְּכָךְ.
if he is liable for it.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Sotah 10b and 36b-37a: Sotah 10b reads Yehudah's admission, 'She is more righteous than I' (Bereishis 38:26), as a public sanctification of Heaven's Name. Yehudah therefore merited that all four letters of the Divine Name appear in Yehudah, with the additional dalet; Yosef, who sanctified the Name privately by resisting Potiphar's wife, received one added letter - the heh of Yehosef (Tehillim 81:6), not a yod. Sotah 36b-37a gives the parallel formulation at the Sea: Yosef's private sanctification is contrasted with Yehudah's public sanctification through Nachshon's descent. Rashi on Bereishis 38:26 adds the Midrashic background to mimmeni: a Heavenly voice declared, 'From Me' these hidden events came, because kings were destined to descend from Tamar. R' Tzadok fuses the two sugyos: public confession is itself Kiddush Hashem, and the tribe's leap into the Sea reveals that confession in national action.

paragraphs.text:
Avodah Zarah 5a presents David as the model for a lone sinner's path to teshuvah, in contrast to Israel as a community. I Divrei HaYamim 5:2 states that Yehudah prevailed over his brothers and provided the ruler while the firstborn right belonged to Yosef. Sotah 10b and 36b distinguish Yehudah's public confession and sanctification of the Divine Name from Yosef's private sanctification, expressed in their names. Rav Tzadok reads the royal strength of Yehudah as the ability to take responsibility for an actual sin and transform its result through teshuvah from love, as opposed to Yosef's guarding against the sin in the first place. This is Rav Tzadok's development of the verses and sugyos, not a direct quotation of all these implications from a single source. The older note's suggestion of an Ohr HaChammah gloss on Zohar I 206a is retained as an unresolved bibliographic lead, not an attested quotation.
Sources: Avodah Zarah 4b–5a; I Divrei HaYamim 5:2; Sotah 10b, 36b; Bereishis 38:26; Takanas HaShavin 11, Seif 4; cf. Ohr HaChammah on Zohar I 206a (unverified bibliographic lead).

paragraphs.text:
The letter hei of this world has an opening below, and its suspended left leg provides another opening for one returning in teshuvah. Menachos 29b states, 'ומאי טעמא תליא כרעיה? דאי הדר בתשובה מעיילי ליה' — Why is its leg suspended? If one returns in repentance, he is brought in. This is the correct location of Rav Tzadok's letter symbolism. The available digital Hebrew witness of Takanas HaShavin 11 reads '(במנחות ק״ט ב)' (109b); the source teaching is verified at 29b. This apparent folio discrepancy must be recorded without claiming a facsimile has been collated. Bereishis Rabbah 85:1 says that while Yehudah's family underwent crisis, Hashem was preparing the light of the Messiah. Pri Tzadik, Bereishis 14 and Shemos 3 expressly connect the emergence of goodness from darkness with teshuvah from love, which transforms deliberate sins into merits. The deed is not characterized as good before repentance: Rav Tzadok describes the subsequent transformation.
Sources: Menachos 29b; available Takanas HaShavin 11 Hebrew reading '(במנחות ק"ט ב)' (unverified against printed facsimile); Bereishis Rabbah 85:1; Pri Tzadik, Bereishis 14; Pri Tzadik, Shemos 3; Yoma 86b.

paragraphs.text:
Machshavos Charutz §7, paragraph 15, explicitly contrasts Yosef's gevurah directed against the forces of the nations and appetite with 'יהודה גבר באחיו': Yehudah's more inward mastery among his own brothers. Peri Tzadik, Pinchas §15 explains the covenantal integrity embodied in Yosef and David's mission to demonstrate teshuvah for the individual. In Siman 11 Rav Tzadok does not minimize Yosef's restraint; he explains why Yehudah's public admission, followed by rectification, supplies a necessary route for someone who has already fallen. This parallel fits after his argument is developed, where the sins can be transformed into merits, rather than being bunched together with the earlier note on the general phrase 'very good'.
Sources: Machshavot Charutz 7:15; Peri Tzadik, Pinchas 15; I Divrei HaYamim 5:2; Sotah 10b; Avodah Zarah 5a; Takanas HaShavin 11, Seif 4.

paragraphs.text:
Rav Tzadok's 'everything is from His true will' must be read only retrospectively, after sincere teshuvah. Devarim 4:35 declares 'אין עוד מלבדו', while Koheles 7:20 describes human frailty. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 5:1, nevertheless insists that an individual freely chooses good or evil; Divine sovereignty cannot license deliberate sin. Pri Tzadik, Bereishis 14 expressly cautions that one should not infer that Hashem desires the deeds of the wicked: the acts become 'טוב מאד' only when rectified through teshuvah from love. Resisei Layla §9 similarly connects the profound Divine understanding of human deeds with the ultimate transformation of wrongdoing into merit; neither passage permits a person to plan a sin. Rav Tzadok's point here is that the very distance once produced by wrongdoing can, through actual teshuvah, lead to deeper closeness.
Sources: Devarim 4:35; Koheles 7:20; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 5:1; Pri Tzadik, Bereishis 14; Resisei Layla 9; Yoma 86b. The older invocation of Resisei Layla §52 concerning Bilaam/Shittim was not verified in the cited section and is not retained as source evidence.

paragraphs.text:
The act of Yehudah's confession supplies a public pattern of teshuvah later exemplified by David. Avodah Zarah 5a teaches that David's episode shows an individual who sins the path to repentance; Sotah 7b links Reuven's confession to Yehudah's precedent, and Sotah 10b presents Yehudah's public acknowledgment as sanctifying the Divine Name. Likkutei Maamarim, Upon Completion of the Talmud §13 explicitly contrasts Yosef's 'לאכפיא' (restraining evil before acting) with Yehudah's 'לאהפכא' (transforming the bitterness of a prior fall). Tzidkat HaTzadik §254 describes David's particular trial as involving desire and kingship; it should not be quoted as saying that David's 'perpetual incompletion' is the teaching's exact language. Rav Tzadok's developed argument here is not that transgression is desirable, but that responsible confession and complete teshuvah can reveal a kind of public Kiddush Hashem unattainable through mere concealment of the failure.
Sources: Avodah Zarah 5a; Sotah 7b, 10b; II Shmuel 12:13; Likkutei Maamarim, Upon Completion of the Talmud 13; Tzidkat HaTzadik 254; Takanas HaShavin 11:4.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Vidui, shame, and Kiddush Hashem: Sotah 7b says, ‘Who caused Reuven to confess? Yehudah,’ with parallels at Bava Kamma 92a and Makkos 11b; Sotah 10b adds that Yehudah’s public admission sanctified Heaven’s Name. Shmuel II 12:13 records David’s ‘I have sinned to Hashem’ and Nasan’s immediate assurance of forgiveness. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1 and 2:2, defines teshuvah as abandoning the sin, regret, resolve, and verbal confession. Berachos 12b deepens R’ Tzadok’s phrase ‘to regret and be ashamed’: Rav teaches that one who sins and is ashamed is forgiven, first from Yechezkel 16:63 and then from Shaul, whose shame over Nov kept him from mentioning the Urim veTumim; ‘tomorrow you and your sons will be with me’ is read as his restoration among the righteous. Vidui therefore converts concealed failure into open submission: shame shows that the sinner no longer identifies with the act, and public confession can become Kiddush Hashem.

paragraphs.text:
Sotah 36b–37a preserves a dispute about which tribe entered the Sea first: R. Meir describes Binyamin, while R. Yehudah describes Nachshon ben Aminadav of Yehudah entering while the other tribes hesitated. The sugya's praise of Yehudah's daring is tied to his subsequent rule. Another Midrashic tradition (Midrash Tehillim on Tehillim 114) says that the Sea saw Yosef's coffin and fled, echoing Yosef's flight from temptation (Bereishis 39:12). Sanhedrin 37b states that one liable to chenek may die by drowning after the cessation of judicial executions; this is the legal analogy employed by Rav Tzadok. Rav Tzadok himself draws the further contrast: Yosef resisted the transgression before it happened, whereas Yehudah, having confessed, willingly entered the water even if punishment was due. Neither the Gemara nor the Midrash explicitly states this entire combined interpretation. The earlier footnote's specific Kli Yakar attribution was not independently located at the claimed Exodus source and is withheld rather than presented as an exact quotation.
Sources: Sotah 36b–37a; Tehillim 114:3; Midrash Tehillim 114:4; Bereishis 39:12; Sanhedrin 37b; Takanas HaShavin 11:4–5. Kli Yakar cross-reference requires original-section confirmation.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: David — “the man who raised up the yoke of teshuvah” (Avodah Zarah 5a) — attained complete rectification. This is malchus, which Yehudah merited by “prevailing over his brothers” in subduing the yetzer to confess after sinning — reckoned greater than Yosef’s mastery, who conquered without any sin and gained but one letter of the Divine Name, whereas Yehudah is called entirely by the Name (Sotah 10b). For Yehudah merited that his very sin become a great merit — the emergence of Mashiach’s light from that deed.

p: (ה) וְזֶהוּ הַתְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
And this is repentance out of love,
שֶׁלֹּא מִיִּרְאַת עֹנֶשׁ,
not from fear of punishment,
דְּאַדְרַבָּא מְקַבֵּל עָלָיו הָעֹנֶשׁ
for on the contrary he accepts the punishment upon himself
בְּרְצוֹנוֹ
willingly
אִם הוּא רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כָּךְ.
if such is the will of the Blessed Name.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מִמֵּילָא
And through this, of itself,
גַּם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַעֲבִיר
the Blessed Name also removes,
חַטָּאתוֹ הַשּׁוֹגֵג גַּם כֵּן
his inadvertent sin as well,
וְנִמְחַל הָעֹנֶשׁ לְגַמְרֵי
and the punishment is entirely forgiven,
וְאַדְרַבָּא זוֹכֶה עַל יְדֵי זֶה
and on the contrary through this he merits
לִישׁוּעָה וָנֵס
salvation and a miracle
וְלִינָּצֵל מֵאוֹתוֹ עֹנֶשׁ,
and to be saved from that punishment,
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה זָכָה גַּם כֵּן לְמַלְכוּת
and through this he also merited kingship,
כְּדְאִיתָא (בְּסוֹטָה שָׁם).
as stated (in Sotah 37a).
כִּי מִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת
For the attribute of kingship
הִיא ה׳ אַחֲרוֹנָה דְּשֵׁם
is the final Hei of the Name,
כַּנּוֹדָע
as is known,
כִּי זֶהוּ מִדַּת מַלְכוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ
for this is the attribute of His blessed kingship,
אֲשֶׁר בַּכֹּל מָשָׁלָה
which rules over all,
גַּם בַּמַּדְרֵגוֹת הַיּוֹתֵר תַּחְתּוֹנִים
even in the lowest levels
הַכֹּל הוּא מֵהַנְהָגָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ
everything is from His blessed guidance
וְאֵין שׁוּם דָּבָר
and nothing at all is
חוּץ לְמֶמְשַׁלְתּוֹ וְהַנְהָגָתוֹ.
outside His dominion and guidance.
וּמַלְכוּת יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא מַה שֶּׁחָלַק
And the kingship of Israel is what He apportioned,
מִכְּבוֹדוֹ לְבָשָׂר וָדָם
of His glory to flesh and blood,
וְזָכוּ לָהּ עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
and they merited it through repentance out of love,
שֶׁנַּעֲשׂוּ גַּם הַזְּדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת
in which even the willful sins became like merits
וְנִתְבָּרֵר דְּאֵין שׁוּם דָּבָר
and it became clear that nothing is
נֶגֶד כְּבוֹד מַלְכוּתוֹ.
against His glorious kingship.
וְאַדְרַבָּא עַל יְדֵי הַחֵטְא
And on the contrary, through the sin,
אַחַר שֶׁהוֹדָה בָזֶה
after he confessed it,
נִתְקַדֵּשׁ שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא
the Heavenly Name was sanctified publicly,
וְגָרַם בּוֹ קִדּוּשׁ שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם
and he caused thereby a sanctification of the Heavenly Name
יוֹתֵר מִמַּה שֶּׁפָּעַל יוֹסֵף
greater than what Joseph achieved.
בִּכְבִישָׁה מֵחֵטְא
by conquering the temptation to sin.
וְזֶהוּ כָּל עִנְיַן הִתְגַּלּוּת
And this is the whole matter of the revelation of
כְּבוֹד מַלְכוּתוֹ
the glory of His kingship,
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה קִדּוּשׁ שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם בָּעוֹלָם
that there be sanctification of the Heavenly Name in the world,
וּלְכָךְ נִתְיַחֵס
and therefore is ascribed.
תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה לִיהוּדָה
repentance out of love to Judah.
וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָאִים
And all Israel are called,
עַל שֵׁם יְהוּדָה
after Judah,
דְּ"מִקֶּרֶב אַחֶיךָ תָּקִים עָלֶיךָ מֶלֶךְ" כְּתִיב
for it is written “from among your brothers you shall set a king over you,”
דְּהַקָּמָתוֹ הוּא מִקֶּרֶב
for his establishment is from within,
וּמֵהַפְּנִימִיּוּת שֶׁל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל
and from the inwardness of all Israel,
רַק שֶׁאֶצְלָם הוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם
only that with them it is hidden
וּבְקֶרֶב לִבָּם
and within their hearts.
וְאֶצְלוֹ הוּא בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת וּבַפֹּעַל
while with him it is revealed and in action.
וְעַל יְדֵי הִתְעוֹרְרוּתוֹ
And through his awakening
נִתְעוֹרֵר גַּם כֵּן תְּשׁוּבָה
repentance is also awakened,
בְּכָל הַלְּבָבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
in all the hearts of the children of Israel,
שֶׁגַּם כְּלַל הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל
for the entire community of Israel too,
הִיא הָרְמוּזָה בְּה׳ אַחֲרוֹנָה דְּשֵׁם
is alluded to in the final Hei of the Name,
כַּאֲשֶׁר שָׁבִים לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת
when they truly return to the Blessed Name
וּמִתְאַחֲדִים בְּמִדַּת מַלְכוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,
and unite in His blessed attribute of kingship,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַכְּפִירָה בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
which is the denial of idolatry,
שֶׁאֵין שׁוּם כֹּחַ שְׁלִיטָה וּמֶמְשָׁלָה
that there is no power of rule or dominion
מִבִּלְעָדָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ,
apart from Him, blessed,
וְכָל הַכּוֹפֵר בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
and whoever denies idolatry
נִקְרָא יְהוּדִי
is called a Jew,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּמְגִלָּה י״ג רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳
as they said in Megillah (13a),
שֶׁזֶּהוּ קְדֻשָּׁתוֹ שֶׁל יְהוּדָה
for this is the holiness of Judah.
שֶׁנִּקְרָא כֻּלּוֹ עַל שֵׁם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
who is called entirely by the Name of the Holy One, Blessed Be He.
וְכֵן כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל
And so all Israel
דִּמְסָרֵי נַפְשַׁיְיהוּ
who give up their lives
עַל קִדּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם
for sanctification of the Name,
לְקַדֵּשׁ שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא
to sanctify the Heavenly Name publicly,
שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׁגִּיחַ בְּמֶלֶךְ בָּשָׂר וָדָם
not to heed a king of flesh and blood

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Primary source, halachic framework, and R' Tzadok: Yoma 86b:3 resolves two statements of Reish Lakish: teshuvah from fear reduces deliberate sins to inadvertent ones, whereas teshuvah from love transforms them into merits. Sforno on Shemos 34:7 reads venakeh in this light: complete cleansing belongs to those who return from love, whose sins are accounted as merits. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2, defines the formal elements of teshuvah as abandoning the sin, removing it from one's thought, resolving never to repeat it, regretting the past, and verbal confession. R' Tzadok's willing acceptance of punishment is therefore not an additional judicial condition or a call to seek suffering; it describes the inner surrender of love, in which the penitent wants only Hashem's will. Resisei Layla section 38 explains 'with all your soul' (Devarim 6:5) as surrendering even one's spiritual self-interest and consenting to lose the soul itself for the Divine will. That parallel clarifies the se'if: the penitent accepts whatever Hashem wills, and precisely this bitul opens the change from shogeg residue to complete merit.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Sotah 36b–37a — Yehudah, the Sea, and kingship: R' Yehudah teaches that the tribes hesitated until Nachshon ben Aminadav and the tribe of Yehudah entered the Sea. Tehillim 69 is read as Nachshon's prayer while the waters reached him, and Hashem then told Moshe, 'Speak to the children of Israel that they travel' (Shemos 14:15). The Gemara concludes that for this reason Yehudah merited dominion in Israel, expounding Tehillim 114:2–3: 'Yehudah became His sanctuary; Israel His dominion; the sea saw and fled.' R' Tzadok reads the descent as willing acceptance of Heaven's judgment: precisely the submission that does not flee punishment becomes the act through which the decree is removed and malchus is revealed.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Zohar — the final heh as Malchus: Zohar, Tzav 56:1 identifies the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven with the final heh of the Divine Name, which is called Malchus. The standard sefirotic correspondence is yud–Chochmah, first heh–Binah, vav–the six middos, and final heh–Malchus (see Sulam on Zohar, Vayikra 285:1). Malchus receives the higher lights and reveals them below; therefore it is the letter associated with the lowest and most manifest realm. R' Tzadok uses this kabbalistic map as the architecture of teshuvah: the final heh reveals that Divine kingship reaches the very place that appeared most distant, so even a fall can become the site of renewed revelation.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Tehillim 103:19 and the reach of Malchus: The full verse reads, 'Hashem established His throne in the heavens, and His kingship rules over all.' In peshat, the heavenly throne is followed by universal sovereignty over every part of creation. Tikkunei Zohar 40b:2 says that no action among the lower realms occurs except through Malchus, applying this verse; Tikkunei Zohar 56b:10 identifies the Shechinah with the same kingship and describes it as ruling even over the realm of the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil. R' Tzadok therefore stresses the lowest levels: evil has no independent sovereignty, though human free choice and responsibility remain fully real. Teshuvah uncovers the deeper rule that was concealed within the apparent opposition.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Berachos 58a — earthly kingship as borrowed glory: The Gemara's exact blessing over a Jewish king is 'Who shared of His glory with those who fear Him,' while over a gentile king it is 'Who gave of His glory to flesh and blood.' The same passage teaches, 'earthly kingship is patterned after heavenly kingship,' and urges one to see kings so that the future distinction can be recognized. Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 224:8, codifies these blessings. R' Tzadok's phrase compresses the two Talmudic formulas; it is not presented as the verbatim text of the berachah. His point is that human sovereignty is never autonomous: Israel's malchus is a portion of Divine glory entrusted to human beings and is legitimate only insofar as it reveals Heaven's kingship.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Sotah 36b and 10b — private and public Kiddush Hashem: Sotah 36b contrasts Yosef, who sanctified Heaven's Name in private and received one added heh in Yehosef, with Yehudah, who sanctified the Name publicly and contains the entire four-letter Name within Yehudah. The Gemara there identifies the public act with Yehudah's descent into the Sea. Sotah 10b supplies the complementary personal model: Yehudah publicly admitted concerning Tamar, 'She is more righteous than I,' and a Heavenly voice affirmed his confession. R' Tzadok joins these two expressions of Yehudah: entering judgment publicly and confessing after failure reveal a greater Kiddush Hashem than hidden mastery alone, because the power of teshuvah itself becomes manifest before others.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Gemara and meforshim on public sanctification and kingship: Sotah 36b:10 contrasts Yosef, who sanctified Heaven's Name privately and received one added letter in Yehosef, with Yehudah, who sanctified the Name publicly and bears the entire four-letter Name within Yehudah. Rashi there identifies Yehudah's public act with the descent into the Sea. Sotah 37a:6 then concludes that Yehudah merited dominion in Israel, expounding Tehillim 114:2, 'Yehudah became His sanctuary; Israel, His dominions.' Maharal, Netivos Olam, Netiv Ahavas Hashem 2:2, explains the contrast as one of spiritual form: Yosef's attachment is hidden, while Yehudah's blessing and Kiddush Hashem are revealed before all. Ben Yehoyada on Sotah 37a adds that the leap did not first create Yehudah's royal destiny; it secured the continuity of that kingship. R' Tzadok joins this national act to the personal act of teshuvah: willing entry into judgment becomes public Kiddush Hashem, and the same submission that accepts the decree becomes the source of rescue, miracle, and enduring malchus.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Peshat, halachah, Kabbalah, and R' Tzadok: Devarim 17:15 commands, 'From among your brethren shall you set a king over yourself.' In its plain halachic use, 'from among' sets a boundary on appointment: Rambam, Hilchos Melachim 1:4, applies it to the king and other positions of authority. R' Tzadok then reads mikerev homiletically as 'from the inward core': the king actualizes a royal point hidden within the people. Berachos 58a, codified in Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 224:8, calls the blessing over a Jewish king 'Who apportioned of His glory to those who fear Him,' while the blessing over a gentile king says 'Who gave of His glory to flesh and blood.' The distinction supports R' Tzadok's point that Israel's kingship participates in Divine glory rather than standing as an autonomous power. The Zohar, Tzav 8:56, identifies the yoke of Heaven's kingship with the final heh; Zohar, Introduction 30:241, identifies Knesses Yisrael with that final heh as it receives and unites the higher powers. Machshavot Charutz 7:18 supplies R' Tzadok's parallel: every Jewish soul includes both Yosef and Yehudah, but Yehudah is Israel's primary name and the root of Knesses Yisrael because his power repairs deficiency and creates renewal after a fall.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Megillah 13a — why 'Yehudi' means rejection of idolatry: Mordechai belonged to Binyamin, yet Megillas Esther calls him a Yehudi. The Gemara answers that anyone who repudiates idolatry is called a Yehudi, and cites Daniel 3:12, where Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah are called 'Jewish men' because they refused the royal idol. Maharal, Ohr Chadash 2:5, explains that the name marks exclusive allegiance to the One God against every competing power. R' Tzadok connects this to Yehudah's name, which contains the Divine Name: the holiness of Yehudah is the recognition that no rule exists independently of Hashem. In Yisrael Kedoshim he similarly treats Yehudi as Israel's name of self-surrender and Kiddush Hashem.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Halachah of Kiddush Hashem: Vayikra 22:32 commands, 'I shall be sanctified among the children of Israel.' Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 5:1–4, defines when a Jew must surrender life rather than transgress: the three cardinal prohibitions, specified cases of public coercion before ten Jews, and a time of persecution, with the detailed distinctions set out there. He names Daniel, Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah among the scriptural models. Thus mesirus nefesh is governed by halachah and is not a general license to seek danger. R' Tzadok invokes its inner root: the Yehudah-point refuses to acknowledge an earthly power as independent of Divine kingship, and that absolute allegiance is the deepest source of public Kiddush Hashem.

paragraphs.text:
Yirmiyahu 50:20 states that the iniquity of Israel will be sought and absent, and the sins of Yehudah will not be found, 'כי אסלח לאשר אשאיר'. Metzudas David explains that the restored remnant has been forgiven so that a search will uncover no guilt. Malbim distinguishes Israel's 'avon', associated with alien worship and distorted belief, from Yehudah's 'chatas', associated with desire. Rav Tzadok interprets this more deeply: when teshuvah from love is completed, even the inadvertent residue ceases to be found in its previous spiritual form, because wrongdoing has been transformed into merit (Yoma 86b). The preceding notes already explain the separate Megillah 13a teaching that repudiating idolatry earns the designation 'Yehudi' and the halachos of Kiddush Hashem. A complementary original parallel is Yisrael Kedoshim 8:16, which connects Yehudah's root to rejection of idolatry and mesirus nefesh. This is Rav Tzadok's exegetical reading of the promise of forgiveness, not the verse's literal assertion that historical acts never occurred.
Sources: Yirmiyahu 50:20; Metzudas David and Malbim ad loc.; Yoma 86b; Megillah 13a; Daniel 3:12; Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 5:1–4; Yisrael Kedoshim 8:16.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Teshuvah from love is not from fear of punishment; on the contrary, one accepts the punishment willingly, if such is Hashem’s will. And through this Hashem removes even the inadvertent residue, and the penalty is wholly pardoned. Indeed he merits deliverance, and even malchus (Sotah 37a).

And so is the way and order always,
שֶׁל כָּל בַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה
of all penitents,
דְּאַף דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
for even King David, peace be upon him,
בְּחַיָּיו לֹא הוֹדִיעֻהוּ
in his lifetime was not informed
מִמְּחִילָה הַגְּמוּרָה
of the complete forgiveness,
לִהְיוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת
that it become like merits,
דִּתְחִלַּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה
for the beginning of repentance
שֶׁמִּצַּד הָאָדָם לְעוֹלָם
from the human side is always.
הוּא מִיִּרְאָה
out of fear.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר (תְּהִלִּים לח)
And therefore he said (Psalms 38),
"עֲוֺנִי אַגִּיד אֶדְאַג מֵחַטָּאתִי",
“I declare my iniquity; I am troubled by my sin,”
וְרֵישֵׁיהּ דִּקְרָא שָׁם
and the beginning of the verse there,
"לְצֶלַע נָכוֹן",
“I am ready to stumble,”
נִדְרָשׁ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין קז)
is expounded (in Sanhedrin 107a),
אַמַּעֲשֶׂה דְּבַת שֶׁבַע
regarding the incident of Bathsheba,
וּמִשֶּׁהִגִּיד עֲוֺנוֹ וְהִתְוַדָּה עָלָיו
and once he declared his iniquity and confessed it,
לֹא דָאַג עוֹד עָלָיו
he no longer worried about it,
דְּוַדַּאי נִמְחַל
for certainly it was forgiven
עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה
through repentance,
שֶׁלֹּא יֵחָשֵׁב עוֹד לְעָוֺן מֵזִיד
so that it no longer be counted as a willful sin,
אֲבָל דְּאָגָתִי מֵהַחֵטְא
but his worry was about the sin,
שֶׁנִּשְׁאַר עֲדַיִן
that still remained,
דְּלָזֶה צָרִיךְ עֵזֶר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
for which he needs the Blessed Name’s help.
לָשׁוּב מֵאַהֲבָה
to return out of love.
וְכֵן אָמַר (שָׁם נ״א)
And so he said (there, Psalm 51),
"פְּשָׁעַי אֲנִי אֵדָע
“my transgressions I know,
וְחַטָּאתִי נֶגְדִּי תָמִיד",
and my sin is always before me,”
דִּילְפִינַן מִינָּהּ (בְּיוֹמָא פ״ו עַמּוּד ב׳)
from which we derive (Yoma 86b).
דְּחוֹזֵר וּמִתְוַדֶּה
that one confesses again.
וְאַפְּשָׁעִים דְּמֵזִיד
And regarding “transgressions,” which are willful,
אָמַר לְשׁוֹן "אֵדָע",
he used the language “I know,”
דְּהַוִּדּוּי הוּא רַק אִידִיעָה
for confession is only an awareness,
שֶׁכְּבָר פָּשַׁע לְשֶׁעָבַר
that he already transgressed in the past,
וְאַף דִּכְבָר נִמְחַל
and although it was already forgiven,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא יִשְׁכָּחֶנּוּ
nevertheless he must not forget it,
וְצָרִיךְ לָדַעַת
and must know it
וְלִהְיוֹת נִכְלָם תָּמִיד
and always be ashamed.
מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל זֶה
before the Blessed Name over this.
אֲבָל "חַטָּאתִי" הוּא "נֶגְדִּי",
But “my sin” is “before me,”
תָּמִיד עוֹמֵד לְנֶגְדִּי מַמָּשׁ,
always standing literally before me,
כִּי לֹא נִמְחַל עֲדַיִן כְּלָל
since it was not yet forgiven at all,
דִּבְחַיָּיו לֹא הוֹדִיעֻהוּ עֲדַיִן
for in his lifetime they had not yet informed him
דְּנֶחְשָׁב לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
that it counted as repentance out of love.
וְלִהְיוֹת נִמְחַל לְגַמְרֵי
and was entirely forgiven.
(וּמַהֲרַשׁ״א בַּחִדּוּשֵׁי אַגָּדוֹת שָׁם
And the Maharsha in Chiddushei Aggados there,
הִרְגִּישׁ קְצָת בָּזֶה
sensed something of this,
אֶלָּא שֶׁפֵּירֵשׁ
except that he explained
דְּמַה דְּחוֹזֵר וּמִתְוַדֶּה
that the one who confesses again.
הַיְנוּ עַל הַשּׁוֹגֵג
means regarding the inadvertent.
וּלְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא מַשְׁמָע
But the Gemara’s wording implies
דְּחוֹזֵר וּמִתְוַדֶּה עַל הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת
that he confesses again the first ones
כְּמוֹ עַל אוֹתָן שֶׁשּׁוֹנֶה בְּאִוַּלְתּוֹ,
like those he repeats in his folly.
וּלְהַחֲשִׁיבָן עֲבֵרָה דְּמֵזִיד
and counts them a willful transgression.
וְגַם לְפִי דְבָרָיו
And also according to his words
הַשָּׁב מֵאַהֲבָה
one who returns out of love,
אֵין חוֹזֵר וּמִתְוַדֶּה
does not confess again.
וְלֹא חִלְּקוּ בָזֶה
yet they did not distinguish in this.
וְנִרְאֶה עִקָּר
And the main view seems
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי
as I wrote,
דְּלְעוֹלָם חוֹזֵר וּמִתְוַדֶּה
that one always confesses again
כְּבָרִאשׁוֹנָה מַמָּשׁ,
exactly as at first,
דְּגַם "אֲנִי אֵדָע"
for even “I know”,
הַיְנוּ דְּחוֹזֵר וּמִתְוַדֶּה
means that he confesses again,
דְּאִי לָאו הָכִי
for if not so
הוּא נִשְׁכָּח מִלֵּב
it would be forgotten from the heart.
וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לְדַעְתָּם עוֹד)
and there would be no need to know them any longer.
כִּי הָעֲבֵרָה שֶׁלּוֹ הָיְתָה בְּחִלּוּל הַשֵּׁם
For his transgression was in desecration of the Name,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שְׁמוּאֵל ב׳ י״ב)
as it is said (II Samuel 12) ",
אֶפֶס כִּי נִאֵץ נִאַצְתָּ" וְגוֹמֵר
“however, because you have utterly scorned,” etc.
וְעַל חִלּוּל הַשֵּׁם אָמְרוּ (בְּיוֹמָא פ״ו עַמּוּד א׳)
and regarding desecration of the Name they said (Yoma 86a)
"לְמִיתָה מְמָרֶקֶת",
“death cleanses fully,”
וְעַל כֵּן לֹא נִתְגַּלָּה
and therefore was not revealed.
גְּמַר מְחִילָתוֹ קֹדֶם הַמִּיתָה
the completion of his forgiveness before death.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם נָתָן הִבְטִיחוֹ
Nevertheless Nathan promised him:
"ה׳ הֶעֱבִיר חַטָּאתְךָ לֹא תָמוּת",
“The Lord has removed your sin; you shall not die,”
וְהַיְנוּ דְּדָוִד מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל
and that is why David, king of Israel.
חַי וְקַיָּם בֶּאֱמֶת
lives and endures in truth.
אֶלָּא שֶׁעֲדַיִן לֹא נִתְגַּלָּה זֶה
Only this has not yet been revealed
בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
in this world
עַד בִּיאַת הַמָּשִׁיחַ מִזַּרְעוֹ,
until the coming of the Messiah from his seed,
וְהוּא דָּוִד בְּעַצְמוֹ
who is David himself,
דְּ"חַיִּים שָׁאַל מִמְּךָ נָתַתָּה לּוֹ",
for “he asked life of You, You gave it to him,”,
כִּי לֹא יִצְטָרֵךְ עוֹד לְמִיתָה מְמָרֶקֶת
for he will no longer need cleansing death.
מֵאַחַר דְּנִתְגַּלָּה דְּהוּא כִּזְכִיּוֹת
since it was revealed that it is like merits.
וְאַדְרַבָּא הוּא קִדּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם
And on the contrary it is sanctification of the Name,
שֶׁאַף בְּדָבָר זֶה
for even in this matter,
שֶׁאֵינוֹ חֵטְא אֶלָּא זְכוּת
which is not a sin but a merit,
רַק לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן דִּבְנֵי אָדָם
only in the eyes of people,
נֶחְשָׁב לְחֵטְא
it is considered a sin,
וְגַם עַל זֶה קִבֵּל עֹנֶשׁ,
and even for this he received punishment,
וְעִם כָּל זֶה הִרְבָּה כָּל כָּךְ בִּתְשׁוּבָה
and with all this repented so much
וְחַטָּאתוֹ נֶגְדּוֹ תָּמִיד
and his sin was always before him
וּבוֹשׁ וְנִכְלָם לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
and he was ashamed and humiliated before the Blessed Name.
וְזֶה נֶחְשָׁב לְקִדּוּשׁ שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם
And this is counted as sanctification of the Heavenly Name
כַּאֲשֶׁר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַרְאֶה
when the Blessed Name shows,
דִּסְבִיבָיו נִשְׂעֲרָה מְאֹד
that “around Him it storms greatly,”
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה
and as they said, of blessed memory,
עַל פָּסוּק "בִּקְרֹבַי אֶקָּדֵשׁ"
on the verse “Through those near Me I am sanctified,”
דִּשְׁמוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְקַדֵּשׁ
that His blessed Name is sanctified,
כְּשֶׁעוֹשֶׂה דִּין בִּקְרוֹבָיו
when He executes judgment on those close to Him,
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה
for through this
"וְעַל פְּנֵי כָל הָעָם אֶכָּבֵד",
“and before all the people I will be glorified,”
שֶׁמִּתְרַבֶּה כְּבוֹד שָׁמַיִם
as Heaven’s glory increases
כְּשֶׁרוֹאִים עַד הֵיכָן
when they see how far
צָרִיךְ לִירָא מִפָּנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ.
one must fear Him, blessed.
דִּמְקֹרוֹבָיו כְּנָדָב וַאֲבִיהוּא לֹא חָטְאוּ כְּלָל
For His close ones, like Nadav and Avihu, did not sin at all,
אֶלָּא בְּדָבָר קַל
but with a minor matter,
שֶׁאֵין רָאוּי לַחֲשׁוֹבוֹ חֵטְא כְּלָל
that should not be considered sin at all,
אֲבָל מִצַּד גְּדֻלַּת כְּבוֹד שָׁמַיִם
yet in light of the greatness of Heaven’s glory.
נֶחְשָׁב גַּם זֶה לְחֵטְא
this too is counted as sin.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: R' Tzadok's order of teshuvah: Resisei Layla section 36 distinguishes two sounds of the shofar. The groan born of dread is teshuvah from fear, while the weeping of a child yearning for his father is teshuvah from love; the order is first groaning and afterward crying. This corrects a possible compression of the parallel: yearning is the higher stage of love, not the initial fear. The underlying Talmudic distinction is Yoma 86b:3: Reish Lakish teaches that deliberate sins become inadvertent sins through teshuvah from fear, but become merits through teshuvah from love. Thus the se'if's claim that teshuvah 'on man's side' begins with fear describes the ordinary human point of entry, not its final measure. Fear enables confession and removes the status of willful rebellion; the complete reversal into merit requires the Divine assistance that awakens love. Resisei Layla section 36 further associates the higher teshuvah with a level beyond ordinary time, where the future is repaired at its root. Takanat HaShavin, Siman 5, likewise explains that the deepest healing reaches the root beneath the manifested sin. David's lifetime uncertainty therefore serves R' Tzadok's broader architecture: pardon can be real before the penitent is shown the final, eschatological disclosure that the fall itself has been incorporated into merit.

paragraphs.text:
Yoma 86b records two opinions regarding sins already confessed on an earlier Yom Kippur. The first bars repeating the confession unless the person has sinned again, invoking Mishlei 26:11. In the Gemara's received text R. Eliezer ben Yaakov praises repeating confession, quoting Tehillim 51:5: 'כי פשעי אני אדע וחטאתי נגדי תמיד' — 'For I know my transgressions, and my sin is continually before me.' Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:8, rules that one repeats the confession even while continuing in repentance. However, Rabbeinu Yonah, Shaarei Teshuvah 4:21, preserves a differing attribution: there R. Eliezer ben Yaakov is said to reject repetition. He cautions against implying distrust in Divine forgiveness or neglecting present failings. This is an actual textual/attribution variant, not identical wording to the received Yoma 86b. Rav Tzadok explicitly considers an explanation he attributes to Maharsha, then argues that renewed vidui truthfully names the former deed even after teshuvah from love; it does not negate the forgiveness or imply the deed was permitted. The primary Maharsha printed page still requires direct collation.
Sources: Yoma 86b; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:8; Shaarei Teshuvah 4:21 (variant attribution); Mishlei 26:11; Tehillim 51:5; Takanas HaShavin 11, discussion of repeated vidui.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Chilul Hashem and the four divisions of atonement: Shmuel II 12:14 describes the public consequence of David's deed. Radak explains that it gave the enemies of Israel an opening to speak disparagingly, so the desecration lies in the public meaning created by the act. Yoma 86a:8 teaches the classic gradation: for neglect of a positive command, teshuvah atones immediately; for an ordinary prohibition, teshuvah suspends and Yom Kippur atones; for kareis or judicial death, teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend while suffering completes; for chilul Hashem, those three suspend and death completes the cleansing. Rambam codifies this in Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4. Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 5:11, also explains that for a prominent Torah figure, conduct that is not intrinsically sinful can become chilul Hashem when observers reasonably speak disparagingly because of it. That halachic category illuminates R' Tzadok's later claim that David's deed, at its hidden root, was merit although to human sight it appeared sinful and produced a public desecration. 'Death scours' here describes the structure and timing of complete kapparah; it is not counsel to seek death or suffering. R' Tzadok's innovation is that the eventual revelation reverses the public meaning itself: David's punishment, lifelong confession, and extraordinary teshuvah become a Kiddush Hashem, showing how exactingly Hashem deals with those nearest to Him and how completely teshuvah can heal.

:8 teaches the classic gradation: for neglect of a positive command, teshuvah atones immediately; for an ordinary prohibition, teshuvah suspends and Yom Kippur atones; for kareis or judicial death, teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend while suffering completes; for chilul Hashem, those three suspend and death completes the cleansing. Rambam codifies this in

, also explains that for a prominent Torah figure, conduct that is not intrinsically sinful can become chilul Hashem when observers reasonably speak disparagingly because of it. That halachic category illuminates R' Tzadok's later claim that David's deed, at its hidden root, was merit although to human sight it appeared sinful and produced a public desecration. 'Death scours' here describes the structure and timing of complete kapparah; it is not counsel to seek death or suffering. R' Tzadok's innovation is that the eventual revelation reverses the public meaning itself: David's punishment, lifelong confession, and extraordinary teshuvah become a Kiddush Hashem, showing how exactingly Hashem deals with those nearest to Him and how completely teshuvah can heal.

sources.ref: Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 5:11

paragraphs.text:
After David says 'חטאתי לה׳', Nasan answers 'גם ה׳ העביר חטאתך לא תמות' (II Shmuel 12:13) — Hashem has removed your sin; you shall not die. Radak interprets this as immediate acceptance of the confession: David will not die the death of the wicked, although the announced consequences will still affect him. Rav Tzadok develops a different, inward aspect of David's enduring life: 'דוד מלך ישראל חי וקיים' appears in Rosh Hashanah 25a as the signal used by Rebbi for the new moon, and the alternating disappearance and renewal of the moon can serve as a symbol of kingship hidden and then restored. Most directly, Rav Tzadok in Machshavos Charutz 20:3 explicitly applies Tehillim 21:5 to David's essential 'חי וקים' and relates complete rectification to a later stage when death is swallowed up. The enduring spiritual root is Rav Tzadok's interpretation, not a denial that David underwent mortality in the ordinary biblical account. The inherited note's Zohar Vayeshev 25:275 folio was not independently collated and is therefore not used as direct textual proof here.
Sources: II Shmuel 12:13; Radak ad loc.; Rosh Hashanah 25a; Tehillim 21:5; Machshavos Charutz 20:3 (Rav Tzadok).

paragraphs.text:
Tehillim 21:5 states: 'חיים שאל ממך נתתה לו אורך ימים עולם ועד' — 'He asked You for life; You gave it to him, length of days forever and ever.' Radak distinguishes length of life in this world from everlasting life in the World to Come. Metzudas David reports the Midrashic interpretation that Mashiach ben David asks for life after seeing Mashiach ben Yosef killed. Rav Tzadok develops this very text in Machshavos Charutz 20:3 and in Kometz HaMinchah II 27:1, connecting David's life and the Tree of Life to his work of teshuvah. This supports the present claim that the promised life will be fully manifest through David's descendant, when the hidden merit becomes visible. The verse, the Midrashic messianic reading, and Rav Tzadok's application are distinct layers and must not be attributed to one another as verbatim statements. A prior cross-reference to specific sections in Siman 15 was not separately collated in this batch, so this footnote now relies on the verified direct Rav Tzadok parallels.
Sources: Tehillim 21:5; Radak and Metzudas David on Tehillim 21:5; Machshavos Charutz 20:3; Kometz HaMinchah II 27:1.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Those near to Hashem and Kiddush Hashem: Vayikra 10:3 records Moshe's words after the deaths of Nadav and Avihu: 'Through those near to Me I shall be sanctified, and before all the people I shall be honored,' followed by Aharon's silence. Rashi, drawing on Sifra, Zevachim 115b, and Vayikra Rabbah 12:2, explains that the Mishkan would be sanctified through Hashem's honored ones; Moshe tells Aharon that his sons have proved even greater than they, and Aharon receives reward for his silence. Ramban preserves that derash and adds a peshat dimension: when judgment is executed upon those closest to the Sanctuary, the people learn reverence for Hashem and His holy place; he also discusses whether vayidom means that Aharon ceased crying or became wholly silent. Chazal and the classical commentators propose several particular failings of Nadav and Avihu, including the unauthorized fire and other lapses proportionate to their stature. R' Tzadok is stressing that proportionality, not erasing every classical account of error: among the exceptionally near, even a slight deviation that would seem negligible in another person bears enormous public weight. He applies the same pattern to David. Divine exactitude toward the righteous creates awe 'before all the people,' while David's acceptance of judgment and lifelong teshuvah turn an apparent chilul Hashem into Kiddush Hashem. The analogy also explains the phrase 'around Him it storms exceedingly' (Tehillim 50:3, expounded by Chazal as exacting judgment with the righteous): nearness increases responsibility because the public reads Hashem's honor through the conduct and fate of those nearest to Him.
