inlineHeadings.text: The theme: This is the rule and order for every penitent: even David, in his lifetime, was not shown the complete pardon that turns sins to merits — because teshuvah, on man’s side, always begins from fear. Hence “my iniquity I declare, I worry over my sin” (Tehillim 38:19): once he confessed the willful avon, he no longer worried over it. It is surely forgiven — but he still “worried over the chatas [the inadvertent residue] that remains,” which needs Hashem’s help to return from love.

p: (ז) וְכֵיוָן שֶׁבְּעָנְשֵׁי דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
And since through the punishments of King David, peace be upon him,
וּבְהַפְלָגַת תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ
and the extremity of his repentance,
נִתְקַדֵּשׁ שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם עַל יָדוֹ,
the Heavenly Name was sanctified through him,
הֲרֵי נֶחְשָׁב אוֹתוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה
that act is considered
קִדּוּשׁ ה׳ בֶּאֱמֶת
truly a sanctification of the Lord,
לֹא חִלּוּל הַשֵּׁם
not a desecration of the Name,
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין צָרִיךְ
and nevertheless he does not need
לְמִיתָה הַמְּמָרֶקֶת
the cleansing death,
רַק אַדְרַבָּא זוֹכֶה עַל יְדֵי זֶה
but rather through this he merits,
לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם
eternal life,
דִּמִּכְלַל לָאו אַתָּה שוֹמֵעַ הֵן
for from a negative you learn a positive,
בְּכָל מָקוֹם בַּתּוֹרָה
everywhere in the Torah,
וְאִם חִלּוּל הַשֵּׁם צָרִיךְ מִיתָה לְכַפָּרָה
and if desecration of the Name requires death for atonement,
מִדָּה טוֹבָה מְרֻבָּה
the good measure is greater:
דִּקְדוּשׁ ה׳ נוֹתֵן חַיִּים
sanctification of the Lord gives life.
וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר "חָטָאתִי לַה׳",
And King David, peace be upon him, said “I have sinned to the Lord,”
כִּי גַם בְּהִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה בַּלֵּב דַּי
for even a thought of repentance in the heart suffices,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי (לְעֵיל רֵישׁ סִימָן ט),
as I wrote (above, beginning of section 9),
וּמִיָּד שֶׁנִּתְחָרֵט בַּלֵּב
and immediately when he regretted in his heart
וְשָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת
and truly returned,
יָדַע וְהִרְגִּישׁ בְּלִבּוֹ
he knew and felt in his heart
דִּכְבָר נִמְחַל
that it was already forgiven.
וְנַעֲשָׂה כִּשְׁגָגוֹת
and made like inadvertent sins.
אֶלָּא דְּהַשּׁוֹגֵג עֲדַיִן נִשְׁאָר
But the inadvertent still remained,
כִּי הַתְחָלַּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה
for the beginning of repentance
שֶׁמִּצַּד הָאָדָם לְעוֹלָם
from the human side is always,
הוּא מִצַּד הַיִּרְאָה
from the side of fear,
דְּעַל כֵּן שַׁיָּיךְ גַּם כֵּן לַמֶּלֶךְ בְּיִחוּד
which is why it especially applies to the king,
דְּבוֹ תֹּקֶף הַיִּרְאָה
in whom is the strength of fear,
דְּכֵיוָן שֶׁכָּרַע
for once he has bowed.
שׁוּב אֵינוֹ זוֹקֵף
he no longer straightens up.
וְזֶה הַתְּשׁוּבָה תַּתָּאָה
And this is the lower repentance,
שֶׁבְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם
of human effort,
הַמְקַדֵּשׁ עַצְמוֹ מְעַט מִלְּמַטָּה
who sanctifies himself a little from below,
דְּ"שׁוּבוּ אֵלַי"
“Return to Me,”
וְאַחַר כָּךְ "וְאָשׁוּבָה אֲלֵיכֶם"
and then “and I will return to you,”
בִּתְשׁוּבָה עִלָּאָה
in higher repentance
שֶׁמִּצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
from the side of the Blessed Name,
הַמְקַדֵּשׁ אוֹתוֹ הַרְבּה מִלְמַעְלָה
who sanctifies him much from above,
וְהוּא הַסִּיּוּעַ
and this is the help
שֶׁמְּסַיְּעִין לַבָּא לְטַהֵר
given to one who comes to purify himself:
בִּפְתִיחָה קְטַנָּה
with a small opening
שֶׁבְּה׳ לְמַעְלָה
in the Hei above,
שֶׁיּוּכַל לִכָּנֵס בַּפֶּתַח הַגָּבוֹהַּ יוֹתֵר
so that he can enter the higher gate,
דַּאֲנִי אֶת דַּכָּא וּשְׁפַל רוּחַ.
for “I am with the crushed and lowly of spirit.”
וְהַבַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה לִבּוֹ נִשְׁבָּר
And the penitent’s heart is broken,
דַּכָּאוּי וְשָׁפָל מִפְּנֵי עֲוֹנוֹתָיו
crushed and lowly because of his sins,
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה
and through this,
מִתְקָרֵב אֵלָיו הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּיוֹתֵר
the Blessed Name draws closer to him all the more,
דְּ"קָרוֹב ה׳ לְנִשְׁבְּרֵי לֵב"
for “the Lord is near to the broken-hearted”
וְיוּכַל לִכָּנֵס
and he can enter,
לְמַדְרֵגָה גְּבוֹהָה בְּיוֹתֵר
a higher level still,
וְהוּא הַמָּקוֹם
and this is the place
שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין
where penitents stand
שֶׁאֵין צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים (יְכוֹלִין לַעֲמֹד).
where perfect tzaddikim cannot stand.
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ
And this is what he told him: ",
גַּם ה׳ (הֶעֱבִיר חַטָּאתְךָ)" וְגוֹמֵר
“The Lord has also (removed your sin),” etc.
דְּכמוֹ שֶׁאַתָּה שַׁבְתָּ לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
for just as you returned to the Blessed Name,
כֵּן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שָׁב אֵלֶיךָ
so the Blessed Name returned to you
וְנִתְקָרֵב לְךָ יוֹתֵר עַל יְדֵי כֵן
and drew closer to you through this.
וְהֶעֱבִיר גַּם הַשּׁוֹגֵג
and removed even the inadvertent.
אַךְ "אֶפֶס כִּי (נִאֵץ נִאַצְתָּ)" וְגוֹמֵר
But “however, (you have utterly scorned),” etc.
וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְגַלּוֹתוֹ עֲדַיִן
and it cannot yet be revealed
בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה בְּחַיֶּיךָ
in this world, in your lifetime.
שֶׁזָכִיתָ לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה הַגְּמוּרָה
that you merited complete repentance out of love.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמַר מִזְמוֹר עַל זֶה
Nevertheless he uttered a psalm about this,
וְאָמַר שָׁם
and said there
"זִבְחֵי אֱלֹקִים רוּחַ נִשְׁבָּרָה (לֵב נִשְׁבָּר וְנִדְכֶּה אֱלֹקִים לֹא תִבְזֶה)",
“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit (a broken and crushed heart, O God, You will not despise),”
שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַקָּרְבָּן הַמְכַפֵּר
which is the offering that atones,
גַּם עַל הַשּׁוֹגֵג
even for the inadvertent,
שֶׁמִּתְקָרֵב עַל יְדֵי זֶה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
as one draws near through this to the Blessed Name
עַל יְדֵי שְׁבִירַת לֵב
through the heartbreak,
שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ עַל יְדֵי הַחֵטְא כְּשֶׁשָּׁב
he has through the sin when he repents,
וְנִמְצָא הַיְרִידָה צֹרֶךְ עֲלִיָּה
and so the descent is for the sake of ascent.
וְרָאוּי לְזַמֵּר
and worthy of song.
וְאַף דַּעֲדַיִן חַטָּאתוֹ נֶגְדּוֹ,
And although his sin is still before him,
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה לִבּוֹ שָׁבוּר בְּיוֹתֵר
for through this his heart is more broken,
וּמִתְקָרֵב בְּיוֹתֵר
and he draws closer,
וְכָּל כָּךְ עַד שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לְתַקֵּן גַּם הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ,
so much so that he merits to repair even the root,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר
as it is said ".
הֵן בְּעָוֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי וּבְחֵטְא יֶחֱמַתְנִי" וְגוֹמֵר
“Behold, I was born in iniquity, and in sin my mother conceived me,” etc.
וְיִיחֵס עָוֹן מֵזִיד עַל הָאָב יִשַׁי שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ וְלֹא חָטָא מֵעוֹלָם כְּלָל
And he attributed willful iniquity avon to his father Yishai, who died only through the counsel of the serpent (etyo shel nachash, Shabbos 55b) and never sinned at all,
רַק מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּעָוֹן מָלֵא דַּאֲפִילּוּ חָסִיד וְכוּלֵיהּ, מַה שֶׁכִּוֵּון לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ

save for that which the Sages of blessed memory expounded on “avon” written in full spelling (Vayikra Rabbah 14:5), that even the pious cannot escape some trace of sin, namely that he intended for his own personal pleasure;

Rav Tzadok derives by an a-fortiori moral reading: if chilul Hashem may require death for completed atonement (Yoma 86a; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4), the sanctification of the Name through profound teshuvah can reveal enduring life. This is a Rav Tzadok interpretation, not a standalone ruling that public sanctification grants biological immortality. The broader principle that the measure of Divine benefit exceeds punishment is used in Sotah 11a. In Kometz HaMinchah II 27:1, Rav Tzadok identifies the Tree of Life with David, cites 'חיים שאל ממך נתתה לו', and calls David 'הגבר הקים עולה של תשובה', a source-checked internal parallel. Machshavos Charutz 20:3 likewise associates David's lasting life with the ultimate rectification of chilul Hashem. The note must follow Rav Tzadok's completed inference 'דקידוש ה׳ נותן חיים', not precede his contrast.
Sources: Yoma 86a; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4; Sotah 11a; Kometz HaMinchah II 27:1; Machshavos Charutz 20:3; Tehillim 21:5.

paragraphs.text: Confession and the inward return: Shmuel II 12:13 places David's entire spoken response in two words, 'I have sinned to Hashem,' and Nasan immediately announces that Hashem has removed his sin. Radak explains the word gam reciprocally: just as David confessed, Hashem accepted his confession, although earthly consequences still remained. The power of an inward turn has a concrete halachic analogue in Kiddushin 49b: a thoroughly wicked man who betroths a woman on condition that he is righteous creates a doubtful kiddushin, lest he have entertained a thought of teshuvah. Rambam, Hilchos Ishus 8:5, and Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 38:31, codify that ruling. This does not erase the formal mitzvah of verbal confession in Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1; rather, the inward resolve can immediately change the person's direction and standing, while complete vidui and repair still follow.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Peshat, Midrash, Kabbalah, and R' Tzadok: Malachi 3:7 says, 'Return to Me and I will return to you.' In the immediate prophetic context, the rebuke concerns neglected tithes; Malbim explains that Israel's return restores the rain and blessing withheld through that neglect. Chazal broaden the verse into a general structure of teshuvah. Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2:2 reads 'Open for Me' as Hashem's request that Israel make one opening of teshuvah like the eye of a needle, after which He opens gates wide enough for wagons. The same reciprocity appears in Yoma 38b and Shabbos 104a: one who comes to purify is assisted from Heaven. The Zohar's Ra'aya Mehemna, Naso 122a-123a, supplies the terminology of teshuvah tata'ah and teshuvah ila'ah, interpreting teshuvah mystically as tashuv heh, the restoration of the lower and upper heh of the Divine Name. R' Tzadok adapts that kabbalistic map to the moral sequence here: the lower return is the person's limited movement from below, rooted in yirah; the higher return is Hashem's answering nearness, which opens love and a degree the person could not produce alone. Pri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Elul 4:1, likewise connects the needle-opening to it'aruta de-letata, an awakening from below. The Midrash is therefore not a promise that effort or the halachic elements of teshuvah may be skipped. It explains the asymmetry of grace: a sincere human beginning is small but real, and the Divine assistance it elicits is vastly greater.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Pesukim, Gemara, meforshim, and halachah: Yeshayah 57:15 joins two apparent opposites: the One who dwells in the high and holy place also dwells with the crushed and lowly, in order to revive them. Malbim identifies the crushed person here with the baal teshuvah and reads the verse as answering objections to the very possibility of repentance: Divine transcendence does not prevent Hashem from drawing near to the contrite. Tehillim 34:19 similarly promises that Hashem is near to the broken-hearted and saves those crushed in spirit. Berachos 34b records a dispute about the resulting rank. R' Abahu says that complete tzaddikim cannot stand where baalei teshuvah stand, reading Yeshayah 57:19, 'peace, peace to the far and to the near,' with the formerly distant person first. R' Yochanan reads 'far' as one who was always far from sin and therefore places the complete tzaddik first. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:4, codifies the penitent's extraordinary closeness without turning the disagreement into a license to sin: a baal teshuvah must not imagine himself remote, for he is beloved and desirable before the Creator and has tasted sin yet separated from it and conquered his inclination. R' Tzadok follows R' Abahu's higher valuation in this se'if. The fall is not itself the advantage; the advantage is the broken-hearted return that converts distance into a deeper nearness. The phrases 'crushed' and 'broken' therefore describe humility and honest dependence on Hashem, not hopelessness or self-destruction. They provide the vessel through which the higher teshuvah, Hashem's answering return, can enter.

Tehillim 51:19 reads 'זבחי אלהים רוח נשברה, לב נשבר ונדכה אלהים לא תבזה' — 'The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and humbled heart, O God, You will not despise.' Radak explains that an offering without a broken heart is not what Hashem desires. The preceding verse (51:18) declares that David cannot substitute an ordinary sacrifice for the heartfelt acknowledgment of his sin. Rav Tzadok's reading in this se'if treats a broken heart as the inner korban through which the repentant person draws close, despite the persistence of sorrow over past wrongdoing. It supports the further point that descent can become a preparation for spiritual ascent; it does not mean that a deliberate violation is transformed into a permissible deed without complete teshuvah. The inherited specific claim about Rashi's discussion of a chatas for deliberate sin was not independently verified and is not repeated as a direct quotation.
Sources: Tehillim 51:18–19; Radak on Tehillim 51:19; Yoma 86b (teshuvah from love); Takanas HaShavin 11, Se'if 7.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Directing permitted enjoyment toward Heaven: Berachos 63a calls “In all your ways know Him” (Mishlei 3:6) a brief passage on which all the fundamentals of Torah depend, and Rava applies it even to situations bordering on transgression. Avos 2:12 states, “All your deeds should be for the sake of Heaven.” Rambam, Hilchos De'os 3:2-3, applies this principle specifically to eating, drinking, marital relations, and procreation: these acts are not to be pursued merely for pleasure, but as part of health, continuity, and the service of Hashem; he adds that one should hope to bring forth a child who will become wise and great in Israel. Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 231, codifies this all-embracing avodah. R' Tzadok's comparison to laying tefillin does not imply that bodily pleasure is intrinsically forbidden. It measures whether the self experiences the act as an isolated gratification or as a transparent fulfillment of the mitzvah. In Yishai's case the deed remained wholly a mitzvah; only the nearly imperceptible inward turn toward self-enjoyment is called avon relative to his extraordinary purity.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Since through David’s sufferings and his prodigious repentance the Name was sanctified, that very act is reckoned a sanctification, not a desecration — so no scouring death is needed. On the contrary, he merits eternal life (for “from the negative you infer the positive”). A mere thought of teshuvah in the heart already sufficed.

p: (ח) וְיִיחֵס עָוֺן מֵזִיד
And he ascribed willful iniquity
עַל הָאָב יִשַׁי
to the father, Jesse,
שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ
who died through the serpent’s enticement,
וְלֹא חָטָא מֵעוֹלָם כְּלָל
and never sinned at all,
רַק מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה י״ד, ה׳)
only what they, of blessed memory, said (Vayikra Rabbah 14:5)
בְּעָוֺן מָלֵא
on “avon” written in full spelling,
דַּאֲפִילּוּ חָסִיד וְכוּלֵּי
“that even a pious person,” etc.
מַה שֶּׁכִּוֵּן לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ,
namely that he aimed at his own enjoyment,
דְּזֶה בָּא עַל יְדֵי עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ
for this comes through the serpent’s enticement
וְשֹׁרֶשׁ יֵצֶר הָרָע שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּעוֹלָם
and the root of the evil inclination in the world
הַמְגָרֶה תַּאֲוָה בַּלֵּב
which provokes desire in the heart
לְכַוֵּן לַהֲנָאָתוֹ
to aim at one’s own enjoyment
לֹא לְשֵׁם מִצְוָה לְבַד
not for the sake of the mitzvah alone.
כְּהַנָּחַת תְּפִלִּין
as in putting on tefillin.
וְדָבָר זֶה הוּא בַּלֵּב בִּלְבַד
And this is in the heart alone,
וְאֵין בּוֹ שׁוּם דָּבָר בַּפֹּעַל
with nothing at all in action,
דְּהֲרֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה בַּפֹּעַל
for the deed in action,
לְהָבִיא נֶפֶשׁ יְקָרָה
bringing a precious soul,
דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם לָעוֹלָם
that of King David, peace be upon him, into the world,
הוּא מִצְוָה גְדוֹלָה
is a great mitzvah
וְאֵין בָּהּ שׁוּם חֵטְא כְּלָל
with no sin at all in it.
שֶׁיִּצְטָרֵךְ תִּקּוּן
that would need repair.
וְכַוָּנַת הַלֵּב לַהֲנָאָתוֹ
And the heart’s intent for its own enjoyment
אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא מִצַּד הַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָּה
is only from the leaven in the dough,
דְּנָחָשׁ הַקַּדְמוֹנִי
of the primeval serpent,
שֶׁיּוֹשֵׁב עַל שְׁנֵי מַפְתְּחֵי הַלֵּב
who sits at the two openings of the heart,
וְדָבָר זֶה נִקְרָא "עָוֺן"
and this is called “iniquity”
שֶׁיִּמָּחֶה לְגַמְרֵי וְאֵינֶנּוּ,
that is wiped out completely and is gone,
וְלֹא נַעֲשָׂה מִמֶּנּוּ
and it was not made from it.
חֵטְא וְשׁוֹגֵג מִקֹּדֶם
a sin or inadvertent error earlier.
גַּם לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לִזְכִיּוֹת
Nor does it apply that it become merits,
אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה
after repentance,
דְּהֲרֵי גַּם מִתְּחִלָּתוֹ זְכוּת הוּא
for from the outset it is a merit,
וַאֲפִילּוּ מַחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה
and even an evil thought
אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְצָרְפָהּ לְמַעֲשֶׂה
the Holy One, Blessed Be He, does not join to deed,
בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
in Israel,
כָּל שֶׁכֵּן זֶה שֶׁאֵינוֹ מַחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה
all the more so this, which is not an evil thought,
דְּאֵיזֶה חֵטְא כְּלָל
for what sin is it at all,
רַק לְגַבֵּי סְבִיבָיו כְּיִשַׁי
only relative to those around Him, like Jesse.
נֶחְשָׁב זֶה לַעֲוֺן מָלֵא
is this counted as avon written plene.
וְיָדוּעַ מֵהָאֲרִ״י זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה
And it is known from the Ari, of blessed memory,
דְּבְכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁנּוֹסַף אוֹת
that wherever a letter is added
מֵאוֹתִיּוֹת הַשֵּׁם הַהֲוָיָה
from the letters of the Name Havayah,
יֵשׁ בּוֹ תּוֹסֶפֶת מַעֲלָה וּקְדֻשָּׁה
it has an added elevation and holiness,
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן אוֹת ו׳
and all the more so the letter Vav,
שֶׁהוּא אוֹת אֱמֶת
which is the letter of truth,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא (בַּזֹּהַר רֵישׁ וַיִּקְרָא),
as stated (in the Zohar, beginning of Vayikra),
וְזֶהוּ "עָוֺן מָלֵא"
and this is “avon written plene” ",
דַּאֲפִילּוּ" וְכוּלֵּי
“that even,” etc..
מִי שֶׁדָּבוּק בֶּאֱמֶת לְגַמְרֵי
for one who cleaves entirely to truth.
וְזֶהוּ דַּרְגָּא דְיַעֲקֹב דְּלָא מֵת
And this is the level of Jacob, who did not die,
כִּי הַמִּיתָה הִיא מִצַּד הַשֶּׁקֶר
for death is from the side of falsehood,
שֶׁהוּא "עַד אַרְגִּיעָה"
which is “only for a moment”,
וְאֵין לוֹ קִיּוּם
and has no endurance,
דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא "כָּזָב"
for which reason it is called “kazav”,
רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר דָּבָר הַפּוֹסֵק
meaning something that ceases,
וְהוּא הַתַּאֲוָה
and it is desire
שֶׁנִּקְרָא "לֶחֶם שֶׁקֶר",
which is called “bread of falsehood,”
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן "שְׂפַת אֱמֶת"
unlike “the lip of truth,”
"תִּכּוֹן לָעַד".
“which is established forever.”
וַעֲוֺן זֶה שֶׁנֶּחְשָׁב לוֹ לְיִשַׁי
And this iniquity that was counted against Jesse
לְפִי גְדֻלָּתוֹ לַעֲוֺן
according to his greatness as iniquity,
נִתּוֹסַף בּוֹ אוֹת הָאֱמֶת
had the letter of truth added to it,
כִּי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה
for the act,
מִלְּבַד מִצְוַת עוֹנָה בְּעָלְמָא
besides being merely the mitzvah of marital duty
וּמִצְוַת "וְלָעֶרֶב אַל תַּנַּח יָדֶךָ"
and the mitzvah of “and in the evening do not rest your hand”
כְּשֶׁהִיא בַּת בָּנִים
when she is of childbearing age,
וּלְהוֹלִיד
and of fathering,
אֲפִילּוּ שֶׁקִּיֵּם פְּרִיָּה וְרִבִּיָּה
even though he had fulfilled “be fruitful and multiply,”,
דְּיֵשׁ מִצְוָה לְכָל אָדָם
since there is a mitzvah for every person,
בִּלְיֵדַת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
in the birth of King David, peace be upon him,
הַמְתַקֵּן הַכֹּל
who repairs everything
עַד דְּיִבָּקֵשׁ עָוֺן וְאֵינֶנּוּ
until iniquity is sought and is gone
וְיִבְלַע הַמָּוֶת
and death is swallowed up,
כִּי יִתְגַּלֶּה הָאֱמֶת הַקַּיָּם לָעַד
when the truth that endures forever will be revealed,
וַדַּאי אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא פְּעֻלַּת אֱמֶת
certainly is nothing but an act of truth,
הֵפֶךְ הֶעָוֺן שֶׁהוּא שֶׁקֶר
the opposite of the iniquity, which is falsehood.
לְהַגִּיד כִּי גַם עָוֺן זֶה דָּבוּק בֶּאֱמֶת
to declare that even this iniquity is attached to truth.
כִּי שֹׁרֶשׁ הַתַּאֲוָה וְהַחֵשֶׁק
For the root of desire and longing
שֶׁל הַמַּשְׁפִּיעַ לַמּוּשְׁפָּע
of the giver toward the receiver,
הוּא בְּעֶלְיוֹנֵי עֶלְיוֹנִים
is in the loftiest of the lofty,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהִמְשִׁיל בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים
and as Song of Songs likens
אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לִכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל
the Blessed Name’s love for the community of Israel
כְּחָשׁוּק לַחֲשׁוּקָתוֹ מַמָּשׁ.
to a lover for his beloved, literally.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Gemara, Midrash, and meforshim: Shabbos 55b lists Binyamin, Amram, Yishai, and Kilav as four people who died solely because death had entered the world through Adam and the serpent. The Gemara finds a Scriptural allusion specifically for Yishai. II Shmuel 17:25 calls Avigayil 'the daughter of Nachash,' although I Divrei HaYamim 2:13-16 identifies her as Yishai's daughter; Nachash is therefore read as a title for Yishai, who died only through the serpent. Rashi on II Shmuel 17:25 records precisely this explanation. Vayikra Rabbah 14:5, a discourse on conception opening from 'When a woman conceives' (Vayikra 12:2), cites Tehillim 51:7 and R' Acha's teaching that even the most pious cannot be wholly without one subtle side of avon in the human process of conception. Ibn Ezra and Radak on Tehillim 51:7 explain more generally that desire accompanies embodied human formation; Malbim distinguishes the material distortion called avon from the appetitive pull called chet. R' Tzadok combines the Gemara and Midrash without contradicting either. In the ordinary juridical sense Yishai never sinned; in the scale of inner purity appropriate to one of Yishai's stature, the faint turn toward personal gratification can still be called avon. Here avon malei means the word avon written plene, with an additional vav; it does not mean an intensified or ‘full-fledged’ transgression. The phrase does not stigmatize marital intimacy or David's conception. It measures how completely even a permitted and commanded act can be directed toward Hashem alone, while preserving the Gemara's unequivocal testimony to Yishai's righteousness.

paragraphs.text:
Vayikra Rabbah 14:5 directly expounds 'הן בעון חוללתי' (Tehillim 51:7). Rabbi Acha says that even the most pious cannot lack 'צד אחד מעון', and the Midrash has David ask: did my father Yishai intend specifically to bring me into the world, or also his own pleasure? This is the correct direct source for the 'בעון מלא' explanation. It does not accuse Yishai of an illicit relationship, nor does it say he had personally violated a prohibition. Bava Batra 17a identifies Yishai among the four who died only through the serpent's counsel. Rav Tzadok interprets the Midrash at a high standard of inward intentionality: even a wholly permitted and meritorious conception may contain a nearly imperceptible human experience of enjoyment; the actual deed remains a great mitzvah. The earlier claim that Niddah 31b itself quotes this verse in this context was not established in the checked Niddah text and is not presented here as verified.
Sources: Vayikra Rabbah 14:5 (exact passage); Tehillim 51:7; Bava Batra 17a; II Shmuel 17:25; Takanas HaShavin 11, Se'if 8.

paragraphs.text:
Berachos 17a asks 'ומי מעכב? שאור שבעיסה ושעבוד מלכויות' — 'What holds us back? The leaven in the dough and subjugation to kingdoms.' Rashi explains 'שאור שבעיסה' as the yetzer hara fermenting the heart. Berachos 61a gives a distinct image: 'יצר הרע דומה לזבוב ויושב בין שני מפתחי הלב' — 'The evil inclination is like a fly sitting between the two entrances of the heart.' Rav Tzadok joins the images to describe a slight self-directed motive intruding into an act that is otherwise a mitzvah. Neither Gemara says that every permitted bodily pleasure is forbidden. The conceptual distinction is between an act dedicated to the Divine purpose and its admixture of private self-importance. The specific inherited attribution to Maharsha concerning the fly having no substance is not independently collated in the printed commentary; it is omitted as a direct claim while the original source images and earlier note text remain archived.
Sources: Berachos 17a with Rashi; Berachos 61a; Koheles 10:2; Takanas HaShavin 11, Se'if 8.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Thought and deed in the Gemara and halachic-moral tradition: Kiddushin 40a contrasts good and evil intention. Hashem joins a good thought to the deed - and, when circumstances prevent the intended mitzvah, credits the intention - but ordinarily does not join an evil thought to an act for punishment, based on Tehillim 66:18, 'Had I regarded iniquity in my heart, Hashem would not hear.' The sugya itself limits the rule: idolatrous thought is treated exceptionally, and Ulla explains another verse by reference to a transgression committed and repeated until it comes to seem permissible. Thus the statement is not permission to cultivate improper fantasies; it distinguishes inward temptation from a completed transgression. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 4:4, warns specifically against looking at forbidden relations while imagining that looking is harmless because no sexual act has been committed, while the juridical equation of thought and deed remains limited. R' Tzadok uses the kal vachomer carefully. Yishai's intent was not an evil plan at all: the marital act was permitted, life-giving, and a mitzvah, and the trace of personal enjoyment was stirred by the universal se'or she-ba-isah rather than chosen as rebellion. Therefore it never became a shogeg that must later be converted into merit. The mitzvah was merit from the outset; only a degree of inward opacity, measured against Yishai's extraordinary closeness, needed to be erased. This preserves both moral responsibility for chosen thought and the se'if's central distinction between an act's halachic status and the purity of its innermost motive.

paragraphs.text:
The text speaks of 'עון' written malei, with an added vav, and calls this 'אות האמת'. Zohar III, Vayikra 2a, expressly expounds 'ונתתם לי אות אמת' (Yehoshua 2:12): 'דא את ו׳ דדא אקרי אות אמת' — 'This is the letter vav, called the sign of truth.' In the immediately following teaching, 'העמק שאלה' is related to the final hei of the Divine Name and 'או הגבה למעלה' to yud. Those distinct letter readings must not be conflated. The current Hebrew manuscript of Rav Tzadok reads 'אות ו׳' and 'עון מלא'; no alternative printed witness reading yud has been produced in this audit. His interpretation connects the added vav to the enduring truth of the good act underlying Yishai's conception of David, while the trace of self-interest remains something to refine. Neither the Zohar nor Rav Tzadok licenses deliberate wrongdoing: the present deed was lawful and meritorious from its beginning.
Sources: Zohar III, Vayikra 2a; Yehoshua 2:12; Takanas HaShavin 11, Se'if 8; Vayikra Rabbah 14:5.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Kazav as something that fails and ceases: Mishlei 12:19 contrasts permanence and transience: “The lip of truth is established forever, but a lying tongue is only for a moment.” R' Tzadok gives the precise linguistic formulation in Pri Tzadik, Kedushas Shabbos 7:11: “Falsehood has no legs or endurance; the meaning of kazav is a thing that stops,” and he continues that the affairs of this world have only temporary existence unless they are joined to the enduring root. This supplies the background to the present sentence. Falsehood is not merely an inaccurate statement; it is an experience cut off from its source and therefore incapable of lasting. Yaakov, whose attribute is emes (Michah 7:20), represents the opposite movement: finite life and action become enduring when attached to Hashem's will. R' Tzadok therefore links “Yaakov did not die” with the permanence of truth and reads the serpent's self-enclosed desire as a kazav precisely because its pleasure immediately expires.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: “Bread of falsehood”: the phrase is Mishlei 20:17, “Bread of falsehood is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel.” Rashi reads it as the momentary sweetness of forbidden intimacy; Metzudas David and the straightforward sense include benefit acquired through deceit. Malbim broadens the image: gain obtained without rightful labor, and even false beliefs fed to the soul, may initially taste sweet but ultimately become gravel and spiritual death. R' Tzadok uses the verse at the level of inward motive. Pleasure detached from the lasting purpose of a mitzvah promises satisfaction yet cannot endure, and is therefore “bread of falsehood.” This does not classify every pleasure as false. The following paragraphs uncover a holy, life-giving root within desire; what must be removed is the concealing claim that private gratification is the act's final purpose.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Yaakov, truth, and enduring life: Taanis 5b records R' Yochanan's statement, 'Yaakov Avinu did not die.' When challenged by the Torah's account of embalming, mourning, and burial, he derives the teaching from Yirmiyah 30:10, which links Yaakov with his seed: just as his descendants are alive, he is alive. Rashi to Bereishis 49:33 notes that the Torah says Yaakov expired but does not use the word death. Ramban there explains that the souls of the righteous are bound in the bond of life and may retain a distinctive attachment to their purified spiritual garment; he does not deny the narrative of burial. The attribute behind this endurance is already assigned to Yaakov in Michah 7:20, 'You will give truth to Yaakov.' Mishlei 12:19 contrasts that permanence with falsehood: the lip of truth is established forever, whereas a lying tongue lasts only for a moment. R' Tzadok reads mortality spiritually as the end of what is false and self-enclosed. Taavah called 'bread of falsehood' promises a satisfaction that immediately ceases; emes joins a finite act to Hashem's enduring will and to future generations. Tzidkas HaTzadik section 147 makes Yaakov's freedom from the serpent's shame the paradigm for this rectification. Thus 'Yaakov did not die' is not merely a claim about biological continuance. It explains why an act wholly directed to building the covenantal seed participates in lasting truth, and why Se'if 8 can uncover an immortal, holy root beneath a desire that the serpent had clothed in transience and embarrassment.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Halachic background to Yishai's act: The Torah separately recognizes procreation and onah. 'Be fruitful and multiply' (Bereishis 1:28) obligates the man in p'ru u'rvu, while Shemos 21:10 establishes the husband's continuing conjugal obligation. Even after the minimum mitzvah of procreation has been fulfilled, R' Yehoshua teaches in Yevamos 62b from Koheles 11:6, 'In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not rest your hand,' that one should continue to build a family. Rambam, Hilchos Ishus 15:16, and Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 1:8, codify this continuing rabbinic duty. Onah is independently binding according to the couple's circumstances (Mishnah Kesubos 5:6; Rambam, Hilchos Ishus 14:1; Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 76), so marital union is not reduced to biological reproduction. Rambam, Hilchos De'os 3:2-3 and 5:4, adds the inward discipline: bodily acts should be directed toward knowing and serving Hashem, and marital life should combine sanctity, mutual willingness, and joy. R' Tzadok therefore identifies several objective layers of mitzvah in Yishai's deed - onah, continued family-building, and the actual bringing of a soul into the world - before the unique result is even considered. The birth of David, the future rectifier of Adam's failure and progenitor of Mashiach, magnifies the deed's truth but does not create its permissibility retroactively. This is why the trace of self-interest cannot turn the act into sin: halachically and teleologically it is mitzvah, while the se'if examines only the refinement of intent appropriate to Yishai's exceptional spiritual level.

This is why the trace of self-interest cannot turn the act into sin: halachically and teleologically it is mitzvah, while the se'if examines only the refinement of intent appropriate to Yishai's exceptional spiritual level.

paragraphs.text: David and Adam's seventy years, verified in the full Midrash and the Kabbalah ZIP: Bamidbar Rabbah 14:12 explicitly says, 'כנגד שבעים שנה שחיסר אדם משנותיו ונתן לדוד בן ישי'—seventy years Adam subtracted from his allotted years and gave to David ben Yishai. Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 19 independently preserves the transfer tradition. Recanati on the Torah, Bereishis §§219–220, corroborates it in the Hebrew Kabbalah archive: 'שבעים שנה חסרו לאדם הראשון לתשלום האלף ונתנן לדוד', then repeats Adam's gift to David in its continuation. These are received aggadic and mystical traditions, not a literal claim stated in the chronology of Bereishis 5:5. Rav Tzadok uses them to explain why Yishai's deed, the birth of David, is an enduring act of truth and a source of eventual rectification of Adam's mortality. The theological application belongs to Rav Tzadok, not to the wording of the Midrash. Yeshayah 25:8 is the prophetic horizon of the swallowing of death. Exact witnesses: midrash-with-meforshim.zip, Bamidbar Rabbah 14:12, complete paragraph; rav-tzadok-kabbalah-2026-10-08.zip, Recanati on the Torah, Bereishis §§219–220; Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 19. Original first-print Recanati facsimile not inspected.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Prophetic horizon and meforshim: Yirmiyah 50:20 speaks of the final restoration after the fall of Babylon: 'The iniquity of Israel will be sought and there will be none, and the sins of Yehudah will not be found, for I will forgive those whom I leave as a remnant.' Radak explains that sincere return and Divine forgiveness leave the accuser with no discoverable charge; the verse is not denial that sin once occurred but a promise of complete removal. Yeshayah 25:8, in a prophecy of Hashem's universal banquet and removal of disgrace, says that He will 'swallow up death forever' and wipe tears from every face. Pesachim 68a contrasts this verse with Yeshayah 65:20, where a hundred-year-old may still die; Ulla applies the promise of death’s abolition to Israel and the remaining mortality to the nations. The classical tradition contains different accounts of the stages of resurrection and the World to Come; R' Tzadok's point here is the shared symbolic axis: sin, falsehood, and death are temporary, whereas truth and the life rooted in Hashem endure. David is placed at that axis because his teshuvah repairs Adam's introduction of death and his royal seed leads toward Mashiach. The 'avon' surrounding Yishai's intention is therefore exposed as a covering, not the deed's essence. When the covering is removed, no independent sin remains to be found, and the birth of the one who will help rectify death is seen as pe'ulas emes, a deed of truth. This does not mean ordinary offenses disappear without teshuvah; it describes the completed clarification produced by teshuvah, in which the false admixture is erased and the holy act that it obscured stands revealed.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: R' Tzadok's larger framework: Tehillim 51:7, 'Behold, in iniquity was I formed,' is read here not as an accusation that Yishai committed an ordinary transgression, but as a disclosure of the primordial mixture that can remain even within a mitzvah. Shabbos 55b explicitly numbers Yishai among the four who died only be-etyo shel nachash, through the serpent's counsel and the mortality introduced through Adam, not through a sin of their own. Vayikra Rabbah 14:5 nevertheless applies the plene phrase be-avon even to the most pious, because embodied conception can contain a minute element of self-directed pleasure. Tzidkas HaTzadik section 147 supplies the closest parallel: the shame that entered after the serpent is evidence that human desire had ceased to be experienced as a transparent mitzvah, whereas Yaakov's rectification of that distortion belongs to the mystery that 'Yaakov did not die.' Pri Tzadik, Miketz 1, develops the same chain explicitly: Yishai's freedom from personal sin, the Midrash's be-avon malei, the serpent's implantation of self-enjoyment, and the work of uprooting that residue through Torah. This is a spiritual genealogy, not inherited halachic guilt. The act is judged as Yishai's mitzvah and David's birth as an immense good; only the nearly invisible inward admixture is called avon relative to Yishai's exceptional level. Se'if 8 therefore explains the 'root' named at the end of Se'if 7: David's teshuvah reaches beneath his visible deed to clarify the ancestral human drive itself, revealing that its ultimate source is holy life-giving desire rather than sin.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Shir HaShirim as the holy root of desire: The rabbinic reading does not treat the Song's language of longing as accidental. R' Akiva declares in Yadayim 3:5 that all the Writings are holy and Shir HaShirim is the Holy of Holies. Rashi's introduction reads it as a sustained parable of a beloved wife who remembers her youthful closeness to her husband while in separation - Knesses Yisrael remembering and seeking Hashem. Shir HaShirim Rabbah consistently identifies the lovers with Hashem and Israel; for example, at 6:1 the nations question Israel about her Beloved, and Israel answers that their mutual cleaving cannot be severed. The Zohar deepens this imagery into the union of the Holy One and the Shechinah, the supernal source from which blessing and souls flow. R' Tzadok's terms mashpia and mushpa belong to that kabbalistic grammar: the giver's urge to bestow and the recipient's readiness to receive originate in a Divine pattern of relationship. He is not collapsing Divine love into physical appetite or declaring every desire holy as experienced. He distinguishes root from distortion. At its root, desire is the movement by which life and blessing pass from giver to receiver; the serpent's residue bends that movement inward toward isolated gratification and shame. The work of teshuvah is therefore not annihilation of the life-force but clarification of it. In Yishai's begetting of David, the future fruit reveals the source: the act participates in the highest yearning to give life, while its minute self-regarding husk can be removed. This prepares Se'if 9, where even the father's pleasure is shown to possess a side of truth because a son brings merit and continuity to his father.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: David ascribes a willful avon to his father Yishai — who “died [only] by the counsel of the serpent” and never sinned (Shabbos 55b). Meaning only the “full iniquity” of the Midrash (“even a chasid [is called an ‘iniquity’]”): the faint self-interest that the se’or she’ba’isah and the primal serpent stir in the heart, so that one aims even slightly at his own pleasure and not for the mitzvah alone. This is only in the heart; the act — bringing David’s precious soul into the world — is a great mitzvah with no sin.

p: (ט) וְעִקַּר חֵשֶׁק הָאֱמֶת דְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
And the essence of the longing for truth of our father Jacob, peace be upon him,
שֶׁאָמַר "הָבָה (אֶת אִשְׁתִּי)" וְגוֹמֵר
who said “Give (my wife),” etc.
לְהַעֲמִיד תּוֹלָדוֹת נִתְכַּוֵּן
he intended to establish offspring,
וְלֹא הָיָה לוֹ שׁוּם מַחֲשָׁבָה
and he had no thought.
וְכַוָּנָה אַחֶרֶת כְּלָל
or intent otherwise at all.
וְעֵרְבּוּב תַּאֲוַת שֶׁקֶר
And the admixture of false desire
דְּלַהֲנָאָתוֹ
for his own enjoyment,
אַף הִיא יֶשׁ בָּהּ צַד אֱמֶת
even it has a side of truth,
כִּי יֵשׁ בְּהוֹלָדַת בָּנִים
for in begetting children there is,
הֲנָאָה לָאָב מִצַּד הָאֱמֶת
enjoyment for the father from the side of truth,
דְּ"בְּרָא מְזַכֶּה אָבָא".
for “a son vindicates his father.”
וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
And King David, peace be upon him,
שֶׁהוּא הַמְתַקֵּן לְחֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן
who is the repairer of the sin of the first man
וְעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ,
and the serpent’s enticement,
וְזִכָּה לְאָבִיו בְּיִחוּד
and in particular vindicated his father,
שֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵר דְּגַם הֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ מִזֶּה
by showing that even self-enjoyment from this,
הוּא הֲנָאַת אֱמֶת
is truthful enjoyment,
אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵינָהּ אוֹתָהּ הֲנָאַת הֶבֶל וְכוֹזֶבֶת
but not that vain, deceptive enjoyment
שֶׁל דִּמְיוֹן הַיֵּצֶר
of the imagination of the inclination
הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מֵעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ
that stems from the serpent’s enticement
הַמְכֻנֶּה בְּשֵׁם "עָוֺן",
which is called by the name “iniquity,”
רַק הַכֹּל נִטְפָּל
but everything is subordinate
לְאוֹת הַוָּ״ו שֶׁבּוֹ,
to the letter Vav in it.
שֶׁהוּא אוֹת אֱמֶת
which is a letter of truth.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם סוֹף סוֹף
Nevertheless, in the end,
מִצַּד הַקְּלִיפָּה הַמַּקֶּפֶת
from the side of the husk that surrounds
וּמְכַסָּה לַפְּרִי וּמַעֲלִימָתוֹ
and covers the fruit and conceals it,
נֶחְשָׁב לְעָוֺן
it is counted as iniquity,
וּכְפִי גֹּדֶל מַעֲלַת וּקְדֻשַּׁת יִשַׁי
and given the greatness of Jesse’s stature and holiness.
נֶחְשָׁב זֶה לְעָוֺן מֵזִיד
this is counted as willful iniquity.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּאִמּוֹ
Unlike with his mother,
נֶחְשָׁב רַק לְחֵטְא
it is counted only as sin,
וְגַם דְּאֶצְלָהּ
and also because with her
אֵין מַעֲשֵׂה מִצְוָה בַּפֹּעַל כָּל כָּךְ,
the act of mitzvah in action is not so much,
דְּנָשִׁים אֵין מִצְוֹת עַל פְּרִיָּה וְרִבִּיָּה
for women are not commanded in being fruitful and multiplying,
רַק דְּהַנִּטְפָּל לְעוֹשֵׂי מִצְוָה כְּעוֹשֶׂה
only that one subordinate to those doing a mitzvah is as one doing,
וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לָהּ לִהְיוֹת עֲדִיפָא מֵהָעוֹשֶׂה עַצְמוֹ.
and it cannot be that she is superior to the doer himself.
וְגַם תִּקּוּנָהּ כְּתִקּוּן הַחֵטְא
And her repair is also like the repair of the sin,
שֶׁמִּתְהַפֵּךְ לִזְכוּת
that turns into merit,
כִּי כְּשֶׁכַּוָּנָתָהּ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם
for when her intent is for the sake of Heaven,
אָז נֶחְשָׁב הַמַּעֲשֶׂה לְמִצְוָה
then the act is counted a mitzvah,
שֶׁהֲרֵי אֲפִילּוּ עֲבֵרָה לִשְׁמָהּ גְּדוֹלָה
for even a transgression for its sake is great,
כָּל שֶׁכֵּן מַעֲשֶׂה דְּנִטְפָּל לְמִצְוָה
all the more an act secondary to a mitzvah
כְּשֶׁהִיא לִשְׁמָהּ.
when it is for its sake.
אֲבָל בְּכַוָּנָה לַהֲנָאָתָהּ
But with intent for her own enjoyment
אֵין גּוּף הַמַּעֲשֶׂה עַצְמָהּ מִצְוָה
the act itself is not a mitzvah for her,
אֶלָּא מִצַּד הַנִּטְפָּל לְעוֹשֶׂה
except from the side of being secondary to the doer,
וְעַל יְדֵי הַתִּקּוּן
and through the repair —
דְּבְרָא מְזַכֶּה לְשָׁרְשׁוֹ בָּאָבוֹת
that the son vindicates his root in the fathers —.
נַעֲשָׂה אֵצֶל אִמּוֹ לִזְכוּת גָּמוּר
it became for his mother a complete merit.
וְכָל חֵטְא דָּוִד הָיָה רַק מִצַּד זֶה
And all David’s sin was only from this side,
כֵּיוָן דְּלֹא הָיָה רָאוּי לְאוֹתָהּ מַעֲשֶׂה
since he was not fit for that act,
אֶלָּא לְהוֹרוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה
but to teach repentance,
וְלֹא שַׁיָּיךְ תְּשׁוּבָה אֶלָּא עַל חֵטְא
and repentance applies only to sin,
וּמֵהֵיכָן יָבוֹא לוֹ חֵטְא
and from where would sin come to him,
כֵּיוָן דִּכְבָר לִבּוֹ חָלַל
since his heart is already hollow,
וְעַל כָּרְחָךְ הוּא רַק מִצַּד שֹׁרֶשׁ יְצִירָתוֹ מֵאֲבוֹתָיו
it must be only from the root of his formation from his fathers
עַל יְדֵי כַּוָּנַת הֲנָאָה לְגַרְמֵיהּ,
through intent of enjoyment for itself.
דַּעֲדַיִן לֹא תִּקֵּן שֹׁרֶשׁ זֶה מִקֹּדֶם
for he had not yet repaired this root earlier.
וְאַף שֹׁרֶשׁ זֶה אֵינוֹ חֵטְא גָּמוּר
And even this root is not a complete sin,
דְּגַם הוּא לֹא חָטָא בֶּאֱמֶת
for he too did not truly sin,
וְכָל הָאוֹמֵר דְּחָטָא אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא טוֹעֶה
and whoever says he sinned is merely mistaken,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת נ״ו עַמּוּד א׳)
as they said (Shabbos 56a),
וְגַם רְאוּיָה הָיְתָה לוֹ
and she was also destined for him
מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית
from the six days of Creation
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין ק״ז עַמּוּד א׳)
as they said (in Sanhedrin 107a).
וַאֲכִילַת פַּגָּה הוּא
And the eating of the unripe fruit is
לְפִי שֶׁלֹּא הִמְתִּין
because he did not wait,
שֶׁיִּקָּחֶנָּה בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא וּבְקִדּוּשִׁין
to take her publicly and with betrothal,
רַק בְּצִנְעָא
but privately,
כִּמְתַכַּוֵּן רַק לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ לְבַד
as intending only his own enjoyment alone
וְלֹא כְּבָא לִקַּח אִשָּׁה
and not as one coming to take a wife.
הָרְאוּיָה וְנִגְזַר לוֹ מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם
who was fit and decreed for him from Heaven.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Midrash, Rashi, Ramban, and R' Tzadok: Bereishis 29:21 records Yaakov's demand to Lavan, 'Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled, that I may come to her.' Bereishis Rabbah 70:18 asks how even an undisciplined person could speak so openly. R' Aivu answers that Yaakov had been told that he would establish the twelve tribes; he was already eighty-four, and his words meant that he must begin producing those generations. Rashi incorporates both the chronological reading - the period associated with his mother's instruction and his service had reached its completion - and the Midrash's inward reading: 'that I may come to her' was said leholid toldos, to beget offspring. Ramban preserves the plain contractual setting. Yaakov was demanding the marriage for which he had served; 'I will come to her' means that he would marry her and continue to complete whatever service remained, not take her and abandon Lavan. The Midrash and peshat therefore address different questions: the latter explains the legal-temporal claim, while the former explains the exceptional candor of a tzaddik. Pri Tzadik, Bereishis 8, reads the Midrash as a restoration of Adam before the serpent: Yaakov did not experience the bodily self-enjoyment that produced shame after the sin, but knew the act only as bringing forth life. Pri Tzadik, Rosh Hashanah 7, Vayigash 11, and Beha'aloscha 6 repeat the same association among Yaakov's pure intention, 'they were not ashamed' (Bereishis 2:25), and 'Yaakov Avinu did not die' (Taanis 5b). This does not make immodest speech a general model. R' Tzadok treats Yaakov's wording as evidence possible only at his unique rung: because no false private claim was present, there was nothing for shame to conceal. The verse thus establishes the standard against which Yishai's nearly imperceptible admixture is measured.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: 'A son brings merit to his father' in its Talmudic setting: Sanhedrin 104a is discussing the kings excluded from the World to Come. Amon is omitted in honor of his righteous son Yoshiyahu; when the Gemara asks why Menasheh is not likewise spared by the merit of his father Chizkiyahu, it answers: bara mezakeh abba, but abba lo mezakeh bara. A son's righteousness can count for the father, whereas a father's righteousness does not automatically rescue a corrupt son. The Gemara cites Devarim 32:39 to teach that Avraham does not simply save Yishmael and Yitzchak does not simply save Esav. Rashi identifies Yoshiyahu and Amon as the case of a son benefiting his father. Maharsha supplies the causal explanation by observing that even some wicked fathers do not want their children to follow their path and may rebuke and train them toward goodness; the son's virtue therefore reveals a merit in the father that was not visible in the father's own conduct. Sotah 10b is not a second primary source for the phrase. Tosafos there cites Sanhedrin 104a while asking how David's prayer could raise Avshalom, a case that seems to run in the opposite direction, and offers qualifications concerning punishment already borne and the power of a father's prayer. Later halachic custom draws on the same principle to explain the special force of a child's Torah, mitzvos, and Kaddish for a parent. R' Tzadok uses the maxim more radically but still causally. David does not transfer an unrelated store of merit to Yishai. David is the fruit of Yishai's own life-giving act, and the fruit clarifies the root: the pleasure of producing a child capable of holiness, continuity, and rectification is itself a true paternal good. The klipah is the father's isolated self-enjoyment; bara mezakeh abba reveals that parent and child were never spiritually isolated in the first place.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Halachic and aggadic background: The Mishnah and Gemara in Yevamos 65b record the dispute between the Sages and R' Yochanan ben Beroka. The Sages exempt a woman from the individually defined command of p'ru u'rvu, deriving the obligation from the language of conquest in Bereishis 1:28 and from the command addressed in the singular to Yaakov in Bereishis 35:11. The halachah follows the Sages; Rambam, Hilchos Ishus 15:2, and Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 1:13, rule that the man is commanded and the woman is not. Exemption is not a declaration that motherhood or her participation is spiritually neutral. The same sugya recognizes her independent interest in children, and the wider halachic tradition treats building and settling the world as an objective good in which both spouses participate. R' Tzadok explains her reward through Makkos 5b. There R' Akiva learns from the Torah's treatment of an additional witness who joins transgressors: if one attached to evildoers is punished with them, all the more does Hashem reward one attached to performers of a mitzvah as a performer. Thus nitpal le'osei mitzvah does not create the man's formal obligation in the woman; it describes her genuine share in the mitzvah-act and its reward. Nazir 23b supplies the comparison to aveirah lishmah. The sugya first states that an aveirah for Heaven is greater than a mitzvah not for its own sake, but after challenging this from the value of doing mitzvos even shelo lishmah, it refines the claim: Yael's aveirah lishmah is comparable to a mitzvah shelo lishmah. Rashi explains lishmah as for the sake of a mitzvah; Tosafos distinguish constructive shelo lishmah, which can mature into lishmah, from self-serving Torah used to attack others. R' Tzadok's kal vachomer is therefore conceptual, not permission to violate halachah. If even an objectively prohibited act performed for a uniquely saving heavenly purpose can possess spiritual value, then certainly a permitted marital act by the woman who enables her husband's mitzvah can become complete zechus when directed to Heaven. His terms avon and chatas measure degrees of inward alignment in this passage; they do not invent separate sacrificial liabilities or diminish the woman's essential role in bringing David into the world.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: 'My heart is a void within me' in peshat, Chazal, Kabbalah, and R' Tzadok: Tehillim 109:22 belongs to David's prayer as a persecuted, impoverished man. Metzudas David reads chalal in its plain sense: his heart has become stricken and emptied by fear and grief; Malbim similarly connects it to the broken heart described earlier in the verse. Chazal deliberately reread the image as an account of inner mastery. Berachos 61b teaches that tzaddikim are judged by the yetzer tov and cites this verse; Rashi explains that David's yetzer hara was like something dead within him. Bava Basra 17a preserves an opinion that David too was among those over whom the yetzer hara did not rule, again deriving it from lev chalal. The Yerushalmi, Berachos 9:5, and the early kabbalistic Sefer HaBahir make the image more active: David could not make peace with the evil inclination, so he slew it in his heart; the Bahir attributes the victory to his uninterrupted attachment to Torah. R' Tzadok frequently cites this cluster. Divrei Sofrim section 28 says that David's heart was entirely clean of base appetite and that his trial with Bat-Sheva was therefore a test of a complete vessel, while Tzidkas HaTzadik section 248 insists that the power of cheshek itself remains the human being's greatness. 'Dead' does not mean that David ceased to possess will, passion, or freedom. It means that the yetzer no longer ruled as an autonomous inner claimant. That creates the se'if's problem: if David's own heart had already been emptied of such false appetite, the point of vulnerability had to lie deeper, in the inherited human root of his formation. His failure then served the purpose described earlier in the volume - to open and demonstrate the road of teshuvah from precisely that root.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Textual clarification and the full Shabbos sugya: The subject of 'he too did not truly sin' here is David, not Yishai. The immediately following formula, 'whoever says that he sinned is merely mistaken,' is the statement of R' Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of R' Yonasan in Shabbos 56a, not Shabbos 55b. The Gemara reads II Shmuel 12:9 with careful limits. David sought to do the evil described but did not commit the straightforward legal offenses attributed to him: Uriah was liable as one who rebelled against the king, though David should have judged him before the Sanhedrin, and David had valid marital capacity with Bat-Sheva because soldiers of the House of David wrote bills of divorce for their wives before battle. Rashi and Tosafos discuss whether those gittin operated immediately or conditionally and how Bat-Sheva's status was resolved. Malbim on II Shmuel 11:3 uses the same halachic framework, arguing that otherwise Bat-Sheva would have remained forbidden to David, their child would have had an invalid status, and David's later marriage and the choice of Shlomo could not stand. The sugya is not saying that David acted flawlessly. It preserves Nasan's rebuke, David's confession, and the punishments in II Shmuel 12, while relocating the wrong from formal adultery and unlawful execution to intention, procedure, scandal, and abuse of royal haste. Classical meforshim are not entirely uniform: Abarbanel reads the narrative's moral charges more literally, whereas Rashi, Tosafos, and Malbim develop the Talmudic defense. R' Tzadok consciously adopts the Gemara's strongest defense because his question is the origin of teshuvah in a heart already called chalal. If the visible deed were ordinary adultery, no ancestral theory would be required. By removing that legal description while retaining real fault, Shabbos 56a allows him to identify the remaining chet as the private, premature mode of taking what should have been received openly, responsibly, and in its Divinely appointed time.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: R' Tzadok's framework for this se'if: The argument is not that every experienced pleasure is holy, but that the power of desire has one created root whose truth or falsehood is determined by its direction. Michah 7:20 assigns emes to Yaakov, and the Midrash and Rashi on Bereishis 29:21 make Yaakov's startlingly direct words a disclosure of wholly purposeful desire: he sought the covenantal generations, not private gratification. Tzidkas HaTzadik section 248 supplies the general rule. The ikkar of a person is the cheshek in the heart; the same force is called yetzer tov when directed to good and yetzer hara when bent away from it. Machshavos Charutz 3:4 develops Yaakov's truth through Yosef: because Yosef's form resembled his father and Yaakov was immersed in Torah, which is called truth, even Yosef's dreams and imaginative pictures proved true rather than deceptive. Se'if 9 applies that grammar to Yishai and David. Sanhedrin 104a's bara mezakeh abba means that a righteous son can disclose and add merit to the father who generated and formed him. David's life therefore reveals that the paternal pleasure surrounding his conception was not empty self-enclosure; it secretly participated in the production of a soul who would rectify Adam and establish the Davidic line. The second half then applies the same distinction to David and Bat-Sheva. Shabbos 56a removes the simple legal picture of adultery, while Sanhedrin 107a says the match itself was destined but taken as an unripe fruit. Divrei Sofrim section 28 and Pri Tzadik, Emor 14, are close parallels: David's heart was fundamentally clear of base appetite, Bat-Sheva was the woman fit for him, and the failure lay in forcing a destined truth before its proper time and form. Teshuvah does not retroactively license haste or secrecy. It separates the enduring fruit from the klipah of self-appropriation, restoring the same cheshek to Hashem's timing, public responsibility, and kiddushin.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Bat-Sheva as the destined but unripe fruit: Sanhedrin 107a places the teaching inside the account of David's requested trial. David asked why the liturgy names the God of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov but not the God of David; Hashem answered that the Patriarchs had withstood trials, and warned David in advance that his own test would concern a married woman. After describing the episode, the school of R' Yishmael interprets Tehillim 38:18: Bat-Sheva daughter of Eliam was fit for David, but he ate her as a pagah, an unripe fruit. Rashi explains that he forced the hour and came to the destined relationship by means of transgression. The metaphor therefore holds destiny and responsibility together. A true future does not make every present path to it true; fruit taken before ripeness is the correct fruit damaged by wrong timing. R' Tzadok develops this repeatedly in Pri Tzadik, including Vayeishev 12, Pekudei 8, Kedoshim 14, Emor 14, and Eikev 19. Divrei Sofrim section 28 adds that the object of David's desire was not foreign to his holy root - Bat-Sheva and the Davidic-Messianic seed were genuinely his future - yet acting before the appointed disclosure made the act appear and function as private appetite. In this se'if R' Tzadok gives 'unripe' a precise social and halachic shape: David did not wait until he could take her befarhesya and through kiddushin. This is not merely a preference for publicity. Open marriage would have aligned personal desire with covenant, community, and recognized responsibility; secrecy isolated the pleasure from those truths. Teshuvah ripens the fruit by returning desire to its proper relationship and time. The adjoining citation to Shabbos 56a establishes that the root and ultimate match were not sinful; Sanhedrin 107a explains why taking them prematurely was nevertheless a genuine failure that required David's confession, suffering, and lifelong teaching of return.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Yaakov’s essential drive was for truth — he intended only to raise offspring, with no ulterior motive. Even the “false,” self-directed pleasure has within it a side of truth, “for a son brings merit to his father.” David, who rectifies Adam’s sin, vindicated his father Yishai in particular: it was clarified that even the self-interest in his begetting was a pleasure of truth — only cloaked by the klipah that conceals the fruit, and so reckoned an “iniquity” befitting Yishai’s greatness.

אֲבָל תִּקּוּנִי
— But my repair —
"וּבְסָתוּם חָכְמָה תּוֹדִיעֵנִי",
“and in the concealed, You make me know wisdom,”
דְּוַדַּאי יֵשׁ בָּזֶה גַּם כֵּן חָכְמָה גְדוֹלָה
for certainly there is in this also great wisdom
מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּרָא יֵצֶר הָרָע בָּעוֹלָם
in that the Blessed Name created the evil inclination in the world,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ "בָּרָאתָ יֵצֶר הָרָע".
as they said “You created the evil inclination.”
כַּיָּדוּעַ דְּהַחָכְמָה וְהִיא הַתּוֹרָה
As is known, wisdom — which is the Torah —
שֶׁהִיא חָכְמַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
which is the wisdom of the Blessed Name
לֹא נִתְּנָה לְאָדָם
was given to man only
אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ יֵצֶר הָרָע
because he has an evil inclination,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּשַׁבָּת פ״ט רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳)
as they said (Shabbos 89a),
וְהוֹלֶכֶת דַּוְקָא לְמָקוֹם נָמוּךְ
and it goes specifically to a low place
וּמִי שֶׁדַּעְתּוֹ שְׁפָלָה
and to one whose mind is lowly,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּתַעֲנִית ד׳ סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳)
as they said (Taanis 7a),
וְדַחָכְמָה מְפֹאָרָה דַּוְקָא בִּכְלִי מְכֹעָר
and wisdom is adorned specifically in an ugly vessel,
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה יוּכַל לְהִתְקָרֵב לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
for through this he can draw near to the Blessed Name
כַּאֲשֶׁר לִבּוֹ דּוֹאֵג וְנִשְׁבָּר בְּקִרְבּוֹ,
when his heart worries and is broken within him,
דְּאָז מְגַלִּין לוֹ סִתְרֵי תוֹרָה
for then they reveal to him the secrets of Torah,
כִּדְתְנַן (בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק אֵין דּוֹרְשִׁין).
as we learned (at the beginning of the chapter “Ein Dorshin”).
וְזֶהוּ "תְּחַטְּאֵנִי בְאֵזוֹב",
And this is “purge me with hyssop,”,
הַיְנוּ שִׁפְלוּת הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מִצַּד הַחֵטְא
meaning the lowliness that stems from the sin,
שֶׁאַחַר כָּל הַיְּגִיעָה בַּתּוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה
that after all the toil in Torah and service,
כְּשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לִידֵי נִסָּיוֹן קַל
when he comes to a minor test
בְּתַאֲוָה וַהֲנָאָה גּוּפָנִית
of desire and bodily pleasure,
רוֹאֶה מַעֲשָׂיו מַעֲשֵׂה בְהֵמָה
he sees his deeds as an animal’s deeds,
עַל יְדֵי הַשִּׁפְלוּת הַזֶּה
through this lowliness
יוּכַל לִטָּהֵר לְגַמְרֵי
he can be purified completely.
וּלְהַגִּיעַ לְמַעֲלָה יוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלָה
and reach a greater level.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ
And as he said afterward
"תָּגֵלְנָה עֲצָמוֹת דִּכִּיתָ",
“Let the bones You crushed rejoice,”
דְּמַה שֶּׁהוּא מִצַּד תּוֹלַדְתּוֹ
for what is from his nature by birth,
מָה לָאָדָם לַעֲשׂוֹת מִזֶּה
what can a person do about it
כֵּיוָן שֶׁנּוֹלַד כָּךְ
since he was born so,
וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא שֶׁיְּצָרוֹ כֵּן
and the Blessed Name formed him so,
וַהֲרֵי זֶה כְּאִלּוּ אַתָּה דִּכִּיתָ,
and it is as if You crushed him,
אֲבָל עַל יְדֵי זֶה דַּיְקָא
but through this very thing,
יָבוֹא לִידֵי גִּילָה
he comes to joy,
כִּי יִשְׁמַע שָׂשׂוֹן וְשִׂמְחָה
for he will hear gladness and joy
עַל יְדֵי זֶה דַּיְקָא
through this very thing.
מַה שֶּׁלֹּא הָיָה לוֹ מִקֹּדֶם
what he did not have before.
וְזֶהוּ הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין
And this is the place where penitents stand,
שֶׁגָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר
which is greater.
כִּי יֵשׁ שָׁם שִׂמְחָה יְתֵרָה
for there is extra joy there.
וְכַיָּדוּעַ הַמָּשָׁל
And as the known parable:
לְמִי שֶׁהָיָה בֶּן יְחִידוֹ מֵרָחוֹק בַּשִּׁבְיָה
one whose only son was far away in captivity,
אֵיזֶה זְמַן בֵּין אוֹיְבִים וּמְצִירִים
for some time among enemies and oppressors,
כְּשֶׁשָּׁב לְבֵית אָבִיו
when he returns to his father’s house
יֵשׁ שִׂמְחָה יְתֵרָה כִּפְלֵי כְפָלַיִם
there is extra joy, many times over,
לְאֵין עֵרֶךְ
beyond measure
מִמַּה שֶּׁהָיָה בִּהְיוֹתוֹ בְּבֵית אָבִיו תָּמִיד
compared to when he was always in his father’s house.
וְלֹא נִפְרַד מִמֶּנּוּ כְּלָל
and never separated from him at all.
וְזֶהוּ אֲפִילּוּ אִם שָׁב
And this is so even if he returned,
רַק כְּמוֹת שֶׁהָיָה מִקֹּדֶם
only as he was before,
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן אִם שָׁב בְּמַעֲלוֹת יְתֵרוֹת
all the more if he returned with extra merits,
שֶׁהִגִּיעוּ לוֹ עַל יְדֵי הַשִּׁבְיָה
that came to him through the captivity,
וְזֶהוּ עַל יְדֵי הַכִּבּוּס
and this is through the washing
דְּ"מִשֶּׁלֶג אַלְבִּין",
of “I shall be whiter than snow,”
שֶׁיָּשׁוּב יָפֶה הַרְבֵּה יוֹתֵר
that he return much fairer.
מִמַּה שֶּׁהָיָה מִקֹּדֶם
than he was before.
וְכֵן בִּקֵּשׁ בִּתְחִלַּת דְּבָרָיו
And so he asked at the start of his words: ",
הֶרֶב כַּבְּסֵנִי" וְגוֹמֵר
“Wash me thoroughly,” etc.
שֶׁיִּכָּבֵס כִּבּוּס מֻרְבֶּה
that he be washed with abundant washing
עַד שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נָחְוַר לְגַמְרֵי
until he is entirely whitened.
גַּם מֵחֵטְא שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה כִּשְׁגָגוֹת
even from sin made like inadvertent sins.
כִּי הִרְגִּישׁ בְּנַפְשׁוֹ
For he sensed in his soul,
הִתְעוֹרְרוּת תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
an awakening of repentance out of love,
שֶׁרָאוּי לְהִתְלַבֵּן
that one deserves to become white
עַל יְדֵי הַכִּבּוּס דִּתְשׁוּבָה
through the washing of repentance
יוֹתֵר מֵאוֹתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא נִתְלַכְלֵךְ.
more than one who was never soiled.
וּבִרְאוֹתוֹ כִּי אַחַר כָּל תְּפִלָּתוֹ
And upon seeing that after all his prayer,
הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לֹא רָצָה לְהוֹדִיעוֹ שֶׁנִּמְחַל
the Blessed Name did not want to inform him that he was forgiven,
וְחָשַׁב אוּלַי זֶה דְּמִצַּד הַתּוֹלָדָה
he thought perhaps this, which is from the side of birth,
בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ
through the serpent’s enticement,
אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְתַקְּנוֹ לְגַמְרֵי
cannot be repaired completely
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כִּזְכִיּוֹת
to become like merits
עַד עֵת קֵץ
until the end of days.
שֶׁיְּבֻלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח
when death is swallowed up forever.
וְעַל כֵּן חָזַר לְבַקֵּשׁ
And therefore he again asked: ",
הַסְתֵּר פָּנֶיךָ" וְגוֹמֵר
“Hide Your face,” etc.
שֶׁהֶעָוֺן יִמָּחֶה לְגַמְרֵי
that the iniquity be wiped out completely,
וְהַחֵטְא הַנִּשְׁאָר מִמֶּנּוּ
and the sin that remains from it
עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה
through repentance out of fear
שֶׁאֵין נִמְחָה לְגַמְרֵי
that is not wiped out completely.
עַל כָּל פָּנִים יַסְתִּיר פָּנָיו
at any rate He should hide His face.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא הִנִּיחַ אֶת שֶׁלּוֹ גַּם כֵּן
Nevertheless he did not let go of his own either,
וְהוֹסִיף לוֹמַר
and added saying ",
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא" וְגוֹמֵר
“Create a pure heart,” etc..
וּבְרִיאָה הוּא יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן
and creation is something from nothing.
וּבְסֻכָּה (נב, סוֹף עַמּוּד א)
And in Sukkah (52a, end of side a)
מִזֶּה שֶׁדָּוִד קְרָאוֹ
from this, that David called it (.
לַיֵּצֶר הָרָע) טָמֵא
(the evil inclination) impure.
וְשֹׁרֶשׁ חֶטְאוֹ מֵאֲבוֹתָיו
And the root of his sin from his fathers,
שֶׁכִּוְּנוּ לַהֲנָאָתָן
who aimed at their own enjoyment,
זֶה אֵינוֹ רַע הַפּוֹעֵל
is not an evil of the doer,
דְּטַעַם הַטֻּמְאַת עֶרֶב
for the reason for the impurity of evening —
דִּבְדָבָר מִצְוָה וּקְדֻשָּׁה
since in a matter of mitzvah and holiness.
לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ טֻמְאָה
impurity does not apply.
רַק לְפִי שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
only because it is impossible in this world
בְּלֹא כַּוָּנָה לַהֲנָאָתוֹ
without intent for one’s own enjoyment,
אֲפִילּוּ חָסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים
even the pious of the pious.
מִזֶּה הֵיפֶךְ הַטָּהֳרָה
from this comes the opposite of purity.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Why the Torah was given to beings with a yetzer hara: Kiddushin 30b states the foundational pairing, 'I created the evil inclination, and I created Torah as its seasoning'; Torah is not merely information about the struggle but the Divinely fashioned means of redirecting it. Shabbos 89a supplies R' Tzadok's more specific proof. When the angels claimed the Torah, Moshe answered from its commandments: they have no parents, commerce, jealousy, murder, adultery, theft, or evil inclination. The Torah's descent to humanity is therefore justified precisely by the low and conflicted conditions in which its wisdom must work. This does not shift moral responsibility to the Creator. Midrash Tanchuma, Bereishis 9, records Kayin's attempted defense, 'You created the evil inclination in me,' but the narrative preserves his accountability; creation of temptation explains the arena of choice, not the choice made within it. The contrast also clarifies 'in the hidden You teach me wisdom.' Rashi on Tehillim 51:8 understands that hidden wisdom as the wisdom to confess truthfully. Radak sees it as the insight by which David recognizes that his inward will was for Hashem even though desire overcame him. Malbim says moral wisdom is planted deep in the soul and must be drawn out from beneath the covering of matter. R' Tzadok combines all three: the yetzer creates the possibility of concealment and failure, while Torah and confession draw wisdom out of that concealment and reveal the act's true root. His claim that Hashem created the yetzer is therefore neither fatalism nor a plea of innocence. It explains why a failure can become the material of deeper Torah, provided the person accepts responsibility and allows the Torah to season, rather than merely suppress, the same power of desire.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Humility, hidden Torah, and the hyssop of purification: The printed author text cites Taanis 4a, end; the passage discussed here is at Taanis 7a. Taanis 7a teaches in two linked images that Torah resembles water, which leaves a high place for a low one, and water, wine, and milk, which keep best in inexpensive vessels. The Gemara illustrates the second teaching when the emperor's daughter mocks R' Yehoshua ben Chananya as splendid wisdom in an unattractive vessel; he answers that royal wine spoils when stored in gold and silver. Rashi explains that Torah endures in him more because of the humility associated with the vessel. Maharal, Netiv HaTorah 2 and Netiv HaAnavah 8, makes the point metaphysical: humility is peshitus, freedom from self-imposed bulk and limitation, and is therefore the fitting receiver of Torah's non-material intellect. Chagigah 13a applies the same qualification specifically to sod: the chapter headings of the Merkavah are transmitted only to an av beis din and, according to the stricter version, only when his heart worries within him. Rambam, Moreh Nevuchim I:34, explains this as humility, submission, and intense fear of sin joined to wisdom; Pri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shevat 2, likewise connects the worried heart with fitness to receive the concealed teachings. The hyssop image has concrete Torah background. Hyssop participates in the purification of a metzora (Vayikra 14:4-7) and in the ashes and sprinkling of the red heifer (Bamidbar 19:6, 18). Rashi and Radak on Tehillim 51:9 therefore hear David asking for purification like that of a metzora or one defiled by a corpse; Rashi on Vayikra 14:4 adds the moral symbolism that one raised like a cedar must lower himself like a worm and hyssop. Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 17, cites that explanation directly: 'Cleanse me with hyssop' means that David's own lowliness becomes the instrument of purity, in accord with Sotah 5a, 'I am with the crushed one.' R' Tzadok's novelty is that the humiliation of discovering bodily weakness is not merely punishment. When it breaks self-certainty without breaking hope, it makes the heart a low place into which Torah and even its secrets can flow.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: The joy unique to teshuvah: In the plain sense of Tehillim 51:10, David asks to hear through prophecy that he has been forgiven. Radak says the message would gladden a soul pained by sin and revive bones crushed by fear of God; Metzudas David connects the crushed bones to Nasan's harsh prophetic rebuke. Malbim keeps the purification imagery of the preceding verse: after the isolation and pain of a metzora, healing produces both outward rejoicing and inward joy. Berachos 34b records R' Abbahu's teaching that complete tzaddikim cannot stand in the place of baalei teshuvah, while R' Chiya bar Abba in R' Yochanan's name disputes it and reserves the highest hidden reward for those who never sinned. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:4, codifies the first view pastorally and ethically: a penitent must not imagine himself distant; he is beloved, and his reward is greater because he tasted sin, separated from it, and conquered a stronger inclination. Yoma 86b supplies the distinction central to this volume: teshuvah from fear reduces deliberate sins to inadvertent ones, whereas teshuvah from love can transform them into merits. The captive-son parable explains the surplus of joy, not the desirability of captivity. Reunion after distance reveals and intensifies a bond that continuous residence never had to display. Accordingly, the Mishnah's warning in Yoma 8:9 that one may not plan to sin and repent remains fully in force. Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 17, gives R' Tzadok's close parallel: 'whiter than snow' is not only removal of stain but the conversion of sins into merits, and beyond that the messianic clarification of 'very good.' In Se'if 10, 'the bones You crushed' are also the givens of birth that David did not choose. Their rejoicing means that teshuvah does not merely work around those givens; by redirecting the inherited power and producing a deeper humility and attachment, it turns the place of crushing itself into the source of a joy and closeness previously unavailable.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: R' Tzadok's map of Tehillim 51 in this se'if: Psalm 51 is David's confession after Nasan's rebuke, and verses 8-12 move from inward truth to purification, renewed joy, erasure of sin, and finally a newly created heart. The classical meforshim establish the range of the opening verse. Rashi reads 'You desire truth in the hidden parts' as David's truthful confession and identifies batuchos with the kidneys, the concealed seat of counsel. Radak says David's deeper will never sought rebellion; his regret proves that desire overpowered a will still directed toward Hashem. Metzudas David makes the verse strikingly close to this siman: Hashem demands truth even in the thoughts of the kidneys, and therefore the father's inward thought matters although the outward act was not sinful. Malbim explains that truth and moral wisdom lie deep within the soul but are covered by materiality, making failure possible. R' Tzadok joins these readings into a doctrine of root-rectification. Pri Tzadik, Balak 14, and Rosh Chodesh Av 3, identify batuchos with the kidneys whose counsel comes 'from afar,' from the hidden root; Torah can disclose true counsel at that depth. Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 17, follows almost the entire sequence used here: hidden wisdom, purification through the lowliness of hyssop, whitening beyond snow, hiding and erasing sin, and a pure heart that makes the penitent like a new creature. Tzidkas HaTzadik section 39 adds that prayer and heavenly mercy can change even a compromised root, because 'create for me' denotes creation ex nihilo. Thus Se'if 10 is not excusing David through birth or the yetzer. It insists that teshuvah must reach beneath the legal act and conscious intention to inherited disposition itself. The same hidden region that carried the admixture also carries the wisdom by which it can be understood, humbled, and recreated.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: From pardon to a newly created heart: 'He will swallow up death forever' is Yeshayahu 25:8, the prophetic promise that death and disgrace will finally disappear. Sukkah 52a links the end of death with the end of the yetzer by portraying Hashem's future slaughter of the evil inclination. David's fear in this se'if is therefore precise: perhaps the inherited trace of Adam and the serpent can be fully converted only when death's root is abolished. His next petitions form an ascending sequence. On 'Hide Your face from my sins and erase all my iniquities' (Tehillim 51:11), Radak explains that David asks that the sins no longer stand before Hashem for remembrance and punishment, and then asks that every iniquity be wiped away. Yet concealment and erasure are still less than positive renewal. Rashi and Metzudas David read 'Create for me a pure heart' (51:12) as protection against future failure; Radak adds Divine support so the yetzer no longer rules. Malbim distinguishes a heart whose material appetite is present by birth from a spirit distorted later by acquired false images: the former requires a new creation, while the latter can be renewed to its original straightness. Sukkah 52a's list of seven names for the yetzer makes David's wording explicit: God called it evil, Moshe uncircumcised, and David impure, inferred from his request for a pure heart. This is a spiritual analogy, not a new halachic status for permitted marital life. Pri Tzadik, Bo 4, applies the name to David's struggle with the admixture of desire; Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 17, says that a pure heart makes him like a new creature and turns the past into merits. Tzidkas HaTzadik section 39 states R' Tzadok's governing principle most sharply: prayer can overturn even the root, for beriah means existence from nonexistence. David therefore asks for more than acquittal. He asks Hashem to create within the very place of inherited self-directed pleasure a heart whose desire is transparent to Divine truth.
