inlineHeadings.text: The theme: “Behold, You desire truth in the hidden parts” (Tehillim 51:8) — even in the concealed depths the act must be pure. “In the secret You teach me wisdom” — there is deep wisdom in why Hashem created the yetzer hara: the Torah, His wisdom, was given precisely because man has a yetzer. And wisdom “goes to the lowly,” is beautiful in a homely vessel, its secrets revealed to a broken heart. Hence “cleanse me with hyssop” — the lowliness that comes from sin.

p: (יא) וְאוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע
And that wicked one,
שֶׁלֹּא הִשִּׂיג מְצִיאוּת טָהֳרָה וּקְדֻשָּׁה
who did not grasp the reality of purity and holiness,
בְּדָבָר זֶה
in this matter,
אָמַר
said
"מִי שֶׁהוּא טָהוֹר וְקָדוֹשׁ וּמְשָׁרְתָיו" וְכוּלֵּי
“He who is pure and holy and His attendants,” etc.
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (נִדָּה ל״א סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳)
as they said (Niddah 31a, end of side a).
כִּי הוּא הָיָה מְשֻקָּע בְּזֻהֲמַת הַתַּאֲווֹת
for he was sunk in the filth of the desires.
אֲבָל אֵצֶל יִשְׂרָאֵל עַם קָדוֹשׁ,
But with Israel, a holy people,
אַף דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם
although nevertheless
גַּם מִטִּפָּה שֶׁהַצַּדִּיק נוֹלָד
even from the drop from which a tzaddik is born
יֵשׁ טֻמְאָה
there is impurity,
מִצַּד עֵרְבּוּב הַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָּה
from the admixture of the leaven in the dough,
אֲבָל עַצְמוּתוֹ לֹא כֵן
yet his essence is not so,
וְעַל כֵּן הַטֻמְאָה רַק לְשָׁעָה
and therefore the impurity is only temporary:
וְטוֹבֵל וּמַעֲרִיב שִׁמְשוֹ וְנִטְהַר
he immerses, his sun sets, and he becomes pure.
וּבִרְחִיצָה קַלָּה הוּא מִתְכַּבֵּס
and with a light washing he is cleansed.
וַחֲכָמִים דָּרְשׁוּ (בְּנִדָּה שָׁם, עַמּוּד ב)
And the Sages expounded (in Niddah there, side b)
"בְּחֵטְא יֶחֱמַתְנִי אִמִּי"
“in sin my mother conceived me”,
לִשְׁנָא דְּדִכּוּיֵי וְטָהֳרָה
as language of cleansing and purity,
אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁפְּשָׁטֵיהּ חֵטְא
although its plain sense is sin,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם זֶהוּ רַק מִצַּד הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
nevertheless this is only from the side of this world,
שֶׁלֹּא נִתְבָּרְרָה עֲדַיִן קְדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל לְגַמְרֵי
where Israel’s holiness is not yet fully clarified,
וְעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר בִּלְשׁוֹן
and therefore it is said in a language,
דְּמִשְׁתַּמַּע לִתְרֵי אַפֵּי
that can be read two ways.
וְהוּא חֵטְא וְגַם טָהֳרָה
both sin and also purity.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁרָאָה בְּמַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ אָז
Nevertheless, according to what he saw in his thought then,
כִּי לֹא נִתְבָּרֵר עֲדַיִן
since it was not yet clarified,
תִּקּוּן הַקּוֹדֵם לְגַמְרֵי
that the earlier repair was complete,
עַל כֵּן בִּקֵּשׁ עַל בְּרִיאָה חֲדָשָׁה
therefore he asked for a new creation,
יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן
something from nothing, ",
לֵב טָהוֹר" לְגַמְרֵי
“a pure heart” completely.
וּבָזֶה יִתְתַּקֵּן הַכֹּל
and thereby all will be repaired.
וּלְפִי שֶׁהַשּׁוֹגֵג כַּפָּרָתוֹ בְּקָרְבָּן
And since the atonement of the inadvertent is by offering,
עַל זֶה אָמַר שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ
about this he said there afterward
"כִּי לֹא תַחְפֹּץ זֶבַח" וְגוֹמֵר
“For You do not desire sacrifice,” etc. ",
זִבְחֵי אֱלֹקִים רוּחַ נִשְׁבָּרָה" וְגוֹמֵר
“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit,” etc.
שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַזֶּבַח הַמְכַפֵּר לְשׁוֹגֵג
which is the sacrifice that atones for the inadvertent
הַנּוֹעֲשֶׂה מִן הַמֵּזִיד
made from the willful
עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה
through the repentance
עַל יְדֵי הַלֵּב נִשְׁבָּר שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ.
through the broken heart he has afterward.
דְּכָל זְמַן דְּלֹא נִתְתַּקֵּן לְגַמְרֵי
For as long as it has not been completely repaired,
לִהְיוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת
to be like merits,
אִם שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
if he truly returns to the Blessed Name
רוּחוֹ נִשְׁבְּרָה בְּקִרְבּוֹ
his spirit is broken within him,
לַאֲשֶׁר הִמְרָה פִּי מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים
for having rebelled against the word of the King of kings,
וְהוּא נִכְלָם וּמִתְבַּיֵּשׁ בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ
and he is ashamed and embarrassed before himself
וְאֵין יָכוֹל לְהָרִים פָּנָיו לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
and cannot lift his face before the Blessed Name,
וּבָזֶה יְכֻפַּר לוֹ גַּם שִׁגְגָתוֹ.
and thereby even his inadvertent sin is atoned.
וּמִן הַשָּׁמַיִם יַעַזְרוּהוּ
And from Heaven they will help him
לְהַגִּיעַ לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
reach repentance out of love,
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לִזְכִיּוֹת
so that it become merits,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת י״ב עַמּוּד ב׳)
and as they said (Berachos 12b)
דְּהָעוֹבֵר עֲבֵרָה וּמִתְבַּיֵּשׁ
that one who commits a transgression and is ashamed.
מוֹחֲלִין מִשָּׁאוּל
is forgiven, as learned from Saul.
וּבְוַדַּאי שָׁאוּל שֶׁבּוּשׁ אָז
And certainly Saul was ashamed then
כִּי הִרְגִּישׁ חֶטְאוֹ
because he sensed his sin,
וְיָדַע שֶׁחָטָא
and knew he had sinned,
בְּוַדַּאי שָׁב וְנִתְחָרֵט כְּבָר עַל זֶה
he surely already repented and regretted this,
וּבְלָאו הָכִי נַמִּי
and even otherwise
כָּל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁעָבַר עֲבֵרָה
every Torah scholar who commits a transgression
וַדַּאי עָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה
certainly does repentance
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם יט עַמּוּד א),
as they said (there, 19a).
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן מָשִׁיחַ ה׳ כְּשָׁאוּל
and all the more the Lord’s anointed, like Saul.
אֲבָל לִהְיוֹת לְעוֹלָם
But as for always being
כָּל תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁמִּצַּד הָאָדָם
every repentance from the human side,
הוּא רַק מִיִּרְאָה
it is only out of fear,
וַאֲפִילּוּ אָדָם גָּדוֹל
and even a great person
שֶׁאֵינוֹ מִיִּרְאַת עֹנֶשׁ
whose (repentance) is not from fear of punishment
רַק מִיִּרְאַת רוֹמְמוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,
but from fear of His blessed exaltedness,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא רַק תְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה
nevertheless it is only repentance out of fear,
דְּנַעֲשָׂה כִּשְׁגָגוֹת
which is made like inadvertent sins.
וְעֲדַיִן צָרִיךְ כַּפָּרָה
and still needs atonement.

paragraphs.text: Bilaam's failure to perceive holiness and the limited nature of bodily tum'ah: Niddah 31a describes Hashem as attending to the conception of a future righteous child. Bilaam objects: 'מי שהוא טהור וקדוש ... יציץ בדבר זה?'—would One pure and holy look at such a thing? The Gemara relates his failure to see the sanctity of procreation to the expression 'שתום העין' (Bamidbar 24:3). Maharal, Netzach Yisrael, ch. 57, explains that the Israelite seed comes from a concealed inward power; Bilaam, attached to zenus and outward desire, cannot apprehend that sanctity. This point was checked against independent complete Hebrew text witnesses (Sefaria and TorahLeshma), not an original Maharal print facsimile. Rav Tzadok's close parallel is Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos, Positive Commandment 2, §253, where 'בלעם כחו בפיו ... במדרגת הדעת ... משמאילים, נגד משה רבינו ... מיימינים וסמא דחיי': Bilaam's leftward daas is contrasted with Moshe's life-giving daas. The quotation was checked against the Rav Tzadok library ZIP and visually against the Har Bracha printed edition, p. 82 (PDF p. 86). Vayikra 15:16–18 separately establishes temporary ritual tum'ah after emission and marital relations; ritual status is not a declaration that lawful, mitzvah-directed marriage is a moral offense. One immerses and awaits evening. Rav Tzadok's conclusion that an easily removed outward covering is not the essential root is his interpretive step, not the ruling of Niddah or Vayikra. Sources: Niddah 31a; Bamidbar 24:3; Maharal, Netzach Yisrael 57; Dover Tzedek, Ner HaMitzvos II §253 (Har Bracha p. 82); Vayikra 15:16–18; Berachos 17a.

Rav Tzadok's close parallel is Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos, Positive Commandment 2, §253, where 'בלעם כחו בפיו ... במדרגת הדעת ... משמאילים, נגד משה רבינו ... מיימינים וסמא דחיי': Bilaam's leftward daas is contrasted with Moshe's life-giving daas. The quotation was checked against the Rav Tzadok library ZIP and visually against the Har Bracha printed edition, p. 82 (PDF p. 86). Vayikra 15:16–18 separately establishes temporary ritual tum'ah after emission and marital relations; ritual status is not a declaration that lawful, mitzvah-directed marriage is a moral offense. One immerses and awaits evening. Rav Tzadok's conclusion that an easily removed outward covering is not the essential root is his interpretive step, not the ruling of Niddah or Vayikra. Sources: Niddah 31a; Bamidbar 24:3; Maharal, Netzach Yisrael 57; Dover Tzedek, Ner HaMitzvos II §253 (Har Bracha p. 82); Vayikra 15:16–18; Berachos 17a.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: The double reading of 'uv'chet yechematni imi' (Tehillim 51:7): Niddah 31b:3 records two views about the time of conception. R' Yitzchak in the name of Rav Ami associates conception with the onset of the menstrual period and cites 'be'avon cholalti'; R' Yochanan associates it with the time near immersion and cites 'uv'chet yechematni imi.' The Gemara explains that chet can be a term of dikuyi, cleansing, from 'vechitte et habayis' (Vayikra 14:52), rendered by the Targum as purification, and from 'techateini b'ezov v'et'har' - 'purge me with hyssop and I shall be pure' (Tehillim 51:9). Rashi on Niddah 31b explains the verse accordingly: the mother conceived after being cleansed from the blood of niddah. Yalkut Shimoni on Nach 765 preserves the same derash in its anthology of this psalm. The derash does not erase the ordinary meaning of chet. The classical meforshim emphasize that meaning from several angles. Rashi on Tehillim 51:7 reads David as acknowledging that human formation occurs through an arena in which many sins can arise, or through parents who are themselves fallible; 'yechematni' denotes heat. Ibn Ezra locates the point in the desire and yetzer planted in the human heart from birth. Radak stresses that sexual desire is natural and hence especially difficult to master, while explicitly refusing to make nature an exemption from responsibility; mastery is greater precisely because the drive is innate. Metzudas David connects David's particular failure with the same kind of desire present at conception. Malbim distinguishes avon, distortion of intellect caused by embodiment, from chet, failure through appetite, whose disposition accompanies conception. R' Tzadok deliberately preserves both sets of readings. In the manifest conditions of this world, where Israel's holiness has not been completely clarified, the verse truthfully says 'sin': bodily origin carries appetite and the se'or's admixture. At its root, however, the same word can mean purification because conception after immersion serves the creation of holy life. The philological two-sidedness becomes a theology of teshuvah: the surface defect is real, but it is not the final identity of the act or the person. Compare Siman 15 §50, where Rav Tzadok explicitly names the "שאור שבעיסה" obstructing Israel's inward will, and §110, where he discusses the "טבור" as the prenatal channel of vitality and relates it to "ובחטא יחמתני אמי". These precise references replace the inherited §§94 and 103, whose actual passages do not establish the two specific claims. The present derash is the seed of that later claim: repair must reach the inherited channel without confusing the channel's admixture with Israel's essential holiness.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: The shogeg offering and the 'sacrifice' of a broken heart: Vayikra 4 establishes the chatas for specified inadvertent transgressions. Rambam, Hilchos Shegagos 1:1, formulates the legal boundary precisely: one who inadvertently violates a negative command involving an act for whose intentional violation one is liable to kareis must bring a sin-offering. Not every mistake therefore carries a korban, and R' Tzadok is drawing an analogy from the Torah's paradigmatic shogeg, not issuing a new rule of sacrificial law. Yoma 86b supplies the transition: teshuvah from fear makes deliberate sins like inadvertent ones, whereas teshuvah from love makes them merits. Once rebellion has been removed, the deed's remaining imprint resembles a shogeg and still calls for kapparah. David's next words answer that need: 'You do not desire sacrifice ... the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and crushed heart You will not despise' (Tehillim 51:18-19). Radak explains that the sacrifice God desires is the broken spirit; a korban without a broken heart is rejected, while a broken heart is accepted even without a korban. Malbim distinguishes the inner ruach, which generates the soul's images, from the outer lev, seat of appetite and the power to govern it: both must be broken away from their old pattern, so that wisdom and fear replace corrupt images and desire is subdued. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2, gives the practical structure beneath that brokenness: abandonment of the sin, removal from thought, resolve not to return, regret, and verbal confession. In Pri Tzadik, Vayigash 8:1, R' Tzadok gives the close parallel to this se'if: fear-based teshuvah cancels the willful status but leaves the ma'aseh and its defect in force, like an act performed unintentionally, and it therefore needs kapparah and refinement; love-based teshuvah receives Divine illumination that repairs the body of the act itself and turns it into merit. The 'broken spirit' is thus not self-loathing and does not replace an actual chatas when halachah obligates one. It is the inward offering of truthful regret and shame appropriate to the residue that fear-based return has not yet transformed. Precisely because the heart is broken before Hashem rather than merely frightened by punishment, Heaven can assist the penitent toward teshuvah from love. Compare Siman 15 §110, where Rav Tzadok connects "ובחטא יחמתני אמי" with the prenatal navel and the inherited root requiring rectification, and §50, which explicitly describes the obstruction as "השאור שבעיסה". The former §§103 and 94 are incorrect point references for those two claims. Here R' Tzadok provides the mechanism of that root-healing: fear removes defiance, brokenness atones for the remaining shogeg-like imprint, and Divine love recreates the deed as merit.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Shaul's shame, repentance, and the limit of pardon: Berachos 12b:9-12 first cites Yechezkel 16:63 for the teaching that one who sins and is ashamed is forgiven, but rejects that proof because a community may be different. It then proves the rule from Shaul. When Shaul tells Shmuel that Hashem no longer answers him 'by prophets or by dreams' (I Shmuel 28:15), he omits the Urim VeTummim because recalling them would expose his destruction of Nov, the city of kohanim. That omission is the evidence of shame. The Gemara then reads Shmuel's 'tomorrow you and your sons will be with me' (28:19) as 'with me in my partition,' proof that Heaven pardoned him. Rabbeinu Yonah, Shaarei Teshuvah 1:22, makes shame a high stage of teshuvah: contemplating Hashem's greatness, patience, and knowledge of one's hidden thoughts changes the radiance of the sinner's face and produces humiliation before the One against whom he rebelled. That is especially relevant here, because R' Tzadok explicitly includes yiras haromemus - awe of Divine exaltedness - within teshuvah from fear. Vayikra Rabbah 26:7 adds that Shmuel offered Shaul a choice: he could flee and survive, but if he accepted the attribute of justice he would be 'with me.' Shaul went to battle knowing that he and his sons would fall; the Midrash praises him for rejoicing in the justice that struck him. His shame was therefore not a passing feeling but acceptance of responsibility and judgment. Berachos 19a:6 adds the presumption used by R' Tzadok: if a Torah scholar transgressed at night, one should assume by day that he certainly repented. The Gemara limits this to matters affecting his own person; in monetary wrongs, repentance may not be presumed until restitution is made. That qualification guards the passage from becoming a license to substitute emotion for repair. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2, likewise requires abandoning the act, regret, resolve, and confession. R' Tzadok's inference concerning Shaul is therefore strong but carefully limited: if an ordinary talmid chacham is presumed to return, all the more so Hashem's anointed king, whose shame and acceptance of judgment are explicit. Yet pardon is not the same as transformation into merit. Pri Tzadik, Vayigash 8:1, explains that fear-based return can leave the deed's imprint requiring kapparah, while love repairs the deed itself. Se'if 11 uses Shaul to show the full dignity and efficacy of shame - genuine forgiveness - while reserving the final conversion of the past into zechuyos for the Divine assistance that brings teshuvah from love.

paragraphs.text: Completion of the Se'if 11 distinction: the same generative act can be commanded and life-giving, while the yetzer's self-centered admixture leaves a temporary, outward trace. Niddah 31a gives Bilaam's failure to recognize Divine attention to holy conception, whereas Vayikra 15:16–18 establishes the separate, short-lived legal category of ritual tum'ah after emission or intercourse. Rav Tzadok does not call permissible marital intimacy a transgression. Berachos 17a's 'שאור שבעיסה' is the obstructing inclination rather than the heart's deepest will; teshuvah from fear may erase rebellious intent, yet completion of kapparah still requires honest inward return. Compare the exact Rav Tzadok parallel in Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash §8: fear-based return leaves a shogeg-like mark in the deed, while love can transform the deed itself. Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos, Positive Commandment 2, §253, Har Bracha printed p. 82 / PDF p. 86, contrasts Bilaam's leftward daas with Moshe's life-giving daas. The Maharal's complementary inward/outward distinction is in Netzach Yisrael ch. 57, directly checked in two Hebrew text witnesses. Detailed Bilaam / tum'ah sources are already treated at note 75, so this note belongs after the completed Se'if 11 conclusion and does not replicate that apparatus in full. Sources: Niddah 31a; Vayikra 15:16–18; Berachos 17a; Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash 8; Dover Tzedek, Ner HaMitzvos II §253; Maharal, Netzach Yisrael 57.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: That wicked one, Bilaam — who never grasped that there could be purity in this matter — sneered, “would One who is holy and pure. And whose ministers are holy and pure, engage in this?” (Nidah 31a) — for he was sunk in the filth of desire. But among Israel, a holy people, the impurity is only temporary — one immerses, the sun sets, and he is pure; a light rinsing launders him.

p: (יב) וְהָרִאשׁוֹן
And the first
הַמְעוֹרֵר כֹּחַ הַתְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
to arouse the power of repentance out of love
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כִּזְכֻיּוֹת
so that it become as merits,
הוּא דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
is David the King, peace be upon him,
דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא
for therefore he is called.
שֶׁהֵקִים עֻלָּה שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה
one who raised up the yoke of repentance.
וִיהוּדָה רֹאשׁ הַשֵּׁבֶט
And Judah, head of the tribe,
שֶׁהִתְחִיל בָּזֶה
who began this,
הָיָה קֹדֶם מַתַּן תּוֹרָה
was before the giving of the Torah,
דְּאֵין הַחֵטְא נֶחְשָׁב לְחֵטְא כָּל כָּךְ,
when sin was not considered so much a sin,
דְּלִבְנֵי נֹחַ לֹא נֶאֶסְרָה קְדֵשָׁה
for to the children of Noah a kedeshah was not forbidden,
דְּהִיא אָמְרָה לוֹ דְּהִיא פְּנוּיָה
for she told him she was unmarried,
אֶלָּא שֶׁהֵם נָהֲגוּ עַצְמָם
but they conducted themselves
כְּדִין יִשְׂרָאֵל
by the law of Israel
(וַאֲפִילוּ בְּדִינֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
(and even by the laws of Israel
אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁקִּדְּשָׁהּ
it is possible he betrothed her,
בִּפְנֵי רֵעֵהוּ הָעֲדֻלָּמִי
before his friend the Adullamite,
וּכְמַאן דְּאָמַר
like the one who says,
דְּחוֹשְׁשִׁין לְקִדּוּשִׁין בְּעֵד אֶחָד
that we are concerned for betrothal with one witness,
וְהִיא לֹא יָדְעָה
and she did not know,
דִּזְקוּקָה לְיִבּוּם
that she was bound to yibum,
וְקֹדֶם מַתַּן תּוֹרָה
and before the giving of the Torah
נָהֲגוּ יִבּוּם בִּקְרוֹבִים
yibum was practiced among relatives
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב רַמְבַּ״ן)
as Ramban wrote)
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם
Nevertheless
אֵין שַׁיָּכוּת לִתְשׁוּבָה כָּל כָּךְ.
there is not so much relevance to repentance.
וְגַם אֵין כֹּחַ הַתְּשׁוּבָה כָּל כָּךְ
Also the power of repentance is not so great,
קֹדֶם מַתַּן תּוֹרָה
before the giving of the Torah,
כֵּיוָן דְּאֵין נָהוּג בְּבֶן נֹחַ
since it is not practiced for a Noahide
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי (לְעֵיל סִימָן א).
as I wrote (above, section 1).
וְגַם דְּשָׁם עַל הָאֱמֶת
And also there, in truth,
לֹא הָיְתָה קְדֵשָׁה
it was not a kedeshah,
וְלֹא הָיָה חֵטְא כְּלָל
and there was no sin at all,
וְאַדְרַבָּא קִיֵּם
on the contrary he fulfilled,
הֲקָמַת שֵׁם הַמֵּתִים
raising up the name of the dead,
וְעַל כֵּן הַמַּתְחִיל
and therefore the one who began.
הָיָה דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
was David the King, peace be upon him.
וְשָׁאוּל זָכָה גַּם כֵּן
And Saul also merited,
לִמְחִילָה גְּמוּרָה
complete forgiveness,
דְּעִמִּי בִּמְחִצָּתִי דִּשְׁמוּאֵל
for “with me in my section,” of Samuel,
עַל כָּרְחָךְ לֹא הָיָה עָלָיו
necessarily there was not upon him,
עוֹד שׁוּם חֵטְא
any further sin,
שֶׁנִּמְחַל עַל יְדֵי הַבּוּשָׁה
for it was forgiven through the shame,
דְּאָזֵיל סוּמָקָא
for the redness departs
וְנִשְׁפַּךְ דָּמוֹ
and his blood is poured out
דְּעָדִיף מִדַּם הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת
which is greater than the blood of the offerings.
לְכַפֵּר עַל הַשּׁוֹגֵג הַנִּשְׁאָר
to atone for the remaining inadvertent sin.
אֲבָל אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּמְחַל לְגַמְרֵי
But although he was completely forgiven
עֲדַיִן לֹא נֶחְשַׁב
still he was not considered
לִהְיוֹת עוֹד כִּזְכֻיּוֹת
yet to be like merits,
בְּלֹא תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
without repentance out of love,
וְעַל זֶה הוּצְרַךְ עוֹד לְעֹנֶשׁ בְּבָנָיו
and for this he still needed punishment through his sons,
שֶׁאָז נִתְקַן לְגַמְרֵי
for then he was completely repaired.
לִהְיוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת
to be like merits.
וְעַל כֵּן יָצְאָה אָז בַּת קוֹל
And therefore a heavenly voice then came forth:
בְּחִיר ה׳,
“chosen of the Lord,”
וַאֲשֶׁר יִבְחַר ה׳ הוּא הַקָּדוֹשׁ,
and “whom the Lord chooses is the holy one,”
שֶׁכָּל מַעֲשָׂיו בִּקְדֻשָּׁה
whose every deed is in holiness.
וְאֵין שׁוּם דָּבָר אֶצְלוֹ מִלְּבַר
and nothing with him is external.
וּבְרָא מְזַכֶּה אַבָּא
And a son brings merit to the father,
שֶׁיָּכוֹל לִזְכּוֹת גַּם לְאַחַר מִיתָה
who can gain merit even after death
מַה שֶּׁלֹּא תִּקֵּן בְּחַיָּיו
what he did not repair in his lifetime.
עַל יְדֵי בָּנָיו אַחֲרָיו
through his sons after him.
לֹא בִּזְכוּתָם לְבַד
Not by their merit alone,
רַק עַל יְדֵי מַה שֶּׁהֵם מְקַבְּלִים עֳנָשִׁים בִּשְׁבִילוֹ,
but through their accepting punishments on his behalf,
וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר
and as it is said,
"אֲבוֹתֵינוּ חָטְאוּ וְאֵינָם
“Our fathers sinned and are no more,
וַאֲנַחְנוּ עֲוֹנֹתֵיהֶם סָבָלְנוּ",
and we bore their iniquities,”
וְקִבְּלוּ עֳנָשִׁים
and they accepted punishments.
וּבָזֶה נִתְכַּפֵּר לָהֶם בְּגַן עֵדֶן
and thereby they were atoned in Gan Eden.
וְעַל כֵּן אוֹמֵר הַבֵּן
And therefore the son says,
"הֲרֵינִי כַּפָּרַת מִשְׁכָּבוֹ"
“I am the atonement of his resting place,”
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּקִדּוּשִׁין ל״א עַמּוּד ב׳)
as they said (in Kiddushin 31b),
וּפֵרֵשׁ רַשִׁ״י
and Rashi explained
דְּכָל עֹנֶשׁ הָרָאוּי לְאָבִיו
that any punishment due his father,
יָבוֹא עָלָיו
will come upon him,
וְיוֹעִיל זֶה לְכַפֵּר נֶפֶשׁ אָבִיו
and this will help atone for his father’s soul
שָׁם בִּמְקוֹם מְנוּחָתוֹ.
there in his place of rest.
וְגַם בְּכַפָּרַת קָרְבָּנוֹת וְעֶגְלָה עֲרוּפָה
And also in the atonement of offerings and the broken-necked heifer
אָמְרוּ (בְּהוֹרָיוֹת ו׳ עַמּוּד א׳)
they said (in Horayos 6a).
דִּמְכַפְּרִין עַל דּוֹרוֹת שֶׁעָבְרוּ הַמֵּתִים
that they atone for past generations, the dead.
וְכֵן בִּתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
And so with repentance out of love,
שֶׁנִּזְכֶּה לָשׁוּב כֻּלָּנוּ בִּמְהֵרָה בְיָמֵינוּ
that we all merit to return speedily in our days
בְּלֵב שָׁלֵם לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
with a whole heart before the Blessed Name,
נִזְכֶּה לְתַקֵּן כָּל הַדּוֹרוֹת הַקּוֹדְמִים
we shall merit to repair all the earlier generations,
שֶׁיִּהְיוּ חַטֹּאות כָּל הַדּוֹרוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת
so that the sins of all generations be like merits.
וְיִהְיֶה תִּקּוּן הַכֹּל
and all be repaired.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Yehudah and Tamar - law, confession, and the root of David: Bereishis 38:14-26 describes Tamar presenting herself as a kedeishah and Yehudah later confessing, 'She is more righteous than I.' The Noahide laws of forbidden relations in Sanhedrin 57b-58a prohibit adultery and specified relatives, but do not make consensual relations with an unmarried, unrelated woman the equivalent of adultery; thus the narrative term kedeishah should not automatically be read as the post-Sinai legal category. R' Tzadok also raises a deliberately hypothetical Israel-law defense: perhaps the transfer of the pledge before Hirah the Adullamite could be viewed as kiddushin before one witness. Kiddushin 65b records the dispute - Rav Kahana says such kiddushin need not be feared, while Rav Pappa says they must be. Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 42:2, rules that one witness does not effect kiddushin even when both parties admit it; the Rema preserves an opinion that is stringent when both admit. The bracketed argument here is therefore lomdus showing how little ordinary sexual wrongdoing need be assumed, not the normative ruling that one witness certainly creates marriage. Ramban on Bereishis 38:8 explains the deeper pre-Torah institution: the ancients knew a great benefit in yibbum, practiced it through the brother and then the nearest family redeemer, and called the wider form ge'ulah. The Torah later limited the legal mitzvah to a deceased childless brother's wife. Ramban on 38:24 stresses that a Noahide widow awaiting this custom was not thereby an eishes ish, and on 38:26 explains that if Shelah did not redeem Tamar, Yehudah was the next family redeemer. Hence 'raising the name of the dead' (Devarim 25:6; Rus 4:10) means preserving the dead man's place and continuity, not necessarily giving the child his personal name. Sotah 10b:11 praises Yehudah's public admission and records the heavenly confirmation, 'From Me these hidden things emerged'; Bava Metzia 59a derives from Tamar's discreet presentation of the pledges that one should accept the furnace rather than shame another publicly. Bereishis Rabbah 85:1 sets the entire episode within providence: while the family was occupied with Yosef's sale and mourning, Hashem was creating the light of Mashiach. R' Tzadok, Likkutei Ma'amarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:13, locates the power of hoda'ah and teshuvah in Yehudah, from whom David emerges; Pri Tzadik, Vayeishev 9:1, develops David and Mashiach as the completion of that power. Yet Yehudah acts before Torah and, on Ramban's account, within a genuine redemptive custom. That is why the se'if honors him as the tribal beginning while reserving the full post-Torah revelation of sins becoming merits for David.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: David as the paradigm of teshuvah: Avodah Zarah 4b-5a first says that neither David nor Israel was naturally suited to the deed attributed to each: David's heart was already 'hollow within me' (Tehillim 109:22), and Israel had just declared at Sinai that it would obey. Their falls therefore became the Torah's answer to despair. If an individual sins, he is directed to David; if a community sins, it is directed to the generation of the Golden Calf. Both cases are needed, because an individual's sin is less public while a community possesses the greater power of collective prayer. The sugya then reads 'the saying of David son of Yishai ... the man raised on high' (II Shmuel 23:1) as David 'who raised the yoke of teshuvah.' The Zohar, Mishpatim 3:248, repeats this teaching and joins it to David's promise, 'I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners will return to You' (Tehillim 51:15): his story opens a path of return for ordinary sinners. Maharal, Tiferes Yisrael chapter 48, treats the individual and communal examples as a disclosure that teshuvah belongs to the providential order of Torah, not as permission to choose sin. The practical definition remains Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2: abandonment of the act, regret, resolve for the future, and confession. Yoma 86b adds the level central here: return from fear makes willful sins like inadvertent ones, while return from love makes them merits. R' Tzadok develops David's distinctive role across his works. Resisei Layla 28 grounds return in the indestructible root of Israel: even after a person has sunk very low, the Divine promise 'I am with you ... and I will return you' preserves the point from which full teshuvah can grow. Tzidkas HaTzadik §254 instead discusses how rectification may demand adopting the opposite conduct in a specific area of prior failure, even where another person's act would be permitted; it invokes David in that discussion. It is not an exact source for a general claim that David's kingship is "inexhaustible longing." The more precise David-and-Mashiach parallel for the present point is Pri Tzaddik, Pinchas §15, which explicitly calls Mashiach ben David the one who raises the yoke of teshuvah. Pri Tzadik, Pinchas 15:2, joins the same Davidic power to Mashiach: the individual who returns awakens thoughts of return in all Israel. In this se'if, David is therefore 'first' not merely chronologically, but because after Matan Torah he reveals the full power of love-based teshuvah to transform the past within the post-Sinai order of Torah into a new source of merit.

paragraphs.text: The physical imagery of shame as atonement, distinct from the source note on Shaul's pardon: Bava Metzia 58b says humiliating another is likened to shedding blood because the red leaves the victim's face and pallor appears. Its prohibition concerns deliberately shaming a fellow person; it is not a requirement that penitents seek humiliation. Rav Tzadok applies that image to spontaneous, sincere shame before Hashem as a metaphorical 'blood offering' surpassing the formal sacrificial image. Berachos 12b establishes Shaul's heavenly pardon after genuine shame; Maharal, Netiv HaTeshuvah 5, explicitly explains that shame indicates withdrawal from and rejection of the sin, rather than stronger identification with it (Hebrew text directly checked in Wikisource and the Machon Yerushalayim-based transcription). Tehillim 51:18–19 names the 'sacrifices of God' as a broken spirit; the phrase does not alter the legal rules of chatas or remove duties of confession, restitution and changed action (Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2). Rav Tzadok's Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash §8, separately explains that fear-based teshuvah may leave a shogeg-like remainder requiring kapparah, whereas love transforms the deed itself into merits. Thus the completed comparison of blushing, 'blood', and remaining shogeg here clarifies why pardon is not yet the final transformation. Sources: Bava Metzia 58b; Berachos 12b; Tehillim 51:18–19; Maharal, Netiv HaTeshuvah 5; Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash 8.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: The seven descendants of Shaul and the declaration 'chosen of Hashem': II Shmuel 21:1-9 relates a three-year famine 'for Shaul and for the house of blood, because he put the Givonim to death.' The Givonim reject money and demand seven male descendants of Shaul; David delivers them, while sparing Mephiboshes son of Yonasan because of his oath. This episode immediately raises two Torah objections: 'Fathers shall not be put to death for children, nor children for fathers' (Devarim 24:16), and a hanged body may not remain overnight (21:23). Yevamos 78b-79a confronts both. R' Yochanan answers that it was preferable for a letter of Torah to be displaced in this exceptional case than for the Divine name to be profaned: the nations had to see that Israel's covenant with converts would be vindicated. The same sugya treats the bodies' extended exposure as a public lesson in the gravity of harming gerim. This is an extraordinary kiddush-Hashem setting, not a general license for courts to punish adult children for a father's crime. Rambam, Hilchos Issurei Biah 12:24, cites the Givonim's pitiless demand for the seven as the reason David excluded them from joining the congregation, so Chazal preserve the moral complexity on both sides. Berachos 12b:13 then offers an alternative proof of Shaul's heavenly pardon. On the verse 'that we may hang them before Hashem in Giv'as Shaul, chosen of Hashem' (II Shmuel 21:6), a heavenly voice declared: 'chosen of Hashem.' Bamidbar Rabbah 8:4 expands the same reading: the human speakers said 'Giv'as Shaul,' and Heaven supplied 'chosen of Hashem.' The ordeal therefore did not fix Shaul eternally as rejected; once justice and public covenantal responsibility were completed, his chosenness was proclaimed anew. R' Tzadok joins this to the language of Bamidbar 16:7, 'the one whom Hashem chooses is the holy one': complete repair reveals that no portion of the person's history remains outside holiness. Yoma 86b supplies the conceptual bridge. Forgiveness removes liability, but only teshuvah from love converts willful sins into merits. Pri Tzadik, Vayigash 8:1, explains that the latter heals the body of the deed, not merely its willful classification. Thus R' Tzadok reads the suffering through Shaul's house and the later heavenly voice not as a contradiction to the pardon already proved in Berachos, but as the final passage from forgiven residue to a past wholly reintegrated as merit.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: 'A son brings merit to his father' - scope and limits: Sanhedrin 104a explains why Amon is omitted from the list: the merit of his righteous son Yoshiyahu benefits the father. It then asks why the righteous father Chizkiyahu does not similarly rescue Menasheh, and answers that a son brings merit to his father, whereas a father does not automatically rescue a sinful son. Responsa Rashba V:49 explains the asymmetry in the world of souls. The child is an effect and continuation of the parent; when that continuation serves Hashem, the source acquires merit through what it produced. Sefer HaChinuch, mitzvah 598, uses precisely this principle to explain yibbum: the descendant established through the widow continues the deceased brother's place and benefits him in the world of souls. This also closes the circle with Yehudah and Tamar earlier in the se'if. Kiddushin 31b:11 states the halachic expression of honor after death: for twelve months, when repeating a parent's teaching, a child says, 'My father, my teacher - I am the atonement for his resting place.' Rashi explains it as accepting upon oneself any punishment due the parent. Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 240:9, codifies this formula within the first year and 'may his memory be a blessing' thereafter. Pri Tzadik, Pinchas 15:2, explicitly says that at times a person's repair comes through children and cites 'a son brings merit to his father.' Horayos 6a:7 gives a communal analogue. From the eglah arufah prayer, 'Atone for Your people Israel whom You redeemed' (Devarim 21:8), Rav Pappa derives that this atonement is fit to include even the generation redeemed from Egypt. Rashi there explains that a communal sin-offering does not die when members of the public die, because the dead can be included in the continuing community's kapparah. This does not mean that every private chatas can be offered after its owner's death. Nor is inherited punishment the ordinary criminal rule: Devarim 24:16 and Yechezkel 18 insist that each person is judged for his own sin, and Sanhedrin 27b limits punishment of descendants to those who continue their ancestors' deeds. The Shaul-Givonim episode is treated in Yevamos 79a as an exceptional kiddush-Hashem case. Eichah 5:7 - 'Our fathers sinned and are no more, and we have borne their iniquities' - describes descendants bearing the historical and spiritual consequences of an inherited breach, not a routine transfer of courtroom guilt. R' Tzadok's point is therefore organic and intergenerational: the parent's unfinished imprint can be repaired through the life, merit, or exceptional suffering of the continuation he brought into being. Resisei Layla 28 supplies the wider frame, describing Israel's generations as branches of one enduring root; later holiness can reach backward because the family and the people are not spiritually isolated units.

The child is an effect and continuation of the parent; when that continuation serves Hashem, the source acquires merit through what it produced.

, uses precisely this principle to explain yibbum: the descendant established through the widow continues the deceased brother's place and benefits him in the world of souls. This also closes the circle with Yehudah and Tamar earlier in the se'if.

:11 states the halachic expression of honor after death: for twelve months, when repeating a parent's teaching, a child says, 'My father, my teacher - I am the atonement for his resting place.' Rashi explains it as accepting upon oneself any punishment due the parent. Shulchan Aruch,
, codifies this formula within the first year and 'may his memory be a blessing' thereafter.
, explicitly says that at times a person's repair comes through children and cites 'a son brings merit to his father.'
:7 gives a communal analogue. From the eglah arufah prayer, 'Atone for Your people Israel whom You redeemed' (

), Rav Pappa derives that this atonement is fit to include even the generation redeemed from Egypt. Rashi there explains that a communal sin-offering does not die when members of the public die, because the dead can be included in the continuing community's kapparah. This does not mean that every private chatas can be offered after its owner's death. Nor is inherited punishment the ordinary criminal rule:
and Yechezkel 18 insist that each person is judged for his own sin, and
limits punishment of descendants to those who continue their ancestors' deeds. The Shaul-Givonim episode is treated in

- 'Our fathers sinned and are no more, and we have borne their iniquities' - describes descendants bearing the historical and spiritual consequences of an inherited breach, not a routine transfer of courtroom guilt. R' Tzadok's point is therefore organic and intergenerational: the parent's unfinished imprint can be repaired through the life, merit, or exceptional suffering of the continuation he brought into being.
supplies the wider frame, describing Israel's generations as branches of one enduring root; later holiness can reach backward because the family and the people are not spiritually isolated units.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The first to arouse the power of teshuvah from love. The kind that turns sins to merits — is David, “who raised up the yoke of teshuvah.” Yehudah, head of the tribe, who began this before the giving of the Torah, acted where the “sin” is barely a sin (a harlot is not forbidden to the Noahides).

p: (יג) וְכֵן הוּא סֵדֶר וְדֶרֶךְ
And so is the order and way of
כָּל הַבָּא לָשׁוּב אֶל ה׳,
everyone who comes to return to the Lord:
בַּהַתְחָלָה הוּא מִיִּרְאָה
at the beginning it is from fear,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ כָּל כֹּחַ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם
for this is all the power of a person’s effort
בַּעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
in the service of the Blessed Name
רַק לְיִרְאָה
only toward fear,
עַל יְדֵי "שִׁוִּיתִי ה׳ לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד"
through “I have set the Lord before me always,”,
שֶׁהוּא כְּלָל גָּדוֹל בַּתּוֹרָה
which is a great principle in the Torah,
שֶׁנִּזְדַּמֵּן בְּרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ
which came about through divine inspiration
בְּפִי רַמָ״א זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה
in the mouth of Rema, of blessed memory.
בְּהַגָּהָה דְּרֵישׁ אוֹרַח חַיִּים
in the gloss at the beginning of Orach Chaim.
שֶׁזֶּה הַתְחָלַת עֲבוֹדָה
For this is the beginning of service
לְאָדָם הַבָּא לָלֶכֶת בְּדֶרֶךְ הַחַיִּים
for a person coming to walk in the way of life:
לָדַעַת וּלְהַכִּיר
to know and recognize
שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נֶכְחוֹ תָּמִיד
that the Blessed Name is always before him
וְצוֹפֶה וּמַבִּיט
and watches and looks,
עַל כָּל דְּרָכָיו וּמַעֲלָלָיו
upon all his ways and deeds,
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה יַגִּיעַ
for through this he will arrive
לְפַחַד וְיִרְאָה מִמֶּנּוּ יִתְבָּרַךְ
at dread and fear of Him, blessed be He.
וְהַכְנָעָה וּבוּשְׁתּוֹ מִמֶּנּוּ תָּמִיד
and submission and shame before Him always.
וְהַמִּתְעוֹרֵר לָשׁוּב אַחַר שֶׁחָטָא
And one who awakens to return after having sinned
הֲרֵי זֶה מַתְחִיל מֵחָדָשׁ
is beginning anew
לִכָּנֵס לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
to enter the service of the Blessed Name,
וְרֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה
and “the beginning of wisdom,”
שֶׁהוּא כָּל הַתּוֹרָה כֻּלָּהּ
which is the whole Torah,
הוּא יִרְאַת ה׳,
is the fear of the Lord,
דְּהוּא תַּרְעָא לְאֵעֲלָא גּוֹ מְהֵימְנוּתָא
for it is the gate to enter into faith,
וְזֶה הַשַּׁעַר
and this is the gate
שֶׁכָּל בַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה גַּם כֵּן יָבֹאוּ בוֹ
through which all penitents also come.
בִּתְחִלַּת תְּשׁוּבָתָן
at the start of their repentance.
וְאַחַר שֶׁשּׁוֹקֵד בִּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ
And after he is diligent in his repentance
וְחַטָּאתוֹ נֶגְדּוֹ תָמִיד
and his sin is before him always
לִהְיוֹת לִבּוֹ נִשְׁבָּר בְּקִרְבּוֹ,
so that his heart is broken within him,
עַל יְדֵי זֶה זוֹכֶה אַחַר כָּךְ
through this he afterward merits
לִמְחִילַת הַשּׁוֹגֵג
forgiveness of the inadvertent.
וְלִהְיוֹת כְּמִי שֶׁלֹּא חָטָא כְּלָל
and to be as one who never sinned at all.
וַעֲדַיִן "טְהָר יָדַיִם יֹסִיף אֹמֶץ",
And still “he that has clean hands grows stronger,”
שֶׁיִּזְכֶּה שֶׁמִּן הַשָּׁמַיִם יְסַיְּעוּהוּ
so that he merit that from Heaven they help him
לְהַגִּיעַ לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
to reach repentance out of love,
עַד שֶׁיָּשׁוּב הַכֹּל זְכֻיּוֹת
until everything turns to merits.
שֶׁזֶּהוּ שְׁלֵמוּת תִּקּוּן הַתְּשׁוּבָה
which is the completeness of the repair of repentance.

items.h: סִימָן יב
Teshuvah through suffering and Divine awakening
תשובה מייסורין והתעוררות מלמעלה

p: (א) הַשְּׁלִישִׁי
The third,
עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
is through suffering,
שֶׁלֹּא שָׁבוּ
in that they did not return
עַד שֶׁנִּתְיַסְּרוּ
until they were afflicted (,
כֵּן הוּא בְּרַשִׁ״י
(so it is in Rashi,
וּלְאַפּוֹקֵי כְּשֶׁעֲדַיִן לֹא בָּאוּ יִסּוּרִין
excluding when suffering has not yet come
רַק יָרֵא שֶׁלֹּא יָבֹאוּ
but he fears it will come,
וְעַל יְדֵי כֵן שָׁב
and therefore returns,
זֶה נִקְרָא מִיִּרְאָה
this is called “from fear,”
אֶלָּא שֶׁהִיא מַדְרֵגָה קְטַנָּה
except that it is a lesser level —
מִיִּרְאַת עֹנֶשׁ,
from fear of punishment,
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם זֶה בִּכְלַל מִיִּרְאָה).
yet even this is included in “from fear”).
וְיֵעָיֵן שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י
And see there in Rashi,
הַחִלּוּק בֵּינֵיהֶם
the distinction between them,
דְּמֵאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה
that from love and fear
נִקְרָאִים בָּנִים
they are called sons
וְעַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
and through suffering.
נִקְרָאִים עֲבָדִים
they are called servants.
וְצָרִיךְ לְעַיֵּן
And it requires study:
כֵּיוָן דְּהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
since the Holy One, blessed be He,
מְקַבֵּל תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ,
accepts his repentance,
וְהַגַּם שֶׁלֹּא שָׁב
and although he did not return,
עַד אַחַר שֶׁבָּא עָלָיו יִסּוּרִין
until after suffering came upon him,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם מִשֶּׁשָּׁב
nevertheless once he returned,
נִקְרָא בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה גָּמוּר
he is called a complete penitent,
דְּ"תָּשֵׁב אֱנוֹשׁ עַד דַּכָּא" כְּתִיב
for “You return man to crushing” is written,
וְדָרְשׁוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי
and they expounded in the Yerushalmi
(פֶּרֶק ב דַּחֲגִיגָה, הֲלָכָה א)
(Chagigah chapter 2, halachah 1)
עַד דְּכַדּוּכָהּ שֶׁל נֶפֶשׁ,
“until the crushing of the soul,”
דַּאֲפִילוּ בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָה מְקַבְּלִין
that even at the time of death they accept.
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן עַל יְדֵי שְׁאָר יִסּוּרִין
and all the more through other suffering.
וּמִקְרָא מָלֵא
And an explicit verse
(בְּפָרָשַׁת וָאֶתְחַנַּן)
(in Parashas Va’eschanan)
"בַּצַּר לְךָ וּמְצָאוּךָ" וְגוֹמֵר
“When you are in distress and it finds you,” etc. ".
וְשַׁבְתָּ עַד ה׳" וְגוֹמֵר
“and you will return to the Lord,” etc.
וּבְטַעֲנָה זוֹ בָּא מְנַשֶּׁה
And with this argument Menasheh came
כְּשֶׁשָּׁב עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
when he returned through the suffering
דְּמֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר
of the king of Assyria,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ
as they said
(בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי פֶּרֶק י דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין, הֲלָכָה ב),
(in the Yerushalmi, Sanhedrin chapter 10, halachah 2),
וְנִתְקַבְּלָה תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ
and his repentance was accepted
לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
according to Rabbi Yehudah.
בְּמַתְנִיתִין דְּשָׁם
in the Mishnah there.
וְתַנָּא קַמָּא דְּפָלִיג
And the first Tanna who disagrees
מִשּׁוּם דְּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ
because he holds
דְּלֹא עָבַד תְּשׁוּבָה
that he did not do repentance,
כַּמְבֹאָר (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין ק״ג רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳)
as explained (in Sanhedrin 103a),
וְהַיְנוּ דְּאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהִתְפַּלֵּל
that although he prayed
לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְהִצִּילוֹ
to the Blessed Name and He saved him.
מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא שָׁב מֵחֲטָאָיו
nevertheless he did not return from his sins.
אֲבָל אִם שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת
But if he truly returned,
אֲפִילוּ מִתּוֹךְ הַיִּסּוּרִין
even from within the suffering,
הֲרֵי אָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין צ״ז סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳)
they said (in Sanhedrin 97b)
דְּגַם גְּאֻלָּה הַשְּׁלֵמָה הָעֲתִידָה
that even the future complete redemption
יוּכְלוּ לִזְכּוֹת
they can merit
עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה
through repentance
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
that comes through suffering,
מִמֶּלֶךְ קָשֶׁה כְּהָמָן
from a king as harsh as Haman,
הֲרֵי דְּנִקְרָא בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה גָּמוּר
so he is called a complete penitent,
הַגָּדוֹל מִצַּדִּיק גָּמוּר
greater than a complete tzaddik,
כָּל שֶׁשָּׁב בֶּאֱמֶת
whoever truly returns.
מֵחֲמַת הַיִּסּוּרִין
because of the suffering.
וְאִם כֵּן וַדַּאי
And if so, certainly
דְּהֲרֵי הוּא מֵעַתָּה
he is from now
בִּכְלַל עוֹשִׂין רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם
among those who do the will of the Omnipresent,
דְּנִקְרָאִים בָּנִים וְלֹא עֲבָדִים
who are called sons and not servants,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא י׳ עַמּוּד א׳)
as they said (Bava Basra 10a),
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן לְרַבִּי מֵאִיר
and all the more according to Rabbi Meir
(בְּקִדּוּשִׁין ל״ו עַמּוּד א׳)
(in Kiddushin 36a).
דְּלְעוֹלָם נִקְרָאִים בָּנִים
that they are always called sons.
וּמָה שֶׁכָּתַב עוֹד
And what he also wrote —
גִּירְסָא אַחֶרֶת וּפֵרוּשׁ אַחֵר
another reading and another explanation —
דְּ"בָּעַלְתִּי" מַשְׁמַע
that “baalti” (I have been master/husband to you) implies
קֹדֶם שֶׁתָּשׁוּבוּ,
before you return,
וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר כַּוָּנָתוֹ
one must say his intention is
דְּעַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה
that through the repentance
מְתַקְּנִים לְמַפְרֵעַ
they repair retroactively
לַעֲקֹר הַחֵטְא מֵעִקָּרוֹ,
to uproot the sin from its root,
כְּמוֹ חָכָם הָעוֹקֵר הַנֶּדֶר מֵעִקָּרוֹ,
like a sage who uproots a vow from its root,
דְּנִמְצָא אִגְלַאי מִלְּתָא הַשְׁתָּא
so it is revealed now.
דְּגַם לְמַפְרֵעַ הָיוּ מְרֻצִּים
that retroactively too they were favored.
וְגַם זֶה צָרִיךְ עִיּוּן
And this too requires study,
דְּתִינַח תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
for it works for repentance out of love,
דְּהוּא כִּזְכֻיּוֹת
which is like merits,
אֲבָל מִיִּרְאָה
but from fear,
דְּכִשְׁגָגוֹת
which is like inadvertent sins,
וְהַשּׁוֹגֵג עֲדַיִן צָרִיךְ סְלִיחָה
the inadvertent still requires forgiveness,
וְלֹא שַׁיָּךְ אַכְּתִי
and it is not yet applicable —
"בָּעַלְתִּי בָכֶם" גַּם מִקֹּדֶם
“baalti bachem” even earlier —.
כֵּיוָן דְּלֹא נֶעֱקַר עֲדַיִן לְגַמְרֵי
since it has not yet been completely uprooted.
וּבְ
And in Sanhedrin (97b)
מַיְיתֵי מִקְרָא דְּ"בָּעַלְתִּי"
it brings the verse “baalti”,
דְּבְּלֹא תְּשׁוּבָה כְּלָל
as without repentance at all,
וְזֶה עִנְיָן אַחֵר
and that is a different matter,
וְשָׁם פֵּרֵשׁ רַשִׁ״י
and there Rashi explained,
דְּ"בָּעַלְתִּי" מַשְׁמַע בְּעַל כָּרְחוֹ וְכוּלֵּי
that “baalti” implies against his will, etc.
וְשַׁפִּיר יְפֹרַשׁ
and it can well be explained
גַּם עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
also through suffering,
דְּהוּא בְּעַל כָּרְחוֹ
which is against his will
וְלֹא מֵאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה
and not from love and fear.
דְּהוּא מֵרְצוֹנוֹ שָׁב
where he returns of his own will.
וְעַל כֵּן פְּשַׁט "בָּעַלְתִּי" מַשְׁמַע
And therefore the plain sense of “baalti” implies
וַדַּאי דְּמְפָרֵשׁ לֵיהּ
that certainly he explains it,
עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
as through suffering,
וְקָרוֹב יוֹתֵר
and closer still
דְּהוּא לְשׁוֹן בַּעַל לְאִשָּׁה
is that it is the language of husband to wife,
וְלֹא אָדוֹן לְעֶבֶד
and not master to servant,
דְּכְשֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְעוֹרְרוֹ
for when the Holy One, blessed be He, arouses him
(עַל יְדֵי הַיִּסּוּרִין שֶׁמֵּבִיא עָלָיו)
(through the suffering He brings upon him)
הוּא מִסִּטְרָא דְּנוּקְבָּא
it is from the feminine side
וְכְאִשָּׁה הַמְקַבֶּלֶת מִבַּעְלָהּ.
like a wife receiving from her husband.
מָה שֶׁאֵין כֵּן בָּנִים הוּא דְכוּרָא
Whereas sons are the masculine,
זֶהוּ כְּשֶׁשָּׁבוּ מֵהִתְעוֹרְרוּת עַצְמָם
that is when they returned from their own arousal,
מֵאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה
out of love and fear,
וְגַם כְּפִי הַנֻּסְחָא אַחֶרֶת דְּרַשִׁ״י
and also according to the other version of Rashi
קְרָא דְּ"שׁוּבִי אֵלַי"
the verse “Return to Me”
הַיְנוּ בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִלְתַתָּא דִּידְהוּ.
is through their own arousal from below.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Yoma 86a and Rashi - suffering as the occasion of return: Rav Yehudah's answer is 'here, from love or from fear; there, through sufferings.' Rashi defines the third case narrowly: 'one who did not return until he was afflicted with sufferings.' R' Tzadok elsewhere clarifies the boundary: one who has not yet been struck but repents because he fears that punishment may come is still returning from fear, albeit the lower fear of punishment. Actual suffering creates the third case because the pressure is already present. Chazal use the same image in Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:3:2: just as oil improves only through crushing, Israel is brought to repentance through crushing. Pirkei deRabbi Eliezer 43 likewise closes its survey of the power of repentance by saying that Israel may return from distress, oppression, exile, and want. These passages describe an awakening; pain itself is not teshuvah. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2, still requires abandonment of the sin, regret, resolution not to repeat it, and verbal confession. This also prevents confusion with the baraisa of the four divisions of atonement earlier on Yoma 86a. There, repentance has already occurred and sufferings are 'memarkin,' completing the cleansing of transgressions punishable by kareis or court death; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4, and Rabbeinu Yonah, Shaarei Teshuvah 4:11, codify and develop that process. Here the sufferings precede the change of heart and provoke it. Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 13:1, makes this very distinction and cites Achav and Menasheh: they returned only after the decree or affliction, yet their return was received. R' Tzadok's question is therefore not whether coercive pain is itself a mitzvah or kapparah, but whether the sincere choice made within that pressure remains permanently branded as a servant's response.

paragraphs.text:
The case of Menasheh separates a desperate request for rescue, genuine repentance, and the further question of one’s portion in Olam HaBa. II Divrei HaYamim 33:10–17 says that after rejecting prophetic warnings, Menasheh was captured by Assyria, taken in chains to Bavel, and “ובהצר לו חלה את פני ה׳ אלהיו ויכנע מאד” — “In his distress he entreated Hashem his God and humbled himself greatly.” His prayer was heard; afterward he removed foreign gods, restored the altar, offered sacrifices, and commanded Yehudah to serve Hashem. The Yerushalmi, Sanhedrin 10:2, expands the ordeal: the idols fail him and the ministering angels seek to obstruct his prayer; Hashem opens a way to receive it lest repentance be closed to others. Pesikta de-Rav Kahana 24:11 offers the parallel wordplay on “ויעתר”; Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 43 also names Menasheh as an example of repentance. These are Midrashic expansions, not details stated in Divrei HaYamim. Nevertheless Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2 disputes his ultimate share: R’ Yehudah invokes his restoration as evidence he has a share, while the Sages answer “למלכותו השיבו, לא השיבו לחיי העולם הבא” — “He returned him to kingship, not to the World to Come.” Sanhedrin 103a preserves a strict view “בגלל מנשה דלא עבד תשובה,” but R’ Yochanan warns that denying Menasheh’s share weakens all penitents and cites a tradition of thirty-three years of return. Thus Rav Tzadok’s strict phrase “מכל מקום לא שב מחטאיו” is the position he is analyzing, not the unopposed verdict of Chazal or a denial of the Chronicles narrative. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2, requires abandonment, regret, future resolve, and confession; 2:1 accepts even late return while distinguishing the ideal of complete teshuvah. In Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah §13, Rav Tzadok himself explicitly presents Menasheh as proof that teshuvah initiated by suffering can be received. Compare Tzidkas HaTzadik §130 and Takanas HaShavin 15:95–96 for his later discussion of spiritual root and the Midrashic tunnel.
Sources: II Divrei HaYamim 33:10–17; Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2; Sanhedrin 102b–103a; Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 10:2; Pesikta de-Rav Kahana 24:11; Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 43; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:1–2; Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 13; Tzidkas HaTzadik 130; Takanas HaShavin 15:95–96.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: The 'king whose decrees are harsher than Haman's': Sanhedrin 97b-98a records the dispute of R' Eliezer and R' Yehoshua over whether redemption depends upon Israel first repenting. R' Yehoshua answers that if they do not repent, the Holy One sets over them a king whose decrees are as harsh as Haman's, Israel repents, and He restores them to the good. Yerushalmi Taanis 1:1 gives the same teaching and joins it to Yirmeyah 30:7, 'it is a time of distress for Yaakov, and from it he shall be saved.' Megillah 14a supplies the historical model: the removal of Achashverosh's ring and its transfer to Haman accomplished more than forty-eight prophets and seven prophetesses, because the decree returned Israel to the good. R' Tzadok repeatedly insists that this is not merely salvation of bodies. In Machshavos Charutz 6:1, the blow itself becomes the cure: Haman's decree brought Israel to complete teshuvah and to a renewed acceptance of Torah from love, so the source of danger became the source of rescue. Resisei Layla 58:3 says 'like Haman' precisely because the harshness is ultimately a provisional appearance whose purpose is to restore the heart to its Father in heaven. Tzidkas HaTzadik 52 adds the radical application used here: Mashiach can arrive in a generation wholly guilty, because God can bring the entire generation to repentance in a single moment and reveal the high root hidden beneath its failures. Siman 12, sections 9 and 11, will develop the same image as the Divine hand concealed within the apparently rejecting hand of Esav. The proof in the present se'if is exact: if return induced by suffering were intrinsically invalid or permanently second-class, it could not be the road to the complete future redemption. Once the response becomes true teshuvah rather than momentary panic, the coercive beginning does not cancel its redemptive power. Primary-text/source checkpoint: the exact "מעמיד להן מלך שגזרותיו קשות כהמן" is confirmed in the Shas ZIP at Sanhedrin 97b (not a separate 98a quotation). The Rav Tzadok parallel was checked directly against both the Reader ZIP and Har Bracha Machshavos Charutz, printed page 26 / PDF page 30; the Resisei Layla discussion was also checked in the ZIP and at printed page 202 / PDF page 206. References beyond these passages are retained with their existing scope.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: 'Where baalei teshuvah stand': Berachos 34b records R' Abahu's teaching that complete tzaddikim cannot stand in the place occupied by baalei teshuvah, deriving it from Yeshayahu 57:19, 'peace, peace, to the far and to the near' - the one who had been far is named first. R' Yochanan disagrees and reads 'far' as one distant from sin from the outset; the Gemara therefore presents a real dispute about comparative rank. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:4, adopts R' Abahu's view and explains that the penitent has tasted sin, separated from it, and conquered a stronger inclination. This does not erase Rambam's distinction in 2:1 between the ideal case of 'complete teshuvah' - the same opportunity and full strength, with abstention solely because of repentance - and a later return in weakness, which is accepted but not the choicest form. R' Tzadok is pressing the aggadic claim at its deepest point: if a person genuinely abandons the sin after suffering awakens him, does the source of the awakening bar him from the baal-teshuvah advantage? Takanas HaShavin 3:1 explains R' Abahu metaphysically. The tzaddik remains within the measured order of Torah, prophecy, and wisdom, while the baal teshuvah broke the world's boundary and, in returning from the place to which he fell, discovers that God was present even there. Resisei Layla 54:9 similarly says that after sin, rescue, and atonement, the penitent can attain a light higher than the joy available through ordinary worldly service. Pri Tzadik, Shelach 14:3, preserves both sides of the Gemara by teaching that each can be true in a different respect. Thus 'greater than a complete tzaddik' here is not a blanket rule that pain automatically elevates. It is the possible rank of the person who uses pain to make a real inward return and then transforms the distance itself into greater closeness.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Israel as sons even after sin: Bava Basra 10a contrasts two modes of relation to God. When Israel does the will of the Omnipresent it is called sons; when it does not, servants. Kiddushin 36a records the fuller dispute on 'You are sons to Hashem your God' (Devarim 14:1). R' Yehudah says the title sons depends upon behaving as sons; R' Meir says, 'either way you are called sons,' and brings verses that call Israel foolish sons, faithless sons, and corrupt sons. Rashi emphasizes the climax: even after the corruption of idolatry they can again be called 'sons of the living God' through repentance. Accordingly, R' Tzadok's argument works on both opinions. For R' Yehudah, the sincere penitent is now doing God's will and should be called a son; for R' Meir, the essential filial bond was never annulled. The Zoharic framework sharpens this second reading. Yahel Or on Zohar II 254b, drawing on Zohar III 36a-37a, explains that even when Israel's deeds are corrupt it remains rooted on the right side; the left may rule over it because of its deeds, but it does not become mixed with that side permanently. He therefore reads 'Return, wayward sons' literally: although wayward, they remain sons and are summoned to return, and he explicitly cites R' Meir in Kiddushin. The exceptional story of Acher marks the danger of believing oneself excluded, while Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1 answers even that despair with 'until the crushing of the soul they receive.' R' Tzadok's wider theology is parallel: Takanas HaShavin 3:1 says the baal teshuvah can return from beyond the ordinary bounds of law because the Divine hand remains extended there, and Tzidkas HaTzadik 52 compares Israel to a rose among thorns whose root remains intact beneath the surrounding damage. The se'if's unresolved difficulty is therefore precise. 'Servant' cannot describe Israel's final essence after true teshuvah; it must name a stage, manner of awakening, or degree of revealed closeness, which the following sections will define. Source-status qualification: the exact primary printed Yahel Or/Zohar folios cited above have not been separately collated in this batch; the attribution is retained as an inherited bibliographic lead rather than independently certified direct quotation.

paragraphs.text:
Yoma 86a compares “שובו בנים שובבים ארפא משובותיכם” (Yirmeyahu 3:22), “Return, wayward sons; I shall heal your waywardness,” with “שובו בנים שובבים כי אנכי בעלתי בכם” (3:14), “Return, wayward sons, for I am your master.” Rashi on Yoma reads the first as return from love or fear, whose penitents are called children, and the second as return after suffering, described by the language of servitude. But this is an aggadic taxonomy of the motive for return; the four divisions of kapparah earlier on Yoma 86a instead address what completes atonement after return. In the biblical verse, Rashi on Yirmeyahu 3:14 explains ba’alti as “אני אדון לכם” — “I am your Master,” who does not leave Israel to enemies. Radak records both renewed marital attachment after estrangement and an alternative sense “I was weary of you”; the verse is therefore broader than this single derashah. Radak on 3:22 likens repentance and forgiveness to medicine for the wounded soul. Rav Tzadok asks why even an accepted baal teshuvah should retain the name “servant,” since Kiddushin 36a reports R’ Meir’s “בין כך ובין כך אתם קרוים בנים” — “Either way, you are called children.” Bava Basra 10a adds a related distinction in how Israel are described. The first awakening through pain can be servile, yet it need not be the penitent’s final identity. In Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah §13, Rav Tzadok explicitly distinguishes three awakenings—fear, love, or suffering—and uses Kayin, Achav, and Menasheh to establish that the third can also be accepted. His reading of “תשב אנוש עד דכא” (Tehillim 90:3), and Adam’s surprise at Kayin’s repentance in Bereishis Rabbah 22:13, illuminate that power. This does not erase the higher level of teshuvah from love, which can transform deliberate sins into merits. The inherited separate note also cited Yahel Or on Zohar II 254b; retain that bibliographic lead for direct collation rather than attributing unverified exact wording.

Radak on 3:22 likens repentance and forgiveness to medicine for the wounded soul. Rav Tzadok asks why even an accepted baal teshuvah should retain the name “servant,” since Kiddushin 36a reports R’ Meir’s “בין כך ובין כך אתם קרוים בנים” — “Either way, you are called children.” Bava Basra 10a adds a related distinction in how Israel are described. The first awakening through pain can be servile, yet it need not be the penitent’s final identity. In Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah §13, Rav Tzadok explicitly distinguishes three awakenings—fear, love, or suffering—and uses Kayin, Achav, and Menasheh to establish that the third can also be accepted. His reading of “תשב אנוש עד דכא” (Tehillim 90:3), and Adam’s surprise at Kayin’s repentance in Bereishis Rabbah 22:13, illuminate that power. This does not erase the higher level of teshuvah from love, which can transform deliberate sins into merits. The inherited separate note also cited Yahel Or on Zohar II 254b; retain that bibliographic lead for direct collation rather than attributing unverified exact wording.

Yoma 86a and Rashi; Yirmeyahu 3:14, 3:22 and Rashi/Radak ad loc.; Kiddushin 36a; Bava Basra 10a; Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 13; Tehillim 90:3; Bereishis Rabbah 22:13; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4; cf. Yahel Or on Zohar II 254b (exact printed wording not yet collated).

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: There are three modes of teshuvah — from love, from fear, and through sufferings. Those who return from love or fear are called “sons”; those who return only once sufferings have struck are called “servants.” Yet even one aroused by sufferings, once he truly repents, is a “complete baal teshuvah” — for “You bring man back to contrition [dakka]” (Tehillim 90:3), which the Yerushalmi expounds “until the crushing of the soul”: Heaven receives the penitent even at the very hour of death, and all the more through lesser sufferings.

p: (ב) וְשׁוּב רָאִיתִי
And again I saw
בְּמַהֲרָשָׁ״א
in the Maharsha
בַּחִדּוּשֵׁי אַגָּדוֹת שָׁם
in Chiddushei Aggados there
שֶׁהִרְגִּישׁ
that he noticed
בְּמַה שֶׁהִקְשֵׁיתִי
what I asked,
מֵהַהוּא דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין
from that passage in Sanhedrin,
וּפֵרֵשׁ כֵּן
and explained thus:
צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר הַגִּירְסָא
one must say the reading
דְּהָרוֹמְיָא
of the contradiction,
דְּ"שׁוּבוּ" מַשְׁמַע בִּתְשׁוּבָה דַּוְקָא
that “shuvu” implies specifically with repentance,
וּ"בָּעַלְתִּי" מַשְׁמַע בְּלֹא תְשׁוּבָה
and “baalti” implies without repentance,
כַּנִּזְכָּר מִסַּנְהֶדְרִין
as mentioned from Sanhedrin,
מְשַׁנֵּי דְּהוּא עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
he answers that it is through suffering;
יֵעָיֵן שָׁם
see there.
וּפֵרוּשׁ זֶה גַּם כֵּן אֵינוֹ מְחֻוָּר
And this explanation too is not clear,
דְּאִי לְסַלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ
for if it were to enter your mind
"בָּעַלְתִּי" מַשְׁמַע בְּלֹא תְשׁוּבָה
that “baalti” implies without repentance
לֹא הָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר
he should not have said
"כָּאן וְכוּלֵּי וְכָאן וְכוּלֵּי",
“here, etc. and here, etc.”
אֶלָּא הָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר
but he should have said
הָכִי נַמֵּי עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה
so too, through repentance,
דְּמַעֲמִיד וְכוּלֵּי
which establishes, etc..
וְעַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
and through suffering.
אֲבָל הַלָּשׁוֹן "כָּאן וְכוּלֵּי"
But the wording “here, etc.”
מַשְׁמַע דְּיָדַע
implies that he knew
גַּם בְּסַלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ
even in the initial supposition,
דְּ"בָּעַלְתִּי" רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה
that “baalti” means through repentance,
רַק דְּהוּקְשָׁה לֵיהּ
only that it troubled him,
דְּבְּאֵיזֶה דָּבָר לֹא דָּמֵי
in what way they are not alike,
דְּעַל זֶה יִפּוֹל לְשׁוֹן הַשִּׁנּוּי
for upon this falls the language of the answer
דְּ"כָּאן" בְּמִין זֶה דְּהַתְּשׁוּבָה
“here” in this type of repentance.
וּ"כָּאן" בְּזֶה
and “there” in that.
וְאִי הַקֻּשְׁיָא דְּלֹא דָּמֵי הוּא
And if the difficulty is that they are not alike,
דְּ"שׁוּבוּ" מַשְׁמַע אַתֶּם
that “shuvu” implies you,
וּ"בָּעַלְתִּי" מַשְׁמַע אֲנִי וְעַל יְדֵי
and “baalti” implies I and through Me,
אִם הַקֻּשְׁיָא
if the difficulty is
לָמָּה פְּעָמִים כֵּן וּפְעָמִים כָּךְ,
why sometimes thus and sometimes thus,
עַל זֶה לֹא תֵּרֵץ כְּלוּם
on this he answered nothing
בִּלְשׁוֹן "כָּאן",
in the wording “here,”
רַק הָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר
he should only have said
הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַמְתִּין לָאָדָם
the Blessed Name waits for a person:
אִם שָׁב מֵעַצְמוֹ מוּטָב
if he returns on his own, good,
וְאִם לָאו
and if not,
"בָּעַלְתִּי בָּכֶם" כָּל כָּךְ.
“I have been master over you” to that extent.
וְאִם הַקֻּשְׁיָא
And if the difficulty is
אֵיךְ בִּמְצִיאוּת
how in reality,
לְהָשִׁיבָם בְּעַל כָּרְחָם
to return them against their will,
זֶה וַדַּאי אֵינוֹ בִּגְדֵר קֻשְׁיָא כְּלָל
this is certainly not a difficulty at all.
כְּלַפֵּי שְׁמַיָּא
with regard to Heaven.
וְגַם הַלָּשׁוֹן "כָּאן וְכוּלֵּי"
Also the wording “here, etc.”,
אֵינוֹ נָכוֹן בָּזֶה
is not right in this,
וְרֵישָׁא דִּ"שׁוּבוּ" וְגוֹמֵר
and the beginning of “shuvu,” etc.
יָדַע גַּם הַמַּקְשֶׁה
the questioner also knew.
דְּהוּא מֵאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה
that it is from love and fear.
וְתוּ יֵשׁ לְדַקְדֵּק
And further one should examine
בַּגִּירְסָא שֶׁלְּפָנֵינוּ
in the reading before us
מִקְרָא דְּ"שׁוּבוּ וְגוֹמֵר, אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבֹתֵיכֶם",
the verse “Return… I will heal your backslidings,”,
לְפֵרוּשׁ רַשִׁ״י וּמַהֲרָשָׁ״א
according to Rashi and Maharsha,
לָמָּה מַיְיתֵי הַאי קְרָא דְּאַחַר כָּךְ
why does it bring this later verse
וְלֹא רֵישֵׁיהּ דִּקְרָא
and not the beginning of the verse
דְּ"בָּעַלְתִּי" עַצְמוֹ
of “baalti” itself,
דְּפָתַח גַּם כֵּן "שׁוּבוּ בָנִים" וְגוֹמֵר
which also opens “Return, children,” etc.
דְּקָרֵי לְהוּ בָּנִים וְאָמַר "שׁוּבוּ".
for it calls them children and says “return.”
וְאִי דְּבָעֵי לְאַתּוֹיֵי "אֶרְפָּא"
And if he wanted to bring “I will heal”,
דְּלְרַשִׁ״י הַיְנוּ מִיִּרְאָה
which according to Rashi is from fear,
לוֹמַר דְּאַף מִיִּרְאָה נִקְרָאִים בָּנִים
to say that even from fear they are called children,
קָשֶׁה הַאי גּוּפָא מְנָא לֵיהּ,
this itself, how does he know it?
דְּהֲלֹא יֵשׁ מָקוֹם לוֹמַר
for there is room to say,
דְּמִיִּרְאָה לֹא
that from fear they are not,
אֵימָא אֵין הָכִי נַמֵּי
say: yes, indeed,
דְּבְּסֵיפֵיהּ דְּ"אֶרְפָּא" לֹא כְּתִיב "בָּנִים".
since at the end of “I will heal” “children” is not written.
וּמִלְּשׁוֹן "מְשׁוּבֹתֵיכֶם"
And from the wording “your backslidings”
אֵין לְדַיֵּק
one cannot infer,
דְּעַל "בָּנִים" דְּרֵישֵׁיהּ קָאֵי
that it refers to the “children” at its beginning,
דְּבְּהַאי קְרָא דְּ"בָּעַלְתִּי" גַּמִּי
for in this verse of “baalti” too
כְּתִיב "בָּנִים" בְּרֵישֵׁיהּ
“children” is written at its beginning
וְלֹא אָמַר
and he did not say,
דְּאֶתְכֶם עַל "בָּנִים" דְּרֵישֵׁיהּ קָאֵי
that “you” refers to the “children” at its beginning,
וְהָתָם נִמְשָׁךְ טְפֵי לְרֵישֵׁיהּ
and there it is drawn more to its beginning,
מִמַּה שֶׁאָמַר "כִּי אָנֹכִי" וְגוֹמֵר
than to what it says, “for I,” etc.
דְּמִלַּת "כִּי" מַשְׁמַע
since the word “ki” implies.
שֶׁקָּאֵי עַל "שׁוּבוּ" דְּלְעֵיל
that it refers to the “shuvu” above.
וּבֶאֱמֶת מֵהַאי טַעְמָא גַּם כֵּן
And in truth for this reason also,
דָּחוּק לְפִי דִבְרֵיהֶם
it is strained according to their words,
שֶׁנִּצְטָרֵךְ לִהְיוֹת סַכִּינָא חֲרִיפָא
that it must be a sharp knife,
מְפַסְּקֵי קְרָאֵי
cutting up the verses,
וּלְשׁוֹן "כִּי" וְגוֹמֵר מַשְׁמַע
while the wording “ki,” etc. implies
דְּפָרוּשֵׁי מְפָרֵשׁ
that it is explaining.
וְהַכֹּל עִנְיָן אֶחָד
and all is one matter.
וְתוּ יֵשׁ לְדַקְדֵּק
And further one should note
כְּפִי הַנֻּסְחָא בַּגְּמָרָא שֶׁלְּפָנֵינוּ
according to the text in the Gemara before us
מַסִּיק לְסֵיפֵיהּ דִּקְרָא
it concludes with the end of the verse
דְּ"בָּעַלְתִּי" וְגוֹמֵר
“baalti,” etc. ",
אֶחָד מֵעִיר" וְגוֹמֵר
“one from a city,” etc.
דְּמַה דְּמַיְיתֵי לְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב כֻּלּוֹ
for its bringing the whole verse
דְּ"וְלָקַחְתִּי" וְגוֹמֵר
“and I will take,” etc.
הוּא לְלֹא צֹרֶךְ,
is without need,
וּבְעֵין יַעֲקֹב הַגִּירְסָא "וְגוֹמֵר",
and in Ein Yaakov the reading is “etc.”
וְגַם מִלַּת "וְגוֹמֵר" הוּא לְמוּתָר
and the word “etc.” too is superfluous.
אִם הָרְמְיָא מִמִּלַּת "בָּעַלְתִּי" לְבַד
if the contradiction is from the word “baalti” alone.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: The textual setting of Se'if 2 is the second of two adjacent derashos on Yoma 86a. First, R' Chama bar Chanina contrasts the beginning of Yirmeyah 3:22, 'Return, wayward sons,' with its conclusion, 'I will heal your waywardness.' Rashi explains that return from love uproots the sin from its beginning, whereas return from fear leaves the former blemish perceptible like the name of an invalid who has been healed. Rav Yehudah then contrasts that entire verse with Yirmeyah 3:14, 'for I am a Master to you, and I will take you one from a city and two from a family,' and the Gemara answers: here from love or fear, there through sufferings. Rashi's principal explanation reads the titles: returners from love or fear are called sons, while those who did not return until suffering struck are called servants. Rashi then records an alternate text: the contradiction is between 'Return to Me and I shall return to you' and 'I am already a Master to you' - the first describes Divine return after human repentance, the second Divine mastery before repentance. Maharsha rejects the need for that alternate text and preserves the standard editions; the next note gives his construction. Maharal, Netivos Olam, Netiv HaTeshuvah 2, offers an important conceptual parallel without relying on the Maharsha's three-clause mapping. 'Return ... I will heal' indicates an awakening that begins within the person; 'I am a Master to you' indicates an awakening initiated by God, who compels the person through suffering. Maharal thus distinguishes love, fear, and suffering as three grades of agency and associates them with Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov: love is inner attachment, fear is the person's own response to an external demand, and suffering is an arousal imposed from above. R' Tzadok accepts the reality of those three modes but tests whether the wording and chosen verses support either Rashi's labels or Maharsha's reconstruction. His wider teaching explains why the textual point matters. Resisei Layla 21 says that only after teshuvah from love will it be disclosed that Israel's sins too were within the Divine order established from Creation; Tzidkas HaTzadik 40 likewise defines the deepest repentance as the illumination in which deliberate sins become merits, while Tzidkas HaTzadik 52 and Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 13, show that suffering can begin a genuine national return. The se'if therefore does not reject repentance born from fear or pain. It asks how an externally forced beginning relates to the later inward return that heals and transforms. The halachic baseline remains Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2: abandonment of the sin, regret, resolution, and confession make the act teshuvah; the aggadic distinctions here concern its mode, depth, and revealed relationship to God, not whether pain automatically atones or whether a fearful penitent is excluded.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Maharsha, Chiddushei Aggados to Yoma 86a - text, source, and R' Tzadok's critique: R' Shmuel Eliezer Edels (1555-1631) wrote Chiddushei Aggados to clarify the non-legal passages of the Bavli. Here he says that Rashi's alternate reading is forced and that 'all the text of the editions' should be maintained. He reads Yoma together with Sanhedrin 97b-98a. There R' Eliezer says that Israel is redeemed only if it repents; R' Yehoshua answers that if Israel does not repent, the Holy One will set over it a king whose decrees are as harsh as Haman's, Israel will repent, and He will restore them to the good. In the following Scriptural exchange R' Yehoshua cites Yirmeyah 3:14, 'for I am a Master to you, and I will take you one from a city and two from a family,' as a promise of redemption not dependent upon an earlier voluntary return. Maharsha combines these passages and maps three phrases in Yoma onto three responses: 'Return, wayward sons' describes voluntary repentance from love; 'I will heal your waywardness' describes repentance from fear of punishment; and 'I am a Master to you' describes compelled repentance through sufferings, when God raises a Haman-like ruler and thereby restores Israel. This reading is theologically close to Maharal's distinction between human arousal and Divine compulsion, but R' Tzadok objects to its syntax. If the initial force of 'I am a Master' is that God acts before Israel repents, the Gemara should have answered explicitly that this too ends in teshuvah - the repentance produced by the harsh king and the sufferings. Its balanced formula, 'here ... and here ...,' implies that both verses were already understood to describe teshuvah and that the unresolved contrast lies in some other detail. His second objection is still more textual. Yirmeyah 3:14 itself begins, 'Return, wayward sons, says Hashem,' before continuing 'for I am a Master to you.' If the problem were simply son versus servant, or return versus no return, why did Rav Yehudah cite the later verse 3:22 - 'Return, wayward sons, I will heal your waywardness' - instead of allowing the apparent contradiction to stand within 3:14 itself? Classical peshat also cautions against turning ba'alti into a technical denial of repentance: Rashi on Yirmeyah understands it as Divine lordship and refusal to abandon Israel to the enemy; Radak records the covenantal-marital sense; Malbim emphasizes renewed attachment even when only a remnant returns. A later discussion in Marit HaAyin to Yoma insists that even repentance from fear restores the legal-spiritual title of son, and cites the Rashba's ruling that Israel remains children even in sin. Consistently, Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:1-2 and 7:4, distinguishes the completeness and rank of repentance without saying that an awakening caused by fear or suffering is unreal once the sinner genuinely abandons the sin. R' Tzadok will therefore retain Maharsha's crucial Sanhedrin background but relocate the contradiction. In Se'if 3 he reads it in the endings of the verses: 3:22 promises healing to all who return from their own arousal, whereas 3:14 concludes that only 'one from a city' truly returns under an arousal from above and brings merit to the rest. This explains both the verses chosen by the Gemara and the phrase 'here ... here' without branding a sincere penitent permanently as a servant.

- text, source, and R' Tzadok's critique: R' Shmuel Eliezer Edels (1555-1631) wrote Chiddushei Aggados to clarify the non-legal passages of the Bavli. Here he says that Rashi's alternate reading is forced and that 'all the text of the editions' should be maintained. He reads Yoma together with

-98a. There R' Eliezer says that Israel is redeemed only if it repents; R' Yehoshua answers that if Israel does not repent, the Holy One will set over it a king whose decrees are as harsh as Haman's, Israel will repent, and He will restore them to the good. In the following Scriptural exchange R' Yehoshua cites

, 'for I am a Master to you, and I will take you one from a city and two from a family,' as a promise of redemption not dependent upon an earlier voluntary return. Maharsha combines these passages and maps three phrases in Yoma onto three responses: 'Return, wayward sons' describes voluntary repentance from love; 'I will heal your waywardness' describes repentance from fear of punishment; and 'I am a Master to you' describes compelled repentance through sufferings, when God raises a Haman-like ruler and thereby restores Israel. This reading is theologically close to Maharal's distinction between human arousal and Divine compulsion, but R' Tzadok objects to its syntax. If the initial force of 'I am a Master' is that God acts before Israel repents, the Gemara should have answered explicitly that this too ends in teshuvah - the repentance produced by the harsh king and the sufferings. Its balanced formula, 'here ... and here ...,' implies that both verses were already understood to describe teshuvah and that the unresolved contrast lies in some other detail. His second objection is still more textual.

itself begins, 'Return, wayward sons, says Hashem,' before continuing 'for I am a Master to you.' If the problem were simply son versus servant, or return versus no return, why did Rav Yehudah cite the later verse 3:22 - 'Return, wayward sons, I will heal your waywardness' - instead of allowing the apparent contradiction to stand within 3:14 itself? Classical peshat also cautions against turning ba'alti into a technical denial of repentance: Rashi on Yirmeyah understands it as Divine lordship and refusal to abandon Israel to the enemy; Radak records the covenantal-marital sense; Malbim emphasizes renewed attachment even when only a remnant returns. A later discussion in Marit HaAyin to Yoma insists that even repentance from fear restores the legal-spiritual title of son, and cites the Rashba's ruling that Israel remains children even in sin. Consistently, Rambam,

and 7:4, distinguishes the completeness and rank of repentance without saying that an awakening caused by fear or suffering is unreal once the sinner genuinely abandons the sin.
