inlineHeadings.text: The theme: R’ Tzadok examines the Maharsha’s reading of the sugya. The Maharsha keeps the standard text and, following Perek Chelek, maps the three clauses onto three teshuvos: “Return, wayward sons” — willful, from love. “I will heal your waywardness” — from fear of punishment; “for I am a Master to you” — the compelled teshuvah when God sets over them “a king like Haman.” R’ Tzadok raises several difficulties with this and with Rashi, and prepares his own reading.

p: (ג) וְעַל כֵּן נִרְאֶה לְפָרֵשׁ
And therefore it seems to explain
דְּעִקַּר הַקֻּשְׁיָא
that the main difficulty,
הוּא רַק מִסִּיּוּם לָשׁוֹן הַנִּזְכָּר
is only from the conclusion of the wording mentioned,
דְּהָתָם כְּתִיב "שׁוּבוּ" וְגוֹמֵר
for there it is written “Return,” etc.
לְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל
to all Israel ",
וְאֶרְפָּא" לְכֻלָּם
“and I will heal” all of them,
וְהָכָא כְּתִיב נַמֵּי "שׁוּבוּ"
and here too it is written “return”.
וּמְסַיֵּם דְּיִקַּח רַק אֶחָד מֵעִיר וְגוֹמֵר
and concludes that He takes only one from a city, etc.
וְגַם לְפִי מַה שֶּׁאִיתָא (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין קי״א רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳)
And also according to what is stated (in Sanhedrin 111a) ",
אֶחָד מֵעִיר מְזַכֶּה כָּל הָעִיר" וְכוּלֵּי
“one from a city grants merit to the whole city,” etc.
מְבֹאָר מִכָּל מָקוֹם
it is nevertheless clear,
דְּרַק אֶחָד הוּא הַזּוֹכֶה וּמְזַכֶּה
that only one is the one who merits and grants merit,
וְאַמַּאי לֹא כֻּלָּם
and why not all of them,
שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר
since it is possible to say
שֶׁיָּשׁוּבוּ כֻלָּם
that they all return
וְיֵרָפֵּא כֻלָּם
and all be healed
וְיִזְכּוּ כָּל אֶחָד מֵהֶם בְּעַצְמוֹ.
and each of them merit on his own.
וְעַל זֶה אָמַר כָּאן
And to this He said here,
מֵאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה
“from love and fear,”
דִּבְהָכִי מִתְקַיֵּם קְרָא
for thereby the verse is fulfilled,
דְּ"שׁוּבוּ" וְגוֹמֵר "אֶרְפָּא" וְגוֹמֵר דִּלְעֵיל
“Return,” etc. “I will heal,” etc. above,
וְכֵיוָן שֶׁשָּׁבוּ בְּעַצְמָם
and since they returned by themselves
מֵאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּידְהוּ
from their own arousal,
כֻּלָּם זוֹכִים לִרְפוּאָה
all merit healing,
כָּל אֶחָד כְּפִי תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ.
each according to his repentance.
וּקְרָא דְּ"בָּעַלְתִּי"
But the verse of “baalti”
דְּמַשְׁמַע בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִלְעֵילָא
which implies arousal from above
הוּא שֶׁיָּשׁוּבוּ,
is that they return,
הַיְנוּ עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
that is, through suffering,
בָּזֶה רַק אֶחָד מֵעִיר
in this only one from a city
שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
returns truly to the Blessed Name
וְלֹא מִשּׁוּם לְהִנָּצֵל מֵהַיִּסּוּרִין
and not merely to be saved from the suffering,
עַל יְדֵי זֶה לְבַד
by this alone,
רַק שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַיִּסּוּרִין הוּא מִתְעוֹרֵר
but through the suffering he is aroused,
וּמִשֶּׁנִּתְעוֹרֵר לָשׁוּב
and once aroused to return
הוּא שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת
he returns truly.
וּמְזַכֶּה כָּל הָעִיר
and grants merit to the whole city.
וַאֲפִילוּ תֵּימָא
And even if you say
דְּלֹא נִיחָא לְמָרֵיהוּ לוֹמַר
that it does not please them to say
עַל כָּל הַשָּׁבִים מִיִּסּוּרִים
of all who return from suffering,
שֶׁאֵינָם בֶּאֱמֶת אֶלָּא אֶחָד בָּעִיר
that they are not true except one in the city,
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּהָכָא מַיְירֵי
one can say that here it speaks.
בִּתְשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה
of complete repentance.
וְלֹא מִבַּעְיָא לְפֵרוּשׁ רַשִׁ״י
And not only according to Rashi’s explanation
דְּ"שׁוֹבָבִים" הַיְנוּ מֵאַהֲבָה
that “shovavim” means from love
(וְיֵשׁ לְדַקְדֵּק לְפִי דְבָרָיו
(and one should examine, according to his words,
אַגִּירְסָא בַּתְרָא דְּמַיְיתֵי
the second reading that he brings,
דְּמוֹקֵי קְרָא דְּ"בָּעַלְתִּי"
that he establishes the verse of “baalti”.
מֵאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה
as from love and fear.
וְהָא כְּתִיב בֵּיהּ "שׁוֹבָבִים"
But “shovavim” is written in it,
דְּלְפִי דְבָרָיו הַיְנוּ מֵאַהֲבָה
which according to his words means from love,
וְלָמָּה מַזְכִּיר גַּם מִיִּרְאָה
so why does he mention fear as well,
וּמְנָא לֵיהּ דְּקָאֵי גַּם אַמִּיִּרְאָה)
and how does he know it refers to fear too)
אֶלָּא גַּם לְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי
but also according to what I wrote
(בַּסִּימָן הַקּוֹדֵם)
(in the previous section),
דְּ"שׁוֹבָבִים" מַשְׁמַע מִיִּרְאָה כִּשְׁגָגוֹת
that “shovavim” implies from fear, like inadvertent sins,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם קְרָא דְּ"לָקַחְתִּי" דִּבְתְרֵיהּ
still the verse of “I will take” that follows it
הַיְנוּ כְּשֶׁיִּזְכּוּ אַחַר כָּךְ
is when they later merit.
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לִזְכֻיּוֹת
that it become merits.
וְכָךְ הַמִּדָּה
And such is the way:
דְּתְחִלַּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה
the beginning of repentance is from fear,
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן כְּשֶׁשָּׁב עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
and all the more when he returns through suffering,
דְּוַדַּאי אֵין תְּחִלָּתוֹ בָּא
for certainly his beginning comes,
אֶלָּא בְּהִתְעוֹרְרוּת יִרְאָה
only through arousal of fear,
וְאַחַר כָּךְ זוֹכֶה לָשׁוּב בֶּאֱמֶת מֵאַהֲבָה
and afterward he merits to return truly out of love,
וּכְדִמְסַיֵּם הָתָם אַחַר כָּךְ "אֶרְפָּא",
as it concludes there afterward “I will heal,”
דְּהַיְנוּ כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי
which, according to what I wrote,
רְפוּאָה גְּמוּרָה
is complete healing.
שֶׁיִּהְיוּ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת
that they become like merits.
הָכִי נַמֵּי הָכָא דִּמְסַיֵּם "וְלָקַחְתִּי",
So too here, where it concludes “and I will take,”
הַיְנוּ שֶׁיִּזְכֶּה אַחַר כָּךְ
it means that afterward he merits
לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
repentance out of love;
זֶהוּ רַק אֶחָד מֵעִיר
this is only one from a city
כְּשֶׁהַהַתְחָלָה בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִלְעֵילָא
when the beginning is by arousal from above.
עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
through suffering.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם
And although nevertheless
שָׁב וּמִתְחָרֵט בֶּאֱמֶת
he returns and truly regrets,
דַּי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כִּשְׁגָגוֹת
it suffices that it be like inadvertent sins,
כִּתְשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה
like repentance from fear,
שֶׁהֲרֵי תְשׁוּבָתוֹ
for his repentance.
מִיִּרְאַת הַיִּסּוּרִין שֶׁבָּאוּ עָלָיו
is from fear of the suffering that came upon him.
אוֹ גַם אִם יִזְכֶּה לִמְחִילַת הַשּׁוֹגֵג
Or even if he merits forgiveness of the inadvertent,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם לְהִתְהַפֵּךְ עוֹד לִזְכֻיּוֹת
still to be further turned into merits,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ שְׁלֵמוּת הַתִּקּוּן הַגָּמוּר
which is the completeness of the full repair
בִּתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
in repentance out of love
עַד שֶׁיִּהְיוּ רְאוּיִים לִגְאֻלָּה שְׁלֵמָה
until they are worthy of complete redemption
בִּמְהֵרָה בְיָמֵינוּ,
speedily in our days,
לָאו כָּל אָדָם זוֹכֶה
not every person merits,
אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי אֶחָד מֵעִיר
but through one from a city
הַזּוֹכֶה לְכָךְ
who merits this
וּמְזַכֶּה כָּל אֶחָיו עִמּוֹ
and grants merit to all his brothers with him
שֶׁיִּזְכּוּ גַּם כֵּן לַתִּקּוּן הַגָּמוּר
so that they too merit the full repair.
עַל יָדוֹ דַּוְקָא
specifically through him.
מָה שֶׁאֵין כֵּן כְּשֶׁשָּׁב בְּעַצְמוֹ
Not so when he returns on his own
מֵהִתְעוֹרְרוּתוֹ,
from his own arousal:
אַף דִּתְחִלָּתוֹ מִיִּרְאָה
although his beginning is from fear,
כָּל אָדָם יוּכַל לִזְכּוֹת
every person can merit
אִם לֹא יִתְרַשֵּׁל בִּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ
if he does not slacken in his repentance,
אַחַר כָּךְ לְמֵאַהֲבָה
afterward toward love.
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן כְּשֶׁתְּחִלָּתוֹ מֵאַהֲבָה
and all the more when his beginning is from love.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Sanhedrin 111a - source, meforshim, and the reach of one person's merit: This teaching appears in the closing aggadah of Perek Chelek, amid discussions of how many will be redeemed. On Yirmeyah 3:14, Reish Lakish first says devarim ki-kesavan, 'the words are literal': only one from a city and two from a family will be taken. R' Yochanan objects, 'It is not pleasing to their Master that you say this about them,' and expounds that one person's merit benefits the entire city and two benefit the entire family. The Gemara repeats the same exchange between Rav Kahana and Rav, making clear that the merciful reading is deliberate and not a casual paraphrase. Rashi explains the objection as: do not diminish Israel so drastically. Yalkut Shimoni on Nach 270:3 preserves this dispute as a midrash on the verse and thereby shows its independent place in the later aggadic source tradition. The peshat traditions need not deny the derash. R' Yosef Kara explains the simple sense as a future gathering of scattered survivors, collected one from this city and two from that family, who will later multiply in Zion. Malbim likewise reads 'one from a city' as the small remnant that God will nonetheless take and restore. Sanhedrin transforms that image of a remnant into collective merit: the few are not merely saved from the many; their merit becomes the means by which the many are saved. R' Tzadok adopts R' Yochanan's derash but gives it a precise role in the Yoma sugya. When suffering produces only a wish that suffering stop, the person has not yet made the pain into return for Hashem's sake. In R' Tzadok’s first explanation, the 'one from a city' is the rare person in whom the arousal from Above becomes a genuine inward teshuvah, and he thereby brings merit to those whose response remains incomplete. A closely related baraisa in Yoma 86b states in R' Meir's name that because of one individual who repents, he and the whole world are forgiven, deriving this from Hoshea 14:5, 'I will heal their waywardness ... for My anger has turned from him' - 'from them' is not written, but 'from him.' Tzidkat HaTzadik 159 asks how one person's repentance can yield forgiveness for others and answers that the exceptional penitent awakens stirrings of teshuvah in their hearts as well; he also warns that not everyone can simply declare himself that singular individual. This supplies the inner mechanism for the present se'if: the one merits the city by beginning a real movement within it. The kabbalistic parallel is Zohar Chadash, Midrash HaNe'elam on Noach, near its conclusion: if even one congregation returns in teshuvah, the merit of that gathering can draw in the entire exile. The individual, congregation, city, and nation are therefore successive circles of one principle - an authentic point of return can become the channel of a collective redemption. The halachic boundary remains important. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2-3, requires each sinner's own abandonment of the sin, regret, resolve, and confession; another person's merit does not perform those acts in his place. The aggadah describes collective favor, rescue, and awakening, not a legal substitution of one confession for another. This also prepares Se'if 4: even after the one has conferred merit, the prophetic call and daily bas kol continue to summon every other person to turn the externally granted opening into his own complete return. R’ Tzadok then offers a second explanation that does not deny the sincerity of the other sufferers’ repentance: the rare individual reaches its completed transformation into merits through love, and brings that completed repair to the others. Sincere fear-based return and even pardon of the remaining inadvertent residue can precede that higher completion. Exact-text qualification from Tzidkas HaTzadik §159: Rav Tzadok says that the universally comprehensive individual whose repentance can awaken every soul is specifically Mashiach ben David, because his soul must encompass all souls ("רק משיח בן דוד הוא יהיה כן"). Other penitents may stir the people or faculties connected to their own spiritual root; they do not automatically secure every individual’s inward teshuvah. The expansive "one from a city" merit in Sanhedrin 111a and Rav Tzadok’s specific metaphysical explanation must be kept distinct from any halachic substitution for each sinner’s repentance.

A closely related baraisa in Yoma 86b states in R' Meir's name that because of one individual who repents, he and the whole world are forgiven, deriving this from Hoshea 14:5, 'I will heal their waywardness ... for My anger has turned from him' - 'from them' is not written, but 'from him.' Tzidkat HaTzadik 159 asks how one person's repentance can yield forgiveness for others and answers that the exceptional penitent awakens stirrings of teshuvah in their hearts as well; he also warns that not everyone can simply declare himself that singular individual. This supplies the inner mechanism for the present se'if: the one merits the city by beginning a real movement within it. The kabbalistic parallel is Zohar Chadash, Midrash HaNe'elam on Noach, near its conclusion: if even one congregation returns in teshuvah, the merit of that gathering can draw in the entire exile. The individual, congregation, city, and nation are therefore successive circles of one principle - an authentic point of return can become the channel of a collective redemption. The halachic boundary remains important. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2-3, requires each sinner's own abandonment of the sin, regret, resolve, and confession; another person's merit does not perform those acts in his place. The aggadah describes collective favor, rescue, and awakening, not a legal substitution of one confession for another. This also prepares Se'if 4: even after the one has conferred merit, the prophetic call and daily bas kol continue to summon every other person to turn the externally granted opening into his own complete return. R’ Tzadok then offers a second explanation that does not deny the sincerity of the other sufferers’ repentance: the rare individual reaches its completed transformation into merits through love, and brings that completed repair to the others. Sincere fear-based return and even pardon of the remaining inadvertent residue can precede that higher completion. Exact-text qualification from Tzidkas HaTzadik §159: Rav Tzadok says that the universally comprehensive individual whose repentance can awaken every soul is specifically Mashiach ben David, because his soul must encompass all souls ("רק משיח בן דוד הוא יהיה כן"). Other penitents may stir the people or faculties connected to their own spiritual root; they do not automatically secure every individual’s inward teshuvah. The expansive "one from a city" merit in Sanhedrin 111a and Rav Tzadok’s specific metaphysical explanation must be kept distinct from any halachic substitution for each sinner’s repentance.

paragraphs.text: Expanded source note: Yoma 86a and R' Tzadok's reading of the two verses: Rav Yehudah sets Yirmeyah 3:22, 'Return, wayward sons; I will heal your waywardness,' against Yirmeyah 3:14, 'Return, wayward sons ... for I am a Master to you, and I will take you one from a city and two from a family.' The Gemara answers: here from love or fear, there through sufferings. Rashi and Maharsha, discussed in the preceding notes, locate the contrast in the titles 'sons' and 'servants,' or in voluntary versus compelled return. R' Tzadok instead asks why the Gemara cited the later verse 3:22 when verse 3:14 itself begins with the same summons, 'Return, wayward sons.' He therefore moves the contradiction to the endings. Verse 3:22 addresses all Israel and promises healing to all who return; verse 3:14 ends with only 'one from a city and two from a family.' The difference is not whether the latter people repent, but how the movement began. Love and fear are an it'aruta di-letata, an arousal initiated by the person, so each returner receives the healing corresponding to his own teshuvah. Suffering is an it'aruta di-le'eila, an arousal initiated from Above. Many seek only relief from pain; the rare 'one from a city' allows the suffering to awaken a return directed to Hashem Himself, and his merit then reaches the rest. This reading also preserves R' Tzadok's insistence in Se'if 1 that teshuvah born amid suffering can be complete once it becomes truthful and inward. The classical commentators help define the derash. Rashi on Yirmeyah 3:14 explains ba'alti as Divine lordship: Israel bears God's Name, and His honor does not permit Him to abandon them to their enemies. Radak records both the covenantal-marital sense - God will take Israel back after divorce - and the Targum's 'I desired you'; Malbim reads the verse as God's attachment to the children even where the earlier generation failed, promising to gather even a tiny remnant. These are peshat and covenantal readings, whereas R' Tzadok is explaining the Bavli's juxtaposition and the spiritual process implied by its answer. His terminology belongs to a larger pattern in his sefarim. Takanat HaShavin 5:4 contrasts the human demand, 'Return to Me,' with the hope that an arousal from Above will first draw Israel; there too, the enduring goal is that the upper awakening be followed by the person's own return. Tzidkat HaTzadik 159 explains that the repentance of a unique individual can benefit the whole world because it awakens thoughts of teshuvah in other hearts, not because his inner act mechanically replaces theirs. Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 14, similarly notices the movement in Hoshea from the singular 'Return, Israel' to the plural 'Take words with you and return,' treating individual return as capable of opening a communal movement. Thus the present se'if is not a theory of automatic atonement through pain. It is a theory of how a Divine interruption becomes human teshuvah, first in the exceptional individual and then, through him, in the community. The author also offers a second, less restrictive reading in the latter half of this paragraph. The many can repent sincerely from fear and can even gain pardon for the remaining shogeg-like trace; “one from a city” then refers to the person who reaches the further completion of love, turning sins into merits and enabling the others to share in complete repair. By contrast, one who begins returning of his own initiative can continue personally from fear to love if he does not slacken. These are alternative explanations, not a blanket claim that almost all sufferers are insincere. Exact-text qualification from Tzidkas HaTzadik §159: Rav Tzadok says that the universally comprehensive individual whose repentance can awaken every soul is specifically Mashiach ben David, because his soul must encompass all souls ("רק משיח בן דוד הוא יהיה כן"). Other penitents may stir the people or faculties connected to their own spiritual root; they do not automatically secure every individual’s inward teshuvah. The expansive "one from a city" merit in Sanhedrin 111a and Rav Tzadok’s specific metaphysical explanation must be kept distinct from any halachic substitution for each sinner’s repentance.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: R’ Tzadok gives his own reading: the whole difficulty is only from the ending of the verse. “Return, wayward sons, I will heal” is said to all Israel — all return and all are healed. But “I am a Master to you, I will take one from a city and two from a family” implies that only one wins and brings merit to the rest.

p: (ד) וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם
And nevertheless,
הַכָּתוּב צוֹוֵחַ "שׁוּבוּ" וְגוֹמֵר
the verse cries out “Return,” etc.
אַף דְּכְבָר "בָּעַלְתִּי" וְגוֹמֵר
even though “baalti,” etc. already
וְעוֹרַרְתִּי הַהַתְחָלָה עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
and I aroused the beginning through suffering,
וְלָקַחְתִּי רַק אֶחָד מֵעִיר הַמְזַכֶּה כֻּלָּם
and took only one from a city who grants merit to all,
שֶׁהוּא מִתּוֹךְ הַיִּסּוּרִין עַצְמָן
who from within the suffering itself,
הִתְעוֹרֵר לָשׁוּב בֶּאֱמֶת מֵאַהֲבָה
was aroused to return truly out of love,
עֲדַיִן גַּם הַשְּׁאָר
still the rest as well
הַנָּבִיא מְעוֹרְרָם בְּשֵׁם ה׳
the prophet arouses in the name of the Lord,
לָשׁוּב עוֹד מֵאַהֲבָה
to return further out of love.
דְּ"שׁוּבוּ בָנִים" לְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל קָאָמַר
for “Return, children” he said to all Israel.
וְ"שׁוֹבָבִים" לְרַשִׁ״י
And “shovavim” according to Rashi,
הַיְנוּ תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
means repentance out of love,
וְגַם לְדִידִי רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר
and even according to me it means
דְּכְבָר הֵם שׁוֹבָבִים
that they are already backsliders-returned,
עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה דְּעַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
through the repentance that came through suffering,
וּמְעוֹרְרָם עוֹד
and He arouses them further.
לַחֲזֹר וְלָשׁוּב עֲדַיִן
to turn back and return yet again.
וְרַק לָבוֹא מֵהַתְחָלַת הִתְעוֹרְרוּת
But to come from the beginning of arousal
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין לְבַד
that is through suffering alone
לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
to repentance out of love,
לֹא כָּל אָדָם זוֹכֶה
not every person merits,
אֲבָל יוּכַל לְהִתְעוֹרֵר אַחַר כָּךְ
but he can be aroused afterward
בְּהִתְעוֹרְרוּת חֲדָשָׁה
with a new arousal
לָשׁוּב בֶּאֱמֶת
to return truly.
שֶׁלֹּא מֵהַיִּסּוּרִין לְבַד
not from the suffering alone.
וְאַחַר דְּ"לָקַחְתִּי"
And after “I took”
עַל יְדֵי אֶחָד מֵעִיר הַמְזַכֶּה כֻּלָּם
through one from a city who grants merit to all,
דְּלֵיכָּא עוֹד יִסּוּרִין
when there is no more suffering,
אוֹ אֲפִילוּ לֹא נִסְתַּלְּקוּ עֲדַיִן
or even if it has not yet departed,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא מִתְעוֹרֵר עוֹד
still he is aroused further.
לָשׁוּב שֶׁלֹּא מֵחֲמָתָן
to return not because of it.
וְדָבָר זֶה בְּיַד כָּל אֶחָד לִזְכּוֹת
And this is in everyone’s hand to merit
גַּם אַחַר הָאַתְחַלְתָּא
even after the beginning,
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
that was through suffering,
וְאַדְרַבָּא נָקֵל עוֹד יוֹתֵר
on the contrary, it is even easier
מֵאַחַר שֶׁכְּבָר הִתְחִיל לָשׁוּב עַל כָּל פָּנִים
since he already began to return in any case.
אַף שֶׁהוּא עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
even though it was through suffering.
וּבַת קוֹל יוֹצֵא בְּכָל יוֹם
And a heavenly voice goes forth every day (,
כֵּן מוּבָא בַּסְּפָרִים
(so it is brought in the books,
וְאוּלַי הוּא בְּאֵיזֶה מִדְרָשׁ,
and perhaps it is in some Midrash,
דִּבְגְּמָרָא
for in the Gemara, Chagigah 15a,
וּבַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי פֶּרֶק ב דַּחֲגִיגָה
and in the Yerushalmi, chapter 2 of Chagigah,
וְרוּת רַבָּה עַל פָּסוּק "לִינִי הַלַּיְלָה"
and Ruth Rabbah on the verse “Stay the night,”
וְקֹהֶלֶת רַבָּה עַל פָּסוּק "טוֹב אַחֲרִית"
and Koheles Rabbah on the verse “The end is better,”
אֵין הַלָּשׁוֹן "בְּכָל יוֹם",
the wording is not “every day,”
רַק דְּאָז שָׁמַע אַחֵר הַבַּת קוֹל)
only that then Acher heard the heavenly voice) ",
שׁוּבוּ" וְכוּלֵּי
“Return,” etc.
וְיָדוּעַ דְּהֵם הַהִרְהוּרֵי תְשׁוּבָה
and it is known that these are the thoughts of repentance
שֶׁנּוֹפְלִים בְּלֵב כָּל אָדָם
that fall into every person’s heart
מִי שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לִהְיוֹת לְבָבוֹ פָּנוּי
who merits to have his heart free
לִשְׁמֹעַ אוֹתוֹ קוֹל הַמְעוֹרְרוֹ.
to hear that voice arousing him.
וְזֶה הַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת לֹא פָסִיק לְעוֹלָם
And this arousal never ceases,
גַּם עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
even through suffering;
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַבַּת קוֹל יוֹצֵא גַּם כֵּן
still the heavenly voice goes forth also.
לְעוֹרְרוֹ לָשׁוּב בֶּאֱמֶת גַּם כֵּן
to arouse him to return truly as well.
וְרַק כְּשֶׁהוּא אֵין שׁוֹמֵעַ
Only when he does not hear
לְקוֹל הַבַּת קוֹל הַמְעוֹרְרוֹ
the voice of the heavenly voice arousing him
וְשָׁב רַק מֵחֲמַת הַיִּסּוּרִין
and returns only because of the suffering,
בָּזֶה הוּא רַק אֶחָד מֵעִיר
in this case it is only one from a city
שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לִזְכּוֹת עַל יָדוֹ.
through whom it is necessary to merit.
אֲבָל בְּיַד כָּל אָדָם הוּא
But it is in every person’s hand,
גַּם אַחַר הַיִּסּוּרִין
even after the suffering,
דְּלֹא נִגְרַע כֹּחוֹ
for his power was not diminished
בְּמַה שֶּׁהָיָה מִקֹּדֶם
by what was earlier
לְהִתְעוֹרֵר גַּם כֵּן
to be aroused also,
עַל יְדֵי שְׁמִיעַת הַבַּת קוֹל דְּ"שׁוּבוּ" וְגוֹמֵר
through hearing the heavenly voice of “Return,” etc.
שֶׁהוּא דְּבַר הַנָּבִיא בְּשֵׁם ה׳
which is the word of the prophet in the name of the Lord.
הַקַּיָּם לְעוֹלָם
that endures forever.
דְּמֵאַחַר שֶׁנִּכְתְּבָה נְבוּאָתוֹ בַּסֵּפֶר
For since his prophecy was written in the book
דְּמִצְטָרֶכֶת לְדוֹרוֹת
because it is needed for the generations,
הֲרֵי הַדִּבּוּר קָבוּעַ וְקַיָּם
the utterance is fixed and enduring
וּפוֹעֵל לְדוֹרוֹת בְּכָל דְּבַר ה׳,
and acts for generations in every word of the Lord,
כְּעִנְיַן "לְעוֹלָם ה׳ דְּבָרְךָ נִצָּב בַּשָּׁמָיִם",
as in “Forever, Lord, Your word stands firm in heaven,”
וְנֶאֱמַר "כֵּן יִהְיֶה דְבָרִי" וְגוֹמֵר
and it is said “so shall My word be,” etc.
"לֹא יָשׁוּב אֵלַי רֵיקָם"
“it shall not return to Me empty,”
"כִּי אִם עָשָׂה אֶת" וְגוֹמֵר "שְׁלַחְתִּיו".
“but it shall accomplish… that for which I sent it.”
וְכָל דִּבּוּרָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ
And all His utterances, blessed be He,
מִפִּי נְבִיאָיו
from the mouths of His prophets
שֶׁנִּכְתְּבוּ בְּתוֹרָה נְבִיאִים וּכְתוּבִים
that were written in Torah, Prophets and Writings
הֵם פּוֹעֲלִים לְדוֹרֵי עוֹלָם
act for all generations
בְּכָל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל
in all the souls of Israel
שֶׁבְּכָל דּוֹר וָדוֹר
in every generation
לְהוֹלִיד בִּלְבָבָם
to bring forth in their hearts,
הִרְהוּרֵי תְשׁוּבָה וְהִתְעוֹרְרוּת לָשׁוּב
thoughts of repentance and arousal to return,
וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַבְטִיחַ
and the Blessed Name promises,
דְּלֹא יָשׁוּב רֵיקָם
that it will not return empty.
דְּסוֹף כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל לָשׁוּב בֶּאֱמֶת
for in the end all Israel will return truly.
וְאַף שֶׁמִּתְקַיֵּם גַּם הַדִּבּוּר
And although the utterance is also fulfilled ",
כִּי אָנֹכִי בָּעַלְתִּי" וְגוֹמֵר
“for I have been master,” etc.
שֶׁמְּעוֹרֵר עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין גַּם כֵּן
which arouses through suffering as well,

paragraphs.text: Yirmeyahu 3:14 and 3:22 — the two prophetic calls underlying the entire discussion. Verse 14 says, “Return, wayward sons ... for I have been a Master to you; I will take you one from a city and two from a family,” while verse 22 says, “Return, wayward sons; I will heal your waywardness.” Yoma 86a places these verses in tension and distinguishes voluntary teshuvah from return awakened through suffering; Sanhedrin 111a interprets “one from a city” mercifully, that one person can bring merit to the whole city. Rashi explains ba’alti as Hashem’s lordship and covenantal claim over Israel; Radak records both the marital sense and the Targum’s sense, “I desired you”; Malbim emphasizes that Hashem gathers even a tiny remnant and restores it to Zion. R’ Tzadok’s point in this se’if is a further stage: even after the arousal from Above and the merit of the exceptional “one,” the command “Return, sons” continues to address every Jew. Collective merit opens the door, but it does not replace each person’s own inward return.

paragraphs.text: Teshuvah from love: Yoma 86b teaches that when one repents from love, intentional sins are transformed into merits; when one repents from fear, they are reduced to inadvertent sins. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:6-7, describes the baal teshuvah as beloved and close to Hashem, and stresses that yesterday he was separated and today he is attached to the Shechinah. R’ Tzadok therefore says that even one initially moved only by suffering can afterward “return again from love.” The first movement may have been compelled by pain, but a subsequent awakening, no longer driven simply by escaping the affliction, permits an inward and freely chosen teshuvah that changes the quality of the past. Rav Tzadok will identify the renewed daily Divine summons later in this seif; its mechanism has not yet been introduced at this anchor.

paragraphs.text: The daily proclamation is not merely an inference from Avos. Sefer Chareidim, Positive Commandments 1:34, explicitly states: "ובכל יום ויום בת קול מכרזת שובו בנים שובבים כדאיתא בזוהר פרשת נשא" — every day a heavenly voice proclaims "Return, wayward children," citing Zohar Naso. This is a direct independently checked Hebrew-text witness for the daily wording; the specific folio and earliest print of the Zohar passage remain to be directly collated and should not be described as already verified. By contrast, Avos 6:2 explicitly speaks of a daily voice from Chorev rebuking neglect of Torah; it does not quote the daily "שובו" proclamation. Chagigah 15a, Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1, Rus Rabbah and Koheles Rabbah describe the singular voice heard by Acher, not independently a daily event. The inherited references to Shelah, Aseres HaDibros, Yoma (Derech Chaim), and Kedushas Levi, Ki Savo 7, are retained as secondary parallels but their precise original printed passages were not collated in this batch. Rav Tzadok interprets the daily summons as a renewed invitation to real repentance; it never replaces the person’s own action. Sources: Sefer Chareidim, Positive Commandments 1:34 (direct Hebrew witness); Avos 6:2; Chagigah 15a; Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1; cited Zohar Naso (attribution via Chareidim).

paragraphs.text: The “bas kol issuing every day, ‘Return, wayward sons!’” is cited by R’ Tzadok from the standard seforim. He notes that in the extant sources — Chagigah 15a, the Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1, Rus Rabbah (on “lodge the night,” Rus 3:13), and Koheles Rabbah (on “better is the end”) — the wording is not “every day” but rather the singular event in which Acher (Elisha ben Avuya) heard the bas kol. R’ Tzadok reads the daily “bas kol” as the perpetual stirrings of teshuvah that the prophetic word, fixed in Scripture, awakens in every generation’s hearts.

paragraphs.text: Rav Tzadok himself defines the daily voice here as "הרהורי תשובה שנופלים בלב כל אדם" — thoughts of repentance that arise in every person’s heart. The important distinction is between a Divine awakening, which can arise without bodily suffering, and a sincere personal decision to return, which remains necessary. The inherited Chassidic parallels — Mekor Mayim Chayim’s citation of the Baal Shem Tov, Meor Einayim on Vayeira, and Kedushas Levi on the degree to which each person perceives a bat kol — are preserved as bibliographic leads; their exact Hebrew in the earliest printed witnesses has NOT been collated here, and none is presented as a verified verbatim quote. Mesillas Yesharim ch. 5 supplies a related practical discussion of moral awakening through reflection and admonition, distinct from Rav Tzadok’s mystical explanation. The securely identified primary wording of the daily proclamation is Sefer Chareidim, Positive Commandments 1:34. It does not require equating Avos 6:2 (a daily rebuke over Torah neglect) with the different "שובו בנים" formula. Sources: Takanas HaShavin 12:4 (Rav Tzadok’s direct words); Sefer Chareidim, Positive Commandments 1:34; inherited parallels for future collation as named above.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 14a: after stating that forty-eight prophets and seven prophetesses were recorded, the Gemara asks whether there were no others and answers that prophets actually arose in enormous numbers. Only “a prophecy needed for the generations was written; one not needed for the generations was not written.” In its plain sense, this explains the canon of Tanach: the recorded prophecies contain an enduring message for later generations. R’ Tzadok draws a stronger spiritual conclusion from the same rule. If the prophecy was written because it is needed for all generations, its speech is not merely historically relevant; it remains an active Divine utterance that continues to awaken the souls for whom it was preserved.

paragraphs.text: Tehillim 119:89, “Forever, Hashem, Your word stands firm in the heavens.” Radak, Ibn Ezra, Metzudas David, and Rambam in Moreh Nevuchim I:15 understand nitzav as permanence and unchanging endurance. Midrash Tehillim and Shemos Rabbah use the verse to teach that Hashem’s word and promise remain standing until fulfilled. The Baal Shem Tov, cited in Tanya, Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah ch. 1, reads it ontologically: the letters of the Divine command that created the heavens remain within them continually, giving them existence at every moment. R’ Tzadok applies that chassidic principle to prophecy. The command “Return” remains “standing” in the world and continually gives life to new stirrings of teshuvah in Jewish hearts.

paragraphs.text: Yeshayah 55:10-11. The prophet compares Hashem’s word to rain and snow: they do not return upward before watering the earth, causing it to give birth and sprout, and producing seed and bread. So too, “My word ... shall not return to Me empty, but shall accomplish what I desired and succeed in that for which I sent it.” Rashi and Radak explain that the Divine promise will certainly be fulfilled; the agricultural comparison emphasizes that its effect may unfold through a process of hidden germination before becoming visible. This precisely supports R’ Tzadok’s language: the prophetic word planted in Tanach acts through the generations, “giving birth” to thoughts of teshuvah, even when its final fruit is not immediately apparent.

paragraphs.text: “In the end all Israel will return in truth” is the formulation of Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:5: “All the prophets commanded concerning teshuvah ... and the Torah has already promised that Israel will ultimately perform teshuvah at the end of their exile, and immediately they will be redeemed.” His source is Devarim 30:1-3: “You shall return to Hashem your God ... and Hashem your God will return your captivity.” This is not merely a hopeful prediction but, in the Rambam’s halachic presentation, a promise embedded in Torah. R’ Tzadok reads Yeshayah’s “it shall not return empty” as the spiritual mechanism of that promise: the words of the prophets continue to work within Israel until the promised collective teshuvah becomes actual and true.

The prophet still cries “Return, sons!” to all Israel, calling them to return further, from love. וְכֵן הוּא בְּמִדְרַשׁ רוּת וְקֹהֶלֶת שָׁם
and so it is in the Midrash on Ruth and Koheles there,
וְהוֹבָא גַּם כֵּן בְּתוֹסָפוֹת חֲגִיגָה שָׁם
and is also brought in Tosafos on Chagigah there,
דְּאַחֵר שָׁמַע בַּת קוֹל זֶה
that Acher heard this heavenly voice
מִאַחוֹרֵי בֵּית קֹדֶשֵׁי הַקָּדָשִׁים
from behind the Holy of Holies,
בְּיוֹם הַכֻּפּוּרִים שֶׁחָל לִהְיוֹת בְּשַׁבָּת
on a Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbos,

it seems the main strength of this arousal,
הוּא בְּיוֹם הַכֻּפּוּרִים
is on Yom Kippur,

דְּכִמְעָט אֵין אֶחָד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל
for there is almost no one of Israel
שֶׁלֹּא יַעֲלֶה בִלְבָבוֹ אָז
in whose heart there does not arise then.
אֵיזֶה הִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה
some thought of repentance.
וְהוּא מִאוֹתוֹ הַקּוֹל "שׁוּבוּ"
And it is from that voice, “Return”
(בָּנִים שׁוֹבָבִים)
(backsliding children)
הַמְפוּצֵּץ
that shatters
וְיוֹצֵא מִסּוֹף עוֹלָם וְעַד סוֹפוֹ
and goes forth from one end of the world to the other
וְנִשְׁמָע לְכָל הַלֵּבָבוֹת מִבְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל

אֲשֶׁר לֹא נִטְמְעוּ עֲדַיִן בְּנִין הָעַמִּים לְגַמְרֵי
who have not yet been completely assimilated among the nations,
דְּאֲפִילוּ אַחֵר
for even Acher,
שֶׁנִּגְזַר עָלָיו "חוּץ" וְגוֹמֵר
upon whom “except” was decreed, etc..
מִכָּל מָקוֹם שָׁמַע הַבַּת קוֹל
nevertheless heard the heavenly voice.
וְלֹא לַחִנָּם שָׁמְעוֹ,
And not for nothing did he hear it,
וְהַיְנוּ שֶׁגַּם הוּא הִתְעוֹרֵר
meaning that he too was aroused,
אֶלָּא שֶׁלִּבּוֹ הִתְעָהוּ
but his heart misled him
לַחֲשֹׁב כִּי חָטָא כָּל כָּךְ

עַד שֶׁאֵין הַתְּשׁוּבָה מוֹעֶלֶת לוֹ עוֹד
that repentance no longer avails him.

דְּזֶה הַפְּתִיחָה
for this opening is
שֶׁמַּרְאִין לוֹ
that they show him
שֶׁאֵין מְעוֹרְרִים אוֹתוֹ לְגַמְרֵי

but on the contrary

although it was to trouble him from the side of “one who comes to defile”
מִכָּל מָקוֹם
nevertheless
אֲלוּ הָיָה בָּא לְטַהֵר
had he come to purify himself
הָיָה גַּם זֶה לְסִיּוּעַ לוֹ.
this too would have been a help to him.
דְּהָיָה לוֹ לִהִתְבוֹנֵן
For he should have reflected:
אֲלוּ לֹא חָפֵץ בְּוֹ ה׳
if the Lord did not desire him,
לָמָה הִשְׁמִיעָהוּ בֶּאֱמֶת
why did He truly let him hear it?,
וְאֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חָפֵץ בְּמוֹת הַמֵּת
And the Blessed Name does not desire the death of the dead,
וְלָמָּה זֶה יְגַלֶּה לוֹ שֶׁנִדְחָה
and why would He reveal to him that he was rejected
אִם לֹא כְּדֵי שֶׁיִתְעוֹרֵר עַל יְדֵי זֶה
if not so that he be aroused through this,
לָשׁוּב עוֹד בְּחֶזְקָה יוֹתֵר
to return with greater strength,
לִהִתְמַרְמֵר לְפָנָיו יוֹתֵר
to be more bitter before Him
וּלְעוֹרֵר רַחֲמָיו רַבִּים עַל עַצְמוֹ
and arouse His abundant mercies upon himself,
וּלְהַרְבּוֹת בְּתְפִּלָּה וּתַחֲנוּנִים
and increase in prayer and supplications,
וְכְּעִנְיַן מַה שֶׁאָמַר ה׳ לְמֹשֶׁה
and as the Lord told Moshe
בְּחֵטְא הָעֵגֶל
regarding the sin of the Calf
לְהוֹדִיעַ עֹנְשָׁם וְחֲרוֹנוֹ עֲלֵיהֶם
to make known their punishment and His anger upon them.
כְּדֵי שֶׁיִתְפַּלֵּל בְּעַדָם
so that he would pray on their behalf.
וְכֵן הוּא אֵצֶל אַחֵר
And so it is with Acher:
לְעִנְיָן זֶה הוֹדִיעוּהוּ
for this purpose they informed him
כְּדֵי לְעוֹרְרוֹ שֶׁיְרַחֵם עַל עַצְמוֹ
in order to arouse him to have mercy on himself
אֵיךְ בֵּן חָבִיב כָּמוֹהוּ
how a beloved son like himself
שֶׁזָכָה כְּבָר לִכָּנֵס בַּפַּרְדֵּס
who already merited to enter the Pardes
וְלְחַפֵּשׁ בְּגִנְזֵי דְּמַלְכָּא
and to search the King’s treasuries,
נִטְרַד בְּפֶּתַע פִּתְאוֹם
was suddenly cast out,
וְלָהָרִים קוֹל בְּכִי וּתַחֲנוּנִים
and to raise a voice of weeping and supplications.
לִפְנֵי אָבִיו שֶׁבָּשָּׁמַיִם
before his Father in Heaven.
וּבְוַדַּאי רַחֲמֵי שָׁמַיִם מְרוּבִּים
And surely the mercies of Heaven are greater,
כְּרַחֵם אָב כָּל בָּנִים
than a father’s compassion for all his children,
שֶׁאַף שֶׁזוֹרֲקוֹ לַחוּץ
for although He throws him out
וְאוֹמֵר שֶׁלֹּא יַנִּיחוּ עוֹד לִכָּנֵס לִבֵיתוֹ
and says they will not let him enter His house any more,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם עֵינָיו צוֹפִּיוֹת כָּל שָׁעָה
still His eyes watch every hour
שֶׁיָּשׁוּב וְיְרַחֲמֵהוּ,
for him to return so He may have mercy on him.
כִּי יֵטִיב מַעֲשָׂיו
when he improves his deeds.
וְאֲפִילוּ אִם נִסְגְּרָה הַדֶּלֶת לְפָנָיו
And even if the door was closed before him
בְּכָל הָעוֹלָמוֹת
in all the worlds,
מִפְּנֵי מִדַּת הַדִּין
because of the attribute of judgment,
יָדוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא פְּרוּסָה
the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, is spread out
תַּחַת כְּנָפֵי הַחַיּוֹת
beneath the wings of the Chayos
לְקַבֵּל בַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה
to receive penitents,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּפְסָחִים קי״ט עַמּוּד א׳)
as they said (in Pesachim 119a).
וְהוּא הַמַּחֲתֶּרֶת בָּרָקִיעַ
And this is the tunnel in the firmament
שֶׁעָשָׂה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמְנַשֶּׁה
that the Holy One, blessed be He, made for Menasheh
לְקַבְּלוֹ בִּתְשׁוּבָה
to receive him in repentance,
מִפְּנֵי מִדַּת הַדִּין
despite the attribute of judgment,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין ק״ג עַמּוּד א׳)
as they said (in Sanhedrin 103a).
כִּי הוּא הָיָה גַּם כֵּן דּוֹגְמַת אַחֵר
For he too was like Acher,
דְּיָדַע כֹּחוֹ וְמָרַד
who knew his Master’s power and rebelled,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי וּמִדְרָשׁוֹת שָׁם
as they said in the Yerushalmi and Midrashim there
בְּטַעַם "חוּץ מִאַחֵר",
regarding the reason for “except Acher,”.
כִּי גַּם מְנַשֶּׁה הָיָה תָּלְמִיד חָכָם גָּדוֹל
for Menasheh too was a great Torah scholar.

paragraphs.text: Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1 (9b): R’ Meir said to Acher, “You have all this wisdom, and you do not return in teshuvah?” He said, “I cannot.” “Why?” “Once I was passing before the Holy of Holies, riding on my horse on a Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbos, and I heard a bas kol issuing from the Holy of Holies saying, ‘Return, O sons — except for Elisha ben Avuya, who knew My power and rebelled against Me.’” (So too Rus Rabbah and Koheles Rabbah, cited in Tosafos, Chagigah 15a.)

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — conceptual parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §120): “So too the yetzer should be met with ‘the left repels and the right draws near’; in Elisha’s case the right also repelled. Although they said (Bereishis Rabbah 9), ‘Very good — this is the yetzer hara,’ all depends on the person: one person’s measure is to subdue and repel the inclination entirely, and another’s is to transform it.” The Elisha discussed there is the prophet, in the context of his treatment of Gehazi, not Elisha ben Avuyah/Acher: §120 expressly cites Sanhedrin 107b and Berachos 10b. It therefore offers a conceptual comparison about repulsion, drawing near, and differing forms of repair; it is not a direct assertion about the bas kol heard by Acher. In the present passage R’ Tzadok himself argues that even the apparent rejection could have awakened Acher to a stronger return. Original printed-edition checkpoint: Har Bracha, Tzidkas HaTzadik §120, printed p.51, supports this as a conceptual parallel, NOT a direct story about Acher. Sanhedrin 107b is the prophet Elisha and Gehazi. The source attribution must not be transferred to Elisha ben Avuyah.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Per the Yerushalmi (and Rus/Koheles Rabbah, cited in Tosafos), it was Acher who heard this bas kol. This comes from behind the Holy of Holies, on a Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbos. The full force of this arousal is on Yom Kippur, when nearly every Jew feels some stirring of teshuvah, from that voice “Return, wayward sons,” which “shatters forth” from one end of the world to the other and is heard by every Jewish heart not yet wholly assimilated. Even Acher heard it.

p: (ו) וּמִלְּבַד מַה שֶּׁאִיתָא
Besides what is stated
(בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין שָׁם עַמּוּד ב)
(in Sanhedrin there, 103b)
עַל כָּל מְלָכִים,
regarding all those kings,
הַפָּנִים שֶׁהָיוּ שׁוֹנִים בְּתוֹרַת כֹּהֲנִים
the interpretations of Toras Kohanim that they would expound,
רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר בְּדַרְכֵי הָעֲבוֹדָה
meaning in the ways of service
לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
to the Blessed Name.
וּבִמְנַשֶּׁה אָמְרוּ
And of Menasheh they said
נֶגֶד שְׁנֵי מַלְכוּתוֹ,
corresponding to the years of his reign,
עַיֵּן שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י
see there in Rashi
דְּכָל שָׁנָה הָיָה דּוֹרְשׁוֹ,
that each year he expounded it,
הֲרֵי גַּם בִּשְׁנוֹת רִשְׁעוֹ
so even in the years of his wickedness
לֹא זָז מִלִּדְרשׁ
he did not cease from expounding
רָזֵי תוֹרָה
the secrets of Torah
בַּעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
in the service of the Blessed Name. (,
וִירָבְעָם — קג
(And Jeroboam — 103,
נִרְאֶה לִי בְּגִמַּטְרִיָּא עֵגֶל
it seems to me by gematria “calf,”
כִּי הָיָה דּוֹרֵשׁ דְּרָשׁוֹת שֶׁל דֹּפִי
for he expounded faulty expositions
לִפְתֹּר דַּרְכֵי עֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
to interpret the ways of service of the Blessed Name.
בְּמַעֲשֵׂה הָעֵגֶל
in terms of the incident of the Calf.
וְאַחְאָב — פה
And Ahab — 85,
אוּלַי לְפִי שֶׁחִדֵּשׁ עֲבוֹדַת הַבַּעַל בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
perhaps because he introduced Baal worship in Israel,
שֶׁעִקַּר עֲבוֹדָתוֹ כְּפִי הַנִּרְאֶה קְצָת הָיָה בַּפֶּה
whose main service, it appears, was partly with the mouth,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר
as it is said
"וְהִשְׁאַרְתִּי" וְגוֹמֵר "כָּל" וְגוֹמֵר "הַפֶּה אֲשֶׁר לֹא נָשַׁק לוֹ".
“And I have left…” etc. “all…” etc. “every mouth that has not kissed him.”
וּכְרִיעַת הַבִּרְכַּיִם
And bending the knees,
זֶהוּ הִשְׁתַּחֲוָאָה הַנְּהוּגָה בְּכָל עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
is the bowing practiced in all idolatry,
וְאִיתֵיהּ גַּם בַּעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
and it exists also in the service of the Blessed Name
בִּכְרִיעוֹת וְהִשְׁתַּחֲוָיוֹת בַּמִּקְדָּשׁ
in kneelings and prostrations in the Temple,
וּבִשְׁעַת תְּפִלָּה דְּכָרַע בְּמוֹדִים
and at the time of prayer, as one bows at “Modim,”
וְכַיּוֹצֵא בְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
and like Rabbi Akiva,
בִּבְרָכוֹת ל״א עַמּוּד א׳
in Berachos 31a,
אֲבָל נְשִׁיקַת פֶּה
but kissing with the mouth
נִרְאֶה דְּנִתְחַדֵּשׁ אָז עַל יְדֵי אַחְאָב
it seems was introduced then by Ahab,
בַּעֲבוֹדַת הַבַּעַל
in Baal worship.
וְאֵין כָּאן מָקוֹם לְהַאֲרִיךְ יוֹתֵר בָּזֶה)
and this is not the place to elaborate further on this.)
עוֹד מָצִינוּ
We also find
(שָׁם קב עַמּוּד ב)
(there, 102b),
אַמְנַשֶּׁה בְּיִחוּד
regarding Menasheh in particular,
אִתְחֲזִי לֵיהּ בְּחֶלְמָא
that he appeared to him in a dream: ".
חַבְרָךְ קָרִית" וְכוּלֵּי
“You called me your friend,” etc.
וְהוּא אָמַר אַכֻּלְהוּ שְׁלֹשָׁה מְלָכִים
And he said regarding all three kings,
וּמִכֻּלְהוּ לֹא בָּא אֵלָיו לִשְׁאֹלוֹ עַל זֶה
and of all of them, none came to him to ask about this,
אֶלָּא מְנַשֶּׁה
except Menasheh,
מַשְׁמַע דְּהוּא הַגָּדוֹל שֶׁבָּהֶם
which implies he was the greatest of them,
וְשֶׁלּוֹ לְבַד הָיָה רָאוּי
and his alone was fitting
שֶׁיֶּחֱרֶה לוֹ
that it should anger him.
עַל מַה שֶּׁקְּרָאוּ חַבְרִין
that they called them friends.
וְכֵן זָכָה
And so he merited
שֶׁנִּקְבַּע הֲלָכָה בִּשְׁמוֹ בַּגְּמָרָא
— that a law was fixed in his name in the Gemara —,
מֵהֵיכָן לִמְשָׁרָא הַמּוֹצִיא
from where is the Motzi permitted,
מַה שֶּׁגִּלָּה בַּחֲלוֹם
what he revealed in a dream
וְנִדְרַשׁ מִשְּׁמוֹ,
and was expounded in his name.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
even though he has no share in the World to Come. (,
דְּשָׁם קו עַמּוּד ב גַּבֵּי דּוֹאֵג
(For there, 106b, regarding Doeg,
גַּם אַחַר שֶׁאָמַר "יִתָּצְךָ לָנֶצַח"
even after saying “He will break you down forever”,
דְּלֹא יִהְיֶה לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
that he would have no share in the World to Come,
הוּצְרַךְ לְבַקֵּשׁ "וְיִסְחֲךָ מֵאֹהֶל"
it was necessary to ask “and uproot you from the tent”
דְּלָא לֵימְרוּ שְׁמַעְתְּתָא בִּשְׁמֵיהּ
that they not say teachings in his name
בְּבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ,
in the study hall,
דְּאַף שֶׁאֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
for although he has no share in the World to Come
אֶפְשָׁר מִכָּל מָקוֹם
it is nevertheless possible
שֶׁשְּׁמַעְתְּתָיו יִהְיוּ נֶאֱמָרִים מִשְּׁמֵיהּ
that his teachings be said in his name
אִלּוּ זָכוּ לְכָךְ,
had they merited this,
וְדוֹאֵג הָיָה זוֹכֶה
and Doeg would have merited it.
לוּלֵי קְלָלַת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם)
were it not for the curse of David the King, peace be upon him.)
וְכֶאֱלִישָׁע אַחֵר
— And like Elisha, Acher —,
דְּשָׁנָה רַבִּי שְׁמוּעָה מִשְּׁמוֹ בְּאָבוֹת
Rabbi taught a teaching in his name in Avos,
אַף דְּהוּא עַצְמוֹ אָמַר עָלָיו
although he himself said of him
(בַּחֲגִיגָה שָׁם עַמּוּד ב)
(in Chagigah there, 15b) ".
לֹא נִין לוֹ וְלֹא נֶכֶד בְּעַמּוֹ" וְגוֹמֵר
“He shall have neither son nor grandson among his people,” etc.
וַעֲדַיִן בִּימָיו הָיָה נִדּוֹן בְּגֵיהִנֹּם
And still in his days he was judged in Gehinnom
עַד שֶׁבָּא רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְהוֹצִיאוֹ מִשָּׁם
until Rabbi Yochanan came and took him out from there,
כִּדְאִיתָא הָתָם
as is stated there,
וּמַשְׁמַע דְּהַשְּׁמוּעָה הָיְתָה שְׁגוּרָה
and it implies that the teaching was current
בְּפִי הַחֲכָמִים בְּבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ
in the mouths of the Sages in the study hall,
עוֹד מִקֹּדֶם בְּחַיֵּי רַבִּי מֵאִיר
even earlier, in the lifetime of Rabbi Meir,
שֶׁנִּגְמַר דִּינוֹ לְמַעְלָה
when his judgment was sealed Above.
שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
that he would have no share in the World to Come.
וְכֵן רַבִּי מֵאִיר עַצְמוֹ
And so Rabbi Meir himself
דְּגָמַר שְׁמַעְתָּא מִפּוּמֵּיהּ
who learned a teaching from his mouth,
לִמְּדָהּ לְתַלְמִידָיו
taught it to his students,
וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים
and some say
דִּבְכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁנִּקְרָא רַבִּי מֵאִיר "אֲחֵרִים"
that wherever Rabbi Meir is called “Acherim” (others)
הוּא הַשְּׁמוּעוֹת
it is the teachings.
דְּגָמַר מִפּוּמֵּיהּ דְּאַחֵר
that he learned from the mouth of Acher.
וְגַם בְּעוֹדוֹ נֶחְשָׁב לְמוֹרֵד
And even while he was considered a rebel
מִכָּל מָקוֹם יָדַע כֹּחוֹ,
nevertheless he knew his Master’s power,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ יְדִיעַת דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֲמִתִּיִּים
which is knowledge of true words of Torah.
וּשְׁמוּעוֹת הַנִּקְבָּעוֹת לְעָלְמֵי עַד
and teachings fixed for all eternity.
דְּדָבָר זֶה אֵינוֹ מִצַּד חָכְמָה אֱנוֹשִׁית
For this is not from human wisdom,
וְדֶרֶךְ חִדּוּד שֵׂכֶל לְבַד
and sharpening of intellect alone,
דְּדְבַר חָכְמָה הַקַּיֶּמֶת לָעַד
for a matter of wisdom that endures forever
אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא הַנִּמְשֶׁכֶת מֵחָכְמָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,
is only that which is drawn from His wisdom, blessed be He.
שֶׁהוּא וְדַעְתּוֹ וְחָכְמָתוֹ הַכֹּל אֶחָד
for He, His knowledge and His wisdom are all one.

paragraphs.text: Three kings — Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2 identifies them as Yerovam, Achav, and Menasheh, and states that they have no share in the World to Come. R’ Yehudah disagrees regarding Menasheh, citing II Divrei Hayamim 33:13, where his prayer is accepted and he is restored to Jerusalem; the Sages answer that he was restored to his kingdom, but not necessarily to life in the World to Come. R’ Tzadok’s point here does not erase that judgment. It sharpens the paradox: these rulers could possess extraordinary Torah attainment while directing their will in rebellion, so their knowledge increases both the enduring Torah that can be preserved and the gravity of their responsibility.

paragraphs.text: Toras Kohanim — the traditional name of the Sifra, the tannaitic halachic Midrash on Sefer Vayikra. Its subjects include korbanos, kehunnah, tumah and taharah, and the laws of kedushah. Sanhedrin 103b records the many “faces” these kings expounded in Toras Kohanim, and Rashi explains that Menasheh renewed and expounded a new mode each year. R’ Tzadok reads “Toras Kohanim” inwardly as the Torah of avodah: Vayikra is the book of approaching Hashem through service and sanctification. Thus the astonishing feature is not merely their scholarship, but their penetration into the very paths of Divine service even during years in which their deeds opposed that knowledge.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 102b: Rav Ashi reached the discussion of the three kings and said, “Tomorrow we will begin with our colleagues.” Menasheh appeared in his dream and challenged him, “You call us your colleagues and your father’s colleagues? From where do you begin ha-motzi?” Rav Ashi did not know. He asked Menasheh to teach him and promised to expound the teaching in his name the next day. Menasheh then answered: from the place where the loaf’s baking first forms a crust. When Rav Ashi asked why scholars of such attainment had served idols, Menasheh replied that, had Rav Ashi lived then, he would have lifted the hem of his garment to run after them. The next day Rav Ashi introduced the discussion as “our teachers.” The passage preserves their Torah attainment while warning against underestimating the historical force of their temptation. Halachic continuation: Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 167:1, codifies the requirement to break the bread where it was well baked; the Rema discusses practical application according to a loaf’s shape. The Sanhedrin 102b dream therefore preserves an operative halachic teaching in Menasheh’s name. The continued Torah transmission is conceptually distinct from the severity of Menasheh’s moral judgment.

paragraphs.text: Acher’s teaching in Avos — Pirkei Avos 4:20 records explicitly in the name of Elisha ben Avuyah: one who learns as a child is compared to ink written on new paper, while one who begins learning in old age is like ink on erased paper. The meforshim explain that early learning is deeply engraved and retained, whereas later impressions are less readily fixed. This is the “teaching in Avos” to which R’ Tzadok refers: despite Acher’s fall, Chazal preserved his true Torah by name within the Mishnah’s chain of ethical teaching.

paragraphs.text: “Neither son nor grandson” — Iyov 18:19 describes the obliteration of the wicked person’s continuity. Chagigah 15b applies the verse to Acher when his impoverished daughter came before Rebbe. Rebbe initially asked whether any of Acher’s seed still remained; she answered, “Remember his Torah and do not remember his deeds.” Fire then descended and touched Rebbe’s bench, demonstrating the enduring claim created by Torah even when its bearer acted disgracefully. This episode supplies the precise background for R’ Tzadok’s separation between Acher’s condemned conduct and the Torah teachings that continued in the beis midrash.

paragraphs.text: Chagigah 15b: “When Acher died, they said in Heaven: let him not be judged in Gehinnom, and let him not enter the World to Come. Let him not be judged — because he engaged in Torah; and let him not enter the World to Come — because he sinned. R’ Meir said: better that he be judged and then enter the World to Come; when I die I will raise smoke from his grave. When R’ Meir died, smoke rose from Acher’s grave a sign he was being judged. R’ Yochanan said: is it a mighty deed to burn one’s teacher? There was one such disciple among us, and can we not save him? If I take him by the hand, who will wrest him from me? He said, “When shall I die and extinguish the smoke from his grave?” When R’ Yochanan died, the smoke ceased from Acher’s grave; the eulogizer said of him: ‘even the guard of the gate did not stand before you, our teacher.’”

paragraphs.text: R’ Meir’s selective reception — Chagigah 15b asks how R’ Meir could learn from Acher when Malachi 2:7 teaches that Torah should be sought from a teacher who resembles an angel of Hashem. The Gemara distinguishes an adult scholar, capable of discrimination, from a child. It describes R’ Meir as eating the date while discarding its pit and, in another image, eating the pomegranate’s interior while throwing away its rind. Rava adds that a talmid chacham is like a nut: even when the shell is soiled, the interior is not made repulsive. R’ Tzadok’s wording that R’ Meir absorbed the teaching and transmitted it means disciplined separation of authentic Torah from corrupted conduct, not an unrestricted license to follow a sinful teacher.

paragraphs.text: “He knew My power and rebelled against Me” — the full expression appears in Ruth Rabbah 6:4, Koheles Rabbah 7:8, and Yalkut Shimoni on Nach §974 in the account of the bas kol heard by Elisha ben Avuyah. It declares: “Return, wayward children … except for Acher, who knew My power and rebelled against Me.” The phrase defines Acher’s rebellion as informed defiance rather than ignorance. In R’ Tzadok’s argument, that same genuine knowledge explains both sides of the paradox: his rebellion was more severe precisely because he knew, while the true Torah contained in that knowledge could still be separated from his choice and preserved.

R’ Tzadok therefore distinguishes a timeless Torah insight from human cleverness: what becomes part of the enduring Torah of the beis midrash testifies that its inner source transcends the personal failure of the speaker.

paragraphs.text: Divine knowledge and wisdom — Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 2:10, formulates that the Creator does not know through knowledge external to Himself: “He is the Knower, He is the known, and He is the knowledge itself — all is one.” R’ Tzadok extends this formulation here to chochmah: Torah wisdom that is eternally true is drawn from the Divine wisdom and is not merely an achievement of autonomous human intellect. This explains how an authentic teaching can possess permanent sanctity even when the individual who received it later rebelled; the enduring truth belongs at its root to Hashem’s wisdom, while the person remains accountable for the direction of his will and actions.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Every Torah insight that a diligent disciple will one day discover was already revealed to Moshe at Sinai through his bond with the supernal Wisdom. A person who reaches that level of da’as and nevertheless rebels is described as one who knows his Master and rebels against Him. The Attribute of Justice may therefore punish such a person by sealing the doors of teshuvah, as happened when Pharaoh’s heart was hardened.

The theme: These three “great ones who rebelled” — Menasheh, Achav, Yerovam — were, even in their wickedness, immersed in Torah: the Gemara counts the “faces” (modes of exposition) each expounded in Toras Kohanim, i.e. in the ways of serving God. Menasheh never ceased expounding the secrets of Torah even in his years of wickedness. He appeared to Rav Ashi in a dream and bested him in halachah.

p: וְזֶהוּ הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה
And this is the words of Torah
שֶׁתַּלְמִיד וָתִיק עָתִיד לְחַדֵּשׁ
that a veteran student is destined to innovate,
שֶׁנִּגְלוּ לְמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
which were revealed to Moshe our teacher, peace be upon him,
מִצַּד דְּבֵקוּתוֹ בַּחָכְמָה הָעֶלְיוֹנָה
by virtue of his cleaving to the supernal wisdom,
שֶׁעַל יָדָהּ זָכָה
through which he merited,
לְקַבָּלַת הַתּוֹרָה לָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
the receiving of the Torah for this world,
וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַגִּיעַ לָהּ
and it is impossible to reach it
אֶלָּא מִצַּד הַיְדִיעָה וּבְדַעַת
except by way of knowledge and awareness,
שֶׁהוּא הַהִתְחַבְּרוּת וְהַדְּבֵקוּת
which is the connection and cleaving
בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
to the Blessed Name.
וּמִי שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵגָה זוֹ
And one who reached this level
וְעִם כָּל זֶה מוֹרֵד
and despite all this rebels,
עָנְשׁוֹ מִצַּד מִדַּת הַדִּין
his punishment, by the attribute of judgment, is,
לִסְתֹּם בְּפָנָיו דַּלְתֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה
to seal the doors of repentance before him,
כְּעִנְיַן פַּרְעֹה
like Pharaoh,
שֶׁאַחַר שֶׁבַּמַּכּוֹת הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת
who after, in the first plagues,
הֶרְאוּ לוֹ יְדִיעַת כֹּחַ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
they showed him knowledge of the power of the Blessed Name
כְּפִי כֹּחַ הַשָּׂגַת הָאֻמּוֹת
to the extent of the nations’ grasp,
וְעִם כָּל זֶה מָרַד
and despite this he rebelled,
הָיָה בַּמִּשְׁפָּט
it was in judgment
לְהַכְבִּיד אֶת לִבּוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ,
to harden his heart afterward,
וְלֹא כִּשְׁאָר הַבָּא לְטַמֵּא
and not like others who come to defile.
דְּרַק פּוֹתְחִין
for whom they merely open.
וּמִדַּת הַדִּין טוֹעֶנֶת
And the attribute of judgment argues
גַּם בְּרִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
also regarding the wicked of Israel
שֶׁיָּדְעוּ וּמָרְדוּ
who knew and rebelled,
לִהְיוֹת הַמִּשְׁפָּט כֵּן
that the judgment should be so,
דְּמָה נִשְׁתַּנּוּ אֵלּוּ מֵאֵלּוּ,
for how are these different from those?
וְאַף כְּשֶׁרוֹצֶה לָשׁוּב
and even when he wants to return
לֹא דַי שֶׁאֵין מְסַיְּעִין
not only do they not help,
אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּצַּד מִדַּת הַדִּין
but by the attribute of judgment
טוֹרְדִין אֶת לִבּוֹ
they trouble his heart.
לְהָסִיחַ דַּעְתּוֹ מֵהַתְּשׁוּבָה
to divert his mind from repentance.
וְזֶהוּ עִנְיַן קַבָּלַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה
And this is the matter of acceptance of repentance:
כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
for when the Blessed Name
מְקַבֵּל לְרָצוֹן
accepts favorably,
אָז מִצְוָה גּוֹרֶרֶת מִצְוָה
then one mitzvah draws another
וּבְכָל עֵת מוֹסִיף וְהוֹלֵךְ,
and at all times he adds and progresses,
דְּכָל שֶׁבָּא לְהוֹסִיף לְטַהֵר
for whoever comes to add to purify,
הַסִּיּוּעַ מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם
the help from Heaven.
הוֹלֵךְ וּמִתְגַּבֵּר גַּם כֵּן
grows stronger as well.
וְאִם הִגִּיעַ לְכָךְ
And if it reached the point
שֶׁמִּדַּת הַדִּין מְעַכֶּבֶת
that the attribute of judgment obstructs,
אָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חוֹתֵר חֲתִירָה
then the Blessed Name digs a tunnel,
הַיְנוּ כְּעִנְיַן הַכְּרוֹז
like the proclamation
"חוּץ מֵאַחֵר".
“except Acher.”
דְּלִפְנֵי מִדַּת הַדִּין
For before the attribute of judgment
מַרְאֶה שֶׁמְּדַחִין אוֹתוֹ
it shows that they push him away,
וּמַכְבִּידִין אֶת לִבּוֹ בָּזֶה
and harden his heart thereby,
וּבֶאֱמֶת הוּא אַדְרַבָּא הִתְעוֹרְרוּת
but in truth it is, on the contrary, an arousal
אִם הִשְׂכִּיל לָדַעַת
if he has the wisdom to know,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ הִתְעוֹרְרוּת דֶּרֶךְ חֲתִירָה
that this is an arousal by way of a tunnel,
שֶׁלֹּא יַנִּיחַ מִלִּדְפֹּק
that he not cease knocking
עַל דַּלְתֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה
on the doors of repentance
לְהִתְקַבֵּל בִּידֵי אָדָם הָעֶלְיוֹן
to be received by the hands of the supernal Adam.
שֶׁתַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַחַיּוֹת
beneath the wings of the Chayos.
הַיְנוּ שֶׁאֵין הַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת
That is, the arousal is not
בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת לִבּוֹ
in the revelation of his heart,
עַל יְדֵי הַבַּת קוֹל "שׁוּבוּ" וְגוֹמֵר
through the heavenly voice “Return,” etc.
רַק מִצַּד הַהִתְבּוֹנְנוּת
but through reflection,
בְּמַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב
in the depths of the heart,
שֶׁהַמַּעֲמַקִּים שֶׁל כָּל זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב
for the depths of every descendant of Yaakov
הֵם דְּבוּקִים בְּשָׁרְשָׁם וּמְקוֹרָם
— are attached to their root and source —
צוּרַת אָדָם הָעֶלְיוֹן
the form of the supernal Adam,
שֶׁהוּא צוּרָתוֹ שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
which is the form of Yaakov our father, peace be upon him.
הַחֲקוּקָה בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד
engraved on the Throne of Glory.
דְּגָדוֹל כֹּחָן שֶׁל נְבִיאִים
For great is the power of prophets,
שֶׁמְּדַמִּים צוּרָה לְיוֹצְרָהּ וְכוּלֵּי
who compare the form to its Former, etc.
הַיְנוּ דְּכָל הַשָּׂגַת הַנְּבִיאִים
meaning that all prophetic perception
אֵינוֹ מִצַּד עַצְמוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ
is not from His blessed essence,
דְּלֵית מַחֲשָׁבָה תְּפִיסָא בֵּיהּ כְּלָל
for thought has no grasp of Him at all,
רַק מִצַּד אֲצִילוּת
but from the emanation
וְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַשָּׂגָה
and extension of perception
שֶׁרָצָה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
that the Blessed Name wished,
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מוּשָּׂג לַנִּבְרָאִים
to be grasped by created beings.
וְהִיא כְּפִי הַשָּׂגַת הַנִּבְרָאִים
and it is according to the grasp of created beings.
וְהוּא הָאָדָם
And this is Adam,
רֹאשׁ וְתַכְלִית הַנִּבְרָאִים
the head and purpose of creation,
וְאֵין שָׁם הַשָּׂגָה אַחֶרֶת
and there is no other perception
בֶּאֱמִתּוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ
of His blessed truth,
אֶלָּא מַה שֶּׁהוּא הַשָּׂגַת הָאָדָם הַשָּׁלֵם לְמַטָּה
except the perception of the complete human below,
שֶׁזֶּה כָּל כַּוָּנַת בְּרִיאַת הָעוֹלָמוֹת כֻּלָּם
for this is the whole intent of the creation of all the worlds,
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה שָׁם אָדָם בַּעַל בְּחִירָה
that there be a person with free choice
שֶׁיַּכִּיר וְיַשִּׂיג בִּבְחִירָתוֹ
who recognizes and grasps by his choice.
שֶׁיֵּשׁ שָׁם אֱלֹקִי בּוֹרֵא וּמַנְהִיג
that there is a divine Creator and Guide.
וְעַל כֵּן הַשָּׂגַת הָאֱלֹקוּת הַמּוּשָּׂג
And therefore the perception of the divinity perceived,
הוּא בְּדִמְיוֹן הַנְּבִיאִים כִּדְמוּת אָדָם
is in the prophets’ imagery as the likeness of a person,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַהַשָּׂגָה הַמּוּשֶּׂגֶת
which is the perception grasped.
כְּפִי כֹּחַ וְדַעַת הָאָדָם
according to the power and mind of man.
וְהוּא יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
And this is Yaakov our father, peace be upon him,
שֶׁהוּא הָאָדָם הַשָּׁלֵם
who is the complete person
שֶׁהָיָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
who was in this world,
דְּמִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵמָה
whose bed was whole,
וְלֹא מֵת
and he did not die,
דְּמָה זַרְעוֹ בַּחַיִּים
for as his descendants are alive,
(אַף הוּא בַּחַיִּים)
(so too is he alive)
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּתַעֲנִית ה׳ עַמּוּד ב׳)
as they said (in Taanis 5b).
הַיְנוּ דְּקוֹמַת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל
That is, the stature of the Assembly of Israel,
זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
the descendants of Yaakov our father, peace be upon him,
שֶׁבְּכָל דּוֹר וָדוֹר
in every generation
הֵן הֵם עַצְמוֹ
is itself,
קוֹמַת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
the stature of Yaakov our father, peace be upon him,
רַק שֶׁמִּתְפָּרֶטֶת וּמִתְחַלֶּקֶת
only divided and subdivided.
לִפְרָטֵי נְפָשׁוֹת הַרְבֵּה
into many individual souls.
וְכָל מִי שֶׁהוּא מִזֶּרַע יַעֲקֹב
And everyone who is of the seed of Yaakov,
אֲפִילוּ הִגְדִּיל עֲוֹנוֹת עַד אֵין קֵץ
even one who multiplied sins without end,
יְדֵי אָדָם הָעֶלְיוֹן
the hands of the supernal Adam —,
הַיְנוּ יַד יָמִין מִדַּת הַחֶסֶד
that is, the right hand, the attribute of kindness —
דְּ"יָדוֹ" כְּתִיב
for “His hand” is written
כִּדְאִיתָא הָתָם (בִּפְסָחִים יד עַמּוּד א)
as stated there (in Pesachim 14a)
וְהוּא הַיָּמִין
and it is the right
שֶׁהוּא יָד סְתָם לְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַחוֹרֵם (בִּמְנָחוֹת ל״ז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳)
that is the unspecified “hand” according to Rabbi Yose the Chorem (in Menachos 37a),
וּלְדִידֵיהּ הָנֵי קְרָאֵי דְּתַנָּא קַמָּא הָתָם
and according to him, those verses of the first Tanna there
(לו עַמּוּד ב)
(36b)
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר מִשּׁוּם דִּמְפָרֵשׁ בְּהוּ אַחַר כָּךְ יָמִין
one can say it is because it specifies in them afterward “right”,
עַל כֵּן קָרֵי לִשְׂמֹאל סְתָם יָד
therefore it calls the left an unspecified “hand,”
אֲבָל יָד סְתָמָא
but an unspecified “hand”
בִּדְלָא מְפָרֵשׁ אַחַר כָּךְ מִידֵּי
where it does not specify anything afterward,
הוּא יָמִין
is the right,
וְהִיא פְּרוּסָה בַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת
and it is spread out in the tunnel
תַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַחַיּוֹת
beneath the wings of the Chayos,
שֶׁבְּעוֹלַם הַכִּסֵּא
in the World of the Throne,
דְּמִתַּמָּן אִתְגְּזָרוּ נִשְׁמָתִין
from where souls were hewn,
שֶׁהִגִּיעַ הַפְּגָם גַּם לַנְּשָׁמָה שֶׁבַּמֹּחַ דִּטְהוֹרָה הִיא
so that the blemish reached even the soul in the brain, which is pure,
וְאֵין אָדָם זוֹכֶה לָהּ
and a person does not merit it
אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן כְּבָר הִגִּיעַ
unless he has already reached.
לְמַדְרֵגַת קְדֻשָּׁה וְטָהֳרָה
a level of holiness and purity.

Megillah 19b gives a RELATED but not identical formulation: "דקדוקי תורה ודקדוקי סופרים ומה שהסופרים עתידין לחדש" were shown to Moshe; its application concerns future rabbinic elaborations including Megillas Esther. Rav Tzadok uses the tradition to distinguish lasting Torah truth, rooted in Divine Wisdom, from merely independent human ingenuity; compare Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 2:10 (directly verified Hebrew).

paragraphs.text: Da’as as connection — the biblical root is “Adam knew Chavah” (Bereishis 4:1), where knowledge denotes intimate union. Pardes Rimmonim 23:4 explicitly explains that da’as is named from this verse because it means joining and unification, and R’ Tzadok himself states later in Takanas HaShavin 15:108 that yediyah is a language of “connection and deveikus.” Thus, in this se’if da’as is not information about Hashem but a bond through which the human mind becomes receptive to supernal Chochmah. That explains why the authentic chidush of a talmid vatik can already be included in Sinai: the disciple uncovers, through deveikus, a facet of the Divine wisdom already rooted in Torah.

paragraphs.text: “One who knows his Master and intends to rebel” — Sifra, Bechukosai, section 2:2, derives this definition from “If you will not listen to Me” and applies it as well to Nimrod and the people of Sedom: their added guilt was that they recognized their Master and deliberately opposed Him. Halachos Gedolos preserves the same teaching in its discussion of the stages of rejecting Torah. R’ Tzadok uses the phrase in its strongest sense: after da’as has become genuine attachment, rebellion is not ordinary weakness or ignorance but a conscious severing of a known bond, and therefore Middas HaDin can claim that the ordinary path of return should be closed.

paragraphs.text: Pharaoh’s hardened heart — Shemos 7:3 announces, “I shall harden Pharaoh’s heart”; after Pharaoh repeatedly hardens himself, the Torah first says explicitly, “Hashem hardened Pharaoh’s heart” at Shemos 9:12, and again at 10:1. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 6:3, explains that a person may sin so greatly and so willingly that the punishment itself is the withholding of teshuvah, enabling full retribution; Pharaoh is his leading example. Ramban to Shemos 7:3 adds that the first refusals were Pharaoh’s own, while the later hardening both punished the earlier evil and prevented fear of the plagues from producing a merely coerced submission. R’ Tzadok reads this as the claim of Middas HaDin against one who has already been shown Divine power and nevertheless rebels. Qualification: Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 6:3 directly presents Pharaoh as a case of penitence withheld as punishment; Ramban, Shemos 7:3 distinguishes his own early hardening from the later Divine hardening and also the Divine aim of making the signs known. These are related but not identical formulations, and Rav Tzadok applies them interpretively to a knowing rebel.

paragraphs.text: “One who comes to defile himself, they open for him; one who comes to purify himself, they assist him” — Yoma 38b, Menachos 29b, and Avodah Zarah 55a, expounding Mishlei 3:34. The academy of R’ Yishmael compares it to a merchant: the purchaser of foul-smelling kerosene is told to measure it himself, whereas those selling fragrant balsam help the purchaser so that all may share its scent. Rabbeinu Yonah to Avos 4:2 explains that “opening” means the sinner is left to the path he chose, while positive choice receives active Heavenly assistance. R’ Tzadok contrasts this normal rule with the exceptional judgment of a knowing rebel: Middas HaDin seeks not merely to leave the path open, but to disturb even his desire to return.

paragraphs.text: “A mitzvah draws another mitzvah” — Pirkei Avos 4:2. Rabbeinu Yonah explains that the reward of a mitzvah includes help and readiness to perform the next mitzvah, while the consequence of sin is increased entanglement in further sin. Rashi to Devarim 22:8 similarly explains the sequence from sending away the mother bird to building a home and making a parapet as “mitzvah draws mitzvah.” R’ Tzadok applies the principle specifically to accepted teshuvah: acceptance is not only the erasure of the past; it becomes visible in a growing current of siyata diShmaya that carries the penitent from one act of purification to the next.

paragraphs.text: The hidden “tunnel” of teshuvah — II Divrei HaYamim 33:13 says of Menasheh, “He prayed to Him, and He was entreated vaye’ater by him.” Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 10:2 relates that the ministering angels closed the windows of Heaven against Menasheh’s prayer, so the Holy One “dug him a tunnel beneath His Throne of Glory” and heard him; the Midrash reads vaye’ater as though vayeichater, “He dug.” The tunnel is a route concealed from the prosecutors and outside the ordinary order of judgment. R’ Tzadok now generalizes Menasheh’s episode: even when Middas HaDin blocks the revealed gates, Hashem can create a hidden passage that preserves the possibility of return.

paragraphs.text: “Return, wayward children — except for Acher” — Chagigah 15a records the bas kol that Elisha ben Avuyah heard after his entry into the Pardes; the same sugya records R’ Meir repeatedly urging him to return. Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1 and Ruth Rabbah 6:4 give the fuller formulation: “except for Elisha ben Avuyah, who knew My power and rebelled against Me.” On the surface the proclamation excludes him. R’ Tzadok offers a deliberately deeper reading: the very fact that the exclusion was addressed to him and heard by him was a concealed summons, challenging him to push past the apparent rejection and prove that no Divine voice can finally abolish the possibility of teshuvah. This interpretation is R’ Tzadok’s theological development of the sugya, not its explicit wording.

paragraphs.text: The image of the Divine hand reaching beneath the wings of the Chayos is explicitly developed in Kol Bo, §66 (the hand beneath the wings receiving repentant sinners), with Yechezkel 1:8, “וִידֵי אָדָם מִתַּחַת כַּנְפֵיהֶם,” as its prophetic language. See also Malbim on Yechezkel 1:8. Rav Tzadok interprets the hidden hand as compassion reaching one apparently refused by revealed judgment; this is an interpretive application, not a claim that the prophet describes a literal physical hand of the Creator. An additional inherited attribution to Zohar Pekudei remains unconfirmed by exact folio and is not relied on as a direct quotation.

paragraphs.text: “No thought grasps Him at all” — the celebrated formulation of Tikkunei Zohar in Patach Eliyahu. Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 4, explains the distinction: no created intellect can grasp the Holy One in His essence, yet through Torah and mitzvos the mind can cleave to His revealed will and wisdom. This is precisely the boundary R’ Tzadok draws here. The prophetic “likeness of Man,” the sefirotic attributes, and Yaakov’s form on the Throne describe the emanated mode Hashem willed creatures to apprehend; they are not a description of His unknowable Essence. The footnote therefore guards the passage against corporeal interpretation while preserving R’ Tzadok’s claim that revealed Divinity is ordered according to the perfected form of man.

p: (ח) אֲבָל יֵשׁ פְּעָמִים
But there are times
אֲנָשִׁים גְּדוֹלִים כְּאַחֵר וּמְנַשֶּׁה
that great people like Acher and Menasheh
שֶׁכְּבָר זָכוּ בְּמַדְרֵגָתָם לִנְשָׁמָה
who already merited, at their level, a neshamah,
וְאַחַר כָּךְ חוֹטְאִים
and afterward sin,
וְזֶה נִקְרָא
and this is called,
יוֹדֵעַ רִבּוֹנוֹ וּמוֹרֵד
“one who knows his Master and rebels,”
שֶׁיּוּכַל לִפְגֹּם
who can blemish
גַּם הַנְּשָׁמָה שֶׁבַּמֹּחַ,
even the soul in the brain,
שֶׁשָּׁם הַחָכְמָה וְהַיְדִיעָה לְרִבּוֹנוֹ.
where lies the wisdom and knowledge of one’s Master.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה
And through this
יוּכַל לְהַגִּיעַ
he can reach,
דְּאֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
that he has no share in the World to Come,
דְּנֶפֶשׁ רוּחַ נְשָׁמָה
for nefesh, ruach, neshamah,
שֶׁהֵם נֶגֶד שְׁלֹשָׁה עוֹלָמוֹת
which correspond to three worlds —,
בְּרִיאָה, יְצִירָה, עֲשִׂיָּה
Beriah, Yetzirah, Asiyah —.
הֵם נֶגֶד שָׁלֹשׁ אוֹתִיּוֹת אַחֲרוֹנוֹת דְּשֵׁם
correspond to the last three letters of the Name.
דְּהַנְּשָׁמָה הִיא נֶגֶד ה׳ רִאשׁוֹנָה
For the neshamah corresponds to the first Heh,
שֶׁהוּא סוֹד עָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי כַּנּוֹדָע,
which is the mystery of the World to Come, as is known,
וְהִיא מֵהַבְּרִיאָה
and it is from Beriah,
דְּרֻבּוֹ טוֹב וּמִעוּטוֹ רַע
whose majority is good and minority evil.
וְהֵם מֻעָטִים מִמַּדְרֵגָה זוֹ דְּרַע
and few are those who fall into this level of evil.
וְכַנְפֵי הַחַיּוֹת
And the wings of the Chayos
הֵם הַחוֹצְצִים
are what divides,
בְּעַד הַהַשָּׂגָה שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מֵהֶם
from the perception above them,
שֶׁהוּא הַשָּׂגַת הַנְּשָׁמָה לַנְּשָׁמָה דְּמֵאֲצִילוּת
which is the perception of the neshamah of the neshamah of Atzilus.
דְּשָׁם אֵין מָקוֹם לָרַע כְּלָל
for there is no place for evil at all.
וְזֶהוּ הַחֵלֶק אֱלֹקִי מַמָּשׁ
And this is the truly divine portion,
שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּכָל אֶחָד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל
that is in every one of Israel,
וּמִי שֶׁזָּכָה לָהּ
and one who merited it
מֻבְטָח שֶׁלֹּא יֶחֱטָא עוֹד
is assured he will not sin any more,
כִּי כְּבָר הִשְׁלִים
for he has already completed
כָּל אוֹתִיּוֹת הַשֵּׁם הַכְּלוּלוֹת בּוֹ
all the letters of the Name included in him,
שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ חַיּוּתוֹ,
from which is his life,
כְּטַעַם "וְאַתָּה מְחַיֶּה אֶת כֻּלָּם",
as in “and You give life to them all,”
וּבִהְיוֹת הַשֵּׁם שָׁלֵם
and when the Name is whole.
אֵין חִסָּרוֹן עוֹד כְּלָל
there is no deficiency any more at all.
וְגַם כַּאֲשֶׁר פָּגַם
And also when he has blemished
וְהַמִּשְׁפָּט לִהְיוֹת שְׂמֹאל דּוֹחָה
and the judgment is that the left pushes away,
וּמִדַּת הַדִּין מְקַטְרֵג
and the attribute of judgment accuses,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַיָּמִין דְּאָדָם דַּאֲצִילוּת מְקָרַבְתּוֹ,
still the right hand of Adam of Atzilus draws him near,
רַק לֹא דֶּרֶךְ הִשְׁתַּלְשְׁלוּת הָעוֹלָמוֹת
but not by way of the chain of worlds —,
דִּבְרִיאָה, יְצִירָה, עֲשִׂיָּה בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת
Beriah, Yetzirah, Asiyah — in revelation,
הַיְנוּ לְהָאִיר לוֹ בַּפֹּעַל
that is, to illuminate him in actuality
בְּמֹחוֹ וְלִבּוֹ
in his brain and heart
וּמֵהֶם לִכְלֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה
and from them to the organs of action
לְסַיְּעָם בַּפֹּעַל לַעֲבוֹדָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,
to help them in practice to serve Him, blessed be He,
רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
only the Blessed Name,
בְּרֹב רַחֲמָיו וַחֲסָדָיו
in His abundant mercy and kindness,
מְעוֹרְרוֹ וּמְסַיְּעוֹ דֶּרֶךְ הֶעְלֵם
arouses and helps him in a concealed way,
שֶׁגַּם בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת לִבּוֹ וּמֹחוֹ עַצְמָם
so that even in the revelation of his own heart and brain,
הוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם
it is in concealment,
וּכְעִנְיָן שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ
and like what we said
מֵהָא דְּ"חוּץ מֵאַחֵר".
from the case of “except Acher.”

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I:57): a mezid can be misled by the evil inclination into imagining the act permissible, whereas a poshea is “one who knows his Master and intends to rebel.” He reads “Hold Your servant back from the willful ... then I shall be clear of great transgression” (Tehillim 19:14) through that distinction. The present passage applies the knowing rebel’s greater responsibility to a person who has already attained the level of neshama and then corrupts it; its conclusion nevertheless preserves the possibility of help through a concealed route.
