inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Sometimes great ones like Acher and Menasheh, who had already attained a neshama in their rung, sin afterward. This is “one who knows his Master and rebels,” able to blemish even the neshama in the mind, the seat of the knowledge of one’s Master, and thereby to reach [the state of] “having no share in the World to Come.” For nefesh–ruach–neshama correspond to the three worlds of Beriah–Yetzirah–Asiyah — the three final letters of the Name — while the neshama corresponds to the first heh, the secret of Olam Haba, drawn from Beriah (mostly good).

p: (ט) וְנִרְאֶה
And it seems
דְּלַתַּנָּא קַמָּא (דִּמְנָחוֹת שָׁם)
that according to the first Tanna (of Menachos there),
דְּסְתָם יָד הוּא שְׂמֹאל
for whom an unspecified “hand” is the left,
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר
one can say
דְּזֶה דְּהַהִתְקָרְבוּת
that this, that the drawing near,
הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַדְּחִיָּה
is through the pushing away,
דְּהֲרֵי כְּשֶׁאָמַר "חוּץ מֵאַחֵר"
for when it said “except Acher”
הֲרֵי בָּא לְדָחוֹתוֹ,
it came to push him away,
וְהוּא מִצַּד הַשְּׂמֹאל דּוֹחָה
and that is from the pushing left,
וְזֶה עַצְמוֹ הוּא כְּדֵי לְקַבְּלוֹ
yet this itself is in order to receive him.
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר
as explained.
וְזֶהוּ "יָדוֹ" כְּתִיב
And this is “His hand” is written,
דְּאֵין שָׁם הִתְגַּלּוּת יַד יָמִין
for there is no revelation of the right hand,
שֶׁהוּא הַחֲסָדִים הַגְּלוּיִים
which is the revealed kindnesses,
דְּאָז הָיָה מָקוֹם לְמִדַּת הַדִּין לְקַטְרֵג
for then there would be room for the attribute of judgment to accuse,
רַק אַדְרַבָּא הַקַּבָּלָה
but on the contrary the receiving,
הוּא עַל יְדֵי יַד הַשְּׂמֹאל הַדּוֹחָה
is through the pushing left hand,
דְּכְשֶׁרוֹאִין שֶׁנִּדְחֶה
for when they see he is pushed away,
נִסְתָּם פִּיּוֹת כָּל הַמְקַטְרְגִים
the mouths of all accusers are shut.
וּבָזֶה הוּא הַקִּרּוּב שֶׁבַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת
and in this is the drawing near that is in the tunnel.
אוֹ אֶפְשָׁר
Or it is possible
דְּהַקִּרּוּב הוּא עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
that the drawing near is through suffering,
כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁהָיָה בִּמְנַשֶּׁה
as was the case with Menasheh,
וְזֶהוּ בְּיַד שְׂמֹאל
and this is with the left hand
שֶׁנִּרְאֶה כְּפוֹגֵעַ בּוֹ מִדַּת הַדִּין לְהַעֲנִישׁוֹ,
that seems like the attribute of judgment striking him to punish him,
וּבֶאֱמֶת הוּא לְהֵטִיב אַחֲרִיתוֹ
but in truth it is to improve his end.
וּלְעוֹרְרוֹ עַל יְדֵי זֶה לִתְשׁוּבָה
and to arouse him through this to repentance.
וְדָבָר זֶה נִקְרָא
And this is called,
קַבָּלָה בַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת
receiving in the tunnel,
כְּשֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְעוֹרְרוֹ
when it is impossible to arouse him,
עַל יְדֵי הַבַּת קוֹל "שׁוּבוּ" וְגוֹמֵר
through the heavenly voice “Return,” etc.
כִּי הוּכְבַּד לִבּוֹ
because his heart has been hardened
עַל יְדֵי מִדַּת הַדִּין
by the attribute of judgment,
הַסּוֹתֶמֶת לְפָנָיו דַּלְתֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה
which seals before him the doors of repentance,
"דּוֹדִי שָׁלַח יָדוֹ מִן הַחוֹר"
“My Beloved sent forth His hand from the hole,”
שֶׁשָּׁם הַשְּׁרָצִים מְצוּיִים
where the creeping things are found,
כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה)
as they said (in Shir HaShirim Rabbah)
עַל פָּסוּק זֶה
on this verse
עַל בִּנְיַן בַּיִת שֵׁנִי עַל יְדֵי כּוֹרֶשׁ,
regarding the building of the Second Temple by Koresh,
וְשָׁם נִקְרָא "דוֹדִי",
and there He is called “My Beloved,”
דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הָיָה בְּאַהֲבָה וְחִבָּה
for it was nevertheless with love and affection.
וְלֹא עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
and not through suffering.
וּכְשֶׁהוּא עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
But when it is through suffering
דְּאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם
from the nations of the world,
כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּמֶלֶךְ קָשֶׁה כְּהָמָן
as they said of a king as harsh as Haman,
זֶהוּ הַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת דְּבַמַּחְתֶּרֶת
this is the arousal in the tunnel
עַל יְדֵי יַד שְׂמֹאל
through the left hand,
שֶׁנִּרְאֵית כְּדוֹחָה
that appears as pushing away,
וְנִרְאֵית כְּמִתְלַבֶּשֶׁת בְּיָדַיִם
and appears clothed in the hands.
יְדֵי עֵשָׂו
of Esav.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהָיוּ נִרְאִים
Just as appeared
יְדֵי יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
the hands of Yaakov our father, peace be upon him,
בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁבָּא לְקַבֵּל הַבְּרָכוֹת
when he came to receive the blessings,
מִיִּצְחָק אָבִיו
from Yitzchak his father,
שֶׁיָּדָיו הֵן הֵם יְדֵי אָדָם הָעֶלְיוֹן
for his hands are the very hands of the supernal Adam,
כִּי צוּרָתוֹ בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד
because his form is on the Throne of Glory,
וּכְשֶׁבָּא לִפְנֵי יִצְחָק אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
and when he came before Yitzchak our father, peace be upon him,
שֶׁהוּא מִדַּת הַדִּין
who is the attribute of judgment.
הוּצְרַךְ לָבוֹא בַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת
he needed to come in the tunnel.
כִּי עֵשָׂו הָיָה לוֹ בְּגָדִים הַחֲמוּדוֹת
For Esav had the precious garments
דְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן
of Adam the first,
שֶׁהָיָה לוֹבְשָׁן כְּשֶׁשִּׁמֵּשׁ אָבִיו
which he wore when he served his father,
הַיְנוּ שֶׁהָיָה פּוֹשֵׁט טְלָפָיו
that is, he would extend his hooves
וּמַרְאֶה הַלְּבוּשׁ שֶׁלּוֹ
and show his garment,
טָהוֹר וְטוֹב לִפְנֵי אָבִיו
as pure and good before his father,
וְהַפְּנִימִיּוּת שֶׁכֻּלּוֹ טָמֵא
while the inner side, which is entirely impure.
אֵינוֹ נִגְלֶה בַּחוּץ
is not revealed outside.
וְזֶה כָּל עִנְיַן עֵשָׂו
And this is the whole essence of Esav:
לְהַעֲרִים לְהִתְעַטֵּף
to deceive by wrapping himself,
בִּלְבוּשׁ שֶׁל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם וְצַדִּיק
in the garb of a Torah scholar and tzaddik,
וְכמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה
and as they said, of blessed memory,
עַל פָּסוּק "אִם בֵּין כּוֹכָבִים" וְגוֹמֵר
on the verse “If you set your nest among the stars,” etc.
דְּעָתִיד לְהִתְעַטֵּף בְּטַלִּיתוֹ
that he is destined to wrap himself in his tallis
וְלֵישֵׁב אֵצֶל יַעֲקֹב
and sit beside Yaakov,
וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מוֹרִידוֹ.
and the Holy One, blessed be He, brings him down.
כִּי הוּא בְּיָדוֹ לְהַעֲלִים פְּנִימִיּוּתוֹ
For it is in his power to conceal his inner side,
וּלְהִתְלַבֵּשׁ בִּלְבוּשׁ הַנִּרְאֶה טוֹב
and clothe himself in a garment that looks good,
לֹא לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן הַגַּשְׁמִי בִּלְבַד
not only to the physical eye.
רַק גַּם בְּכָל הָעוֹלָמוֹת
but also in all the worlds.
וְיִצְחָק אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
And Yitzchak our father, peace be upon him,
הָיָה נְבִיא ה׳ וְטָעָה בּוֹ,
was a prophet of the Lord and erred about him,
וְרַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּעַצְמוֹ
and only the Blessed Name Himself
הוּא שֶׁיּוֹרִידוֹ
is the one who brings him down,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "מִשָּׁם אוֹרִידְךָ נְאֻם ה׳",
as it is said “From there I will bring you down, says the Lord,”
שֶׁהוּא לְבַדּוֹ אֲשֶׁר יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב
for He alone looks at the heart
וְיוֹדֵעַ פְּנִימִיּוּתוֹ.
and knows his inner side.

paragraphs.text: An unspecified “hand” as the left — Menachos 37a records the first Tanna’s position that the right hand is called “his right hand yad yemino” but is not called simply yad without qualification; the sugya applies this to the placement of tefillin on the left arm. R’ Yosei HaChorem challenges the premise from Bereishis 48:17, while R’ Nasan derives the left arm by linking “you shall bind them” to right-handed writing, and Rav Ashi expounds yadkhah as yad kehah, the weaker hand. Rashi to Shemos 13:9 and Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 27:1, codify the practical halachah that tefillin are placed on the left arm. R’ Tzadok takes the Tanna’s linguistic rule beyond its halachic setting: yad without an openly stated “right” signifies the concealed left side of din.

paragraphs.text: “The left repels and the right draws near” — Sotah 47a and Sanhedrin 107b warn that rejection must never be total: one hand may distance, but the stronger right hand must remain ready to receive. The Gemara contrasts this balance with Elisha’s rejection of Geichazi and Yehoshua ben Perachyah’s rejection of his disciple “with both hands.” The same page applies the formula to the yetzer, a child, and a wife. In R’ Tzadok’s reading, the Acher proclamation is itself a left-handed rejection whose hidden right hand remains present; the apparent exclusion is therefore not the cancellation of teshuvah but the concealed means by which the door is kept open.

paragraphs.text: Menasheh’s suffering as an awakening — II Divrei HaYamim 33:10-13 relates that after Menasheh ignored prophetic warning, the Assyrians seized him with hooks, bound him in bronze, and carried him to Bavel; “when he was in distress, he entreated Hashem ... humbled himself greatly ... and prayed,” and Hashem restored him to Jerusalem. Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 10:2 describes the captivity more sharply: his captors placed him in a heated copper vessel, and only when every idol failed did he remember the verses his father had taught him, especially Devarim 4:30-31, promising return “when you are in distress.” The later “tunnel beneath the Throne” was thus preceded by suffering that cracked the hardened exterior and awakened the memory of Torah. R’ Tzadok therefore calls the punishing left hand itself the first stage of Divine reception.

paragraphs.text: A “king whose decrees are harsh as Haman” — Sanhedrin 97b records the dispute whether redemption depends upon voluntary teshuvah. R’ Yehoshua answers that if Israel does not return, the Holy One raises a king whose decrees are as harsh as Haman’s, “and Israel repent, and He restores them to the good.” The pressure is not an alternative to teshuvah but the external instrument that exposes Israel’s buried will to return. R’ Tzadok develops this very source in Machshavos Charutz §6 together with Megillah 14a, where the removal of Achashverosh’s ring accomplished what forty-eight prophets had not: Haman’s threat awakened the nation. Here the hostile ruler is the garment of the hidden Divine hand.

paragraphs.text: “The hands are the hands of Esav” — Bereishis 27:22 describes Yaakov’s voice emerging through hands made to appear like Esav’s. Bereishis Rabbah 65:20 contrasts the two powers: Yaakov rules through voice, prayer, and Torah, whereas Esav rules through the hands; Gittin 57b identifies “the hands of Esav” with the violent empire that destroyed the Temple and exiled Israel. R’ Tzadok reverses the image inwardly: when suffering comes through the hands of Edom, the external agent is indeed Esav, but the concealed purpose may be the hand of the “supernal Man” using that garment to awaken teshuvah. This does not excuse the oppressor; it identifies the redemptive intention hidden beneath the historical instrument.

paragraphs.text: Yaakov’s form engraved above — Bereishis Rabbah 68:12 states that the angels ascend to view Yaakov’s image above and descend to see him sleeping below, and Chullin 91b gives the related angelic ascent/descent tradition. Ramban, Bereishis 33:20, explicitly writes “שאיקונין של יעקב חקוקה בכסא הכבוד,” then explains its sod in connection with the dwelling of the Shechinah in Eretz Yisrael. Rav Tzadok applies these sources to the statement “כי צורתו בכסא הכבוד”; the description of Yaakov’s earthly hands as the hidden “supernal Man” is Rav Tzadok’s symbolic argument, not a literal bodily description of Hashem.

paragraphs.text: Yitzchak is identified with Gevurah/din in Pardes Rimmonim 23:3:6, whose explicit language is “גבורה מדת יצחק מדת הדין הקשה.” It also summarizes Sha’arei Orah, Gate Six, on the attribute as the heavenly power of justice. Thus Rav Tzadok’s identification “שהוא מדת הדין” is grounded in classical symbolic language. The further explanation of Yaakov’s concealed approach through Esav’s garments is Rav Tzadok’s application to the blessing narrative, not itself a direct quotation from the Pardes.

paragraphs.text: Yaakov’s hidden approach — Bereishis 27:15-35 describes Rivkah clothing Yaakov in Esav’s garments and Yitzchak later saying, “Your brother came b’mirmah and took your blessing.” Targum Onkelos renders b’mirmah as b’chochmeta, “with wisdom,” emphasizing a divinely directed strategy rather than ordinary falsehood; Rashi likewise glosses b’mirmah simply as “with wisdom.” R’ Tzadok’s word machteres is his own conceptual bridge to the hidden “tunnel” of teshuvah: strict justice sees only Esav’s outer garment and therefore cannot prosecute, while the blessing is secretly transferred to Yaakov, its truthful inner recipient. The comparison explains the concealment; it is not a halachic identification of Yaakov with a burglar.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Even according to the view that “yad [unspecified] hand” means the left, the drawing-near comes precisely through the repelling: the very “except for Acher” that came to repel is itself the means of receiving him. For when Justice sees him repelled, its mouth is stopped, and that is the “tunnel.” Or the drawing-near is through sufferings, as with Menasheh — the left hand that appears to strike him with Justice, but is truly to better his end and rouse him to teshuvah.

p: (י) אֲבָל הָאָדָם
But a person,
אֲפִילוּ נָבִיא גָּדוֹל כְּשְׁמוּאֵל
even a great prophet like Shmuel,
יִרְאֶה לָעֵינַיִם
sees only what is before the eyes,
וְכֵן מַלְאָכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת
and so do the ministering angels,
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיוֹדְעִים
and although they know
מַחֲשָׁבוֹת שֶׁבָּלֵּב
the thoughts of the heart
לְפִי דֵּעַת הַתוֹסָפוֹת (שַׁבָּת י״ב עַמּוּד ב׳)
according to the view of Tosafos (Shabbos 12b)
דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "שֶׁאֵין",
the passage beginning “she’ein,”
גַּם בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה יֵשׁ פְּנִימִיּוּת
even in thought there is an inner side
שֶׁהוּא הָאֱמֶת שֶׁבְּעַצְמיּוּתוֹ,
which is the truth of his essence,
וְחִיצוֹנִיּוּת
and an outer side
מַה שֶׁמְּרַמֶּה אֶת עַצְמוֹ גַּם כֵּן
by which he deceives himself too,
לַחֲשֹׁב הַכֹּל לְפָנִים
to think everything is inward,
וּפְנִימִיּוּת הַלֵּב
and the inner side of the heart
אֵין מַכִּיר אֶלָּא הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
none recognizes but the Blessed Name
(וְעַיֵּין בְּסֵפֶר מִשְׁנַת חֲכָמִים לְרַבִּי מֹשֶׁה חַאגִּיז סִימָן צב).
(and see Mishnas Chachamim by Rabbi Moshe Chagiz, section 92).
וּבְעוֹלָם הַעֲשִׂיָּה
And in the world of action
הַכֹּל לְפִי רוֹב הַמַּעֲשֶׂה
everything goes by the majority of deeds,
וְלְפִי הַהִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁבַּפֹּעַל
and by the revelation in practice,
דְּעַל כֵּן יֵשׁ לְעֵשָׂו כֹּחַ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
which is why Esav has power in this world
עַל יְדֵי מִקְצָת מִצְווֹת קַלּוֹת
through some light mitzvos
שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה לְפָנִים
that he does outwardly
וּלְהִתְיַיֵּהֵר
and to be haughty,
וְכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא י׳ עַמּוּד ב׳)
as they said (Bava Basra 10b).
וְהַהִיפֶּךְ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
And the opposite with Israel,
דְּחִיצוֹנִיּוּתָם לֹא כֵּן
for their outer side is not so,
דְּעַל כֵּן אֵין נִגְלִים
which is why they are not revealed,
לְקַבֵּל רוֹב טוֹבָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
to receive most good in this world,
וְרַק הַפְּנִימִיּוּת כֻּלּוֹ אֱמֶת
and only the inner side is entirely truth,
"בִּלְתִּי לַה׳ לְבַדּוֹ",
“to the Lord alone,”
וְכְמוֹ שֶּׁאִיתָא (בְּרָכוֹת י״ז עַמּוּד א׳)
and as stated (Berachos 17a)
"רְצוֹנֵנוּ לַעֲשוֹת רְצוֹנְךָ" וְכוּלֵּי
“It is our will to do Your will,” etc.
לוּלֵי הַמְעַכְּבִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
were it not for the obstructions in this world
לִהִתְגַּלּוֹת הַפְּנִימִיּוּת
to the revelation of the inner side.
דְּרָצוֹן לַפֹּעַל הַמַּעֲשֶׂה
of will into the act of deed.
וּמִדַּת הַדִּין
And the attribute of judgment
הוּא הַמְנַהִיג עוֹלָם הַזֶּה
is the one who governs this world,
כִּידוּעַ דְּ"אֱלֹקִים" בְּגִטְמַרִיא "הַטֶּבַע",
as is known that “Elokim” in gematria equals “nature,”,
וְכֵן הוּא הַכֹּל בְּמִדַּת הַדִּין
and so everything is in the attribute of judgment,
וּכְשֶׁדִּינָא יָתִיב
and when “the court sits”
אָז כָּל צְבָא הַשָּׁמַיִם עוֹמְדִים
then all the host of Heaven stand
מִיָּמִינוֹ וּמִשְׂמאלוֹ
on His right and on His left,
מַיְמִינִים וּמַשְׂמִאִילִים
some ruling for, some against,
שֶׁהֵם הַבֵּית דִּין שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה
who are the court above.
וְהֵם אֵין יוֹדְעִים הַפְּנִימִיּוּת
and they do not know the inner side.
וְעַל כֵּן כְּשֶׁבָּא יַעֲקֹב
And therefore when Yaakov came
לְקַבֵּל בְּרַכַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה מִיִּצְחָק
to receive the blessing of this world from Yitzchak,
הוּצְרַךְ לִלְבֹּשׁ בִּגְדֵי עֵשָׂו
he needed to wear Esav’s garments,
כִּי הוּא הָיָה אוֹהֵב עֵשָׂו
for he loved Esav
מִצַּד הַלְּבוּשׁ הַנִּגְלֶה מִמֶּנּוּ
on account of the garment revealed from him.
לִפְנָיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
before him in this world.
וְכֶּשֶׁלָּבַשׁ יַעֲקֹב אוֹתוֹ לְבוּשׁ
And when Yaakov wore that garment,
וְהוּא כֻּלּוֹ אֱמֶת
being entirely truth
וְאֵין יָכוֹל לְרַמּוֹת
and unable to deceive,
וְלַהַרְאוֹת הַלְּבוּשׁ נֶגֶד הַפְּנִימִיּוּת
or show the garment contrary to the inner side,
מֵמִילָא
automatically
אוֹתוֹ הַלְּבוּשׁ דְּעֵשָׂו נֶהֱפַךְ אֶצְלוֹ
that garment of Esav was turned around with him
לְהַרְאוֹת הָאֱמֶת דְּעֵשָׂו שֶׁבְּאוֹתוֹ הַלְּבוּשׁ,
to show the truth of Esav that was in that garment,
וְהוּא הַלְּבוּשׁ שֶׁלּוֹ מִאוֹתָם שֶׁבִּירוּרוֹ שֶׁלֹּא כֵּן בַּפֹּעַל
and this is his garment, represented by those whose actual conduct does not reflect their inner truth.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם "אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָטָא יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא" בְּפְנִימִיּוּת
and nevertheless “even though he sinned, he is Israel,” in the inner side.
וְעַל כֵּן הֵרִיחַ בּוֹ יִצְחָק
And therefore Yitzchak smelled in him
רֵיחַ בּוֹגְדָיו
the smell of his “betrayers” (garments)
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין ל״ז עַמּוּד א׳)
as they said (Sanhedrin 37a),
אֲבָל עַל יְדֵי הַאָרַת הַפְּנִימִיּוּת דִּיעֲקֹב
but through the illumination of Yaakov’s inner side,
בְּבִיאָתוֹ אֵלָיו
at his coming to him,
שֶׁנִּכְנַס עִמּוֹ רֵיחַ גַּן עֵדֶן מִמַּעְלָה
— in which the fragrance of Gan Eden from Above entered with him —,
הַרֵּיחַ הַטוֹב שֶׁבָּפְנִימִיּוּת בּוֹגְדָיו
the good fragrance of the inner side of his “betrayers,”
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר
and therefore he said:
הַיָּדַיִם וְכֹּחוֹת הַפְּעוּלָה יְדֵי עֵשָׂו
the hands and powers of action are the hands of Esav.
וְהַקּוֹל שֶׁהוּא הַפְּנִימִיּוּת — קוֹל יַעֲקֹב
and the voice, which is the inner side — the voice of Yaakov.

paragraphs.text: Shmuel and Eliav — I Shmuel 16:6-7 relates that when Shmuel saw Eliav, his imposing appearance led him to say, “Surely Hashem’s anointed is before Him.” Hashem answered: “Do not look at his appearance or at the height of his stature ... for man sees with the eyes, but Hashem sees into the heart.” Rashi explains that Eliav was rejected because of his anger, and reads Hashem’s answer as a correction of Shmuel’s claim to be “the seer.” Radak says that Eliav looked fit for kingship outwardly, while Hashem knew that his heart was unfit; and Malbim contrasts visible qualities with the hidden dispositions required for kingship. R’ Tzadok uses this episode as the paradigm for the limit of every created knower: even the greatest prophet evaluates what has entered revelation, whereas Hashem alone knows the deepest point of the heart before it has become conscious thought or deed.

paragraphs.text: Elokim and nature — both א-להים and הטבע have the numerical value eighty-six. The Shelah, Torah Ohr to Terumah §27, uses this equivalence to describe the Divine Name Elokim as the concealed governance revealed through the stable order of nature. R’ Tzadok himself makes the same point in Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 2:44: Elokim signifies mastery over all the forces of nature, and therefore equals ha-teva in gematria. The equation does not identify nature as an independent power; it means that what appears as impersonal law is itself Hashem’s hidden rule through the middah of din. This is precisely R’ Tzadok’s argument here: the world of outward action is administered through measurable consequence, while its inner Divine intention may remain concealed.

paragraphs.text: The Heavenly Court to the right and left — I Melachim 22:19 records Michayahu’s vision of Hashem seated upon His throne “and all the host of heaven standing by Him on His right and on His left.” Chazal ask how “right” and “left” can apply before Hashem and explain: those on the right advocate merit, while those on the left advocate liability. Rashi to Bereishis 1:26 cites this vision to explain Hashem’s consultation with the heavenly retinue. The angels judge from what is available within the created order of evidence and manifestation. R’ Tzadok’s point is that such a court cannot penetrate the innermost will known only to Hashem; mercy may therefore have to enter the judicial order in a concealed garment that even the prosecuting forces cannot challenge.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 44a states concerning Achan, “אף על פי שחטא ישראל הוא,” comparing the sinner to a myrtle surrounded by thorns that remains a myrtle. This directly explains Rav Tzadok’s phrase that outward conduct can resemble Esav while an Israelite’s inner identity remains. Rashi on Bereishis 1:1 also transmits the Midrashic reading that Creation is “for the sake of Torah” and “for the sake of Israel,” called reishis; Shabbos 88a links Creation’s endurance to Israel’s acceptance of Torah. Those are contextual parallels to the inward importance of Israel, not exact statements that the external garment itself is a mitzvah. The former historical 531 cited Sanhedrin 44a as a separate note at this same phrase; its distinct source and interpretive content are incorporated here without repeating the source twice.

This directly explains Rav Tzadok’s phrase that outward conduct can resemble Esav while an Israelite’s inner identity remains. Rashi on Bereishis 1:1 also transmits the Midrashic reading that Creation is “for the sake of Torah” and “for the sake of Israel,” called reishis; Shabbos 88a links Creation’s endurance to Israel’s acceptance of Torah. Those are contextual parallels to the inward importance of Israel, not exact statements that the external garment itself is a mitzvah. The former historical 531 cited Sanhedrin 44a as a separate note at this same phrase; its distinct source and interpretive content are incorporated here without repeating the source twice.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 37a offers two adjacent but distinct homilies: Reish Lakish says that even the “empty ones” among Israel are full of mitzvos like a pomegranate, and R. Zeira interprets Bereishis 27:27, “וירח את ריח בגדיו,” as “אל תקרי בגדיו אלא בוגדיו.” The specific begadav/bogdav wordplay directly supports Rav Tzadok’s “ריח בוגדיו”; the pomegranate teaching is a contextual companion, not the wording of the same quotation. Bereishis Rabbah 65:22 separately associates the scent with Gan Eden and describes repentant offenders. Rav Tzadok unites these traditions to explain the fragrance of inward holiness.

paragraphs.text: The fragrance accompanying Yaakov — Bereishis 27:27 says that Yitzchak “smelled the fragrance of his garments” and blessed Yaakov. Rashi asks how goatskins, which normally have an unpleasant odor, could produce such fragrance and answers, following Bereishis Rabbah 65:22, that the scent of Gan Eden entered with Yaakov; “the field that Hashem blessed” is interpreted as a field of apples or the supernal garden. This source complements the Gemara’s derashah on begadav/bogdav cited in the existing note: the outward garment may be associated with betrayal, yet the inward fragrance reveals the holy root. R’ Tzadok reads the blessing scene as a disclosure of this paradox — Esav’s visible clothing is transformed by Yaakov’s inner truth until even the judge of externals perceives the scent of the hidden Edenic source.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Man — even a prophet as great as Shmuel — “sees to the eyes”; and so do the angels. Even in thought there is an inner core (the true self) and an outer shell (with which one deceives even himself); the inmost heart, only Hashem knows. And in the world of Asiyah everything goes “by the abundance of the deed” and the outward manifestation — which is why Esav has power in this world, through a few “light mitzvos” he does for show and boasts of.

p: (יא) וְזֶהוּ הָעֵצָה
And this is the counsel,
נֶגֶד מִדַּת הַדִּין
against the attribute of judgment,
שֶׁמִּדַּת הָרַחֲמִים
that the attribute of mercy
מַעֲלֶמֶת רַחֲמֶיהָ
conceals its mercy,
מִתַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַחַיּוֹת
beneath the wings of the Chayos,
שֶׁאֵין נִרְגָּשׁ
so that it is not sensed
לְכָל הַמַּלְאָכִים
by any of the angels
וּבֵית דִּין שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה
or the court above.
בְּכָל הָעוֹלָמוֹת
in all the worlds.
וְזֶהוּ "יָדוֹ" כָּתִיב
And this is why “yado” is written (singular),
שֶׁאֵין כָּאן אֶלָּא יָד אֶחָד
for here there is only one hand,
כִּי יַד יָמִין
since the right hand,
מִתְלַבֶּשֶׁת תּוֹךְ הַיָּד שְׂמֹאל
is clothed within the left hand,
וּכְבָיָכוֹל
and, as it were,
אָדָם הָעֶלְיוֹן
the Supernal Man.
מִתְלַבֵּשׁ בְּבִגְדֵי עֵשָׂו
clothes Himself in Esav’s garments.
עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה
Along the lines of what our Sages, of blessed memory, said
עַל פָּסוּק "חָמוּץ בְּגָדִים",
on the verse “red of garments,”
שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לוֹבֵשׁ אָדוֹם כְּמוֹתוֹ
that the Holy One, blessed be He, wears red like him
כְּשֶׁיָּבוֹא לִנְקֹם מִמֶּנּוּ
when He comes to take vengeance on him.
וּלְכַלּוֹתוֹ לְגַמְרֵי
and to destroy him completely.
וְכֵן בְּכָל דּוֹר וָדוֹר
And so in every generation,
כְּשֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהוֹשִׁיעַ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
when it is impossible to save Israel
בְּאֹפֶן אַחֵר
in another way,
כִּבְיֵמֵי הָמָן
as in the days of Haman,
דְּהֻחְזְרוּ לְמוֹטָב
they were returned to the good
עַל יְדֵי זֶה
through this
מָה שֶׁלֹּא הוֹעִיל לָהֶם
which did not avail them,
אַרְבָּעִים וּשְׁמוֹנָה נְבִיאִים
forty-eight prophets,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּמְגִלָּה י״ד רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳)
as they said (Megillah 14a) ".
גְּדוֹלָה הֲסָרַת טַבַּעַת" וְכוּלֵּי
“Greater was the removal of the ring,” etc.
וּבְכָל מָקוֹם "הַמֶּלֶךְ" סְתָם בַּמְּגִלָּה
And everywhere “the king” appears unqualified in the Megillah,
בְּמַלְכּוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם
it is the King of the world,
הַכָּתוּב מְדַבֵּר
of whom Scripture speaks,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּמִדְרָשׁ אֶסְתֵּר),
as they said (in Midrash Esther),
כִּי מַלְכּוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם
for the King of the world —
הִתְלַבְּשׁוּת הַקְּדֻשָּׁה
the clothing of holiness,
בִּלְבוּשׁ שַׂק דְּהָמָן
in the sackcloth garb of Haman,
לִהְיוֹתָם יְשֵׁנִים מִן הַמִּצְוֹת
since they were asleep to the mitzvos,
וְלֹא הָיָה אֶפְשָׁר לְעוֹרְרָם
and it was not possible to arouse them
אֶלָּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה
except in this way:
שֶׁיִּשְׁלַח יָדוֹ מִן הַחוֹר
that He stretch out His hand from the hole
בְּהִתְלַבְּשׁוּת הַהֵפֶךְ.
in the clothing of the opposite.
שֶׁהַגְּזֵרָה לְהַשְׁמִיד וְלַהֲרֹג וְגוֹמֵר
For the decree was to destroy and to kill, and so on,
וּבֶאֱמֶת הָיְתָה הַכַּוָּנָה לְהֵפֶךְ
yet in truth the intention was the opposite:
לְרוֹמֵם וּלְגַדֵּל קֶרֶן יִשְׂרָאֵל
to raise and magnify the horn of Israel
וְלַהֲרֹג וּלְאַבֵּד אֶת הָמָן
and to kill and destroy Haman
וְזֶרַע עֲמָלֵק
and the seed of Amalek.
וְכָל אוֹיְבֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
and all the enemies of Israel.
וְכֵן לֶעָתִיד
And so in the future,
אִם יִצְטָרְכוּ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם
if they should need, Heaven forbid,
לְמֶלֶךְ קָשֶׁה כְּהָמָן
a harsh king like Haman,
יִהְיֶה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְלַבֵּשׁ בְּקִרְבּוֹ,
the Blessed Name will be clothed within him,
דְּ"לֵב מְלָכִים בְּיַד ה׳",
for “the heart of kings is in the hand of the Lord,”
וְעַל יְדֵי אוֹתוֹ הִתְלַבְּשׁוּת
and through that clothing
בִּלְבוּשׁ עֵשָׂו
in the garb of Esav.
יַאֲבִידוּ מִן הָעוֹלָם
they will destroy (him) from the world.
וְכֵן בְּכָל נֶפֶשׁ פְּרָטִי
And so with every individual soul,
דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹמֵר אֱמֶת לְעוֹלָם
for the Blessed Name keeps truth forever:
הֵם זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב
they are the seed of Yaakov,
שֶׁכֻּלּוֹ זֶרַע אֱמֶת
who is entirely a seed of truth,
שֶׁלֹּא יִדַּח מֵהֶם נִדָּח
that no one be cast out from them,
וּמְעוֹרְרָם תָּמִיד לִתְשׁוּבָה
and He always arouses them to repentance
עַל יְדֵי הָאַרְבָּעִים וּשְׁמוֹנָה נְבִיאִים
through the forty-eight prophets
שֶׁנִּקְבְּעָה נְבוּאָתָם לְדוֹרוֹת
whose prophecy was fixed for the generations
בְּדִבְרֵי נְבוּאָתָם
through the words of their prophecy
בְּהַזְהָרַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה
in the warning of repentance
מַרְעֶמֶת וּמַרְעֶשֶׁת
thundering and shaking
בִּתְמִידוּת
constantly.
בִּלְבָבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
in the hearts of the children of Israel.
וְכֵן כָּל מָקוֹם
And so wherever
שֶׁחִדְּשׁוּ סוֹפְרִים אַחַר כָּךְ
the scribes later innovated,
כָּל דִּבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה הַמְקֻדָּשִׁים
all the sanctified words of our Sages, of blessed memory,
וְאַף שֶׁאַחֲרֵיהֶם
and even those after them
אוֹתָם שֶׁהָיוּ חֲכָמִים בֶּאֱמֶת
who were truly wise,
שֶׁכָּל דִּבְרֵיהֶם דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹקִים חַיִּים
whose every word is the word of the living God,
דִּבְרֵיהֶם פּוֹעֲלִים בְּכָל הַדּוֹרוֹת
their words work in all generations
וּבְכָל הַלְּבָבוֹת
and in all hearts,
לְעוֹרְרָם מִשְּׁנָתָם
to arouse them from their sleep,
וְאַשְׁרֵי הַמִּתְעוֹרֵר עַל יְדֵי זֶה לְבַד
and fortunate is the one aroused by this alone.
שֶׁאֵין צָרִיךְ יוֹתֵר
who needs nothing more.

paragraphs.text: Justice joined with mercy in Creation — Bereishis Rabbah 12:15 explains the shift from “Elokim” in Bereishis 1:1 to “Hashem Elokim” in Bereishis 2:4: the world could not endure under strict din alone, so the Holy One joined the middah of mercy to it. Rashi to Bereishis 1:1 states this as: initially it arose in thought to create with din; seeing that the world would not endure, He gave precedence to mercy and joined it to din. Maharal clarifies that this is not a change of mind, God forbid, but two levels of the created order: din defines the truth and structure of existence, while mercy grants the possibility of endurance and repair. R’ Tzadok applies that cosmic pattern to teshuvah: the visible order judges the deed, but the merciful power sustaining the world preserves the hidden point from which return remains possible.

paragraphs.text: “Crimson garments” — Yeshayah 63:1-4 portrays the Divine warrior coming from Edom with blood-colored garments, proclaiming that the day of vengeance and the year of redemption have arrived. Rashi explains that the prophecy speaks in the imagery of human warfare “to convey to the ear what it can hear”: the Shechinah is depicted as clothed in garments stained by the defeat of Edom, while the subject is Hashem’s personal vengeance against Edom and its heavenly power. The anthropomorphic garment therefore does not describe His essence, God forbid, but the form in which His judgment becomes visible within history. Rav Tzadok reads the image inwardly: the red garment appears to belong to Esav and strict din, yet the One clothed within it is the “supernal Man,” whose purpose is Israel’s redemption. The very appearance of Edomite power can thus become the external clothing through which Edom is ultimately destroyed.

paragraphs.text: The decree and its reversal — Esther 3:13 formulates Haman’s decree “to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate all the Jews.” The second royal letter deliberately repeats the same verbs, now granting the Jews power “to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate” the forces attacking them (Esther 8:11). The Megillah then states the governing principle: “v’nahafoch hu — the opposite occurred,” so that the Jews ruled over those who hated them (Esther 9:1). The reversal is deeper than a fortunate change of events. The language of destruction itself is transferred from Israel to Amalek, revealing that the threatening decree had become the instrument of its own undoing. This is Rav Tzadok’s meaning that holiness was clothed in Haman’s garment: within the visible decree lay a concealed Divine intention to awaken Israel, elevate its horn, and turn the power of “destroying” against Haman and the seed of Amalek.

paragraphs.text: A harsh king and the King’s heart — Sanhedrin 97b teaches that if Israel does not awaken to teshuvah, the Holy One may raise over them “a king whose decrees are as harsh as Haman’s,” through whom they return to the good. Mishlei 21:1 supplies the inner principle: “Like channels of water is the heart of a king in the hand of Hashem; He turns it wherever He desires.” The meforshim explain that a ruler may experience his plans as his own, while Providence directs their course toward an end he neither sees nor intends. Thus the teaching does not absolve a wicked ruler of responsibility; Haman chooses hatred and is punished for it. Yet his freely chosen wickedness is enclosed within a higher governance that redirects its consequences. Rav Tzadok calls this Hashem’s clothing within the harsh king: the external garment is Esav’s coercive power, but the hidden hand bends that power toward Israel’s teshuvah and the eventual destruction of the persecutor himself.

paragraphs.text: Resisei Layla §36 (Har Bracha ed., p. 70): “חסד שבמשפט” — “kindness within judgment.” Rav Tzadok explains that judgment itself may call for mercy toward Israel, so that compassion and justice are not competing forces. Here the kindness remains concealed within the apparently harsh external rule of Esav. The parallel illuminates the relationship between chesed and mishpat; it does not directly describe the concealed hand beneath the wings of the Chayos.

paragraphs.text: “Hashem keeps truth forever” and the “seed of truth” — Tehillim 146:6 praises the Creator as “the One who keeps truth forever,” meaning that His covenantal faithfulness is not cancelled by delay or concealment. Yirmiyahu 2:21 calls Israel “entirely seed of truth,” even while rebuking the nation for having outwardly become like an alien vine. The contrast itself is Rav Tzadok’s point: deformation in conduct does not erase the original planting. Michah 7:20 associates truth specifically with Yaakov — “You will grant truth to Yaakov, kindness to Avraham” — and the meforshim explain that “truth” signifies the sure fulfillment of the covenant promised to his descendants. Rav Tzadok combines these verses ontologically. Israel is the seed of Yaakov, whose root is emes; therefore Hashem’s fidelity to truth includes continuously arranging means by which that root will again appear. Teshuvah is not the invention of a new identity but the reemergence of the true seed beneath its foreign growth.

paragraphs.text: II Shmuel 14:14: “וְחָשַׁב מַחֲשָׁבוֹת לְבִלְתִּי יִדַּח מִמֶּנּוּ נִדָּח” — “He devises designs so that no banished one will be cast away from Him.” The wise woman of Tekoa uses this in pleading for Avshalom’s return. Machshavos Charutz §9 (Har Bracha ed., pp. 72–73) applies the verse to the enduring שורש האמונה, root of faith, in Jewish souls and to the eventual awakening of those who have strayed. Resisei Layla §35 similarly treats awakening through the great shofar. Peri Tzadik, Nasso §15 is a complementary discussion of Yaakov’s enduring truth, not a direct repetition of the verse. The point is the possibility of return, not exemption from teshuvah.

paragraphs.text: The authority of the soferim and rabbinic enactments — Devarim 17:11 commands Israel not to turn aside from the rulings of the authorized Torah court. Shabbos 23a asks how one may bless “Who commanded us” over the rabbinic mitzvah of Chanukah lights and answers: Rav Avya derives the command from “lo tasur,” while Rav Nechemiah cites “Ask your father and he will tell you; your elders and they will say to you” (Devarim 32:7). Rambam, Hilchos Mamrim 1:1-2, accordingly includes the received interpretations, enactments, decrees, and safeguards of the Great Court within the Torah’s obligation to heed the sages. Rav Tzadok’s phrase “what the soferim innovated” does not mean arbitrary invention detached from Sinai. It refers to Torah authority drawing forth the practical form needed by a later generation. Their sacred words can therefore serve as a further Divine awakening after the era of prophecy.

paragraphs.text: “The words of the living God” — Eruvin 13b records the heavenly declaration concerning Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel: “These and those are the words of the living God,” even though practical halachah follows Beis Hillel. Gittin 6b similarly applies the phrase to differing interpretations that disclose complementary dimensions of one event. Rashi to Kesubos 57a explains that honest Torah reasoning is not falsehood merely because another sage reaches the opposite ruling: each view articulates the rationale that applies to the reality as that sage understands it, and changing circumstances may reveal the relevance of a different rationale. Rav Tzadok carefully limits his statement to those “who were sages in truth.” Their words possess life because they are genuine apprehensions within Torah, not personal rhetoric. Once articulated in holiness, they continue supplying later souls with the precise thought capable of awakening them from spiritual sleep.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: This is the “stratagem” against the Attribute of Justice: that the Attribute of Mercy hides its mercy beneath the wings of the chayos, unfelt by all the angels and the Heavenly Court in all the worlds. Hence “yado” [singular]: the right hand is clothed within the left. The “supernal Man” clothes himself in “Esav’s garments” — as the Sages said on “crimson garments” (Yeshayah 63:1), that God “wears red like [Edom]” when He comes to avenge and utterly destroy him.

p: (יב) וּזְמַן תְּשׁוּבָה לַכֹּל
And the time of repentance for all,
הוּא בַּעֲשֶׂרֶת יְמֵי תְּשׁוּבָה
is in the Ten Days of Repentance,
שֶׁאָז נִקְרָא בְּהִמָּצְאוֹ
when He is called upon “while He is near,”
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה י״ח עַמּוּד א׳)
as they said (Rosh Hashanah 18a),
שֶׁהוּא מָצוּי אֵצֶל כָּל יָחִיד
that He is available to every individual,
כִּי אָז הוּא בְּיִחוּד הַזְּמַן
for then it is especially the time
שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְעוֹרֵר כָּל יָחִיד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל
that the Blessed Name arouses every individual of Israel
בְּחַדְרֵי לִבָּוֹ
in the chambers of his heart
לָשׁוּב אֵלָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ.
to return to Him, blessed be He.
וְהַהַתְחָלָה עַל יְדֵי קוֹל הַשּׁוֹפָר בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה
And the beginning is through the sound of the shofar on Rosh Hashanah,
דִּפְשׁוּטוֹ
whose simple meaning,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב רַמְבָּ"ם
as the Rambam wrote,
"עוּרוּ יְשֵׁנִים מִתַּרְדֵּמַתְכֶם",
“Awake, you sleepers, from your slumber,”
וְ"הֲיִתָּקַע בַּשּׁוֹפָר וְעָם לֹא יֶחֱרָדוּ"
and “Shall the shofar be blown, and the people not tremble?”,
הִיא תְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה
is repentance from fear,
שֶׁהוּא כָּל הַתְחָלַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה
which is the whole beginning of repentance,
שֶׁמִּצַּד הָאָדָם
from the human side,
וְזֶהוּ פְּעֻלָּתוֹ
and this is its effect.
בִּלְבָבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
in the hearts of the children of Israel.
וְכֵן פּוֹעֵל לְמַעְלָה
And likewise it effects Above
בְּקִיּוּם מִצְוָה זוֹ
through fulfilling this mitzvah,
דְּהַשְׁמָעַת קוֹל שוֹפָר
of hearing the sound of the shofar,
שֶׁהוּא "הַקּוֹל קוֹל יַעֲקֹב",
which is “the voice, the voice of Yaakov,”
קוֹל פָּשׁוּט הַמְעוֹרֵר
a simple voice that arouses
עַל הַפְּנִימִיּוּת הַנֶּעְלָם
the hidden inner side,
שֶׁכָּל רְצוֹנֵנוּ
that all our desire
רַק לַעֲשוֹת רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,
is only to do His will, blessed be He,
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה
and through this,
יַעֲלֶה זִכְרוֹנֵנוּ לְפָנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ לְטוֹבָה
our remembrance will rise before Him, blessed be He, for good,
כִּי יִסְתַּלֵּק כֻּרְסְיָא דִּדִינָא
for the throne of judgment will be removed
וְיֵשֵׁב עַל כִּסֵּא רַחֲמִים
and He will sit on the throne of mercy
לְהִתְנַהֵג בַּחֲסִידוּת
to conduct Himself with kindness
וּמוֹחֵל עֲוֹנוֹת עַמּוֹ,
and forgive the sins of His people,
כִּי מַבִּיט עַל הַפְּנִימִיּוּת
for He looks at the inner side.
וְלֹא עַל חִיצוֹנִיּוּת הַמַּעֲשִׂים הַנִּגְלִים
and not at the outer side of the revealed deeds.
וְשִׁבְעָה יָמִים
And the seven days
שֶׁבֵּין רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים
between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur
הֵם יְמֵי תְּשׁוּבָה
are days of repentance
לְתַקֵּן כָּל מָה שֶׁפָּגַם בְּכָל הַשָּׁנָה
to rectify all that he blemished throughout the year
(אוֹ הַשָּׁנִים שֶׁעָבְרוּ)
(or the years that passed),
כָּל יוֹם יוֹמוֹ
each day its own day,
כִּידוּעַ מִהָאֲרִי זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה
as is known from the Arizal, of blessed memory.
בְּסֵפֶר הַכּוָּנוֹת
in Sefer HaKavanos.
וְהַיְנוּ דְּשִׁבְעָה יָמִים אֵלּוּ
That is, these seven days,
שֶׁהֵם כּוֹלְלִים כָּל יְמֵי הַשָּׁבוּעַ
which include all the days of the week,
הֵם נֶגֶד שִׁבְעָה יְמֵי הַבִּנְיָן
correspond to the seven days of building,
הַכּוֹלְלִים שֶׁבַע מִדּוֹת הַיְדוּעִים
which include the seven known attributes,
שֶׁהוּא כְּלָל קוֹמַת אָדָם
which is the whole stature of man.
בְּכָל מִדּוֹתָיו וּפְעֻלּוֹתָיו הַנִּגְלוֹת
in all his traits and revealed actions.
דְּהַנִּסְתָּרוֹת
For the hidden ones,
הֵם שָׁלוֹשׁ רִאשׁוֹנוֹת
are the first three,
שֶׁנֶּגְדָּם שְׁנֵי יָמִים דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה
to which correspond the two days of Rosh Hashanah,
שֶׁהוּא קוֹמַת הָרֹאשׁ
which is the stature of the head:
חָכְמָה שֶׁבַּמֹּחַ,
Chochmah in the brain,
וְכֶּתֶר שֶׁעַל גַּבֵּי הָרֹאשׁ
and Keser atop the head,
הוּא הָעֹמֶק רֵאשִׁית דְּמַחֲשָׁבָה
which is the depth, the beginning of thought,
הַנֶּעְלָם מִהָאָדָם עַצְמוֹ
hidden from the person himself,
מְקוֹם לֵידַת הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה
the place of the birth of thought,
דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא "יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן"
for which reason it is called “something from nothing”,
וְ"הַחָכְמָה מֵאַיִן תִּמָּצֵא" כַּנוֹדָע
and “wisdom is found from nothing,” as is known,
וְהֵם קְדֻשָּׁה אַחַת וְיוֹמָא אַחֲרִיתָא
and they are one holiness and “another day,”
כִּי הָאַיִן אֵין תְּפִיסָה בֹּו
for there is no grasping of the Ayin
אֶלָּא מִצַּד הַיֵּשׁ הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מִמֶּנּוּ.
except from the side of the Yesh that is drawn from it.
וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים
And Yom Kippur,
הוּא נֶגֶד הַבִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב
corresponds to Binah in the heart.
דְּ"לֵבָבוֹ יָבִין וָשָׁב וְרָפָא לוֹ" כַּנוֹדָע
for “his heart will understand, and he will return and be healed,” as is known.
וְהֵם תִּקּוּן הַנֶּעְלָמוֹת
And these are the rectification of the hidden things:
הַהַתְחָלָה בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה
the beginning on Rosh Hashanah,
בְּתְשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה
with repentance from fear,
וְהַגְּמָר בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים
and the completion on Yom Kippur
בְּתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
with repentance from love,
תְּשׁוּבָה עִלָּאָה
higher repentance,
תְּשׁוּבָה דְּאִתְחֲזְיָא לְחַפָּאָה עַל כָּל עוֹבָדוֹי
repentance worthy to cover over all his deeds,
וְשִׁבְעָה יָמִים שֶׁבֵּינַתַיִם
and the seven days in between
הוּא בְּתִקּוּן הַנִּגְלוֹת
are in the rectification of the revealed things.
בְּמִדּוֹת וּמַעֲשִׂים
in traits and deeds.

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Vayeishev §11: “שהמכוון שזהו התפלה שיתפלל להש״י שיעזוב רשע דרכו ... שגם כח התשובה הוא ביד השי״ת” — “The intent is that one pray to Hashem to abandon the wicked path ... for even the power of repentance is in Hashem’s hands.” This explains why a person must petition Hashem for the very strength to return, as Rav Tzadok develops here. The parallel explains Divine help in personal repentance; the particular ten-day calendar is established by the surrounding discussion, not by these words alone.

paragraphs.text: The shofar as an awakening to teshuvah — Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 3:4, writes that although the command of shofar is a decree of Scripture, it contains an allusion: “Awake, sleepers, from your sleep; arise, slumberers, from your slumber; examine your deeds, return in teshuvah, and remember your Creator.” Amos 3:6 supplies the prophetic image: “Shall a shofar be sounded in a city and the people not tremble?” Pesikta de-Rav Kahana §24 applies this verse to the shofar of Rosh Hashanah and explains that Hashem does not desire the death of the wicked but sends the warning call so that they may awaken. Rav Tzadok therefore identifies this first movement as teshuvah from fear: the sound enters from without, shakes the person out of spiritual sleep, and begins the human response. Yet the Rambam’s language already points beyond fear alone — to self-examination, remembrance of the Creator, and the recovery of one’s true purpose.

paragraphs.text: “The voice, the voice of Yaakov” — Bereishis 27:22 contrasts Yaakov’s voice with Esav’s hands. Bereishis Rabbah 65:20 develops the contrast: Yaakov’s power is in his voice — Torah and prayer — and when that voice is heard in the synagogues and study halls, the hands of Esav do not rule. Rav Tzadok, Resisei Layla §52, similarly calls Torah and prayer “the sword of the mouth,” the spiritual weapon of Israel. In this se’if the shofar is identified with that same voice, but in its simplest and most inward form: not articulated words, but a plain cry preceding speech. The sound reaches the point of Yaakov that is prior to the complications of outward conduct. Thus the mitzvah does not merely announce judgment; it allows the essential Jewish voice to emerge, weakening the external “hands of Esav” and disclosing the soul’s bond with Hashem.

paragraphs.text: The hidden will of Israel — Berachos 17a records R’ Alexandri’s prayer: “Master of the worlds, it is revealed and known before You that our will is to do Your will; and what prevents us? The leaven in the dough and the subjugation of the kingdoms.” Rashi explains the “leaven” as the evil inclination within the heart. The statement distinguishes the deepest ratzon from the forces that obstruct its appearance in action. Rav Tzadok repeatedly builds upon this teaching; see Resisei Layla §20, where even when Israel is “asleep from the mitzvos,” the heart remains awake and the true will remains attached to Hashem. The shofar’s simple voice reaches this pre-verbal ratzon. It does not excuse wrongdoing, because the external barriers must still be overcome through teshuvah; rather, it reveals the point from which genuine teshuvah becomes possible — the inward will that never consented to permanent separation.

paragraphs.text: Remembrance through the shofar — Rosh Hashanah 16a teaches: “Recite before Me kingship, remembrance, and shofar verses: kingship, so that you accept My kingship; remembrance, so that your remembrance rise before Me for good — and through what? Through the shofar.” The shofar is therefore not only a warning heard below; it is the means by which Israel’s remembrance ascends Above. Rambam, Commentary to Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 4:5, cites this teaching as the structure of the Rosh Hashanah service. Sefas Emes explains that the shofar’s voice is uniquely Israel’s own voice and brings the words of remembrance inward, “before” Hashem. Rav Tzadok reads this remembrance as the disclosure of the concealed inner identity. What is remembered is not a selective forgetting of deeds, but the covenantal root beneath them — the true Yaakov-point that can now awaken, repent, and redirect the revealed life.

paragraphs.text: From the throne of judgment to the throne of mercy — Tehillim 47:6 says, “Elokim ascends with the teruah; Hashem with the sound of the shofar.” Yalkut Shimoni on Tehillim §754 explains: when the Holy One sits upon the throne of judgment, He is called Elokim; when Israel sounds the shofar, He rises from the throne of judgment and sits upon the throne of mercy, as indicated by the Divine Name of mercy in the second half of the verse. The change does not imply change in Hashem Himself, God forbid. It describes the mode through which His unchanging will is manifested toward the world. Rav Tzadok connects the transition to the shofar’s revelation of Israel’s inward truth: once the hidden desire to return is sounded, judgment itself can agree that the person is not exhausted by the visible record of failure and that mercy should guide the process of repair.

paragraphs.text: The heart beneath the visible appearance — I Shmuel 16:7 teaches, “Man sees what is visible to the eyes, but Hashem sees into the heart.” In context, Shmuel was impressed by Eliav’s outward appearance, while Hashem disclosed that kingship depended upon the hidden heart. Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 7:7, cites the verse to distinguish human judgment, which must proceed from available evidence, from Divine knowledge of inward truth. Rav Tzadok does not mean that revealed deeds are irrelevant; throughout his writings, teshuvah requires their repair. His point is that Rosh Hashanah judgment includes a dimension inaccessible to any created court: Hashem sees whether the sins express the soul’s final desire or are foreign garments covering a will that remains directed toward Him. The shofar gives voice to that hidden heart, allowing mercy to address the person according to the root from which return can grow.

paragraphs.text: Shaar HaKavvanot, Derushei Rosh HaShanah, end of the introduction, records R. Moshe Galanti’s report of the Arizal’s practice: each of the seven weekdays between Rosh HaShanah and Yom Kippur corresponds to that weekday throughout the preceding year and is an opportunity for focused teshuvah. The reported kabbalistic practice includes personal fasting, but this is not a general obligation to fast. It illuminates Rav Tzadok’s “כל יום יומו,” the correction of each corresponding day.

paragraphs.text: “Wisdom is found from ayin” — Iyov 28:12 asks, “And wisdom, from where me-ayin is it found, and where is the place of understanding?” On the level of peshat, the verse emphasizes that the source of wisdom is hidden from ordinary human discovery. Kabbalistic interpretation reads ayin as the concealed level above articulated Chochmah, often associated with Keser: wisdom flashes into consciousness from a source that the thinker cannot yet grasp as a defined “something.” Chazal also read the verse ethically — Sotah 21b says Torah endures in one who makes himself “as nothing.” Rav Tzadok uses both resonances. Rosh Hashanah repairs the head and the primordial point of thought: Chochmah as the first knowable flash, and Keser as its unknowable birthplace. Teshuvah therefore begins not only by correcting particular ideas, but by returning the faculty of thought to the Divine ayin from which a new and truthful beginning can emerge.

paragraphs.text: Binah, the heart, and teshuvah — Yeshayah 6:10 joins the stages: “his heart understands, and he returns, and he is healed.” Megillah 17b cites this verse to explain why the blessing of teshuvah follows the blessing of understanding in the Amidah: understanding opens the path to return. Rosh Hashanah 17b derives from the same verse that teshuvah tears up a decree; the continuing discussion distinguishes the individual’s deadline from the community’s continuing power of return. In biblical and rabbinic usage, the heart is not merely the seat of emotion; it is the inward faculty that integrates knowledge into lived recognition. Rav Tzadok therefore associates Yom Kippur with Binah of the heart. The flash of awakening that began at Rosh Hashanah becomes comprehended, absorbed, and transformed into loving return. Healing is the final word of the verse because true Binah does not remain abstract: it reunites the divided person and restores the deeds and middos to their source.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III, Acharei Mos 69b (Zohar, Achrei Mot 40:237) locates Yom Kippur’s joy, illumination, and the sweetening of judgments in the “supernal Mother,” the source from which its streams flow. That is the direct background to R’ Tzadok’s association of Yom Kippur with Binah and higher repentance. The lower/higher repentance distinction also appears in Zohar, Nasso 4:47, where lower repentance is called heh. Here R’ Tzadok describes a beginning from fear at Rosh Hashanah and completion through love at Yom Kippur; his precise day-structure assigns Rosh Hashanah to Keser and Chochmah, and Yom Kippur to Binah. The correspondence concerns both repentance’s quality and the hidden roots repaired by these days.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The time of teshuvah for all is the Ten Days of Teshuvah, when [Hashem] is called “found.” Near to every individual — for then, in particular, He rouses every Jew in the chambers of his heart to return. The beginning is the sound of the shofar on Rosh Hashanah: on its plain level, as the Rambam wrote, “Awake, sleepers, from your slumber” — teshuvah from fear (the whole beginning of teshuvah that comes from man’s side).

And the Shabbos in between,
נִקְרָא שַׁבַּת תְּשׁוּבָה
is called Shabbos Teshuvah,
שֶׁבֹּו מַפְטִירִין "שׁוּבָה יִשְׂרָאֵל",
on which we read as haftarah “Shuvah Yisrael,”
שֶׁהוּא הִתְעוֹרְרוּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה
which is the arousal of repentance
בִּלְבָבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
in the hearts of the children of Israel
עַל יְדֵי קְרִיאַת דִּבְרֵי הַנְּבִיאִים

who warn about it.

and draws his spirit to himself, as is known.
וּבְשַׁבָּת זֶה בְּיוֹתֵר
and on this Shabbos especially.

שֶׁמִּצַּד הָאָדָם
from the human side.

בְּכָל הַלְּבָבוֹת

And although the Bas Kol that arouses to repentance

goes out every day,
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בַּעֲשֶׂרֶת יְמֵי תְּשׁוּבָה

and all the more so on Shabbos,

and all the more so on Yom Kippur,
לֹא הִגִּיעַ עֲדַיִן שְׁעַת אִתְעָרוּתָא
the hour of arousal had not yet arrived
לְלֵב "אַחֵר"
for the heart of “Acher”
שֶׁנִּדְחָה כָּל כָּךְ
who was rejected so much,
עַד יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים שֶׁחָל בְּשַׁבָּת

and even this

for the place also causes

some holiness to enter the heart.

came to him by way of the rejecting left,

as mentioned above,

paragraphs.text: Shabbos Shuvah and its haftarah — Hoshea 14:2-3 begins, “Return, O Israel, unto Hashem your God, for you have stumbled through your iniquity; take words with you and return unto Hashem.” Rambam, Hilchos Tefillah 13:19, records that on the Shabbos between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur the haftarah is “Shuvah Yisrael.” Beis Yosef, Orach Chaim 428, treats this as the fixed practice and notes that the halachic sources themselves call the day Shabbos Shuvah. The reading is therefore not merely a name for the Shabbos. The prophet supplies the congregation with the very words of return — recognition of stumbling, confession, prayer, and trust in Divine healing. Rav Tzadok emphasizes the performative effect of sacred reading: the prophetic call heard publicly becomes an awakening within the Jewish heart.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos as return to the source — Beitzah 16a teaches that an additional soul is granted on the eve of Shabbos and departs after Shabbos, reading “Shavas va-yinafash” as the soul’s expanded life and subsequent withdrawal. Kabbalistic and chassidic literature describes Shabbos as “the ascent of the worlds”: their inward life rises from weekday dispersion and action toward its source. Rav Tzadok develops this directly in Resisei Layla §27 and §42, and in Peri Tzadik, Sefer Kedushas Shabbos 1:8, where the ascent enables the soul to unite with the source of its vitality. Takanas HaShavin 15:51 interprets “va-yinafash” as a person drawing breath and spirit inward and explicitly identifies this with the worlds’ return to their root. Thus Shabbos is intrinsically related to teshuvah: both are forms of hashavah, restoring what had spread outward to the place from which its true life comes.

paragraphs.text: “Shabbos Shabbason” — Vayikra 16:31 calls Yom Kippur “a Shabbos of complete rest,” immediately after the promise, “On this day He shall atone for you, to purify you.” The designation is repeated in Vayikra 23:32 together with the command of affliction. The doubled expression marks a cessation deeper than ordinary weekday rest: work ceases, bodily self-assertion is subdued, and the person stands before Hashem for purification. Rav Tzadok reads this doubling in the language of the Divine Name. Ordinary Shabbos restores the revealed order to its source; Yom Kippur reaches the more concealed root of understanding and inward return. When both sanctities coincide, the two movements of return are intensified together.

paragraphs.text: The two hehs and two levels of teshuvah — Zohar III 122a (Raaya Mehemna; Nasso 4:28–29) associates teshuvah with Binah and confession with Malchus, and reads teshuvah as tashuv heh, the return of the heh to the vav and the restoration of the Divine Name. Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah ch. 4, explicitly distinguishes the return of the lower heh, teshuvah tataah, from that of the upper heh, teshuvah ilaah. It explains the first heh as expanded inward understanding and the final heh as Malchus and Divine speech. The lower return repairs the person’s revealed life and submission; the higher return restores inward understanding, love, and union at their source. Rav Tzadok applies this kabbalistic structure to sacred time: the ordinary Shabbos is associated with the final heh and the return of the revealed worlds, while Yom Kippur is associated with the first heh, the concealed mother-source from which a new spirit of purity descends.

paragraphs.text: The printed author text cites Menachos 109b; the passage paraphrased here is at Menachos 29b. Menachos 29b reads Yeshayah 26:4 as teaching that this world was created with a heh and the World to Come with a yud. The heh resembles a portico: whoever wishes may leave. Its detached leg provides a further opening through which a penitent can be admitted. Why not return through the broad opening below? The Gemara answers that return requires assistance, citing Reish Lakish: one who comes to purify himself is assisted. It then asks about the letter’s crown: Hashem promises to bind a crown for the one who returns. The detached leg and the upper opening are therefore one feature, not two successive openings in the Gemara’s argument. R’ Tzadok applies the image of the two hehs homiletically: the lower heh corresponds to Shabbos and teshuvah from fear, and the upper heh to Yom Kippur and the higher teshuvah from Hashem’s side.

paragraphs.text: “Return to Me, and I will return to you” — Malachi 3:7 presents teshuvah as a reciprocal movement. Human beings first turn from estrangement toward Hashem; Hashem’s “return” then means a renewed revelation of closeness and assistance. Yechezkel 36:25-27 describes that Divine side of the process: “I will sprinkle pure water upon you,” give a new heart and a new spirit, and place My spirit within you so that you walk in My statutes. This is not a replacement for human choice, but the response that enables a partial awakening to become deep and enduring. Rav Tzadok calls the first movement teshuvah from man’s side and the second the higher teshuvah “from Hashem’s side”: after the lower opening, a spirit of purity is aroused within the hearts of Israel.

paragraphs.text: “Before Hashem you shall be purified” — Vayikra 16:30 is expounded in Mishnah Yoma 8:9 and Yoma 85b. R’ Elazar ben Azaryah derives that Yom Kippur atones for sins between man and Hashem, whereas interpersonal wrongs require appeasing the injured person. R’ Akiva then declares: “Fortunate are you, Israel! Before Whom are you purified, and Who purifies you? Your Father in Heaven,” comparing Hashem to a mikveh that purifies the impure. The verse therefore has two complementary meanings. One must enter honestly “before Hashem,” including repairing obligations to others; yet the ultimate purifying power is Hashem Himself. Rav Tzadok hears in R’ Akiva’s formulation the higher teshuvah: Israel turns toward purification, and the Father in Heaven awakens and completes it from Above.

paragraphs.text: The Kohen Gadol “within the innermost” — Vayikra 16:2 limits entry beyond the paroches, and Vayikra 16:12-17 prescribes the Kohen Gadol’s unique Yom Kippur service there with incense and blood. The chapter concludes that he atones for the innermost sanctuary, the Tent of Meeting, the altar, the kohanim, and “all the people of the congregation” (16:33-34). Mishnah Yoma 5:1 describes his entry into the Holy of Holies with the incense pan and the cloud of ketores. Chazal call this place lifnai ve-lifnim, “within the innermost,” because it lies beyond the ordinary modes of access and representation. Rav Tzadok connects the bat kol’s emergence from there with its content: the innermost sanctuary is the site where the hidden bond of all Israel is represented and where atonement reaches beneath the visible record of sin to the covenantal root.

paragraphs.text: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah §14:3): R’ Levi teaches that teshuvah reaches the Throne of Glory, citing “Return, O Israel, unto Hashem your God.” Rav Tzadok then reports Rabbeinu Chananel’s explanation: even if one has committed sins whose damage reaches the Throne of Glory, teshuvah is effective for them. He applies this to faults reaching the mind and the root of the neshamah, and goes on to distinguish individual from communal return and the assistance of Torah and prayer. The parallel thus illuminates the present passage’s inward purification: higher teshuvah reaches even the hidden root injured by sin; it does not merely repeat that the penitent ascends to a high place.

paragraphs.text: Atonement joined to inward teshuvah and love — Mishnah Yoma 8:8 teaches that death and Yom Kippur atone together with teshuvah, while Yoma 85b discusses the scope of Yom Kippur’s independent power. Yoma 86b distinguishes teshuvah from fear, through which intentional sins become like errors, from teshuvah from love, through which intentional sins can become merits. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:6-7, describes this higher return as restoring closeness: the person who had been distant becomes beloved, desired, near, and a friend. Rav Tzadok’s “depths of the heart” therefore means more than emotional intensity. It is the revelation that the soul’s deepest will belongs to Hashem, followed by a loving redirection of the very powers that had been misused. Yom Kippur’s pardon becomes fully manifest when the day’s Divine purification awakens that genuine inner return.

paragraphs.text: Acher on Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbos — The precise source is Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1 (9b). Elisha ben Avuyah told R’ Meir that he once rode before the Holy of Holies on Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbos and heard a bas kol emerge from the Holy of Holies: “Return, wayward children — except Elisha ben Avuyah, who knew My power and rebelled against Me.” The Bavli, Chagigah 15a, records the general statement “Return, wayward children, except Acher,” but does not include the Yerushalmi’s distinctive conjunction of Yom Kippur, Shabbos, and the Holy of Holies. The Yerushalmi reads לפני בית קודש הקדשים (before the Holy of Holies), whereas Rav Tzadok’s Hebrew here reads אחורי בית קדשי הקדשים (behind the Holy of Holies); the textual witnesses are left distinct. Rav Tzadok highlights the conjunction of sacred day and place. At the strongest convergence of sacred time and sacred place, even the person who believed himself excluded heard the call of return. The tragedy was not that no call reached him, but that he interpreted the warning as an absolute closing of the gate rather than as the very pressure calling him to break through despair.

paragraphs.text: Hashem receives those who return — Tehillim 90:3 says, “You return man unto crushing, and say: Return, children of man.” Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1 applies this verse directly to Acher’s final illness. When he asked R’ Meir whether a penitent is accepted, R’ Meir answered that a person is received “until the crushing of the soul”; Acher then wept and died, and R’ Meir understood that his teacher had departed through teshuvah. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:4-7, rules that a baal teshuvah must never imagine himself permanently distant: he is beloved and desired before the Creator, and teshuvah brings near those who had been far removed. Rav Tzadok therefore treats even repentance awakened by mortal suffering as genuine return, though the degree of its inwardness determines what further atonement is needed.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The Shabbos between is called “Shabbos Teshuvah,” when we read [the haftarah] “Return, O Israel” — the arousal of teshuvah in Jewish hearts through the reading of the prophets’ words that warn of it. For Shabbos is always a time of teshuvah, the time of the worlds’ return to their place, as a man restoring his soul and drawing his spirit back into himself — and this Shabbos especially. And Yom Kippur, called “Shabbos Shabbason,” is the “first heh” of the Name — whereas every [ordinary] Shabbos is the “lower heh.”

p: (יד) אַף עַל גַּב דְּאֵין מִיָּדִי מַצִּיל כָּתִיב
Even though “there is none to deliver from My hand” is written,
וְלֹא אַבְרָהָם מַצִּיל יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ
and Avraham cannot save Yishmael his son,
כְּדִאיתָא (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין ק״ד עַמּוּד א׳)
as stated (Sanhedrin 104a),
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא אוֹהֲבוֹ
and even though he loves him
וְרוֹצֶה לְהֵטִיב לוֹ
and wishes to benefit him,
אֵין יָכוֹל בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא
he cannot in the World to Come,
דְּלֹא כְּהָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
for unlike this world,
הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
the World to Come
שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד נוֹטֵל חֶלְקוֹ הָרָאוּי לוֹ.
is where each one takes his own fitting portion.
וְאִלּוּ "אַחֵר" לֹא שָׁב כְּלָל
And had “Acher” not repented at all,
עַד שֶׁבַּמִּשְׁפָּט
so that in judgment
הָיָה אוֹבֵד כָּל חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁלּוֹ
he would lose his whole portion in the World to Come,
וַדַּאי הֵם לֹא יָכְלוּ לַעֲשוֹת לוֹ כָּלוּם
surely they could do nothing for him;
רַק שֶׁשָּׁב מִתּוֹךְ יִסּוּרֵי מִיתָה
but since he repented amid the pains of death,
בָּזֶה אָמְרוּ
in this they said, ".
אֶחָד מִעִיר וּשְׁנַיִם מִמִּשְׁפָּחָה" מַצִּילִין כֻּלָּם
“one from a city and two from a family” save all.
כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְקַבֵּל שָׁבִים
For the Blessed Name accepts those who return,
לְעוֹלָם כָּל שֶׁשָּׁב וְמִתְחָרֵט
always, whoever returns and regrets,
דְּאַף דְּנַעֲשָׂה רַק כִּשְׁגָגוֹת
even though it was done only as if inadvertently,
דְּצָרִיךְ עֲדַיִן כַּפָּרָה
so that it still requires atonement,
דִּי לוֹ בְּדָבָר מוּעָט לְכַפָּרָה
a small thing suffices for atonement.
כְּקָרְבָּן
like a sacrifice.
וְכֵן תַּעֲנִית דְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים
And so the fast of Yom Kippur,
שֶׁבָּא עַל זֶה לְכַפֵּר
which comes for this, to atone,
אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה כִּשְׁגָגָה
after the repentance that was made as an inadvertent sin,
דְּמִעוּט חֶלְבוֹ וְדָמוֹ
for the diminishing of his fat and blood
נֶחְשָׁב כְּקָרְבָּן
is counted as a sacrifice,
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן הַמִּיתָה
and all the more so death,
שֶׁנִּשְׁפַךְ דָּמוֹ לְגַמְרֵי
where his blood is spilled entirely.
דְּמְכַפֶּרֶת עַל זֶה
which atones for this.
וְרַק שֶׁמִּדַּת הַדִּין מְקַטְרֶגֶת
But the attribute of judgment accuses,
נֶגֶּד הַיוֹדֵעַ רִבּוֹנוֹ וְמוֹרֵד
one who knows his Master and rebels,
דְּהָא דְּנֶחְשָׁב כִּשְׁגָגָה אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה
for that it is counted as inadvertent after repentance
הוּא לְפִי שֶׁהַחֵטְא הָיָה
is because the sin was
רַק עַל יְדֵי רוּחַ שְׁטוּת שֶׁהִתְעָהוּ וְהֶעֱלִים מִמֶּנּוּ
only through a spirit of folly that misled him and concealed from him
יְדִיעַת רִבּוֹנוֹ
knowledge of his Master,
בְּאוֹתָה שָׁעָה וָעִידָן דְּיֵצֶר הָרָע
at that hour and time of the evil inclination;
אֲבָל זֶה שֶׁיוֹדֵעַ וְמוֹרֵד
but this one, who knows and rebels,
יֵשׁ מָקוֹם לִטְעֹן נֶגְדּוֹ
there is room to argue against him
שֶׁלֹּא יֵחָשֵׁב לִשְׁוֹגֵג עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה
that he not be counted as inadvertent through repentance
כָּל שֶׁלֹּא הִגִּיעַ לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
so long as he did not reach repentance from love.
שֶׁיֵּחָשְׁבוּ לִזְכִיּוֹת
by which sins are counted as merits.
וְעַל זֶה הוֹעִילוּ
And in this they helped,
רַבִּי מֵאִיר וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yochanan,
שֶׁעוֹרְרוּ מִדַּת הַדִּין
who aroused the attribute of judgment,
בְּשָׁעַת פְּטִירָתָן
at the time of their passing,
דְּיָדוּעַ
for it is known
דְּבִיוֹמֵי דְהִילּוּלָא דְצַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים כָּאֵלּוּ
that on the hillula days of such complete tzaddikim,
יֵשׁ שִׂמְחָה גְּדוֹלָה בָּעוֹלָמוֹת עֶלְיוֹנִים
there is great joy in the upper worlds,
וּמֵרוֹב הַשִּׂמְחָה
and from the abundance of joy
בְּטֵלִים כָּל הַמְקַטְרְגִים
all the accusers are nullified,
וְאֵין שָׂטָן וְאֵין פֶּגַע רָע
and there is no Satan and no evil mishap,
וְהָרַחֲמִים גוֹבְרִים
and mercy prevails;
וְאָז יְכוֹלִים לְהַעֲלוֹת
and then they can raise
כַּמָּה נְשָׁמוֹת הַדְּחוּיוֹת
many rejected souls
מִפְּנֵי קִטְרוּג
because of accusation,
וּמִדַּת הַדִּין שֶׁגָּבְרָה עֲלֵיהֶם
and the attribute of judgment that overpowered them,
וְעַל כֵּן יָכְלוּ לְזַכּוֹתוֹ.
and therefore they were able to merit him.
וְלֹא שֶׁבְּכֹחָם הִצִּילוּהוּ,
And it is not that by their own power they saved him,
רַק שֶׁפָּעֲלוּ
but that they brought about
דְּנִתְקַבְּלָה תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ
that his repentance was accepted
בְּכֹחַ הָרַחֲמִים רַבִּים
by the power of the abundant mercies
שֶׁנִּתְרַבּוּ בָּעוֹלָמוֹת עֶלְיוֹנִים
that increased in the upper worlds.
עַל יְדֵיהֶם
through them.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 104a explains why Amon was omitted from the list of kings excluded from the World to Come: his son Yoshiyahu’s merit benefited him. Menashe, however, was not exempted through his father Chizkiyahu. The rule is: a son can benefit his father, but a father does not benefit his son. The Gemara cites Devarim 32:39, “there is none that can deliver from My hand”: Avraham cannot deliver Yishmael, nor Yitzchak Esav. The verse “He has no son nor grandson among his people, and no remnant in his dwellings” (Iyov 18:19) occurs instead in Chagigah 15b, when Acher’s daughter appears before Rebbe; her appeal to her father’s Torah then draws a vindicating sign. These passages must not be joined into a reversed rule of inherited merit. R’ Tzadok’s present qualification is that Acher’s deliverers could act only because he himself had begun to repent under the sufferings of death; they did not create a portion in Olam Haba for someone who had never returned.

paragraphs.text: “One from a city and two from a family” — Yirmiyahu 3:14 promises, “I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and bring you to Tziyon.” Sanhedrin 111a records two readings. Reish Lakish initially takes the verse literally, while R’ Yochanan insists that “one from a city merits the entire city, and two from a family merit the entire family”; Rav gives the same response to Rav Kahana. Yoma 86a places this verse in the laws of teshuvah and distinguishes a return arising from love or fear from a return forced through suffering. Rav Tzadok combines the sugyos: Acher’s own deathbed return created the opening, while the merit of the two great sages could then carry and elevate one who had already begun to return. Their merit did not manufacture a share in Olam Haba for someone wholly detached from it; it activated the communal power Chazal locate in “one” and “two.”

paragraphs.text: Fasting as a korban — Berachos 17a records Rav Sheshes’s prayer after a fast. When the Beis HaMikdash stood, a sinner brought a korban whose fat and blood were offered and he was atoned; now, through fasting, “my fat and blood have diminished,” and Rav Sheshes asks that this diminution be regarded as though offered upon the mizbeiach. Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah ch. 2, cites this passage to explain that in the absence of an offering, a properly directed fast can serve as the gift brought after teshuvah to restore favor. Rav Tzadok applies the same imagery specifically to the Yom Kippur fast: the bodily diminution does not replace teshuvah, but functions as its sacrificial completion after the willful sin has already been reclassified through return.

paragraphs.text: Death as the completion of atonement — Mishnah Yoma 8:8 teaches that death and Yom Kippur atone together with teshuvah. Yoma 86a sets out the “divisions of atonement”: some sins are forgiven immediately through teshuvah, others require Yom Kippur, more severe sins require suffering, and desecration of the Divine Name is held in suspension until death completes the cleansing. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4, codifies this structure and states that for chillul Hashem, teshuvah, Yom Kippur, and suffering suspend the judgment, while death brings the final atonement. Rav Tzadok’s comparison of death to the complete pouring out of blood is therefore not a claim that death automatically saves without repentance. It is the final meruk, the complete cleansing, once a real movement of teshuvah has already begun.

paragraphs.text: The “spirit of folly” — Sotah 3a states: “A person commits a transgression only if a spirit of folly enters him,” deriving shetus from the Torah’s spelling of tisteh. The teaching does not remove responsibility; it explains how a person who truly knows Hashem can act against that knowledge. At the moment of sin, desire creates a temporary concealment in which the consequence and the person’s deeper allegiance are no longer fully present to consciousness. Berachos 17a expresses the same structure in the prayer, “Our will is to do Your will; what prevents us? The yeast in the dough and the subjugation of the kingdoms.” Rav Tzadok uses this to explain why ordinary teshuvah from fear can reduce a deliberate sin to the category of inadvertence: the return uncovers that the act was produced by a distorting spirit rather than by the soul’s deepest will. Acher, however, was described as one who “knew My power and rebelled,” so the Attribute of Justice could argue that his case required a deeper answer.

paragraphs.text: Cf. Siman 11 §1 and §3 (in this volume). Teshuvah from fear uproots the earlier evil intention, so that willful sins become inadvertent ones: a deed remains, but without the prior intention and desire for evil. Siman 11 §3 carefully reads “the iniquity of Israel shall be sought and there shall be none” as the removal of deliberate evil through this first return; the continuation, “the sins of Yehudah shall not be found,” describes the remaining deed healed and transformed into merit through love. The present paragraph adds the particular objection against the knowing rebel: the Attribute of Judgment can contest treating his deliberate rebellion as mere folly until a deeper return from love answers that accusation.

paragraphs.text: R’ Meir and R’ Yochanan on behalf of Acher — Chagigah 15b relates that after Acher died, the Heavenly Court said that he should neither be judged nor enter Olam Haba: his Torah shielded him from judgment, but his sins barred his entry. R’ Meir declared that it was better for him to be judged and afterward enter Olam Haba; when R’ Meir died, smoke rose from Acher’s grave. R’ Yochanan then objected: “There was one among us and we cannot save him? If I take him by the hand, who can remove him?” He said that when he died he would extinguish the smoke, and at his passing the smoke ceased. The Gemara describes the effect of their passing; Rav Tzadok explains its mechanism. Their intervention could operate because Acher’s own final tears constituted a beginning of teshuvah, allowing their merit to shift the case from absolute exclusion toward judgment, cleansing, and eventual restoration.

paragraphs.text: The hilula of a tzaddik — In its ordinary Aramaic usage, hilula means a wedding celebration. Kabbalistic and chassidic sources use the term for the passing of a perfected tzaddik because the life’s avodah reaches its bond and culmination Above. The Idra Zuta, Zohar III 287b-296b, depicts the final day of R’ Shimon bar Yochai as an overwhelming revelation of Torah and attachment rather than merely a moment of loss. Rav Tzadok, Peri Tzadik, Lag BaOmer §1, explains that R’ Shimon’s day of passing is called his hilula because the Torah he revealed was then received and fixed in the hearts of Israel of his generation. Thus Rav Tzadok’s language here is not a general denial of mourning. It identifies the death of a wholly righteous person as a moment when the completed Torah and avodah of that soul become newly active in the upper and lower worlds.

It identifies the death of a wholly righteous person as a moment when the completed Torah and avodah of that soul become newly active in the upper and lower worlds.

paragraphs.text: “There is no Satan and no evil mishap” — The phrase comes from I Melachim 5:18, where Shlomo describes the state of rest surrounding the building of the Beis HaMikdash. Shemos Rabbah 15:26 places Shlomo’s absence of an adversary alongside comparisons of his throne and Hashem’s throne, and describes the Avos praying for Israel during generations of diminished light. Zohar, Emor 25:126, similarly calls Shabbos the “day of the King’s hilula,” when distress, wrath, and pressure are forgotten from the world. Rav Tzadok applies this pattern to the hilula of a complete tzaddik. The abundance of revealed joy and union does not erase justice; it removes the dominance of prosecution, allowing the deeper Divine will of mercy and restoration to be heard. In that opening, souls whose ascent had been obstructed by accusation can be reconsidered and raised.
