inlineHeadings.text: The theme: R’ Tzadok saw in the Asarah Maamaros (Rema mi-Fano, Maamar Chakor Din I, end of ch. 18) that all “negatives for which one is not lashed” are like a positive commandment in this. [That they are] atoned by teshuvah alone: a lav she-bichlalus, one derived from a positive, one with no action, one nitak la-aseh, and one given over to payment where he fulfilled the positive or paid. And though an olah also effects their atonement, “here we deal with atonement that comes of itself.”

p: (ח) וּמָצָאתִי בְּסֵפֶר מִשְׁנַת חֲכָמִים (סִימָן ב אוֹת ו)
And I found in the book Mishnas Chachamim (siman 2, letter 6),
בְּשֵׁם אָבִיו
in the name of his father,
הִרְגִּישׁ מֵהָא דְּעוֹלָה דוֹרוֹן
he sensed a difficulty from that an olah is a gift,
וּמְכַפֵּר אַהַנִּתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה
and yet atones for the one severable by a positive.
דְּגַם נִתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה דַּי בִּתְשׁוּבָה
since even for one severable by a positive repentance suffices.
וְהוּא דָּחָה זֶה
And he rejected this,
דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר בְּסְתָם עוֹלָה קָאָמַר
for one can say it speaks of an unspecified olah,
דְּהוּא עַל חַיָּבֵי עֲשֵׂה
which is for those liable for a positive.
הַמָּצוּי בְּכָל יוֹם בְּכָל אָדָם
which is common every day in every person.
אֲבָל הֵבִיא רְאָיָה מִכָּל מָקוֹם
But he brought proof nevertheless,
מֵהָא דְּחַיָּבֵי עֲשֵׂה מְמַשְׁכְּנִין
from that those liable for a positive are seized for collateral,
וּבְ
and in Tosafos (Rosh Hashanah 6a)
סוֹף דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "יַקְרִיב"
at the end of the passage beginning “yakriv”,
הַטַּעַם דְּמִתְכַּפֵּר בִּתְשׁוּבָה
the reason is that he is atoned by repentance,
וְקָפָסִיק וְתָנֵי "כָּל חַיָּבֵי עֲשֵׂה"
and it states categorically “all those liable for a positive”,
אַף אַהַנִּתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה
even regarding the one severable by a positive.
יַעֲיֵּן שָׁם
see there.
וְאֵינוֹ מֻכְרָח
But it is not necessary,
דְּהָא עוֹלָה לָאו חוֹבָה הִיא
for an olah is not an obligation,
וְ
and Rashi (Arachin 21a).
כָּתַב דְּמֵהַאי טַעְמָא מְמַשְׁכְּנִין
wrote that for this reason they are seized.
וְנֶהִי דְּתוֹסָפוֹת לָא נְהִירָא לְהוּ זֶה
And although this does not seem right to Tosafos,
דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אִי מְכַפֵּר לָא פָשַׁע
since in any case, if the offering brings atonement, he will not neglect bringing it,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם זֶה אֱמֶת דְּאֵינוֹ חוֹבָה
nevertheless this is true, that it is not an obligation,
דְּהָא לָא כְּתִיב קְרָא לְחִיּוּבָא
for the verse does not write it as an obligation,
עַל הָעוֹבֵר לְהָבִיא
upon the transgressor to bring.
אֶלָּא דְּאִי מֵבִיא מִתְכַּפֵּר
but that if he brings, he is atoned.
וּלְפִי זֶה גַּם אִי לָאו הַנִּתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה
And according to this, even if a prohibition severable by a positive,
צָרִיךְ לְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים לְכַפֵּר
needs Yom Kippur to atone,
יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים מִיהַת גוֹמֵר כַּפָּרָתוֹ,
Yom Kippur at least completes his atonement.
וְאַחַר יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים מִיהַת אֵין צָרִיךְ מִידִי
and after Yom Kippur at least he needs nothing.
וְלָא דָּמֵי לְחַיָּבֵי חַטָּאוֹת וַאֲשָׁמוֹת
And it is not like those liable for chataos and ashamos,
דְּאֻמְעַט (בִּכְרִיתוֹת כ״ה עַמּוּד ב׳)
for it is excluded (in Kerisos 25b):
"חַטָּאים דְּבַר קָרְבָּן",
“sinners who have a sacrifice,”,
דְּזֶהוּ בְּקָרְבָּן חוֹבָה דְּחַטָּאוֹת וַאֲשָׁמוֹת
which refers to an obligatory sacrifice of chataos and ashamos,
אֲבָל עוֹלָה דְּאֵינוֹ חוֹבָה
but an olah, which is not an obligation,
לָא מִקְרֵי "חַטָּא בַּר קָרְבָּן"
is not called “a sinner who has a sacrifice”,
לְהַצְרִיכוֹ לְכַפָּרָתוֹ אַחַר יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים
so as to make him need it for his atonement after Yom Kippur,
וְשַׁפִּיר חָיְישִׁינַן דְּפָשַׁע
and we properly worry that he may neglect it.
וּמַמְתִּין עַד אַחַר יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים לְהִתְכַּפֵּר
and waits until after Yom Kippur to be atoned.
וְתוֹסָפוֹת דְּנָקְטִי "לֹא זָז" וְכוּלֵּי
And the Tosafos that cite “he does not move,” etc.
הַיְנוּ בְּסְתָם עוֹלָה דְּאַעֲשֵׂה
mean an unspecified olah for a positive,
וְאֵין הָכִי נָמֵי דְּאַהַנִּתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה
and indeed regarding the one severable by a positive,
חָיְישִׁינַן דְּיַמְתִּין עַל יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים
we worry he will wait for Yom Kippur,
וְלָכֵן עֲדַיִן דָּבָר זֶה צָרִיךְ יִשּׁוּב וְהֶכְרֵעַ.
and therefore this matter still needs resolution and decision.

paragraphs.text: Rav Tzadok, Pri Tzaddik, Ki Tavo §8: "כל המביא דורון לת"ח כאלו מקריב ביכורים" — one who presents a gift to a Torah scholar is regarded as bringing bikkurim. He explains: "דאכילת ת"ח כקרבנות שהת"ח חשיב כמזבח" — a Torah scholar’s eating is likened to offerings because the scholar is likened to the altar. This is an illustrative parallel for a doron as an expression of closeness, not proof that an olah for a lav ha-nitak la-aseh lacks a distinct atoning role. The latter question remains open in Rav Tzadok’s concluding sentence.

paragraphs.text: Sefer Mishnas Chachamim §2, letter ו — background and argument: This work on the 613 mitzvos was composed by R. Yosef Hochgelernter, son of R. Yaakov Yitzchak, and is arranged with the analytical divisions Yavin Shemuah and Tzafnas Paneach. R’ Tzadok quotes a teaching recorded in the father’s name: if Zevachim 7b calls the olah a doron, yet an olah also addresses a lav ha-nitak la-aseh, teshuvah must already have completed its essential kapparah. The author limits “doron” to the ordinary olah for neglect of an aseh; R’ Tzadok then tests that distinction through the coercion passages in Rosh Hashanah and Arachin.

paragraphs.text: Rosh Hashanah 6a: “‘he shall bring it’ (Vayikra 1:3) — teaches that they compel him to bring his offering”; the discussion concerns a voluntary olah. Tosafos (s.v. yakriv): “for every positive commandment too they compel performance, as it says in the chapter Naarah she-Nispatesah (Kesubos 49b). And if you ask: regarding that which we learned in the chapter ha-Omer Mishkali (Arachin 21a), ‘those liable for chataos and ashamos are not distrained, but those liable for olos and shelamim are distrained in order to compel them to bring.’ And if you ask: and for olos, why does he need distraint more than for chataos and ashamos, seeing that in the first chapter of Zevachim (6a) it says that olos too atone for those liable for a positive commandment? One may answer: since we say elsewhere (Yoma 86a) that if he did teshuvah he does not stir from there until they forgive him, he is already atoned by teshuvah — and it is not like chataos and ashamos.”

paragraphs.text: Vayikra 1:3; Arachin 21a; Rashi; Rambam, Hilchos Maaseh HaKorbanos 14:1, 17: An ordinary olah may begin as a neder or nedavah; once undertaken, beis din may distrain and compel the owner until he says “I desire.” Rashi contrasts this with chataos and ashamos, for which no distraint is needed because their owners require them for kapparah. This sharpens R’ Tzadok’s distinction: the sin itself does not create a compulsory olah-debt; the obligation arises only after the person vows or designates it. Thus coercion cannot prove that teshuvah alone fully atones for every lav ha-nitak la-aseh.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86a; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4; Kerisus 25b: The fourfold atonement framework distinguishes a regular lav, for which teshuvah suspends and Yom Kippur atones, from sins requiring further cleansing. Obligatory chataos and definite ashamos remain due even after Yom Kippur because they are “sins subject to a korban.” R’ Tzadok contrasts that continuing sacrificial debt with a voluntary olah: once the relevant completion of kapparah has occurred, the olah is not still owed as a compulsory korban, so one may suspect that the sinner will delay and rely upon Yom Kippur instead of bringing it.

items.h: סִימָן יד
Teshuvah for neglected positive commandments
תשובה על ביטול מצוות עשה

p: וְלָשׁוֹן ״אֵינוֹ זָז מִשָּׁם״ וְכוּלֵיהּ, שֶׁדִּקְדֵּק בּוֹ בְּ״תוֹסְפוֹת יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים״ בְּשֵׁם מוֹרֵנוּ הָרַב רַבִּי יוֹסֵף טְרָאנִי עַיֵּין שָׁם
And the expression "he does not move from there," etc., which was analyzed carefully in Tosefos Yom HaKippurim in the name of the Maharit, see there;

יֵשׁ לוֹמַר לְפִי דַּעַת רַבֵּנוּ מֹשֶׁה בֶּן מַיְמוֹן וְכָל הַמְפָרְשִׁים בְּהָא דְּ״הֵיכִי דָּמֵי בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה״ וְכוּלֵיהּ ״שֶׁבָּאת״ וְכוּלֵיהּ ״בְּאוֹתָהּ״ וְכוּלֵיהּ כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ דִּתְשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה מֵהַמּוּבְחָר צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת דַּוְוקָא שֶׁבָּאת וְכוּלֵיהּ

one can say, according to the opinion of the Rambam and all the commentators regarding the Talmudic statement, "What is the case of a penitent?", etc., "that it comes to him," etc., "with that same woman," etc., according to its plain meaning that a complete and choice repentance requires specifically that it comes to his hand again, etc.

נִרְאֶה דְּזֶהוּ רַק בְּעוֹבֵר עַל לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ״שֶׁבָּאת דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה לְיָדוֹ וְנִיצּוֹל״, דְּלֹא כָּל שַׁעְתָּא מִתְרַחֵשׁ דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה לְפָנָיו וּבְאוֹתוֹ הַגָּווֶן וְהָעִנְיָן שֶׁעָבַר

It appears that this applies only to one who transgressed a negative commandment, as it says, "an opportunity to sin came to him and he resisted," for an opportunity to commit that sin does not present itself at every moment in the same manner and circumstances in which he previously transgressed.
וְגַם צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת אוֹתָהּ עֲבֵירָה עַצְמָהּ דַּוְוקָא שֶׁכְּבָר טָעַם טַעַם אִיסּוּר הַהוּא וְהַיֵּצֶר מְסִיתוֹ וּמִתְגַּבֵּר נֶגְדּוֹ בָּזֶה יוֹתֵר, וְלֹא תַּאֲוַת כָּל עֲבֵירוֹת שָׁווֹת

And it also needs to be specifically that very same transgression, since he has already tasted the taste of that prohibition and the evil inclination incites him and presses more strongly against him in this regard, and the desire for all transgressions is not equal.

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּעוֹבֵר עַל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה, דְּבִיטּוּל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה הוּא בָּא מִצַּד עַצְלוּת וּקְרִירוּת שֶׁאֵינוֹ רוֹצֶה לְהַטְרִיחַ גּוּפוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת הַמִּצְוָה וְכָל הַמִּצְוֹת שָׁווֹת בָּזֶה

Whereas when transgressing a positive commandment, the nullification of a positive commandment comes from laziness and coldness, where one does not want to trouble his body to perform the mitzvah, and all commandments are equal in this regard.

וְאֵין לְךָ רֶגַע שֶׁאֵין מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה מוּכֶנֶת לִפְנֵי הָאָדָם לְקַיְּימָהּ כְּגוֹן לִימּוּד תּוֹרָה וֶאֱמוּנַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ דְּ״אָנֹכִי הַשֵּׁם״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְאַהֲבָתוֹ וְיִרְאָתוֹ וְכַדּוֹמֶה

And there is no moment when a positive commandment is not ready before a person to fulfill it, such as Torah study and faith in the Blessed Name from "I am Hashem," etc., and loving Him and fearing Him, and the like.
וְגַם הַתְּשׁוּבָה עַצְמָהּ, שֶׁהוּא שָׁב וּמִתְחָרֵט עַל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה שֶׁבִּיטֵּל, הִיא עַצְמָהּ מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה
And the repentance itself, where he returns and regrets the positive commandment that he nullified, is itself a positive commandment.
וַהֲרֵי לְפָנָיו מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁהוּא מְקַיְּימָהּ עַתָּה, וְאֵין צָרִיךְ שֶׁתָּבוֹא לְיָדוֹ דַּוְוקָא אוֹתָהּ מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה עַצְמָהּ
So behold, before him is the positive commandment of repentance which he is fulfilling now, and there is no need for that specific positive commandment itself to come to his hand.
וְגַם לְגִירְסָא דִּילַן ״שֶׁבָּאת פַּעַם אַחַת וּשְׁתַּיִם״, יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּבְמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה אֵין צָרִיךְ לָזֶה וְאֵין צָרִיךְ בֵּירוּר עַל יְדֵי בִּיאָה לְיָדוֹ כְּלָל

And also according to our text "that it came once and twice," one can say that for a positive commandment there is no need for this, and there is no need for verification through the opportunity presenting itself again at all;
דְּרַק בִּדְבַר עֲבֵירָה דְּהַתְּשׁוּבָה אַאוֹתָהּ עֲבֵירָה בְּיִחוּד שֶׁלֹּא יִתְקְפֶנּוּ יִצְרוֹ שַׁיָּיךְ זֶה
for only regarding a matter of transgression, where repentance concerns that particular transgression, so that his inclination should not overpower him, is this applicable.
אֲבָל בְּמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה, כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי, דְּבְכָל קִיּוּם מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה סַגִּי, אֵין צָרִיךְ בָּזֶה בֵּירוּר כְּלָל שֶׁתָּבוֹא לְיָדוֹ

But regarding a positive commandment, according to what I wrote, since any fulfillment of a positive commandment suffices, there is no need in this for any verification through that opportunity presenting itself.

דְּאֵין לְךָ אָדָם מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְקַיֵּים כַּמָּה מִצְוֹת בְּכָל יוֹם, וַאֲפִילּוּ הָרֵיקָנִין שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל מְלֵאִים מִצְוֹת כְּרִימּוֹן, וַאֲפִילּוּ פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסוֹף חֲגִיגָה)

For there is no person in Israel who does not fulfill several commandments every day, and even the empty ones in Israel are as full of commandments as a pomegranate, and even the transgressors of Israel, as they said at the end of Chagigah.

paragraphs.text: Tosafos Yom HaKippurim, Yoma 86a, s.v. avar al aseh, by R’ Moshe ibn Chaviv. The following paraphrases the complete discussion cited here. The Maharit, in his derashos (folio 232, as cited there), asks what “he does not stir from there” adds—how long would one otherwise have thought that atonement was suspended? He also asks how “Return, wayward sons” proves immediacy when “I will heal your waywardness” speaks of the future. After referring to the Maharit’s answer, the author questions his assumption that the passage concerns a stubborn offender who relapsed. He proposes an explanation along the lines of Rashi and Rambam. In discussing the baraisa about accepting people who return, Tosafos Yom HaKippurim interprets the first view as withholding permanent reliance on their renewed reliability without periodic examination, lest they relapse; another view distinguishes private return from public return. The accepting view, cited in Bechoros 31a, accepts return in either case: “Return, wayward sons” includes someone still called wayward because he returned privately rather than openly. Rambam rules likewise at the end of Hilchos Teshuvah 3:14. Thus, when one neglects a positive commandment and repents privately, we do not wait for public return before pardon: “he does not stir from there.” The future “I will heal” means that the Holy One will help the person who has returned privately to return publicly as well. The author then raises a further difficulty: Jeremiah’s context concerns return from idolatry, as Rashi explains, so how can it establish a rule about a positive commandment? He suggests that the verse addresses Israel’s leaders, who failed to rebuke their generation’s idolatry and thereby neglected the positive commandment “you shall surely rebuke.” Once they repent by rebuking privately, even before rebuking openly, “I will heal your waywardness” applies. This is his proposed way of deriving the positive-commandment case from the verse.

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:1: “What is complete teshuvah? One to whose hand came a matter in which he had transgressed, and it is possible for him to do it again, yet he separated and did not do it because of teshuvah — not out of fear and not from failure of strength. How so? One who had relations with a woman in sin, and after time secluded himself with her, he still in his love for her and in his bodily vigor, and in the same province in which he transgressed, yet he separated and did not transgress — this is a complete baal teshuvah. This is what Shlomo said, ‘and remember your Creator in the days of your youth’ (Koheles 12:1). And if he repented only in his old age, at a time when it is impossible for him to do what he used to do — although it is not choice teshuvah, it avails him, and he is a baal teshuvah.” And the language in the Gemara, Yoma 86b, which Rabbeinu mentions below: “What is a baal teshuvah? Rav Yehudah said: for example, one to whose hand came a matter of transgression a first time and a second time, and he resisted it. Rav Yehudah indicated: with that same woman, at that same period, in that same place.” The Rambam continues in the same halachah that even one who repents on the day of his death and dies in repentance has all his iniquities forgiven. The recurring test therefore belongs to the description of choice, complete teshuvah; repentance still avails when that test is unavailable.

paragraphs.text: Constant positive commandments. Rambam, Sefer HaMitzvos, aseh 1, 3, and 4, counts faith from “Anochi,” love from Devarim 6:5, and fear from Devarim 10:20; Hilchos Talmud Torah 1:8 requires every Jewish man to establish Torah study by day and night from Yehoshua 1:8. Biur Halachah 1:1, quoting Sefer HaChinuch, describes six mitzvos whose obligation is constant and says that every moment one contemplates them he fulfills an aseh. This supplies the halachic background to Rav Tzadok’s word “prepared”: unlike the recurrence of a particular forbidden temptation, faith, love, fear, and Torah study are immediately available modes of present obedience.

paragraphs.text: Teshuvah as an aseh: Ramban to Devarim 30:11 reads “this commandment” as the return described in 30:1–2, through heart and speech. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1, formally defines verbal vidui as the positive commandment when one repents. Rav Tzadok (Takanat HaShavin 9:1) distinguishes genuine inward return, through which one may be deemed righteous, from the separate positive commandment of confession. Here his argument is that the present actual act of returning is itself obedience and therefore does not require the original neglected aseh to recur before teshuvah can take effect. Sources: Ramban on Deuteronomy 30:11; Mishneh Torah, Repentance 1:1; Takanat HaShavin 9:1.

paragraphs.text: Chagigah 27a, translated: “Reish Lakish said: the fire of Gehinnom has no power over the sinners of Israel — derived a fortiori from the golden altar: just as the golden altar, which has upon it only the thickness of a gold dinar, yet for many years the fire has no power over it — the sinners of Israel, who are ‘full of mitzvos like a pomegranate,’ as it is written, ‘like a slice of pomegranate is your temple rakatekh’ (Shir HaShirim 4:3) — read not ‘rakatekh’ but ‘reikanin shebakh’ the empty ones among you — all the more so.” R’ Tzadok invokes this to show that every Jew always has fulfilled positive commandments to his credit, so the “recurrence test” is unnecessary for atoning a nullified aseh.

HaKippurim scrutinized (citing the Mahari“t: why”he does not stir," and how does one derive. Immediacy from “Return, wayward sons” when “I will heal their waywardness” reads as future?).

p: וּלְעִנְיַן שֶׁלֹּא יְבַטֵּל עוֹד שׁוּם מִצְוָה, זֶה גַּם כֵּן אִי אֶפְשָׁר
And regarding not nullifying any commandment again, this too is impossible.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּזְבָחִים ז עַמּוּד א) ״עַל מְנָת שֶׁאֵין מְחוּיָּב כְּלוּם – פְּסוּלָה, שֶׁאֵין לְךָ אָדָם מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְחוּיָּב עֲשֵׂה״

And as they said in Zevachim 7a, "If it is offered for someone who is not liable for anything, it is invalid, for there is no person in Israel who is not liable on account of neglecting a positive commandment."
וּמַשְׁמַע אֲפִילּוּ עַל מְנָת שֶׁהִקְרִיב כְּבָר עוֹלָה בְּאוֹתוֹ יוֹם, גַּם כֵּן אֵין לְךָ וְכוּלֵיהּ שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְחוּיָּב עֲשֵׂה מִשְּׁעַת הַקְרָבַת עוֹלָה עַד עַתָּה

And this implies that even if he already offered an olah on that very day, there is still no person, etc., who is not liable for neglecting a positive commandment between the time of that olah and now.

דְּאִי אֶפְשָׁר לִינָּצֵל בְּכָל שָׁעָה מִבִּיטּוּל עֲשֵׂה כְּמִצְוַת תַּלְמוּד תּוֹרָה וְכַדּוֹמֶה מִמִּצְוֹת הַתְּמִידוּת, שֶׁכְּשֶׁמְּפַנֶּה רֶגַע אַחַת לִבּוֹ לַבַּטָּלָה, מְבַטֵּל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה וְאֵין לְךָ אָדָם נִיצּוֹל מִזֶּה

For it is impossible to be saved at every moment from nullifying a positive commandment such as the commandment of Torah study and similar continuous commandments, because when one turns his heart to idleness for a single moment, he nullifies a positive commandment, and there is no person saved from this.
דְּעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת ה עַמּוּד א) ״פִּשְׁפֵּשׁ וְלֹא מָצָא – יִתְלֶה בְּבִיטּוּל תּוֹרָה״
Therefore they said Berachos 5a, "If he examined and did not find a sin—he should attribute it to the neglect of Torah study."
דְּדָבָר זֶה מָצוּי אֵצֶל כָּל אָדָם, אֲפִילּוּ צַדִּיק גָּמוּר שֶׁפִּשְׁפֵּשׁ וְלֹא מָצָא לוֹ שׁוּם חֵטְא, וּמִסְּתָמָא שׁוֹקֵד עַל הַתּוֹרָה כָּל הַיּוֹם
For this matter is common with every person, even a completely righteous person who examined and found no sin, and presumably studies Torah diligently all day long.

וְעִם כָּל זֶה יוּכַל לִתְלוֹת בְּבִיטּוּל תּוֹרָה אֵיזֶה רְגָעִים, אִם לֹא יְחִידִים הַשְּׂרִידִים כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי וַחֲבֵרָיו תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים הָאֲמִיתִּים, שֶׁכָּל שִׂיחָתָם וְהִרְהוּר לִבָּם גַּם בְּמִילֵי דְּעָלְמָא הַכֹּל דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה

Yet despite this he could attribute it to the neglect of Torah study for some moments, except for unique individuals, the remnants, such as Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai and his colleagues, the true Torah scholars, whose every conversation and thought of their heart, even in worldly matters, is entirely words of Torah.
וּכְפִי הַנִּרְאֶה דְּעַל כֵּן תִּיקְּנוּ בַּתְּפִלָּה בִּרְכַּת ״הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ״ שָׁלֹשׁ פְּעָמִים בְּכָל יוֹם, וַאֲפִילּוּ צַדִּיק גָּמוּר
And apparently, this is why they instituted in the prayer the blessing of "Hashiveinu" three times every day, even for a completely righteous person;
דְּאֵין לְךָ שֶׁאֵין מְחוּיָּב עֲשֵׂה בְּבִיטּוּל תּוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה, דְּעַל זֶה מְבַקְּשִׁים ״הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ לְתוֹרָתֶךָ וְקָרְבֵנוּ״ וְכוּלֵיהּ
for there is no one free of liability for neglecting the positive commandments of Torah study and service, for regarding this we request "Return us to Your Torah and draw us near," etc.
וְ״הַחֲזִירֵנוּ״ וְכוּלֵיהּ הוּא עַל בִּיטּוּל מִצְוַת תְּשׁוּבָה עַצְמָהּ
And "And bring us back," etc., is regarding the nullification of the commandment of repentance itself.

וְאַף דִּכְבָר שָׁב שַׁחֲרִית וְנִתְכַּפֵּר מִיָּד, וּלְתַנָּא קַמָּא דְּבָרַיְיתָא (יוֹמָא פ״ו עַמּוּד ב) אַחַר שֶׁנִּתְכַּפֵּר וְנִמְחַל אֵין לוֹ לְהַזְכִּירָם עוֹד אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן שׁוֹנֶה בָּהֶם, וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לָשׁוּב וְלַחֲזוֹר וְלָשׁוּב עַל חֵטְא אֶחָד

And although he already repented in the morning and was atoned immediately, and according to the first Tanna of the Baraisa Yoma 86b after he is atoned and forgiven he should not mention them again unless he repeats them, and there is no need to repent and return and repent over a single sin;

בָּזֶה חוֹזְרִים וּמְבַקְּשִׁים לָשׁוּב בְּכָל פַּעַם עַל מַה שֶּׁהוֹסִיף לַחֲטוֹא מִשַּׁחֲרִית לְצָהֳרַיִם וּמִצָּהֳרַיִם לְעַרְבִית, דְּאֵין לְךָ אָדָם שֶׁנִּיצּוֹל בְּכָל שָׁעָה וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי:

nevertheless in this we return and request to repent every time for what he additionally sinned from morning to noon, and from noon to evening, for there is no person who is saved at every moment, as I wrote.

paragraphs.text: Zevachim 7a: “Rava said: a chatas slaughtered on behalf of someone who is not liable for anything is invalid, for there is no person in Israel who is not liable on account of neglecting a positive commandment.” The surrounding sugya discusses a chatas offered with a changed beneficiary and distinguishes one liable for a chatas from one liable for an olah. Rav Tzadok draws on its principle of liability for an omitted aseh: even if a person already offered an olah earlier that very day, further omissions may arise between that offering and the present moment. His examples are Torah study and the other constant commandments. His language here is an inference about fresh liability, rather than a separate ruling about an olah made subject to a formal condition.

paragraphs.text: Berakhos 5a: “Rava—and some say Rav Chisda—said: If a person sees that sufferings befall him, he should examine his deeds, as it says, ‘Let us search our ways and examine them, and return to Hashem’ (Eichah 3:40). If he examined and did not find a sin, he should attribute them to neglect of Torah study, as it says, ‘Happy is the man whom You afflict, Hashem, and teach him from Your Torah’ (Tehillim 94:12). If he attributed them to neglect of Torah study and did not find that fault, it is known that they are afflictions of love.” Rav Tzadok applies the Torah-neglect stage even to an ordinarily righteous, diligent scholar, while expressly excepting the rare scholars whose worldly speech and thought are themselves Torah. This supplies his explanation for renewed daily return without treating the Gemara as denying the possibility of afflictions of love.

paragraphs.text: The “conversation” of true Torah scholars. Sukkah 21b derives from Tehillim 1:3, “and his leaf does not wither,” that even the conversation of talmidei chachamim requires study. The teaching follows R’ Shimon’s report that two halachos were learned from Rabban Gamliel’s seemingly incidental conversation. Rashi to Tehillim 1:3 explains that even what appears secondary or waste-like in a sage serves a purpose; Maharal, Tiferes Yisrael ch. 59, calls such speech the “leaf” that clothes and expresses the inner fruit of wisdom. Rav Tzadok limits the stronger claim—that worldly speech and thought are themselves Torah—to rare, fully integrated scholars such as R’ Shimon bar Yochai and his circle. It is therefore an exceptional spiritual level, not a general dispensation for ordinary idle conversation.

paragraphs.text: Hashiveinu in the three daily prayers. Berakhos 26b records two accounts of the institution of prayer: the Avos instituted the prayers, or the prayers were instituted corresponding to the daily offerings. In the former account too, the Sages aligned them with the offerings. Megillah 17b describes 120 elders, including prophets, establishing the eighteen blessings in order, and explains the placement of teshuvah after understanding. The Hashiveinu blessing asks: “Return us, our Father, to Your Torah; bring us near, our King, to Your service; and restore us in complete teshuvah before You” (Siddur Ashkenaz, weekday Shacharis Amidah, Teshuvah). Rav Tzadok reads the three clauses as an accounting for Torah, avodah, and teshuvah itself. His subsequent answer to the repeated-confession objection explains why the recurring prayers address new omissions since the previous prayer.

paragraphs.text: Repeating confession after forgiveness. Yoma 86b records a dispute. The tanna kamma says that sins confessed on one Yom Kippur should not be confessed again unless they were repeated; R’ Eliezer ben Yaakov says repeated confession is praiseworthy, citing Tehillim 51:5, “my sin is always before me.” Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:8, rules that one confesses them again even while remaining steadfast in teshuvah. Rav Tzadok deliberately argues here even according to the tanna kamma: the three daily requests are not needless repetition of one already-forgiven act, because fresh omissions accumulate between Shacharis, Minchah, and Maariv. His proof therefore does not depend on rejecting the Rambam’s ruling.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: That one should not nullify any further mitzvah is likewise impossible — as they said (Zevachim 7a) that an olah brought “on condition that I owe nothing” is invalid, since there is no Jew who does not owe a positive commandment. Indeed, even “on condition that he already offered an olah that day” fails. For from that offering until now he inevitably nullified some positive commandment (the constant mitzvos, like Torah study — the moment one lets his mind go idle he nullifies a positive commandment).

p: וְהִסְמִיכוּ לָזֶה בִּרְכַּת ״סְלַח לָנוּ״, דְּמִיָּד אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה בָּאָה הַסְּלִיחָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּמְגִלָּה י״ז עַמּוּד ב׳)
And they juxtaposed to this in the Shemoneh Esreh the blessing of "Forgive us" (Salach Lanu), for immediately following repentance comes forgiveness, as they said in Megillah 17b;
וְהַיְינוּ עַל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה דְּמוֹחֲלִין מִיָּד, שֶׁעַל זֶה מִתְוַודֶּה וּמְבַקֵּשׁ בְּבִרְכַּת ״הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ״, וְעַל זֶה הַסְּלִיחָה בָּאָה מִמֵּילָא כַּדִּין תֵּיכֶף לַתְּשׁוּבָה

and this refers to a positive commandment for which they pardon immediately, concerning which one confesses and petitions in the blessing of "Return us" (Hashiveinu), and on this forgiveness comes automatically by law immediately following repentance.
וְכֵיוָן שֶׁנִּפְתְּחוּ שַׁעֲרֵי סְלִיחָה וּמְחִילָה, מוֹסִיף לְבַקֵּשׁ עַל סְלִיחַת חֵטְא וָפֶשַׁע שֶׁהֵם הַחֲמוּרוֹת
And once the gates of forgiveness and pardon have been opened, he continues to petition for the forgiveness of "sin and transgression" (chet va-fesha), which are the severe offenses;

וּלְכָךְ מְסַיֵּים ״הַמַּרְבֶּה לִסְלוֹחַ״, דְּהַסְּלִיחוֹת בְּרִיבּוּי: גַּם מִלְּבַד מַה שֶּׁהַדִּין נוֹתֵן לִסְלוֹחַ, הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּרוֹב רַחֲמָיו וַחֲסָדָיו מִתְפַּיֵּיס בְּתַחֲנוּנִים לִמְחוֹל גַּם עַל הַחֲמוּרוֹת בְּלֹא יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים וְיִסּוּרִין, וְלֹא דֶּרֶךְ וִיתּוּר רַק עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה וְהַתְּפִלָּה

and therefore he concludes "Who abundantly forgives," for the pardons are in abundance: even beyond what strict law dictates to forgive, the Blessed Name in His abundant mercies and kindnesses is appeased through supplications to pardon even for the severe offenses without Yom Kippur and suffering—not by way of arbitrary waiver, but through repentance and prayer;

וּכִצְלוֹתֵיהּ דְּרָבָא וְרַב הַמְנוּנָא זוּטֵי (בִּבְרָכוֹת י״ז עַמּוּד א׳): ״וּמַה שֶּׁחָטָאתִי מָרֵק בְּרַחֲמֶיךָ וְלֹא עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין״, וְהַיְינוּ גַּם בְּאוֹתָם הַצְּרִיכִין יִסּוּרִין לְמָרֵק הַכַּפָּרָה

and like the prayer of Rava and Rav Hamnuna Zuti in Berachos 17a: "and what I have sinned, scour in Your mercies and not through suffering," which refers even to those offenses that ordinarily require suffering to scour and complete atonement.
וְזֶהוּ בִּרְכַּת ״סְלַח״ שֶׁהִסְמִיכוּ לְ״הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ״, דְּזֶה צָרִיךְ לְבַקֵּשׁ בְּכָל יוֹם הַסְּלִיחָה לְהִנָּצֵל מִיִּסּוּרִין
And this is the blessing of "Forgive us" which they juxtaposed to "Return us," for this one must request every day: forgiveness in order to be saved from suffering;
וּבִרְכַּת ״הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ״ עַצְמָהּ הִיא עַל בִּיטּוּל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה תּוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה וּתְשׁוּבָה הַמְפוֹרָשׁ בָּהּ, דְּדָבָר זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהִנָּצֵל בְּכָל יוֹם וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי

while the blessing of "Return us" itself is for the neglect of the positive commandments of Torah, service, and teshuvah made explicit in it, since from this failure it is impossible to be spared every day, as I wrote.
וְאִם כֵּן שַׁפִּיר מוּכְרָח מִזֶּה דִּלִמְחִילָה אַמִּצְוַת עֲשֵׂה עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה אֵין צָרִיךְ לִתְנַאי שֶׁתָּבוֹא לְיָדוֹ

And if so, it is well proven from this that for the pardon of a positive commandment through repentance, there is no need for the condition that the opportunity to fulfill that commandment present itself again;

וְיֵשׁ לְהַכְרִיחַ נַמֵּי כֵּן מֵהָא דִּזְבָחִים (שָׁם ז׳ עַמּוּד ב׳) דְּ״עוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן״, דְּ״הֵיכִי דָּמֵי, אִי דְּלֵיכָּא תְּשׁוּבָה וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְאִי דְּאִיכָּא תְּשׁוּבָה וְכוּלֵיהּ״, וּמָה רְאָיָה, דִּלְמָא שֶׁשָּׁב וְלֹא בָּא לְיָדוֹ וְנִיצּוֹל

and one can likewise prove this from that passage in Zevachim 7b that "an olah is a tribute-gift," where it asks: "What are the circumstances? If there is no repentance, etc., and if there is repentance, etc."; for what proof is there? Perhaps it refers to one who repented, but it did not yet come to his hand again and he was saved from it?

וּמְבוֹאָר בְּרַבֵּנוּ מֹשֶׁה בֶּן מַיְמוֹן דַּאֲפִילּוּ לֹא נִיצּוֹל, מִכָּל מָקוֹם תְּשׁוּבָה מוֹעֶלֶת וְלֹא לְגַמְרֵי, וּבְוַדַּאי דְּיָצָא מִכְּלַל ״זֶבַח רְשָׁעִים תּוֹעֵבָה״ כֵּיוָן דְּהַשְׁתָּא מִיהַת שָׁב וּמִתְחָרֵט, וְעַל זֶה בָּאָה הָעוֹלָה לִהְיוֹת נִמְחָל מְחִילָה גְּמוּרָה

And it is explained in the Rambam (Hilchos Teshuvah 2:1) that even if he was not tested and saved, repentance nevertheless avails, though not completely; and certainly he has departed from the category of "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination" since now, at any rate, he repents and regrets, and for this the olah comes to effect complete pardon.
וְעַל כֵּן צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דִּבְעֲשֵׂה מוֹדֵי דְּלָא שַׁיָּיךְ זֶה, וְהַיְינוּ דְּמַיְיתֵי בָּרַיְיתָא דְּ״לֹא זָז מִשָּׁם וְכוּלֵיהּ״

Therefore one must say that regarding an aseh he agrees that this requirement of facing the test does not apply, and that is why the Gemara cites the Baraisa that "he does not move from there before he is pardoned, etc.";
וּלְשׁוֹן ״לֹא זָז״ בָּא לִרְמֹז דְּאֵין צָרִיךְ שֶׁיָּבוֹא לְיָדוֹ וִיקַיֵּים, רַק מִיָּד נִמְחָל
and the expression "does not move" comes to intimate that there is no need for it to come to his hand and he fulfill it, but rather he is immediately pardoned;
וַאֲפִילּוּ יוֹסִיף לַעֲבוֹר אַחַר כָּךְ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם עַל הַקּוֹדֵם נִמְחַל לְגַמְרֵי, וּבְמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה הוּא תְּשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה כָּל שֶׁמִּתְחָרֵט בִּשְׁעָתוֹ לְגַמְרֵי

and even if he should transgress again afterward, nevertheless for the past he is completely pardoned, and for a positive commandment it is considered complete teshuvah so long as he regrets sincerely at that moment.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 17b explains the order of the Amidah: teshuvah follows understanding because “his heart will understand, and he will return and be healed.” The Gemara asks, “If so, let healing follow teshuvah,” and rejects that order from “let him return to Hashem and He will have mercy on him, and to our God, for He abundantly forgives” (Yeshayah 55:7). It then distinguishes the healing of forgiveness from the later healing of illness. Thus pardon follows teshuvah. R’ Tzadok applies that sequence here to the neglected positive commandment: the return requested in Hashiveinu is followed at once by its pardon.

paragraphs.text: Berakhos 17a: “Rava, after his prayer, would say thus: ‘My God, before I was formed I was unworthy, and now that I have been formed it is as if I had not been formed; I am dust in my life, all the more so in my death; behold I am before You like a vessel full of shame and disgrace. May it be Your will, Hashem my God, that I sin no more, and what I have sinned before You scour in Your abundant mercy — but not through sufferings and evil illnesses.’ And this is the confession of Rav Hamnuna Zuti on Yom Kippur.” R’ Tzadok cites this to show that even severe sins can be scoured “in Your mercy” — through teshuvah and prayer — rather than through suffering. Bava Kamma 50a warns that one who says the Holy One is “vateran” forfeits his life, citing Devarim 32:4: “all His ways are justice.” Rav Tzadok therefore stresses that this merciful scouring is not an arbitrary waiver; teshuvah and tefillah are the divinely established means through which mercy operates within justice.

paragraphs.text: Zevachim 7b: “And Rava said: an olah is a gift. How so? If there is no teshuvah — then ‘the offering of the wicked is an abomination’ (Mishlei 21:27). And if there is teshuvah — but it was taught: ‘one who transgressed a positive commandment and repented does not stir from there until they forgive him’! Rather, learn from this that the olah is a gift.” Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:1, distinguishes teshuvah gemurah—facing the same sin with the same ability and refraining—from a lower level of teshuvah that nevertheless avails and makes one a baal teshuvah; even deathbed teshuvah brings forgiveness. Rav Tzadok therefore treats the later test as perfection of teshuvah, not a prerequisite for its present effect; his special application to a missed positive commandment is his own analysis.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The daily liturgy's juxtaposition of Hashiveinu and Salach Lanu. For a positive commandment, pardon is granted immediately upon repentance without requiring the test of facing the identical temptation (she-ba'as l'yado). The opening of the gates of forgiveness in Hashiveinu allows the petitioner in Salach Lanu to plead for severe offenses (chamurot), where Hashem, in His abundant mercy (HaMarbeh li'slo'ach), is appeased through supplication to pardon even without Yom Kippur and suffering.

p: וּמִיהוּ כָּל זֶה לְשִׁיטַת הָרִאשׁוֹנִים, אֲבָל לְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל (אוֹת ט׳) דְּגַם בַּחֲמוּרוֹת כֵּן, קָשֶׁה הַלָּשׁוֹן ״לֹא זָז מִשָּׁם״ דְּמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה

However, all this follows the approach of the Rishonim; but according to what I wrote above section 9 that even for severe transgressions this is so that one is termed a tzaddik immediately upon repentance, the expression "he does not move from there" regarding a positive commandment is difficult.
וְאוּלַי הָא גּוּפֵיהּ קָא מַשְׁמַע לָן בָּזֶה, דְּאֵין צָרִיךְ לְעוֹלָה לְמָרֵק הַכַּפָּרָה
And perhaps this itself is what it comes to teach us: that he does not need an olah to scour and complete the atonement;

וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּבָאָה עַל חַיָּיבֵי עֲשֵׂה, וְעַל כֵּן יֵשׁ מַה אֵיזֶה צוֹרֶךְ לְתִיקּוּן הָעֲשֵׂה דְּבִיטֵּל, וְקָא מַשְׁמַע לָן דְּאֵינָהּ רַק דּוֹרוֹן, שֶׁמִּדַּת דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ לַחוֹטֵא אַף שֶׁנִּמְחַל לְהָבִיא עוֹד דּוֹרוֹן לְהִתְרַצּוֹת

and even though the olah comes for those liable for omitting a positive commandment, so that there is some need to rectify the positive commandment he neglected, it comes to teach us that it is merely a tribute-gift (doran), for it is proper etiquette (derech eretz) for a sinner, even after he has been pardoned, to bring a gift to appease the King;

וְהַתְּפִלּוֹת שֶׁבִּמְקוֹם תְּמִידִין תִּיקְּנוּם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּבְרָכוֹת כ״ו עַמּוּד ב׳), הֵם בִּמְקוֹם הָעוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן לִמְחַיְּיבֵי עֲשֵׂה בַּזְּמַן הַזֶּה, וְהָעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב בִּתְפִלָּה הוּא בִּמְקוֹם עֲבוֹדַת הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת בְּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ בְּפֹעַל

and the prayers, which were instituted in place of the daily offerings (temidin) as they said in Berachos 26b, stand in place of the olah of tribute for those liable for positive commandments in this era, and the service of the heart in prayer takes the place of the sacrificial service in the Beis HaMikdash in practice.

וְכָךְ רָאוּי לְעֶבֶד שֶׁחָטָא בְּהִתְעַצְּלוּת עֲבוֹדָתוֹ: אַחַר שֶׁנִּתְחָרֵט וַאֲדוֹנוֹ מָחַל לוֹ, יֵשׁ לוֹ לְהוֹסִיף מִשֶּׁלּוֹ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת עֲבוֹדָה לְרַבּוֹ מַה שֶּׁלֹּא נִצְטַוָּוה, לְהַרְאוֹת חִשְׁקוֹ וּרְצוֹנוֹ בַּעֲבוֹדַת רַבּוֹ, וְשֶׁהוּא מוּכָן וְזָרִיז מֵעַתָּה לַעֲבוֹדָתוֹ

And so it is fitting for a servant who sinned through laziness in his service: after he regretted and his master pardoned him, he should add on his own initiative devotion in serving his master beyond what was commanded, to demonstrate his longing and desire for his master's service, and that he is now prepared and zealous for his service;

אֲבָל אֵין זֶה מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְהַצְרִיכוֹ זֶה לְתוֹעֶלֶת הַמְּחִילָה שְׁלֵימָה, דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מוֹחֵל מִיָּד, וְאֵינוֹ זָז אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה וְהַחֲרָטָה מִמְּקוֹמוֹ לְהוֹסִיף לְהִשְׁתַּדֵּל בְּאֵיזֶה עֲבוֹדָה לְצֹרֶךְ הַמְּחִילָה, אֶלָּא מוֹחֲלִין מִיָּד תֵּיכֶף שֶׁנִּתְחָרֵט וְשָׁב בְּלִי זִיזָה לְעִנְיָן אַחֵר וּפְעוּלָּה אַחֶרֶת

but this is not from the side of the Blessed Name to require this of him for the efficacy of full pardon, for the Blessed Name pardons immediately, and the sinner does not need to move from his place after teshuvah and regret to exert himself in further service for the need of pardon; rather, they pardon immediately, the moment he regrets and repents, without moving to any other matter or action;
וְדַיֵּיק זֶה מִקְּרָא דְּ״אֶרְפָּא״ מִיָּד
and he derived this from the verse “I will heal,” immediately.
וּמֵהָכָא הוּא דִּדָיְיקִינַן בִּזְבָחִים שָׁם דְּ״עוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן״, וְלָא תֵּימָא תְּשׁוּבָה תּוֹלָה וְעוֹלָה מְמָרֵק הַכַּפָּרָה וְלָא קָרֵינַן בֵּיהּ ״זֶבַח רְשָׁעִים תּוֹעֵבָה״

And from here is what we infer in Zevachim (7b) that an olah is a tribute-gift, and do not say that repentance suspends and the olah scours the atonement without it being termed "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination";

דְּגַם בַּחֲמוּרוֹת דְּצָרִיךְ יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים אוֹ גַּם יִסּוּרִין אוֹ גַּם מִיתָה לְמָרֵק הַכַּפָּרָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם בִּתְשׁוּבָה לְבַד לֹא מִבַּעְיָא דְּיָצָא מִכְּלַל שֵׁם רָשָׁע, אֶלָּא אֲפִילּוּ צַדִּיק גָּמוּר נַמֵּי מִיקְרֵי כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל (אוֹת ט׳) מִן הַמְפוֹרָשׁ (בְּקִדּוּשִׁין מ״ט עַמּוּד ב׳) ״עַל מְנָת שֶׁאֲנִי צַדִּיק אֲפִילּוּ רָשָׁע גָּמוּר – שֶׁמָּא הִרְהֵר תְּשׁוּבָה״, וְרָשָׁע גָּמוּר מַשְׁמַע גַּם בְּכָל עֲבֵירוֹת הַחֲמוּרוֹת

for even in severe offenses where one requires Yom Kippur, or also suffering, or also death to scour the atonement, nevertheless through repentance alone, not only has he departed from the designation of wicked, but he is even called a complete tzaddik, as I wrote above section 9 from what is explicit in Kiddushin 49b: “on condition that I am a righteous man, even if he is completely wicked—perhaps he contemplated repentance in his heart,” and “completely wicked” implies even regarding all the severe transgressions;
וּמִיָּד שֶׁשָּׁב הֲרֵי הוּא נִקְרָא צַדִּיק אַף שֶׁמְּחוּסַּר כַּפָּרָה עֲדַיִין, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן דְּלָא קָרֵינַן בֵּיהּ ״זֶבַח רְשָׁעִים תּוֹעֵבָה״
and immediately upon repenting he is called righteous even though he still lacks full atonement, and all the more so we do not apply to him “the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination”;

עַל כֵּן מַיְיתֵי שָׁם לְשׁוֹן הַךְ בָּרַיְיתָא דְּ״לֹא זָז וְכוּלֵיהּ״, דִּמְבוֹאָר דִּתְשׁוּבָה מְכַפֶּרֶת לְגַמְרֵי מִיָּד בְּלֹא הוֹסָפַת עוֹד דָּבָר, וְכֵיוָן דִּבְלֹא תְּשׁוּבָה אִי אֶפְשָׁר, עַל כֵּן כָּל עוֹלָה רַק לְדוֹרוֹן

therefore it cites there the text of this Baraisa of “he does not move, etc.,” from which it is clear that repentance atones completely and immediately without the addition of any further element; and since without repentance the offering cannot be acceptable, perforce any olah is solely a tribute-gift.

וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב שָׁם לִפְנֵי זֶה דְּעוֹלָה מְכַפֶּרֶת אַעֲשֵׂה, וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַבִּי שְׁלֹמֹה יִצְחָקִי דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״עוֹלָה וְכוּלֵיהּ אֵינָהּ וְכוּלֵיהּ כַּפָּרָה מַמָּשׁ וְכוּלֵיהּ״ יְעוּיַּן שָׁם, וּבְתוֹסָפוֹת דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״עוֹלָה״, צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דְּגַם לְהַךְ דּוֹרוֹן קָרֵי ״כַּפָּרָה״

And what was written there prior to this, that an olah atones for a positive commandment—see Rashi there (s.v. olah, etc., "it is not, etc., actual atonement, etc.", see there) and Tosafos (s.v. olah)—one must say that to this tribute-gift too it applies the term “atonement”;
אַף שֶׁכְּבָר נִתְכַּפֵּר לְגַמְרֵי, מִכָּל מָקוֹם בַּהֲבָאַת דּוֹרוֹן הוּא מוֹסִיף אַהֲבָה, וּמִמֵּילָא גַּם הַכַּפָּרָה בְּתִיקּוּן הַקּוֹדֵם הִיא בְּיֶתֶר שְׂאֵת

for even though he was already completely atoned, nevertheless through bringing the tribute he increases love, and consequently the atonement in rectifying the past is achieved with greater elevation;
וְאֶפְשָׁר דִּבִתְשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה דִּזְדוֹנוֹת כִּשְׁגָגוֹת, עַל יְדֵי הָעוֹלָה שֶׁאַחַר כָּךְ מִתְאַהֵב לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְנַעֲשָׂה כִּזְכֻיּוֹת
and it is possible that in teshuvah from fear where intentional sins become like inadvertent ones, through the subsequent olah he becomes beloved to the Blessed Name and they become like merits;

וְאֶפְשָׁר גַּם בִּתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה לֹא מִיָּד נַעֲשָׂה כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, רַק דִּבְהָא עֲדִיפָא מִתְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה, דְּמִיָּד שֶׁשָּׁב נִמְחָה הֶעָוֹן לְגַמְרֵי וְאֵינוֹ כִּשְׁגָגָה גַּם כֵּן, רַק הוּא כְּמוֹ שֶׁלֹּא חָטָא כְּלָל

and it is also possible that even in teshuvah from love they do not immediately become like merits, but in this it is superior to teshuvah from fear: that as soon as he repents the iniquity is utterly erased and is not even like an inadvertent sin, but he is as though he never sinned at all;
וְעַל יְדֵי דּוֹרוֹן הָעוֹלָה בְּחַיָּיבֵי עֲשֵׂה (וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים וְיִסּוּרִין בְּחַיָּיבֵי לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה וּמִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין) הוּא שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה כִּזְכֻיּוֹת
and through the tribute of the olah in positive commandments and Yom Kippur and suffering in negative commandments and capital offenses, it is transformed into merits;

וְשַׁפִּיר אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכְּבָר כִּיפֵּר לְגַמְרֵי בִּמְחִילָה גְּמוּרָה וְהוּא רַק דּוֹרוֹן, כֵּיוָן דְּעַל יְדֵי הַדּוֹרוֹן נִתְקַן הַקּוֹדֵם יוֹתֵר, קָרֵי לֵיהּ גַּם כֵּן ״כַּפָּרָה״ עַל הַקּוֹדֵם

and rightly so: although he was already completely atoned with full forgiveness and it is merely a tribute, since through the tribute the past is rectified further, it is likewise termed “atonement” for the past.

paragraphs.text: Berakhos 26b; Taanis 2a; Rambam, Hilchos Tefillah 1:1: Berakhos teaches that the fixed prayers correspond to the daily offerings; even the view that the Avos instituted prayer agrees that the Sages aligned it with the korbanos. Taanis derives ‘service with all your heart’ (Devarim 11:13) as prayer. Rambam codifies daily prayer as a positive command, while the number of prayers, their prescribed wording, and their fixed time are not prescribed by Torah law. Rav Tzadok joins these layers: the Amidah replaces the tamid and olah service, while avodah shebalev expresses the servant’s renewed desire after forgiveness.

paragraphs.text:
Kiddushin 49b teaches that a man who conditions marriage on being a tzaddik may create doubtful kiddushin even if previously wicked, “שמא הרהר תשובה בדעתו” — perhaps he inwardly resolved upon teshuvah. The possibility is crucial; the Gemara does not establish that this particular man has in fact repented (cf. Rambam, Hilchos Ishus 8:5). Rav Tzadok distinguishes the moment of genuine return, when the person is no longer called a rasha, from completion of every subsequent stage of kapparah. His exact parallel in Poked Akarim 4:8 says “אפילו רק הרהר תשובה בלב הוא מיד צדיק גמור ... מצד השם יתברך די בכך,” while also affirming that Torah’s atonement obligations, including korban or suffering where applicable, remain. This resolves why “זבח רשעים תועבה” cannot be applied to a genuinely repentant person even when further cleansing or tribute may follow.
Sources: Kiddushin 49b; Mishneh Torah, Hilchos Ishus 8:5; Poked Akarim 4:8; Zevachim 7b; Yoma 86a; Mishlei 21:27.

paragraphs.text: Zevachim 7b; Yoma 86a: Rava proves that an olah is a gift: without teshuvah it is “the offering of the wicked”; with teshuvah, the baraisa says that one who violated a positive commandment “does not stir” before being forgiven. Yoma quotes “Return, wayward sons”; the continuation of that cited verse is “I will heal your waywardness” (Yirmiyahu 3:22; compare Hoshea 14:5). R’ Tzadok reads this healing as taking effect with the return itself. His argument distinguishes the sinner’s immediate righteous status, which can coexist with incomplete atonement for severe sins, from the complete present pardon of an aseh; its olah therefore follows as a gift.

paragraphs.text: Zevachim 7b, Rashi and Tosafos; Yoma 86b: Rashi compares the olah to a gift brought when greeting the king after appeasement; it does not produce the initial pardon. Tosafos adds that it nevertheless atones for an aseh more than a chatas, because that atonement is its fixed function. Yoma distinguishes teshuvah from fear, which makes willful sins like inadvertent ones, from teshuvah from love, which makes them merits. Rav Tzadok’s further staging is his own possible proposal: the gift-olah may deepen love and elevate the repaired past—either advancing fear-based return toward merit, or turning a sin already erased through love into a positive source of closeness. Thus “kapparah” here means added rectification, not delayed initial forgiveness. Compare Rav Tzadok, Pri Tzaddik, Vayishlach §4:3, on Yaakov’s gift to Esav as part of a further clarification of good and evil. This is an analogy about the possible effect of a gift, not a source for the olah’s halachic atonement. Sources: Pri Tzaddik, Vayishlach §4:3 · Zevachim 7b · Yoma 86b · Rashi on Zevachim 7b:7:1 · Tosafot on Zevachim 7b:7:1

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The spiritual purpose of the olah as a tribute-gift (doran). Since repentance alone grants immediate pardon for a positive commandment, the subsequent offering is an act of pious devotion (derech eretz) that demonstrates renewed zeal, paralleled today by the daily statutory prayers. This tribute elevates the quality of the pardon: in teshuvah from fear, it transforms sins from inadvertent errors into merits (zechuyos); in teshuvah from love, where the sin is already erased as though it never existed, the tribute completes the ascent into absolute merits.

p: אַךְ לְשׁוֹן הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי (פֶּרֶק ח׳ דְּיוֹמָא רֵישׁ הֲלָכָה ז׳) ״הָאוֹמֵר אֵין עוֹלָה מְכַפֶּרֶת וְכוּלֵיהּ אֵין מְכַפֶּרֶת לוֹ״ עַד כָּאן, עַיֵּין שָׁם
However, the wording of the Yerushalmi Yoma 8:7: “One who says, ‘An olah does not atone,’ etc.—it does not atone for him,” thus far, see there;

מַשְׁמַע דְּבָאָה לְכַפָּרָה מַמָּשׁ, דְּאִי רַק לְדוֹרוֹן, וְהַכַּפָּרָה הַמְּתוֹסֶפֶת עַל יָדוֹ הוּא מִמֵּילָא עַל יְדֵי הַדּוֹרוֹן שֶׁהֵבִיא, אִם כֵּן אֵין הֲבָאָתָהּ לְכַפָּרָה וְשַׁפִּיר קָאָמַר ״אֵינָהּ מְכַפֶּרֶת״

implies that it comes for actual atonement; for if it were only a tribute, and the additional atonement achieved through it occurs automatically through the tribute he brought, then its presentation is not for atonement and he has stated accurately that “it does not atone”;

וְכֵן אֲפִילּוּ אָמַר ״אִי אֶפְשִׁי שֶׁתְּכַפֵּר״, הֲרֵי מִכָּל מָקוֹם הֵבִיא הַדּוֹרוֹן, וְלָמָּה לֹא יֵצֵא הוֹסָפַת הַכַּפָּרָה הַבָּאָה עַל יְדֵי הֲבָאַת דּוֹרוֹן אֲפִילּוּ בְּלֹא רְצוֹנוֹ לְכַפָּרָה, כֵּיוָן דְּבֶאֱמֶת אֵינוֹ כַּפָּרָה רַק דּוֹרוֹן

and likewise, even if he said "I do not wish it to atone," behold in any event he brought the tribute, so why would the added atonement that comes through presenting a tribute not take effect even without his desire for atonement, since in truth it is not an atonement but a tribute?
וּבִכְרֵיתוֹת (ז׳ עַמּוּד א׳) אִיתָא אַחַטָּאת פְּלוּגְתָּא דְּאַבַּיֵּי וְרָבָא עַיֵּין שָׁם, וְעוֹלָה לֹא נִזְכַּר
And in Kerisos 7a the dispute of Abaye and Rava is taught regarding a sin-offering (chatas), see there, and an olah is not mentioned;
וְנִרְאֶה דְּתַלְמוּדִין לְטַעְמֵיהּ דְּעוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן, וְהַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי פָּלֵיג עַל זֶה, וְעַיֵּין בְּכוֹרוֹת (כ״ו רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳) וּבְרַבִּי שְׁלֹמֹה יִצְחָקִי יְעוּיַּן שָׁם
and it appears that our Talmud the Bavli follows its reasoning that an olah is a tribute, whereas the Yerushalmi disputes this; and see Bechoros 26b and Rashi, see there.

וְעַיֵּין בְּפֵירוּשׁ הַפְּנֵי מֹשֶׁה (פֶּרֶק א׳ דִּשְׁבוּעוֹת הֲלָכָה ו׳) דִּמְפָרֵשׁ הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חֲנַנְיָה בַּר הִלֵּל שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ: ״לֹא כּוּלָּהּ מִן הַדֵּין בַּר נָשׁ מֵימַר לְמַלְכָּא לֵית אַתְּ מֶלֶךְ״, בָּא לַחֲלוֹק אַדִּלְעֵיל וְלוֹמַר דְּאִיפְּכָא מִסְתַּבְּרָא, וּדְבְקָרְבָּן מְכַפֵּר בְּעַל כָּרְחוֹ דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הִקְרִיב, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם

And see in the commentary of Pnei Moshe Shevuos 1:6 who explains that which Rabbi Chananyah bar Hillel stated there afterward: “It is not within the power of a man to say to the King: ‘You are no King’,” that he came to dispute the preceding statement and to say that the reverse is logical, that a sacrifice atones against his will since he offered it in any event, see there;
וְרָצָה לוֹמַר: זֶהוּ פְּשִׁיטַת תַּלְמוּדִין הַנִּזְכָּר דְּעוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן, וְדַוְוקָא בְּעוֹלָה קָאָמַר
and he meant to say: this is the premise of our Talmud mentioned above that an olah is a tribute, and he stated it specifically regarding an olah.
אַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת פֵּירוּשׁוֹ דָּחוּק וְרָחוֹק מְאוֹד בְּעֵינַי בְּמַשְׁמַע לְשׁוֹן הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי, וְגַם פֵּירוּשׁ הַקָּרְבַּן הָעֵדָה שָׁם בָּזֶה דָּחוּק
But in truth, his explanation is very forced and far-fetched in my eyes according to the meaning of the Yerushalmi's language, and the explanation of the Korban HaEdah there on this is also forced.
וּלְדַעְתִּי פָּשׁוּט בְּהֵיפֶךְ מִדִּבְרֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם, דְּרַבִּי חֲנַנְיָה בַּר הִלֵּל אַדִּלְעֵיל קָאֵי, לְפָרֵשׁ טַעְמָא דְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים מְכַפֵּר בְּעַל כָּרְחוֹ

And in my opinion, the plain meaning is the exact opposite of both their words: that Rabbi Chananyah bar Hillel refers to the earlier statement, to explain the reason why Yom Kippur atones against one's will even if one denies its atonement:

דְּכַפָּרָתוֹ מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְהִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹר פְּנֵי מַלְכוּתוֹ, וְלֹא וְכוּלֵיהּ שֶׁאֵין לוֹמַר ״אֵינְךָ מֶלֶךְ״, דִּבְעַל כָּרְחוֹ הוּא מוֹלֵךְ עָלָיו וְעַל כֵּן בְּעַל כָּרְחוֹ הוּא מְכַפֵּר

for its atonement is from the side of the Blessed Name and the revelation of the light of the presence of His Sovereignty, and one cannot say "You are not King," for He reigns over him against his will, and therefore grants him atonement against his will;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן קָרְבָּן דְּבָא לְכַפֵּר עַל יְדֵי מַעֲשֶׂה דִּידֵיהּ, בְּדִידֵיהּ תַּלְיָא שֶׁלֹּא יִתְכַּפֵּר עַל יְדֵי זֶה, דִּבְיַד הָאָדָם לְהַתְנוֹת עַל מַעֲשָׂיו בִּפְעוּלוֹתָיו כִּרְצוֹנוֹ

whereas a sacrifice, which comes to atone through his own action, depends upon him that he should not be atoned through it, for it is in the power of a person to place conditions upon his actions and deeds as he wills;
וְאַדְּרַבָּא, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי חֲנַנְיָה בַּר הִלֵּל מְסַיְּיעִים וּמַסְכִּימִים עִם הַקּוֹדֵם
and on the contrary, the words of Rabbi Chananyah bar Hillel support and agree with the preceding ruling!
וְשׁוּב מָצָאתִי בְּ״יְפֵה מַרְאֶה״ שָׁם (בְּיוֹמָא סִימָן ג׳) דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״מְכַפֵּר״ פֵּירֵשׁ כֵּן, וְלֹא יָדַעְתִּי לָמָּה נָאדוּ הֵם מִפֵּירוּשׁ זֶה הַפָּשׁוּט וּבָרוּר:
And then I found in Yafeh Mareh there Yoma, section 3, s.v. mechaper that he explained thus, and I do not know why they strayed from this simple and clear interpretation.

paragraphs.text: Yerushalmi Yoma 8:6 (modern paragraph numbering; cited by Rav Tzadok as chapter 8, opening of halachah 7), parallel to Yerushalmi Shevuos 1:6: the teaching distinguishes saying that an olah does not atone, which does not block its normal effect, from an explicit refusal, “אי איפשי שתכפר לי,” in which case “אינה מכפרת לו על כרחו” — it does not atone against his will. The ensuing comparison with Yom Kippur concerns the different status of its atonement, which cannot be negated by withholding assent. Rav Tzadok’s question is how this volitional condition fits the Bavli’s view that an olah follows forgiveness as a doron. The Shevuos parallel varies in wording; the two texts should not be silently harmonized. Sources: Jerusalem Talmud, Yoma 8:6; Jerusalem Talmud, Shevuot 1:6.

paragraphs.text: Kerisus 7a: “One who says, ‘Let my chatas not atone for me’—Abaye says it does not atone; Rava says it atones.” The Gemara qualifies this: if he says not to offer it, all agree it does not atone. They disagree when he says, “Let it be offered, but let it not atone”; Rava initially argues that once he consents to its offering, atonement follows automatically. The discussion then says, “Rava retracted,” and establishes from the baraisa that a chatas does not atone for one who says it should not atone for him. The dispute is about a chatas, not an olah. Rav Tzadok’s inference from the omission of olah is his own comparison with the Bavli’s gift model; it is not an additional explicit ruling of this passage.

paragraphs.text: Bechoros 26b, continuing the question begun on 26a, asks whether an owner might delay bringing an olah, since it is not primarily for atonement, “or perhaps, since an olah too atones for a positive commandment, he does not delay it.” Rashi explains the first side as “he does not bring it for a sin,” and the second by citing Yoma 36a: over an olah one confesses the sin concerning shichechah and pe’ah. Yoma’s baraisa also includes leket and maaser ani in R. Yose HaGelili’s formulation, while R. Akiva says an olah comes for an aseh and a negative commandment attached to an aseh. Thus the Bavli can speak of an olah as not primarily a sin-offering and still call its effect “atonement”; the passage does not by itself equate that effect with the complete pardon or scouring atonement under discussion here.

paragraphs.text: Yerushalmi Shevuos 1:6 parallels the Yoma discussion but includes a reversal formula, “Does it not stand to reason that the opposite is so?” Pnei Moshe reads that reversal as follows: a sacrifice should atone because the person did offer it, whereas refusal of the King’s rule should prevent Yom Kippur from atoning. Korban HaEdah reads the reversal differently: the voluntary olah depends on its owner’s consent, while Yom Kippur, fixed by Hashem, atones against his will and displays Hashem’s kingship. Rav Tzadok’s objection concerns the reading of the Yoma sequence: he takes R’ Chananyah’s statement to explain and support the preceding rule that Yom Kippur atones against one’s will, rather than overturn it. He reports that Yefeh Mar’eh on Yerushalmi Yoma, siman 3, s.v. mechaper, explains it this way; that attribution is retained as Rav Tzadok’s report, not as a quotation independently checked against Yefeh Mar’eh in this pass. Compare Peri Tzadik, Purim §1, which discusses the day’s intrinsic atoning power even when persecution forcibly prevents its observance, following the view that “the essence of the day atones,” while requiring awareness of the day. This is a related distinction between the day’s Divine efficacy and prevented ritual performance, not a claim that the Purim passage itself proves the Yerushalmi’s kingship interpretation.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The Yerushalmi’s ruling on conditional atonement (ha-omer ein olah mechaperes). In Yerushalmi Yoma 1:7, one who declares that his olah should not atone does not receive atonement, implying that the Yerushalmi views the olah as an actual atoning agent rather than a mere gift. R' Tzadok rejects the interpretation of the Pnei Moshe and Korban HaEdah regarding Rabbi Chananyah bar Hillel's statement ("a mortal cannot tell the King: 'You are no King'"). Instead, following the Yafeh Mareh, he demonstrates that Rabbi Chananyah bar Hillel refers to Yom Kippur, which atones against one's will because Hashem's sovereign kingship is absolute; whereas a sacrificial offering depends upon human action and intent, allowing man to stipulate whether his deed shall take effect.

p: וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים מוּכְרָח מֵהַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דְּעוֹלָה לְכַפָּרָה
And in any event, it is proven from the Yerushalmi Yoma 8:7 that an olah is brought for actual atonement;
וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דִּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ דִּמְמָרֶקֶת הַכַּפָּרָה, דּוּגְמַת יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים בְּחַיָּיבֵי לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה
and one must say that it holds that it scours and completes the atonement, analogous to the function of Yom Kippur for those liable for negative commandments.
וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר לְדִידֵיהּ, הַלָּשׁוֹן ״לֹא זָז״ וְכוּלֵיהּ בַּבָּרַיְיתָא דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּחַיָּיבֵי עֲשֵׂה, דְּמַיְיתֵי לַהּ גַּם שָׁם (עַיֵּין שָׁם), הוּא לְטַעְמֵיהּ שָׁם וְשָׁם

And one can say according to the Yerushalmi, the phrase "he does not move from there, etc." in the Baraisa of Rabbi Yishmael regarding those liable for an aseh Yoma 86a, which it also cites there (see there), is consistent with its own reasoning in both places:
דְּעוֹלָה מְכַפֶּרֶת אַהִרְהוּר וְלֹא אַעֲשֵׂה
that an olah atones for sinful contemplation (hirhur) and not for omission of a positive commandment;
וְהִרְהוּר עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה לָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה, וּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ דְּאֵינוֹ בִּכְלַל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה דְּ״לֹא זָז״ וְכוּלֵיהּ
and contemplation of idolatry is a negative commandment lacking physical action, which it holds is not included in the positive commandment category of "he does not move, etc."
וְהַיְינוּ טַעְמָא דְּפָלֵיג אַתַּלְמוּדִין גַּם בָּזֶה דְּלֹא בָּא אַעֲשֵׂה, מִשּׁוּם דְּאַעֲשֵׂה ״לֹא זָז״ וְכוּלֵיהּ וְלֹא צָרִיךְ לְעוֹלָה

And this is the reason that it disputes our Talmud Bavli in this as well, holding that it does not come for a positive commandment, because for a positive commandment "he does not move from there before being pardoned" and does not require an olah at all;
אֲבָל הִרְהוּר (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה) דְּהוּא כְּלָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה צָרִיךְ לְעוֹלָה, וּמְמָרַקְתּוֹ קוֹדֶם יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים
whereas contemplation (of idolatry), which is classified as a negative commandment lacking action, requires an olah, and it scours his atonement prior to Yom Kippur;
וּשְׁאָר לָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה בִּכְלַל כָּל לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה דְּצָרִיךְ יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים
while other negative commandments lacking action are subsumed under ordinary negative commandments, requiring Yom Kippur.
וְהָא דְּלֹא חָשֵׁיב חֲמִשָּׁה חִלּוּקֵי כַּפָּרָה, דְּהִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה תּוֹלָה וְעוֹלָה מְמָרֶקֶת
And that it does not enumerate five categories of atonement, where for sinful contemplation repentance suspends and the olah scours:
מִלְּבַד דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּלָא מַיְירֵי מֵעֲבֵירָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב
besides the fact that one may answer that the Baraisa does not deal with transgressions confined to the heart;
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּלָא מַיְירֵי מִכַּפָּרַת קָרְבָּנוֹת
one can also say that it does not deal with the atonement of sacrifices at all,
כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלָא חָשֵׁיב חַיָּיבֵי חַטָּאוֹת וַאֲשָׁמוֹת
just as it does not enumerate those liable for sin-offerings (chata'os) and guilt-offerings (ashamos),
דְּנַמֵּי אֵינָן בְּלֹא תְּשׁוּבָה דְּ״זֶבַח רְשָׁעִים תּוֹעֵבָה״, דְּהַתְּשׁוּבָה תּוֹלָה וְהֵן מְמָרְקִין הַכַּפָּרָה בְּלֹא יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים

which likewise cannot atone without repentance, since "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination" (Mishlei 21:27), where repentance suspends and they scour the atonement without requiring Yom Kippur,
כְּפִי הַנִּרְאֶה מִלְּשׁוֹן הַמִּשְׁנָה דְּיוֹמָא (שָׁם פ״ה עַמּוּד ב׳): ״חַטָּאת וְאָשָׁם וַדַּאי מְכַפְּרִין, מִיתָה וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים מְכַפְּרִין וְכוּלֵיהּ״
as appears from the wording of the Mishnah in Yoma 85b: "A sin-offering and an unconditional guilt-offering atone; death and Yom Kippur atone, etc.";

וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בַּגְּמָרָא דִּמְכַפְּרֵי כַּפָּרָה גְּמוּרָה, וְגַם יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים אֵין מְכַפֵּר בְּלֹא הֵם, דְּגַם אַחַר יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים צָרִיךְ לַהֲבִיאָן לְמָרֵק כַּפָּרָתָן עַל יָדָם דַּוְוקָא

and see there in the Gemara (Yoma 85b) that they effect complete atonement, and Yom Kippur does not atone without them, for even after Yom Kippur one must bring them to scour atonement specifically through them;
וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכִי לָא חֲשָׁבִינְהוּ בַּהֲדֵי חִלּוּקֵי כַּפָּרָה, וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּלָא מַיְירֵי הָתָם מִכַּפָּרַת קָרְבָּנוֹת
and even so, it did not enumerate them among the four categories of atonement; perforce, it did not deal there with the atonement of sacrifices,
וְעַל כֵּן לֹא נָקַט גַּם כַּפָּרָה דְּעוֹלָה
and therefore it likewise did not include the atonement of an olah.
וּמַתְנִיתִין דְּנָקַט ״חַטָּאוֹת וַאֲשָׁמוֹת מְכַפְּרִין״ וְלֹא גַּם עוֹלָה, יֵשׁ לוֹמַר מִשּׁוּם דְּהָנֵי אֵין בָּאִין אֶלָּא לְכַפָּרָה וּפְסִיקָא לֵיהּ
And the Mishnah, which cited "sin-offerings and guilt-offerings atone" and not an olah as well, one can say is because these are brought solely for atonement and the matter is definitive;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן עוֹלָה דְּבָאָה נְדָבָה גַּם כֵּן, וְלֹא פְּסִיקָא לֵיהּ לוֹמַר דִּמְכַפֶּרֶת, כֵּן נִרְאֶה בָּזֶה בְּשִׁיטַת הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי
whereas an olah is brought as a voluntary freewill gift (nedavah) too, so it is not definitive to state that it atones; thus it appears regarding the position of the Yerushalmi.

(וּלְפִי זֶה מוּכָח מֵהַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דְּלָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה בִּכְלַל לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה, וּבְהָא דְּאֵין מוּכְרָח דְּתַלְמוּדִין פָּלֵיג עֲלֵיהּ, יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּאֵין לְאַפּוֹשֵׁי פְּלוּגְתָּא מִמַּה דְּלָא אַשְׁכְּחַן):

And according to this, it is proven from the Yerushalmi that a negative commandment lacking physical action is included in the category of negative commandments; and in this matter, where it is not compelled that our Talmud disputes it, one should maintain that we do not multiply disputes beyond what is explicitly found.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: וּשְׁאָר לָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה בִּכְלַל כָּל לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה דְּצָרִיךְ יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים

paragraphs.text: Yerushalmi Yoma 8:7:2 (42a; parallel Shevuos 1:6) derives atonement for contemplation of the heart from Yechezkel 20:32 and Iyov 1:5. The following baraisa, Yoma 8:7:4, gives immediate forgiveness after teshuvah for an aseh, and teshuvah suspending until Yom Kippur for a lav. For intentional offenses carrying kareis or court-imposed death it says teshuvah and Yom Kippur atone half, and suffering the other half; for chillul Hashem it describes teshuvah and Yom Kippur, suffering, and death as successive parts of the cleansing. Kiddushin 40a distinguishes ordinary unfruitful evil thought from thought of idolatry, citing “that I may seize the House of Israel in their heart” (Yechezkel 14:5). Rambam, Hilchos Avodah Zarah 2:3, forbids following thoughts that uproot Torah principles and rules that this prohibition carries no lashes. Rav Tzadok’s classification of idolatrous contemplation as a lav she-ein bo maaseh, and his conclusion that teshuvah suspends while the olah completes its atonement before Yom Kippur, are his analysis of these sources; the Yerushalmi does not state that additional category expressly.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 85b: the Mishnah states that a chatas and a definite asham atone. The immediate Gemara distinguishes their complete atonement from an asham talui and explains that those owing a chatas or definite asham must still bring it after Yom Kippur, whereas those owing an asham talui are exempt. Zevachim 7b, discussing the olah, excludes an offering without teshuvah as “the offering of the wicked is an abomination” (Mishlei 21:27). Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1, likewise says sin- and guilt-offerings atone only after teshuvah and verbal confession. Rav Tzadok explains that the baraisa’s general categories do not enumerate sacrificial completions. He then qualifies the Mishnah’s list: chatas and asham are brought only for atonement, while an olah can also be brought voluntarily, so the Mishnah does not describe every olah categorically as an atoning offering.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: According to the Talmud Yerushalmi, an olah burnt offering functions as an actual instrument of atonement (le-khapparah mamash) rather than a mere gift, scouring and completing atonement prior to Yom Kippur in a manner analogous to Yom Kippur's effect on negative commandments. For an ordinary positive commandment (aseh), repentance alone grants immediate pardon ("does not move from there before he is pardoned"), so no sacrifice is required. However, for sinful contemplation of idolatry (hirhur avodah zarah)—which carries the status of a negative commandment lacking physical action (lav she-ein bo ma'aseh)—repentance suspends and the olah scours the atonement. The Tannaitic list of four categories of atonement omits sacrificial offerings entirely, just as it omits chatas and asham, focusing strictly on the calendar and existential vehicles of atonement (repentance, Yom Kippur, suffering, and death).

items.h: סִימָן טו
Rectification of the covenant and the return to holiness
תיקון הברית

p: וְהִנֵּה עָוֹן
And behold, the sin
דְּהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה
of wasting seed
הָיָה נִרְאֶה לִי לִפְשׁוֹט
seemed to me to be resolvable
דְּהוּא גַּם כֵּן בִּכְלַל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה,
as also included in a positive commandment,
שֶׁהֲרֵי לֹא מָצִינוּ עָלָיו
for we do not find regarding it
שׁוּם אַזְהָרָה בַּתּוֹרָה בְּהֶדְיָא.
any explicit warning in the Torah.
וְהַתּוֹסָפוֹת
And the Tosafos
(סַנְהֶדְרִין נט, רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב)
(Sanhedrin 59, beginning of side b)
דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "וְהָא"
in the passage beginning "vehah"
כָּתְבוּ
wrote
דְּמִי שֶׁמְּצֻוֶּה עַל פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה
that one commanded about procreation
מְצֻוֶּה שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׁחִית זֶרַע,
is commanded not to destroy seed,
עַיֵּין שָׁם.
see there.
מִשְׁמַע דְּהוּא בִּכְלַל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה
It implies it is included in the positive commandment
דִּפְרוּ וּרְבוּ,
of "be fruitful and multiply,"
וּמִשּׁוּם הָכִי נֶעֱנְשׁוּ עָלֶיהָ
and for that reason they were punished for it
בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל
in the generation of the Flood,
דְּגַם בְּנֵי נֹחַ הָיוּ מְצֻוִּין אָז עַל זֶה.
since the sons of Noach were then also commanded about this.
וְאִם כֵּן הִיא בִּכְלַל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה,
And so it is included in a positive commandment,
דְּאַף שֶׁעוֹבֵר בְּקוּם וַעֲשֵׂה
for even though one transgresses by an act
נִתְבָּאֵר לְעֵיל (אוֹת יג)
it was explained above (letter 13)
דְּסַגִּי בִּתְשׁוּבָה לְבַד.
that teshuvah alone suffices.
וְשָׁם כָּתַבְתִּי כֵן מִדִּנַפְשִׁי
And there I wrote so on my own
מִסְּתִימוּת לְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא,
from the unqualified wording of the Gemara,
וְעַתָּה רָאִיתִי כֵן
and now I have seen so
גַּם בְּסֵפֶר מִשְׁנַת חֲכָמִים
also in the book Mishnas Chachamim
(סִימָן ב אוֹת ו) עַיֵּין שָׁם.
(siman 2, letter 6); see there.
וְאַף עַל גַּב דִּבְנִדָּה
And although in Niddah
(יג, עַמּוּד ב)
(13b)
יָלְפִינַן לֵיהּ מִקְּרָא
we derive it from the verse
דְּ"לֹא תִנְאָף"
"You shall not commit adultery"
"לֹא יְהֵא בְּךָ נִיאוּף,
"let there be no adultery in you,"
בֵּין בַּיָּד בֵּין בָּרֶגֶל",
whether by hand or by foot,"
הָיָה נִרְאֶה לִי לִפְשׁוֹט
it seemed to me to be resolvable
דְּאֵין זוֹ דְּרָשָׁא גְמוּרָה,
that this is not a full derivation,
וּלְהִיּוֹת הַלָּאו אָתֵי לְהָכִי
and that the negative comes for this
וּלְהִיּוֹת בִּכְלַל מִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה
and be included in a negative commandment
דְּגוּף הַלָּאו בְּנִיאוּף גָּמוּר,
only when the negative itself concerns actual adultery,
וְכמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר
and as he said
בְּסֵפֶר הַמִּצְוֹת לָרַמְבַּ"ם
in the Rambam's Sefer HaMitzvos
(מִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה שמ"ז)
(negative commandment 347)
דְּנִכְפְּלָה בָּזֶה אַזְהָרָה,
that the warning was doubled here,
וְהֵבִיא כֵן מֵהַמְּכִילְתָּא
and he brought so from the Mechilta:
"לֹא תִנְאָף, לָמָּה נֶאֱמַר" וְכוּלֵּי,
"'You shall not commit adultery' - why is it said?" etc.,
עַיֵּין שָׁם,
see there,
וְכֵן הוּא בְּסֵפֶר הַחִנּוּךְ
and so it is in Sefer HaChinuch
(מִצְוָה לה),
(commandment 35),
וְלֹא כָתְבוּ שָׁם
and they did not write there
מֵאִסּוּר הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה כְּלָל,
anything of the prohibition of wasting seed at all,
וְעַל כָּרְחָךְ
so of necessity
דְּהִיא אַסְמַכְתָּא בְּעָלְמָא.
it is merely a support-text.
וְהָרַמְבַּ"ם
And the Rambam
(פֶּרֶק כא מִהִלְכוֹת אִסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה, הֲלָכָה יח)
(Forbidden Relations, chapter 21, halachah 18)
כָּתַב שֶׁאִסּוּר גָּדוֹל הוּא
wrote that it is a great prohibition
וְלֹא כָתַב שׁוּם מִקְרָא מִן הַתּוֹרָה עַל זֶה.
and wrote no verse from the Torah for it.
וְאַף שֶׁכָּתַב שָׁם
And though he wrote there
דְּהוּא כְּאִלּוּ שׁוֹפֵךְ דָּמִים
that it is as if he sheds blood,
וְהוּא מֵהַגְּמָרָא (שָׁם, יג, עַמּוּד א),
which is from the Gemara (there, 13a),
וְשָׁם אִיתָא גַּם כֵּן
and there it also says
"כְּאִלּוּ עוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה",
"as if he worships idols,"
וּבָזֶה בְּוַדַּאי
and by this surely
אֵין רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר
he does not mean
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כְּמוֹ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה מַמָּשׁ,
that it is literally like idolatry,
וְהָכִי נָמֵי לְעִנְיַן שְׁפִיכַת דָּמִים
so too regarding bloodshed
לֹא אָמַר אֶלָּא "כְּאִלּוּ"
he said only "as if"
וְלֹא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בִּכְלַל אַזְהָרַת שְׁפִיכַת דָּמִים,
and not that it is included in the warning against bloodshed,
דְּהֲרֵי אֲפִילּוּ עַל עוּבָּרִין וְכוּלֵּי
for even regarding a fetus, etc.,
שֶׁלֹּא הוֹצִיא רֹאשׁוֹ
that has not emerged its head,
אֵין חַיָּיבִין עָלָיו בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל.
there is no liability for it among Israel.
וַאֲפִילּוּ בְּנֵי נֹחַ
And even the sons of Noach,
דְּחַיָּיבִין עַל הָעוּבָּרִין,
who are liable for a fetus,
דַּוְקָא עוּבָּרִין אִתְרַבִּי
only fetuses are included
(בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין נט, עַמּוּד ב)
(in Sanhedrin 59b)
מֵ"הָאָדָם בָּאָדָם",
from "a man within a man,"
אֲבָל הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה
but wasting seed
אֵינוֹ בִּכְלַל אַזְהָרַת שְׁפִיכַת דָּמִים,
is not included in the warning against bloodshed,
וְכַדְּמוּכָח מִדִּבְרֵי תּוֹסָפוֹת הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
as is proven from the words of the aforementioned Tosafos
דְּאַזְהָרָתוֹ רַק מִשּׁוּם מִצְוַת פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה.
that its warning is only due to the commandment of procreation.

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Sefer HaMitzvos, Negative Commandment 347, treats “lo tin’af” as a warning against actual adultery. His Mechilta quotation distinguishes the death penalty already stated from its scriptural warning; he also explains that “lo tin’af” warns both parties, whereas Vayikra 18:20 addresses the man. Sefer HaChinuch 35 likewise treats actual adultery and the repeated warning. Neither entry derives wasteful emission from this warning. Rav Tzadok infers that the Niddah exposition is an asmachta; that inference is his, rather than an express statement by Rambam.

paragraphs.text: Niddah 13a; Bereishis 38:10; Rambam, Issurei Biah 21:18; Sanhedrin 57b. Niddah derives liability to death from Onan—“it was evil in the eyes of Hashem… and He put him to death”—and compares the sin to bloodshed and idolatry. The Rambam codifies it as a “great prohibition” and repeats the bloodshed comparison, but does not place it under the homicide prohibition. Sanhedrin derives a Noahide’s liability for killing a fetus from “the blood of man within man”; R’ Tzadok distinguishes a fetus from seed that has not entered fetal existence. The comparisons therefore express extraordinary severity, while Tosafos’ operative source remains the duty of procreation.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: R’ Tzadok’s opening approach — that the sin of wasteful emission of seed falls under a positive commandment (not a negative), since the Torah states no explicit prohibition against it. Tosafos (Sanhedrin 59b) derives its prohibition from the positive commandment of procreation (“one who is commanded in ‘be fruitful and multiply’ is commanded not to destroy seed”), which is why the generation of the Flood — including the Noahides — was punished for it. As a positive commandment (even though transgressed by an act), it was explained earlier (Siman 13) that teshuvah alone suffices.

paragraphs.text: Sefer Mitzvot Katan 292 places the prohibition among the seventh division’s mitzvos connected with circumcision. It cites “lo tin’af—lo tehaneh la-af,” the warning to one who facilitates adultery, and Onan’s death. The hand-and-foot exposition is in Niddah 13b, whereas the Semak’s received wording here uses af. Rav Tzadok asks whether the Semak intended an independent, formally enumerated full lav, or scriptural support within his practical compendium.

paragraphs.text: Semak, Introduction and §292; Semag, Negative Commandment 126. The Semak’s introduction explicitly directs readers to the Sefer HaMitzvos of R’ Moshe of Coucy—the Semag—and presents the Semak as a seven-day practical handbook of obligations relevant in exile, not merely a fresh count of the 613. Its framework also includes rabbinic obligations. The Semag discusses wasteful emission within Negative Commandment 126 and cites Niddah material there; the separate facilitating-adultery derivation appears at the end of §103. Those distinct locations must not be conflated. Rav Tzadok therefore suggests that the Semak may list the subject separately for practical study while remaining aligned with the Semag’s formal classification.
