inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The Semak places destruction of seed among Torah prohibitions and cites a reading of lo tinaf different from the received Gemara. Rav Tzadok considers whether this need mean a full negative commandment, but acknowledges that the Semak’s plain wording resists that reconciliation.

p: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם
And in any case,
נִרְאֶה גַּם לִפְנֵי דִּבְרָיו
it appears, even according to his words,
אֵינוֹ מִהַלָּאוִין הַלּוֹקִין,
that it is not among the negatives punishable by lashes,
מֵאַחַר שֶׁכָּתַב
since he wrote
דְּבִכְלָל זֶה גַּם כֵּן
that included in this too
אַזְהָרָה לָעוֹקֵב וְכוּלֵּי,
is a warning to one who abets adultery, etc.,
אִם כֵּן הוֹי לָאוֹ שֶׁבְּכְלָלוּת.
then it is a general negative.
וְאִם כֵּן
And so,
הָא אִיכָּא הָרֶמָ"ע
there is the Rema MiFano
בְּעֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת
in Asarah Maamaros
הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל (אוֹת יג)
mentioned above (letter 13)
שֶׁכָּתַב
who wrote
דְּגַם לָאוֹ שֶׁבְּכְלָלוּת
that even a general negative
בְּכְלַל עֲשֵׂה בְּזֶה.
counts as a positive commandment in this regard.
וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר
And although one can say
דְּכָאן הוֹי גַּם כֵּן לָאוֹ שֶׁנִּתָּן
that here too it is a negative that was given
לְאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין,
for a warning of court-imposed death,
דְּהַאַזְהָרָה קָאָי
for the warning refers
בְּנִיאוּף דְּאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ גָּמוּר,
to actual adultery with a married woman,
וְלַהַזְהִיר הָאִשָּׁה
and (the verse) warns the woman
דְּלֹא נִפְקָא לֵיהּ מִ"לֹא תִתֵּן שְׁכָבְתְּךָ"
for it is not derived from "you shall not give your seed,"
וְכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בְּסְמַ"ג שָׁם
as he wrote in the Semag there
וּבְסֵפֶר הַמִּצְוֹת שָׁם,
and in Sefer HaMitzvos there,
עַיֵּין שָׁם.
see there.
וּבְכָהַיָּא גַּוְנָא
And in such a case,
דְּיֵשׁ בְּכָלָּלוֹ אַזְהָרָה
where included within it is a warning
לְאִסּוּר דְּמִיתַת בֵּית דִּין,
for a prohibition of court-imposed death,
חֲשִׁבִינַן לֵיהּ גַּם כֵּן
we also consider it
נִתָּּן לְאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין
given for a warning of court-imposed death,
שֶׁלֹּא לִלָּקוֹת
so that one is not lashed
אַף בְּהָאִסּוּר הַנִּכְלָל בּוֹ
even for the prohibition included in it
שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין,
that carries no court-imposed death,
וְכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ
as they said
(בְּעֵירוּבִין יז, עַמּוּד ב)
(Eruvin 17b)
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת
and see there in Tosafos,
סוֹף דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "לָאוֹ"
end of the passage beginning "lav,"
וּבְתוֹסָפוֹת (סַנְהֶדְרִין סג, עַמּוּד א)
and in Tosafos (Sanhedrin 63a)
דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "מִשּׁוּם"
the passage beginning "mishum"
(פה, סוֹף עַמּוּד א)
(85, end of side a)
דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "הַכֵּהוּ",
the passage beginning "hakehu,"
וּבָלָאוֹ שֶׁנִּתָּן לְאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין
and regarding a negative given for a warning of court-imposed death
נִתְבָּאֵר שָׁם
it was explained there
מֵעֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת
from Asarah Maamaros
דְּאֵינוֹ בִּכְלַל זֶה.
that it is not included in this (rule).
נִרְאֶה לִי
It seems to me
דְּלֹא אָמַר אֶלָּא
that he said (it) only
כְּשֶׁאוֹתוֹ הָאִסּוּר עַצְמוֹ
when that very prohibition
נִתָּּן לְאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית הַדִּין,
is given for a warning of court-imposed death,
אֶלָּא שֶׁהִתְּרוּ בּוֹ לִמְלָקוּת
only that they warned him for lashes
וְלֹא לִמִיתָה,
and not for death,
דְּבִכְהַיָּא גַּוְנָא הוּא עִקָּר הָא
for in such a case this is the essence of that
דְּנִתָּּן לְאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין
which is given for a warning of court-imposed death
(בְּמַכּוֹת יג, עַמּוּד ב)
(in Makkos 13b)
וְבָרַמְבַּ"ם
and in the Rambam
(פֶּרֶק יח מִהִלְכוֹת סַנְהֶדְרִין, הֲלָכָה ב)
(Sanhedrin, chapter 18, halachah 2)
עַיֵּין שָׁם.
see there.
אֲבָל כְּהָאִי דְּאָמַרְנוּ
But in the case we described,
שֶׁאוֹתוֹ הַעִנְיָן אֵין בּוֹ מִיתָה כְּלָל,
where that matter has no death at all,
רַק הוְאִיל
only since
בְּחֵלֶק הַלָּאו שֶׁלְּאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין
in the part of the negative that is for a warning of court-imposed death
אֵין בּוֹ מַלְקוּת,
there are no lashes,
גַּם בְּאִידָךְ שֶׁבְּכִלָּלוֹ
also in the other part within it
לֹא שַׁיָּךְ מַלְקוּת
lashes do not apply,
כִּיוָן דְּלֹא נִתָּּן הַלָּאו לְאַזְהָרַת מַלְקוּת,
since the negative was not given for a warning of lashes,
דָּבָר זֶה מַה שֶּׁאֵין לוֹקִין עָלָיו
this, that one is not lashed for it,
אֵינוֹ מִפְּנֵי חֹמֶר שֶׁבּוֹ
is not because of its severity
וְשֶׁיִהְיֶה עָנְשוֹ חָמוּר,
or that its punishment be severe,
דְּהֲרֵי בְּהַהִיא לֵיכָּא עוֹנֶשׁ מִיתָה הַחָמוּר כְּלָל,
for in that case there is no severe death penalty at all,
בְּכָהַיָּא גַּוְנָא
in such a case
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר
one can say
דְּלֹא אָמַר הָעֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת
that the Asarah Maamaros did not say
לְהַעֲדִיפוֹ מִשָׁאָר לָאוִין שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין כְּלָל,
to make it superior to other unlashed negatives at all,
דְּלֹא אָמַר אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין
for he said it only when they are not lashed
לְהַחֲמִיר בְּעָנְשָׁם
in order to be stricter in their punishment,
כְּמְבוֹאָר בְּדִּבְרָיו שָׁם, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
as is explained in his words there; see there.
וְאִם כֵּן שַׁפִּיר
And so, properly,
הַךְ פִּטּוּר
this exemption
דְּמִשּׁוּם נִתָּּן לְאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין,
that it was given for a warning of court-imposed death,
אֲפִילּוּ אִי נִפְטַר רַק מִשּׁוּם זֶה
even if he is exempt only because of this,
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר
one can say
דְּלָעֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת
that according to the Asarah Maamaros
הוּא בִּכְלַל עֲשֵׂה בְּזֶה,
it counts as a positive commandment in this regard,
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן
and all the more so
דְּהוּא לָאוֹ שֶׁבְּכְלָלוּת גַּם כֵּן
that it is also a general negative
דְּפָטוּר בְּלָאוֹ הַכִּי
that is exempt in any case,
וְלֹא יִגְרַע כֹּחוֹ
and its force is not diminished
מִשּׁוּם דְּיֵשׁ בְּכָלָּלוֹ
because there is within it
גַּם אַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין,
also a warning of court-imposed death,
כִּיוָן דְּלֹא קָאֵי הַמִּיתָה בֵּית דִּין אַפְרָט זֶה.
since the court-imposed death does not apply to this particular case.

paragraphs.text: Shevuos 47b; Aruch, s.v. עקב; Semag, Lavin §103. Shimon ben Tarfon asks, “From where is the warning to the okeiv after an adulterer?” and derives it from “lo tinaf,” read “lo tanif” — do not cause or facilitate adultery. The Aruch, cited by the Semag, explains the okeiv as one who goes about “on his heels” to procure a woman for another man’s adultery. Since the Semak includes both the adulterous act and the assisting conduct beneath the same Scriptural expression, Rav Tzadok treats the warning as a composite prohibition rather than as a dedicated lav for wasteful emission.

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Sefer HaMitzvos, Shoresh 9; Hilchos Sanhedrin 18:2; Rema mi-Fano, Chakor Din I:18. A lav she-bichlalus is one Torah negative that embraces several distinct prohibited acts or meanings. Rambam explains that when two or more prohibitions issue from one undifferentiated lav, the verse is counted as one commandment and does not generate ordinary lashes for each branch; he codifies that a lav she-bichlalus does not carry lashes. Rema mi-Fano consequently includes it among the lighter non-lashed prohibitions whose atonement follows the category of an aseh. This is the formal bridge Rav Tzadok uses here.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra 18:20; Sefer HaMitzvos, Negative Commandment 347; Semag, Lavin §103. “To your fellow’s wife you shall not give your emission” is phrased to the male adulterer and therefore does not by itself warn the married woman. Rambam cites the Mechilta that “lo tinaf” was repeated to warn both parties—“the man and the woman”—while the first verse warns the man alone. The Semag likewise places “lo tinaf” alongside the adultery warning and also records its separate derashah concerning the okeiv. This is why Rav Tzadok can view the same broad expression as containing both a capital adultery warning and a distinct noncapital branch.

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 17b; Tosafos ad loc.; Tosafos, Sanhedrin 63a and 85a. Eruvin supplies the model for a verse whose scope may contain both a capital and a noncapital branch. R’ Yonasan objects to lashes for crossing the Shabbos boundary because “al yetzei ish mimkomo” could also function as the warning for carrying from one domain to another, a capital Shabbos offense; the Gemara invokes the rule that a lav given as the warning for court-imposed death does not carry lashes. Rav Ashi ultimately distinguishes the wording “yetzei” from “yotzi,” but Rav Tzadok cites Tosafos for the broader analytical issue: when one Scriptural warning encompasses a death-bearing act and another act with no death penalty, the lighter branch may also lack lashes because the shared lav was not formulated as an ordinary warning for lashes.

paragraphs.text: Makkos 13b; Rambam, Hilchos Sanhedrin 18:2. Rava explains the dispute concerning a lav ha-nitan l’azharas misas beis din where the offender was warned for lashes rather than execution: R’ Akiva holds that even then the capital-warning lav does not produce lashes. This is Rav Tzadok’s “primary” form: the very act now before us is itself the capital offense. He contrasts it with the derivative form, where the particular branch has no death liability at all.

p: וּבְתְשׁוּבָה כָּתַבְתִּי עוֹד
And in a responsum I wrote further
דְּאֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר
that one can say
דְּדִּיוּק לְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא שָׁם
the precise wording of the Gemara there,
"לֹא תִהְא בְּךָ נִיאוּף,
"let there be no adultery in you,
בֵּין בַּיָּד בֵּין בָּרֶגֶל",
whether by hand or by foot,"
דְּדַוְקָא מְנָאֵף בְּיָד אוֹ רֶגֶל,
is that specifically one who commits adultery by hand or foot,
שֶׁמַּכְנִיס הָאֵבֶר
who inserts the organ
תּוֹךְ יָדוֹ אוֹ בֵּין רַגְלָיו
into his hand or between his legs
עַל דֶּרֶךְ הַכְנָסָתוֹ בָאִשָּׁה
in the manner of insertion into a woman,
שֶׁדּוֹמֶה לְנִיאוּף דְּאִשָּׁה,
which resembles adultery with a woman,
הוּא דְּאִתְרַבִּי אִסּוּר מִּ"לֹא תִנְאָף",
that the prohibition of "you shall not commit adultery" is extended,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ דֶּרֶךְ נִיאוּף,
for this is the way of adultery,
אֲבָל הַמְהַרֵהֵר וּמִתְקַשֶּׁה
but one who fantasizes and becomes aroused
וּמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה
and emits seed in vain
אֵינוֹ בִּכְלַל הַזֶּה,
is not included in this,
וְאִסּוּרוֹ רַק מִשּׁוּם מִצְוַת פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ.
and its prohibition is only due to the commandment of procreation.
וְרָאִייָה מִהָא
And proof from that
(דִּיְבָמוֹת עו, עַמּוּד א)
(in Yevamos 76a)
"מַנּחִיה לֵיה אֲבִי פוּקְרִי וּמַקְרִי" וְכוּלֵּי,
“they place it by his anal opening and induce an emission,” etc.,
"מַעֲבִירִיה קָמֵּיה בִּגְדֵי צְבוֹעִין" וְכוּלֵּי,
"they pass colored garments before him," etc.,
עַיֵּין שָׁם
see there
וּבְבֵית שְׁמוּאֵל
and in Beis Shmuel
(סִימָן כה, סְעִיף קָטָן ב)
(siman 25, small subsection 2)
וּבְבְּכוֹר שׁוֹר
and in Bechor Shor
(בְּנִדָּה שָׁם)
(on Niddah there)
מַיְיתֵי לָהּ לִלְמוֹד מִשָּׁם
he cites it to learn from there
דְּהוּתַר הַךְ אִסּוּר
that this prohibition was permitted
לְצֹרֶךְ כְּהָאִי גַוְנָא,
for such a need,
עַיֵּין שָׁם.
see there.
אֲבָל לֹא בִּיאֲרוּ הַטַּעַם בְּאֶמֶּת
But they did not truly explain the reason
לָמָה הוּתַר אִסּוּר דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא,
why a Torah-level prohibition was permitted,
וְלַסְמַ"ק בְּלָאוֹ,
and according to the Semak, a negative,
מִשּׁוּם צֹרֶךְ הַבְּדִיקָה דְּשָׁם.
because of the need for the examination there.
וְלִפְי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי נִיחָא,
But according to what I wrote it is smooth,
דְּשָׁם דְּמִקְּרִי
for there, where he is induced
עַל יְדֵי הַחִמּוּם אוֹ הַהִרְהוּר
through heating or fantasy
וְלֹא כְּדֶרֶךְ הַמְנַאֲפִים,
and not in the manner of adulterers,
אֵין אִסּוּרוֹ מִשּׁוּם לָאוֹ דְּ"לֹא תִנְאָף"
its prohibition is not due to the negative "you shall not commit adultery"
גַּם לַסְּמַ"ק,
even according to the Semak,
רַק נִלְמָד מִמִּצְוַת פְּרִיָּה וְרִבִּיָּה,
but is learned from the commandment of procreation,
וְאִם כֵּן שָׁם
and so there
דְּהַבְּדִיקָה הוּא לְצֹרֶךְ מִצְוַת פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה
the examination is for the need of the commandment of procreation,
לְהַכְשִׁירוֹ בָּקָּהָל
to qualify him for the community,
מִשּׁוּם הָכִי הוּתַר.
therefore it was permitted.
וְלִפְי זֶה
And accordingly,
גַּם לַסְּמַ"ק
even according to the Semak
לֹא כָּל מוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה בְּלָאוֹ,
not every emission of seed in vain is a negative,
וּבְלָאוֹ הַכִּי
and in any case
הוּא יָחִידָאָה
he is a lone opinion
נֶגֶד רַמְבַּ"ם וְסְמַ"ג וְסֵפֶר הַחִנּוּךְ.
against the Rambam, the Semag, and Sefer HaChinuch.

paragraphs.text: Yevamos 76a: [regarding one whose membrum was punctured, to determine his fitness to marry into the congregation] “Rava son of Rabbah sent to Rav Yosef: let our master teach us, how do we act [to test whether emission opens the puncture]? He said to him: we bring warm barley bread and place it abei pukri [near the orifice] and he emits — and we observe him. Abaye said: is everyone Yaakov our father, of whom it is written (Bereishis 49:3) ‘my strength and the first of my vigor,’ [meaning] that he never saw an emission in his days?! Rather, Abaye said: we pass before him colored garments [‘of a woman, and he muses upon a woman and emits’]. Rava said: is everyone Barzilai the Gileadi [steeped in licentiousness]?! Rather, it is clearest as we said originally.”

paragraphs.text: Beis Shmuel, Even HaEzer 25:2, considers a diagnostic case in which a woman’s blood may have come from her husband and tentatively permits emission to determine its source. He cites the examination in Yevamos 76a, but says the proof can be rejected and leaves the matter tzarich iyun. Rav Tzadok also cites Bechor Shor on Niddah 13a as a precedent for inducing emission to determine fitness to enter the congregation. He observes that the reason for setting aside the usual prohibition still requires explanation; his own procreation-based explanation follows.

p: וְשׁוּב רָאִיתִי
And afterward I saw
בְּתְשׁוּבוֹת פְּנֵי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
in the responsa Pnei Yehoshua
(חֵלֶק בְּ, הַנִּדְפָּס מִחָדָשׁ, סִימָן מד)
(part 2, newly printed, siman 44)
דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "וְהַשְׁאֵלָה הַשֵּׁנִיּה"
the passage beginning "and the second question,"
כָּתַב גַּם כֵּן
he also wrote
דְּהַךְ דְּרָשָׁא דְּ"לֹא תִנְאָף"
that this derivation of "you shall not commit adultery"
בִּלְתִּי סָפֵק
is without doubt
דְּהוּא אַסְמַכְתָּא בְּעָלְמָא.
a mere support-text.
וְהֵבִיא רְאָיָה מִרַמְבַּ"ם הַנִּזְכָּר
And he brought proof from the aforementioned Rambam
שֶׁלֹּא כָתַב דְּלוֹקִין עַל זֶה,
who did not write that one is lashed for this,
וְאֲפִילּוּ מַכּוֹת מִרְדּוּת
and not even disciplinary lashes
לֹא כָתַב אֶלָּא בְּנִידּוּי וְכוּלֵּי,
did he write, only excommunication, etc.,
דְּדָבָר זֶה
for this matter,
שֶׁאֵינוֹ תַקָּנַת חֲכָמִים זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה
which is not a rabbinic enactment, of blessed memory,
רַק נִלְמָד מִקְּרָאֵי
but is learned from verses
וְאֵין בּוֹ לָאוֹ
and has no negative commandment,
אֵין לוֹקֶה מַכּוֹת מִרְדּוּת,
does not receive disciplinary lashes,
וְכְּמוֹ לָשׁוֹן הָרַע וְכַיּוֹצֵא בּוֹ,
like slander and its like,
יְעֻיֵּן שָׁם בְּאָרֶךְ.
see there at length.
וּמַה שֶׁכָּתַב
And what he wrote:
מִדְּאֵין לוֹקִין אֵין רְאָיָה,
from the fact that they do not lash, there is no proof,
דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר מִשּׁוּם
for one can say it is because
דְּהוּא לָאוֹ שֶׁבְּכְלָלוּת
it is a general negative
אוֹ נִתָּּן לְאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין
or given for a warning of court-imposed death
כְּמֹאמַר לְעֵיל.
as stated above.
וּמַה שֶׁכָּתַב
And what he wrote,
דְּגַם מַכַּת מִרְדּוּת אֵין לוֹקֶה
that one also does not receive disciplinary lashes
בְּאִסּוּר דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא כְּהָאִי גַּוְנָא
for a Torah-level prohibition of this kind,
אֶלָּא בְּאִסּוּרִין דְּרַבָּנַן,
but only for rabbinic prohibitions,
לֵיתָא,
is not so,
דְּגַם בְּאִסּוּר חֲצִי שִׁיעוּר דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא
for even in the Torah-level prohibition of a half-measure
וְאֵין בּוֹ לָאוֹ
that has no negative commandment
מְבוֹאָר בְּרַמְבַּ"ם
it is explained in the Rambam
(פֶּרֶק א מִהִלְכוֹת חָמֵץ וּמַצָּה [חו"מ], הֲלָכָה ז)
(Hilchos Chametz uMatzah, chapter1, halachah7)
דְּלוֹקֶה מַכַּת מִרְדּוּת,
that he receives disciplinary lashes,
עַיֵּין שָׁם.
see there.
וּמַה שֶׁכָּתַב מִלָּשׁוֹן הָרַע,
And what he wrote from slander,
שָׁם יֵשׁ לָאוֹ
there is a negative there,
דְּהוּא בְּכְלַל "לֹא תֵלֵךְ רָכִיל"
that it is included in "you shall not go about as a talebearer"
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב
as he wrote
(פֶּרֶק ז מִהִלְכוֹת דֵּעוֹת, הֲלָכָה ב)
(Hilchos Deos, chapter 7, halachah 2)
אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה,
except that it has no action,
וּמְבוֹאָר שָׁם
and it is explained there
(בְּפֶּרֶק א מִהִלְכוֹת חָמֵץ וּמַצָּה, הֲלָכָה ג)
(in chapter 1 of Chametz uMatzah, halachah 3)
בְּלָאוֹ דְּ"בַּל יֵרָאֶה"
regarding the negative of "it shall not be seen"
שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה
that has no action
דְּלוֹקֶה מַכַּת מִרְדּוּת.
that one receives disciplinary lashes.
וְהָא דְּלֹא כָתַב בְּהִלְכוֹת דֵּעוֹת
And that he did not write in Hilchos Deos
דְּלוֹקֶה מַכַּת מִרְדּוּת
that one receives disciplinary lashes
גַּבֵי לָשׁוֹן הָרַע וְרָכִילוּת,
for slander and talebearing,
אוּלַי מִשּׁוּם דְּפָּרִיצֵי בָּהֵו כּוֹלֵּי עָלְמָא
perhaps because everyone is lax about them
וְלֹא מִשְׁמַע כָּל כָּךְ לְאִינָשֵׁי,
and it does not register so much with people,
וְגַם אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְיַסֵּּר הַכֹּל,
and also it is impossible to discipline everyone,
אוֹ דְּסָבִירָא לֵיהּ לְחֹמֶר הָאִסּוּר
or he holds, due to the severity of the prohibition,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב (שָׁם הֲלָכָה ג)
as he wrote (there, halachah 3):
"לֹא נִתְּנָה לִכְפָּרָה בְּמַכַּת מִרְדּוּת".
"It was not given for atonement through disciplinary lashes."
אֶלָּא דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם
But in any case,
לֹא בָּא לְכַפָּרָה כְּמַלְקוּת דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא,
it does not come for atonement like Torah-level lashes,
דְּכִיוָן שֶׁלָקָה הֲרֵי הוּא כְּאָחִיךָ
for once he has been lashed he is "your brother"
רַק לְרַדוֹת הָעוֹבְרִים
but only to subdue the transgressors
שֶׁלֹּא יִפְרְצוּ,
so they not break loose,
וְאִם כֵּן כָּל שֶׁכֵּן
and so all the more so
אִי חָמִיר טָפֵּי
if it is more severe
אוֹ פָּרִיצֵי טָפֵּי
or people are more lax
דְּרָאוּי לְיַסֵּּר וּלְרַדוֹת.
it is fitting to discipline and subdue.
אֲבָל בְּלָאוֹ הַכִּי
But in any case
אֵין דְּרָכוֹ שֶׁל רַמְבַּ"ם לִכְתֹּב
it is not the Rambam's way to write
בְּכָל אִסּוּרִין כֻּלָם
in all prohibitions, all of them,
דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא אוֹ דְּרַבָּנַן
Torah-level or rabbinic,
עוֹנֶשׁ מַכַּת מִרְדּוּת,
the punishment of disciplinary lashes,
וְיֵשׁ הַרְבּה דֻּכְוֹתֶיה
and there are many like it
אַף דּוֹדַאי יֵשׁ בָּהֶו עוֹנֶשׁ מַכַּת מִרְדּוּת
where, though surely they carry the punishment of disciplinary lashes,
לֹא פִּירֵשׁ בְּחִבּוּרוֹ,
he did not specify in his work,
וְכָתַבְתִּי מִזֶּה כְּבָר בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר.
and I already wrote about this elsewhere.

paragraphs.text: Responsa Pnei Yehoshua, II, §44 (s.v. veha-she’eilah ha-sheniyah). The responsum addresses a patient whose physicians believed that emitting seed could cure him. Pnei Yehoshua permits it when the medical benefit is certain, explaining that the comparisons to bloodshed and forbidden relations express severity rather than the formal law of yehareg ve’al ya’avor. He further calls the derashah from “lo tinaf” an asmachta, arguing from Rambam’s omission of both Torah lashes and makkos mardus. Rav Tzadok accepts neither proof: the absence of Torah lashes can follow from lav she-bichlalus or lav ha-nitan l’azharas misas beis din, and Rambam’s silence about makkos mardus is not itself dispositive.

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Chametz uMatzah 1:7: eating any amount of chametz on Pesach is prohibited by Torah law, although the prescribed liability requires a kezayis; deliberate consumption of less than that amount receives makkos mardus. This directly supports Rav Tzadok’s response that disciplinary lashes are not confined to newly enacted rabbinic prohibitions.

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Chametz uMatzah 1:3, assigns makkos mardus for retaining chametz without an act, although Torah lashes do not apply. Hilchos Deos 7:2 places lashon hara within “lo telech rachil,” and 7:3 describes its exceptional gravity. Rav Tzadok compares these cases when considering why Rambam does not specify disciplinary lashes for lashon hara. His proposed explanations concern that omission; they are not additional rulings stated by Rambam.

paragraphs.text: Makkos 23a; Devarim 25:3; Rambam, Hilchos Sanhedrin 24:4. The Mishnah expounds “veniklah achicha le’einecha”: once the offender has received the Torah-prescribed lashes, he is again “your brother,” expressing judicial atonement and restored standing. Makkos mardus has a different function. Rambam describes the court’s extraordinary authority to strike or otherwise discipline when needed to strengthen Torah observance and prevent breach. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes fixed Torah lashes, which complete a formal kapparah, from discretionary chastisement intended to subdue ongoing transgression and protect the communal fence.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Pnei Yehoshua likewise treats the lo tinaf derivation as an asmachta, arguing from the Rambam’s omission of lashes. Rav Tzadok challenges the force of that proof and the claim that disciplinary lashes apply only to rabbinic prohibitions.

p: וּבְהָאִי דְּאָתִינַן
And in our case
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר
one can say
כִּיוָן דְּכָתַב נִידּוּי
that since he wrote excommunication,
דְּעֲדִיפָא מִמַּכַּת מִרְדּוּת
which is stronger than disciplinary lashes,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (פְּסָחִים נב, עַמּוּד א)
as they said (Pesachim 52a),
וּבְזֶה יֵשׁ חִיוּב נִידּוּי
and for this there is liability for excommunication
אֲפִילּוּ בְּמַקְשֶׁה עַצְמוֹ לְבַדוֹ
even for one who merely arouses himself alone,
כָּל שֶׁכֵּן בְּמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה,
all the more so one who emits seed in vain,
לֹא שַׁיָּךְ לִכְתֹּב עוֹד מַכַּת מִרְדּוּת,
it is not relevant to write disciplinary lashes as well,
דְּתְּרֵּי לֹא עָבִידְנַן,
for we do not do two (punishments),
וּבִמְקוֹם שֶׁכָּתַב מַכַּת מִרְדּוּת אֵין מְנַדִּין,
and where he wrote disciplinary lashes they do not excommunicate,
וְהָכָא דְּמְנַדִּין וְעָבְדִי בֵּיה
and here, where excommunication is imposed, applying
הַחָמוּר (לָכֵן)
the graver penalty, therefore
לֹא כָתַב מַכַּת מִרְדּוּת.
he did not write disciplinary lashes.
אֲבָל מִדְּלֹא מַיְיתֵי כְּלָל בְּזֶה
But from his not citing at all here
קְרָא דְּ"לֹא תִנְאָף"
the verse "you shall not commit adultery,"
מִשְׁמַע וַדַּאי
it surely implies
דְּלֹא סָבִירָא לֵיהּ
that he does not hold
שֶׁיִהְיֶה בָּזֶה לָאוֹ גָּמוּר.
that this is a full negative.
וְשׁוּב מָצָאתִי
And afterward I found
בְּפִירוּשׁ הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת לָרַמְבַּ"ם
in the Rambam's commentary on the Mishnah
(פֶּרֶק ז דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין)
(Sanhedrin, chapter 7)
מִשְׁנַת "הַבָּא עַל הַזָּכוּר"
on the Mishnah "one who lies with a male"
כָּתַב:
he wrote:
"וּמִי שֶׁבָּא דֶּרֶךְ אֵבָרִים" וְכוּלֵּי
"and one who comes by way of limbs," etc.
(זֶה כָּתַב גַּם בְּחִבּוּרוֹ בְּפֶּרֶק כא מִהִלְכוֹת אִסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה)
(he wrote this also in his Yad, chapter 21 of Forbidden Relations)
"אוֹ מְשַּׁמֵּשׁ בְּאֵבֶר מִאֵבָרָיו
"or uses one of his organs
לְכַוּנַת הַנָאָה
for the purpose of pleasure
בְּאֵיזֶה אֵבֶר שֶׁנָּגַע מִאֶבָרֵי גוּפוֹ,
with any organ of his body that touched,
כְּאוֹתָם הַמִּתְעַנְגִּים בְּיָד וְרֶגֶל,
like those who take pleasure by hand and foot,
וְזֶה הַמַּעֲשֶׂה מִהַזְּנוּת
and this act, of promiscuity,
קוֹרְאִין אוֹתוֹ חֲכָמִים
the Sages call
מְנַאֲפִים בְּיָד וְבָרֶגֶל וְכֵן וְכוּלֵּי,
committing adultery by hand and foot, and so on, etc.,
כָּל זֶה אָסּוּר
all this is forbidden
וּמִכִּין לָעוֹבֵר מַלְקוּת,
and the transgressor is struck with lashes,
וְכָל אֵלּוּ נִכְלָלִין בְּשֵׁנֵי לָאוִין וְכוּלֵּי:
and all these are included in two negatives, etc.:
'לֹא תִקְרְבוּ לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה' וְכוּלֵּי,
'do not approach to uncover nakedness,' etc.,
'לִבְלַתִּי עֲשׂוֹת כְּחֻקוֹת' וְגוֹמֵר.
'so as not to do the practices,' etc.
וְכֵן אָסּוּר לְהָרִיחַ בֻּשָׂמִים
And it is likewise forbidden to smell perfumes
שֶׁעַל הָעֶרְוָה וְכוּלֵּי,
on the nakedness, etc.,
אֲבָל אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב עַל זֶה מַלְקוּת
but he is not liable to lashes for this,
אַעֲפִּי שֶׁאָמַר 'לֹא תִנְאָף לֹא תִהְנֶה לָאַף',
although it says 'you shall not commit adultery; you shall not benefit the nose,'
לִפְי שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין מִדְּרָשָׁא",
because one is not lashed from a derivation,"
עַד כָּאן.
end of quote.
וְהִנֵּה גַּם הוּא גוֹרֵס
And behold, he too reads
הָא דְּ"לֹא תִהְנֶה לָאַף" שֶׁבְּסְמַ"ק הַנִּזְכָּר,
"you shall not benefit the nose" as in the aforementioned Semak,
אֲבָל הוּא מְפָרֵשׁ
but he explains it
לְהָרִיחַ מִבֻּשָׂמִים
as smelling perfumes,
שֶׁמֵּרִיחַ וְנֶהֱנֶה בְּאַפּוֹ.
that he smells and benefits with his nose.
וּמִכָּאן לָקַח אִסּוּר זֶה
And from here he took this prohibition
שֶׁכָּתַב
that he wrote
(בְּפֶּרֶק כא מִהִלְכוֹת אִסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה, הֲלָכָה ב)
(in chapter 21 of Forbidden Relations, halachah 2)
וְדִּמִכִּין עַל זֶה מַכַּת מִרְדּוּת
and that one is struck with disciplinary lashes for this
כִּיוָן דְּנִלְמַד מִקְּרָא,
since it is learned from a verse,
וְהָרַב הַמַּגִּיד שָׁם
and the Maggid Mishneh there
צִיּן לְשַׁבָּת (סב, עַמּוּד ב)
cited Shabbos (62b)
וְשָׁם נִזְכָּר עוֹנֶשׁ הַנָּשִׁים
where the punishment of the women is mentioned,
הַמְתִּיזוֹת בֻּשָׂמִים
who sprinkle perfumes
לְהַכְנִיס יֵצֶר הָרָע בַּבַּחוּרִים,
to bring the evil inclination into young men,
וְהָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר זֶה,
and he should have said this,
אֲבָל מַה שֶּׁאָמַר
but what he said
הוּא עַל הָאֲנָשִׁים הַמְרִיחִים
is about the men who smell
לֹא לָקַח מִהַנִּזְכָּר
he did not take from the aforementioned
רַק מִהַהִיא דְּ"לֹא תִהְנֶה לָאַף"
but only from that of "you shall not benefit the nose"
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בְּעַצְמוֹ בְּפִירוּשׁ הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת הַנִּזְכָּר,
as he himself wrote in the aforementioned commentary on the Mishnah,
וְהָרַב הַמַּגִּיד לֹא רָאָה פִּירוּשׁ הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת
and the Maggid Mishneh did not see the commentary on the Mishnah
וְגַם לֹא הָיָה לְפָנָיו הַנֻּסְחָא בַּגְּמָרָא כֵּן
and also did not have the Gemara reading so before him
רַק כְּלָפָנֵינוּ
only as before us
וְלֹא בְּאֵיזֶה בָּרַיְיתָא אַחֶרֶת,
and not in some other baraisa,
וְעַל כֵּן הוּצְרַךְ לְבַקֵּשׁ מִמֶּרְחָק.
so he had to seek from afar.
וּמִלָּשׁוֹן פִּירוּשׁ הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת מִשְׁמַע
And from the wording of the commentary on the Mishnah it implies
דְּדִּרְשָׁא גְּמוּרָה דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא הוּא,
that it is a full Torah-level derivation,
דְּלֹא כָתַב דְּהוּא אַסְמַכְתָּא
for he did not write it is a support-text
רַק דְּמִדְּרָשָׁא לֹא מַלְקִינַן,
only that we do not lash from a derivation,
וְהַיְנוּ עַל דֶּרֶךְ חֲצִי שִׁיעוּר
which is like a half-measure,
דְּאַעֲפִּי שֶׁאָסּוּר מִן הַתּוֹרָה לְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
for although it is forbidden by the Torah according to Rabbi Yochanan
מִרִיבּוּיָא דְּכָל,
from the amplification of "kol,"
אֵין לוֹקִין.
one is not lashed.
וְכַיּוֹצֵא בּוֹ
And similarly,
דְּאֵין עוֹנְשִׁין מִן הַדִּין
that we do not punish from logic,
אַעֲפִּי שֶׁקַל וָחוֹמֶר הוּא אַחַת מִשּׁלֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה מִדּוֹת
although a fortiori reasoning is one of the thirteen principles
שֶׁהַתּוֹרָה נִדְרֶשֶׁת,
by which the Torah is expounded,
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן דְּרָשָׁא כְּהָאִי גַּוְנָא
all the more so a derivation of this kind
שֶׁאֵינוֹ מִּשְׁלֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה מִדּוֹת.
that is not among the thirteen principles.
וְטוֹבָא יֵשׁ כְּהָאִי גַּוְנָא
And there are many of this kind
דְּנָפַק לֵיהּ מִדְּרָשָׁא דְּקָרְאָא
derived from a scriptural derivation
וְהוּא אִסּוּר דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא וְאֵין לוֹקִין,
that are Torah-level prohibitions without lashes,
וְאַף שֶׁדְּרָשׁוּהוּ מִגּוּף לְשׁוֹן הַאַזְהָרָה,
and although they derived it from the very wording of the warning,
אֵין עִקָּר אַזְהָרַת הַלָּאו
the main warning of the negative is not
אֶלָּא עַל נִיאוּף מַמָּשׁ כְּפָשְׁטֵיהּ.
except on actual adultery in its plain sense.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 52a — nidui compared with makkos mardus. Rav Yosef punished Rav Nasan bar Asya for violating the second festival day. In one version he chose excommunication and explained that it was more severe than lashes; the alternate version chose lashes for a Torah scholar because excommunication was too severe for him. Rav Tzadok uses this comparison to suggest why Rambam records nidui here without also listing makkos mardus: the more severe sanction may replace the lesser one. The Gemara itself compares their severity; the broader rule that both are not administered together is Rav Tzadok’s inference.

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Peirush HaMishnayos, Sanhedrin 7:4; Issurei Biah 21:2; Mekhilta de-Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai 20:13 — limb-contact and the nose-derashah: Rambam places limb-based gratification under Vayikra 18:6 and 18:30, but separately derives the ban on smelling an ervah’s perfume from “lo tinaf—lo tehaneh la’af,” stating that Torah lashes do not follow from a derashah. Issurei Biah nevertheless assigns makkos mardus to intentional smelling or gazing. Shabbos, cited by the Maggid Mishneh, describes women using perfume to arouse men. Rav Tzadok distinguishes that case from Rambam’s exact nose-derashah and treats the latter as a Torah prohibition without Torah lashes. In Se’if 8 Rav Tzadok draws a further conclusion from Rambam’s wording: “hand and foot” can describe limb-based contact with an ervah rather than wasteful emission. Mekhilta de-Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai preserves separate “lo tinaf” interpretations concerning pleasure through the nose and sin through hand, foot, eye, and heart. That Midrash supports separating the derashos, but it does not state Rav Tzadok’s precise physical interpretation.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 74a; Sanhedrin 54a — a Torah prohibition without Torah lashes. R’ Yochanan rules that chatzi shiur is prohibited by Torah law because it can combine into the full measure, deriving inclusion from “all fat,” although the prescribed Torah punishment requires the full measure. Sanhedrin discusses the rule “ein onshin min hadin”: even a valid legal inference does not automatically create a corporal penalty without an explicit penal source. Rav Tzadok applies the same structure here. “Lo tehaneh la’af” may establish a Torah-level prohibition, while the plain warning of “lo tinaf” remains directed to actual adultery; therefore no Torah lashes follow from this secondary derashah.

p: וְהִנֵּה רַמְבַּ"ם וְסְמַ"ק עַצְמָם
And behold, the Rambam and the Semak themselves
לֹא הִרְאוּ מָקוֹם הַמַּאֲמָר
did not show the source of the saying
"לֹא תִהְנֶה לָאַף",
"you shall not benefit the nose,"
וְרַק בְּסְמַ"ק שָׁם
and only in the Semak there
צִיּן הַמַּצִּין מַרְאֵה מָקוֹם לְנִדָּה,
did the annotator cite a source in Niddah,
לִפְי שֶׁשָּׁם מַיְיתוּ מִמִּקְרָא זֶה
because there they cite from this verse
לְאִיסּוּר הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה.
for the prohibition of wasting seed.
וְצָרִיךְ לִדְחֹק וּלְפָרֵשׁ
And one must stretch and explain
לִפְי דִּבְרָיו
according to his words
דְּרוֹצֶה לוֹמַר
that he means
שֶׁלֹּא יִגְרוֹם הַנָאָה
that he not give pleasure
לְמַלְאָךְ הַמַּשְׁחִית הַנִּקְרָא "אַף",
to the destroying angel called "af,"
כִּידוּעַ בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ
as is known in the holy Zohar
(פָּרָשַׁת בְּרֵאשִׁית נז, רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א)
(Parashas Bereishis 57, beginning of side a)
דְּבְּעָוֹן זֶה יָהִיב חִילָא וְתוֹקְפָא לְרוּחָא מְסָאֲבָא
that through this sin one gives strength and power to the impure spirit,
עַיֵּין שָׁם,
see there,
וְהוּא דָּחוּק.
but that is forced.
וְיוֹתֵר נִרְאֶה
More likely
כְּפִירוּשׁ רַמְבַּ"ם הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל,
is like the aforementioned explanation of the Rambam,
אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּבָרַיְיתָא דְּנִדָּה שָׁם
except that it is not in the baraisa of Niddah there
וְדִּמְסַיֵּם עַל זֶה בְּיָד וְבָרֶגֶל
and since it concludes on this "by hand and foot,"
אִי אֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר כֵּן.
it is impossible to say so.
וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר
And we must say
דְּלִפְי דַּעַת הָרַמְבַּ"ם
that according to the Rambam
הָיָה הַגִּירְסָא
the reading was
"דָּבָר אַחֵר, אֵלּוּ הַמְנַאֲפִים בְּיָד וְבָרֶגֶל",
"Another matter: these are the adulterers by hand and foot,"
וְזֶהוּ דֶּרֶשׁ אַחֵר.
and this is a different derivation.
(וְאוּלַי גַּם בְּסְמַ"ק יֵשׁ חִסּוּר לָשׁוֹן
(And perhaps in the Semak too there is a missing phrase,
וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר תְּחִלָּה כְּלָשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא
and one must first say the wording of the Gemara,
וְאַחַר כָּךְ "דָּבָר אַחֵר, לֹא תִהְנֶה לָאַף",
and afterward "another matter: you shall not benefit the nose,"
וְאֶפְשָׁר שֶׁדָּבָר זֶה לוּקָּח מִמָּקוֹם אַחֵר
and it is possible that this matter was taken from another source,
וּמֵאִיזֶה בָּרַיְיתָא אַחֶרֶת
and from some other baraisa,
וְאֵינוֹ בְּבָרַיְיתָא דְּנִדָּה כְּלָל,
and not in the baraisa of Niddah at all,
אֲבָל רָאִיתִי בְּסְמַ"ק
but I saw in the Semak
כְּתָב יָד יָשׁין עַל קָלָף
a handwritten manuscript on parchment
מִשְׁנַת קט
from the year 109
גַּם כֵּן הַגִּירְסָא כַּדִּפְוּס.)
that also has the reading as in the printed edition.)

Rav Tzadok is addressing this difference in the received texts, rather than simply translating the printed Gemara.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I, Bereishis 56b–57a (core passage 57a; Bereshit 97:2–6) — giving power to the spirit of impurity: (with the Sulam translation): “‘for the wickedness of man was great’ (Bereishis 6:5) — they committed all the transgressions, yet the measure of their guilt was not complete until they spilled blood in vain upon the earth. And who are they? They are those who corrupt their way (their seed) upon the earth. And this is what is written, ‘only evil all the day’ (ibid.); it is written here ‘only evil,’ and it is written there (Bereishis 38:7) ‘and Er, Yehudah’s firstborn, was evil in the eyes of Hashem.’ R’ Yosi said: is not ‘evil’ [the same as] ‘wicked’? He said to him: no — ‘wicked’ [applies] even [to] one who raised his hand against his fellow though he did nothing to him, as it says, ‘and he said to the wicked one, why do you strike your fellow’ — ‘struck’ is not said, but ‘strike.’ But ‘evil’ is called only one who corrupts his way and defiles himself and defiles the earth, and gives power and might to the spirit of impurity called ‘evil,’ as it says ‘only evil all the day’; and he does not enter the palace of Hashem and does not see the face of the Shechinah, since through this sin the Shechinah departs from the world. … Come and see: when a person is defiled (through this sin), he is not remembered by the Holy One for good, and at all times he is remembered for evil, from that spirit of impurity called ‘evil.’” Rav Tzadok cites this passage only to supply the spiritual idea behind a possible reading of “Af”; the Zohar itself does not interpret the Semak’s wording. Compare Peri Tzadik, Kedoshim §12, where Rav Tzadok likewise discusses pegam ha-bris in Zoharic terms while stressing that teshuvah cleanses the defect and reveals Israel’s underlying holiness.

p: וְהִנֵּה.
And behold.
מִפִּירוּשׁ הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
From the aforementioned commentary on the Mishnah
מְבוֹאָר פִּירוּשׁ אַחֵר
another explanation is evident
עַל הָא דְּבְּיָד וְרֶגֶל גַּם כֵּן,
of "by hand and foot" as well,
דְּאֵין רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר
that it does not mean
עַל הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה בְּיָד וְרֶגֶל,
wasting seed by hand and foot,
רַק עַל הַמַּכְנִיס וְמַמְעֵךְ
but on one who inserts and presses
בְּאֶצְבּעוֹת יָדָיו אוֹ רַגְלָיו
with the fingers of his hands or feet
בְּאִשָּׁה כְּדֶרֶךְ נִיאוּף.
in a woman, in the manner of adultery.
וְאַף דְּבְּנִדָּה שָׁם
And although in Niddah there
מִקָּמֵּי הָכִי אִיתָא
just before this it says
לָשׁוֹן "הַמְנַאֲפִים בְּיָד"
the wording "those who commit adultery by hand"
עַל פָּסוּק "יְדֵיכֶם דָּמִים מָלֵאוּ"
on the verse "your hands are full of blood,"
דְּקָאָי אַעָוֹן זֶה
which refers to this sin,
דְּשָׁיַּךְ "דָּמִים מָלֵאוּ",
to which "full of blood" applies,
וְכֵן הוּא בְּרַמְבַּ"ם
and so in the Rambam
(בְּהִלְכוֹת אִסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה שָׁם)
(Forbidden Relations, there)
לָשׁוֹן זֶה עַל עָוֹן זֶה,
this wording is on this sin,
שָׁם נָקַט רַק יָד
there he mentions only "hand"
וְכֵן בַּקָּרְא כָּתִיב רַק "יְדֵיכֶם",
and so in the verse only "your hands" is written,
אֲבָל בְּרֶגֶל מַמָּשׁ לֹא מִשְׁתַּכַח לָהּ,
but with an actual foot it is not found,
וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים
and in any case
לָאוֹ אוֹרְחֵיהּ
it is not his way
לְשַׁפְשֵׁף בְּאֵבֶר
to rub with the organ
לְהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה,
to waste seed,
וְלֹא הָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר "רֶגֶל" אֶלָּא "יְרֵכַיִם".
and he should not have said "foot" but "thighs."
וְאַף דְּמָצִינוּ בְּכַּמָּה דּוּכְּתֵי בְּקְרָאֵי
And although we find in several places in Scripture
דְּקָרְאוּ גַּם לִירֵכַיִם "רְגָלִים",
that they called thighs too "feet,"
כְּבָר אָמְרוּ
they already said
(בְּיְבָמוֹת קג, סוֹף עַמּוּד א)
(Yevamos 103, end of side a)
בְּכוּלְהוּ דְּהוּא לִלְשָׁנָא מַעְלִיָּא
regarding all of them that it is a refined expression,
וְלֹא שַׁיָּךְ כְּלָל הָכָא
and it does not apply at all here
גַּבֵי הַמְנַאֲפִים בְּעַצְמָם
regarding the adulterers themselves,
דְּשַׁפִּיר הָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר בְּזֶה "יְרֵכַיִם".
for he properly should have said "thighs" here.
גַּם מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ "רֶגֶל" לָשׁוֹן יָחִיד,
Also, that they said "foot" in the singular,
וּבְחַד יָרֵךְ לֹא מִשְׁתַּכַח לָהּ
and with one thigh it is not possible
לְהַקִּיף הָאֵבֶר כְּבָיָד,
to encircle the organ as with a hand,
וְהָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר לָשׁוֹן רַבִּים.
and he should have said the plural.
וְגַם מִהָא דְּדָרַשִׁינַן עַל "לֹא תִנְאָף",
And also from this, that we derive from "you shall not commit adultery,"
וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה אָמְרוּ
and our Sages, of blessed memory, said
דְּאֵין נִיאוּף אֶלָּא בְּאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ,
that adultery is only with a married woman,
רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר
meaning
דְּאֵין הָכִי נָמֵי
that indeed
גַּם הָכָא בְּאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ קָאָי,
here too it refers to a married woman,
אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְנַאֵף מַמָּשׁ בְּאָבְרוֹ
except that he does not commit actual adultery with his organ
רַק בְּיָד וְרֶגֶל,
only by hand and foot,
וְאַיִּידִי דְּמַיְיתֵי לְעֵיל
and since earlier he cites
מְנָאֵף בְּיָד דְּמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה,
one who commits adultery by hand, i.e., emits seed in vain,
מַיְיתֵי גַּם כֵּן מִין אַחֵר מִמְּנַאֲפִים בְּיָד וְרֶגֶל
he also cites another kind of adulterers by hand and foot
וְלֹא קָאָי אַקּוֹדֵם.
and it does not refer to the earlier one.
וְאַף דְּבָרִי"ף
And although in the Rif
(פֶּרֶק שְׁמוֹנָה שְׁרָצִים)
(chapter "Shemoneh Sheratzim")
הַגִּירְסָא כְּדְתַנָּא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל וְכוּלֵּי
the reading is "as taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael," etc.,
וְמַיְיתֵי לָהּ אַדְּלֵעֵיל,
and he cites it on what precedes,
וְכֵן הָא דְּמְסַיֵּם עָלָיו "קָרֵי בֵּיהּ" וְכוּלֵּי
and so that it concludes on it, "read in it," etc.,
מִשְׁמַע כֵּן כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל,
it implies so, as I wrote above,
וְגַם בְּהָרַב הַמַּגִּיד
and also in the Maggid Mishneh
(בְּהִלְכוֹת אִסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה)
(Forbidden Relations)
הֶעֱתִיק הַלָּשׁוֹן דְּתַנָּא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
he copied the wording "taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael,"
עַיֵּין שָׁם.
see there.
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר
One can say
לִפְנֵי רַמְבַּ"ם
that before the Rambam
הָיָה הַגִּירְסָא תַּנָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
the reading was "Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael"
בְּלֹא "דְּ" כְּלָפָנֵינוּ,
without the "d" (of "de-"), as before us,
וְמְפָרֵשׁ לָהּ עִנְיָן בְּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ,
and he explains it as a matter of its own,
וְלֹא זָכַר עַל זֶה הַדֵּּרֶשׁ מִּ"לֹא תִנְאָף",
and he did not mention for this the derivation from "you shall not commit adultery,"
כִּי דְּאַדְרָשָׁא לֹא מַלְקִינַן,
since we do not lash on a derivation,
וְהוּא מַיְיתֵי עַל זֶה לָאוֹ גָּמוּר
and he cites for this a full negative,
דְּ"לֹא תִקְרְבוּ" לְמַלְקוּת גַּם כֵּן כַּנַּזְכָּר.
"do not approach," for lashes as well, as stated.
וְהָא דְּדָרְשׁוּהוּ גַּם כֵּן מִּ"לֹא תִנְאָף"
And that they also derived it from "you shall not commit adultery"
הוּא לְהַחְמִיר עָלָיו,
is to be stricter about it,
לֹאמַר שֶׁקָרָא אָחַשָּׁבָה לְהָאִי כְּמְנָאֵף מַמָּשׁ.
to say that Scripture considers this like actual adultery.
וּבְחִבּוּרוֹ לֹא כָתַב רַמְבַּ"ם זֶה
And in his composition the Rambam did not write this
(אִסּוּר הַמִּשְׁמוּשׁ וְכוּלֵּי)
(the prohibition of fondling, etc.)
דְּאִסּוּרוֹ וְחִיוּב מַלְקוּת הוּא לָמֵד
for its prohibition and liability to lashes he learns
מִכְּלָל חִיבּוּק וְנִישּׁוּק,
from the category of embracing and kissing,
וּמִקָּל וָחוֹמֶר
and by a fortiori reasoning,
דְּעַל כָּל פָּנִים הוֹי קְרִיבָה
that in any case it is approaching
וְלֹא צָרִיךְ לְפָרֵשׁ,
and there is no need to specify,
וְהַחוֹמֶר שֶׁבּוֹ
and the severity in it,
שֶׁדְּרָשׁוּהוּ מִקְּרָא דְּ"לֹא תִנְאָף"
that they derived it from "you shall not commit adultery,"
אֵין בּוֹ נִפְקָא מִיּה לְדִינָא.
makes no practical difference in law.

paragraphs.text: Niddah 13b; Yeshayah 1:15; Rambam, Issurei Biah 21:18 — two adjacent formulations: The Gemara first explains “your hands are full of blood” as referring to “those who commit adultery with the hand,” and immediately afterward records the academy of R’ Yishmael’s exposition of “lo tinaf” as adultery “with hand or foot.” Rambam applies the first formulation specifically to wasteful emission and likewise speaks only of the hand. Rav Tzadok argues that this does not determine the second teaching: if it begins a separate unit, Rambam’s Peirush HaMishnayos can read “hand and foot” as sexual contact with a forbidden woman. The separation of the two clauses is Rav Tzadok’s analysis; the printed Gemara itself places them consecutively.

paragraphs.text: Yevamos 103a — “feet” as a euphemism for the thighs or private area: While defining the anatomical boundary of regel for chalitzah, the Gemara tests verses that seem to use “feet” for the upper leg or private area. It first explains Devarim 28:57 by the birthing position, and then calls the expressions in II Shemuel 19:25, I Shemuel 24:4, Shoftim 3:24, and Shoftim 5:27 “lishana ma’alya,” refined euphemistic speech. Rav Tzadok’s point is that this convention does not naturally explain a technical description of the offenders themselves: there the baraisa could have stated “thighs” directly if that were its intended physical mechanism.

paragraphs.text: Rashi on Shemos 20:13 and Devarim 5:17 — ni’uf denotes adultery with a married woman: Rashi states that the Torah’s term ni’uf refers specifically to relations with an eshes ish, citing the formulations of Vayikra 20:10 and Yechezkel 16:32. Rav Tzadok applies that lexical rule to the derashah in Niddah: “with hand and foot” would still concern an eshes ish, although the prohibited act is performed through other limbs rather than intercourse. Neither Rashi nor the cited verses spell out that extension; it is Rav Tzadok’s inference from the continued use of the word ni’uf.

paragraphs.text: Rif, Shabbos 39b, reads ‘as taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael,’ connecting the hand-and-foot teaching with the preceding ‘adulterers with the hand.’ Maggid Mishneh, Issurei Biah 21:18, likewise has a connective ‘for it was taught.’ The received Niddah 13b begins simply ‘the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught.’ Rav Tzadok therefore proposes that Rambam read the teaching independently. This is his reconstruction of Rambam’s text, not a manuscript report supplied by those commentators.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok reads the Rambam’s Commentary on the Mishnah as distinguishing emission of seed from a separate form of prohibited contact with a woman using the hands or feet. He argues that the latter’s legal warning and lashes arise from prohibited approach, rather than from the lo tinaf derashah alone.

p: וְלִפְי זֶה
And accordingly,
לְרַמְבַּ"ם לֵיכָּא שׁוּם דֶּרֶשׁ
according to the Rambam there is no derivation
מִקְּרָא דְּ"לֹא תִנְאָף"
from the verse "you shall not commit adultery"
עַל מוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה.
regarding one who emits seed in vain.
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּפִירוּשׁ הַמִּשְׁנָה,
And see there in the commentary on the Mishnah,
אַחַר כָּךְ כָּתַב:
afterward he wrote:
"וְכָבָר הִזְהִירוּ חֲכָמִים הַרְבּה עַל הַהַרְהוּר" וְכוּלֵּי,
"And the Sages already warned greatly about (sinful) thought," etc.,
"וְהִאֱרִיכוּ לָשׁוֹן
"and they lengthened the wording
לְאַיֵּּם וְלַהַפְחִיד
to threaten and frighten
כָּל הַמַּקְשֶׁה עַצְמוֹ לְדַעַת
anyone who arouses himself intentionally
וְהַמוֹצִיא שִׁכְבַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה,
or emits seed in vain,
וְבִיאֲרוּ שֶׁכָּל זֶה אָסּוּר
and they clarified that all this is forbidden
אֲבָל אֵינָם מְחַיְבִין מַלְקוּת
but they do not obligate lashes
בְּשׁוּם דָּבָר בְּכִיוֹצֵא בּוֹ",
for anything like it,"
עַד כָּאן.
end of quote.
הִנֵּה יִיחֵס אִסּוּר זֶה לַחֲכָמִים
Behold, he attributes this prohibition to the Sages
שֶׁבִּיאֲרוּהוּ,
who clarified it,
וְלֹא מַיְיתֵי עָלֶיהָ שׁוּם דֶּרֶשׁ מִקְּרָא
and he cites for it no scriptural derivation
כְּדְמַיְיתֵי לִפְנֵי זֶה עַל הַמְרִיחַ כְֻּנַזְכָּר.
as he cited before this regarding smelling, as mentioned.
(וְמַה שֶׁכָּתַב
(And what he wrote,
דְּאֵינָם מְחַיְבִין מַלְקוּת,
that they do not obligate lashes,
נִרְאֶה דְּרוֹצֶה לוֹמַר
it appears he means
גַּם מַכַּת מִרְדּוּת וּמַלְקוּת דִּרַבָּנַן.
also disciplinary lashes and rabbinic lashes.
דְּשָׁם לִפְנֵי זֶה כָּתַב
For there before this he wrote:
כְּשֶׁיִתְיַחֵד עִם הָעֶרְוָה
when one secludes himself with a forbidden relative
אוֹ עִם פְּנוּיָה
or with an unmarried woman
מַלְקִין לְשִׁנְיֶהֶם,
they lash both,
וְהוּא מִהַגְּמָרָא (קִדּוּשִׁין פא, עַמּוּד א)
and it is from the Gemara (Kiddushin 81a),
וְרוֹצֶה לוֹמַר מַכַּת מִרְדּוּת דִּרַבָּנַן,
meaning rabbinic disciplinary lashes,
וְכַמָּה שֶּׁאָמַר רַשִּׁי
and as Rashi said
דִּמְלָקוּת דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא לֵיכָּא
that there are no Torah-level lashes
אֲפִילּוּ בְּיִחוּד דְּעֶרְוָה
even for seclusion with a forbidden relative,
דְּמַיְיתֵי (שָׁם פ:, עַמּוּד ב)
for which he cites (there, 80b)
רֶמֶז מִן הַתּוֹרָה,
a hint from the Torah,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין בּוֹ אַזְהָרַת לָאוֹ,
in any case there is no negative warning in it,
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן יִחוּד דְּפְנוּיָה
and all the more so seclusion with an unmarried woman,
דְּהוּא מִגְּזֵירַת בֵּית דִּינוֹ שֶׁל דָּוִד
which is from the decree of David's court,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין כא, רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב).
as it says (Sanhedrin 21, beginning of side b).
וְהֲרֵי דְּקָרֵי גַּם לְמַכַּת מִרְדּוּת שָׁם
And behold, he also calls disciplinary lashes there
בְּסָתָם "מַלְקוּת",
simply "lashes,"
וְאִם כֵּן כָּאן שֶׁמִּיעֵט מִמַלְקוּת
and so here, in that he excluded lashes,
הַיְנוּ גַּם מִמַּכַּת מִרְדּוּת הַקּוֹדֵם,
that is also from the previous disciplinary lashes,
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר לָשׁוֹן "אֵינָם מְחַיְבִין",
and therefore he said "they do not obligate,"
דְּהַיְנוּ שֶׁהַּחֲכָמִים לֹא חִייְבוּ עַל זֶה מַלְקוּת,
meaning the Sages did not obligate lashes for this,
וְזֶהוּ מַכַּת מִרְדּוּת שֶׁמִּחִיוּב חֲכָמִים.)
and that is disciplinary lashes, which is by obligation of the Sages.)

paragraphs.text: Rambam’s Commentary on Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:4 groups warnings against sinful thought, deliberate arousal, and wasteful emission, then says that these are forbidden but do not carry lashes. The surrounding exposition cites scriptural prohibitions and assigns lashes to other conduct. Rav Tzadok infers that Rambam does not derive this offense from ‘lo tinaf’; his further suggestion that the exemption includes disciplinary lashes is likewise an inference, not an express distinction in the quoted sentence.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 81a states that seclusion receives lashes; Rashi explains these as disciplinary lashes. Rav Ashi excludes the married-woman case to avoid suspicion about her children, while Mar Zutra lashes and announces that only seclusion occurred. Rambam’s Commentary on Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:4 follows the exclusion. Thus the unqualified word ‘lashes’ can denote rabbinic discipline; the author applies that usage to Rambam’s later exemption.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 80b attributes to Rabbi Yochanan in Rabbi Yishmael’s name a Torah allusion: a son may be secluded with his mother, implying prohibition with other forbidden relatives. The verse’s plain subject is idolatrous enticement. Rav Tzadok distinguishes that Torah allusion from an express negative warning that carries ordinary lashes; this legal inference belongs to his discussion.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 21b reports David’s decree after Amnon and Tamar. The Gemara explains it as seclusion with an unmarried woman, since seclusion with forbidden relatives was already prohibited. Avodah Zarah 36b distinguishes that Torah-level prohibition, David’s decree concerning an unmarried woman, and the later decree concerning a non-Jewish woman. Yad Ramah on Sanhedrin 21b expressly explains that ‘seclusion and the unmarried woman’ is one connected decree. This supplies the rabbinic classification invoked here.

p: וְמִיהוּ כָּל הָרִאשׁוֹנִים
However, all the Rishonim
מְפָרְשִׁי לָהּ
explain it
(לְנִיאוּף בְּיָד אוֹ בְּרֶגֶל דְּנִדָּה יג, עַמּוּד ב)
(the adultery by hand or foot of Niddah 13b)
עַל מוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה,
as referring to wasting seed,
וְגַם בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ
and also in the holy Zohar
(פָּרָשַׁת וַיֵּשֶׁב קפח, עַמּוּד א)
(Parashas Vayeishev 188a)
דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "וַיֵּרַע"
the passage beginning "vayera"
אִיתָא:
it says:
"וְאַפִּיק זֶרְעָא לִמְגַּנָא בְּיִדָא אוֹ בִּרְגְלָא",
"and he emitted seed in vain by hand or by foot,"
הִזְכִּיר גַּם כֵּן לָשׁוֹן "בְּרֶגֶל"
it also mentions the wording "by foot"
עַל הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה.
regarding wasting seed.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם
And in any case,
כֵּיוָן דְּהוּא רַק מִדְּרָשָׁא
since it is only from a derivation,
אֶפְשָׁר דְּלְכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא
it is possible that for everyone
לֹא חָמִיר מַעֲשֶׂה לְעִנְיַן תְּשׁוּבָה,
the act is not severe regarding teshuvah,
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן לָעֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת
and all the more so according to the Asarah Maamaros,
דְּלֹא גָּרַע מִלָּאוִין שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין.
which is no worse than negatives that are not lashed.
וְאַפִּילּוּ תֵּימָא
And even if you say
דְּלֹא כְּהָעֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת,
that it is not like the Asarah Maamaros,
וְגַם זֶה דְּלֵיכָּא לָאו מְפֹרָשׁ
and even this, that there is no explicit negative,
כִּיוָן דְּאִסּוּרוֹ מִן הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁלֹּא לַעֲשׂוֹת
since its prohibition is from the Torah, not to do,
וְעוֹבֵר בְּקוּם וַעֲשֵׂה
and one transgresses by an act
וְלֹא בְּבִטּוּל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה
and not by neglect of a positive commandment
כְּשֵׁב וְאַל תַּעֲשֶׂה
by sitting passively
לֹא דָּמֵי לְמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה,
it is not like a positive commandment,
עַל כָּל פָּנִים
in any case,
בְּצִירוּף יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים
together with Yom Kippur
מִיהַת מְכַפֵּר
at least it atones
כְּמוֹ שֶׁיִתְבָּאֵר בְּחֲלוּקָה הַשֵּׁנִית.
as will be explained in the second section.
וְאַעֲפִּי שֶׁמְבוֹאָר
And although it is stated
(בְּאֶבֶן הָעֶזֶר, רֵישׁ סִימָן כ״ג)
(Even HaEzer, beginning of section 23),
דְּעָוֹן זֶה חָמוּר מִכָּל עֲבֵרוֹת שֶׁבָּתּוֹרָה,
that this sin is graver than all sins in the Torah,
עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּבֵית שְׁמוּאֵל
see there in Beis Shmuel
דְּלָאו דַּוְקָא
that it is not literal
וְאִסּוּר כָּרֵת (דְּנִדָּה) חָמוּר מִמֶּנּוּ.
and a karess prohibition (of Niddah) is graver than it.
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּבֵית יוֹסֵף
And see there in the Beis Yosef
דְּהֵבִיא זֶה מִהַזּוֹהַר
who brought this from the Zohar,
וְהוּא (בְּפָּרָשַׁת וַיֵּשֶׁב שָׁם):
which is (in Parashas Vayeishev there):
"דְּבְּכָל חוֹבִין דְּאַסְתָאֲב בַּר נָשׁ בְּהָאִי עָלְמָא דָא
"Of all the sins in which a person becomes defiled in this world,
אִיהוּ חוֹבָא דְּאַסְתָאֲב בֵּיה יָתֵר
this is the sin through which he is more defiled
בְּהָאִי עָלְמָא וּבְעָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי",
in this world and in the world to come,"
עַד כָּאן.
end of quote.
וְאַף דְּסְתִימוּת לְשׁוֹן הַזֹּהַר וְשׁוֻלְחָן עָרוּךְ הַנִּזְכָּר
And although the unqualified wording of the Zohar and Shulchan Aruch mentioned
חָמוּר מִכָּל עֲבֵרוֹת מַמָּשׁ,
is "graver than all sins" literally,
אֶפְשָׁר מִכָּל עֲבֵרוֹת שֶׁכִּיוֹצֵא בּוֹ קָאֲמְרוּ,
it is possible they mean from all sins like it,
שֶׁאֵין עֲלֵיהֶם אֲפִילּוּ אִסּוּר לָאוֹ מְפֻרָשׁ
that have not even an explicit negative prohibition
וְלֹא מִהַחֲמוּרוֹת מֵהֶם.
and are not among the more severe ones.
וְמִיהוּ בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ
However, in the holy Zohar
(פָּרָשַׁת וַיְחִי ריט, עַמּוּד ב)
(Parashas Vayechi 219b)
אִיתָא:
it says:
"וּלְהַאי טָרְדִין בְּהוּא עָלְמָא יַתִּיר מִכּוּלְהוּ" וְכוּלֵי,
“and this one is banished in that world more than all the others,” etc.,
"וְכוּלְהוּ סָלְקִין וְהָאִי לָא סָלִיק.
"and all of them ascend, but this one does not ascend.
וְאִם תֹאמַר שָׁאָר חַיָּיבִין דְּקָטִלִי בַּר נָשׁ וְכוּלֵּי.
And if you say, other sinners who kill a person, etc.,
אִינִין קָטִלִי בַּר נָשׁ אַחֲרָא
those kill another person,
וְהָאִי קָטִיל בְּנוֹי וְכוּלֵּי",
but this one kills his own children, etc.,"
עַיֵּין שָׁם.
see there.
וְהִנֵּה מִשְׁמַע
And behold, it implies
דְּעוֹנְשוֹ חָמוּר מִרוֹצַח גָּמוּר שׁוֹפֵךְ דָּמִים,
that his punishment is graver than a full murderer, a shedder of blood,
אֲבָל הוּא דָּבָר
but it is a matter
שֶׁלֹּא נִתָּּן לִיאָמֵר
that cannot be said
שֶׁיִהְיֶה אִסּוּר זֶה חָמוּר מִשְׁפִיכַת דָּמִים מַמָּשׁ
that this prohibition be graver than actual bloodshed
שֶׁחַיָּיבִין עָלָיו מִיתָה,
for which one is liable to death,
וּבְהַהִיא אֲפִילּוּ מַלְקוּת לֵיכָּא.
while for this there are not even lashes.
וְרוֹצַח יֵהָרֵג וְאַל יַעֲבוֹר,
A murderer: let him be killed rather than transgress,
וּבְהַהִיא פְּשׁוּטָא
and in this case it is obvious
דְּלֹא אָמַרְנַן "יֵהָרֵג וְאַל יַעֲבוֹר",
that we do not say "let him be killed rather than transgress,"
וְמוֻתָּר לְצֹרֶךְ רְפוּאַת גּוּפוֹ
and it is permitted for the need of healing his body,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר בְּתְשׁוּבוֹת פְּנֵי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ שָׁם,
as stated in the responsa Pnei Yehoshua there,
וְהֵבִיא רְאָיָה מִמִּשְׁנָה
and he brought proof from a Mishnah
(סוֹף פֶּרֶק ז דְּאָהֳלוֹת)
(end of Ohalos, chapter 7)
שֶׁמְּחַתְּכִין הַוָּלָד בְּמֵעֶיהָ
that one cuts up the fetus in its mother's womb
שֶׁחַיֶּיהָ קוֹדְמִין.
because the mother's life takes precedence.
עַיֵּין
See
שָׁם.
there.

paragraphs.text: Niddah 13b’s ‘by hand or by foot’ follows the teaching about adulterers with the hand. The connective readings in Rif and Maggid Mishneh support their linkage. Zohar, Vayeshev 17:182–183 (I 188a), explicitly says that seed is emitted in vain ‘by hand or by foot,’ then describes exclusion from the curtain and the countenance of the Ancient of Days. This directly supports the identification accepted here; the author’s preceding reconstruction of Rambam remains a separate proposal.

paragraphs.text: Asarah Maamaros, Chakor Din I:18, treats several prohibitions without lashes as lighter for atonement, including a collective prohibition and a prohibition without an act, alongside specified other categories. It does not put every prohibition lacking lashes in that class: the continuation expressly excludes, among others, warnings attached to capital offenses and offenses of kareis. Rav Tzadok’s placement of the present offense within the lighter class is his application.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86a distinguishes repentance for a positive commandment, repentance together with Yom Kippur for a negative commandment, and the further process for kareis or court-imposed death. Rav Tzadok argues here that even under the alternative classification, repentance together with Yom Kippur suffices. Yoma itself does not identify this particular offense within its hierarchy.

paragraphs.text: Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 23:1, calls the offense ‘more severe than all transgressions’; Beit Yosef cites the Zohar. Beit Shmuel 23:1, through Chelkas Mechokek’s quotation of Sefer Chassidim 176, says this cannot be a literal ranking: that source prefers the lesser wrong when the stated alternative is a forbidden relationship, while still requiring atonement. Rav Tzadok’s further restriction of the phrase to offenses of a comparable legal class is his proposed interpretation.

paragraphs.text: Zohar, Vayechi 25:192–194 (I 219b), calls the offender evil, describes exclusion from the Shechinah, and compares killing another person with killing one’s own children. It says that others ascend while this one does not. Rav Tzadok does not dismiss this language; he distinguishes its spiritual obstruction from the formal legal status of intentional murder, court punishment, and the atonement hierarchy. That reconciliation is his analysis, not a qualification stated in this Zohar passage.

The responsum’s passage reproduced in the Har Bracha edition speaks of treatment that will certainly benefit the patient, and explains the comparisons with murder or forbidden relations as expressions of gravity rather than automatically imposing their rule of martyrdom. His condition concerns certainty of benefit; the quoted words do not state that this must be the only available treatment.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Ohalos 7:6 permits dismembering a fetus in a dangerous labor because the mother’s life takes precedence. Once the greater part has emerged, it forbids displacing one life for another. The cited responsum argues by comparison; the Mishnah does not classify semen as a fetus. Sanhedrin 74a supplies the distinct martyrdom rule for actual murder. Rav Tzadok uses the contrast to resist making the Zohar’s comparison a legal equation.

p: אֲבָל שָׁם לִפְנֵי זֶה
But there, just before this
בֵּאֲרוּ בְּעָנְשׁוֹ
they explained his punishment:
דְּלָא חָמֵי אַפֵּי שְׁכִינְתָּא
he does not see the Shechinah’s face,
וְכֵן (בְּפָרָשַׁת וַיֵּשֶׁב שָׁם)
and likewise (in Parashas Vayeishev there)
דְּלָא עָאל
he does not enter
וְלָא חָמֵי סֵבֶר אַפֵּי עַתִּיק יוֹמִין
and does not see the countenance of the Ancient of Days,
וְכֵן (בְּפָרָשַׁת בְּרֵאשִׁית שָׁם)
and likewise (in Parashas Bereishis there)
דְּלָא עָאל בְּפַלְטְרִין
he does not enter the palaces
וְלָא חָמֵי אַפֵּי שְׁכִינְתָּא
and does not see the Shechinah’s face,
וְכֵן (בְּפָרָשַׁת אֱמֹר צ, עַמּוּד א)
and likewise (Parashas Emor 90a)
רֵישׁ דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "וְלָא".
at the start of the passage beginning “v’la.”
הִנֵּה עִם כָּל תֹּקֶף הַטֻּמְאָה
Behold, with all the force of the impurity
שֶׁבַּעֲוֹן זֶה
of this sin,
לֹא אָמְרוּ בְּזֶה
they did not state regarding it
עֶנְשֵׁי גֵּיהִנֹּם חֲמוּרִים בְּיוֹתֵר
especially severe Gehinnom punishments
מִבִּשְׁאָר עֲבֵירוֹת,
beyond other sins;
רַק כָּל חֹמֶר שֶׁבּוֹ
rather all its gravity
בְּהֶעְדֵּר הַמַּעֲלָה
lies in the loss of the privilege
דִּרְאִיַּת פְּנֵי שְׁכִינָה
of seeing the Shechinah’s face
וּמְנִיעַת הַכְּנִיסָה
and being barred from entering
לְמַדְרֵגוֹת עֶלְיוֹנוֹת.
the higher levels.
וְכֵן לְשׁוֹן "הָאִי לָא סָלֵיק" הַנִּזְכָּר
Likewise the wording “this one does not ascend,” cited above,
רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר
means
שֶׁאֵין עוֹלֶה לְמַעְלָה עֶלְיוֹנָה,
that he does not ascend to a higher place,
וְכַאֲשֶׁר מְסַיֵּם שָׁם גַּם כֵּן
as it concludes there too:
דְּלֵית לָן חַיָּיבַיָּא
we have no sinners
דְּלָא חָמֵי אַפֵּי שְׁכִינְתָּא
who do not see the Shechinah’s face
בַּר מֵהַאי.
except this one.
וּבְפָרָשַׁת וַיַּקְהֵל (רִיד, סוֹף עַמּוּד ב)
And in Parashas Vayakhel (214b, end)
דְּלֵית חוֹבָא דְּקַשְׁיָא
there is no sin as harsh
קַמֵּיהּ קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא
before the Holy One, Blessed is He,
כְּהָאי וְכוּ',
as this one, etc.;
עַל חוֹבָא דָא כְּתִיב
of this sin it is written
"וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי ה'" וְגוֹ'.
“and it was evil in the eyes of Hashem,” etc.
הִנֵּה בְּכָאן פֵּרֵשׁ
Here he clarified
שֶׁקֹּשִׁי חֵטְא זֶה מִכָּל הָעֲבֵירוֹת
that this sin’s harshness beyond all other sins
הוּא קַמֵּיהּ קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא דַּוְקָא,
is specifically before the Holy One, Blessed is He,
דְּמַיְיתֵי עַל זֶה
for he cites on this
קְרָא דִּבְעֵינֵי ה'
the verse “in the eyes of Hashem,”
דְּלָא נִמְצָא כֵּן
which is not found thus
בְּחֵטְא אַחֵר,
with any other sin;
וְכֵן בְּעֵר נֶאֱמַר
and so of Er it says
"רַע בְּעֵינֵי ה'",
“evil in the eyes of Hashem,”
וּבְכָל הָנֵי דּוּכְתֵּי
and in all these places
בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ
in the holy Zohar
מַיְיתֵי גַּם כֵּן
he also cites
מִקְרָא הַנִּזְכָּר,
the aforementioned verse,
וּכְלַפֵּי עֵינֵי ה' דַּיְקָא
and specifically toward the eyes of Hashem
עָוֹן זֶה חָמוּר וְרַע יוֹתֵר מִן הַכֹּל.
this sin is graver and worse than all.

paragraphs.text: The passages invoked here are Zohar, Vayechi 25:192–194, Vayeshev 17:183, Bereishis 97:4, and Emor 11:33: they connect the designation ‘evil’ with exclusion from divine proximity. Emor expressly rejects extending its warning to an otherwise permitted union merely because the woman cannot conceive. Mishpatim 3:167 uses similar Shechinah language in its own discussion of failing to produce fruit. The author infers a distinction between loss of higher ascent and the legal hierarchy of punishment; that distinction is his interpretation of these warnings.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok reads the Zohar’s exceptional severity chiefly as exclusion from the divine presence and higher spiritual levels. He distinguishes this loss of closeness to God from a claim that the offense receives harsher Gehinnom punishment than all other sins.

p: וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר לְפִי זֶה שַׁפִּיר,
And accordingly one can say well,
דְּדַוְקָא הוּא נֶגֶד כָּל עֲבֵירוֹת כֻּלָּם
that it is specifically in contrast to all sins
בְּעִנְיַן הַטֻּמְאָה הַמְרַחֶקֶת
in the matter of the impurity that distances
מִפְּנֵי שְׁכִינָה
from before the Shechinah
וְכַלְפֵּי שְׁמַיָּא דַּוְקָא,
and toward Heaven specifically;
אֲבָל מִצַּד הָאָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
but from the human side in this world
וַאֲפִילּוּ מִצַּד עוֹלַם הַמַּלְאָכִים
and even from the angels’ world
וַדַּאי כָּל הָעֲבֵירוֹת
surely all the sins
שֶׁהֶחְמִירָה תּוֹרָה
that the Torah treated severely
בְּאַזְהָרָתָם וּבְעָנְשָׁם
in their warning and punishment
הֵם חֲמוּרִים יוֹתֵר.
are graver.
וְדָחֵי הָא מִקַּמֵּי הָא
And one overrides the other,
כְּדִבְרֵי סֵפֶר חֲסִידִים
as in the words of Sefer Chasidim
שֶׁמֵּבִיא בְּבֵית שְׁמוּאֵל שָׁם,
cited in Beis Shmuel there,
אוֹ לְעִנְיַן יֵהָרֵג וְאַל יַעֲבֹר
or regarding “be killed rather than transgress”
וּלְהִתְרַפְּאוֹת
and regarding healing
לְדָחוֹתָהּ מִפְּנֵי פִּקּוּחַ נֶפֶשׁ;
overriding it for saving a life;
דְּכַּשֶּׁעוֹשֶׂה אוֹתָם מִצַּד הַדִּין
for when one does them by law
שֶׁנִּדְחֶה מִפְּנֵי דָּבָר אַחֵר הֶחָמוּר
because overridden by another, graver matter
שׁוּב גַּם בְּעֵינֵי ה' אֵינוֹ רַע.
it is no longer evil even in Hashem’s eyes.
וְגוּף חֹמֶר הָאִסּוּרִים
And the actual gravity of prohibitions
לְעִנְיַן דִּחוּי וְכַיּוֹצֵא
regarding overriding and the like,
בְּכָל דָּבָר דְּנָפְקָא מִינָּהּ לְדִינָא
in anything with practical legal difference,
וּלְגַבֵּי הָאָדָם
and from the human standpoint,
הוּא כְּפִי חֻמְרֵי הָאַזְהָרוֹת וְהָעֳנָשִׁים
follows the severity of the warnings and punishments
הַמְפֹרָשִׁים בַּתּוֹרָה
stated explicitly in the Torah,
שֶׁאֲנַן רוֹאִים
where we see
שֶׁהֶחְמִירָה בְּאֵיזֶה דָּבָר,
that it was severe about a given matter;
וְגַם לְעִנְיַן עָנְשֵׁי שָׁמַיִם בְּגֵיהִנֹּם
and also regarding Heavenly punishments in Gehinnom
וַדַּאי הֵם חֲמוּרִים יוֹתֵר
they are surely graver
וְאִם כֵּן הוּא עֹנֶשׁ שָׁמַיִם.
and so it is a Heavenly punishment.
אֲבָל חֹמֶר עָוֹן זֶה
But this sin’s gravity
הוּא רַק בְּעֵינֵי ה' לְבַדּוֹ
is only in Hashem’s eyes alone
וּלְעִנְיַן הַהִתְקָרְבוּת לְפָנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ,
and regarding drawing near to Him, blessed is He,
וַהֲרֵי זֶה עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא
which is like what is stated
(בְּיוֹמָא כט, עַמּוּד א)
(Yoma 29a)
הִרְהוּרֵי עֲבֵירָה קָשִׁים מֵעֲבֵירָה.
“sinful thoughts are harsher than sin.”
וְאַף דְּרַשִׁ"י שָׁם פֵּרֵשׁ
And although Rashi there explained
קָשִׁים לַגּוּף (לְהַכְחִישׁוֹ),
harsher on the body (to weaken it),
כָּל הָרִאשׁוֹנִים לֹא פֵּרְשׁוּ כֵּן,
all the Rishonim did not explain so,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב גַּם כֵּן
and as also wrote
בְּסֵפֶר כַּד הַקֶּמַח לְרַבֵּנוּ בַּחְיֵי
in Kad HaKemach by Rabbeinu Bachya
(אוֹת טָהֳרַת הַלֵּב)
(entry “Purity of the Heart”)
לְפָרֵשׁ כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ
to explain it literally
לְעִנְיַן קֹשִׁי הַחֵטְא וְטֻמְאַת הַנֶּפֶשׁ,
as the sin’s harshness and the soul’s impurity,
וּלְפִי שֶׁהַהִרְהוּר בַּלֵּב
because the thought in the heart
וּמְטַמֵּא הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַשִּׂכְלִית
defiles the intellectual soul
הַשּׁוֹכֶנֶת שָׁם,
which dwells there;
יְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ.
see there at length.
וּבְוַדַּאי שֶׁמַּעֲשֵׂה הָעֲבֵירָה עַצְמָהּ בִּפְעַל
And surely the act of sin itself in deed
חֲמוּרָה הַרְבֵּה יוֹתֵר לְכָל דָּבָר
is far graver in every respect
מֵהַהִרְהוּר.
than the thought.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁטֻּמְאָתָהּ בַּנֶּפֶשׁ קָשָׁה יוֹתֵר
Although its impurity in the soul is harsher,
זֶהוּ רַק לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
that is only before Hashem, blessed is He,
הַבּוֹחֵן לִבּוֹת
who examines hearts,
שֶׁיִּרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב לְבַד,
who sees the heart alone,
וְהוּא מִצַּד הַנִּסְתָּרוֹת
and it belongs to the hidden things
אֲשֶׁר אֵין גָּלוּי אֶלָּא לִפְנֵי ה' אֱלֹקֵינוּ,
known only to Hashem our God;
וְלָנוּ וּלְבָנֵינוּ
but for us and our children
הוּא לַעֲשׂוֹת אֶת כָּל דִּבְרֵי הַתּוֹרָה,
it is to do all the words of the Torah,
וְאֵין לָנוּ אֶלָּא כְּפִי מִשְׁפַּט הַתּוֹרָה
and we have only the Torah’s law
מַה שֶּׁהֶחְמִירָה בְּאַזְהָרוֹתֶיהָ.
as to what it treated severely in its warnings.

paragraphs.text: Beit Shmuel 23:1, quoting Chelkas Mechokek and Sefer Chassidim 176, shows that ‘more severe than all sins’ is not an absolute practical ranking; the quoted comparison still requires atonement for the lesser wrong. The author combines that hierarchy with the medical discussion cited above. His conclusion is that conduct displaced by a genuinely overriding rule is not evil in God’s eyes; the mystical warning does not create an additional rule of martyrdom or overturn the Torah’s legal priorities.

Rashi explains this physically: desire weakens the body more than the completed act. The author then contrasts that explanation with other readings, including Kad HaKemach’s account of the soul; his statement about the greater practical severity of the deed is part of his own reconciliation.

paragraphs.text: Kad HaKemach, ‘Purity of the Heart,’ distinguishes bodily and intellectual traits and explains that thought can directly defile the intellectual soul. It also records other explanations of Yoma’s saying. In particular, it reports Ramban’s restriction of the severe punishment-reading to thought after an act, then disputes it and allows punishment for deliberately maintained thought even before action. Rav Tzadok adopts the inward-stain explanation while developing his own distinction between concealed impurity and practical legal severity. Compare Chovos HaLevavos, the author’s introduction, on inward prohibitions, including sinful thoughts, known fully only to the Creator; that parallel does not itself establish the present hierarchy of punishment.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok distinguishes hidden impurity before God from the Torah’s revealed legal measures of severity. He compares sinful thought with sinful action: damage within the soul can be profound without displacing the practical hierarchy established by explicit warnings and punishments.

p: וְעָוֹן זֶה גַּם כֵּן נִמְשָׁךְ מִהַהִרְהוּר,
And this sin too stems from sinful thought,
וְכְמוֹ שֶׁחִבְּרָם רַבֵּנוּ מֹשֶׁה בֶּן מַיְמוֹן
and as Rambam connected them
בְּפֵרוּשׁ הַמִּשְׁנָה שָׁם יַחַד
together in his Commentary on the Mishnah there,
וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (בְּנִדָּה שָׁם)
and likewise they said (in Niddah there)
כָּל הַמֵּבִיא עַצְמוֹ לִידֵי הִרְהוּר
whoever brings himself to sinful thought
אֵין מַכְנִיסִין אוֹתוֹ
is not admitted
בִּמְחִיצָתוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא,
within the partition of the Holy One, Blessed is He;
כְּתִיב הָכָא "וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי ה'" וְכוּ',
it is written here “and it was evil in the eyes of Hashem,” etc.;
עַיֵּין שָׁם.
see there.
וְהִנֵּה קָרְא דְּ"וַיֵּרַע"
Now the verse “and it was evil”
עַל מוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה קָאֵי
speaks of wasting seed,
שֶׁהָיָה דָּשׁ בְּפָנִים וְזוֹרֶה בְּחוּץ,
for he threshed within and scattered outside;
וְמַיְיתֵי זֶה עַל הִרְהוּר,
yet it is cited regarding sinful thought,
מְבוֹאָר מִזֶּה
which makes clear
דְּעִקָּר חֹמֶר עָוֹן זֶה
that the main gravity of this sin
וּמַה דְּרַע בְּעֵינֵי ה'
and its being evil in Hashem’s eyes
הוּא מִפְּנֵי הַהִרְהוּר.
is because of the thought.
וּלְפִי שֶׁמַּחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה
And since an evil thought
אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְצָרֵּף לַמַּעֲשֶׂה
the Holy One does not join to a deed,
אֵין נֶעֱנָשׁ עָלֶיהָ
one is not punished for it
אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁיָּצָא לַפּוֹעַל בְּמַעֲשֶׂה
unless it emerges into action
בְּהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה
in wasting seed,
שֶׁהוּא נִמְשָׁךְ וְבָא מִהַהִרְהוּר.
which stems and comes from the thought.
וְגַם מַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ "מֵבִיא לִידֵי הִרְהוּר"
And what they said, “brings to sinful thought,”
הַכּוָּנָה בְּהִרְהוּר הַיּוֹצֵא לַפּוֹעַל בְּמַעֲשֶׂה
means thought that emerges into action
כְּמַעֲשֵׂה עֵר וְאוֹנָן דְּמַיְיתֵי,
like the deed of Er and Onan, whom it cites;
וּסְתָם מְהַרְהֵר הַמֵּבִיא עַצְמוֹ לְכָךְ
and an ordinary thinker who brings himself to this
שֶׁהוּא הַמַּעֲמִיק בְּהִרְהוּרוֹ
is one who delves into his thought
וְאֵינוֹ פוֹסֵק
and does not stop,
סוֹפוֹ לָבוֹא לְהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה.
who ends up wasting seed.
וּמִדְּנַקְטָה עַל שֵׁם הַהִרְהוּר
And since it is phrased in terms of thought
מַשְׁמָעוֹ דְּזֶהוּ עִקָּר הַחֹמֶר שֶׁבּוֹ
it implies this is its main gravity,
וּמִשְׁוּם דְּהִרְהוּרֵי עֲבֵירָה קָשִׁים כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּזְכַּר לְעִל.
because sinful thoughts are harsh, as noted above.
וּמִטַּעַם זֶה
And for this reason
בְּלָאוֹ הַכִּי לֹא קָשֶׁה
there is anyway no difficulty
מִסֵּפֶר חֲסִידִים שֶׁמֵּבִיא בְּבֵית שְׁמוּאֵל שָׁם,
from Sefer Chasidim cited in Beis Shmuel there,
דְּלְעִנְיַן בִּיאַת עֲרָיוֹת אוֹ נִדָּה
for regarding forbidden relations or Niddah
מִתּוֹךְ אוֹתוֹ הַהִרְהוּר עַצְמוֹ
arising from that same thought
פְּשִׁיטָא דְּחָמוּר טְפֵי,
it is obvious it is graver,
דְּהֲרֵי מִצַּד הַהִרְהוּר אֵין חִלּוּק,
since as to the thought there is no difference,
וְהָכָּא אִיכָּא עוֹד חֹמֶר
and there is further the gravity
מַעֲשֵׂה הָעֲבֵירָה עַצְמָהּ.
of the deed of the sin itself.
וְלֹא אָמְרוּ דְּחָמִיר מִכָּל עֲבֵירוֹת
They did not say it is graver than all sins
אֶלָּא בְּאוֹתָם שֶׁאֵינָם בְּפֶגָם הַבְּרִית
but only those not involving damage to the covenant
אוֹ שֶׁאֵין בָּאִים מִתּוֹךְ תּוֹקֶף הַעְמָקַת הַהִרְהוּר
or that do not come from intense dwelling on the thought
כְּעָוֹן זֶה,
as with this sin,
רַק מִתּוֹךְ פְּגִיעַת הָעֶרְוָה לִפְנָיו.
but from encountering nakedness before him.
וְהָא דְּאֵין מַכְנִיסִין לְמַחִיצָּתוֹ
And the “not admitted to His partition”
הַיְינוּ לְפַרְגּוֹדָא דְּבַזֹּהַר הַנִּזְכָּר,
refers to the curtain of the Zohar cited above,
וְמִתְבָּאֵר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְּתִי
and it is clarified as I wrote
דְּכָל הַחֹּמֶר הוּא מִצַּד
that all the gravity stems from
הִרְהוּרֵי עֲבֵירָה הַקָּשִׁים.
the harsh sinful thoughts.
וְעַל הִרְהוּרֵי עֲבֵירָה שֶׁבָּלֵּב
And for sinful thoughts in the heart
וַדַּאי דְּסָגִי בְּתְשׁוּבָה שֶׁבָּלֵּב לְבַד,
surely repentance in the heart alone suffices,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְּתִי (בְּאוֹת יג)
as I wrote (in entry 13)
וְכָל הַחֹּמֶר שֶׁבּוֹ הוּא רַק קוֹדֶם שֶׁשָׁב
and all its gravity is only before he repents;
אֲבָל אַחַר דְּלֵבָבוֹ יָבִין וָשָׁב
but after “his heart understands and he returns,”
הֲרֵי נִטְהַר הַלֵּב וְרָפָא לוֹ.
the heart is purified and healed.

paragraphs.text: Rambam’s Commentary on Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:4 groups thought, deliberate arousal, and wasteful emission. Niddah 13b separately says that one who brings himself to sinful thought is not admitted into God’s compartment, linking ‘it was evil in the eyes of Hashem’ with ‘evil shall not dwell with You.’ Rav Tzadok reads the citation of the act’s verse in a teaching about thought as evidence of their connection. The specific claim that the act realizes sustained thought is his explanation of that sequence.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 40a says that a bad thought is not ordinarily joined to a deed, distinguishing a thought that bears fruit from one that does not. The continuation separately discusses idolatrous thought and habitual transgression; it is not an unrestricted declaration that every unperformed thought has no consequence. Rav Tzadok applies the fruit distinction here to thought issuing in an act, and the following discussion explains his account of deliberately prolonged thought.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok traces this offense’s distinctive spiritual damage to sustained sinful thought that leads to action. He argues that repentance in the heart can repair that inner damage, and reads the verses about shovavim in that light.

p: וְעִקָּר לְשׁוֹן שׁוֹבָבִים דְּבַּקָּרָא
And the root of the term “shovavim” in the verse
הַנִּדְרָשׁ עַל הַמְּחִילָה מִיַּד
expounded as immediate pardon
מוֹרֶה עַל הַהוֹלֵךְ שׁוֹבָב בְּדֶרֶךְ לִבּוֹ
indicates one who wanders astray in his heart’s way;
וּמִקָּרְא דְּ"וַיֵּלֶךְ שׁוֹבָב" וְגוֹ' (בְּיָשַׁעְיָהוּ נַז)
and from the verse “and he went wayward,” etc. (Isaiah 57)
נֶאֱמַר שְׁתֵּי פְּעָמִים "הַצַּדִּיק אָבָד"
it says twice “the righteous one perishes,”
שֶׁהִיא כֻּלָּה מְדַבֶּרֶת בְּעָוֹן זֶה בְּיִחוּד,
for it all speaks of this sin in particular,
שֶׁהַחוֹטֵא בוֹ הוּא אוֹבֵד
for one who sins in it loses
מַדְּרֵגַת וּמִדַּת צַדִּיק
the level and attribute of tzaddik,
הַרּוֹמֵז לְשׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית כִּנְדָּע.
which alludes to guarding the covenant, as is known.
וְכֵן מִקָּרְא דְּ"הַנִּחָמִים בָּאֵלִים" וְגוֹ'
And likewise the verse “who inflame themselves among the terebinths,” etc.,
הָאָמוּר שָׁם
stated there,
דָּרְשׁוּהוּ (בְּנִדָּה יג, עַמּוּד א)
they expounded (in Niddah 13a)
עַל זֶה,
about this,
וְהַחוֹטֵא בְּזֶה נִקְרָא שׁוֹבָב,
and one who sins in this is called wayward,
וְעָלָיו נֶאֱמַר
and of him it says
"שׁוּבוּ" וְגוֹ' "אֶרְפָּא" וְגוֹ'.
“Return,” etc., “I will heal,” etc.

paragraphs.text: Yeshayahu 57:1 mentions the tzaddik as lost and again as gathered away. Niddah 13a expounds 57:5’s ‘those who slaughter the children’ concerning the spilling of seed. The chapter later speaks of wandering in the heart’s way and healing. Rav Tzadok connects this cluster with tzaddik, yesod, and the covenant; that spiritual correspondence is his interpretation, not the plain wording of the chapter.

p: אַךְ בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (וַיְחִי שָׁם)
But in the holy Zohar (Vayechi there)
תָּנָן אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה
we learned: Rabbi Yehudah said:
לֵית לָן חוֹבָא בְּעָלְמָא
we have no sin in the world
דְּלָא אִית לֵיהּ תְּשׁוּבָה
that has no repentance
בַּר מֵהַאי,
except this one;
הִנֵּה מַגְרַע כֹּחַ חֵטְא זֶה
Here this sin is placed in a worse position
דְּלָא מְהַנְיָא לֵיהּ תְּשׁוּבָה כָּלָּל.
in that repentance does not help it at all.
וְכָבָר צָוְחוּ עַל זֶה קַמָּאֵי
And the earlier authorities already cried out against this,
שֶׁהֲרֵי אֵין לְךָ דָּבָר
for there is nothing
שֶׁעוֹמֵד בְּפְּנֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה.
that stands before repentance.
וּבְפָרָשַׁת נֹחַ (סב, רישׁ עַמּוּד א)
And in Parashas Noach (62a)
כָּל חוֹבוֹהִי דְּבַר נָשׁ וְכוּ'
all of a person’s sins, etc.,
תָּלְיִין בְּתְשׁוּבָה
depend on repentance,
וְחוֹבָה דְּאוֹשִׁיד זֶרְעָא וְכוּ'
and the sin of one who spills seed, etc.,
נִכְתָּם עֲוֹנֵךְ וְכוּ'
“your iniquity is stained,” etc.,
בַּר בְּתְשׁוּבָה סַגִּי,
except through great repentance,
עַד כָּאן.
end of quote.
וְהֲנֵי שָׁלוֹשׁ מִלּוֹת "בַּר וְכוּ'" מוּקָפִים,
Those three words “bar v’chu’” are enclosed in parentheses,
כִּי בְּסְפָרִים יְשָׁנִים אֵינוֹ,
because in old printings it is absent,
וְנוֹסַף מִתּוֹךְ אֵיזָה נוּסַחָא אַחֲרָא כָּתָב יָד
and was added from some other manuscript version,
כִּי בְּרֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה (שַׁעַר הַקֻּדִּשָּׁה פֶּרֶק יִז)
for Reishis Chochmah (Shaar HaKedushah, chapter 17)
כָּתַב
wrote
דְּבִמְקַצָּת נוּסָחוֹת בְּסִפְרֵי כָּתָב יָד
that in some manuscript versions
כָּתוּב בַּר בְּחִילָא דְּתִיוֹבְתָא תַּקִּיפָא.
it reads “except through the power of strong repentance.”
וְזֶה נִרְאֶה כְּסוֹתֵר הַלָּשׁוֹן
This seems to contradict the wording
דְּפָרָשַׁת וַיְחִי הַנִּזְכָּר
of Parashas Vayechi cited above
שֶׁסָתַם בְּעַד הַתְּשׁוּבָה לַגְמַרְי.
which shuts the door on repentance entirely.
אֲבָל גַּם (בְּפָרָשַׁת וַיַּקְהֵל שָׁם)
But also (in Parashas Vayakhel there)
אַחַר שֶׁהֶאֱרִיךְ בְּגוּף פְּגָם הַפּוֹגֵּם בַּבְּרִית
after elaborating on the damage of one who damages the covenant,
אָמַר
it says:
וְהָנֵי מִּלֵּי כַּד לָא עָבִיד תִּיוֹבְתָא שְׁלֵמָתָא
“and this applies when he does not do complete repentance,
תִּיוֹבְתָא דְּחָזִייָא לְחַפְיָא עַל כָּל עוֹבָדוֹהִי",
repentance fit to cover all his deeds,”
עַד כָּאן.
end of quote.
אַךְ עַדַיִן צָרִיךְ טַעַם
Yet a reason is still needed
עַל שֶׁהֶחֱמיִר בְּתְשׁוּבַת עָוֹן זֶה כָּךְ כָּל,
for why repentance for this sin is treated so strictly,
שֶׁכְּפִי מַה שֶׁכָּתַבְּתִי הוּא קַל
when by what I wrote it is lighter
אֲפִילּוּ מִלָּאוִין הַלּוֹקִין לִדְבֵרֵי הַכֹּל,
than even negative commandments punished by lashes, by all opinions,
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן מִחַיָּיבֵי כָּרִיתוֹת
and all the more so than those liable to karess
וּמִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין
and court-imposed death
לְעִנְיַן הַתְּשׁוּבָה.
as regards repentance.
וְכָבָר נִזְכַּר לְעִל (סִימָן ט)
It was already mentioned above (entry 9)
מִהָא (דְּקִדּוּשִׁין מִט, עַמּוּד ב)
from the passage (Kiddushin 49b)
דְּאֵין לְךָ רָשָׁע בְּשׁוּם עֲבֵירָה
that there is no wicked person in any sin
שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה נֶחְשָׁב צַדִּיק גָּמוּר
who would not be deemed fully righteous
עַל יְדֵי הִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה בַּלֵּב בְּלַבְּדוֹ
through a thought of repentance in the heart alone
בְּרֶגַע אֶחָד,
in a single moment,
דְּשָׁם סְתָמָא אָמַר אֲפִילּוּ רָשָׁע גָּמוּר,
for there it says without qualification “even a completely wicked person,”
מַשְׁמַע בְּכָל עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם
implying any sins in the world,
וְאֵין אֶחָד יוֹצֵא מִן הַכָּלָל.
with none excluded.
וְגַם (בְּנִדָּה שָׁם, עַמּוּד א)
And also (in Niddah there, 13a)
קָרֵי לֵיהּ רָשָׁע שָׁעָה אַחַת לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם,
it calls him “wicked for one hour before the Almighty,”
וְמַשְׁמַע
and it implies
דְּהַכּוָּנָה מִשְׁוּם דְּהַתָּם לָא בָּא
that the meaning is that there he did not come
לְהַזִּיד לְהַרְשִׁיע וְלַעֲבֹר כָּלָּל,
to sin deliberately and be wicked at all,
רַק מִתּוֹךְ שֶׁיִּאחַז בְּאַמָּה
only that by his holding his organ
חוֹשֲׁשִׁין שֶׁיִתְחַמֵּם וְיָבוֹא לְהִרְהוּר
we fear he will become aroused and come to sinful thought
וּלְהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה.
and to wasting seed.
וּבְוַדַּאי אִם יִאָּרֵע לוֹ כָּךְ
And surely if this happens to him,
חֶזְקָתוֹ שֶׁיִהְיֶה אַחַר כָּךְ לִבּוֹ דוֹאֵג עַל זֶה
the presumption is that afterward his heart will worry over it
וְיִהְיֶה שָׁב וּמִתְחַרֵּט בַּלֵּב עַל כָּל פָּנִים,
and he will repent and regret in his heart at least,
וּבְכַהֲדָא סָגִי
and that suffices
שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה נִקְרָא רָשָׁע עוֹד בְּכֹּל.
so that he is no longer called wicked at all.
אֶלָּא דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם בְּשָׁעָתוֹ מִיהַת הוֹי רָשָׁע,
Nevertheless in its moment he is at least wicked,
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר
and therefore it says
דְּלָא יִהְיֶה רָשָׁע גַּם שָׁעָה אַחַת.
that he should not be wicked even for one hour.

The qualification cannot be established by silently changing Vayechi’s text; it emerges from the further witnesses and interpretations that follow.

paragraphs.text: Zohar, Vayakhel 27:388 (II 214b), expressly limits the preceding warning to one who has not performed complete repentance, ‘fit to cover all his deeds.’ The local context concerns damage to the covenant and burial in a coffin; it even continues with a caution about the body’s remaining intact. Reishit Chokhmah 17:23–24 interprets the covenant as kol, embracing the other attributes, so its damage calls for repair of the whole stature. Rav Tzadok extends that comprehensive account; neither source’s severe warning should be quoted without its repentance qualification.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 49b allows for repentance when a complete sinner betroths on condition that he is righteous. Rambam, Ishus 8:5, explicitly codifies doubtful kiddushin: perhaps he repented inwardly. Maris HaAyin distinguishes an immediate change of status and beginning of atonement from its later completion. It also records a dispute about one who owes restitution: whether return of the property is required for that status or a resolve to return it suffices. The author’s general argument about the availability of repentance must be distinguished from a finding that any particular person’s atonement is complete.
