Rav Tzadok explains it through the expectation that this person will regret and return afterward; that account of his presumed subsequent repentance is the author’s inference, not a clause stated by Niddah.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok sets apparently restrictive Zohar passages beside passages allowing powerful or complete repentance. He asks how their severity can be reconciled with the ordinary categories of atonement and with the possibility of becoming righteous through a sincere thought of repentance.

p: וְאִיבְרָא מָצִינוּ לָשׁוֹן זֶה [בְּפֶרֶק ה' דְּעֵדֻיּוֹת מִשְׁנָה ו'] גַּבֵּי עֲקַבְיָא,
And indeed, we find this phrasing in the fifth chapter of Eduyot, Mishnah 6, regarding Akavya ben Mahalalel,
וְשָׁם לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי.
and there what I have previously written does not seem to apply.
אֲבָל גַּם לְעִנְיַן מַעֲשֵׂה הָרֶשַׁע לִכְאוֹרָה לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ שָׁם "שָׁעָה אַחַת",
However, also regarding an act of actual wickedness, seemingly “one hour” is not applicable there,
דְּאִם יַחֲזוֹר בּוֹ מִדַּעְתּוֹ בְּשֶׁקֶר לְהוֹרוֹת בְּהֵיפֶךְ,
for if he retracts his opinion deceitfully to render legal decisions to the contrary,
עַל כָּרְחֲךָ יִהְיֶה כָּל יָמָיו כֵּן מוֹרֶה בְּהֵיפֶךְ מִמַּה שֶּׁהוּא הָאֱמֶת כְּפִי דַּעְתּוֹ.
perforce he would spend the rest of his days teaching contrary to what he considers truth according to his conviction.
וְהָיָה קְצָת אֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר מִשּׁוּם דְּאִם הָיָה מַטְעֶה אוֹתָם שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה חוֹזֵר בֶּאֱמֶת,
And it might have been tentatively possible to suggest that had he misled them without sincerely retracting,
וַדַּאי דְּלֹא הָיָה חוֹזֵר אֶלָּא לְשָׁעָה,
he certainly would have retracted only temporarily for the hour,
וְאַחַר שֶׁיִּתְמַנֶּה אַב בֵּית דִּין הָיָה חוֹזֵר לְדַעְתּוֹ הָרִאשׁוֹנָה,
and once appointed head of the court (Av Beit Din) he would have returned to his original stance,
וּמִשֶּׁעָלָה שׁוּב לֹא הָיוּ מוֹרִידִין אוֹתוֹ בִּשְׁבִיל זֶה שֶׁנֶּחְלַק עִם הַחֲכָמִים בְּאֵיזֶה דִּינִים,
and having once ascended, they would not demote him simply because he disputed with the sages on specific rulings,
וְרַק לְכַתְּחִלָּה לֹא רָצוּ לְמַנּוֹתוֹ עַד שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר,
and only ab initio did they decline to appoint him unless he retracted,
אֲבָל אֵין בָּזֶה כְּדֵי לְהוֹרִידוֹ אַחַר שֶׁנִּתְמַנָּה כְּלָל,
yet there is insufficient cause here to depose him once installed,
וּ"מַעֲלִין בַּקֹּדֶשׁ וְאֵין מוֹרִידִין",
for “we elevate in holiness and do not downgrade,”
וְשַׁפִּיר הָוֵי פְּעוּלַּת הָרֶשַׁע רַק שָׁעָה אַחַת,
so that the transgressive act would genuinely endure for merely one hour,
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר לְשׁוֹן "רָשָׁע שָׁעָה אַחַת".
and therefore he phrased it “wicked for one hour.”
אֲבָל אֵין זֶה מְחֻוָּור כְּלָל,
However, this interpretation is not compelling or clear at all,
דַּהֲרֵי הֵם בִּקְשׁוּ מִמֶּנּוּ לַחֲזוֹר בֶּאֱמֶת וְלֹא לְהַטְעוֹתָם,
for behold, they asked him to retract sincerely and not to deceive them,
וּ"שְׁאֵרִית יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יַעֲשׂוּ עַוְלָה וְלֹא יְדַבְּרוּ כָזָב" (צְפַנְיָה ג, יג),
and “the remnant of Israel shall not do iniquity, nor speak lies” (Zephaniah 3:13),
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן אָדָם גָּדוֹל כַּעֲקַבְיָא בֶּן מַהֲלַלְאֵל חָלִילָה שֶׁיַּטְעֶה אוֹתָם.
and all the more so a sage as venerable as Akavya ben Mahalalel would never, Heaven forbid, mislead them.
וְאִם הֶחֱשִׁיב זֶה לְמַעֲשֵׂה רֶשַׁע לַחֲזוֹר מִקַּבָּלָתוֹ וּמַה שֶּׁהוּא שֶׁלֹּא כַּדִּין לְפִי דַּעְתּוֹ,
And if he considered it an act of wickedness to abandon his received tradition and act contrary to law in his judgment,
לֹא הָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר "שָׁעָה אַחַת",
he should not have formulated it as “one hour,”
וּמֵהֵיכָא תֵּיתֵי לוֹ לוֹמַר לְעִנְיַן שֶׁלֹּא יַטְעֶה אוֹתָם דָּבָר שֶׁלֹּא בִּקְשׁוּ מִמֶּנּוּ,
and whence would he formulate a response about not deceiving them concerning something they never even suggested,
וְלֹא יַעֲלֶה עַל לֵב שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה זֶה שֶׁיִּצְטָרֵךְ לוֹמַר שֶׁלֹּא יַעֲשֶׂה כֵּן.
since it would never enter anyone's mind that he would ever do so, that he should need to declare he would not act thus.
וּבְלָאו הָכִי יֵשׁ לְעַיֵּין מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ לוֹ: "חֲזוֹר בְּךָ וְכוּלֵי וְנַעֲשֶׂךָ אַב בֵּית דִּין וְכוּלֵי",
And regardless of this, it requires scrutiny why they said to him: “Retract, etc., and we will appoint you Av Beit Din, etc.,”
שֶׁנִּרְאֶה כִּמְבַקְּשִׁים שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר כְּדֵי שֶׁיַּעֲשׂוּהוּ אַב בֵּית דִּין,
which makes it appear as though they were asking him to retract for the specific incentive of making him Av Beit Din,
וְאֵיךְ סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּם שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר בִּשְׁבִיל שְׂרָרָה?
and how could it enter their minds that he would compromise his stance for the sake of political prestige?
וְאִם כַּוָּונָתָם הָיָה שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר בֶּאֱמֶת לְבַטֵּל דַּעְתּוֹ מִפְּנֵי הַמְּרֻבִּים,
And if their intention was that he retract sincerely, nullifying his view before the majority,
לֹא הָיָה לָהֶם לוֹמַר הָא דְּ"נַעֲשֶׂךָ אַב בֵּית דִּין".
they should not have added the clause “and we will make you Av Beit Din.”
אִם בַּדִּין הוּא שֶׁיְּבַטֵּל דַּעְתּוֹ וְיַחֲזוֹר בּוֹ,
If halakhic law required that he nullify his view and retract,
גַּם זוּלַת זֶה הָיָה לָהֶם לוֹמַר גַּם כֵּן מִקּוֹדֶם שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר;
they should have instructed him to retract even without any mention of office;
וְאִם אֵינוֹ בַּדִּין שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר,
and if it was not halakhically incumbent upon him to retract,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ [שָׁם מִשְׁנָה ז']: "אֲנִי שָׁמַעְתִּי מִפִּי הַמְּרֻבִּים וְכוּלֵי",
just as he himself subsequently declared (ibid., Mishnah 7): “I heard my traditions from the mouth of a majority, etc.,”
גַּם בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁיַּעֲשׂוּהוּ אַב בֵּית דִּין לֹא סָלְקָא דַּעְתֵּיהּ שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר שֶׁלֹּא כַּדִּין.
then even to be appointed Av Beit Din it would never enter his mind to retract contrary to the law.
וּמַשְׁמָעוּת הַלָּשׁוֹן דְּאָמְרוּ לוֹ שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר בִּשְׁבִיל זֶה שֶׁיַּעֲשׂוּהוּ אַב בֵּית דִּין,
Yet the plain syntax implies that they urged him to retract precisely so that they might make him Av Beit Din,
וְזֶה צָרִיךְ בֵּיאוּר.
and this demands explanation.
וְגַם מַה שֶּׁאָמַר: "מוּטָב לִי לְהִקָּרֵא שׁוֹטֶה וְכוּלֵי" צָרִיךְ בֵּיאוּר,
And likewise his reply, “It is better for me to be called a fool, etc.,” requires explanation,
דְּמֵהֵיכָא תֵּיתֵי יִקְרָאוּהוּ שׁוֹטֶה
for why on earth would anyone label him a fool
עַל שֶׁלֹּא רָצָה לַחֲזוֹר שֶׁלֹּא כַּדִּין בִּשְׁבִיל הַשְּׂרָרָה?
for refusing to abandon his halakhic integrity for the sake of public office?
וְאִם הֵם נֶחְלְקוּ עִמּוֹ בָּזֶה גּוּפֵיהּ,
And if they differed with him over this very premise,
שֶׁהָיוּ סְבוּרִים שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְבַטֵּל דַּעְתּוֹ לְדַעַת הָרַבִּים
holding that he was obligated to subordinate his opinion to the collective majority
וְהוּא סָבוּר שֶׁאֵין לוֹ לְבַטֵּל,
while he held that he had no right to surrender his received tradition,
לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ לִקְרוֹתוֹ "שׁוֹטֶה" בִּשְׁבִיל זֶה
one still cannot call him a “fool” on that account,
אִם הוּא לְפִי דַּעְתּוֹ אֵינוֹ רַשַּׁאי לַחֲזוֹר.
seeing that according to his own reasoned conviction he was not permitted to retract.
גַּם צָרִיךְ בֵּיאוּר מַה שֶּׁאָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ:
Furthermore, what he stated afterward requires elucidation:
"שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ אוֹמְרִים: בִּשְׁבִיל שְׂרָרָה חָזַר בּוֹ",
“lest people say: he retracted for the sake of office”;
וּמַה עִנְיַן "שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ אוֹמְרִים"
and what relevance has public perception, “lest people say,”
אִם בְּלָאו הָכִי אֵין רַשַּׁאי לַחֲזוֹר בּוֹ כְּלָל?
if irrespective of public talk he is entirely prohibited from retracting at all?
וּבְתוֹסְפוֹת יוֹם טוֹב שָׁם נִדְחַק
And in Tosafot Yom Tov there he was pressed to resolve this
דְּ"חֲדָא וְעוֹד" קָאָמַר, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
explaining that Akavya was presenting a compound two-fold rationale (“one reason, and furthermore another”), see there.
אֲבָל פְּשַׁט הַלָּשׁוֹן "שֶׁלֹּא וְכוּלֵי",
However, the literal phrasing “lest, etc.” (shelo),
וְלֹא אָמַר "וְשֶׁלֹּא",
and not “and lest” (veshelo),
מַשְׁמַע דַּחֲדָא מִילְּתָא הוּא
implies that it is a single unified thought
וְסִיּוּם דְּבָרָיו הָרִאשׁוֹנִים.
and the direct continuation and conclusion of his opening statement.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Eduyos 5:6 records the offer to make Akavya Av Beis Din if he recanted four rulings. He preferred being called a fool all his life to becoming wicked before God for a moment, so that people would not say he changed for office. Chagigah 2:2 identifies the first of each pair as Nasi and the second as Av Beis Din. The author now questions how the momentary language and the concern about office fit together.

paragraphs.text: Menachos 99a illustrates ‘ascend in holiness and do not descend’ with silver and gold tables; the Mishnah on 99b describes marble and gold. Megillah 9b gives the closer personal example: Rabbi Yosi says a substitute Kohen Gadol may subsequently serve neither in that office, because of hostility, nor as an ordinary kohen, because one does not descend in holiness; Rabbi Meir states a different formulation of the substitute’s continuing status. Extending the principle to an Av Beis Din is the author’s analogy in a tentative scenario that he immediately rejects, not the subject of either Gemara.

paragraphs.text: Tzefaniah 3:13 describes the purified remnant speaking neither falsehood nor deceit. The author invokes it against his tentative deception scenario. In Eduyos 5:6, Rabbi Yehudah disputes the report that Akavya was excommunicated and praises his wisdom and fear of sin; Bartenura’s wording emphasizes humility. Tosafos Yom Tov offers more than one explanation of the excommunication dispute: one treats deliberate disrespect as incompatible with that stature, while another concerns a lesser court’s authority. These are contextual portraits, not direct answers to the author’s grammatical question.

paragraphs.text: Tosafos Yom Tov on Eduyos 5:6 reads ‘one reason, and moreover another’: Akavya would not recant falsely for office; even if he sincerely changed his mind, he would decline appointment lest people suspect ambition. The first reason concerns wrongdoing before God, the second public suspicion. Rav Tzadok finds that division forced: the Mishnah says ‘so that they should not say,’ without an additional ‘and,’ making it sound like the completion of the first explanation. This textual objection, and the puzzle about ‘one moment,’ belong to his developing argument.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Akavya ben Mahalalel’s refusal of office raises a difficulty about being wicked “for one hour.” Rav Tzadok questions explanations based on a false retraction and asks why concern for reputation, fidelity to one’s received teaching, and the offer of office are joined in the Mishnah.

p: וְעַל כֵּן נִרְאֶה דְּבֶאֱמֶת,
Therefore it appears that in truth,
הֲרֵי אָמְרוּ [שָׁם מִשְׁנָה ז']:
behold they related (ibid., Mishnah 7):
דִּבִשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ אָמַר לִבְנוֹ: "חֲזוֹר בְּךָ וְכוּלֵי,
that at the hour of his passing he instructed his son: “Retract, etc.,
מוּטָב לִדְחוֹת דִּבְרֵי הַיָּחִיד וְכוּלֵי".
it is better to abandon the words of an individual, etc.”
וּמִמַּה שֶּׁאָמַר לוֹ: "וְלָמָּה לֹא חָזַרְתָּ?", אָמַר לוֹ וְכוּלֵי,
And from the fact that his son asked: “And why did you not retract?”, and Akavya replied to him, etc.,
מְבוֹאָר דְּלֹא אָז הוּא שֶׁנִּתְחַדֵּשׁ לוֹ דָּבָר זֶה,
it is evident that this principle was not a novel revelation that occurred to him only then;
רַק כָּךְ הָיָה דַּעְתּוֹ מֵעוֹלָם:
rather, such was his established outlook all along:
דְּהוּא אֵין יָכוֹל לְבַטֵּל דְּבָרָיו שֶׁשָּׁמַע מֵהַמְּרֻבִּים,
that he himself could not set aside traditions he personally heard from a majority,
אֲבָל הַשּׁוֹמֵעַ מִמֶּנּוּ יֵשׁ לוֹ לִדְחוֹת דְּבָרָיו.
whereas one who heard it merely second-hand from him should abandon the isolated opinion.
וּמַה שֶּׁאָמַר לוֹ בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ,
And the reason he instructed him only at the hour of death,
לְפִי שֶׁכָּל יְמֵי חַיָּיו הָיָה בְּנוֹ אֶצְלוֹ וּבְבֵיתוֹ וְלֹא הָיָה מוֹרֶה לְעַצְמוֹ,
was because throughout Akavya's lifetime his son resided with him in his home and did not issue independent rulings,
וְעַל כֵּן לֹא הֻוצְרַךְ לוֹמַר לוֹ זֶה אֶלָּא בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ.
and therefore he did not need to instruct him regarding this until the moment of his demise.
וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לוֹ תַּלְמִידִים אֲחֵרִים כְּלָל אֶלָּא בְּנוֹ לְבַד,
And one must say that he had no other disciples at all except his son alone,
דְּאִם לֹא כֵן, הָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר זֶה עוֹד בְּחַיָּיו לְהַתַּלְמִידִים כְּשֶׁפֵּירְשׁוּ מִמֶּנּוּ
for otherwise, he should have said this during his lifetime to his disciples when they departed from him,
אוֹ בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ גַּם לְתַלְמִידָיו.
or at the hour of death to his disciples as well.
וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּאָז כָּל הַתַּלְמִידִים הָיוּ לוֹמְדִים לִפְנֵי הַסַּנְהֶדְרִין וְהָאַב בֵּית דִּין שֶׁהָיָה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל,
And perforce, at that era all students studied before the Sanhedrin and the presiding Av Beit Din in Israel,
וְהוּא, שֶׁלֹּא נִתְמַנָּה אַב בֵּית דִּין, הָיָה יוֹשֵׁב בָּדָד בְּבֵיתוֹ
while he, not having been appointed Av Beit Din, sat secluded in his home
וְלֹא לָמַד אֶלָּא עִם בְּנוֹ לְבַד.
and studied with his son alone.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: אֲבָל הַשּׁוֹמֵעַ מִמֶּנּוּ יֵשׁ לוֹ לִדְחוֹת דְּבָרָיו.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Eduyos 5:7, Bartenura, and Tosafos Yom Tov - Akavya's received tradition: The Mishnah continues: “בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ... אֲנִי שָׁמַעְתִּי מִפִּי הַמְרֻבִּים... אֲבָל אַתָּה שָׁמַעְתָּ מִפִּי הַיָּחִיד וּמִפִּי הַמְרֻבִּין; מוּטָב לְהַנִּיחַ דִּבְרֵי הַיָּחִיד וְלֶאֱחֹז בְּדִבְרֵי הַמְרֻבִּין.” At death Akavya instructed his son to leave Akavya's ruling for the majority's. Akavya had not formed a private opinion; he preserved a ruling received from a group. Tosafos Yom Tov, citing Raavad, explains either that the earlier authorities were divided, or that each side regarded its transmitters as the majority. Bartenura notes that Akavya says “better,” not simply “obligatory,” because his own mesorah also came from many; his son, however, heard Akavya as an individual against the public tradition. Rav Tzadok thus distinguishes between a teacher's fidelity to what he personally received and a listener's duty to follow the operative majority. Compare Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Novellae to the Rif, Shabbos 22:2: “The rule of an individual and the many applies even to laws for the Messianic era, for Scripture says, ‘incline after the many.’” There he distinguishes the general majority rule from rules giving precedence to named Amoraim. The parallel establishes majority authority; it does not decide which account of Akavya’s received tradition is correct.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok proposes that Akavya could retain his own received tradition while directing students to follow the majority. On this reconstruction, the offer of office concerned his public teaching, and his refusal guarded against the appearance that he had compromised his convictions for rank.

p: וּלְפִי זֶה יֵשׁ לוֹמַר: מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ: "חֲזוֹר וְנַעֲשֶׂךָ אַב בֵּית דִּין",
And according to this we can explain: what they meant by “Retract and we will make you Av Beit Din”
אֵין רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר שֶׁהוּא יַחֲזוֹר לְעַצְמוֹ,
was not that he himself should personally abandon his conviction;
רַק לְפִי שֶׁהָיָה שׁוֹנֶה לִבְנוֹ כֵּן,
rather, since he was teaching his son thus,
וּכְשֶׁיִּתְמַנֶּה אַב בֵּית דִּין יִשְׁנֶה גַּם לְתַלְמִידִים כֵּן;
when installed as Av Beit Din he would teach the public disciples likewise;
וְאַף שֶׁהַתַּלְמִידִים יִשְׁמְעוּ דִּבְרֵי הַמְּרֻבִּים,
and even though the students would hear the words of the majority,
אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּגָּרְרוּ אַחַר דַּעְתּוֹ
it was likely they would be drawn after his personal stance
בִּהְיוֹתוֹ אַב בֵּית דִּין וּמוּפְלָא שֶׁבַּסַּנְהֶדְרִין וְגָדוֹל שֶׁבְּכָל חֲכָמִים,
inasmuch as he would be Av Beit Din, the foremost of the Sanhedrin, and the greatest of all the sages,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [שָׁם מִשְׁנָה ו']: "שֶׁאֵין כָּל עֲזָרָה נִנְעֶלֶת וְכוּלֵי",
as they stated (ibid., Mishnah 6): “No man in the Temple courtyard ever matched his wisdom and piety, etc.,”
וְיִרְבּוּ אַחַר כָּךְ הַנִּגְרָרִים אַחֲרָיו עַד שֶׁיִּתְבַּטְּלוּ דִּבְרֵיהֶם.
and subsequently those following him would multiply until the majority ruling was undermined.
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: "חֲזוֹר וְכוּלֵי",
And regarding this they urged: “Retract, etc.,”
הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא יִלְמוֹד לְתַלְמִידִים כְּדַעְתּוֹ,
meaning that he should not instruct students according to his minority view,
וְיֹאמַר לָהֶם שֶׁיִּסְמְכוּ אַהַמְּרֻבִּים,
and should instruct them to rely upon the majority,
וְזֶהוּ כַּדִּין וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר גַּם הוּא בְּעַצְמוֹ לִבְנוֹ.
and this was entirely in accordance with halakhah, precisely as he himself ultimately told his son.
וְלֹא בִּקְשׁוּ שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר בְּעַצְמוֹ
They never demanded that he personally retract in his own private practice
וְיֹאמַר מַה שֶּׁהוּא שֶׁלֹּא כַּדִּין כְּפִי דַּעְתּוֹ וּשְׁמוּעָתוֹ,
or affirm that which he deemed contrary to law based on his received tradition;
רַק שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר בְּעִנְיַן לִימּוּדוֹ לְתַלְמִידִים,
only that he agree to pedagogical restraint in instructing students,
וּבָזֶה הָיָה דַּי לָהֶם לְמַנּוֹתוֹ אַב בֵּית דִּין,
and with this compromise they were fully satisfied to appoint him Av Beit Din,
דְּאֵין עוֹד חֲשַׁשׁ תַּקָּלָה לְתַלְמִידִים,
since there would no longer be any concern of public legal stumbling for the disciples,
מֵאַחַר שֶׁהֲגַם שֶׁהוּא בְּעַצְמוֹ לֹא יַחֲזוֹר מִשְּׁמוּעָתוֹ,
seeing that even though he himself would not surrender his personal tradition,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם יֹאמַר לְתַלְמִידִים שֶׁיַּנִּיחוּ דַּעְתּוֹ וְיִתְפְּסוּ דַּעַת הָרַבִּים.
he would nevertheless direct the students to set aside his view and uphold the ruling of the majority.
וְאִם כֵּן, הֵם בִּקְשׁוּ מִמֶּנּוּ דָּבָר שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת בַּדִּין
If so, they merely requested of him a course of action that he was legally bound to observe
כְּפִי דַּעַת עַצְמוֹ גַּם כֵּן,
even according to his own personal conviction,
וְגַם הוּא מֵעַצְמוֹ הָיָה עוֹשֶׂה כֵּן כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
and which he himself indeed practiced on his own, as noted above.
רַק לְפִי שֶׁהֵם בִּקְשׁוּ זֶה מִמֶּנּוּ וּכְדֵי לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ אַב בֵּית דִּין,
Only because they requested this of him as an explicit condition for appointing him Av Beit Din,
נִמְנַע מֵהַטַּעַם שֶׁסִּיֵּים: "שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ אוֹמְרִים וְכוּלֵי".
did he refuse, on account of the concluding rationale: “lest people say, etc.”
וְזֶה הָיָה עִיקַּר טַעְמוֹ,
And this was his paramount reason:
דְּמֵאַחַר שֶׁעַד עַתָּה לֹא לִמֵּד לְתַלְמִידִים רַק לִבְנוֹ בִּלְבַד כְּשִׁיטָתוֹ,
for since until then he had taught no disciples except his son according to his methodology,
וְלֹא יָדְעוּ שֶׁדַּעְתּוֹ בֶּאֱמֶת שֶׁאֲחֵרִים יִגָּרְרוּ אַחַר הַמְּרֻבִּים,
and the public did not know that he genuinely held that others must follow the majority,
אִם עַתָּה עַל פִּי בַּקָּשָׁתָם יַעֲשֶׂה כֵּן כְּשֶׁיִּתְמַנֶּה אַב בֵּית דִּין,
if he were now to adopt this public policy upon their request when installed as Av Beit Din,
יֹאמְרוּ שֶׁבִּשְׁבִיל הַשְּׂרָרָה חָזַר שֶׁלֹּא כַּדִּין.
people would gossip that he compromised his principles unlawfully for the sake of public office.
וַהֲרֵי מָצִינוּ חֲכָמִים אָסְרוּ כַּמָּה דְּבָרִים מִפְּנֵי הַחֲשָׁד,
And behold, we find that the Sages prohibited numerous matters solely to avert suspicion;
וּבְשַׁבָּת (כ״ג סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳) אִיתָא:
and in Shabbat (23a) it is taught:
"מְנָא תֵּימְרָא דְּחָיְישִׁינַן לַחֲשָׁד וְכוּלֵי",
“From where do we derive that we are concerned with suspicion? etc.”
וְהַיְינוּ מִקְּרָאֵי דְּמַיְיתֵי דְּגַם הַתּוֹרָה חָשְׁשָׁה לַחֲשָׁד גַּבֵּי פֵּאָה,
and this is derived from the biblical verses cited showing that the Torah itself feared suspicion regarding leaving pe'ah in the field,
וּבְפֶרֶק שְׁלִישִׁי דִּשְׁקָלִים [מִשְׁנָה ב'] יָלְפִינַן מִקְּרָא דְּ"וִהְיִיתֶם נְקִיִּם מֵה' וּמִיִּשְׂרָאֵל" (בַּמִּדְבָּר לב, כב), עַיֵּין שָׁם.
and in the third chapter of Shekalim (Mishnah 2) we derive this from the verse: “And you shall be clear before Hashem and before Israel” (Numbers 32:22), see there.
וּמֵאַחַר דְּגַם מִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְקַיֵּים דִּבְרֵי חֲכָמִים נִקְרָא רָשָׁע
And since anyone who disregards rabbinic decrees is branded wicked,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּנִדָּה (י״ב עַמּוּד א׳),
as they stated in Niddah (12a),
כָּל שֶׁכֵּן בָּזֶה דְּנִלְמַד מִקְּרָא,
all the more so regarding this duty derived directly from Scripture,
הָעוֹבֵר וּמֵבִיא עַצְמוֹ לַחֲשָׁד הֲרֵי זֶה רָשָׁע לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם גַּם כֵּן
one who violates this and subjects himself to public suspicion is deemed wicked before the Omnipresent as well,
אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין שָׁם בֶּאֱמֶת שׁוּם מַעֲשֵׂה רֶשַׁע כְּלָל.
even though in objective truth no transgressive act was committed at all.
וְאִם כֵּן שַׁפִּיר מַה שֶּׁאָמַר "שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ אוֹמְרִים וְכוּלֵי"
And if so, his statement “lest people say, etc.”
הוּא נִמְשָׁךְ לְטַעַם אֶל הַקּוֹדֵם,
is a direct thematic continuation of his preceding words,
דְּמִפְּנֵי כֵן יִהְיֶה נֶחְשָׁב רָשָׁע לַמָּקוֹם גַּם כֵּן.
explaining that on account of this very suspicion he would be reckoned wicked before the Omnipresent as well.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: מִכָּל מָקוֹם יֹאמַר לְתַלְמִידִים שֶׁיַּנִּיחוּ דַּעְתּוֹ וְיִתְפְּסוּ דַּעַת הָרַבִּים.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Chagigah 2:2; Eduyos 5:6; Sanhedrin 88b - the Av Beis Din shapes public Torah: Mishnah Chagigah identifies the zugos: “הָרִאשׁוֹנִים הָיוּ נְשִׂיאִים, וּשְׁנִיִּים לָהֶם אַב בֵּית דִּין”; Bartenura explains that their recurring disputes were between each generation's Nasi and Av Beis Din. Eduyos praises Akavya: “שֶׁאֵין עֲזָרָה נִנְעֶלֶת... בְּחָכְמָה וּבְיִרְאַת חֵטְא כַּעֲקַבְיָא.” Sanhedrin describes unresolved questions rising through the courts and being decided by vote - “רַבּוּ הַמְטַמְּאִים טִמְּאוּ; רַבּוּ הַמְטַהֲרִין טִהֲרוּ” - and a qualified judge being promoted toward the Great Sanhedrin. This is the institutional background for Rav Tzadok's inference: appointing Akavya would place an exceptionally authoritative teacher at the center of national transmission, not merely grant him honor. Rav Tzadok therefore reads the Sages' request as directed to what he would teach the students, lest reverence for him eventually displace the operative majority. The claims that Akavya taught only his son and that appointment would change the course of transmission are Rav Tzadok’s reconstruction. Neither the Mishnah nor Sanhedrin explicitly reports that biography.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 23a; Shekalim 3:2; Niddah 12a - avoiding reasonable suspicion: Shabbos asks, “מְנָא תֵּימְרָא דְּחָיְשִׁינַן לַחֲשָׁד?” and answers that the Torah required pe'ah at the field's end, among other reasons, “מִפְּנֵי הַחֲשָׁד.” Shekalim requires the treasurer to enter without anything that could conceal coins, because “אָדָם צָרִיךְ לָצֵאת יְדֵי הַבְּרִיּוֹת כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לָצֵאת יְדֵי הַמָּקוֹם,” citing “וִהְיִיתֶם נְקִיִּים מֵה׳ וּמִיִּשְׂרָאֵל.” Bartenura explains the pargod chafut as a garment with a folded hem in which money could be concealed; the Mishnah also excludes tefillin and an amulet. The point is a concrete opportunity for concealment, rather than a ban on every garment that happens to be folded. Niddah adds Rava's premise that one who disregards the Sages' requirements is termed a rasha. Rav Tzadok combines these sources: even an honest act may violate the duty to remain clean before Israel when it knowingly creates credible suspicion. Compare Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Novellae to the Rif, Berachos 1:5: one must “take care and flee from suspicion.” Akavya's “that they not say” is therefore not concern for reputation alone; preventable suspicion itself becomes a temporary spiritual fault.

p: אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת, הַךְ חֲשָׁדָא אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא לְשָׁעָה וּבַתְּחִלָּה,
However in truth, this suspicion would persist only for an hour and at the outset,
אֲבָל אַחַר כָּךְ, כְּשֶׁיִּרְאוּ שֶׁמַּחֲזִיק וְעוֹמֵד כֵּן בַּחֲזָרָתוֹ לְגַבֵּי הַתַּלְמִידִים,
yet afterward, when the public saw that he consistently maintained this posture toward the students,
וַדַּאי דְּלֹא יַחְשְׁדוּהוּ עוֹד;
they would certainly no longer suspect him;
שֶׁאִם הָיָה רַק מִפְּנֵי הַשְּׂרָרָה,
for had his concession been solely for the sake of political rank,
אַחַר שֶׁנִּתְמַנָּה הֲוָה לֵיהּ לַחֲזוֹר לְדַעְתּוֹ הָרִאשׁוֹנָה,
once installed he ought to have reverted to his original stance,
דְּשׁוּב לֹא יַעֲבִירוּהוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל.
since they would no longer remove him from office, as I wrote above.
וְזֶה וַדַּאי לֹא יַחְשְׁדוּהוּ שֶׁמַּחֲזִיק אַחַר כָּךְ בַּחֲזָרָתוֹ
And they certainly would not suspect that he maintained this concession subsequently
כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יֹאמְרוּ שֶׁחָזַר מִפְּנֵי הַשְּׂרָרָה,
merely so that people should not say he retracted for the sake of power;
דְּהַחֲשָׁד וּלְזוּת שְׂפָתַיִם עַל חֲזָרָתוֹ מִפְּנֵי הַשְּׂרָרָה
for suspicion and slanderous talk regarding retracting for the sake of office
אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר לְעוֹלָם וְיוֹרֶה שֶׁלֹּא כַּדִּין מִפְּנֵי שְׂרָרָה,
arises only if one permanently abandons the truth and rules unlawfully for personal honor,
דַּהֲוֵי חֲשָׁד אַמַּעֲשֵׂה רֶשַׁע לְהַכְשִׁיל רַבִּים בְּהוֹרָאָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ כַּדִּין לְפִי דַּעְתּוֹ.
which would constitute suspicion of active wickedness in causing the public to stumble through erroneous rulings.
אֲבָל אִם אַחַר כָּךְ חָזַר לְהוֹרָאָתוֹ,
However, if he subsequently reverted to his authentic halakhic ruling,
הֲרֵי אַדְּרַבָּה, עַל יְדֵי הִתְמַנּוּתוֹ לְאַב בֵּית דִּין מַחֲזִיק הוֹרָאָתוֹ
behold, on the contrary, through his appointment as Av Beit Din he would champion his tradition
וְיִמְנַע רַבִּים מִמִּכְשׁוֹל כְּפִי דַּעְתּוֹ;
and prevent the public from stumbling according to his view;
אַף שֶׁהִטְעָה אֶת הַחֲכָמִים בַּמַּה שֶּׁאָמַר לָהֶם שֶׁחָזַר בּוֹ וְנָהַג עִמָּהֶם מִנְהַג רַמָּאוּת,
and even though he would have misled the sages by claiming to retract, practicing deception,
וְעָבַר עַל "מִדְּבַר שֶׁקֶר תִּרְחָק" (שְׁמוֹת כג, ז) וְעַל "שְׁאֵרִית יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יְדַבְּרוּ כָזָב",
violating “Distance yourself from falsehood” (Exodus 23:7) and “the remnant of Israel shall not speak lies,”
מָצִינוּ כְּהַאי גַּוְונָא שֶׁהָיוּ מַטְעִים לַחֲכָמִים כְּדֵי לְהַעֲמִיד הַדִּין עַל אֲמִיתּוֹ.
we find precedents where sages intentionally misled colleagues in order to establish halakhah on its true foundation.
עַל דֶּרֶךְ הַאי דִּיבָמוֹת (קט״ז סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳):
Along the lines of that in Yevamot (116b):
"אָמְרוּ לָהּ: סְפְדִי וְכוּלֵי, וְיַלְּפוּהָ שִׁקְרָא",
“they said to her: Eulogize your husband, etc., and they taught her to state a falsehood,”
אִינְהוּ כְּרַבָּנַן סְבִירָא לְהוּ וְכוּלֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
because they held like the Rabbis to permit her to remarry, see there.
וְאַף לוֹמַר שֶׁקֶר כְּהַאי דְּשַׁבָּת (קט״ו רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳):
And even to state an outright untruth, like that in Shabbat (115a):
אָמַר לָהֶם: אֲתָא אִיגַּרְתָּא מִמַּעַרְבָא וְכוּלֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י.
he told them: “A letter arrived from the Land of Israel, etc.,” see there in Rashi.
וּבְעֵירוּבִין (נ״א עַמּוּד א׳):
And in Eruvin (51a):
"לֹא תְּנָא לֵיהּ כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי אֶלָּא כִּי הֵיכֵי דְּלִיקַבְּלָהּ מִינֵּיהּ".
"He had not learned it as Rabbi Yosi's teaching; he presented it that way only so that the other would accept it from him."
וְכֵן הַאי דְּקִדּוּשִׁין (מ״ד עַמּוּד ב׳):
And likewise in Kiddushin (44b):
"אַפְּכוּהָ וְשַׁדְּרוּהָ וְכוּלֵי", עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י וְכַדּוֹמֶה.
“they inverted the names and sent the query, etc.,” see there in Rashi and similar instances.
וְהֲגַם דְּזֶה לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ בְּיָחִיד נֶגֶד רַבִּים,
And although this rationale does not strictly apply to an individual against a majority,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין בָּזֶה חֲשָׁד שֶׁל מַעֲשֵׂה רֶשַׁע וּלְזוּת שְׂפָתַיִם
nevertheless there is no suspicion of wickedness or malicious slander here
אִם הוּא עוֹמֵד עַל דַּעְתּוֹ וְרוֹצֶה לְהַחֲזִיק שְׁמוּעָתוֹ מִפִּי רַבִּים גַּם נֶגֶד הַמְּרֻבִּים עַל יְדֵי הַטְעָאָה.
if he stands firm on his received tradition from earlier authorities even against his contemporaries through tactical deception.
וְכֵיוָן דְּיֵשׁ שָׁם דָּבָר שֶׁל זְכוּת בְּמַעֲשֶׂה זוֹ שֶׁהוּא עוֹשֶׂה כַּדִּין,
And since there is an aspect of righteousness in this action in that he rules correctly according to his tradition,
וְעוֹד מִתְכַּוֵּין לְמִצְוָה,
and furthermore he intends for a mitzvah,
לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ חֲשָׁדָא.
genuine moral suspicion does not apply.
וְאִם כֵּן, אִלּוּ לֹא הָיָה חוֹזֵר בֶּאֱמֶת, וַדַּאי שֶׁהָיָה אַחַר כָּךְ חוֹזֵר לְדַעְתּוֹ;
If so, had he not retracted sincerely, he would certainly have returned to his stance afterward;
וְאִם כֵּן, כְּשֶׁיִּרְאוּ שֶׁעוֹמֵד בַּחֲזָרָתוֹ וַדַּאי שֶׁלֹּא יַחְשְׁדוּהוּ עוֹד שֶׁעָשָׂה מִפְּנֵי הַשְּׂרָרָה,
and if so, when the public saw that he adhered to his retraction, they would no longer suspect him of acting for prestige,
יֵדְעוּ שֶׁהַחֲזָרָה בֶּאֱמֶת.
and would know that his retraction was genuine.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: וְעָבַר עַל "מִדְּבַר שֶׁקֶר תִּרְחָק" (שְׁמוֹת כג, ז) וְעַל "שְׁאֵרִית יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יְדַבְּרוּ כָזָב",

paragraphs.text: Shemos 23:7; Tzefaniah 3:13; Shevuos 30b–31a; Sforno on Shemos 23:7; Malbim on Tzefaniah 3:13. “מִדְּבַר שֶׁקֶר תִּרְחָק” means “Distance yourself from a false matter.” Shevuos applies it to safeguards against judicial falsehood. Tzefaniah describes a remnant that neither wrongs nor speaks falsehood and has no deceitful tongue. Sforno warns against a judge’s wording that a dishonest litigant could exploit; Malbim distinguishes wrong in deed, false speech and calculated deception. Tzefaniah’s full wording is “שְׁאֵרִית יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יַעֲשׂוּ עַוְלָה וְלֹא יְדַבְּרוּ כָזָב וְלֹא יִמָּצֵא בְּפִיהֶם לְשׁוֹן תַּרְמִית” — “The remnant of Israel shall do no wrong, speak no falsehood, and no deceitful tongue shall be found in their mouths.”

paragraphs.text: Compare Kometz HaMinchah II §1 (Sefaria 2:1): “In arithmetic there is a false calculation through which one cannot reach the truth unless he first assumes several falsehoods; they are a path through which to reach the truth. So too in Torah,” followed by the teaching that a person understands Torah through first stumbling in it. This concerns intermediate assumptions and error in learning; it does not itself permit deceiving another person. Peri Tzadik, Vayetzei §1, conversely emphasizes Yaakov’s fear of even a trace of falsehood. These parallels illuminate the tension; the legal examples and their limits are developed in the following phrases.

paragraphs.text: Yevamos 116b; Meiri - satisfying a disputed condition without fabricating the underlying case: Rabbi Yehudah required a woman who reported her husband's death to appear in mourning; the Chachamim did not. When a woman came before his court, advisers told her, “סִפְדִי בַּעְלִיךְ, קִרְעִי מָאנִיךְ, סִתְרִי מַזְיֵיךְ.” The Gemara asks, “אַלְּפוּהָ שִׁיקְרָא?” and answers, “אִינְהוּ כְּרַבָּנַן סְבִירָא לְהוּ... כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלִישְׁרְיָהּ.” The Meiri formulates the limit: when a recognized beis din permits the matter without that condition, one may guide the litigant to appear before the stricter beis din in a manner that satisfies its condition, and this is not treated as מיחזי כשיקרא. No evidence of the husband's death was invented; the advisers held that she was already halachically permitted and arranged the presentation so Rabbi Yehudah would also permit her. Rav Tzadok cites this as the milder model: an external appearance is adjusted to secure what the advisers understand to be the true ruling. It does not establish permission to falsify facts on which the דין itself depends.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 115a; Rashi - an invented report used to stop a real violation: The Gemara permits preparing vegetables on Yom Kippur only “מִן הַמִּנְחָה וּלְמַעְלָה מִפְּנֵי עָגְמַת נֶפֶשׁ.” When Rabbah saw his household beginning too early, “אָמַר לְהוּ: אֲתַאי אִיגַּרְתָּא מִמַּעְרָבָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן דְּאָסַר.” Rashi explains his purpose in four words: “כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלִיקַבְּלוּ מִינֵּיהּ” - so they would accept the correction from him. Unlike the Yevamos case, this was an outright invented report, but it was used to stop conduct that was genuinely premature under the very rule being discussed. Rav Tzadok therefore treats it as the stronger precedent for a pedagogic falsehood directed toward immediate compliance with the דין. The source still does not say that any mitzvah-purpose permits lying; its force is narrower: Rabbah did not distort the halachah, gain personally, or create false evidence. He used a claimed authority to make his household heed the correct restriction.

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 51a; Kiddushin 44b with Rashi - altered attribution to secure an honest ruling: In Eruvin, Rabbah told Rav Yosef to rely on his identification of their Shabbos residence and attributed the rule to Rabbi Yosi. The Gemara clarifies: “לָא תְּנָא לֵיהּ כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי, אֶלָּא כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלִיקַבֵּל לַהּ מִינֵּיהּ, מִשּׁוּם דְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי נִימּוּקוֹ עִמּוֹ.” In Kiddushin, after Shmuel and Karna disputed a minor's betrothal, the scholars “אַפְכוּהָ שַׁדְּרוּהָ לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב.” Rashi explains that they reversed the names because Rav loved Shmuel; by placing Karna's ruling in Shmuel's name they could test whether Rav would concede to the substance rather than react to the speaker. These cases concern attribution, not manufactured legal facts. Rav Tzadok uses them to show that Chazal sometimes separated a teaching from its stated source so the listener would evaluate or accept the correct דין. He then states his own limit: this technique does not resolve an individual-versus-majority dispute; it only removes the specific suspicion of a wicked act when the actor sincerely seeks to preserve what he regards as the lawful tradition.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok argues that continued public adherence to the majority would eventually dispel suspicion that Akavya had retracted for office. In developing this argument, he compares specific cases of misleading statements used to uphold a received halachic judgment, without treating them as a general permission to deceive.

p: וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּזֶה טַעַם הַחֲכָמִים
And it can be suggested that this was the rationale of the sages
שֶׁאָמְרוּ לוֹ: "חֲזוֹר וְנַעֲשֶׂךָ אַב בֵּית דִּין", וְלֹא חָשׁוּ לַחֲשָׁדָא;
who proposed to him: “Retract and we will make you Av Beit Din,” and harbored no fear of public suspicion;
דְּלֹא מָצִינוּ חֲשָׁשַׁת חֲשָׁד בְּכָל מָקוֹם,
for we do not find concern for suspicion applied everywhere,
וְכֵן הָא דְּיָלְפִינַן מִקְּרָאֵי הַנִּזְכָּרִים לְעֵיל,
and likewise that which we derived from the verses cited above,
אֶלָּא לְעִנְיַן חֲשָׁד גָּמוּר שֶׁיִּשָּׁאֵר בְּדַעְתָּם כֵּן;
applies strictly to permanent, enduring suspicion that remains fixed in their minds;
אֲבָל חֲשָׁד לְשָׁעָה וְאַחַר כָּךְ יִתְבָּרֵר לָהֶם הָאֱמֶת וְיָסוּר הַחֲשָׁד,
whereas regarding fleeting, temporary suspicion where the truth will emerge and remove the doubt,
לֹא מָצִינוּ לָחוּשׁ לָזֶה.
we do not find that halakhah mandates concern.
וַעֲקַבְיָא חָיֵישׁ שֶׁלֹּא לֵיעָשׂוֹת שָׁעָה אַחַת וְכוּלֵי,
Yet Akavya took care not to become wicked for even a single hour, etc.,
דָּיֵיק שַׁפִּיר לוֹמַר "שָׁעָה אַחַת",
and was remarkably precise in declaring “one hour,”
דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם בְּאוֹתוֹ שָׁעָה שֶׁיַּחְשְׁדוּהוּ וְיַחֲזִיקוּהוּ הַבְּרִיּוֹת לְרָשָׁע,
for at least during that brief hour when people suspected him and deemed him wicked,
נַעֲשָׂה רָשָׁע גַּם לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה מִיהַת,
he would be considered wicked before the Omnipresent at that moment as well,
דַּהֲרֵי אָז אֵינוֹ נָקִי מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל,
for at that moment he was not clear before Israel,
וְעָבַר בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה עַל מַה שֶּׁאָמְרָה תּוֹרָה: "וִהְיִיתֶם נְקִיִּם וְגוֹמֵר".
violating at that instant the biblical mandate: “And you shall be clear, etc.”
וּמִיהוּ, לֹא דָּמֵי הַךְ לְהַהִיא דְּנִדָּה הַנִּזְכֶּרֶת לְעֵיל,
However, this case does not compare to that of Niddah mentioned above,
דְּשָׁם הָוֵי מַעֲשֵׂה חֵטְא וְרֶשַׁע גָּמוּר בִּשְׁעָתוֹ,
for there it constitutes an act of actual sin and complete wickedness at the time,
אֶלָּא שֶׁאַחַר כָּךְ יָשׁוּב.
save that he will subsequently repent.
וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּלֹא דָּמֵי לְהָא דְּ"אֶחֱטָא וְאָשׁוּב – אֵין מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ וְכוּלֵי"
And even though it is not equivalent to “I will sin and repent, for which one is not granted opportunity to repent”
בַּמִּשְׁנָה יוֹמָא (פ״ה עַמּוּד ב׳),
in Mishnah Yoma (85b),
דְּהָכָא אֵין בָּא לַחֲטוֹא,
for here he does not deliberately set out to sin,
רַק דְּמִתּוֹךְ שֶׁאוֹחֵז בַּאֲמִתּוֹ חָיְישִׁינַן דְּיָבוֹא לְחִמּוּם
rather merely by grasping his organ we fear he might reach seminal arousal
עַל יְדֵי הִרְהוּר וּגְרִיַּית יֵצֶר הָרָע שֶׁיִּתְקְפֶנּוּ,
through involuntary thought and the incitement of the evil urge overpowering him,
וְאֵין חוֹטֵא עַל סְמַךְ שֶׁיָּשׁוּב,
and he does not sin relying in advance on repentance;
רַק אָנַן אָמְרִינַן בְּעַצְמֵנוּ כֵּן
rather we merely say of our own assessment
דְּוַדַּאי הוּא שֶׁיָּשׁוּב אַחַר כָּךְ וְיִתְחָרֵט,
that it is certain he will repent afterward with remorse,
מֵאַחַר שֶׁלֹּא בָּא לַעֲבוֹר בִּזְדוֹנוֹ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
seeing that he did not set out to transgress willfully, as mentioned above.
מִכָּל מָקוֹם בִּשְׁעָתוֹ מִיהַת
Nonetheless, at that very moment
עוֹבֵר עַל דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹצֶה שֶׁיֶּחֱטָא הָאָדָם גַּם לְשָׁעָה
he violates that which Hashem does not want a person to transgress even for an hour,
אַף שֶׁיָּשׁוּב.
even though he will subsequently repent.
(וְאֶפְשָׁר דְּעַל כֵּן אֵין מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ לָשׁוּב,
(And it is possible that on this account he is not granted the opportunity to repent,
אֶלָּא דְּבְיוֹמָא פ״ז עַמּוּד א׳ אָתוּ עֲלַהּ מִטַּעַם אַחֵר,
save that in Yoma 87a they explain it through a different rationale,
וְדַוְוקָא בִּשְׁתֵּי פְּעָמִים, עַיֵּין שָׁם).
and specifically when committed twice, see there).

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: וְעָבַר בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה עַל מַה שֶּׁאָמְרָה תּוֹרָה: "וִהְיִיתֶם נְקִיִּם וְגוֹמֵר".

paragraphs.text: Bamidbar 32:22; Mishnah Shekalim 3:2; Shabbos 23a with Bartenura and Rashi - the scope of suspicion: Moshe told Gad and Reuven that after fulfilling their public obligation they would be “וִהְיִיתֶם נְקִיִּם מֵה׳ וּמִיִּשְׂרָאֵל.” Shekalim applies this to the Temple treasurer: “אָדָם צָרִיךְ לָצֵאת יְדֵי הַבְּרִיּוֹת כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לָצֵאת יְדֵי הַמָּקוֹם.” He entered without anything that could appear to conceal coins; Bartenura explains the suspicion that later wealth came from the chamber. Shabbos likewise requires a Chanukah light at each of two differently facing entrances when townspeople might see one entrance and infer that the mitzvah was neglected; Rashi identifies that concrete inference. These cases create an appearance liable to remain. Rav Tzadok's limitation - that Chazal did not generally legislate for a momentary suspicion certain to be disproved - is his own inference, not an explicit rule in the sources. Akavya nevertheless accepted the stricter personal standard: during that interval he was not yet “clean before Israel.” The Ohr Zarua LaTzadik parallel on avoiding suspicion is quoted at its earlier occurrence in this discussion.

paragraphs.text: Niddah 13a; Maharal, Netiv HaPerishus 3 - an actual aveirah for “one moment”: Rabbi Eliezer taught: “מוּטָב שֶׁיּוֹצִיא לַעַז עַל בָּנָיו... וְאַל יַעֲשֶׂה עַצְמוֹ רָשָׁע שָׁעָה אַחַת לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם.” The conflict is between avoiding public suspicion and avoiding contact that may produce prohibited arousal. The Gemara asks, “וְכָל כָּךְ לָמָּה?” and answers that the concern is an actual emission for no purpose, citing Onan: “וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳ אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה.” Maharal explains the comparison to a flood: wasting the human power of generation undoes the divinely ordered gathering from which future life proceeds, parallel to the Flood's undoing of the gathered waters. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes the cases. Akavya's deed may be innocent while observers temporarily misunderstand it; in Niddah the feared act itself is sinful at that moment. Later regret can repair the person, but it does not make that moment a non-act. He borrows Rabbi Eliezer's phrase “one moment” while separating objective wrongdoing from temporary public suspicion.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Yoma 8:9; Yoma 87a with Rashi; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 4:1 - relying on future repentance: The Mishnah states: “הָאוֹמֵר אֶחֱטָא וְאָשׁוּב, אֶחֱטָא וְאָשׁוּב, אֵין מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה.” Yoma explains the repetition: “כֵּיוָן שֶׁעָבַר אָדָם עֲבֵירָה וְשָׁנָה בָּהּ... נַעֲשֵׂית לוֹ כְּהֶיתֵּר.” Rashi says that after repetition the sin feels permitted, obstructing repentance. Rambam lists “הָאוֹמֵר אֶחְטָא וְאָשׁוּב” among the severe acts that impede teshuvah because the future remedy is built into the present decision to sin. Rav Tzadok distinguishes Niddah: the person does not intend to transgress on condition that he later repent; Chazal fear that contact may awaken the yetzer, and Rav Tzadok predicts later regret after an unplanned lapse. His bracket asks whether even this may impede teshuvah, while noting that Yoma formally emphasizes repetition. In Takanat HaShavin 10:8 he explains that one who plans to sin in order to become a baal teshuvah cannot reach full regret, because the sin never appeared truly evil. Resisei Layla 38 likewise distinguishes mistakenly treating an aveirah as a mitzvah from knowingly relying on later repentance.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok distinguishes suspicion that will be dispelled from an actual transgression that is later repaired by repentance. He proposes that the sages did not require Akavya’s additional stringency about momentary suspicion, while the warning in Niddah still concerns a real offense at the time it occurs.

p: וְאַף לְמַאן דְּאָמַר בִּבְרָכוֹת (ל״ד עַמּוּד ב׳):
And even according to the authority in Berakhot (34b) who states:
"בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין – צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים אֵינָם עוֹמְדִים",
“In the place where penitents stand, completely righteous people cannot stand,”
דְּעָדִיף מִצַּדִּיק גָּמוּר,
holding that a penitent is superior to the righteous,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא בְּאֵלֶּה חָפֵץ ה'.
nevertheless, Hashem takes no delight in the sinful deed itself.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה ב׳):
And as they stated in Bereishit Rabbah (end of Parashah 2):
"אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ בְּאֵיזֶה מֵהֶן חָפֵץ וְכוּלֵי,
“I know not in which of them He delights, etc.,
כֵּיוָן דִּכְתִיב וְכוּלֵי",
since it is written, etc.,”
וְאֵינוֹ חָפֵץ בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶם שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים.
and He does not desire the deeds of the wicked.
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּיְפֵה תֹּאַר בְּשֵׁם יֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים
And examine there in Yefeh To'ar in the name of some commentators
דְּהַךְ אַגָּדָה סְבִירָא לַהּ דְּצַדִּיק גָּמוּר עָדִיף מִבַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה, יְעֻיַּין שָׁם.
who suggest that this Midrash maintains that a tzaddik gamur is superior to a ba'al teshuva, examine there.
וּתְמִיהָה, דְּהֵבִיא בְּעַצְמוֹ הַפְּלוּגְתָּא מִפֶּרֶק "אֵין עוֹמְדִין" (בִּבְרָכוֹת שָׁם),
And this is astonishing, for he himself cited the dispute from the chapter Ein Omedin (Berakhot 34b),
וַהֲרֵי שָׁם רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ הוּא דְּאָמַר זֶה
and behold there it is Rabbi Abbahu who asserted
דְּ"בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה וְכוּלֵי" דְּבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה עָדִיף,
that “in the place where penitents, etc.” a ba'al teshuva is superior,
וְהוּא עַצְמוֹ בַּעַל הַהַגָּדָה שֶׁבִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה הַנִּזְכֶּרֶת לְעֵיל, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
and he is the very author of the midrashic teaching in Bereishit Rabbah cited above, see there.
אֲבָל לְדַעְתִּי פָּשׁוּט לְהֵיפֶךְ:
However, in my opinion the plain meaning is the exact reverse:
דְּרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ לְטַעְמֵיהּ דְּבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה עָדִיף,
for Rabbi Abbahu was following his consistent view that a ba'al teshuva is superior,
וּמִשּׁוּם הָכִי אָמַר דְּ"אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ בְּאֵיזֶה חָפֵץ".
and on that account said “I know not in which of them He delights.”
דִּלְמַאן דְּאָמַר צַדִּיק גָּמוּר עָדִיף
For according to the one who holds a tzaddik gamur is superior,
פְּשִׁיטָא דְּחָפֵץ יוֹתֵר בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶם שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים;
it is obvious that He desires the deeds of the righteous more;
אֲבָל לְדִידֵיהּ דְּבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה עָדִיף
but according to Rabbi Abbahu that a ba'al teshuva is superior,
הָיָה אֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹצֶה יוֹתֵר בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶם שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים
one might have contemplated that Hashem desires the deeds of the wicked more
כְּדֵי שֶׁיָּשׁוּב אַחַר כָּךְ וְיַגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵגָה גְּדוֹלָה יוֹתֵר,
so that he subsequently repents and reaches a far more transcendent station;
וְהֻוצְרַךְ לִלְמוֹד מִקְּרָא דְּאֵין חָפֵץ וְכוּלֵי,
and therefore he was required to deduce from Scripture that He takes no pleasure, etc.,
כִּי "הָאֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם יָשָׁר" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, כט)
for “God made man upright” (Ecclesiastes 7:29)
שֶׁלֹּא יֶחֱטָא כְּלָל,
that he should never sin at all,
וְאֵין רוֹצֶה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה רָשָׁע אֲפִילּוּ שָׁעָה אַחַת.
and He does not desire that a person be wicked even for one hour.
אֲבָל הָכָא אֵין כָּאן מַעֲשֵׂה רֶשַׁע בֶּאֱמֶת כְּלָל,
Yet here with Akavya there was no transgressive act in truth at all,
רַק שֶׁהַבְּרִיּוֹת חוֹשְׁדִין אוֹתוֹ לְשָׁעָה;
merely that the public would suspect him temporarily;
כֵּיוָן דְּאַחַר כָּךְ יִסְתַּלֵּק הַחֲשָׁד
and since the suspicion would subsequently dissipate,
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּאֵין חָשׁוּב רָשָׁע לַמָּקוֹם כְּלָל אֲפִילּוּ בִּשְׁעָתוֹ.
one might argue that he is not considered wicked before the Omnipresent even at that moment.
אֶלָּא שֶׁעֲקַבְיָא הֶחְמִיר עַל עַצְמוֹ
However, Akavya adopted a stringent standard upon himself
לְהַחְשִׁיב גַּם זֶה לְרִשְׁעוּת "שָׁעָה אַחַת",
to reckon even this appearance as wickedness for “one hour,”
דִּבְאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה שֶׁהַבְּרִיּוֹת מַחֲשִׁיבִין אוֹתוֹ לְרָשָׁע
in that during the hour when the public regards him as wicked
הוּא כְּרָשָׁע לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם.
he is accounted as wicked before the Omnipresent.
וּבָזֶה יָדַע שֶׁאֲחֵרִים יַלְעִיגוּ עָלָיו
And in this he knew that others would scoff at him
וְיֹאמְרוּ שֶׁהוּא "חָסִיד שׁוֹטֶה" בָּזֶה,
and claim that he was a “pious fool” in this attitude,
לְהַנִּיחַ הִתְמַנּוּת אַב בֵּית דִּין בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין גְּדוֹלָה שֶׁל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל,
in forfeiting appointment as Av Beit Din of the Great Sanhedrin of all Israel,
שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּזֶה וַדַּאי מַעֲלָה וְהִתְעַלּוּת גָּדוֹל לַנֶּפֶשׁ גַּם כֵּן
which assuredly brings immense elevation and transcendence to the soul as well,
כֵּיוָן שֶׁהוּא מַעֲלָה בַּקֹּדֶשׁ.
since it is an ascension in holiness.
דְּעַל כֵּן גְּדוֹלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מָצִינוּ שֶׁהָיוּ מִתְאַוִּים לַנְּשִׂיאוּת,
Therefore we find that great leaders of Israel yearned for the presidency,
וְקָרֵי לַהּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (כ״ח רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳): "כָּסָא דְּמוֹקְרָא",
and it is called in Berakhot (28a): “a cup of aromatic caraway,”
וּכְוַדַּאי לֹא חָמְדוּ לְכָבוֹד בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
and certainly they did not lust for transient worldly honor,
רַק לְהַמַּעֲלָה דִּקְדוּשָּׁה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לְנַפְשֵׁי יִשְׂרָאֵל.
rather for the spiritual elevation that accrues to Jewish souls.
וְהַחֲכָמִים שֶׁאָמְרוּ לוֹ: "חֲזוֹר וְכוּלֵי"
And the sages who suggested to him: “Retract, etc.”
הָיוּ סְבוּרִים דְּאֵין כְּדַאי לְהַנִּיחַ זֶה בִּשְׁבִיל חוּמְרַת חֲשָׁשַׁת הַחֲשָׁד דִּלְשָׁעָה.
held that it was inappropriate to forfeit this holy office over the stringency of a fleeting suspicion.
וְעַל זֶה אָמַר: "מוּטָב לִי לְהִקָּרֵא שׁוֹטֶה וְכוּלֵי",
And regarding this he replied: “It is better for me to be called a fool, etc.,”
דִּבְשְׁבִיל זֶה שַׁפִּיר שַׁיָּיךְ לוֹמַר דְּיַחְשְׁבוּהוּ לְשׁוֹטֶה;
for on this account it was fully appropriate to anticipate they would brand him a fool;
דְּמָצִינוּ "חָסִיד שׁוֹטֶה" בְּסוֹטָה (כ״א עַמּוּד ב׳)
for we find the archetype of the “pious fool” in Sotah (21b)
כְּשֶׁדּוֹחֶה דָּבָר גָּדוֹל בִּשְׁבִיל אִיסּוּר קַל, עַיֵּין שָׁם,
as one who pushes away a monumental mitzvah on account of a minor stringency, see there,
כֵּן נִרְאֶה בָּזֶה.
and such appears to be the dynamic here.
וּמִתְבָּאֵר שַׁפִּיר גַּם מִשָּׁם
And it is thus lucidly established from there as well
דְּמַשְׁמָעוּת לָשׁוֹן זֶה דְּ"שָׁעָה אַחַת"
that the import of this expression “one hour”
הַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁאַחַר כָּךְ יִתְגַּלֶּה דְּגַם עַתָּה לֵיכָּא רִשְׁעוּת,
applies where it will subsequently be revealed that even right now no true wickedness existed,
וְזֶהוּ בַּהַהוּא דְּנִדָּה
and this is identical to the case in Niddah
רַק עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה לְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם.
which is rectified solely through repentance to repair the past.

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 34b; Bereishis Rabbah 2:5; Yefeh To’ar; Maharal, Netiv HaTeshuvah 4; Peri Tzadik, Shelach 6 - higher teshuvah does not make sin desirable: Berakhot records R’ Abahu’s teaching: “מָקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין, צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים אֵינָם עוֹמְדִין”; R’ Yochanan instead ranks the complete tzaddik higher. Bereishis Rabbah has R’ Abahu ask, “אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ בְּאֵיזֶה מֵהֶם חָפֵץ,” and conclude: “בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים חָפֵץ, וְאֵינוֹ חָפֵץ בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶן שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים.” Yefeh To’ar cites an explanation that the uncertainty concerns repentant sinners versus complete tzaddikim, with the conclusion favoring the latter. Rav Tzadok argues oppositely: because the same R’ Abahu ranks baalei teshuvah higher, one might mistakenly infer that Hashem desires the fall which produces their later ascent. “עָשָׂה הָאֱלֹקִים אֶת הָאָדָם יָשָׁר” rejects that inference. Maharal explains that R’ Abahu values the baal teshuvah’s greater overcoming after attachment to sin, while R’ Yochanan values never having that attachment. Peri Tzadik states the boundary explicitly: one might think “שֶׁיְּקַלְקְלוּ מִקּוֹדֶם וְאַחַר כָּךְ יַעֲשׂוּ תְשׁוּבָה,” but “לְכַתְּחִלָּה בְּוַדַּאי חָלִילָה לַחְשׁוֹב כֵּן.” Teshuvah can transform a past fall; Hashem’s original desire remains uprightness.

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 28a with Rashi; Sotah 21b - nesius, public responsibility, and chasid shoteh: When R’ Elazar ben Azarya was offered the nesius after Rabban Gamliel’s removal, his wife warned that he too might be removed. He answered: “לִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ אִינִישׁ יוֹמָא חֲדָא בְּכָסָא דְמוֹקְרָא, וּלְמָחָר לִיתְּבַר” - use a precious goblet for one day even if it breaks tomorrow. Rashi explains that it is an expensive glass cup whose owner should use it for the opportunity and distinction it affords. When Rabban Gamliel was restored, the Sages preserved a share of leadership for R’ Elazar because “מַעֲלִין בַּקֹּדֶשׁ וְאֵין מוֹרִידִין.” This supplies the background for Rav Tzadok’s inference that nesius may represent genuine elevation through serving and teaching Klal Yisrael, not merely worldly honor. Sotah defines “חָסִיד שׁוֹטֶה” through one who refuses to look at a drowning woman in order to rescue her. His error is allowing a secondary concern to displace an immediate, greater obligation. Rav Tzadok applies the category analogically: the Sages could view refusal of the Av Beis Din position because of a temporary suspicion as sacrificing a major public Torah responsibility for an unusually remote stringency. Akavya’s “better to be called a fool” means that he knowingly accepted that criticism rather than relax his personal standard. The spiritual reading of nesius and its application to Akavya are Rav Tzadok’s analysis, not explicit statements of either Gemara.

paragraphs.text: Niddah 13a with Rashi and Maharal - actual momentary sin versus a suspicion later disproved: The Sages objected that one who does not hold himself while urinating may appear physically impaired, causing aspersions on his children. R’ Eliezer answered: “מוּטָב שֶׁיּוֹצִיא לַעַז עַל בָּנָיו... וְאַל יַעֲשֶׂה עַצְמוֹ רָשָׁע שָׁעָה אַחַת לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם.” The Gemara asks, “וְכָל כָּךְ לָמָּה?” and identifies the concern as an actual forbidden emission, citing Onan: “וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳ אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה.” Rashi explains that contact produces warmth and may cause the emission. Maharal explains the comparison to bringing a flood upon the world: wasting man’s generative power reverses the divinely ordered preservation of future life, paralleling the Flood’s undoing of creation’s order. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes this case from Akavya’s. In Niddah, the feared deed itself is wrong at that moment; later teshuvah repairs the past but does not reveal that no aveirah occurred. Akavya would not actually corrupt a ruling: observers would temporarily suspect that he had recanted for office, while his later conduct could reveal that their suspicion had never described his deed. Rav Tzadok extends the phrase “one moment” from objective wickedness later repaired to a momentary public judgment later disproved. That extension is his analysis, not an explicit equation made by Niddah.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The elevated standing of a baal teshuvah does not mean that God desires the original sin. Rav Tzadok uses Rabbi Abbahu’s teachings to explain this distinction, then returns to Akavya’s willingness to forgo a sacred office rather than accept even momentary suspicion.

p: וְעַיֵּין בְּרֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה שָׁם כָּתַב
And examine in Reishit Chokhmah there, where he wrote
דְּלָא מַהֲנֵי תְּשׁוּבָה תַּתָּאָה,
that lower repentance (teshuva tata'ah) does not suffice,
דְּהַיְינוּ סוּר מֵרָע לְבַד,
which is merely turning away from evil alone,
אֶלָּא צָרִיךְ תְּשׁוּבָה עִילָּאָה
rather one requires supernal repentance (teshuva ila'ah)
[בִּצְעָקָה שֶׁמִּלִּבּוֹ, עַיֵּין שָׁם].
(through an outcry emerging from the depths of his heart, see there).
וּבְשֵׁם הָרַב יְהוּדָה חַלְגְּוָאָה בְּסֵפֶר צָפְנַת פַּעְנֵחַ כָּתַב
And in the name of Rabbi Yehudah Chalgava in Sefer Tzafenat Pane'ach he wrote
דִּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ קָשָׁה מִפְּנֵי שֶׁצָּרִיךְ סִיגּוּפִים הַרְבֵּה שֶׁיִּלְאֶה לַעֲשׂוֹתָם,
that repentance for this sin is difficult because it requires so many mortifications that a person becomes weary of performing them,
וְעוֹד תֵּירֵץ: דְּצָרִיךְ עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה לְתַקֵּן כָּל הָאֵבָרִים.
and he further resolved that through repentance one must rectify all bodily limbs.
וּבְשֵׁם הָרַמַ״ק בְּסֵפֶר אֵילִימָה כָּתַב
And in the name of the Ramak (Rabbi Moshe Cordovero) in Sefer Eilimah he wrote
דְּצָרִיךְ דָּבָר שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מִמְּקוֹם הַתְּשׁוּבָה, יְעֻיַּין שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ.
that this requires reaching a realm that transcends the place of standard repentance, examine there at length.
וְכָל זֶה אֵינוֹ מַסְפִּיק לְיַישֵׁב גּוּף הַדָּבָר
And all this is insufficient to resolve the substantive core of the question
שֶׁהֶחְמִירוּ בִּתְשׁוּבַת עָוֺן זֶה כָּל כָּךְ,
as to why they treated repentance for this sin with such extreme gravity,
וְהוּא נֶגֶד אַרְבָּעָה חִלּוּקֵי כַּפָּרָה שֶׁהָיָה רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל דּוֹרֵשׁ;
for this contradicts the four divisions of atonement that Rabbi Ishmael expounded;
דִּכְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְפִי דַּעְתִּי
for according to what I have formulated in my opinion,
אֵין צָרִיךְ לְכַפָּרַת עָוֺן זֶה סִיגּוּפִים וְיִסּוּרִין מְמָרְקִים כְּלָל,
atonement for this sin requires neither physical mortifications nor scouring afflictions at all,
וְאֵין בּוֹ חֹמֶר לְכָל הַיּוֹתֵר מִשְּׁאָר מִצְוֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה לְעִנְיַן כַּפָּרָה.
and at most it bears no greater severity than other negative commandments regarding atonement.
וּבִשְׁלָ״ה (שַׁעַר הָאוֹתִיּוֹת, אוֹת קְדֻשָּׁה)
And in the Shelah (Sha'ar HaOtiyot, letter Kedushah)
הֵבִיא תֵּירוּץ הָרֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה דְּצָרִיךְ בָּזֶה לְתַקֵּן כָּל אֵבָרָיו.
he cited the resolution of the Reishit Chokhmah that one must rectify all his limbs in this transgression.
וְהוּא כָּתַב לְתָרֵץ
And the Shelah himself proposed to resolve
לְפִי שֶׁהָרָגִיל בְּחֵטְא זֶה הוּא חָטָא בּוֹ כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים,
because one who is habituated to this sin has stumbled in it multiple times,
וְעַל כֵּן תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ קָשָׁה לַעֲשׂוֹת הַסִּיגּוּפִים עַל כָּל פַּעַם, יְעֻיַּין שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ.
and therefore his repentance is arduous because he must perform mortifications for each individual occurrence, examine there at length.
וּכְבָר קְדָמוֹ גַּם בָּזֶה הָרֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ
And the Reishit Chokhmah himself already preceded him in this argument subsequently
בְּדִבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל: "וְצָרִיךְ לְהַתְמִיד", עַיֵּין שָׁם.
under the heading “And one must persevere,” see there.
וְזֶה וַדַּאי אֵין מַסְפִּיק,
And this resolution is assuredly insufficient,
אֲפִילּוּ נוֹדֶה לְגוּף צֹרֶךְ הַסִּיגּוּפִים לְקַבָּלַת תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ;
even if we were to concede the very necessity of physical mortifications for the reception of his repentance;
מִכָּל מָקוֹם דִּבְרֵי הַזֹּהַר מְבוֹאָר
nevertheless the language of the Zohar makes it clear
דִּמְדַבְּרִים מִגּוּף חֵטְא זֶה בְּעַצְמוּתוֹ
that they are speaking of the intrinsic nature of this sin in its essence,
וְלֹא מִצַּד רִבּוּי הַפְּעָמִים,
and not merely on account of the multiplication of offenses,
שֶׁזֶּה אֶפְשָׁר גַּם בַּחֲטָאִים אֲחֵרִים שֶׁהוּרְגַּל כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים.
for repetitive habituation is equally possible across other transgressions.
וְכֵן בְּחֵטְא זֶה שֶׁשָּׁב וְנִיחַם מִיָּד אַחַר פַּעַם הָרִאשׁוֹן וְלֹא חָטָא יוֹתֵר,
And likewise in the case of this specific sin where one repented with remorse immediately after the first time and never sinned again,
וּבַזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ לֹא חִלְּקוּ בֵּין פַּעַם אֶחָד לְהַרְבֵּה,
and yet in the holy Zohar they drew no distinction between a single occurrence and many,
וְאֵין נִרְאֶה כְּלָל דְּאָתֵי מִכֹּחַ רִבּוּי הַחֲטָאִים.
and it is completely unapparent that the stringency derives merely from the accumulation of sins.

paragraphs.text: The quoted distinctions in Reishis Chochmah are “אֵין הַדָּבָר תָּלוּי בִּתְשׁוּבָה תַּתָּאָה ... דְּהַיְינוּ בְּסוּר מֵרַע” — “The matter does not depend on lower repentance ... that is, turning from evil”; and “עַד שֶׁיַּגִּיעַ לִתְשׁוּבָה עִילָּאָה” — “until he reaches higher repentance.” Its report of Tzafnas Paneach says “תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ קָשָׁה עַד מְאֹד ... צָרִיךְ סִיגּוּפִים הַרְבֵּה” — “His repentance is exceedingly difficult ... he requires many mortifications.” The whole-stature explanation describes the blemish as “כְּאִלּוּ פָּגַם כָּל הַשִּׁיעוּר קוֹמָה” — “as though he blemished the whole stature,” requiring a correspondingly forceful return. These quotations retain the distinction between the cited explanations and the objection Rav Tzadok now raises.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: וְאֵין בּוֹ חֹמֶר לְכָל הַיּוֹתֵר מִשְּׁאָר מִצְוֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה לְעִנְיַן כַּפָּרָה.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86a; Tosefta Yoma (Lieberman) 4:6–8; Shaarei Teshuvah 4:6; Takanat HaShavin 13:1 - the four categories govern basic atonement: R. Elazar ben Azaryah answers: “שְׁלֹשָׁה הֵן, וּתְשׁוּבָה עִם כָּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד.” For a negative commandment, “תְּשׁוּבָה תּוֹלָה וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים מְכַפֵּר”; for kareis or a court-imposed death penalty, teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend punishment and suffering completes the cleansing; chillul Hashem requires death for the final cleansing. The Tosefta has a related graded account, but its final formulation divides the atoning functions into thirds and differs from the Bavli’s wording. The formulation quoted here is Yoma 86a; the two witnesses should not be presented as identical. Rabbeinu Yonah adds an important distinction: even after repentance has atoned for a neglected positive commandment, an olah may still “תּוֹסִיף עַל כַּפָּרָתוֹ וְיוֹסִיף לְהִתְרַצּוֹת” - increase acceptance and reconciliation. Thus forgiveness, completed kapparah, and fuller spiritual restoration are related but not identical. Rav Tzadok makes this distinction earlier in Takanat HaShavin 13:1, describing the later offering as “דורון בעלמא” after forgiveness. His argument here is that R. Yishmael’s scheme was stated comprehensively for Torah transgressions. Unless this sin falls into kareis, death, or chillul Hashem, extraordinary mortifications cannot become a new condition for basic kapparah. “Upper” or “complete” teshuvah may describe full rectification of the spiritual damage, but it cannot silently become a fifth category replacing the explicit order of Chazal.

footnotes.heAnchorPrefix: וְאֵין נִרְאֶה כְּלָל דְּאָתֵי מִכֹּחַ רִבּוּי הַחֲטָאִים.

paragraphs.text: Shlah, Shaar HaOtiyot, Kedushah; Reishis Chochmah 17:22, 24; Rokeach; Rambam, Hilchos De’os 3:1; Zohar, Vayakhel 214b; Peri Tzadik, Ki Savo 12 - repetition and intrinsic repair: The Shlah explains that this concealed sin is easily repeated, so the penitential regimen would have to correspond to every occurrence; the sinner’s years can therefore be consumed by teshuvah while “בְּרֹב לֹא תַּשְׁלִים.” Reishis Chochmah similarly requires persistence year after year, remembering “כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים הִכְעִיס אֶת בּוֹרְאוֹ.” The background is the Rokeach’s teshuvas ha-mishkal and related disciplines, which prescribe practices proportionate to the act; they are not R. Yishmael’s four categories of kapparah. Rambam, Hilchos De’os 3:1, supplies a general limit: “אָסְרוּ חֲכָמִים שֶׁיְּהֵא אָדָם מְסַגֵּף עַצְמוֹ בְּתַעֲנִית” — “The Sages forbade a person to afflict himself through fasting.” This does not reject every targeted correction, but it shows that self-mortification is not automatically the essence of teshuvah. Rav Tzadok’s textual objection is that the Zohar speaks about the sin itself: “וְהָנֵי מִילֵי כַּד לָא עָבַד תְּיוּבְתָא שְׁלֵימָתָא... לְחַפְּיָא עַל כָּל עוֹבָדוֹי,” without distinguishing one occurrence from many. Reishis Chochmah likewise explains an intrinsic blemish to the whole spiritual stature. In Peri Tzadik, Ki Savo 12, Rav Tzadok quotes this Zohar and adds: “עַל יְדֵי תּוֹרָה יֵשׁ תַּקָּנָה לִפְגָם זֶה,” together with prayer and crying. Repetition may increase the burden, but it cannot explain the Zohar’s unique characterization of the sin itself.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok surveys explanations requiring higher repentance, repair of every limb, or repeated mortifications for this offense. He finds them insufficient to explain the Zohar’s distinctive severity, especially where a person repented immediately after a single occurrence.

p: וְעַיֵּן שָׁם
And see there
בְּרֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה
in Reishis Chochmah
וְכֵן בְּשְׁנֵי לֻחוֹת הַבְּרִית
and likewise in Shnei Luchos HaBris,
שֶׁהֵבִיאוּ רְאָיָה
who brought proof
דְּמְהַנְיָא תְּשׁוּבָה מִדּוֹר הַמַּבּוֹל,
that repentance helps, from the generation of the Flood,
שֶׁנַּח הִתְרָה בָּהֶם
since Noach warned them
שֶׁיָּשׁוּבוּ
to repent,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ
as stated in the Midrash
וּבְרַשִּׁי בְּחוּמָשׁ עַיֵּין שָׁם.
and in Rashi on the Chumash; see there.
וְנִרְאֶה
And it seems
דְּהֵבִינוּ
that they understood
דְּמַה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזּוֹהַר
what they said in the Zohar,
דְּלָא מְהַנְיָא תְּשׁוּבָה
that repentance does not help,
הַיּוֹנָה שֶׁהוּא לַגְמַרְי
to mean it is entirely
כְּאִלּוּ לֹא שָׁב כָּלָּל,
as if he had not repented at all,
וְכְאִלּוּ עַדַיִן עוֹמֵד בְּרִשְׁעוֹ.
and as if he still stood in his wickedness.
וְזֶה וַדַּאי דָּבָר תָּמוּהּ וְזָר מְאוֹד,
This is surely a puzzling and very strange matter,
וְאֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא
and even if you say
דְּלָא תִּקֵּן הַקָּדוֹם בְּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ כָּלָּל,
that he did not repair the past through his repentance at all,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם
in any case,
כָּל שֶׁהָיוּ שָׁבִין
as long as they were repenting
וְלֹא הָיוּ חוֹטְאִים עוֹד,
and no longer sinning,
וַדַּאי שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ נִעֱנָשִׁים
surely they would not have been punished
בְּעוֹנֶשׁ הַמַּבּוֹל
with the Flood
לְכִלָּיוֹן הָעוֹלָם כֻּלָּם
for the destruction of the whole world,
בְּשִׁבְּבוֹ יֹאבְדּוּ גַּם לַגְמַרְי.
on account of which they would perish entirely.
וּבְבִנֵי נֹחַ בְּלָאוֹ הַכִּי
And regarding Noachides anyway,
לֹא מָצָאוּ שֶׁנִּתְנָה לָהֶם תְּשׁוּבָה
we do not find that repentance was granted them
לְכַפָּרַת הַקָּדוֹם כָּלָּל,
for atonement of the past at all,
וְכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְּתִי (לְעִל, אוֹת א) מִזֶּה
as I wrote above (entry 1) on this
בְּשֵׁם הַמִּדְרָשׁ וְהָרִאשׁוֹנִים.
in the name of the Midrash and the Rishonim.
אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם
Nevertheless
הַתְּשׁוּבָה מוֹעֶלֶת לָהֶם
repentance does avail them
לְבַטֵּל הַעוֹנֶשׁ הַנִּגְזָר
to cancel the decreed punishment,
כְּדַאֲשַׁכַּחֲנַן בְּאַנְשֵׁי נִינְוֵה,
as we find with the people of Nineveh,
וְהַזּוֹהַר מְדַבֵּר בְּתְשׁוּבָה
while the Zohar speaks of repentance
שֶׁהִיא מוֹעִילָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
that avails Israel
שֶׁיִּמָּחֵל עָוֹן הַקָּדוֹם
so that the past sin is pardoned
וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה כְּאִלּוּ לֹא חָטָא מֵעוֹלָם,
and it is as if he never sinned,
וְעַל זֶה אֵין רְאָיָה מִדּוֹר הַמַּבּוֹל.
and for that there is no proof from the generation of the Flood.

paragraphs.text: Reishis Chochmah, Shaar HaKedushah 17:25; Shlah, Shaar HaOtiyos, Hilchos Bi’ah 1:35; Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 5:6; Rashi, Bereishis 6:14 — Noach’s warning proves that return could avert the Flood: Reishis Chochmah writes: “וּרְאָיָה שֶׁגַּם... יֵשׁ לָהֶם תְּשׁוּבָה, שֶׁהֲרֵי דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל... נִתְעַכֵּב נֹחַ בַּעֲשִׂיַּת הַתֵּבָה כְּדֵי לְהַכְרִיז לָהֶם שֶׁיַּחְזְרוּ וְיַעֲשׂוּ תְּשׁוּבָה.” The Midrash itself says, “מֵאָה וְעֶשְׂרִים שָׁנָה הָיָה מַתְרֶה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל, שֶׁמָּא יַעֲשׂוּ תְּשׁוּבָה,” and describes Noach repeatedly explaining the Ark until they refused to return. Rashi states the purpose even more briefly: “אוּלַי יָשׁוּבוּ.” The Shlah uses this as a challenge to an absolute reading of the Zohar: “וְעַל כָּל זֹאת רָצָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שֶׁיַּעֲשׂוּ תְּשׁוּבָה וְיִמְחֹל לָהֶם.” Background: the long construction made the approaching judgment visible and gave the generation time to abandon its corrupt conduct. The texts establish that an opportunity to turn from the evil course was offered before the decree was carried out. Rav Tzadok next examines the extent of what that proof establishes.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Ha’azinu 4:1; Takanas HaShavin 1:4 — Noahide teshuvah and the difference between future healing and retroactive atonement: Tanchuma distinguishes Israel’s covenantal gift of atonement: “עוֹשֶׂה תְּשׁוּבָה, נוֹשֵׂא לוֹ פָּנִים. יָכוֹל לַכֹּל? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: אֵלֶיךָ, וְלֹא לְאֻמָּה אַחֶרֶת.” Rav Tzadok cites this passage together with the Ramah miPano and R. Yitzchak Abarbanel in his opening siman. There he supplies the distinction governing the present se’if: “וְרַק רְפוּאָה לְהַבָּא זֶה יֵשׁ גַּם בְּגוֹיִם,” whereas “תִּיקּוּן הַקּוֹדֵם” means that the prior sin itself is removed—“יְבֻקַּשׁ עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ.” In other words, a Noahide can cease the evil and thereby no longer be subject to a decree whose basis is continuing wickedness; this is real return from the present course. The special Torah chiddush of kapparah for Israel goes further: it can transform the relationship to the past, ultimately leaving the person “כְּאִלּוּ לֹא חָטָא מֵעוֹלָם.” Rav Tzadok therefore reads the earlier authorities precisely, not as denying all moral change to the nations, but as denying the uniquely Jewish power of teshuvah to uproot and repair the former act itself.

paragraphs.text: Yonah 3:8–10; Taanis 16a. Nineveh was commanded, “וְיָשֻׁבוּ אִישׁ מִדַּרְכּוֹ הָרָעָה” — “Let each person turn from his evil way.” Scripture then says that God saw their deeds, that they had turned from their evil way, and did not bring the threatened calamity. Taanis stresses that the verse mentions their deeds, rather than their sackcloth and fasting.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok distinguishes averting a threatened punishment from obtaining pardon for the past. He argues that the call to the Flood generation to repent establishes the former, but does not by itself resolve the Zohar’s difficulty about the full repair of an Israelite’s earlier sin.

p: אַךְ מִאַרְבָּעָה חִלּוּקֵי כַּפָּרָה
But from the four divisions of atonement
דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל,
of Rabbi Yishmael,
שֶׁכָּלַל בָּהֶם כָּל הָעֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה,
which included all the sins in the Torah,
וַדַּאי מִבְוֹאָר
it is surely clear
דְּמְהַנְיָא תְּשׁוּבָה לְכַפָּרַת הַקָּדוֹם גַּם כֵּן
that repentance does atone for the past too,
עַל כָּל פָּנִים
at least
בְּצִירוּף יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים.
together with Yom Kippur.
וְעִייֵן שָׁם בְּשְׁנֵי לֻחוֹת הַבְּרִית
And see there in Shnei Luchos HaBris
דְּבָרוֹקַח כָּתַב
that the Rokeach wrote
דְּבַעֲבֵירָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ עוֹנֶשׁ מִיתָה
that for a sin carrying the death penalty
צָרִיךְ סִיגּוּפִים הַשּׁוָּים לַמָּוֶת,
one needs self-mortifications equal to death,
וְהַמּוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה חַיָּיב מִיתָה,
and one who wastes seed is liable to death,
עַד כָּאן.
end of quote.
וְתָמוּהּ
And it is puzzling
דְּבָרוֹקַח כָּתוּב זֶה
that the Rokeach wrote this
עַל חַיָּיבֵי מִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין
about those liable to court-imposed death,
עַיֵּין שָׁם (בְּהִלְכוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה סִימָן יא)
see there (Hilchos Teshuvah, siman 11)
בָּא עַל אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ,
regarding relations with a married woman;
אֲבָל .
but ...
בְּחַיָּיבֵי כָּרִיתוֹת
regarding those liable to karess
(שָׁם סִימָן ז וְסִימָן יד)
(there, siman 7 and siman 14)
אַף דְּהִצְרִיךְ גַּם כֵּן לְסִיגּוּפִים
although he also requires self-mortifications
וְיִסּוּרִין מְמַרְקִין,
and cleansing sufferings,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא כָּתַב שָׁם
nonetheless he did not write there
קָשֶׁה כַּמָּוֶת כָּלָּל,
“harsh as death” at all,
עַיֵּין שָׁם,
see there,
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בְּהַהִיא
and all the more so regarding that case
דְּגַּם כָּרֵת לֵיכָּא.
where there is not even karess.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86a; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4; Shaarei Teshuvah 4:6. The baraisa states “שְׁלֹשָׁה הֵן, וּתְשׁוּבָה עִם כָּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד” — “There are three, and repentance accompanies each one.” Repentance effects immediate forgiveness for a positive-commandment failure; with a negative commandment it suspends while Yom Kippur atones; with kareis or court-death offenses repentance and Yom Kippur suspend while suffering cleanses; with desecration of the divine Name death completes the cleansing. The later agents do not replace repentance.

paragraphs.text: The severe wording quoted from Zohar, Vayechi 219b, is “לֵית לָן חוֹבָא בְּעָלְמָא דְּלָא אִית לֵיהּ תְּשׁוּבָה, בַּר מֵהַאי” — “There is no sin in the world without repentance except this one.” The qualification in Vayakhel 214b is “וְהָנֵי מִילֵי כַּד לָא עָבַד תְּיוּבְתָא שְׁלֵימָתָא ... לְחַפָּאָה עַל כָּל עוֹבָדוֹי” — “These words apply when he has not performed complete repentance ... to cover all his deeds.” Reishis Chochmah explains why merely ceasing the act is not the whole repair of its spiritual damage. The Flood and Nineveh establish that return can avert punishment; Rav Tzadok distinguishes that from complete repair of what preceded.

paragraphs.text: Compare Resisei Layla §41: Israel can “repair what preceded until deliberate sins become merits.” Machshavos Charutz 15:5 makes the particular qualification explicit: “For this sin in particular, concerning which the Zohar states that repentance does not help, this means that through repentance alone it is impossible completely to repair what preceded, except together with Torah.” This supports repentance’s efficacy while distinguishing it from the complete repair discussed by the Zohar. This parallel is retained here once, rather than repeated in the following Rokeach notes.

paragraphs.text: Shelah, Shaar HaOtiyos, Hilchos Bi’ah 1:49; Rokeach, Hilchos Teshuvah §§7, 11 and 14, as quoted and compared by Rav Tzadok. The Shelah writes: “אִם יֵשׁ עוֹנֶשׁ מִיתָה, צָרִיךְ לַעֲשׂוֹת לוֹ סִגּוּפִים הַשָּׁוִים לְמִיתָה; וְהַמּוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה חַיָּב מִיתָה” — “If there is a punishment of death, one must undertake mortifications corresponding to death; and one who emits seed in vain is liable to death.” This is the Shelah’s application.

paragraphs.text: Rav Tzadok tests it against the Rokeach’s adultery case in §11, with suffering “as harsh as death,” and the differing regimens for niddah and kareis in §§7 and 14. He distinguishes a formal Torah punishment from an instance of heavenly death or a severe warning. The inference is his legal objection to the Shelah’s application; it does not deny the gravity of the sin. The §11 wording cited for this comparison is “שֶׁהוּא כְּמִיתָה, יִסְבּוֹל צַעַר קָשֶׁה כְּמִיתָה” — “Because it is like death, he should bear suffering as harsh as death.” Its exact historical printing remains subject to the source qualification recorded for this Rokeach material.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The four divisions of atonement affirm that repentance can repair past sin. Rav Tzadok questions the use of the Rokeach’s disciplines for capital offenses to establish the same requirement here merely from the language “liable to death.”

p: וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב
And what he wrote
דְּחַיָּיב מִיתָה
that he is liable to death
הוּא מֵהַגְּמָרָא דְּנִדָּה (שָׁם, עַמּוּד א)
is from the Gemara in Niddah (there, 13a),
וְלָמְדוּ מִקְרָא דְּאוֹנָן,
which derived it from the verse about Onan;
עַיֵּין שָׁם.
see there.
וְיֵשׁ לְעַיֵּין קְצָת
One should examine somewhat
מָה רְאָיָה מַיְיתֵי
what proof he brings
מִקֹּדֶם מַתַּן תּוֹרָה,
from before the giving of the Torah,
דְּהָיוּ בִּכְלַל בְּנֵי נֹחַ
since they were included among the Noachides
דְּאַזְהָרָתָן הִיא מִיתָתָן,
whose warning is their death,
וְהָיוּ חַיָּיבִין מִיתָה בִּידֵי אָדָם
and were liable to death at human hands
עַל זֶה גַּם כֵּן,
for this too,
דְּהָרֵי קֹדֶם מַתַּן תּוֹרָה
for before the giving of the Torah
נִצְטַוּוּ "פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ"
they were commanded “be fruitful and multiply,”
דְּזֶה בִּכְלָלוֹ.
which includes this.
וְהָא דְּלָא חָשִׁיב לֵיהּ
And that he does not count it
בְּשֶׁבַע מִצְווֹת בְּנֵי נֹחַ,
among the seven Noachide commandments,
וּמִשּׁוּם דְּלָא נִשְׁנָה בְּסִינַי
is because it was not repeated at Sinai,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (נט, סוֹף עַמּוּד א),
as stated in Sanhedrin (59a, end),
הַיְינוּ מִסִּינַי וָאֵילָךְ
meaning from Sinai onward
דְּנִטְּלָה מֵהֶם,
it was taken away from them,
וְכמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר רַשִׁ"י (שָׁם, עַמּוּד א)
and as Rashi said (there)
רֹאשׁ דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "לָזֶה"
in the passage beginning “la-zeh,”
וְכמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בְּטוּרֵי זָהָב אֶבֶן הָעֶזֶר (סִימָן א, סְעִיף קָטָן ב)
and as the Taz wrote on Even HaEzer (1:2),
וּבְטוּרֵי אֶבֶן (בְּרֹאשׁ מִלּוּאִים לַחֲגִיגָה)
and in Turei Even (beginning of Miluim on Chagigah)
דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "לֹא לְתֹהוּ"
passage beginning “lo l’sohu,”
וּבְמִשְׁנֶה לַמֶּלֶךְ (פֶּרֶק י מֵהִלְכוֹת מְלָכִים),
and in Mishneh LaMelech (Hilchos Melachim, ch. 10);
יִעַיְּינוּ שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ,
see there at length;
וְעַל כֵּן נֶעֶנְשׁוּ בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל.
and therefore they were punished in the generation of the Flood.
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּמִשְׁנֶה לַמֶּלֶךְ
And see there in Mishneh LaMelech
שָׁם לִפְנֵי זֶה
just before this,
הֵבִיא מֵרַמְבַּ"ן וְרַשְׁבַּ"א (נִדָּה שָׁם, עַמּוּד א)
where he cites Ramban and Rashba (Niddah there)
דְּגַם מִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְצֻוֶּה "פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ"
that even one not commanded “be fruitful and multiply”
אָסוּר בְּהַשְׁחָתַת זֶרַע,
is forbidden to destroy seed,
דְּהַכֹּל לָקוּ בַּמַּבּוּל,
since all were punished in the Flood,
וְדָזֶה דְּלָא כְּתוֹסָפוֹת סַנְהֶדְרִין הַנִּזְכָּר
and this is unlike Tosafos in Sanhedrin cited above
דְּהוּא בִּכְלַל "פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ",
that it falls under “be fruitful and multiply,”
אֶלָּא דְּלָא יָדַע
but he did not know
הֵיכָן רְמִיזָא אִסּוּר זֶה לְבֶן נֹחַ
where this prohibition is hinted for a Noachide
וְגַם אַמַּאי לָא מְנָאוֹ
and also why they did not count it
בִּכְלַל שֶׁבַע מִצְווֹת בְּנֵי נֹחַ,
among the seven Noachide commandments,
וְהִנִּיחַ בְּקֻשְׁיָא,
and he left it as a difficulty;

that whoever transgresses the words of the Sages is likewise liable to death,
עַיֵּין שָׁם לְעִנְיַן הַיָּשֵׁן קוֹדֶם תְּפִלַּת עַרְבִית,
see there regarding one who sleeps prior to the Evening Prayer,
וְכֵן בְּעֵירוּבִין [כא עַמּוּד ב] לְעִנְיַן נְטִילַת יָדַיִם,
and likewise in Eruvin (21b) regarding washing the hands,
וְאַף דְּקָרוּ לְהוּ שָׁם "חֲמוּרוֹת" מֵהַאי טַעְמָא, עַיֵּין שָׁם,
and even though they designated them there as 'grave' matters on this account, see there,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם וַדַּאי אֵין לְדַמּוֹתָם לְחַיָּיבֵי כְּרֵיתוֹת
nevertheless one certainly cannot equate them to those liable to excision
לְעִנְיַן חֹמֶר הַתְּשׁוּבָה וּלְהַצְרִיךְ יִסּוּרִין מְמָרְקִין,
with respect to the severity of repentance so as to require scouring afflictions,
וְלֹא חֲמִירֵי מִבִּיטּוּל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא כְּלָל.
and they are not graver than the omission of a biblical positive commandment at all.
וְלֹא אָמַר אֶלָּא בְּחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת וְחַיָּיבֵי מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם
And he spoke exclusively of those liable to excision and those liable to death at the hands of Heaven
שֶׁחִיְּיבָתַן תּוֹרָה לְעֹנֶשׁ הַחֵטְא,
whom the Torah itself formally sentenced as the statutory penalty for the sin,
וְלֹא בְּחַיָּיבֵי מִיתָה שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַבָּנַן,
and not of those designated as 'liable to death' by rabbinic formulation;
וַאֲפִילּוּ שֶׁנִּמְצָא שֶׁנֶּעֶנְשׁוּ כֵּן,
and even where it is found historically that individuals were punished thus,
כָּל שֶׁלֹּא קָבְעָה תּוֹרָה הָעֹנֶשׁ לַחֵטְא
so long as the Torah did not fix this specific punishment to the sin
כִּבְכָל חַיָּיבֵי מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם שֶׁמָּנוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה.
as it did with all the statutory liabilities to death at the hands of Heaven enumerated by our Sages of blessed memory.

paragraphs.text: Niddah 13a; Bereishis 38:9–10; Rashi — Onan and the Gemara’s phrase “liable to death”: The Gemara states: “כל המוציא שכבת זרע לבטלה חייב מיתה, שנאמר: וירע בעיני ה׳ אשר עשה וימת גם אותו” — “Anyone who emits seed in vain is liable to death, as it is stated: ‘What he did was evil in Hashem’s eyes, and He put him to death also.’” The verse concerns Onan, who “שחת ארצה לבלתי נתן זרע לאחיו” — destroyed [his seed] upon the ground so as not to provide offspring for his brother. Rashi explains: “דש מבפנים וזורה מבחוץ,” intercourse was begun normally but completed externally. Background: the Gemara cites a narrative of punishment by Heaven; the verse does not formulate a permanent beis-din penalty or list this act among the Torah’s fixed chayavei misah. That distinction drives Rav Tzadok’s question. Since Onan lived before Matan Torah, when the patriarchal family still stood within the legal framework of Bnei Noach, how can his death by Heaven establish the exact post-Sinai classification for a Jew? Earlier in this siman (15:1–4), Rav Tzadok likewise notes that the Rambam calls the act an “איסור גדול” and cites the Gemara’s comparisons, but does not identify a distinct Torah death-penalty. Se’if 23 therefore accepts the Gemara’s severity while investigating what kind of “death liability” the proof from Onan actually establishes.
