paragraphs.text: Sefer Chasidim §167; Rokeach, Hilchos Teshuvah §§7, 11, 14, as compared by Rav Tzadok; Orchos Tzadikim 26:103; Menoras HaMaor, Hilchos Teshuvah 18; Kesubos 33b - two different measures of suffering: The Rokeach tradition contains two distinct formulations. For adultery, Orchos Tzadikim preserves: since the act carries court-imposed death, “יִסְבֹּל צַעַר הַקָּשֶׁה כַּמָּוֶת,” including an hour in snow or ice throughout the winter and comparable summer suffering. By contrast, Menoras HaMaor states for kareis-level arayos: “יֵשֵׁב בַּקֶּרַח כְּשִׁעוּר צְלִיַּת בֵּיצָה וְגוֹמְעָהּ,” with fasting between three and forty days. The first imitates the gravity of the written punishment; the second measures pain against the duration and pleasure of the act. Rav Tzadok uses this contrast to explain why the ice prescribed for wasted seed may suffice once: its function is hamishkal, not a substitute for death. He nevertheless flags a difficulty in the Rokeach's language comparing such suffering to lashes. Kesubos distinguishes “הַכָּאָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהּ קִצְבָּה” from unlimited coercive flogging; fixed Torah lashes are lighter than death, while unlimited beating can be harsher. Therefore one cannot create a single hierarchy from the words “lashes,” “kareis,” and “like death.” The total context - duration, repetition, purpose and accompanying restrictions - determines whether a regimen corresponds to punishment, breaks desire, or supplies post-forgiveness ritzui.

paragraphs.text: Responsa of Maharam of Rothenburg, penitential order; Rashi on Bereishis 7:4; Sefer Chasidim §176; Tzidkas HaTzadik 262 - why forty days correspond to formation: The penitential order attributed to Maharam, quoted here by Rav Tzadok, says that one who wasted seed should fast forty days “כְּנֶגֶד יְצִירַת הַוָּלָד,” sit in winter water for the egg-roasting measure, avoid meat, wine and hot food, and confess with a firm resolution not to return. Rav Tzadok proposes that its “וְיָשַׁב” should read “אוֹ יָשַׁב,” because Sefer Chasidim explicitly offers ice or forty summer fasts as alternatives. The forty-day symbolism has an established source: Rashi explains the Flood's forty days as “כְּנֶגֶד יְצִירַת הַוָּלָד,” because that generation corrupted human formation. Rav Tzadok nonetheless rejects the idea that Maharam is treating wasted seed literally as fetal bloodshed. The same penitential collection assigns forty fasts to relations with an immersed unmarried woman, where no destroyed fetus is involved. He therefore reads the number as a measure of bodily pleasure: the whole body is heated toward procreation, and forty days of restraint answer the forty-day process of formation; the winter water directly counters the immediate heat. The Tzidkas HaTzadik §262 analogy is quoted with the earlier ice-or-fasting discussion and is not repeated here. The number forty is thus a symbolic measure of ritzui, not proof of misah bidei Shamayim or a fifth category of basic kapparah.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok reads the winter and summer disciplines in Sefer Chasidim as alternative ways to counterbalance the offense’s pleasure. He proposes a corresponding textual correction in Maharam and explains the forty-day measure through fetal formation, without making it a formal murder penalty.

p: וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים נִרְאֶה טַעַם סִיגּוּפֵי עָוֺן זֶה לָ"רוֹקֵחַ" וְסִיעָתוֹ מִשּׁוּם "תְּשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל".
And at any rate, the rationale for the penances for this iniquity according to the Roke'ach and his school appears to be because of "commensurate repentance"
וְטַעַם "תְּשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל" עַצְמוֹ, שֶׁלֹּא הֶרְאָה לוֹ "רוֹקֵחַ" מָקוֹר
And the underlying reason for "commensurate repentance" itself, for which the Roke'ach did not indicate a source
(כִּלְשׁוֹן "תְּשׁוּבַת הַבָּאָה" שֶׁמֵּבִיא מִגְּמָרָא דְּיוֹמָא [פ״ו עַמּוּד ב׳],
(unlike the concept of "repentance that presents itself," which he cites from the Gemara in Yoma [86b],
וּ"תְשׁוּבַת הַגֶּדֶר", הֲגַם דְּהוּא לֹא מַיְיתֵי מִגְּמָרָא, הוּא מְבוֹאָר בְּפֶרֶק "זֶה בּוֹרֵר" [כ״ה עַמּוּד ב׳]
and "protective repentance," which, although he does not cite it from the Gemara, is elucidated in the chapter "Zeh Borer" [Sanhedrin 25b]
בִּמְשַׂחֲקֵי בְּקוּבְיָא דַּאֲפִילּוּ בְּחִנָּם לָא עָבְדֵי,
regarding dice players, who must reform to the point that they do not play even for free,
וּמַלְוֶה בְּרִבִּית אֲפִילּוּ לְגוֹי לֹא מַלְוֶה,
and moneylenders with interest, who must not lend even to a non-Jew,
וּמַפְרִיחֵי יוֹנִים אֲפִילּוּ בַּמִּדְבָּר לָא עָבְדֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
and pigeon racers, who must not race even in the wilderness, see there.
וּ"תְשׁוּבַת הַכָּתוּב" הוּא מִדְּבָרִים שֶׁצָּרִיךְ יִסּוּרִין מְמָרְקִין לְחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת וְחַיָּיבֵי מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין;
And "scriptural repentance" is derived from those matters where scouring afflictions are required for those liable to spiritual excision and capital punishment;
אֲבָל לִ"תְשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל" לֹא נִמְצָא שׁוֹרֶשׁ בַּגְּמָרָא),
yet for "commensurate repentance," no explicit root is found in the Gemara),
הוּא מֵהָא דְּעוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן.
is from that principle that a burnt-offering serves as a appeasing gift
וְהָאֲרִיזַ"ל אֵין מְפָרֵשׁ הַדּוֹרוֹן כְּמִשְׁקַל הֲנָאָה,
And the holy Ari does not explain the gift as matching the weight of the pleasure,
וְעַל כֵּן קָבַע תַּעֲנִיּוֹת הַרְבֵּה גַּם לַעֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁאֵין כָּל כָּךְ הֲנָאָה,
and therefore he established numerous fasts even for transgressions that do not involve so much physical pleasure,
וְכֵן לְמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה הוֹסִיף עַד פ״ד תַּעֲנִיּוֹת,
and likewise for one who emits semen in vain, he increased the requirement up to eighty-four fasts,
כִּי אֵין הַדּוֹרוֹן כְּפִי מִשְׁקַל הַהֲנָאָה דַּוְוקָא,
because the gift is not necessarily strictly according to the weight of the pleasure,
וּבְוַדַּאי דְּאֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים.
and certainly both these and those are the words of the living God
וּבַשְּׁלָ״ה שָׁם רָמַז גַּם כֵּן לְדִבְרֵי הָרוֹקֵחַ וְהָאֲרִ"י בְּתִיקּוּן עָוֺן זֶה
And in the Shelah there, he likewise alluded to the words of the Roke'ach and the Ari regarding the rectification of this iniquity
(וּתְמִיהָה שֶׁכָּתַב זֶה אַחַר מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב דְּצָרִיךְ יִסּוּרִין כְּמִיתָה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל,
(and it is astonishing that he wrote this after having written that one requires afflictions equivalent to death as mentioned above,
וַהֲרֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם – הָרוֹקֵחַ וְהָאֲרִ"י – לֹא כָּתְבוּ בָּזֶה אֶלָּא מִסְפַּר תַּעֲנִיּוֹת, וְלֹא יִסּוּרִין כְּמִיתָה כְּלָל),
seeing that both of them—the Roke'ach and the Ari—prescribed for this nothing more than a tally of fasts, and not afflictions akin to death at all),
וּדְאֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים,
and that both these and those are the words of the living God,
וּכְשֶׁרוֹצֶה לְתַקֵּן הַפְּגָם בְּיוֹתֵר וּבְעוֹלָם יוֹתֵר עֶלְיוֹן צָרִיךְ תְּשׁוּבָה בְּיוֹתֵר, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
and when one wishes to rectify the spiritual blemish more intensely and in a higher realm, he requires a greater degree of repentance, see there
וְהַיְינוּ כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי: צָרִיךְ דּוֹרוֹן יוֹתֵר לִהְיוֹת רָצוּי גַּם בָּעוֹלָמוֹת הָעֶלְיוֹנִים בְּיוֹתֵר,
And this is consistent with what I wrote: one needs a greater gift to become acceptable in the most elevated spiritual worlds as well,
וְגָבֹהַּ מֵעַל גָּבֹהַּ.
transcending high above high
וְכָל אֶחָד דִּבֵּר לְפִי מַדְרֵגַת הַשָּׂגָתוֹ,
And each authority spoke according to the level of his spiritual perception,
וְכַיָּדוּעַ מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב הָרַמַ״ע בְּהַקְדָּמַת סֵפֶר "פֶּלַח הָרִמּוֹן",
and as is known from what the Rama of Fano wrote in the introduction to the book Pelach HaRimmon,
דְּקַבָּלַת הָרַב מֹשֶׁה קוֹרְדּוֹבֵירִי וְהָרִאשׁוֹנִים נֶגֶד קַבָּלַת הָאֲרִ"י כְּמַדְרֵגַת הַפְּשָׁט נֶגֶד הַסּוֹד, עַיֵּין שָׁם.

that the Kabbalah of Rabbi Moshe Cordovero and the early masters stands in relation to the Kabbalah of the Ari as the level of Peshat (plain meaning) stands in relation to Sod (mystical secret), see there

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86b; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:1; Tzidkas HaTzadik 73 — teshuvas haba’ah tests the transformed choice: Yoma defines the complete returnee: “הֵיכִי דָמֵי בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה? ... שֶׁבָּאת לְיָדוֹ דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה פַּעַם רִאשׁוֹנָה וּשְׁנִיָּה וְנִיצַּל הֵימֶנָּה,” specifically “בְּאוֹתָהּ אִשָּׁה, בְּאוֹתוֹ פֶּרֶק, בְּאוֹתוֹ מָקוֹם.” Rambam codifies the principle: “זֶה שֶׁבָּא לְיָדוֹ דָּבָר שֶׁעָבַר בּוֹ ... וּפֵרַשׁ וְלֹא עָשָׂה מִפְּנֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה,” while desire and strength remain. This is not a punishment imposed on the body, but evidence that the inner decision has changed under equivalent conditions. Rav Tzadok therefore says the Rokeach can point to an explicit Gemara for teshuvas haba’ah, whereas the proportional suffering of teshuvas hamishkal lacks such a direct Talmudic formulation. The safeguard against deliberately recreating a forbidden test, and the providential meaning of a returning test, are explained in the earlier Tzidkas HaTzadik §73 parallel. Thus teshuvas haba’ah verifies freedom from the former hold of the sin; it is not the source for a fixed number of fasts.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 25b — the protective fence. The rehabilitation examples require dice-players to cease “אֲפִילּוּ בְּחִנָּם” — “even for free”; interest-lenders to refrain “אֲפִילּוּ לְגוֹי” — “even to a non-Jew”; and pigeon-racers to desist “אֲפִילּוּ בַּמִּדְבָּר” — “even in the wilderness.” These are the separate examples for teshuvas hageder. They build a boundary beyond merely ceasing the former prohibited act. They do not by themselves derive the later gift model of teshuvas hamishkal.

paragraphs.text: Zevachim 7b. Rav Tzadok then seeks a conceptual source for the Rokeach’s separate teshuvas hamishkal. Zevachim states: “עוֹלָה — דּוֹרוֹן הִיא” — “The olah is a gift.” Rava reasons that without teshuvah the offering is “זֶבַח רְשָׁעִים תּוֹעֵבָה,” while after teshuvah the sinner has already been forgiven; the olah therefore enters afterward as a gift of renewed favor. Rav Tzadok proposes that the Rokeach understood proportional counter-suffering in the same post-forgiveness category: pleasure was used to rebel, so an opposite exertion becomes a fitting doron and restores willing service. The earlier Rokeach discussion applies the gift logic even to lesser prohibitions. The §262 parallel on absorbed pleasure is quoted with the preceding ice-or-fasting discussion. The source is therefore the logic of ritzui, not a new indispensable condition of basic mechilah.

paragraphs.text: Shelah, Shaar HaOtiyos, Hilchos Bi’ah 1:49–50; Reishis Chochmah, Shaar HaTeshuvah 7; Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah 3; Rema MiPano, introduction to Pelach HaRimon — different depths of one true repair: The Shelah sets out the Rokeach’s four forms of repentance and accepts both the Rokeach’s regimen and the Arizal’s tikkunim as “אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹקִים חַיִּים,” and states “וְאִם רָצָה לְתַקֵּן בְּיוֹתֵר, אָזַי צָרִיךְ תְּשׁוּבָה בְּיוֹתֵר, וְכוּלֵּי הַאי וְאוּלַי” — “If he wishes to repair more deeply, he then requires deeper repentance, and even then, perhaps.” Rav Tzadok articulates the application here in terms of a higher world. Tanya records the Arizal’s figure explicitly: “פ״ד תַּעֲנִיּוֹת,” and presents the dispute whether repeated acts require repeated series like separate chata’os or can be addressed like one olah covering several positive-commandment failures. Its accepted practical compromise is three series, yet it sharply limits fasting when health or Torah study will suffer and permits redemption through tzedakah. The number is therefore a kabbalistic form of ritzui and tikkun, not a simple measurement of physical pleasure. Rav Tzadok uses this to explain why the Arizal can require more than the Rokeach without contradicting him: the doron reaches additional spiritual worlds. Rav Tzadok cites Rema MiPano’s introduction to Pelach HaRimon, which he presents as treating the Ramak and earlier kabbalists in relation to the Arizal as progressively deeper levels rather than mutually exclusive systems. At the same time, Rav Tzadok questions the Shlah’s phrase “יסורין כמיתה”: the actual Rokeach and Arizal schedules cited here prescribe fasts, not literal death-like suffering. Greater tikkun must not be confused with a formal Torah punishment category.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok connects the Rokeach’s commensurate repentance with the appeasing gift of an olah. He explains differing prescriptions of the Rokeach and the Ari through different levels of spiritual repair, while distinguishing these gifts from afflictions required for essential atonement.

p: וְיָדוּעַ אַרְבַּע מַדְרֵגוֹת פַּרְדֵּ״ס שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּהַשָּׂגַת הַתּוֹרָה
And it is known that the four levels of PaRDeS present in the comprehension of the Torah
הֵם נֶגֶד אַרְבָּעָה עוֹלָמוֹת אֲצִילוּת, בְּרִיאָה, יְצִירָה, עֲשִׂיָּה וְנֶגֶד אַרְבַּע אוֹתִיּוֹת הַשֵּׁם,
correspond to the four worlds of Atzilut, Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah, and to the four letters of the Tetragrammaton,
וְכָל אֶחָד הִשִּׂיג כְּפִי מַדְרֵגַת הַשָּׂגָתוֹ,
and each master apprehended according to the level of his perception,
וְעַל פִּי דַּרְכּוֹ דִּבֵּר בְּעִנְיַן הָרִיצּוּי
and in accordance with his own pathway spoke concerning spiritual appeasement
לְאוֹתָן מַדְרֵגַת הַשָּׂגָה שֶׁנִּתְגַּלּוּ עַל יְדֵי הָאֲרִיזַ"ל,
relative to those levels of perception that were revealed through the holy Ari,
שֶׁלֹּא נוֹדְעוּ עֲדַיִן מִקּוֹדֶם וְלֹא הָיוּ יְכוֹלִים לְהַגִּיעַ לְכָךְ,
which were not yet known previously and which earlier generations could not attain,
וְעַל כֵּן הָיָה דַּי לָהֶם מִתִּיקּוּן שֶׁנִּתְגַּלָּה אָז
and therefore it was sufficient for them to employ the rectification revealed then
כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁהָיָה הַצֹּרֶךְ אָז לַמַּדְרֵגָה שֶׁהָיוּ יְכוֹלִים לְהַגִּיעַ.
commensurate with the need of that era for the level they were capable of attaining
וְרִיצּוּי הַדּוֹרוֹן הוּא כְּדֵי שֶׁיּוּכַל לְהַגִּיעַ לְתַכְלִית הַמַּדְרֵגָה שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר לְצַדִּיק גָּמוּר לְהַגִּיעַ,
And the appeasement of the gift is designed to enable one to reach the ultimate spiritual rank accessible to a complete tzaddik,
עַל יְדֵי הָרִיצּוּי הַגָּמוּר שֶׁ"הֱבִיאַנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ חֲדָרָיו" (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים א, ד).
through absolute favor, reflecting: "The King has brought me into His chambers" (Song of Songs 1:4)
וְכָל תִּיקּוּנֵי תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁל הַקַּדְמוֹנִים כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי
And all the rectifications of repentance outlined by the early masters, as I have written,
אֵינָם לְעִכּוּב הַכַּפָּרָה לְגַמְרֵי,
do not fundamentally withhold or delay essential atonement,
רַק לְהַגִּיעַ גַּם כֵּן לָרִיצּוּי הַגָּמוּר.
rather serve to enable one to attain ultimate, complete favor as well
וְאַף בְּחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת וּמִיתַת בֵּית דִּין
And even regarding those liable to excision and capital punishment,
אֵין הַסִּיגּוּפִים שֶׁקָּצְבוּ לְיִסּוּרִים הַמְּמָרְקִים לְבַד,
the penances they prescribed were not aimed at serving as the scouring afflictions alone,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּדִבְרֵי הָרוֹקֵחַ שֶׁקָּצַב מִלְּבַד זֶה לִ"תְשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל",
just as I wrote regarding the words of the Roke'ach, who established requirements beyond this for "commensurate repentance,"
שֶׁהוּא בִּמְקוֹם הַדּוֹרוֹן עַל פִּי דַּרְכּוֹ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
which stands in place of the propitiatory gift in his system, as mentioned above

paragraphs.text: Or HaChaim, Shemos 32:6; Shaarei Kedushah I 2:8; Shaar Maamarei Razal, Tractate Shabbos §8; Etz Chaim, Shaar 42, chapter 4, mahadura kama (Sefaria 42:17); Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:44; Resisei Layla 35; Tzidkas HaTzadik 134 — PaRDeS, ABiYA, and ascent from one level of attainment to another: PaRDeS is the familiar acronym for peshat, remez, derash, and sod—the plain, allusive, homiletical, and esoteric dimensions of Torah. Or HaChaim makes the correspondence used here explicit: “הַפְּשָׁט אוֹרוֹ מֵאִיר בְּעוֹלַם הָעֲשִׂיָּה, רֶמֶז בְּעוֹלַם הַיְּצִירָה, דְּרָשׁ בְּעוֹלַם הַבְּרִיאָה, סוֹד בְּעוֹלַם הָאֲצִילוּת”—peshat illumines Asiyah, remez Yetzirah, derash Beriah, and sod Atzilus. Shaarei Kedushah presents the four modes of Torah-study as vehicles for the soul’s ascent, while Shaar Maamarei Razal and Etz Chaim relate the worlds to the four letters of Havayah: yud to Atzilus, the first heh to Beriah, vav to Yetzirah, and the final heh to Asiyah. These worlds are graded modes of Divine disclosure, from revealed unity to increasingly differentiated and concretized reception; a teaching may therefore be true on one level without exhausting a higher one. Rav Tzadok develops this in Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:44. Hashem did not establish unrelated systems; “אוֹתוֹ הַסֵּדֶר שֶׁבָּאֲצִילוּת הוּא עַצְמוֹ בִּבְרִיאָה... בִּיצִירָה... בַּעֲשִׂיָּה”—the same order repeats from Atzilus through Asiyah, though it descends into different forms of being. He also maps the worlds within the person: the hidden root of unified attachment corresponds to Atzilus; apprehension in which knower and known remain distinct to Beriah; the heart and ruach to Yetzirah; and recognition embodied in action to Asiyah. Resisei Layla 35 adds that Atzilus is what Hashem makes apprehensible of His otherwise unlimited light, and “כְּפִי מִדַּת הַשָּׂגָתָם הוּא... מִדַּת הַהַשָּׂגָה הַנֶּאֱצֶלֶת”—the revealed apprehension corresponds to the recipients’ attainment. Rav Tzadok therefore does not treat earlier authorities as mistaken: each spoke truth from the chamber and capacity then accessible. Tzidkas HaTzadik 134 supplies the direct teshuvah parallel. There is no fixed end to a person’s levels, and “כְּפִי מַעֲלַת הָאָדָם וְהַשָּׂגָתוֹ כָּךְ הִיא תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ.” A sin may have been genuinely repaired “בְּכָל דַּרְגִין וְעוֹלָמוֹת” on the lower level, leaving no trace there; yet upon ascent it becomes newly visible according to the higher standard and calls for deeper teshuvah. This is the bridge in this se’if: the earlier tikkun sufficed for the level then revealed, while the Arizal’s disclosures opened a higher chamber and therefore a fuller ritzui. The correspondences come from the cited sources; their application here is Rav Tzadok’s analysis.

paragraphs.text: Shir HaShirim 1:4; Yalkut Shimoni, Shir HaShirim §982; Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah 6 — “The King brought me into His chambers”: Shir HaShirim says, “הֱבִיאַנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ חֲדָרָיו.” Yalkut Shimoni applies the verse to R’ Akiva, who entered Pardes and emerged in peace, and also interprets the chambers as the hidden treasuries of heaven, Gan Eden, and “חַדְרֵי תוֹרָה.” Tanna DeBei Eliyahu compares it to a king taking his beloved by the hand into innermost rooms and teaches that each talmid chacham has inner chambers in Torah. These readings illuminate Rav Tzadok’s use of the verse. It is not a source for a formal requirement to perform a particular fast or mortification. It is the image of complete ritzui after forgiveness: the penitent is not merely released from liability but restored to intimate access and higher Torah-attainment. The Midrashic link to R’ Akiva’s entry into Pardes also echoes the PaRDeS framework at the beginning of this se’if.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86a; Zevachim 7b; Rokeach, Hilchos Teshuvah — kapparah, yissurin memarkin, and the separate doron: Yoma distinguishes the stages of atonement by category: for kareis and court-death offenses, “תְּשׁוּבָה וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים תּוֹלִין, וְיִסּוּרִין מְמָרְקִין” — repentance and Yom Kippur suspend, while suffering completes the cleansing. Zevachim, by contrast, calls the olah “דּוֹרוֹן הִיא”: without teshuvah the offering is rejected as a sacrifice of the wicked, while after teshuvah the person has already been forgiven; the offering restores favor. The Rokeach’s teshuvas hamishkal prescribes measured fasts or suffering corresponding to the transgression. Rav Tzadok’s chiddush is to separate these functions. He does not deny Yoma’s required cleansing where it applies; he argues that not every mortification listed by the early pietists is that indispensable stage. Some are an additional doron — a discipline of appeasement and repair that elevates the penitent beyond mechilah toward complete ritzui. This distinction is Rav Tzadok’s analysis, not an explicit statement of Yoma, Zevachim, or the Rokeach.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Within his account of differing spiritual attainments, Rav Tzadok explains why an appropriate gift can vary with the level of closeness being sought. He maintains that these further rectifications seek complete favor and do not themselves withhold the basic pardon of repentance.

p: וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים נִרְאֶה דְּבַעַל "הַתַּנְיָא" לָמַד זֶה
And at any rate, it appears that the author of the Tanya derived this
(שֶׁמּוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה חַיָּיב מִיתָה)
namely, that one who emits semen in vain is liable to death
מִדִּבְרֵי הָרוֹקֵחַ וְסֵפֶר חֲסִידִים שֶׁסִּידְּרוּ תַּעֲנִיּוֹת וְסִיגּוּפִים לִתְשׁוּבָה עַל זֶה,
from the words of the Roke'ach and Sefer Chassidim, who structured fasts and mortifications for repentance over this;
וּלְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי אֵינוֹ רְאָיָה כְּלָל מִיהַת.
yet according to what I have written, this constitutes no proof whatsoever
וְאַף דִּבְסֵפֶר חֲסִידִים שָׁם הֵבִיא בָּזֶה מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ:
And even though in Sefer Chassidim there he cited the dictum:
"דִּכְאִלּוּ מֵבִיא מַבּוּל וּכְאִלּוּ שׁוֹפֵךְ דָּמִים",
that "it is as if he brings a flood and as if he sheds blood,"
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דִּלְעִנְיַן הַסִּיגּוּף לְדוֹרוֹן תָּלוּי גַּם כֵּן כְּפִי חֹמֶר הֶעָוֺן
it can be said that regarding the penance for a gift, it depends also upon the intrinsic severity of the sin,
וְאַף עַל פִּי דְּאֵין בּוֹ כָּרֵת.
even if it does not carry the formal penalty of excision
וְגַם בְּמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה,
And likewise with positive commandments,
אַף שֶׁהַתּוֹרָה אָמְרָה דֶּרֶךְ כְּלָל "הָעוֹלָה מְכַפֶּרֶת לְדוֹרוֹן עַל כָּל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה",
even though the Torah stated as a general rule that the burnt-offering atones as a gift for all positive commandments,
עַתָּה שֶׁאֵין לָנוּ קָרְבָּנוֹת מִסְּבָרָא וַדַּאי יֵשׁ חִלּוּק בֵּין עֲשֵׂה חֲמוּרָה לְקַלָּה
now that we lack sacrificial offerings, by logical deduction there certainly exists a distinction between a severe positive commandment and a minor one
בְּעִנְיַן סִיגּוּפִים שֶׁעוֹשִׂים לְרִיצּוּי דּוֹרוֹן.
with respect to the penances performed for the appeasement of a gift
אֲבָל אֵין בָּזֶה עִנְיָן לְיִסּוּרִין מְמָרְקִין דְּחַיָּיבֵי כְּרֵיתוֹת שֶׁהֵם מְעַכְּבִין הַכַּפָּרָה,
Yet this bears no relation to the scouring afflictions of those liable to excision which hold back essential atonement,
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי דְּהוּא רַק מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה
and all the more so according to what I wrote, that this falls merely under a positive commandment,
אוֹ מִ"וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ" (בְּרֵאשִׁית ב, כד)
either from "and he shall cleave unto his wife" (Genesis 2:24)
אוֹ בִּכְלַל "פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ" (שָׁם א, כח).
or within the commandment to "be fruitful and multiply" (ibid. 1:28)
הִנֵּה גַּם בְּמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה דְּחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת,
Now, even regarding a positive commandment that carries excision (such as circumcision or the Paschal offering),
דְּנִתְבָּאֵר [לְעֵיל אוֹת י״ג] בִּפְשִׁיטוּת מִלְּשׁוֹן הָרַמְבַּ״ם דְּהוּא בִּכְלַל חַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת,
which was explained above in section 13 as plainly emerging from Maimonides' phrasing to be included in the category of excision,
וְכֵן הוּא גַּם כֵּן בַּ"עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת" שָׁם בִּפְשִׁיטוּת,
and as is likewise stated in Asarah Ma'amarot there as obvious,
רָאִיתִי עַתָּה בְּ"תוֹסְפוֹת יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים" [בְּיוֹמָא פ״ה סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳]
I have now seen in Tosfot Yom HaKippurim on Yoma 85b
שֶׁכָּתַב בְּיִשּׁוּב דִּבְרֵי רַמְבַּ״ם [פֶּרֶק א מֵהִלְכוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה הֲלָכָה ב] מִקּוּשְׁיַת הַ"כֶּסֶף מִשְׁנֶה" שָׁם,
who wrote to resolve the words of Maimonides (Laws of Repentance 1:2) against the challenge of the Kessef Mishneh there,
מֵהָא דִּשְׁבוּעוֹת [י״ב סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳]
based on the passage in Shevuot 12b
דְּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם "הַאי עֲשֵׂה הֵיכִי דָּמֵי וְכוּלֵי"
that what the Gemara asked there, "What are the circumstances of this positive commandment, etc.?"
קָאֵי אַעֲשֵׂה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כָּרֵת דְּמֵחֲמוּרוֹת, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
refers specifically to a positive commandment carrying excision, which is categorized among the grave transgressions, see there
וּמְבוֹאָר דִּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ דְּגַם מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כָּרֵת בִּתְשׁוּבָה לְבַד נִמְחָל,
And it is clear that he holds that even a positive commandment carrying excision is forgiven through repentance alone,
כִּדְמַיְיתֵי בַּגְּמָרָא שָׁם עַל זֶה הָא דְּ"לֹא זָז וְכוּלֵי", עַיֵּין שָׁם.
just as the Gemara cites in this connection the ruling that "he does not move from his place before he is forgiven, etc.," see there

paragraphs.text: Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah ch. 1; Rokeach, Hilchos Teshuvah §20; Sefer Chasidim §167 — Severe penitential regimens do not by themselves determine the formal atonement category: The Baal HaTanya writes that the classic mussar works, foremost the Rokeach and Sefer Chasidim, prescribe numerous fasts and mortifications for sins carrying kareis or beis-din death, and likewise for wasteful emission of seed, which he classifies as death by Heaven from the deaths of Er and Onan; for the purpose of avoiding heavenly suffering he therefore treats it like kareis. The Rokeach, as quoted by Rav Tzadok, prescribes forty fast-days together with practical safeguards against renewed arousal, while Sefer Chasidim prescribes cold-water mortification. Rav Tzadok is not denying that these Rishonim regarded the offense with extraordinary severity. His precise argument is methodological: the quantity and harshness of a teshuvah regimen may be intended to restore favor and refine the person in proportion to the damage, and therefore cannot alone prove that the offense belongs legally to the kareis-or-death class whose essential kapparah requires yissurin. The classification as death by Heaven is explicit in the Tanya; the inference that it was derived from the Rokeach and Sefer Chasidim is Rav Tzadok’s own reconstruction.

paragraphs.text: Niddah 13a; Yeshayah 57:5; Bereishis 6:12; Sefer Chasidim §167 — “As though he brings a Flood” and “as though he sheds blood”:  Niddah describes conduct likely to cause wasteful emission as though it brings a Flood upon the world, linking it to “all flesh had corrupted its way,” and R’ Yitzchak and R’ Ami compare the emission itself to bloodshed through the derashah that reads shochatei, “those who slaughter children,” as sochetei, “those who squeeze out.” Rashi on Niddah 13a, s.v. ke-ilu mevi mabul, explains that the Flood generation corrupted through heated passion and was punished measure for measure with heated waters. Sefer Chasidim turns these images into penitential practice, prescribing immersion or sitting in icy water to cool the bodily heat that produced the sin. These statements explain why a doron-oriented tikkun may be unusually demanding. Rav Tzadok nevertheless distinguishes an aggadic comparison expressing destructive spiritual potential from a formal Torah category of homicide, kareis, or statutory death; that distinction continues his analysis from the opening se’ifim of this siman.

Rav Tzadok nevertheless distinguishes an aggadic comparison expressing destructive spiritual potential from a formal Torah category of homicide, kareis, or statutory death; that distinction continues his analysis from the opening se’ifim of this siman.

paragraphs.text: Zevachim 7b; Rashi, s.v. olah doron hi; Yoma 86a; Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah ch. 2 — The olah restores favor after the sinner has already been pardoned: Rava reasons that an olah cannot effect the first pardon for neglect of a positive commandment: without teshuvah, “the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination,” while after teshuvah the offender “does not move from his place until he is forgiven.” The olah is therefore a doron. Rashi compares it to one who offended a king, secured appeasement through an advocate, and then brings a gift when admitted again before the king. Iggeres HaTeshuvah applies this distinction to voluntary fasting after genuine teshuvah: the fast is not the essence of forgiveness, but a means of becoming as beloved and welcome as before the sin. Rav Tzadok adopts the same structure here. Basic mechilah follows the halachic category of the offense; the additional regimen may vary with its severity because it seeks fuller ritzui and renewed closeness. The Tzidkas HaTzadik §134 parallel on a deeper repentance after ascent is retained at the earlier discussion of the levels of attainment. It does not retroactively invalidate the earlier forgiveness.

paragraphs.text: Tosafos Yom HaKippurim on Yoma 85b, as quoted by Rav Tzadok; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:2 and 1:4; Kesef Mishneh; Shevuos 12b — An aseh whose neglect carries kareis: The Rambam distinguishes the general categories of atonement and states that one who violates a positive commandment and repents is forgiven immediately. The Kesef Mishneh discusses how this formulation relates to the sugya in Shevuos, which asks what type of positive commandment remains for the Yom Kippur scapegoat to atone after teshuvah has already atoned. Tosafos Yom HaKippurim explains the sugya’s “this aseh—what are its circumstances?” as referring to an unusually severe positive commandment whose neglect itself carries kareis, such as the obligations of Korban Pesach or circumcision. On his reading, the rule “he does not move from there until he is forgiven” still follows the mitzvah’s positive-command form, even where kareis marks the gravity of its neglect. Rav Tzadok invokes this as direct support for the governing distinction of Siman 15: severity may enlarge the need for ritzui, safeguards, and later purification without automatically transferring the offense into the atonement schedule of a full negative prohibition or a kareis transgression. This is the view he draws from Tosafos Yom HaKippurim; it should not be presented as an uncontested reading of every Rishon or Acharon.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The number or severity of penitential fasts does not, in Rav Tzadok’s analysis, establish a formal liability to death or kares. He distinguishes the gravity relevant to an appeasing gift from afflictions that hold back essential atonement, then examines a different opinion about positive commandments carrying kares.

p: וְאִיבְרָא שֶׁהוּא כָּתַב זֶה אַלִּבָּא דְּרַמְבַּ״ם,
And indeed, he wrote this according to the stance of Maimonides,
וּכְבָר תָּמְהוּ עָלָיו שֶׁלֹּא רָאָה דִּבְרֵי רַמְבַּ״ם עַצְמוֹ [שָׁם הֲלָכָה ד]
and commentators have already expressed wonder at him for failing to notice the explicit words of Maimonides himself (ibid., Halakhah 4),
שֶׁכָּתַב דַּוְוקָא מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ כָּרֵת "לֹא זָז וְכוּלֵי".
who specified that only for a positive commandment that does not carry excision does "he not move, etc." apply
גַּם מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב שָׁם דִּקְרָא "שׁוּבוּ בָנִים וְגוֹמֵר" (יִרְמְיָה ג, כב) דְּיָלְפִינַן מִינֵיהּ דַּעֲשֵׂה נִמְחָל מִיָּד
Furthermore, what he wrote there—that the verse "Return, backsliding children, etc." (Jeremiah 3:22), from which we derive that a positive commandment is forgiven immediately,
קָאֵי בַּעֲשֵׂה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כָּרֵת,
applies to a positive commandment carrying excision,
דִּבַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה מַיְירֵי כִּדְמוֹכְחֵי קְרָאֵי
because it is addressing idolatry as the surrounding verses demonstrate
(דְּכָל הַפָּרָשָׁה שָׁם בְּיִרְמְיָה ג קָאֵי אַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שֶׁעָבְדוּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם),
(for the entire passage there in Jeremiah 3 addresses the idolatry they served, see there),
וּמַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ עֲשֵׂה בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה דְּתוֹכָחָה שֶׁלֹּא הוֹכִיחוּ,
and that one can identify a positive commandment regarding idolatry in the obligation of rebuke which they neglected,
אוֹ הֵיכִי דְּלֹא יָדְעוּ לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה בְּלָאו אֶלָּא בַּעֲשֵׂה, יְעֻיַּין שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ,
or in a case where they were unaware of the negative prohibition against idolatry and knew of it only as a positive duty, examine there at length,
תָּמוּהַּ מְאֹד;
is exceedingly astonishing;
דְּאַעֲשֵׂה דְּתוֹכָחָה לֵיכָּא כָּרֵת,
for on the positive commandment of rebuke there is no excision,
וְרַק הָעוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה בְּכָרֵת וְלֹא מִי שֶׁאֵין מוֹכִיחַ.
and only the one who actually serves idols incurs excision, not the one who merely fails to rebuke
וְאַף דְּנֶעֱנָשׁ מִטַּעַם עֲרֵבוּת כְּשֶׁלֹּא מִיחָה,
And even though a person is punished under the principle of mutual responsibility (areivut) when he fails to protest,
הֲרֵי מְפוֹרָשׁ [בִּשְׁבוּעוֹת ל״ט רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳]
behold it is explicit in Shevuot 39b
דְּגַם רְשָׁעִים דְּעָלְמָא שֶׁהָיָה בְּיָדָם לִמְחוֹת וְלֹא מִיחוּ אֵין נֶעֱנָשִׁים אֶלָּא בַּדִּין הַקַּל, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
that ordinary wicked people who had the ability to protest and did not protest are punished only with the lesser penalty, see there
וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב דְּיָדַע רַק בַּעֲשֵׂה,
And as for what he wrote, that the offender was aware only of the positive commandment,
מִלְּבַד דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר כֵּיוָן דְּכָרֵת דִּילֵיהּ עַל הַלָּאו נֶאֱמַר וְלֹא עַל הָעֲשֵׂה,
aside from the fact that one may argue that since its excision was stated regarding the negative prohibition and not the positive commandment,
וְהוּא יָדַע מֵהַכָּרֵת אַף עַל גַּב דְּלֹא יָדַע מֵהַלָּאו, מִכָּל מָקוֹם כּוֹרֶת דִּילֵיהּ חָמוּר;
and he knew of the excision even if he was unaware of the negative prohibition, his liability to excision remains severe;
בְּלָאו הָכִי נַמֵּי, הֲרֵי גַּם שׁוֹגֵג דְּחַיָּיבֵי כְּרֵיתוֹת חַיָּיב חַטָּאת,
even without this, behold an inadvertent offender of an act carrying excision is liable to a sin-offering,
וְהַיְינוּ עִם הַתְּשׁוּבָה, דְּאִי לָאו הָכִי "זֶבַח רְשָׁעִים תּוֹעֵבָה" (מִשְׁלֵי כא, כז),
and that offering functions only alongside repentance, for otherwise "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination" (Proverbs 21:27),
וְרַק עוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן אֲבָל חַטָּאת לָאו דּוֹרוֹן,
and only a burnt-offering is a gift, whereas a sin-offering is not a gift,
דְּאֵין לוֹ כַּפָּרָה בִּתְשׁוּבָה לְבַד וַאֲפִילּוּ עִם יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים עַד שֶׁיָּבִיא חַטָּאת,
in that he has no atonement through repentance alone, nor even with Yom Kippur, until he brings a sin-offering;
וְאִם כֵּן, אֵיךְ אָמְרוּ עַל זֶה דְּמוֹחֲלִין מִיָּד?
and if so, how could they say concerning this that he is forgiven immediately?
וּמִי עָדִיף יָדַע בַּהַכָּרֵת וַעֲשֵׂה וְשָׁגַג בְּלָאו, מֵאִלּוּ שָׁגַג בַּכֹּל דְּלֹא נִתְכַּפֵּר עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה לְבַד?

And why should one who knew of the excision and the positive command but erred regarding the prohibition be superior to one who was mistaken about everything, who is not atoned for by repentance alone?

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86a; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4; Minchas Chinuch, mitzvah 364, s.v. ובס״ד נתחיל לכתוב חילוקי כפרה (Sefaria 364:1:5) — the Rambam limits immediate pardon to an aseh without kareis: Rabbi Yishmael’s formulation in the Gemara says generally that one who violated an aseh and repented is forgiven immediately. The Rambam adds the decisive qualification “she-ein bah kareis,” excluding such positive commandments as milah and the Korban Pesach, whose neglect carries kareis. The Minchas Chinuch likewise places an aseh carrying kareis within the more severe atonement category. Rav Tzadok therefore reads the Rambam’s wording as substantive, not incidental: the objective punishment attached to the neglected command determines its seder ha-kapparah. Compare the preceding se’ifim, where immediate mechilah is distinguished from the further stages of kapparah, ritzui, and doron.

paragraphs.text: Yirmiyahu 3:6–22; Tosafos Yom HaKippurim to Yoma 85b–86a, s.v. Amar Rabbi Yehudah — the idolatry setting of “Return, wayward children”: The prophecy repeatedly describes worship “upon every high mountain,” “under every leafy tree,” and adultery “with stone and with wood”; the call “Shuvu banim shovavim, erpa meshuvoseichem” therefore arises in an explicit avodah-zarah context. In Rav Tzadok’s account, Tosafos Yom HaKippurim asks how this verse can prove that an ordinary aseh is forgiven immediately and suggests either that the aseh was the failure to rebuke the idolaters, or that the sinner knew only a positive formulation of the prohibition. Rav Tzadok’s first objection is that failure to rebuke has no kareis of its own. The separate objection about ignorance of the lav is developed in the following phrases and explained with the chatas argument.

paragraphs.text: Shevuos 39b; Shabbos 54b–55a; Rambam, Hilchos De’os 6:7 — arvus, protest, and derivative punishment: Shevuos distinguishes the principal sinner from others who could have protested: in ordinary transgressions, the sinner receives his own judgment, wicked members of his family a severe derivative judgment, and other wicked people who failed to protest only the lighter judgment. Shabbos and the Rambam nevertheless teach that one able to rebuke who remains silent is “seized” for the other’s sin and may be punished severely. Rav Tzadok’s point is categorical: arvus can create real liability, but it does not make the non-protester the direct idolater or assign the non-protester the idolater’s kareis. This distinction also prepares the continuation in Se’if 37, where he returns to the deaths decreed for failure to protest in Shabbos 55a.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Kerisus 6:4 states the exact rule: “חַיָּבֵי חַטָּאוֹת וַאֲשָׁמוֹת וַדָּאִין שֶׁעָבַר עֲלֵיהֶן יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים, חַיָּבִין לְהָבִיא לְאַחַר יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים” — “Those liable for sin-offerings or definite guilt-offerings, over whom Yom Kippur has passed, must bring them after Yom Kippur.” Its following rule about contingent guilt-offerings is different. This is the direct source for the distinction being used here.

rich.text: Mishnah Kerisus 6:4 states the exact rule: “חַיָּבֵי חַטָּאוֹת וַאֲשָׁמוֹת וַדָּאִין שֶׁעָבַר עֲלֵיהֶן יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים, חַיָּבִין לְהָבִיא לְאַחַר יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים” — “Those liable for sin-offerings or definite guilt-offerings, over whom Yom Kippur has passed, must bring them after Yom Kippur.” Its following rule about contingent guilt-offerings is different. This is the direct source for the distinction being used here.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra 4:27–35; Mishnah Yoma 8:8 and Kerisus 6:4; Rambam, Hilchos Shegagos 1:1 and Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1; Zevachim 7b — a chatas completes kapparah and is not merely a doron: An inadvertent violation of a lav whose intentional violation carries kareis obligates a chatas. The Rambam rules that the offering itself cannot atone without teshuvah and verbal confession; conversely, teshuvah and Yom Kippur do not cancel the outstanding korban obligation. This differs from an olah, which Zevachim describes as a gift brought after the basic pardon. Rav Tzadok uses that formal distinction as a test of the proposed reading: if the deed objectively belongs to the kareis/chatas class, knowing the kareis while being unaware of the lav cannot transform it into a light aseh that is forgiven immediately. This continues his distinction in Se’ifim 34–35 between essential kapparah and the additional doron of complete ritzui.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok challenges the claim that repentance alone immediately completes atonement for a positive commandment carrying kares. He examines the Rambam’s express limitation and rejects attempts to prove the claim from neglect of rebuke or incomplete knowledge of the prohibition of idolatry.

p: וּמִיהוּ גּוּף דְּבָרָיו אֱמֶת, דִּקְרָא בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה קָאֵי.
Nevertheless, the core of his observation is true: the verse does address idolatry
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם [בְּיוֹמָא פ״ו עַמּוּד א׳] סוֹף דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל: "עָבַר עַל עֲשֵׂה",
And see there in Yoma 86a, at the end of the heading: "Avar al aseh,"
הוּקְשָׁה לֵיהּ אֵיךְ מַיְיתֵי דְּהַאי קְרָא אַעֲשֵׂה וְשָׁם קָאֵי אַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה,
where he was troubled as to how the Gemara cites this verse for a positive commandment when there it addresses idolatry,
וְתֵירֵץ דְּקָאֵי אַאוֹתָם שֶׁלֹּא הוֹכִיחוּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
and resolved that it refers to those who failed to rebuke, see there
הִנֵּה הֲדַר בֵּיהּ בְּעַצְמוֹ מִתֵּירוּץ שֵׁנִי הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל וְתָפַס תֵּירוּץ הָרִאשׁוֹן.
Behold, he himself retracted the second resolution mentioned above and embraced the first resolution
וְהַגַּם דְּמִזֶּה אֵין רְאָיָה לַעֲשֵׂה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כָּרֵת כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי,
And although from this there is no proof for a positive commandment carrying excision as I have written,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם לִדְאַתָאן עֲלַהּ נִרְאֶה שַׁפִּיר לִלְמוֹד מִשָּׁם;
nevertheless, for the thesis we are establishing, it is entirely proper to derive from there;
דַּהֲרֵי מְבוֹאָר [בְּשַׁבָּת נ״ה עַמּוּד א׳] דְּנִגְזַר "מִמִּקְדָּשִׁי תָּחֵלּוּ" עַל שֶׁלֹּא מִיחוּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם,
for behold it is elucidated in Shabbat 55a that the decree "begin at My sanctuary" was executed against those who failed to protest, see there,
הֲרֵי דְּנִתְחַיְּיבוּ מִיתָה לַשָּׁמַיִם עַל זֶה,
which demonstrates that they became liable to death by Heaven on account of this,
וַהֲרֵי זֶה חַיָּיב מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם דּוּגְמַת מוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה דְּיָלְפִינַן מֵאוֹנָן,
and this constitutes a liability to death at the hands of Heaven parallel to emitting semen in vain, which we derive from Onan;
וַחֲזֵינַן דְּגַם עֲשֵׂה דְּחַיָּיב מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם כְּהַאי גַּוְונָא,
and we see that even a positive commandment carrying death at the hands of Heaven of this kind,
מַה שֶּׁרָאִינוּ מִי שֶׁנִּתְחַיְּיבוּ מִיתָה עַל זֶה – מַהֲנֵי לֵיהּ תְּשׁוּבָה לְבַד.
in cases where we observe people incurring death for it, repentance alone avails
וְגַם בְּעִיקָּר דִּפְשִׁיטָא לְהוּ דְּכָל מוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה חַיָּיב מִיתָה,
Furthermore, regarding the foundational premise taken for granted by authorities that anyone who emits semen in vain is liable to death,
אַף דְּבַגְּמָרָא אִיתָא סְתָם,
even though in the Gemara it is stated without qualification,
צָרִיךְ יִשּׁוּב;
it requires careful resolution;
כֵּיוָן דְּמֵאוֹנָן יָלְפִינַן לַהּ,
since we derive it from Onan,
וְשָׁם מְבוֹאָר בַּכָּתוּב דְּהָיָה שֶׁלֹּא לְהָקִים זֶרַע וּלְבַטֵּל מִפְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה.
and there it is made explicit in Scripture that his motive was to avoid raising seed and to nullify procreation
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דַּוְוקָא בְּבִיטּוּל מִצְוַת פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה,
One can argue that liability to death applies specifically when linked to nullifying the commandment of procreation,
דְּמָצִינוּ עֹנֶשׁ זֶה גַּם בְּחִזְקִיָּה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל,
for we find this specific penalty also with King Hezekiah as mentioned above,
וְגַם עֵר שֶׁמֵּת עַל חֵטְא זֶה אָמְרוּ [בִּיבָמוֹת ל״ד עַמּוּד ב׳] שֶׁרָצָה שֶׁלֹּא תִּתְעַבֵּר, עַיֵּין שָׁם,
and also regarding Er who died for this sin, they stated in Yevamot 34b that he sought to prevent her conceiving, see there,
וּבִטְּלוּ מִפְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה;
and thus they nullified procreation;
אֲבָל כְּשֶׁאֵין בָּטֵל מִפְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה,
however, when one does not neglect the obligation of procreation,
בָּזֶה אֵין לִלְמוֹד מִשָּׁם דְּחַיָּיב מִיתָה כְּלָל.
one cannot derive from there that he is liable to death at all
וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּהַגְּמָרָא מַיְיתֵי לַהּ אַ"אוֹחֵז וּמַשְׁתִּין",
And even though the Gemara cites this verse regarding one who holds his organ while urinating,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם כֵּיוָן דְּעִיקַּר הֶעָוֺן בִּכְלָלוֹ מִצְוַת פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה,
nonetheless, since the underlying root of the iniquity in its general scope connects to procreation,
מַיְיתֵי לְעִנְיַן חֹמֶר הֶעָוֺן
it cites it to illustrate the grave severity of the iniquity,
אַף דְּבָזֶה לֵיכָּא חִיּוּב מִיתָה,
even though in this specific instance there is no formal liability to death,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הֶעָוֺן חָמוּר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ גַּם חִיּוּב מִיתָה.
yet the sin is fundamentally grave in that within its broader rubric a liability to death also exists

paragraphs.text: Tosafos Yom HaKippurim on Yoma 85b–86a, s.v. avar al aseh, as reported here by Rav Tzadok; Yirmiyahu 3:6–22 — the author’s first answer and Rav Tzadok’s reading of his retraction: The source verse for immediate forgiveness of an aseh, “Return, wayward children; I will heal your waywardness,” appears in a prophecy whose surrounding verses explicitly describe idolatry on the high places and under the leafy trees. Tosafos Yom HaKippurim therefore asks how a verse spoken in an avodah-zarah setting can prove the rule for an ordinary positive commandment. His first answer identifies the relevant aseh as the bystanders’ failure to rebuke the idolaters; his second treats the worshippers as people who knew the Divine command only through its positive formulation. As explained in the expanded notes to Se’if 36, Rav Tzadok rejects the second answer because ignorance of the lav does not remove the deed’s objective kareis and chatas classification. Here he observes that the later discussion returns to the first answer—failure to rebuke—and takes that as the author’s operative resolution. The conclusion that this constitutes a retraction is Rav Tzadok’s reading of the sequence; it is not an explicit statement by Tosafos Yom HaKippurim.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 54b–55a; Yechezkel 9:4–6; Rashi; Petach Einayim; Rambam, Hilchos De’os 6:7 — “From My sanctified ones shall you begin” and punishment for failing to protest: The Gemara describes righteous people in Yerushalayim who groaned over the public abominations and had fulfilled the Torah “from alef to tav,” yet did not protest. Middas HaDin argued that, although Hashem knew the sinners would not listen, the righteous themselves could not know that with certainty; the protective mark was therefore reversed, and “u-mi-mikdashi tacheilu” is read as “begin with My sanctified ones.” Rashi and the surrounding sugya frame their fault as the neglected obligation to protest, while the Rambam rules generally that one who can rebuke and remains silent is “seized” for the sinner’s wrongdoing. Petach Einayim on Shabbos 55a reports Yashresh Yaakov’s question about the duty to rebuke even when refusal is known, and his distinction that the neglected positive commandment does not ordinarily carry death. Chida then offers a different distinction involving the power to compel changed conduct. Those are separate voices in the discussion; Petach Einayim must not be presented as simply codifying the death liability. Rav Tzadok uses the episode as an actual instance of death decreed from Heaven for neglect of an aseh and argues that teshuvah alone can nevertheless address the aseh-category. His formulation should not be mistaken for a codified rule that every failure to rebuke carries a statutory misah bidei Shamayim; the Gemara recounts an exceptional communal judgment, and Rav Tzadok draws an analogy from the severity of its consequence.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 10a; Yevamos 34b; Bereishis 38:7–10; Machshavos Charutz 15:4 — Chizkiyahu, Er, and the common element of frustrating procreation: Yeshayah told Chizkiyahu that he would die because he had not married and engaged in peru u-revu; Chizkiyahu’s prophetic knowledge that unworthy children would emerge did not permit him to neglect the command. Yevamos explains that Onan prevented conception because the offspring would be attributed to his brother, while Er acted so that Tamar would not become pregnant and lose her beauty; “He slew him also” links their deaths to the same conduct. Rav Tzadok identifies the common denominator as the intentional diversion of the generative act away from establishing seed. Compare Machshavos Charutz 15:4: “The first mitzvah is procreation, so that the species should actually endure,” as Adam was commanded before the sin; after separation and failure he returned “to beget, in his likeness and image, Sheis,” and “the end is embedded in the beginning.” Its context contrasts physical offspring with writing Torah, the final mitzvah, as enduring spiritual offspring and repair. This is the conceptual frame of the parallel. That parallel supplies conceptual background for his emphasis here on procreation as the root-purpose of the faculty. It does not independently prove his narrower halachic claim that literal death-liability applies only when peru u-revu is actually frustrated.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis 38:8–10; Niddah 13a; Rambam, Hilchos Issurei Bi’ah 21:18; Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 23:1 — Onan as the source of the Gemara’s unqualified death-language: Rabbi Yochanan states without qualification that one who emits seed in vain is liable to death and proves it from Onan. The narrative, however, gives a particular motive: Onan repeatedly spilled the seed “lest he give seed to his brother,” directly frustrating Yehudah’s command to establish offspring for the deceased Er. The Rambam and Shulchan Aruch codify a broad prohibition against wasteful emission and stress its exceptional gravity, but they do not derive in these passages a separate formal death-penalty category for every circumstance. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes two questions: the prohibition and severity are general, while the literal death-liability inferred from Onan may depend on the additional element of deliberately defeating procreation. This proposed limitation is Rav Tzadok’s chiddush; Niddah itself applies Rabbi Yochanan’s statement in general language and does not articulate the qualification.

paragraphs.text: Niddah 13a; Rashi; Rambam, Hilchos Issurei Bi’ah 21:18–19 — why the Gemara cites the death-statement regarding one who holds himself while urinating: The immediate sugya is not a husband refusing conception. It forbids a man from holding the organ while urinating because stimulation may lead to wasteful emission, and Rabbi Yochanan’s death-language from Onan is introduced to explain the extreme caution. Rashi on Niddah 13a explains the stimulation and the Flood comparison, and the Rambam similarly places strict safeguards around conduct that can lead to emission. Rav Tzadok acknowledges that this context appears broader than actual nullification of peru u-revu. His answer is that Chazal may cite the most severe consequence found within the general class in order to establish the gravity of every instance, even when the particular case does not itself carry literal death-liability. Thus he is not reducing the prohibition; he is separating an aggadic statement of class-wide severity from the narrower formal question governing the order of kapparah in this siman. This distinction is his interpretive proposal and is not expressly stated by the Gemara or the Rambam.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok finds limited support for his distinction between a fixed Torah penalty and other acts punished by Heaven. He also questions whether the cases of Er and Onan establish the same death liability where the offense is unconnected with an intention to prevent procreation.

p: וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים
In any case,
כְּפִי מַה שֶׁהֵבִינוּ כֻּלָּם
according to what everyone understood
דְּדִבְרֵי הַזּוֹהַר דְּאֵין לוֹ תְּשׁוּבָה
that the Zohar’s “no repentance”
הַיְינוּ לְגוּף מְחִילַת הָעָוֹן וְהַכַּפָּרָה
means the very pardon and atonement of the sin,
וַדַּאי הוּא דָּבָר תָּמוּהּ וְזָר,
it is surely puzzling and strange,
וְכָל מַה שֶּׁכָּתְבוּ בְּזֶה
and all that they wrote on this
הֵם דְּבָרִים דְּחוּקִים וְרְחוּקִים.
is forced and far-fetched.
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן כְּפִי פְּשִׁוּטַ הַלָּשׁוֹן
And all the more so by the plain wording
דְּאֵין לוֹ תְּשׁוּבָה כָּלָל,
that there is no repentance at all,
דְּזֶה וַדַּאי דָּבָר שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר,
which is surely impossible,
דְּהֲרֵי אִיסּוּר אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ
for the prohibition of a married woman
וַדַּאי חָמוּר מִמֶּנּוּ,
is surely graver than it,
וְכִמְבוֹאָר גַּם כֵּן בְּסֵפֶר חֲסִידִים
as is also explained in Sefer Chasidim,
הַמּוֹבָא בְּחֵלְקַת מְחוֹקֵק וּבֵית שְׁמוּאֵל
cited in Chelkas Mechokek and Beis Shmuel
וְנִזְכָּר לְעִל.
and mentioned above.
וּמַעֲשֵׂה דָוִד בְּבַּת שֶׁבַע
And the incident of David and Bas Sheva,
שֶׁהָיָה בְּאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ,
which involved a married woman,
אָמְרוּ (בְּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ד, סוֹף עַמּוּד ב)
they said (Avodah Zarah 4b):
שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה רָאוּי לָכָךְ
that he was not fit for this,
אֶלָּא לְהוֹרוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה
but to teach repentance,
שֶׁאִם חָטָא יָחִיד וְכוּ׳,
that if an individual sins, etc.;
עַיֵּין שָׁם;
see there;
הֲרֵי דְּגַם לְאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ הַחָמוּר
so even for the graver case of a married woman
מְהַנְיָא תְּשׁוּבָה
repentance helps,
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן לְזֶה.
and all the more so for this one.
אֲבָל כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְּתִי לְעִל
But according to what I wrote above
בְּתְשׁוּבָה שֶׁסִדְּרוּ רוֹקַח וַהָאֲרִי״זַל
about the repentance order of the Rokeach and the Arizal,
דְּאֵינָם לְעַכֵּב הַכַּפָּרָה
that they do not hold up the atonement
רַק לְדוֹרוֹן,
but only an appeasing gift,
וְכָל אֶחָד כְּפִי מַדְרֵגָתוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּזְכַּר לְעִל,
each according to his level, as stated above,
נִרְאֶה לִי פָּשׁוּט
it seems clear to me
דְּגַם הַזּוֹהַר כּוּנָתוֹ
that the Zohar too means
לְעִנְיַן הַרִּצּוּי דּוֹרוֹן,
the appeasement by gift,
שֶׁיִּתְרַצֶּה לְגַמְרֵי
that he be fully accepted
לַעֲלוֹת וְלֵיָּרָאוֹת פְּנֵי ה'
to ascend and see Hashem’s face
בְּמַדְרֵגוֹת עֶלְיוֹנוֹת
at the higher levels
כְּצַדִּיק גָּמוּר שוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית
like a complete tzaddik who guards the covenant
שֶׁלֹּא חָטָא מֵעוֹלָם.
and never sinned.
וּבְכָל הָעֲבֵירוֹת הוּא כֵּן,
And with all sins it is so:
דְּבִתְשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה מֵאָהֲבָה
through complete repentance out of love,
זָדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוּ כְּזְכוּיוֹת
deliberate sins become like merits,
וְעֲלֵיהֶם חָיֹה יִחְיֶה,
“and through them he shall surely live,”
וְהַיְינוּ אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הָרְאוּיָה
meaning after proper repentance
וְהַבָּאַת הַדּוֹרוֹן אַחַר כָּךְ
and then bringing the gift,
חוֹזֵר לִהְיוֹת מְקֻרָּב וְבֶּן בַּיִת
he returns to being close, a member of the household,
כְּבָתַּחִלָּה בְּעוֹז יוֹתֵר,
as at first, with even greater strength,
מֵאַחַר שֶׁגַּם הָעֲבֵירוֹת עוֹלִים לְחֶשְׁבוֹן מִצְוֹת.
since even the sins ascend to the account of mitzvos.
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ בַּזּוֹהַר
And about this the Zohar says
דְּבְּעֲבֵירָה זוֹ לֹא מְהַנְיָא תְּשׁוּבָה
that for this sin repentance does not help
לִהְיוֹת כְּזְכוּיוֹת וְכַמַּקְדָּם לְגַמְרֵי,
to become like merits, entirely as before,
אֲפִילּוּ אַחַר כָּל הַדּוֹרוֹנוֹת.
even after all the gifts.
וְהַרּוֹקֵּחַ וְהָאֲרִי״זַל דִּבְּרוּ
The Rokeach and the Arizal spoke
כְּפִי מַדְרֵגָתָם,
according to their own level;
מְהַנְיָא תְּשׁוּבַת כָּל אֶחָד
each one’s repentance helps
לְאוֹתָה מַדְרֵגָה שֶׁהִשִּׂיג שֶׁיוֹעִיל.
for the level that he attained.
וּמַעֲלַת רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאִי
And the stature of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
בְּהַשָּׂגָתוֹ וּמַה שֶׁגִּלָּה לַחֲבֵרַיו
in his attainment and what he revealed to his colleagues
גְּבוֹהָה מִכֻּלָּם,
is higher than all;
כִּידוּעַ מִזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ
as is known from the holy Zohar,
מַה שֶׁאָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ
what he said about himself
וְכֵן עַל כָּל בְּנֵי דּוֹרוֹ
and likewise about all of his generation,
שֶׁאָמַר שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה כְּדָרָא דָא
that he said there will not be one like this generation
וְשֶׁלֹּא יִתְגַּלֶּה עוֹד כֵּן
and that such will not be revealed again
עַד בִּיאַת מָשִׁיח.
until the coming of Mashiach.
וְכְּפִי הַשָּׂגַת מַדְרֵגָתָם
And according to their level of attainment
אָמְרוּ שֶׁבְּחֵטְא זֶה אֵין תְּשׁוּבָה מוֹעִיל
they said that for this sin repentance does not avail,
שֶׁיוּכַל לְהַגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵגָה גְּבוֹהָה כָּזוֹ
to reach such a high level,
שֶׁאֵין יָכוֹל לְהַגִּיעַ לְזֶה
which none can reach
אֶלָּא צַדִּיק גָּמוּר שוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית
except a complete tzaddik who guards the covenant
שֶׁלֹּא פָּגַם מֵעוֹלָם כָּלָל.
who never damaged it at all.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86b, interpreting Yechezkel 33:19, distinguishes repentance from fear, which makes deliberate sins like inadvertent ones, from repentance from love, which makes them like merits. Sefer HaIkkarim IV:25 explicitly asks why repentance should yield positive merit rather than merely erase guilt. Its answer stresses Divine grace and generosity, and the love through which the penitent reaches the Torah’s intended end. It should not be reduced to a claim that effort independently earns the cancellation of the past.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok proposes that the Zohar’s “no repentance” concerns full restoration to an exceptional level of divine closeness, rather than the denial of pardon. He relates the different penitential prescriptions to different spiritual attainments, reserving the highest level described here for an unblemished covenant.

p: וְרַשְׁבִּ״י וַחֲבֵרָיו
And Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his colleagues
הָיוּ יְחִידִים בְּדָבָר זֶה,
were unique in this matter,
שֶׁעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ (בְּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה, רֹאשׁ פָּרָשָׁה לִה)
which is why they said (Bereishis Rabbah, start of ch. 35)
"לְדֹרֹת" חָסֵר,
"ledoros" is written defectively,
פָּרַט לְדוֹרוֹ שֶׁל חִזְקִיָּה וְשֶׁל רַשְׁבִּ״י
excluding the generation of Chizkiyah and of Rashbi,
שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ צְרִיכִין לְאוֹת קֶשֶׁת
who did not need the sign of the rainbow
נֶגֶד עוֹנֶשׁ מַבּוּל
against the Flood punishment
הַבָּא עַל פְּגָם הַבְּרִית.
that comes for damaging the covenant.
וְעַל חִזְקִיָּה אָמְרוּ (סַנְהֶדְרִין צד, עַמּוּד א)
And of Chizkiyah they said (Sanhedrin 94a)
דְּבִקֵּשׁ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ מָשִׁיח.
that the Holy One, Blessed is He, wished to make him Mashiach.
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּזְכֶּה לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם,
That is, that he merit eternal life,
דְּעַל מָשִׁיח נֶאֱמַר
for of Mashiach it is said
“חַיִּים שָׁאַל מִמְּךָ נָתַתָּה לֹּו” וְגוֹ׳,
“he asked You for life; You gave it to him,” etc.,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סֻכָּה נב, עַמּוּד א)
as they said (Sukkah 52a):
“אֵינוֹ מְבַקֵּשׁ אֶלָּא חַיִּים” וְגוֹ׳.
“he asks only for life,” etc.
וְדָבָר זֶה אַי אֶפְשָׁר
And this is impossible
אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי שְׁלֵמוּת קְדֻּשַׁת הַבְּרִית,
except through the completeness of the covenant’s holiness,
וְכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְּתִי לְעִל (רֹאשׁ סִימָן ו)
and as I wrote above (start of siman 6)
בְּאוֹתָם שֶׁמֵּתוּ בְּעִטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ,
about those who died through the serpent’s counsel,
דְּזֶהוּ עִטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ
that this is the serpent’s counsel:
שֶׁיֵּשׁ עַדַיִן שֹׁרֶשׁ תַּאֲוָה גּוּפָנִיּת בַּלֵּב
that there is still a root of bodily desire in the heart
בְּעִנְיָן זֶה.
regarding this matter.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשּׁלוֹם
Not so Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him,
דְּהָיָה נָקִי מִזֶּה
who was clean of this
וְלֹא רָאָה קֶרִי מֵעוֹלָם,
and never experienced an emission,
דְּרְאוּבֵן רֵאשִׁית אוֹנוֹ,
for Reuven was his first-fruit of strength,
לֹא מֵת;
and he did not die;
וְכֵן אֵלִיּהוּ מַלְאַךְ הַבְּרִית חַי לְעוֹלָם.
and likewise Eliyahu, angel of the covenant, lives forever.
וְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי גַּם כֵּן
And Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi too
לֹא נִרְאָה הַקֶּשֶׁת בִּימָיו
no rainbow was seen in his days,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (כְּתוּבוֹת ע״ז עַמּוּד ב׳),
as they said (Kesubos 77b),
נִכְנַס חַי לְגַן עֵדֶן,
he entered Gan Eden alive,
וְרַשְׁבִּ״י שָׁם שָׁאֲלוּ עַל זֶה,
and Rashbi there inquired about this,
דְּלוּלֵי זֶה
for without this
לֹא הָיָה יָכוֹל לִכָּנֵס לִמְקוֹמוֹ וּמַחִיצָתוֹ שֶׁל רַשְׁבִּ״י
he could not enter Rashbi’s place and partition
וְלַהַשִּׂיג מַדְרֵגָתוֹ,
and attain his level,
וְגַם לֹא הָיָה אֵלִיּהוּ הַמַּכְרִיז לְפָנָיו “פַּנוּ מָקוֹם”.
nor would Eliyahu have proclaimed before him “make room.”
וְרַשְׁבִּ״י נִסְתַּלֵּק בְּמִלַּת “חַיִּים”
And Rashbi departed with the word “chayim”
עַד הָעוֹלָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסוֹף הָאִידְרָא זוּטָא דְּהַאֲזִינוּ)
unto eternity, as stated at the end of Idra Zuta in Haazinu,
וְדִּשְׁמַעוּ קוֹל “אֹרֶךְ יָמִים” וְגוֹ׳ “וְחַיִּים שָׁאַל” וְגוֹ׳.
and they heard a voice: “length of days,” etc., “he asked for life,” etc.
וְהַיְינוּ דְּזָכָה לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם
That is, he merited eternal life,
שֶׁיִּזְכֶּה בוֹ מָשִׁיח כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּזְכַּר,
as Mashiach will merit, as mentioned,
וְכִיעַקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשּׁלוֹם
and like Yaakov Avinu
דְּלֹא מֵת רַק לְמַרְאִיֿ הָעַיִן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
who did not die, only in appearance in this world.
וְכֵן רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּנוֹ
And likewise his son Rabbi Elazar,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא פד, עַמּוּד ב)
as they said (Bava Metzia 84b)
דְּנָפַק קָלָא מִעִילִיּתֵיהּ,
that a voice came out of his upper chamber,
וְכֵן נִתְבָּאֵר לְעִל (סוֹף סִימָן ו) בְּרַבִּי
and so it was explained above (end of siman 6) regarding Rebbi,
וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן גָּדוֹל מִמֶּנּוּ
and Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon is greater than he,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְּתִי שָׁם מִגְּמָרָא דְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא שָׁם.
as I wrote there from the Gemara in Bava Metzia.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר רַשְׁבִּ״י (סֻכָּה מה, עַמּוּד ב)
And therefore Rashbi said (Sukkah 45b):
“בְּנֵי עֲלִיָּה מוּעָטִים”,
“the people of the elevated class are few;
וְאִם שְׁנַיִם הֵן אֲנִי וְבִנִי הֵן”,
if there are two, they are I and my son,”
וְמַסְקִינַן שָׁם
and the Gemara concludes there
דְּהֵם דְּעָייְלִי בְּלָא בַּר לְקַבֵּל פְּנֵי שְׁכִינָה
that they are those who enter, without permission, to receive the Shechinah’s presence,
וּמִשּׁוּם הָכִי נִקְרָאִים “בְּנֵי עֲלִיָּה”
and therefore they are called “sons of the elevated class”
שֶׁהֵם כְּבְנֵי בַּיִת לִכָּנֵס כִּרְצוֹנָם.
as they are like household members, entering at will.

paragraphs.text: The rainbow is the protective covenantal sign, not itself a Flood punishment. Rav Tzadok connects the absence of the sign to the exceptional protection supplied by kedushas habris; the Midrash does not itself formulate that full causal explanation. Etz Yosef is cited as related commentary; its exact wording has not been independently collated.

paragraphs.text: Sukkah 52a; Tehillim 21:5. After seeing Mashiach ben Yosef slain, Mashiach ben David says, “I ask of You only life.” Hashem answers that David had already prophesied the request: “Life he asked of You; You gave it to him, length of days for ever and ever.” This immediate setting is the request to survive. Rav Tzadok reads the verse’s enduring-life language within his further account of complete covenantal repair; that causal account is not independently stated in this Gemara.

paragraphs.text: Bava Basra 17a; Shabbos 55b. The four who died “through the serpent’s counsel” are Binyamin, Amram, Yishai and Kilav. The tradition distinguishes their mortality from death caused by their personal transgression. Rav Tzadok refers here to the beginning of Siman 6 for his identification of the remaining serpent-root with bodily desire. That inward identification is his explanation of the tradition, not the Gemara’s express definition of the phrase.

paragraphs.text: II Melachim 2:11 describes Eliyahu’s ascent; Malachi 3:1 and Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 29 connect the angel of the covenant with the covenantal and redemptive tradition. Rav Tzadok joins these distinct sources in a single explanation of enduring life through covenantal purity. None of these passages by itself states that Yaakov’s bodily purity caused the non-death teaching or that Eliyahu’s title caused his ascent.

paragraphs.text: Kesubos 77b relates R’ Yehoshua ben Levi’s Torah study among sufferers from ra’atan, his entry into Gan Eden, Eliyahu’s announcement, and Rashbi’s rainbow question. The Gemara says that no rainbow had appeared, but R’ Yehoshua answered otherwise to avoid claiming credit. Bereishis Rabbah 35:2 gives a different setting involving Eliyahu and access to Rashbi; the two narratives should not be silently merged.

paragraphs.text: Petach Einayim on Kesubos 77b, s.v. azal ashkechei, first suggests that a rainbow might have appeared in a distant region. In its concluding bracketed reconsideration, Chida calls that explanation strained and instead understands the distant community as deserving a rainbow although Rashbi’s merit prevented it from appearing. The withdrawn regional proposal is not his settled conclusion. Haflaah, s.v. bar Livai, separately interprets the reply as an admission of what R’ Yehoshua’s own deeds would have warranted, without taking credit for the protection. Rav Tzadok’s equation of access to Rashbi’s chamber with the same degree of kedushas habris remains his interpretation.

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 84b. R’ Elazar b’Rashbi’s wife reports keeping his body in the attic for between eighteen and twenty-two years. The narrative describes blood when a hair was pulled, a voice from the attic deciding disputes, and his eventual burial beside his father. It also recounts the comparison with Rebbi. These are the reported wonders behind the citation; the voice is not merely an unspecified heavenly echo.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok links the exceptional covenantal purity of Rashbi and his circle with the absence of a rainbow, enduring life, and entry into the divine presence. He reads the accounts of Chizkiyahu, Yaakov, Eliyahu, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi within that spiritual framework.

p: וְדָבָר זֶה זוֹכֶה רַק מִי
And this is merited only by one
שֶׁלֹּא טָעַם טַעַם חֵטְא מֵעוֹלָם,
who never tasted the taste of sin,
כְּאָדָם הַרִאשׁוֹן קֹדֶם הַחֵטְא
like the first Adam before the sin,
שֶׁהָיָה מִשְׁכָּנוֹ בְּגַן עֵדֶן,
whose dwelling was in Gan Eden,
וְשָׁם הָיָה יָכוֹל לֶאֱכֹל מֵעֵץ הַחַיִּים
and there he could eat from the Tree of Life
וְחַי לְעוֹלָם.
and live forever.
וְאַחַר הַחֵטְא גֻּרַשׁ מִשָּׁם
After the sin he was expelled from there
“פֶּן יִשְׁלַח יָדוֹ” וְגוֹ׳,
“lest he send forth his hand,” etc.,
דְּעַל זֶה לֹא הוֹעִיל לוֹ תְּשׁוּבָה
since for this repentance did not help him
שֶׁיוּכַל לְתַקֵּן הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ דְּעִטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ
to repair the root of the serpent’s counsel
וְלְבַטֵּל גְּזֵירַת הַמָּוֶת;
and cancel the decree of death;
עַיֵּן (לְעִל סִימָן ג)
see (above, siman 3).
וְגַם בְּאוֹתָם מֵאָה וְשְׁלֹשִׁים שָׁנָה
And also in those 130 years
שֶׁיָּשַׁב בְּתַעֲנִית לָשׁוּב מִחַטְאוֹ
in which he sat fasting to repent of his sin
הוֹלִיד רוּחוֹת שֵׁדִים וְלִילִין
he fathered spirits, demons and lilin
מִשִּׁכְבַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה
from wasted seed
דְּחָזֵי לְאָנְסוֹ
that came involuntarily,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּעֵירוּבִין יח, עַמּוּד ב)
as they said (Eruvin 18b),
וְקָרְאוּ לֵיהּ שָׁם חָסִיד גָּדוֹל.
and they call him there a great chasid.
אֶלָּא דְּאֲפִילּוּ חָסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים וְכוּ׳,
But even the greatest of chasidim, etc.,
שֶׁעַדַיִן לֹא נִטְהַר הַלֵּב מִתַּאֲוָה גּוּפָנִיּת
whose heart was not yet purified of bodily desire,
שֶׁלֹּא לְהוֹצִיא בָּשָׂר
so as not to emit bodily substance,
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּא לִידֵי טֻמְאָה בַּלַּיְלָה לְאָנְסוֹ.
through which he came to impurity at night involuntarily.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהִיא לְאָנְסוֹ,
Although it was involuntary,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוֹלִיד בְּזֶה רוּחוֹת שֵׁדִים וְלִילִין
still he thereby fathered spirits, demons and lilin
וְהוֹסִיף כֻּח בְּסִטְרָא דְּמַסָּאֲבָא
and added strength to the side of impurity,
רַחֲמָנָא לִצְלַן.
may the Merciful One save us.
וּבְוַדַּאי
And surely
שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהִרְהֵר בְּיוֹם
it was not because he had sinful thoughts by day
וְעָבַר עַל “וְנִשְׁמַרְתָּ מִכָּל דָּבָר רָע”
and transgressed “guard yourself from any evil thing,”
שֶׁלֹּא יְהַרֵּהַר וְכוּ׳,
that one should not have sinful thoughts, etc.,
אַף שֶׁעַדַיִן לֹא נִתְּנָה תּוֹרָה
although the Torah had not yet been given
לְהַזְהִיר עַל זֶה,
to warn about this,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא הַרֵי קוֹרְאִין אוֹתוֹ חָסִיד גָּדוֹל,
for otherwise they would not call him a great chasid,
וְגַם זֶה לֹא הָיָה קֶרִי לְאָנְסוֹ
and this would not have been an involuntary emission
כֵּיוָן דְּהוּא בְּהִרְהוּרוֹ הֵבִיא עַצְמוֹ לְכָךְ,
if by his thought he had brought himself to it,
וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ וַדַּאי נִזְהָר בְּתַכְלִית מִכָּל שֶׁמֶץ הִרְהוּר.
so of necessity he surely guarded fully against any trace of sinful thought.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis 2:8–9; 3:22–24; Ramban on Bereishis 3:22. The Tree of Life stands in the garden, and after the sin access is guarded lest Adam eat and live forever. This directly supplies the tree-and-life connection. The further distinction concerning repentance and the serpent-root is developed by Rav Tzadok below.

paragraphs.text: This parallel helps distinguish genuine repentance from the further reversal of mortality. It must also be read alongside, rather than quoted as an independent proof of, the present se’if’s stricter formulation about one who never tasted sin. The serpent-counsel tradition in Bava Basra 17a and Shabbos 55b was already identified in the preceding se’if.

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 18b; Bereishis 5:3. The Gemara first describes the spirits, demons and lilin produced during Adam’s years under ban, then challenges this from R’ Meir’s account of his great piety, fasting, separation and fig-garment discipline for 130 years. Its resolution is explicit: the occurrence was involuntary. Thus the designation “great chasid” and the involuntary occurrence belong to the same passage. The conclusion about an untransformed bodily root is Rav Tzadok’s further reading.

paragraphs.text: Machshavos Charutz 15:10 connects Adam’s 130-year account with the repair of generative power through Avraham and Sarah. Compare the more fully quoted 20:13 parallel in the preceding note on repentance and the death decree. These are Rav Tzadok’s own metaphysical accounts, not separate Talmudic rulings assigning deliberate guilt to an involuntary event. Here he distinguishes the occurrence’s described spiritual consequences from conscious consent or willful transgression.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Adam’s repentance did not, in Rav Tzadok’s account, remove every root of bodily desire or undo the decree of death. The involuntary emissions during his years of penitence illustrate a remaining condition of the body, which the author distinguishes from deliberate sinful thought.

p: אֲבָל גַּם בְּאֹנֶס גָּמוּר
But even in total compulsion
מִטּוֹרַח הַדֶּרֶךְ
from the strain of the road,
כְּהַאי דְּחָסִיד אֶחָד (בְּשַׁבָּת קכ״ז עַמּוּד ב׳)
as in the case of a certain pious man (Shabbos 127b),
גַּם כֵּן יֵשׁ בּוֹ טֻמְאָה
there is still impurity in it
וְצָרִיךְ טְבִילָה,
and immersion is required,
וְגַם לִדְבָרֵי תּוֹרָה
also for words of Torah,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת כב, עַמּוּד ב).
as they said (Berachos 22b).
וְשָׁם אִיתָא
And there it says
בְּמַעֲשֵׂה דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָא דְּרָאָה קֶרִי,
in the incident of Rabbi Yehudah who had an emission,
מַשְׁמַע בְּשֵׁנָה וְלָאֲנְסוֹ
implying in sleep and involuntarily
וְלֹא בְּתַשְׁמִישׁ הַמִּטָּה,
and not in marital relations,
וְהוּא נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן חָסִיד אֶחָד בְּסָתָם
and he too is called “a certain chasid” without name,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּתְּמוּרָה טו, סוֹף עַמּוּד ב)
as they said (Temurah 15b, end)
וְמַיְיתֵי לָהּ רַשִׁ״י שַׁבָּת שָׁם.
and Rashi cites it in Shabbos there.
וְהַקָּרוֹב דְּהַיְינוּ עוֹבָדָא דְּשַׁבָּת,
Most likely it is the same incident as in Shabbos,
שֶׁלֹּא לִתְלוֹת רָאִיית קֶרִי לְאָנְסוֹ
so as not to attribute an involuntary emission
בְּאוֹתוֹ הַגּוּף הַקָּדוֹשׁ שְׁתֵּי פְּעָמִים אוֹ בְּשְׁנֵי חֲסִידִים.
to that same holy body twice or to two chasidim.
וְטַעַם טְבִילָה לִדְבָרֵי תּוֹרָה
The reason for immersion for words of Torah
מְבוֹאָר בְּבְּרָכוֹת שָׁם
is explained in Berachos there:
לִפְנֵי שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לִלְמוֹד בְּאֵימָה בְּיִרְאָה בְּרֶתֶּת וּבְזִיעָה,
because one must learn with awe, fear, trembling and sweat,
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל “מִכָּאן”
and see Rashi there, in the passage beginning “mikan,”
שֶׁבָּעַל קֶרִי אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא מִתּוֹךְ קַלּוּת רֹאשׁ וְזַחוּת הַדַּעַת.
that an emission-sufferer arises only from lightheadedness and arrogance.
וְאִם כֵּן
Then
דְּגַם לְאָנְסוֹ צָרִיךְ עַל כָּרְחֲךָ לוֹמַר
even for an involuntary one we must say
דְּגַם זֶה מִקַלּוּת רֹאשׁ.
that this too stems from lightheadedness.
וְאַף דְּחָלִילָה לְקַדּוֹשֵׁי עֶלְיוֹן
Although, heaven forbid, the exalted holy ones
שֶׁיִהְיֶה לָהֶם שׁוּם רֶגַע קַלּוּת רֹאשׁ חָס וְשָׁלוֹם
could have no moment of lightheadedness, God forbid,
בְּהַקֵּיץ וְלֹא זַחוּת דַּעַת,
when awake, nor arrogance,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם
nevertheless
כָּל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא נִצְלוּ מֵעִטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ לְגַמְרֵי,
as long as they were not entirely rescued from the serpent’s counsel,
לְהִיוֹת לֵב בָּשָׂר כְּלָעָתִיד
to be a heart of flesh as in the future,
וְכִיעַקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשּׁלוֹם
like Yaakov Avinu,
גַּם בְּמַה דְּחָזֵי לְאָנְסוֹ בְּשֵׁנָה
even in what comes involuntarily in sleep
לֹא נִצְלָה מִהַרְגֵּשׁ הֲנָאָה גּוּפָנִיּת בְּשָׂעָתוֹ בְּשִׁנָּתוֹ,
he was not spared the sensation of bodily pleasure at that moment in his sleep,
וְגַם זֶה נִחְשָׁב לְקַלּוּת רֹאשׁ וְזַחוּת דַּעַת,
and this too counts as lightheadedness and arrogance,
וְגוֹרֵם תּוֹלֶדֶת כֹּחוֹת טֻמְאָה רַחֲמָנָא לִצְלַן.
and generates offspring of impure forces, may the Merciful One save us.
וְעַל זֶה תִּקְנוּ חֲכָמִים הַטְּבִילָה
For this the Sages instituted immersion
אוֹ רַחֲצָה בְּתֵּשַׁע קַבִּין,
or washing with nine kavim,
שֶׁבְּכָךְ הוּא נִטְהַר
by which he is purified
מֵאוֹתוֹ רוּחַ הַטֻּמְאָה
from that spirit of impurity
וְזַחוּת הַדַּעַת הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מִזֶּה.
and arrogance that flows from it.
וְיוּכַל לִדָּבֵק בְּמָאוֹר וּקְדֻּשַׁת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁהוּא עֵץ חַיִּים,
Then he can cling to the light and holiness of the Torah, which is a Tree of Life,
כִּי עַל יָדָהּ דְּבוּקִים בְּחַיֵּי עוֹלָם
for through it people cling to eternal life;
הִיא הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁנִּקְרֵאת כֵּן (שַׁבָּת י, לג)
it is the Torah that is so called (Shabbos 10a, 33b),
וְכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר “וְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם נָטַע בְּתוֹכֵּנוּ”.
as it says, “and eternal life He planted within us.”
וְעַל יְדֵי הַתּוֹרָה יוּכַל לְתַקֵּן גַּם כֵּן הַכֹּל,
Through Torah he can repair everything too,
דְּעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא טז, עַמּוּד א)
about which they said (Bava Basra 16a):
“בָּרָא יֵצֶר הָרָע, בָּרָא תּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין”.
“He created the evil inclination; He created Torah as its spice.”
וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא קָרָאוֹ רַע
And the Holy One, Blessed is He, called it evil,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סֻכָּה נב, עַמּוּד א)
as they said (Sukkah 52a)
מִקְרָא דְּ“כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם רַע מִנְּעֻרָיו”
from the verse “for the inclination of man’s heart is evil from his youth,”
שֶׁהוּא בְּחֵטְא דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל
which concerns the sin of the Flood generation,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ מִצַּד שֹׁרֶשׁ הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע שֶׁבָּבְּרִיאָה
this being from the root of the evil inclination in creation
שֶׁבְּעִטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ,
that came through the serpent’s counsel,
שֶׁהוּא מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
which is from the side of Hashem, blessed is He,
שֶׁבָּרָא עֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע
who created the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil
וְהַבְּחִירָה לָאָדָם לֶאֱכֹל מִמֶּנּוּ,
and gave man the choice to eat from it,
שֶׁמִּזֶּה נִכְנָס הַרְגֵּשַׁת תַּאֲוַת הַגּוּפָנִיּוֹת לַלֵּב
through which the feeling of bodily lust entered the heart
וְלֹא כְּמִקֹּדֶם דְּלֹא יִתְבּוֹשָׁשׁוּ.
unlike earlier, when they felt no shame.
וּבְמַתָּן תּוֹרָה נַעֲשׂוּ חֵרוּת מִיֵּצֶר הָרָע,
And at the giving of the Torah they became free of the evil inclination,
דְּעַל יְדֵי הַתּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין יוּכְלוּ לְתַקֵּן זֶה,
for through Torah, the spice, they can repair this,
וְכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב רַמְבַּ״ם (בְּסוֹף הִלְכוֹת אִסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה)
and as Rambam wrote (at the end of Hilchos Issurei Biah)
דְּאֵין הַתַּאֲוָת אֶלָּא בְּלֵב פָּנוּי מִדִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה.
that lust exists only in a heart empty of words of Torah.

Rashi on Bereishis 49:3 and Yevamos 76a supply Yaakov’s exceptional bodily-purity standard, as discussed in the preceding se’if. The inference concerning sensation in sleep is his present interpretation; neither the future-heart verse nor the Yaakov passages independently formulates it.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 22a–b; Rambam, Hilchos Krias Shema 4:8. The sugya distinguishes forty se’ah, nine kav and exemption according to its different cases; it should not be reduced to one water requirement for everyone. Rambam states that Ezra’s Torah-study enactment did not spread throughout Israel and lapsed, and that Jews read Torah and Shema in this state because words of Torah do not contract impurity. Rav Tzadok’s explanation of the inner purification therefore does not by itself reinstate that former prerequisite.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 10a and 33b call Torah “eternal life” in contrast with temporal activity: the former contrasts leaving study for prayer, and the latter records Rashbi’s response to ordinary labor after the cave. The phrase “and eternal life He planted within us” is from the blessing after the Torah reading. Rav Tzadok uses this language to describe Torah as the spiritual Tree of Life; the water discussion belongs to the preceding note.

paragraphs.text: Bava Basra 16a explicitly says, “The Holy One, Blessed is He, created the evil inclination; He created Torah as its antidote.” It is the companions’ reply to Iyov’s attempt to excuse conduct through the way people were created. Kiddushin 30b gives the related first-person formulation, “I created the evil inclination, and I created Torah as its antidote.”

paragraphs.text: Bereishis 2:25 and 3:7 set the absence of shame before the sin against the subsequent awareness of nakedness. Bereishis 6:5 describes the evil thoughts before the Flood; 8:21 gives “the inclination of man’s heart is evil from his youth.” Sukkah 52a cites that latter verse as Hashem’s name “evil” for the inclination. Rav Tzadok connects these stages with the serpent-root and bodily desire. The textual sequence and the name are explicit; that unified inward account is his interpretation.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 146a says that the serpent’s pollution ceased from Israel when they stood at Sinai. Avos 6:2 reads charus, “engraved,” as cheirus, “freedom,” and identifies the person occupied with Torah as free. Midrash Tanchuma, Eikev 8, distinguishes teachings about freedom from the Angel of Death, exile and suffering, and describes the loss after the sin. Rav Tzadok brings these traditions together in his account of freedom from the evil inclination and its repair through Torah; the sources do not all use one identical list.
