inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok offers a comforting reading of the address to the fleeing sages: a painful interruption can become the occasion for renewed strength in Torah. He connects this pattern of bitterness leading to gain with the Exodus, the Sea, and the release of hidden holy vitality.

The theme: Moshe leads Israel away from the Sea’s extraordinary but temporary revelation toward the work of acquiring Torah inwardly. Rav Tzadok interprets the bitterness at Marah and the rising after repeated falls as occasions for a deeper, enduring return.

p: וּבֶאֱמֶת זֶה הָיָה רַק לְפִי שָׁעָה,
Yet in truth, that sublime spiritual revelation was only for a temporary hour,
מַה שֶּׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עָשָׂה בְּעַצְמוֹ מִצַּד אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָּא לְבַד,
being an unearned gift that the Holy One wrought Himself solely via an awakening from Above,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְאַתֶּם תַּחֲרִישׁוּן" (שְׁמוֹת יד, יד).
as it is stated: “and you shall hold your peace” (Exodus 14:14).
וְאֵין זוֹ הַשָּׂגָה שֶׁהִגִּיעוּ לָהּ מִצַּד הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם וִיגִיעָתָם,
And this was not an enduring attainment that they achieved through personal exertion and inner labor,
שֶׁהוּא הָעִיקָּר שֶׁנִּקְבָּע בַּלֵּב בְּקִנְיָן דְּ"יָגַעְתָּ וּמָצָאתָ – תַּאֲמִין" (מְגִילָּה ו עַמּוּד ב);
which is the primary divine consciousness established in the heart through integrated acquisition: “if you have toiled and found—believe it” (Megillah 6b);
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מְצִיאָה שֶׁבְּלֹא יְגִיעָה אָמְרוּ "אַל תַּאֲמִין",
whereas regarding a find that comes without prior labor they warned: “do not believe it,”
אַף שֶׁנִּדְמֶה לוֹ שֶׁמָּצָא אֵינוֹ דָּבָר הַמִּתְקַיֵּים "יָתֵד בְּמָקוֹם נֶאֱמָן",
for even though it seems to him that he has found it, it is not an enduring stake in a firm wall,
וְ"הֲתָעִיף עֵינֶיךָ בּוֹ וְאֵינֶנּוּ" (מִשְׁלֵי כג, ה).
and “should you blink your eyes at it, it is gone” (Proverbs 23:5).
דְּעַל כֵּן הִסִּיעָן לְהַרְאוֹתָם
Therefore Moses moved them away to demonstrate to them
דְּאוֹר זֶה אֵינוֹ קְדוּשָּׁה דִּקְבוּעָה וְקַיָּימָא בַּלֵּב שֶׁלֹּא תִּנָּתֵק עוֹד;
that this light was not yet an immutable sanctity permanently etched in the heart that could never be severed;
וּמִיָּד שֶׁנָּסְעוּ מִשָּׁם וְנִסְתַּלֵּק אוֹתוֹ אוֹר,
and the moment they journeyed from there and that supernal light departed,
"הָלְכוּ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים [בַּמִּדְבָּר] וְלֹא מָצְאוּ מָיִם" (שְׁמוֹת טו, כב),
“they went three days in the wilderness and found no water” (Exodus 15:22),
וְאָמְרוּ [בְּבָבָא קַמָּא פב עַמּוּד א]: "אֵין מַיִם אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה".
and our Sages expounded in Bava Kamma (82a): “Water refers to nothing other than Torah.”
וּמִסְפַּר שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים
And the measure of three days
עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי סוֹף בְּרָכוֹת פֶּרֶק ט הֲלָכָה ה]:
is in line with what they taught in the Jerusalem Talmud (end of Berakhot 9:5):
"אִם תַּעַזְבֵנִי יוֹם – אֶעֶזְבְךָ יוֹמָיִם".
“If you abandon Me for one day, I will abandon you for two days.”
כְּמוֹ בְּעִנְיַן הַחֵשֶׁק וְהָאַהֲבָה אָמְרוּ
Just as in the dynamics of spiritual passion and divine love they stated
דְּטִיפָּה שֶׁיּוֹרֶדֶת מִלְּמַעְלָה עוֹלוֹת כְּנֶגְדָּהּ טִפָּתַיִם מִלְּמַטָּה,
that for one drop that descends from Above there ascend two responsive drops from below,
דְּהָאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא מִתְגַּבֵּר וְהוֹלֵךְ;
in that the awakening from below steadily increases;
וּבְעִנְיַן הָרִיחוּק וְהָעֲזִיבָה – בְּהֵיפֶךְ:
so in the dynamics of alienation and abandonment, it operates in the reverse:
כְּשֶׁמַּתְחִיל בַּעֲזִיבָה, "הַבָּא לִיטַּמֵּא פּוֹתְחִין לוֹ" (יוֹמָא לח עַמּוּד ב),
when one begins to turn away, “for one who comes to defile himself, an opening is made for him” (Yoma 38b),
וְיֵצֶר הָרָע מִתְגַּבֵּר וְהוֹלֵךְ.
and the evil inclination progressively gathers strength.
וְהֵם שָׁלֹשׁ מַדְרֵגוֹת דְּ"הֵלֶךְ", וְ"אוֹרֵחַ", וְ"אִישׁ" (סֻכָּה נב עַמּוּד ב),
And these correspond to the three stages of the urge: a “traveler,” a “guest,” and a “man” (Sukkah 52b),
וּבִתְלָתָא הָוֵי חֲזָקָה וְנַעֲשָׂה בַּעַל הַבַּיִת.
and with three occurrences a legal presumption (chazakah) is established and it becomes the master of the house.
וְעַל כֵּן אַחַר אוֹתָם שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים
Therefore, after those three days without Torah
"בָּאוּ מָרָתָה... כִּי מָרִים הֵם" (שְׁמוֹת טו, כג),
“they came to Marah... for they were bitter” (Exodus 15:23),
שֶׁכְּבָר נַעֲשׂוּ גַּם הֵם מָרִים.
in that they themselves had already turned bitter.
וְשָׁם הָיְתָה הַהַתְחָלָה לְקַבָּלַת תּוֹרָה,
And there at Marah was the true beginning of the laborious acceptance of the Torah,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ דְּעֶשֶׂר מִצְווֹת נִצְטַוּוּ שָׁם (סַנְהֶדְרִין נו עַמּוּד ב),
as our Sages stated that ten commandments were commanded to them there (Sanhedrin 56b),
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "שָׁם שָׂם לוֹ חֹק וּמִשְׁפָּט" (שְׁמוֹת טו, כה).
and as it is stated: “There He made for them a statute and an ordinance” (Exodus 15:25).
וְכֵן "וַיּוֹרֵהוּ" דָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה
And likewise “and He showed him” (vayorehu) was expounded by our Sages
מִלְּשׁוֹן הוֹרָאָה וְתוֹרָה,
as stemming from the language of instruction (hora'ah) and Torah,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַתּוֹרָה לִהְיוֹת תַּבְלִין לְיֵצֶר הָרָע,
for this is the essential root of the Torah: to serve as a curative spice against the evil inclination,
כְּדָבָר הַמְתַבֵּל שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה אֶת הַמַּר מָתוֹק.
like a spice that seasons and transforms the bitter into sweet.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: כַּמָּה דְּבָרִים מָרִים שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם שֶׁאַתֶּם מַמְתִּיקִין
And as they taught: how many bitter things exist in the world that you sweeten,
כְּתֻרְמוּסִין שֶׁשּׁוֹלְקִין זַיִ״ן פְּעָמִים,
such as lupines which they boil seven times to remove their toxicity,
וְאָמְרוּ [בְּבֵיצָה כה עַמּוּד ב]:
and they stated in Beitzah (25b):
"תֻּרְמוֹס מְקַטַּע רַגְלֵיהוֹן [דְּשׂוֹנְאֵיהֶם שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל]".
“the lupine cuts down the feet of Israel's adversaries.”
וְאִיתָא עַל פָּסוּק (שׁוֹפְטִים י, ו): "וַיַּעַבְדוּ אֶת [הַבְּעָלִים וְגוֹמֵר]",
And it is brought in the Midrash on the verse: “And they served the Baalim, etc.” (Judges 10:6):
דַּאֲפִילּוּ כְּתֻרְמוֹס הַזֶּה לֹא עֲשָׂאוּנִי
that the Holy One lamented: “Not even like this lupine did you treat Me,”
לְעָבְדוֹ אַחַר שֶׁעָבְדוּ זַיִ״ן עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה.
to serve Him after having served seven varieties of idolatry.
שֶׁהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ: "שֶׁבַע יִפּוֹל צַדִּיק וָקָם" (מִשְׁלֵי כד, טז),
Which operates on the principle: “A righteous man falls seven times, and rises up” (Proverbs 24:16),
דְּעַל יְדֵי הַנְּפִילוֹת הוּא קָם,
for precisely by virtue of the falls does he rise,
שֶׁהַיְרִידָה לְצוֹרֶךְ עֲלִיָּה
in that the descent is for the purpose of a greater ascent,
כְּשֶׁזּוֹכֶה אַחַר כָּךְ לְהִתְעוֹרֵר מִתּוֹךְ מְרִירוּת הַנְּפִילוֹת וְלָשׁוּב אֶל ה',
when he subsequently merits to awaken from the bitterness of his falls and return unto Hashem,
וְכַנּוֹדָע דְּנַעֲשָׂה הַכֹּל כִּסֵּא אֶל הַקְּדוּשָּׁה,
and as is known, everything is then converted into a throne for holiness,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "עֲלֵיהֶם חָיֹה יִחְיֶה" (יְחֶזְקֵאל לג, יט),
as it is stated: “he shall surely live by them” (Ezekiel 33:19),
דִּזְדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוּ זְכִיּוֹת,
in that willful sins are transformed into merits,
שֶׁעַל יְדֵיהֶם דַּיְיקָא בָּא לַמַּדְרֵגָה הַגְּדוֹלָה
for specifically through them does he arrive at that supreme stature
דִּ"מְקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין" (בִּבְרָכוֹת לד עַמּוּד ב).
of “the place where penitents stand” (Berakhot 34b).

paragraphs.text: Bava Kamma 82a reads three days without water as three days without Torah. It attributes the original arrangement of readings to the prophets among them, so Israel would not remain three days without Torah. Ezra’s later enactment specifies three readers and ten verses. The original institution and Ezra’s arrangement are distinct stages in the account.

paragraphs.text: Yerushalmi Berachos 9:5:20 gives the Torah-study maxim “Abandon me for one day; I shall abandon you for two,” illustrating it through travelers leaving Tiberias and Tzippori in opposite directions: each walks a mile, making two miles of separation. Bava Kamma 82a supplies the three Torah-less days. Peri Tzadik, Vayigash 11:1, describes Yaakov’s fear of interrupted Torah in Egypt and the promised ascent from it. The Yerushalmi itself does not identify Marah’s three days with three stages of the inclination.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 247b, Ra’aya Mehemna, Pinchas, says that no drop descends from above without two drops ascending to meet it. Its immediate context is the three faculties of memory, thought and imagination. HaSulam, Pinchas §665, preserves the wording but tentatively identifies the unit beginning “the secret of the matter” as an incorporated marginal gloss. Ta’anis 25b gives a related image in handbreadths, varying with the soil, rather than the exact drops wording. Applying the image to love and an increasing awakening from below is Rav Tzadok’s exposition.

paragraphs.text: Sukkah 52b describes the inclination’s advance from traveler to guest to man established in the house; it also gives the study-hall remedy that can dissolve stone and shatter iron. Peri Tzadik, Metzora 1:1, applies the first stage to persuasion into idleness and interruption of Torah. The association with threefold chazakah is Rav Tzadok’s analogy, not a legal acquisition of the soul by the inclination. Shabbos 104a separately distinguishes opening the way to impurity from assisting one who comes to purify himself.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 30b and Bava Basra 16a give Torah as the remedy or spice created for the inclination. Tzidkas HaTzadik §242 explains seasoning desire until it becomes good; §12 distinguishes purification for future conduct from atonement for the past. Resisei Layla 35:2 discusses awakening from worldly imagination toward Torah’s truth, while Yisrael Kedoshim 10:22 distinguishes written and Oral Torah in reaching the inclination’s root and its settled hold in the heart. These are different aspects of Rav Tzadok’s transforming-spice account.

paragraphs.text: Beitzah 25b compares Israel unfavorably with a lupine boiled seven times and finally eaten: after serving the seven listed foreign cults, Israel still did not serve Hashem. Tanchuma, Bereishis §7, likewise uses bitter lupines made edible as an image of sweetening. The sevenfold food preparation and the rebuke over idolatry are the sources; the following comparison with seven falls and a greater rise is Rav Tzadok’s development.

paragraphs.text: Mishlei 24:16 says that the righteous falls seven times and rises. Yoma 86b distinguishes repentance from fear, making intentional sins like inadvertent ones, from repentance from love, making them merits. Berachos 34b preserves Rabbi Abahu’s ranking of penitents alongside Rabbi Yochanan’s different ranking. Peri Tzadik, Nitzavim 1:1 and Vayeilech 1:1, reads the fall as becoming the cause of a greater rise; Resisei Layla 52:2 links renewed Torah acquisition with stumbling.

paragraphs.text: Machshavos Charutz 15:5 gives a more specific comparison: retrospective repair, especially of the covenantal blemish discussed there, requires Torah joined to repentance. This is Rav Tzadok’s treatment of that case, not an added condition quoted from Yoma. Here “when he merits” is essential: elevation comes through awakening from bitterness and returning to Hashem, not through the fall alone.

p: וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר לָהֶם לְנַחֲמָם:
And this is what the sage told them to comfort them:
דִּכְזַיִת שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּמְקוֹם מָרָה,
that the essential olive-bulk of liver is situated specifically at the site of the bile,
שֶׁמְּקוֹם הַמְּרִירוּת – שָׁם עִיקַּר הַחַיּוּת,
for in the very place of bitterness—there resides the core of life,
כִּי יִתְרוֹן הָאוֹר דַּיְיקָא מִן הַחֹשֶׁךְ.
because the preeminence of light emerges specifically out of darkness.
וּמִשְׁכַּן הַנֶּפֶשׁ דִּקְדוּשָּׁה הוּא בַּכָּבֵד,
And the seat of the holy Nefesh is within the liver,
שֶׁשָּׁם עִיקַּר מִשְׁכַּן נֶפֶשׁ הַבַּהֲמִית,
where lies likewise the primary seat of the animal soul,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ [פָּרָשַׁת פִּינְחָס רכד סוֹף עַמּוּד א]:
as our Sages stated in the holy Zohar (Parashat Pinchas 224a):
"כָּבֵד סַמֶּ״ךְ-מֵ״ם וְנָחָשׁ (דָּא בְּדָא וְאִיהוּ חַד)",
“the liver is Samael and the Serpent—one intertwined with the other and forming a single entity,”
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם (רכד עַמּוּד ב) בְּאֹרֶךְ;
and examine there (224b) at length;
וְסִיֵּים [שָׁם רכה רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א]:
and the Zohar concludes there (225a):
"מִן כָּבֵד נָפְקִין כָּל מַרְעִין וְכוּלֵי".
“from the liver emerge all illnesses, etc.”
וְהוּא מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ [בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא נח עַמּוּד ב]:
And this corresponds to what they stated in Bava Batra (58b):
"בְּרֵישׁ כָּל מַרְעִין אֲנָא דָם",
“At the head of all illnesses am I, blood,”
וְרוֹצֶה לוֹמַר הַכָּבֵד שֶׁכֻּלּוֹ דָּם
which refers to the liver which is entirely blood,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא [בְּחֻלִּין קט סוֹף עַמּוּד ב],
as it is taught in Chullin (109b),
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא [בִּבְכוֹרוֹת נה סוֹף עַמּוּד א]:
and as stated in Bekhorot (55a):
"זַכְרוּתָא דְּדָמָא – כַּבְדָּא",
“the masculine source-potency of blood is the liver,”
שֶׁהוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ דָּם לַנֶּפֶשׁ הַבַּהֲמִית,
which is the fountainhead of blood for the animal soul,
וְעִיקַּר חַיּוּתוֹ בִּמְקוֹם מָרָה,
and its essential vitality resides at the site of the gall bladder,
שֶׁמִּשָּׁם נִמְשָׁךְ כָּל הַמַּרְעִין וְהַחוֹלָאִים כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל,
whence are drawn all afflictions and maladies as mentioned above,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב גַּם כֵּן רַשִׁ״י [בְּסוֹטָה ה עַמּוּד א].
and as Rashi likewise commented in Sotah (5a).
אֲבָל זֶהוּ מִצַּד הַקְּלִיפָּה הַקּוֹדֶמֶת וְסוֹבֶבֶת וּמַקֶּפֶת לַפְּרִי,
However, this dynamic stems from the impure shell that precedes, surrounds, and encases the fruit,
וּ"בְרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא וַהֲדַר נְהוֹרָא" (שַׁבָּת עז עַמּוּד ב),
mirroring “first darkness and then light” (Shabbat 77b),
שֶׁשָּׁם הוּא גַּם כֵּן שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַחַיּוּת שֶׁל הַנֶּפֶשׁ דִּקְדוּשָּׁה.
for there precisely is anchored also the vitality of the holy soul.
וְהַדָּם שֶׁבַּכָּבֵד הוּא עֲכִירַת הַדָּם
And the blood within the liver represents turbid, coarse blood
שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ הַכַּעַס וּרְצִיחָה וְכָל מַחֲלָה וְכָל תַּקָּלָה וְכָל קְטָטָה וּמִינֵי פוּרְעָנֻיּוֹת
from which emerge wrath, bloodshed, every sickness, every moral stumbling, all strife, and all manner of afflictions
הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מִמְּרִירוּת הַמָּרָה שֶׁאֶצְלָהּ.
drawn forth from the bitterness of the bile adjacent to it.

paragraphs.text: Chullin 46a concludes that an olive-bulk of liver must remain at each of two sites: the gallbladder and the place of its principal attachment. Rashi explains the latter; Rambam, Hilchos Shechitah 8:21, and Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De’ah 41:1, codify both. Rav Tzadok highlights one site for his homily without giving an exhaustive ruling.

Rav Tzadok’s consolation through interrupted Torah and renewed vitality is a related but distinct explanation.

paragraphs.text: Koheles 2:13 compares the superiority of wisdom over folly with light over darkness. Machshavos Charutz 7:2 develops renewed longing through intermittent distance; Resisei Layla 17:1 describes hidden light sought within darkness; Kedushat Shabbat 7:6 applies the pattern to repentance. The emergence of greater light from darkness is Rav Tzadok’s exposition of the comparison, not a claim that suffering or sin is intrinsically desirable.

paragraphs.text: Zohar, Pinchas 39:209–215, describes the brain ruling over the heart and the heart over the liver. It identifies liver and lobe with Samael and the serpent, recording also a male-and-female variant. In the sacrificial sequence they receive first, consuming the offering’s fats; their veins are associated with the ishim and their forces. The heart receives confession and prayer, ascending with the smoke, and brings the priest’s intention of unification and the Levites’ joy toward the brain. The brain in turn brings the offering toward the One concealed from all.

paragraphs.text: The lobe’s female counterpart first approaches a person as something insignificant and then becomes attached little by little. The heart is principal in holiness; its two counseling kidneys are likened to two cherubim. A broken spirit, confession and prayer are brought to the heart, which advocates for the liver, binding the levels in the offering. Vidui here means confession; eimurim u-fedarim are sacrificial portions and fats.

paragraphs.text: The concluding contrast is explicit: from the liver issue illnesses and blows throughout the limbs; from the heart, “the purest of all,” issue good, health, strength, joy and the completeness the limbs need. Pinchas 40:216 continues with the offering distancing impurity and drawing holiness near. This sacrificial and symbolic setting governs the two quotations here.

paragraphs.text: The Zohar’s liver–heart–brain hierarchy describes coarse vitality brought toward the heart’s holiness and the brain’s inward intention. Rav Tzadok infers that the liver, though the seat of the animal life-force, is also where the holy nefesh must govern and refine that vitality. Peri Tzadik, Re’eh 1:1, similarly connects liver and gall with governing the inclination. Identifying this locus as a holy root is his interpretation of the process, not an equation of unrectified impulses with holiness.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 61b gives the liver’s anger and gall’s calming drop; Bava Metzia 107b associates gall with illness. Nedarim 22a and Shabbos 105b condemn destructive anger and its conduct. Peri Tzadik, Re’eh 1:1, explicitly acknowledges the apparent reversal between the liver’s immediate anger and gall as its bitter root. Rav Tzadok applies these images to murder, quarrel and calamity; clarification and disciplined use of strength are distinguished from surrender to rage.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: The location of life beside bitterness becomes, for Rav Tzadok, an image of consolation: light emerges from darkness. His account of the liver places the holy soul’s vitality alongside the surrounding animal forces, like fruit emerging through its enclosing shell.

p: וְ"הָאֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם יָשָׁר" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, כט),
And “God made man upright” (Ecclesiastes 7:29),
דְּאַדְּרַבָּה, מְרִירוּת הַמָּרָה מַמְתִּיקוֹ כְּשֶׁמִּשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ כַּהֹגֶן וְכָרָאוּי,
for, on the contrary, the bitterness of the bile sweetens him when he utilizes it properly and fittingly,
שֶׁזּוֹרֶקֶת רַק טִיפָּה וּמַנִּיחַתּוּ;
in that it secretes merely a single drop and soothes the liver;
וּמַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן כְּשֶׁשּׁוֹטֶפֶת וְעוֹבֶרֶת
unlike when it overflows and floods uncontrollably
עַל יְדֵי הִתְגַּבְּרוּת כֹּחוֹת הָרָע שֶׁבַּדָּם הֶעָכוּר שֶׁבַּכָּבֵד
through the surging of the powers of evil in the turbid blood of the liver
וְחַרְבָּא דְּמַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת שֶׁבַּמָּרָה (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כ עַמּוּד ב).
and the venomous sword of the Angel of Death that rests in the bile (Avodah Zarah 20b).
וְכָל הַחֲטָאִים מִתְיַיחֲסִים לַנֶּפֶשׁ,
And all sins are attributed scripturally to the Nefesh,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (וַיִּקְרָא ד, ב): "נֶפֶשׁ כִּי תֶחֱטָא",
as it is stated: “If a soul (nefesh) shall sin” (Leviticus 4:2),
דְּשָׁם הוּא הִתְגַּבְּרוּת נֶפֶשׁ הַבַּהֲמִית,
because there is the locus of the surge of the animal soul,
שֶׁהוּא נַפְשׁוֹת אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם שֶׁאֵין קְרוּיִים אָדָם
which corresponds to the souls of the nations who are not titled Adam,
הַמַּלְבֶּשֶׁת וּמַקֶּפֶת לְנֶפֶשׁ הָאָדָם דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל.
enclothing and surrounding the authentic human soul of Israel.
וְזֶהוּ הַמֵּ״ם דְּאָדָ״ם,
And this is the letter Mem of Adam (אָדָ״ם – Marah),
שֶׁהִיא מַדְרֵגָה הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה שֶׁבּוֹ עִיקַּר הַמְּרִירוּת.
which is the lowest rung wherein resides the core of bitterness.
וּמִשָּׁם הַתְחָלַת הַכְּנִיסָה לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה
And from there begins the entry into words of Torah,
שֶׁעִיקָּרָהּ יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם,
whose very foundation is the fear of Heaven,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשַׁבָּת לא עַמּוּד א]:
as our Sages stated in Shabbat31a:
אִי יִרְאַת ה' אוֹצָרוֹ – אִין,
“If the fear of Hashem is his storehouse, yes (he may enter)”
וְהוּא בַּלֵּב כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּיוֹמָא עב עַמּוּד ב] עַל פָּסוּק (מִשְׁלֵי יז, טז): "וְלֶב אָיִן".
and its seat is in the heart, as they expounded in Yoma (72b) on the verse: “and he has no heart.”
וְכֵן בַּתּוֹרָה עִיקָּרָהּ בַּלֵּב,
And so too the Torah has its primary core in the heart,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (דְּבָרִים יא, יח): "וְשַׂמְתֶּם אֶת דְּבָרַי אֵלֶּה עַל לְבַבְכֶם וְעַל נַפְשְׁכֶם",
as it is stated: “Therefore shall you lay up these My words in your heart and in your soul” (Deuteronomy 11:18),
שֶׁמִּן הַלֵּב נִמְשָׁךְ אַחַר כָּךְ לַנֶּפֶשׁ
in that from the heart it is subsequently drawn down into the Nefesh,
שֶׁהוּא כֹּחוֹת הַמַּעֲשֶׂה בַּפּוֹעַל הַבָּא מֵהַנֶּפֶשׁ
which represents the active faculties of deed proceeding from the Nefesh,
שֶׁהוּא כֹּחַ עוֹלָם הָעֲשִׂיָּה;
which embodies the spiritual power of the World of Action;
וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר (שָׁם ל, יד): "כִּי קָרוֹב אֵלֶיךָ הַדָּבָר מְאֹד, בְּפִיךָ וּבִלְבָבְךָ לַעֲשֹׂתוֹ".
and concerning this it is stated: “For the word is very near unto you, in your mouth, and in your heart, that you may do it” (ibid. 30:14).
וּפֶה הוּא הַכּוֹלֵל וּמְחַבֵּר שְׁנֵיהֶם,
And the mouth is that which integrates and bridges both dimensions,
דַּעֲקִימַת שְׂפָתָיו הָוֵי מַעֲשֶׂה (סַנְהֶדְרִין סה עַמּוּד א),
for the physical articulation of the lips is halakhically deemed an action (Sanhedrin 65a),
וְעִיקָּרוֹ מֵרוּחַ הַחַיִּים שֶׁבַּלֵּב;
and its root flows from the spirit of life residing in the heart;
וְתַרְגּוּם לְ"נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה" (בְּרֵאשִׁית ב, ז): "לְרוּחַ מְמַלְּלָא",
and Onkelos translates “a living soul” (Genesis 2:7): “a speaking spirit,”
שֶׁהוּא מְחַבֵּר נֶפֶשׁ וְרוּחַ.
which unifies Nefesh and Ruach.
וְ"שִׂפְתֵי צַדִּיק יִרְעוּן רָצוֹן",
And “the lips of the righteous nurture goodwill,”
"יִרְעוּן" לְשׁוֹן חִיבּוּר וּדְבֵיקוּת,
“feed/shepherd” (yir'un) being an expression of union and cleaving (re'ut),
וְגַם לְשׁוֹן לִימּוּד דַּעַת לְהָרָצוֹן שֶׁבַּלֵּב,
and also an expression of imparting conscious knowledge to the will in the heart,
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַדִּבּוּר פֶּה הוּא נִכְנָס גַּם כֵּן לַלֵּב.
in that through speech of the mouth, holiness penetrates likewise into the heart.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ "לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ",
And afterward it descends into practical deed, “to do it,”
כִּי רְבִיעִית דָּם שֶׁחַיֵּי הָאָדָם תְּלוּיִין בּוֹ
for the quarter-log of blood upon which human life depends,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשַׁבָּת לא סוֹף עַמּוּד ב], עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י,
as our Sages stated in Shabbat (31b), see there in Rashi,
הוּא דָּם הַזַּךְ וְהַצָּלוּל שֶׁבַּלֵּב
is the pure, refined blood within the heart,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת [סוֹטָה ה עַמּוּד א] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל: "אָדָם";
as Tosafot wrote in Sotah (5a, heading: “Adam”);
וּמִמֶּנּוּ תוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים לְכָל הַגּוּף,
and from it proceed the conduits of life to the entire body,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (מִשְׁלֵי ד, כג): "מִכָּל מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ, כִּי מִמֶּנּוּ תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים",
as it is stated: “Keep your heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life” (Proverbs 4:23),
דְּעַל יָדוֹ מִזְדַּכֵּךְ גַּם הַדָּם הֶעָכוּר שֶׁבַּכָּבֵד.
for through it the turbid blood of the liver is refined as well.

paragraphs.text: Koheles 7:29 says that God made the human being upright, while human beings sought many devices. Rav Tzadok invokes the verse here for the originally constructive capacity whose bitterness becomes destructive through misuse. The created uprightness and its subsequent distortion remain distinct.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 61b states that gall casts a drop into the angry liver and calms it. Peri Tzadik, Re’eh 1:1, distinguishes anger’s immediate manifestation in the liver from its bitter root in gall. Rav Tzadok’s present contrast is between proper measure that preserves life and an excess that overwhelms it; the ethical balance is his interpretation of the bodily imagery.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra 4:2 speaks of a nefesh that sins. Yevamos 61a derives a specific corpse-under-covering law from “you are Adam,” also considering scriptural uses of adam for non-Jews and distinguishing contact and carrying. Its legal derashah does not deny human status. Sotah 5a supplies Adam as efer, dam, marah—ash, blood and gall. Kedushat Shabbat 7:32 places nefesh’s struggle in the liver and ruach’s in the heart. The surrounding animal garment and the mem/marah correspondence are Rav Tzadok’s spiritual exposition.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 31b speaks of the life-bearing revi’is of blood; Rashi explains that life depends on it. Sotah 5a uses the person’s single revi’is in an argument for humility. Tosafos, citing Rabbenu Chananel, identifies clear blood upon which the heart is founded, not all the blood in the body. Mishlei 4:23 supplies “from it are the issues of life”; Rosh Chodesh Av 6:1 links this to Torah entering the heart, and Kedushat Shabbat 7:32 distinguishes liver/nefesh from heart/ruach. The heart’s refinement of lower vitality is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok traces the movement from the lower soul’s bitterness toward fear of God and Torah in the heart. Speech joins heart and action, allowing the heart’s refining vitality to reach the bodily powers represented by the liver.

p: וְזֶהוּ שֶׁנִּתְבַּשְּׂרוּ בְּמָרָה (שְׁמוֹת טו, כו):
And this is the glad tidings they were promised at Marah (Exodus 15:26):
"אִם שָׁמוֹעַ תִּשְׁמַע [לְקוֹל ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ וְגוֹמֵר], כָּל הַמַּחֲלָה אֲשֶׁר [שַׂמְתִּי בְמִצְרַיִם לֹא אָשִׂים עָלֶיךָ], כִּי אֲנִי ה' רֹפְאֶךָ".
“If you will diligently hearken to the voice of Hashem your God... I will put none of these diseases upon you which I have brought upon the Egyptians; for I am Hashem that heals you.”
כִּי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה רִפְאוּת לַשֹּׁרֶךְ (מִשְׁלֵי ג, ח),
For words of Torah are “health to your navel” (Proverbs 3:8),
הוּא הַטַּבּוּר,
which is the umbilical cord,
שֶׁמִּשָּׁם חַיּוּתוֹ בִּתְחִלַּת הַיְצִירָה בְּבֶטֶן אִמּוֹ,
whence flows one's physical vitality at the inception of formation in his mother's womb,
דְּטַבּוּרוֹ פָּתוּחַ וְהוּא יֶרֶךְ אִמּוֹ (נִדָּה ל עַמּוּד ב),
in that his navel is open and he is as the thigh of his mother (Niddah 30b),
וּמִשָּׁם בָּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָרָע שֶׁבַּתּוֹלָדָה
and from there enters the hereditary root of evil at birth,
דְּ"בְחֵטְא יֶחֱמַתְנִי אִמִּי" (תְּהִלִּים נא, ז).
for “in sin did my mother conceive me” (Psalms 51:7).
וְעַל כֵּן, אַף דְּלֹא יָשִׂים הַמַּחֲלָה,
Therefore, even when He promises not to place the disease upon you,
הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא לְהַנִּיחַ לְהִתְגַּלּוֹת,
meaning not allowing it to break forth into active sickness,
צָרִיךְ רְפוּאָה לְשׁוֹרֶשׁ הַמְּרִירוּת שֶׁיִּתְמַתֵּק לְגַמְרֵי.
a person still requires healing for the root of bitterness itself so that it be sweetened completely.
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר [שָׁם רכה רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א]:
And this is what our Sages stated in the Zohar (III, 225a):
"לֵב אִיהוּ זַכִּיךְ מִכּוּלָּא, מִמֶּנּוּ נָפְקִין כָּל טָב וְכָל בְּרִיאוּתָא דְּשַׁיְיפִין וְכוּלֵי",
“the heart is the most pure and refined of all; from it proceed all goodness and all health of the limbs, etc.,”
שֶׁדָּם הַזַּךְ שֶׁבּוֹ, הוּא הַדָּלֶ״ת דְּאָדָ״ם,
in that the refined blood within it, which is the letter Dalet of Adam (Dam - דָּ״ם),
הוּא הַמַּבְרִיא וּמְרַפֵּא לְכָל מַרְעִין שֶׁמִּכָּבֵד וּמָרָה.
is that which restores to health and heals all sicknesses emerging from the liver and the bile.
וְהָאָלֶ״ף דְּאָדָ״ם
And the letter Aleph of Adam (אָדָ״ם – Efer - אֵפֶר)
הוּא מַדְרֵגָה הָעֶלְיוֹנָה שֶׁבּוֹ,
is the highest, transcendent spiritual level within him,
וְהוּא נְשָׁמָה הַטְּהוֹרָה שֶׁהִיא חֵלֶק אֱלֹהַּ מִמַּעַל,
which is the pristine Neshamah that is an actual portion of God from Above,
וְאַלּוּפוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם גָּנוּז בְּגַוָּוהּ (אַלֶ״ף).
and the Master (Aluph) of the universe is concealed within its core (represented by the letter Aleph).
וְעָלֶיהָ אָמְרוּ שֶׁהִיא "אֵפֶר",
And concerning it they stated that it is “ash” (efer),
כִּי גּוּף הָאָדָם נִבְרָא עָפָר מִן הָאֲדָמָה מִמְּקוֹם הַמִּזְבֵּחַ שֶׁמִּלְּמַטָּה,
for the body of man was formed of dust from the ground taken from the site of the earthly Altar,
וְהַנְּשָׁמָה מִמְּקוֹם מִזְבֵּחַ שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה,
while the soul was hewn from the site of the supernal Altar Above,
שֶׁשָּׁם מִיכָאֵל עוֹמֵד וּמַקְרִיב נִשְׁמוֹתֵיהֶם שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים
where Michael the Archangel stands and sacrifices the souls of the righteous,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת [בְּסוֹף מְנָחוֹת קי עַמּוּד א] מֵהַמִּדְרָשׁ.
as Tosafot recorded at the end of Menachot (110a) from the Midrash.
וְהֵם נַעֲשִׂין אֵפֶר,
And these souls become holy ash,
וְזֶהוּ חֲזָרָתָם לִמְקוֹרָם,
and this represents their return to their divine Source,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בַּגּוּף: "וְיָשׁוּב אֶל הֶעָפָר כְּשֶׁהָיָה",
as stated regarding the body: “and it returns to dust as it was,”
וְזֶהוּ תִּיקּוּנוֹ לְכַלּוֹת זוּהֲמָתוֹ.
and this dissolution constitutes its essential rectification to eradicate its contamination.
כֵּן בַּנְּשָׁמָה,
So too regarding the Neshamah:
שֶׁהֲגַם שֶׁהִיא טְהוֹרָה,
for even though it is fundamentally pure,
מִצַּד חִיבּוּרָהּ אֶל הַגּוּף בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
yet by virtue of its physical attachment to the body in this world,
אַף שֶׁהַצַּדִּיקִים זוֹכִין בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְהַעֲלוֹתָהּ מַעְלָה מַעְלָה,
even though the righteous merit through their holy deeds in this world to elevate it higher and higher,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם "אֵין אָדָם צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה טּוֹב וְלֹא יֶחֱטָא" (שָׁם ז, כ).
nevertheless “there is not a righteous man upon the earth that does good and sins not” (ibid. 7:20).
וּמַה שֶּׁהוּא לְמַטָּה "עָפָר",
And that which in the lower earthly realm is physical “dust” (afar),
הוּא בְּרוּחָנִיּוּת "אֵפֶר",
is in the spiritual realm transcendent “ash” (efer);
דְּעַל זֶה אָמַר אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "וְאָנֹכִי עָפָר וָאֵפֶר" (בְּרֵאשִׁית יח, כז),
concerning which Abraham our father, peace be upon him, proclaimed: “and I am but dust and ashes” (Genesis 18:27),
שֶׁהוּא מִצַּד הַגּוּף וְהַנְּשָׁמָה.
which refers to the dual dimensions of the physical body and the supernal soul.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא [פָּרָשַׁת פִּינְחָס רכה עַמּוּד א]:
And as they stated in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas 225a):
רְפָאֵל דְּאִיהוּ אֵפֶר, דְּהַיְינוּ אֵפֶר שִׂכְלִית.
the Archangel Raphael is “efer” (ash), meaning the supernal intellectual ash.
כִּי אָמְרוּ [בְּקֹהֶלֶת רַבָּה ג, כ] עַל פָּסוּק (קֹהֶלֶת ג, כ): "הַכֹּל הָיָה מִן הֶעָפָר",
For our Sages stated in Kohelet Rabbah (3:20) on the verse: “All are of the dust”:
אֲפִילּוּ גַּלְגַּל חַמָּה שֶׁהוּא מַדְרֵגָה הַיּוֹתֵר עֶלְיוֹנָה בַּעֲשִׂיָּה הַגּוּפָנִית,
even the solar orb, which is the highest physical body in the World of Asiyah,
שֶׁנִּבְנָה כֻּלּוֹ מִיְסוֹד הֶעָפָר אֲפִילּוּ זֶה הַמָּאוֹר הַגָּדוֹל,
was constructed entirely from the element of earth, even that great luminary;
וְהוּא כֻּלּוֹ אֵשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּנְדָרִים ח עַמּוּד ב]
and it is entirely fire as stated in Nedarim (8b)
עַל פָּסוּק (מַלְאָכִי ג, יט): "וְלִהַט אֹתָם הַיּוֹם הַבָּא",
on the verse: “and the day that comes shall burn them up” (Malachi 3:19),
שֶׁיּוֹצִיא הַחַמָּה מִנַּרְתִּיקָהּ,
that Hashem will extract the sun from its sheath,
וְהָאֵשׁ שׂוֹרֵף הֶעָפָר וְנַעֲשָׂה אֵפֶר,
and the fire burns the elemental dust and it becomes ash,
וְגַם הוּא נִקְרָא "עָפָר" כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּפֶרֶק כִּסּוּי הַדָּם, חֻלִּין פח עַמּוּד ב].
and that ash is likewise called “dust” as stated in chapter Kissui HaDam (Chullin 88b).

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 101a:10 answers the Marah question conditionally: if Israel listens, the disease is not imposed; if not, it may be imposed, yet Hashem remains the healer. Rashi to Shemos 15:26 gives both a homiletic answer and the preventive physician teaching Torah and mitzvos to avoid illness; Kli Yakar retains the preventive comparison. Mekhilta, Vayassa 1:26–27, separately presents Torah as life and healing and Rabbi Yitzchak’s World-to-Come healing. These approaches illuminate the question without making them one identical answer.

paragraphs.text: Niddah 30b:18 describes the fetus with its mouth closed and navel open, nourished by what its mother eats and drinks. Chullin 58a:11 records opposing views: Rabbi Eliezer calls the fetus part of its mother, while Rabbi Yehoshua does not. The case concerns offspring conceived before its mother became a tereifah and its fitness for the altar. Rav Tzadok borrows the image for the inherited root; it is not a statement that every legal use of “fetus as its mother’s thigh” is settled.

paragraphs.text: Mekhilta, Tractate Vayassa §1, records differing identifications of the tree at Marah and the principle that Hashem heals bitter with bitter. It also interprets the tree as Torah, the Tree of Life, whose words are life and healing. Kli Yakar to Shemos 15:26 connects Torah’s initially difficult or bitter appearance with its sweet end, healing bodily and spiritual illness. These are the parallels for the completed distinction between preventing illness from appearing and healing its root.

paragraphs.text: Peri Tzadik, Ki Tavo 12:1, says that Torah repairs the covenantal blemish and cites “healing for all his flesh.” It distinguishes Torah/Chochmah from repentance/Binah and also discusses prayer, crying and humility; the paths are not reduced to one method. Divrei Chalomot §22 gives a separate bitter-with-bitter instance concerning Yavin, Sisera and Yael, an exceptional act for Heaven and later transformation into merit. It is a qualified comparison, not a literal exposition of the Marah promise.

Avraham’s “dust and ash” in Bereishis 18:27 becomes his pairing of body and neshamah. The refined ash signifies removal of what adhered through embodiment, not destruction of the pure soul.

paragraphs.text: Zohar, Pinchas 40:223, describes union within the fourfold order: Michael is intellectual water, Gabriel intellectual fire, Uriel intellectual air or wind, and Raphael ash, “that is, intellectual dust”—עפר שכלית. The Holy One unites water with fire and wind with dust, “making peace in His heights”; without His presence the angels have no strength. Rav Tzadok’s quotation here has אפר שכלית, “intellectual ash.” The source’s dust reading and the author’s ash wording are distinguished within the shared fourfold context.

paragraphs.text: Chullin 88b provides the legal and linguistic overlap. Beis Hillel permits ash for covering blood because Bamidbar 19:17 calls it “dust of burning”; Beis Shammai distinguishes that qualified phrase from ordinary dust. The sugya permits a traveler on a ship to burn a garment for ash and later connects Avraham’s “dust and ash” with red-heifer ash and sotah dust. It does not identify dust and ash physically in every respect.

Beis Hillel permits ash for covering blood because Bamidbar 19:17 calls it “dust of burning”; Beis Shammai distinguishes that qualified phrase from ordinary dust. The sugya permits a traveler on a ship to burn a garment for ash and later connects Avraham’s “dust and ash” with red-heifer ash and sotah dust. It does not identify dust and ash physically in every respect.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Healing at Marah means, in Rav Tzadok’s exposition, more than preventing an outward illness: the underlying bitterness must also be repaired. He moves through the symbols of blood and ash in Adam to the soul’s return to its source, pictured through the supernal altar and the relation of dust to ash.

p: וְהוּא מַדְרֵגָה הָעֶלְיוֹנָה שֶׁבֶּעָפָר שֶׁבְּגַלְגַּל חַמָּה,
And this is the supreme level of dust residing within the solar orb,
וְכֵן אֵפֶר וְדֶשֶׁן הַמִּזְבֵּחַ.
and likewise the ash and fat-cinders (deshen) of the Altar.
וּבָרוּחָנִי וְשִׂכְלִי שֶׁהוּא כֹּחַ הַנְּשָׁמָה,
And in the spiritual and intellectual realm which is the potency of the Neshamah,
הוּא מַדְרֵגָה הָאַחֲרוֹנָה דְּ"נֵר ה' נִשְׁמַת אָדָם" (מִשְׁלֵי כ, כז),
it constitutes the lowest terminal point of “the candle of Hashem is the soul of man” (Proverbs 20:27),
שֶׁהִיא כֻּלָּהּ אוֹר הַמֵּאִיר,
which is entirely an illuminating light,
דְּ"אוֹהֲבָיו כְּצֵאת הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בִּגְבֻרָתוֹ" (שׁוֹפְטִים ה, לא);
as “they that love Him are as the sun when it goes forth in its might” (Judges 5:31);
וְהִיא עָפָר שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה אֵפֶר
and it is spiritual dust that was transformed into ash
מִמֶּנּוּ נִמְשָׁךְ הָרְפוּאָה דִּסְלִיחָה לַגּוּף הַחוֹטֵא,
from which is drawn down the healing of forgiveness for the sinning body,
כְּשֶׁיָּבִין וְיַשְׂכִּיל בְּרוּחוֹ וְשִׂכְלוֹ
when a person understands and perceives through his spirit and intellect
לְהַגְבִּיר כֹּחַ הַשֵּׂכֶל וְהַנְּשָׁמָה הַטְּהוֹרָה,
to empower the faculty of the intellect and the pristine Neshamah,
וּ"לְבָבוֹ יָבִין וָשָׁב" (יְשַׁעְיָה ו, י).
and “his heart will understand, and he returns” (Isaiah 6:10).
וְכַיָּדוּעַ דְּאַרְבָּעָה מַלְאָכִים [שֶׁבְּרַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא שָׁם] הַנּוֹשְׂאִים הַכִּסֵּא,
And as is known that the four archangels (in Ra'aya Meheimna ibid.) who bear the Throne,
הֵן הֵם נֶגֶד גִּימֶ״ל (שְׁלוֹשָׁה) אָבוֹת וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם רַגְלֵי הַמֶּרְכָּבָה.
correspond to the three Patriarchs and King David, peace be upon him, the four legs of the divine Chariot.
וּרְפָאֵל נֶגֶד דָּוִד שֶׁהֵקִים עוּלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה,
And the Archangel Raphael corresponds to David who raised the yoke of repentance,
וְ"שָׁב וְרָפָא לוֹ".
fulfilling “and he returns, and is healed for him.”
וְאַף צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים צְרִיכִים רְפוּאָה מֵעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ,
And even completely righteous people require healing from the instigation of the Serpent,
שֶׁמִּזֶּה לֹא נִמְלְטוּ גַּם צַדִּיקִים הַיּוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלִים שֶׁמֵּתוּ בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ,
from which even the greatest tzaddikim were not spared, who died solely through the instigation of the Serpent (Shabbat 55b),
דִּלְזֶה אֵין רְפוּאָה עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
for which mortality there is no complete healing through repentance in this world
עַד לֶעָתִיד, דִּ"מַחַץ מַכָּתוֹ [שֶׁל עוֹלָם] יִרְפָּא" (יְשַׁעְיָה ל, כו)
until the ultimate future, when “He heals the stroke of the world's wound” (Isaiah 30:26)
וִ"יבֻלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח" (שָׁם כה, ח).
and “He will swallow up death forever” (ibid. 25:8).
וְעַל כֵּן אֲפִילּוּ צַדִּיקִים צְרִיכִים לַחֲזוֹר לְעַפְרָם שָׁעָה אַחַת קוֹדֶם תְּחִיַּת הַמֵּתִים,
Therefore even the righteous must return to their dust one hour before the resurrection of the dead (Shabbat 152b),
וְנַעֲשִׂים "תַּרְוַוד רָקָב",
and become a “ladleful of decomposed remains” (tarvad rakav),
דְּהַגּוּף מִן הַנִּקְבָּרִים, וּמִ'קֶּבֶר' נַעֲשָׂה 'רָקָב'
for the body is among those buried, and the letters of kever (קבר, grave) are rearranged as rakav (רקב, decay);
וְהַנְּשָׁמָה מִן הַנִּשְׂרָפִין,
while the soul belongs to those consumed by divine fire,
דְּגַם נִשְׁמוֹתֵיהֶן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים הַקְּרֵבִין עַל גַּבֵּי הַמִּזְבֵּחַ,
for even the souls of the righteous offered upon the supernal Altar,
הַיְינוּ שֶׁהֵם לְאִשֶּׁה רֵיחַ נִיחוֹחַ לַה',
become a fire-offering of pleasing aroma unto Hashem,
כִּי נִדְבָּקִים בִּמְקוֹרָן דְּהֵם חֵלֶק אֱלֹהַּ
for they cleave to their Source, being a divine portion,
וַ"ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֵשׁ אֹכְלָה הוּא" (דְּבָרִים ד, כד).
and “Hashem your God is a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy 4:24).
וּמַה שֶּׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לִידָּבֵק מִצַּד הָעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ
And whatever part cannot be united on account of the Serpent's instigation
שֶׁנִּקְלַט גַּם בָּהּ בִּהְיוֹתָהּ בַּגּוּף,
which was absorbed into the soul as well while dwelling in the body,
הוּא נַעֲשָׂה אֵפֶר.
is burned away to become ash.
וּמִזֶּה בָּא הָרְפוּאָה אַחַר כָּךְ,
And from this process emerges the ultimate healing afterward,
שֶׁהוּא חוֹזֵר לִהְיוֹת נִכְנָס לְהָרָקָב שֶׁל הַגּוּף
for it [the ash] again enters the body’s decomposed remains
וְקָם בִּתְחִיַּת הַמֵּתִים בְּרִיָּה חֲדָשָׁה קְדוֹשָׁה וּטְהוֹרָה,
and rises at the resurrection of the dead as a new, holy, and pure creation,
שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ עוֹד שׁוּם זוּהֲמָא מֵעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ
possessing no longer any contamination from the Serpent's instigation,
שֶׁנִּכְלָה עַל יְדֵי שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה עָפָר וָאֵפֶר.
which was completely annihilated through having been reduced to dust and ashes.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra 6:3–4 and Mishnah Tamid 1:4 describe defined acts of altar service. The kohen scoops from the inner consumed coals and deposits them at the prescribed place east of the ramp; accumulated ash is carried to a pure place. Menachos 110a supplies the distinct heavenly-altar image, and Peri Tzadik, Tzav 4:1, links altar fire with Torah’s refining light. The refined remainder’s incorporation into service is Rav Tzadok’s symbolic use of efer and deshen, not a uniform legal status for every kind of ash.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 17b:10–12 uses “his heart understands, and he returns and is healed” for the order of understanding and repentance, expressly identifying the healing here as forgiveness, not illness. Rosh Hashanah 17b:8–9 cites it for repentance tearing a decree within a discussion of scope and conditions. Sha’arei Teshuvah 2:10 requires a settled undertaking to obey Torah, not understanding alone. Takanas HaShavin 6:9 connects David’s return with the heart and this verse. These sources illuminate strengthening the intellect and pure neshamah toward the healing of forgiveness.

paragraphs.text: A full ladle of decomposed human remains, melo tarvad rakav, is a technical measure in Mishnah Oholos 2:1 and Nazir 49b–51a, not ordinary grave soil. Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 34:10 pictures the remainder mixed with earth like leaven in dough before renewed life. Yerushalmi Nazir 7:2:5–7 both expounds kever/rakav and links a ladleful of altar earth with Adam’s formation, retaining legal conditions for decay. The wordplay is a rabbinic derash, not historical etymology.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok links the soul’s remaining ash with healing through repentance and eventual resurrection. Bodily decay and the soul’s return to its source remove what remains of the serpent’s defilement, after which the ash rejoins the body as a new, holy creation.

p: וְנִשְׁמָתָן שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים הַנִּשְׂרֶפֶת בְּאֵשׁ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם,
And regarding the soul of the wicked which is burned in the fire of Gehenna,
לְכַלּוֹת עָוֺן וּלְהָתֵם פֶּשַׁע שֶׁהָיְתָה מְשׁוּקַּעַת בָּהֶם,
in order to consume iniquity and terminate the transgression in which it was immersed:
שָׁרְשָׁם שֶׁבִּקְדוּשָּׁה, שֶׁהוּא הָאֵפֶר הַנִּשְׁאָר,
their indestructible root in holiness, which is the surviving ash,
תִּיקּוּנוֹ שֶׁיּוּכַל לַחֲזוֹר לִקְדוּשָּׁה לְגַמְרֵי
its rectification—enabling it to return to holiness completely
וּלְהִתְגַּבֵּל עִם רָקָב הַגּוּף לָשׁוּב לִחְיוֹת חַיֵּי עוֹלָם בִּקְדוּשָּׁה –
and be kneaded together with the dust of the body to live eternal life in sanctity—
הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי הַצַּדִּיקִים,
occurs exclusively through the mediation of the righteous,
כָּל אֶחָד עַל יְדֵי אֵיזֶה צַדִּיק שֶׁמִּשָּׁרְשׁוֹ,
each soul through that specific tzaddik from whose spiritual root it stems,
שֶׁהוּא אֵפֶר תַּחַת כַּפּוֹת רַגְלָיו.
being scattered as ashes beneath the soles of his feet.
וְעַל יְדֵי שֶׁנּוֹגֵעַ בַּצַּדִּיק נִמְשָׁךְ בּוֹ חַיּוּת,
And through coming into contact with the righteous, living vitality is drawn into it,
כְּעִנְיַן הָאִישׁ שֶׁנָּגַע בְּעַצְמוֹת אֱלִישָׁע וַיֶּחִי (מְלָכִים ב יג, כא).
mirroring the corpse that touched the bones of Elisha and revived (II Kings 13:21).
כִּי בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהָרָע גּוֹבֵר,
For in this world where evil predominates,
הַטֻּמְאָה שֶׁהוּא חֵלֶק אָדָם רָע וְסִטְרָא אָחֳרָא הִיא מְטַמֵּא אֲחֵרִים בְּמַגָּע,
impurity, which is the domain of evil and the Other Side, defiles others through physical contact;
אֲבָל הַקְּדוּשָּׁה אֵינוֹ מְקַדֵּשׁ בִּנְגִיעָה בְּעָלְמָא.
whereas holiness does not automatically sanctify through mere touch alone.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם מָצִינוּ גַּם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה:
And nonetheless, we find even in this world a precedent:
"כָּל הַנֹּגֵעַ בַּמִּזְבֵּחַ יִקְדָּשׁ" (שְׁמוֹת כט, לז),
“Whatever touches the altar shall be holy” (Exodus 29:37),
לְעִנְיַן פְּסוּלִין שֶׁאִם עָלוּ לֹא יֵרְדוּ (זְבָחִים פג עַמּוּד ב);
regarding disqualified sacrifices: that if they ascended the Altar, they shall not descend (Zevachim 83b);
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם זֶה לֹא לְכָל פְּסוּלִין,
and nonetheless even this applies not to all disqualified offerings,
רַק לְאוֹתָן שֶׁהָיוּ פְּסוּלָם בַּקֹּדֶשׁ.
rather strictly to those whose disqualification occurred within the Sanctuary.
וּלְעָתִיד יִשָּׁאֵר רַק אוֹתָם שֶׁהָיָה פְּסוּלָם בַּקֹּדֶשׁ,
And in the ultimate future there shall endure only those whose disqualification occurred in holiness,
דְּהַיְינוּ זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁשָּׁרְשָׁם בִּקְדוּשָּׁה,
namely the seed of our father Jacob, peace be upon him, whose root is in holiness,
רַק אַחַר כָּךְ נִפְסְלוּ עַל יְדֵי מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם.
only that subsequently they became disqualified through their outward deeds.
וְהַצַּדִּיקִים הֵם הַכֹּהֲנִים הַנִּגָּשִׁים אֶל ה'
And the righteous are the priests who draw near unto Hashem
הָעוֹמְדִים עַל גַּבֵּי הַמִּזְבֵּחַ שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה;
standing atop the supernal Altar Above;
וּכְשֶׁהָרוּחַ מְפַזַּרְתָּן תַּחַת רַגְלֵיהֶם,
and when the celestial wind scatters the ashes beneath their feet,
הֲרֵי הֵם נוֹגְעִים בַּמִּזְבֵּחַ
behold those ashes touch the Altar
וְנַעֲשׂוּ קֹדֶשׁ וְלַחְמוֹ שֶׁל מִזְבֵּחַ וְלֹא יֵרְדוּ עוֹד,
and become consecrated as holy and as the bread of the Altar, never to descend again,
שֶׁגַּם הֵם עוֹלִין לְאִשֶּׁה רֵיחַ נִיחוֹחַ לַה',
for they too ascend as a fire-offering of pleasing aroma unto Hashem,
וְאֶפְרָן נַעֲשָׂה דֶּשֶׁן הַמִּזְבֵּחַ שֶׁל מַעְלָה מִנִּשְׁמוֹתֵיהֶם שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים,
and their ash becomes the sacred deshen of the supernal Altar alongside the souls of the righteous,
וְהַמְחוּבָּר לְטָהוֹר – טָהוֹר.
and that which is joined to the pure is pure.

paragraphs.text: Daniel 9:24 concerns seventy weeks for the people and the holy city, restraining transgression, ending sin, atoning for iniquity and bringing everlasting righteousness. Rav Tzadok’s “לכלות עון ולהתם פשע” recombines its vocabulary rather than quoting its sequence verbatim. Malachi supplies the distinct burning-day image. Applying these terms to consuming the soul’s sinful admixture is Rav Tzadok’s purification account.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 44a says of Israel’s sin, “Although he sinned, he is Israel,” likening the myrtle among thorns to a myrtle still. Peri Tzadik, Pesach 8:1, applies enduring affiliation even to the wicked son; Resisei Layla 44:1 develops the enduring root. The remaining ash is not innocence or automatic acquittal. It is the point from which complete repair and future restoration remain possible.

paragraphs.text: Malachi 3:19–21 places the burning day, healing sun and ashes beneath the righteous one’s feet together; Nedarim 8b describes the same sun healing and judging. The claim that the surviving ash can itself be repaired through a righteous person of its spiritual root is Rav Tzadok’s eschatological synthesis, beyond the plain image of defeat beneath the feet.

paragraphs.text: II Melachim 13:20–21 reports the corpse touching Elisha’s bones, reviving and standing. Sanhedrin 47a:8–9 uses the event in its discussion of burial beside the righteous and states, “He stood on his feet, but did not go home.” The source gives that limitation without specifying a duration. Rav Tzadok uses the exceptional miracle as a paradigm of life drawn through contact with the righteous, not as an ordinary law of physical transmission.

paragraphs.text: Chaggai 2:11–14 asks whether sacred flesh carried in a garment sanctifies food touched by the garment; the priests answer no. They then affirm impurity from one defiled by a corpse. The first question concerns secondary touch, not a universal denial of sanctity through every direct contact. Rav Tzadok extends the structure of these defined laws to spiritual influence.

paragraphs.text: Shemos 29:37 supplies the altar-touch verse. Zevachim 83a:15 states that the altar sanctifies what is fit for it; 84a:7 gives Rabbi Shimon’s principle that what became disqualified within sacred status is accepted by the sacred. The Mishnah records disagreements, including Rabbi Yehudah’s particular rulings. The category concerns sacred status and fitness, not every disqualification or merely a physical location inside the Sanctuary.

paragraphs.text: Resisei Layla §5 calls Gehinnom’s judgment “immersion in desires.” It teaches retaining faith that enjoyment comes from Hashem and drawing weekday enjoyment into holiness through Shabbos delight. This is a qualified comparison for an existing capacity drawn into holiness. It does not say that fire burns desires out or state the present sequence of ash, contact with a tzaddik and resurrection.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Kelim 12:2 supplies the maxim that attachment to the impure is impure and attachment to the pure is pure. Its setting is attached fittings and implements; individually, the fittings are pure. Bava Kamma 92b:13 already uses the rule for association with one’s kind. Rav Tzadok applies it to the remnant joined to the righteous through shared root and elevation, not automatic consecration by casual physical proximity.

inlineHeadings.text: The theme: Rav Tzadok concludes with the future restoration of the surviving holy root through the righteous. The ashes beneath their feet are likened to an offering whose disqualification arose in holiness and which remains on the altar; joined to the pure, they become holy once more.
